# TO THE MOST NOBLE
## *And Most Distinguished Man*
# JACOB DUPAN,
## MOST UPRIGHT SENATOR
## OF THE REPUBLIC OF GENEVA
->& *Most Deserving Consul*.<-

->THE BROTHERS DE TOURNES, JEAN ANTOINE AND SAMUEL,<-
->SEND THEIR WARMEST GREETINGS.<-
<note>original: "S. P. D." stands for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a standard Latin greeting in formal letters meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

**G**reat are the obligations by which we are bound to you, most Distinguished Man, and we seek neither to erase them nor to balance them with any worthy compensation. We are unable to repay our debt, and we have no thought of truly remunerating those exceptional tokens of goodwill which you—having served for many years as <term>Consul</term><note>The highest elected magistrate in the Republic of Geneva.</note> and <term>Praetor</term><note>A high-ranking judicial officer; in Geneva, this was the "lieutenant de la justice."</note>, and as a most wise protector <insert>❦</insert> of our Geneva—have so magnificently bestowed upon us. We mention these things lest you should think in your mind that these labors of ours are being consecrated to your Honor merely as a return for your favors. We are led by a far different spirit, driven solely by the brilliance of your virtues.

<summary>In this dedication, the De Tournes brothers, famous Genevan printers, present the collected works of Paracelsus to Jacob Dupan, a prominent local statesman. They frame the gift not as a repayment for his past support, but as a tribute to his virtuous character and public service.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Dupan, De Tournes, Geneva, dedication, patronage, consul, praetor, 17th-century printing</keywords>

# THE EPISTLE.

<term>Theophrastus Paracelsus</term><note>A famous and controversial 16th-century Swiss physician, alchemist, and philosopher who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, the most celebrated Physician and easily the Prince of <term>Chemists</term><note>In the 17th century, the term "Chemicus" referred to both chemistry and alchemy, which were not yet distinct fields.</note>, is now presented to you. He is not merely patched together with crude little commentaries, but adorned with new and remarkable additions. We hang this work in your sanctuary as a <term>votive offering</term><note>original: "anathema," here used in the classical sense of an object consecrated or hung in a temple as a gift to a deity.</note> most worthy of a man of your high station; nor do we believe so great a man offends your <term>authority</term><note>original: "fasces," the bundled rods and axe symbolizing the power of high-ranking Roman magistrates, here referring to Dupan’s role as Consul.</note> if—after having once been known to princes and having excited the highest admiration—he now looks upon the sun once more and seeks your patronage. And you, surely, will not allow this <term>Horn of Amalthea</term><note>original: "Amaltheæ cornu," a reference to the Cornucopia or "horn of plenty," signifying that Paracelsus’s work is an inexhaustible source of knowledge.</note> and this boundless storehouse of every kind of learning to lack your protection. Indeed, it is the duty of either a Prince or a Consul to support, with their own authority, those illustrious men who come forth into the light for the great benefit of mankind. 

If indeed, most Honorable Man, a <term>Chief Physician</term><note>original: "Archiater," a title for a high-ranking or royal doctor.</note> so famous—forgetting his own jurisdiction—knocks upon the proud doors of sacred <term>Justice</term><note>original: "Themidis," referring to Themis, the Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note> and shamelessly breaks into her secret inner chambers, he will nonetheless find rest under your name, because of the grace with which you embrace all <term>guardians of wisdom</term><note>original: "sapientiæ Antistites."</note>. You are so fashioned after every example of humanity that you reject nothing unless it is separated from what is honorable and just. Those who know you intimately know that what we say is most true, and they revere and look up to the admirable harmony of your virtues, which are <insert>to be shared with</insert> and linked one with another. We, however, most Distin—

<summary>The publishers present Paracelsus’s collected works to Jacob Dupan, arguing that a statesman of his rank has a duty to protect such a vast "horn of plenty" of knowledge. They acknowledge that while Paracelsus (a doctor) might seem out of place in the realm of a legal official, Dupan’s universal virtue and wisdom make him the perfect patron.</summary>

# THE EPISTLE.

...most distinguished [Sir], those great ornaments of your soul, by which you raise your head to the heavens and set it among the stars, we—well aware of our own insignificance—keep silent about. For we would only be attempting the most vain task if we tried to show you to yourself by acting as a mirror. But you, Excellent and Virtuous Man, do not only shine with your own brilliance; other honors are added to you, which dazzle the sharpness of our eyes with their overwhelming abundance of light. 

For you have an elder brother, a man of great age, blessed in his children and blessed in his grandchildren's offspring, to whose mind old age has brought no wrinkles, taken away no vigor, nor removed any praiseworthy impulse. He is—as is plain to everyone—a bright star of the <term>sacred council</term><note>original: "sacri synedrij." In Geneva, this likely refers to the Council of Two Hundred or the Consistory, the city's governing and religious bodies.</note>, whose <term>innate</term><note>original: "αὐτόχθων" (autochthon), a Greek term meaning native to the soil or inherent.</note> vigor of mind is neither bent by the weight of business nor burdened by any mass of affairs. 

From this venerable old man there is also a noble lineage; there are noble children who outshine all others in the civic dignities of <term>Geneva</term><note>original: "Geneuensibus."</note>. Among them, famous even above the heavens, is that most distinguished Senator and <term>Former Consul</term><note>original: "Exconsul."</note>, who—after he initiated many into the mysteries of wisdom as a prelude to that virtue whose purest rays he now emits—now stands against the pride of the age in his great works, sailing only toward justice. His name is admired by all...

<meta>This page concludes the dedicatory epistle to Jacob Dupan, which began on the previous page. The text moves from praising the recipient's family to justifying the printers' work and offering a final blessing for his leadership in Geneva.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE

Furthermore, it is not out of place to mention that those driven by the sting of envy will accuse us of audacity, as if we have unworthily placed our names at the gateway <note>original: "propylæo," a Greek-derived word for a monumental entrance, used here metaphorically for the preface of the book.</note> of this edition. Truly, fair judges of such matters will feel otherwise; they will not unwillingly admit that the world of letters <note>original: "rem literariam," often translated as the "Republic of Letters," referring to the international community of scholars.</note> has been advanced somewhat by our labors. For who among the learned is unaware that printers—using the black-colored children of Cadmus <note>original: "Cadmi filiolis atricoloribus." This is a poetic way of describing printed letters. Cadmus was the mythical figure credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece; "black-colored" refers to the ink.</note>—restore to their former splendor the works of great men that reek of the decay of long ages? They rescue them from the goddess of death <note>original: "libitinâ," referring to Libitina, the ancient Roman goddess of funerals and burials; here it means saving works from being forgotten or lost to time.</note> and thus entrust them to posterity. This fact is surely too well known for it to be worthwhile to linger longer on its proof; and perhaps we have already detained you too long, **Most Distinguished Sir**, calling you away with this rambling speech while you are occupied with the highest affairs of state.

Only one thing remains: we shall petition the Eternal Deity with humble prayers that in these sorrowful and turbulent times—in which heroes are scarcely equal in number to the seven gates of **Thebes** or the mouths of the fertile **Nile** <note>The authors are using a classical trope: both the city of Thebes and the Nile Delta were famous for having seven openings, implying that true leaders are now very rare.</note>—He may permit you, in the fullness of your years, to remain present and preside over our affairs. May you therefore, **Most Distinguished Sir**, long grace our **Geneva** with your good fortune, and enjoy the years of **Nestor** <note>original: "Nestoreos annos." Nestor was the legendary Greek king known for his great age and wisdom; to wish someone "Nestorean years" is to wish them a very long and productive life.</note> amid the most abundant fruits of your most just administration. **Farewell**, along with all your household, you great ornament of the **Republic**.

---

-> *Given at Geneva, June 1, 1658.* <-

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page begins the "Preface to the Reader" by Frederick Bitiskius, the editor of this 1658 edition of Paracelsus’s works. It follows the dedication to Jacob Dupan and serves to explain the delays, corrections, and additions made to this specific collection compared to previous printings from Frankfurt.</meta>

## FREDERICK BITISKIUS
### SENDS GREETINGS TO THE READER.

<margin>Why the works of Paracelsus appear so late.</margin>
<margin>Reasons for printing them.</margin>
<margin>The Frankfurt edition is remarkably defective.</margin>
<margin>The purpose of the preface.</margin>
**A**t last, Kind Reader, there appear—promised more than two years ago—the works of THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus, a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, easily the Prince of Chemists. They are produced at the expense of the De Tournes Brothers <note>A famous family of printers originally from Lyon, then Geneva.</note>, who are most zealous for the public good, and are more complete and corrected than the Frankfurt editions. Perhaps they come later than your hope and expectation, as it was their intention to anticipate those; however, grave prejudices against the author began to spread after the plan for printing was announced, which caused them to suspend the hand already applied to the labor and break the thread of the web they had begun. For this reason, they hesitated for some time, doubtful in mind whether to proceed as they had started or to step back. Eventually, men most skilled in both branches of Medicine <note>Refers to the traditional Galenic medicine based on herbs/humors and the newer "Chemical" medicine championed by Paracelsus.</note> were called into council. They exhorted the printers with one voice and one pen to despise the insults vomited by envy against the author and to finish the work for which they had girded themselves. They said that Chemistry <note>original: "Chymia." At this time, the term encompassed both what we call chemistry and alchemy.</note> rises daily to a more sublime peak of glory, and that the most outstanding physicians throughout Europe labor in cultivating it. Even in Paris, they noted, by royal munificence a two-year public curriculum is taught annually despite the barking of the critics <note>original: "Momis," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism.</note>. Furthermore, they argued that the learned men of our age—whose eyes are freed from the spell of boasted antiquity—now distinguish the excellent from the futile and the genuine from the false, looking upon Theophrastus with greater respect than in the past. Thus, the printers should proceed safely, and the literary world would feel and express gratitude to them. Stirred by so many incentives and persuaded by such authorities, they took up the press again with an eager hand. Moving with an unhindered foot from the starting line to the finish, they collected these three volumes and made them public for your sake, Reader. They were always anxious with a remarkable solicitude that the works should appear perfect in every part (as much as was in their power). For they were warned by more diligent readers of Paracelsus’s writings about several treatises omitted in the Frankfurt edition, and that the author's meaning was corrupted in many places by the translator in the Latin version. This was due both to the Belgian translator <note>Likely referring to Gerard Dorn, who translated many of Paracelsus's German works into Latin.</note> not understanding the German idiom and to his lack of focused intention, being a man skilled in Law rather than the <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>Alchemical practice and theory.</note>. Therefore, they requested my effort in collating the Latin copy with the German. I contributed this work gladly, though not unaware of my own meager ability, both so that I might examine with a more exact eye the writings of an author worshipped by many like a god and detested by others more than a dog or a snake (mindful of the Apostolic precept to "test all things, hold fast to what is good" <note>A reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:21.</note>), and so that I might show my inclination toward public study by this public token. I have therefore undertaken this province, and I thought it would be worthwhile if, in this preface, I first briefly showed what has been provided in this edition beyond its predecessors, and then declared, by weighing them in a just balance, what value should be placed on the things said by some too heatedly (and often less truly) concerning the life and monuments <note>The written legacy or works.</note> of the Author.

<margin>The first part of the preface.</margin>
<margin>Both Surgeries were added to this edition. The tenth book of the Archidoxes.</margin>
As pertains to the first point: since this work has fallen into the hands of men who love literary utility, they have sought out all the genuine offspring of Theophrastus’s genius with singular care so that you should lack nothing. They rejected the forged works that take pride only in his name, of which a huge number are in circulation. Regarding the *Surgeries* <note>Paracelsus's "Grosse Wundarzney" (Great Surgery Book), which was highly influential.</note>, which were neglected by the Frankfurt printers—representing no small part of his glory and certainly the first monument of his lofty mind, dedicated to the Emperor and celebrated even by the praise of his adversaries—they decided these should not be omitted and established them as the third volume. Also standing joined to its brothers is the *Tenth Book of the Archidoxes* <note>A key alchemical text by Paracelsus; the tenth book was often considered the most secret or "highest" part of his doctrine.</note>. This was the Author’s most dear and precious pledge, extorted from him rather than obtained, and he almost sufficiently grieved that it was written so clearly, fearing the cruel hand of envy, even when it first saw the light of day. Like a treasure long buried in the earth and finally found under a prosperous star, this little book alone will be for the wise man a light to illuminate whatever shadows of silence or obscurity Theophrastus had hidden elsewhere.

<summary>In this preface, Frederick Bitiskius explains that the new edition of Paracelsus's works was delayed by controversy but eventually completed with better translations and the addition of previously omitted texts like the "Surgeries" and the "Tenth Book of the Archidoxes." He criticizes previous editions for their errors and claims this version is a more accurate representation of Paracelsus's alchemical and medical genius.</summary>

<keywords>Paracelsus, Bitiskius, De Tournes Brothers, Frankfurt edition, Chemistry, Alchemy, Surgery, Archidoxes, Latin translation, medical controversy, 17th-century printing</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by Frederick Bitiskius, the editor of the 1658 Geneva edition of Paracelsus’s works. It transitions from discussing the printers' hesitations to the specific features of this new edition, including a portrait, a glossary, and the editor's efforts to correct the Latin text against the German originals.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

## PREFACE.

Furthermore, so that they might satisfy the curious eyes of those asking in what sort of "home" <note>A metaphorical way of referring to the body or physical appearance.</note> such a narrow mind dwelt, the publishers have seen to it that a portrait of the Author, sketched by the most gifted brush of Tintoretto <note>Jacopo Robusti, known as Tintoretto (1518–1594), a titan of the Venetian Renaissance.</note>, be engraved and included here. It differs somewhat from the one attached to the German Edition; however, since this one was made by a more celebrated artist with a more refined hand—depicting a younger Theophrastus while he was following the Mars of the Venetians <note>original: "Venetorum Martem"; this refers to Paracelsus’s service as a military surgeon or soldier in the wars of the Republic of Venice.</note>—it expresses his face to the life. Because it was acquired with greater difficulty and at a higher price, there is hope it will be even more pleasing to those who contemplate it than the previous version.

<margin>The Will.</margin>
The remaining items joined to the preface, although not written by him but about him, will bring no small benefit and pleasure to the reader. The included Will <note>Paracelsus’s last will and testament, which Bitiskius uses to defend the author's character.</note> will serve as a defense or a "sponge" to wipe away the impudent slanders blustered against the Author regarding his uncertain father <note>Accusations of illegitimacy.</note>, his supposed beggary, and the rumors of recurring troubles with guardians or his sudden death.

<margin>A small Dictionary.</margin>
As for the small Dictionary we have added, its use to students of these books needs no words to explain; it will silence the complaining cries about obscurity and the "novelty of terms" <note>Paracelsus was famous for inventing a brand new vocabulary for chemistry and medicine, which frustrated traditional scholars.</note>, and will provide an excellent shortcut for those who previously had to collect terms explained scattered here or there, waiting until "one book opened another."

<margin>The Letter of Severinus the Dane.</margin>
We thought it wise to place before all the rest the Letter of Petrus Severinus the Dane <note>Peder Sørensen (1542–1602), a Danish physician whose influential work "Idea Medicinae" helped systematize Paracelsian thought for a learned audience.</note>, a most learned man and a disciple of the great Theophrastus. It raises the Master with well-deserved praise and paves the way to many things that have until now been inaccessible to those of moderate learning.

<margin>Comparison with the German Copy.</margin>
I have compared the Latin context of the book itself with the German with as much diligence as I could. If I noticed that the translator had wandered from the Author's intent, I took every effort to bring it back as closely as possible. I restored certain omissions—sometimes entire lines, occasionally two or three—to their proper places. I corrected errors in spelling, commas, and periods which sometimes disturbed a very clear meaning; and whatever seemed to me to be twisted askew, I bent back toward the right path to the best of my ability. Nevertheless, I avoided any pretense of rising up through another's lapse, or building a trophy to my own glory out of someone else's errors. For that reason, I left untouched and committed to the press just as they were many things that were not entirely out of tune with the Author’s sense—partly at the urging of others, and partly because my own nature refuses to recommend its own work by neglecting the efforts of another. Nor would I want these things said to build a cover for my own yawning <note>Sluggishness or boredom.</note>, or to wash away the fault of ignorance with a beautiful excuse: there are, without doubt, many things in these works that outpace the slowness of my own wit, and there were things that escaped my diligence. I am certain that your kindness will cover the former and your humanity will excuse the latter; I truly promise this to myself and earnestly ask that you do so. Indeed, I feel myself unworthy here too—that, as I descend into the arena for Theophrastus with a bold attempt of my limited wit to join battle with forces formidable for their numbers (or even their mere abundance), the reader might help my weakness failing under such a labor, and bring auxiliary hands to one facing such numerous legions. But, considering that every mark of a "prevaricator" <note>A legal term for a dishonest advocate who betrays their client’s cause.</note> must be avoided, I implore you with a patient ear to keep a mind untainted by preconceived opinions and observant of the balance in a cause not yet fully examined, while I try to wash away so many and such great monstrous insults fabricated and piled upon **THEOPHRASTUS**.

<margin>The huge number of enemies of Theophrastus.</margin>
I try, I say—for who could feel certain of the outcome, or not fear that, with so many spears hurled from the loud mouths of so many adversaries, he might be conquered and overwhelmed, if not by the force of arguments, then by their sheer volume? Here, a mob of Aristotelian Philosophers <note>Followers of Aristotle’s traditional natural philosophy taught in universities.</note> declaims, and with indignant faces and noisy voices, they clamor that Theophrastus did not depart from the schools moved by the weight of reason, but that he flew away out of ignorance of Peripatetic doctrine <note>Aristotelianism.</note> and a light-headed mind.

<margin>Aristotelians.</margin>
<margin>Galenists.</margin>
There, the followers of Galen <note>The dominant medical tradition for 1,500 years, based on the four humors.</note>—the larger flock of modern physicians—thunder a menacing speech. They charge him with irreverence toward gray-haired antiquity, blaming him because he was the first to deny and despise the oracles of Apollo <note>A poetic reference to traditional medical wisdom, as Apollo was the god of healing.</note> that had been celebrated for so many centuries and established by happy success and outcome; and that he instead brought forth and exalted his own little fables, manufactured in his own brain.

<margin>The Common Crowd.</margin>
The most fickle common people shout along with these—people who are like wax to any impression. Having been taught to sing the same song by those masters, they rashly condemn him without knowing the cause.

<margin>A reader who is his own master is desired.</margin>
<margin>The writer of the Preface does not adhere to Paracelsus in everything.</margin>
How could I dare to clash with such numerous enemies of such great authority, being unequal in strength and resources, unless I were certain of the protection of Truth—at whose sight alone the innumerable battle-lines of falsehoods are put to flight? And unless I were fully persuaded of the integrity of your mind, Kind Reader—corrupted by no prejudices—which I appoint as the judge of this dispute? (So that, having weighed the arguments on both sides, you may freely pronounce what the enemies bring against **PARACELSUS** and what I bring in his favor as worthy of blame or praise.) Yet, I want to remind you here in the entryway <note>In the introduction or "vestibule" of the book.</note>, lest you think I am so addicted to the party of Paracelsus that I would fight for his defense at every turn and on every occasion—receiving the spears launched at him always with my own side exposed, and that access to his heart is only open through my own chest. Not at all. I have never sworn an oath to the words of any Master (I always except the Great Master <note>God.</note> and His disciples); I have made no man’s cause my own; nor is it my intent at present to fight for the words and deeds of **PARACELSUS** as if for "altars and hearths." <note>original: "pro aris & focis"; a classical idiom meaning to fight for one's most sacred possessions, home, and religion.</note>

<summary>Bitiskius describes the features of this edition, including a portrait by Tintoretto and a glossary, while defending Paracelsus against his academic critics (Aristotelians and Galenists) and clarifying his own role as an objective editor rather than a blind follower.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Frederick Bitiskius’s defense of Paracelsus, addressing the philosopher's personal character, his human failings, and the reliability of his primary critics—specifically Johannes Oporinus and Thomas Erastus. Bitiskius acknowledges that while Paracelsus was not perfect, much of the slander against him stems from unreliable sources or corrupted manuscripts.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>Paracelsus was excessively burdened by his Adversaries.</margin>
<margin>Who Oporinus was and what faith is to be placed in him.</margin>
<margin>Who Erastus was and what faith [to have] in him.</margin>
<margin>The Author's writings were corrupted.</margin>

*...in his mind. For he was indeed a man, and since it is human to err—as much to stray from the truth in doctrine as to fail in morals—I by no means think him to have been a stranger to this mortal fragility. For I would not wish to whisper about <term>PARACELSUS</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist.</note> what the schools shout with full throats from their pulpits, and what so many authors chant in their writings concerning Hippocrates: namely, that the "divine old man" could neither deceive nor be deceived. Far be such blasphemy from our mouths, attributing to a man that which God has reserved for Himself as the absolute Truth. We present <term>PARACELSUS</term> to you, not as an Achilles washed in the Stygian waves <note>Referring to the River Styx; Bitiskius means Paracelsus was not immortal or invulnerable.</note> and therefore invulnerable; but rather as one immersed in the abyss of original sin, and therefore imbued with the tint of many vices, his body often exposed and vulnerable—even pierced and wounded—by the arrows of his accusers. I confess his life was not exempt from every stain: but I utterly deny it was marked by as many foul stigmas as his enemies falsely brand upon him. Regarding his writings, they are sprinkled with certain doctrines that an exact and rigid censor might not approve; but I contend that very many of them admit a kinder interpretation, and therefore should by no means be rejected—unless we think a beautiful and elegant body should be entirely destroyed because of a few blemishes.*

*Nor should it be passed over that the antagonists owe nearly all the battering rams with which they strive to strike <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> <note>Paracelsus’s chosen name.</note> to <term>Oporinus</term> <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568), a famous printer and scholar who served as Paracelsus's secretary for two years and later wrote a scathing letter about his habits.</note>, the amanuensis of <term>Paracelsus</term>, who followed the example of Aristotle in being unjust toward his teacher. He, unmindful of the benefits bestowed upon him and ignorant of the value of the doctrine instilled by his Master, rushed against him with a sharp pen and punctured his name with most hostile marks. But he finally came to his senses, and the man whom he had pursued with insults while alive, he followed with veneration when dead. The infamous bites he took at his teacher’s reputation turned into the remorses of conscience, and a repentance—alas, too late—closed the wounds of the dead man which he had inflicted while he breathed. It would have been desirable if, while the author still lingered among the living, <term>Oporinus</term> had returned to his senses; then, I believe, we would have had <term>PARACELSUS</term> confessing with an honest mouth that he had won no victory from any enemy more pleasing than this. And indeed, it is a triumph worthy of an ever-green crown when enemies, having fallen to the ground of their own accord, lick up and swallow what they spat out at the innocent; and, having regained a better mind, they seriously—though late—mourn their preceding madness as if it were the agitation of the Furies. A witness to this unfeigned repentance is <term>Toxites</term> <note>Michael Toxites (1514–1581), a physician and poet who became a major editor and defender of Paracelsus’s works.</note>, the celebrated Doctor of Medicine and faithful interpreter of <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>, in the preface to the Testament. Another witness is <term>Conringius</term> <note>Hermann Conring (1606–1681), a polymath who was generally critical of Paracelsus, making his admission of Oporinus’s change of heart more credible.</note>, an adversary of Paracelsus, whose testimony is all the more credible because it comes from an enemy; he affirms that <term>Oporinus</term>, after the death of <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>, stood as his admirer and worshiper, though he had previously been a despiser and hater. This is clear from the letter begged from him by <term>Weyer</term> <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician known for his work on demons; he published Oporinus’s private letter to damage Paracelsus’s reputation.</note>, which Oporinus took very poorly when he learned it was being worn away in the hands of the common people, testifying to his grief in many ways. This single confession and revocation by <term>Oporinus</term> knocks from the hands of the adversaries all the weapons with which they promised themselves they would utterly destroy the memory and esteem of <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>; therefore, those who fight with them in the future will deserve laughter, not opposition.*

*As for the other part of the arrows with which the author is attacked, drawn from the quiver of <term>Erastus</term> <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss theologian and physician who wrote a massive four-volume critique of Paracelsian medicine.</note>, his capital enemy, it must be known that many things brought forward to his ignominy rely solely on the authority of the adversary. Consequently, they do not deserve faith as they are unworthy of security, since frequently in his writings, led by a blind passion for contradicting <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>, Erastus contravened the clearest truth. It must be added, finally, that certain things were undoubtedly changed, added, mutilated, and perverted in his writings by the adversaries or rivals of <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>, which the Author, if alive, would not recognize as his own. For he left many posthumous manuscripts which, handled by the hands of the envious or those swelling with a false persuasion of doctrine, saw the light long after his death. Their deceit has substituted entire treatises under his name, such that it is only clear to those most skilled in the doctrine and style of <term>PARACELSUS</term> which were written by him. We ourselves have excluded several from this edition which were inserted in the German edition but relegated to the spurious by those learned in the Chemical art; we leave the judgment to the Reader as to what should be thought of a page here or a few periods there.*

<margin>A response is given to the objection concerning his uncertain origin.</margin>

*Having premised these things, I now move forward to catch the first spear hurled at the man even as he drew his first breath. It targets his obscure and unknown origin, noting that he was born of an uncertain and wandering Father, and a mother from a brothel. They please themselves wonderfully when fighting with their own ghosts; for from a supposed fiction, under a dark cloud of birth craftily concealing a crime, they reason thus: "What wonder if <term>PARACELSUS</term>, born of parents whose blood was reddened by crimes, was bruised everywhere with foul spots and emulated the vices of his parents? Crows come from a crow, even if the chicks mimic the color of swans; as long as the father's blood boils in the veins, the crimes of fathers and grandfathers will effervesce; and the offspring is often liable to more serious things, even if wearing the masked face of an honest man" (so that the foulness of the lineage...*

<header>PREFACE.</header>
<meta>catchword: each</meta>

# PREFACE.

...may hide his wickedness. But even if we grant that the fruit does not fall far from the tree, and that "an evil egg comes from an evil tree," <note>original: "mali corni malum ouum." A variation of the proverb "a bad crow lays a bad egg," implying that character is inherited.</note> what does this have to do with our <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term>, <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> who was not only born to parents joined in lawful marriage, but was also distinguished by a noble lineage and integrity? Since his Last Will and Testament provides clear testimony regarding their lives and their passing, I, in performing my duty, reject and demolish this first objection. From this, the reader may perceive with a single glance how far a hateful lust for criticism drove <term>Erastus</term> <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who was one of the most fierce critics of Paracelsus’s medicine and theology.</note> headlong, for he denied that <term>PARACELSUS</term> descended from the <term>Bombast von Hohenheim</term> family, attempting instead to brand a man of noble birth as the bastard of some common woman and a vagabond of unknown home.

<margin>On Drunkenness.</margin>
Everyone condemns his drunkenness, and they reproach him for having lived too much among cups and tankards. Yet this is a vice of his nation, not the man, handed down in an uninterrupted thread from the age of <term>Tacitus</term> <note>The Roman historian Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD) famously described the ancient Germans' tendency to drink heavily in his work *Germania*.</note> to our own; perhaps it is contemporary with German sincerity, and I know not if it be joined by some bond of kinship. <term>Maier</term> <note>Michael Maier (1568–1622), a German physician and alchemist.</note> denies that it is considered a vice among Germans if someone, indulging his nature among friends, drowns his sadness in repeated cups of wine, and, smoothing his brow, waters his vitals with that sweet liquor. And indeed, very many of that nation seem to indulge quite freely in <term>Father Liber</term>, <note>original: "libero Patri." An epithet for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> while remaining otherwise of most upright life and pure of crime. If the virtue of the most wise <term>Socrates</term> and the severe <term>Cato</term> was more than once warmed by wine, why is it surprising if <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> rendered his own colder temperament more vigorous by the same means? (For they say he was castrated by a hog when he was three years old). It is established by experience that wine sharpens the wit for many and pours in subtle concepts; and I believe that stupendous vigor of mind—by which, when well-watered, he easily produced sublime and abstruse things—flowed from there. For those ideas do not smell of a hangover, but of a purified mind, once the thickest vapors have been dissipated by sleep a few hours after drinking, leaving only the noble spirits to shape these excellent concepts.

They add that he was a perpetual inhabitant of public inns, and that ivy was no more fixed to the taverns than he was himself. <note>An ivy bush was a traditional sign hung outside a tavern.</note> And while they everywhere call him a runner and a wanderer, here alone do they grant him "constancy" and "stability."

<margin>On his wandering and staying in inns.</margin>
Truly, this needs no response, as his adversaries are reprehending things they would extol with praise if they knew the cause. That unquenchable greed for searching out the secrets of nature and enriching his mind with the furniture of recondite sciences did not allow him to remain long in one and the same place. Instead, like <term>Mercury</term>, it placed under him the little fires for traversing all lands, nations, and cities, so that he might confer face-to-face with men who search into nature—especially Chemists—and obtain through one or two conversations what they had found through long labors and nightly vigils. For those with experience know with what great sweat barely one or two truths are dug out from the bosom of nature, and how deep is that "well of <term>Democritus</term>" <note>Democritus famously said that "truth lies at the bottom of a well."</note> which must be dried up by the fires of the <term>Spagyrists</term>. <note>Spagyric is a term for alchemical medicine involving the separation and recombination of plant or mineral components.</note> Therefore, by my reckoning, he deserves praise if he traveled through many regions out of a desire for learning. Let whoever pants for solid science and burns with the love of knowing the innermost secrets of things wander as that Author did. Let them seek out where men grown grey in this study are to be found, and receive from a friendly mouth in the space of one little hour what those men possess through so many expensive labors. Not every land bears everything: he who seeks frankincense should go to the Arabs; he who seeks rhubarb, to the Chinese. Betony should be sought in shady places, the grape in sunny ones; the carline thistle in mountainous areas, and sundew in the marshes. We are not all born under one star, nor did the most wise Moderator of the universe appoint one single man as the dispenser of all His goods; rather, He distributed His treasures to different men and various regions according to His good pleasure. By this necessity, the Parent of nature bound men together by Law, so that He might join them by need, wanting us to require each other's work and to seek from neighboring regions what our own lack. This, then, and no other reason, is what impelled him to change his seat so frequently and forced him to be a guest in public houses; for it would have been quite ill-advised to rent private ones for the short time he stayed in each city.

<margin>On Poverty.</margin>
They also criminalize his poverty, which is often the companion of virtue and an indicator of a mind pure from fraud and hands free from plunder. I know not if one of the philosophers spoke rashly when he called a rich man either "unjust or the heir of the unjust," since most people, puffed up by the bladders of illicit arts, emerge from the whirlpool of poverty, or succeed those who, having scraped together goods through right or wrong, escaped the supposed disgrace of want. I hold these little objections as worth hardly anything at all, nor would I deem them worthy of a response, were it not pleasing to see the adversaries warring among themselves. Lest he should grant <term>PARACELSUS</term> the knowledge of the "gold-making stone," <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> <term>Gesner</term> <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss physician and naturalist.</note> imagines him struggling with poverty and squandering the modest money acquired through cures on drinking bouts, until he had to apply his medical hand again to earn more when it failed. But <term>Oporinus</term> <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568), a famous printer who served as Paracelsus’s secretary for a time.</note> contradicts this in a letter to Doctor Weyer, where he says the following: *He was a prodigal squanderer of money, and indeed so often destitute of it that I knew not even a penny remained to him; yet on the very next day, he would show that he had a well-furnished purse, so that I often wondered from where it had been supplied to him.*

<summary>Bitiskius defends Paracelsus against charges of illegitimacy, habitual drunkenness, and aimless wandering, arguing that his travels were a noble pursuit of hidden natural knowledge and that his drinking was a cultural trait that did not impede his genius.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus’s character. The previous page refuted accusations of his common birth and habitual drunkenness, attributing his behavior to national custom rather than personal vice. This page addresses his alleged greed and medical competence.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...nearly every month he saw to it that a new garment was made for himself, and he would give the previous one to the first person he met. From where could this continuous and inexhaustible prodigality flow, if not from the perennial fountain of the <term>elixir</term>? <note>The "Elixir of Life" or "Universal Medicine," a substance in alchemy capable of curing all diseases and prolonging life.</note> To whom else has such a fertile spring, never and nowhere ending, been found, than to the possessor of the <term>Stone</term>? <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> Nor was he hunting for empty little glories when he claimed for himself a greater treasure than that of Pope Leo or the Emperor Charles V: for, by the unanimous consensus of the Philosophers, the veins of those blessed mines never fail.

<margin>The objection is resolved.</margin>
However, it is of no importance what his detractors respond—that it was not fitting for a <term>Croesus</term> <note>A reference to the king of Lydia, legendary for his immense wealth.</note> to bargain for small rewards for his cures, to demand promised payments, or to be angry with a Marquis and a Canon who refused him. For, as <term>Maier</term> <note>Michael Maier (1568–1622), a German physician and counselor to Rudolf II, known for his alchemical writings.</note> sincerely noted, in love and in <term>Chemistry</term> nothing is safe; in both, rivals are to be feared. These rivals, not being received with the same goodwill, envy your fortune; and being unable to bear one more successful than themselves, they often plot against your life and leave nothing untried to remove the hated man from their midst. Therefore, he very excellently and wisely feigned poverty in such cases and concealed his opulence. Indeed, he is accused of imprudence—and not without cause—for the fact that only once, in the presence of his servant Francis (as the latter's letter to Neander testifies), he performed a <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectionem." In alchemy, the act of casting the Philosopher's Stone into a crucible of molten base metal to transform it into gold.</note> and gave the resulting Sun <note>original: "Solem." In alchemical language, "Sun" refers to gold.</note> to him to be sold.

<margin>On palliative cures.</margin>
Thus falls the lie based on this argument concerning his seeking payment from <term>palliative cures</term> <note>Treatments that merely mask symptoms or provide temporary relief rather than a true cure.</note> and swindling the sick of their silver for illnesses that were only somewhat eased but remained infamous for their recurring attacks. This is further torn down by the testimony of Francis, who says: "With equal industry, I knew him to heal, for free, lepers, those with dropsy, epileptics, those with gout, those afflicted by the venereal disease, and countless other sick people; something which the Galenic Doctors were unable to imitate."

In this, he asserts that <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> cured the aforementioned conditions fundamentally and without any reward. And this lie is finally completely overturned by the example cited by Planis-Campis, a Parisian Surgeon. **THEOPHRASTUS** was staying in Nuremberg, where he was attacked by the physicians of that city and proclaimed a loud-mouthed deceiver. To come to the aid of his struggling reputation, he approached certain men of the highest authority in that Republic and promised to produce a specimen of his skill to remove the infamy and assert his art, with no fee stipulated or accepted. At the command of these men, who lent him a willing ear, several "elephants" <note>original: "elephantiacos." Refers to those suffering from "elephantiasis," a term often used historically for a severe, disfiguring form of leprosy.</note>—who were segregated from the communion of other men and thrust into an infirmary—were chosen by the judgment of others. **THEOPHRASTUS**, by the singular power of his remedies, cleansed them from the foul Greek leprosy and restored them to their former health. That most ample and celebrated city preserves the illustrious testimony of these cures in its Archives, and thus preserves the name of **PARACELSUS** forever living in them, immune to the deceptive stain of greed.

<margin>On the Lie.</margin>
How thick a veil of hatred is drawn over their sight—a hatred conceived from tender years and matured with increasing age—those who are blinded by it prove most evidently when they lean on their own weapons. For a certain learned man, daring to proclaim **PARACELSUS** a total liar because he boasted of having traveled through Denmark and yet called Stockholm a city of Denmark, shows himself to be most ignorant of Danish history. He does not know that while **THEOPHRASTUS** was traveling in those regions, Sweden was still under the rule of the Danes, and it was only some years later, when Christian IV was in power, that it wavered and finally fell away when the purple cloak was stripped off. <note>The translator is referring to the Kalmar Union, where Denmark, Norway, and Sweden were under a single monarch. Sweden’s final break from the union occurred under Gustav Vasa, though the author's historical chronology here is a bit confused regarding the specific kings.</note> Therefore, he could have called it a city of Denmark, just as today we call Warsaw a city of Poland for the sole reason that it obeys the King of the Poles, although it is situated in Masovia, outside the soil of Greater or Lesser Poland. Let the same judgment apply to so many other objections, almost every one of which betrays either the ignorance or the rashness of his enemies. 

One critic, joking so as to prove Paracelsus’s lack of knowledge, accuses him of a failure of memory—and indeed one so great that he forgot the names of herbs to be reported to his disciples. This is a weak argument drawn from a weakness of memory; for we know men of the most refined judgment and the sharpest intellect who lack the happiness of a good memory, yet they hold a place in the Republic of Letters that is not to be despised. It is scarcely permitted to anyone to be so fortunate that these three faculties of the soul <note>Usually identified as memory, intellect, and will.</note> fall to them in a perfectly equal degree of excellence. But Neander fights against this joke, affirming that the steward of the mind's delights was so obedient to the man that, when ordered to bring forth an entire passage of Galen, he produced it immediately. The same is also proven by the herbal written by **THEOPHRASTUS**, of which Toxites makes mention in the preface to the *Testament*.

<margin>The second part of the Preface.</margin>
Having now surveyed the things brought forward by his adversaries against the life and morals of **THEOPHRASTUS**, let us now also hear their complaints concerning his writings. The famous anatomist of our century, Bartholin, complains in a letter to Bogdan that not a single line has flowed from his pen which a jealous circle of detractors has not defiled with their spite and wished deleted. This also happened to **PARACELSUS**; looking at his rising fame with a grim eye, the physicians divined—not falsely—that as much would be taken from their own fame as was added to his.

<margin>Why the physicians were hostile to Paracelsus.</margin>
And indeed, since he professedly opposed the trivial doctrine of the medicators and their method of curing,

# PREFACE.

*...they correctly guessed that if, by the weight of his reasoning or the success of his cures, his method were to be approved and theirs rejected, it would result in glory for him and disgrace for them. Therefore, to avert the looming disaster, they decided to oppose him as skillfully as possible, and to defame whatever came from his hand or pen. Not content with accusing his life of being full of outrages, they charged his writings with being works of darkness, ignorance, empty talk, impiety, and a jumble of illicit things; they condemned them to the flames, intending them as a pleasing <term>holocaust</term> <note>In this context, a "burnt offering" or ritual sacrifice.</note> to the spirits of <term>Aristotle</term> and <term>Galen</term>.* <note>Aristotle and Galen were the ancient Greek authorities whose teachings dominated philosophy and medicine for centuries; Paracelsus famously challenged their dominance.</note>

<margin>Bright and eminent minds in favor of Paracelsus.</margin>
*But on the opposite side, not a few men of more sincere character and more sublime intellect admired and held his writings in high esteem, and giving public signs of their appraisal, they recorded it in their own works. Among these, let <term>Ramus</term> <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), an influential French humanist and logician.</note> come forward first, a most sharp and learned man; in his oration concerning Basel, placing THEOPHRASTUS among the chief ornaments of that city, he said:*

<margin>Ramus.</margin>
> **He entered so deeply into the innermost vitals of nature, and explored and perceived the powers and faculties of metals and plants with such incredible sharpness of mind, that medicine seems to have been born for the first time with him, enabling the cure of all diseases—even those considered desperate and incurable in the opinion of men.**

<margin>Quercetanus.</margin>
*To him let <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist who championed Paracelsian medicine.</note> be added, a man of multifaceted knowledge and experience and a Royal Physician, who reports that THEOPHRASTUS teaches many things in the medical art almost by divine inspiration, which a grateful posterity can never sufficiently admire or praise.*

<margin>Gellius Zemeus</margin>
*Indeed, <term>Gellius Zemeus</term> <note>A 16th-century Dutch physician.</note> bursts out with these words: "Among the Germans there now exists a certain young man, THEOPHRASTUS, whose equal the world does not produce; I do not remember having read anyone more learned."*

<margin>Barthius</margin>
*What does <term>Barthius</term> <note>Caspar Barthius (1587–1658), a German scholar.</note> say in Scholtz’s Medical Epistle 80? "I think highly of Theophrastus," he says, "he performed admirable things; but I have not yet heard of anyone who perfectly understands him or can do what he himself did."*

<margin>Smetius.</margin>
*One may add to these <term>Smetius</term> <note>Henricus Smetius (1537–1614), a Flemish physician.</note>, who asserts that PARACELSUS was a hardworking and industrious seeker of hidden things, a man of great skill, and admirable in the preparation of medicines.*

<margin>Melchior Adamus.</margin>
*And let us close this line of witnesses with <term>Melchior Adam</term> <note>A German biographer (1575–1622) known for his lives of famous scholars.</note>, who testifies that he was endowed with a most sharp and almost divine intellect, and that no mortal ever unearthed such difficult, secret, and hidden things in the whole of Philosophy. He freed many from leprosy, gout, dropsy, and other incurable and desperate evils; and every day for two hours at Basel, he interpreted both active and speculative Philosophy with the greatest diligence and to the great profit of his listeners—teaching a doctrine which he had attained not from <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The "Father of Medicine," whose traditional methods Paracelsus often rejected in favor of chemical remedies.</note>, but from experience.*

<margin>Response to the objection regarding obscurity.</margin>
*I could bring forward more praises of THEOPHRASTUS, but since the reality of the situation and the products of his intellect speak for themselves, I will not linger on these further and instead turn to answer the objections of his adversaries. The first fault they find is that of obscurity—that at the very threshold he pours a mist over even the sharpest eyes. They claim the cause of this is the vast number of unknown words, invented without any clear necessity. To them I respond: it is uncertain, and they have not yet established by firm reasoning, whether this defect of vision arises from the weakness of the eye, from an insufficiently illuminated object, or from a sudden and excessive arrival of light. Indeed, <term>owls</term> <note>original: "noctuae"</note> cannot bear bright light because of the tenderness of their eyes, and they experience the same "obscurity" when suddenly brought out from a dark prison into the middle of the day as they do when moving from the brightest sun into a dark cave. Perhaps those complainers, raised in the shadows of the schools, are made dim-sighted by the sight of the beam of true philosophy, because the eye of a mind unaccustomed to such delicate structure is dazzled by the new light rising with more brilliant rays.*

<margin>The reasoning for the writing style of the Egyptians and Pythagoreans.</margin>
*If, however, it is not far from the truth that obscurity arises for those less accustomed to reading him, or for those who seek the hidden meanings in the deepest recesses without any profound meditation, let them know that it was the custom of the ancient sages—especially the <term>Egyptians</term> and <term>Pythagoreans</term>—to use a style of writing where they hid all the most beautiful things under the coverings of words, numbers, or enigmatic figures. In this way, they skillfully concealed them from the common folk, so that being unseen, they would not be envied. It is reasonable to believe that THEOPHRASTUS imitated such great men; namely, so that he might offer for sale a knowledge earned by his own sweat only to those willing to sweat for it.*

<margin>The Galenists do not want to change their doctrines.</margin>
*For he saw the whole army of Doctors, nursed on the milk of <term>Galenic</term> discipline, who were unwilling to exchange the foods they had been used to since their tenderest years for new ones, even if they were more nourishing, for fear of damaging their health.*

<margin>Nor the Aristotelians.</margin>
*He saw the crowd devoted to <term>Aristotle</term> had so greedily drunk in the opinions of their Master that, having turned them into their very juice and blood (however faulty), no scalpel could be found to draw them out or separate them. He noticed that no thanks were given to him for detecting and uprooting the errors of the ancients and substituting the truth (still unknown) in their place. Struck with deep inward sorrow and indignant that the world should be blind while its eyes were open and healthy, he acted so as not to bury the talent entrusted to him by the Father of Lights, nor yet to <term>throw pearls before swine</term>.* <note>A biblical reference (Matthew 7:6) meaning to offer something valuable to those who do not understand or appreciate its worth.</note>

<summary>This page defends Paracelsus’s intellectual legacy by citing endorsements from major scholars like Ramus and Melchior Adam, while refuting the common criticism that his writing is intentionally "obscure" or confusing.</summary>

# PREFACE.

<sig>¶ ¶ 2</sig>

## PREFACE.

<margin>Why he wrote obscurely.</margin>
<margin>Obscure things are made clear.</margin>
*...he chose a style of writing removed from the common sort, hoping that his late-born descendants, being more keen-sighted in the light of nature—once the fog of the authorities of antiquity had been dispersed—would perceive and embrace with their whole soul those things which his own contemporaries rejected with all their might. Nor did this conjecture fail him, since most ingenious men, following in his footsteps with experience as their companion or guide, have in our age and that of our fathers uncovered many things which he wished to remain hidden. A path that was impassable before this century has been so smoothly paved that, with the ruts and the frequency of impediments removed, they have left only a few things for our own diligence to clear away. Therefore, the complaint about obscurity is a testimony of supine negligence; for those who wail that their jaws are tired from chewing for themselves, and who shun the labor of those who bring complaints about difficulties in this regard, clearly desire food that has been pre-chewed. If, walking the path of nature, they turn over these volumes with repeated reading, they will discover the waters of truth scattered here and there; they will perceive with a grateful ear the harmony of his sayings and their sweet concord; and finally, they will notice the clear light of day dissipating the shadows they had wrongly believed in.*

<margin>Aristotle’s obscurity.</margin>
*Nor did he sin more gravely than <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose works were famously difficult and subject to centuries of commentary.</note>—if indeed he sinned at all—who so greatly veiled his opinions in ambiguity of words that up to this point there has been more labor in the schools over extracting his meaning than over the certainty of the things themselves. He hints at this, and nods to our own words, in the letter given to Alexander, where he promises the King that no one will perceive the sense of his physics except from his own living voice as a teacher; hence those tears shed over the buried mind of the author. I could, with the same bolt, bar the nonsense regarding the unheard-of novelty of his words, found in no language, or the abuse of others which, through figures of speech, were twisted with a stubborn neck from their ancient meaning to a new one with remarkable audacity and force, were there not other obstacles at hand.* <margin>Response to the objection concerning unknown words.</margin> *It should by no means be taken ill that <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> <note>Paracelsus's given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> fabricated new terms for new things previously unknown in the schools, since necessity compels one who labors under a lack of an <term>etymon</term> <note>A root word or origin.</note> to mark a thing with some name so that it may be more easily distinguished hereafter. By what word used in the schools, I ask, would he have defined that universal <term>first matter</term> <note>The primordial substance from which all things are created.</note>, composed of the three principles, and producing all things by the vegetative power of the general form it already possesses, when that matter is entirely unknown to the philosophers of the school?* <margin>What the first matter is to the Chemists. Aristotle is noted.</margin> *For he did not mean <term>Aristotle’s</term> matter—always raging with unexhausted lust, an unformed harlot of insatiable pleasure, never satisfied by any embraces and always burning for new couplings. Our chaste matron, joined to her spouse by an indissoluble knot as long as the fates allow, clings to his friendly side and, with a luxuriant but legitimate fecundity, blesses the marriage bed with an almost innumerable offspring. Why, therefore, should it not be permitted to call that anonymous matter <term>Iliastes</term>?* <margin>What is Iliastes, Archeus, Ares, and Lestias.</margin> *Why should it not be lawful to call the force producing all things from <term>Iliastes</term>, the dispenser of all things, the <term>Archeus</term>? Or <term>Ares</term>, the spirit peculiar to each species, granting a nature and form different from others? What, finally, prevents that hidden and glowing smoke of the earth, from which plants are dissolved, rot, and ferment, from being named <term>Lestias</term>? Since such things have not reached the knowledge of the professor's chairs, and common philosophy is mute concerning them, why shall we not impose names unknown to them upon things at the chemical furnace, to avoid the labor of tedious circumscription?*

<margin>Response given to Sennert and others.</margin>
*But many of them are "barbarous," says <term>Sennertus</term> <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a physician and chemist who attempted to bridge the gap between Galenic medicine and Paracelsian chemistry.</note> of great name, and many others; or, if any are used in medical practice, they have suffered a "backward-stretching" <note>original: "opisthotonum"</note> at the hands of <term>Theophrastus</term> through tropes or symbolism. It is surprising that they did not see what philosophy cherishes in its own bosom along with common Medicine, before stretching their sight to distant things; unless perhaps their aging doctrine, with the defect of the eyes most familiar to declining age, labors more sharply to discern distant things than those close at hand. For what tastes more of barbarism than those barbarous words expressing the modes of <term>syllogistic figures</term> <note>Mnemonic names used in logic to remember types of valid arguments.</note>, which they use so freely?* <margin>The terms for syllogistic figures are barbarous.</margin> *The very sound has something so ungrateful to the ears that <term>Felapton</term>, <term>Bocardo</term>, and <term>Ferison</term> <note>Technical names for specific types of logical syllogisms.</note> suggest the names of Furies or Fates to the mind. And when they give us the origin of their terms explained, then we also promise to do the same on our part. Now, "being," "essence," "entitative," "quantitative," "individuific," "identitative," "potentiality," "thisness," <note>original: "haecceitas"</note> "essentity," "receptivity," "Petreity," "sororeity"—are these not clearly un-Latin, and as far from the purity of Latinism as they are from abstract matter? And yet the whole of philosophy bristles, sown all over with such things as if with briars.* <margin>Others similarly.</margin> *What if that very Medical faculty, and other sciences and arts, following the example of Chemistry, have incurred no blame? In what matter did <term>PARACELSUS</term>, following in their footsteps, commit a crime? Has not the new art of diseases assigned names to its humors, while it named the fiery one "yellow bile," the earthy one "black bile," and the watery one "phlegm"?* <margin>Medicine has invented new names of this kind.</margin> *Why, not retaining the common words, did it not designate bile by the name of "gall," melancholy by the name of "feculent blood" or "earthy humor," and phlegm by the name of "undigested" or "watery" humor? Has it not spoken metonymically, usurping the cause for the effect, when it called the disease "cholera" when bile broke out above and below, and called the disturbances of the black humor "hypochondriac melancholy"? Has it not...*

<summary>This page defends Paracelsus against charges of obscurity and the use of "barbarous" neologisms, arguing that new chemical and natural concepts required new terminology, just as traditional logic and medicine created their own technical vocabularies.</summary>

# PREFACE.

<meta>catchword: delicate</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>Theology.</margin>
Theology introduced the terms of the Church consistory; the word <term>sacrament</term> <note>original: "sacramenti"; here meaning a sacred rite, but originally referring to a Roman soldier's oath of allegiance.</note> was borrowed from a military symbol. Have not the theologians introduced Trinity, Incarnation, Transubstantiation, and <term>Impanation</term> <note>The theological theory that the body of Christ is present in the bread of the Eucharist without changing the substance of the bread.</note> into the Latin language? What of the fact that genus and species, act and potency, form, motion, and so on, are understood quite differently in a proper Latin sense than they are when used
<margin>Philosophy.</margin>
<margin>Mathematics.</margin>
*logically, physically, and metaphysically*? Geometers and even experts in optics drew the word "ray" from the sun into their own arts. And to say nothing of astronomy and other arts filled with terms invented at will, *Algebra*—while it considers numbers in a different way than common *arithmetic* does—devised <term>squares, squared-squares, sursolids, bisursolids, etc.</term> <note>original: "cenſos, cenſi-cenſos, ſurſolidos, beſurſolidos"; these are archaic terms for powers of numbers (e.g., x², x⁴, x⁵, x¹⁰).</note> along with <term>cossic signs</term> <note>Early algebraic symbols used before modern notation was standardized.</note>. It borrowed the name "root" from plants, and "square" and "cube" from the Geometers. If it was permitted for other faculties to forge new words at their pleasure, or to bring words forged elsewhere back to the anvil and, having impressed them with a mark of their own kind, transfer them to their own use, shall **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Referring to Paracelsus, whose full name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> be reproached for applying new little words to recent productions of genius or art, or to previously unknown minerals of nature he detected? Or for transplanting wild shrubs into his own gardens? **THEOPHRASTUS**—and after him *Severinus*—are weighed down by scandal for having used the words *tincture*, *economy*, and *root* to describe the power and origin of actions, not realizing that these words move the mind far more powerfully than the word "virtue" or "power." For the name "tincture" represents to the imagination not just a bare impression, but the very *manner* of the impression.

<margin>What a Tincture is to Chemists.</margin>
Because, just as a tincture first takes away the color from a cloth and then imprints its own, so do those powers of which they speak mark the character of their own faculties and erase the former state.

<margin>What a Root is.</margin>
As a root is the beginning of the trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, so the cause of a disease—upon which the effects, accidents, signs, and symptoms depend in their becoming and their finished state—best enjoys the name of "root."

<margin>What Economy is.</margin>
"Economy" is not badly attributed to any internal organ, because there, through digestion, heterogeneous things are separated, individual things are arranged in their proper place, and once the things fit for nutrition are preserved and cleansed, the refuse is swept away. Therefore, there is no reason why adversaries should be offended that **PARACELSUS** inserted and cultivated these "little plants" and others, drawn from natural or artificial things, which strike the imaginative faculty more vehemently for the sake of conceiving them in the mind alone.

<margin>Response to the objection regarding his ignorance of the Latin language.</margin>
But the reasons brought forward are by no means sufficient for them; they bring up another reason for these invented names that are foreign to common use: namely, his ignorance of the Latin language, which is the key and instrument of all erudition. If they said he had *neglected* a language previously known and understood, they would obtain what they want with plain ease; but to say he never *possessed* it is not the same. Indeed, having had the most learned teachers and men excelling in all liberal doctrine, an auditor—if he were like a wooden post—would have profited nothing without a full knowledge of the Latin language, since at that time all disciplines were delivered in it. However, the reason for his contempt was the uncertainties—or to speak more truly, the dreams—which the leaders of ancient philosophy consigned to posterity in their books. Thus, he preferred to abstain entirely from unrolling their works rather than to waste useless effort in a daily reading of great labor and no profit. For this reason, his library was confined to scarcely one or two books, as he himself intended to drink purer waters from the source itself, proceeding on the same straight path as the very first authors.

<margin>Theophrastus reads the book of nature.</margin>
Therefore, he betook himself to that famous "Book of Nature," most full of every kind of wisdom, inscribed by the finger of the Divine Master, to be turned over with a more diligent mind. In this reading, however, what was required was not paper leaves, but the attention of the senses, a sharp genius, assiduous meditation, tireless experience, and finally, the blessing of God.

<margin>What it means to learn from the light of nature.</margin>
And this is the way in which someone is illustrated by science from the "light of nature," which, being unknown to *Sennert*, provided him an occasion for mocking **THEOPHRASTUS** and *Croll*. The former asserts that those taught by the light of nature are instructed by the Holy Spirit; the latter asserts that a singular influence of the stars concurs and is required. Both are true. For the divine blessing, which we implore in all our labors, as well as inspiration, does not always happen through an open and perceptible revelation; rather, we often see the effect when we did not feel it in the making. The concurrence of the stars radiates doctrine into the mind when the spirit, flowing into the lower parts, affects the bodily parts within us. For the air—which enters us like the nearest vessel receiving the influx, drawn in by the first breath after leaving the prison of the mother's womb—tempers the vital and animal spirit. The soul then uses these spirits in forming icons or species, and affects them according to the nature of the matter of the air, which then, being swallowed under a favorable constellation, imprints the firmest traces, to be seen throughout the entire interval of a passing life. Whence, for **THEOPHRASTUS**, born under a favorable aspect of the stars and learning from the light of nature, the Roman tongue was a "wooden" thing; since he was not in need of it as an instrument, he derived secret cognitions from the spring of nature by means of the senses, reason, and experience. Up to this point, there have been reproaches; but behold, here are laments and almost tears on account of the offended or "flayed" ears, which are too tender, caused by an unpleasing style, unpolished and unrefined by any tool, which he uses to cough up not only Latin but also the Swiss-German he drank in with his mother's milk. Oh...

<margin>
The labor of the Orator compared with the Philosopher.
</margin>
*O delicate eardrum that is wounded by this harsh sound! O tender stomachs nurtured in the Ciceronian temple <note>Referring to the followers of Marcus Tullius Cicero, who prized perfectly polished Latin above all else.</note>, in whom this cruder food produces <term>indigestion</term> <note>original: "apepsiam"; a Greek-derived term for the inability to digest food.</note>! Among philosophers, these critics require the elegance of an orator with an attentive ear, discerning the purer dictions like precious metals by their very ring. But let those people listen to Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who famously defended the "barbarous" Latin of medieval thinkers if their ideas were sound.</note>, the glory of Italy and the Phoenix of his age: "To have failed to join eloquence with wisdom," he says, "is perhaps so far from a fault that to have joined them is a sin." And it should be a cause for shame that they have censured PARACELSUS for his ignorance, or rather his neglect, of the choice of words, the flow of periods, and the sound of clauses. Let that labor fall to the spectacle and pomp of rhetoricians; the simple truth is what a philosopher must seek and propose. It is permitted for rhetoricians to measure the proper circuits of their sentences and to ejaculate from a rolling tongue little droplets sweeter than <term>Hyblaean honey</term> <note>Honey from the Hyblaean Mountains in Sicily, famous in antiquity for its sweetness.</note>; it is for them to weigh the burden of every single word and to place them most conveniently so they do not produce harshness. While the rhetoricians are busy rounding their sentences or arranging them in a <term>quincunx</term> <note>An arrangement of five objects, like the dots on the five-side of a die; used here to mean a rigid, artificial pattern.</note>, the philosophers admire and investigate the reason for the circular figure in the primary bodies of this universe. While those men hunt for the sound of words, arrange them, and place them neatly in order, these men contemplate and examine the admirable harmony of nature, its stupendous arrangement, and its orderly succession. While those men adorn their speech, comb it, smear it with the tricks of a slave-trader <note>original: "mangoniis"; referring to the practice of "furbishing" or "doctoring" goods (or slaves) to make them look better than they are.</note>, curl it with locks, and deck it out with their finery, these men—using the <term>chymiatric</term> <note>Chemical-medical art, specifically Paracelsian alchemy.</note> art—strip away the superfluous garments with which nature covers the innermost powers of things as if with wrappings; and having removed the clothing, they finally exhibit to the eyes of all a naked **Diana** without her dress <note>In mythology, seeing the goddess Diana naked was a dangerous revelation of divine truth; here, it means seeing nature's secrets directly.</note>. Therefore, for a philosopher to gather curious garlands of eloquence and to study artificial elegance rather than the native form of things is plainly unbecoming and should not be required of him. We do not indeed despise a speech that clearly explains the feelings of the mind and runs along without stumbling; indeed, we grant the festivities of a playful wit and concepts seasoned with salt <note>A metaphor for wit or intellectual sharpness.</note>, if they come from a ready <term>Minerva</term> <note>Meaning "natural intelligence" or "inspiration."</note>. But eloquence that tastes of bitten fingernails <note>A metaphor for labored, over-thought writing.</note>, smells of Demosthenes' lamp <note>Demosthenes, the Greek orator, was said to study by lamp-light with such intensity that his speeches smelled of oil rather than natural grace.</note>, or finally prepares a seduction for the eyes with makeup, we condemn in a philosopher along with Pico; nor do we seek a laurel crown in this <term>must-cake</term> <note>original: "mustaceo"; a laurel-decorated cake mentioned by Cato, often used in the proverb "to seek a laurel in a must-cake," meaning to seek fame in trivial things.</note>. I add that no one here has found the Goddess of Persuasion so favorable that*
<margin>
The diversity of styles.
</margin>
*he could boast of having pleased everyone. Among the eloquent themselves, some hunt for a flowery kind of speech, others for the simple and naked; some distinguish their work with metonymies, figures, and tropes; others call a spade a spade <note>original: "scapham nominant scapham"; literally "they call a skiff a skiff."</note>. Some like the Asiatic style; others the Laconic; others the "Politic," as they call it. Some love to speak in the purest Latin, others grammatically; some require and embrace the natural placement of words, others the transposed. The river of Cicero, running most widely with perpetual evenness, smiles on some; but it displeases Brutus and seems insipid to him. Some prefer the little streams of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), known for a concise, "staccato" Neo-Stoic style of Latin.</note> gliding in a narrower channel, conspicuous for the rippled surface of the waves and playing everywhere with little flowers on the bank; yet these are rejected by no fewer people. And if things are brought back to a just balance, almost every subject to be discussed requires its own form of speaking: here the style must be loosened, there it must be tightened. Since, therefore, there is such a diversity of tastes, and not all great men have the approval of everyone for their speech, we should be moved very little if THEOPHRASTUS <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus.</note> the Philosopher, for whom such things were by no means a concern, did not satisfy everyone in this regard.*

<margin>
Response to the objection regarding the ignorance of Logic.
</margin>
> *But they reply that the name of "Philosopher" fits him less than that of "Orator," as one who was supposedly ignorant and a despiser of the other parts of philosophy, and especially of **Logic**—the art of arts, the inventor of sciences, the guiding star of truth, and the rudder of the mind in the knowledge of things. Let us grant that he was ignorant of it (though this is not conceded); let us not deny that he despised it. But whether he did so wrongly must now be weighed more accurately. How, I ask, can anyone easily believe that Logic is the directress in the investigation of things,*
<margin>
Logic does not know itself.
</margin>
*and thus the notifier of all truth, who knows that Logic has not known itself until now, nor has it known to what genus it owes its origin? For how great (oh, the shame!) are the battles even to this day in its very inner sanctum over whether it originates from the family of arts, of sciences, or of lower "habits"; or whether it constitutes a body mixed from all these? How many skirmishes are there between those who relegate it to the rank of handmaidens and those who place it in the honorable seat of Ladies? And shall she guide the eyes of my mind, or pour light upon my dimness, who until this day has remained blind and uncertain whether she should join herself to the male or the weaker sex, or to a composite hermaphroditic third? Let her apply a polished mirror, eyeglasses, or an eye-salve as a support for her weakened eyes, and having attentively considered every part of her own body, let her establish something certain about her own status; and afterwards, let her seek the name of "leader" or "surgeon of the eyes" under some pretext. No less inept is the title "art of arts" or "science of sciences," which implies that all arts and sciences are either discovered or perfected by its help.*
<margin>
It does not find or perfect the arts.
</margin>
*I would wish they would point out any art or discipline discovered by a Logician, or raised to a more eminent height. The vote of my senses and experience bids me believe that whatever arts have been unearthed, practiced, and advanced, were done so by men who were unrefined in this "artificial logic" of which we speak;*
