<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the intellectual establishment. While the previous page defended Paracelsus's "unpolished" writing style as being more truthful than empty rhetoric, this page shifts to a direct attack on Scholastic Logic—the foundation of university education at the time—arguing that it is an sterile, "crippled" tool that fails to produce actual scientific discovery.</meta>

## PREFACE.

<meta>Digitized by Google</meta>

and conversely, those who are excessively devoted to this [Logic] are so inept at everything else because of their excessive subtlety, to the point that the proverb about "purely pure Logicians" <note>original: "puris putis Logicis"; a common Renaissance-era jibe meaning that those who know only logic are mere fools in practical matters.</note> deserves its reputation. <margin>Scholastic physics is not science.</margin> The "physics" that walks about the famous Schools as a distinguished science has, until now, only been such "in potential." It claims to bring forth form into action, yet it relies on no efficient cause except for those things found by chance or luck—which Aristotle, for that reason, conveniently (and truly) placed within the order of natural causes. 

The common crowd of philosophers has indeed toiled with wicked labor so that, from their own brains—which have long been in the sharpest pains of labor—that long-desired offspring might finally emerge. They used Logic as a midwife and even borrowed time from Astronomers (perhaps to cast a birth chart <note>original: "Thema Genethliacum"; an astrological chart drawn for the moment of birth.</note> and choose a lucky hour for the delivery). But thus far, it has been in vain; whether through the misfortune or the unskilled hands of the midwife, I know not. For from this laboring mountain, nothing has emerged but a ridiculous mouse <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*: "The mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse is born."</note>. Unless, perhaps, the instruments of Logic themselves are to be blamed for their imperfection, and the failure to extract science from the womb of the "dura mater" <note>A play on words: "Dura mater" is the tough outer membrane of the brain, but here the author also implies a "harsh mother" (the mind) struggling to give birth to knowledge.</note> should be attributed to them. 

Since Philosophy uses definition, division, demonstration, and the syllogism as its primary forceps—but forceps with one leg missing—it is no wonder that, with such inept tools, it has not reached its target. <margin>Logic is an imperfect instrument.</margin> It lacked the help of Definition because that requires both a "genus" and a "specific difference"; yet these must be sought from the "substantial form" <note>In Scholastic thought, the "substantial form" is the internal essence that makes a thing what it is.</note>, which remains hidden from them to this day, with the sole exception of man. Division was of no greater use, since things cannot be separated into species except by the diversity of those same forms, which they have not yet perceived. In "a priori" <note>Demonstrating from cause to effect; starting with the reason something exists.</note> demonstration it was blind, for the cause that gives being to a thing is unknown; it substituted a phantom and a "non-being" for "prime matter" <note>The fundamental, formless substance of the universe in Aristotelian physics.</note>, and while bickering over "secondary matter," it remained ignorant of the "end" or purpose because the properties of things were not known. As for the "efficient cause" (especially the equivocal kind), they are still disputing it. It is beneath the dignity and pride of science to allow "a posteriori" <note>Demonstrating from effect back to cause; the author implies that Scholastics were too proud to learn from physical evidence.</note> demonstration. The remaining Syllogism and Topics—along with the whole of Dialectic properly so-called—cannot extend a helping right hand to science, as they are occupied only with probabilities, not with things that can be demonstrated or are of certain truth. 

Now, what do those figures of the syllogisms and their "modes" contribute to science, or indeed to any knowledge of things? <margin>The figures of the Syllogism are useless to science.</margin> The greater part concludes negatively, and therefore brings no positive knowledge; the rest conclude particularly, and no conclusions of that "brand of flour" <note>original: "cuius farinae"; a Latin idiom meaning "of that sort."</note> constitute axioms in the sciences, since axioms must be general—nor is science granted concerning particulars and individuals. Therefore, only "Barbara" <note>A mnemonic name in Scholastic logic for a syllogism where all three propositions are universal and affirmative.</note> remains, the "midwife" of the sciences, which concludes universally by the force and power of universal premises. But look at this syllogism in Barbara: *Every stone is an animal; Every man is a stone; Therefore, every man is an animal.* A true consequence and an evident demonstration follow from false antecedents. This testifies that the conclusion does not necessarily cohere with the premises, nor does it flow naturally from them; it shows that in Logic alone, "the apples fall far from the family tree" <note>original: "procul à ſtemmate poma cadere"; a variation of the proverb "the apple doesn't fall far from the tree," used here to mean Logic produces weird, unnatural results.</note> and a noble eagle is hatched by cowardly doves. 

Indeed, I know the falsehood of the proposition and the assumption, as well as the truth of the consequence, not from Logic, but from my senses and natural reason. By these things it is clear that all that magnificent apparatus of "forms" is vain and foolish, as are the ridiculous shouts of those who, in their disputes, do nothing but cuckoo "In form! In form!" Furthermore, if Logic bestows the knowledge of truth—to the point that a philosopher without Logic is like a body without an eye, an eye without a pupil, or a pupil without a ray—what is the reason that Thomas Aquinas, Albertus Magnus, and Duns Scotus <note>The three most influential medieval Scholastic theologians and philosophers.</note> hardly agree in their opinions, if the truth (which is one) was agreed upon by them as the most subtle and excellent Logicians? <margin>Thomas Aquinas, Albert, and Scotus do not agree.</margin> Why does Erasmus, the light and pillar of literature, assert that it is easier for someone to extricate himself from a labyrinth than from the entanglements of the Nominalists, Realists, Thomists, Ockhamists, and Scotists? <note>These were the competing "sects" or schools of Scholastic philosophy that dominated universities.</note> He claims no one understands these things unless he has wasted thirty-six years on the physics and "otherworldly" Aristotelian and Scotist matters. 

They ought to be warned that, if they wish to be heard as Teachers of Truth, they should at least hide those "barbarous" disagreements of theirs (which are the mark of Barbarians, not Teachers) from the common people. Or, if they wish to enjoy the title of Logicians by merit, they should diligently examine the "topical places" <note>original: "locos topicos"; standard categories or themes used in dialectical argument.</note> of their Dialectic to find a "middle term" that might reconcile those extremes by which they are divided. Moving from a greater altercation to a smaller one, they might elicit a conclusion to such great lawsuits. Otherwise, it is hardly bearable that they accuse THEOPHRASTUS <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus.</note> and after him Severinus <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), a major Danish physician and follower of Paracelsus.</note> because they placed "disease" in the category of substance. <margin>Disease in Substance.</margin> 

At this point, Curtinus, Conringius <note>Hermann Conring (1606–1681), a famous German polymath and fierce critic of Paracelsian medicine.</note>, and many other enemies of the name of PARACELSUS burst into laughter; they ironically call the Chymists "good logicians" and scold them with lashes of the tongue they in no way deserve. They claim that [the Paracelsians] have placed diseases under the category of substance—which they have trampled upon so often—simply because of the narrowness of the [ten Aristotelian] categories. Yet diseases are so far from being stabilized in one of those ten "little huts" <note>original: "tuguriolis"; a mocking term for Aristotle's ten categories of being.</note> that, on the contrary, any one of them is more widely spread than all those little houses taken together. Indeed, these categories are contained within almost any disease, as is clear to anyone who considers the disease of a stone in the bladder, or an obstruction from...

### PREFACE.

...whether [the blockage] was caused by a stone—to speak in the manner of the Schools <note>The author is likely finishing a medical metaphor from the previous page, using a "stone" (calculus) as a pun for both a physical ailment and the "calculations" of logic.</note>—or some other cause, it will become clear to anyone who examines it. For this system occupies all the **Categories** <term>Predicaments: The ten categories of being defined by Aristotle, such as substance, quality, and quantity, which formed the basis of Scholastic logic.</term>, and yet something is always left over from poor health that must be housed elsewhere. The Masters themselves do not deny that those "chambers" are too narrow, and are not grand enough palaces to house the entire universe of things. I shall pass over the **Transcendentals** <term>Transcendentals: Concepts like "Truth" or "Goodness" that were thought to transcend Aristotle's ten categories.</term> which, because their size exceeds the "penny for lodging" <note>A metaphor for the basic classifications of logic; these grander concepts do not fit into the cheap, small boxes of Scholasticism.</note>, could find no "Where" <note>original: "Ubi"; one of Aristotle's categories referring to location.</note> to reside within the system. I will say nothing of incomplete, collateral, or intentional beings; I at least pity the **Concrete** things, which are treated poorly by this zeal for "virtue." Because these things did not wish to walk about as naked "Qualities" out of modesty, but rather clothed in a proper "Habit"—lest they feel the "Passion" of the cold through "Action"—they were left without a comfortable "Site," and were forced to live as outcasts from the category of "Relation," wandering wherever they were permitted to choose a seat and inhabit <margin>Abstract things do not exist in the world.</margin> this entire Theater of the World. <note>The author is satirically personifying Aristotle's categories—Quality, Habit, Passion, Action, Site, and Relation—as tenants who cannot find a home in the rigid Scholastic system.</note> This is the reason why, in the world today, one never sees "heat" or "coldness," "fatherhood" or "sonship," "whiteness" or "blackness" [as abstracts]; instead, one sees the hot and the cold, the father and the son, the white and the black. From this it is clear that they have established their dwellings not in real entities, but in things converted into "forms" by the force of reason, and they have preserved them this way until now. I pass over the "figure" of **Galen**, the specific "modes" for each figure discovered by **Ramus** <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572) was a famous reformer of logic who challenged Aristotelianism.</note>, and many other things. From these, I could easily show that the "Vacuum" (which was supposedly expelled from nature) has actually taken refuge in the common figures and modes of the syllogism—did my pen not hurry from such playfulness toward more serious matters. Therefore, if **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist.</note> despised and made nothing of this uncertain art or science (choose your term)—which is crippled in its instruments, ambiguous in its conclusions, and staggers and falters everywhere—he should be forgiven, for he sought and possessed a solid doctrine. Even if it is granted that he gave no specimen of Logic in his writings, or even that he was ignorant of it, this added detail contributes nothing to the study to which he dedicated himself. Nevertheless, his books testify to any fair judge, and the unanimous experts of the higher sciences agree, that he was not merely lightly brushed with **German philosophy**, but was thoroughly saturated by it. <margin>Paracelsus: a master of true philosophy.</margin> I know that many do not include him in the catalog of philosophers because he did not speak a single word about those most subtle and thorny questions with which they enclose all science as if with hedges. For how (they say) could he deserve the name of "philosopher" if he does not examine the intricate reasons of the **Modals** <term>Modal logic: A complex branch of logic dealing with necessity and possibility.</term> as if they were his own fingers? If he does not imagine "imaginary spaces" or know whether God inhabits them? If he does not define whether **Plato’s** "Ideas" gave birth to **Aristotle’s** "Universals," or whether the latter, with a wider mouth, swallowed the former? Or finally, if he does not comprehend with what dexterity <margin>He despised thorny and useless questions.</margin> a finite quantity can be divided into infinite parts? He considered this philosophy to be trifling—the idle speculations of "fantasists" inhabiting a brain for fear of a vacuum—and believed it stood as far from the true method of philosophizing as the imaginary stands from the real, or the useful from the futile. 

But such things "sharpen and polish the mind in a wonderful way," they respond. They sharpen it, I admit; but to the ruin of that venerable Goddess, **Truth**, who is so pierced through by these untimely "points" that her narrowed face is so scarred everywhere that she is no longer <margin>Truth is not recognized.</margin> recognized. They "polish" the mind, I grant; but they make it so slippery that it can thereafter be constrained by no chains of reason, nor caught and held by any hand of argument. Instead, like an eel, the mind slips away through its own "distinctions," leaving no exit for its own understanding or that of anyone else. Such subtlety is fatal to any opinion, and nothing has placed greater obstacles in the path of the simplicity of the **Gospel** than **Scholastic Theology**, which is filled with as many useless questions as it is subtle ones. This "transcendent elevation" of wits and "sharper-than-is-just" acumen has brought no less harm to **Physics**. For this reason, the "Noble Pole"—a priest of Nature who became famous under the name of **The Cosmopolite** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and "servant of nature."</note>—persuades the student burning with a desire for knowledge of Nature to flee these over-subtle things and walk in simplicity. <margin>The advice of the Cosmopolite.</margin> I must highly revere him, not only for our shared fatherland and his supreme knowledge of natural things, but especially for the more-than-snow-white honesty of his spirit, which is visible everywhere in his writings; he is to be recommended to all true lovers of physics. 

And so, to finally encompass in a single word what good Logic and that "subtle" philosophy bring: I say they grant a facility for arguing or thinking "probably" on either side of a question, and for ingeniously doubting everything, even the most obvious truths. They provide sweet nourishment for minds flitting about and residing in imaginary "super-celestial" space. Finally, this science is the most convenient of all for establishing the doctrine of **Pyrrho** <note>The ancient Greek founder of Skepticism.</note> and the schools of the **Skeptics**. 

Let us now try, as much as we are able, to stop the continuous wailing of the Physicians regarding the atrocious insults [of Paracelsus], <margin>Objection: regarding the insults and vanity.</margin> or at least to moderate them. For they complain that the volumes of **PARACELSUS** are filled with nothing but mockery of doctors, whom he treats as guilty of ignorance, stupidity, and murder on almost every page under the name of "Humorists" <term>Humorists: Doctors who followed the traditional Greek theory that health is governed by four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</term>. They complain that he raises himself to the very stars with insolent pride, claiming that he alone found the spring of true medicine and drank from it in a great gulp; that he is the "true physician" produced from the **Light of the Greater World** <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "Macrocosm" or the universe.</note>, while the others flit about like shadows; that **Avicenna**, **Averroes**, and **Galen** should follow in his footsteps; and finally, that he is the **Monarch of the Medical Art**, appointed by God and Nature...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus (Theophrastus), responding to common criticisms of his character and his "monarchical" claims over the field of medicine. <header>PREFACE.</header>

# PREFACE.

<margin>Response to the first point.</margin>
*...chosen. To address the first point first: they do not provide the cause for his bitterness* <note>original: "stomachus"; literally "stomach," but in Latin idiom, it refers to irritation, anger, or a sharp tongue.</note> *near death, which was nothing other than the insults, persecutions, and injuries from the doctors living at that time. By provoking and aggravating* THEOPHRASTUS *with these things, they triggered those sharp rebuttals. Indeed, these doctors took it poorly that a new teaching—one harmful and fatal to their Ancient system—was being brought forth by* PARACELSUS. *They did not think it was enough to satisfy their minds by merely banning his books from being printed; they also sought to gnaw at his reputation with a "malicious tooth,"* <note>original: "theonino dente"; a classical reference to Theon, a poet known for his biting, slanderous wit.</note> *spreading rumors that this new "Healer-ling" was nothing but a traveling quack, a bellows-blower* <note>original: "ciniflonem"; literally "hair-curler" or "ash-blower," a derogatory term for an alchemist or low-level laborer.</note>, *a seller of smoke, an ignorant man, a seeker of profit from superficial cures, one who sought to bring back an empirical sect that had been expelled centuries ago, and finally, one who set up a play of infernal magic. What spirit, even the mildest, would not be inflamed with anger when pricked by these thorns? What even Angelic patience, when so virulently wounded, would not be driven to fury? To* THEOPHRASTUS, *struck to the very heart, revenge seemed sweet if he could unsheathe his pen against those who everywhere sharpened their tongues against him; he judged it legitimate to reproach those men with the truth, since they were staining his name with so many lies.*

<margin>
Not all Chemists approve.
</margin>
*There are some among the followers of* THEOPHRASTUS *themselves who, not approving of that wagon-load of insults, say that a blameless way of life meets a suppressed reputation better than any defensive speech. they say that patience is the victor over slanderers, that silence is a barrier against injuries, and finally, that noble deeds shut the mouth of envy itself. We do not deny that it is a noble way of healing this evil—to restore a reputation wounded by a viper’s bite through integrity of life; it is a beautiful revenge to avenge injuries through the steady harmony of honesty. It is a victory worthy of a trophy if one can convict impious accusers of lying by as many actions as they have tongues, so that at last, blushing in their hearts rather than their faces, they might fall silent and proclaim our innocence and confess their own fault. We grant that there are those whom tolerance recalls to the path of reason, from which contradiction and opposition had diverted them. There are those who, persuading themselves that the enemy is conquered, no longer insult him; and a cold silence in the face of rebuke tempers the bile of some. The lion casts away his anger once the enemy is floored, and spares the one he could have killed. But little dogs pursue a man who is running away, and hares insult a dead lion. It is a virtue only of the most noble minds to be conquered by the gentleness of character, and to set aside anger when it is easily received from an adversary.*

<margin>
The nature of Theophrastus's enemies.
</margin>
*But* THEOPHRASTUS *encountered enemies of a far different nature—men who persecuted him not only in person with words and deeds, but also in his absence through letters and writings, laboring as much as they could to have him driven from cities, so much so that it was safe for him to set a firm foot nowhere. Patience would have profited him little or nothing; instead, it would have further provoked the fury and the sarcasm he sought to quiet. Therefore, I think he deserves pardon if he blunted these blades with similar weapons. As for that boasting of his—while not everyone praises it—they nonetheless offer legitimate excuses for it: namely, that his free, Swiss spirit* <note>original: "helueticum"; Paracelsus was born in Einsiedeln, Switzerland. The author links his bluntness to a national character trait of independence.</note> *preferred to speak out what he felt about himself rather than press it restlessly under a silent breast for too long.*

<margin>
Response to the second point. Dissimulation is rejected.
</margin>
*For what use to me are those "Tiberian" spirits* <note>A reference to the Emperor Tiberius, known for his secretive and deceptive nature.</note>, *or the disciples of the "Political Doctor" from Italy* <note>Likely a jab at Machiavellian political thought, implying cunning and deceit.</note>, *who hide a massive ambition in their hearts while feigning humility in their faces? Who wish to seem to reject the breeze of fame, which they actually catch with gaping mouths? They are so far removed from praising themselves that, while a flattering tongue strokes their pride, they cry out that their modesty is being wounded—yet all the while, deep in their hidden bosoms, they embrace the most eloquent heralds of their own praise, like Alcibiades. Our* THEOPHRASTUS *was furthest removed from this vice of dissimulation; he preferred to admit to a magnificent opinion of himself rather than incur the disgrace of a faked sincerity.*

<margin>
By what name the title "Monarch" fits Theophrastus. What a true Physician is.
</margin>
*Nor do I see a reason why he should be so criticized because, by preferring himself to others, he affected a "Monarchy" in the Medical Faculty. Every art and discipline has its "Monarch"—that is, a most excellent craftsman or Master who excels all others. And one may affirm, without flattery, that* THEOPHRASTUS *was such a man in the matter of Medicine. For since this entire study is directed toward practice, and leaves behind a sensible work—namely, health—one should not call "Doctor" the man who can merely discuss medicine elegantly and neatly; nor the one who knows how to present to the eyes the number, production, and connection of external, antecedent, and conjoined causes, or the nature of diseases and symptoms; nor the one to whom all the names of herbal lore and their different shapes are known; nor even the one whose exact observation of anatomy has shown the composition, site, form, or use of the most delicate and subtle parts. Rather, the true Doctor is he who knows how to conquer, drive away, and cure the most stubborn diseases, and who knows how to recall health from its exile by a "right of return."* <note>original: "post-liminio"; a legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile or captivity.</note>

<margin>
Theophrastus cured the most stubborn diseases.
</margin>
*In this regard, even his antagonists are forced to admit, however unwillingly, that* THEOPHRASTUS *carried every point. His own epitaph bears witness to this, as do the words of* Oporinus, <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a famous printer and briefly Paracelsus's secretary. Though he later criticized Paracelsus, his testimony regarding his medical successes remained influential.</note> *his own assistant, whose words survive: "In curing ulcers, even the most desperate ones, he performed miracles, without any prescribed diet or observed regimen being followed." And a little further down: "He boasted of his Laudanum* <note>Paracelsus's "Laudanum" was a secret, potent medicine, different from the later opium-based tinctures; he treated it as a "sovereign" remedy.</note> *in such a way that he did not hesitate..."*

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus (referred to here by his name Theophrastus), specifically addressing his medical successes and responding to theological criticisms. It transitions from a defense of his character to a comparison between his errors and those of Aristotle, arguing for a charitable interpretation of his work.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...he dared to affirm that by the use of [his medicine] alone, he could restore the living from the dead; and this he demonstrated in actual practice several times while I was with him. Conrad Gessner <note>A famous Swiss physician and naturalist, often considered the father of modern bibliography.</note> agrees with this, saying: *I hear many were easily cured by him in desperate illnesses, and malignant internal organs were healed by him.* The testimony of the aforementioned Francis confirms this, and they render the proof complete, both through countless other instances and the example cited by Melchior Adam in his description of Paracelsus's life: he asserts that Albertus Bazaus, Physician to the King of Poland, visited a sick man with THEOPHRASTUS whom few hoped would survive due to a lack of strength and pulse, with his chest also suffering; and THEOPHRASTUS also admitted that the patient was "given up for dead" <note>original: "conclamatum esse"; a Roman funeral term for the final call to the deceased, meaning the case was hopeless.</note> if he were to proceed according to the method of the "humorists" <note>Physicians who followed the traditional Galenic system based on the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note> using their medications; but he added that his own remedies were more effective and could revive this dejected health; and with the said medicine administered, within the space of a few hours he expelled everything from the <term>bowels</term> <note>original: "alvum"; referring here to the purging of the digestive tract.</note> and restored health. It is no wonder then if he justly claimed the title of Monarch of Medicine for himself; and he possesses it, not to be snatched away by any of the physicians of past ages. 

But indeed, while I give no ground for this complaint, on the other hand, I cannot help but join the intense choir of Sacred Theologians, <margin>Theophrastus is accused by the theologians.</margin> being forced to concede that he is most justly accused of one or two errors committed in the explanation of Biblical passages. Therefore, just as I am an advocate for learning Medicine, Natural Philosophy, and Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiæ"; in this era, the term covered both chemistry and alchemy.</note> from him, so I would suggest to no one that the mysteries of faith should be extracted from his books. Yet I do not think any more severe judgment should be passed on his writings for this reason than on those of <margin>Aristotle's absurd doctrines.</margin> Aristotle the Stagirite, for although his works abound with enormous and most impious doctrines, their author is designated the "Philosopher" par excellence and the "Genius of Nature." For what can be imagined more absurd or more injurious to the Divine Majesty than to grant eternity to the world, thereby establishing something co-eternal with God? Aristotle thinks the Deity, or the first intelligence, has no care for worldly things, but is tied to the first sphere, toiling to the point of pouring sweat in revolving it and carrying along the other spheres, while the assembly of lesser intelligences struggles in vain; he is equipped with no knowledge of particulars, and therefore is neither all-knowing nor to be invoked. He teaches that no punishments are to be expected by the wicked, just as no reward is to be expected by the upright; that the soul is mortal, since all forms of bodies perish. And yet, with these and other absurdities, he is celebrated as the greatest of philosophers, and his authority is held as law in the schools, his sayings as oracles; so that it was not without reason that Luther, a zealot for God's cause, says grievingly in the history by Sleidanus:

> Aristotle is held in highest esteem by the Scholastic theologians, and nothing said by him is so absurd and foreign to our religion that they do not defend it, or clothe it with some interpretation, however far-fetched, so that his honor and the reputation of his name may remain intact.

It is not our intention to force THEOPHRASTUS’s earth-bound opinions to the plumb line of sacred truth; but for one investigating the reason for his deflection from the right path, no other occurs than the <margin>The cause of Theoph.'s deviation.</margin> dim light <note>original: "creperum... divinae lucis"; 'creperum' implies the uncertain light of dusk or dawn.</note> of divine light detected by the great men of that age, but by him—who died in the forty-first year of the past century [1541]—it was seen at least from a distance, not clearly perceived. But if the fates had granted a longer life, Christian charity—which commands us to judge nothing but good of the dead—compels us to believe that, illuminated by nearer rays, he would have recognized the truth along with his errors. It happened to Tertullian and also to Origen—men of eminent genius, if ever there were any—that by loosening the reins of reason not subject to faith, they fell into a whirlpool of foul errors in a headlong course; yet it is the opinion of the most Christian men, whose hearts burn with love for their neighbors, that they recovered themselves by swimming out before death and returned to the river flowing with the milk and honey of celestial truth. Saint Augustine also wrote retractations of his youthful errors, and I conjecture, not without reason, that THEOPHRASTUS would have done the same if the renewing light of the Gospel had fully bathed him while he still enjoyed the breath of life; since in his writings he frequently corrected a previous opinion, having been made more learned by experience or reason, fearing nothing of the mockery of critics <note>original: "Zoilorum"; referring to Zoilus, a classical grammarian known for his spiteful criticism of Homer.</note>. 

His enemies attribute that to inconstancy and forgetfulness of previous teaching, and Helmont <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont, a Belgian chemist and physician who followed but also criticized Paracelsus.</note> censures him because, after often mocking the "humorists," he soon seems to join them elsewhere. But these things did not please Helmont’s palate because THEOPHRASTUS did not, as he did, entirely cast out "humors" from nature, but he only rebuked the laziness of physicians <margin>Why he approves and disapproves of humors.</margin> who claim that any ill health depends on them, that they are generated from any foods, that there are four and neither more nor fewer, and that almost all diseases proceed from their imbalance. Therefore, if by changing a previous opinion he often amended it, and openly, without blushing, confessed a preceding error, let it be a constant sign of integrity, not instability. For why should it be a sin to follow the banners of truth by abandoning a recognized error, and to give oneself to the royal road after wandering? Day teaches day, and daily...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus's character and intellectual method. While the previous page focused on his medical miracles and desperate cures, this section transitions into a philosophical justification for why Paracelsus (Theophrastus) changed his opinions over time and why he often presented his findings as "bare assertions" without the detailed logical proofs expected by traditional academics.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>We learn by growing old.</margin>
*We grow old by learning. The pupils of the soul are sharpened by new rays of light while those of the body grow dull; and modest truth flees the gaze of the young, but reveals itself willingly to those of a grander age who, having laid aside the <term>praetexta</term> <note>original: "praetexta"; the purple-bordered toga worn by Roman boys, here symbolizing the immature state of youth.</note>, discover it for themselves. A noble nature is not confounded by a rustic shame, but blushes with modesty—the color of virtue—when it realizes it has embraced a shadow instead of a body, a painted face instead of a natural one. It burns with a more vehement love the further it perceives itself to have been from the sought-after object, having been deceived by the mere appearance of truth.* <margin>The allurements of truth.</margin> *Truth has this peculiar quality: it is sought by as many suitors as it happens to find spectators; even those who seem to have declared open war against it kiss it in their innermost hearts. Indeed, endowed with so many charms and shining with so many graces, it snatches up with sweet violence anyone who is independent and not baited by the seasonings of false opinions. It possesses those it has snatched, and feeds those it possesses with the ambrosia and nectar of every kind of knowledge, binding them to itself for life. And will there still be someone who thinks an author worthy of reproach because, having renounced his first impressions, he has exchanged a false opinion for a true one? Will anyone think him marked by the stain of inconstancy because he washed away that stain of error? He who shows himself constant in absurdities and persists obstinately in errors ill-deserves the praise of constancy.* <margin>Constancy in the love of truth.</margin> *He alone should be called constant who always and everywhere, from wherever or however it comes, opens the doors of his mind to the Truth, receives it greedily, treats it honorably, and finally binds it to himself in the tightest bond. That false and masked ghost of this virtue—which surrounds already-conceived opinions with such a strict siege that all hope of escape is cut off—brings an unspeakable obstacle to the sciences, preventing them from moving forward. But a philosophical mind is always ready to yield to better reasons and to concede to the truth; indeed, it rejoices to go out or run to meet it when seen from afar, with the desire for knowing adding spurs. He always has it engraved before his eyes and in his tenacious memory that whatever is said against the will of truth is forbidden. He is so far from hiding, veiling, covering, or protecting the errors of his own writings that, on the contrary, he voluntarily confesses, opens, attacks, and conquers them. If this were engraved in the living character of the minds of today’s authors—who labor under a <term>cacoëthes scribendi</term> <note>A Latin expression derived from Greek, meaning an "insatiable itch for writing" or a bad habit of writing incessantly.</note>—and if it were attached to the titles of their volumes and diligently observed, the skirmishes of pens and tongues would have already bid us a final farewell. Therefore, the habit familiar to THEOPHRASTUS <note>The author uses Paracelsus’s given name, Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> of changing his opinion whenever a newly perceived light revealed the darkness of the past night, is entirely free from blame; indeed, it should be inscribed in everlasting metal and imitated by every true philosopher.*

<margin>Objection concerning bare assertions.</margin>
*The adversaries now proceed, arguing that lest the "Monarch" <note>A title Paracelsus sometimes used for himself, "Monarch of Physicians," which his critics found arrogant.</note> should seem to have assumed the name in vain, he actually strove to usurp it when he wanted his opinions—supported by no columns of reason—to be held as the firmest and most impregnable fortresses, and his sayings to be held as rules. Thus, they say, he busied himself with representing a resurrected <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>The followers of Pythagoras were famous for the "ipse dixit" (he himself said it) rule, accepting the master's word as absolute truth without requiring further proof.</note> to us. We forgive the detractors here and elsewhere, as they are utterly ignorant of the way of writing used by philosophers who have mastered reason. THEOPHRASTUS was more occupied in finding the secrets of nature than in publishing what he found; he did not always strengthen his opinions with heaps of arguments, lest he be forced to reveal many things in his proofs that must still be hidden from the common crowd of Physicians. For there are three kinds of things which <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the "Hermetic" corpus of Egyptian-Greek wisdom and alchemy is attributed.</note> wished the disciples of his philosophy to keep hidden from the world, bound by testament and oath.* <margin>Three things are hidden by philosophers.</margin> <margin>First.</margin> *First, those things that would bring more calamity than benefit to the human race; for this reason, they wrapped their <term>elixir</term> in the coverings of riddles and <term>griffins</term> <note>original: "gryphorum"; refers to intricate puzzles or complicated enigmas that protect secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, so that the profane "cattle" might be kept away from the stalls, and lest a sword be put into the hands of the wicked by this revelation—a sword dangerous to themselves and others, like one in the hands of a madman.* <margin>Second.</margin> *Next, he commanded that many precious things be preserved by the heirs of philosophical labors, lest they be thrown to dogs or given to bastards when they are owed to legitimate sons. For this reason, the most excellent remedies—vying with that "Universal" one—are only passed hand-to-hand or whispered in the ear, to be preserved in Pythagorean silence until the final breath, and only then to be committed to the trust of another of proven integrity.* <margin>Third.</margin> *Finally, he ordered that the general process of nature in composing and resolving mixtures—the knowledge of the universal spirit with the common matter of things underlying it (that is, the fountain of all generation and corruption, and the spring of all virtues and faculties visible in the three kingdoms of nature)—be hidden with all zeal. A corrupt world does not deserve the revelation of such great mysteries, noted only by a passing pen by that scribe of the divine majesty. For although the torches are pressing near, the times have not yet arrived in which nothing will be so hidden that it is not revealed and finally exposed to the sight of all.*

<margin>Objection concerning Plagiarism.</margin>
*Behold, kind reader, the reasons why THEOPHRASTUS did not labor much in proving his science. He preferred to be accused of ignorance and vain boasting, and to suffer the loss of his reputation, rather than to scatter the secrets of philosophers among the unworthy common people with an itching pen. The crowd sings, the pulpits resound...*

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus against his academic and professional rivals. # PREFACE.

<sig>¶¶¶ 2</sig>

<margin>Crato.</margin>
Reports *resound* that **PARACELSUS** has brought forth a new and previously unheard-of doctrine; but **Crato**, the Imperial Physician, along with **Germain Courtin** of Paris, command silence. Crato, indeed, so that no glory should redound to **PARACELSUS** as if he were the first inventor of his own doctrine, asserts that he himself saw a book in the library of Marcus Singmoser (Secretary of the most sacred Imperial Council), written by a monk two hundred years ago. Crato used this book for many months, and claims it clearly handed down everything that **PARACELSUS** and his followers now carry about like <term>Eleusinian mysteries</term> <note>original: "Eleusina sacra"; these were the secret religious rites of ancient Greece. Here, the author uses the term to mock the idea that Paracelsus's "secrets" were stolen from hidden ancient sources.</note>, so evidently that it could deceive no one. Truly, why he did not make public those mysteries which reveal such great things, he does not add a reason; perhaps charity suppressed it, fearing that the celebrated name which **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> had acquired by this plagiarism would go to ruin. Certainly, the heart of **Crato** burned with such feeling toward this man; but why did that same charity not spur him to look toward the public good rather than the private glory of one man? Why did he not bring a torch to drive away the darkness of the night reigning in the writings of **THEOPHRASTUS**? Some wish these volumes to have belonged to **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary alchemist; the author is skeptical that Paracelsus's work is merely a copy of Valentine's.</note>; but these, having no agreement with the **Theophrastic** works (excepting the doctrine of the three principles), have been unable to manifest these <term>Eleusinian mysteries</term> until now.

<margin>Courtin's objection.</margin>
**Courtin**, however, charges him with a greater crime: that like a thief in the night, he broke into antiquity, stole the universal "seeds" <note>original: "spermate"; referring to the concept of *panspermia*, where the seeds of all things are hidden in matter.</note> of **Anaxagoras**, and produced them on the stage dressed in different colors. That wrinkled material had been driven out of the <term>Lyceum</term> <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> by **Aristotle**, the "God of Philosophers," and the daughter had died long ago with her parent; but now, led back from the underworld and recalled into these breezes in a wonderful way, she is reborn through a discarded <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The transmigration of souls; the idea that an old, dead philosophy is inhabiting a new body.</note>. To **Paracelsus**, indeed, and the entire **College of Chemists**, the authority of men is of little concern; anyone who fights against them with such weapons is forced to yield the field and <term>concede defeat</term> <note>original: "herbamque porrigere"; literally "to reach out the grass," an ancient Roman expression for surrendering.</note>. With a single experience, they destroy a hundred of **Aristotle's** skillfully crafted reasons; they prove all things by fire, and little concerned with whose image the coin bears, they examine the material and weigh it exactly on the scales.

<margin>Democritus and Epicurus often bring forth truth.</margin>
They very often find that **Democritus**, though laughing, spoke the truth; and that **Epicurus**, in his "soaked mind," cherished sound opinions from a "wine-filled tongue" and brought forth sober sentences. They find that the latter discovered in wine the same truth that the former claimed was hidden at the bottom of a well. These most rigid defenders of truth compel the **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note> himself to halt his step and stand before the tribunal of truth to plead his cause and explain the reasons for his doctrine. Therefore, an opinion is not rendered worse simply because it fell into oblivion with its author after being rejected by the <term>Stagirite</term> <note>Aristotle, named for his birthplace, Stagira.</note>; nor is the assertion of **Anaxagoras** to be condemned just because it did not meet with Aristotle's approval.

<margin>Courtin harasses Chemistry.</margin>
But the most eloquent **Courtin** continues in his oration against **PARACELSUS**, which is entirely shaped by the ferocity of the **Peripatetic** and **Galenic** discipline. Harassing **Chemistry** in wondrous ways, he dreams that she is led by him in a submissive triumph, although he is plainly destitute of the strength of arguments. He merely inflates his dissertation with bombastic words and brings forth weapons from **Aristotle's** armory that are held in contempt by the <term>Chymiatrists</term> <note>Physicians who used chemical remedies.</note>.

<margin>Eloquent Courtin.</margin>
Not unaware that the deformity of a face is often made tolerable by artifice, and that <term>deception</term> <note>original: "mangonium"; the art of furbishing or dressing up goods—like slaves or horses—to hide defects.</note> not infrequently makes up for a defect of nature, he omits nothing to dress his oration elegantly. He runs through all the gardens of the orators to pluck little flowers, lights up all the lamps of rhetorical figures, seeks out the trappings of ornamental words, curls his periods with perpetual curling irons, and equips every part of his speech with whatever allurements he can find, so that he may win majesty for his disciplines and capture the goodwill of minds.

<margin>Courtin assumes various masks of emotion.</margin>
Then, soon after, striking fear with a furrowed brow, he inveighs against **PARACELSUS**. He attacks with massed engines of argument, hurls his catapults with great force, thunders, lightens, and stirs up storms of waves so that they might swallow the tossed and shaken little ship of **THEOPHRASTUS**, which is all but shipwrecked. Finally, with his face composed into cheerfulness, he wittily mocks the **Spagyrics** <note>Alchemists.</note>. He unfolds a cloud of words, now striking them with continuous irony and pretending to extol them so that they might fall more heavily, now dissolving into laughter, now biting with a sharp tooth while flattering. In a word, he assumes and re-assumes so many personas that he yields nothing to the actor **ROSCIUS** <note>A famous Roman comic actor.</note>.

*But let us contemplate with what scimitar the exultant **Courtin** has cut down the palm branch—the sign of victory. Let us weigh for a moment some of the reasons brought forward both against the doctrine of **PARACELSUS**, as well as those brought in favor of his own.*

<margin>One and another of Courtin's arguments are examined.</margin>
He feels quite rightly that one must labor at first to destroy the foundations and principles of any science if we wish the rest of the building to fall on its own. Therefore, he rejects the three **Chemical** principles as if they were cornerstones, using the argument that they are not contrary to one another—which are necessarily required (as he says) for any generation—and he substitutes **Aristotle's** "primary matter, form, and privation" in their place. Nothing is said here in support of **THEOPHRASTUS'S** opinion except the demonstration of <term>salt, sulfur, and mercury</term> <note>The three primary substances (Tria Prima) which Paracelsus argued were the foundation of all matter.</note>—performed a thousand times before one's eyes and visible in the resolution of mixtures even to the <term>bleary-eyed and barbers</term> <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus"; a Latin idiom meaning "everyone," including the most common or uneducated people.</note>. These principles are never to be destroyed by his "reasons without reason," even if his supporters burst with effort. Relegating him now to whether form and privation in...

<meta>This page continues the intellectual defense of Paracelsus, specifically transitioning from biographical defenses against plagiarism to a philosophical critique of his detractors' Aristotelian foundations. ## PREFACE.

<margin>The opposition of form and privation is refuted.</margin>
It is pleasing to inquire whether "form" and "privation" <term>privation</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present. For example, blindness is the "privation" of sight.</note> are contrary to one another in the common subject of matter, or not. Setting aside those *arguments* by which others have already struck *privation* from the register of *natural principles* for good (lest I seem to be doing work already done), it seems to me that this cleverly invented opposition should be rejected by right: *Because contraries are always under the same genus; but form refers to substance, from which privation is excluded*, as noted by **Sennertus**, with the agreement of **Courtin** in his *Epitome of Physics, book 1, chapter 3*. Next, because *substance, or a part of substance as such, has no contrary; and substantial form is a constitutive part of substance, and is considered here as such, without regard yet to the qualities flowing from it; therefore, it is contrary to nothing, and certainly not to privation.* It follows from this also: since things oppose one another through accidents—*qualities, etc.*—and almost all of these proceed from form, while none proceed from privation, the latter, being stripped of weapons, cannot oppose the former. Moreover, opposition only exists between two real and positive beings; *but privation is nothing but the negation of a Being, namely, of a future form, which is itself still nothing, except in potential: that is, it can only potentially exist.* Just as in a glass filled with water (to use a palpable example) there is wine—namely, if the clear water is poured out and the wine is poured in—so the future form is in the matter if, when the present form is expelled, that one succeeds it; but this "to be" is actually "not to be," or to be nothing. Therefore, since *privation in its formal concept implies nothing but the absence of a thing which can be, but is not; and the material concept, denoting the capacity of a subject for a new form, is falsely attributed to it (since it depends solely on the disposition of the matter and should be attributed to it and spoken of it),* I do not see how it can be contrary to an *actual Being*, or even to act itself, since *there are no real attributes of a Non-being or a Fictional Being.* I wonder that **Sennertus**, in the place cited above, states that *matter sometimes constitutes one natural thing with one form (these are his words), and sometimes another thing with another, and that it is the subject of those contraries in turns,* when nevertheless it is a received opinion denied by no one that *matter can never naturally exist, nor could it ever have existed, without form. No one can ever provide a state in which matter, without form, constitutes a thing alone with privation; because at the very same instant that one form departs, another occupies the matter: and thus privation is always excluded, and no succession by turns is given, and consequently no battle.*

<margin>The unhappy privation.</margin>
It is also ridiculous when they say that *privation disposes matter and adds a sting so that it desires a new form, which is the cause of its own destruction; and this assertion weakens a rule confirmed by all nature: that nothing seeks the cause of its own death.* A truly unhappy suitor!—who, from all eternity (if one believes **Aristotle**), has wooed matter and instilled a love that changes by the hour, and supplied the provocations of new desires, in the hope of one day possessing the abundance of a future mistress; yet until the present, he has withered with envy because of the happiness of his rival. And although *matter has urged and persuaded the change of husbands, he [Privation] has nevertheless always been excluded, while his most hateful enemy [Form] was received with open arms.* It is incomprehensible how a vain hope has not long ago weaned him, with "Vatinian" contempt <note>original: "odio vatiniano"; an ancient Roman expression for a fierce, unyielding hatred, named after Publius Vatinius.</note> or hatred succeeding his lost love.

<margin>The definition of place as a continuum is refuted.</margin>
**Courtin** goes further and says that **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Paracelsus</note> defined "place" most falsely when he established a vacuum <term>vacuum</term><note>A void or empty space containing no matter.</note> for a body. Our author, seeing that place cannot be conceived without space deprived of all body (unless we admit the penetration of bodies), *said that the places of mixed things are the elements, insofar as they are entirely free from the jurisdiction of another.* **Courtin** believes a great occasion for laughter is supplied to him here; and therefore, stuffing his entire speech with mocks and rebukes regarding these things, he himself, with **Aristotle**, *defines place as the surface of the surrounding body.* Truly, this *lynx-eyed mole* <note>original: "lynceus talpa"; a sarcastic oxymoron combining the lynx, famed for sharp sight, and the mole, noted for blindness.</note> does not see that he has defined not "place" itself, but the "boundary" by which place is circumscribed. For that boundary is a surface; and a surface cannot be a place, since *an analogy is required between the place and the thing located within it, and since a body to be placed has three dimensions, the place requires the same; but a surface consists of only two, and therefore is unsuitable for receiving a body.*

<margin>No absurdities in nature.</margin>
*But a vacuum entirely possesses the nature of three dimensions, namely length, breadth, and depth; which, in the abstract, belong to a vacuum or to place properly speaking, but not to bodies. For we speak with very little accuracy when we say a body "has length," etc. Rather, it should be said that a body "is long," because only concrete things exist in nature, never abstract ones: hence, granting these formulas of speech to mathematics, we banish them from the boundaries of physics. For it must be held that the terms of Mathematics do not always suit the expression of natural things, nor even do their demonstrations, as I shall make most evident in my "Philosophizing Chemist" [Chymicus Philosophans], where I shall solve the "Achilles" argument <note>original: "Achilleum... argumentum"; likely referring to Zeno's paradox of "Achilles and the Tortoise," used here to discuss the infinite divisibility of space.</note> (as it seems to many), drawn from geometry to prove that a continuum is infinitely divisible, which leads to the absurdity of granting that a diagonal line is equal to the side of a square, unless that infinity*

...infinite division is admitted. But to return to the matter at hand: <margin>The first absurdity from Courtin's definition of "place."</margin> Courtin does not notice how many absurdities he runs into with this definition. For it must be conceded that the highest heaven, being surrounded by no body, is not "in a place"; and since "place," according to him and Aristotle, limits what is located within it, that heaven will be without a limit, and thus infinite. <margin>The second absurdity.</margin> They are forced to establish another absurdity: namely, that the ultimate heaven is deprived of a convex surface, and thus a spherical body exists without an external surface. All these things they do just to keep Aristotle’s definition "patched up and protected" <note>original: "sartam tectamque," a legal phrase meaning kept in good repair.</note>. I would go further and show many more of his absurd and inept arguments by examining them, were it not outside my purpose to follow and repel the trivial reasons with which he attacks **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus.</note>, as the narrow boundaries of a Preface do not allow it, and the running of the printing press prevents it. <margin>Nature ignores the decrees of Aristotle.</margin> It matters little, then, that the "Walkers" <term>Walkers</term><note>A play on "Peripatetics," the followers of Aristotle who famously walked while teaching.</note> are jubilant, as Courtin says, that they have whipped the opinions of the Chemists out of their schools; for nature has excluded the decrees of the schools from the boundaries of her kingdom since the very birth of the world, and daily she beats and casts out their vain assertions and empty words with clubs. Indeed, the times are approaching when our *pyrotechnia* <term>pyrotechnia</term><note>The art of fire, referring here to chemistry and alchemy.</note> will finally set fire to the Lyceum itself; constructed of straw and wood, the buildings of scholastic arguments will be reduced to ashes, while only the sun, the refined gold, and the hard adamant <note>A legendary stone of indestructible hardness, often associated with diamond.</note> remain untouched by the flame. <margin>The shoemaker should stick to his sandal.</margin> This same Courtin treats the degrees of fire, the nature of Mercury and gold, and other things unknown to him—like a blind man talking about colors—and therefore these things require no response, as they collapse under their own weakness. <margin>Objection regarding Magic.</margin> I approach the final insult, which is horrifying even to think about: all the aforementioned things are of no importance compared to this one, yet it is the most subtle and crafty invention of our enemies: accusing the writings of **PARACELSUS** <margin>The cause of the accusation.</margin> of "ceremonial magic" and other nefarious arts. When I look for the cause, I find no other than certain things he spoke of quite freely, and certain words he used which are terrifying to the common crowd. Because for a long time the opinion has prevailed among the ignorant that all Magic, Cabala, Chaomancy, etc., are the inventions of the Devil—delicacies with which he baits and feeds his slaves—they could not help but immediately accuse **PARACELSUS** of incantations and sorcery, as he mentions these things frequently. But if they had weighed with a more diligent scale the sense in which he used those words, they would have judged more soberly and not condemned the man with such a headlong sentence. Oh, what a crime! To wipe the name of an innocent man from the book of life with a sacrilegious hand and a single stroke of the pen, without examining the cause, and to inscribe it upon Charon's coin <note>A reference to the coin placed in the mouth of the dead to pay the ferryman of the underworld.</note>. For what else is a "magician," in the sense they mean, than suitable fuel for the fire, a brand of hell, a total slave to Lucifer, and a perpetual enemy and adversary of God his Creator? <margin>A Christian should be treated more gently.</margin> Those educated in the school of Christ ought to fear the penalty of retaliation from that just Judge, who reserved the power of condemnation for Himself alone. Everything should have been recalled to a more exact balance before anything so harsh was pronounced against a Christian, and before flames and fires were decreed by a wicked mouth. They say he wrote of Magic: but others have done the same, and no fault was given to them, nor did they suffer such persecutions. The name of that Magic ought to be a terror to no one, for he speaks of *natural* magic, not *superstitious* magic, which he warns in various places in his volumes must be fled from and abhorred. <margin>What natural Magic teaches and why.</margin> There is a "natural magic" which diligently investigates the virtues and powers of all nature and happily achieves them; it joins agents with passives in the proper manner, place, time, weight, and measure; it disposes the lower things, as if they were receptacles, so that they may be open to the influences of the celestial bodies; it marries the heavens with sublunary things; and with the equipment of this round fabric <note>The universe.</note> it instructs man, the **microcosm**, so that it may produce effects admirable to the mind and stunning to the eyes. <margin>The Magi from the East.</margin> The Wise Men from the East, who are called "Magi" in the Holy Scriptures, were taught by this science that that new star presaged something new, and they knew that Christ the Savior was born in Judea. <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin> By the benefit of this science, **Dionysius the Areopagite** perceived the Author of the world suffering when Christ was crucified. <margin>Moses.</margin> **Moses** was instructed in this, for the divine page testifies that he was well-versed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (which was nothing other than natural magic, highly cultivated by that people). Nor is anyone so destitute of mind, or so impious, as to dare to refer these men to the infamous catalog of sorcerers. Not a few other names he used have fallen into misuse, and arts that were once praiseworthy signify nefarious and execrable things today. <margin>What he understands by Geomancy, Pyromancy, Chaomancy.</margin> **THEOPHRASTUS**, according to his custom, accepted a different meaning for Geomancy, Pyromancy, and Chaomancy than is commonly held. He did not use them as foolish instruments for divining the future—which depends on man's free will or the secret decree of the Almighty made before the ages—but he valued them highly insofar as natural effects can be foreseen from natural causes through them. Or he even accepted and used them for the arts that produce magnetic and sympathetic cures. <margin>Who is a Chaomantic? A Geomantic?</margin> And in this way, any common person practices **chaomancy** <term>chaomancy</term><note>The study of the "chaos," which Paracelsians defined as the air or atmosphere.</note> who, from the winter rain, a corrupted spring, and diseases...

<margin>
When the Physician is a Chaomantic.

Geomantic.

Pyromantic.
</margin>
...predicts the future of one infected with contagious diseases. He should be called a Geomantic <term>Geomancy</term><note>Literally "earth-divination," but here referring to the study of terrestrial influences on health.</note>, not only he who, from the poisonous vapors rising from the earth, foresees and predicts the plagues of that region; but also he who discerns the fertility of the soil from its barrenness by considering the depths of the lands. The Physician understands Chaomancy <term>Chaomancy</term><note>Divination or medical insight derived from the air (Chaos) or the atmosphere.</note> when, intending to dissipate a swelling of the spleen, he applies a sympathetic remedy: applying the spleen of a beast over our own [spleen] region until it warms up, and then exposing that beast's spleen to the air or smoke to dry out, he cures the man's swelling spleen. A Physician is to be called a Geomantic who, after warming water-pepper <note>Original: "persicaria," a plant used in folk medicine.</note> over a bruise and committing it to the earth, dissolves the clotted blood in the body. He employs Pyromancy <term>Pyromancy</term><note>Divination or healing through fire.</note> who, by plucking and burning hairs from the crown of an Epileptic during the height of a seizure, heals the budding illness. These remedies, alien to all superstition and impiety, are brought forward by great men—men not accused of the crime of infernal magic—indeed, by the Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the traditional medical authority whose views often clashed with Paracelsus.</note> themselves, and are accepted and commended by these authors; yet when brought forward by **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Paracelsus.</note>, they are exploded and rejected as damned. The common crowd of practitioners is often offended by such remedies and calls them "unnatural" because, being ignorant of the reason or medium by which they are performed,
<margin>The Schools are ignorant of the medium.</margin>
they recognize none at all. And although many chatter much about the "virtual contact" of things and sympathy, nonetheless, because they have stopped at speculation, they have never investigated what that contact is, how great it is, or by what logic it operates. Being content to have named it and observed it in natural things, but little concerned with its application, they agitate nothing further; it is no wonder if they are stunned to the point of amazement by a new way of uprooting an illness. Regarding the **Homunculus**
<margin>The Homunculus is a speculation.</margin>
of **THEOPHRASTUS**, there is no small murmur among them; it is surprising that these curious men have not perceived it to be a subtle speculation of genius, rather than the impious practice of a reckless Deucalion <note>In Greek mythology, Deucalion repopulated the earth by throwing stones; the author argues Paracelsus's "little man" is a philosophical concept, not a literal attempt to play God.</note>. To those for whom the manner of human generation (proceeding from the seed of both sexes) has been declaimed until they are hoarse and instilled until they are nauseous, it can find nothing obscure. By "Cabala"
<margin>What the Cabala is.</margin>
**THEOPHRASTUS** understood nothing other than the illustration of divine mysteries through natural things as far as possible, and the demonstration of the Archetype [the divine pattern] everywhere in the physical copies of this world. On this subject, Pico della Mirandola—a man above titles and praise—and Petrus Galatinus—most learned in every branch of literature and doctrine—wrote many things, defending them against the envious tooth of ignorance; their works should be consulted. Finally, Naudé <note>Gabriel Naudé (1600–1653), a French librarian and scholar who defended famous men against charges of magic.</note>—a man of almost infinite reading and learning, as well as a most polished wit—
<margin>Naudé defends Theophrastus from the accusation of Magic.</margin>
vindicated **PARACELSUS** from the crime of infamous Magic; he liberally exempted him from this accusation, along with others who were spoken of ill by the gossip of the unskilled. If those sublime and happy spirits had any care for mortal affairs or any sense of rest in their ashes, they would surely pour out immortal thanks for such an immortal benefit. For since the "true life," according to Cicero <note>Original: "Tullium," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>, is not that which is enclosed in the narrow confines of this body, but that which lives in the memory of all ages, and which posterity gazes upon and cherishes with reverence: has not Naudé given them life, if he restored their fame—that is, their posthumous life? His adversaries wanted their memory damned to eternal darkness and obscurely handed over to oblivion; but by his benefit, they have crossed the waters of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> and attained a name that will never die. May his memory be inscribed in a sacred temple, more lasting than marble, and cherished by the children of our children, because he taught that men who were despised and hated for unjust reasons should be so honored.

<margin>
The objections regarding the air are now answered.
</margin>
I seem to have followed through on everything now, and not only washed away the things for which **PARACELSUS** was being reproved, but also demonstrated that the light, weightless arguments of his adversaries—concocted at will—yield more to his honor than to his disgrace; even though they labor to overturn his glory, won through so many exhausted labors and through so many obstacles and precipices, as if applying siege engines against it. If, however, any other accusation remains, which I in my ignorance might have passed over with a dry pen without response, and of which Dorn <note>Gerhard Dorn, a key defender and editor of Paracelsus.</note> warns Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus, a major critic of Paracelsian medicine.</note> in letters sent to him: it must be weighed by his detractors with an exact scale whether they actually understand what they are blaming, since it happens every day to very many people that they
<margin>The adversaries do not understand what they blame.</margin>
disapprove of what they do not understand. For fools, consumed by the preconceived opinion of their own acquired doctrine, are persuaded that nothing escapes the keenness of their genius, nothing excels their sublimity, and nothing can dull their sharpness or delay their subtlety; they arrogantly claim the faculty of judging and pronouncing sentences on anything whatsoever with excessive license. But what is so stupid as that
<margin>Their stupid presumption.</margin>
imagination that no science is so widely extending that it cannot be contained within the narrow limits of one head, and that nothing is so implicit that its "idea" is not explicitly formed in the fictitious folds of a wonderful brain? Does it not reek of a hypochondriac disease to believe that all the more kindly influences concentrated upon them when they were born, that all things sublunary and superlunary conspired, and that all of nature finally stretched every nerve so that they might be a specimen of its powers, a mirror of all perfection...

The author contrasts the "eagle-like" intellect of great thinkers with the "crawling" minds of envious traditionalists.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

...of perfection, and would produce in themselves the very epitome of every kind of science and wisdom? Before them, truly, the immature age sent nothing similar or equal into the air, nor will an exhausted future ever bring forth anything like it. If those men, being of sound mind, had studied the philosopher's warning <term>Know thyself</term><note>The famous Socratic and Delphic maxim "Nosce te ipsum," urging self-awareness of one's own limitations.</note> and had begun a comparison of their own soul's faculties with others, they would confess with me that <margin>Minds more sublime than ours.</margin> a massive volume could be composed of things unknown to their own imagination. They would see that there are minds which, compared to us crawling upon the ground, are like eagles in the high heavens, attaining through play what we cannot reach with any exertion of strength. They would perceive that these more fortunate offspring of nature precede our slowness by so many parasangs <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, used here to mean "by a great distance."</note> that their footsteps escape the sharpest sight of those who try to follow. Consequently, they would feel more modest about themselves and would by no means strive to defile with envious mouths the labors of others—labors untouched by their own insights and surpassing their understanding.

I believe satisfaction has been given to honest minds, but not to the half-learned who are swollen with the wind of their own self-esteem, <margin>The author has labored to satisfy honest minds.</margin> or those rotting with the poison of envy, or finally those maliciously blind in whose very marrow hatred for **THEOPHRASTUS** <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> has taken such deep root that it cannot be torn up or eradicated by any machinery of reason. For who can persuade those who stubbornly close their eyes that the day has dawned? Who can recall to righteousness those born and made with such grim eyes that they view every rising glow of another's glory with hostility, their very nature resisting, and remove a malice almost sucked in with their mother's milk? There are those who seek and find spots on the sun, and knots in a bulrush <note>original: "in scirpo nodos"; a Latin proverb meaning to look for difficulties or flaws where none exist.</note>, and who are pleased by nothing unless it was born from themselves. To these, I confess, I have not labored to give satisfaction.

Instead, I have written for those who, by their own example, are conscious of human weakness and understand in how many and how great ways men can fall away from the standard of reason or morals. I believe every doubt has been removed for them, and the glory due to **THEOPHRASTUS** has been asserted. The false accusations with which he was charged have been refuted, and the <margin>Truth triumphs.</margin> serpentine tongues that stung his reputation have been pulled out. I hope, therefore, that with the unbridled lust for slander restrained and the right of truth preserved, truth will at last stand victorious; it will lead falsehood, conquered and bound, in triumph. Truth shall rise clothed in splendid rays and present itself to the sight of all, while falsehood and its authors seek eternal hiding places. 

There remain still the reasons why **THEOPHRASTUS**, moved by conviction, departed from the decrees of the Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over a millennium.</note>. However, <margin>Subject of the second preface.</margin> because these require a treatment in a more extended style, we reserve them for the preface of the second Volume, lest this current work grow into too great a mass, exceeding the laws of a preface.

## A WRITTEN LETTER
# TO THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.
### *In which the logic of the order and names, and indeed the method of the whole Adept Philosophy, is concisely and learnedly demonstrated.*
### BY
# PETER SEVERINUS THE DANE,
## Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine.

->*PETER SEVERINUS sends Torches and Lamps<note>original: "Lampades & Lucernas." This refers to the passing of the "light" of knowledge from teacher to student.</note> to THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.*<-

I have read your books of Philosophy, THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS, in which I have recognized the divinity of your Genius and the admirable majesty of your contemplations. And although I know that the minds of other Philosophers have been entangled in the same difficulties, it has nevertheless been granted to few to ascend with an equal sharpness of mind to the innermost shrines of the <term>Mosaic mysteries</term><note>The belief that Moses held a secret, divine understanding of the physical world (a "Christianized" version of ancient natural philosophy).</note>. We admire the piety of Orpheus, the majesty and hidden science of the whole of creation in Pythagoras, the humanity of Socrates, and the eloquence and subtlety of investigations in Plato. But we congratulate you—even more so in this our century—that all these qualities, or certainly most of them, have fallen to you alone. Nor do I doubt that you have received the treasures of these secrets from living and vibrant streams, and not from dead and silent letters (as we are accustomed to do); and thus, by a certain divine coupling, you have recalled the universal <term>Consonance of the Muses</term><note>The harmonious unity of all sciences and arts.</note> and the sciences from the entire circumference of the circle back to a single center. O blessed soul, consecrated to such a predestination! 

Yet we, whom you have left far behind, lament the obscurity of your commentaries; we accuse the unheard-of novelty of your names <note>Paracelsus famously invented his own vocabulary (e.g., "Archeus," "Iatrochemistry"), which frustrated contemporaries.</note>, we require consistency and evenness of treatment, and we desire the truth of the <term>mechanical preparations</term><note>The actual laboratory work and chemical recipes for creating medicines.</note>. Who doubts that these difficulties can weary even steady minds? They have plainly overcome the intellects of this century. Therefore, we fear lest your pious and friendly purpose be greatly detracted from by your obscured authority; and lest the truth (may God avert the omen!), which now shines only slightly through the shadows, should be neglected and cast aside, causing us to slide back into the ancient confusion of darkness and errors. 

O source of truth and wisdom, look upon our affairs and the hearts of those who, with pious desire and burning prayers, struggle day and night against this imminent <term>metamorphosis</term><note>Here, a negative transformation or a descent back into ignorance.</note>. You who are light, and shine in the darkness, illuminate our eyes, so that having received the light we may live in you, and through pious love and mutual duties, we may be able to conspire toward union, having rejected the multitude and <term>fornication</term><note>Likely used here in the biblical sense of "spiritual adultery" or the pursuit of false, impure philosophies.</note>. And because you have said, "to him who knocks, it shall be opened," the door would surely stand open to us, provided there were not lacking those who would knock properly at the due times. Let us arise, then, sons of the Muses who care for the truth, and with long-lasting patience let us strip off the darkness and impurity of our minds; for a purified mind, like a lightning bolt, reaches the innermost parts of things once the shadows are overcome. Then, finally, it will be permitted to draw nourishment from the inner shrines and guarded treasures of the Philosophers. For previously, oppressed by a deep lethargy, we were unable to separate the husks and shells from the kernel; why then, being blind or dim-sighted, do we define splendor by its obscurity—just as those suffering from fever blame even the sweetness of sugar for bitterness? Why [do we define] the novelty of all things...
