<meta>This page continues Severinus’s introductory letter to Paracelsus. Following the previous page's praise of Paracelsus’s "divine coupling" with the sciences, Severinus now defends Paracelsus’s difficult writing style, his use of strange terminology, and the deliberate obscurity used to protect sacred knowledge from the unworthy.</meta>

# LETTER FROM SEVERINUS TO PARACELSUS.

Do we not watch in wonder when new things, unheard of by us, are proposed? This power is granted to Philosophers: because they have become masters of things, they are also able to dispense names at their own will and to clothe their offspring as they please. For it is a sacrilege to look upon <term>Diana</term><note>In mythology, Actaeon was punished for seeing the goddess Diana naked; here, it signifies that the naked truth of nature is too powerful or sacred for the unprepared to witness directly.</note> naked. We certainly would not blame the changed laws of order or the variety of treatment if we knew the narrowness and the misery of poverty in our own methods—we who write nothing solid or known, but only "inverted thefts" <note>original: "furta inuersa"; likely referring to plagiarism or the reshuffling of old ideas without new insight.</note>. Everything is so hidden and wrapped in thick darkness because we have not joined our Muse to ourselves in a holy marriage. For it is by her benefit that we are admitted to the sacred banquets of the Muses, where we drink <term>ambrosia and nectar</term><note>The food and drink of the gods, representing divine knowledge or immortality.</note> even to the point of intoxication; from this opulence and incomprehensible liberality, we bestow gifts upon mortals. If we cannot contain such great riches and such inexhaustible treasures within our small huts and narrow limits, is it any wonder? Indeed, those things which the Philosophers wished to write according to a certain law and method were published in such an orderly fashion that they have taken away from us all hope of imitation. Thus he wrote the book of *The Great Surgery* <note>original: *Chirurgiæ Magnæ*</note>, the *Paramirum*, the *Paragranum*, *On Tartar*, *On the Diseases of Insanity*, and *On Contractions*. 

Sometimes they deliberately invert the order when they propose the secret mysteries of nature to the "sons of wisdom," mindful of the oath and the command that it is not permitted to "give what is holy to the dogs" <note>A biblical reference (Matthew 7:6) commonly used by alchemists to justify hiding their secrets from the uninitiated or "vulgar" readers.</note>. As <term>Geber</term><note>An 8th-century Islamic polymath and alchemist, often cited as a founding father of the craft.</note> says: "We have scattered our science not in a continuous series of speech, but in different chapters; because if it had been handed down continuously, the honest and the wicked alike would have unworthily usurped it." In this way were written the *Archidoxa of Preparations*, *On Long Life*, *On the Vexation of Alchemists*, and *On the Tincture of the Philosophers*. 

There is also another reason for the order, when we bring our meditations, received from the light of the mind, into the light of day. Here, inventions are joined with admirable continuity: amplifications are added, doubts arise, recollections of new and unknown contemplations are presented, and the reasons for things previously understood are confirmed. By this variety and abundance, with incredible sweetness, they soothe the souls of those who have become the priests and ministers of the Muses. For the senses and dull rays of others cannot penetrate or be joined to them, because they have no proportion. For the Philosophers, while they resonate this lyre, are separated from the body and climb to the innermost shrines of the mind; they receive and return the riches reserved for you. 

In this, they demonstrate the divinity of our soul and its continuity with the <term>Ideas</term><note>Platonic "Forms" or the perfect blueprints of reality.</note> and the <term>First Unity</term>, as well as its immortality and its knowledge of all things before it became a guest of this foul and dark dwelling <note>Referring to the physical body as a temporary, dim residence for the divine soul.</note>. Therefore, mindful of piety and duty, while they strive to communicate these things to their "sons," they groan and lament that they must adapt such great majesty of things to such light and abject garments <note>The "garments" are human words, which Severinus considers inadequate for divine truths.</note>. With all the variety they can muster—Metaphors, metonymies, Allegories, Enigmas, inversions, new resolutions, and compositions—they try to excuse this "poverty of names." Let there be room for such liberality; the entire method of writing used by Philosophers is **magical**. For they attempt to exhibit the hidden mechanics of invisible things openly to the senses in a visible form, just as the invisible nature of spirits is represented by the same industry in a visible form in mirrors. Conversely, they hide visible and manifest things and dazzle the eyes, so that those who see may not see, and those who hear may not hear, and in this way they walk about invisibly. 

We have manifest examples of this in the booklet *On Elemental Diseases*, such as on *Gout*, *Apoplexy*, *Mania*, *Epilepsy*, *Dropsy*, *Colic*, *Hectic Fever*, *Diarrhea*, etc. There, indeed, with a wonderful variety, he exposed the generation and hidden structure of those diseases—now Astronomically, now Philosophically, now Alchemically, at other times Necromantically, Hydromantically, or Pyromantically. And in the Physical exposition, he sometimes borrows transformations from the family of minerals, at other times from the province of metals and marcasites, and sometimes he takes garments and habits from the stage of herbs. And if, in a flowing comedy, he describes famous persons, places, and times with names chosen at his own will, he deserves praise and forgiveness. 

Thus, he chose to call the principles, the Abysses, the roots, and the minerals—from which the beginnings of all things are drawn—by the names *Ares*, *Iliados*, *Idæos*, and *Iliastros* <note>These are technical Paracelsian terms for the fundamental cosmic and spiritual principles of matter.</note>. He would have deserved equal grace if he had called them *Gut.* or *Bmi.* <note>Severinus argues that the specific sounds of the words matter less than the principles they represent.</note> Again, because by a vital and constant agitation he promotes these seeds—lying hidden and quiet—onto this worldly stage for their vigils and destined duties, he names it the *Archeum* <note>The internal, animating force or "inner alchemist" that directs life processes.</note> or the *Vulcanos* <note>The inner fire of nature.</note>. If he had called them *Parmenones* or *Syros* <note>Common names for slave characters in Roman comedy; Severinus implies the name is secondary to the function.</note>, he would have had nature with equal...

->¶ ¶ ¶ ¶<-
->favor<-

<meta>This page continues the defense of Paracelsus’s writing style. Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), a Danish physician and follower of Paracelsian "Vitalism," explains that the apparent inconsistency in Paracelsus’s terminology is not due to ignorance, but rather a reflection of the fluid and "theatrical" nature of life itself. The catchword from the previous page was "joined," leading into this page's discussion of nature's shifting roles.</meta>

# LETTER FROM SEVERINUS TO PARACELSUS.

...joined by favor. Sometimes, as the face of things changes, Nature switches roles and duties, fitting the "garments" of roots or mechanical arts to different places; and vice versa. For a single set of "characters" is not enough to represent the variety of so decorous and rich a comedy. Furthermore, it is a sacrilege to confuse the quiet flow of the mind with a heavy and turbulent <term>precision of words</term><note>original Greek: ἀκριβολογία (akribologia); referring to an overly pedantic or rigid use of language that stifles actual understanding.</note>: in this way, in the little book *On the Procreations of the Element of Water*, he altered the meaning of the <term>Iliadus</term><note>In Paracelsian thought, "Iliadus" refers to the first matter of the elements or a type of vital force; here Severinus explains why the term's meaning shifts between books.</note>. Likewise, he marvelously varied the naming of the "element" in the book *Philosophy to the Athenians*, in the *Paramirum*, the *Greater Surgery*, *On Degrees and Compositions*, and in nearly all his books.

Is this any wonder? In any given nature there are a thousand gifts, an infinite conspiracy and influx of duties and properties, which proceed silently under the hidden command of predestination and complete their assigned task; and because they become citizens and inhabitants of the most diverse "commonwealths," they also assume different habits, manners, and signatures. Thus, he frequently changed the names of the temperaments and of the <term>Three Primes</term><note>The *Tria Prima*: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed were the fundamental components of all matter.</note>. Truly, for the sons of wisdom—who know how to penetrate with the sharp edge of the mind into the quiet **Liturgy of Nature**—he appears admirable in this variety once the shells and husks have been cast aside; yet he entangles the counterfeit wits of the <term>Sophists</term><note>Here meaning conventional academic philosophers who argue for victory rather than truth.</note> in confusion.

But it is unjust to spend more hours on these matters; I will resolve the business in a few words by contracting the vastness of the subject. He who can truly name things is a <term>Magus</term>; to him, it will matter little <note>original: "Davusne loquatur an Heros"; a reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, meaning it doesn't matter if a lowly servant or a hero is speaking.</note> **whether a servant or a hero speaks**. Even with his eyes closed, he will most easily distinguish the differences of this hidden comedy from the duties and properties of the characters, however much the <term>Choragus</term><note>The leader of the chorus or the producer of a play; here used metaphorically for God or Nature directing the "play" of the world.</note> has delighted in their mutable variety. This man, having become master of things through powerful wisdom, will establish individual things flourishing with a unique condition of properties—things which have very rarely entered the commonwealth of mortals. He will have an infallible confidence in immortality and will, as far as is lawful, move things that are standing still.

Forgive me, wise ones, if I have set these things forth too plainly. As for the riddles of the "preparations" <note>Referring to chemical/alchemical recipes.</note>, they are not so locked up that they cannot be opened, if someone can draw the keys from the inner chambers of Theory—especially if, by constant inspection of natural works perfected by the service of fire and heat, he polishes these keys (which would otherwise be covered in rust). He who follows the literal and external sense will run in vain.

Why then did he write, if he did not want to be understood literally? Why did he despoil so many, led astray by vain hope, of their great wealth and resources? To say nothing of the loss of time and the burden of labors. He wrote these things for the **Sons of Wisdom**, not for the "Sophistic" alchemists fascinated by the hunger for gold, nor for the goldsmiths, nor the furnace-tenders of the mines, nor the servants of names, languages, and external surfaces. Therefore, if they "put their sickle into another man’s harvest," they are punished by the highest right. If he had written these things more clearly, the furnace-makers, skilled goldsmiths, street-peddlers, and alchemists would now surpass all physicians and would have prostituted the Art, to the great injury of Nature.

I ought to answer these things in your name, venerable Father, as best I could, to those who do not fear to call you a "buffoon" or a "street-peddler" with sacrilegious and nefarious daring—calling you ignorant of all Philosophy because you despised the naked and empty subtleties of languages. Those who pursue the management of your life with viperous hatred, exaggerating human vices, establish an unfair law against themselves with great rashness. No one lives without vices; he is best who is weighed down by the least of them. **They do not see the bag that hangs behind their back** <note>A reference to Aesop's fable: humans carry two bags; one in front with their neighbors' faults, and one behind with their own.</note>. I could satisfy them in a far different way, but their ears and dull senses could not yet bear it; they must be nourished with milk. For it is safer to cure a "ulcerous" disposition of the soul by a <term>gradual process</term><note>original: "epicrasin"; a medical term for an evacuative treatment that works slowly and gently.</note>; he himself found a mild mitigation for a <term>consuming ulcer</term><note>original: "vlceri æstiomeno"; likely referring to a gangrenous or "eating" sore (phagedenic).</note>. 

Let them read his books more calmly, for he composed several Hymns while living quietly a few years before his death, and they will be milder; the fervor of his age and the impulse of such a noble soul deserve pardon. One thing remains which has delayed us most: they say you despised antiquity and the dogmas of the ancient sages, and that you established a "monarchy" by introducing entirely new things. Even those who hail you as teacher and father profess this. Indeed, in many places, with a flowing pen and by a certain impulse rather than deliberate counsel, you seem to have written so. Yet in other places, you praised **Hermes**, the Egyptian sages, **Archelaus**, **Plato**, and **Hippocrates**. That you did not adapt your commentaries to their laws, names, and methods is excused by philosophical liberty. You imposed that burden upon us; through immense meditations and long vigils, we have discovered the harmony. 

The nature and properties of the **Natural Balsam**, which is the foundation—

<meta>This page concludes the letter from Petrus Severinus to Paracelsus. The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the shifting terminology in Paracelsian philosophy, linking Paracelsus's work to the ancient lineage of Hermetic and Alchemical masters. The catchword "the t..." from the previous page completes the phrase "the theme" in the first line.</meta>

# LETTER FROM SEVERINUS TO PARACELSUS.

...the theme and subject of all your natural books, just as we have seen described in the works of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy and "Hermetic" philosophy is attributed.</note> and in all those philosophers who joined their small but fertile volumes into the "book of truth"—such as Geber, Alphidius, Plotinus, Senior, Rosinus, Morien, Villanova, Raymond Lully, and Isaac <note>Severinus is listing a "Who's Who" of medieval and Renaissance alchemists and philosophers to prove that Paracelsus belongs to an established, prestigious tradition.</note>. Your **Three Principles** <note>The "Tria Prima": Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which Paracelsus identified as the fundamental components of all matter.</note>, indeed, are so clearly established, depicted, and declared in the writings of Raymond, Isaac, Geber, and others, that it would be tedious to list every instance. We even find the names themselves in Raymond, along with their functions and properties in his *Book of Mercuries*, or rather in the concluding section of his *Testament*.

But the talent you received from these masters you have returned with great interest. You have set forth individual, fertile "offspring" that others overlooked; in this way, you have revealed many specific remedies for diseases. Is it any wonder? The principles of truth are fertile. Likewise, we have seen the conditions and roles of the **supernatural Balsam** <note>In alchemy, "Balsam" refers to a preservative, life-sustaining essence within the body.</note> and the **celestial body**—which you discuss in all your magical and Cabalistic meditations—described by that same Hermes, the monarch of the threefold philosophy, and by Orpheus, Pythagoras, Plato, Synesius, Iamblichus, Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, and the other Platonists. However, you have explained these properties more clearly, drawing from the sacred springs with deep and profound variety.

Therefore, we give thanks to you, and we bear witness that you have not lived in vain, nor did you come without purpose, for you have established a memory for your name that is immune to oblivion. And, if that difficult <term>Adech</term><note>original: "adech"; a Paracelsian term for the "inner man" or a vital spiritual force that shapes destiny. Here, Severinus suggests it acts as a force of fate or death that might "prune the branch" of life.</note> did not completely cut short your progress—if what you desired so often with prayers and holy hope has come to pass for you—then we are satisfied to remain in silence. Temper the bitter cups of Poppy and Nettle with the healing virtue of the Melissa <note>Balm-gentle or lemon balm, used here as a metaphor for transforming suffering into sweetness.</note>, so that we too, having finally overcome and dismissed mortal things, may ascend with the assembly of the Blessed to the **Highest Good**—the principle and source of all things—and enjoy eternal bliss through the knowledge and experience of it.

->To Him, the Only One, be praise, honor, and glory<-
->forever and ever, AMEN.<-

# LIST OF THE BOOKS
## CONTAINED IN THE FIRST VOLUME OF THE WORKS
### OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.

I. ***Paramirum*** <note>original: "Paramirum", a title coined by Paracelsus likely meaning "Beyond Wonder."</note> ***concerning the Five Entities of all diseases: that is, in what way any disease can arise from five causes. It comprises five books:***
> *The first deals with the **Entity of the Stars** upon inferior bodies, page 7.*
> *The second, with the **Entity of Poison**, page 12.*
> *The third, with the **Natural Entity**, page 17.*
> *The fourth, with the **Spiritual Entity**, page 22.*
> *The fifth, with the **Entity of God**, page 26.*

II. ***Another Paramirum, which is completed in five parts:***
> *In the First & Second parts, the **Origin of all diseases** is treated: how they are naturally generated from the dissolution of the **Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur** of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the "Macrocosm" or the universe.</note>, pages 31 & 48.*

## VOLUME ONE
# OF MEDICINE
## THE PARAMIRUM OF THEOPHRASTUS
### ON
### MEDICAL INDUSTRY.
# THE TEXT OF THE PARAMIRUM
# OF THEOPHRASTUS
### [of] Hohenheim on Medical Industry.
# THE FIRST BOOK OF PROLOGUES.

---

### NUMBER I.
### PROLOGUE I.

<margin>Five modes of healing</margin>
**I**t is in your interest to know first, Reader, that all diseases in general are usually cured in five ways. Therefore, we begin our medicine from the cure of the diseases themselves rather than from the knowledge of their causes: because the cure points out the causes of the diseases to us, as if with a finger. Let this then be the summary, this the primary argument of our book: that five cures exist in total: which is the same as if you said five arts, or five faculties, or five medicines in all, or five Doctors. Any one of these faculties is separately sufficient for the healing of all diseases. For by five ways, as has been said, five faculties of medicine are found: each of which by itself ought to be marked with that degree of the skilled, sufficient, and industrious physician, who is able to conveniently heal every accident or affliction <term>pathema<gloss>original Greek: παθέμα; referring to a condition of suffering or disease</gloss></term> in either medicine <note>This likely refers to the two "medicines": the physical and the spiritual, or the internal and external, which Paracelsus often distinguished.</note>, as a single sufficient master of the degree of the five faculties. Truly, whoever strives to learn, experience, or attain this degree of any faculty for daily operation <margin>Things a Physician must know.</margin>—for him, beyond the fact that it is right for him to have an exact account first of his own soul, and then also of the sick body, he must apply himself entirely and diligently to this study, so that he may hold the solid foundation of his faculty. He must understand and know much more from within himself than from the patient; he must have the base of his science situated in himself, and not placed in an external subject. He must not overflow or wander from one cause into another; he must not fluctuate within himself like other states of mind, or waver in a disorderly fashion. For indeed, any single faculty is in and of itself a perfect inquiry and comprehension, both in theory and practice, as well as in physics <note>In this context, "physics" refers to *physica*, the study of nature and the natural world.</note>, regarding the knowledge of causes as well as the cure of diseases. And with these things, we wish the introduction to our first medical book to be finished and concluded.

<summary>This page serves as the formal introduction to Paracelsus’s "Paramirum," where he asserts that there are five distinct ways or "faculties" of healing, each sufficient on its own to treat all diseases. He emphasizes that a physician's knowledge must be rooted in a deep, internal understanding of these faculties rather than just observing the patient's symptoms.</summary>

<keywords>Paracelsus, Paramirum, five modes of healing, medical industry, medical theory, pathema, medical faculties, Hohenheim</keywords>

->PARAMIRUM ON THE FIVE<-

# NUMBER II.
## SECOND PROLOGUE.

<margin>Twofold medicine.</margin>
**N**ow indeed, just as we have shown in the aforementioned words that there are five different faculties—each of which exists and stands separately without the other—and as we have taught that anyone instructed in even one of them emerges as a sufficiently suitable doctor of all diseases for both types of medicine: so also this must be laboriously noted: we are not speaking equally of five cures for five causes appearing in every disease. Instead, we are describing five entirely different types of healing: any one of which individually addresses all causes of disease, as will be handed down more clearly hereafter. In the beginning, if you wish to be a doctor, reflect on this: medicine is twofold: <term>Clinical<gloss>original: Clinicen; referring to internal medicine practiced at the bedside</gloss></term> or <term>Physical<gloss>original: Physica; the study of natural causes and internal remedies</gloss></term>, and <term>Surgical<gloss>original: Chirurgica; from the Greek for 'hand-work,' referring to external treatments and operations</gloss></term>. This is not because they have two different origins, but rather from a distinction of their types, the logic of each being contained within itself. For fever and plague indeed arise from the same source, yet they are distinguished from one another.

<margin>Distinctions between fever and plague.</margin>
For one part goes into the internal decay, such as fevers, which fall under clinical medicine; the other results in the plague, which is to say it turns from the center toward the surface. Truly, for a prompt understanding of what has been said, so that you may grasp the logic of both medicines, attend to this: Every affliction that goes from the center to the surface is a matter for physical consideration. But that which happens from the perimeter toward the center is assigned to the surgeon.

<margin>What the physical and surgical look toward.</margin>
But observe this also: Whatever departs by the secretion of nature into the established <term>emunctoria<gloss>organs or channels that carry off waste, such as the sweat glands or kidneys</gloss></term> of the body—all of that is "physical" in terms of consideration. But that which occupies non-natural waste-outlets is surgical. Furthermore, whatever is visible according to its location is considered a wound. But that which remains hidden and concealed, that evil belongs to the physical doctors. And by this status, doctors are separated. But as it pertains to their "sects," the matter requires more accurate consideration. These men are indeed distinguished by their ranks, but their sects are five, and they perform their healings in five ways. Indeed, there are five origins of all disease causes, which even a single sect considers. This is the same as saying that those five origins must be known to any sect. Nevertheless, by reason of the cure, five sects are enumerated:

<margin>Five sects of Physicians</margin>
as for the understanding and knowledge of causes, however, only a single sect exists. And by this discourse, it has pleased us to define the ranks and statuses of doctors.

---

# NUMBER III.
## THIRD PROLOGUE.

**F**urthermore, just as the five sects of Doctors are found in this way, named by their faculties—behaving in such a way that none operates in the likeness of another, yet the power of any sect is such that it can heal the five aforementioned origins of all diseases—so first the names of the five sects themselves must be learned. Once these are defined, we shall descend from that preamble to a further knowledge of medicine.

<margin>Natural Physicians.</margin>
Those who belong to the first faculty or sect are called NATURALISTS: for this reason, they heal only according to the nature of plants themselves, as they agree with their symbols or concordances. Thus they cure the cold with heat, the moist with the dry, fullness with emptying, and the empty with filling, just as nature herself teaches that anything is chased away by its opposite. And the advocates of this sect were <note>Paracelsus is listing the giants of traditional medieval medicine, whom he often critiqued.</note> Avicenna, Galen, and Rhazes, as well as their interpreters and others like them.

<margin>Specifics</margin>
Those of the second sect are usually called SPECIFICS, because they cure all diseases through a specific form, or through a <term>Specific Essence<gloss>Latin: Ens specificum; the unique internal power or "virtue" of a substance</gloss></term>. For example: a magnet attracts iron to itself, not by the benefit of elementary qualities <note>i.e., not because it is "hot" or "dry"</note>, but by a specific power. Thus these doctors heal all diseases by the specific power of medicines. From this class come those who are otherwise called "experimenters," or called "empirics" by some for the sake of mockery, as well as all those called Naturalists insofar as they deal with purgations. For those who purge the bodies [which power flows from a specific form and is not assigned to the Naturalists] step out from their own sect into another.

<margin>Characterals.</margin>
The third are called CHARACTERALS. Indeed, they heal all encountered diseases with certain characters <note>original: 'characteribus'; these refers to signs, talismans, or spoken words</note>, which is recognized both from their books and their very method of curing. Their operation happens like this: if someone commands someone else to run, and the one commanded runs, this operation happens through the word. In the same way, the cure is perfected

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence as the catchword "cura" (cure) indicates the start of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus distinguishes between internal (physical) and external (surgical) medicine based on the direction of the disease's movement. He introduces the first three medical sects: the Naturalists (using opposites), the Specifics (using essential powers), and the Characterals (using words or signs).</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the description of the five sects of medicine (the "Five Ways") and introduces a foundational theoretical section that Paracelsus calls a "Parenthesis," which explains the origins of all diseases. He begins a sharp critique of traditional medical authorities.</meta>

->ON THE ORIGINS OF DISEASES. 3<-

...cure through <term>characters<gloss>original: characteres; these are mystical signs, seals, or sigils believed to hold celestial power</gloss></term>. The authors and masters of these were Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century polymath and theologian known for his work in the natural sciences and alchemy</note>, the Astrologers, the Philosophers, and many others.

<margin>The Spirituals.</margin>
The fourth are called **SPIRITUALS**, so named because they know how to gather the spirits of herbs and roots in such a way that they heal and redeem the sick person whom they [the spirits or the disease] have occupied or weakened. It is as if a judge puts someone in shackles: he alone exists as the doctor for the prisoner. For both the shackles and the keys belong to the judge, and he may restore them when he wishes. In this way, the sick—being as if bound—are liberated by the spirits of herbs, if those spirits either decay or are consumed, as their Little Book will indicate. Many unnamed people belonged to this sect, as did Hippocrates himself along with others.

<margin>The Believers.</margin>
The fifth are called **BELIEVERS**, because they drive away and heal diseases through faith: so that if someone believes in the truth and obeys, they are healed. Christ himself with his disciples performed this. Concerning these five sects, five <margin>Concluding books.</margin> concluding books will be published in succession; for the better understanding of which, we will instruct you more plainly in that same place.

### NUMBER IV.
### FOURTH PROLOGUE.

<margin>Their division.</margin>
**M**oreover, we will divide the five books already mentioned into two parts. One will be the practice of the body [internal medicine]; the other of wounds [surgery]; and each indeed will be appropriately marked out by its own Canons and paragraphs. Indeed, we adapt this preamble or forecast to both parts, so that it pertains to both orders. But before we arrange the five promised books: we will provide for you, the Doctors of both orders and of each individual Sect, one <term>Parenthesis<gloss>In this context, a foundational theoretical section that stands apart from the specific "Five Ways"</gloss></term>, distinguished as its own section, by which we wish to define the "Medical Parenthesis." Its place will be set between the present prologues and the five mentioned books of conclusions: so that it is connected with none of these, nor appropriated to either of them: but stands alone by itself. And indeed, this Parenthesis will teach you the origins of all diseases from which they flow: which a Doctor of any Sect rightly and deservedly ought to have known and explored. If he has done this, then he can, by his own free will, devote himself to whichever Sect he wishes, and use those foundations in his work, according as he understands the origins of diseases through the explanation of this parenthesis. <margin>Commendation of the Parenthesis.</margin> Since this Parenthesis is the indication or exposition of all disease-causing factors; it rightly precedes the five books of conclusions, because it is right for healing to have a certain cause—that is, a man skilled and intelligent in those things which are necessary for healing. In this Parenthesis, five partitions will be established, called **TREATISES**: <margin>Subdivision of the Parenthesis.</margin> <margin>Chapters of the Treatises.</margin> Indeed, there will be five, on account of the five things from which all diseases arise. Every Treatise will again be distributed into its own chapters, so that in this way the foundation of origins, all accidents, and diseases, and their kinds, may be more easily understood along with that from which they are born. And all these things will be determined in two chapters, according to the understanding of the two orders of Medicine, following one another in individual sects, and distinguished by defined rules. The end of the five treatises will also be the end of the chapters and rules of the Parenthesis itself. These five books of the conclusions of the foundation of healing in the five sects will follow next.

# SECOND BOOK OF PROLOGUES.
### NUMBER V.
### FIRST PROLOGUE.

**W**e will now therefore establish the Prologue of our Parenthesis in this way. At the beginning, I declare to both you Doctors and Surgeons, that if you are going to read this parenthesis of ours, from which a true doctor is made, you should not think us ignorant and unskilled in your books simply because we do not pull the same yoke with you. For we do not act with you for this reason: that your style, as well as your practice and knowledge of causes, are by no means approved by us, being as if erroneous, as we are about to say in more detail hereafter. Furthermore, we are not a little offended partly by the scarcity of miracles, and partly by the multitude of sick people abandoned by you. <margin>Why Paracelsus departs from the Doctors.</margin> As for the fact that you boast so much of your patron doctors, the <term>Chaldeans<gloss>referring here to ancient Mesopotamian medical-astrological traditions</gloss></term> as well as the Arabs and Greeks: that does not move us much. <margin>What kind of doctors the Arabs and Chaldeans were.</margin> For even their own published writings testify that the fate of the sick, whom they once undertook to cure, was the same as yours today, the greatest part of whom die. Furthermore, their writings do not break, correct, or annihilate us: of which indeed there is no knowledge among you. For you ought not to think that they fight against us: since on the contrary they act much more clearly for us.

<summary>Paracelsus defines the final two medical sects—the Spirituals and the Believers—and introduces his "Parenthesis," a foundational theoretical bridge explaining the origins of disease. ### NUMBER VI.

## SECOND PROLOGUE.

<margin>
Explanation and division of the Parenthesis: The Five Beings (Entia).
</margin>

**I**n a fair manner, we explain to you the **Parenthesis** <note>Paracelsus uses "Parenthesis" to mean a foundational theoretical insertion or framework that brackets his medical system</note> in which all the foundations of the Physician are placed, and upon which the basis of **Avicenna**, **Rhazes**, **Averroes**, **Hippocrates**, and **Galen** is founded. You must understand these things regarding the dual orders of both Physicians and Surgeons: that in this Parenthesis, both Theory and Practice are contained, necessary for the knowledge of all diseases as well as their cures. We will construct a brief explanation of these as follows. Our mentioned Parenthesis consists of five Treatises; and the subject of each Treatise is an **<term>Ens</term>**. Pay attention to this: there are five **ENTIA** which bear and beget all diseases. These five **ENTIA** signify five origins. Take it this way: there are fivefold origins or causes, from which any single cause emerges that is powerful enough to generate all diseases—those that ever were, those that are now, or those that will be hereafter. You Physicians ought to have paid attention to these **ENTIA**, rather than believing that all diseases flow from one **Ens** or one origin. You should be entirely persuaded that five parts or five **ENTIA** exist, from any

<margin>
The five entities of diseases.
</margin>

one of which individual diseases arise. Take a demonstration of this from an example: let one disease be placed in our midst, namely the **plague** <note>original: "pestis"; often used by Paracelsus as a general term for severe infectious or epidemic disease</note>. It is asked: from where does it arise? You answer: "From the dissolution of Nature." You speak, therefore, as Naturalists. But the Astronomer places the cause of this in the motion or course of the heavens. Which of these is true? I conclude thus: both are true. One operation or origin is indeed from Nature; one is likewise from the stars; and besides these, there are three others. For Nature is one **Ens**; the Star is also one **Ens**. Thus, you must know that there are five plagues—not according to their types, essences, forms, or species—but according to their origins from which they are produced, whatever type they may eventually be. We say, therefore, that our body is subject to five **ENTIA**; and each individual **Ens** contains all diseases under itself, and exercises a certain power with them over our body. For there are five kinds of dropsy, and just as many of the **royal disease** <note>original: "morbi regii"; a traditional term for jaundice</note>, and just as many of fever, and just as many of cancer. This is also true of others.

<margin>
From where the plague comes.
</margin>

<margin>
The five plagues.

### NUMBER VII.

## THIRD PROLOGUE.

<margin>
What an Ens is.
</margin>

**J**ust as the five **ENTIA** have been enumerated, so further you physicians must observe what an **<term>Ens<gloss>A "Being" or "Entity"—an active, governing force or influence that determines the state of the body</gloss></term>** is known to be. An **Ens** is a cause or a thing that has the power of governing the body. You, however, led into error against us, determine that the plague arises from the humors—that "gold" which lies hidden inside the body. This opinion is very erroneous. Rather, pay attention to this: what is that thing which contaminates the body with poison? And not: how does the infected body behave? Do you not remember this: that either all diseases, or at least any single one, emerge from outside the body itself? It is entirely right that the body should be either inflamed or affected in some other way. For the body is never the cause of disease to itself. Besides this, they [the Entia] dispose themselves toward the body; the body cannot struggle against them, but it is entirely necessary for it to suffer being weakened by them. For these [Entia] have such power over the body that they can affect it according to their own nature. And every single **Ens** is so constituted that all diseases without exception are subject to it. Therefore, fivefold fires govern our body...

The fivefold governors of our body.

...govern, or rather overhang the body in such a way that it can be attacked and weakened now by this one, now by that. <margin>Spiritual Entity.</margin>

## NUMBER VIII.
### FOURTH PROLOGUE.

**S**ince we have thus far made mention of the five **ENTITIES**, it is now consequential that we investigate what those **ENTITIES** are. Indeed, even if our ancestors and predecessors were returned to this vital breath, they would greatly admire this medicine of ours; however, we will say nothing about that. Nor will their remedies be a cause for contempt to us; but we will rather seek out or "suck out" <note>A metaphor for extracting the essential truth or active power (the "marrow") from older medical traditions.</note> their sinew and marrow. As a beginning to our **Parenthesis**, therefore, so that we may finish the little book of prologues and more certainly understand the very **ENTITIES** that govern, rule, and compel our body, let these things be established.

<margin>Entity of the Stars.</margin>
The first treatise of the **Parenthesis** teaches what essence and power the stars contain within themselves. That power acts upon our body in such a way that the body is voluntarily subject to whatever impression and operation they have. This power of the stars is called the **ENTITY OF THE STARS** <note>original: "Ens Astrorum"</note>: which is counted as the first of all those things to which we are subject.

<margin>Entity of Poison.</margin>
The second force or power that violently alters us and casts us into diseases is the **ENTITY OF POISON** <note>original: "Ens Veneni"</note>. Concerning this you will note: even if the star itself is healthy within us and does not harm the body by any injury, nevertheless the **ENTITY** of poison can inflict harm upon us. Just as we are subject to it, so we must expect its impression, nor is it permitted to decline its power.

<margin>Natural Entity. Our body is thus fourfold.</margin>
The third force is that which itself wears down and weakens our body, even if the two previously named **ENTITIES** are healthy and fortunate within us. And this is called the **NATURAL ENTITY** <note>original: "Ens Naturale"</note>. This **ENTITY** is understood when the body itself weakens us through its immoderation or debility from a poor **<term>Complexion<gloss>In this context, the physical constitution or the internal balance of the body's nature.</gloss></term>**. Thus from this, many and diverse—indeed, all diseases—arise without exception, even while the other **ENTITIES** are in themselves well-situated and disposed.

## NUMBER IX.
### FIFTH PROLOGUE.

**T**here is no reason, however, for you to wonder at our prologue in this **Parenthesis**. For wonder comes from ignorance and lack of skill. But if you are entirely inclined to wonder: I ask you to unroll this parenthesis by reading, which will put an end to your wonder. Although we do not fear your style at all—as one who looks at us with squinted and distorted eyes. You seem to yourselves to have all the medications for fevers, or (as they call them) **Recipes**, most skillfully prepared. But whatever those may be, it is certain that by their use you are so far from achieving your wish that the outcome becomes a terror to yourselves. If you consider their foundation, you will notice yourselves that you are more slight than if you were merely ignorant. For you look back at something other than what you ought. You divide the kinds of fevers into nearly 70 species: yet you do not pay attention to the fact that fevers are numbered five times 70 <note>Paracelsus argues that since there are 5 Entities, every disease—like fever—has 5 different versions based on its origin.</note>. For you spend your talent and mind on the **Natural Entity** alone...
<margin>How many species of fevers.</margin>

<header>THE PARAMIRUM: CONCERNING THE FIVE ENTITIES</header>

Beyond that, you do not think at all that there are four others still. If that natural **ENTITY**, which you posit, were the principle or cause of sickness or fever, your opinion might have some weight. But you consider that [natural cause] as the disease itself; and so you entangle yourselves in error. Repeat this to yourselves whenever it happens—or has happened—that it could be asked of you who have treated those with fever: were they healed by your work or not? For, if the feverish person is inflamed by the Star: he is either killed or restored by the same. You may medicate however you wish, and even give the patient a whole pharmacy to drink; yet you will attempt everything in vain, just as the treatise **ENTITY OF THE STARS** demonstrates.

<margin>All entities must be understood by the physician.</margin>
Take care, therefore, that the **ENTITIES** are not unexamined or unknown to you; so that you can understand what you are doing, and whether you are helping the sick or rather harming them. This theory is clearly set before you within physical limits. You cling to this one alone, and touch only the Natural **Entity**. This happens by such a certain error that you cannot at all understand what the natural **ENTITY** is in truth; and this is for the reason that you mix everything together and cannot distinguish what should be chosen and where.

## NUMBER 10.
## SIXTH PROLOGUE.

**S**o then, listen further to us. Since the power over our bodies is distributed into five domains, to whose force our bodies are subjected and by which they are driven into diseases—namely, the **ASTRAL ENTITY, POISONOUS ENTITY, NATURAL ENTITY, SPIRITUAL ENTITY, and DIVINE ENTITY**—five treatises of this parenthesis <note>Paracelsus refers to this systematic section as a "parenthesis," meaning a necessary explanatory digression or foundational block within his larger work.</note> will follow in this order: namely, in what way the **Astral ENTITY** has dominion over the human body, so that it either sickens it or kills it. And so also for all the others.

<margin>A declaration concerning the style he uses.</margin>
But before we begin the parenthesis itself, I would have it known that we will use a gentile <note>original: "gentili seu Ethnico". Paracelsus uses "gentile" or "ethnic" to refer to a secular, naturalistic approach based on observation rather than scripture.</note> or ethnic style in writing, though we are descended from a Christian man. The reason why we do this is **FAITH**. For if we were to write as a Christian, then those four **Entities**—the *Astral, Poisonous, Natural, and Spiritual*—would have to be omitted, nor could they be described by us. For that is not a Christian style, but an ethnic one. But the last **ENTITY** is of the Christian style, with which we shall also conclude. Yet this gentile style, which we use in describing the four entities, will burn no stain into our faith; rather, it will more readily sharpen our intellect. We name it the gentile style because it sets aside the faith of Christ; and yet we profess this: that all of you who search and follow the nature of the four Entities were born Christian. Why we call the other four Entities gentile or profane, but the last one divine, we will recount in part in this treatise. And yet, so that we may perfectly understand the true foundation of truth itself, we will more fully derive and define that **Entity** of **FAITH** in the final book of conclusions. In that book, we will bid farewell to the profane style <note>original: "nuntium mittemus", an idiom meaning to dismiss or formally break off a relationship</note>, and we will persevere hereafter in faith as **FAITHFUL** ones, to whom paganism is of no concern. Let you Christians also strive for the same with us, and judge us finally by the "Faithful" books.

->**CHAPTER I.**<-

**A**s we write for you concerning the Astral **ENTITY**, this first task falls to us: that we rightly consider the essence, form, and properties of the Stars. Once this is provided, the path by which the *Astral Entity* is drawn forth will follow. Regarding this matter, you have extracted a foundation from Astronomical doctrine, yet you pay little attention to true evidence, nor do you weigh what was necessary to consider. Indeed, you profess that the heaven itself constitutes a body or a star. But this is vanity. For man, once bodily established, is henceforth formed by nothing other than the *Entity of the Seed* <note>original: "Ente Seminis" (mistranscribed as "feminis" in the Latin text due to the long 's'); this refers to the inherited biological blueprint from the parents.</note>, without any concurrence of the stars. To this, you respond that the stars themselves moderate, dispose, fashion, and imbue bodies according to their own nature. That sense is certainly distorted. For why this is not so is shown to you by the *Entity of the Seed*. Therefore, we will no longer argue against this opinion of yours: as it falls and vanishes by its own resolution. Nevertheless, as a foundation for our Explanation, we will grant you this declaration: Adam and Eve received their bodies through creation, and [humanity continues] through the *Entity of the Seed* until the destruction of the world. And even if no star, nor any planet, had ever been or were now in nature, children would nonetheless have been born and tempered by the generation of their parents just as has happened otherwise. Surely one would have been born Melancholic, another Choleric; this one faithful, that one unfaithful. So also one would have been upright, another wicked: because these natures of men consist in the Entity of properties, and do not flow down from the stars. For these fill no part of the body—that is, they infuse no temperament <term>complexionem: the specific balance of humors in an individual</term>, no color, no nature, and no substance.

<margin>
That the heaven disposes and fashions itself into bodies.
</margin>

->**CHAPTER II.**<-

<margin>
The two Entities of man: of the Seed and of Virtue.

**W**e advise every Physician to establish two Entities in man: the *Entity of the Seed* and the *Entity of Virtue*. And although we add nothing private here: nevertheless, be mindful of this doctrine, so that you may read and observe these things in their proper place. Here we use such an axiom that fits the *Astral Entity* like the beginning of a text. And since it is our purpose to teach in what way the *Astral Entity* can harm us: you first have need of explanation and knowledge that the stars—whether they be Planets or any other stars of the firmament—build nothing in our body, and produce nothing in our color, beauty, morals, virtues, or other properties. And you ought to eliminate this opinion from your minds, which you have cherished for so long, by which you have made judgments about men and made the men themselves from the nature and position of the stars. Although we do not initiate a longer discourse here against our adversaries—especially because the end of this Explanation we have begun is not to respond to every objection head-on—nevertheless, hereafter there will be such a great abundance of paper and ink for us that we may, Jehovah willing and favoring, expend them on this matter. Now therefore, after you have understood that those stars give us neither nature nor properties—

<margin>
The reason why the stars kill our bodies.
</margin>
...to instill other qualities: now turn your mind to the opposite—the reason why these same stars weaken and kill our bodies. Let us not think that because we are "offspring of Saturn" <note>original: "soboles Saturnia"; a reference to the astrological belief that those born under the influence of Saturn are predisposed to certain temperaments or lifespans.</note>, we therefore have a longer or shorter life. This is vanity. Indeed, the movement of Saturn affects no man’s life, neither prolonging nor shortening it. For even if Saturn had never ascended into the sky or the firmament, humans would still have been born in the same way. And even if no Moon had ever been created, humans of that same nature would have emerged. Indeed, be persuaded of this: even if Mars is fierce and cruel, it is not because of Mars that **Nero** <note>The Roman Emperor, used here as a historical archetype of cruelty.</note> existed as his offspring. Although both are indeed of the same nature, one borrowed nothing from the other. Look: **Helena** and **Venus** were certainly of one nature; yet Helena would have been an adulteress even if Venus had never been born. And although Venus is older than Helena, you must believe that harlots lived even before Helena.

### CAP. III.

<margin>
Humans cannot live without the stars.
</margin>
**B**eyond what has been mentioned so far, you see that much more could be recounted concerning these things. But since mention of these occurs in the *Entity of the Seed* and the *Entity of Virtue* <note>original: "Ente Seminis & Virtutis"; Paracelsus refers back to his system of five causes of disease.</note>, we cut short this discourse here. Nevertheless, you ought to consider that the firmament and the stars are completely established in such a way that humans and animal creatures cannot thrive without them. Yet, they are by no means created *by* the stars. Understand this from the following example: A seed cast into the earth brings forth its fruit from itself, for it holds the <term>Entity of the Seed</term> <note>The inherent biological blueprint or life-force within a seed.</note> hidden within it. Meanwhile, if the Sun did not warm the seed, it would not sprout. Yet you must not think that this seed is generated by the Sun, or the firmament, or anything else. Hold this to be true: the heat of the Sun establishes the proper timing—just as if you wish to digest something and bring it to its proper operation or effect, it must be done through <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "digestio"; in Paracelsian natural philosophy, this refers to the ripening, maturation, or chemical transformation of a substance by heat, not just stomach digestion.</note>. Thus, digestion does nothing other than operate through time. The thing itself which is being digested holds its own operation within itself.

<margin>Digestion.</margin>
Take this as what "digestion" is: without it, a fetus cannot grow. For it is increased by digestion itself—that is, in the womb. Therefore, for this work, the fetus needs no star, no planet. The womb itself is to it as a planet and a star. The seed has need of digestion; this happens in the earth. But the earth itself has no digestion without the Sun. Yet the womb is a digestion even without any stars. And although the Sun might never shine, and Mercury himself might run backward, children are still born, they still grow, and the Sun and digestion are not taken from them. <margin>Stars do not incline.</margin> Indeed, the stars possess absolutely no power to <term>incline</term> <note>original: "inclinandum"; a direct attack on the common astrological maxim "the stars incline, but do not compel." Paracelsus argues they don't even incline us.</note> a human according to their nature, nor is the human held by any law to receive such an inclination. Understand this again in this way: of two soldiers, equally fierce and wrathful, which one gives nature or character (to use this word) to the other? None. Of twins extremely similar to each other, which one bestowed this similarity on the other? Neither. Why then do we call ourselves "Jovial" or "Lunar" <note>influenced by Jupiter or the Moon.</note> because of the same reasoning as the example of the twins? A fetus is one, like a seed in its substance; it is a twin as a seed, and not the "offspring of the Sun," as is traditionally said of twins.

### CAP. IV.

**H**aving demonstrated these things, know that we wish further to bring this parenthesis to the <term>Astral Entity</term> <note>original: "Ens Astrale"; the second of Paracelsus's five entities, dealing with environmental and atmospheric influences on health.</note>, so that you may fully understand how the stars harm and kill us. Hitherto you have been persuaded that the stars "incline" us, and that we are fashioned by this inclination according to the character of the stars. From this, it happened that you composed great books on this matter—on the art by which the stars can and should be resisted. Yet that writing is a mere shadow. Nor does it concern us in what sense you understand that proverb, *The wise man rules the stars*.

<margin>
The stars are most free.
</margin>
However, in the sense that we accept it, it is admitted thus: The stars compel nothing in us, they fashion nothing, they form nothing, they resemble nothing, they incline nothing. They are, in themselves, most free; and we are likewise most free. And yet note, we cannot live without the stars. <margin>To what extent we need the stars.</margin> For both cold and heat, and the digestion of those things by which we live, proceed from them. Only the human character does not. And they benefit us only so much, or we have need of them only so much, as we have need of cold and heat, food and drink, and air. Beyond that, they are not in us, nor are we in them. But if they are indeed similar to us, or we to them—or if they are not as we are, and we are not as they—why then do we labor over those long-winded propositions and disputes? Surely the Architect fashioned it so. Who knows what lies hidden in the firmament which might benefit someone, though we are ignorant of it? For neither the brightness of the Sun...

# ON THE ENTITY OF THE STARS.

<margin>The influence of blood in the fetus.</margin>
...neither the skill of **Mercury** nor the beauty of **Venus** <note>Mercury was traditionally associated with intellect and craft, Venus with physical beauty.</note> provides us with anything. Only the splendor and rays of the **Sun** are of use to us, for it produces the crops and the summer, which provides our yearly harvest. But to conclude this discussion, so that you may understand the beginning of this digression, take note of this: if a fetus—conceived or born under the most beneficial and noble planets and stars—should take on a different or entirely contrary nature, whose fault would that be? It is surely the fault of the one from whom that blood flowed, just as is taught concerning generation. Similarly, you should judge that the stars themselves do nothing here, but only the blood. Even if a child's birth is matched to a planet’s appointed hour, that child still holds its nature from the blood. Often, good traits coincide with good stars and bad with bad; but only one of these acts as the true cause, not both. This is the <term>Entity of the Seed</term> <note>original: "Ens feminis"; refers to the hereditary power or "life-entity" contained within the reproductive seed, which Paracelsus argues is the real source of a person's traits, as opposed to astrological influence.</note>.
<margin>Entity of the Seed.</margin>

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Fortune comes from diligence, not from the stars.</margin>
Before we descend to our main subject, we will present to you something concerning the aptitude and ability of the body. After you have weighed and decided everything, you might think that a man’s fortune and his diligence flow to him from the stars—so that one person grows faster than another, this one in arts and learning, that one in wealth, another in power and the like. You ascribe all these things to the stars, from which you believe they were received. We overturn all of this and interpret the matter in this way: Fortune itself comes from **diligence**; diligence comes from the **spirit**. Just as every man has a certain genius or spirit, so is he diligent toward this or that thing. And as he is diligent in this or that thing, so he becomes "fortunate." So that you may recognize this genius, know that it is like the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "inner alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believed directed the growth and functions of the body.</note>; just as is taught concerning the Archeus, we will not linger here lest we wander from our purpose.

You also make many assertions about the diversity of forms among men—how from the first **Adam** through so many centuries and among so many millions of men, no one has ever had a face equal to another, except for **Twins**, whose similarity is miraculous and admired. You credit this to the stars and their wonderful motion. This matter is presented to us as if wrapped in a veil. Rather, know this (which we understand more aptly regarding the limit of life): the **Entity of the Seed** was so created by God that all forms, colors, and species of men—of which there is no number—must be fulfilled. Once these have been produced and fulfilled,
<margin>The origin of the diversity of forms in man.</margin>
then, in due course, men will come forth again, exhibiting the same faces presented by those who died long ago. When the day of the **Final Judgment** <note>The end of the world in Christian theology.</note> approaches, then all the colors and characters of men will have been exhausted. For that day is set precisely at the point when all colors, forms, species, and characters have already passed, and no one else can be born without being similar to someone who came before. At that time, the hour of the world's first circuit will be finished. Do not let yourselves fall into the speculation of establishing multiple ages of the world or dividing the world into parts. For if all the colors and characters of men have flowed out, and no new forms can be produced but only similarities, then the true age of the world will have ended.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>What the body must beware of.</margin>
<margin>Life is fire.</margin>
But to what end are these thoughts? Surely so that you may more clearly and lucidly understand what we want and have proposed. By this guidance, the <term>Astral Entity</term> <note>The "Ens Astrale"; the influence of the atmosphere and the heavens on human health.</note> is to be understood by you in this way: There is one certain thing, which is not seen, which protects and preserves us—and all those things that live and feel—in life. And this flows forth from the stars. We explain it thus: A fire that burns has need of wood. Without it, there is no fire. In this way, consider that **life is fire**. And yet it does not live without wood. Observe this as well: although this is a crude and heavy example, it is suitable enough for you. Namely, the **body is the wood**. Its **life is the fire**. Now, life lives from the body. The body, in turn, needs to have something so that it is not consumed by life, but endures in its own substance. This is the very thing about which we are explaining this "Entity" to you. And this flows from the stars, or the firmament. You assert, and not falsely, that if there were no air, all things would fall downward, and whatever had life within it would be suffocated and perish. But accept in turn that there is still one thing that sustains the body, which in turn preserves the life of the body. Its lack or destruction would be no more tolerable than the loss of air. For in it, and from it, the air itself is nourished. If this were not so, the air would dissolve. From this thing, the firmament lives. If it were not in the firmament, the firmament would perish. We call this <term>M</term> <note>original: "M."; likely standing for *Mysterium* or the "Manna" of the stars, a subtle spiritual nourishment Paracelsus believed was extracted from the air to sustain the "balsam" of life.</note>. For in the universe, nothing was created above this; nothing is more primary than this; nothing is more important for the contemplation of a **Physician**. Note this well, then, so that we may indicate this **M** to you: not because...

# PARAMIRUM TREATISE I.

...that it arises from the firmament, or was born in it, or is transmitted to us by the same. For none of these things are so. But in what way this is to be received by you: it is right that you be mindful of those things which are indicated concerning the first created thing, and which in the present discourse will be further handed down concerning **M.**

### CHAPTER VII.

After you have received from us the explanation of **M.**, now attend further to this example. That which is a hardened and closed-up <term>hypocautum</term> <note>original: "hypocautum"; a room heated from below by a furnace. Paracelsus uses it here as an analogy for an enclosed environment.</note>, it conceives such an odor within itself as you have sent into it. That odor does not arise from the room itself, but from you. Now take notice. Whatever people are present in that place, they smell this odor, just as you have prepared it. And it can happen that you might excite both all diseases and similarly their cures in that chamber for those who dwell in it. Note this. The air, which is inside, does not proceed from you. But the odor emanates from you. But understand further: we speak of the air in such a way that we recount to you the *Astral Entity* <note>original: "Ens astrale"; the influence or "being" of the stars as it affects the physical world.</note>. You explain that air arises from the motion of the firmament, which we deny. Not equally, however, concerning the wind, as Meteorology proves.

<margin>Air [was created] before all creatures by the Highest Good.</margin>
Air flows down from the Highest Good <note>God</note>, and that existed prior to all creatures. After it, there are other created things. The firmament itself lives from the air, as do all creatures. Therefore air is not produced from the firmament. For the firmament is preserved by air just as man is. And even if all the firmaments were to stand still, the air would nevertheless exist no less. But if indeed the world were to perish in that rest and stillness, the cause of this thing would be this: that the firmament lacked air, and this had perished. And then this would be a sign that it was all over for man himself as well. All elements would be dissolved. For in the air, all things are sustained. This is the *Great M.* Now we say to you, that this *Great M.* is such a thing from which all created things live, and they draw out their life in it and from it. But this *Great M.* can be so altered and poisoned that man draws this poison into himself. For since his life is in it and dwells there, necessarily his body also will be alterable and contaminable by that same thing which lies hidden in the *Great M.*: just like the air changed in the heated room, of which we discussed a little while ago. So then there is something that defiles this *M.*: which itself then both remains in the body and is separated from it.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>The stars have change.</margin>
Thus, therefore, let the *Entity of the stars* be understood. The stars themselves possess their various natures and properties: just as people do on earth. These same stars have their change in themselves, namely of better, worse, sweeter, more acidic, more bitter. If they indeed persist in their goodness, nothing of evil emanates from them. But in depravity, their malignancy emerges. Remember indeed, that the same [stars] surround the whole world, just as a shell <note>original: "putamen"</note> surrounds an egg. Air enters through the shell, and penetrates it first, proceeding to the center of the world. Thus again you should judge: whatever stars are poisoned, the same infect the air with their contagion. Thus, wherever this virus reaches, there these diseases emerge according to the condition of the malicious star. For that power is not such that it can contaminate the universal air of the whole world. It infects at least one part of it, according as its force is strong. The same reasoning also applies to the goodness of the stars. This therefore is the *Astral Entity*, that is, the odor, breath or vapor, or sweat of the stars mixed with the air, just as the course of the stars makes it manifest. For from here come forth cold, heat, dryness, humidity and the like, which are indicated by their properties. From here therefore conclude, that the stars themselves incline nothing <note>A rejection of the idea that stars force human will or "incline" the soul to specific sins; they only affect the physical environment.</note>: but by their breath at least they infect and contaminate **M.** through

<margin>The stars incline nothing.</margin>
which we are further poisoned and afflicted. And such is the nature of the *Astral Entity*, which disposes our bodies to both good and evil in this way. Whichever man, according to his natural blood, is so tempered that he is opposed to that breath, he becomes sick from it. But he who has not acquired a contrary nature, nothing harms him. Neither does he feel the injury who has received so strong and noble a temperament against it that he is sufficient for overcoming the poison by the nobility of his blood: or he who has taken medicine resistant to the poisonous vapors of the heavens. From here also conclude this: all created things are opposed to man, and man in turn to these same things.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>How the exaltations of the stars harm the celestial bodies.</margin>
So that you may drink in a fuller knowledge of these things: it should be known that we do not accuse summer and winter alone as if they were harmful to our bodies, as we hinted in the previous examples; but we make the source any planet and star, whenever it climbs so far to its <term>exaltation</term> <note>original: "exaltationem"; in astrology, the position where a planet's influence is most powerful.</note> that it penetrates **M.** and tempers it according to its own nature. Thus **M.** becomes excessively salty from some; from others it becomes more "arsenicated," or "sulphurated," or "mercurialized." For their exaltations are either poison or health to our bodies; unless this perhaps prevents it: that the vapor, on account of distance, does not reach us. Take proof of this from here. If the exaltation of
<margin>The powers of the arsenic stars.</margin>
arsenic stars reaches the face and center of the earth, and especially the water: then by its power it contaminates all the water with arsenic. ### CHAPTER XI.

In likeness to what has been said, our bodies represent lakes, and their members represent the fish. # SECOND TREATISE OF THE PARAMIRUM

### *First Section.*

As we have now explained, the **Astral Entity** affects us both within and outside the body, namely according to diseases that do not go outside the body, and those that depart into its surroundings. So likewise, for your knowledge, it is required that we recount how poison is situated in each star. For this belongs more to the faculty of Astronomy than to Medicine.

<margin>Fivefold poisons of dropsy.</margin>
Whatever comes of this, the poisons that produce <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: hydropisis; an old medical term for the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water, known today as edema.</note> are fivefold. They are indeed under one genus, but they differ in five natures. Thus, one is the poison of the stars; the other four belong to the other Entities; yet each produces dropsy, just as there are fivefold sulfurs and other similar things.

### *Second Section.*

Truly, by what means you may know from which Entity the dropsy arises, and by what remedies it may be cured: this is read as handed down in the medications for diseases. These things having been handed down thus far, we wish to conclude the Entity itself, adding this: you will think in vain of healing astral diseases as long as the diseased star dominates. For its power is superior to the physician. From this you ought to gather that it is altogether right, as those who would serve as upright physicians, that you carefully observe the times, and do not attempt the cure of any disease before the convenient time, since every effort would be futile.
<margin>The star’s power is superior to the physician.</margin>

# SECOND PARENTHESIS.
## SECOND BOOK AND PAGOYUM <note>A term coined by Paracelsus, likely referring to a specific division, region, or "treatise-block" within his philosophical system.</note> OF THE TREATISE ON THE ENTITY OF POISON.
### CHAPTER I.

After the treatise on the Astral Entity has been completed thus far, order demands that we now discourse upon the Entity of Poison, which is the second source from which our bodies are affected. Yet, mindful of the first foundation we leaned upon in delivering the Astral Entity, we still apply our efforts to it: namely, that our bodies are violated by five Entities and led to suffer. Nevertheless, so that we may tread a easier and shorter path:

<margin>The basis of the Entity of Poison.</margin>
we shall not resume the aforementioned preface, but we shall establish the basis and truth of the *Entity of Poison* in this way. It is confirmed among all that our bodies require conservation—that is, a certain vehicle by whose benefit they may thrive and be nourished. Wherever this is lacking, life itself goes into exile. Equally, however, it must be noted that the very same one who fashioned or created our bodies likewise procreated the foods themselves: with the same facility, indeed, but not with equal perfection. I wish this to be understood thus: the body was given to us empty of poison. But that which we offer to the body in the place of nourishment has poison joined to it. Thus the body was created perfect, but the other [the food] was not.
<margin>The body is empty of poison.</margin>
<margin>Foods are poisons to themselves.</margin>
From this, observe that other animals and fruits are food for us. Therefore, they are also poison. To themselves, indeed, they are neither food nor poison, but in respect to themselves, and insofar as they are creatures, they participate in perfection equally with us. Insofar as they are taken as food for us, to that extent they are poison to us; by which reasoning that which is by no means a poison to itself is a poison to us.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>How things were established as good and bad.</margin>
Each single thing is perfect in itself and made good for itself and for its own purpose. But if we look at external uses, then it was established as both good and evil. Consider it thus: the ox, which feeds on grass, receives poison and health from it. For the grass has both in itself: nourishment and medicine. To the grass itself, however, the grass is not a poison. So also for man: whatever he eats and drinks exists as both poisonous and healthful for him at the same time. Yet that which he eats is not a poison to itself. And take this which we propose in two ways. One concerning man himself, excluding the nature of animals and plants. The other concerning the intake. But we shall weave this even more clearly for easier understanding: one thing in man is the great nature; the other is the poison that is brought into that nature. And so that we may complete this parenthesis for your benefit, recall to yourselves that God established all things perfect for themselves; but for others, they are imperfect, on account of and for their use. And in this, the foundation of our second *Entity*, namely poison, shall rest. But we wish to be understood further in this way: that God indeed appointed no <term>Alchemist</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "internal alchemist" (often associated with the stomach or the "Archeus") is the biological force that separates the nutritious essence of food from the poisonous waste products.</note> for man or for creatures for his own sake...
