It marks a major transition in the book where Paracelsus moves from discussing the "natural" or "heathen" causes of disease to the "Entity of God" (Ens Dei), shifting his writing style to a Christian perspective.</meta>

# PARAMIRUM TRACTATE V. FIFTH BOOK <note>The original Latin includes the phrase "Non Pagoyus," an obscure term likely meaning "not a dream" or referring to a non-secular division of his philosophy.</note>

...we wished to indicate this so that you might understand how violently and commandingly the *Spiritual Entity* <term>Ens Spirituale: the spiritual force within a person that can influence health or disease</term> dominates the body, such that by this power, many diseases and all their various kinds can be channeled into a human being.

<margin>The Spiritual Entity is the cause of many diseases.</margin>
In these cases, you should not apply remedies meant for natural diseases, but you should heal the spirit itself. For it is the spirit that is sick. Next, note this as well: many fall ill from spirits through the power of the will, even those who have not been afflicted through figures, images, or other mediums—as is common among neighbors. And yet, the will in these people is so powerful that it can ignite and injure the spirit of another. This happens through the medium of their *Dreams*: specifically in this way. If they sleep, then all their intentions are carried out and fulfilled in others, so that your spirit leads the spirit of another to you while you sleep; and you, while sleeping and unaware, injure him as if through a dream, and this occurs through the medium of your word, which goes out from the sleeper without him being conscious of it.

<margin>The effectiveness of the dreams of the envious.</margin>
For the dreams of envious people are made real if they encounter one another effectively, whether by hand or by mouth: as is more clearly taught in the treatises on *Dreams*. For it is not a dream if it arises from the spirit, unless perhaps it happens as I have indicated. For it arises from the spirit itself, which we have already mentioned.

## Part I.

Thus you should now understand that a hand can injure a man even if he is not physically grasped, as was said above. So the mouth strikes with words the one whom you seek. However, let these things be understood in this way: that all of this happens through a certain medium, and specifically through the power of the spirit.

## Part II.

Similarly, note that faith works nothing here, but the will alone. To bring or introduce anything here regarding faith would be closer to foolishness than wisdom. Let this be an example: Two men cannot strike each other through faith or belief, but only through the deed itself. In the same way, two spirits of the will arise, not from belief, but from the glowing heat <note>original: "incandescentia," referring to a burning intensity of will or passion</note> of their men. These two fight without belief, truly, by the deed itself and by the forces expended—just as more is indicated regarding *Faith* and the will, as well as regarding the Vitonissae <term>Vitonissae: a term used by Paracelsus to describe spiritual or supernatural entities, often associated with witchcraft or spectral influences</term> and incantations.

# PARENTHETICAL TEXT ON THE FIFTH ENTITY.

---

### TRACTATE ON THE ENTITY OF GOD.

#### CHAPTER I.

**A**fter we indicated in the earlier parts—at the beginning of our books, to be sure—that we had decided to write four books in the "Heathen" <note>original: "Ethnico," meaning a secular or natural philosophy style that does not rely on Christian revelation</note> manner and style for this reason: that any Christian man who writes in any way other than the tenor of our Faith, writes as a heathen. Now, therefore, in this Parenthesis of ours, we shall set aside that heathen custom and ritual, and we shall use a Christian style throughout in completing this fifth book on the **ENTITY OF GOD**, so that you may no longer hold our "heathenism" against us.

<margin>A protestation against the charge of degenerate visitation.</margin>
Even though, once this Parenthesis is finished, we shall annex five books of practice <note>original: "Praxeos," referring to clinical or applied medicine</note> so that this book may be completed and perfected, I would nevertheless have you forewarned: we shall finish this fifth book itself in a Christian style, and we shall treat the four following books, which we indicated at the beginning, with the characteristic "heathen" way of speaking. This is easily permitted to us without bring shame upon our Christian confession, because the Heathen rite proceeds for it and from it, just as it was predestined by God. Although diseases themselves also arise from nature, according to the four previously mentioned Entities, it was nonetheless right for us to investigate their cures through faith and not through nature. As this fifth book of practice will make more plain. Therefore, we shall not be afraid to list the four Entities, even if they exist as "Heathen." You, however, must extract the true and complete foundation of healing from the fifth book, in which genuine medicine is produced. We establish the other four books of practice not for Christians, but for the nations. For we strive to propagate the foundations of medicine to all people: we confer a portion to the Turks, a portion likewise to the Saracens, a portion to Christians, and a portion to Jews, as these books shall declare.

#### CHAPTER II.

**W**hile we are composing these things for Christians, we would have them be advised to diligently study this fifth Parenthesis: from which they will learn how they ought to both seek and cure all diseases from this point of instruction.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the "Ens Dei" or "Entity of God," the final and most significant cause of disease in Paracelsus's medical philosophy. After discussing the natural and spiritual causes, he now addresses the theological dimension of illness—specifically the concepts of divine timing (the "hour") and the role of the physician as a servant of God's will.</meta>

# ON THE ENTITY OF GOD

<margin>
Health and diseases are from God.
The order of diseases is twofold: Nature and Scourge.
</margin>
And in this way: It is known to you that both health and disease are sent by God, and not by men. Indeed, you must divide human diseases into two orders: namely, into **Nature** and into the **Scourge** <term>Flagellum: a divine punishment, trial, or "whip" meant to correct the soul</term>. That which is natural belongs to the first, second, third, and fourth Entities. The Scourge is the fifth. <note>Paracelsus organizes all pathology into five "Entities" (Entia): 1. Ens Astrale (stars), 2. Ens Veneni (poison/environment), 3. Ens Naturale (constitution), 4. Ens Spirituale (spirit/will), and 5. Ens Dei (God).</note> Regarding this, it must be noted that God has set before us punishment, an example, and a conscience within diseases, so that we may understand from them that all our affairs are worth nothing, and that we are not solidly grounded in any science, nor do we know the truth. Rather, our weakness shines through everywhere: and our power and knowledge are as nothing. But to come to the point: it must be known that God both grants health and sends disease, and at the same time shows the remedies owed to them. As for how these matters stand in Medicine: believe me, all things are established and predestined upon this point of our explanation. That point is *time*. Regarding this, pay attention: it is necessary that all diseases be healed in the favorable hour of time, and not according to our own will or thought. The meaning of this saying is this:

<margin>No physician knows the limit of health.</margin>
surely no physician can know the boundary of health. For this is in the hand of God. And every disease is a <term>purgatory</term> <note>original: "purgatorium"; Paracelsus views the suffering of illness as a temporary state of cleansing or trial, similar to the theological Purgatory, but experienced during life.</note>. Therefore, no physician can heal unless it happens that God remits this purgatory. Indeed, the physician must be one who works and labors within the predestination of the purgatory.

---

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Every disease is a purgatory.</margin>
**W**e have said that every disease is a purgatory. Every physician must therefore be carefully on guard not to rashly presume he knows the hour of either health or of his own medical operation. For all of this is placed in the hand of God. Unless predestination is such as you physicians presume it to be, then you will heal the sick person with no medicine. But if the hour of predestination is at hand, you restore the sick to health. Note this here: if a sick person is offered to you, God has sent him to you if he recovers under your care. If not, he was not sent to you by God. For if the time of the hour of redemption <note>meaning the time when the patient is "redeemed" or released from their suffering</note> is near, then at last God refers the sick person to the physician; but never before that time. And whatever arrives earlier has no foundation in this.

<margin>Unskilled physicians are the demons of the purgatory.</margin>
<margin>Whether a physician effects anything by his art.</margin>
**Therefore, unskilled physicians are the demons of the purgatory, sent to the sick by God. The wise physician belongs to those to whom God has brought the hour of health.** Then this also must be impressed upon you: that predestination can by no means be hindered, even if the physician is most noble and most skillful. That hour must be at hand which is the end of the purgatory. And to the one for whom a physician of happiness and health is not sent by God, no health is granted by God. Since God sends the physician to the sick in this way, now consider among yourselves whether the physician effects anything by the benefit of his art, or not. Think of it thus: that God created both the medicines for diseases and, besides these, the physician himself; but He delays these for the sick person until the established hour of time arrives. And only then does the course of both nature and art proceed. Never before that, unless the time has approached.

---

### CHAPTER IV.

**T**herefore you should have reflected and recalled that you profess yourselves to be Christians, above nature and set over it; but the power of your art is withdrawn from you (even if you sometimes walk in the right way) until the hour of time has arrived. For the hour of time is the hour of your operation: and not before, even if the hour of art were at hand. Since we testify to you that God is the cause of all diseases, accept it in this way: that He created equally what is against us and what is useful and beneficial, for the reason that we have our purgatory; just as we will inform you more at length concerning <term>purgatory</term>.

<margin>Why God does not take away diseases from us without medicine.</margin>
And although He, as the one who created diseases for us, could easily take them away from us without any medicine if the hour of time were at hand and the end of the purgatory were approaching; yet the reason why He does not do so is because He wishes to do nothing without men or their labor. If He performs miracles, He performs them humanly and through men. If He heals miraculously, He executes it through men. Thus He also accomplishes this very thing through physicians. But because there are two kinds of physicians—namely, those who heal miraculously and those who heal through remedies—distinguish them thus: He who believes, works through a miracle. But since belief <note>original: "credulitas"; Paracelsus uses this to mean active faith or religious conviction</note> is not so strong in everyone, and the hour of purgatory has passed, yet faith is not present: then the physician executes a miracle which God would perform wonderfully if belief flourished in the sick person; just as these things are more clearly explained in the 5th book, <term>On the Divine Care, or the Care of the Faithful</term> <note>original: "de cura Deifica vel fidelium"</note>. But so that we do not leave this question bare to you, for the sake of a richer understanding, turn your mind to the following explanation.

He argues that physicians act as divine instruments, and that even miraculous healing is channeled through human effort or faith.</summary>

# TREATISE V OF THE PARAMIRUM

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Why cures were successful in the time of Hippocrates.</margin>
**Y**ou must know, therefore, that in the times of Hippocrates, Rhazi, and Galen, treatments were very successful and fortunate. The reason is that the purgatories <note>The Latin *purgatoria* here carries a double meaning: both the medical act of "purging" the body of ill humors and the spiritual "purgatory" or cleansing of the soul through suffering.</note> in those centuries were small. But both now and hereafter, because evils grow stronger in heaps, treatments are rendered more and more unsuccessful every day. For this reason, there have never been worse doctors in the world than there are today. For the "purgatory" is too violent to be calmed by any doctor. Indeed, if the doctors of old were to return to us from the grave, their entire art would be blind and worth nothing. Even if this is true, a new punishment has also been added. Therefore, in this treatise, we employ a Christian style, by which we may be led to a true understanding: namely, that all diseases <margin>All diseases are scourges.</margin> are scourges, examples, and signs or warnings that God may take them away from us through faith—in a Christian manner, not through medicines in the pagan fashion, but in Christ. For the sick person who places his hope in medicine is hardly a Christian. But he who trusts God for the outcome is truly a Christian, for he commits to God the manner by which he may be healed, whether that happens miraculously through the saints, or through his own effort, or through doctors, or even through old women <term>Anus: elderly women, often implying folk-healers or midwives who used traditional herbal lore</term>. <margin>God is the supreme physician.</margin> You Christians ought to hold to this: that God must be regarded as the supreme physician. He is the most high—not infinite <note>Paracelsus likely means God's action in the physical world is specific and defined, rather than a vague, "infinite" abstraction.</note>—but the most powerful and mighty, without whom nothing happens. Pagans and infidels cry out to men for help. You, on the contrary, cry out to God; He will send you a healer at the opportune time, whether that be a saint, a physician, or someone else.

### CHAPTER VI.

**S**ince we have now demonstrated that it is God who grants both health and disease at the same time, we will not introduce the mention of recovering health in this place. For this is not as proper a place for that discussion as the fifth book of *Practice*. Rather, we will establish an explanation here of how <margin>How the Entity of God can inflict diseases.</margin> the Entity of God is powerful enough to afflict all men with diseases, beyond that which happens from the motion and order of nature, as we have taught concerning the four previously described Entities. We will prefigure this for you briefly in this way. You know that in this world, man is subject to God along with all other creatures. From this, therefore, you must confess that it is God who makes created things fortunate or unfortunate. Furthermore, take note that God holds a double punishment in His hand: one which concerns life, and the other which concerns death. The causes of these will be explained elsewhere. The punishment that follows death will be omitted here. That which is imposed during life belongs here. We shall say it this way: Remember that death flowed from sin because of one man <note>Adam</note>, who did not commit the sin himself <note>Paracelsus refers here to the "Great Judgment" of the heavens/stars influencing the Fall, a complex alchemical-theological view.</note>, but because of the great judgment of the heavens, just as we shall discuss death in the *Book of Death*. Furthermore, note that this cause, which pronounced the judgment of death upon us, does nothing further against us. It is the Creator who acts. Whatever does not side with the Adversary <note>The Devil</note>, He punishes—not because of the person's own sin, but at least as a sign. Also, so that those whom He considers His own may be distinguished; and these are subject to no physician. For God wants His own people to be marked with the sign of the Adversary <note>Meaning they suffer worldly afflictions like the "scourge" of disease as a test of faith.</note>. But there are others whom God affects with punishment out of their own right faith and petition. These are subject to the physician by this peculiar permission.

### CHAPTER VII.

**F**rom this you can gather that no medicine stands against death, but only against disease. The physician must have known this thoroughly. For no theologian will reveal this to the Physician. And although diseases are indeed produced from the four Entities, yet this is not a reason to fight against the will of God. At the very least, the hour and the time must be considered. Therefore, you must take diligent care here that you do not attempt to medicate in any way unless the hour of the harvest is at hand, in which either God or you may reap; all of which is explained more clearly in the *Book of Death*. <margin>How medicine and the sick relate to one another.</margin> How medicine and the sick relate to one another must be carefully noted by you physicians: because diseases leap upon us by divine command and from no other cause, as the *Archidoxis* <term>Archidoxis: one of Paracelsus's major works on the "mighty mysteries" of nature and alchemy</term> proves. Also, because natural medicines were similarly created from divine providence; and because, as was also said above, no sick person can be healed unless the hour of the harvest—that is, the divine command—is present, as predestination demonstrates. Here, then, how will Medicine fit into such things, so that a doctor can rightly profess himself to be a Physician? In this way, surely: he is the servant and minister of nature. But God is the Lord of nature. Thus, it follows further that the Physician can heal no one unless God <margin>The Physician heals no one unless God sends him.</margin> sends him to that place. So also note attentively that Hellebore <note>A potent and dangerous medicinal plant used as a purgative.</note> leads to vomiting. But that it should be useful when taken from just any doctor is a vain thought. The reason: it is not predestined for every doctor that the medicine given by him be effective for the health of the patient to whom it is given. For the art...

# ON THE DIVINE ENTITY

True medicine flows from God, as do the dosage and the practice, and the principles; then both the sick person is sent to Him <note>God</note>, and He to the sick person. And whatever city supports a good doctor who heals many: this city has reason to proclaim its good fortune more justly than one that supports a bad doctor. This we also understand regarding the holy doctors, whom we in no way exclude here.

## CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>
Why medicine and the doctor were created by God.
</margin>
**B**ut so that you may know the reason why God created both medicine and the doctor—though He Himself nonetheless heals, and works through the doctor, rather than healing by Himself without the doctor's help—consider this explanation: these are surely the secrets of God. He does not wish the sick person to know that God is the doctor; rather, He wishes that the art and practice may thus have their own progress. He wants man to perceive His help not only in miracles, but also to observe the same in God's creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to created things like herbs, minerals, and natural elements used in medicine.</note>, which heal through the supreme master of medicine <note>This refers to the skilled physician acting as God's instrument.</note>, and all this by His permission in its own time, as was also mentioned before.

<margin>
The causes of diseases cannot be investigated.
</margin>
Now furthermore, understand this also: the causes of diseases arising from the divine power—that is, from His Entity—cannot be investigated so as to know by whom or in what way they are inflicted, in the same way that this can be fundamentally known in the case of the four <term>Entities (Entia): The five fundamental origins of disease according to Paracelsus: astral, poisonous, natural, spiritual, and divine.</term>. An example of this is as if someone having cloth were to shape a tunic for himself according to his own will. So God also deals with us, in a way so secret that no doctor can perceive whether that sick person lies ill by divine power or not. For He so silently mixes His power and punishment with the four Entities that no one understands it to be anything other than one of those four Entities. And this is the very reason why some diseases of the four Entities cannot be cured by any help. For the "hour of the end" is not yet present; the time is not yet at hand, nor the count of days. They therefore continue and last until the hour of death, by which all diseases are ended. Where such a remarkable change occurs that no disease remains any longer, but it is changed just as white is changed into black. For as long as the disease lasts, there is no death. Let these things be said to you as a reminder of purgatory <note>original: "purgatorii." Paracelsus links the medical concept of "purging" the body to the spiritual "purgatory" or cleansing of the soul through suffering.</note> and the hour of the end, as befits Christians.

## Section I.

**J**ust as we discuss the Entity of God with you, so you ought to firmly decide for yourselves that it is the height of vanity if you place any trust in those arts in which you are thoroughly skilled. For to do that is to have acted like a pagan. You must always direct yourselves toward the Entity of God. And this is the Christian way, joined with successful outcomes. For a doctor who is not also a Christian makes the will of God (that is, predestination) of no account, as the *Archidoxis* <note>One of Paracelsus's major works on the "Arch-secrets" of nature and medicine.</note> will show you.

## Section II.

**B**ut if an objection could be raised against us concerning pagan doctors, whether they be Christians or infidels (for there is but one sect of all those who do not use faith), that they themselves heal the sick no less successfully than faithful doctors: this can neither break nor weigh down our Entity, for this reason. For if it is necessary for something to happen or to cease: then it must entirely be accomplished by those who either are able or are present there. The difference in this matter is this: the faithful man does not work against nature like the pagan. The pagan wants, and insists, that the medicine succeed or not, as if he were a kind of god. The faithful man, once he has taken care of the things pertaining to medicine, then, if it does not succeed, commits the matter to the hour and the time that will be pleasing to God. For medicine itself is the "plow" of doctors, which God has not forbidden; because private utility dominates, and the Public Good is nothing. Then He also makes the harvest difficult for the pious; all for the praise of His creation, and so that the virtues He created may shine forth—which is surely a cause more powerful than all those we established before, as the *Musalogium* <note>Likely a reference to a Paracelsian text on the spiritual or "musical" harmonies of the soul and body.</note> demonstrates.

## CONCLUSION.

->The aforementioned Parenthesis <note>A "parenthesis" refers to an explanatory digression inserted into the main text.</note> of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> regarding the Five Entities.<-

**A**fter we have shown you the Parenthesis which we inserted into the Prologue and the five books of practice, we shall now establish its end here. And just as you have understood the Parenthesis, so you have found that there are five Entities. These are very effective and powerful for introducing any diseases, even when each one is considered on its own. Next, however, the Parenthesis being finished, the work begins, which proceeds to be divided into five books, as the Prologue following the conclusion shows. Without these [Entities], you will be so occupied that you would not think the practice was established upon the diseases of only one origin; but rather in five...

He concludes his introduction to the Five Entities, emphasizing that faithful physicians must trust divine timing ("the hour") rather than just their own skills.</summary>

know that the ways proposed are divided, as was also said above. Indeed, if you doctors of the <term>Natural Entity (Ens Naturale)</term><note>The Natural Entity refers to diseases arising from the physical makeup of the body and its environment, rather than spiritual or divine causes.</note> along with your accomplice astronomers perhaps do not indulge us, it will move us not at all, nor will the Theological writings themselves. In these two parts, it befits a wise man to be thoroughly refined and polished: namely, that he be an artist <note>In this context, "artist" (artifex) refers to a skilled practitioner or craftsman of medicine.</note>, and not a purple-clad fantasist.

# PROLOGUE TO THE FIVE BOOKS
## OF THE PRACTICE OF THE PARAMIRUM
### OF THEOPHRASTUS OF HOHENHEIM begins.

->To the fair and impartial Reader, Greetings.<-

<margin>The books of Paracelsian Practice were never found.</margin>
*KIND Reader, since Theophrastus Paracelsus, in the short prologues of this Paramirum, and especially in the preceding conclusion, expressly and clearly promises that he wishes to describe five books of practice pertaining to this Paramirum, to be placed after the parenthesis: a suspicion could arise in your mind as if those books were suppressed by the envy of certain people, since they are entirely missing here, and do not follow the finished medical parenthesis according to the author’s promise. For this reason, it seemed especially necessary to preface a few things, and to inform you, the suspicious reader, that those five practical books were never found with these theoretical ones. For in those papers in which the author had designated this Theory, he wrote no more, but ended it with this title "Prologue to the five books of practice," so that he left nearly three quarto sheets of paper blank: as is evident from the author's own autograph <note>An "autograph" is a manuscript written in the author's own hand.</note>, which is kept with the distinguished master Dr. Johann Homel II in the Styrian town of Pettau <note>Modern-day Ptuj, Slovenia.</note>. Whether Paracelsus actually recorded and completed that practice in another separate book is known to no one. He had this very familiar habit of least of all binding related and akin books into one work. Whence it can easily happen that those books lie hidden and stored in another place, as yet unexplored. I, however, for all I know, have never found anything from anyone who has seen those five practical books or knows where they are stored. Meanwhile, if God and Fate favor us at some time, so that they may be unearthed somewhere and come to our hands: they will by no means be withheld from the public literary world. In the meantime, let us be content to use and enjoy these things which fortune has offered us. For I myself, along with many others, grieve and complain that the others are missing. For there is no doubt that Paracelsus would have described said five modes of healing all diseases solidly and most skillfully, namely by what method any disease can and should be healed industriously: either according to the Natural or rational method, or according to experience from the Specific Form of things, or through Characters and Images, or Spiritually, or finally through the Christian faith. Therefore, what is missing here, the diligent reader will be able to collect and complete from other books of Paracelsus, in which he has shown such cures in detail and scattered throughout.*

*The other Paramirum, which now follows, is entirely different from the aforementioned, nor does it look to the preceding ones, and was arranged in another way by the author himself, just as he did in several other books: some of which exist described by him a second and third time in different arrangements. To the following Paramirum, however, these books are numbered:*

On the causes and origin of diseases from the three first substances <note>The "Three Primes" (Tria Prima): Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>. Book one and two.
On the causes and origin of diseases from **Tartar** <note>Tartar refers to stony or calcified deposits in the body, which Paracelsus believed caused many illnesses.</note>, six Treatises, which are held as the third book of the Paramirum.
On the cause and origin of diseases of the **womb**. Book Four.
The books on the cause and origin of **invisible diseases** are held as the fifth part or book.

# THE PARAMIRUM WORK
## OF AUREOLUS THEOPHRASTUS BOMBAST OF HOHENHEIM, SWISS HERMIT, called Paracelsus the Great.

->*Written in honor of the distinguished and excellent Joachim von Watt, Doctor and Consul at St. Gallen.*<- <note>Joachim von Watt (1484–1551), also known as Vadianus, was a celebrated Swiss humanist, physician, and politician who led the Reformation in St. Gallen.</note>

### BOOK I.

<margin>Praise of Joachim von Watt.</margin>
Since nothing can be truly and solidly understood without a knowledge of principles and precepts, it is only right, distinguished sir, that this work, the *Paramirum*, should be inscribed to you above all others. You, Master Doctor Joachim von Watt, promote every path leading toward the truth more than any other, and uniquely support those who walk and cultivate those paths. It is right, I say, that I consecrate this work to you before all others because of the strange errors that have arisen in the medical art. Among all the citizens of our Swiss fatherland, you are its most excellent practitioner; you rightly hold the prize of praise, such that I appoint you as the judge over this work of mine before all others. For I know you to be a fair critic, and I hope you will be so here: one who is not ashamed to reject recognized errors and to agree with the shining truth. This was my reason for looking to you first. And so that I might not spend the time I pass in the city of St. Gallen in vain, I chose to awaken your reputation and your knowledge and wisdom in natural things to judge this work, so that the perpetual memory of both of us might flourish among all those who admire medicine. For you have been found to be not only a preserver and a primary member in receiving and propagating the truth that looks toward eternity, but you also shine as a generous steward and administrator of the things of the body, in which that eternal spirit dwells. Therefore, by every right, it was fitting for me to dedicate this *Paramirum*, my work, to you, which begins thus:

<margin>Man consists of three substances.</margin>
First of all, the Physician ought to know that man can consist of <term>three substances</term><note>These are the "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. Paracelsus believed these were the fundamental building blocks of all matter, representing different states of being (solidity, combustibility, and volatility).</note>. For although he was created from nothing, he was nonetheless made into "something." This "something" is divided into three. These three constitute the whole man, and they are the man himself; man is the same as those three, from which and in which he possesses all his things—both good and bad—as far as the physical body is concerned. From this it follows that the doctor must know their division and recognize their composition, preservation, and dissolution. For in these three consists the whole, the half, and the smallest part of both health and sickness. Thus, here may be found how much and how great the health is, and what weight of disease exists. For the doctor must not deny that sickness consists in <term>weight, number, and measure</term><note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom (11:20): "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight." Paracelsus applies this theological concept to the physical and chemical reality of the body.</note>. <margin>In what sickness consists.</margin> If it consists in this way, then above all else, the foundation of these things, from which they manifest themselves, must be established. And this is the most necessary thing of all: that it be properly examined at the very beginning. According to these things, death is also found in that state if life is cut off from those three; yet their binding together is life and the man himself. Thus, from those three substances proceed all causes, origins, and understandings of diseases; furthermore, also the signs and properties, and whatever else the doctor needs to know. Therefore, it is necessary that these three be most correctly understood by the doctor and weighed according to all their properties—what they are like and how they make people healthy or sick. For the science of how a man is healthy and how he is or becomes sick is one and the same. Just as sickness arises from health, so health comes from sickness. Therefore, not only must the origins of diseases be known, but also the restorations of health. However, ignorant doctors have slipped into the light of nature and obscured it; leaving these three substances of nature unexplored, they have adopted a foreign foundation, which their own brains supplied to them through fantasies without any...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "naturæ" (of nature) indicates the next page begins with a discussion of the "light of nature."</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus dedicates the "Paramirum" to the scholar Joachim von Watt and introduces his foundational theory: the human body is composed of three primary substances, and all health and disease must be understood through their balance and measure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book I of the Paramirum. Paracelsus moves from his dedication to Joachim von Watt into the philosophical core of his medical theory, emphasizing that true medical knowledge comes from the "Light of Nature" and the transformative power of fire (alchemy) rather than abstract reasoning.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>
<header>PARAMIRUM BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN.</header>

<margin>The Light of Nature.</margin>
...by the testimony of the light of nature. Nor did those men consider that no physician can have a known foundation, either of diseases or of man, unless he has received enough testimony from the light of nature. That light is the "great world" <note>The macrocosm—the universe—which Paracelsus believes must be studied to understand the "little world" of the human body.</note>. For just as gold is tested seven times through fire: so also seven times and more the physician ought to be tested through fire—that is, the fire tests these three substances <note>The *Tria Prima*: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which Paracelsus viewed as the fundamental components of all matter.</note>, which it presents as pure and naked, clean and simple. This is because, since fire is not applied, nothing of proven value is present. 

<margin>Fire tests all things.</margin>
Fire tests all things: that is, if the impure is separated, the three pure substances are presented. Thus also the Physician is tested: not that he himself should be burned, but that his art, theory, and practice should be initiated or "baptized" in the fire. For these things do not reveal themselves before the eyes of the unlearned <note>original: *rusticorum*, literally "peasants" or "rustics," used here to mean those without philosophical insight.</note>, nor are they so easily grasped. Therefore fire is that which brings forth what is obscure and drags it into the sunlight. And in such a way the science of medicine ought to be presented.

<margin>Medicine consists through fire.</margin>
Now it follows, because God created medicine, therefore it consists through fire. So also He created the physician, so that he might be born from the fire. Now indeed the physician is from medicine, not from himself; therefore it is necessary that he undergo the examination of nature, which nature is the world itself and all its capacity. And what nature itself teaches him, he ought to refer to his own wisdom, yet seeking nothing in his own wisdom, but in the light of nature alone; and afterward, he should store that doctrine in the storehouse of memory. Now indeed the Physician is visible through his works; nature itself is also manifest, with nothing hidden. 

<margin>Fire makes the physician and is the treasure of medicine.</margin>
The causes of health and sickness must also be so conspicuous, and nothing should lie hidden in obscurity. Therefore fire is named first, in which those things that were hidden are dissolved, so that they may become conspicuous. From this sight, the science of medicine is born. For so it testifies. Because the physician is a physician from medicine, and not without it: let him be of it, not against it; then there is a need that he consider that and study in that which constitutes him, not in that which he promises from himself. Thus in the nature of Medicine is placed wisdom, art, Theory, Practice, etc. These are not situated in the physician himself. By which the error is abundantly refuted—whatever is not found in nature, but is established and proposed from prejudice alone. For the teacher is in the fire, not in the disciple himself. But this is still much more intelligible: In man there is nothing inside that makes him a physician, even if he has a brilliant talent in himself. 

For in him there is no art: but he exists as a vacuum like an empty chest, skillfully made. Yet it is suitable for storing those things which are brought into it, namely the treasures of our hands. So therefore that brilliant talent is without all experience, art, and medical science. But what we learn and experience, these things we preserve in it, and bring back out at the proper time. 

<margin>The consideration of the Physician.</margin>
But now contemplate two examples, so that you might more easily understand the physician. The first exists such: The Glassmaker—from whom did he receive his art? Not from himself, certainly: because his own reason could not penetrate it. But after he took the subjects of the art and threw them into the fire: then at last the light of nature showed him the glass. This art is preserved in this chest. The reasoning for the physician is the same. It follows then to the second example. The Carpenter <note>original: *tignarius*</note>, who builds a house, can achieve this art from the storehouse of his wisdom if he has an ax and wood ready. But it is not the same for the Physician. For even if he has both the medicines and the patient, he nonetheless lacks the science and the knowledge of things. If, however, he has this ax and wood, then he might indeed be a Physician. Therefore it is necessary that he first be a craftsman who can prepare the ax. Furthermore, his own talent helps him to learn to use them. 

<margin>The goodness of talent is the small chest of medicines. Fire teaches medicine.</margin>
In the same way, the brilliance of talent is the small chest of medicines and of science itself. But the treasure to be stored in it comes forth from the fire. Therefore just as the glassmaker learned the art of making glass from fire, when before he did not know what he was doing, but had stored away the discovered art: so likewise fire teaches the science and art of medicine. And this is the testing of the physician. This is true: the unskilled part (that is, those who are not born from nature) do not wish to acknowledge their teacher, but hold their own reason as medical wisdom and rely upon it. Which must rightly be said to have built on sand. Whatever fire teaches, that cannot be understood or proven without fire. 

<margin>Wisdom is twofold: of experience and of industry.</margin>
For wisdom is twofold: one, which we draw from experience. The other, which we gather from our own industry. The wisdom of experience is again twofold: one is the foundation and master of the physician. The other is his error and seduction. The first is that which he receives from the fire, while he practices the Vulcanian art <note>The "Vulcanian art" refers to alchemy, named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and smithing.</note> in transmutation, fixation, exaltation, and reduction.

<margin>The preparation of experience.</margin>

Paracelsus asserts that a physician's talent is merely a container that must be filled with knowledge gained from nature and "Vulcanian" (alchemical) practice.</summary>

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>II.</margin>
...reduction and perfection, and the other works annexed to these. In this experience, those three substances are tracked down—to find out what the nature, property, or composition is of whatever is contained in all things throughout the whole world. The other way, however, is that which attains something by chance, without the aforementioned experience. In that way, what is found to be right once is not confirmed to be always right, such that one could trust or stand upon it. This building lacks a foundation; it is a structure built upon error, glossed over with fictitious sophistry. For such a person would think to himself: who grants you this experiment? Surely this one. Who gave it to him? Another, and so on back to the very first, from whom all received it: then the matter returns to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here Paracelsus uses the name to represent the alchemist/chemist who works with the furnace to reveal the hidden nature of matter.</note> and the spagyrist <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe an alchemist who "separates and recombines" substances to create medicine.</note>. Thus you should know that we ought not to become learned in medicine from this kind of hearing or reading, but by the same method the first man taught. Even so should we. Let him who taught the first, teach us as well. To that end, <margin>Our teacher is Vulcan.</margin> the nature of Vulcan and our own nature becomes the teacher. For if someone says: *Do this, and you will be safe*: then certainly necessity demands that you know who said that. Then the matter returns to him who is health <note>original: *salus*, meaning both "health" and "salvation."</note> itself. So in this business too: let us penetrate to Medicine itself, that is, into nature; otherwise, we will by no means be Physicians. For if I want the foundation to stand: I must speak and teach not about invisible things, but about entirely visible things. For it is of great account to a Physician that we have had God moving before our eyes visibly and palpably, so that we have heard our Savior himself, the foundation of all truth. Yet Medicine itself stands before us much more conspicuously and visibly: which we ought to grasp visibly, not through a dream—palpably, not in shadow. Truly, all these things were believed to be unobservable by those who lacked the "eyes of fire." From which then emerged that total destruction <note>original: *panolethria* (Greek), meaning complete ruin or a "universal plague" of ignorance; Paracelsus uses it to describe the collapse of true medical knowledge.</note> upon which even that wandering and unstable medicine is established. <margin>The four humors.</margin> It is hard to believe that four humors are stored in man according to their explanations. The matter rests on faith alone. But medicine ought to be established not in faith, but in the eyes. Nothing persists in faith except diseases of the soul and eternal salvation. On the contrary, all medicine of the body stands as something visible, without any faith. It is the same with this "total destruction" as it is with erroneous religions: where not everyone who says, *Lord, Lord*, will be heard immediately. That is, if you are not a Physician, yet you affect its use: if, offering your experiment, you say, *do this, do this*: then it turns out badly again. For medicine does not hear you: nor are you the true shepherd of these sheep. Yet this answers you: <margin>Who is a Physician.</margin> *Not you: the sick have need of a physician* <note>A reference to Matthew 9:12.</note>, whom they themselves also know. For he was created for their sake. Therefore, only he who is called is a Physician: for him, medicine is produced from the earth: it knows him, extols him, and helps him. Therefore, this foundation remains: the three substances are to be <margin>Substances must be known entirely.</margin> known and explored by us: and that not from our own brains, nor from hearing, but from the experience of Nature's dissolution, and the investigation of those properties. For man is taught by the "great world" <note>The macrocosm or universe.</note>, not by man. This is the concordance that makes a physician whole: if he has known the world, and from it, man—who are one thing, not two. I leave the rest to experience.

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>The three substances of the body: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt.</margin> There are three substances that bestow its own body upon everything: that is, every single body consists of three things. The names of these things are *Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt*. If these three are compounded, then they are called a "body": nor is anything added to them except life and what coheres with it. Thus, if you take a certain body in your hands, you then invisibly have three substances under one appearance or form. We must discuss these three. For here three substances exist under one form, which give and make all health. For if you hold wood in your hands, then by the judgment of your eyes you have at least one body. And knowing this is of no use to you. The rustics <note>Paracelsus uses "rustic" (*rusticus*) to refer to those who see only the surface of things without understanding the underlying chemical/spiritual reality.</note> know and see the same. You must descend and penetrate so far as to know that you are pressing in your hands Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. If you perceive these three things by <margin>The eyes of the physician.</margin> sight, touch, and feel—each one separated from the other—then at last you have obtained those eyes with which a Physician ought to see. These eyes must be as sharp in seeing through these three as the rustic certainly sees raw wood. Let this example serve you so that you may know man himself also in these three, no less than the wood itself: that is, that you hold man himself to be formed in a similar way. If you see his bones, you see like a rustic. But if you hold his Sulfur separately, his Mercury separately, and his Salt separately, then you see through to what the bone is, and if it is sick, what defect it has, from what cause, and...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine is found through alchemical experience (fire/Vulcan) and the observation of nature's visible structures rather than abstract faith or the traditional theory of the four humors. He introduces the "Tria Prima"—Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt—as the three fundamental substances that compose all physical matter, including the human body.</summary>

...and how it suffers. Thus, the outward appearance belongs to the rustics <note>Paracelsus uses "rustics" to refer to the unlearned or laypeople who only see the surface of things.</note>; the contemplation of the internal parts, this is the secret that belongs to Physicians. Now, if it is necessary for these things to be made visible—and without this visibility medicine remains crippled—then indeed nature must be led to the point where she strips herself bare and reveals herself. Therefore, observe into what ultimate matter those things pass, and into how many kinds. You will surely find those three substances separated from each other in just as many kinds. The rustic does not care for this; yet the Physician cares. The mere experimenter <note>One who tries remedies by trial and error without understanding their underlying nature.</note> also neglects it, but not the Physician. The vagabond <note>original: "erro." Referring to an unstable person or a medical quack who wanders without a foundation.</note> makes nothing of this; yet the Physician values it most highly. For before all else, those three substances and all their properties in the Great World <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe at large.</note> must be known. Then he will find the same and similar things in man as well. Now, he understands what he has in his hands, and recognizes what he governs.

<margin>Wood possesses these three substances.</margin>
Therefore, so that you may know these things more clearly, begin with wood. It is a body in itself. Let it be burned. That which burns is sulfur; that which smokes is Mercury. The ash that remains is Salt. The burning itself confuses the understanding of the rustic. But to the Physician, it provides the beginning and the path to medical eyes. Thus, three things are found here—neither more, nor fewer—with each one separated from the other. Furthermore, it must be noted concerning these three,

<margin>All things possess the substances of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt in an equal manner.</margin>
that all things possess them in an equal manner. Even if they are not immediately visible to the eyes in one way, they are nonetheless revealed through art <note>The "art" here is alchemy, specifically the process of separation.</note>, which brings them to that point and places them before the eyes. That which burns is sulfur. Besides sulfur, nothing blazes. That which smokes is Mercury. Nothing is sublimated <note>Turned into vapor or "lifted up" by heat.</note> except Mercury alone. That which turns to ash is Salt. Nothing turns to ash unless it be salt. That which becomes ash is the substance—that is, the part from which the wood is constituted. And although it is the ultimate matter, not the first matter <note>Materia prima: the fundamental, unformed substance of the universe.</note>, it nonetheless bears witness to the first matter (of which it is the ultimate state) while it is joined to the living body. Although in a living body nothing at all appears except the "rustic spectacle" [the outward appearance], separation nonetheless reveals the substances. I am not speaking here of the first matter, since I am treating Medicine, not Philosophy. Just as we have reviewed concerning salt, so know regarding smoke: that it bears witness to Mercury, which is lifted up and sublimated by fire. And although its first matter is not visible here, the ultimate matter of the first is nonetheless visible. Thus, this Mercury is the second substance of the thing. Likewise, that which burns and appears bright or fiery to the eyes, that is sulfur. It is consumed because it is volatile. Now this which is fire is itself surely the third substance, which constitutes the whole body.

<margin>Man is composed of salt, sulfur, and Mercury.</margin>
From these things a Theory must now be inaugurated: what Mercury, what sulfur, and what salt may be—whether in wood or in other things—so that they may thus be compared with the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," meaning Man, who is a miniature reflection of the whole universe.</note>. Now you have it concerning man: his body is nothing besides sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. In these three things his health is placed, as well as sickness and whatever is connected to them. And just as these are only three, so they alone become the causes of all diseases—not the four much-celebrated humors <note>The traditional medical theory that health depends on four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Paracelsus famously rejected this Galenic system.</note>, qualities, or other similar things. However, although not all things burn (such as stones), alchemy nonetheless demonstrates that both these, and metals, and all other things believed to be incombustible, can be made flammable. Even if many things are not sublimated, nonetheless art again proves they can be brought to that point. The same things are understood regarding salt. For what is not evident to the eyes of rustics is plain in the art—that is, in the art of separation—from which the thing is afterwards placed before the eyes. The aforementioned art bestows the knowledge of these things: that the condition of all things is no different.

<margin>The nature of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</margin>
Now if we wish to speak of the properties and nature of these three, the matter must be judged so: that Nature is situated either in Mercury, or Sulfur, or Salt, whether it be good or bad, healthy or sick. For each and every substance has its own nature. Now, if a meeting into one body occurs, then the natures come forth under one form; nonetheless, they ought to be attributed to their own substance and not to the whole in common. For the natures are good. Now, if they are not present, disease is present. From this, therefore, you can know what departs from the substance: for the withdrawal of one is the arrival of another. As many diseases (as many natures), so many are the numbers of diseases. Speaking of these natures, we have need of knowledge of the first matter. Since indeed the first matter of the world was the *FIAT* <note>original: "FIAT" (Latin for 'let it be done'). The divine command of creation from the Book of Genesis.</note>, who will attempt to explain how this "let it be" happened? Nonetheless, we have some knowledge of this through the fire of Vulcan <note>Alchemical fire.</note>, by which we can declare those first three: namely by sulfur, because they agree; by Mercury, because they are also similar; by Salt, because they are of one operation. But although these things are in the Great World, nonetheless they are to be understood similarly concerning the Small World: yet with this distinction, because man has his own first matter in the *Limbus* <note>A Paracelsian term for the primordial "matrix" or "chaos" from which man was created.</note>, which—

He argues that these three, rather than the traditional four humors, are the true causes of health and disease in both the Macrocosm and the human Microcosm.</summary>

<page-num>35</page-num>

-># ON THE THREE PRIMARY SUBSTANCES<-

<margin>
All diseases consist in the three substances.
</margin>

Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt are [the essence] of the four elements, gathered together into one human being. Therefore, the Physician must know that all diseases consist in these three substances, and not in the four elements <note>Paracelsus is famously rejecting the traditional Galenic theory that diseases are caused by an imbalance of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) or their corresponding humors.</note>. As for what power the elements themselves have, or what they are, that does not concern medicine because of the humors. For they are the matrices <note>In Paracelsian thought, a 'matrix' is a womb or source where things are formed and nurtured.</note>. In what way this is so, a specific chapter indicates. Therefore, the Physician alone must have these three things known and explored. For in these, the causes of all diseases lie hidden.

Now, since a man cannot see these things in himself as long as he enjoys life, but only after destruction <note>Referring to the death or chemical breakdown of the body.</note>, he must therefore fix his mind on those things that are dissolved. For these substances consist in the body in a precious and adorned state as long as they live and are healthy. Sulfur, Mercury, or Salt do not fall ill as long as they "live" [remain in their vital state], but only when they are dissolved. Therefore, the mind must rightly be focused on their separation.

<margin>
Life hides the three substances.
</margin>

Look at a ruby <note>original: "carbunculum." While this can refer to an inflammatory tumor, Paracelsus uses it here as an example of a beautiful mineral to illustrate alchemical composition.</note>, most beautiful and pleasant, of wonderful virtue and nature. Yet it is nothing else but Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. If it were separated, then these things are detected; namely, something formless, if it were deprived of its life <note>Paracelsus believed even minerals possessed a form of "life" or vital force that held their chemical components together in a specific form.</note>. Attribute it to life, then, that you do not see these things. For life is that veil which hides these substances. Likewise, look at a man: how beautiful and graceful he is if he lives; if he dies, how great a destruction occurs. Or if even one limb dies in him, how clearly and sensibly it passes into these three substances. That which is such through death is also such through life, but more ornate, more refined. So also the Cedar tree: as long as it lives, it stands beautiful. But when cast into the fire, then what its life concealed is revealed through it. And this is the truth of all things. I wish all these things, which could be demonstrated in many ways, to be understood only for the sake of their principles, from which diseases are born. For if these three are one and not separated, then health is well. If indeed they are dissolved from each other—that is, separated and segregated—then one putrefies, another burns up [Sulfur], the third vanishes by another way [Mercury]: and these are the true principles of diseases. For as long as the body remains one, diseases are absent. But if, on the contrary, the body is dissipated, then that finally comes forth which the Physician needs to know. And just as if twenty men were in one alliance, you would know them all as a group; but if they are separated, you would say they are separated in this or that way, noting from them what you recognize in each. So here also you must know all things. In separation, you see more exactly what has been separated. Unless this happens, what else remains but the principle of death—that is, the destruction of the entire kingdom?

Now, so that you may understand the argument at the foundation of this chapter, know this: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt are the three substances mentioned, but hidden by the presence of life. In the separation of life, they are uncovered and manifested. From which you will now understand both their genera and species, so that all have now been named. And if one, two, or more diseases occur, you can say: "This is the disease, and this is what excited it." And as was the example of the alliance of unity, constituted of many parts: if it is broken, then you say, "This man or that man did it, through this or that way." You do not say "cholera, melancholy, or phlegm" <note>original: "cholera, melancholia, phlegma." These are the traditional Galenic humors. Paracelsus argues that naming the chemical "man" or substance responsible is more accurate.</note> did it, but rather you assert, "this man did it." So you must understand the same thing here. For if it is said, "this [substance] did it," that is said more correctly than "cholera did it." For a disease, in all its parts, can be compared to nothing more fittingly than to a man. And let this be said to you, Physicians: the hinge of the matter is this, that the thing which is a disease should be called a "man," with all the properties belonging to a man.

<margin>
A disease should be called by the name of a man.
</margin>

Thus you embrace the three elements, the three substances, the four stars, the four lands, the four waters, the four fires, the four airs, and all the conditions, manners, properties, and natures of a man, without which there is no disease. You indeed forgot these when you wrote that diseases arise from the four humors—which never had any affinity with the elements or the "four and three" things. It is right to speak with that property, so that all "manly" natures are found in the disease, and it is named a "man," as one who is fashioned from the perfect *limbus* <note>original: "limbo." In Paracelsian philosophy, the *Limbus* is the primordial "chaos" or "extract" from which all things, including man (the Microcosm), were created.</note>, just like the diseases themselves.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
Three humors.
</margin>

**B**ut these things require a more detailed explanation: because diseases are fashioned in this way, and they must be understood "manfully" <note>Paracelsus uses "viriliter" (manfully/as a man) to suggest that a disease has its own individual character, anatomy, and life-cycle, much like a human being.</note>. The matter stands thus: Sulfur is a humor. Mercury is a humor. Salt is a humor. Thus there are three of them. These three humors are bodies. In this place, "body" is humor, not a foreign thing. It is the body itself that the Physician must treat. And though you may wish to say that this is the cause which [brings] disease...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that all diseases are rooted in the Tria Prima (Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt) rather than the four Galenic humors. He explains that life acts as a veil hiding these substances, which only become visible through "separation" (death or fire), and asserts that a disease should be treated as a complete, individual entity or "man."</summary>

<page-num>36</page-num>
->### PARAMIRUM BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES<-

<margin>Humor produces no disease.</margin>
...that [humor] should give birth to disease: this we will by no means concede. For humor produces no disease. That which produces disease is something else: namely, the Substantiated Being <note>original: "Ens substantiate." This refers to the actual essential reality or "being" of a thing, rather than its outward appearance or secondary qualities.</note>. Now it is necessary that whatever stirs up diseases must be masculine or virile—that is, astral—originating from the whole limbus <note>The "limbus" in Paracelsian thought is the primordial chaos or the great reservoir of matter from which all things were created.</note>; yet humor, as it is commonly understood, has nothing of the stars within itself. Therefore, it cannot give birth to diseases. For this reason, a disease ought rightly to be called "virile," because of the masculine nature which creates and imprints it <note>In this context, "masculine" or "virile" refers to the active, formative, and energetic principle, while the "humor" is the passive material.</note>. Now, pay attention to what those three things are which are called the causes and progenitors of diseases here.

<margin>The power of Sulfur.</margin>
The first is <term>Sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the principle of combustibility, heat, and growth.</note>. Judge its power in this way: it never proceeds toward its own evil by itself unless it is Astral—that is, unless a spark of fire is thrown into it. For then, awakened by the spark, it flourishes. For is not burning a virile act, or a virile operation? Without this, nothing happens. Therefore, if any disease is declared to be from sulfur, then first of all that sulfur must be named according to its specific type; next, its masculine operation must be named, and who it was that ignited it.

<margin>Species of Sulfurs.</margin>
There are many kinds of Sulfurs: <term>Resin</term>, <term>gum</term>, <term>Botin</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for turpentine or coniferous balsam.</note>, <term>Lard</term>, <term>fat</term>, <term>butter</term>, <term>oil</term>, <term>burning wine</term> <note>original: "vinum ardens," referring to distilled alcohol.</note>, etc. There are also some sulfurs of wood; some of animals; others of men; some of metals, such as <term>oil of gold</term>, <term>Luna</term> (silver), <term>Mars</term> (iron), etc. Some are of stones, such as <term>liquor of Marble</term>, <term>Alabaster</term>, etc. Some are feminine, and some belong to all other things, all designated by their own peculiar names; and afterward, the fire falling into them (which alone is the "star") brings its own name. Now this operation is the "sinning matter" <note>original: "materia peccans," a traditional medical term for the material cause of a disease.</note> on the one hand.

<margin>The power of Salt.</margin>
Furthermore, concerning salt, it must be known that it exists by itself as a material humor, which does not itself bring on disease unless its "star" is joined to it. Truly, its star is its "resolution" <note>The process of dissolving or breaking down a solid into a liquid state.</note>, which makes it masculine. For it shows itself no less tumultuously than <term>spirit of Vitriol</term> <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>, <term>Tartar</term>, <term>Alum</term>, <term>Nitre</term> (saltpeter), etc., if it is resolved. But how could such a nature be sent into humors without a "star"? About this, all physicians everywhere have remained silent. And even if they had never committed any other error than omitting the "star" in all causes and cures, it would certainly be abundantly clear from that one fact that they have built upon moss and sand.

<margin>Species of salts.</margin>
Know, therefore, that there are many salts. Some are <term>calces</term> <note>Powders produced by roasting or calcining a mineral.</note>; some are ashes; some are <term>Arsenical</term>; some are <term>Antimonial</term>; some are <term>Marcasitical</term> <note>Derived from marcasite or iron pyrites.</note>, and other similar things. From all these are produced and born (just as the "body" of the salt is) peculiar diseases, which then also take on the private name and nature of each.

<margin>The power and authority of Mercury.</margin>
Understand the same regarding <term>Mercury</term> <note>The principle of liquidity, volatility, and transformation.</note>. It is not virile by itself unless the "star of the Sun" exalts it. Otherwise, it does not ascend. Indeed, its preparations are many, but its body is only one. Yet its body is not like sulfur or salt, which have many bodies from which they return various salts and sulfurs. Here there is only a single body, which the "star" itself nevertheless changes in various ways and into various natures. From this, many diseases are born from the same source. Therefore, its masculine nature is from the star, by which it is led into diseases. If all diseases are contained in these three, under their own name and title, know then: that which is sulfurous must be reduced to sulfur so that it may burn. And that which is <term>Mercurial</term> should be reduced to sublimation, if it is suited for it. And that which is from salt should be reduced to salt, as much as belongs to it. Here, therefore, are contained the general causes of diseases, as we have categorized above.

<margin>General causes of diseases.</margin>
In these things, therefore, consists what we said before: namely, that man is placed in three things, and these three have a middle body, that is, a living body. For before this life is the <term>first matter</term> (*prima materia*); after this life is the <term>final matter</term> (*materia ultima*). And this is a certain "middle" between the first and the last; and it is for the sake of this very thing that the Physician and medicine were created. Furthermore, although the "middle body" is the head [the primary focus], it is not itself the subject; rather, only these three substances are, if one sets aside the life, essence, and nature, to which we have nothing to add or take away. Now, as for what exists as our subject, it is broken within itself in three ways.

<margin>The ways in which our subject is broken.</margin>
First, by itself. If this happens, then life casts itself down. For the principle of life is like that of peace. Where there is peace, there is concord. And as soon as concord is dissolved, peace also perishes. The same is true of life. If those three substances do not wish to remain undivided among themselves, then life flies away, leaving the body lifeless and dissolved. *Secondly*, if it is dissolved by violence—either in birth, or in upbringing, or by our own will, by which we invite and lead the stars against us, not unlike a city that provokes its own Lord onto its neck. *Thirdly*: if it neither dissolves nor separates itself, but remains united, and we do not cause it by external force, then the third way is at hand: namely, the *End*. Thus all things have their end; and though they may be the best, strongest, and most beautiful, in time they all obtain their...

<meta>The catchword "tur" at the bottom refers to the continuation of the word "fortiuntur" (they obtain/achieve) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases are caused by the active "astral" force within Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury, rather than by passive humors. He describes how these three substances define the living body and how their harmony or discord determines health, life, and death.</summary>

->## ON THE FIRST THREE SUBSTANCES<-

...to this end, man himself is also devoted: he will never leap over the number of years [allotted to him].

<margin>Why such various species of things were created.</margin>
Next, the cause must be weighed: why, indeed, were three things created instead of one, and why are there so many and such various species of them, which are nearly infinite? For there are so many species that the resin of Rhaetia <note>A Roman province in the central Alps.</note> is not the same as that of Noricum <note>A region roughly corresponding to modern Austria.</note>; nor is the almond oil of Naples the same as that found near Lake Como. So also, those things in the mountains differ from those born in the plains; which I do not wish to describe at greater length here. The cause of this multiplicity and variety is this: because Christ said, *every kingdom divided against itself will perish* <note>original: "omne regnum in se diuisum, peribit." Matthew 12:25.</note>. Therefore, if things are destined to perish, it is necessary for internal wars to be stirred up within their own members, and thus the body is dissolved and killed; and this happens in a great many ways. For the species [of destruction] are unsearchable. This is the foundation of diseases—not the humors. Thus, there are also various medicines, and for that reason, various destructions. Medicine itself is fleeting; it is born with man and dies with him. For these are the "Platonic Years" <note>A reference to the "Great Year," a cosmic cycle after which the celestial bodies return to their original positions; here used to mean a cycle of renewal.</note> in which all things are renewed. Arnold <note>Likely Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> handed down a few things regarding this, as arguments of that understanding, but he slips away from the purpose too quickly. He who knows the heads of the kingdom’s destruction is fit to be admitted to the knowledge of my demonstrated foundation. As a conclusion to this, so that all diseases may be known, there will follow Three Books regarding the three established points: in which those diseases—which are signified and occur through themselves, through us, and through the end of time—will be explained, along with how they come to be.

<margin>What a physician requires to know man and his diseases.</margin>
Regarding such matters, it is so arranged that if a physician wishes to know man and perceive his diseases, he must have perceived the diseases of all things which nature suffers in the "Great World" <note>The Macrocosm (the universe) as opposed to the Microcosm (man).</note>. For nature suffers so that we may see it: it suffers one thing in this genus, another in that; but in man, it suffers all things. For if man was truly fashioned out of the *limbus* <note>The primordial "chaos" or raw material of creation.</note>, he was certainly fashioned with this end: that he should carry and bear all his own goods and evils with him. Therefore, a middle path was established by God, lest we follow those two [extremes], according to that measure and order prefigured from the beginning. Since these things are external, the physician must also learn them externally, and find the correspondences in preparing and separating diseases from visible things. He must reduce those bodies through the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>Alchemy, specifically the process of separating (Greek: *span*) and recombining (*ageirein*) substances to find their essence.</note> into their "ultimate matter"; then he will find which substance gives birth to the disease.

---

<margin>To what extent Arab and foreign physicians are to be believed.</margin>
If he has reduced all these things, then he has the knowledge of all diseases. But if he is familiar only with his own region, he cannot be the physician for any foreign patient. For a physician exists only in things known, not unknown. Therefore, he must not allow himself to be seduced either by the Arabs, the Barbarians, or the Chaldeans <note>Paracelsus frequently attacked the authority of ancient Greek and medieval Arabic medical traditions, such as those of Galen and Avicenna.</note>—just as we should not. Let any man believe another only as much as he has experienced for himself in the fire. For he does not know how to trust Medicine if it has not been proven through fire. Indeed, a physician is born through fire, as has been said. Learn therefore Alchemy, which is otherwise called <term>Spagyria</term>. It teaches how to discern the false from the true. Such is the "Light of Nature" <note>The innate wisdom or intelligence found within the natural world, accessible through observation and experiment.</note>, so that testing may be done in all things, and one may walk in the light. From this light of nature, we ought to know and chatter, not from fantasy, in which nothing is birthed except the 4 humors and their compositions, their increase, status, and decrease, and other trifles of this sort, which do not emerge from a brilliant mind filled with a treasury of good, but from a fictitious and completely unproven foundation.
<margin>Spagyria</margin>

## CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The complexions are refuted and overturned.</margin>
Now, however, an objection is raised concerning the <term>complexions</term> <note>The four temperaments (Sanguine, Choleric, Phlegmatic, Melancholic) that were the basis of traditional medicine.</note>, as when it is said: *This man is Sanguine, or Choleric, or Phlegmatic, or Melancholic*; yet none of these is true. This is proven by many causes. The most general is this: because life bestows that which they call "complexions." If, therefore, life confers it, and not the three substances, then it is not to be considered by the physician. For life, and that which adheres to life, is by no means subject to the physician. And even if such complexions were present, the consideration of them would not pertain to the physician. For that which passes away with life does not fall under medical theory. The physician should remember this deeply. Nor does this error concern only the healthy body, but it also pertains to the sick. For they derive diseases from what they believe to be present in a healthy body. Furthermore, one of the causes is this: that the whole body does not allow these four complexions to exist in man, because they are "species." In no species is there a complexion, but rather the nature of its own substance. Nature, however, is not a complexion. For if I say: *This is hot*, that is not its complexion; its nature has this from its substance, just as colors do. This, however, produces neither sickness nor health; it is necessary for something to be either hot or cold, etc., in its own nature. But this has nothing to do with the living body. Moreover, regarding what is usually said about *customs, character, and natures*...
<margin>Whether customs, character, etc. arise from complexion.</margin>
