<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s critique of traditional medieval medicine. Having argued that diseases do not stem from the four humors, he now asserts that the "complexions"—the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a person—are irrelevant to the physician. He shifts the cause of disease to the stars (astronomy) and the "inner virtues" of substances.</meta>

<page-num>38</page-num>
->### PARAMIRUM BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES.<-

...common usage suggests that disease arises from one’s <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine a person's temperament and health.</note>: but this is also false. For these things come from the stars, not from complexions. Bile does not stir up anger; rather, <term>Mars</term> <note>In medical astrology, the planet Mars was thought to govern "choleric" or angry behavior and the secretion of bile.</note> does. From this it follows that bile is poured out or overflows, just as a stomach is filled by too much drink. In this way, Mars pours out the bile. To judge the nature of these things belongs to the Astronomers, not the Physicians—though the latter have forgotten them. Therefore, he who does not perfectly grasp the principles and the related branches of his art is easily led headlong into error.

<margin>Complexions are not the causes of diseases.</margin>
From these things, understand now that you are mistaken in thinking that complexions are subject to the Physician, or that they become the matter or cause of diseases. For such things are inherent to life itself, not to the physical body.

<margin>What and of what kind the conditions of diseases are.</margin>
But if indeed a disease is hot or cold, moist or dry, do not say on that account that the disease is of that particular "complexion." For these are the *conditions* of the diseases, not their complexions. A complexion consists of two qualities together: namely, in hot and moist, or hot and dry; and likewise in cold and moist, or cold and dry—tending toward the nature of the elements, which need not be discussed here. These sorts of disease conditions are either hot or cold, but are neither moist nor dry at the same time; or they are moist and dry, but neither hot nor cold at the same time. Rather, they are such that the condition is either hot alone, or cold alone, or dry alone, or moist alone. And that condition exists in only one quality, not in two.

I say that <term>Mania</term> <note>A state of intense madness or frenzy, which Paracelsus classifies as "pure heat."</note> is heat; but it possesses neither moisture nor dryness. Likewise, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydropisis," a swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note> is moisture, having neither heat nor cold joined to it. And so it is with the rest. In this way are illnesses constituted. This must likewise be considered in medicine, <margin>The double complexion is rejected in Medicine.</margin> so that a "second degree"—that is, a double or twin complexion—is not admitted. Instead, every thing maintains its own single condition: namely heat, cold, dryness, or moisture. For in diseases, these cannot exist together; there must be only one. Because that which is double or twofold is subject to life [the spirit], it is not subject to the Physician.

<margin>Complexion concerns the Physician not at all.</margin>
To give an example: If a thing is beautiful, bright, and well-colored, what does that matter to a Physician? Nothing. In the same way, complexions do not concern him. For they are the garments of nature and they adorn her; they are not to be examined by the Physician at all. But if you truly wish to know why heat exists alone, and likewise cold alone, moisture alone, and dryness alone—then consider that which stands alone. That which is alone is without life, and it abandons life. Therefore, a disease is now at hand. Furthermore: bodies are set on fire by the stars; otherwise, they would not fall ill. The stars stir up internal wars. And so, if the body is now set on fire, it invades at least one quality, not two. For it is cast into either heat, or cold, or moisture, or dryness. Whichever one it is cast into, that is what the physician must weigh and examine. But the matter will be clearer in an example: Suppose someone inflicts a wound or a tumor on another, or cuts off a foot, etc. This blow itself is certainly neither hot, nor cold, nor moist, nor dry in its essence; it is simply a blow. Understand in the same way that all diseases are like this in the beginning, and arise in this manner. If this happens inside the body, what else is it but a wound, where neither heat, nor cold, nor moisture, nor dryness need be considered?

<margin>Incarnatives.</margin>
Therefore, the true and genuine art is to "Incarnate" <note>From "incarnare," meaning to make flesh grow. Paracelsus refers to medicines that promote the healing of tissue.</note>. Whether those <term>Incarnatives</term> are hot, cold, moist, or dry should not move you. If they are flesh-making, that is enough for you. Leave the rest aside. And although it happens that wounds grow hot, become inflamed, and turn feverish, these things are not the disease itself. <margin>The cure of wounds or blows is done without regard for complexion.</margin> Attack the disease itself: it requires no cooling, no binding. These points are brought forward to demonstrate your erroneous and mangled art, because you are not at all instructed in Incarnatives, as was your duty. The same things likewise happen in dropsy. Use those specific things which drive out the dissolved salt, and pay no regard to whether they are hot or cold. For medicine is not founded on these [qualities], just as colocynth <note>A powerful bitter purgative made from a desert vine.</note> and Turbith <note>A root used as a laxative.</note> purge without respect to complexion. For they do not have that power from their complexion, but from their "masculine nature" <note>In alchemy/early medicine, "masculine" often refers to a substance's active, essential power or virtue.</note>. Therefore, all virtues of things are <term>Arcana</term> <note>Secret or hidden spiritual powers within nature that act directly on a disease.</note>, so that they cure the diseased parts in the same way they were made and born. They are made without complexion; they are healed without complexion. And remember this as most true: because as nature approaches, it also recedes. That fire is extinguished by water does not happen because of cold, but because of moisture. Thus, that fire heats is not because of dryness, but because of heat. That which governs the disease always remains so: not because it is a "sinning matter" <note>A reference to the "peccant humor" of Galenic medicine.</note>, but as a color that adds nothing and takes nothing away. Disease is present like a sword, which cuts without any complexion.

<margin>Persian fire.</margin>
It happens that sulfur is ignited and blazes as if in <term>Persian fire</term> <note>original: "ignis Persicus," a historical name for various skin inflammations, likely shingles or erysipelas.</note>. Now, what will be the medicine for this? Truly, to extinguish it, as one does a fire. But because your treatment begins with cold things and camphor, a doubtful outcome must be expected. This one foundation must be considered here...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the "complexion" (the balance of humors) is irrelevant to treating disease, which he compares to a simple wound or a fire. He asserts that medicines work through their "Arcana" (hidden virtues) rather than through qualities like heat or cold.</summary>

He concludes a thought here that we must "consider" (completing the word *considerandum* from the previous page's catchword) how to truly quench a disease rather than just suppressing it.</meta>

<page-num>39</page-num>
->## FROM THE THREE FIRST SUBSTANCES ##<-

...one had to consider what could extinguish the invisible fire. For to extinguish is the goal: to merely cool is poisonous, because it drives the disease back and stirs up other evils. God does not demand that we act this way; rather, like perfect medicine which is maintained in good order, we should strive for that which our eyes show us in water and fire <note>Water naturally extinguishes fire; Paracelsus argues medicine should work with the same clear, natural logic</note>. Thus, our eyes must be opened in the art of medicine so that we may perceive in a medicinal and "fiery" way those things which a peasant sees clearly. We are driven to this foundation when we are about to begin a cure.

<margin>The four complexions are to be entirely rejected.</margin>
Therefore, it is with good reason that we must abandon the <term>complexions</term> <note>The traditional belief that health depends on the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note> and the four <term>humors</term> <note>Blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. For these are to be considered very little here. Those who have involved Medicine in so many obscurities have done this. It is indeed true that a disease must be either hot or cold. For what exists without colors? In the same way, nothing exists without these qualities. And yet, those are nothing more than signs, and by no means the diseases themselves. He who takes the signs for the matter itself stands in his own way. What does it matter that the forehead burns, that the head is inflamed along with the whole body, that the urine is red, the pulse fast, the liver thirsty, and other similar things? These certainly signal the disease at the very least, but they are not the matter itself.

For they are something other than the matter; they misrepresent the disease itself. <margin>Colic</margin> In the case of colic arising from <term>constipation</term> <note>original: *constipatione*</note>, what is felt? Severe griping pains, burning, paralysis, thirst, vomiting, and the like. Yet let none of these things distress or delay you. If you remove the constipation, then all the other symptoms will be resolved. <margin>Stone</margin> Consider the "stone" <note>A kidney or bladder stone, called a *calculus*</note> and the symptoms it induces. Do you wish to remove those symptoms? Then remove the stone. You will remove this neither by hot nor cold things, without regard for complexions or humors; you will remove it with the knife alone. And let these lessons be established for you not in one case, but in all. Let the "knife" be the <term>arcanum</term> <note>A secret, powerful remedy that goes straight to the essence of a disease</note> of the stone. Therefore, recognize the *arcana* for what they ought to be. I say this: he who thinks that cold things are owed to hot, or moist to dry, does not understand the nature of disease. For return to the case of <term>mania</term>. What else helps this but the lancing of a vein? For in this way the patient recovers. And this is its *arcanum*, not indeed camphor, nor water-lily, nor sage, nor marjoram, nor enemas, nor cooling things, nor this, nor that, but bloodletting <note>original: *phlebotomia*</note> alone. If this is true in mania, it will be true in other diseases as well. Nor will there be a new law for these.

<margin>No one should be called "Melancholic."</margin>
But if someone truly wants to say of a healthy man that he is "Melancholic," he speaks falsely again. For the light of Nature does not know what "Melancholy" is. But if you were to say: *this man, by his character, is Saturnine or Lunatic*, you would speak correctly. <margin>Character comes from the stars, not from melancholy.</margin> Indeed, our character and the properties of our natures are formed by the stars, and Melancholy <note>Referring here to the supposed humor of "black bile"</note> is not poured into the body by the stars. Therefore, if it is not from the stars, it should not be accepted into Medicine nor set up as a pillar to support the weight of the profession. If its seat is in the Spleen, then the Spleen belongs to <term>Saturn</term>, by which it is ruled. Now indeed, Saturn and the spleen together produce the disease of the spleen; and yet those [traditional doctors] mention nothing of the Spleen, nor of Saturn, but only of "melancholy." But even the <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A fever that recurs every four days, traditionally linked to black bile</note> is fashioned and established by Saturn, and proceeds according to his impression. Where then is "Melancholy" here? Thus your "humor" is false, and is nothing. Likewise they talk nonsense about the <margin>Melancholy is not to be accepted in medicine.</margin> "phlegm of the brain"—an error much cruder than the former, and hardly worthy of being touched upon here. The same is also true of bile and blood. Where does that leave the Kidney, Lung, Stomach, and the rest, and especially the Heart? If they were going to manufacture humors at all, certainly the heart before everything, then also the lung, the liver, and the kidneys would each need some peculiar humor; and they do have them. For every single member in the body contains its own humors; but not of the kind <margin>Humors in every member.</margin> that those four [traditional humors] present. Rather, they show themselves as the members themselves do—each one for itself, and one does not answer for another. The Spleen guards its own place; so too the kidneys; so the lung; so the region where bile is; so the seat of phlegm; so the border of Melancholy, and so on. But let it be far from us to divide the body into four pillars of humors as if into four Elements. It is indeed true that there are four Elements. <margin>What an element is.</margin> But if you ask what an element is, I respond: *it is the matrix of its fruit* <note>The "matrix" is the mother-source or womb from which something grows</note>. For example, the Earth is the matrix of its fruit, as is evident. Its fruit cares for neither the cold nor the dryness of the earth, and by itself it is also nothing. There, it is necessary for all four elements to meet. we say the same also of water, air, and earth. But as you discourse about these, it is clear that the Elements themselves are not yet known by you. If you had understood them, then certainly you would have divided the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe</note> more aptly; which, however, you explain in a quite crude manner.

## CHAPTER V.

**N**ow, since the "ultimate matter" proves this, that all things in the universe consist of three substances...

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the traditional theory of the four humors and complexions, arguing that diseases should be treated by finding their specific "arcanum" (remedy) or by understanding planetary influences like Saturn, rather than balancing hot and cold qualities. He redefines "Elements" as the mother-sources (matrices) of things and insists that every organ has its own unique vital juices.</summary>

<page-num>40</page-num>
->### PARAMIRUM, BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES ###<-

...reside, which are themselves the true subject of the physician; yet the middle body is nothing like them, because of its wondrous structure and its transformation. However, that change or transformation is nothing other than how a painter depicts an image on a wall, or expresses it in a wooden statue. There, no one sees the wood, but rather the beautiful <term>icon</term> <note>original: "iconem"; here meaning a representational image or portrait</note>. Yet a damp sponge with a little effort wipes away everything the painter added of his own.

<margin>An elegant comparison of life drawn from pigments.</margin>
Life is exactly like this. Once sculpted by God and gathered into <term>three substances</term> <note>Paracelsus’s "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which he believed made up all matter</note>, and afterward illuminated, life is a smoke that grants us the ability to stand, walk, move, and so on. But all these things are wiped away by a single sponge. Now, it must be fully understood here that we should not be led astray by life and its outward appearances. For that painter is quite ingenious who has smeared those three substances with colors, so that in one the Sun, in another the Moon, in a third Venus, etc., appear depicted. This one is fair, that one is dark, another is colored differently. And this is the highest mastery of the painter, who has so skillfully adorned his statues. But from these aforementioned things, you should take nothing for the cure. They are merely colors and pigments, not mixed with oil or glue, but light, like a shadow or the air. Meanwhile, it is true that certain colors in the human being himself ought to be noted. But those are painted on by death.

<margin>The pigments of death.</margin>
For death, too, has its own pigments. If death invades and fixes itself, then life gives way, and then those pigments show themselves. What do these indicate? Death and its diseases. These two colors are indeed necessary to know, but they provide you with no knowledge toward curing the disease. For they are merely signs.

<margin>The deceptive nature of signs.</margin>
The nature of signs is deceptive and uncertain, just like a word from the tongue, which flies out either in earnest or in jest. Because these colors are present in these things, you must not judge that the disease is subject to you based on them. For neither heaven nor earth are with you in that. This is above all else. Nothing else is to be known or thought of, however, except that all things consist in that image: that is, all things are fashioned into a form. In this form itself is the <term>anatomy</term>. Man is a fashioned thing.

<margin>The anatomy of diseases.</margin>
His form is his anatomy, which is among the most necessary things for a physician to know. For so also are there "anatomies" of diseases: that is, <term>Hydrops</term> <note>An old term for edema or dropsy, the swelling of soft tissues due to fluid</note> is fashioned in such a way that it fits its own form. Therefore, it is not enough to have knowledge of the anatomy of a man; one must also know the anatomy of the dropsy, just as if it stood there fashioned and painted in its own shape. The same is true for all other diseases. We must study the anatomy of this fashioned form. For without this, nature will never 

<margin>The anatomy of herbs.</margin>
witness us as Physicians. Set before yourselves the example of roses and lilies. Why did God express them in such a shape and form, as he did other similar things? It is because he created both the Physician and his medicine from the earth, so that he might know what comes forth from the earth in its own anatomy. If he knows their anatomies, he must afterward also know the anatomies of diseases; then he will find the <term>concordance</term> <note>The "harmony" or "agreement" between a plant's nature and a disease's nature; the basis of "like cures like"</note>—which things are similar to each other and belong together. From this concordance of two anatomies, the physician grows, and without it, he is nothing.

<margin>The physician arises from the concordance of anatomies.</margin>
Blessed would be that hour in which he who is hindered by no misery could labor in this study. Pay attention to this: every single thing that benefits the <term>matrix</term> <note>The womb, or more broadly, the creative "womb" of any organ</note> possesses the anatomy of the matrix; and whatever diseases that matrix feels are contained in that anatomy. Therefore, the anatomy of diseases, as well as of other natural things, ought to be held in the highest regard.

<margin>Anatomy is to be held in the highest regard.</margin>
Thus we ought to know God from his great works, and conclude deep within ourselves that such varied images exist for that one cause, for which the forms of diseases are also wonderful. And he who understands the anatomy of the "roses" of diseases <note>Likely referring to skin eruptions or "rosy" symptoms</note> ought to rejoice deeply at the sight, because God has displayed such medicine to his eyes, which looks back at him and helps him effectively and swiftly. Similarly, one must feel the same regarding lilies, Lavender, and all other things.

<margin>What colors are.</margin>
But what are colors? Nothing but food for the outward eyes. Diseases can indeed agree with them if they pass into their "ultimate matter." The same is true regarding taste. For what else is taste than a part of anatomy? It designates nothing other than the agreement of similarity. From which follows the distribution of this taste to all members in the body, so that sweet is joined to its own sweet, and bitter to bitter, just as degrees of sweetness, acidity, bitterness, etc., embrace each other. Who is the physician who would seek the medicine for the liver in Gentian, Agaric, or Colocynth? <note>These are famously bitter herbs; Paracelsus is arguing that the medicine's "anatomy" or quality must match the organ's need</note> No physician would.

<margin>The order and line of anatomy.</margin>
Who is the physician who would seek the medicine for bile in Manna, Honey, Sugar, or Polypody? No physician would. Like belongs to like: yet in the order of anatomy, nothing cold is given against hot, and nothing hot against cold; but only in the line of anatomy. That order would be confused if we sought our health in contraries: just as if a father, when his child asks for bread, should by no means hand him a serpent instead of bread. Truly we have a Father in heaven who created us, and he would not fail to provide the things necessary for our request...

<meta>The catchword "ria" at the bottom of the page indicates the next page begins with "necessaria" (necessary).</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that life and disease are like "pigments" on a statue, and true medicine requires understanding the "anatomy" (essential form) of both the disease and the cure. He rejects the traditional Galenic method of treating "contraries" (like using cold to treat heat) in favor of a "concordance" where the medicine matches the disease's inner nature.</summary>

<page-num>41</page-num>

...but instead offered serpents? Wormwood would certainly be a bad medicine in place of sugar <note>original: "Zuccaro"</note>. Therefore, just as a child is handed what they ask for, and not poison, so it is here: the gallbladder asks for its own, the heart for its own suitable thing, and the liver for its own proper thing. This must be the column upon which the Physician stands, so that in his <term>anatomy</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "anatomy" not just to mean the study of bones and organs, but the inner structural essence and spiritual correspondence between a medicine and a disease</note> he provides to each thing that which agrees with it by similarity. For the bread that an infant eats has its own anatomy, and the child eats its own proper body. So <margin>The disadvantages of ignorance in anatomy.</margin> every single medicine must also have the anatomy of its own disease. For one who is unskilled in this anatomy, it is very difficult to follow and grasp what is right. But it is easy for the one whose integrity is small, who is moved by neither crime nor infamy. These people are the enemies of the light of nature.

<margin>The anatomy of the eyes.</margin> Look at the eye in the head, with what wondrous craftsmanship it has been fashioned; and how the middle body has so marvelously impressed its anatomy into this image and instilled its own "taste" into it. From the image and the taste proceeds the knowledge of the medicine itself. Now pay attention to the anatomy of the diseases that happen to it: *Cataracts, Spots, White Opacities, and Darkened Vision* <note>original: "Cataracta, Macula, Albugo, Scotomia"</note>. Why is this? Now, if you have simple spectacles, look into them so that you may find the likeness of the disease in its anatomy. For example: Diseases descend from <term>transmutation</term> <note>the process of one substance changing into another</note>. Now transmute those ocular anatomies; and in that transmutation, look into the anatomy of the taste and the appearance or image—though less at the image, and more at the taste. And if you have obtained the joining and agreement of those things: what blind person would beg God for bread, only to have poison substituted for it? Therefore, be grounded and skilled in anatomy; then you will by no means provide stones instead of bread. For you ought to know that you are the father of the disease, not its teacher or master. Feed it, therefore, just as a parent feeds his own son. And just as a father is moved toward his son to sustain him according to his need, and to provide him with what the son himself is made of; likewise, the Physician ought to be moved toward his patient. As you understand this example, so also the other examples in the treatment of other patients should be similar. Whatever is <margin>Note.</margin> transmuted, you must transmute the same, and strive so that the healthy anatomies are brought into agreement with one another. Afterward, if diseases occur, take <margin>Theophrastus’s composition of recipes.</margin> care to compose them in both transmutations. And thus recipes <note>original: "recepta"</note> ought to be set down and composed, not in the manner of charlatans with long sheets of paper full of syrups, theriacs, and other things in which no anatomy appears, but only pure fantasy.

Am I not therefore right to separate myself from that process of "hereditary" *Recipes*, as they are called? Indeed, I am right. For although many virtues and efficacies are sometimes found in some of those remedies regarding health (though often dangerously), the outcome from them is only because they happened to stumble upon some Anatomy by chance, or they mixed in some principal ingredient received from a true and healthy physician—which veils and covers their own "theory." And then that principal ingredient is deprived of its own dignity, while the added trifles claim it and keep it. This is the "mastery" of such men. How foully you err, you whose foundation is mossy and overgrown, and who is forced to prop it up daily so that the earthly foundation can be preserved? Truly, the props are full of sophistry, flatteries, stroking of egos, and frequent additions; and they simulate more gestures than court fools, though there is no count to them.

Let this be the question: *Whether wine and oil <margin>Whether wine and oil are suitable for a wound?</margin> are suitable for a wound?* Just as Christ speaks concerning the wounded man near Jericho. Of course, you are able to deny it. But it must be true: not a figure of speech, not a metaphor, not a jest or a joke. Now if it is a foundation, and it is a medicine, you are professing your own foolishness. For from it you can heal nothing, which the Samaritan nevertheless did. And even if that event had not truly happened, Christ (as he who is truth itself) would not have wanted to point to a foolish medicine, but rather to an Anatomy and a certain <term>arcanum</term> <note>a secret, powerful medicinal virtue or "inner stars" of a substance</note>. Far be it from us to say that Christ did not correctly name the simple things of nature. Because this is a secret for wounds, now look at yourselves and see how much you are lacking or falling short. The matter comes back to this: there must be enough in the wine and oil; otherwise, there will be no foundation in medicine. Pay attention, therefore, to the preparation, to the virtue, to the time and hour, to the property, and whatever else pertains to this. For if you agree that a grain cannot bear fruit unless it is first cast into the field and rots, then the other must also be true: namely, that the wound is the field, and the oil and wine are the seed. Now you divine: what will the fruit be?

### CHAPTER VI.

**N**ow these things clearly bring to light those arts which cut and separate the body of wine, which is not a <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the "little world"; the idea that the human being contains the entire universe within them</note>: that is, it must happen in the experience of life...

He criticizes traditional, complex recipes as "fantasy" and explains the healing power of the Samaritan's wine and oil as a secret medicinal seed planted in the "field" of a wound.</summary>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>PARAMIRUM BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES</header>

### PARAMIRUM BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES

<margin>Experience must take place in life.</margin>
...it must. And this is the truth: to experience in life what resides in the middle of the body, to dissolve one thing and lead it into another. Do not build upon that which belongs to [outward] life; rather, turn away from what is primary toward the other, and inquire within it. That [true] life arises from the arts <note>Paracelsus refers here to the "art" of alchemy or chemical transformation</note>, not for the service of the soul—that is, it is not the soul's lodging in this life. In this life, the arts and the foundation that is proposed are unearthed. For consider the weakness of the first life: if it proceeds into the operations of its own <term>arcana</term> <note>secret healing essences</note>, then the first life is compelled to die.
<margin>A living rose is useless.</margin>
For there is nothing in it that is of use to man. In its first life, the <term>Rose</term> is great and beautifully refined in its taste. As long as it retains this, it is of no use to <term>Medicine</term>. It must undergo putrefaction <note>the alchemical process of breaking down a substance to release its essence</note> and die within it, to be born anew. Only then can you discuss its medical powers; only then may you administer it. For if the stomach leaves nothing un-putrefied—which is what a man ought to be—then nothing will remain un-putrefied which ought to become medicine. Therefore, care nothing for the first life, nor seek anything within it. Its entire temperament, and whatever belongs to it,
<margin>What is not subject to the Physician.</margin>
perishes, and nothing remains. That which does not remain, which does not pass into a new birth, is not a subject for the <term>Physician</term>. Let all his labor be this: that it be led into a new birth. From this, finally, emerge the true <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercurius</term>, and <term>Sal</term> <note>The "Three Primes": Sulfur (the soul/flammability), Mercury (the spirit/volatility), and Salt (the body/solidity)</note>, in which all
<margin>What the secrets of things are.</margin>
secrets, foundations, works, and cures lie hidden. Once the second life is introduced, the primary matter is already visibly present; you see its ultimate form if the first life of the middle body has departed. From this middle life, a new life must begin, which is subject to no death, except for the single end in which all things perish. And because the death of frailty weighs upon it, no new life remains [otherwise].

Now, these things must be considered beforehand in man, and must be founded upon this. For in the exposition and separation of any "middle body," the primary matters are manifested. He who knows these from the new life knows the subject of that life. There are two subjects. One is the sick man; he is not reduced to a new life, but the "middle" remains to him. The other is the medicine. It protects the middle life through its own new life. For this reason, the <term>arcana</term> are placed in the new life—not in the first, nor the middle. But also consider that the <term>Anatomy</term>
<margin>How many types of anatomy: What is Local Anatomy? What is Material Anatomy?</margin>
of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>Man as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note> is investigated in two ways, and neither is done poorly. One is <term>Local</term>; the other is <term>Material</term>. <term>Local</term> is when a man is dissected by himself: where one observes what bones, flesh, veins, etc., are, and what seat they occupy.

But this is the least of all things. The other is more powerful: namely, that by which a new life is introduced into man after the first middle life, into a transformation. In this, one observes what blood is, and what kind of <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Salt</term> are present; likewise what the heart is, what its sulfur, what its mercury, and what its salt are. The same applies to the brain and all the members of the whole body. This is the true and genuine <term>Anatomy</term>. And this is the foundation of the beginning: thus must the <term>Physician</term> be born. Yet this "birth" is hard to understand, and this speech is hard to hear for those who will not dismiss their own fantasies—those who trust their own brains rather than the way of truth itself. Therefore, this one piece of advice is given: that we be educated and live in the arts; otherwise, who will believe us or trust us with a man? This is the discovery of the primary matter. This is the matter that indicates the disease to us. This we must know thoroughly. Once this is done, we shall then attain the transformed <term>Anatomy</term> with easy effort.

But besides this, yet another <term>Anatomy</term> follows. That is the anatomy of diseases, as we have often said. It is superfluous to recount it here. Thus, three Anatomies are to be celebrated in man. The first is <term>Local</term>. This indicates the image of man, his proportion and nature, and whatever is connected to these. The second demonstrates living sulfur, volatile <term>Mercury</term>, and sharp salt in every member. The third teaches how

it was held to be invisible, and yet it is present. For it must be reduced to such a state that it can be seen by the eyes. For if the **Light of Nature** <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lux Naturae) is a central concept for Paracelsus, referring to the innate wisdom or divine intelligence present in the natural world that a physician must learn to read.</note> is to be light, then it must be conspicuous, not obscure, and not dark. <margin>From where diseases should be named.</margin>
By virtue, therefore, of **Anatomy**, which is founded in the light of nature, it is right and just that diseases also be named according to the light rather than according to the darkness. That is, let anatomy yield and provide the names of the diseases. In this way, every disease is named intelligently and correctly according to the art. 

<margin>Fever is not correctly named.</margin>
It is erroneous and without reason that **Fever** is called "Fever" <note>original: 'Febris'</note>. For this name is derived from the "fervor" <note>heat or boiling</note> of the fever. But heat is merely a sign of that disease, not the matter, nor the cause. A name, however, ought to proceed from the matter and the property and the nature of the substance itself. Just as a nettle is truly a nettle because it burns <note>In Latin, 'urtica' (nettle) is related to 'urere' (to burn)</note>. But more truly, it is the **salt of urine**. For they share one and the same **Anatomy**. Therefore, "Fever" is a name that tastes of its master’s folly. For it is a disease of **ignited sulfurous nitre**. From this it shakes the body, from this it strikes with horror, and from this it gives intervals of rest. These and other names you will find in their own proper chapters. 

So too the name of **Apoplexy** <note>a sudden loss of consciousness, often a stroke</note> proclaims the wisdom of the one who named it; for according to Medical reason, it ought not to be called Apoplexy, but 

<margin>Apoplexy is rightly called cachymial Mercury.</margin>
**sublimated cachymial Mercury** <note>'Cachymia' is a Paracelsian term for an imperfectly formed mineral or ore; he argues the disease is caused by a specific chemical volatility resembling mercury.</note>. For such is its matter, its cause, and the substance at fault. The signs, truly, are only to be considered so that through them the body and the substance may be denoted. But he who wrongly introduces signs as causes errs in his entire practice. Indeed, there are many bodies and species which either heat or cool. Therefore the name "fever" is false, but "Nitrous" is not. To this, fever proceeds from the principle of humors <note>The traditional Galenic theory that health depends on balancing four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Paracelsus rejected this.</note>, from which it nevertheless ought not to proceed. 

<margin>The falling sickness, the "green" disease.</margin>
Although names should more justly be given from the art of healing, such as the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note> or the "**green disease**" <note>original: 'viridellus morbus'</note>. For that species of the falling sickness is cured by the "green" remedy. If these things are not done according to the prescription with discernment, an error is committed. For **Anatomy** preserves these distinctions. 

Do not let it disturb you that your peasant-like eyes do not show these things to you. For the physical body obscures those eyes. But for this reason, science is at hand, upon which the **Physician** must rely. 

<margin>What the physician's eyes should be like.</margin>
It reveals more to him than to the peasant. For if he wishes to know or see no more than a peasant, he certainly seems neither called nor created for **Medicine**. The peasant was not chosen for this, but the Physician was chosen. 

<margin>Who the physician is.</margin>
The cause lies in the science in which the Physician must be proficient. For the Physician is he who publicly reveals the miracles of God. If he is present for this purpose, it is right that he use these things correctly, not wickedly; truly, not falsely. For what is hidden in the sea that he should not disclose? Nothing. What lies hidden in the sea that should not be discovered by him? Nothing. He ought to bring things out into the open—not only from the sea, but also from the earth, from the air, from the firmament (that is, from fire)—so that all may truly behold the wonders of God, why they exist, and what they portend. 

Because, however, all things are not explained, it is a sign that the required understanding is absent. What is the cause that the profession is composed of such great folly and, at the same time, such thin art, which yet desires to be held in such high esteem? It is this: that it is not alone; the same blindness, the same cataract <note>original: 'glaucoma'</note>, occupies other professions as well. For just as we do not know the whale, that monster of the sea, so the other profession <note>likely referring to Theology</note> does not recognize who the **Beast of the Apocalypse** or **Babylon** may be. Therefore, these are related blindnesses, which nevertheless ought to be corrected. 

<margin>Medicine and Theology are inseparable.</margin>
And just as the blindness of the physician in cases of this kind is the destruction of the sick man, so likewise the other blindness is the death of the soul. **Christ** spoke wonderfully and of unheard-of things. **Medicine** is also wonderful. As the one, so the other must also be tracked and investigated. For these two professions will never suffer a divorce. And just as the body is the dwelling place of the soul, so the one clings to the other, and one repeatedly reveals the other.

And although it is not shaped in exactly the same way, the seed-bed is nevertheless present—namely, the body—and it is fashioned within us according to what it is. Just as a seed is truly a tree, but it is brought to perfection in the earth. So the **stomach** is also a sculptor

...belongs to him who visibly makes that which is invisible. Regarding these matters, therefore, observe the example of nourishment in this manner:

<margin>Our food is what we are.</margin>
Whatever serves as our food is that very thing which we ourselves are. In this way, we eat our own selves; such is also the nature of medicine, though a distinction is maintained regarding its specific disease. And that which is yielded through health, that very thing replaces the limb within its own member. Let this be no wonder to you. The reason: A tree flourishing in a field would not be a tree unless it had its own food. <margin>What is food?</margin> What is food? It is not merely filling or fattening, but the **restoration of form**. <margin>What is hunger?</margin> What is hunger? It is the indicator of the arrival of death, in the destruction of the limbs. For the **form** was sculpted by God himself within the mother’s womb. This sculpture remains in the shape of an **image**. However, it perishes and dies without the application of an external form. He who does not eat does not grow; he who does not eat does not live. Now, if the growing person is increased by food, and the **craftsman** <note>original: 'opifex'. Paracelsus often refers to an internal "Archaeus" or alchemist that builds the body.</note> of the form is inside him, who extends his own form—if he possesses a form without which he can do nothing—it follows then that the nourishment of the sculpted image contains within itself the form into which it may pass, and which it may increase and extend. <margin>Rain is the tree and plant.</margin> Rain contains the tree within itself, as does the liquid of the earth. Rain is its drink; the liquid of the earth is the food by which it grows. Now, what grows here? Nothing else but this: as much as is added to the tree in its growth, that much of the bark and wood is made from the rain and liquid. The **shaper and molder** <note>original: 'formator ac plastes'</note> is himself in the seed; the wood, bark, etc., are in the liquid and the rain. That craftsman existing within the wood can fashion wood out of these two things. It happens likewise with herbs. The seed is nothing. It holds at least a beginning within itself, in which the form, the craftsman, the nature, and the property reside. If it must grow, then the rain, the matter, and the liquid produce the herb itself. Therefore, within this herb are stalks, leaves, and flowers.

Thus, every form of all growing things exists externally in their nourishment. And if we are deprived of this, we never grow, but die in a deserted form. If we ascend to full growth, that form must be preserved so that it does not fail. For within us, there exists a certain **essence** similar to fire. That essence feeds upon both our form and our image. Therefore, if we did not add to it and build up the form of our body, then it would be extinguished in a deserted image. Thus, it is necessary that we eat ourselves, lest we die from a defect of form. In this way, we eat our own fingers, our own body, blood, flesh, foot, brain, heart, etc. That is, every **morsel** <note>original: 'bolus'</note> that we swallow contains within itself all our members, whatever the whole man contains and holds enclosed within himself. From these things, some have raised a doubt, because it was indicated that the members and the body require nourishment. But they stop at this: why they have need of nourishment, and for what purpose? These people have not understood what nourishment is in a human, what happens, and by whom it is done. Therefore, that internal craftsman takes nothing for the image except what is suitable—that is, what becomes "wood." The rest he casts out in the manner of excrement, with only the likeness remaining.

<margin>Change is the restoration of form.</margin>
But this also must be weighed accordingly. In all things, nutrition is established for the sake of the form alone. As summer approaches, the time of hunger presses upon the trees; and then they promise leaves, flowers, fruit, etc. From these things, what is perceived if their forms take in nothing from the outside? They do not have it within themselves. For if they did, then even if cut off and cast down, they would bestow it just as much as those fixed in the earth. Therefore, they are fixed in the earth so that the form may enter and be fashioned, which is the mastery and gift of trees. A human, indeed, does not have need of this same thing. For he does not put forth his fruits in the same way as trees. According to its fruits, the creature is different. From this, know that all things live for the sake of the preservation of their form; and because of its consumption, they feel hunger and thirst, so that the image may be replaced and supplied. You see no differently that fat and grease increase from food. Unless it is supplied, that part of the image is abolished. Likewise with another part. Although it is so arranged that when a defect pertains to the principal parts, sudden death rushes in. For life does not remain when the interior image of the whole body fails. Thus, from humans, humans grow; that is, <margin>Nourishment is man.</margin> **Nourishment is man**, and likewise it returns a man, which is to say, his image. Thus we eat ourselves. And unless we ate ourselves in this way, our body would vanish, along with the life in between, and whatever is in us. In this way, there are truly two humans: <margin>The double man.</margin> the **Visible** and the **Invisible**. The Visible is double: namely according to the body and the soul. The Invisible is simple, namely according to...

...according to the body. Let this be an example of it: from the wood that lies before us, a sculptor can carve an image if he removes what must be removed. In this same way, a statue exists within a man, which at first glance did not appear as such. This is how human nourishment behaves: once in the body, it goes into its own members. It does not remain in one part, but is worked upon with the greatest skill. For the Highest of the Heavens fashions man—that is, He arranges the limbs as far as the man extends. Now, if we know that we eat and drink our own selves—and likewise that every tree and every living creature eats itself—we must further understand what emerges from this regarding Medicine, as will be discussed hereafter. And even if we never eat bones, veins, or ligaments, and rarely eat brain, heart, pancreas, or membranes, nonetheless know this: it is not bone that generates bone, nor brain that generates brain. Rather, any morsel of food is all of these things together. If the **form** exists here invisibly, then the bone will also be present. 

Bread is blood. Who sees this? It is fat. Who beholds it? Who grasps it? It is lard. Yet no one either feels or sees it. And yet, it is generated from there; so industrious a craftsman <note>original: "artifex". Paracelsus refers to the 'Archeus', an internal alchemist or vital force that separates the useful parts of food from the waste.</note> works in the stomach. He who can make iron from sulfur—for iron is sulfur—is himself present here daily, and daily fashions for man that for whose sake He created him. Likewise, if He can produce a diamond from salt, or gold from Mercury, He can also do this in man. For He has far greater care for man than for other things. Therefore, He forges for him whatever is necessary. You, at least, be the workman: supply the material to Him, and let Him separate and form it as He wills. He is perfectly aware of measure, number, weight, proportion, length, and all other things.

<margin>The spermatic and alimentary man.</margin>
But pay attention: every single creature is double. One part is from the seed <note>original: "sperme"</note>, the other from nourishment. The seed is the beginning. Once it is cast, it immediately craves its nourishment. The seed itself is the creature; this nourishment belongs to it. The seed has the freedom of the human form, so that what it eats becomes human, and becomes human limbs. Therefore, man is destined for the consumption of his form through death, which is caused by the seed. <note>Paracelsus suggests that the biological "seed" from our parents carries the necessity of mortal decay (Justice), while food provides the grace to continue living (Mercy).</note> He is compelled to endure this death in that which provides and suffices as nourishment. Thus, it is not enough for a man to be born from a mother's womb; he must also be born equally from nourishment itself. Whatever concerns the nature of human life regarding the soul is separate from nourishment. For that property of the soul's life <margin>Life from the soul.</margin> arrives with the soul, not with the body; as far as morals and character are concerned, it arises from the man according to his own wisdom. Here, however, whatever is present from nourishment is the body—according to which neither virtue, nor anger, nor honesty, nor wickedness are judged. What the body is, is well known to the Physician. He who fashions the body in the mother's womb also fashions it in the stomach. For this architect applies himself continually to his work, so that he does nothing else but repair and mend that which has been made—that is, he preserves that form which is diminished, dissolved, broken, and dissipated in one way or another, day by day, here and there. Such things are observed in many ways in healthy bodies as well as sick ones. For health, in its integrity and state, requires preservation no less than a disease requires a cure.

It is clear from these things that by this reasoning we have two bodies: which are indeed one body, but created in a twofold way—in seed and in nourishment—and the alimentary body is similar to the spermatic one. From this, it is right for us to recognize that as soon as we are thrust out from the mother's womb, we live by the sole grace and mercy of God, and we produce our body further not from the mother's womb, but from nourishment. For we receive one body out of **Justice** <note>original: "iustitia". Referring to the natural law of biological inheritance.</note> from a father and mother. Lest it perish and die, we sustain it out of **Grace** through prayer to God, when we pray:

> *Give us this day our daily bread,*

which is the same as if we were to say, *Give us today our daily body.*

<margin>A double body: of Justice and of Mercy.</margin>
<margin>A double medicine: of Justice and of Mercy.</margin>
For the body received from the mother nourishes itself until the hour of death. And therefore, we pray for the daily bread. But that which gives us our body is "daily." Thus we have two bodies: of Justice and of Mercy. Likewise, there are two medicines: of Justice and of Mercy. That is, we are called to each body: to that which is given by father and mother, and to that which is bestowed upon us by nourishment. For this reason, we are taught by Christ to be anxious for our daily bread; as if He were saying:

> *Your body received from your mother is nothing. Today, yesterday, long ago it would have belonged to death. Therefore, bread shall henceforth be your body. Therefore, take care that you never live hereafter out of Justice from father and mother, but from the body of Mercy. For that reason, pour out prayers to your heavenly father for the giving of daily bread—that is, concerning your body. And then He will give you the body—that is, the body of Mercy.*

In this we live henceforth, and...

Of the **Body of Justice** <note>original: "corpore Iustitiae". Paracelsus uses this term to refer to the biological body we inherit from our parents and Adam, which is subject to the "justice" of mortality and original sin.</note> we retain nothing except the very beginning of our birth. Therefore, we eat our own selves out of grace and mercy. For a man ought to think this way: even if he has come forth from his mother's womb, he is no longer merely the son of his mother and father, but is the son of Him who provides his nourishment. Thus, He is our heavenly Father—not only according to that justice which He bestowed upon Adam and his descendants, but He is our Father daily from the moment we lose the body of our corporal and mortal parents. For we retain nothing from our mortal parents except the seed. All other things flow from the heavenly Father. We belong to Him; we pray to Him for our body, and not for the "body of justice." For if the **Body of Grace** <note>original: "corpus gratiae". This is the body built and maintained daily by the food God provides through nature.</note> did not exist, the other body of justice would collapse at any moment. Therefore, see what the body truly is: we eat our own selves, yet not out of "justice," but out of grace and prayer.

## CHAPTER VIII.

Therefore, we must diligently consider who and what we are, if we no longer live from our mother’s body, but from the **Body of Bread** through grace, and not justice. John the Baptist alluded to this when he testified to the Jews that *God is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones.* <note>Matthew 3:9</note> What else is this but saying that bread is made from stones, as if from the earth? This bread produces the bodies of the children of Abraham, who later must acknowledge that they live from the Body of Grace. Thus, we possess a body made of the bread of nourishment. I declare this so that I may further confirm my proposition: namely, that man has his **Anatomy** on the outside, which the physician must understand. The physician should form his knowledge so that he can penetrate through it to the understanding of the **Three Substances**, <note>The "Three Substances" (Tria Prima) are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the fundamental building blocks of all matter in Paracelsian chemistry.</note> to know what they truly are. From this body follows the **Regimen** <note>term: Regimen (A prescribed way of life or medical system)</note> and diet, which provides a new occasion to describe the diseases of fullness or satiety, immoderation, and the poor quality of foods that do not benefit our body. Although it is established that our stomach transforms what is ingested into us and for us, nevertheless, our petition looks toward bread, and further toward the fact that all things are clean and subject to us. Indeed, whatever is more closely related to bread is the more healthy for the body, provided it is used in a settled measure in all things. In this way, we are renewed and made young. And just as we sow the seeds of nourishment, so shall we reap.

And from the body of justice we indeed have and retain one disease. Though justice does not produce diseases, any more than the bread for which we pray does. <margin>John the Baptist lived without disease.</margin> Just as John the Baptist and several others lived without diseases for this reason. But as luxury is committed in bread, so it is also applied to the gift of justice; thus, in both parts, an excess of measure and order is committed, from which diseases and similar things afterward arise. We would never be afflicted by these if we lived according to the Law and the Prayer. <note>Refers to the Lord's Prayer ("Give us our daily bread").</note> Thus we conceive diseases from the mother's womb. And because it is necessary for us to be born again, we also conceive those diseases again—that is, through our daily bread. Therefore, if we must fundamentally speak and write about the **Regimen**: <margin>A rule and diet must be prescribed.</margin> we can prescribe no other Regimen or diet than that one must remain within the law of justice and of the food for which we pray. In this law, all health is continually preserved and guarded from diseases. But if we do not keep this regimen, then we will not retain our healthy body. However, because God is beneficent and does not take vengeance for such offenses and contempt for the regimen He gave, He created the **Physician**, who is like unto Himself, just as Christ said to his disciples: *Forgive sins as often as the sinner groans.* <note>A paraphrase of the mandate for mercy and forgiveness.</note> So also the Physician should be ready to heal as often as diseases fall upon us. <margin>It is the duty of Physicians to be able to heal all diseases.</margin> By the power of this command, Physicians heal every disease, even lepers. This is how medicine stands, and the Physician with it: that they heal and preserve the body by the virtue of Him who also preserves the soul in the body.

Therefore, it is an arduous and exceptional thing to administer the office of medicine; <margin>The Physician's province is hard.</margin> it is not a matter as light as some have been persuaded. For just as Christ commanded his disciples: *Go, cleanse the lepers, make the lame walk, give sight to the blind, etc.,* so these things pertain no less to Physicians than to the Apostles. Now, he who is unskilled in healing leprosy does not understand the power of medicine. He who does not restore the feet of the lame is unworthily called a Physician—and so on for all other things. Therefore, let it be established by those who know that the Physician is appointed by God, not merely <margin>For which diseases the Physician is primarily appointed.</margin> for catarrh, headaches, abscesses, or toothaches, but rather for Leprosy, Apoplexy, Epilepsy, and similar diseases, with none excepted. If we cannot cure these, then both our art and wisdom...

...wisdom fails us, though it is necessarily required here. Without the blessing of God, nothing succeeds. Indeed, all medicine is found upon the earth. But that which ought to penetrate, or "touch the nerve" (as they say), is lacking. That is to say: the medicines have indeed grown until the harvest, but the reapers have not yet arrived. If the reapers of true Medicine were to arrive, without the interference of false **sophistry** <note>original: "sophistica". Paracelsus uses this to describe the traditional, theoretical medicine of his time (based on Galen and Aristotle), which he viewed as empty wordplay.</note>, then we would cleanse the lepers, restore sight to the blind, and so on. For all this power is in the earth and is growing there. But ambition and the boasting of sophistry do not allow the mysteries of nature and the **great works of God** <note>original: "magnalia Dei"</note> to burst forth. They judge medicine to be just as they are themselves: men whose science and integrity would barely fill a single **dram** <note>original: "drachma vnica". A small unit of weight; Paracelsus is insulting the tiny amount of actual knowledge held by mainstream doctors.</note>. They cloak their own ignorance

<margin>The excuses of physicians.</margin>
with this response: *This disease is incurable.* By this, they not only betray their own stupidity but also a lie. For God never sent any disease for which He did not also create a medicine. But it is the habit of our ignorance to forget that God has granted us a body, and continues to grant it daily. Would He not, therefore, also have conferred medicine upon us, by which we might heal occurring diseases at His appointed time? And concerning this medicine, hardly anyone has easily given it a thought; but here our opposing party torments itself greatly.

<margin>Why the sick need a physician</margin>
Although many things could be recounted in this place—namely, that God wills that sick men live upon the earth no less than the healthy, and that for the sake of one man He often strikes a whole legion and weakens them with diseases—nonetheless, out of His grace, He has always communicated suitable medicine, and said that the sick have need of a physician.

Now, if they need a physician, they need him for this reason: to be healed by him. Unless this happens, why else would they have need of him? They have need of one who heals them, and does not let the sick lie there or merely flatter them. And these things prove that it is lawful for us to be able to heal whatever is sick, whether it be leprosy, blindness, or lameness. For all are sick and stand in need of a physician. It is indeed true that a man who uses his eyes for gambling, falsehood, and deceptions has no need of them. Likewise, he who uses his tongue petulantly for cursing has no need of it. If God deprived such a person of that member, and he said to the physician, *I am sick, my eyes have need of a doctor,* then in those schools they will answer that *he has no need of them,* just as a lecher has no need of his feet. But these matters belong to God, not to man. It is not beside the point that a physician might be excused, not in just one but in all diseases that hinder some evil; for those who are thus afflicted are even considered more blessed than the wicked who are healthy. For those whom God loves, He chastises—yet in such a secret way that it is discovered by no physician.

Now indeed, so that we do not forget the secrets and the great faithfulness of God, you ought to understand how illustrious a medicine has been created by <term>God</term> <note>Paracelsus emphasizes God as the "Arch-Physician" from whom all natural healing properties flow.</note>. For it heals not only those diseases we have mentioned so far, but also those that are inherent from birth: such as congenital blindness, paralysis, etc. If medicine does not ascend to this height, then surely many pages in medicine are still blank. Although most of them are filled, they are filled with empty trifles. And yet, those things which especially ought to have been moved have not yet been moved. For if we turn our eyes to the stupendous miracles of nature, we shall see births and outcomes that are plainly admirable: such as that a **lion is born dead** <note>This refers to a widespread medieval belief that lion cubs were born dead and only came to life after three days when the father lion roared over them—often used as a metaphor for the Resurrection.</note>, and achieves life by the loud cry of its parent, which is a much greater thing than obtaining sight. Truly, the lion has not only this, but many other things which we do not yet know or have explored. In these things, nature prefigures for us how much we lack in the secrets of nature. Therefore, we wrongly extol ourselves so much with our honors, since we have not yet leaped over those boundaries which we think we passed long ago. The day of our jubilation is a day of misery and very bitter. For here there is not even a beginning, to say nothing of the hidden things of nature. And those who say these things are received with hisses. And yet, all those books which they bring forward and boast of are mere trifles. Your works testify to this: that your doctrine is worth nothing. You seize the key of wisdom and science, yet you do not enter its inner chambers. In this way, surely, those things required for a Physician must be understood, just as it has been proposed successively in all the chapters, and thus is most firmly founded in the nature of things. For nature itself does not lie open even to its own secrets; indeed, scarcely at all. A marvelous thing was the degeneration or variation of peoples, since there was originally only one Adam, from whom we were all produced so differently. What was the cause of this? Only the secrets of nature, which itself also produced giants; which...

This provides a small "kitchen profit" which allows the idle to live contentedly at home, unconcerned with the art itself. But if such great profit comes from urine, why perform more laborious works, when they practice medicine solely for the sake of scraping together coins?

# BOOK SECOND,
## CHAPTER I.

<margin>Every seed is threefold</margin>
**N**ow you shall understand from my words how three substances come together into one body; attend to this example. Every seed is threefold: that is, it is one seed in which three substances exist and grow. And just as only one seed appears at hand, so these three seem to be only one. Now, every thing is united in the seed, not divided, but it is the very conjunction of unity. As in a walnut, there are wood, bark, and roots. These three things are indeed different, yet joined in one seed. So also is man. In the beginning, he is one seed, whose **outer shell** <note>original: "cortex"</note> is the sperm. No one has ever seen the seed itself because of its smallness and subtlety. Now, men are born from the seed. If generation begins, then these three things grow, each one mixed and united in its own nature into one body, not three: as a man grows,

<margin>Man is one, and threefold.</margin>
he turns into bones, flesh, and blood. Although these are three, yet it is at least one growing thing. Thus these three constitute one body, and they themselves are invisible within it. So these three substances grow out, mixed in unity, joined until their appointed time: like a tree, which first grows into a pith. That pith is a triple substance, but at least one wood. And that these three substances are in it is demonstrated by Art <note>Paracelsus often uses "Art" to mean Alchemy, the process of laboratory separation.</note>, Nature, and Death, by which any thing is separated and moves apart as it ought to be. Thus you have the principle of these things: that they coalesce among themselves and are one, and each has its own office for completing the body.

<margin>The office of the three substances. Of Sulphur also threefold.</margin>
Furthermore, know this: what the office of each might be. From **Sulphur** <term>Sulphur: In Paracelsian thought, one of the "Three Primes" (Tria Prima) representing the principle of combustibility, growth, and oily substance, not just the yellow mineral.</term> the body grows; that is, the whole body is Sulphur, and a Sulphur so subtle that it is consumed invisibly by fire. Now, there are many kinds of Sulphur. Blood is one Sulphur, flesh is another, the principal organs another, the marrow another, and so on. But indeed, there is "volatile" Sulphur. The bones, which are themselves varied, are Sulphurs, but made from "fixed" Sulphur. And in the separation performed through science, each Sulphur is found as it truly is. Now, the solidification of the body is from **Salt** <term>Salt: The principle of stability, structure, and solidity in the Tria Prima.</term>: that is, without salt nothing tangible would be present. For from Salt the diamond has its hardness and iron has its own; from it lead has its softness, and alabaster its own, and so forth. All freezing and coagulation is from Salt. Therefore, one salt is in the bones, another in the blood, another in the flesh, another in the brain, and similarly in others. For as many kinds of Sulphurs as there are, there are also just as many Salts.

<margin>How many kinds of Salts. Also of Mercury.</margin>
The third is **Mercury** <term>Mercury: The principle of fluidity, spirit, and "liquor" in the Tria Prima.</term>; it is the liquor. All bodies have their own liquors in which they consist, so that the blood has one liquor, the flesh another, the bones another, and the marrow another. Therefore, it has Mercury. And yet it is at least one, which has as many various species and differences as there are Sulphurs and Salts. Thus, as man has need of a body, so he necessarily requires a compaction—that is, a solidification—and likewise a liquor. And these three are man, who is only one body. Therefore, you perceive that there is only one body, but three things.

<margin>The nature of Sulphur, the nature of Salt, the nature of Mercury.</margin>
So, being composed as one, they constitute one body, and yet they are three. Therefore, Sulphur burns away, for it is pure Sulphur. Salt turns into **alkali** <term>alkali: the solid, ash-like residue left after a substance is burnt and its salts are extracted</term> because it is fixed. Mercury evaporates; not burning indeed,

but

...but receding by the power of fire. Thus, from these three all dissolutions arise: just as a tree, when its moisture departs, withers away. Hence, if the **sulphur** <note>original: "sulphur"; in Paracelsian chemistry, Sulphur represents the principle of combustion and growth.</note> is taken away, no form remains. If the **salt** <note>original: "sal"; the principle of stability and solidification.</note> is removed, no coagulation remains, but the tree collapses and flows away, like a barrel deprived of its hoops. If this be a body, it is made of at least one nature, such as a **pear** <note>original: "pyrus".</note>. This is the same as saying that a pear tree of only one kind bears pears. This should be understood in the same way regarding other trees. You should know, moreover, that however many kinds of fruits there are, there are just as many various species in the **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmo"; the "little world," meaning the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>. From which it follows that he who knows the pear also knows its tree, as well as its three <margin>The necessary knowledge of the three substances.</margin> pear-like substances. The same must also be understood regarding diseases. It must be so established with these that, if you see a disease, you say: "this is a pear, this is an **apple**" <note>original: "pomum".</note>: that is, those three substances ought to be as well known to you as they exist in the disease as they are in that tree. Therefore, if these three things produce pears of one kind, not of three; and in their **ultimate matter** <note>original: "ultima materia"; the final, physical form a substance takes.</note> they have three substances: then diseases must also be known by an equal rationale, because they have a sulphurous body, a **mercurial** <note>original: "mercurialem"; the principle of liquidity and volatility.</note> liquor, and their coagulation from salt: which three are born from three others. Therefore, a suitable **medicine** <note>original: "Medicina".</note> must be a fire which consumes—that is, a fire of essence—and without fire there is no Medicine. For just as fire consumes the sulphur of the tree, so that neither sulphur nor tree remains, so it is necessary for medicine to be a consumption, not only in the sulphur, but also in the liquor and the salt. For in diseases there are **volatiles** <note>original: "volatilia"; substances that easily evaporate or change state.</note>: and though fixed things may indeed be encountered, they are nonetheless subject to medicine so that they become volatiles.

<margin>Diseases must be noted and expressed by name.</margin> Now truly, speaking of the nature of these things—that is, of diseases—a single name is enough, just as with fruits, as has been said: "This is a pear." For by that name all things are comprised. "This is an apple." Again, by this name all things are contained. The same is the comprehension of diseases. For if you see **leprosy** <note>original: "leprā".</note>, say: *This is leprosy*: for that is enough. Nor should one attend here to its coldness, or heat, or moisture. For from those qualities <margin>Qualities in diseases are not to be considered.</margin> nothing is born or generated in bodies and substances that is required for knowledge: since medicine in Leprosy proceeds as if in a Regeneration: all of which things happen without such considerations. For you are not going to make a certain tree by looking at its color, or form, or any similar thing, but only its **seed** <note>original: "semen".</note>. For all other things finally follow by themselves. For they are the substances of the ultimate matter, that is, their lives. And therefore, nothing of importance is placed in the qualities themselves. Do likewise also in **jaundice** <note>original: "icteritia".</note>. If you call it by its name, judge no further whether it be cold or moist. For its cure behaves like an axe that fells a tree: or like a fire that consumes all volatile things. And just as the example is in fire, that it consumes all things: so also medicine must be constituted. One must not estimate where there is heat or cold: but simply that which the nature and property of the **arcana** <note>original: "arcanorum"; the secret, restorative healing essences within natural substances.</note> demand must be taken away and removed. For just as there is something that snatches away life: so also something or some cause exists which takes away diseases. If you pluck a pear from a tree, the tree is now empty. By these same names and causes you ought to pluck and cut out diseases: not being occupied with the <margin>Diseases which are to be cut out.</margin> substance and body of the pear, but its stalk, by which it is fastened. From this, now understand more closely what medicine is, and in what knowledge it consists.

But now attend to these examples. In certain successions, winter and summer are changed so that one follows the other repeatedly, now cold, now heat. Look for the same in the body. But no one would call this a disease. One expels the other of its own accord. For man is subject to both summer and winter. And although during winter he might be surrounded by a circle or boundary of fire so that he felt no winter: nevertheless, winter itself still executes its operations in him, as does any month according to its measure. And this is hindered by no exclusion. In the same way, man is affected by summer. Why, then, does the physician refuse to know such things, and refuse to weigh the celestial courses on a similar scale? As if nature had erred. Which error they themselves strive to correct, with a most unsuccessful outcome. These causes may indeed seem to lead to diseases, since as winter, so also the heat of summer is adverse to man: but in truth they are not diseases. For thus the stars also rise, with days interspersed, stirring up cold and heat. Similar things happen through fevers, etc. What else moves such things but a **celestial cause**? Yet the Physician assigned such things to the microcosm itself by his own judgment, since he had not admitted heaven itself into consideration. Whence he is rightly entangled in errors. Then also this...

He also argues that many bodily states are natural reflections of celestial and seasonal cycles rather than diseases to be "cured" by traditional means.</summary>
