Having introduced the Three Primes—Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt—on the previous page, he now attacks the traditional Galenic system of "degrees" and "humors," replacing them with a chemical and theological model of disease based on the behavior of these three fundamental substances.</meta>

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>ON THE THREE PRIME SUBSTANCES</header>
<sig>E 2</sig>

# ON THE THREE PRIME SUBSTANCES

<margin>A single degree of cold, as of the other qualities.</margin> They <note>The traditional Galenic physicians of Paracelsus's time.</note> forbid it, lest we surely increase the degrees; that is, what you can achieve with the first degree, you should not attempt to perform with the third or fourth. They say, of course, that the stomach cannot bear something too weak: otherwise, the colder a thing is by one degree, the more convenient and useful it will be, so that the dose may be reduced. But this is no slight error when they say: "This is colder than that by one or two degrees," when in fact there is only one single degree of coldness itself.

It would be much more accurate if they spoke thus: "This herb has one half-ounce of cold; but that one weighs two ounces of cold," provided that an equal weight of each is taken. From which follows this: "Take of cold, as you find it, one drachm. Administer it in a fever." But because they choose specific herbs—for example, not **purslane** <note>original: "portulacam"; a cooling herb.</note>, but **water-lily** <note>original: "nenufar".</note>; not **chamomile**, but **pepper**—by this very act they reveal that they seek neither cold nor heat, but the **arcana** <note>original: "arcana"; secret healing essences or "mysteries" within substances.</note> themselves, which are nevertheless taken for the degrees themselves. If they only knew that there is only one cold, one heat, one moisture, and one dryness, they would not find it difficult to abandon their current path. If indeed reason and experience dictated that double or triple versions of hot, cold, dry, or moist existed, I would gladly concede to their opinion.

<margin>Humors are not to be placed in any bodies.</margin> These things said so far aim at this: that it may be known that great errors have been committed until now in judging the degrees, as well as in the **complexions** <note>original: "complexionibus"; the traditional balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a person.</note> of things which are not rightly understood, because all things were considered as one in those four. For they established four **humors** <note>The traditional fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, when in truth there exists only the single liquor of **Mercury**; of which not only four natures, but species and properties, or manifestations, are found to be nearly infinite. Yet Mercury alone is not the cause of these, but the other two <note>Sulfur and Salt.</note> concur with it. For every single disease exists from these three according to their composition.

<margin>How diseases arise.</margin> What the cause of the remaining two might be is handed down in special chapters. For diseases arise just as **Lucifer** <note>Referring to the fall of the rebel angel in Christian theology.</note> did in heaven: namely, from his own pride and elation, which afterwards stirs up all internal wars. As if <margin>The wondrous nature of Mercury.</margin> **Mercury**, on account of its liquor—which exists as something truly great and wondrous—exalts itself. For God created it above all wonders. If it now ascends and does not remain in its proper degree, then that is the beginning of discord. The same is the logic for **sulfur** and **salt**.

---

<margin>From what ulcerations come.</margin> For if **salt** exalts and separates itself, what else is it but a corroding and consuming thing? Wherever its pride dominates, there it gnaws and eats away. From this gnawing are then born ulcerations, cancer, gangrene, and so on. If salt remained in its proper seat, a human being would never at any time suffer ulceration in the body. If **sulfur** swells with ambition, it then melts the body, just as the Sun melts snow. And **Mercury** itself, by its own subtlety, proceeds and ascends to such an extent that it induces sudden and instantaneous death whenever it exalts itself beyond its degrees. For it was so ordained by nature that it should stay within its degrees without pride. Yet there are as many "heads" as there are senses, which by some force break through their established limits. Now indeed, <margin>The contrariety of the body's principles is fatal. The equal excellence of all things. Greed made gold more excellent than silver.</margin> because nothing among carnal creatures ought to be eternal, it is necessary for those things to be exalted and separated in so many ways through those manifold gifts, virtues, and operations which they possess. And just as a kingdom destroys itself, so also does health. Therefore, it should be known that the goodness and excellence of every single thing is entirely the same as any other. Thus a **carbuncle** <note>A red gemstone, often a ruby or garnet.</note> is no better than a **pumice** stone, nor is a **fir** tree more ignoble than a **cypress**. The light of Nature proves this. But he who made gold more excellent than silver was compelled to do so by greed. For no less a gift was given to silver than to gold. Therefore, those things were so established not from the wisdom of nature, but from human judgment.

Now, if **Death** sees the imminent dissolution of the kingdom <note>i.e., the human body.</note>, she rushes in; just as a kingdom that is about to fall comes into the hands of foreigners. So if those three substances loosen their union and concord, then Death stands nearby, and by her industry she gradually tames and seizes one of them after another, until finally, having overcome some, she occupies the whole kingdom, from which she can then be ejected by no help. But if that does not happen, and Death only lies in wait for this or that substance in part, then a medicine is at hand, which comes as an aid to nature and restores it to wholeness. Thus, whatever salt has eaten away, **comfrey** <note>original: "consolida"; a plant used historically to heal wounds and bones.</note> heals; and as much as has departed through the dissolution of sulfur, **saffron** <note>original: "crocus".</note> restores and replaces; and that which Mercury has made too thin, **gold** thickens. And by this help, nature is succored. But just as any kingdom is not occupied without manifest and irreparable damage, so also the flesh which has been eroded by salt is replaced as "dead" <note>original: "fatua"; meaning tasteless, silly, or in this context, non-functional/scarred tissue.</note>, and does not...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases are caused when the Three Primes (Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt) "rebel" and overstep their natural bounds, much like Lucifer’s fall. He rejects the Galenic system of degrees and humors, proposing instead that medicines like gold, saffron, and comfrey act by restoring the balance of these three substances.</summary>

...nor can a loss, once accepted, be equally repaired. The same is true of the rest. For this reason, greater care must be applied so that these bodies are maintained in their integrity. They are completely corrupted by a simple cause; by a slight occasion, the sharpness of the air <note>original: "asperitas auri"; likely referring to the environmental influence or "sharpness" of the atmosphere on the body's balance.</note> acts against them. For God has established these things with us in this way: we have possessed medicine from the very beginning of things until now, and from this time forward we shall possess it until the end of the world, with the very same force, power, and virtue that He conferred and imparted to His Apostles for healing the sick. This healing proceeds from the unique virtue of the divine mandate.

<margin>
The shared lot of Physicians and Apostles.
</margin>
<margin>
The allegory of Jonah.
</margin>
Therefore, physicians have received the same mandate as the Apostles. If they live under this mandate and are bound to it, it is necessary that they act according to it, and that they learn and recognize the true and genuine foundation. But many "adulterers" exist: that is, many transgress that mandate, and many despise and scorn it. To what shall I compare this? Surely to that saying of Christ: "A wicked and adulterous generation," which desires to see signs but does not wish to perform them. Therefore, no sign shall be given to it except the sign of **JONAH**, hidden in the belly of the fish. So too should they have searched in the earth, just as the Jews sought the resurrection in the whale.

<margin>
How the three substances are reduced to the four Elements.
</margin>
<margin>
What the Elements produce.
</margin>
<margin>
The Spagyrist.
</margin>
Furthermore, this art is so manifold, and the mentioned three substances—**Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt**—are so certain, that they can be taught according to four generations; that is, they can be referred back to the nature of the matrices and the Elements. Or rather: all things are born from the four Elements. From the Earth come herbs, wood, and the like. From Water come metals, stones, and their minerals. From the Air comes dew and <term>Tereniabin (a medicinal manna or "honey-dew" believed to fall from the sky)</term>. From Fire comes thunder, lightning, snow, and rain. But these matters I leave to the study of Meteors, which is established from the light of nature itself. Let us now proceed further. The <term>Microcosm (the human being as a "little world" reflecting the universe)</term> itself, if it goes into its own dissolution, becomes earth; the virtue of which is so wonderful that it most readily produces fruits from itself which are sown within it. This is the preparation that the physician ought to know. Thus, from this very body arises the second Element, Water. Since this water is the matrix of minerals, the <term>Spagyrist (an alchemist who separates and recombines substances)</term> produces a Ruby from it. Likewise, this preparation brings forth the third Element, Fire, from which hailstones arise; and the fourth, the Aereal Element, which, when enclosed in a glass vessel, distills dew for itself from its own ascending spirit. Many have begun to write about this generation, but they have despaired in the actual work. For it is not fitting for a pig to be occupied in a field planted with turnips. But another transmutation remains after this, which bestows all kinds of Sulfurous, Mercurial, and Saline substances, just as it is fitting to demonstrate to the world of these Microcosms. And many have indeed labored diligently to find within man his health, the water of life, the philosopher’s stone, the arcanum, the balsam, potable gold, and the like. In this they acted rightly. For all those things lie hidden within him, and they also exist in the external world. As they are in the external world, so they are assimilated in our internal world. Do not be persuaded of anything else but this: nothing exists so black that it does not have some whiteness within it; and conversely, nothing is so white that it does not foster blackness. The same is true of the other colors. Therefore, just as these colors are produced, so too are those things previously mentioned. Salt is white, yet it contains all colors within itself. Sulfur burns; therefore it contains all oils. Mercury flows; therefore it encloses all humors within itself. And so it is with the rest, which we refer back to philosophy.

<margin>
What the healing of wounds is.
</margin>
<margin>
Man is Mumia.
</margin>
In this way, man is his own physician. For if he helps his own nature, then nature provides him with the necessary things and bestows a garden upon him according to the account of his whole <term>Anatomy (here meaning the structural and functional map of the body's inner nature)</term>. For if we unroll the condition of all things from the bottom up, we find that our Nature itself exists as our physician; that is, it has within itself all those things which it needs. I ask you to observe wounds in passing. What is missing from a wound? Nothing except the flesh itself. This must grow from within; it cannot be added from without. Therefore, the healing of wounds is nothing but a defense, so that nature is not overwhelmed by external injuries, but can proceed unhindered in its own action. Thus it heals itself, smoothes itself, and arranges itself, just as the <term>Surgery (the manual art of healing)</term> of skilled physicians teaches. For man himself is <term>Mumia (the innate vital force or "balsam" that heals the body)</term>. *Mumia* is the balsam that heals wounds. Mastic, gums, and litharge do not contribute even a tiny bit to the generation of flesh, except insofar as they defend nature, lest it be disturbed in its operation. This is also the principle of internal diseases. If nature defends itself, then it alone [heals] all...

This regarding the power of medicine must be understood in a twofold way: namely, the medicine of the Great World <note>the Macrocosm or the universe</note> and the medicine of Man. The others are the healers. These use the knowledge of Nature itself. For example, if someone is wounded, two methods are established for healing the wound: Defense and Curation. Defensive treatment was handed down above. Healing is "curative" if a wound becomes internal <note>original: "ventricosum," literally "having a belly" or cavity</note>, such that medicines must be applied that generate flesh. Once this kind of medicine is placed into the wound, Nature rises up from within and digests the medicine in the wound so that it becomes flesh: thus, the wound itself acts like a stomach. For without a "stomach" <note>the capacity to process and transform matter</note>, none of these things can happen. But these things are explained more fully in the study of surgery. By the same reasoning, you can understand regarding other diseases how one kind of knowledge resides in the physician, and the other in the nature of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the "small world," meaning the human being</note>.

Now, in these matters, it must be understood that man and those external things foster a certain consensus and similarity among themselves while they mutually affect and admit one another. From this you can understand with what strength nature resists death, so much so that it calls upon and summons the heaven itself and the earth, and all their virtues and powers, to its aid. And in exactly the same way as you have learned that the soul—having gathered all its strength and calling upon God himself with all its heart and all its power—struggles to resist the devil: so nature has an equal concern to assemble and employ all the defenses which were ordained by God for the defeat of death. For nature is shaken and struck by such a horror of cruel and bitter death, which stands fiercely before its eyes—death which our eyes do not see, nor our hands touch, yet nature sees and feels it.

<margin>The wisdom of Nature</margin>
Nature herself, however, sees it, touches it, and knows it. Therefore, she summons to herself all celestial and earthly virtues so that she may resist that formidable enemy.

<margin>
How horrible death is.
</margin>
For death is truly terrifying, cruel, and bitter. If he who made death—namely Christ on the Mount of Olives—trembled so greatly at the sight of it that a bloody sweat flowed from his whole body, and he prayed to the heavenly Father for it to be taken and moved away: it is not without cause that nature herself should tremble violently in its presence. For the greater the knowledge of death, the greater the caution, preservation, and the search for medicine which the wise man pursues.

### CHAPTER III.

And such is the "great composition": <term>Great Composition</term> <note>Paracelsus's term for a medicine that unites the powers of the entire universe</note> that is, true medicine, as has been said, proceeds from heaven, earth, from all elements, and from all their powers. And this is that composition in which the physician must sweat while learning: this is the true Recipe <note>original: *Recipe*, the traditional command 'take' at the start of a prescription</note>. These are the "simples" <note>medicinal plants or ingredients</note>—not in number, but in their composition—from which the entire external man is composed. When this is joined and united, all Remedies, Medicines, and <term>Arcana</term> <note>secret, powerful healing essences</note> are joined within it; in this, all powers are enclosed. And these strengths can struggle against the diseases that afflict man. As for those powers which do not afflict the present man, their secrets either work among themselves or remain at rest. 

Consider this example of the wood in the hands of the sculptor. That craftsman carves infinite forms and images from a single piece of wood. In the same way, the body of man produces infinite diseases, and yet there is only one body from which they are all "carved." Now, just as one image of wood is burned and consumed by fire no less than another, so in the "great composition" there is a similar medicine which, like fire, purifies and separates the impure from the pure. But because ambiguous remedies are often proposed, even if they are taken in the proper order, the hope they offer is never free from danger.

Thus, in this great composition, the entire world—namely the virtues of heaven and earth—and the whole man of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>Man viewed as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note> is established. That is, just as the world exists within him as if in a drop, so man himself—with all his limbs, joints, nature, and property—consists of both the healthy and the bad, the sick and the good. Thus, if he takes these same things, he takes his own <term>Limbus</term> <note>the primordial "matrix" or matter from which man was created</note> from which he was born; he takes his very self, and unites his physical body with that from which it is made, into that which it lacks. And this composition stands above other medicines just as the Sun stands above all the stars. What is the Sun other than the Moon? What is night other than day? Except that they are distinct, the Sun for its own light, and the day for its own. In this way, the heaven is distinguished from the earth, and all flowers, roots, gems, and stones are distinguished. Similarly, it is worth the effort for the Physician to know the differences between medicines, no differently than if he were separating darkness from light, or day from night.

<margin>
Which medicines are to be distinguished.
</margin>
For it is fitting for a physician to distinguish medicines in the same way that Moses describes in the Book of Genesis: how Jehovah separated one thing from another—today this, tomorrow that, the day after another. So we too must consider that we have a matter in our hands clearly similar to what God had; we must possess the knowledge of separating and distinguishing the black from the white, the clear from the obscure—that is, the medicine from the mud in which it lies buried. For that is how God created it.

But what should be said of its operation? This very thing: it must be made clear. For God does not want it to be known in any other way than as the axe that cuts down the tree. Thus He requires His work in medicine to be considered: and with equal efficacy and power that...

<margin>The fixed period of all things.</margin>
So far, then, after health itself has been described in this manner—along with man and his diseases—under a general Theory and Physics, from which all chapters (especially those assigned to diseases) are deduced and founded upon this general Theory: now, furthermore, we must also treat of death and its accidents, such as time, etc. A constituted and prefixed time is set for all things, namely, how long they ought to endure, whether that be for good or for ill. For so even the Saints have their prescribed goal, which being finished, they cease to live on this earth. There is also a limit for the wicked. All things are bound by God to a defined time. The boundary of this time is death. It sits at our side and waits for our internal battles, seizing the opportunity of where it might break in. lest it neglect any moment of chance, but continually obeys its celestial Lord. <margin>What and of what sort humans are.</margin>

And even if the whole world were to rely on one person; before God, however, that person is nothing, nor does their dignity stand in the way. Thus our life is constituted, truly, like a treasure that is not at all safe. If we indeed guard it diligently by all means and labors, what shall we gain by that industry? This, namely: that under the most accurate and sharp-eyed guardianship, it shall be stolen from us. Is it not indeed a faithful guardianship if a sick man lying down flees to God and implores Him for help? If he solicits a Physician and cries out for aid to be provided? And yet, when he hoped for it least, he is cut down and snatched away. Is he not a sufficiently fortified King who, gathering all his forces and undertaking a battle against the enemy, surrounds and almost buries himself on all sides most firmly with a rampart and ditches, and fights surrounded by equipment both horse and foot as if by a bronze wall? And yet he, when he thinks all things are most safe and secure, is pierced through by a rushing bullet.

<margin>What things follow death.</margin>

It is the bailiff and the minister who invites us to the judgment of God. ### CHAPTER IV.

And although we have indicated death, which is the ultimate goal of all things, this treatise is not yet finished; necessity demands that we dwell longer on these matters so that what has been proposed may become more clearly open. Therefore, proceeding further in a general way, we shall speak of the three substances lifting themselves up in pride—that is, leaping beyond the rank appointed for them in their **exaltation** <note>In alchemy, an "exaltation" is the raising of a substance to a higher power; here, Paracelsus uses it to describe a pathological over-activity where a substance "gets above itself"</note>—and in what manner that surely happens. First of all, we shall speak of Mercury. Since it is understood that Mercury is a liquor within man, and a manifold one at that—from which cause also manifold natures proceed from it—I would now have you know that there exist three modes and ways of its separation. The first way by which Mercury rises is **Distillation**. The second is **Sublimation**. The third is **Precipitation**. <margin>Three ways of separating Mercury.</margin> And although various species exist within these modes, there is no need to enumerate each one. It is enough that the principal ones be handed down here. Just as besides the three ways mentioned, three other modes remain: so also in the body itself. And this is the **Operation of Nature**.

Now it must first be taught what it is that drives Mercury into these three orders: that is, leads it into that path by which it is sublimated, distilled, and precipitated. For it does not do this of itself; rather, it is necessary that it take something from the outside, through which it may rise and be separated by a "divorce" from the other two <note>The other two substances: Sulfur and Salt</note>. For example: Pride was not in the nature of Lucifer, but he took it from elsewhere. Therefore he lifted himself up above others. So here too, this thing is something other than its nature: which ought to be understood in this way. That which moves Mercury from its rank <margin>From what Mercury is separated.</margin> is heat, and through heat it rises. Now this heat belongs to the **Digestive power**; and is therefore **Accidental** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing’s nature but happens to it externally</note>. If this heat is intense and full, being then more powerful than the Mercury, it elevates it—that is, it prevails and agitates it, like wood which is ignited and burns from the intense heat of the Sun. Thus Mercury itself also rises <margin>Three species of Mercury from the fervor of heat.</margin> from an external and foreign heat. Now this heat drives it in three ways, according to the knowledge of its mistress, **Mechanics** <note>Paracelsus views the mechanical/chemical processes of the body as a form of "craft" or internal engineering</note>. Thus there is another heat which emerges from the commotion of the body, no weaker than the former, yet more variable, and not as certain as the first. Yet by whatever reason it is stirred up, it ignites the Mercury and brings it to an ascent. Besides these, know that there exists also a third kind, stirred up by the stars: as when a certain ignited star indicates a presage of sudden death, or of other Mercurial diseases this year, at that time, and so forth. Thus there are three foreign heats capable of lifting Mercury: from whose ascent diseases then follow, that is, the "precipitations of pride" into death. Therefore it is necessary for the Physician to know and be able to distinguish the heat of exercise and the heat of the stars. For thus he will be able to protect his patients and prescribe for them a certain regimen and preservation based on this consideration.

Furthermore, observe the manner in which Mercury is ignited. There are three modes. For it is ignited either in the dry or in the depressed, which can be either moist or dry. Now Mercury lies in the whole body, in all the members. As many members: so many species of Mercury. <margin>In how many ways Mercury is ignited. How many species of Mercury.</margin> To this, recognize that there are many parts in the body with their own offices: and thus, this is the office of Reason, this of vision, this of hearing. Whence various kinds of its diseases emerge. From this one it plunders reason; from that one it takes away the veins; from another it takes the tongue. Thus the heat begins. Invading the body, if it ignites it, then to where <meta>Catchword: potissimum (chiefly/most especially)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how the "Three Substances" cause disease. Having introduced Mercury as the principle of liquidity and volatility, the text now details how external or internal heat causes Mercury to "circulate" or "precipitate" within the body, leading to specific categories of illness like gout, insanity, or skin diseases. It then transitions to the second substance, Salt.</meta>

# FROM THE THREE PRIMARY SUBSTANCES

->C 2<-
<meta>catchword: aforesaid</meta>

it primarily invades a location, and there it begins its operation—that is, it begins to ignite, as if that place were a hearth in which the **Mercury** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, Mercury represents the volatile, fluid, and "spirituous" principle of the body, not just the liquid metal.</note> lay. For example, if heat were to arise from satiety or fullness, and that fullness of heat were so subtle that it equaled the spirit of wine, it would be raised up so far that it would penetrate into the brain along with that spirit. Then, because a sufficiently strong heat exists, the Mercury wanders further than its proper boundary, and whatever it touches, it strikes and harms. The same must also be understood regarding the heart. If heat should occupy the heart, then the heart would be like a hearth from which it would eject its own Mercury. Wherever that Mercury reaches, a disease is generated there.

Thus, in strong <term>complexions</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to an individual's specific balance of humors and substances; their physical constitution.</note>, in which there is daily excess or immoderate exercise, or even a star composed as we have described, then the entire body is moved—that is, all its members are established in heat. From this it happens that the whole Mercury is carried up and down, and is distilled through the body no differently than in a **Pelican** <note>An alchemical vessel designed for "circulatory" distillation, where the vapors condense and flow back into the base.</note>. But if it climbs to the highest degree, it then completes its wickedness—that is, if it is certainly intensified and made subtle. Whether this happens in the body by distilling, or by sublimating, or by precipitating, so that it reaches its supreme essence, it is then cast down from its "throne," and thereafter a disease of the body and instantaneous death occur. For before that time, it does not break out there, but has a little space for ascension, circulation, and preparation, until it reaches the extremes. Only then does it slide back and get thrown down to the depths.

So too, if a certain star should seize and inflame its own part of the body, it will not strike until it has ascended to the ultimate subtlety. And then it gives birth to its diseases. Thus Mercury is driven into its "exaltation" by external heat, which is nothing other than a failing—that is, a nursery of diseases.

<margin>The effects of the ignition of Mercury.</margin>
Thus, as has been said, three ways or modes exist: One brings on sudden death and its various types. This is the **distillation** of Mercury. Another induces **Podagra** (gout in the feet), **Chiragra** (gout in the hands), and **Arthritis**. That is the **precipitation** of Mercury. The third produces **Mania** and **Phrensy** (delirium). That is the **Sublimation** of Mercury. To each of these, as well as to their specific types, peculiar chapters have been assigned in their own books, where they are explained more clearly. Thus the "ultimate matter" of things that transcend their proper degree is manifold. For there are various Mercurial types, various functions, various parts, and of all these, various natures, modes, and properties. If these are joined or coincide, they give birth to various diseases, distinguished by different signs, behaviors, and other characteristics.

<margin>The miraculous utility (effects) of Mercury.</margin>
Through its preparation, Mercury becomes so subtle that, because of its inner power of nature, no one can resist it. The reason is that the other two substances <note>Salt and Sulfur</note>, because of the intensity of the heat by whose force they are repressed, are unable to tame it. Hence it is made so subtle that it penetrates both flesh and bones, and thus it transudes and pervades not only through the pores, but even outside of them. From these then arise pustules, the "French disease" <note>original: "morbus gallicus"; a historical term for Syphilis</note>, leprosy, and similar diseases, and they draw their matter and primary cause from there. In what ways this happens is declared in the proper chapters. By this heat of its own, just as it ascends, so in many ways it also excites cold, burning heat, stiffness, and shivering whenever its <term>paroxysm</term> <note>The sudden onset or worsening of symptoms.</note> is imminent. For whenever such a sharp and subtle poison attacks nature itself, then nature is seized by a kind of dread. That dread is the trembling of the body, arising from the fear of cold and heat, which run together. For there is an obstruction and a fluctuation of vapors, just like in a closed pot that boils over and lifts itself up. Cold is truly the matter and cause of any fear. But when the burning heat increases and prevails, the receding cold then gives way to inflammation. And these things have been handed down concerning the wonderful nature of Mercury. Because the various aspects of its nature cannot be more fully described in this place for the sake of brevity, we defer the greatest part of this discussion to our other volumes.

### Chapter V.

<margin>How many ways Salt is changed.</margin>
Since this treatment of Mercury is in some part exact and finished, we shall confer the same right to **Salt**, which is the other part of the three substances. Regarding this, know first that if it should go into its "pride" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the substance becoming overactive or agitated</note>, it is varied in four ways: namely, into **Resolution**, **Calcination**, **Reverberation**, and **Alkalization**. Now the nature of salt is varied, and therefore the types of its preparation and its modes are also various. Many salts are calcined; many are reverberated, alkalized, and resolved. All of these things happen within a human being with no less certainty than they do outside of him in the science of alchemy.

<margin>The resolution of salt.</margin>
At the beginning, however, it is necessary to know what that thing is by which salt is broken down, so that in...

<page-num>58</page-num>

...the aforesaid preparation may rise to the highest grade, from which it should have remained distant. The causes of this are threefold. The first is the **immoderation of food**, by which digestion is destroyed, the parts of the body are led toward excess, and the flesh is rendered too "slippery"—that is, the flesh is made too tender, soft, and marrow-like, and the blood is supplied in an overly luxurious manner. As soon as these abound, the **Salt** <note>In Paracelsian thought, Salt is the principle of stability and physical form. When "corrupted," it causes diseases of the skin and structural tissues.</note> cannot remain in its own essence and integrity, as it properly should. It is just as when a field is too rich and luxurious; it affects the crops so that they rot more quickly. This also happens if the field is flooded by excessive rain, so that the seeds are soaked with abundant moisture and rot, or degenerate into another nature.

<margin>The salts by which it is broken.</margin>
This must be understood similarly regarding other matters. Thus, excessive luxury also excites and drives Salt toward its own "exaltation" <note>An alchemical term meaning to raise a substance to a higher state of power or purity; here, it implies a dangerous over-activity.</note>. This happens most greatly and readily if sexual excess arises from itchy, sweaty, and blood-stirring stimulation. From this, the Salt is greatly increased and becomes wild. From this commotion, the body conceives a "cold spirit"—that is, a wind or gas. This converts the Salt into another nature, more powerful than the rest. For if an abundance of seed is directed into a certain passage, then the nature of the Salt perishes, and too much liquid is contracted, so much so that the Salt passes into excess—that is, into another nature.

The same things also happen due to the **stars** <note>Paracelsus believed the "macrocosm" of the heavens directly influenced the "microcosm" of the human body.</note> falling upon the Salt and its parts. Just as the wind dries things out, so do the stars. As the sun melts hail, so it melts salts. For salts are situated in the body in no different a way than hail lies in the fields. Since their nature is such that they should remain in that state, yet they cannot sufficiently resist external forces, it happens that they are broken and separated. The same logic applies to Salt, which cannot resist. Therefore, when some contrary force attacks, it is easily altered by an abundance of flesh, fat, blood, or tender substance. The same occurs through sexual intercourse, and similarly through the influence of the stars.

Now, indeed, there are some salts which, seized by such changes, melt too much in this manner. If they are liquefied, the nature of the heat existing in the body is such (as we also said regarding **Mercury**) that it attempts to eject the liquefied or resolved Salt outside the body. For that internal heat of the body leaves no resolved Salt within the body but eliminates and ejects it for many reasons. This is true not only of resolved salts but also of those that are **calcined** and **reverberated**. From this, it happens that sweat is salty. For sweat is nothing other than Salt resolved in this way. From this it follows that some sweat flows from the blood, some from the flesh, bones, and marrow; this is confirmed by the fact that different natures of salts exist. For from these arise <term>serpigo</term> <note>A "creeping" skin eruption like ringworm.</note>, <term>impetigo</term> <note>A contagious skin infection characterized by crusting sores.</note>, itching, <term>scabies</term> <note>A general term for itchy skin diseases or mange.</note>, and similar kinds, which are taught in the books on **Surgery** and which we will pass over for now.

<margin>The calcination of salt.</margin>
But if the salts of nature are **calcined** <note>Calcination is the alchemical process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a dry powder or ash.</note>, they become like this: if they lose their liquid, the Salt is then calcined in its own essence. If it loses its moist temperament, the Salt is left behind as a calcined substance, just as in the preparation of **Alum**, **Vitriol**, and other similar things. For you ought to understand this preparation in the same way. Thus, as calcination begins, the moisture departs through sweat. That moisture gnaws and bites at the skin; this itching is then followed by scabs and ulcers. For eventually, if the Salt is without moisture, it breaks out to where it was meant to be driven, and it eats away a hole for itself in that place of the body where it lies hidden. There is more on this in the *Surgery*.

<margin>The reverberation of salt.</margin>
But that which is **reverberated** <note>Reverberation refers to a process of intense, reflected heat in a furnace. In the body, Paracelsus uses it to describe a specific internal "distillation" of salts.</note> is a different kind of salt—namely, a liquid, moist one. In its "Anatomy," it is distilled up and down; this operation is called *Reverberation*. For no external heat or excess can enter into its substance; rather, just as water can never be mixed with oil, so other things cannot be united with this. Thus, spirits fly about above and below this Salt, fluctuating now upward, now downward, until a certain mucilage or viscosity is formed. At that time, it acquires a sharpness greater than is proper. Thus it breaks through: that is, the internal heat drives its substance out of the body. While this happens, holes and other external ulcers are brought upon the body. Thus Salt behaves and operates according to its nature; from this operation, various and manifold diseases arise, which I call **aeruginous wounds** <note>Wounds resembling "aerugo" or verdigris—the green rust found on copper.</note> in my *Surgery*. For any such "rust" is expelled from the interior to the exterior through the pores and performs its work in the air.

<margin>All wounds come from salt.</margin>
Therefore, understand further: no ulcer or other external disease occurs unless it is stirred up by **Salt**, which works together with the air outside on the skin and draws everything out toward the air.

**Salt, Sulfur, Elements, Congelated, Coagulated, Dissolved, Resolved, Morphea, Leprosy**

<margin>What the types of wounds are.</margin>
...entice. From which it can be gathered that salt behaves now in this way, now in that. Hence, ulcers are also called and classified as dry, moist, flowing, or purulent. Although these appear in various ways—partly with the erosion of the substance of the intermediate body, and partly from diet, food, and similar things—it is of no use to treat those details here. For in this way, wounds of salt are generated: wandering, foreign, corroding, cancerous, deep, putrid, dry, and so on. Many other non-cavernous conditions arise as well, such as alopecia <note>original: "alopecia"; patchy hair loss</note>, pustules, scars, condylomata <note>original: "condylomata"; wart-like growths</note>, and even **Morphea** <note>A skin disease causing discolored patches, often a precursor to or subtype of leprosy in older medical texts</note>, **Leprosy**, and all their species. And as the type of salt is, so is the type of pain. Furthermore, whatever the nature of the "star" <note>Paracelsus believed celestial influences (stars) governed the behavior of the internal minerals in the body</note> is, it exerts itself accordingly in its exaltation <note>The state where a substance reaches its peak power or activity</note> and moves the body. Moreover, it must be known that when they take on various forms—as in cancers, fistulas, gangrenes, and corrosions—that very thing happens because of the salt, the nature of which is such. For salt gives the form to all of these, just as they are revealed through the light of nature. As the salt behaves, so it brings on the disease: whether acute, long-lasting, brief, or lethal. All these differences are explained in their own specific chapters.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>From what sulfur is separated.</margin>
**T**he same reasoning applies to **Sulfur**: it is separated and exalted by four things. These are the four Elements. Its nature exists as follows: If it is occupied by the moist element, then it also becomes moist in likeness to it, just as it receives that impression from the Element of Water. Similarly, if it is invaded by the Element of Air, it then becomes dry and takes on a degree of dryness. For in the Element of Water resides humidity, and in Air resides dryness. Thus, sulfur takes on two natures of exaltation.

<margin>Humidity and dryness from air.</margin>
But you should judge the same regarding the two remaining Elements, namely Fire and Earth. If Earth dominates the sulfur, it then renders it cold and preserves it so. Likewise Fire—that is, the firmament <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "firmament" or stars are often identified with the Element of Fire</note>. This makes the sulfur hot, once it has impressed heat upon it.

<margin>Heat from fire.</margin>
Thus, the four Elements are the craftsmen who lead the sulfur to its transformation, so that, having slipped from its proper duty, it degenerates into the arousal of diseases. Various types of these are created—such as cold, hot, moist, or dry—and in every type there are various species, depending on the nature of the sulfurous matter altered within the body and limbs.

<margin>Double cold.</margin>
<margin>Coldness from the earth.</margin>
Thus sulfur becomes cold, and through that Element, it is rendered either volatile or fixed. Now, this cold is manifold: *Congelated and Resolved; Coagulated and Dissolved.* Out of these four Elements, that cold emerges; yet all are grouped under the name of the Element of Earth. For a part of the cold is produced from water, a part from fire, a part from earth, and a part from air. Thus, every single Element contributes some part of the cold. Meanwhile, however, only "Cold" is named as an Element, and for those reasons, I refer the reader to philosophy. Now, consider these colds, which have their essence in coldness. For there is but one single coldness, not many; yet the weight varies—that is, there is more coldness in one than in another. Whence, although one appears colder than another, there exists only one uniform cold. But it is divided according to its substance: into hardness and humidity.

<margin>Double hardness. Humidity, also congelation, unites humidity and hardness.</margin>
Hardness is twofold: *Congelated* and *Coagulated*. Humidity is also twofold: *Dissolved* and *Resolved*. Congelated cold comes from "igneous" <note>fiery</note> cold, such as frozen water, snow, hail, etc. In the same way, congelation occurs in sulfur, proceeding from the Element of Fire, crowded with specific diseases and their species, which are not undeservedly compared to snow, frost, and hail, and are of a similar origin. This is produced in part by the stars and is said to be born from "cold fire." For the firmament is fire.

<margin>The source of coagulation.</margin>
Furthermore, coagulation is another kind of coldness, which has its origin in water. This cold is indeed different, yet it is of the same degree as the igneous cold. If this proceeds to its operation, then whatever is attacked by this cold is coagulated.

<margin>How coagulation and congelation differ.</margin>
Coagulation differs from congelation in this: the former is fixed, while the latter is volatile. For whatever proceeds from the cold of the Element of Water is all coagulated and a "cold coagulate."

<margin>Coldness produced by individual Elements.</margin>
In this way, you see coagulated things such as corals, alums, entalia <note>original: "Entalia"; fossilized shells or dentalium used in pharmacy</note>, and similar vitriols, salts, aluminous things, etc. Of the same kind are diseases born from cold coagulate—that is, from the cold of water. In a similar way, cold is born from the air. This, according to its substance, is neither congelated nor coagulated, but is wind. And just as the North Wind or the West Wind brings cold into the heat through and from itself, so also this is the nature of the Element of Earth: to exhibit something of cold in the air and wind. Whence even in the body, such "true-colds," "chaos-colds," <note>referring to the atmosphere or 'chaos'</note> and "air-colds" are detected—without substance, without stability, and without being seen—accompanied by their own peculiar types and species of diseases.

accompanied. Thus, the earth itself, which is truly called earth, has a peculiar generation of diseases produced from itself, just as cold herbs grow upon the earth, such as **Nightshade** <note>original: "Solatrum"</note>, **Rose**, **Lettuce**, **Purslane**, and so on. <margin>Fire in all four Elements.</margin>
In no less a way, you ought to know this concerning the Element of Fire—that is, concerning heat—so that you may similarly seek fire in the four Elements. For if any disease should arise from sulfur, it would entirely possess the nature of one of these four. Sulfur, to be sure, persists in its own office by itself. From this, it happens that the sulfur burns, behaving no differently than if a lightning bolt were hurled from heaven into a tree and consumed it. Such an invisible operation of the firmament exists within our bodies. And just as the sulfur of the tree burns it, so too does the same ignite within a man. And as you see the little flame and the **stinging nettle** <note>original: "vrticámque"</note> spring from the earth, you see with what forces they press on if they touch the physical body. Similar generations are also crafted in man himself; all of which are designated under their own headings. From the fire: this is of "impression" <note>A Paracelsian term for an effect caused by celestial or atmospheric influence</note>. So also in the cold, the Element of water has its own coagulation, such as the coagulation of saltpeter and the like.

<margin>Moisture is fourfold according to the number of the four Elements.</margin>
Similarly, you have moisture from the four Elements: that is, one in water, one in earth, and finally one in air; yet these are only of one degree of the Element and are the cause of its diseases. Four types of these exist: this moist thing is from the moisture of fire; that moist thing is from the moisture of air; the third is from the moisture of earth; and the fourth is from the moisture of water, together with the species contained within them.

<margin>Dryness is fourfold, from the four elements.</margin>
The reasoning for dryness is the same: it is fourfold. These four types also emanate from the Elements, just as was said of the others. For certain drynesses are from fire; some from water; several from air; and some from earth. What sort these are, dry diseases sufficiently declare. For thus these four types exist in the highest rank of diseases: namely, cold, hot, dry, and moist. Therefore, every disease rightly begins and is understood in these degrees. And although in this Theory the diseases do not follow one another according to order, they will nevertheless be explained in a just and ordinary series where their Practice <note>The clinical application of the theory</note> is handed down. Briefly, however, most things are touched upon here because they are treated more fully in many places elsewhere, as in the book on **Complexions and Degrees**, and other natural works which properly refer to Philosophy.

<margin>Not all diseases are from the elements.</margin>
Now, indeed, we cannot deny that singular diseases sometimes arise which are not from the Elements, even if they appear somewhat similar to them. For example, if salt is calcinated <note>Reduced to powder by heat</note> and ignited by bodily moisture, it can happen that it inflames its own sulfur in which it consists; and this happens not just in one way, as mentioned before, but in all other ways. To this, it must be answered that such things are known from their signs, which distinguish all of them. But he who does not know the certain differences will not conveniently discern the signs themselves; just as will be explained in its proper place concerning **internal wars** <note>original: "bellis intestinis"; Paracelsus uses the metaphor of civil war to describe diseases where the body's internal principles fight each other</note>. Therefore, pay attention to our other books, not indeed according to the division...

## Chapter VII.

<margin>What specific diseases are.</margin>
**F**urthermore, it is true that besides all these, yet another genus of diseases exists. Two of these are handed down in this chapter. One arises from the seed of the sperm; the other from the *specific form* <note>The "specific form" is the unique internal blueprint or essence that makes a thing what it is</note>. These themselves must also be diligently noted so that they may be correctly distinguished from other diseases. Now, it is known to you how all things consist in those <term>Three Firsts</term> <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the foundational chemical principles in Paracelsian thought</note>, or substances, as has been said. In those, however, another and singular kind of accident exists, which does not pertain to those things handed down so far. It is of this sort: namely, some things move sweat, others loosen the bowels, others burn, and so on. These must be weighed very deeply. For they are called **specific illnesses**. Nor are they derived from the previously mentioned causes, but they are implanted in us and are of our own intimate nature; so that this man sweats this way, that man is loose in this way, and so on.

<margin>What are the diseases of the seed?</margin>
Now, regarding the sperm <note>original: "spermate," referring here to the "seed" or biological blueprint of a person</note>, it must be held that many more generations <note>procreations or formations</note> occur than are recognized. The causes of these have been ignorantly attributed elsewhere. For camphor, and <term>spermaceti</term> <note>A waxy substance from sperm whales, used in early medicine</note>, and many similar things prove this. From these are raised the diseases of the bladder and kidneys. For even if <term>Tartar</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to stony or calcified deposits in the body, like kidney stones or gouty crystals</note> or "the stone" exists—that is, the matter itself—it does not congeal into a stone without the nature of those things. For the "coldness of the seeds" or their "diaphoretic heat" <note>heat that induces sweating</note> congeals it. Such then is the coagulation. But heat or cold has its own peculiar Anatomy and Physiology, according to the division mentioned above. Just as with the previous points, so these too must be understood equally; whatever will be worthy of knowledge besides these will be handed down in their own proper chapters. This is now a peculiar chapter: which is also separated in this way from other diseases. Whatever is inborn or implanted, we cannot take away from the root. Now, the **specific form** and the "seed of the sperm"—that is, its very nature—are implanted in us. Therefore, it is right for the root to sustain its own sprout. If anyone were born blind, that would not be "congenital" in the sense of a missing root. For although one may not have sight, sight is nonetheless within him, even if it is not in the suitable and correct place.

<margin>Is sight lacking in the blind?</margin>
This is the reason why he is blind, and thought to be born blind, even though he has sight within himself: just as if someone showed six fingers on one hand and only four on the other; then the fingers would simply not exist in their proper place. Thus, no skilled physician could say, *"This blind man is incurable."* For Nature exists as a most skillful and truly wonderful thing. Therefore, because sight is present, it can be driven and arranged to its own proper place. This is something that cannot be done with fingers. For these are the substance of the body, but that <note>sight</note> is a "wind" <note>a spiritual or vital force</note>, destitute of a body. Therefore, it can be moved from its place, which is least permitted in a transposed body. Furthermore, regarding those things handed down in this chapter, that is not the entire reason: for they are inborn things, just as hardness is to iron, or whiteness to chalk. From which it can be understood that they are to be accepted just as they happen. For no one can prevent snow from falling. But this can be avoided: that it does not harm a man. And therefore, since the sperm is the <term>Limbus</term> <note>The "Limbus" in Paracelsian terms is the primordial "marrow" or chaotic extract from which all elements and man were created</note> in the four Elements, it will also contain its powers within itself. These powers are rightly and deservedly called **Impressions** by men. For they truly are impressions.

<margin>Sperm is the Limbus.</margin>
<margin>The "impression of the heaven" is an invention of astronomers.</margin>
But note here the error of the astronomers of this sort. They say that the "impression is made from heaven." This is nothing. For the heaven imprints nothing on us. We have received an image created by the hand of God. According to that image, whatever we may be like, we are nonetheless the work and likeness of the hand of God, without any intermediary, with all our members. Now, whatever conditions, or properties, and behaviors we bring forth, we received all those things with the breath of life; they were implanted in us with that very breath. But the diseases by which we are afflicted emerge from the three mentioned substances in that manner which we have explained. In this regard, the stars do have something they "imprint," just as fire imprints on wood or straw, or as saffron imprints something on water. Know then, that an "impression" is that which we cannot propel away from ourselves, just as...

->PARAMIRUM BOOK II: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES<-

...just as diseases are, introduced into the body from the outside via the <term>Limbus</term> <note>The "Limbus" in Paracelsian thought refers to the "divine chaos" or the prime matter from which all things were created; it is the "clay" of the universe</note>. Such an impression also becomes specific within the seed, from which we are indeed driven, yet we cannot in turn expel those influences. But as for what they add regarding "inclination" <note>The astrological belief that the position of planets at birth "inclines" or pushes a person toward certain behaviors or fates</note>, that likewise amounts to nothing.

<margin>The fictitious inclination of the Astronomers.</margin>
For what they profess—that a man is inclined toward Mars, Saturn, the Moon, etc., or toward theft and similar things—is pure fanaticism and nonsense. Indeed, we can more conveniently say it this way: Mars imitates the man. For man is more powerful than Mars and all the planets. He who has truly examined the heavens and knows man speaks nothing of this sort. Instead, he judges that man exists as someone so noble and great before God that his image, with all his actions, both good and evil, is depicted and expressed in the heavens. This, however, is by no means an "inclination." And although they might moderate their error in some part by saying, *the stars do not compel* <note>original: "astra non necessitare"</note>, this is at least an ingenious veil. The heavens have two divisions from man: one, that man is depicted in the heavens themselves. From this, it is falsely concluded that this or that man is "Saturnine" <note>Influenced by the planet Saturn, traditionally associated with gloom or sluggishness</note>. This is the same as if someone were depicted and portrayed in a painting, and afterward people said the image conferred its own inclination onto the original person, so that whatever he did, he did by the power of the image. The other division is the "prelude." For the heavens are so adorned that the future works, actions, and manners of all men are exhibited and represented within them. And this prelude they call "inclination," as if they were saying he is forced and impelled by the prelude to do this or that. All preludes are merely prophecies that presage the future. But inclination, impression, constellation, and the like—this is the very mud that the Astronomers have cast over their own eyes.

<margin>The arrogance of the Astronomers.</margin>
If this is pointed out to them, they snarl. But if their errors are relegated to the class of superstitious arts and true sciences are brought forward, they are not ashamed to say that such science is "Necromancy."

Pay attention, therefore, that nature depends on these two things. One is in the seed. This must be properly understood from the first Theory. Even if substance and bodies are not present, nevertheless generations can proceed from them. Likewise, where a specific sickness is present, consider that it cannot be turned away at the root. Its "accidents" <note>The outward symptoms or secondary characteristics of a disease</note>, however, can be conveniently removed. For it often happens that a specific laxity is within the stomach and intestines; so also a specific leprosy may cling within the blood. According to the art, this is the same as saying that Colocynth, Turbith, or Scammony <note>These are all powerful herbal purgatives used in Renaissance medicine</note> were in the belly; and it would be said by someone, *he has that specific Scammony, or Colocynth, or Spurge, or Agaric, or whatever else it may be*. Or thus: *He has a specific "little flame" or specific water, which now exists as innate Leprosy or Morphoea <note>A skin condition involving localized patches of hardened skin</note>, or something similar*. For in this way, a specific fatness often occurs—that is, it happens that someone becomes fat when food is by no means the cause. So too a specific thinness occurs, such that many grow slender with no amount of food helping. And the Physicians have by no means included these things in specific science, but have babbled the same things as the unskilled Astronomers, saying, *this is Melancholy, etc. This is Saturn; this is the nature of his Ascendant* <note>The "Ascendant" is the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>. For man assumes nothing from the Ascendant; he was created from the Limbus and by the hand of God; not by the Ascendant, nor the planet, nor the constellation, or similar things. As if these things truly forced him to either grow fat or waste away! In these diseases, it is necessary to have certain knowledge so that they may be properly distinguished from the primary interpretation of other diseases. For they are often weighed incorrectly, as we shall teach in its proper place, especially where their "aversion" <note>The method of turning away or curing the disease</note> is discussed: where we deal principally with the seed of the sperm and specifics.

### CHAPTER VIII.

**N**ow, indeed, beyond all these, there exists in man an invisible body, which is by no means constituted from the three mentioned substances <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>.

<margin>The invisible body in man; from where it comes.</margin>
That is, man has a body not produced from the Limbus. Its origin is from the breath of God. And just as any inspired breath or vapor in our hands is nothing, so also in our eyes, that body is nothing. Although in this place I am forced to use the kind of language that must be granted to me as a Physician and understood in the sense that Philosophy itself reveals concerning man. Which is this: We know from Holy Scripture that we shall rise again in this body on the day of the last judgment and give answer for our sins. Now, truly, that body committed the sin, which is nothing before our eyes. From this, it can be gathered that it is *that* body which will be resurrected. For we are not going to give an account of the sicknesses of our bodies, or their health and similar things, but rather of those things which proceeded from the heart, which alone concern the man.

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the idea that stars and planets "incline" humans toward specific behaviors, arguing instead that the heavens merely mirror human action. He introduces the "invisible body," a spiritual form given by God's breath that is separate from the physical body and is the part of man held accountable at the Resurrection.</summary>

<keywords>Limbus, astrology, inclination, specific diseases, invisible body, resurrection, breath of God, purgatives, Saturn, Mars</keywords>

--- Page 98 ---
<meta>This page concludes the philosophical foundation of the "Three Prime Substances" and the "Two Bodies" of man, transitioning from a critique of astrological fatalism to the theological and medical necessity of moderation, ending with a dedication to Joachim von Watt.</meta>

->### From the Three Prime Substances<-

And this too is a body, not indeed from the <term>Limbus</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "Limbus" to refer to the "great chaos" or the prime material of the physical universe from which the human body was fashioned.</note>, but produced from the Spirit or breath of God. Since we are to see God our Savior in our flesh, it is consistent that the body born from the Limbus will appear there as well, for it is truly flesh. Who could be ignorant of those things which will occur in the <term>glorification</term> <note>original: "clarificatione"; referring to the state of the "glorified body" after the resurrection in Christian theology</note>, which shall be established by the mouth of God, where one body will be made like the other? Therefore, we shall rise in the flesh. For now, however, we know of at least one flesh, not two—yet there are two bodies, though only one flesh, and that one is taken from the Limbus, which is the subject of diseases.

Furthermore, know concerning this body that, besides hunger, thirst, and other things due to the natural body by right, it possesses a stimulating and instigating nature toward those things that transcend the limit. The flesh from the Limbus is indeed a nature that remains within its own mode, measure, and justice. Whatever exists beyond this proceeds from evil, not from nature. That excess, therefore, flows from the <term>impalpable body</term> <note>The "impalpable" or "sidereal" body is the spiritual/invisible part of man that Paracelsus distinguishes from the physical flesh.</note>, which oversteps both measure and nature. For whatever is administered to nature departs or diverts into natural places and channels for natural operations. For example, whatever food is given for natural necessity descends into the belly and is subsequently emitted through the stool, which is as it should be. So too the seed of Nature diverts into its own field—namely, the womb—and there produces fruit. But whatever is beyond these things proceeds from evil.

<margin>
A passage of St. Paul explained regarding how it should be understood by wives.
</margin>
I would not wish to appear a wicked Christian who opposes Paul, who commands that the lust of women be satisfied <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:9 regarding marriage as a remedy for "burning" with passion.</note>. This was not said by him as if it were a just and pure work, but at least so that adultery might be avoided, into which they might be precipitated for the sake of satiating pleasure. These things were spoken for the sake of avoiding a worse evil. The same applies to men. Since, however, this discussion concerns that which happens beyond nature from the "other" man <note>the spiritual/invisible man</note>, and not from the one who is of the Limbus, it must be rightly weighed and explained by the physician.

The physician must do this so that he may build two bodies and two men from this knowledge, which he may then set against the astronomers who subject the body to the stars. This body, I say, was created from the mouth of God and not from the stars—so that man may be tested as to what he wills or does not will, in what good or evil he desires to walk, how much he venerates God, and what he trusts in Him.

<margin>
God’s noble beneficence.
</margin>
Thus, man still has one body, which is that body to which Adam and Eve in paradise added perfection by the eating of the apple, according to which he was made "whole"—understand this as the knowledge of good and evil. From this now follows eating more abundant than nature requires, and drinking more lavishly than thirst demands. God is so kind that He sets before us according to our desire: good wines, beautiful women, choice foods, and glittering money, so that through these we may be tested—to see what manner of life we keep, and whether we hold to or overstep the boundary of nature. For here there is a certain association of these two bodies—namely, of the breath of God and of the Limbus—having the likeness of a marriage. From this it is gathered that the violation of this union belongs to a wicked and adulterous nation that observes no limit. For the <term>insensible body</term> <note>the spiritual body</note> made a promise that it would not burden the natural body or act beyond measure. If this is not done, what else is it but adultery, which exists as a maximum debt before God? But it is not fitting for me to say more on what pertains to this purpose. Rather, let us conclude with these things the universal Theory, the origin of Physics and Surgery, and the cause of all diseases. After this general comprehension, the following books will provide more information and understanding in each specific chapter separately. And since the declaration of these matters demands a singular Philosophy, I shall finish in those places—God willing, who even now has shone upon us by His grace—and I shall exhort you to recognize that medicine from this Philosophy, so that everything which God has bestowed upon medicine may be fulfilled in it.

## Epilogue to Dr. Joachim von Watt <note>Joachim von Watt, known as Vadianus (1484–1551), was a Swiss humanistic scholar, physician, and reformer.</note>

**T**hus, Most Excellent Master von Watt, I could not omit bringing forth the first book of my *Paramirum* <note>The *Opus Paramirum* is one of Paracelsus’s major works, the title implying something "beyond wonder" or "above marvelous."</note> works. In this, through long labors by day and night, I have striven for this one thing: to instruct and inform the students of Medicine by this discourse of mine. From this, more fruit will emerge than we currently imagine. There will be no shortage of those who will accuse me of pride and ambition in these matters. Some will argue it is madness. Some will blame it on ignorance. But I hold this one thing against them: as much as anyone knows in the art, so much does he judge of <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus.</note>. He who is corrupted in Philosophy should know himself to be unfit for this Monarchy of medicine.
