<header>PARAMIRUM, BOOK 1. ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES.</header>

*...is one who will never honor Theophrastus with praise. Whoever is in error in astronomy will hold all my sayings in no regard. They say my Physics, Meteorology, Theory, and Practice are intricate, new, wonderful, and unheard of. But how could I not seem wonderful to someone who has never walked under the sun? Truly, the multitude of followers of either Aristotle, Ptolemy, or Avicenna does not terrify me. Rather, the ill-will that now flourishes everywhere terrifies me—as does the unjust law, ritual, and order (or custom, as they call it) of Jurisprudence. To whom a gift is given, he possesses it. To one who is not called, it is not my place to call him. May God be with us, our protector and preserver forever. Farewell.*

# ON THE ORIGIN AND CAUSE OF DISEASES OF BOTH PROFESSIONS,
## By Aureolus Theophrastus Paracelsus, to Master <term>Joachim Vadian</term>, Physician. <note>Joachim Vadian (1484–1551) was a Swiss humanist, physician, and the reformer/mayor of St. Gallen. He was a close contemporary and correspondent of Paracelsus.</note>
### THE THIRD BOOK OF THE PARAMIRUM.
### To the Reader.

*Although I suffer from a great lack of quiet time, skilled and kind Reader, and no one comes forward to provide it, nevertheless—since the excellent Master Joachim Vadian, Doctor of Medicine and the <term>Consul</term> <note>original: "consul"; refers to Vadian's role as the Burgomaster or Mayor of St. Gallen.</note> and Physician of the city of St. Gallen, is present with me—I could not pass by without composing and writing down, as was fitting, a general Theory of both medicines <note>Paracelsus refers here to "both medicines": the physical (earthly) and the spiritual or "astral" medicine.</note> from my own experience. And even though I began this same work with great diligence some time ago in Basel, hoping it would certainly be of use to many (though when the truth comes forth, many violent and healthy and fierce winds usually arise), I have believed more and more every day that I would discover this: that those who love the soul would also love the body, and those who spare the soul would also take account of the body. But the outcome was very much against this sentiment of mine. A very swift wind rushed in here. Therefore, I would have you be attentive, honest Reader. Beware, however, of making any judgment immediately from the first, second, or third chapter; rather, continue your reading all the way to the end, and compare that which I encompass in these few pages with your own experience. Let those whom I touch upon and criticize here not move you at all. Weigh and estimate each thing with a fair scale, corrupted by the favor or friendship of no one. For even more books (with the help of divine grace) will subsequently come forth, built upon this very foundation, which will bring you more pleasure. Acknowledge and learn this. Given at St. Gallen on the 15th day of March, in the year of salvation 1531.*

---

# THEOPHRASTUS VON HOHENHEIM, ON THE CAUSE AND ORIGIN OF DISEASES.
## BOOK THREE.
### TRACTATE THREE.

<margin>A physician without philosophy is worth nothing.</margin>
Will any of the Philosophers who occupy themselves with natural things not burst into laughter when they see that Physicians have forgotten and omitted most of those things—and the most necessary ones—which, having been dug out from the foundations of Philosophy, present themselves in the very pains and diseases themselves? Yet these physicians leap over all these things; they do only one thing, which is to set the hook to catch money, or to press their petty disputes with peasants and laymen. Yet it was more fitting for them to engage in disputation with the Philosophers themselves, because of their shared subject matter. As long as they do not act in accordance with Philosophy, they remain ignorant of what their true subject is. Furthermore, because they do not agree with the Philosophers, nor dare to fight against them in mutual combat, let it be a conviction to you that whatever they themselves treat or attempt is erroneous and fruitless. For it is quite disgraceful for a physician to be called a Physician, and to profess himself as such, while being ignorant and unskilled in Philosophy. From this, how many errors arise...

<summary>Paracelsus introduces the third book of his Paramirum with a dedication to Joachim Vadian, arguing that true medicine must be rooted in philosophy rather than profit or tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Joachim Vadian, St. Gallen, medical philosophy, medical theory, critique of physicians, 1531, Paramirum</keywords>

--- Page 100 ---
<meta>This page continues from the introduction to the Third Book of the Paramirum. Paracelsus moves from his dedication to Master Joachim Vadian into the core philosophical argument: that diseases can arise from the "excrement" or waste products inherent in the three prime substances (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) that make up all matter.</meta>

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>FROM THE THREE PRIME SUBSTANCES</header>

...will be clearly revealed to you in what follows.

<margin>No nourishment exists without excrement.</margin>
Although the preceding Book was also established and titled concerning the cause and origin of diseases, one thing still remains beyond the matters above, which itself has the force of a cause and generates diseases in various ways. It is worthwhile for you to understand this properly and to weigh it accurately according to Philosophy itself: namely, that all things contain the three substances. <note>original: "tres substantias"; Paracelsus refers to his "Tria Prima"—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—which he believed were the fundamental building blocks of all material reality.</note> Now, however, in those three there is a certain egestion, dross, or excrement. For nothing provides nourishment that does not contain some dross and the excrement of its own digestion within itself.

This, truly, must be understood more articulately in this way: All things that either exist or grow contain within themselves their own dross or dung. Just as such things exist in man, so they exist in every single thing through itself. The same was said in the beginning regarding the three prime substances of the body. This, however, now further explains the diseases of those three primes—namely, what egestion, dross, or excrement generates within us. To understand this, do not be moved by the fact that the ancients were silent on such matters. For the cause of this is that they understood nothing in any of these things. What wonder is it, then, if they handed down no perfections or more accurate accounts in this matter? Now, therefore, I shall further bring forth from Philosophy what I wish for you to understand here.

<margin>Whatever lives requires nourishment.</margin>
You ought to know, moreover, that all things grow and live, and for that reason have need of food and nourishment. If, therefore, they have need to eat, it is necessary that they also possess a stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"; in Paracelsian thought, this refers not just to the organ of the stomach, but to any internal "alchemist" or processing site within an organ that separates useful matter from waste.</note> and its power. From this, it is now established that they, just like man, eat both pure and impure things. Yet they do not have their own emunctories <note>An "emunctorium" is an organ or canal that carries off waste from the body, such as the sweat glands or the nose.</note> like a man does; rather, what they eat, they retain inside. The good is separated from the bad and converted into the nourishment of that thing. The bad recedes from that anatomy and has its own peculiar anatomy, and the dross itself remains in that thing. Thus, in that thing, the dross and the nourishment are retained together. Regarding this dross, which is thus left behind in the nourishment, I shall now discourse, while nonetheless recalling most points back to Philosophy itself.

Regarding this matter, know that this nourishment, together with the dross, is eaten and drunk by man at the same time. From this it follows that the nature of man separates them in turn, and does not leave them joined within himself. But because it is twofold, two things are produced: namely, Nature and Dross. Although the human stomach does not separate these two—for it separates at least its own

<margin>What the stomach separates.</margin>
dross from the pure, but not the dross of natural things. For that is so united with the nourishment that the stomach does not have the force or power to separate this union; instead, it mandates this duty to a more subtle stomach, which is in the <term>mesaraics</term> <note>The mesaraic (or mesenteric) veins, which Paracelsus viewed as part of a secondary digestive system that further refined nutrients.</note>, in the liver, in the kidneys, in the bladder and intestines, etc. In these stomachs, those drosses are separated. From this, conclude that our stomach—that is, the first stomach, continuous with the throat—separates at least that which putrefies and does not putrefy, that which is crushed and not crushed. Now, indeed, nothing is crushed or broken except that which is not flesh, not marrow, and not bone. Therefore, whatever is not man, is dross. What is man, is not dross. But the drosses of those things are not the drosses of man. Thus, they are also not broken down; they are not "man." Therefore, they remain and exist within the man. For that reason, they are "coctilia" <note>Literally "things to be cooked" or "digestible." Paracelsus is arguing that these foreign wastes remain in the body and must be "cooked" or processed by internal organs.</note>.

So, because things are present in man which ought not to be in him—which are not his own dross, nor the man himself, but exist as the dross of natural things (that is, of food and drink, as was said before)—it is necessary to describe what those nutrients do and set in motion within the body. Moreover, the reason why these things seem foreign and marvelous is due to the ignorance of those who wonder at them. Now, those diseases which are thus generated are different and distinct from those described in the first book. Although it remains true that all drosses are and remain in those three substances, just as other things are, they are nevertheless separated and distinct from others just as much as a man and his dross are distinguished, as is demonstrated in its proper place. So too, the diseases that are generated from the man are distinguished from those that arise from the dross by the very same distinction. Thus, something far different and singular must be understood in these diseases arising from dross.

<margin>The humors are not the causes of diseases.</margin>
And although the ancient writers, with their affected styles, produce <term>cholera</term>, <term>phlegm</term>, and <term>melancholy</term> <note>These are three of the four "humors" (along with blood) of Galenic medicine, which Paracelsus famously rejected in favor of chemical and mineral causes.</note> very grandly as the causes of diseases, because these things lack reason and a foundation, who would greatly care for or value them? While they comment upon and extol these things, they by no means consult the foundations of Philosophy itself, so that they might see from there that they can by no means maintain their position with their humors. Consider diligently, indeed, by what evidence they could prove that from phlegm, melancholy, or blood...

<sig>F 3</sig>

<summary>Paracelsus introduces the concept of diseases caused by "stercus" (dross/excrement) inherent in all matter. He argues that the body contains multiple "stomachs" or refining sites that must separate these foreign wastes from human tissue, and he begins to reject the traditional Galenic theory of the four humors as the cause of illness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s argument from page 65. Having established that all things contain "dross" or excrement, he now refutes the traditional medical view that diseases like kidney stones come from the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). Instead, he introduces his theory of "Tartar"—the stony waste product of digestion.</meta>

<page-num>66</page-num>

### PARAMIRUM BOOK III: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES

They claim that these sorts of generations are produced from Blood and Bile, even though such natures do not actually exist within those humors. But in what way can something become something else, when it is not that thing itself? These diseases are *Stone, Sand, Clod, and Slime*. <note>original: "Calculus, Arena, Bolus, Viscus"; Paracelsus is categorizing different types of solid deposits found in the body, which he calls 'Tartar'.</note> Now, my dear fellows, since you have explained your humors to us, I would love to hear how *Stone, Sand, Clod*, and *Slime* can be created when none of them exist in the beginning? If stone, sand, etc., are to be formed in a human at all, then the things from which they are generated must be present within him. If they are not present, they certainly will not be made, because they do not exist. Even if they insist on many examples to confirm these things outside of the four humors, their foundation and reasoning in this matter are just as weak and shaky as they are in all other things. Here is the knot of the problem: if these men were Philosophers instead of Poets, if they were Anatomists instead of Clerics, and if they were truthful instead of triflers, then they would certainly proceed much more correctly and soundly in evaluating the diseases of these things, which are outside the human condition and nature.

On the contrary, you should know that this body, which generates and brings forth these diseases, is complex: namely, it produces stone, sand, clods, and slime. These are the four "dungs" of natural things. And all the nutrients that natural things eat and drink follow these four types—becoming either stone, sand, clod, or slime. In the end, all these are "coagulation," which is to say, their ultimate state of being; or, finally, they all become stone through this process of hardening. First, however, it must be demonstrated that these dungs have their "ultimate matter" <note>The final, solid form a substance takes after all its processes are complete.</note> in the form of stone. It happens like this: Human waste, in its ultimate matter, undergoes putrefaction <note>decay or rotting</note>. But the ultimate matter of natural things <note>referring here to the mineral or "tartaric" elements in food</note> is coagulation <note>hardening or thickening</note>. Here, then, they are opposites. For human digestion has its own "emunctories" <note>organs or channels that carry off waste</note>. Whatever passes out of these is excreted by the force of putrefaction. That process rouses its own expulsive power. For the power of expulsion resides in the dung and excrement itself, not in the nature of the human being. However, that power is by no means present in natural things. If such things exist, they are "coagulative," and for this reason: because they take their nourishment from things similar to themselves.

<margin>Nourishment is similar to itself.</margin>
For the plantain plant eats plantain, the sweet flag eats sweet flag, and so it goes for the rest. <note>Paracelsus believed that every plant or creature extracts a specific "essence" from the environment that matches its own nature.</note> Now, in the beginning of this nutrition, all things are in a state of coagulation, and that state resolves itself into nourishment. Therefore, that which is not digested by the one who eats it returns to the coagulation from which it came.

<margin>Resolution is twofold.</margin>
For that "resolution" <note>the breaking down of a substance</note> departs from the state of coagulation in two ways. One way is that which never coagulates again: this is nourishment. The other way is that which does coagulate: this is the dung. For just as in a human being, that which is not "human" becomes dung, so it is here. Therefore, the resolution is manifold: in the form of stone, in the form of sand, in the form of a clod, or in the form of slime. From these four come the stones and sands which ought to be called the "ultimate matter" of the dung of nourishment—that is, in natural things. This ultimate matter is explained in two ways: One, through itself in the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," meaning the human body.</note>; the other, through the human being within himself, that is, in those diseases which this Book will treat. The ultimate matter of those things which are made through themselves are the "bricks of the earth." For all these things have a need to eat. In the beginning, however, there is only slime; yet it is of such a nature that as soon as it is cast out of the body, it coagulates. The four elements drive it out, not the things that grow. For growing things sustain themselves within themselves. Know therefore, that what dries up contains dung within itself; that which is separated is nourishment without its body.

<margin>Duelech is a spongy stone.</margin>
He who prepares wood makes *Duelech* <note>A Paracelsian term, likely derived from Persian/Arabic, referring here to a porous or spongy stone, often specifically a bladder stone.</note> from it. He who prepares a herb creates Alabaster and similar things from it. These are the ultimate matters of the dung of natural things.

<margin>Heat from sulfur; ashing from salt; smoking from Mercury.</margin>
For everything that burns contains Sulfur within itself. If it turns to ash, it has Salt. If it gives off smoke, it has Mercury. <note>These are the Tria Prima: the three fundamental spiritual-material principles Paracelsus believed made up all matter.</note> Now, if it contains these three, it also has excrements similar to these: not useful, but stony; not smoking, but coagulated; not turning to ash, but persisting in a solid form. Understand it this way: if wood yields ash, and ash yields salt, and salt yields stone, then know that the "Mechanic" <note>The *Archeus*, or internal alchemist of the body, who directs digestion and separation.</note> establishes these things in the body and manifests his ultimate matter within the body. Which of the peasants sees oil in wood? No one. Who looks for water in a stone? No one, except a Physician. So, in turn, he will seek in that which is not, so that it may be; that is, wood in oil, or stone in water. This is now the wise, "Adept Philosophy." <note>True alchemical or medical knowledge that goes beyond surface appearances.</note>

<margin>There are 4 types of Tartaric diseases.</margin>
As has been understood, then, there are four types of these: *Stone, Sand, Clod, and Slime*. It is necessary to look for these four in the body—that is, in the nourishment. For nourishment is the body. If they enter the body, they are born in that same place, just as the spirit works who is the "Mechanic" of that place—that is, the craftsman of those things. This Book, therefore, in its own category...

<meta>catchword: category (genere)</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that stony diseases like kidney stones (Tartar) do not come from the four humors, but are the solid, "coagulated" waste products of nourishment. He identifies four types of this waste—stone, sand, clod, and slime—and attributes their formation to an internal "Mechanic" or alchemist within the body.</summary>

### FROM THE THREE PRIMARY SUBSTANCES

<sig>F 4</sig>

...the category of Tartar is rightly assigned. For any "final matter" <note>original: "ultima materia"; the final state of a substance after it has been processed by the body’s internal "alchemist."</note> of growing things, if they are separated within the body, is called Tartar. Thus Tartar is also called stone or pebble, sand, clod, and slime, depending on its form. Therefore, the proper Book of Tartar follows here, explaining how it and its various types are to be understood and perceived. From what has been said so far, it is concluded that Tartar is at the very least the excrement of food and drink, which is coagulated in this way by the human spirit. Unless these excrements are mixed with their own natural expulsive power and cast out in that mixture, then from them is generated that which will be described hereafter.

<margin>What is Tartar?</margin>
<margin>Tartar is taken in with external things.</margin>
Thus we both eat and drink tartar: once it has entered us, unless it is mixed with our other waste and excreted with the bulk of it, it remains stuck in the body. From this, many different diseases emerge in numerous ways, which until now have been explained by neither ancient nor modern doctors—not because of their malice or ill-will, but rather out of their lack of skill and ignorance.

<margin>From what matter is Tartar made? Tartar from edibles.</margin>
Next, it must first be understood how we take in tartar through legumes, such as barley, peas, and so on. For all these things contain tartar within themselves. It is certain that tartar is formed from their mucilage or slime which they produce, and from their thick substance, which is born solely from the "final matter"—that is, from the part that is sweet. For this reason, all foods cooked with mucilage are also presented <note>or "offered as a treatment"</note> against the stone. <note>original: "adversus calculum"; while Paracelsus usually views these as causes, traditional medicine used mucilaginous plants to "smooth" the passage of stones.</note> But if the stickiness is removed through cooking, then the danger is broken, because that matter (which would otherwise stick and glue itself down) passes out with the other excrement. Thus, Bitumen, <term>slime</term> <note>original: "viscus"; a sticky, glue-like substance.</note>, mucilage, and the "gluten" of legumes are nothing other than the material of dung, which turns into stone or sand in the body whenever it reaches its final state. Have the same conviction regarding dairy products. These supply a <term>bolar</term> <note>original: "bolarem"; referring to "bolus," a medicinal clay or a thick, clod-like mass.</note> matter, that is, a clay-like substance. Understand it this way: all dairy contains "clods" within it. From this clod, tartar is made, unless it is driven out with other waste. Similarly, meat and fish also contain these clods. Know therefore, that legumes produce their waste in a slimy way; but fish, meat, and dairy produce it in a "bolar" way, which is to say, like clay. From these two sources, observe two types of waste. Aside from these, no other tartars are born from food except the tartar of the clod and the tartar of the slime, along with their subspecies, just as legumes, meat, grain, and herbs are categorized. For stalks, roots, and grains are all understood to fall under the category of "legumes" here. The doctor, therefore, in prescribing a diet for such diseases, must work to ensure that these types of tartar and waste are mixed with the putrefaction and excrement of the stomach and their own expulsive power. Without this preparation, no regimen or diet can be established by any other way. For abstinence alone does nothing. Furthermore, this separation happens nowhere else except within the human being.

<margin>Tartar from drinks.</margin>
<margin>Beer generates a double tartar.</margin>
Similarly, in the drinking of wine or water, or whatever goes by the name of drink, we have double excrements. First, it should be known that those drinks prepared from tree fruits, such as pears and apples, are comparable to wine and water. Beer, however, and anything extracted from legumes, contains both kinds of tartar: that of the grain and that of the water from which it is made. Therefore, such drinks have their "correction" <note>their remedy or balancing factor</note> in the fact that they pass through the body quickly and do not stay long. Indeed, the less they are digested, the better.

<margin>When Tartar is produced more, when less.</margin>
<margin>Why Tartar is less in some and more abundant in others.</margin>
For a "strong" digestion is actually a rapid operation for generating the stone; a "light" digestion is less so. No light digestion ever gave birth to a stone or to tartar. Hot and powerful digestions are so rapid and thorough that they omit nothing from being separated. This is the reason why more tartar is found in one person than in another; it depends on whether the places of digestion and separation are stronger or weaker. Furthermore, concerning a sick person of this type, know that there are two tartars in them, named according to the nature and condition of that region. Hence it often happens that a certain medicine works for these types of tartar in one region but less so in another. The cause of this is the varied properties of the wines and waters that those regions produce and bring forth.

<margin>The variety of Tartar from the variety of things.</margin>
Furthermore, you see how tartar is born in wine, and a "slimy stone" is born in water; sometimes these separate by themselves and stick to the vessels, sometimes less so. However they may be separated, true tartar always remains in them, and is never fully drawn out or extracted. In solid foods this does not happen in the same way, but only in drinkable things, which possess a large amount of excrement but are too weak to hold onto it. Thus, they separate from themselves. Now, one kind stays in wine, another in water. So also their final matters...

<meta>Catchword: "à se" (from themselves)</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus explains that "Tartar" (internal stony deposits) originates from the waste products of food and drink, categorizing them into "slimy" (from legumes) and "clay-like" (from meat and dairy). He argues that strong digestion can paradoxically increase stone formation by separating these wastes too efficiently if they aren't properly expelled.</summary>

<page-num>68</page-num>
<header>THE PARAMIRUM, BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES</header>

...are distinct from one another. Regarding the fact that a stone <term>calculus|A hard mass or "stone" formed in the body, such as a kidney stone</term> is generated here, or sand <term>arena|Fine, grainy deposits often found in the bladder or kidneys</term> there: this proceeds entirely from the condition and nature of that region, such that both stone and sand are available. Many times the stone is expelled with the waste while the sand remains; and conversely, the sand is cast out while the stone is left behind. This happens in this region, but less so in that one. For there are countless and diverse people in whom tartar is produced, and in all of them peculiar and diverse natures or types of generation are found, as will be declared in their own chapters.

<margin>Few are without tartar.</margin>
We therefore drink tartar with wine, with water, and with the juices of trees. Unless it is excreted and separated due to weak digestion, it is impossible to find any person who is not affected or burdened by tartar, in whatever part of the body it may occur. This must be carefully noted.

The same must be judged concerning the nature of coagulation <note>The process of a liquid becoming solid or semi-solid</note>, hardening, form, appearance, etc.—namely, that they are produced according to the condition of the specific location, food, and drink. For thus it happens that a Swiss man is seized by a Nuremberg or Westerburg stone due to the legumes and grains of those places. Likewise, these nations can in turn feel "Swiss stone" from the dairy products of Switzerland. The same is true for Swabians, Bavarians, Alsatians, Franks, etc., as they consume the drinks of others. So too, a foreigner who travels in Portugal, Apulia, England, or Sweden—if he then resides in Germany, he may feel the separation of a stone that was delayed for many years over the course of time.

<margin>The error of some regarding tartar.</margin>
Let us now close this first Treatise, having sufficiently defined how we take in tartar from the outside and do not generate it from within ourselves, as is clear from what has been said. Therefore, those who think otherwise about the generation of stones dwell in obvious error and ignorance. It is a sign of a weak foundation when those who are ignorant of the nature of nutrients and the resulting waste conclude that the viscous <note>Sticky or thick</note> substance of food is the cause of tartar, yet they do not add what that viscosity is, or how, when, or from where the stone is born. For it is not enough to say that the earth produces trees and brings forth herbs; one must add by what reasoning and in what way. Even peasants know the former; but for doctors, the knowledge of earthly things ought to be deeper and more perfect. Indeed, you propose "coagulation," but you are ignorant of what it is. You suggest some kind of heat, but you omit from where the stone arises and what it primarily is. All these are arguments for your stupidity and lack of skill, which you reveal everywhere, confessing that you are not yet well-versed in the principles of medicine. It would be a waste of time to spend it on such trifles, of which you make yourself especially worthy.

### SECOND TREATISE OF BOOK III
<note>While the page header says Book I, the text here marks a new internal division as the Second Treatise of Book III. Paracelsus's internal book numbering is often complex and non-linear.</note>

<margin>What a thing consists of indicates its nature.</margin>
**S**ince the nourishment of natural things and plants is drawn from resolved stones, into which they are later coagulated again, it must first be known that what arises from stones (as Philosophy demonstrates, though it is not the place to prove it here) degenerates back into stones through the excessively swift and subtle heat of digestion. Digestion itself separates such things but does not generate them. For it cannot generate stones since it is not a stone itself. But where stones are present, it can separate them. Once this separation from the nourishment and waste has been made, they proceed into their own operation, according to the spirit present there, which is the **spirit of salt** <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, the "spirit of salt" is the active force that governs solidity and coagulation</note>. This spirit takes its origin from the waste: one part goes into a "solar stone" and ash; another into a different stone, and another form and cause, as will be more clearly taught in the following sections.

<margin>The spirit of salt alone coagulates tartar.</margin>
From this, be persuaded that the **spirit of salt** itself coagulates and forms the tartars. It establishes this coagulation and formation according to the place where it is located. For it exists in the whole body. So too does the spirit of sulfur; so too the spirit of mercury. But these have nothing to do with these wastes and tartaric diseases. They neither add nor take anything away from them; they separate nothing and form nothing. <margin>From what material tartar is made.</margin> The **spirit of salt** alone performs this. Since it finds the matter of the stone, it works upon it like the heat of the sun—which the spirit of salt resembles. If it finds mucilage or slime <note>original: "viscum"</note>, it then dries it out. And whatever is in the process of coagulation, that very thing it becomes, according to its office. Because [the other spirit] is not the spirit of salt, it cannot change stony materials into stones. The same is true for other stones. For there is no other thing that holds this right. Only the **spirit of salt** converts stony matter into stones—that is, leads it into its final matter <note>original: "ultimam materiam"</note>. There is proof of this in foods as well. These, no heat, no fire...

He rejects traditional medical explanations of viscosity, insisting that only this specific chemical force can transform food waste into stone.</summary>

# TREATISE II ON DISEASES FROM TARTAR. 69

No digestion can reduce food into its ultimate matter <note>The "ultimate matter" refers to the final state of a substance after it has been fully processed by nature or alchemy</note>, except only the stomach of man, which has this power. Because of this, many errors are committed in the **Vulcanian art** <term>Vulcanian art|The art of alchemy or chemistry, named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and the forge</term>, by which the ultimate matter is not reduced by the right path.

There are many who use putrefaction; but that is not the way to the ultimate matter, rather it is a deviation. Therefore, it is not the heat of the body that provides this, but the **spirit of salt** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to a specific digestive or corrosive force, not necessarily table salt</note>. Only the philosopher <note>The "philosopher" here refers to a natural philosopher or alchemist who understands the hidden laws of nature</note> knows what kind of thing this is, but the physician knows it least of all. Since Philosophy teaches these things in this way—which the physician also ought to accept—I leave those things aside here and move further to the "separation," how it happens in the following parts, and how the types of tartar arise from it, and by what means it is reduced by the spirit of salt.

<margin>The reason and method of generating tartar.</margin>
In the beginning, whatever we eat and drink, the mouth receives. Truly, the mouth holds it no differently than a funnel: whatever is poured into it flows down into the vat placed beneath. This passage made through the mouth is not in vain; the mouth itself retains some tartar. This is because there is a heat of digestion in the mouth—not of "complexion" <note>The balance of the four humors</note>, nor of the Elements, nor of humors, but of digestion alone. The heat of digestion is another power entirely. The function of this specific heat is more significant and greater. Therefore, whatever we put into the mouth is no less in a state of digestion than if it were in the stomach. It is possible to "eat in the mouth" and contain the food there, without swallowing anything into the stomach, except what is digested in the mouth. For eating in the stomach provides "rustic" (coarse) nourishment, but eating in the mouth is "noble" nutrition.

<margin>What is eating in the mouth and eating in the stomach?</margin>
Those who eat in the mouth do not defecate. But those who eat in the stomach do. However, those eating in the mouth do urinate. And thus many of the saints sustained themselves; although men thought they ate nothing because they produced no dung, yet the mouth alone is enough to nourish the entire body. Thus, by that power, the mouth digests and separates the "natural excrement" (waste). But this waste, because it finds nowhere to cling, is glued to the teeth. 

<margin>Why tartar does not cling to the throat.</margin>
For the other parts constituting the mouth—such as the throat, the tongue, the uvula, and the gums—are too moist and smooth for the tartar to be able to cling to them. Thus, tartar is generated on the teeth. And not from drink alone, but also from food, according to its nature and condition. If there were some permanent cavity or capacity in the mouth, then the waste would separate into many more types of tartar, just as many types are indeed found elsewhere. These forms cannot be made into "coagulations" (solid stones) in the mouth because of the slipperiness of the place.

<margin>The effect of dental tartar and the sharp nature of tartar.</margin>
Therefore, let there be nothing else in the mouth but the first separation of natural waste, which clings to the teeth. From this later follow putrefaction of the gums, erosion of the teeth, pains and torments, and the like—surely from the nature of the **acrimony** <note>A sharp, biting, or corrosive quality</note> which is added to every tartar. Therefore, you must compare the paroxysm <note>A sudden, intense attack of pain</note> of the teeth from tartar with the paroxysm of the "stone" <term>stone|A calculus, such as a kidney stone or gallstone</term> in the vessels; as more will be said about these in a specific chapter.

<margin>Tartar in the opening of the stomach.</margin>
That matter from the mouth is then derived into the "mouth of the stomach" <note>The cardia or the esophagus</note>. Here it must be known: that which descends does not slip down to the bottom of the stomach immediately and in a moment. But in the opening of the stomach, another digestion occurs, similar to that which was in the mouth. Where this happens, tartar clings no less to it than to the teeth. 

<margin>What diseases come from tartar of the stomach's orifice.</margin>
For the material from which the stomach is built has received this nature and aptitude to conceive tartar and admit its adherence. Once this happens, singular diseases arise, such as **burning of the throat** <note>Heartburn or acid reflux</note>, tightness of the diaphragm, and other compressions and tortures. Even paroxysms arise, similar to the paroxysms of the stone. 

<margin>Tartar from raised vapor.</margin>
At this point it must be repeated that it often happens that by the vapor and smoke of the food rising from the stomach, such tartar is also generated. Just as when wine is distilled, the tartar is so subtle that it ascends along with it. For that is not the right way of separating the "ultimate matter" of its waste. Therefore, it flies through at the same time. However, if another and true "industry" <note>A specific alchemical technique</note> is applied, then the tartar is separated in "burning wine" <note>original: "vino ardente"; this refers to distilled alcohol or brandy</note> no differently than in other wine; which they then call **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine|Ethanol or concentrated alcohol</term>, which is the tartar of wine—that is, it is the tartar of wine which has been dried out with the waste products. It is generated in this way. 

<margin>Distillation makes all things sharper.</margin>
Therefore, if this happens in the stomach—that it boils up and raises the tartar—then in that process it acquires more acrimony. For every single thing distilled and digested is sharpened in its nature. Now indeed, the pain or burning of the throat happens from many causes. For sometimes it is calcined tartar, sometimes salt, and similar alkalis, according to their nature. 

<margin>Causes of burning in the throat.</margin>
Nature generates and manufactures all these things; nothing is more foolish than man himself. From this, the magnitude and multitude of pains emerge, if they burn and boil in this way, like lime from water. It also often happens that a heat of this kind is induced in the mouth of the stomach either by food, or by drink, or by salt: all of which

### TREATISE III ON THE ORIGIN OF DISEASES FROM TARTAR

must be noted. For since tartar is of a single nature, it also conceives a uniform paroxysm <note>A paroxysm is a sudden attack or increase in symptoms, such as a "fit" of pain or coughing</note> from ingested food, drink, or from cooling, or exercise, and similar causes. Add to these the paroxysm of the stone <note>original: "calculi"</note>, which also follows its own nature and condition.

<margin>The empty labor of physicians regarding tartar.</margin>
In this way, then, it is introduced into the stomach. More often, however, it happens that tartar is found at the "mouth of the stomach" <note>The cardia or upper opening of the stomach</note> in the aforementioned manner, and with it stones of various shapes, which excite pains similar to those produced by bile. These are indeed "purged" by the followers of Avicenna and Galen <note>Followers of the traditional Greco-Arabic medical authorities whom Paracelsus frequently criticized</note>, but they are not actually driven out. It also happens in the stomach that tartar adheres there from stones, boluses, and the like, just as it does on the teeth; but not truly from slime. These stones or tartars of the stomach break down its power, and change and alter it into various diseases and pains, just as a special chapter has been assigned to these diseases below. Nor do these things only happen; but sometimes stones also clog the passages so that the bowels are restrained. Is it not fair, then, to bring forth and explain here those things which for so many centuries lay hidden, suppressed through ignorance? For see the ancient errors: How many patients are distressed by purges, when no necessity demands that humors and viscosities, and other things sticking in the stomach, be led out? For not only do those things help nothing; but the matter itself becomes more dangerous day by day. For they do not lead out or drive out the tartar by purges. Unless you know how to reduce calcined <note>Calcination is the alchemical process of heating a substance to reduce it to a dry powder</note> tartar into sand and grasp its transmutation, all your effort and entire endeavor will be spent in vain.

<margin>The various works of tartar.</margin>
Just as you now see the types of tartar in the stomach, which are various and can adhere to the stomach and thus be coagulated by the **spirit of salt** <term>spirit of salt|In Paracelsian thought, a specialized digestive or acidic force that can harden soft waste into stone</term>: so now observe further, that burning, compression, boiling, and other diseases behaving thus—as if some millstone, or fire, or stone, or trunk were pressing down—all these, I say, proceed from tartar. This alone confounds and annihilates all the rules of the ancients. For they never understood nor knew the "reduction" of tartar <note>The process of breaking it down chemically</note>, much less do they know it today. Therefore, they practice medicine with certain shame and disgrace, and with their recipes they slaughter men before their appointed time. They discovered things that ought not to have been discovered. But they have no other wisdom. Reduce the tartar, and you will extricate yourself from the disease.

<margin>Tartar from food and drink.</margin>
To understand the matter more clearly, there are at least two ways in which tartar is born in any man, yet distinct from each other. One way it is born from food, the other from drink. That which comes from food goes to the intestines and is excreted from here through the bowels. The other hastens to the liver and bladder, and thus withdraws. Of the first, we shall speak before; of the second, later.

<margin>What is the goal of tartar from food</margin>
<margin>What is the goal of tartar from drink</margin>
<margin>What are the primary seats of tartar.</margin>
In the beginning, recall to yourselves what was said above: namely, that tartars are generated in the mouth, in the mouth of the stomach, and in the stomach. Now, these diseases are specifically distinguished from those we shall describe hereafter. Namely, those tartars which are united from both food and drink become one mixture. This must be observed. For the stone that is produced there from the tartar of food is easier to dissolve than the other which is born from drink.

<margin>How the tartar from food differs from the tartar of drink.</margin>
The explanation for that which comes from drink is one thing; that which comes from food is another: and yet, compared to all other stones and tartars, they have another nature and property. These differences, for that reason, deserve to be specifically noted in the cure. For that second kind is easier to treat.

<margin>The difference of tartar according to location.</margin>
For the further it is from the mouth to the emunctories <term>emunctories|The organs or passages in the body that serve to carry off waste products, such as the kidneys or pores</term>, the harder and firmer is the coagulation by the spirit of salt. For subsequently, the tartar is more and more distilled, refined, and precipitated; and the further it penetrates, the more accurately it must be attended to. Thus, that which is in the mouth is the easiest to treat. That which is in the mouth of the stomach is second. The third, and the most stubborn of the three, is that which resides in the bottom of the stomach. Henceforth, that which is further from the stomach in the intestines is even more persistent; but the most firmly fixed is that in the liver, kidneys, and bladder. For that which is in the intestines is from food. Therefore, it is milder than that in the urinary passages. Consequently, there follows a further division of those twin paths, with their conditions and natures.

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
And would that, as was right, these things had been provided and explained long before me: then certainly they would have applied their labor more laudably, and brought more benefit than they do with their trifles, with which Galen, Rhazes, and Avicenna with their commentaries grow so insolent and are carried away.

<margin>The duty of the separating power.</margin>
Just as the separating power <note>Paracelsus refers to the "Archeus," a vital force or "inner alchemist" that sorts nutrients from waste</note> is established in the stomach, which discerns the putrid from the impure, and the dung from the nourishment: so also a double dung is produced from food, namely from edible things and from drinkable things.

<margin>Drinkable foods. Edible drinks.</margin>
Take this in such a way that you understand there are many foods which, besides being foods, also exist as drinks; likewise, there are many drinks which are also foods, and lead to that which they nourish by drink. Whence one generation of tartar follows, not two. And

-># ON DISEASES FROM TARTAR, TREATISE III.<-

Although the origin comes from two things [food and drink], the mixture forms at least one single kind. It is divided into its own species according to the nature of each. And although at this point it might be argued that more of the cause comes from drink than from food, there is no need to assume this, for drink does not enter the body except in the form of drink or food. For in its journey, "drink" must also be understood in this way: that is, if it arises from the liquid part of the foods; that is, the liquid which is in the food.

<margin>Tartar of the intestines.</margin>
Furthermore, observe this general rule regarding the intestines: all waste from the stomach passes through them. Now, there is a long delay within the intestines before it exits, so it stays in that place for a long time. There, the tartar sticks together, as has been said. It stirs up various diseases in the belly, the number of which exceeds infinity. From this, colic is largely born, as well as griping <note>original: "tormina"</note> and twisting of the upper and lower belly, obstructions, flows <note>likely referring to diarrhea or dysentery</note>, and the like. You must know precisely that this tartar produces fits <note>original: "paroxysmos"; sudden attacks of symptoms</note> similar to a stone in the bladder; that is, they are of the same type of fit. Therefore, just as a stone causes pain in its own location, tartar also causes agony. And what is displayed by the bladder in stone-forming disease <note>original: "lithiasi"</note> and painful urination <note>original: "stranguria"</note> is manifested by the intestines in colic and griping. And as you know that no one is paralyzed <note>original: "resolui"</note> in the limbs below the waist by a bladder stone, you should also know here that a similar paralysis occurs in all limbs. This tartar does not wander only downward or upward, but through the whole body. Therefore, in its own specific chapter, pay careful attention to the origin of Colic.

<margin>Movement of intestinal tartar.</margin>

<margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin>
But a great error was committed by the ancients in the description of this disease. For it has often happened that this tartar has caused such great constipation in the intestines—specifically when it adhered to some intestines like the tartar of wine <note>the crusty sediment found in wine casks</note>—and being inserted into the fat and soft parts, it was subsequently piled up and emitted nothing of itself. In such cases, neither purges, nor syrups, nor enemas <note>original: "clysteria"</note>, nor anything else could be of help.

<margin>Obstruction of the intestines from a tartar stone.</margin>
Many times a coagulation also occurs, which, through the length of time and continuous layering, grows to the point that at last a stone grows into a massive bulk. This stone, allowing nothing to pass by, violently closes and locks the <term>monoculum</term> <note>the "one-eyed" intestine; the cecum or blind gut</note> where it usually grows. This formation is similar to flint, to which mud sticks one layer after another until at last a large stone is made from it; for such is its growth in water. Because there are many kinds of tartar—such as lime, <term>Duelech</term> <note>a Paracelsian term for a specific type of painful, stony deposit</note>, others that are rough, smooth, Mercurial, Aluminous, etc.—so too are many various types of "Colic" (as they call them) generated. But be very careful not to mistake tartar for simple Colic or gas <note>original: "ventositatibus"</note>. This is a famous error. It is a very shameful thing that so many Italian and French physicians—<margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin>especially those living in Montpellier, Salerno, and Paris, who all compete for the prize and look down on everyone else—yet know and can do nothing. They are clearly caught out, for all their art is hidden in their tongues, which produce nothing but babbling. They do not fear to order enemas even if they bring about death, and yet they think everything is perfectly cured. They boast loudly of their accurate and subtle anatomies, and yet they have not yet observed that tartar sticks to the teeth—to say nothing of other more serious things. These are the "sharp-eyed" physicians who need no spectacles for their noses! What, I ask, is your "first-hand observation" <note>original: "autopsia"</note> and Anatomy? In which you have not even the slightest skill? These men are imitated by the German "cuckoos" and thieving physicians who look on like fools; as do the recently hatched idiots. And when they have looked through everything, they know a little less than nothing. Thus they are, as it were, strangled by waste and corpses. When this is done, they sing a Requiem <note>a mass for the dead</note>. I wish they would actually visit the sick.

Therefore, note that the liver takes pleasure in nothing but what is its own—that is, the nourishment. The rest, which is superfluous, runs through and hastens to the urinary passages. For just as rain falls drop by drop, if it is generated—not all the water at once, but that generation is drop by drop, and it falls in the same way, as is taught in Mechanics—so it happens likewise with the matter of nourishment belonging to the liver. And just as colic is generated in the intestines, so here other pains arise, according to the nature of that <gloss>9</gloss> place in which the tartar is located. It also frequently happens that the collection there is too great, so that because of this tartar, the nourishment cannot pass through. Therefore, with the nourishment left in the stomach, vomiting follows, along with a lack of appetite for food, wasting of the limbs <note>original: "tabes membrorum"</note>, a fit <note>original: "paroxysmus"</note> of the stone, etc. That is, it is like a certain fever with cold and heat, such as the plague, pleurisy, and other similar diseases; yet all of these are at least one fit of tartar, just as erysipelas <note>A bacterial skin infection, though here likely referring to any red, inflammatory rash</note> largely derives its origin from tartar.

<margin>The placement of nourishment.</margin>
Know likewise that if this matter of nourishment and urine meet in one passage and proceed to their paths, then in that transit the nourishment is extracted. From which it follows that it is necessary for both the urine and the nourishment to pass through all those small veins that constitute the liver. Now indeed, the urine runs ahead of the nourishment into the liver, being pressed through the veins. If it lingers there too long and does not flow through quickly and easily, but is affected and dried by the swift heat of digestion, then tartar is left behind in the liver. Although this material may be retained, it behaves just as if it had been dried out by the sun. However, it is not merely dry; the **spirit of salt** <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, the active principle of salt that causes solidification and coagulation</note> is present. It joins together and coagulates the matter into tartar, according to that form of which the prime matter is capable. <margin>What are the paths of urine?</margin>
So then the urine, passing to the bladder, hastens through peculiar paths directed from the liver into the kidneys. These paths or passages contain nothing other than raw and immature urine. And just as the excrements of the stomach are not yet dried in the stomach itself, nor in the intestines, but first receive their form in the **caecum** <note>original: "monoculo"; literally "the one-eyed [gut]"</note>, at that hour of drying in which the expulsive virtue is generated in them: so also it should be known concerning the urine, that the closer it is to the bladder, the more subtle and formed it becomes. This is not because those intermediate passages draw their own nourishment from the urine, but because heat cooks it more perfectly and thereafter purifies and clears it more and more. This same thing also happens to the dung of the intestines. For the intestines take no nourishment from drink, but draw this from other places and parts. But the reason why both the dung and the urine are thus prepared is that each thing gradually matures until it reaches its own native place. So also is drink, and so is urine, which gradually matures until it flows into the bladder: for there it is perfectly matured and purified; just like a pear, which begins to grow in the month of May. If it reaches autumn, it is mature. Before that time it is not yet mature, nor is it even truly a pear.

# TREATISE IV ON DISEASES FROM TARTAR

Therefore, understand in this way: in those pathways that lie between the liver and the <term>emunctorium</term> <note>An organ that carries off waste; here referring to the urinary tract or bladder</note>, many types of tartar are generated that are sharper, more violent, and more powerful than those in the stomach, the mesenteric veins, and the liver.

<margin>Those diseases which arise here.</margin>
For in those cases, the urine is sometimes found by testing to be quite pure and clear. Yet, the clearer it appears, the harder and sharper the generation of tartar actually is. From this, obstructions are then stirred up, occurring alongside attached scales, leaves, grit, sand, and stones, and other similar things by which the urine is contaminated. Thus also in the loins many types of <term>Erysipelas</term> <note>original: "Erysipelae"; a red, spreading skin inflammation</note>, <term>Phlegmons</term> <note>original: "Phlegmones"; deep-seated bacterial inflammations</note>, <term>Abscesses</term> <note>original: "Apostemata"</note>, and ulcerations are produced, which nevertheless never come to light, and are neither seen nor recognized.

<margin>Reproof of the doctors.</margin>
In these cases, therefore, it would be necessary for a man to be dissected before an anatomy lesson <note>The author suggests practical observation of the disease is better than theoretical anatomy</note>, and for this tartar to be properly examined and considered. But these blockheads, even if they were to look at it with their own eyes, they still stand there as stupid as **a calf before a Bishop** <note>An idiom meaning to be utterly confused or dumbfounded</note>, and they say of that wine, "This is a certain viscosity." Look, master Doctor, is dung not also red earth?

<margin>The kidneys are not nourished by urine.</margin>
Furthermore, it is established from both physical and anatomical principles that the kidneys do not grow or receive nourishment from the urine. Instead, they are nourished in the manner described in the specific chapter on the head. It is also certain that in the kidneys, the urine does nothing else but wipe away and wash out the filth.

<margin>Urine is the balm of the kidneys.</margin>
For urine is the balm of the kidneys, which without urine would easily rot. For this reason, we are dealing here with the urine, and not with the nature and condition of other things. Thus, the urine is afterwards clarified even more and rises to its redness; that is, it "approaches autumn" <note>The author uses seasons to describe the chemical ripening or color changes of bodily fluids</note>. But there is also a certain cavity and space ready at hand, to which it can easily cling like a barrel, if the <term>spirit of salt</term> <note>original: "spiritus salis"; an alchemical term for a mineral acidic force that causes solids to precipitate out of liquids</note> pursues the tartar too swiftly, so that it is separated from its own excrement—that is, the urine.

<margin>The different types of kidney tartar.</margin>
For then either a leafy tartar, a sandy tartar, or a stony tartar is generated: all of which differences are drawn from the kidneys, whose property is in that place. Take such an example from the inner secrets of Philosophy: If someone drinks water that produces flints—and the tartar of that water is separated and extracted from the waste—and then that spirit of salt comes upon it, then a stone is generated from that tartar, not a leaf, not a scrap, not sand. But if it separates from sandy water, then sand is produced. The same applies to the other forms. Although it also happens that it sometimes sticks to its own mud and dregs, these are distinguished very quickly. Unless that happens, then dry tartar adheres; when this occupies and closes off the entire place, it brings on death. In other cases, it turns to stone, according to the nature of the water. If that water is fit for producing many stones, then its tartar also brings forth many. If it produces large or rough ones, etc., the tartar also produces such types according to all those differences.

<margin>Where the stones get their color.</margin>
The stones absorb their colors from the urine and the juice of the kidneys. Sometimes they retain their own distinct and primary colors, such as blue, red, purple, yellow, saffron, and so on.

<margin>Green, blue-gray, and black stones.</margin>
Green, blue-gray <note>original: "cyaneus"</note>, and black are not generated, because those colors are separated in the opening of the stomach, where they perish. Furthermore, those colors are otherwise rare and infrequent. Therefore, as is the custom of the region and the nature of the food and drink, so is it right that we too can find the form, the kind, and the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>A sudden attack or fit of the disease</note> according to all the ways that tartar contains it and in which it is innate.

<margin>Tartar of the bladder.</margin>
Thus, the urine is then carried forward into the bladder. In this place also, the generation is such that it can easily be attached. For it has enough of both space and matter for that; yet it does not remain but is scraped and dragged away. However, the "walls," leaves, and scraps are not scraped away, as they are too wide. Nevertheless, grains are distinguished, which grow there in the manner of sand or stone. Know, moreover, that the sandy form arises solely from the nature of the region—that is, from the nature of the food and drink of that region. From this you can now easily understand where a stone or sand comes from, after you have considered the kinds of stone and sand, etc., of that region, such as pumice, flints, and others. For no form is produced from anywhere else than from the general nature of stones in that region. Furthermore, the coagulation occurs solely from the spirit of salt, which persists in that condition and form. Now, just as it happens that one, two, or more stones, and likewise much sand, are made or born in one place at the same time, so hold this brief rule for all of them.

<margin>When there are many stones: and what they are. Why multiple infants are born.</margin>
If one or more stones are born, the cause is the same as why two or three infants are born. For here one similar matter is present, one likeness. Two or three infants are born for this reason: because nature was ordered toward one infant. But now it happens that a double nature and double seed are collected in one shell, just as...

In this way they grow, with one being more abundant than the other. This is why one is larger or smaller than the other. Indeed, their size, shape, and likeness cannot be strictly defined. 

So it should also be held as certain regarding the bladder stone <term>calculus</term> <note>A stone formed in the bladder or kidneys</note>: they are not generated one after another—that is, one growing for so many years and then a new one beginning. However, concerning gravel and sand, the common rule is that they grow perpetually. For they are not equated to the specific generation of stones.

Enough has been said so far regarding the generation of tartar in the urinary passages and the manner in which it occurs. If this account seems brief, it is because of the specific chapters where each genus and species is presented individually. Meanwhile, the passages have been indicated: namely, those leading from the mouth to the stomach, from the stomach to the anus, and from the stomach again to the liver, kidneys, and bladder. Furthermore, regarding urine and the waste of the intestines, nothing has been omitted.

Beyond these things, another type of tartar must be recognized. <margin>Tartar of the principal organs differs from the tartar of excrement.</margin> This concerns the principal organs whenever they are burdened by tartar, from whatever causes or materials. This tartar contains its own peculiar diseases. The reason is that it does not emerge from the tartars already mentioned; rather, it is a "foreign" tartar born specifically in those locations. And although it has its origin and cause in food, it does not consist of the nature of excrement as previously shown, but is driven through other pathways. For this reason, it must rightly be separated from the others. Just as its kind is different, it also occupies specific organs, as will be taught in its own book.

First, however, it was proposed above regarding Treatment <note>original: "Curatione"</note> that stones must be expelled through "reduction" <note>An alchemical term meaning to break a solid back down into its constituent liquid or softer parts</note>. There the art is placed in the preparation of those things that reduce the stone, but do not transmute or precipitate it. 

Yet there is another treatment for this, which will be handed down shortly. At this point, it should be known that it often happens that one <margin>Tartar as a disease.</margin> stone is expelled, in whose place another is later substituted—just as one child is born after another. In such a case, the cause is none other than the first cause, which can return a second time or more. From this, one must conclude that tartar is a foreign disease of growing things, arising from the earth and its liquids. These liquids are of the sort from which a mass, stone, glue, and sand are born; these in turn descend into us with legumes, grain, herbs, wine, water, or meat and, as has been said, grow upon us or are glued to us. <margin>The most effective remedy for tartar.</margin> Against this sticking, there is no more effective medicine than butter and olive oil, as the regimen for those things demonstrates.

### FOURTH TREATISE
#### The Fourth Tartar

Let us proceed to the generation of tartar as it occurs in other organs, such as the lungs, gallbladder, heart, spleen, brain, and kidneys. To understand how generation occurs in these parts, learn from this general rule: everything that exists within a human being needs food and its daily required nourishment. That nourishment remains in the state it was in when it was taken into the stomach. 

Once it is drawn to its proper places, then you must know that every single part in the body acts as its own stomach <note>original: "ventriculo"; Paracelsus envisions each organ having its own digestive capacity</note> for itself, separating or casting away from itself whatever is not good or what it does not desire. No organ performs this office of "cooking" <note>The ancient view of digestion as a form of heat-based cooking</note> for another. The stomach alone works for the sake of the whole "commonwealth" of the body. <margin>Each part has its own stomach; the main stomach is a public servant.</margin> And just as it works in the urine for the sake of the liver, kidneys, and bladder, it also undertakes this for the benefit of all other parts. 

However, through the main stomach, not all things are sufficiently separated; instead, every single organ undertakes a new preparation. It seizes what it considers suitable and akin to itself, but separates and shakes off the useless. Those things thus separated are also excrements, for which various exits have been established. Thus, the lung is purged through the arteries; the brain through the nostrils; <margin>The paths through which each excrement is led out.</margin> the spleen through the hemorrhoidal veins; bile through the stomach; the kidneys through the bladder; and the heart into the "chaos" <note>original: "chaos"; a Paracelsian term referring to the atmosphere or the air into which the heart's "spirituous" wastes are exhaled</note>. 

Therefore, just as the principal parts of nutrition terminate separately in their own passages, so these excrements of the principal organs are the material from which the generations of tartar are established, according to their own natures. For they are very subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" means refined, gas-like, or microscopic</note> if they lose themselves and manifest there. Concerning their condition, consider this example: as if something...

### TREATISE IV ON TARTAREOUS DISEASES, 75

If something is distilled to the highest degree and further refined into a state of volatility so that it appears to be without a body—yet in truth, nothing is made without a body. And if it should indeed seem to be so, a body is always found by a skilled and proven craftsman. It is the same here: since tartar is found neither in the stomach (due to excretion) nor in the urine, it is instead found as a volatile body. It permeates the other aforementioned members like "burning wine" <note>original: "vini ardentis"; i.e., alcohol or distilled spirits</note> ascending, so that it is thought to be without a body. Yet it is not without one. Even if it is placed in a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized alchemical glass vessel used for "circulating" or continuous distillation, where the vapors condense and flow back into the base.</note> and circulated, it still contains the tartar within itself.

<margin>Even volatile things have a body.</margin>
The same applies to those substances. Therefore, if they fall into the appropriate places of the aforementioned members, then at last the **twin craftsman** <note>This refers to the *Archeus*, the internal "chemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believes resides in each organ to govern its functions.</note> is present. He is the one who can separate the body from the volatile part, which the other craftsmen—namely, the stomach, liver, etc.—cannot do at all. In this way, any single thing is truly found in its congruent places according to its own property and "exaltation" <note>In alchemy, 'exaltation' is a process that raises a substance to a higher state of purity or power.</note>; this is evident from this common example: One man and one woman are bound in one marriage. If these two, as they are joined, come together, no adultery is committed. The reason is that the <term>anatomy</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "anatomy" not just for physical structure, but for the inherent spiritual and functional "map" or destiny of a thing.</note> and the concord are as one, and nothing violates it. But if they do not come together, the love is not solid and firm, but wavering like a reed in the water. For the man who goes wooing elsewhere does not have his legitimate spouse according to the tenor of Anatomy. Likewise, the woman who goes wooing does not have her legitimate husband. For to every human being, a certain libido or pleasure is innate from God to prevent them from becoming an adulterer. Therefore, the commandment applies to those who are joined by no such bond:

<margin>Dual marriage.</margin>
that they should keep that commandment as if they were joined. Thus, there are two marriages: one of those whom God joins, as mentioned above; the other, which men join themselves. The first keep faith without a commandment. The second do so minimally, being bound by the commandment. So it is in our present proposal. If any thing is brought into the conjunction and concordance of its own anatomy, then it brings forth whatever it has. If that does not happen, it cannot be forced to separate. Therefore, if one wishes to explore the secrets of nature, the **twin master** must always be added to them, and according to that mastery, all things must be handled and observed with it. Otherwise, all things that are produced will be blind and obscure.

<margin>Why lung tartar is scarcer than in other parts.</margin>
Thus, it must first be known that if those things are to be brought to their destined places, a portion is detained in the lungs. Before I begin to explain that, I would wish you to be forewarned: there is little tartar there, and it does not aggregate in such a heap as in the other passages of the urine or the intestines. The cause is that what the lungs "eat and drink" is very little indeed. For if you were to measure the multitude of things a man ingests—and from that mass you subtract both the dung and the urine—certainly very little will be found remaining in the body. If, therefore, all the members (of which there are many) must be nourished from that tiny quantity, certainly in that distribution, very little will fall to the lungs. And therefore, from that very thin mass, no such "solemn," manifest, and daily operation or species of tartar could proceed as occurs in the urine and intestines. Therefore, these things must also be observed more accurately according to its generation. But for the understanding of these things,

<margin>Why it is more harmful than other more abundant tartar.</margin>
this must also be known: that on the contrary, such a small amount inflicts more damage than a large amount of something else. Add to this: that in matters of this kind, the <term>spirit of salt</term> <note>The active mineral principle Paracelsus believes resides in the body, which can either prevent or cause the "stony" solidification of tartar.</note> cannot prepare itself for operation as often. For here it is not as powerful as in other passages; instead, it is forced to rest to some extent. Where there is no multitude [of matter], there its power does not abound. For the multitude of the spirit of salt arises from the multitude of matter.

Concerning the tartar of the lungs, we shall therefore hand down these things next. You often see that in the lungs of both animals and men, <term>calculi</term> <note>Stones or hard mineral deposits.</note> are found, similar to grains of millet. Furthermore, veins enter into the lungs. These veins do not have a similar anatomy to the blood veins of the other principal parts. Therefore, a peculiar treatment is owed to these veins in this place. The

<margin>Lung veins are the stomach.</margin>
veins of the lungs are the "stomach" of the lungs. In these veins, the lung separates the pure from the impure, and what it finds unsuitable for itself, it rejects. The [main] stomach

<margin>Lung veins are the stomach.</margin>
does not know this separation; yet the lung knows it. Hence it also happens that a peculiar excrement is found in the lungs—that is, inserted into the "pipe" <note>The trachea or bronchial tubes.</note> itself—which are its only stomach, created by God for this use: so that excrement may be <term>pelicanized</term> <note>Processed or circulated, as if in a pelican vessel.</note> and articulated in them until it falls into the lungs themselves. <margin>The stomach of the brain.</margin>
Similarly, there is also a specific stomach dedicated to the brain. However, this stomach is *outside* the brain, not inside it. Once the brain has received this, it begins its stomach-like operation. Just as the stomach (I speak of the first one) is the primary corruptor of all members when it does not perform its duty uprightly and well, so too must we understand the stomachs of the individual members: many diseases are born from their weakness. Yet, all these have thus far been taught by no one, but have been erased by oblivion and ignorance.

But these other stomachs, which are of such great importance, they have not even caught a scent of. From this, one can correctly conclude that many diseases exist which are born from these ventricles, but which doctors have wrongly categorized under other headings, caring little for what they do or what reality they are treating. It is therefore right that a special book be written about such diseases, which is why I set these things apart.

This tickles you so pleasantly that even in other matters, whatever you merely guess in passing, your decrees must be followed simply. And deservedly so: for as the flock is, so is the king. Pay attention, therefore, so that you recognize whether diseases of the gallbladder come from a stone or without one. Know also that the gallbladder has no greater enemies than these wastes. It rarely falls ill if tartar does not concur, whether separated or not. Believe this also: the stone in its paroxysm expels the bile in many ways and modes that are not appropriate to describe here. Thus, here too it strives for the same: it produces jaundice, paralysis, distortion, colic, compression of the chest, vomiting, indigestion, and so on. And for all these things, the physicians are not ashamed to say <margin>Rebuke of the physician.</margin> that it is "cholera" <note>yellow bile</note>.
