<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s radical redefinition of female anatomy. Having previously established the woman as a unique "monarchy" or "Microcosm" tied to the macrocosmic world, he now specifically attacks the prevailing medical theories of his time regarding menstruation, pregnancy, and the origin of breast milk.</meta>

<page-num>94</page-num>
<header>THE PARAMIRUM, BOOK IV. ON THE ORIGIN.</header>

This flower is then followed by the fruit, which is the offspring. Do you doctors not know that every flowering tree flowers because of the fruit that is about to burst forth? Even a tree that has no fruit within it does not flower. Yet, according to your opinion, a woman flowers and yet contains no fruit within herself. That is to say: by your judgment, virgins flower; but where is their fruit? There is none. Therefore, that flow is merely excrement <note>original: "excrementum" — in this context, it refers to biological waste or a byproduct, not necessarily feces</note>.

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
Although this error is very crude, it excessively defiles both the Galenic and Avicennist physicians along with their followers, who say that *a virgin flowers without a man, from whom the flower emerges*. For if she is said to flower at all, then she must necessarily push forth fruit as well. From this, it would follow that children are born without men. O foolish Doctors! <note>original: "O bliteos Doctores!" — 'bliteus' is a term for something tasteless or stupid, derived from the name of a bland herb</note> What good do you draw from your unexplored science? You contradict yourselves, as is the custom of men of your sort. Do you not know that the womb is nothing other than a *Microcosm*? <note>term: <term>Microcosm</term> (Microcosma) — a miniature world that contains the same structures and laws as the great universe (Macrocosm)</note> If, therefore, it must give birth, it must be cleansed for that purpose. This cleansing is such that all filth is pushed out through the established channels. Unless that purification is complete and all dead matter departs, the womb does not admit conception. It remains pure until the fading of the milk; this milk is not produced from the menses, but emerges from the breasts, which are destined and consecrated for this use.

<margin>Menstruation does not occur during pregnancy and lactation.</margin>
And as long as pregnancy and breastfeeding last, no such waste exists. For all things are tranquil and yield to this time. During this period, nothing impure is born that needs to be excreted. For such is the nature of woman: as soon as she conceives, she is transmuted, and all her parts behave as they do in summer, when no snow, frost, or winter storms prevail, but all things smile, pleasant and lovely. The womb itself is bathed in this kind of loveliness and summer joy. Therefore, all waste products rest quietly until winter returns and its frost and snow reappear. For then the waste products seethe once again. Here, however, it is necessary to understand the time of birthing, and what condition or proportion it holds. This is what the physician must discuss.

<margin>Milk is not from the menses.</margin>
For if he is ignorant of this, whatever he brings forth will be worth nothing. It is a blind induction to claim that the menses produce milk, and that it becomes the nourishment of the fetus. Fools! Question nature first before you write commentaries on books. Each and every one of these things is explained more clearly in Philosophy, in the place where the generation of man is taught.

From these things, therefore, learn the anatomy of the womb and what the entire body of a woman is: that the fetus in the womb draws its nourishment from the breasts and, even outside the womb, coaxes from them the best and most noble milk—not at all that waste product which they call the *menses*.

<margin>The menses as poison.</margin>
Since no poison more foul or harmful is found upon the earth than that, how could it serve as nourishment for the fetus? How ignorant and unrefined is the saying, *that a human is nourished by that poison*, when nothing more virulent exists in the body than that waste, nor can it be offered to others? For it admits no other transformation for the better. That is to say: no poison becomes food, but remains poison. What father is there who would hand his son stones or a serpent instead of bread? No one. Much less God Himself; consider this diligently.

<margin>How and why the menses cease in pregnancy and breastfeeding.</margin>
This, however, is true: that nature rests and is suppressed according to its "poison," just as the sun stood still and was fixed in the time of Joshua. So too is every movement of nature halted from the time of conception until the infant ceases to live in that way and is fed and nourished in the manner of other men. Indeed, it is also true that what is ejected during birth is useless. You think milk is produced from that; yet a "mole" <note>term: <term>mola</term> — a 'false conception' or 'uterine mole,' a mass of tissue that grows in the womb but is not a viable fetus</note> could more easily result from it.

<margin>Nutrition is from good juice. The fetus is nourished by its own.</margin>
And this is a sign of divine faithfulness: that filth of this kind does not harm the fetus, and that the fetus is rendered safe and secure from it. And yet you are not ashamed to say the fetus is nourished by those things. For nothing anywhere is ever nourished by filth, but rather by pure juices, whether they be trees, herbs, or roots. All things desire to be nourished and sustained by subtle liquids, such as dew and rain. Of all these, the fetus is the most worthy in terms of its nourishment. There is more in an infant than in a herb of the field. Furthermore, the infant's nature is of the softest and most tender kind. Therefore, it is entrusted to the care of the womb and the breast until it attains a more solid strength for food.

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
Now, what else is that flow in a tree but its own seed? For all things purge themselves through foam. <note>original: "spuma" — foam or dross. Paracelsus views menstruation as the "scum" rising to the top of a purifying liquid, which is then discarded</note> In the same way, nature herself is cleansed through foam, so that a purer and more exquisite food is supplied to the fetus. You, however, assert the opposite: that this foam becomes food, and that milk is produced from the menses and retained in the womb until the fetus is brought into the light; at which time the menses...

# OF THE DISEASES OF THE WOMB

...that the menstrual flow turns into milk. It is abundantly clear from such things what kind of "philosophical liquor" <note>original: "Philosophicę liquore" — Paracelsus is mockingly referring to the theoretical foundations his opponents use to explain biology.</note> you are stained with. Pay close attention: that which overflows is the "foam" of a cooked substance, which the fetus eats in the mother’s womb and which flees from the breasts. See now how these excrements are foamed out. Do you not understand that if a drink had to be skimmed of its foam, nothing would be left of it? These Stoics <note>In this context, Paracelsus uses "Stoics" as a derogatory term for rigid, traditionalist university doctors who follow ancient rules without observation.</note> are truly austere.

It is therefore fair and appropriate that both diseases and health be presented as a unique monarchy, since they are distant from the afflictions of men by such a great interval. This is not just by reason of the breast, or the womb, or the menstrual flow itself, but also with respect to the whole body, which was built for the sake of the breast (or nipples), the womb, and the menstrual flow. Therefore, if the body was built for these things, it must also be built according to their nature, and not according to an alien nature—that is, a male one. And although it often happens that one and the same medicine is useful for both men and women—as occurs in the plague and in fevers—it must nevertheless be known that all such things happen entirely through a power that is either narcotic and numbing, or diaphoretic <note>term: <term>Diaphoretic</term> — a substance that induces sweating, often used in older medicine to "break" a fever.</note>; these are not applied according to the true origin and method of appropriate remedies. For this reason, because they are not drawn from the legitimate order, it happens that they are beneficial today but less so tomorrow; they help in the plague, but in another disease, they do not. More will be said of these in their proper places. But because one must heal by a correct and legitimate method, it is right that women, with their specific diseases and their specific health, be separated entirely from men.

<margin>The woman is like a tree; the man is the fruit.</margin>
An example shall be given. The woman is like a tree bearing its fruit. The man is like the fruit which the tree bears. Understand it this way: a tree needs many things for its support while it brings forth that for which it exists. Now, just as many injuries can provoke the tree, but only a few can provoke the pear (the fruit), so it is with the woman compared to the man. In respect to the man, the woman is what the fixed tree is to the pear. The fruit indeed falls away, but the fixed tree remains. Furthermore, the tree has the care of other fruits yet to come and a longer-lasting life. Therefore, it is compelled to endure and suffer many things for the sake of the fruits, so that they may be born soundly and successfully. Therefore, if you wish to be good physicians, weigh carefully what this example teaches and how it is to be understood. For if you do otherwise, you shall never be skilled physicians. Meditate on this "monarchy" separately; you will see that what is specifically necessary for the tree is not at all necessary for the pear, and what is necessary for the pear is not necessary for the tree. Although this is an external lesson, the same principle is considered to hold for the man and the woman. From this, you will also gather that the difference between the male and the female is the same as that between the pear and the seeds enclosed within it. By whatever condition these two differ from each other, boys and girls differ similarly; for which I refer you to Philosophy.

<margin>Woman is not from the Limbus.</margin>
Have you never considered within yourselves that "man" [humanity] is from above, namely from the Limbus <note>term: <term>Limbus</term> — in Paracelsus's theory, the "Great Limbus" was the primordial "extract" of all created things from which God formed Adam.</note>, but only the male, not the female? The woman is the second creature, not the first, nor created with the first. Therefore, she is below the man. If, therefore, she is the second creature and not from the Limbus, she will also be different in her body. For if she were of the same body as Adam, she would also have been created from the Limbus. But because she had to manage a different monarchy, she was made after the man, from living flesh that was flesh. From that flesh, another flesh was created, just as flesh was made to come forth from the Limbus (which was not flesh before it was made so). Thus, the woman is from the flesh of the man. But that flesh did not remain "woman" [as a part of man]; rather, she separated from the man as much as the man separated from the clod of earth from which he was created. And this is the reason for establishing a "New Theory" concerning the woman and referring her to a specific Physics <note>term: <term>Physics</term> — here meaning the study of the natural laws and physical composition of a body.</note>, and thus for refuting those who judge and estimate man and woman by the same likeness—even though these doctors otherwise present themselves impressively, except for those things pertaining to the womb (which provides the place and nourishment for the fetus).

<margin>Reproof of the physicians.</margin>
<margin>Which authors are to be admitted.</margin>
Now, consider the needs of the fetus: the whole body is required for it, and not a single drop of blood remains in the body that does not become necessary for the womb. Therefore, they have undeservedly separated the blood from her. But they themselves did not understand the matter, nor do their "chicks" <note>original: "pulli" — a mocking term for the students or followers of established medical authorities.</note> want to grasp it today. How sweetly it tickles you whenever you insist: "Galen says this, Avicenna says that." By this means, you have certainly covered yourselves well and hit your mark! But do you really think that because those men said those things, they are therefore true? First, prove that the author is truthful and blameless, and only then make him "authentic." But that labor will cost you dearly. Because faith is given to those putrid authors, and their words are held as Gospel—and you yourself are no more "wiped clean" [discerning] than they—you rightly melt away along with those lying authors. For like is easily joined with like.

<page-num>96</page-num>

### PARAMIRUM BOOK IV: ON THE ORIGIN

...and the devil often brings both together. Because it is established that a different condition and monarchy <note>Paracelsus uses the term "monarchy" to describe a self-governing biological system or realm of influence within the body.</note> prevails in a woman, it is now necessary to establish two monarchies: that is, one monarchy of the woman and another of the man. From this follows a different knowledge of the heavens and a "Microcosmic" agreement <note>original: "Microcosmica consensio" — the belief that the human body (the Microcosm) reflects the movements and structures of the universe (the Macrocosm).</note> existing within both, which has been overlooked by those blind-sighted doctors mentioned before.

<margin>Jaundice in a woman is different than in a man.</margin>
Since the human body is now separated so that one belongs to the woman and another to the man, by reason of this connection, a distinction must also be proposed in diseases. This is so that those things said thus far may be understood more clearly and readily. Consider an example of this kind: let there be one case of jaundice <note>original: "icteritia"</note> that occupies a man, and let there be another that afflicts a woman. Now, let the signs and prognosis for both cases of jaundice be the same, and let everything else be so similar that they seem to belong to one genus or species. One might not establish one species for the man and another for the woman, but after considering all circumstances and evidence, might think it is one species of disease—that is, one thing. Consequently, it would then seem that one cure and one medicine should be applied. Yet, that cure will not work. I will propose the reason to you.

<margin>What "Hermaphroditic" medicines are.</margin>
Some medicines are indeed "Hermaphroditic" <note>In this context, Paracelsus means "universal" medicines that are effective for both sexes, as opposed to "specific" medicines that only work for one.</note>, being beneficial to both sexes; a special book has been written about these, which I will exclude here. But regarding the course of a true regimen, understand it this way: a woman has jaundice like a man, but besides that, she has something else as well. That is, the "body" in which this jaundice exists is a *profluuium* <note>While usually meaning a "flow" or "discharge," Paracelsus here uses "profluuium" to describe the specialized internal environment or "liquor" of the female body.</note>.

<margin>What a *profluuium* is.</margin>
What is a *profluuium*? It is not the waste matter or the menses themselves; rather, it is the whole body from which the menses emanate. That body retains the name of "profluuium" when it becomes diseased. In other contexts, it is the "liquor of the Microcosm." This liquor is subject to jaundice, occurring in such a way that the cause is the same in the man and the woman, yet the "body" [the underlying substance] is not the same. For in a similar way, you might dye both a peacock and a piece of wood a yellow color; the color is indeed the same—that is, the disease is the same—but those two bodies are different. And although they present one color and one sign, the medicine must be directed toward the bodies, not toward the color. Just as wood is mastered by an adze, and iron by a hammer, you must know that the body itself must be similarly subject to the eyes of the physician. Unless he proceeds in this way, he will never expel the disease. For even if he insists on medicines that remove the color, the body itself is nevertheless left behind as it was.

<margin>Species of jaundice.</margin>
For if the liquor of the Microcosm turns toward its own flow, it becomes white. What is this other than "white jaundice"? For the other kind is yellow. White does not proceed from yellow unless it is stopped. Thus there are many effusions—red, white, yellow, and black—all of which should be understood under one heading.

Furthermore, since the body must be attacked—not the colors alone, but the body and the colors together—the medicine must therefore be separate and distinct. And even if you use Hermaphroditic medicines, whether simple or compound, you do not possess or employ them through true art, but out of madness or unskilfulness (as will be deduced more fully in its proper place). For we cannot be persuaded otherwise than that you at least mix and confuse them. If it succeeds, you have hit upon the thing by chance. This is the true art: that you do not add male medicines to female ones, nor female to male; but that you keep each monarchy within its own Anatomy and do not mix them. Indeed, that which is mixed is such that it is not rendered perfect by either side.

<margin>To whom Hermaphroditic remedies should be given. The power of Plantain.</margin>
Any single Hermaphroditic medicine should be administered alone and separately, not as a compound. This is how the matter stands: Plantain <note>original: "Plantago" — a common herb used to treat inflammation and bleeding.</note> checks dysentery in both men and women. It is indeed Hermaphroditic. And yet it separates itself, having a place in the Anatomy of both, and serves both monarchies. There are many others like it, though their number is not very great. If it is applied to a man, then the female "secret" <note>original: "arcanum" — the hidden medicinal virtue or essence.</note> within the herb lies dormant. If it is applied to a woman, the male part dies away.

<margin>Whence "experiments" arose.</margin>
From these Hermaphroditic medicines, "experiments" <note>By "experimenta," Paracelsus refers to empirical remedies found through trial and error rather than derived from the "canonical" or theoretical rules of ancient medicine.</note> were born. Therefore, in other simple medicines, no "experiment" exists, but only "canonical practice." However, to say that Hermaphroditic experiments are sufficient is far from the truth. Why do experiments help? They help because the disease does not always attack "canonically" [according to the rules], but against the canon. For that reason, they are useful. But that which attacks canonically must also be treated canonically; no mere experiment does anything here. Similarly, that which does not attack canonically cannot be removed by canonical care; here, only an experiment is useful.

<margin>A reprimand of physicians.</margin>
But many things ought to be investigated regarding these matters, which are deferred to a more suitable place. From this, recognize that it is a great error for writers to claim that all diseases arise "canonically," and for that reason, they propose a "canonical cure" everywhere. This is followed then by...

He introduces the concept of "Hermaphroditic" medicines—universal remedies that can work for both sexes—but warns that true medical art requires understanding the specific anatomy of each sex.</summary>

->**OF THE DISEASES OF THE WOMB**<-

...then comes the standard treatment, upon which their errors are built. Furthermore, if the standard treatment seems to be less than effective, there follows the *Treasury of the Poor* <note>original: "Thesaurus pauperum" — a very popular medieval medical manual of simple recipes</note> and other easy-to-obtain remedies. "Use this," they say, "it has been proven in many cases. Indeed, this is effective: for this person testifies to it." In this way, their error is manifest: they do not understand the difference between standard medical care and mere anecdotal experiments. Observe truly these blind doctors.

Furthermore, learn from the example of jaundice <note>original: "icteritia"</note> or similar diseases: there is not just one "yellowness," but many; and because of this, many types of jaundice exist. And while bile indeed expresses that color, there is not only one single color within it; rather, all shades of yellow lie hidden in it, as is taught in its own chapter. Now, female bile is one thing, and male bile is another. Thus, the colors are also different. Therefore, if they are different, the medicines must also be different. If the medicines are divided, the medical practice will also be divided. *Assa* <note>A Paracelsian term likely referring to a specific transformative process or substance</note> is the promoter of the color. *Ressella* is the remover of them. *Rearea* is the experiment. However, the principal matters in these things are not these "hermaphroditic" experiments that remove colors; rather, they must be treated from the foundation so that the body obeys and complies. For bodies are changed in standard diseases: just like an object being dyed, whose tint never vanishes, but the body and the color remain inseparable as one. When things are established in this way, medicine must not behave in the aforementioned manner, but must proceed from its own "monarchy" to attack the body. In the restoration of the body, health itself is restored, and thus the disease departs.

<margin>The nature of diseases is twofold.</margin>
For there is a twofold nature in all diseases: *With a body, and Without a body.* Because this distinction has not been observed until now, let it be proof to us that they have wandered astray in their cures. Because there is one bile in a woman (which nevertheless has all the conditions and properties of bile), that bile cannot be mastered in standard diseases except through its own "monarchy"—that is, through the kind of medicine which is organized and cast into a different Anatomy and Physics than the medicine of men. Therefore, what the "male" centaury plant <note>original: "centaurea mascula"</note> achieves in men, the "female" centaury plant achieves in the same degree for women.

<margin>The providence of God.</margin>
For this was of such great importance to God that He attributed to women their own peculiar monarchy. And just as He transposed them from men into a different body and nature, so He also assigned to them specifically their own world and nourishment. He appointed the physician for this purpose: to scrutinize and know these things, and not to follow Avicenna or Galen <note>Two of the most famous ancient medical authorities, whom Paracelsus frequently criticized for being outdated</note>. For Divine Providence anticipated those fabricated wits, saying that He Himself created the Physician. This is the same as if it were said: *That Physician can do what I myself created. Any other who pushes himself forward is a fraud.* Now, discern by the light of nature which of us is the counterfeit and which is the genuine.

Just as all things that are born are distinct because of these two monarchies, as has been said, so also the firmament, the earth, water, and air are divided into these two monarchies so that each may protect its own nature. Consequently, understand now that the food which a human eats and the food <margin>Nutritious foods differ from medicinal ones.</margin> of Medicine are by no means one and the same thing—that is, they are not of one condition or nature. The reason is this: every food that is eaten is simple. And although it is indeed divided into two monarchies, that distinction concerns only the medicinal powers, not the food or nourishment itself. Although food taken from their own monarchy is healthier for women in many things than food from the monarchy of men, this happens because of the cause of disease, not the nourishment. A "Smith" and "Craftsman" <note>This refers to the *Archaeus*, the internal alchemist or life-force Paracelsus believed governed the body's functions</note> lives in the stomach; he fashions human flesh from it. He is equipped with two natures, even though the digestion is only one. One nature is in him so that, if he works in a man, he produces male flesh. If he works in a woman, he generates female flesh.

<margin>The Archaeus in the body.</margin>
This Archaeus, however, prepares for the human within their own monarchy. Therefore, no worry about providing nourishment troubles the physician; he only needs to concern himself with providing the medicine, so that it may be led into its own monarchy. For as far as nourishment is concerned, the Archaeus in the stomach masters and subdues it, and from it fashions and forms what is needed. And just as a blacksmith fabricates whatever he wishes from his iron, so does the Archaeus. The logic for medicine, however, is not the same. <margin>Food is the human.</margin> Medicine must be brought forth from its own monarchy so that it is kept in its own nature. For in that place, the Archaeus cannot change it into something other than what it is. Everything we eat is the human being himself. If a human eats and ingests it, he makes out of it what he himself is; that is, flesh and blood. For we are those things. But we are *not* medicine; rather, this medicine expels one disease, and that one another, according to how we are afflicted. It must be given and handed to us from that specific species and genus. For the stomach does not produce from it what we need unless it first receives that which is supposed to be beneficial. If it does not, then by its own power, the stomach rejects it. And for that reason, the body and its diseases are two things in one.

<header>PARAMIRUM BOOK IV. ON ORIGINS</header>

According to this standard, the regimen <note>A "regimen" refers to a prescribed way of life, including diet and medical habits, to maintain or restore health.</note> must also be established so that it is divided according to its own monarchy <note>Paracelsus uses "monarchy" to describe a distinct biological realm or sovereign system within the body—specifically the separate "realms" of male and female biology.</note>. For a single regimen should not be given simply to produce blood and flesh; rather, its purpose is to expel that which has corrupted or contaminated the blood and flesh. Therefore, there is one medicine at hand, and one food: that is to say, the regimen produces blood and flesh, yet not simply from nourishment, but through medicine.

Understand it in this way: the regimen is both *nourishment* and medicine. For a body that is diseased will not grow, but rather diminishes. Therefore, if you wish for it to be increased, the regimen must be a medicine that acts to ensure the body accepts food as nourishment. For this reason, the monarchy in a sick person must be maintained by both food and medicine, insofar as it pertains to the disease. If the body were healthy, such a measure would not be necessary.

<margin>Medicinal foods.</margin>
However, it is true that we do not simply place those things which are both food and medicine—such as *Lettuce, Chard, turnips*, etc.—into the account of this monarchy, but we distinguish them to some extent. It is established that they coincide with a certain medicine, and this power in that monarchy must be separated in such a way that a woman is given her own chard, and a man is given his own. From the neglect of this distinction, it follows that the firmament and the astral motions <note>Paracelsus believed that the movements of the stars influenced the "inner heaven" of the human body.</note> are impacted, and they stir up a certain dissolution in the opposite body outside of its monarchy. Consequently, in women, their "time" <note>Referring to the menstrual cycle.</note> is interrupted; in men, "other flesh" grows. What is convenient and healthful for the man in this regard turns out to be damaging and harmful to the woman. For establishing a regimen for a healthy person is a greater task than for a sick one: the healthy person requires a multifaceted knowledge that looks after all the limbs, whereas the regimen for the sick is minimal, and the secrets of all things are most powerful there.

<margin>The physician's duty in prescribing</margin>
Now, he who prescribes a regimen of health in such matters should divide the monarchy itself, and consider the motion of the heavens and the condition of the persons; only then will he anticipate the movement that is within the food. For food has its own "star" <term>star (astrum) <gloss>The inherent celestial or vital power within a substance that governs its effects</gloss></term> just as the heaven does; therefore, it even resists the heaven. He who does not understand this is caught in obvious error. For he will not be anticipating what is already present, but what is yet to come. Indeed, the whole art is placed in this: that what is yet to come may be prevented. The physician must have full knowledge of this. If he does not, his art is mere butchery and robbery.

Since the first matter <note>original: "prima materia" — the raw, original state of a substance before it is transformed by the body.</note> of human flesh and blood is one thing—that is, food and drink—there are nonetheless two "ultimate matters" produced from that single first matter: namely, male flesh and female flesh. These are as different from one another as meat and fish; yet, neither the first matter nor the ultimate matter is easily recognized. For God, who joined man and woman, established "one flesh" there—that is, He joined them into one flesh so that they might eat one food and drink one drink, not two. Therefore, they even share one first matter. However, the Archæus <term>Archæus <gloss>The internal "alchemist" or vital force that separates nutrients from waste and directs the body's growth</gloss></term> is different. He enters the monarchy of that which is eaten; though those who are joined eat from a single pot. If a theory is needed here, understand it this way: there is a necessity in these things concerning that which is transmuted. It is proper to know how this happens, and what the Archæus does, if from that which is one, he produces male flesh and <margin>The Archæus is one thing in a man, another in a woman.</margin> menstrual flesh, which differ by a great margin. Assume this about them: because diseases are born from and invade through food, it is right that this be known fundamentally in the ultimate matter, not in the first—unless perhaps the first matter, in its own powers, becomes "hermaphroditic," <note>That is, a mixture of male and female qualities that hasn't been properly separated by the body's internal processes.</note> or becomes some medicine belonging to a divided monarchy, concerning either the man or the woman. For then that must be taken away and excluded, just as a disease is taken away by the same process. For if the defect clings to the ultimate matter rather than the first, then it is detected in the ultimate, not the first. Therefore, look for diseases there as well, because the ultimate matter in this place is broken within itself and stirs up diseases for itself. Hence, its theory must rightly be directed toward the rule of this Physics. And thus, finally, his Physics will achieve its goal. We see and recognize that our subject is placed in the ultimate matter, not the first. From this <margin>The ultimate matters of men and women differ.</margin> it follows that we must know how great an interval exists between the ultimate matters of women and men, so that we may separate and distinguish them by that same interval in the Monarchy. Unless it is done in the manner described, it is certain that a chronic or fatal disease will be birthed and maintained in that place.

Furthermore, other things must be passed down concerning the matrix <term>matrix <gloss>The womb or uterus</gloss></term>, namely how it ought to be known according to the Microcosmic <note>The "Microcosm" is the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note> nature; specifically, as a small, third, and indeed ultimate creature, which nevertheless retains the nature of the Microcosm. Know, therefore, that it is a matter of general knowledge that the vessel which conceives, forms, and protects the infant is called by the common name **Matrix**. Although the woman is all of that, it is nonetheless right that the seed, for whose sake—

### ON DISEASES OF THE WOMB.

...woman was created, let this name <note>The name "woman," which Paracelsus derives here from her biological function.</note> be primarily preserved. For it is because of this vessel that woman exists, and not for the necessity of any other member or part. To understand the <term>matrix</term> <note>The womb or uterus.</note> more correctly, know that the whole woman is the earth, and all the elements. This womb is like a tree, growing from the earth. The fetus is the fruit bursting forth from the tree. And just as a tree is rooted in the earth, and thus exists along with the earth in the air, in the water, and in the fire—all of which the field provides—so too in the woman there are four fruits, four Elements, and both the upper and lower spheres. In the middle of all these, the tree is fixed, and it is for the sake of this tree that woman was made.

<margin>Woman was created solely for the sake of the womb.</margin> <note>The original Latin margin uses "mamma" (breast), but the text and Paracelsian theory treat the breast and womb as a single integrated system of the "maternal monarchy."</note>

<margin>In woman, all things are present.</margin>

Just as the earth and its fruits exist with the Elements for the sake of the tree, to sustain it, so too all the members of a woman, with all their natures and properties, exist for the sake of the womb. Therefore, the knowledge of such a creature must begin in this way, so that we may learn to recognize our subject as it pertains to medicine. But let us continue. Just as a tree draws nourishment for its body and growth from the four fruits, the four Elements, and the upper and lower spheres—without which it cannot thrive, and which it changes and alters in various ways until it becomes a tree and is preserved—so too in the woman, the womb, like a tree, draws to itself from all parts of the entire body whatever is necessary for its own preservation. In this way, the womb is sustained by the body of the woman in every form, just as a tree is sustained by all the Elements and fruits. From this it follows that because the womb seizes its own nourishment, it is also necessary that at its appointed time—namely, every month—it must eject and cast off its waste, as was said above. If you consider it in this way, as if the womb were like a sea and like a tree, you will easily recognize what its diseases and what its defects are.

<margin>In the Microcosm, all minerals are present.</margin>

This is how the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—a philosophical concept that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note> or "lesser world" behaves, containing within its body all the minerals of the world. From this, you should understand that the body seeks its medicine from the world, for the body is the world itself. From this it is again clear that *all minerals are useful to man, if each is applied to its corresponding mineral located within the body of the Microcosm.* Whoever lacks knowledge of these things is by no means a Philosopher, nor a Physician. First, if a Physician says that <term>Marcasite</term> <note>A general term used by Paracelsus for metallic ores and minerals, particularly iron pyrites.</note> is useful for this or that, it is absolutely necessary that he first knows what the Marcasite of the world is, and what the Marcasite of the Microcosm is. This is a matter of Philosophy. Furthermore, if he wishes to speak as a physician, he will say: *Marcasite is a disease to man; and therefore it helps or heals man.* If the skin of the body is eaten away, and a limb develops an ulcer from that erosion, what else is that but a Mineral? For it is like a salt, and belongs to the same grade and genus as salt. Now, <term>Colcothar</term> <note>A reddish-brown powder (iron oxide) produced by heating vitriol; it was used as a drying and healing agent.</note> heals that opening.

<margin>What Colcothar is and to whom it belongs.</margin>

Why? Because Colcothar is a salt that "eats" into the opening. Similarly, Mercury also heals its own ulcers, as do other Arsenical minerals. You can learn that these things are true even from your external senses, and recognize the differences between them through experience: namely, that this kind of salt heals, while that one is of another kind and nature. Those things belonging to this class do not solidify wounds at all; rather, <term>Comfrey</term> <note>Latin: *Consolida*; a plant used to "consolidate" or knit together wounds and bones.</note>, <term>Mumia</term> <note>The vital life-force or an alchemical preparation thought to contain the essence of life and healing.</note>, and <term>Balsams</term>—which are not salts—heal wounds. Why is that? Wounds are not caused by salt. Therefore, neither salts, nor vitriols, nor Mercuries, nor Arsenics are helpful. Because these "holes" or erosions are caused by salt, and Balsams, Mumia, and Comfrey are not salts, they are not effective for curing those specific openings. If these things happen externally on the skin, it must be known that the internal body also possesses these minerals, and must be understood according to them, and not according to the "humors." <note>Paracelsus famously rejected the ancient Greek theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile), preferring to explain disease through chemistry and minerals.</note>

<margin>Knowledge of the three substances is necessary.</margin>

Thus the body itself consists of these three substances <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the "Tria Prima" or three primary materials of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>, as do all material things. For this reason, one must also consider the "first" and "last" matter, where the former must agree with the latter. For all things exist in a state of correspondence. He who is ignorant of this correspondence is unjustly called a *Doctor and author of medicine*. Indeed, he heals none of the sick unless they recover on their own, to the good fortune and reputation of the physician; for beyond this, they deserve no other reputation.

In this way, then, the womb conceives its diseases from the "earth" of the body. And just as a tree that is corrupted by the earth loses its greenery, its nature, its power, and even its fruits and apples, the same happens to a woman. Unless her body is good, healthy, and balanced, then the entire womb itself becomes corrupt, sterile, unhealthy, unfit, and filled with every kind of disease. Therefore, by the same method that the earth and its fruits are to be understood, you shall also examine the Microcosmic woman. And what the earth loses in the tree, it also corrupts in the womb. What happens to trees also happens to the womb. If something foreign occupies a tree, it corrupts it...

<summary>Paracelsus uses the analogy of a tree growing in the earth to describe the womb's relationship to the female body. He argues that diseases are caused by mineral imbalances and that physicians must understand the chemical "Microcosm" of the body to provide cures.</summary>

# PARAMIRUM, BOOK IV: ON ORIGINS

<margin>The fetus is affected by the womb.</margin>
<margin>The womb is affected in two ways.</margin>
This also occurs naturally in the womb. If a color other than the natural one is applied to a tree, then its fruit is also tinted and discolored. So it is with the womb. Hence, many conditions emerge within it for which infants are forced to pay the price, becoming either distorted and monstrous, or varied and spotted in their coloring, or affected in some other way. The cause of all these outcomes is the womb. For what a man performs with his hands when tinting and coloring a tree, a woman performs through her **imagination**, as will be discussed more extensively in its proper place. From this, one may now gather that the womb becomes either healthy or sick depending on how it is influenced by that in which it is established. It follows the impulse of its environment. Therefore, when we are to judge its diseases, we shall first examine all the minerals of the body; then the four Elements, the fruits, the firmament, and both spheres <note>Paracelsus refers to the "upper sphere" of the heavens/stars and the "lower sphere" of the earthly body.</note>. If we judge all these correctly, the conditions of the womb will easily reveal themselves. For first of all, pain shows itself, and of this, the womb bears witness. He who does not know these types of minerals will not be able to discern the faults of the womb. For if <term>Cachimia</term> <note>An impure mineral ore or the "immature" state of a metal.</note> can produce goiters in trees, and talc can generate worms, they can likewise stir up the same in the uterus, so that goiters, ganglia, and nodules are born; from this example, you may easily judge other diseases as well. But if you cannot conveniently speak in this way—claiming, for instance, that a disease is generated from melancholy or phlegm—you must attribute it entirely to the minerals from which a goiter grows, whether it be fibrous, venous, or fleshy. Thus, it is necessary that all diseases be discovered through this cause.

<margin>The origin of fools and other monsters.</margin>
<margin>The quality of the fruit.</margin>
But regarding the precedence or the eruption of species within minerals, it must be decided and judged in this way: whichever species gains mastery also governs the "tree" of that "earth"—that is, the womb fixed within the body. This being established, know once again: if any nature flows into a species, it is not removed until that species is consumed or overcome by a foreign mixture. Hence, fools, the mindless, the goitrous, and other monsters are later born, whether according to their nature, their person, their limbs, or their proportions. These things happen according to diseases in other matters as well. Now, since this condition is deposited in the womb, should not a different Theory be established? And although it is true that the parent himself, through these mineral species, can generate children similar to himself—insofar as his own "species" exists implanted in the seed—one must nevertheless know that the womb undergoes a double fate. One arises from the woman herself. This concerns the tree. A good tree bears good fruit. Such a fruit is healthy in the body and in the earth, and is also fertile or fruitful. Then, the tree is also good, and from it comes good fruit. The other fate consists in the generation of children: that is, a healthy seed produces healthy fruit. Thus, the seed and the tree are two distinct things here, divided into two parts. The tree of the earth puts forth its fruit perpetually, even without seed. However, the "tree" of the woman does not do so, unless seed is applied to the tree by the man. From this, it is clear that the greatest importance is placed in the seed. Unless the seed is healthy in itself, it will never be improved by the goodness of the tree. Therefore, what happens to the tree also happens to the seed. It is necessary for both to be good. If both are good, only one good outcome remains: the fruit. Therefore, other accidental factors also concur, which affect the womb during the planting of the seed; these diseases are to be judged according to the properties of the man, not the woman. Thus, the womb is now divided: into diseases that are its own, and those conceived from the man.

<margin>How male diseases in a woman are to be cured.</margin>
<margin>Jaundiced seed makes the woman jaundiced.</margin>
And this, finally, is the true and skillful Theory, born from the light of nature itself and not from a fanatical brain. Diseases that affect women because of men require "male" remedies. From this, it is established that male remedies for <term>nephritis</term> <note>Kidney disease.</note> also remove nephritis in women. For what reason? Not because there was a single cause for the disease in both, as some have thought, but because the woman had become sick by being affected by the man. Therefore, the male remedy was also beneficial. However, for what she suffers from her own self, such a remedy is of no use; rather, medicines must be drawn from her own <term>monarchy</term> <note>Paracelsus's term for the unique biological and functional domain of the female body.</note> and no other. For this reason, a remedy was sometimes helpful and sometimes less so. And this is the truth not of one, but of all diseases. For you must believe this: that seed drenched in <term>icteritia</term> <note>Jaundice; a yellowing of the skin and eyes.</note>, when cast into the womb, excites jaundice in the woman. The reason is that the seed, once attracted, proceeds to its own "anatomy." Therefore, if a woman is seized by this kind of jaundice, she wishes and ought to be cured entirely with male medications. For the body is so greedy for the emission of seed that it moves and compels all its joints and all its members to that work. From this, it is manifest that if the said members separate, each one carries away with it the anatomy of its own place regarding sicknesses, and by this act contaminates itself.

<summary>Paracelsus explains that the womb (matrix) can be diseased either through its own mineral imbalances or through the "contagion" of the male seed. He argues that diseases contracted from the male require masculine remedies, as the woman's body absorbs the male's specific anatomical ailments during conception.</summary>

<header>DISEASES OF THE WOMB.</header>
<sig>I 3</sig>

### DISEASES OF THE WOMB.

<margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin>
...contaminate, and thus establish the beginning of the generation of that disease. Ignorant physicians think it a great defense whenever they cry out that this or that medicine, in this or that place, has cured this specific disease, in women as well as in men. But reason proves that they speak here without skill. For if they testify to such things even concerning young girls who have not yet experienced a man, they surely confirm our opinion of their ignorance even more seriously. For they are unaware that girls are heirs to their father's goods as well as his diseases through his seed. And since they have received these evils from the father, they are likewise healed by paternal remedies. This is the pure and simple ignorance and lack of skill of those men, because they have known neither the origins and causes of diseases, nor their modes of operation. While they repeatedly pour out their "humors," <note>Paracelsus is mocking the traditional Galenic focus on balancing the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note> they closely imitate the example of John of Garland, <margin>John of Garland.</margin> who did the best he could and wrote a commentary on Alexander. Although that work is worth nothing and of no value, he nevertheless did what <note>John of Garland (c. 1190–1252) was a famous grammarian; Alexander likely refers to Alexander of Villedieu, whose grammar John commented upon. Paracelsus uses them as examples of useless academic pedantry.</note> he could.

<margin>The body of the disease is one thing, the woman another.</margin>
Now, however, it must also be understood how these two things come together; namely, that which comes from the man and the body of the woman. Therefore, there are two bodies which do not permit mutual mixing without the destruction of one or the other. These two bodies are the body of the disease and the body of the woman, which is to suffer within its <term>anatomy</term> <note>In Paracelsian terms, "anatomy" refers not just to the physical structure, but to the internal spiritual and elemental blueprint of a person.</note>. Now, the body of the woman is a whole and is not broken. For where the body is anatomically broken, medicine will profit nothing. For no help remains for a broken body, just as burnt or broken wood, turned to charcoal and crushed, is never restored. However, the body of the disease—that is, what is present from the man—is a body of disease; not a body of the "first matter," but only of the "ultimate matter." Furthermore, these two bodies are distinct. The body that comes from the man is like a spirit. That which is from the woman exists as something corporeal. Now, spirit and the corporeal can exist together just like air in a body, or in water, wood, or stone. <margin>How do spirit and body coexist?</margin> But if the air is corrupt, then the wood also becomes diseased from it—not because the wood or stone themselves fall ill, but because that which is within the wood or stone is diseased, yet is neither wood nor stone. That thing is indeed the air. Thus it is clear that the air is diseased, not that physical body; and one should not think the wood is sick, but the air itself. So it is in this case also: when a man is diseased in his seed, the disease of the seed is like "air." Thus the disease conducts itself within the woman’s body according to its anatomy, like air in a foreign body; though with this difference: that here colors are added which are not added when they meet with air. But understand it as if a color exists. They are taken up if they are foreign to that body in which they are found. For this must be observed accurately: because four bodies <note>Likely referring to the four elements or the "four pillars" of Paracelsus's medicine.</note> consist within one substance, in which diseases lie, not in the manner of a humor, but in the manner of a body; and not as if there were a humor in that body, but a <term>liquor</term> <note>A subtle, vital fluid, distinct from the gross "humors" of medieval medicine.</note>. Consider these things, you whose art this is. <margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin> Because you have not yet recognized any body consisting of the four elements, you are necessarily doubtful about the seat of the plague, whether it be in the blood or the flesh. For you do not know that blood is a fourfold body. You do not even know that a stone is a fourfold body. Learn this, therefore, before you place the red biretta <note>The "tiaram rubeam" or red cap worn by doctors of medicine as a sign of their rank.</note> upon your head.

He is well instructed by science who has discovered what makes an <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note> and what makes a body. For he has recognized that blood does not produce those things which are not of the nature of blood—namely, such miraculous bodies. He is also industrious and skilled who knows by what means a woman conceives from a man in another body. Why is this? Understand it in this way. Heaven makes one man different from another, and a man different from a woman. The <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the stars.</note> can do this, the star can do this, the course of the heavens can do this. So the man also, by a similar reasoning as has been said, is the star, firmament, and heaven of the woman. And just as heaven makes a different kind of person, so the man also makes a "different" woman—that is, another nature and property in those things which pertain to the order of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The concept that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the "macrocosm" of the universe.</note>. Through influence and impression, the woman is "constellated" by the man; her own stars recede from her, and the stars of the man are received in their place. He who knows these things stands upon the path of true medicine. But he who knows nothing of the stars will find none of this even plausible. <margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin> For who is a more capital enemy to nature than he who judges himself wiser than she, when she is our supreme school and discipline? Such is the labor of the ancient writers, who added so many vain commentaries concerning the diseases of women. For they never mentioned, even by a single word, that transformation which is instituted in the interior of the woman’s body by the stars of the man, according as these two microcosmic natures are mutually affected by one another. For the inferior receives an impression from the superior, and therefore inclines toward the manner of the superior...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases of the womb often originate from the "stars" or spiritual influence of the man, which "constellate" the woman's body like the heavens influence the earth. He scolds traditional physicians for focusing on humors and failing to understand the fourfold elemental nature of the human body.</summary>

nature. These things must be described in two ways through the power of Theory and Physics. For if the body is to be weakened by the star of the man, then he infects that which is inclined toward him by his own impression. And just as the stars of heaven incline and compel regarding diseases, so too does this male "course" incline, so that it may reach the body of another woman, generating those diseases which are referred to another branch of Physics. In these matters, you physicians are blind, since you pursue not the art itself, but filthy lucre <note>Paracelsus frequently accused the medical establishment of his day of being more interested in profit than in true healing.</note>.

<margin>The source of suffocation of the womb.</margin>
Ponder this "heaven," which comes from the man, with zeal and diligence. For from it many diseases are born, which have been wrongly attributed to other origins and causes. Take, for example, **suffocation of the womb** <term>suffocatio matricis: historically known as hysteria, it was believed the womb could move or "suffocate" the woman</term>. From where does it come, if not from the heaven of the man, who כך constellates the body of the woman? This is the first origin of this disease. If this influence is to be brought into action, then the man is in the **falling sickness** <term>caducus: epilepsy or the "falling sickness"</term>; that is, his own star is falling. And even if this does not actually happen to him, there is still an "inclination." For in this way, the stars also inflict diseases upon men from which the stars themselves do not suffer. If this constellation becomes a conjunction or an impression, then the "suffocation" emerges, which is similar to the falling sickness. Truly, this has been the ignorance of all the academic schools.

<margin>Reprimand of physicians.</margin>
The alumni of these schools have commented much on the falling sickness and the suffocation of the womb, yet they have shamefully failed to indicate what kind of body it has from the "four falling sicknesses," or in which place it lies hidden. Because they were silent on these things, it is no false suspicion that they were much more ignorant and unskilled regarding the essence of the disease. Therefore, their commentaries are mere opinions and prejudices.

<margin>How the man acts upon the woman.</margin>
The first duty that falls to a physician is to describe the body and the substance. This is the foundation from which one can be judged a master in the medical art. The same applies here. If a man is so constellated in his own "heaven" that he contains such a conjunction within himself, then it must necessarily break out. Now, he has two bodies—that is, two subjects: his own body and the body of the woman. If the inclination turns back upon the man himself, then his star and his will are weak and have vanished. But if it does not turn back upon the man himself, but toward the woman, then the falling sickness pervades her—not the specific kind the man has, but the falling sickness of the womb. For here the body is different, not one that can be compared to the man's. For two inclinations are present: one of the external heaven, reflecting the man’s heaven; the other of the man’s heaven, which is the suffocation of the womb. Therefore, three different "falling sicknesses" shine forth from this: the man’s is masculine, the woman’s is feminine (though both are from one heaven, for the condition of this heaven is masculine), and the third belongs to the interior body, which receives its heaven from the man.

Know therefore from these things that these matters are propagated in a hereditary manner—if not in the father or the mother, then in the fruit <note>the "fruit" refers to the child or offspring</note> itself. This is one thing: that a man does not infect himself with the true "falling sicknesses" of the interior heaven, except in the form of a **fainting spell** <note>original: "syncopen"</note>. But he infects the woman with the suffocation of the womb.

<margin>A girl is affected by suffocation in two ways.</margin>
In a girl who is born, suffocation is imprinted in two ways: in the manner of a virgin, and in the manner of a woman. The virginal type is similar to a fainting spell, attacking with some early signs of the falling sickness. Suffocation, however, is more than just fainting. Concerning these diseases, specific chapters have been established in their proper place, especially for understanding the **Mechanical** <note>the "Mechanicus" in Paracelsian terms refers to the practical application or the "workman" of nature</note> aspects, which we will not describe at length here.

Now, what has been said about "suffocation" must similarly be understood regarding "precipitation" <note>likely referring to a sudden onset or "falling" of humors or spirit</note> from the man—that is, from his heaven. For all those many diseases which the womb receives—more than are even encompassed under masculine names—proceed from the heaven of the man. And although they do indeed arise in the woman's body from the earth, the firmament, the air, and the water (as has been said many times before), the greatest cause is the heaven of the man. For just as the plague is a disease generated from the heavens beyond the nature of man, and yet it begins in the man and its final matter is in him, so it is also in this case. Now, precipitation is from the star whence **apoplexy** <term>apoplexia: a sudden loss of consciousness, often a stroke</term> flows. The flow of the womb is from the star whence **dysentery**, **lientery** <term>lienteria: a form of diarrhea where food passes undigested</term>, and **diarrhea** arise; these direct and end themselves in the womb according to that body of the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: the human being seen as a miniature version of the entire universe</term>. From this you can see that it is worth the effort for a physician to consider all things according to their first origin—how one thing proceeds from another and into another.

<margin>All things must be explored according to their origin.</margin>
Afterward follows the **monarchy** <term>monarchia: the sovereign power or ruling principle of a particular natural system or disease</term> with its interpretation. Unless you define diseases in this way within the four bodies according to their species, and explain the first principle of things, and—persevering in **anatomy** <term>anatomy: for Paracelsus, this means the structural and occult makeup of a thing, not just dissection</term>—separate the creature into man and woman, and likewise the medicine itself, then the art will surely represent nothing else but stale and juiceless cinnamon, melting and dissolving in the mouth like a shaggy cap. Thus the arts and sciences smile upon those who love them—that is, those to whom God has imparted them. Even if you were to be exceptionally skilled in these: [to you]...

He critiques mainstream physicians for ignoring these celestial origins and emphasizes the need for a gender-specific understanding of medicine based on these "first origins."</summary>

<page-num>103</page-num>
# ON DISEASES OF THE WOMB.

...you shall not keep these things to yourself alone, nor use them to flatter yourself: but you shall impart them to those for whose sake all medicine was created.

<margin>The physician alone is the most accurate observer of man.</margin>
Since, therefore, the physician is the only one who can most greatly extol and celebrate God, it is right that he should also be the most skilled and wisest of all. For who is there anywhere who can more accurately know what and of what kind man is, and how sublime he was made by God, than the physician himself? He alone can vividly illustrate the works of God above all others—namely, how noble the world is, and how much more noble man himself is; and in what way one proceeds and comes into being from the other in a versatile series. And he who is unskilled in these things should not boast of anything regarding medicine. For man appears to be fashioned with such great labor and in such a miraculous way that if one were to unroll his substance and nature through deeper contemplation, he would be found truly vast. And this indeed is the greatest thing,

<margin>Whatever is in the world is also in man.</margin>
which they ought to meditate upon constantly: namely, that nothing exists in either heaven or earth that does not also flourish in man. For these are the heavenly virtues <note>virtutes: here meaning powers or inherent properties</note> which shall be moved. For God, who is in heaven, is in man. For what and where is heaven, if not **Man**? If we are to enjoy this, we must confess that it is within us.

<margin>Man is heaven itself, the seat of God.</margin>
And therefore, as if from mouth to mouth, He perceives beforehand what we desire. For He is closer to our hearts than either our tongue or our thoughts. He established for Himself His own spacious and beautiful heaven, noble and best. For He truly dwells in heaven, that is, in man. For He Himself also testifies that He dwells in us, and that we exist as His temple. If He is in us, therefore, let us adore Him there where He stays—namely, in the heavens, which is to say, in man. Therefore, let the physician diligently weigh and consider what he handles with his hands. For he takes upon himself the care of the noblest and greatest subject: the noblest, I say, and one in whom so very much is situated.

But if he knows neither the world, nor the elements, nor the firmament: what, I ask, shall he know of man, who is everything that fills heaven and earth? What, since man himself exists as heaven, and that earth, and this air, and this water? He who established these things also established both <term>monarchies</term> <note>monarchia: in Paracelsian terms, a "monarchy" refers to a specific realm of nature or a sphere of influence (e.g., the realm of the body vs. the realm of the elements)</note>, and created medicines within His monarchies,

<margin>From where the physician must learn.</margin>
just as He also created the physician himself. But He created him such that he should learn from creatures: he should not trust in his own speculation or imagination, but should acquire knowledge for himself from individual natural things. For these are his teachers. For neither the foundation nor any knowledge of these things is drawn out from man himself <note>Paracelsus argues that medical knowledge comes from studying nature, the "great world," not just from looking at the human body in isolation</note>. Yet this is true: God appoints a physician for Himself whenever He wishes. For such is the power of Him who created all things. He allows him to be born when it seems timely not to man, but to God Himself. For He has reserved this for His own judgment.

Just as we see, therefore, that trees produce their good or bad fruits from the earth according to the influence of heaven (for there are few years in which the earth alone has dominion and produces its fruits according to nature, even if it is very good; so strong and powerful is the influence upon things being born). So too must it be determined regarding the body of a woman, that she is not without "inclination." Now, this knowledge is not slight: that a good soil brings forth good fruits, provided that no hindrance is brought in from external things—that is, from the external heaven. Understand it this way: we cannot look after the earth by itself, but must allow it to be adapted to the state and condition of the heaven—unless perhaps someone should come forward who is skilled in the <term>medical philosophy</term> of natural things. So it is on the part of the woman: it is similar, or rather, even more so. For she can be guarded so that she is not infected by the "lower heaven," that is, by the man. If infection is not introduced, she can bear good fruit from it,

<margin>How it is to be understood that a good tree bears good fruit.</margin>
because the earth is fertile and good. It matters much, however, that we understand correctly how a good tree bears good fruit. The genuine sense is this: a tree that is of a good nature brings forth good fruits. Moreover, that tree of an upright nature is stronger than every evil nature, and is so fixed in goodness that it cannot be violated by any evil nature. This example, therefore, fits in every part that allegory of Christ saying: **A good tree bears good fruit**. For this was said in a good sense, drawn from nature. From that good progeny, proceeding from nature, Christ chose His disciples for Himself.

<margin>Judas from a bad progeny.</margin>
But from that source whence evil comes forth, He took the twelfth disciple, Judas. For an Apostle of upright nature would never have betrayed Christ. But he did so, who was set apart from an evil nature. Since Christ so diligently instills in us the concept of a good and evil nature, we must therefore unroll it from nature itself. When a good nature is offered to us, effective medicines are at hand. When an evil nature is encountered, the same thing happens to us as happened to Christ with Judas. And this method or allegory must by no means be neglected. For from it alone...

<sig>I 4</sig>
biles,

<summary>Paracelsus describes the physician as a witness to God's glory who must learn from nature (the Macrocosm) to understand man (the Microcosm). He equates the woman to fertile earth and the man to an influencing "heaven," using the biblical allegory of the good tree and Judas to explain natural predisposition to health or corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physician’s duty to understand the hidden structures of human nature. It expands on the idea from the previous page that man acts as a "heaven" to woman, exploring how "good" and "bad" natures are joined and how a physician must discern the internal state of a patient just as Christ discerned the hearts of his disciples.</meta>

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>PARAMIRUM, BOOK IV: ON ORIGINS</header>

# PARAMIRUM, BOOK IV: ON ORIGINS

From this foundation, and from no other, arise all diseases, both curable and incurable.

Because Christ himself foresaw that it is so situated in nature that there is a "good" and "bad" nature to be chosen—even regarding eternal salvation—it is certainly worthy of a physician to know what a good or bad nature is. For this reason, I propose the following discourse here.
<margin>What constitutes a good or bad nature.</margin>
A woman, who possesses a healthy and upright nature, can be either preserved or not preserved by the <term>lower heaven</term><note>lower heaven: Paracelsus often refers to the husband or the male influence as the "lower heaven" that acts upon the woman, who represents the "earth" or "nature."</note>, which is to say, by her husband. For you see that natures which are otherwise good in faith can be inclined and persuaded toward good or evil by the "herald of the word" (the preacher).
<margin>The mouth of the preacher is a kind of heaven.</margin>
For the mouth of the preacher is a kind of heaven and an inclination. Just as he is a heaven, so too the man is the heaven of the woman; not through the mouth, however, but through that by which "the two are one flesh." Preachers of a depraved nature persist in that depravity and seduce the people through it. But the upright keep the people in their duty. Therefore, a woman must retain her own good nature, provided she is with a man who possesses a similar goodness.
<margin>Like produces like. The sense of Christ's words.</margin>
For in this way, when good is joined with good, it can beget nothing of evil. It was in a purely natural sense and manner that Christ spoke of marriage when he said: *What God has joined, let no man separate.* <note>original Latin: "Quos Deus iunxit, hos homo non separet." Matthew 19:6.</note> For he was indicating this: "You separate spouses by divorce and decide according to your own will. Why? Because surely your joining is of yourselves. You are of a depraved nature." Therefore, you also judge marriage depravedly. But a marriage that is from God is the joining of those through whom the chosen children of God are born. This you shall by no means separate. This is the same as if he had explained: "God joined the marriage (or the fathers and mothers) of Peter, John, Judas, Bartholomew, Simon, Philip, etc., and these remained bound by one bond. From these were born Peter, Judas, John, Philip, and the rest. For their good nature joined their fathers, mothers, and ancestors, all of a good character. And therefore, they shall not be separated from one another." Because Christ so diligently introduces this concept of "good nature" and chooses his own from it, it is fitting that a good nature also be recognized by the physician, so that he may preserve it in its proper state—namely, by bringing the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the human body as a "little world"</note> and <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the universe or "great world"</note> into harmony. Nor should he preserve them only according to their virtues <note>virtutes: here meaning spiritual powers</note>, but also according to the bodily matters of which we speak here. This knowledge is arduous and of great importance.
<margin>What kind of people the disciples of Christ were said to be.</margin>
Because Christ chose his disciples in this manner, it is also fitting for a king to be such, and it is proper for the people to create their magistrates by this standard. For a bad nature, feigning goodness, is a "Judas": he too had shown himself upright toward the poor, but he sought nothing but his own profit. Therefore, elections should not be made from the external appearance of speech, but from the innermost integrity of nature. For a bad nature has more "good" in its mouth than a good one. A good nature consists in works and actions; a bad nature, by contrast, performs nothing but promises much. Nothing is to be judged by the mouth; it must be judged by the heart. Indeed, the heart never enters the mouth except through works. Understand all these things as meaning that it is fitting for a physician to recognize a good nature in its goodness. Because that nature is situated in the heart, it is right for the physician to judge it. This is also how Christ speaks of marriage: *What God joins, let no man separate:* that is, if the marriage consists of a good nature, you shall not separate that union, but it shall remain unshaken, and you shall never dissolve it.

Now, just as the nature of a marriage is discerned to be upright or bad by its "conjunction," know that the very same thing must be sought in the nature of things. For whatever is good in it, nothing but good is begotten from it. Just as all things in the universe are distinct from one another—such as the Sun, Moon, Night, Day, Devils, and Angels—so this dual nature is also detected among men.
<margin>Nothing good flows from evil.</margin>
The nature that belongs to darkness, in whatever face or manner it exhibits itself, is always dark and evil. Nothing good is established from it, just as nothing good comes from the devil.

If, therefore, the case is such with nature, it will certainly seem that nothing whatsoever can be contributed to the good. I repeat this here because I established earlier that a good tree—that is, a woman—remains good if she was of a good nature in the beginning. If she is such, she will not be made worse by the "lower heaven" of her husband; that is, from any good nature, healthy and good fruits will be born.

The logic of the heart is the same, though this does not pertain to the physician here. However, this distinction must be held in medicine: that often a certain soil bears good fruit (that is, good seed is cast into it), yet it nonetheless degenerates. Therefore, a thing must be referred back to its own nature: namely, so that the soil and the seed agree. For this is that "marriage" which man does not separate, which is to say, what God has joined. For seed cast upon a rock perishes; that is, it wastes away, not being of itself...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the physician must discern a patient’s inner "nature" (good or bad) just as Christ judged the hearts of his disciples. He uses the metaphor of marriage and soil to explain how a woman's health (nature) interacts with her husband's influence (the lower heaven).</summary>
