# ON DISEASES OF THE WOMB

evil. A good nature is constantly preserved, so that it is not driven into the hatred of God: even if it fails with such a heart, as is the property of a good nature. So it is also in medicine: if any one of those [with a good nature] is seized by a disease, then he rises again by the power of medicine; but a bad nature collapses. From this, curable and incurable patients are found. Certainly, if they were compared to one another, they would be like Peter and Judas. The latter, who did not rise but hanged himself, remained as such.

<margin>
When diseases are incurable.
</margin>
Much indeed has been said until now about incurable diseases, but the foundation has not yet been touched upon, precisely because of the nature [of the patient]. A good nature also dies itself unless it receives a "resurrection"—that is, the help of medicine. Here, the ignorance of physicians converges; through a lack of skill, they pronounce as incurable that which was entirely curable. Thus, first, we must consider here the <term>heaven of the lower sphere</term><note>In Paracelsian thought, the "lower sphere" usually refers to the microcosm of the human body, specifically the reproductive organs in this context, which are influenced by celestial bodies.</note>. Then, the upper and lower spheres together, as one heaven. Furthermore, the nature and condition. Then the body. Finally, the <term>matrix</term><note>original: "matrix". While literally "womb," in this context it refers to the entire reproductive and generative system of a woman as a spiritual and physical organ.</note> by itself. In these, the entire Theory is contained. A similar nature must also be sought in medicine. For the art of composition proceeds from a foundation emerging from anatomy—not indeed from <term>degrees</term>, <term>complexions</term><note>Paracelsus is rejecting the traditional Galenic medicine of his time, which focused on balancing the four "humors" and their qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness), known as degrees and complexions.</note>, and experiments, but from "anatomies," which ought to be the beginning and the end for every physician. For without these, he will not be a composer of medicines. Art is its own indicator through such things, and nothing hides itself. For he knows from anatomy alone that man and woman must be joined. Equally, it is fitting for the physician to know that medicine and diseases must be joined according to their natures.

<margin>
Many diseases, many medicines.
</margin>
For if the physician knows this—that medicine heals disease—it is also fitting for him to know this: since many diseases are contained within a single one, many medicines also exist, which are both divided from one another and gathered into one. And this must be done through anatomy.
<margin>
The highest medicine.
</margin>
Although this is also true: that a single Medicine is given, in which all "anatomies" are present, of all diseases together and of all medicines; for medicine is the highest of all things. In its own time, the heaven will also fall back to that point, so that at least one disease may spread, and only one medicine may remain.
<margin>
Reproof of physicians and pharmacists.
</margin>
And this only the <term>astronomer</term> and the Physician understand. But because the sophistry that has prevailed until now has not yet been eliminated, no one scrutinizes these secrets. For the <term>dregs of the pharmacists</term><note>original: "pharmacopœorum fex". Paracelsus frequently criticized pharmacists for preparing medicines incorrectly or using poor quality ingredients.</note> pollute and contaminate the true preparation of medicine.

<margin>
How the center of the womb and the womb itself affect each other. Comparison of the sun's ray and the spirit of disease.
</margin>
But to return to the beginning and start the conclusion, learn further from this how the <term>Center of the matrix</term> and the whole or entire matrix are joined together; and pay attention to the manner in which one infects the other. Namely, in this way: just as the Sun by its subtlety penetrates glass and heats what is enclosed inside the glass—and just as fire is introduced through a furnace into a room, with the objects placed within remaining unharmed—so the spirits of diseases "persuade" or penetrate the center of the womb, not through the pores or channels themselves. And therefore, believe that little faith should be given to that vanity which, in great and acute diseases, claims there is a passage through the pores. For all diseases of this kind are only <term>spirits</term><note>In this context, "spirit" refers to an invisible, non-material force or essence, similar to a gas or a radiation, rather than a ghost.</note>, not exiting the body otherwise than as heat from the Sun. What the Sun burns, the spirit of the Sun burns. Observe the difference in this: just as the Sun heats through glass, and fire through a furnace, yet they do not heat through the skin of a man in the same way. The heat that emerges in those diseases is the heat of the body, which, increased by something foreign, boils over in its own fluids. For it ejects vapors through the pores, just as is the nature and condition of all boiling things. The spirit of the disease, of which we speak here, must be understood from the center of the womb in such a way that it is a different and diverse substance from the sun. It is the substance of the womb, and the sun is its substance; just as those three natures and centers are distinguished. If, therefore, the womb fosters a disease, the first thing is that the disease becomes a body, which itself collapses. Afterward, its vapor overflows, or a spirit is poured out from it, which is like nothing but the scent breathing out from musk or a rose. It "persuades" and penetrates, visible or palpable to no one. Such are all diseases exiting from the womb into the body. Those which are truly brought from outside the body into the womb exist bodily with their own bodies, as is explained in its proper place.
<margin>
Colored spirits of the womb.
</margin>
Now, in addition to these things, know that the spirits persuading from the womb into the body are colored—that is, they contain the power of colors. The cause is: just as the spirit of <term>vitriol</term><note>Vitriol: a historical term for various sulfate minerals (like copper or iron sulfate), used here to describe how a spirit can have a specific chemical "tinge" or property.</note> tints, and yet is a spirit; so also spirits tint or color diseases and seize the body in all places, no differently than if they were the body themselves.

Although many diseases may fall upon the womb, it often happens that one part is healed by another: as when the center of the womb is sick, it is many times cured by the womb; and so, in turn, the womb by the center. Thus, just as one hurts and offends the other, so with equal power one can heal...

Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires "anatomy"—the understanding of the inner essence of organs—rather than the superficial theories of his contemporaries.</summary>

# PARAMIRUM BOOK IV. ON THE ORIGIN
<page-num>106</page-num>

<margin>Disease and health share one root.</margin>
can heal. Where diseases arise, there also the root of restoring health is placed. For from the same root from which the disease emerges, health also must sprout forth. And so vice versa. Now, if it is possible for a disease to be born from itself, it will also happen that health emerges from itself. If we can become sick by accident, we can also be restored by accident. In that which we fall ill, in that same thing we also recover. Therefore, if the stars <note>original: "astrum". Paracelsus believed the "inner stars" or astral influences within the body governed health.</note> afflict us, the same will also return us to health. If a <term>plethora</term><note>An overabundance of bodily fluids (humors), thought to cause illness.</note> casts us down, the same will also refresh us. For every help remains within its own goal and should not be sought in another's.

If, therefore, in the body of the <term>Microcosm</term><note>The human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note> the same will be no less true—namely, that exterior health overcomes interior sickness—that is: the health of the body amends the central disease, and the central disease overcomes the corporal disease of the <term>matrix</term><note>original: "matrix". Refers to the womb, but also to the generative spiritual essence of a woman.</note>. For if the heaven is able to weaken from the outside this healthy body of ours, which we have taken from the earth, then likewise it can heal and preserve that body which weakness afflicts or is about to afflict. The reasoning here is altogether similar. Wherefore Hippocrates rightly handed down, if he spoke in this sense:

> *That it is power which drives out diseases.*

<margin>Hippocrates is praised.</margin>
This is the same as if he had said, *one power always drives out another.* Thus power is a celestial force, not from medicine, but is an invisible medicine; just as if someone recovers by his own guidance, without medicines, he is said to have recovered through power. This power is celestial <term>Astronomy</term><note>In this context, the study of the "stars" or spiritual forces within the human body.</note>; therefore it heals the sick. Those who do not recover in this way, using medicines, are healed through <term>arcana</term><note>Secret, powerful spiritual or chemical remedies that contain the concentrated "virtue" of a substance.</note>.

<margin>What are arcana?</margin>
An **arcanum** is not a power, but a force and potential more powerful than power. Although this is an old error of physicians, that they have named potential forces "powers." From which it has happened that they understood neither Hippocrates nor his commentaries.

Therefore, these things having been handed down, I wish for the **Monarchy** <note>The total system or "kingdom" of nature governing a specific subject.</note> regarding women to be concluded in general, and to be considered by physicians above all. Although I would wish this matter to be entirely finished with these aforementioned things. Furthermore, indeed (*God willing*), we shall hand down each disease of women—which they either endure in common with men, or suffer as peculiar and their own without the custom of men—separately and individually: for this one purpose, that this Monarchy of the Microcosm may be rightly and properly known and understood, with the definition and explanation added of all things and causes, as necessity demands; and with Masculine, Anatomical, and <term>Archimeic</term><note>Likely referring to the "Archeus," the internal "alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believed governed the body's functions.</note> instruction and the origin of worldly intelligence; outside of the consideration of which, no one is or can be a physician.

<margin>A reproof of physicians.</margin>
Indeed, I do not deny that I depart far from other physicians in the explanation of this monarchy. But I do so by right. For those men have been discovered sufficiently enough, that they not only treat ignorantly and without any foundation, but that they also write outside all light of nature—even though it does not befit a physician to comment on anything that is not similarly proven and established by the light of nature itself. For if he ought to take medicine from the earth, it is necessary that the earth itself be the Physician, not the man. Then he also will draw his doctrine from the earth, so that he may certainly use that which the earth provides for defined and necessary things. If he neither does nor knows this, by all his scribbling he achieves nothing else than the seduction of both himself and the patient.

Even though those men are raised to such a height of dignity and majesty that they are placed not last among the four columns of the Academies—upon which they build I-know-not-what, as if no one were permitted to move or speak anything against that order—nevertheless, know this about them: those very men who placed those columns freely confess that they were placed so by them, yet they do not know whether it was done correctly or not. The responsibility is left to anyone to defend. However, so that they might do it, they say they were persuaded and compelled because of certain experiments and reasons. Whether any foundation is situated in these, they do not inquire more curiously, but command the response to those to whom these things belong. But, O good God, how fragile and wavering these columns are! How futile this foundation is! Over which, nevertheless, they build I-know-not-what oracles, shouting repeatedly,

> *that those who are set over the Academies as the fourth member cannot err.*

But in truth, it is foully erred in this, while you are placed as columns. And they even take Christ as a support for themselves, saying,

> *the sick have need of physicians.* <note>A reference to Matthew 9:12.</note>

Because they arrogate this name to themselves, they are not troubled about any further perfection. But if they had truly weighed this properly—namely, that God created the physician and produced medicine from the earth, *so that He might be honored through it*—then they would have raised a circular question in their schools:

> *whether you were created by God, or indeed by the Devil:*

this is: whether you profess the truth or a lie. So indeed about the creator...

He launches a scathing critique of academic physicians, accusing them of ignoring the "light of nature" and relying on fragile institutional authority rather than true medicinal foundations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the polemic against academic physicians from the previous page, specifically targeting the university establishment. It then transitions into the formal title page and preface of Paracelsus's work on "Invisible Diseases," expanding his medical theory beyond the physical body to the spiritual or "invisible" aspects of human health.</meta>

# DISEASES OF THE WOMB.

It would certainly be established by your creator for everyone. For that claim—that God calls wretched schoolmasters, agents, pharmacists, laymen, monks, and the like to be doctors—is pure nonsense. As for you, *Leipzig, Tübingen, Vienna, and Ingolstadt* <note>These were major university centers of the time, representing the academic medical establishment that Paracelsus frequently attacked for being too theoretical and disconnected from nature.</note> created you. And you are just like these creators of yours. We do not deny, of course, that you have caught a scent of something in Astronomy, a bit in Philosophy, and even a little in Logic; but that is neither hot nor cold. If the Astronomer would banish his fortune-telling into exile, the Philosopher his "rational" theories, and the Logician his trifles, it might actually be possible for you to grasp some foundation of medicine.

Now, however, because you defend your cause by citing the authorities of Machaon, Apollo, Aristotle, Galen, Averroes, Avicenna, Rhazes, Mesue, etc. <note>A list of ancient and medieval authorities in medicine and philosophy whose works formed the core of university education.</note>, it is far off the mark. Your first duty is to find out whether those men lied or not. Once that is settled, they will either be accepted or rejected. If their writings were flutes or pipes, he would be a fine and industrious organist who could compose some little song upon them. But it is just as it is with the Geometers: they mix their speculations with circles and various instruments that move and advance themselves. But when you look closely, they collapse and are confounded along with their instruments. They are wooden hobby-horses. If you were to mount them to go on a journey, you would laugh at their vanity. 

If you did not use God as a pretext, veiling your madness through Him, you would certainly be found far vainer and more ignorant than all the Alchemists and soothsayers. Relying on that pretext, you keep chanting: *"God does not want this, God sent this—who can resist His judgment or power?"* For all things are placed in His hand. But why do you use such things as a pretext? Doubtless because you have come forth from a corrupt nature. Thus you constantly carry the word of the Lord in your mouth, while omitting this necessary part: *"the sick have need of a physician."* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 9:12.</note> But why is that? Here you fall silent. And if you were to give an answer, it would at least be done so that you might extort money and trust from men. But the heart of the doctor is far distant from his tongue. Weigh these things among yourselves, and answer squarely.

### AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

<margin>W</margin> *e have hitherto completed three books from the light of nature <note>original: "luce naturae". Paracelsus uses this term to describe knowledge gained through the direct observation of the natural world rather than from books.</note>, and in them we have explained the conditions and diseases of the visible, bodily part of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the whole universe.</note>, and we have written them down with singular diligence and experience, and with sufficient demonstration of philosophical and experimental evidence. Although in those books the sufferings of the visible body of the <term>Microcosm</term> are treated accurately and abundantly enough, and everything in every chapter is effectively established and confirmed to such an extent as could be drawn from the light of nature itself—with nothing omitted or neglected—nevertheless, not even in this way have all the diseases of the visible part of the <term>Microcosm</term> that fall upon the body been enumerated.* 

*For even if everything has been described that occurs visibly to the eyes and palpably to the hands—diseases of the kind that have been laboriously extracted from the solid foundation of philosophy, so that any skilled person can engage with them without error (even though the <term>Humorists</term> <note>Followers of the traditional medical theory based on the four "humors" or bodily fluids; Paracelsus was their primary opponent.</note> have conducted their whole discourse in the midst of errors)—yet in those books we have only encompassed the ailments of half the human being, namely, the part that is visible. Thus, use and necessity demand that we further undertake to describe the other half of the human being, so that in this way the whole and complete human might stand within the knowledge and contemplation of the physician.* 

*Although that part is invisible, it is nonetheless palpable. And that which is palpable is not visible; this is likewise true in the light of nature: a blind man who feels something does not see what he feels. So also in the contrary: we see and we feel, but what we feel, we do not perceive. And just as feeling something seems marvelous to a blind man, so to our eyes it is marvelous that they do not perceive what the hands touch. Pay close attention to this example. For a man is not born blind in vain: rather, he is an example and a monument to us, showing that we too, though we have sharp eyes, are in the dark within the light of nature. For that reason...*

He introduces his work on "Invisible Diseases," arguing that doctors must understand the invisible, spiritual half of the human being to truly treat the whole person.</summary>

It establishes the "Light of Nature" as the essential tool for a physician to perceive the invisible forces that govern the human body, bridging the gap between physical symptoms and their spiritual or "invisible" origins.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
# PREFACE TO THE BOOKS

...it should be considered worthily deserving of consideration.

<margin>Man without the light of nature is nothing.</margin>
O men who are not merely of the earth, how much do we truly profit in the knowledge of natural things without the light of nature? From this light <note>original: "lux naturae"; a central concept in Paracelsian thought referring to an innate, God-given intuition or intellectual illumination that allows one to understand the secrets of the natural world.</note> I now bring forth that which extends from the visible to the invisible, which is no less admirable in the latter than in the former. That I may dwell upon this light of nature: *the invisible is visible*. Whatever the eyes see (just as it is set forth in the other visible half) requires very little further demonstration. For the eyes themselves behold this great world; they lead it into Philosophy in such a way that, when the eyes are applied, it is perceptible to the sight.

<margin>Whatever we see is but half of what is made.</margin>
For whatever is constituted from it is visible. Yet, that which is further taken up in the following books regarding this subject is not visible. To ensure, therefore, that the invisible is rendered visible is a labor of no small effort. To expand upon this more widely, know that the world, and whatever we see and touch in its entire universal scope, is at least half of the world's part. However, that which we do not see is just as much in terms of quantity, nature, and property. The cause is this: that there is yet another "half-man" in whom the invisible world operates. In this sense, two worlds constitute two men in one body <note>This refers to the concept of the Microcosm (man) reflecting the Macrocosm (universe), where man possesses both a physical body and a "sidereal" or spiritual essence.</note>. So marvelous are the creatures, to be weighed so deeply in the light of nature according to that which God made invisible within them. Likewise, it is also according to this that we know things visibly. By this very craftsmanship, God illustrates His wonders and the discipline of the light of nature, so that by gazing upon them we do not merely feed our eyes, but rather greatly admire those natural things which the eye does not grasp, but which we investigate through the inquiry of the mind. These things nevertheless stand as clearly before us as a pillar stands before the face of a blind man. Furthermore, since in the light of nature those things which are otherwise invisible are rendered so clearly visible, we propose to explain next how our eyes might be opened, using this example as a guide: *The moon is a light*, but it does not teach us to distinguish colors. As soon as the sun rises, however, all colors are both seen and distinguished clearly.

<margin>The light of Nature is most excellent.</margin>
The light of Nature is similar, being much brighter than the light of the sun. And as the light of the moon is to the splendor of the sun, so the light of nature is raised above all sight and the power of the eyes. In this light, *invisible things become visible*. You must perpetually hold onto this: that one light always exists more splendidly than another.

We yield our faith to works. And we are compelled to yield it. For he who believes less lacks works; works testify to that from which they proceed. If the works are visible, but that from which they proceed is invisible, you ought to believe; they are only invisible because we do not walk in that light through which things are rendered visible. The same thing happens here as happens to those who hear a ringing bell on a dark night. They do not see the bell itself, and yet they perceive its work; that is, they certainly hear it. But if you are eager to see that from which the sound is emitted, it is necessary that this happen through a certain light. The Moon is indeed a light, but a dimmer one. The Sun exhibits individual things most clearly of all. Therefore, it is not fitting for us to be content with that light which merely shows the works and makes them visible; rather, we must proceed further and consider that the thing which performs the works is more significant and greater than the works themselves. Therefore, its light must also be more significant and brighter. For every single thing has its own light through which it is seen; every single light also renders its own object visible, which remains unseeable in the presence of an alien light. If, therefore, the works lead us further than to merely stop at the works themselves, surely he who refuses to follow this guide can never be led to faith in the works. If we believe in the work, we shall also believe in the master of the work. For that faith is dead which does not walk from the works to the master. Splendid buildings certainly please us. But how much more should their Architect please us? Buildings teach us nothing; rather, the knowledge of them flows from the craftsman. Take this example: Christ was the light of the world, but invisible, for He was a man; His works testify to that. Those who appraised His works by that light saw much more clearly than all the stars of the firmament can shine. Our eyes saw the works by the light coming from the sun, but that same light could not show the Master. And therefore, those who wished to know Him and hold Him as visible as He was, had need of that light which would illuminate Him, of which it was said by the Apostles: *Here we shall build three tabernacles* <note>A reference to the Transfiguration (Matthew 17), where Christ's divine nature was briefly made visible to his disciples in a burst of supernatural light.</note>. Thus, every single thing has its own light. And for those who are blind to the primary light, invisible things appear before their eyes like a steep mountain in the middle of a thick night. Thus, we find in nature a certain light capable of rendering us as perceptive as neither the Sun nor the Moon can. These things are brought forward by us for this purpose: that we may know that we behold man and all universal creatures only by at least a half-part, and because of this, we should consider a handle for proceeding further to be extended to us.

<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin>
Therefore, just as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 1st-century judge of the Areopagus converted by St. Paul; in the Middle Ages, he was legendary as an astronomer who recognized the supernatural darkness at the Crucifixion as a sign of God's suffering.</note> could not see by his own light those works which were performed under the cross of Christ, even though he was most skilled in the astronomical firmament itself—and yet he brought himself beyond the work itself to perceive the Architect of the world—so we also must by no means stop at the sight of the work alone. For he who seeks and knocks, finds. But regarding works, the matter must be understood thus: although we detect diseases in ourselves, of which...

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES.

*The origin [of these diseases] cannot be known from this visible body: yet these diseases are nothing but works. They do not command us to speak of things that are beyond our grasp, but rather to light a torch through which we might be able to speak. This is within our intellect. Therefore, while we pursue this, the outcome clearly reveals that another "half-man" is also present: and that man is not constituted of blood and flesh alone, but that an additional, different body is added, which itself appears far too brilliant for our dull eyes. And it is in this [body] that those diseases reside, along with all their invisible causes.*

<margin>Explanation of the upcoming consideration.</margin>
*It is our purpose to comment further on these causes, and on this body in which they operate: so that a knowledge of these diseases and their causes may truly constitute a whole and perfect Physician. For just as it was previously taught concerning visible or corporeal diseases, so now the incorporeal ones are proposed—which are yet, as has been said, simultaneously corporeal. We are compelled to venture this by that "work" which, beyond itself, also bears witness to its own creator; and it teaches by what method the work is produced, and who it is by whom it is produced. How this is to be investigated is set forth individually in these books. For in this field it must be known that, wherever any works are eventually performed, they are performed for this sole reason: that we might inquire into and learn their causes. For all works are made by GOD. Indeed, it is our duty to investigate how they pertain to us. For they are manifested for no other end than that GOD might hint at something to us through them, and testify by His divine providence,* <margin>The purpose of divine works.</margin> *that many wonders are hidden in His secret treasuries. From these we may recognize His profound and incomprehensible wisdom, which lacks both limit and measure: so that He might not only dazzle our dull eyes, but furthermore bring forth His illustrious and greatest "Magnalia" <note>original: "Magnalia"; a term frequently used by Paracelsus to refer to the "Great Works" or miracles of God hidden within the natural world.</note>. Therefore, because He places these works before our eyes, it is right that we should inquire into them more accurately. For we were not created to sleep, but to keep watch, and to be prompt and ready for all His works.*

<margin>The idea that a man’s body is besieged by the devil is jarring to reason.</margin>
*To a man who walks only in the visible light of nature, it is a stumbling block—indeed, an object of indignation and hatred according to physical sense—that a man can truly be besieged by the Devil, and so ruled and governed by him that the external sense can judge nothing else except that this besieged man is not a man at all, but a pure Devil. Is this not a stupendous work of GOD, that a man living upon the earth should appear to foster a Devil within himself? Especially since man is the image of GOD, and not of the Devil, differing from the Devil as much as a stone differs from wood. Furthermore, it is also incredible that since man is the image of GOD, redeemed from the Devil through CHRIST, he could nonetheless be snatched away and confined in such a horrendous prison, and have no prerogative prepared for him from the merit of his redeemer. Should not an entire chapter be spent explaining why this happens? Now, however, there is only this "work," and through this work we are led to believe that a far greater cause for the matter exists. GOD wants us to know this cause: and He commands that we do not look upon that work simply or in passing, but that we search and investigate entirely more deeply why it has been placed before our eyes. For if we have the leisure and the spirit to inquire into what uses the wool of a sheep or the bristle of a pig might serve; if we can bring any single thing into its proper order, and make raw foods savory to the palate through proper cooking, and build heated rooms against the winter, and raise roofs against the rains (all of which serve only the delights of the body): why, I ask, should we not also undertake an intent meditation on that thing whose possession is a benefit not to the body, but to eternity itself? For whatever harms the body breaks the domicile of the eternal.*

<margin>The custom of the Devil.</margin>
*If the devil now dwells in that domicile, he destroys and lays it waste. Therefore, the cause must now be rightly investigated as to why he has become a "work" in this instance. If visible reason does not grasp it, one must turn to the invisible. If this is brought toward the right light, it is offered to us no less clearly than the visible itself. Thus, because the number [of diseases] is drawn from the works—from which every Theory and Practice flows—those diseases will follow in their respective verses, showing how those spiritual diseases are able to exist within us; yet that spirit is visible to its own light, seeing as it constitutes the [other] half of man.*

*Thus I would have you warned, reader, that in understanding all the following diseases, you must put on a "visible understanding." For all works are visible. Therefore, their causes must also be visible. Do not let it confuse you that these things are not all found in the open light of the Sun. Rather, think how secret God is, even outside the Sun. And if you find these things to be such, know that in this place we have undeservedly called invisible things "invisible." For it is clear from the works themselves that they have emerged from another work. Thus a house is a work, and it is visible. The Architect is also a work, and is himself visible. This Architect, the Sun ☉ <note>The sun symbol (☉) here represents the "Light of Nature" or the creative force of God acting as a divine architect.</note> of God, is the house; it is the work of the Architect. Thus it must also be understood that we see works placed visibly before our eyes. If we know the maker of the work, he too will be visible to us. In eternal things,* <margin>Eternal things are revealed through faith; worldly things through the light of reason.</margin> *faith makes all things conspicuous. In invisible corporeal things, the light of nature makes all things visible. Therefore, do not be terrified or disgusted whenever you hear that some thing can become visible: nor believe that it is not already visible. That which is to be visible,*

PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF INVISIBLE DISEASES.

the case is the same for you in that place, so that the Infant, who is in conception, now exists as visible. And although it may be invisible: *what does that take away from the visible?* And with these things, Reader, we put an end to the preface, adding a solemn declaration that you should not judge us before the final note <note>original: "colophonem"; the concluding statement or finishing touch of a book.</note> is added. For here, because such illustrious hidden things appear, they invite and compel us to investigate them further; especially because not only I myself, but many others, bring forth and reveal various things in these matters. And yet, because that light is being shaken out, contemplations of this kind regarding the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a philosophical term referring to the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note> are labeled by most as deceptive, Diabolical, Sorcerous, Augural, and superstitious—certainly by force and public injustice, as will be proven in the books that follow. Farewell.

---

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING
# BOOKS.

**N**ow indeed, so that you may know what we shall deliver in the following pages: know that Philosophy is twofold. So also, medicine is twofold. One part has been handed down concerning Corporeal diseases. Next, the Incorporeal ones shall be treated—why they are invisible and how they are to be made visible. The treatise is completed in four books. The first will contain *diseases which faith gives, and as much as faith can comprehend.* The second will treat the *impressions of the hidden heaven—specifically in what manner and by what reason it acts upon us.* The third will define the *diseases of the imagination, and how it operates without any physical matter.* The fourth will determine the *secrets of natural virtues, which operate beyond all bodily reason through the property of their own body.* And so, just as these things are the works of nature, they shall also be investigated by me. But truly, because one book—namely on Healing—would be missing, it is therefore annexed after the four mentioned books; from which anyone will be able to be abundantly satisfied.

---

# THE ENTRANCE TO THE FIRST BOOK,
## CONCERNING MATTERS BEFALLING MAN
## FROM FAITH.

<margin>What is faith?</margin>
**I**t is entirely necessary that these matters be founded upon the doctrine of Christ. For they are completely inscrutable to human reason, insofar as it flows from Adam. Just as that doctrine is now proposed, so it must be accepted with solid faith. Indeed, the virtues of faith are never searchable by man out of himself. For in this, faith is the highest light, indicating the foundation of what we ought to understand in that faith. Thus God Himself also bestowed upon us a foundation and principle for learning natural medicine in herbs, stones, the movement of the heavens, and other similar things; while we observe these, we are swept away into <margin>Inquiry follows wonder.</margin> great admiration, which is then followed by the investigation of nature. And thus you experience what lies hidden in eyebright <note>original: "eufragiâ"; a herb traditionally used to treat eye ailments, here used as an example of hidden natural power.</note> and in other things. For the works themselves are the causes and movers which rouse us to seek the genuine meaning. Therefore, be persuaded that not all things are placed in those objects merely to know what pertains to the visible body—for that is only one part—but that they also consist in the words of the supreme scripture, which contains that object through which we can investigate those things that look toward my proposal concerning faith.

<margin>What is the Gospel?</margin>
It is known and explored by you that the Gospel delivers a brief synopsis of the virtue and power of faith, in which place it has this sentence: *if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, and from that faith and in that faith you say to this mountain, "you mountain, throw yourself into the sea," it shall be done.* Thus it must be established: our strength, which consists in the solidity of blood and flesh, is quite weak and fragile; but true and durable strength rests in faith alone. And with the same ease <margin>How great is the strength of faith.</margin> that we can lift a grain of mustard seed with our hands and throw it into the sea, with no weight (or the very least) hindering us, with that same readiness we can cast huge mountains into the sea through our faith.

Regarding faith, therefore, it must be held as certain that wonderful operations are performed through it, such as this visible body would not dare to attempt or meditate upon even once. Look at Samson: his strength was not in so small a body, but that virtue was his faith. So also was the faith of Joshua and similar men, who all serve as proof to us that this earthly body of ours possesses no strength, but all fortitude, which we ought to enjoy and work with, must be placed in faith. And in this way, the virtue of faith is to be understood.

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>ON INVISIBLE DISEASES.</header>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES.

...to be understood, take heed.

<margin>How powerful spirits are.</margin>
But let us proceed with these matters. This same thing is possible for spirits, who are able to cast Mount Olympus into the Red Sea. These same beings are also capable of scattering the ocean even over Mount Etna <note>Mount Etna is a famous volcano in Sicily; Paracelsus uses these landmarks to illustrate the literal, physical power he believes spiritual forces possess.</note>. They can do similar things in other instances as well, by the permission of God. From this, gather the following: spirits do not have a body; and for that reason, they have neither blood nor flesh. And yet, they are distinguished by such great strength. <margin>Spirits possess faith.</margin> It is faith that provides this, which they possess. Therefore, let the sum of the Gospel be this, as if Christ had said: "What are you humans with your strengths? Nothing. However, I show you from where you ought to summon your strength: namely, from faith." If you have only as much faith as equals a grain of millet: behold, you will be so robust that you will not yield in strength even to spirits. Now indeed, although you are men, your strength and fortitude will be similar even to the spirits themselves, as it was also for Samson <note>A biblical judge endowed with supernatural strength through God's spirit.</note>. From this, note how we become spirits through faith. For whatever we strive for beyond this earthly nature, faith provides all of it, which works through us like a spirit; nor are we weaker than the spirits themselves. Therefore, the words of Christ can also be understood in this sense: if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, and you are earthly spirits: how much more will you achieve if your faith were like a melon? With what great strength will we surpass the spirits if our faith were the size of a gourd?

<margin>Through faith, man is superior to spirits.</margin>
Thus, therefore, a man can do all these things through faith, and he retains this strength for himself in this world; and through this virtue of faith, he excels above the spirits, whom he also readily conquers, so that all are subjected to him. For through faith, one fights against spirits, who otherwise would attack us with a far more atrocious assault. Through faith, they are lulled to sleep and put to flight. Through faith, we tame and restrain most of them. This should be understood in a similar sense as if a large loaf of bread were placed upon a table. Even if our faith were no larger than a tiny, worn-away crumb of it: nevertheless, we would rise up strong and powerful enough against the spirits. How much more, truly, if we were to eat a large fragment from that bread? For we propose that faith is like that entire loaf of bread. Indeed, one ought to know that this faith, transferred into us from the first creation, preserved Abraham himself, Moses, and all other similar men in their strength. From this, those men emerged so wonderful, and so often worked beyond human strength. But know also concerning those who lacked this faith—

<margin>Disadvantageous confidence.</margin>
—and trusted in this fragile and human fortitude, wisdom, and virtue. These were conquered and overcome by spirits, and reduced to such ignominy that they bent their knees to the victorious spirits as if to powerful kings, and worshipped them as gods. Is this not indeed strength—to be cast down and routed without provisions or arms by that which has neither flesh, nor blood, nor bones? For what else is their strength but faith? For besides it, the spirits have nothing else.

<margin>Faith strengthens and empowers all devils.</margin>
Furthermore, take heed further concerning this strength, that it also flourishes in devils; regarding which, note this divided explanation. Everyone has faith: and from it, they have their power. From this, two things follow: Use and Abuse. Use exists of itself. Abuse is that which I shall speak more of. The devils abused their faith; therefore they were cast out of heaven. However, faith was not taken away from them for that reason; rather, the permission of God was placed in opposition to them. Therefore, if faith was not taken away from them: even they will have the power of demolishing mountains into the sea, and doing other similar things. These same beings also have the power, through their faith, to introduce diseases. And just as the Sun shines upon the good and the bad without distinction: so also the devil can act against men. And therefore, he can produce either good or bad signs. For as long as he retains faith: so long does he also possess its virtue.

<margin>The history of Samson.</margin>
Just as faith is understood concerning spirits: so let it also be established concerning men, that we are able to harm one another invisibly, and to employ faith rightly or wrongly, just as God permits it to us. However, those blows and wounds which are inflicted by this virtue cannot be proven or shown in any other way than Samson would have demonstrated how he laid low and destroyed such a great crowd of people with a single jawbone. For that slaughter was and is by the permission of God; and anyone who has the faith of Samson—of whom there are many—could produce the same slaughters if God permitted such strength to be directed into action, which is, however, by no means useful.

Although, however, that faith is a prerogative among us, so that we can put the devils and spirits themselves to flight in that virtue, and cast mountains into the sea: nevertheless, we ought not to tempt the deed itself for that reason. One must at least believe, and rest in this confidence. Samson believed; there was a need; for that reason, it happened. But if even—

<summary>Paracelsus argues that faith is a literal source of power that allows humans to rival or exceed the strength of spirits and devils. He explains that even fallen spirits retain the power of faith, using it to cause disease, while humans must use their faith according to God's will to protect themselves and overcome spiritual forces.</summary>

<page-num>112</page-num>

->BOOK I. ON ORIGINS<-

...or if in this very hour there were a similar necessity, certainly more Samsons <note>Samson was a biblical judge known for his supernatural strength; Paracelsus argues that such miracles are not just historical events but possibilities inherent in the power of faith.</note> would appear in the world. But it is fitting for us to believe the Scripture and the Gospel, and likewise to know that we are capable of these things; yet we should not emulate the example of the man who plucked out his own eye so that he would not be offended by it <note>A reference to Matthew 5:29. Paracelsus suggests that while faith gives us the power to perform such radical acts, we should not seek to replicate them without divine necessity.</note>. What we believe must not be confirmed by any works. For he who hastens to works departs from faith by his haste and hurries toward damnation. For God did not speak these things so that we should desire to do them, but at least so that we might know what the efficacy of our faith is. 

<margin>The virtue of faith is not to tempt.</margin>

Moreover, God himself displayed certain examples of this in the Old Testament, just as the power of faith has been uniquely declared to us in the New Testament. And although it is true that while we dwell here, we walk in the flesh, nevertheless our faith, which we cast upon the Creator of all things, is so effective and great that its power can be expressed by no words. 

<margin>How great the power of faith is, even in the weak.</margin>

Indeed, faith itself is taken away from no one, except from him who casts it away of his own accord. Therefore, it operates in two ways: In good men toward good; in evil men, conversely, toward evil. 

<margin>The twofold nature of faith.</margin>

There is no need to write anything here concerning the good. But concerning the evil, take heed of these things.

Therefore, if we have conceived through faith, but afterwards obstruct it with evil matters, the Holy Scripture calls this "tempting" in its own idiom. For in that case, we tempt God and expend faith upon things for which it was never given. For we strive to prove whether faith is truly such as it is preached to be. But we must beware of such temptations; we must believe that the matter was tested long ago. If we do not look for the "works" of the words, we remain pure in faith. Furthermore, we pray to God specifically for this: that he lead us not into temptation—that is, that he not indulge us in temptation. 

<margin>The danger of temptation.</margin>

For whoever's temptation God complies with, let that person be anxious for their own soul. Because of this, when something does not happen and succeed according to one's wish, it is a liberation from evil. For God does not even indulge the spirits themselves so that they are granted their wishes; otherwise, nothing would be left unturned or un-conquered. Nevertheless, those spirits are no less capable of it, and we are capable along with them. For we are able to strike all mountains and hills out of the way so that we might walk on a level plain—yet it does not happen. For God wants them to stand in that place, so that you may proceed safely wherever you wish. In the same way, a carpenter <term>tignarius: a builder or carpenter</term> knows how to build a house in a meadow and is able to do so. If the owner of the meadow permits it, the house is built. Otherwise, not at all. And let this be an example of the abuse of the powers of faith.

### *How faith weakens and harms the body.*

But why indeed do I mention such things when I have not yet touched upon what I intended: namely, how it happens that faith weakens the body? For thus far we have treated at least the strengths and efficacy of faith. Now, therefore, we shall approach the second point—abuse—in this manner. A physician has good remedies in his power. Depending on what sort of man he is, he employs them accordingly. With them he can heal the sick, or with them he can kill. For if he can administer lemon balm <note>original: "melissa"; a common herb used for calming and healing.</note> for health, he can also administer arsenic for death. 

<margin>Good and evil are worked through faith.</margin>

But how are these things to be understood? In this way: through the virtue of our faith, we humans can work good or evil, provided that the Master grants this power to the "carpenter." Our faith is no different than a craftsman's tool. He forges <note>original: "cudit"; literally to strike or hammer, as a blacksmith does at an anvil.</note> a knife, with which he strikes his neighbor and wounds his body. Without the knife and similar instruments, he cannot wound his neighbor. By a certain similarity, turn this toward faith, which we decide to abuse, degenerating from that purpose for which it was granted to us. For then we apply the power of our faith to an evil path and decline from the right way, and we believe this to be such-and-such, or that to be another thing. Thus, the vice of the abuse of our faith is the cause. It also forges weapons which we believe to be this or that.

Now truly know this: we can rightly and deservedly call that which has been fabricated—like the knife or the weapon—a "spirit." 

<margin>What sort of things spirits are.</margin>

For a spirit can do without hands or feet whatever a human does. If it operates in a similar way, then there is no longer any difference between them. But a brief instruction must be placed first regarding this "forging" or fabrication: that faith requires such an order. If an epidemic disease <note>original: "morbus Epidemicus"</note> should fall upon us, and we judge it to be a punishment and a vengeance, then that is what it becomes. And even though it may be natural in origin, faith nevertheless renders it unnatural, and leads it to a point where no one can extricate themselves from it according to natural signs. Whence it happens that all natural help appears to be in vain. Those weapons which faith forges and fabricates persuade us of this. For if we can designate good things through those weapons, we can also perpetrate evil through them. And just as a mountain is cast into the sea, so here [the power] of faith also...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the dual nature of faith, explaining how the same spiritual force that allows for miraculous strength can also be used to generate disease or harm if misdirected.</meta>

<page-num>113</page-num>

# OF INVISIBLE DISEASES

<margin>Let us follow the spirits through faith, to see into what power they lead.</margin>
...also the seed is destroyed. For faith in itself can produce all kinds of herbs, namely the invisible nettle, and the invisible celandine <note>original: "Chelidoniam"; celandine was a herb commonly used in alchemy and folk medicine, often associated with sight or the liver</note>, etc. And so, whatever thing earthly nature brings forth, the strength of faith can also produce. In the same way, this same faith can also produce all diseases. But the difference in this is that God either permits these things or forbids them to happen. It is within our power to stab one another and to threaten many other dangers, but we ought to abstain. In this way, faith can do the same according to its own powers. For in physical things, examples are established of what they are in their own powers, so that they can cause both good and evil. Thus faith can do the same in its own powers. For we are made similar to the spirits, to whom all these things are possible, so that they may do invisibly that which the body performs visibly.

Let it be understood, therefore, that faith cannot be taken from us by itself: and that it takes the place of an instrument (like a weapon) suitable and convenient for all things. Just as the earth can harm a man, so too can it poison him: and all of this comes from the virtue of faith—that faith, indeed, by which we cast mountains into the sea. For that cast would be harmful, to hurl a mountain into the sea <note>A reference to Matthew 21:21; Paracelsus warns that such immense power can be used for destruction as easily as for miracles</note>.

<margin>Using faith to harm men.</margin>
But if we abuse faith and believe that which turns to the harm of our neighbor, then it happens so. Through our intense and serious faith, men are killed by prayers, and are rendered distorted and paralyzed. Natural diseases are turned into unnatural ones. But if superstitions of this kind flourish in a certain region, then the same happens to the Physician as happened to Christ in his own country, where he could not perform many signs and miracles. For they did not believe in those things which faith required; rather, they unfortunately believed in one another: to which Christ yielded. For God wills that we walk in the true and right way. If we walk in this way, we can make ourselves healthy through faith, which nevertheless God by no means wants. He requires this: that we carry faith inwardly and believe that the possibility is within us. But these things must never be subjected to external eyes: because he certainly wants those things to be secret and hidden—that is, in faith, not in proof. Therefore, even medicines were created for us, which exercise the works of divine charity in us, and allow faith to rest with works: through which faith we could easily cross the wave with a dry foot <note>original: "sicco pede"; an idiom meaning to accomplish a difficult task easily or miraculously, like the Israelites crossing the Red Sea</note>. But why God permits some to inflict diseases on others through the virtue of faith, and now to heal, now to weaken men through superstition—let God be the judge of that.

-> The Distinction of Faith. <-

<margin>Faith of this kind.</margin>
**F**urthermore, so that faith may be properly distinguished, know that it is not that faith in Christ which saves; but at least it is that innate faith which we have in God the Father. Therefore, saving faith is not included here. Concerning that, nothing has been treated so far. For that faith proceeds from Christ and is reflected back to Christ. For He does not say this: "if you believe in me, mountains will roll themselves into the sea"; but He implies this: "if you believe in me, through me you shall be saved." Christ Himself, as the Son of God, freed no one from death and diseases. But insofar as He was the second person of the Deity, He performed those things by His power. As long as He walked on earth, He had this one goal of His office: that He might free us from the Devil, the earth, and hell. But so that He might make His will known even to the unrefined common people, who were not capable of understanding the scripture and other testimonies: hence He performed signs and miracles, which were for God alone to do: so that they might see and believe because of the works that He was the Son of the most high God. But here at the same time, pay attention to how healing is distinct.

<margin>What kind of healing belongs to Christ and what kind to faith.</margin>
Those whom Christ heals, or others heal through the name of Christ, these are healed through the power of God: by no means through their own faith, but on account of prayers poured out to Christ, they obtained His mercy, by which He snatched them from diseases and all evils.

But why do I say these things? Truly our mind and purpose is that you may understand from this that those who are not healed through prayers and vows, and through the mercy of Christ, and yet recover in a marvelous way: those, I say, make themselves healthy through their own faith. It is my purpose to speak of this healing or recovery. For we ought not to be healed through our own faith, but through divine mercy. For in this way, we can give sight to no one born blind by faith, nor restore any dead person to life. But nevertheless, we obtain that this may be done through mercy. If, however, we direct our faith simply and nakedly, so that we may thrust a mountain into the sea, and thus stir up the spirit within us: then by that deed we fall into pride, by which we shake off prayers and the expectation of mercy, constituting ourselves as Gods, and abusing the power and virtue of faith...

<margin>...on account of a vice</margin>

# BOOK I: ON THE ORIGINS

<margin>What the permission of God brings about.</margin>
...we render each other paralyzed and unhappy. For this reason, God also often permits this to us, so that we might see the force and efficacy of our faith, and thus believe ourselves to be either sick or healthy. This is truly a desperate life: one in which we live for our own stubbornness and malice, having forgotten our God and His mercy. This ultimately leads us into despair.

Furthermore, know that from these diseases, which today are common to the whole world, one has always followed another since the beginning of the world. From this, it also happened that new, foreign, and rare diseases were believed to have appeared among various peoples, and they judged these to be singular punishments and scourges. Because of this, in those narrow straits of affliction, they especially called upon those who were the greatest and most excellent men among them to preserve the people from these plagues. Falling thus into superstition, they did not consider that any given plague ought to be removed by another way.
<margin>From which first authors the superstition of faith arose.</margin>
Thus, therefore, faith fell into abuse: the Egyptians stood forth as the primary authors of this abuse. The same later grew among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note> as well,
<margin>Aesculapius and Machaon.</margin>
and established idolatry, which lasted a long time until at last Aesculapius and Machaon <note>In Greek mythology, Aesculapius was the god of medicine, and Machaon was his son, a healer in the Iliad. Paracelsus views them as the founders of "natural" medicine.</note> came forth. They developed and weighed the natural course of medicine to such an extent that they discovered that diseases of this kind were purely natural. They afterwards published these findings, described and explained in books, and taught that nature alone operates here, rather than a plague of punishment. By this discovery, they put the abuse and superstition to rest in great part; just as this care belongs most especially to physicians. In the meantime, however, this kind of superstition had also taken root among Christians. And just as the Gentiles venerated their Apollonian priests, so Christians inverted their names: instead of "Apollonists," they worshipped "Antonnists" <note>Followers of St. Anthony, often invoked against "St. Anthony's Fire" or ergotism.</note> and "Wolfgangists" <note>Followers of St. Wolfgang.</note>. Rising up by the power of faith, they "hurled the mountain into the sea," <note>A reference to Matthew 21:21. Paracelsus argues that Christians used the power of faith to create new forms of superstitious healing and harm.</note> and they shamefully forgot all mercy and prayer to God, except for where they retained some small amount of it for external show and pretense.

Now, as the state of things is today, we dash the "mountain" against one another—into the leg, into the belly, etc.—and no limb within us is left safe from this mountain, nor is there any disease into which
<margin>Superstition concerning the saints.</margin>
that mountain is not brought and mixed. From this, naturally, diseases become "unnatural." Now, however, just as one threw the mountain into the sea by believing, he must also cast it out and restore it to its place by believing. This is the medical art in diseases of this kind.

It is inevitable that some superstition arises from the abuse of faith. And while we toss the mountain, we also occupy ourselves with mountains; that is, we establish the Saints as mountains, and we strike each other with them. Now, we cannot truly displace the saints from their station. Therefore, Faith "sculpts" the saints for us, and by its power, hurls them into the sea in which we believe. And just as Faith sculpts and fashions the saints, so those who hurl the saints into the sea also express and shadow forth that sculpture. From this, wooden images and statues arise. And just as the body plays and gesticulates with these, so faith emulates it; from the power of that "spiritual saint," a spiritual trickery <note>original: "dolum," meaning a device or deception</note> is fashioned, which is hurled at us in the same way as if you were to seize the head of St. Dionysius, the wheel of St. Catherine, or the hook of St. Wolfgang <note>These are the traditional iconographic attributes of these saints: Dionysius is often shown carrying his own head, Catherine with a breaking wheel, and Wolfgang with an axe or hook.</note> and dash them into a peasant's face. For when the saints have rendered diseases unnatural in this way, a completely similar mode exists. For the body and its spirit in faith always walk joined under one yoke, and the one fits and agrees with the other equally.

Who, then, would dare to deny this? Since the 
<margin>Faith, the invisible man.</margin>
strength that God put into this earthly body is spent on these wooden tricks, why should not the strength of faith—which is surely the "invisible man"—be spent on gods of this sort? For whatever the body shows and does, faith performs the same with no less activity. From this, conclude now that the diseases or healings of these saints are not made by the devil himself, but by ourselves. The devil, however, is greatly delighted by such things. For it is
<margin>How great is the power of faith.</margin>
once and for all established that faith can do exactly what the body can. Just as a lead bullet shot from a gun can pierce a man, faith can do so much more easily than the body itself. Let this example be an instruction to you. You are visible and corporeal. Yet there is also another, and he is your very self, but not visible. Therefore, what your body dares, that other dares as well—you the visible, he the invisible. Therefore, know of faith that images have their origin and cause in this appearance: specifically, that a man fashions a wax image in the name of his enemy, and wounds or injures it in that body. Thus the invisible man has invisibly wounded his enemy. Because truly...

He introduces the concept of the "invisible man" (the spiritual self) which can exert physical effects, such as harm, through belief and sympathetic magic.</summary>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

<margin>Where incantations originate.</margin>
But truly, that God permitted this is a sign that we have that power; and at the same time, it is a monument to who we are. Not indeed so that we should perform such things, for whoever dares to do so tests and tempts God. And yet, woe to the soul of him to whom this is permitted. It is surely from this power and foundation that sorcerers <note>original: "incantatores," referring to those who use chants or spells</note> perform their deceptions: painting an image on a wall and driving a nail into it. Their spirit later does the same through the power of faith that "moves mountains," and it drives an invisible nail into the enemy unless God averts it. From this also arose "lovers" who enchanted women and fashioned wax images, which they melted by applying candles or torches, and thus fulfilled or satiated their lust. That is to say, their own spirit also wantoned with an invisible torch. Thus the Egyptians and the Chaldeans, who were like them, fashioned images according to the face of the firmament and the movement of the stars; but all did so in the context of such powers which, through their own simplicity, they did not even understand. They made images that moved and spoke by themselves. In this way, they forgot the impossibility of nature, but not of the powers, as was stated above.

<margin>The final cause of divine permission.</margin>
Therefore, it must be clearly and precisely understood how wonderfully faith operates when God permits it. For if I wished to commit such things to writing and even slightly flatter those practitioners of deceptions by recounting how much they achieved through their incantations by God’s permission, a truly marvelous chronicle would certainly be established. Yet God permitted all these things for this reason alone: so that through these works we might see that we ourselves are also able to cast a vast mountain into the sea, and that we ourselves are spirits and invisible men. These things have been brought forward and drawn out by me so that we might investigate how any "saints" are manufactured in faith, similar to those the potter fashions. Their virtue and power, however, is to weaken or heal men in every way and reason, just as the doctrine of images holds—namely, that faith accomplishes all these things if we wish to abuse it, just as the body itself can produce effects according to its own powers if it wishes to abuse them. To put the matter more briefly: Faith renders a man invisible; he then forges and works that which the body would manufacture if it could. For in this way, he is turned into spirit, for whom all these things are easy to perform. And our bodily strength is not taken away from us unless it happens through divine providence. The matter, therefore, is similar to a case where God might cast someone into a disease 

<margin>When the worship of statues began.</margin>
for this purpose: so that his strength and insolence do no harm. Hence He makes him paralyzed in hands and feet. In the same way, He also paralyzes the faith of these wicked men. But to hasten to the conclusion, you know it is understood that the "signs" <note>miraculous tokens or healing wonders</note> of the saints were already customary long ago, even before the birth of Christ; therefore, they cannot be judged to have originated from Christians. For they are too ancient, like an ancestor <note>original: "avi," which can mean grandfather or a long-standing tradition</note>; yet the Christian faith knows no such ancestry. But those men to whom God permits such things through faith—by the efficacy and power of that faith which they have decreed to abuse for evil—might dare to place a hoopoe <note>The hoopoe bird was frequently associated with magic and the occult in medieval lore</note> upon a stake or a spindle, of which they themselves are then the judges. Because faith gave them the hoopoe, it sits there as if by God’s will.

<margin>The Christians' James has succeeded the Pagans' Apollo.</margin>
Therefore, they do not tire of adoration, forgetting that God did not commend His shepherd Peter to anyone in that manner. Thus, according to the custom of the ancient Egyptians and pagan <note>original: "Ethnico"</note> ritual, Apollo has become Saint James, and the one is the same as the other. For Apollo and those like him were introduced through the power of faith; it is not as if that spirit was actually called "Apollo," or as if the spirit at Saint James’s shrine is called "James." For no one ever knew the names of those spirits substituted in those places, except for one "watcher" <note>original: "speculatorem," perhaps referring to a visionary or a sorcerer who monitors spiritual forces</note> who, in the power of faith, cast a mountain there. Whatever name that man had, the spirits also rightfully assume, according to the movement of the mastery of him who tempted God. He who desired to produce signs through faith, and proceeded to tempt God constantly and continually, forgot this: that it is not lawful to demand signs of faith, but rather one should believe, yet not so that the sign is forced to happen. <margin>What kind of signs should be asked for by Christians.</margin> We ought to ask for those signs which reach us from the mercy of God. Those are Christian signs, having come forth from Christ and being born in Him. Therefore, whatever emanates from mercy, charity, and faithfulness, consider this to be Christian. The rest, which I have touched upon so far concerning faith, consider to be such that neither Apollo nor James is truly with them. Both the Gentiles and the Christians have been deceived by these things.

<margin>Superstitious health.</margin>
But they also do not remember that no one can bring health upon themselves by believing, unless they are sick through the abuse of faith. This refers to the "health of superstition." To heal is a work that testifies to its maker. It is fitting, however, that all healing flow from the mercy of God. Now, therefore, healing is a work of mercy, as is confirmed by the example of the physician. God created us, and just as for the tongue,

the tongue, just as He placed his delight in the eyes, and granted us the aptitude to rule and govern those members according to our will and pleasure. For by divine providence, it was already known beforehand what kind of diseases would arise from them.

<margin>Medicine was created from the foreknowledge of God.</margin>
According to this foreknowledge of His, God created medicine and its skilled craftsmen—that is, **Physicians** <term>Medicos: medical practitioners or doctors</term>—who would recognize those diseases and provide their remedies.

Now judge for yourselves: *was this done through faith, or through divine mercy, since mercy already existed before man was created?* For when all things were already created, man was brought forth last of all.

Thus, you ought to know that health flows from medicine, but medicine was created from the mercy of God. Likewise, that which flows from the Son of God is taken from the same origin: namely, that His mercy already existed before human faith. Therefore, the works of healing are not works of faith, but works of mercy.

<margin>What kind of work healing is:</margin>
But if faith should at any time produce signs <note>original: "signa," meaning miracles or wonders</note>, then remember that Gospel in which Christ predicted: *they themselves shall perform signs.* This is to be understood as if Christ were saying: *not out of my mercy, but out of the virtues of faith, they shall establish Apollo and James, according to the tenor and measure of the strength of their own faith.* <note>Paracelsus likely refers to the blending of classical "healing" figures like Apollo with biblical figures like the apostle James, showing how human belief can channel power into specific forms.</note>

<margin>The Devil does not work in the place of men.</margin>
Here another mention of their faith must be made, *namely how a common opinion has prevailed among them, as if the Devil himself performs such things in the place and name of men.* This is in no way to be admitted. One must indeed believe this about the power of the Devil: that he can indeed perform such signs through the force of the faith he possesses, but he does so through himself, in those whom he has permission from God to influence. The Devil himself cares nothing for signs of that kind.

<margin>The mercy of God plagues the Devil.</margin>
The mercy of God, which He promised to us, offends and bites him. His sole purpose is to shake and tear this mercy away. He permits us to commit evils; he allows us to abuse faith and to carry out everything within our strength.

<margin>The wondrous cunning of the Devil.</margin>
Besides all these things, if he does not think the heap of our evils is large enough, he adds to them. Yet this is not the only goal of his labor. His primary fixed aim is to drive us into despair of the mercy of Christ (of whom he is the sworn enemy) and to demolish and overturn our faith directed toward Christ, as well as our hope and charity. For through those things, we can bring damnation upon ourselves; without them, we are undivided in all things. And although a certain playful accessory might be made through those spirits among the fictional gods of the Gentiles and Christians—namely under the appearance of a diabolical religion—it would be the same as if a sturdy peasant stood next to a goldsmith, so that what the goldsmith carved in gold, the peasant himself fashioned out of dung. Therefore, the Devil also imprints his own signs and marks <note>original: "charagmata," from the Greek for an engraved mark or brand</note> upon calves and pigs: which is an indication that his power is greatly narrowed and restricted, and that he cannot operate freely in faith according to his own whim. Otherwise, he would have long ago uprooted and laid low everything from its deepest foundation, and would show himself far more atrocious and fierce than any thought could grasp.

## *On the Disease of St. Valentine, or the so-called falling sickness.*
<note>St. Valentine's Disease is a historical name for Epilepsy.</note>

<margin>Epilepsy or the falling sickness.</margin>
Furthermore, understand now that the natural course of men, which the Elements and the stars provide, produces a certain disease that strikes a man down and induces a spasm in him, convulsing the limbs, hands, and feet, and even distorting the eyes and other parts with cruel and horrendous signs.

<margin>From where it was introduced.</margin>
It is not clear by what reasoning this disease first invaded man. In ancient times, it was believed to have been sent by the gods <note>original: "diuis," referring to minor deities or spirits</note> whom we may have offended on earth by some injury. And because these gods could not be avengers on this earth due to their lack of physical presence, they sent this punishment and vengeance down from heaven. This persuasion once passed into belief. Faith then cast the mountain into the sea with such force that eventually, for the sake of that faith, a "little man" <note>original: "virunculus," a homunculus or invisible spirit</note> was fabricated to work invisibly in this matter.

<margin>The superstitious aversion to the falling sickness.</margin>
And just as someone seizes a man by the hair, shakes and vibrates him, and tosses him from one corner to another: so too has faith operated. Therefore, if medicine helped at all here and cured that natural disease of convulsion, faith certainly extended its operation further than anything that could be taken away from the sickness; and thus in that way, it cast the Physician into despair. Furthermore, observations have been made by some of the people that the planets, the new moon, the fourth day, and the full moon, and similar movements of the stars, have stimulated and increased this disease.

<margin>Astronomical superstition.</margin>
From which infected men are divided:
