### *On the Diseases with wounds and ulcers called the punishment of St. Quirinus, and the vengeance of St. John.*

<margin>The natural cause of the disease of St. Quirinus.</margin>
**I**n the same way, nature itself also brings about a certain natural tearing of the flesh and skin through a corrosive force, or a "strong salt" stored within the human body. Now truly, because these types of salts are manifold, they likewise cause disturbances in the body in many ways. And just as it is the nature and property of corrosive salt to inflict pains, so the common people judged such a disease to be a divine punishment before the true foundations of medicine were laid open. This opinion lasted until the birth of Christ. For since St. Quirinus <note>St. Quirinus of Neuss was a Roman martyr often invoked against the bubonic plague and skin ulcers.</note> was believed by the people to be holier than all others, they called all their diseases the punishments of this saint—as if no other <margin>St. Quirinus's disease.</margin> **master craftsman** <note>original: "daedalus," referring to an expert creator or designer</note> of diseases existed besides him. Furthermore, those priests decreed that ulcerous legs in particular were the punishment of St. Quirinus. To this, a remedy was added: a <margin>Its cure</margin> small image was to be sculpted in faith, which would strengthen and heal the leg, according to the height of their faith. St. John was regarded in a similar way; they introduced a shadowy <margin>The disease of St. John's vengeance.</margin> little man for him too, because he was believed to be the patron of that votive temple. The same honor was shown to other saints as well, who, because of the superstition of the ignorant masses, were required to be the guardians and makers of all evils. However these things may be arranged, to me—who knows that every cult of adoration and the priesthood itself was founded upon these vanities—this opinion of the mind remains: that <margin>Why the Devil introduced such superstitions.</margin> the Devil himself mixed his playful wickednesses everywhere, not so that many miracles might be performed, but so that fornication, greed, and other similar vices would not die out. By these things, the people were driven into a "faith" where they constantly believed and agreed to everything, and under that pretext, they multiplied all kinds of crimes, especially fornication and lust. For these are the impulses of Satan. Therefore, he always joins himself closely to these superstitions, so that by his inspiration he may continually strengthen and promote such a priesthood. Otherwise, no one would make a fuss about the signs themselves, whether they were great or small. But Satan, so that he can always keep his workshop and his wares nearby, diligently and curiously searches for the place where such miracles are most likely to be performed, so that he may insidiously insert himself into them.

### *On the Natural fire, which in later centuries was called the fire of St. Anthony.*

**S**o nature also has a fire kindled within itself, produced by the **sulfur** <note>Paracelsus viewed "Sulfur" as one of the three primary chemical principles of the body, representing combustibility and heat.</note> of man, not unlike the lightning of the sky, the shooting of stars, or the igniting of fire in mines. Even if this disease has not been correctly described by Physicians according to its nature, <margin>The disease Erysipelas.</margin> nature itself has manifested it through the acceptance of applied remedies, so that it is now abundantly clear that this disease was naturally born. But when the preachers of "penitential diseases" defined these things as their oracles, the people—though they resisted at first—were finally forced to believe. Thus, a violent persuasion prevailed that St. Anthony was the "Lord of Fire," even though he was never a blacksmith, never blew upon a fire, nor knew a lake or an anvil. And they forgot that he is the master of no element. If he were still among the living, he would be forced either to borrow fire or strike it himself. Furthermore, he is not **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire and blacksmithing.</note>, nor did he ever extinguish Mount Etna. Yet today, they command the poor man to extinguish everyone's rotting and oily leg. Even if he did something similar while living on earth, they find no support for their claims in this. For whatever was done through him will be contained in the book of saints, not scattered among sorcerers. Through this credulity, however, the matter was brought to the point where faith fabricated a certain "fictional Anthony" who rightly deserves to be called Vulcan. He blows the fire and stirs up the flames exactly like a most industrious blacksmith putting iron into the hearth. In these matters, everyone must diligently pay attention to how the conditions of such diseases lose their natural character. For all knowledge is placed in the removal of the natural course.

# BOOK I. ON ORIGIN

<page-num>118</page-num>

...she was of strange appearance and possessed a singular character.

When commanded by her husband to do this or that: if it was not convenient, she would bark back, stir up a rebellion against the man, and put on a shocking face, pretending to be sick. To make this deception persuasive, she devised and lied about a certain illness that seemed suitable. Thus, she began to dance, swearing that she could not stop herself from dancing. For she knew her husband detested nothing more than dancing. Therefore, to play the role she had taken on effectively and to confirm the likeness of the disease, she invented a specific type of it, repeatedly leaping and dancing, flying upward, singing, and emitting I-know-not-what screeching sounds. Once these acts were finished, she would twitch slightly in her limbs and then fall asleep. She marketed this dance as a disease, not revealing her malice to her husband, who was otherwise credulous by nature. From this point forward, it happened that other women later adopted the same character, one after another establishing the practice and driving others toward the same mischief. Eventually, it reached the point where the common people believed this to be a "penitential disease" <note>A disease sent as a punishment for sin that requires penance.</note>; and from this evidence, they fashioned a cause for themselves, or a helper—a saint—who might conquer that disease.

<margin>Magor, a pagan God: succeeded by St. Vitus.</margin>
Faith first fell upon <term>Magor</term> <note>A term likely referring to a pagan or "Gentile" spirit or deity of Germanic origin.</note>, a spirit of the pagans. As that belief faded, <term>St. Vitus</term> succeeded to his place, to be deified in this land after his death. From him, the name was transferred to the disease, so that it was called <term>St. Vitus's dance</term> <note>original: "Viti chorea"; historically known as "dancing mania," a social phenomenon where groups of people danced erratically.</note>. Gradually, therefore, and more and more every day as that opinion was strengthened among all people, the disease was granted its own "citizenship" in the community. Moreover, that faith seized those who delighted in dancing; it later stabilized the disease so that it remained perpetually alongside that faith.

<margin>The power of superstition.</margin>
From this, one may judge the power of preconceived notions. If something is marketed by opinions as being true, then certainly that assertion produces such solid faith that it is immediately held as established and settled. In this manner, many diseases occur—not only this dance, but others whose kinds or species are beyond numbering. Thus, some have persuaded themselves that they are possessed; while they believed this, it eventually happened to them in reality. In the same way, they first preached about <term>St. Valentine's dance</term> <note>original: "Valentini choream"; often associated with epilepsy or "falling sickness" in this period.</note>, into which they were finally thrown headlong themselves.

<margin>St. Dionysius. Patron of the French Sickness.</margin>
From this origin, many diseases first flowed forth which now leap upon us daily in the same way, yet did not exist before. This also happened with the <term>French Sickness</term> <note>original: "lue Gallica"; Syphilis, which broke out as a major epidemic in Europe in the late 15th century.</note>, for which they blamed <term>St. Dionysius</term>. Something similar happens in the plague: the greatest cause of which is almost always that the people, driven into despair, have persuaded themselves that it happens by fate and is 

inevitable.

<margin>How one is freed from the plague.</margin>
Through this despair, they have reduced faith to such a narrow strait that it is no less impossible to help them with medicines than it is to swallow a great mountain. These people are so powerful in their faith that they even infect the very heavens with poison; this then infects others with the plague according to the strength of their faith. In many such matters, faith performs that which would otherwise not happen at all. Thus, we create sad diseases and many hardships for ourselves; we are so degraded by these kindled evils that we almost perfectly resemble that man who, even if he were protected by the strongest armor, was struck dead by fear as soon as he saw a limping little boy standing against him with a smoking gun <note>original: "sclopeto"; an early form of firearm.</note>.

<margin>Man even against the stars.</margin>
The same thing happens to us in this case—we who are otherwise powerful enough even against the stars themselves. But as soon as we are struck by trepidation, then the force of faith is hurled against us like a <term>lightning-bolt</term> <note>original: "fulminaria glans"; literally a "lightning-ball" or "thunder-bullet."</note>, so that we must then endure whatever evil we have mutually cast upon ourselves. Thus, in many more ways than we can express, chains and bonds overwhelm us, in which we toss about miserably. If we were to leave our faith unchanged, and not attempt to test that which Christ himself affirmed to be possible; if we did not drive our faith into temptation or spend it on those things of which we have spoken, but rather sought the faith of mercy: what, I ask you, could possibly cause us affliction anywhere in this world?

So, too, other works of faith are found which are clearly similar to adopted ones, as in <term>St. Vitus's dance</term>, which themselves arise from stubborn and imaginative men. These people manufacture a cause for themselves out of an envious heart, favoring no one with their own good, and they pluck a certain saying from Holy Scripture which they twist and interpret according to their own brains. Once they have done this, they place such powerful faith in their own explanation that its virtue reflects back upon them and occupies them, hardening them so much that, for the sake of one risk to their interpretation, they dare to recklessly lose their lives.

<margin>The obstinacy of the Anabaptists.</margin>
An example of this obstinacy is found in the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>A radical religious group during the Reformation who practiced adult baptism and were often persecuted.</note>, who are driven by the abuse of an insane faith to the point that they would rather perish and die for a concept once it is conceived. Their superstition and sect cannot be described by a more fitting sense or a more convenient name than <term>incantation</term>: not because they are enchanted by other men, but because they compel themselves into such a faith that, by the force of this faith and not for the sake of truth itself, they would even leap into the fire...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases like St. Vitus's Dance and the plague are often caused or worsened by human imagination, social suggestion, and "insane faith" rather than purely physical agents. He uses the example of a rebellious wife faking a dancing fit to show how human behavior can be codified into a recognized "disease" through superstition.</summary>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

<page-num>219</page-num>

->ON INVISIBLE DISEASES<-

...let them surrender themselves to the fire. For to enter the fire on account of the will of God is of a greater and worthier cause than either a second or a third baptism <note>A critique of the Anabaptists, whose name means "re-baptizers," as they insisted on adult baptism even for those baptized as infants.</note>. For this reason, God commanded no one to die. He who despises death for the sake of His word must be greatly overflowing with the Holy Spirit, so that he may die in such a godly manner. However, those who heap up faith for themselves as a "work"—specifically so that their faith is not without works—whip themselves toward these works through their faith, as if they were saying: *If God is unwilling to produce signs through us, then we shall produce them from ourselves.* Thus, they have nothing left but to die in that stubbornness: a death that is just as if the spirit of faith were to begin a leaping-about in a dance. For those among these men who are seized by that "leap" are so far cast down from reason that they nurture the same nature as the <term>Anabaptists</term>, namely, preferring to die and be burned because of a conceived opinion rather than to yield from it.

<margin>For what cause martyrdom should be undergone.</margin>

It is surely something other than our own stubbornness that ought to lead us to that martyrdom. Let anyone take up this Horrendous example for themselves: how miserably they cast a vast mountain upon their own backs, and therefore plunge themselves deep into the sea, so that by believing, they bring upon themselves the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>Original: "fonticum morbum," a term usually referring to epilepsy; here used metaphorically for a self-induced spiritual collapse.</note> until they die and perish. What is this "foundation of scripture" other than a rash persuasion, which is then stabilized by a following faith? And these are those signs and wonders which they perform, of which Christ spoke. But if they were to labor, and eat the bread of their own labor, and be as inclined to give to their neighbor as to take away, and if they fulfilled the six works of mercy <note>Feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, sheltering the traveler, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and visiting the prisoner (Matthew 25).</note> and did other things: then certainly their superstition would enter into a different order. And if they were killed for causes of that kind, who would not hold them to be martyrs? Because if they risked their lives for the sake of works of mercy, certainly no random flame would consume them; rather, they would more often escape death, and not be so lightly burned and pass away. But the "articles" <note>Doctrinal points or creeds.</note> for the defense of which they spend their lives testify too clearly concerning the "works" of their faith—that these things are not very acceptable to God. For because of those very articles, they would be readily roasted on a grate or boiled in a pot of oil. They ought to have considered diligently that they were made to be redeemed from many punishments, and not to offer themselves to death everywhere, but rather that they had wonderfully extricated themselves from chains and prisons several times. Because they had pleased God, He wished to use their works longer. But the lives of these men—

---

—are not prolonged at all, but fall straight into death. And an evident distinction also falls between these men and the saints. For the saints went toward death <note>Implying they accepted it when it came</note>, whereas these men throw themselves into the fire by "dancing." Even if we did all those things which they have done, and embraced their entire doctrine, we would not yet have persisted in the six works of mercy, the foundation of which is *charity toward one's neighbor*. But what kind of "work" is this: to be idle, and gluttonous, and full of every treachery?

<margin>The character of the Anabaptists.</margin>

They neither clothe the needy, nor do they care for the sick. They have this one single sign of their life: *to cast down their eyes and look at no one.* And should this kind of faith not be called a seductress, and be referred to the number of these diseases, just as we wrote above concerning faith? For if you compare their histories with the saints, presumption will easily shine forth from their brow everywhere—a presumption by which they lead themselves into a certain "faith," believing they are indeed throwing a mountain into the sea, but not throwing it out again. To die on account of faith is a godly thing. But to die on account of "articles" which they themselves have established is a death born of superstition. Nor is that death very precious which is undergone for the sake of such things. For if you are burned up, what works follow you at last? Where do the fruits of the saints remain? For to be baptized twice is not a fruit of the saints. To despise and slander everyone is not a fruit of the saints; to pray for your enemies who afflict you with ignominy is no fruit of the saints. For if even a resurrected Paul were to inspect your articles, he would not let you go without disgrace. And would you endure to pray for this? Rather, ask him to pray for you. For you are the disgraceful ones, not those for whom you pray. Justly, therefore, all those before whose eyes such men appear ought to judge thus: that these men believe too much, and abuse their faith (which ought to have been directed toward God) for their own works, and they forget this: to know themselves. For they are so persuaded that they have been led there by faith that they cannot stop. Thus they are entangled in a disease, just like those who are seized by <term>St. Vitus's Dance</term> <note>Original: "chorea Viti." The author views the religious zeal of the Anabaptists as a clinical equivalent to the dancing plague.</note>. If their paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms.</note> presses upon them, they must rush headlong into that insanity. If all of us were fashioned according to their character, no hungry person anywhere would be fed, no naked person clothed, no sick person healed, and no exile received into hospitality. For all these things proceed from a greater foundation. Meanwhile, they themselves flee from labor so that their neighbor might also have something.

The author argues that true faith is found in practical works of mercy and charity rather than in stubborn adherence to self-made doctrines or the seeking of a meaningless death.</summary>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

## INTRODUCTION TO THE THIRD BOOK

<margin>The analogy between the visible and invisible man.</margin>
**I**t was sufficiently declared in the first Preface that man is twofold: visible and invisible. I have not proposed to write here about the visible, except perhaps where something must be brought forward by way of comparison. For what is more fitting to be presented as a likeness than things which are already similar? I shall deal further, then, with the invisible body; concerning its principle, consider this example. The visible body extends its operations into all things; man sees all its motions and whatever it does. Now, truly, that which is seen is at least half of the work; the other half, which the invisible body completes, no one sees. For example, a carpenter <note>original: *tignarius*</note> builds a house with two bodies: one invisible, in the <term>Idea</term> <note>In this context, an "Idea" is not just a thought, but a formative blueprint or spiritual pattern that precedes physical creation.</note>, and the other visible, through visible action. So here also you ought to know that the body has the power of establishing, fabricating, and constructing whatever the Idea provides. Thus, the invisible body can also build and perform all similar things—each of these bodies according to its own property and the logic of its creation. I will give a case: the carpenter builds a house, for his body was predestined for that task in its creation. Secondly, note another example: a pregnant woman, looking at that house, might conceive of it with such a strong <term>Imagination</term> <note>The "power of imagination" was believed in the Renaissance to be a physical force capable of molding the fetus or causing disease.</note> that it aligns with her will—matching the very will the carpenter has for building the house. Now the woman's imagination builds a house internally within her invisible body, just like the one she conceived in her mind. For whatever the Idea offers to the body to be constructed, the body returns to it; and whatever the imagination holds out to the eyes to be seen, the eyes push back into the imagination. Thus the eyes look at the house. Even if the house were removed from all sight, you would still see the house. Indeed, this example declares the property of each body according to its creation.

Furthermore, the body has its own wood and tools with which it erects and establishes all things. All these things exist in the invisible body as well. Nor is there any craft that does not see all its own proper instruments within its imagination. And just as the image of any person can see those things, it perceives them with the same clarity within the invisible body. For the visible body learns from the invisible. Therefore, since all these things are established in the invisible body, that body also uses them all in every way and manner, just as the visible body does. However, the visible body cannot work unless it is helped by the <term>spheres</term> <note>original: *globis*; referring to the macrocosm of heaven and earth which provide the "ground" or material for any action.</note>—that is, by heaven and earth.
<margin>Whatever is done requires a subject.</margin>
For in them and upon them all things are perfected. A painter who wishes to paint needs a physical wall. A stonemason about to work requires the physical ground. A blacksmith requires an anvil on the earth. To summarize these points: whatever man works or establishes, it is necessary that he establish it upon some thing. For without that "thing," his art is nothing. Now, no art is conferred upon us by God unless He adds everything necessary for its perfection.
<margin>Every art receives what is necessary from God.</margin>
This is because the craftsman is within himself, equipped both with art and with all the instruments necessary for fabricating whatever can ever be devised—whether it be in the art of conquest, or painting, or smithing, or weaving. For all these things, the art itself is ready and industrious. Now, what does it lack? Nothing, except the "spheres" upon which it may work—that is, the wall on which it may paint what it wishes. It suffers from no other defect. The art itself is so subtle and excellent that it can express through imitation everything that the eyes see and grasp, even if its own visible body cannot do so.
<margin>The excellence of art.</margin>
So inventive and ingenious is art that it can paint a fly on a wall upon that flat surface which it has. There is a single sharpness and a single subtlety between sight and painting: so that it can even sketch a spider's web with the same subtlety with which the eyes can see it or the spider can weave it.

<margin>The fetus: the foundation of imagination.</margin>
So that these things may be more easily understood regarding pregnant women—and lest, wandering further, I forget the "ground" or the "plane"—note that the fetus, hidden in the womb, is that very ground and that "sphere." For this reason, it is currently impossible for men to achieve the mastery of this craftsmanship in their own imagination <note>The author argues that men lack the "internal ground" (the womb/fetus) to manifest their imaginations into physical reality in the same way.</note>. For this cause, no mention will be made of men here, but only of women, in whom this art is greatest. However, although in cattle also the imagination expresses all the colors with which they are marked (rather than natural generation), nevertheless their imaginations are, as it were, too dark and intoxicated, reflecting a foolish dream. For the highest contemplation that cattle conceive during the time of gestation consists only of that refraction which occurs in water, if they see themselves in it. For every imagination becomes strongest through water. Although sometimes...
<margin>The imagination of cattle is lighter than that of humans.</margin>

It argues that the human spirit contains all the tools of any trade, but requires a "ground" (like a womb or a wall) to manifest its work.</summary>

### BOOK III. ON THE ORIGIN

Sometimes, indeed quite often, this flows from custom, just as happens in regions **prone to goiters** <note>original: *strumiparis*; referring to areas where goiters—swelling of the neck—were common due to environmental factors</note>: in these places, the cause is taken more from a customary imagination than from other natural factors. Now, to insist upon my proposal: the reason why the infant is the soil or the earth upon which that which the imagination makes is built, is this. The body we see is the woman’s. The <term>Species</term> <note>In this context, *species* refers to the outward form or mental image that the imagination projects.</note> of the imagination is also hers. For the woman is both of these. Therefore, she cannot build upon herself, but upon another. For he who builds, builds so that he may enjoy the building. But no one enjoys themselves <note>The author means that a builder requires an external object or space to manifest their work; they cannot be both the architect and the foundation simultaneously.</note>. Because it is built upon the earth, it is taught by that very structure that the earth is the earth. Thus the buildings of the imagination demonstrate what the "earth" is within the mother's womb. It is observed, moreover, that those buildings are constructed upon the infant. Therefore, the fetus is also the earth; and that in which it lies is the outer sphere and globe, which we call heaven.

<margin>The woman is the craftsman of the imagination: the fetus is the recipient of the work.</margin>
<margin>How forms are impressed upon the fetus.</margin>
Thus, therefore, the woman is the craftsman in her imagination: the infant is the wall in which the work is completed. Now we must speak of the hand that sketches the image. Understand this briefly in this way. The hand is invisible, as are the instruments: and yet these two are perpetually joined. Now, as you know, the cow follows the calf; that is, any craftsman follows the workshop and looks out from the floor upon which he builds: so also the hand proceeds with its instrument to the cell in which the fetus is hidden. And just as a craftsman chooses a place for himself which, by permission of the true master, is free: so also consider that the imagination with its hand is a servant; and that the body is not the master in the exercise of the art, but at least in supplying a place suitable for the future structure. Furthermore, conceive of it as if the body said: *Build this here, so that it may be continually in my sight:* then at that command the hand goes to the stated place, and looking into it, says, *Here it can be.* Thus, therefore, in that place named by the imagination, the work is built, just as the imagination itself conceived it. Which we shall say even more clearly. A woman who has conceived an image of this kind (suppose that she has caught sight of a **tortoise** <note>original: *testudinem*; birthmarks were often thought to resemble animals seen by the mother during pregnancy</note>) and impressed it upon herself: in that imagination, she touches her knee with her hand, so that both bodies are moved together most famously in one moment. But now the image is in the fetus, and the maker of the image seizes the knee with the hand: thus a tortoise is built upon the infant’s knee, no differently than if some master commanded a painter thus: "paint me a tortoise on this branch." Take the matter in this way. To wherever the touch of the imagination proceeds, there also the invisible body with its instruments proceeds, and builds that which happened upon its mind.

But to instruct you regarding color, how it, though it be invisible, nevertheless becomes visible: observe this example. You see that every single seed is gifted with its own heat before it <term>putrefies</term> <note>In alchemy, "putrefaction" is not just rotting, but a necessary stage of breakdown that allows a new form or color to emerge from matter.</note> in the earth. After the putrefaction, they will finally burst forth. So also man, in the corporeal body, knows how to express colors after the putrefaction of those things: that is, he who can putrefy lead, produces from it red, yellow, and white. He who can putrefy silver, produces blue. Now these visible corporeal things, the invisible body itself also possesses invisibly within itself. For whatever exists in the world, the eyes can see. And whatever they see, the invisible body also possesses. For example: just as the said things putrefy through man: so also the invisible body putrefies them, and takes them from the visible in the world, and stores them invisibly within itself, until it renders them visible in the fetus. Here see two examples: one visible and the other invisible: and yet both are one.

<margin>How a magnet attracts iron.</margin>
The first: A magnet attracts iron to itself without hands, without feet. And just as the magnet attracts the visible to itself: so also bodies are attracted to themselves invisibly through the imagination. Not that the body itself enters; but that enters which the eyes see, yet which is not palpable, such as are form and colors, and that without damage to the body: just as the second example teaches, which is this. <margin>How amber attracts vitriol to itself.</margin> Upon a small tablet made of leaden ash, or **bismuth** <note>original: *biſmuto*; an early reference to the metal bismuth, often associated with lead or tin in this period</note>, place yellow **amber** <note>original: *succinum*</note>, and at an interval of three spans from it, set down **vitriol** <note>original: *vitriolum*; a term for various sulfate minerals</note>: then the vitriol loses both its color and its sharpness, and in the preparation of the amber, both the color and the sharpness are found, yet the vitriol still appears as common vitriol to the eyes. For in this way many colors and virtues are translated into other bodies in those things where the colors are of the highest nature.

Thus, if it is possible for the body to be able to pluck and eat a herb: it will also be possible for the imagination to eat along with it: just as the imagination helps to build a house. For no one would dare to declare that the visible body alone built it, but it is necessary that the invisible be joined with the visible and the work be undertaken together. Wherefore also the imagination is powerful, so that it can eat in that appetite along with the pregnant woman. And since the earth is corporeal; but the imagination...

This page delves into the mechanics of this "architectural" power and uses analogies from alchemy and nature (such as raining frogs and the birth of worms) to explain how invisible forces manifest in the physical world.</meta>

...however, the architect in that place: therefore that **appetite** <note>In Paracelsian terms, *appetitus* refers to a driving desire or instinctive attraction that moves the imagination.</note>, with colors, forms, and figures joined to it, can most expressly depict and shade that thing. This is to be understood in a similar way as if oil and water were mixed together, and verdigris <note>original: *æs viride*; a green pigment or crust formed on copper</note> were thrown into this mixture, and both were to drink in that color: or as if copper were slipped into the **stomach of Vulcan** <note>original: *stomachum Vulcani*; a common alchemical metaphor for the furnace or the transformative power of fire</note>; then two bodies are produced, each with its own proper color. For in the woman, there is no division. Whatever one body can seize and do, the other can do as well. Whatever can be thought with the consent of the body: that happens. But since bodily examples are understood with pain and difficulty, consider a more illustrious example for yourselves: namely, that a man, according to the mode of celestial motion, can give himself over to the long-lived life of **Saturn**: or make himself a son of the **Sun**: that is, if he were the offspring of the **Moon**, and lived according to the nature of the Moon both in sickness and in health: he could then degenerate from her and become solar. Truly, these things happen through a certain **attractive force**, which works miraculously. For it is just as possible to draw away forms and natures from invisible things as it is easy to grasp some body with the hands. For just as it can happen that the body plucks and grasps a corporeal thing with the hands: so with the same ease the appetite of the imagination seizes the same. For every external thing has two bodies: the visible and the invisible. Therefore, it seizes whichever body is its own. And just as many things are taken by the body where an exalted imagination does not concur: so many things are also taken by an **exalted imagination** where an exalted body does not concur.

<margin>
Frogs 
which 
fall in 
rains.
</margin>
But furthermore, consider such an example. They say it rains frogs. Understand how that happens. The things that make rains are the invisible bodies of man; just as the earth is a visible body. Frogs, however, are made in an earthly way, and come forth from the earth, from which the visible body has its origin. Now, truly, it is against nature for it to rain frogs. The reason is: because they are born from the earth, not from rains. However, that they come from rains happens because they come forth from the invisible body, which consists of a similar generation as the earth. And therefore, frogs are visible to the earth from their cause and origin: but the rest are invisible. It happens in this way. The superior body has an **attractive virtue** <note>A "virtue" in this sense is an inherent power or quality</note> within itself to attract toward itself from the earth. But the earth also has an attractive force to attract toward itself from the heavens. The earth draws the invisible to itself and renders it visible. Heaven lures the visible from the earth and makes it invisible: Although each of these returns to where it was taken from, to our sight it is the same as it was before. Now, the Sun projects toward itself that which is related to its own **magnet**: so also every single star draws according to its own magnetic nature. Thus, a certain "frog-like" substance is attracted through the impregnating nature of the sky. And in the same way a mark is generated in the fetus: so also is the generation of frogs. For the imaginative power in the sky is the earth, the infant is; and that which falls down upon it from the sky is that which that star has imagined, and which it has lured according to the nature of the **pregnant magnet**. Thus, all those things must be ascribed to pregnant powers, which—by what the eyes see—draw to themselves through the magnet, and generate that which they behold in the fetus: just as was said of these things before.

<margin>
The true 
generation 
of worms 
by the 
attraction 
of semen.
</margin>
Furthermore, it must be known that in a similar way, entire semen is sometimes attracted, from which **worms** are afterwards born in women. This matter should rightly be a wonder to all, that such rare and unusual worms are carried in the womb of a woman, where the **workshop for generating the likeness of God** <note>The human womb, designed to create humans in the *imago Dei*</note> is placed. Now, a worm is not according to the likeness of God: nor is it from the semen of the man: furthermore, it could not have been brought in or led down into those places through food or drink. For the understanding of this, know the **pregnant nature** (so I call it) of the woman. If the hour of conception were pressing: and appetite were to overcome the imagination: and the imagination were the man, and were to flourish in that appetite: and the attractive force were to rise into its exaltation: now the sperm will be attracted invisibly into the workshop of conception, taken from that place where it was stored. A worm, however, is generated in natural heat. Thus, kinds of worms of this sort grow up in the body of the woman. Wherefore no one should wonder at this, thinking about the invisible body which is nothing greater than the image in the fetus. As this example teaches.

<margin>
The power 
of 
appetite.
</margin>
Whatever the body either sees or appetites in a pregnant nature, this is perfected in the fetus. For the interior body behaves in this work just like a painter toward a parent. The father does his work corporally. Here, what he has perfected corporally, the painter depicts. In the same respect that these two hold toward each other, so also...

### BOOK III: ON THE ORIGIN

...even congenital marks <note>original: *adnatæ maculæ*; birthmarks</note> in relation to those things from which they originated. Moreover, that such things are fully formed in the maternal womb occurs through a power of this kind: just as a **magnet** <note>The magnet was a favorite Renaissance metaphor for invisible, "sympathetic" forces acting at a distance.</note> hidden within a pregnant woman draws things equally to itself—exactly as a magnet draws iron—along with the body and other elements. It does not act like **amber** <note>original: *succinum*; known for its static electric properties, believed to "draw out" forces.</note>, which draws out the strength from vitriol; nor even like **Amethyst**, which is born in iron-rich stones and draws **Misy** <note>A metallic mineral, often an oxidized iron or copper ore, used in ancient medicine and alchemy.</note> from stones into its invisible body, and grows and increases with it in the same way as the Misy with which it lay.

<margin>Worms are hatched by heat.</margin>
They say that heat hatches worms, just as a hen hatches chicks from an egg. This should be understood equally regarding us humans: that we also are prepared through heat of this kind. Yet, heat is not the primary cause, although it must necessarily be provided; rather, it is the **nature and property of the female** that provides this, which is granted to women alone. That operation is not a function of the bodily heat itself, but rather of the **invisible nature** of which we have spoken. That nature is from the **stars**; and it is this very **Sun**—not the one in the heavens—that "cooks" the human being. Just as the Sun in the firmament warms the whole earth, so that other Sun warms the body. From this it follows that our earthly nature has nothing to do with the fetus in respect to these matters; instead, the **internal star** alone accomplishes such things. From this it is also concluded: just as you see the Sun scorch, blacken, and whiten things suited to receive those colors, similarly other things are created through these impressions. Now, it is no different with the fetus in the womb, except that such colors are branded upon it by that internal Sun. Therefore, concerning what has been said, know how the stars of a woman perform such operations. For **man is more than the stars** and the imagination of man. For imagination proceeds from the root of man, and man moderates the star. From this it is clear that the star is the craftsman, but it carries out what the imagination commands in this manner.

<margin>Man commands all things contained within himself.</margin>
For man has dominion over all things that are within him, whether it be appetite or will. For every single appetite is a consent and a kind of command, so that it may be carried out just as it exists in the image. Man is even **above his own star**, just as God is above the firmament, where He commands that this happen here, that there, a comet appear here, a star or other sign appear there. Surely, such is this dominion: such also is the imagination of the woman, so that whatever she hungers for in her external body is designated in the fetus. For the fetus is the **face of heaven**, the body is the **earth**, and man is the **begetter of those signs**, just as God is in the firmament. And such signs are made as swiftly as a spark struck from the air. And just as a hand violently strikes that spark from flint, and there stirs up fire where fire was not; so also the appetite demands fire, and in that striking, all thoughts are directed toward the fire. Therefore, an invisible hand can strike a shadowy fire into the fetus, according to what the thought or imagination of that woman might be. For her interior imagination is similar to the **eyes of a Basilisk** <note>A mythical serpent-like creature believed to kill with its gaze.</note>. 

<margin>The Basilisk who kills with its sight.</margin>
The Basilisk kills the one it looks upon for this reason: its **strong imagination** discharges poison along with its sight, so that the sight and the poison become one. So it is also with women. Whatever they see during the time of pregnancy and ardently desire, that is then reflected back into them along with their sight, and is imprinted upon their own fruit in the womb. For nothing else lies beneath them but this fruit. Thus also, just as with the Basilisk—if it sees itself in the Sun, its own poison is reflected back, by which it is then poisoned—similarly, these things are born in the eyes and in the **chamber of the imagination**, which the eyes refract onto the fruit of the womb, which is subject to this "tree" and over which she has dominion. For outside her body, that imagination is of no efficacy. Therefore, it is brought into action in that place where it rules. If this were not so, then she could also imprint such things on others by imagining them, just as she imprints them on the fetus. And just as through this power of the eyes, they discharge **menstrual blood** <note>A common medieval/Renaissance belief was that a menstruating woman's gaze could dim or stain a mirror.</note> onto a mirror; so in that hour they can also cast a certain stain into the eyes of another, just as the Basilisk discharges its poison through its eyes onto another.

Furthermore, concerning the imagination, take further note of what is commonly said: That if a woman at that time imagines for herself a learned and wise man, such as **Plato** or **Aristotle**; 

<margin>Whether anyone can be rendered more learned and wise through imagination.</margin>
or a military man, such as **Julius [Caesar]** or **Barbarossa** <note>Frederick Barbarossa, the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>; or an outstanding craftsman, such as **Hans Hoffhammer** <note>A famous 16th-century organ builder.</note> on the organs, or **Dürer** of Nuremberg in paintings; that she will then give birth to an offspring of that kind, who reflects the aforementioned men. Truly, whoever devised this, his brain was obsessed by a **great fool** <note>original: *grandi morione*; implies the theorist was a buffoon or possessed by folly.</note>. For such things require not just appetite and desire, but also the **knowledge** of those arts and wisdom; just as knowledge is present if they see a fish, or a strawberry, or something similar. If they had the knowledge of those things, and from this a **strong imagination**...

<summary>This page explains how a mother's internal "star" and "sun" (the imagination) physically shape the fetus, using analogies like the magnet and the deadly gaze of the basilisk. However, the author argues that while physical marks can be imprinted, complex traits like wisdom or artistic skill cannot be "imagined" into a child without actual knowledge of those fields.</summary>

...if a strong power <note>original: *fortis*; the text continues the sentence from the previous page.</note> were to approach: then we would least of all contradict them. However, so many things are required for such an operation that no proof of it has ever yet been seen. This much is true: if a woman listens to a craftsman—such as a musician or a learned man—and takes delight in him, then that impression is passed on to the fetus. And although she herself might not understand or be skilled in the matter, she nonetheless governs that process from which it follows that the fetus emulates what she desired. Yet this emulation is not of "perfect" <note>meaning comprehensive or innate</note> learning, but rather of "persuaded" learning, which lacks a solid foundation. The fetus is indeed rendered capable of such things, but in an inconstant and fluctuating way. This is indeed possible, and it remains in the fetus just like an imprinted mark <note>original: *stigma*; a birthmark or sign</note> or a skin blemish—if, for instance, during those hours the woman is tormented by a desire for stealing, for wooing, or other similar acts.

<margin>Imagination disposes the fetus toward theft and lust.</margin>

<margin>By imagination, some foods are made more pleasing than others for the future.</margin>

For this is perfected in the fetus and is born into it, and that propensity lasts through the entire course of its life. From this, many opinions of many men have arisen—namely, that the causes of these outcomes are the **Planets**—when in truth, it is the fault of the **imagination** alone. By this reasoning, many things are born into the offspring which break out in later years, so that a great malice of youth is detected almost everywhere. Since it is also commonly admitted that some people are periodically moved toward certain foods more ardently than others, or feel a heavy aversion to them, it should be known that all these things are stimulated by an external appetite through the **human star** <note>original: *astrum hominis*; a Paracelsian term for the internal spiritual force or "inner heaven" that governs a person's constitution.</note> given to the fetus, without any addition of things placed outside the human being. For the **imagination is the star itself.**

<margin>How an impression can be made externally through imagination.</margin>

It was said a little earlier that women are able to imagine in such a way that, through their desire, certain things with their own forms, colors, and figures might also be imprinted upon the body of another stranger—just as they are on their own fetus—unless that obstacle of which we spoke stands in the way. Therefore, when the imagination is aroused, the **menstruum** <note>original: *menstruum*; here referring not just to biological menses but to a formative "maternal matter" or vital solvent capable of being shaped by the spirit.</note> becomes the matter of that work, which is subject solely to the spirit of women, and from which **specters** <note>original: *spectra*; mental images or apparitions made manifest.</note> take their body. Take note of this example: the imagination of women is so powerful that they have imagined such "menstruum" even into the middle of the heavens, and by the power of imagination, they have fixed from it that which they previously saw painted and outlined before them. Later, however, those forms and figures fell back down into humans through that imagination, imperceptibly and wonderfully. This happened for no other reason than that the imagination generated its own "menstrual body" in such a way that it fell upon men, no differently than it would fall upon an infant enclosed in the womb. Although foul superstition has added the idea that the **Devil** adorns, paints, and tints works of this kind, that is as far as possible from the truth. If the foundation of these incidental signs <note>original: *signorum*; marks or omens</note> is to be uncovered and fully manifested, know that women in childbed <note>original: *puerperæ*</note>, if they are occupied with such an imagination, produce "asterisks" or "little crosses" and other similar things from such matters—which should seem a wonder to no one. For if it were agreeable to reason that the "menstruum" be more clearly uncovered and explained according to its powers, many more miracles would be produced, which are better omitted here. For many **Epidemic diseases** and others like them have arisen and been stirred up from this source alone. However, in the place where I shall produce the "privileges of women" <note>likely referring to a specific section of his medical theory regarding the unique biological and spiritual rights/functions of women</note> which they possess during the time of pregnancy, childbed, and the menstrual flow, I will satisfy your every desire regarding these matters.

<margin>Parts of the human body.</margin>

Know regarding all these things that at the time of man's creation, his body was founded both invisible and visible, and both parts were taken from the **Limbus** <note>original: *limbo*; the primordial "chaos" or reservoir of matter from which God created the universe.</note>. For one part is earthly, the other celestial. Therefore, the celestial operation is no less than the earthly. To the earthly body, commands were given for building and working with the hands. Therefore, more is enjoined upon this body in terms of practical knowledge than upon the invisible one. And whatever the external body performs, those works are complete. But the works of the invisible body are like certain **shadows** of the body. For although the external body completes its works through imagination, yet at least that is corporeal. But what is perfected in this place <note>the invisible realm</note>, the imagination can destroy through the invisible body. And just as a shadow can be understood in relation to a man, so too are the impressions of the fetus—distinct, however, from other shadows in this: that this shadow is constant and does not vanish.

<margin>How great the power of invisible or incorporeal things is, even over the body.</margin>

For if a sound can destroy hearing, or the Sun can so abolish sight that corporeal diseases are stirred up from it, the imagination will also be able to do the same. And just as someone can gaze at another standing before him with his eyes in such a way that the person flees from his position—or as one can command another, "Do this," which is nonetheless a "bare word" and yet performs what was commanded—because that word departs from the body, so also does one body drive away and put to flight another even beyond thirty miles. In which however...

What the Cabalistic art proves.

Now, the **Olympic spirit** <note>In Paracelsian thought, the Olympic spirit refers to the celestial or astral part of the human spirit that connects us to the stars and governs the imagination</note> completes these works, pulling the shadow away from all bodily works. Within this Olympic spirit, the **Cabalistic art** <note>A form of mystical interpretation often involving the secret powers of letters and spirits</note> is situated with its associated fields. This art proves that the force of imagination is effective in many more things if the conjunctions of the Olympic spirits are united. In the same way that visible bodies can be joined, the Olympic spirits of creation—which are the "stars" within the human body—can also be joined. These matters are described in the books of *Gabalia* <note>Likely a reference to a specific (perhaps lost or pseudonymous) magical text on the Cabala</note>.

<margin>
How a lame fetus is born from parents who are not lame.

But we must continue here with the discussion of diseases born from the imagination. Regarding those who are born lame from the mother’s womb—even when the parents, both father and mother, are not the cause of this—their lameness is induced from nowhere else than that the "inner man" of the imagination is bent. For if the physical body itself can be bent or distorted, the **inner star** <note>original: *astrum*; referring to the spiritual or astral body</note> can also be so. For both are one man—two parts of a single whole. Therefore, it often happens that the body is distorted or lame even though no prior cause of disease existed, while the interior body is entirely healthy and agile. Conversely, the interior body is also often contracted and distorted while the external body remains safe and unharmed. Now, every body reflects the fetus, and the fetus receives the character of that body and is born accordingly. When such a "monster" <note>Historically used to describe any congenital disability or unusual birth</note> is brought into the light, think to yourselves that the imagination distorted and deformed the fetus; whether this came from a spontaneously sparked imagination, or from the sight of an external form which afterward passed into its nature. 
<margin>
The imagination of a pregnant woman produces many monsters.
</margin>
Indeed, many such monsters are brought forth, produced by the imagination alone, with the physical nature of the body causing none of it.

<margin>
Succubus and incubus from the imagination. The nature of the seed of succubi and incubi.
</margin>
Although this is also true: the imagination itself is the cause of the **succubus** and **incubus** <note>Male and female demons believed to visit people in their sleep</note>, for the reason that the imagination gives birth to these things, and then they are drawn forth. To understand this, you must first know where the seed <note>original: *sperma*</note> of the incubus and succubus originates. It comes from the strong and persistent imagination of all those who woo in their thoughts and spirit. Because it arises from imagination, it is not true and natural seed, but is like a **foolish salt** <note>original: *sal fatuus*; a Paracelsian term for a substance that mimics the appearance of a thing but lacks its vital, life-giving power</note>.

---

For any seed that is to be the beginning of a fetus cannot be produced from imagination alone, but is generated by the operation of those parts destined for this task in creation. I offer this example: Unless a grain is cast into the earth and decays, it produces no fruit. Likewise, this seed must be cast into its own "earth," to which it is destined, so that it may decay in its place by its own earth; otherwise, no fetus is born from it. It is no different than if you were to cast a grain of wheat into a swamp; something similar to a "foolish wheat" <note>deformed or sterile stalks</note> might be produced, but not true wheat. And just as the seed for the coming year must be cultivated with labor this year to produce future crops—for seed cannot be cast into a field without labor—so too can no natural seed be made prolific without the natural order of conception. Therefore, conclude from this: *the incubus and succubus are the seed of foolish salt, produced from imagination without the natural order.* Thus, that seed is not natural, but a "foolish" thing. 
<margin>
Thomas Aquinas is criticized.

Therefore, **Thomas Aquinas** is not without blame, for he accepted a "foolish thing" as something perfect <note>Aquinas argued that demons could physically father children by stealing human seed; Paracelsus argues these encounters are purely imaginary/astral projections</note>.

<margin>
What "Heroic Love" is.

What is this love? It is nothing other than when someone, through fantasy, fashions a woman for himself in his mind, and by "having a matter" with her, satiates his love. From this comes the discharge of a "deaf" and "foolish" seed, which is unfit for the generation of children. Nevertheless, from that seed, the **Incubus and succubus** are born. But you must note one more thing here: such an imagination is the mother of shameless lust. This is why, if such lovers meet through an intense imagination, they are not at all fertile. For the imagination governs this seed

The lustful are infertile.

The cause of a mole.
</margin>
in such a way that nature is weakened by foreign elements. This is the primary cause of many cases of sterility and the **mole** <term>mola: a false pregnancy where a mass of tissue, rather than a fetus, grows in the uterus</term>. To continue speaking of the generation of the incubus and succubus: you must know that those seeds are carried away by nocturnal spirits. These spirits transfer them to those places where they can be hatched—namely, to snakes, worms, toads, and similar impure animals. For there, driven by those spirits, a union

<margin>The power of imagination.</margin>
The imagination is a hard and stubborn thing. If the mind were to repeat and bring back in order every single point that has been handed down in this book most briefly and clearly—namely, how many and how great are the forces that arise through the imagination of both men and women—I have no doubt that every <margin>The duty of the Magistrate.</margin> magistrate would strenuously compel the idle and lazy to work. They would provide for those who cannot command their own imagination, so that so many crimes and foul works might henceforth be abandoned. If it must one day be purged again on the Last Day: woe to those "pastors" <note>Referring to both religious and civic leaders responsible for the moral health of the community.</note> who have poorly fed the flock of sheep over which they were placed, for they were ordained for their sake.

And with these words, I now conclude this third book of mine on invisible things, founded upon manifold experience and drawn from the very faculty in which all these things become visible. It is derived so solidly and effectively from the very **light of nature** <note>term: light of nature (Lumen Naturae); in Paracelsian philosophy, this is the innate wisdom or intuition granted by God to understand the natural world.</note> that not even the smallest false letter can be found in it. This is true even if no more books were to follow, should God so advise. Therefore, with these few points proposed, lengthy interpretations and a profuse text have been enclosed within these brief verses.

Many other children are also born who are connected to the aforementioned origin to some degree; however, I omit them here for the sake of avoiding fear, since they can be understood in part from what has already been said. But concerning children who are legitimately born and yet, as has been said, are burdened by certain **maternal impressions** <note>original: "annafsentiis". This Paracelsian term refers to marks, deformities, or traits impressed upon a fetus by the mother's imagination or desires during pregnancy.</note>: receive this foundation regarding the union of these two. <margin>Gold and silver in a single metal.</margin> Gold or silver is sometimes generated within a single ore or metal. Even if that were a "monster" of nature, the gold nevertheless truly lives. Therefore, monsters of this kind are no less human, even if they are horrendous in appearance. For at the hour of their conception, their mixture was confused and not separated in nature. Indeed, nature is so subtle in the formation of a fetus that <margin>The subtlety of nature in forming the fetus.</margin> no separator could be so skillful in the refining of gold. For in the same way, an infant breaks forth from the liquids of the sperm, just like well-purified **saltpeter** <note>nitre; used here as an alchemical analogy for crystallization and purity.</note> which bubbles up like crystal and segregates itself from the dross in which it lies; or like a **pearl** <note>original: "unio"; a large, high-quality pearl.</note> which emerges from its own "sperm." But if something heterogeneous falls into it, then both grow together, and no one can discern one from the other—like quicksilver and gold, or silver and copper, or even more so like silver and tin. In that way, they remain invisibly narrowed and joined. But referring these matters to my other books, which treat more copiously of the generation of man, I now finish here.

<header>OF DOCTOR THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS OF HOHENHEIM</header>

# BOOK FOUR ON
->INVISIBLE THINGS.<-

->PREFACE TO THE READER.<-

<margin>Through what means Mahomet and Apollo rose up.</margin>
**R**ead this fourth book of our proposal diligently, skilled reader. For in it, hidden things are revealed which exhibit themselves visibly through their works—not merely so that you might be aware of natural secrets, but also so that you may learn from this how fraudulent their use has been until now. For through these invisible virtues of nature, Mahomet rose up, as did the primary god of the heathens, Apollo. These figures, making an incursion among the nations, stirred up such superstition and "idolomania" <note>A term coined to describe a madness or obsession with idols/idolatry.</note> that people superstitiously worshipped a body that was either already rotting in the earth or preserved with balsam. Those sects and their cults also cast their roots into the New Testament and introduced a lamentable schism; so much so, that not only was everything widely defiled by foul superstitions, but crimes and every kind of outrage rushed in all at once. And all these things were not only stirred up by sectarians and ministers of the temples, but were fostered by them with all their might. My purpose, however, is to describe natural things. If these are included in these volumes, many things will undoubtedly become known from them which have until now lain deeply hidden and have been correctly and truly recognized by no one.

<margin>Asmatheus.</margin>
For if it is permitted for a Physician to reduce gold all the way to its "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: The purest, most concentrated medicinal force extracted from a substance through alchemy.</term>, and to defame in his writings the Sophist <note>Paracelsus uses "Sophist" as an insult for traditional university-trained doctors who relied on old books rather than experience.</note> Avicenna and his accomplices, then perhaps it will also be permitted for a certain impostor to rise up in Medicine and pronounce thus concerning medicine of that sort: "Nature does not provide this; Asmatheus <note>Likely a reference to Asmodeus, a demonic figure, used here to represent a spiritual or non-natural force that people mistakenly credit for healing.</note> works it." This is something that could be done with little effort. For the Sophist physicians grant such things out of their own ignorance. Therefore, O Reader, the virtues of nature are immense. For who would be so confident as to dare to estimate how much and how great a power she possesses?

<margin>The infinite Wisdom of God.</margin>
For all these powers flow from divine wisdom. But who shall reach the end of this wisdom? For Scripture says it is without number, and proclaims its immense height and incomprehensibility.

<margin>What the Light of Nature is.</margin>
What, then, shall man do in the hidden depths of the earth? What will he achieve for himself, and what will he think, if he looks out into the sublime light of nature itself to see what his status is in relation to divine wisdom? Nothing else, surely, than the interval by which he is distant from the lowest point of the earth to the farthest peak of the sun—and through this again to a "new sun," seven times clearer and more splendid than that one. Even so, he will in no way reach even the very beginning of divine wisdom. Because, however, the **Light of Nature** <term>Lumen Naturae: The "Light of Nature," Paracelsus's term for the innate knowledge and life-force provided by God to help humans understand the physical world.</term> is like a crumb from the Lord’s table to be gathered by all nations, and because that light of nature has departed from the Jews, it is right not to cease, but to read and seize upon this wisdom as long as even the smallest crumb falls. Although this search may be too deep for us, therefore let praise, glory, and honor be to the eternal God, the supreme benefactor, who allows the light of nature to shine for us, so that we may walk rightly and fundamentally in natural things.

## INTRODUCTION TO THE FOURTH BOOK.

<margin>How man is a microcosm.</margin>
<margin>In man all things are contained.</margin>
**E**very single thing which must be properly explained by the light of nature must be traced back to the revelation of the first creation. For every principle is the cause of what follows, just as their nature is; for like does not beget unlike. Such also is the creation of heaven and earth, made not only according to form and figure, but also according to natural powers and properties. From the creation of all these things, man himself was fashioned, made by the hand of God according to His likeness. But where does this discourse lead? Solely to this: that you may understand that man is a **microcosm** <term>Microcosm: 'Little world'; the philosophical concept that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</term>, not indeed according to his physical form and substance, but according to all the virtues and operations which the greater world possesses. Thus from man flows the noble name of Microcosm; which is the same as saying that all celestial motions, all earthly natures, all watery properties, and all airy conditions truly exist within man himself. Within him thrives the nature of all the fruits of the earth, of all metals, the power of water, as well as the entire constellations and the four winds of the world. For what is there anywhere on earth whose nature and virtue man does not exhibit within himself? To such an extent is he subtle...

He begins the introduction by defining man as a Microcosm, containing all the powers, elements, and celestial influences of the universe within himself.</summary>

<page-num>130</page-num>
# BOOK IV. ON ORIGINS

The slime <note>original: "limbus"; in Paracelsian philosophy, the "Limbus" is the primordial "great mystery" or the reservoir of all matter from which God created the universe and man.</note> was subtle and sharp, from which God fashioned man according to His own likeness. Indeed, every naturalist <note>original: "Physico"</note> must consider this: that God created man, who was formed in His image, out of a most noble compound, the like of which shall never exist at any time in the future. His excellent works prove this. For even the heavens themselves cannot be so excellent in their powers, nor can the earth or any other element be so noble, that the body of man does not either equal or surpass them. All those wonders are present within man.

<margin>
Mummy <note>original: "mumia"; for Paracelsus, this is not just an Egyptian corpse, but the vital, curative balsam or "life-force" that remains in the flesh even after death.</note> contains all things in itself.
</margin>
All the powers of herbs and trees are found in "mummy." In truth, not only are the virtues of things growing from the earth detected in it, but furthermore, all the natures of waters, all the properties of metals, all kinds of marcasites <note>A term used then for various metallic ores, often iron pyrites.</note>, and all species of gems are found there. Why do I list these things individually here? All things are found in man; all are found no less effectively in mummy. As far as the eyes see the form, and as far as the hands touch the body—what, I ask, is lacking or missing from this compared to anywhere else?

<margin>
Naturalists are rebuked.
</margin>
Truly, one cannot keep from laughing when unrolling the commentaries of those who call themselves "Masters of Nature." These writings sound as if they were felt and touched, yet from them, one can see that the light of nature was never even glimpsed through a lattice window <note>original: "trasennam"; a screen or window-blind</note>. Instead, they built their foundations upon fragments supplied to them by spirits. And it is especially to be lamented that spirits laid such foundations upon which philosophers have built their knowledge of nature. From now on, let the same not happen again; instead, let it be built upon that base from which all things arise and flow. And although those spirits might still suggest more particulars to us:

<margin>
The light of nature alone must be observed.
</margin>
we must not follow their schools, but rather the light of nature itself must be more closely observed and grasped.

And to summarize all these things: whoever seeks opopanax <note>A fragrant gum resin used in incense and medicine.</note> will find it in this mummy.

<margin>
The power of mummy.
</margin>
And so it is with all other things. For whoever is able to explain and divide man—that is, to separate from each other those things that ought to be separated—his desire will be satisfied in all things. From man, he brings forth those things which could only with difficulty be elicited through Vulcan <term>Vulcan: In alchemy, this refers to the "internal fire" or the chemist/alchemist who uses heat to transform and refine substances.</term> and external means. For if someone seeks lemon balm <note>original: "Melissam"</note>, he finds it here. If someone seeks antimony, he finds it here. In this mummy, all things are natural, but until now they have escaped human knowledge. It is therefore right and proper to speak and discourse further on "microcosmic" <note>Referring to the "Microcosm," the idea that man is a "little world" containing everything found in the vast universe (the Macrocosm).</note> matters, so that those things may be explained which happen through invisible nature—things which the unrefined public usually considers to be witchcraft, illusions, and diabolical acts, even though they are purely and entirely natural, and are unearthed from a natural foundation. For in the limbs of man, a double nature must be established: namely, a tangible acting power, and an impalpable power.

<margin>
A double body.
</margin>
For this visible body has its natural operations, but the invisible body has them as well. Whatever afflictions this visible body suffers, it also has medicines for them established in the same place; and from where it can be harmed, it can also be healed. Know this regarding invisible powers: the thing that generates such a firm imagination <note>In this context, "imagination" is a creative, formative power of the mind/soul that can physically affect the body.</note> must not be something thin or contemptible. Where such foundations are laid, many things are undoubtedly stored. And just as the power of the lily opens and exerts itself, so also the invisible body puts forth its virtue. Therefore, if those wonders are in the body, just as they shine forth—and are confirmed by the testimony of eyes, tongue, and ears—certainly something fixed regarding them will also be in that microcosmic body. Thus, the greatest things can be produced from mummy, just as you see cloves shining from their little trees and celandine <note>original: "chelidoniam"; a flowering plant in the poppy family.</note> standing proud in the garden. While they live, they smile most gracefully and lovably upon everyone. But when dry and dead, they have no grace; and yet their virtues are still present. Thus, even if no one sees the mummy with their eyes, its virtue has not vanished. For life only carries away that which provides mutual recognition among men. But that from which life proceeds remains in the mummy. Thus you ought to know that these two natures in man, the visible and invisible, are endowed with various strengths and powers: that is, what the visible body provides in medicine, and what the invisible body likewise provides. For just as the visible body speaks, and no one sees the speech itself; and just as the eyes see, yet no one sees the sight itself; so understand similarly that the visible body, if it is "mummy," still has the invisible body with it. For this reason, it can perform admirable things, just as if it were alive.

<margin>
What is mummy?
</margin>
Mummy is this: if a man is stripped of life, then his flower breaks out in natural powers and secrets.

<summary>Paracelsus explains that man is a microcosm containing every herb, mineral, and celestial virtue, specifically located in the "Mumia" (the vital essence of the body). He argues that man has both a visible and an invisible body, both of which possess natural, non-magical healing powers.</summary>

<page-num>131</page-num>
### ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

<margin>The miracles of mummy.</margin>
So that you may understand these things, note that two operations can break forth from mummy here. One is: what the mummy does, which the living man was able to do. The other is: that the parts of the Mummy are a complete medicine. Understand these things more clearly and accurately in this way: You have discovered how a living body, through the power of medicine, can restore the sick to health. In the same way, you can know that the same thing can also happen in dead mummy. By which paths, however, must be known above all. For from this many Mummies have emerged which have performed miracles. Similarly, in another way, the same mummy was distributed, just like to people flocking together for a festival <note>original: "Enccœnia"; likely referring to the Feast of Dedication or a public fair.</note>. In such cases, its nature was not truly weighed by the people, but superstition and faith extolled it; and so, in the name of the Saints <note>original: "Diuorum"; Paracelsus often uses this term to refer to the cult of saints which he critiques as being misunderstood natural phenomena.</note>, these virtues were esteemed as miracles, as if one of the Saints worked such things beyond the measure of nature—yet these matters had been purely natural occurrences. This happened because nothing had been handed down regarding these forces, and the invisible body produced wonderful operations. Nor did they consider this: that even a magnet attracts a great mass of iron.

<margin>Man is a magnet.</margin>
And note that man himself is also a magnet, and in the manner of a magnet—just as it attracts iron—so he himself attracts and entices people. For observe this example of the perverse custom of men: If by chance a foreign man of rare appearance should arrive from somewhere, everyone rushes to him in competition, and they run to gaze at the stranger. They are accustomed to doing the same even at the sight of an unusual bird or dog, and other similar things. Now, just as nature has implanted such a quality in this or that person, on account of which a rush of people is moved, so she also grants a similar thing to a dead body. Thus anyone ought to be persuaded: Whatever nature gives while living, she gives the same when dead. 

Whence, if a mummy is buried, and nature stirs such a rush or gathering through miracles of healing this or that disease, then it should seem to you the same as if one centurion <note>A military recruiter.</note> in Lyons were enlisting a soldier and hiring him with counted crowns <note>original: "coronatis"; a type of currency.</note>; while another in Trent distributed Rhenish gold; and a third finally in Saxony did the same with groschen marked with a sword; and yet this soldier would flock to this one, and another to that one, to be enlisted. For all these are natural and human dreams, and certain superstitions of the living. Exactly the same thing happens to the mummy. For this one counts or weighs out fevers, that one the plague. And yet its reason is one, its nature is one. And just as it does not happen to everyone to be a centurion and count money, so also not every mummy can produce signs. However, the things I propose to you concerning this Mummy and explain naturally, those you ought to read and learn diligently.

<margin>Mummy held as a holy thing.</margin>
Therefore, let it be our purpose to declare the Mummy; specifically that Mummy which allows its work to flow out from the earth. This has been held as holy by many and has stirred up a congregation of people. And not for that reason alone: but also because, due to its powers given by nature, it was deservedly an object of admiration for healing people. Before I explain the matter itself, this must be stated first: many mummies have been sold under various pretexts in public gatherings, and presented and adored as Saints, since the people did not weigh how much greater the works of the Saints are, and how much more sublime their work is than these natural effects. They themselves will hasten to your aid, if only it has seemed so to God and been so ordained. And they have no need for promises, or vows, or gifts. For no reward was paid to Christ.

<margin>Both the dead and the living should be called upon.</margin>
Therefore, weigh this diligently. If you go to a city, you do the same as if you implored a doctor. He heals you by prescribing medicine. And when you have recovered, he orders that you pay the pharmacist for the jar. Is this not natural? Indeed. It is compared in the same way with those bodies also. For this is clear from the light of nature: that Doctors exist not only above the earth, but also within the earth; and that this is the manner and order of nature, that not only the living are called into service <note>original: "asciscantur"; to be received or adopted into use.</note>, but also the dead.

In this way, gods were born to the gentiles. In the same way also to Christians and Turks, while shaking off the true God, the only redeemer, from their souls, they placed all their protection in bodies of this kind. Even if this is indeed natural, it is nevertheless not right or proper. For God created the doctor to move above the earth, not within it. Thus He created medicine *from* the earth, not *in* it. And the living must be given place, not the dead.

<margin>The fraud of the devil regarding mummy.</margin>
But the fact that they follow those things with such great superstition is because of levity and seduction, to which Satan instigates and entices. However, when those bodies or mummies first emitted their powers, Satan himself also mixed in his own dung <note>original: "stercora"; used metaphorically for corruption or lies.</note>. And since men did not understand that those works were...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the healing powers of certain corpses (mummies) are natural "magnetic" forces rather than divine miracles. He warns that while these forces are real, mistaking them for the work of saints is a form of superstition encouraged by the devil.</summary>
<keywords>mummy, vital force, magnetism, natural healing, superstition, religious critique, Satan, medical theory</keywords>
