<page-num>132</page-num>
# BOOK IV. ON ORIGIN

<margin>Nature is finite.</margin>
...that these things are natural: he <note>Likely referring to the "invisible body" or the deceptive influence mentioned previously.</note> persuaded them that these things are produced by the saints <note>original: "diuis"; Paracelsus uses this term to refer to the Saints of the Church, whose physical relics were often credited with miracles.</note>, and flow from those for whom he afterwards even established initiates and priests, and in the same effort propagated his own crimes. But the condition of Nature is this: now it is autumnal, that is, it bears nothing; now it is summery, that is, it produces a harvest. Thus, along with this harvest of the saints, many have been gathered into the granary: and thereafter neither signs nor any works followed. But why? Surely because nature has an end and does not last forever, while the holy live eternally. Moreover, just as a rose breaks forth or rises in its own time, and at nearly the same moment falls again: so it goes with these bodies: today they flourish, tomorrow they wither. For all things are natural: and for that reason, they rise and fall with nature. Therefore, I would wish everyone to be diligently warned here to attend carefully to this book, and weigh what nature can do within her own powers.

But if we seek signs from the Saints which are free from deceit and disguise: we must not look to their bodies, nor follow natural things. For the body is nothing other than earthly nature: and whatever it performs, it is all naturally implanted within it, no differently than sneezing is to mustard, or blistering to the buttercup <note>original: "ranunculo"; the juice of the buttercup or crowfoot plant was historically used to cause skin irritation or blisters.</note>. Here there is no divine work.

<margin>The Saint who helps.</margin>
Although out of simplicity and ignorance regarding natural faculties occupying us, most things of this kind were believed to be supernatural. Toward this we were especially driven by natural Masters, Philosophers, and Physicians, who held a name without the reality. Therefore, distinguish between the Natural and the Divine: and thus the body will remain a natural body, while the Saint will be a Saint. If a Saint has worked a miracle in any of us: he does it without his body. For he does those things in the name of Christ.

Now consider what part his body has in this business—the one whom you implore for help, who has long since been dead and is with God. Suppose he does bring you aid: yet for that reason he will not be clothed in his body again, but will leave it among the worms, and will work in the name of Jesus. If therefore he works without a body: why do you seek it in the body? Let the dead bury the dead; you, have to do with the living. Nature is joined to nature: so too the Saints are joined to one another. If a Saint is to hear and heal you (for I suppose this can happen), then he will not summon you to his tomb; but the goal <note>original: "meta"; used here to mean the meeting point or destination.</note> is situated there in your breast and heart. How then could you be more closely joined to a Saint than if you stand upright? It is not within our power to penetrate to the Saints: it is necessary that they descend to us. Moreover, they have made a divorce from their bodies, and for that reason cannot carry us there. For if the body had to be with the Saint, then it would not be upon the earth; but together with its Saint, it would fly up to heaven through the window of the chamber.

<margin>Who first attributed natural works to the Saints.</margin>
Furthermore, the undertakers <note>original: "vespillones"; used pejoratively here to refer to those who profit from the burial and veneration of bodies, such as certain clerics or shrine-keepers.</note> were the first to call the natural works of the body "divine." For what purpose they did this is clear enough from their splendid temples and monasteries. Preaching about the Saints, they pointed the finger only at the body: where Satan incited them so that he might sustain them; and he spread a mist over the light of knowing nature, lest by chance it be betrayed that these are not the works of the saints, but of nature itself; lest, I say, it be known that the body and the nettle are defined by the same explanation. For the body also is a nettle <note>A metaphor suggesting the body has its own inherent "sting" or biological properties, independent of the soul.</note>.

<margin>John the Baptist worked no miracles.</margin>
If bodies are now established as holy, let no one doubt that the Turks themselves are as well-fortified as the Christians. But meanwhile, Christians shamefully forget that John the Baptist—who nonetheless came forth most holy from his mother's womb—works nothing anywhere with his body. Who, if the body itself were a saint, would rightfully fill many chapels. But let all of you recall that wonderful composition of nature from which man was made. And give credit for everything to this clod of earth.

To further instruct you briefly concerning the body and the saints: now learn how they differ among themselves. Once and for all, this is true: the body is buried in the earth, while the saint is raised into heaven. Therefore, whatever that which is in the earth performs, it is natural. Likewise, what that which is in the heavens performs, it is supernatural. Now, if the body must rise again on the day of final judgment and give an account of its life: it is necessary that the same body first be glorified. But what is glorification, if not the removal of natural powers? And in what does a saint differ from me or another, except in this: that he is glorified? That is, he has nothing natural anymore, while I am most full of nature.

<margin>How Saints differ from us, the living.</margin>
For if a saint existed and yet had natural powers, who could disentangle themselves from such a saint? For the power of nature is so wonderful that it can rightly be judged divine by the people. It is hard to say and difficult to understand: namely, that a saint walks above the earth and, not excluded from natural powers, produces signs; should that be credited to nature or to divinity? Unless it be that he might establish his works in the name of Jesus.

<summary>This page argues that miracles attributed to the physical bodies and relics of saints are actually natural biological phenomena. Paracelsus insists on a strict separation between the earthly "natural" body and the "glorified" heavenly saint, criticizing the religious veneration of remains as a misunderstanding of nature's inherent powers.</summary>
<keywords>relics, saints, nature vs divine, John the Baptist, glorification, miracles, medical philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 132, where Paracelsus argues that the "miracles" attributed to the physical remains of saints are actually natural phenomena inherent in the human body, which contains the powers of the entire cosmos.</meta>

<page-num>133</page-num>
-> ON INVISIBLE DISEASES. <-

...would establish. Otherwise, who would consider his walking upon water to be the work of a saint? <note>Paracelsus is distinguishing between natural laws and divine miracles; he argues that some "miracles" are actually natural, though misunderstood.</note> Country folk are indeed prone to believing; however, it would be difficult to persuade me of this here on earth. Who is glorified, whom death might leap over, if death is not the beginning of that glorification? But whatever has not been glorified must be considered a natural creature. Whatever of the earth clings to us shall be taken away. Therefore, the elements themselves will be dissolved, and all things that consist of them. If these perish, what will become of the nature of the body, forged from these elements? All things will eventually be glorified. Where then will the bodies go, and their appendages, which concern those natural secrets destined to be destroyed through glorification? Before glorification, one does not know the other, unless the testimony of Christ is present. For fire will consume bodies, but not the saints <note>original: "diuos"; here referring to the glorified, holy state of the soul as opposed to the corruptible physical body.</note>. Know then, that what bodies perform in the sick is a purely natural labor, no different than what a physician would do, or if you were to go to the baths of <term>Pfäfers</term> <note>original: "Piperinas"; refers to the famous thermal baths at Bad Pfäfers in Switzerland, which Paracelsus studied for their natural healing properties.</note>. In the same way those baths perform their natural operations upon you, so you also wash yourself at the tomb of that body. For God established natural works in a wondrous way. Therefore, it is right for us to be constantly mindful of His wisdom, which can never be fully uncovered by any scrutiny. For in the end, it is true that we contain within ourselves natural powers no fewer or weaker than those contained by heaven and earth themselves. If a magnet, which appears to be a dead thing, can draw iron to itself: a dead man can also attract the living to himself.

<margin>Man is no less powerful than heaven and earth themselves.</margin>
If beggars are permitted to come into the sun: the same access will be given to man. If the planets can govern a man according to their will: a dead body will also be able to do the same. And all these works are invisible: and yet they are natural. For just as nature distributes herbs: so here too will be a similar distribution.

Now, that only the glorified being is a saint, while the body in the tomb is not glorified: its decay and the worms prove this. For whatever is glorified is not subject to these conditions. Therefore, the body in the tomb retains the nature of all the planets and stars; no limit can be reached regarding this nature and these powers within us. And the more deeply we search, the more wonders are discovered.

<margin>By what power the bodies of saints attract men</margin>
Thus this body also retains all the properties of the element of water, from which all mines originate. Therefore, the body possesses a magnet: and its power is a magnet. For every magnet exists within the nature of iron and consumes iron, just as these bodies consume one another. In the same [body], all the powers of the element of earth remain. Therefore, in it is also the power of Lavender, and of all things born of the earth. In the same way, the nature of air remains in it. For which reason it is also <term>Manna</term> <note>In the Paracelsian system, "Manna" refers to a celestial, nourishing balsam or essence found within natural substances.</note>. Now, since the firmament itself and the other elements are considered by you to be quite wonderful: are not bodies also admirable?

<margin>Mummy, the wonder of nature</margin>
And would these not be sufficient reason for me to take up the description of corporeal nature, specifically because this kind of <term>Mummy</term> <note>original: "Mumia"; in early medicine, this refers to the vital force or medicinal substance remaining in a corpse, not an Egyptian mummy.</note> exists? In which the powers of both the lower and higher spheres lie hidden? So that, by weighing the nature of the body in this way, I might bring it into the light? For while I do this, I touch or violate no relics of the saints: but I am dealing with nature. I also hope that in this way I have done something pleasing to the saint himself, within the light of nature. For a saint is such a distinguished thing that if they could feel shame in any way, they would not dare to stand before God even for a moment if they wished to handle such crude things and bring nature into the sanctuary. Nor shall anyone reproach me with the thought that I am a despiser of the saints or a mocker of the miracles produced by them. For I am so well-versed in both nature and the saints that I am perfectly able to distinguish these things from one another with great exactness. Furthermore, if I examine the miracles of the saints in both the Old and New Testaments, it is easy for me to see clearly which are holy and which are less so. Therefore, I praise and worship God among the saints, because in glorification there are such wonderful powers of raising the dead, restoring sight to the blind, and cleansing lepers—and that in the name of Christ, which is above all firmaments and elements. Here I am not unaware that nothing ought to be criticized. And although some may complain about me, that I am plundering the tombs of the saints: yet this accusation will only echo from the "kitchen" <note>A metaphor for base, material interests or the greed of those who profited from relic-based pilgrimages.</note>, with which not even Christ Himself ever agreed. What then shall I do? But concerning the saints more specifically...

<meta>catchword: ...also</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the healing powers of relics are purely natural properties of the human body (Mummy) rather than supernatural miracles, asserting that the physical body contains the same powers as the stars and elements.</summary>
<keywords>Mumia, Mummy, Magnet, Saints, Glorification, Nature, Elements, Pfäfers, Manna, Firmament</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 133, where Paracelsus asserts that the supposed miracles performed by the remains of saints are actually natural "magnetic" properties of the human body rather than divine interventions.</meta>

### BOOK IV. ON ORIGINS

...and the book will be completed.

Here one must carefully attend to the words of Christ when he says: *They shall perform great signs.* <note>Referencing Matthew 24:24, where Jesus warns of false prophets performing wonders.</note> For whom else does he imply but those who guard and preach about the dead? Or is it not "giving signs" when they say: *Behold the gathering of a great multitude hurrying near.*? Why then should this be considered as nothing? Look at the extraordinary offerings. And should this not be considered a good and Christian work? Yet these madmen do not remember that the pagans do the very same things, though they have no dealings with Christ. "Look," they say, "at the great number of crutches; behold the wax images with spears and weapons; see the candles and the vials." Read the miracles recorded on the tablet, and so on. Even if all these things truly happened, the basis and origin is the pure and simple body. Therefore, consider it no different than a journey to the thermal baths. <note>Paracelsus frequently compared pilgrimage sites to medicinal baths, arguing both work through natural chemistry.</note> For in both cases, the matter can turn out well or poorly; it is the same path that carries both the paralyzed and the healthy to and fro. 

Now, it would be too cheap an honor for the saints if they merely gave new crutches in exchange for old ones and sent away so many lame people whose feet were exhausted and bruised from traveling such distances. If a work is truly to be the work of a saint, it is necessary that the person believe in Christ, or that the work possess a peculiar quality that is distinct from the usual habits of other saints. As much as our faith in Christ and the Saints dictates, I hope they would not allow these [superstitions]. If it were necessary for a Saint to exist within a physical body, then no body would be more useful to us than that of Christ himself—if his dead body were of the same power as it was when he was living. But it is not so. For this reason, he rose again and ascended into heaven, as the Apostles testify. If the body of Christ in the earthly tomb performed no signs, it is much less possible for any other body to do so. Therefore, one must not deviate from the example of our predecessor <note>Referring to Christ as the model.</note> but must follow in his footsteps. 

But since things have now reached the point where natural works are exalted above the Body of Christ himself and are worshiped as miracles, this confirms the word of Christ, who said: *they shall perform great miracles.* These should be accepted by us in no other way than how the first inventors of medicine were regarded as gods by the people because of their miracles and works of healing, before anyone knew what <term>Rhubarb</term> was. <note>original: "Rhabarbara"; in the 16th century, the potent medicinal effects of exotic plants like rhubarb seemed miraculous until their natural properties were understood.</note> It is the same with these bodies, because it was uncertain that the <margin>Why the first physicians were worshipped as gods.</margin> remains of Berthold <note>original: "Betholdi"; likely referring to the relics of a local saint such as Berthold of Regensburg.</note> were buried here. Think instead of the non-glorified body, which is nothing other than a natural thing. Therefore, whatever 

<margin>Natural things act simply.</margin> is earthly, and acts naturally, must be earthly. For this reason, nature works for the credulous and the incredulous, the good and the bad, the honest and the dishonest, whoever and whatever they may be. Whoever devours <term>Colocynth</term> is driven to the stool. <note>original: "Colocynthidem"; the bitter apple, a violent purgative. Paracelsus argues that just as a laxative works on everyone regardless of their piety, so do the "miracles" of relics.</note> For every natural operation was so ordained by God that it happens without respect of persons, without imagination, without faith, and neither in the name of Jesus nor without it; but rather, nature acts simply and in its own way. Search the scriptures regarding this; they will instruct you more clearly.

However, so that you may understand the nature of the body more explicitly—specifically whether it is the whole body or some part of it—there are two paths to follow here. One is what is said: "Here such-and-such a body is buried," or what is affirmed: "Here the head or another limb of such a body is preserved." Now, if this body has a "magnet" within itself, it draws the common people to it; it heals those it can heal, and those it cannot heal, it dismisses. The other path is when this "magnet" is hidden or buried secretly, <margin>Mumia which draws men by force.</margin> and afterwards it is boasted with a great cry: *Here a wonderful sanctuary is celebrated!* <note>Paracelsus uses "Mumia" to describe the natural life-force or "balsam" remaining in a corpse that exerts a physical attraction.</note> In this way, the magnet exerts itself and pulls men away from the plow with such speed that not even a compass needle could be incited more swiftly. These are the origins of pagan superstition; and thus hidden <term>Dedication Festivals</term> <note>original: "Encænia"; festivals of consecration or dedication, often associated with the opening of a shrine.</note> are established through natural impressions. It is done secretly because that body was once wicked and criminal, and therefore they did not dare to boast of it as a Saint, knowing however that it contained a magnet and much "quicksilver" <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury. Paracelsus believed mercury and other minerals within the body governed its physical influence.</note> for anointing men. 

Thus, men are enticed to such a corpse no differently than a vulture. How the vulture and the corpse it seeks match and agree in their natures should be firmly engraved in your minds. For just as a vulture gasps for a corpse so that they are joined even across the sea, it must be understood by the same forces that men flock to that body. For God sets before us an example in nature so that we may recognize it in such matters: that according to nature, we follow a corpse so naturally constituted, just as vultures do. This example taken from nature cannot be rejected. For Christ himself said: *Where the corpse is, there the eagles will be gathered.* <note>Matthew 24:28. Paracelsus interprets "eagles" here as those drawn to the spiritual "body" of Christ, contrasting it with the "vultures" drawn to earthly relics.</note> Is this not the same as saying: *No bird flies higher than the eagle. So among men, none fly higher than those I have redeemed by my death. For these fly even unto heaven itself.*?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the "miracles" associated with saints' relics are actually natural magnetic attractions inherent in the human body, comparing their effects to medicinal herbs like rhubarb or colocynth. He warns that worshiping these natural phenomena as divine signs is a form of superstition that confuses physical "mumia" with true spiritual power.</summary>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

...fly. *The eagles, however, descend from the heights toward me to the body—that is, the carcass on the ground.* <note>Paracelsus is interpreting Matthew 24:28: "Wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered."</note> Understand now: when we fall away from Christ and follow a "carcass" of this kind <note>meaning a dead sect or physical relic</note>, has not the word of Christ been precisely verified? For we are eagles, no less than John the Evangelist himself. <note>In Christian iconography, St. John the Evangelist is symbolized by the eagle because of his "high-flying" spiritual insight.</note> Who flies higher toward the kingdom of heaven than we do? And what is the body other than a carcass? Or what else would Christ have hinted at by "the eagle" than what has been said? Now, from the body of a Saint, you may even establish a carcass. Yet these carcasses are putrid. Therefore, my purpose here is to treat natural things. We shall gather these into a specific book so that the things handed down thus far can be explained more conveniently. For these matters are of greater concern to us than Philosophy. And yet, this also drove me: the fact that true Philosophy had not yet been rightly discovered. For matters of this sort should have been perceived and understood long ago by the Heathens, as well as by the Physicians. However, the reality itself reveals that they have learned nothing at all from the light of nature. <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lumen Naturae) is a central Paracelsian concept referring to the innate knowledge found within the natural world, as opposed to knowledge from books.</note> Otherwise, they could not have passed over these things with such neglect.

<margin>Critique of Physicians and Philosophers.</margin> Indeed, such as the masters they had, such also are their works. They built their foundation upon their own spirit. And just as wandering scholars <term>vagantes scholares: poor, traveling students of the medieval period who often lived by begging</term> scrape together fragments, so these men have begged from spirits here and there: here some spelt, there wheat; here oats, elsewhere barley; in some places morsels, in others porridge. These they later threw together, stuffed into a single pot, and from that mishmash they cooked up a "Philosophy" that fits together no better than if one mixed bran with sand or some other absurd thing. This is how Aristotle published his Philosophy; this is how Pliny became an Herbalist. From these collections and fragments, Galen and Avicenna also grew bloated. And if the chattering spirits of Necromancy <note>original: "spiritus Nigromantici"</note> had not existed, from where could those fools have scraped together their Philosophy? These are truly those philosophies and medicines founded upon visions. It seems the same to me as if a Physician were to judge urine through a magnifying glass. They think they have achieved a great thing if they know whether a tunic is blue or green; and they snatch a consultation about a patient's health from the greased nail of a thumb. When Horehound <note>original: "Marrubio"</note> is offered to them, they do not know if it is "water-waste" or "heart-wort." <note>original: "vitica sit. vel cardiaca"</note> When Burnet <note>original: "pimpinellâ"</note> is held out, they do not know if it is Rampion or Dock. <note>original: "rapunculuſne sit an lapathum"</note> The cause of this ignorance and ambiguity is that the spirits were unwilling to confess the fundamental truth to them.

Here, therefore, while the so-called wise men were hardened, the vulture followed the carcass.

You should also know that the "charity" of men is not the thing to be looked at, as when people say: *This man, while he lived on earth, performed many good works, and therefore it is right that God should repay them by allowing the working of such signs.* For who knows, before God, what is truly good or evil? <margin>Divine signs seen in good deeds...</margin> Therefore, we must judge nothing by this standard. Even if God were to perform a sign through some body, it does not follow that the body itself should be worshiped. Let there be an example: Someone is murdered somewhere. If, a long time later, it happens that this body bleeds in the presence of the standing murderer <note>Paracelsus refers to "cruentation," the medieval belief that a victim's corpse would bleed if the killer approached it</note>, it cannot be concluded from this that *this body is alive*. Rather, it is indicated by that bleeding that the spilled blood demands vengeance from God and the magistrate. Similarly, let us suppose someone had destined many goods for a certain Brothel <note>original: "Lupanari"</note>, specifically for the purpose that the prostitutes should not sin on the Sabbath day. If he then dies, and no one deigns to bury the dead man except those little harlots: does the body become more worthy because of this? You should not understand these things in any other way than if someone had a faithful companion who died, and you kept his image with you and preserved it above other things. What does this benefit the one who died? Or why does he become more worthy because you value his image so much? If such a thing happens and the dead man is buried: let it happen, and leave the body alone. For it is a sign that the earth will consume him. If someone crosses a river with dry feet, who shall judge how that happens, even if it truly occurs? What does that deed have to do with the body? The body is not the cause. For the carcass of the deceased cannot do it. If it cannot do it again, it did not do it the first time. That which is within a human produces the effect: namely, his spirit, which went out from God. Therefore, if the body dies, the spirit proceeds to Him from whom it came—from God, back to God. The body, however, because it was taken from the earth, returns to it. Thus, everything returns to its "first matter." <term>prima materia: the foundational substance from which a thing is made</term> With these things so established, what, I ask, shall we seek in the body, since the human being is not "whole" in that state? Who eats a bone that is not salted? Who sees by a lamp that is not burning? Indeed, many are thought to be "divine" <note>saints</note> whose good deeds are actually quite rare. And many of their neighbors may far exceed them in merit, but they do not possess this "magnet" and are destitute of that nature. This...

<meta>catchword: qui (who/which)</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus critiques traditional medicine and philosophy (Aristotle, Galen, Avicenna) as being built on "scraps" and deceptive visions rather than the "Light of Nature." He argues that miracles associated with dead bodies are natural phenomena or spiritual signs, rather than proof of the corpse's holiness, emphasizing that the spirit returns to God while the body returns to dust.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section concerning the distinction between true divine miracles and natural phenomena that are often mistaken for the supernatural. Paracelsus is establishing that many "miraculous" healings attributed to saints are actually the result of natural virtues implanted in the human body by God at birth.</meta>

<page-num>136</page-num>
->### BOOK V. ON THE ORIGIN<-

<margin>
Vulcan produces miracles; you have the magnet.
<note>original: "Vulcanis miracula edit magnetē habēs." Vulcan refers to the alchemical "inner craftsman" or the power of fire/transformation in nature.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Christ heals without a medium.
</margin>
...who possesses nature—even if he were a dog—would nevertheless produce miracles, and good ones at that. For that is how that constellation moves.

<margin>
The power of the Mumia is implanted from the mother’s womb.
<note>original: "Mumiæ vis ex vtero materno inditur." Mumia is a central Paracelsian term referring to the vital, balsamic force or "life-grease" within a living body that allows for healing and preservation.</note>
</margin>
Note well, indeed, that these things are implanted in us in the mother's womb. And just as roses bring their scent from the earth with them, so we too bring this property with us. Thus also <term>witches and magi</term> <note>Paracelsus often viewed magic as a natural, albeit hidden, science of the imagination and will.</note> are born; they do not become such through study or art. Thus even the dead can be such as they were when living. For if such a nature is born into the world, a peculiar power remains in the bodies. And although the spirit is separated from the bodies, that which is its innate virtue and property nevertheless remains in the bodies and lies hidden in the earth, like <term>saffron in a box</term>. The earth is furnished with such bodies no differently than a pharmacy is with jars. Regarding these signs, unless Christ himself had also foretold them, who, I ask, would be so bold as to want to search so deeply into the secrets of nature? Because such signs occur and bring portents with them—through fasting, through prayers, and through familiar spirits—the omens of the celestial signs also concur. Even the misery of the earth itself agrees, such as thirst, famine, plague, and the uprising of father against son and son against father, and so on. Who among men would not fly into nature and investigate the reason for these events more accurately? For it is admitted that not everything proceeds from the Devil. Nor do all things flow down from the stars; and not all things are produced in the name of Christ. If, therefore, Christ does not wish to support these things by helping, then these natural good works are timely for them to deceive the incautious common people. For if such things emanated from Christ, the blind would indeed see, and the dead would be raised. But the Son of God does not wish to help. Therefore, they seize the works of the Father—that is, natural virtues—and they sell them under the name of the Son. Because they deal with the works of the Father, they produce signs only in the summertime.

<margin>
The works of the "saints" fade in their own autumn.
<note>original: "Diuorū opera suo autumno exsoles sunt." Here "divorum" (saints/gods) refers to those who perform wonders through natural means rather than true divine grace.</note>
</margin>
When autumn approaches, however, all those things fall away and wither. For they only hold a natural course, according to which they also exist. When that time is finished, the grace of these "saints" also ends. In all times, it could easily be understood that truly divine works must be Christian and durable without such an autumn; they are not taken from the nature of things but are spoken in the name of Jesus: *Rise, take up your bed and go.* <note>original: "surge, lectum tuum accipe & abi." A reference to Mark 2:11.</note> This is what it means to heal: to throw away the crutches and to free the captives whom we did not bind. For all diseases weigh upon us from the creation of God the Father; it is right, therefore, that they be healed again by that same creation—unless it happens that the Son of God frees and heals, who requires no creaturely means to perfect the work, but operates according to divine power.

<margin>
Medicine is not what the eyes see.
</margin>
So, enough has been explained regarding these matters thus far. As a finishing touch, we shall also reveal the manner in which those things happen, so that we may see men becoming healthy, not from natural forces <note>meaning the "natural" forces of traditional medicine like herbs</note>, because they neither drink syrups, nor swallow boluses, nor devour sweets, nor anoint their limbs. In all these things, <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek physician representing the establishment medicine Paracelsus rejected.</note> is inferior, for he could do nothing without prescribed medicines. For those things heal invisibly; and there is no other difference between them than prescribing and not prescribing. Nothing is situated in the act of prescribing: for what the teeth chew is by no means the medicine. Indeed, no one sees the medicine. And because it is not seen, there is no need for a "body" for the medicine. Its corporeal form exists only so that our eyes may see it. For the incorporeal is not within our power. If death can creep in, and throttle and kill us, medicine can do the same. Nothing of importance is situated in the body, but in the virtue.

<margin>
The power of the quintessence.
</margin>
Therefore the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia." The "fifth essence" or most concentrated and purified extract of a substance, believed to contain its essential medicinal power.</note> was discovered, which indeed reduces twenty pounds to one ounce; yet that ounce far exceeds the power of the twenty pounds. Because of this, the less "body" there is, the more virtue there is in the medicine. And if visible man can reduce these twenty pounds into an ounce, the invisible ones <note>referring to spiritual or natural forces</note> can do so much more easily. If the splendor of the sun can penetrate glass, or if fire can penetrate a furnace while the body itself remains outside, the body of man can also pour out and extend its virtue widely, even while he himself remains still in his place and—just like the sun—does not penetrate. Therefore, nothing is ascribed to the body itself, but only to the forces emanating from it, just as the scent from fragrant musk remains even while its body stays in its place. In this investigation, multiple experiments have also been found regarding <term>mumia</term> itself, so that it may be said: "This part of the man is useful for this, that part for another." I shall not hand these down until I explain mumia in the <term>secret school</term>. At that place, I will share with you those things which are lacking here. For they have such deep mysteries hidden within them that an entire book would scarcely suffice for their explanation. But because it is better that they not all be revealed, so that the evils emanating from them might be avoided, it will be more appropriate to be silent about them here than to speak. With these things said, this fourth book on invisible things is concluded.

<margin>
Epilogue.
</margin>

...we wish it to be concluded. From this, you have learned how natural bodies, through their own infinite virtues, perform many miracles among the people. Because of this, the authors of these works were held as gods and worshipped by some, while by others these same works were believed to be the deeds of the Devil. # THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS
## OF HOHENHEIM, DOCTOR
### BOOK FIVE ON
### INVISIBLE THINGS.

->PREFACE TO THE READER.<-

<margin>The pursuit of medicine.</margin>
I do not doubt, indeed, that I shall be little approved by those various sects born and fashioned from their own brains, whose followers have no experience in true wisdom, nor do they hunt for the foundation of truth with any zeal. Even if they overflow with pride and self-esteem, let us set no value on them. For who would magnify the levity of those whose heart breathes only through constant arrogance? Whose praises and accusations are approved or rejected only by their own accomplices. For where does a reed grow, except in places blown through by the wind? Indeed, their rashness breaks out daily with new growth; they forge their own praise for themselves and are busy possessing what they never actually hunted for with any study. They are accustomed to moving mostly among the blind, being <term>one-eyed</term> <note>original: "lusci." A reference to the proverb "In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king."</note> themselves, so that, according to the <margin>The operation of characters.</margin> old proverb, they might rule over them. It is my purpose here, however, to hand down an account of <term>characters</term> <note>original: "characteribus." In Paracelsian thought, these are symbolic marks, seals, or celestial signatures that carry specific spiritual or natural powers.</note>—namely, by what means they operate within us. I do not do this so that I might provide a shortcut for the heralds, those declaiming from their chairs, or the itinerant quacks; but rather to inform the learned and the skilled how ineptly and injuriously those things have been explained by others for a long time. I wish to testify with what violence those things have been suppressed through ignorance—things which ought rather to have been rescued from the foul swamps. To the point of <margin>Characters are not illusions.</margin> nausea, they bark out that these things are magical, sorcerous, and illusory, though they themselves do not know even the slightest bit about them. May a curse be upon them! For they have forgotten the oath pledged to God, they have taken up another baptism, and they have brought shame upon marriage; whence now their own <margin>Basel is mentioned:</margin> virtue also fades away. Basel nourished me in its Academy, but I was accused by it as if I were offending very many people by my teaching. But how could I offend wise men, I who have rescued and liberated from scandal those who had already fallen and perished? But if even one of my own disciples should be offended by this, what could be the cause of this offense? This, to be sure: that he thinks he knows before he listens. Indeed, who anywhere does not thus offend with a scandal the one who flatters himself so much with the wisdom he already possesses? He offends himself who values himself so highly and <margin>The method of judging things.</margin> judges that which he has not understood even in a dream. But you, Reader, be one who wishes to know useful things; do not judge your faith by your own judgment, but whatever you judge, prove it according to experience. For he who esteems himself most highly will be humbled all the more easily, the more sublime he judges himself to be. For this reason, the virtues of names and words are also handed down. How these come to be is the purpose of our instruction. Here we shall also define the limits of what must be either added to or taken away from these things. Therefore, Reader, judge nothing until you have first drunk from the foundation.

# INTRODUCTION TO THIS BOOK.

Every single work that is directed toward the strengthening and lifting up of our frailty proceeds from God. For who can be found who would undertake to prop up a house about to fall, when he greatly hates its lord and owner? Our body is the sustainer of God’s soul. Its guardianship is a bodily protection. But who procures the sustenance of the body for a man more diligently than God himself? He wishes our life to be prolonged; therefore, he also provides for us with various aids and protections. Nay, even so that our life...

<meta>This page continues Book Five, moving from the preface into a discussion on how Divine Providence utilizes even our enemies and harmful nature for our benefit. It establishes the theological foundation for the medicinal use of toxic or "hostile" substances.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>BOOK V. ON THE ORIGIN</header>
<meta>catchword: would command</meta>

<margin>Safety for Christians even from enemies.</margin>
God sometimes compels even those things which are most opposed to us to defend and protect us. For salvation and fortune shall emerge from our enemies, and from the hands of those who hate us <note>This is a paraphrase of the "Benedictus" from the Gospel of Luke (1:71): "Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us."</note>. Therefore, if any good is bestowed upon us by our enemies, let us receive it as if it proceeded from God. For God drives and compels our enemies so that, whether they are willing or unwilling <note>original: "nolentes volentes"</note>, they do us good. For so the Scripture foretells it shall be: that safety and health emerge from the hands of all who wish us ill. Thus the spears of those who wish to pierce us are broken; those very lances become a medicine for us.

<margin>All good comes from God.</margin>
From wherever help is at hand for us, it is sent by God. For it is He who breathes life into our body and protects it; there is no other God besides Him. But if you should be driven headlong into a ditch and are pulled out by a robber, there is no reason for you to feel grateful to the robber; it was the command and instinct of God that drove the robber there. Do you truly think this is not the same help as if one of the twelve Apostles had rescued you? Whatever contributes to the long duration of your "house"—in which the soul lives—God has provided. He has decreed to keep you safe longer. And even if the Devil himself had performed it, He would still have produced safety out of the hands of your enemies and all those who hate you. For it is similar with the robber: to whom you would only be of use in a lonely pit. He seeks your wealth. However, he does not take it unless he first takes your life <note>The meaning here is that the robber would normally kill to steal, but God intervenes to change the outcome.</note>. Now, the fact that he both saves your life and lets you go once saved, this is divine governance. Therefore, God compels him to be a help to you. Divine providence is so concerned for us that safety emerges from everywhere. For this, thanks be to God. What is a greater source of envy to our enemy than that we resist so firmly and know that he himself pulled us out of the ditch? For this, therefore, let us praise God, not him; and let us be fully persuaded that he is compelled to do us good, and that by divine command. Let us close this discourse: safety from the hands of our enemies.

<margin>The thistle, though thorny, is yet healthy for man.</margin>
Consider the thistle among the thorns. It has such hatred toward us that it does not allow us to touch it because of its thorns. But if we have penetrated to the thistle, it pricks us with no less sharpness, lest by some chance we reach the medicine which it holds within itself. But what does God do? He commands the fire. The fire draws the medicine out of the thistle and softens its stings; it reduces the whole thing to ashes, which are afterward gathered by the Physician from the mud and filth. In this way, the evil is tamed and the good is separated. Indeed, who could hate the thistle when it provides us with so many benefits? For even if it is an enemy to the body, it is nonetheless compelled to bestow health upon it. Who can hate a woman, whatever her temperament may be? For the earth is occupied by her fruits <note>Paracelsus likely refers to the "fruit of the womb," implying the necessity of women for the continuation of humanity regardless of personality.</note>. And therefore, God prolongs her life, even if she be made of pure bitterness. Therefore, God prefigures these things so they may be an example to us, that we should judge nothing else of our enemies than that they are under the hand of God, no differently than the thistle and thorn are under the power of the fire.

<margin>The benefits of a harmful fire.</margin>
And just as fire tames these things so that they may serve us for baking bread, so God also deals with our enemies. Bread yields to our benefit and works toward the prolongation of our life, even though fire itself is also our enemy, pursues us, and desires to devour and consume whatever is cast into it. And yet, we are the ones who rule over it, and we hold it, as it were, in our hands. Therefore, good things also proceed to us from the fire. We do not desire to enjoy the hatred of the fire itself; it is enough for us to have command over it and to be able to order it to be of use and profit. And we may enjoy these benefits proceeding from it, and it is right that we give thanks to God, who safely delivered and ordained us from the power of fire, so that this same enemy of ours might cook our food to the highest delights of the palate.

<margin>Benefits of the hostile serpent.</margin>
Look at serpents. They burn with such atrocious hatred toward us that they hiss at the very first sight of a man. But what good is hidden in this enemy? A great deal. After the head and tail have been cut off, no nobler medicine is found anywhere in the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," the most purified and potent form of a substance in alchemy.</note> for <term>morphea</term> <note>A skin condition involving discolored patches, sometimes associated with leprosy in historical texts.</note> of the skin. If, therefore, God has so established this enemy that he in whom lethal poison lurks becomes safety for us, without doubt He will also drive our greatest and most capital enemy to do us good against his will. By that very deed, the enemy declares that he has God as his Lord. Nor is the Scripture empty which promises that safety and health shall be procured from our enemies and from the hands of all those who hate us. For God is faithful in all His words and works. God is so faithful toward us and all who walk according to His will that before He would abandon us, He would rather give orders to the Devil <note>The sentence concludes on the next page with "to protect us."</note>...

<vocab>God, enemy, safety, Thistle, Fire, Serpents, medicine, providence, Devil</vocab>

<summary>Paracelsus explains that God uses hostile forces—enemies, thorns, fire, and venomous snakes—to provide healing and protection for humanity. He argues that even the most "evil" things are under God's command and can be transformed into medicine through alchemical and divine processes.</summary>

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>ON INVISIBLE DISEASES.</header>
<sig>M 4</sig>

# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES

<margin>Help from the Devil himself comes from God.</margin>
...would command <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "even if the Devil himself had performed it, He would still have produced safety out of the hands of your enemy."</note>, so that He makes all things work together for our good. At the very least, God declares His power and omnipotence in this way, protecting those who love Him so that they are not harmed by their enemy, but are instead helped by him. Therefore, if we love God with all our heart, we must not doubt that if the Devil were to heap up gold and silver for us, if he were to help us, if he were to offer us medicine, or if he were to snatch us from chains and prisons, all these things would be done by divine mandate and powerful command.

There is yet one thing I wish to instruct you upon: namely, how many and how great are the remarkable benefits bestowed upon wicked people through the Devil—knowingly and undoubtedly—and this without a direct command from God, though He permits it. The Devil can easily provide these things, moved by our earnest and sinful entreaties, so that he sometimes heals great diseases, frees people from great hardships, removes them from prisons, and performs other similar feats. This happens even if there is no good whatsoever in such a person, nor any good originating from them. But why do these things happen? Doubtless, God wills that the truth of His Scripture remains: that good is provided to everyone by their enemies. Just as God extends life to a great age for those who love Him, He likewise permits the Devil to protect those of an unjust and impious life through similar entreaties; He even heals them in wondrous ways through words, names, consecrations, and so on. Therefore, both those who love God and those who cling to the Devil shall say at the last judgment: *Good things came to us from our enemies, dwelling in the elements and the abyss of hell.* For it must be admitted that Scripture is true for both the good and the bad alike, and that God is not consumed by envy or hatred for anyone, but heaps up His mercy until the final judgment.

<margin>Medicines serve the evil and the good alike.</margin>
And just as He allows winter and summer to shine upon all equally, He also allows these things to be driven by their own motion. He declares this abundantly enough in medicines, which purge and strengthen everyone in the same way—the faithful and the unfaithful, the upright and the superstitious, those who love God and those who hate Him.

Therefore, things of this sort produce neither faith nor any unbelief if God is considered according to His mercy. Does not Scripture preach about the "shaking of the celestial powers" when it says, *they shall be moved in their time*? <note>A reference to Matthew 24:29 or Luke 21:26, regarding the "powers of the heavens" being shaken.</note> What are these "celestial powers" <term>virtutes coelestes: in this context, Paracelsus refers to invisible, spiritual forces or influences that operate beyond the natural laws of the visible world</term> to be understood as here? These are surely the forces that seem to help us in an invisible and supernatural manner. Did not our chief enemy <note>The Devil</note> descend from heaven? He is therefore "celestial," not earthly. We humans, however, are not celestial but earthly. We did not descend from above, but emerged from the earth below. But if we are born again, then we too shall be moved along with the celestial powers. For what are those protections I write about here if not celestial powers? Who gives and distributes them if not God alone? He gives to the good by command, and to the wicked by permission. And in whom could this produce any superstition, since these things flow entirely and truly from this source alone? Or to whom could they be a stumbling block? Therefore, these things can offend no one, unless that person is already evil and offended within themselves. If someone is perhaps so simple-minded as to think a scandal is being set for their simplicity here, let them first learn this and search the Scriptures, as they were commanded, so that they may recognize and know every matter from its foundation. For the sake of such a person's simplicity, God will not cease His work—neither that which is done by His command, nor that which is done by the permission of the Devil.

<margin>The purpose of invisible works.</margin>
<margin>Nothing is to be ascribed to the Devil.</margin>
This must be held as a corollary for everyone: whatever happens in this way from invisible things does not happen without a manifest cause. Rather, a handle and an incentive are offered to us to investigate and weigh the true and genuine causes more deeply; these things are by no means to be ascribed to the Devil. For it is God without whom the power of the Devil is nothing. Look at the Governor <term>Praetorem: a high-ranking magistrate or judge</term> in a city, how he has his officers <term>lictores: attendants or executioners who carried out a magistrate's orders</term> who obey him and see that all his commands are finished. Who would take such an officer to be the Governor himself? No one. Therefore, that power will not be assigned to the officer, for it is the will of the Governor. You should judge these matters in the same way here. All things must be sought in God, for all things flow from Him. That which is by "permission" should be valued in the manner of a permission. But the divine will must be sought above all—namely, how either divine mercy or wrath is directed toward us. For this is the sum of the matter: we are to have help altogether, whether we are good or bad. As medicine itself testifies, its help is not the praise of the Physician, but of God. The physician has at least the "grace of the art" <note>original: "Gratiam saltem artis"</note>, but not the power of the help itself. For here, nothing is his own except the skill alone.

Therefore, all these things were said so that...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that all healing and help, even when delivered by the Devil or used by wicked people, ultimately originates from God's command or permission. He asserts that medicines and "celestial powers" function as universal tools of divine mercy that operate regardless of a person's faith or moral standing.</summary>

<page-num>140</page-num>
# BOOK 5. ON ORIGINS
<meta>catchword: pull out.</meta>

<margin>All things are to be received from God alone</margin>
Let us not value the one whom we see simply because he is the one who helps. Otherwise, thanks would have to be returned to the physician, not to God; honor would have to be returned to the grass and the hay, and to the boxes and jars of the pharmacists. That would indeed be impious and superstitious. For if we wished to proceed in this way, it would eventually lead us to look toward the devil rather than toward God. That would be enormously false and unjust. Instead, let us constantly meditate in our hearts on this: that God created medicine and placed it before our eyes so that we might seriously consider it. Therefore: if some good is bestowed upon us by the <term>characters</term> <note>These are "characteres," or specialized magical and astrological symbols often inscribed on talismans in Paracelsian medicine to channel celestial influence.</note> which I describe, then let that be the same to you as if it were hay or grass.

<margin>How one should feel regarding characters.</margin>
Even if they were of the pure devil himself, let them be to you the same as the jars of the pharmacists. Establish this solid foundation: *Salvation from our enemies, and from the hands of all those who hate us* <note>A reference to the Song of Zechariah in Luke 1:71.</note>. Think thus to yourself: God created me, God delivered me. Whatever good is bestowed upon me, whether it flows from enemies or friends, let all praise and thanks for it be given to God. In this way, all things are to be traced back to their first origin.

<margin>How great is the pride of some physicians.</margin>
Pay attention, I pray, to the proud physician. If you give thanks to God for the help provided, rather than to him, he will be greatly indignant. For he is by no means satisfied with thanks given for the art itself. But how will his pride harm you? God will not deprive you of medicine for this reason. In such a case, whatever help is brought to you, whether by spirits or other invisible means, give thanks to God for it. If one spirit or another no longer wishes to help you, let him go. When one departs, another will succeed him. Do not desert God for this reason. In all invisible things, our judgments are blind. Therefore, whatever serves to prolong our life must be received as being in God. For He strives to make Himself known to us through various works, and desires to be honored in all things, in whatever way they reach us.

All things are contained within their own order. This order proceeds from a command. Who, indeed, leaves his horse in a pit and does not <insert>pull it out</insert>, even if it is a <term>double Sabbath</term>? <note>A "double Sabbath" likely refers to a high holy day or a festival that coincides with the weekly Sabbath, increasing its religious strictness.</note> Is it not true that this permission was established by Christ, so that help might be provided? Should anyone be allowed to violate this command? Now, if it is permitted to violate the command of the Sabbath so that the death of a horse might be averted, much more can the command of God be broken for the sake of saving a human.

<margin>How healing by characters might be a sin.</margin>
Understand the matter this way. The command states that you should not despise the physician, nor the medicine itself. It is added that these are produced from the earth. But suppose it is the Sabbath, and you heal your neighbor with characters, which—strictly speaking—are not born from the earth with their own powers; in this, you have violated the Sabbath. For you are not precisely following the command. Yet, this violation extends no further than if you had saved a horse on the Sabbath day. You performed a work of assistance and brought the help that your art taught you. Regarding the help itself, there is no sin. For it did not come from you, but from God. The Art itself might be regarded as a violation of the Sabbath, yet it was established and granted by the words of Christ when He used the example of pulling a horse out of a pit.

<margin>David eating the consecrated bread.</margin>
Direct your mind also to this: that David entered the temple with his companions and ate those loaves which it was a religious duty not to eat <note>The "Showbread" or Bread of the Presence, reserved for priests (1 Samuel 21).</note>. But in a time of hunger, he ate under the pressure of necessity, and he ate without sin. Therefore, necessity has an excuse in Scripture.

<margin>Necessity excuses.</margin>
It is right for necessity to be averted by whatever is at hand, whether it be the Devil, a Spirit, a Physician, a thief, or whatever else is present. Now, truly, there was much more significance in those loaves which David ate with his people than there is here in the Art. One must be covered by the response of the other. For there are commands that must be kept by everyone. But Christ Himself shows us this limitation: that it is permitted for us to avert the danger of a beast. Therefore, much more a human. Because it was permitted for David to eat the loaves to curb his hunger, they were no longer what they were before, when they were in the sole power of the priests.

<margin>How the Devil's help becomes ours.</margin>
The same reasoning applies to the Art. Suppose the Art is entirely of the Devil. If that Art is placed in my hand, the help is also in my hand. Thus, it is no longer the Devil’s, but mine. Then at last I can bring help to the sick and give thanks to God.

For this reason, I take it upon myself to explain what those things are which are called "magical," and are defamed by other similar names. It is certain that a command has been given to us that we should bring help and assistance to one another. Would it be impious if I said to the Devil standing before me: "Go and pull the horse out of the ditch in my name"?

<summary>This page argues that healing is a divine gift that transcends religious law (like the Sabbath) and the source of the cure (even if magical or demonic), using the biblical examples of David and Christ's teachings to justify "necessity" in medicine.</summary>

<page-num>141</page-num>
# ON INVISIBLE DISEASES
<header>ON INVISIBLE DISEASES</header>

<margin>When the help of the Devil occurs.</margin>
...pull out. <note>original: "extrahe"; this completes the thought from the previous page about pulling a horse from a pit on the Sabbath.</note> If that should happen, who could rightly accuse me of the law of superstition? Indeed, let my faith rather be judged as proven by this: that I dare to command such things of the Devil or another spirit. But if he were to pull a horse out of one pit and cast it into another, only then could I be called superstitious, for that is the kind of superstition that returns a profit or reward to him. For here you should attend to a singular point concerning alliances: if the Devil brings someone to the point of beginning such matters with superstition—as will be said later regarding ceremonies and other things—then it is truly the case that both the help and the art hang from his hand, and he who could have been the rightful master has become a servant. 

<margin>The devil is the servant of all the faithful.</margin>
For it is fitting that the Devil obeys every faithful person. If he is able to perform a task, what harm is there in trying it? However, these men seek the praise and honor of the Devil, not of God. And here lies the trick and the deception of the <term>art</term> <note>In this context, "art" refers to alchemy, magic, or the specific "spagyric" medicine practiced by Paracelsus.</note>. For the Devil does not have the power over this art that he has over the ceremonial arts which others use. Therefore, if this art is employed as it is in itself, it is not a violation of the commandment. Nor will it be the property of the Devil; rather, like just plunder, it is taken away from him, just as the children of Israel captured many things. For gold and silver cannot be taken from him by his permission, but must be snatched from his back and from any spirit that possesses them. For he follows us with wide-open jaws, seeking whether he can extort his own plunder back from us.

<margin>The purpose of the arts. Mary Magdalene.</margin>
Whatever we are capable of in the arts ought to be spent for the praise and honor of God, in this way: that it matches the deed of Mary Magdalene, who poured precious ointment on the head of Christ. According to human understanding, that ointment could have been spent far more conveniently and usefully than being poured out in such a way. Yet Christ gave testimony for her, saying that *she has done a good work*. Therefore, even if we do not always act according to human intellect, if we walk in true charity with these matters, we shall obtain the same excuse alongside the pouring out of this ointment. Is it against the divine command to help? Not at all. Yet to reconcile with the Devil and superstitions is contrary to the divine word. Even if we were to heal men through false gods, it would still be a wicked thing. For we see that this produces false signs. And truly, false signs arise from false gods.

<margin>Where the error regarding "characters" comes from.</margin>
However, the source of <term>characters</term> <note>These are "characteres," specialized symbols or sigils used in Paracelsian medicine to focus celestial or natural influences.</note> does not come from false gods, nor does it have anything of superstition in itself. Although it is true that all superstitious signs proceed from natural forces, those forces should rightly be ascribed to the honor of God. The power of the "light of nature" <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lumen Naturae) is a central concept for Paracelsus, referring to the innate wisdom and healing power placed by God within the physical world, discoverable through observation and experience.</note> should be revealed, and superstition relegated back to its own place. For even if superstition is cast aside, nothing is taken away from those natural forces. They never belonged to the false gods; it is as if someone were walking around in borrowed clothes. 

Nevertheless, I declare that not all things have been commanded to the human condition. Indeed, various sects that cloak themselves under the name of Christ constrain the Gospel with such tight nets that, if Christ had not proposed the example of the horse in the pit, it would be legal for no one to eat or drink on the Sabbath. Instead, it would be necessary either to observe the Sabbath by worshipping all things in heaven and hell through religion, or to have no clear understanding of the Sabbath at all. Therefore, this narrow way of thinking should be cast far away, as it is not consistent with Scripture. For in this way, they would eventually justify Judas and condemn Christ, just as the <term>Anabaptist</term> <note>A radical reformist sect that Paracelsus often criticized for what he saw as their extreme and literalist interpretations of scripture.</note> sectarians have done for the most part. 

<margin>Anabaptists resist.</margin>
Thus, a matter should not be judged as "magic" simply because it cannot be understood by a dull and foolish intellect. 

<margin>Something is not "Magic" just because it is not understood.</margin>
Nor should we flatter the devil by offering him that honor. For what affects him more sweetly in all superstitions than if glory is given to him as if he were the author? We must seek out various things everywhere so that we may experience various wonders and learn the secrets of God in manifold things. It would have been enough for us if He had commanded us to obtain health through fasting and prayers. But He did not wish this; instead, He established other means for us to investigate, and He allows us to wander the earth so that we may learn many things in it. And when we have tested all things, we must retain what is good. It is right for us to remember these things and constantly turn them over in our minds. For it is necessary that both good and evil come forth. If we bring them out and distinguish them from one another, we shall retain the good and omit the evil. 

<margin>The arts of the devil are to be learned, but he himself is to be omitted.</margin>
What else is indicated to us here but that we should, if we can, learn all the arts of the devil? Let us use the arts, but omit the devil. We are permitted to learn all arts; all things are given to be tested so that what is good may be kept. For we were born onto the earth so that the lesser might learn from the greater. For God endowed the devil with many arts...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that physicians should utilize the "Light of Nature" and various "arts"—including symbols and sigils—for healing, asserting that these powers belong to God rather than the Devil. He emphasizes that the "arts" themselves are neutral tools that should be reclaimed from superstition and used for the praise of God, much like the plunder taken by the Israelites.</summary>

Paracelsus is expanding his argument that the power behind healing and natural wonders—even when mirrored by the Devil or pagan magicians—ultimately resides in the "Light of Nature" granted by God.</meta>

<page-num>142</page-num>
# BOOK V: ON THE ORIGIN
<header>BOOK V: ON THE ORIGIN</header>

<margin>The Devil is much more learned than men.</margin>
...elevated us higher to the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lumen Naturae) is a central Paracelsian concept: it is the intuitive and observable knowledge of the physical world that God allows humans to discover through experience and science, distinct from spiritual revelation.</note>. If we truly understood these things, we would never offend God. And although our arts are not identical to yours, many are nevertheless related to you. <margin>Words act even as herbs.</margin> For if one uses a word instead of a herb, that word functions as the herb. Yet let no one suppose that words of this kind are devils. They are his own <term>species</term> <note>Here, "species" refers to the outward forms or manifestations of natural forces.</note>; and <term>characters</term> <note>Written symbols or sigils believed to hold natural or celestial power.</note> are his compounds and syrups. Such things are born in those regions where he himself acts, about which more must be said.

<margin>Moses creates serpents.</margin>
We must carefully attend to what the Scripture says concerning Moses: *how by divine command he performed great miracles before King Pharaoh throughout his entire kingdom.* From a cast-down rod, a serpent was born. The magicians, daring the same, performed similarly, and no less skillfully than Moses himself. And although Scripture strikes these men with harsher names, nothing truly resides in the names themselves.

<margin>Pharaoh’s magicians did not simply offend God.</margin>
For the art itself knows how to declare names differently. But what happened? When the magicians had produced many serpents, then Aaron’s serpent devoured all the others. Why? Clearly, God claimed dominion here for himself alone, nor did he suffer anything to be introduced into his power by human arts—even though he initially turned a blind eye to it. What else does this signify but that, in respect to God, our entire world is as nothing? It shows that we are not truly masters of any art on this earth, but are always compelled to wait and see what God permits us or refuses us. 

In this way, many other signs were subsequently manifested before Pharaoh, all of which the magicians emulated equally. These men performed such things through art. Moses and Aaron, however, acted without art <note>Paracelsus distinguishes between "art" (human technique/alchemy) and "miracle" (direct divine intervention), though both operate on natural substances.</note>. The matter stands in exactly the same way with those sick people who were healed by Christ and his Apostles; physicians, emulating this very thing, have also healed many thousands of the sick. To attach the name of <term>Venefici</term> <note>original: "Veneficorum." Historically meaning "poisoners" or "sorcerers." Paracelsus is defending his unconventional medical practices against accusations of witchcraft.</note> to them for this reason seems quite unjust. For that art proceeded from the light of nature. A similar art existed even among those Egyptians, which has not yet been extinguished in the light of nature. 

For if nature has such power that it can make copper from iron, and can create gems from liquids, it can certainly do much more according to its greatest secrets. Therefore, those magicians by no means offended God by their art itself, but rather by the wickedness and recklessness of their daring, done as an insult to Moses and Aaron. For they seemed to be saying: "What are these two men saying, that they were commanded by God? They do this by art, just as we do." See the evidence of this here. Therefore, their art vanished so that Moses and Aaron might be revealed. 

Does not the Scripture itself testify that God says: "Am I not he who made the mute, and the deaf, and the blind, and those who see?" What else is this saying but that he is the creator of all things? If we are born deaf and mute, shall we remain so for that reason? He is the one who teaches us to speak. For how could infants learn to speak by their own strength if God did not wonderfully contribute his help? Now, if we are able to speak and hear, we possess the instruments for knowing divine works, at least as far as God permits us. For what use is it for someone to see, if they are ignorant of what they see? What is the end for which man was created, if not to learn and experience both evil and good, but to retain only the good? If we hold no experience of these things, then we have discovered nothing concerning God. 

Or is it truly an ornament to a man if he knows nothing? <margin>An ignorant man is of no value.</margin> No man of skill ever remained in deceptions, nor has anyone ever seen such a man polluted by superstitions. For where do superstitions flourish, if not among the ignorant and unskilled? Where does pride dominate, if not among the unlearned? <margin>A rebuke of physicians.</margin> Where does folly reign, if not among those who, standing firm in their own "wisdom," neglect to investigate the wisdom of God further? 

Therefore, if any art is eventually brought into the open which they cannot grasp with their beet-like and spongy brains, they immediately cry out that it is "magical" and "superstitious." They use this "art" and this foundation simply so that their folly does not become public, and so they themselves—the "supreme masters"—are not exposed as frauds. Therefore, it is right for everyone to know that any help flows from God. <margin>All help is from God.</margin> It is not possible for the Devil, nor a magician, to provide it on their own. And even if this cannot be grasped by human reason, it does not conflict with Scripture. In what way each thing happens, and what abuses are committed here, must also be passed down: to this end, that we may know the means delivered by God—through which we work and obtain such things—from their very foundation. For if someone led a person wandering from the path back onto their way, would they not be restored to a sufficiently right goal? Surely those who know and are able to perform these works are doing [God's] work.

<margin>We are born naked and without arts.</margin>
Because we humans are born naked into this world, and we bring neither arts nor wisdom with us, fixing our hope on the grace of God alone: therefore He himself provides...

<meta>catchword: provides</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the "arts" used in healing and transformation are natural gifts from God, using the biblical contest between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians to show that while human art is secondary to divine power, it is not inherently evil. He rebukes ignorant physicians who label effective but misunderstood natural arts as "superstition" to hide their own lack of skill.</summary>
