He is now explaining that while humans appear to learn skills from their environment, the true source of all "arts" (sciences, crafts, and medical knowledge) is God, who operates through spiritual intermediaries.</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>
# OF INVISIBLE DISEASES
<header>OF INVISIBLE DISEASES</header>

<margin>God alone is our teacher.</margin>
God provides for us, yet He grants nothing to us out of His own motion except for life itself. As for all other matters, whether we are made healthy or infirm, He commits all of that to Nature itself. He commands parents to teach us to speak. Furthermore, as we grow, we are compelled to learn everything with great labor, and we do not produce even the smallest <term>art</term> <note>In the 16th century, an "art" referred to any skilled craft, science, or branch of knowledge, such as medicine, metallurgy, or music.</note> from within ourselves. Therefore, if we must learn everything, it is necessary that the thing which teaches us humans must not be human itself. For man is, from the very beginning, unrefined and ignorant. Thus, for those who wish to learn, the first foundation must be placed in God; He alone must be established and recognized as our God, who both teaches and provides whatever serves our needs.

<margin>After creation, man receives all things through a medium.</margin>
And if we wish to examine all things, we will surely understand that all things have been brought about through a certain <term>medium</term> <note>An "intermediary" or "middle-man" through which power or knowledge flows.</note> ever since the creation was finished by God. For instance, when God the Father created heaven and earth, He created them to be intermediaries from which that which our body must master would flow to us. In this way, man was made the master of medicine, the master of fields, meadows, and vineyards: not because he received this from the earth or the Sun itself, but because God, according to the orchestration of these intermediaries, bestowed those things. For so it pleased Him. In like manner, we do not possess the knowledge of the arts from within ourselves, but we have these also through some medium.

<margin>Spirits are also a medium by which one is instructed.</margin>
This medium consists of the **invisible spirits**: just as a field brings forth its own fruits, so these spirits give the arts out of themselves. And regarding these intermediaries—whether they reach us as Angels or others so appointed by God—it is no different than when the Angel, saluting Mary, rendered her "full of <term>Grace</term>" <note>original: *Gratia*. A reference to the Annunciation (Luke 1:28). Paracelsus compares the inspiration of a scientist or artist to a divine message delivered by an angel.</note>. In this way, gifts are communicated to us in secret: and let each person diligently guard the gift attributed to them by God—this person one gift, that person another—and hold it as an "angelic salutation," which is one and the same as that gift.

<margin>All arts are more perfect in the spirits.</margin>
Now then, how could we either cultivate the earth or, as was said, rule over it, if we did not have a certain light that was above man to teach us? Moreover, all arts are indeed perfect within the spirits, whether they be good or evil. From those spirits, the arts descend to us. For they, like an intermediary, confer those arts upon us (just as the Sun confers summer and brightness), so that we may know something on this earth. For from ourselves, we know nothing. Therefore, if it is necessary for the knowledge of the arts to be transferred entirely from them to us, it is necessary that we have a certain <term>affection</term> <note>A natural inclination or "attraction" toward a specific subject or craft.</note> toward them.

<margin>One must learn from spirits, both evil and good.</margin>
This disposition must reside in God, without any other intermediary. From here, the commands of God later go forth: *“You, Angel, or spirit, teach this man this thing, and that man that thing, so that he may have this endowment from you.”* From this it follows that we are "called" and driven by this affection, one toward this thing, another toward that. Thus, thereafter, the command is carried out and given through the angel or spirit: the power of learning that which we desire is conferred upon us. And if we do not persist in this path—even if we were to occupy ourselves with our own fantasies until we went mad—we would not even learn how to melt raw lead. Therefore, God fashions and makes us such as it has pleased Him for us to be. To one man He suggested the **invention of printing**; another He taught the **craft of smiths**; to another He imparted the **art of Music**, and so consequently He bestowed on each person something peculiar that would serve human uses. And in establishing all these things, He employed such an order that now, after the first inventors, others might continually teach the same things to others. And so, that which is impossible for a man to learn from himself, he draws and attains from others in the prescribed order. Just as Mary, from the salutation spoken to her, became immediately full of grace: so also are gifts distributed among us in the same way. And whatever we find anywhere, it all flows from this principle. Therefore, let no one be concerned through which intermediaries these things are derived to us; but rather let there be a firm persuasion that from wherever they are suggested to us—whether by evil or good spirits—they do so because they are compelled by the express command of God. For God wills all things to obey Him, and He wills His majesty and omnipotence to shine forth no less in hell than in the heavens. The same God also wills and commands this: that whatever dwells in either the heavens or hell should serve and comply with us, His chosen ones.

<margin>Demons have nothing of themselves.</margin>
Now truly, since both the good and evil spirits are all **creatures**, that which they are capable of will also be a "created" thing. Thus, they have nothing of themselves; but rather all things, whatever they may be, are from God. These things being so established, which man, and by what right, shall say that he learns from the Devil, since the Devil is not God? No one can help but confess that not even the smallest bird flies on the earth unless it is sent by God; and thus not even a lowly nettle springs up unless it happens by the express command of God. If it displeased God for us to enjoy it, He would surely cut it off in a single moment. Now, because He does not cut it off, it is clearer than light from this fact, that...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that all human knowledge and skills are divine gifts mediated by invisible spirits (angels or otherwise). He emphasizes that humans are born ignorant and can only learn through God's ordained "Light of Nature," which even utilizes "evil" spirits to fulfill God's will.</summary>

man.

He does not hate us, but out of divine faithfulness favors us greatly. Furthermore, what evil is there in these <term>arts</term>? <note>Referring to the sciences and crafts discussed on the previous page.</note> Nothing indeed, except what we ourselves corrupt. To pray and to fast is indeed good. For through this, Satan is expelled. Likewise, it is good to knock and to ask. Thus all things are good for us and suitable to be employed for our benefit; but it is by no means good if we pray and fast like the <term>austere</term>, <note>original: *Tetrici*; Paracelsus likely refers to the "gloomy" hypocrites mentioned in Matthew 6:16.</note> that is, that our face must be washed in such a way as if we were ignorant of the fact that the heart, and not the mouth, must be moved. From this it follows that fasting and prayers turn into evil for them. Not because fasting and praying are evil in themselves, but because that which is added to them is evil. From this, conclude that *God confers such gifts upon us through a greeting, namely to each according to his vocation.* For since we ourselves are anxious for these same things, the matter must not be conducted in an austere way—that is, there is no need for ceremonies. For it would be wicked if, having obtained such good things, we were unwilling to turn to God from ourselves without a <term>medium</term>. <note>An intermediary or ritualistic "middle-man."</note> Our affairs collapse, however, because we attempt to obtain good things

Nor should any ceremonies be employed either before or after, but we should follow precisely in the footsteps of Mary. For if she did not err, neither shall we err if we follow her as a proven leader; all other ways are erroneous and doubtful.

But while we speak of ceremonies, it

Therefore, let the same depart from us in the same way. But if we pollute the gift of God by employing ceremonies, we are driven headlong into pride, which God seriously hates. While we speak of ceremonies, we wish all to be understood in the same sense. For they are the cause of the invented name of "superstition," with which we are accustomed to be burdened. But we will show you some examples. From Christ, a doctrine and order have been handed down to us, to which we are permitted neither to add nor to take away anything. This pertains to every single human being.

Now, as much as he has the power to distribute, so much he pays out. That payment is in the hands of God, ratified only so far as the divine will allows. For if anything needs to be obtained from God, He will certainly fix His eyes on the heart, not on ceremonies. And whatever He has bestowed upon us, He by no means wants it spent on ceremonies, but on labors. For He bestows nothing else but that by which we may love God with all our heart, with all our strength, and with our whole soul; and by which we may also help our neighbor as ourselves. If, therefore, what God imparts to us is to be spent on this, then all ceremonies rightly fade away. Now, just as ceremonies have prevailed in all things and corrupted their own power, so they have also contaminated the <term>magical art</term>; <note>For Paracelsus, "magic" was the study of the hidden forces of nature and the "Light of Nature," which he believed should be practiced through faith, not ritual.</note> that is, the subject I am now treating has long since been reduced to such a state that without ceremonies it seems to be of no further consequence. For by the same reasoning as we deal with God without the manifestation of the heart, so also must we act in this art. For we are all capable of the same power, and no one is inferior to another. But that this power proceeds less effectively is due to the author, Satan, who strives for this one thing: that we do not use the power given by chance without first employing ceremonies.

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s critique of religious and magical rituals. While the previous page established that all gifts come from God without the need for intermediaries, this page explains how Satan used "ceremonies" to distract people from God and lead them toward the worship of servants—both spiritual and human.</meta>

-># ON INVISIBLE DISEASES<-

<margin>
Why Satan introduced ceremonies.
</margin>
What, then, are the ceremonies of those <term>arts</term> <note>Referring to magical or ritualistic practices.</note> after all? They are hypocritical fasts and feigned prayers. Just as the Pharisees used to deceive the eyes of the people with their pretenses, so here too the Devil mimics and introduces that Pharisaic ritual through numbers, specific times, abstinence, consecrations, blessings, holy water, and other similar things. Through these tricks, Satan has instilled a belief in the hearts of men, leading them to believe that anyone who intends to obtain anything from God must forget God himself and instead use these ceremonies entirely. They believe that only in this way can a successful outcome be hoped for. Now, as for what place these things should hold, let the theologians judge. For just as men interact among themselves by abusing their own power, so too is the situation with those aforementioned spirits.

<margin>
What ceremonies consist of.
</margin>
I would not want anything to be said too harshly here regarding the <term>power of Peter</term>. <note>A reference to the "Power of the Keys"—the authority to bind and loose—traditionally attributed to St. Peter and the Church hierarchy.</note> I only advise this: that each person should nourish and cherish a calm and peaceful heart within themselves. The reason I bring these matters forward is that <term>characters</term> <note>Magical signs, sigils, or astrological symbols.</note> are neither words nor names. However, those who follow ceremonies have confused them with words and names, specifically so that respect would be given to the spirits—as if nothing could succeed without imploring them. This is the same as if they were to say: unless you flatter Peter, you will have no standing for grace before God.

<margin>
Both Peter and spirits are servants of God.
</margin>
<margin>
Whom ceremonies concern.
</margin>
Yet since it is certain that Peter and the spirits are servants of God—who are compelled to carry out whatever is commanded by God—it follows by every reason that if Christ commands Peter to loose something, he is forced to do it. Conversely, if He commands him to bind, the same applies. And if he does so, this work is ratified in heaven and on earth. For such is his office, and his ministry is inclined toward all of God’s commands. Now, even if we were to treat Peter as a God, he would not agree to this unless he were specifically commanded by God first. Know therefore that ceremonies are aimed only at Peter. They behave similarly toward the spirits; they are directed so that the One who is meant to command is erased by forgetfulness, and His servants, whose job it is to minister, are substituted in His place. In whatever way such a household is governed, when the Lord is absent, **the cats play with the mice**; <note>original: *cati cum muribus ludunt*; a variation of the proverb "while the cat's away, the mice will play," here implying that the spirits act out when the true Master (God) is ignored.</note> the servants do whatever and however much they please. Because of this abuse, the art itself should by no means be held in contempt; rather, the superstition lies in the fact that the art is expended upon the servants. And this is evident from the art itself, which in this case is so mangled that by itself it can neither help nor provide any counsel. Such "housekeeping" spreads in all homes if the Master is away for a long time. The servants, lusting after power, are forced to devise various things to veil their own recklessness. But since these servants do not have the same power and strength as their Master, and yet are implored for help and urged to produce signs, they must seek various excuses and diversions, such as: "you did not fast or pray correctly," or "you did not confess properly." "This is why you suffered that loss," etc. Thus the followers of ceremonies are handled and "seasoned" with that **tasteless salt** <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 5:13; salt that has lost its flavor and is fit only to be trampled.</note> which is useful for nothing except to be thrown into the mud.

<margin>
How God sometimes overlooks ceremonies.
</margin>
Now, because faith or trust works in this way upon the servants, many results often follow—that is, even if the matter only concerns the servants, many things still have successful outcomes. But when faith and power are cast upon one who has no mandate to provide help, God acts as a just judge; He employs various means and takes many things into account through His instrument, overlooking many things—not indeed out of respect for the servant, but out of respect for the man himself. And this is the most powerful reason why God confirms the faith of a <term>transgressor</term>. <note>Here, one who uses the "wrong" ritualistic methods but still has sincere faith.</note> For He is a free agent. Let no one fall into temptation; let no one look for help from elsewhere. All things must be asked for and obtained from God. Whatever He then commands His **Divine ones** <note>original: *Diuis*; referring to the saints or celestial spirits.</note> to do, let that be done and be welcome, whether it is provided by this one or that one, by a spirit, an angel, or a devil. For in this way, even the spirits are commanded to teach and to help, so that benefits might overflow to us from enemies as well as friends.

<margin>
Spirits promulgated the arts.
</margin>
<margin>
The Divine ones are powerless if God refuses.
</margin>
<margin>
Solomon's mirror and Moses's book of the consecration of numbers.
</margin>
It is manifest by the light of nature that the spirits gave these arts to the public. Once this was accepted as fact by everyone, people began to invoke the spirits themselves, as if they came to help of their own accord and by their own will; they did not consider that the spirits do such things only because they are compelled by divine command. Then, from the institution and magical teachings of the Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians, the distinct names of these spirits were published, whom the superstitious worshipped and honored as gods. However, if anyone demands much from the Divine ones, they can provide nothing if God does not nod His head. For they are mere servants. Thus, having preserved these names, even when the spirits could not bring help, men began to play along with the spirits and established peculiar ceremonies in fasting, praying, and other similar things—just as there is the **Mirror of Solomon** and **Moses's Book of the Consecration of Numbers**. <note>These were famous Renaissance grimoires (books of magic) falsely attributed to the biblical Solomon and Moses.</note>

...they finished. This thereafter grew stronger and stronger every day: since they were clearly persuaded that they would obtain something certain through institutions of that kind. However, they achieved nothing other than empty nettles and other ravings: such as all the works of servants are, with whom the Lord has no business. 

<margin>Visible and invisible Popes. Our faith is no longer in our own hand.</margin>
And so recognize the Popes, both invisible and visible <note>Paracelsus likely refers here to both the earthly hierarchy of the Church and spiritual entities or "masters" who claim authority over the soul.</note>, who sell themselves as lords, not servants, and consider how much any priesthood should be valued.

Now, this is the condition and nature of faith: that once released from our hands, it is no longer in our power. Then those things happen which we mentioned. But furthermore, its powers are to be reviewed, and they are various. 

<margin>Types of faith.</margin>
For men say: "This man, through a blessing, knows how to be wounded so that he cannot be struck or pierced by anyone"; "That one can walk across a sharp sword"; "Another knows how to protect himself from a musket ball," and so on. This is one way. The second is this: one can cure this or that disease by consecrating <note>Performing a ritual blessing or making an object "holy" to effect a cure.</note>, such as **inflammations, arthritis, hemorrhages, fevers, etc.** And so thirdly: one can compel this or that herb through incantation to do this or that; likewise, this man knows how to reconcile or dissolve love. How these relate to these four types will be explained hereafter. First of all, however, it must be held that many wicked superstitions converge in these things, brought and introduced by the ancients, and especially by desperate scoundrels, who mixed in many things less Christian and religious—certainly not without the impulse and suggestion of the Devil himself—which could not be recounted here without causing offense. 

<margin>Mount Venus.</margin>
One thing, however, of ancient origin is about the so-called **Mount Venus** <note>original: "mons Veneris"; refers to the Venusberg of German folklore, a subterranean kingdom of sensuality and magic.</note>: from which they boast they have taken away <term>characters</term> <note>Magical signs or sigils believed to hold power.</note> of this sort. This is not entirely false in every respect. For just as witches meeting on the 

<margin>Bructerus.</margin>
**Bructerus** <note>The Brocken, the highest peak in the Harz Mountains, legendary site of the Witches' Sabbath.</note> set up their intercourse and assemblies, and obtain and learn from demons their arts which they then practice; so equally for their men, Mount Bructerus is their own, which they also call "Venusian" (nor yet is that the Mount of Venus about which a certain kind of species is shown in that type of game called ***Karnöffel*** <note>A 15th-century card game often used as a metaphor for social or religious disorder.</note> by the Germans); in it they also meet similarly, and the Devil subjects himself to them in the form of a woman, and teaches them those characters with these usual ceremonies. What powers these have and where they emanate from will be explained later. In these matters, however, no one should place any trust. For this is not the foundation of that art, 

---

but they are mere indulgences, sought without any virtue or efficacy. Many such adulterated and "Venusian" ravings have been spread by fanatics and tricksters.

But to weigh and reveal this power: do you think, I ask, that Satan can, by all his power, prevent and turn aside the possibility of me being either wounded or pierced through? 

<margin>The devil cannot prevent piercing. The weakness of the devil.</margin>
This can by no means happen. God alone and unique has this power. Such is the weakness and impotence of the Devil that he cannot even mold an unbreakable pot, let alone say anything about a man. Indeed, he cannot even pull a loose tooth; I say nothing of him being able to cure a more serious disease. Nor can he make any little herb other than what it is, or add or take away anything from it. So he cannot join two people together, much less reconcile them with love or hatred. 

<margin>Formulas of superstitions.</margin>
Concerning these four articles, observe the four ways. The first of them, concerning wounds and blows, is such: He who saved **St. Lawrence** <note>original: "D. Laurentium"</note> from being burned on the iron grate; He who protected **St. John** in the oil from burning; He who pulled the three boys safe and unscorched from the glowing furnace—He knows this art and imparts it to those He favors. If this is imparted to him who uses characters: then it is a sign and testimony of an invitation to the final judgment of God: where it will be for the divine sentence to pronounce for what cause He established and confirmed their superstition. By such characters, who but God alone could know how to cure diseases? He can command the spirits to be like herbs and act similarly with them. But why God permits these things in this way lies within His own judgment. Spirits can by no means perform such things by themselves, whether God permits or commands it. Indeed, if they conjure herbs, they do not instill any other power in them than what was there before. If these are sometimes more or of greater efficacy than their natural measure, it should be 

<margin>Why incantations actually happen.</margin>
attributed to the previous articles. Therefore, it should be known that such added virtues of medicines come at least as a covering for them. And by the power of characters, to establish either friendships or enmities is a work of the imagination. For it is a patched-up art: which snatches scraps from all arts and sews one "patchwork coat" <note>original: "centonem"; a metaphor for a work compiled from various sources, like a quilt of scraps.</note> from them. Whether it be more or less, 

<margin>The art of characters is a collection.</margin>
everything is born from the collections of the said things, as this book will hand down. And it is right for every single person to remember these things.

# OF INVISIBLE DISEASES

...anyone, before he degenerates from his true origin and fails in the middle, as has been declared.

<margin>Spirits can do whatever the body can do.</margin>
This is certainly most true, if the power of nature is to be explained to its fullest extent: that invisible spirits can accomplish everything that the visible body can. For if the visible body knows how to fashion for its own protection a breastplate <note>original: *lorica*; a piece of armor</note> against any blows—under which the visible and invisible body may lie hidden and protected—by the same pressing necessity, the invisible body can also make an invisible breastplate for itself. By this, it may protect and defend itself as an invisible body, and the visible one along with it. For this is clear from the light of nature. In the same way, the invisible body can also take away diseases from the visible one, and inflict other similar ones upon it by the same effort—evidently so that honor for these wonders <note>original: *magnalia*; great or miraculous works</note> may be ascribed to another greater being. For in this way it measures where there is no fate; in this way, that which was not deposited is found. For if malignant spirits are able to prepare such prey for themselves, they do not hesitate. And when they perceive the frivolity of such men, they silently thrust themselves in as companions. Finally, whatever they provide for us, whether they teach us arts or bring help: consider all those things in this context as if they flow from a divine command, and not merely from permission.

<margin>Trust in God must be effectual.</margin>
Indeed, our trust in the majesty of God must be so firm and solid that we do not fall away from it even the slightest bit in any distress, but must perpetually cling to Him. Since, therefore, these spirits are very often "Teachers of Arts," who frequently thrust themselves in under the appearance of some command to teach difficult and subtle matters, or secret sciences in all arts, or to confer great reputation, abundant eloquence, and profound wisdom: therefore, those who wallow in sins, yet nevertheless wish to be held as genuine Apostles, should watch themselves carefully. These people are easily forced into this school. But those who dare to put their own spirit before the Holy Spirit: their study and purpose is to shatter that which can be shattered by no reason. From this, one can perceive the stubbornness of those heads in defending their own views: they who establish, defend, and magnify those articles of faith which the Apostles nevertheless received and believed with a simple sense: such as the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>A radical Reformation group practicing adult baptism, often viewed as social and religious subversives in this period.</note>, <term>Bohemians</term> <note>Followers of the Hussite movement or the Moravian Brethren in the Czech lands.</note>, and <term>Trinitarians</term> <note>Likely referring here to Anti-Trinitarians or those who overly intellectualized the mystery of the Trinity.</note>. And with these things said so far, let it be enough to have explained what should be thought concerning <term>characters</term> <note>original: *characteribus*; magical or astrological signs used in talismans and healing.</note>: with which it seemed convenient to end the fifth book.

***

->TO THE READER.<-

*Even though, benevolent Reader, this following book **On the Generation of Man** would be more conveniently joined with the Philosophical books—since it does not treat the **Origin of Diseases** in the same way and manner as the other books of this first part—it nevertheless seemed not ill-advised to subjoin it to this work, the **Paramirum**. This is because the other Philosophical books to which it should have been added are not at hand at this time, and are rather missed. Furthermore, the material itself which the author treats here pertains principally to Medical matters. For it explains the generation of the physical body, which is the immediate subject of medicine.*

*Furthermore, the benevolent Reader must be warned again that this book also (like the first **Paramirum** on the **Five Entities**) was not completed by the author: but that he ceased writing in the middle of a page next to the title, **On the Interior Man**. This is known from Paracelsus's own autograph manuscript, which the aforementioned Dr. Johannes Homelius the younger, Physician at Ptuj <note>original: *Pettauii*; a town in modern-day Slovenia.</note> in Styria, still keeps with him along with the **Paramirum** on the **Five Entities**. Moreover, the remaining three books, which Paracelsus mentions in the fourth preface (namely, on the human-like creatures living in the Elements of water, earth, and fire), were not found with him. It could easily be that they were never written by the author according to this arrangement and division. Because, however, he compiled and published a private Philosophical book elsewhere on **Nymphs, Pygmies, Salamanders, etc.**, the diligent reader can repair what is missing here from that work, and be satisfied with this.*

-># THE BOOK ON THE GENERATION<-
->## OF SENSIBLE THINGS IN REASON:<-
->## BY THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS THE GERMAN.<-

->## THE FIRST BOOK OF THE PREFACES OF THEOPHRASTUS TO THE GERMAN BOOK.<-

->### THE FIRST PREFACE OF THEOPHRASTUS.<-

<margin>The ancients are rebuked.</margin>
**W**e must diligently consider, above all else, which commentaries and bewitching philosophical books—written by those who profess themselves to be worldly gods—are currently in the public eye, and what objections may be raised and brought from them against our following text. For although those authors appear quite ridiculous to us, and we accept them only with a grain of derision, nevertheless, because they were compiled with the greatest labor and born of sharp judgment, it pleases us to subject them to our consideration and to respond to the authors themselves as is due. First, however, we are moved by a just calling out of our predecessors in Philosophy who, with laborious effort, described the **Generation of man**. Even if the Light of Nature <note>The "Light of Nature" (*Lumen Naturae*) is a core Paracelsian concept referring to the innate wisdom and divine intelligence present within the natural world, accessible through observation rather than just scripture.</note> denied them nothing, it seems that she also granted them nothing. For whatever they handed down did not (as our Philosophy does) spring from the light of reason, but rather from the subtleties of that interior sense which we have conceived from within ourselves. To these, we offer this response: they wrote only from their own brains, and not from experience or ocular <note>visible or firsthand</note> knowledge.

<margin>Without experience, nothing is worthy of the light.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle is censured.</margin>
For experience and science alone are worthy of bringing anything into the light—not "autodoxia" <term>autodoxia: a Greek-derived term for self-styled opinion or unfounded personal belief</term> and presumed experience. The sharp fantasist Aristotle left behind many monuments concerning **Generation**. He, however, was wretchedly misled in nature itself and remained wonderfully ignorant of natural Philosophy. Yet he was sharp in his erroneous opinions that strike against nature; he established his sentiment with quite plausible momentum, confirmed it with prudent reasons, and illustrated it with artistic and pleasant sentences. If all these things were exactly as they are in nature, just as his flattering words suppose, who would ever desire a clearer light in nature? So too his other followers, interpreters, and disciples have striven for the same sharpness and subtlety, so that they might fortify and establish their opinions with many detours and with artistic and ingenious arguments. Yet all these things, in the foundation of nature, are nothing but smoke and a crushed, wilted flower.

<margin>Eternal bliss is the highest good; next to this is the knowledge of nature. Avicenna.</margin>
We, however, are so convinced that besides the eternal bliss of man, nothing more noble or excellent exists anywhere than to have known nature and to have learned from her, as from a mistress, the entire foundation of Philosophy. Just as we establish this, we conversely condemn those ingenious subtleties that boast of being Philosophy, yet are nothing else than a beautiful opinion, painted and adorned with its own "flowers." Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina, whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard university text Paracelsus famously burned.</note> (under whose name we include all Physicians), along with his followers, predecessors, and successors, proposes a very beautiful doctrine concerning human seed and its generation. And although they have all sweated strenuously in one effort to proclaim certain worthy and arduous things about the generation of man, nevertheless, their entire Philosophy reeks of those Physicians who are not born of true Philosophy.

<margin>Philosophy is the mother of Physicians.</margin>
For Philosophy is the mother of the good and noble Physician. Yet this habit clings to them constantly: to exist as Physicians while lacking the foundation upon which a Physician is built. Therefore, to speak truly, they have an end, but no beginning. Whatever is not material, they treat as material; and they judge and assume the beginning only by the manner of the end, and they thrust all the blame upon nature if they have understood something incorrectly. But why should the commentaries of such wavering men trouble us excessively? Though they do not flow from the fountain of Philosophy, they nevertheless confer everything upon nature with undiscerning judgment. To touch upon the foundations of those who fight against us—both the living and the dead—we must first know regarding the Astronomers that they seem to attack us with pictures, figures, "kings," and very effective rules <note>original: *canonibus*; formal rules or laws of calculation</note>.

<margin>Physicians are rebuked.</margin>
Yet we shall receive all these things as a passing breeze that eventually vanishes by itself. For what they value most, we judge to be of no price, especially when we recall that they, for the sake of their plausible opinion, merely describe how the Planets and stars beget and form children. For some say that the stars confer upon them their nature, complexion, and virtues. Why we take it upon ourselves to explode their foolishness...

<summary>Paracelsus begins his treatise by critiquing traditional authorities like Aristotle and Avicenna for prioritizing theoretical speculation over firsthand experience. He asserts that true medical and philosophical knowledge must spring from the "Light of Nature" rather than the "smoke" of academic tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Generation, Light of Nature, Aristotle, Avicenna, experience vs theory, medical philosophy, Astronomers, human seed</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of Paracelsus's treatise on human generation. The previous page established that he intends to challenge established philosophical authorities by relying on the "Light of Nature" rather than traditional academic subtleties.</meta>

<header>ON THE GENERATION OF MAN</header>

<margin>
The stars have no power in the generation of man.
</margin>
...since they are of so little importance: It is for your sake, however, and not our own, that we strictly affirm this: neither Planets nor Stars have any cooperation whatsoever in this case. The demonstration of this will be brought forth later in its own chapters; for it is certain that those scholars will by no means be satisfied with this present preface of ours. Nevertheless, in the text itself, they will find what they desire to satisfy themselves. Neither shall the doctrines, writings, and monuments of the **vicars of the gods** <note>original: *vicariorum diuorum*; Paracelsus likely refers to the "god-like" academic authorities such as Aristotle and Galen whose works were treated as sacred in universities.</note> trouble us, whether they work for us or against us. For we never attributed so much to Aristotelian subtleties that we would not attribute twice as much to the specious arguments of these men. And yet, we do not credit the honor of their wisdom to the Gods or to the Light of Nature, but rather to private utility and to wandering spirits, with whom doubt and ambiguity—rather than a sober Philosophy—are accustomed to dwell. In the meantime, let this preface serve as an excuse in some part, until we approach the text itself.

### THE SECOND PREFACE.

NOW, if we wish to begin the text itself concerning the **Generation of man**, we must first establish a certain hypothesis from which the arguments of our treatise may be drawn. We shall place the foundation upon this: that we are able to teach and demonstrate the very things that we see. In the generation of man, two things especially occur to us which are not observed in all other generations. For whatever appears here to the senses is at least male and female. From this pair, the generation of the fetus is perfected, reflecting the same and uniform likeness with the parents who generated it. This being established in the preface, we shall dismiss and examine the objection concerning those who are not born according to a form similar to ours, such as the **One-eyed**, **Cyclopes**, and other similar beings. This manifold and diverse generation provides us with an occasion so that we may, through philosophizing, hold the opinion that not all men in the universe, according to all their various forms, descend from a single parent and progenitor, but rather from many.

<margin>
*Bipedal Cyclopes, and the one-eyed, for they are from one father;*
</margin>
As, for example: those who are bipedal <note>two-legged/standard humans</note> are born from their own private source; from another private source the Cyclopes; and from another again the one-eyed are generated. Those who say that so many men, of such varying forms, were produced from **incubation** <note>the act of "brooding" or hatching</note> or from the **mother's gaze** <note>This refers to the theory of "maternal impression," the belief that what a pregnant woman saw or imagined could physically alter the fetus.</note> cannot be dismissed without a laugh. For perhaps those things were put forward as jokes to move men to laughter. Otherwise, if we accept such things seriously, we can by no means agree with them without certain proof. Yet Philosophy makes this certain for us: if a fetus should change its form through the mother’s gaze so that it is similar to neither father nor mother, then that fruit remains sterile, and he was the first and last to receive that form.

<margin>
*Forms do not all come from one.*
</margin>
But setting this aside here, we terminate our preface with this sentiment: that there is altogether something else from which each individual form is born, and that all things do not proceed from one. For it is outside the law of nature for a one-eyed child to be born from a male and female Cyclops, and conversely, for a Cyclops to be produced from a male and female one-eyed parent. Let the same judgment apply to other forms as well, whose various marks, both known and unknown, exist in nature. It would indeed be much more probable to say that fierce and wild men issued forth from the birth of bipedal men and were born from such a father, than what was proposed in the previous argument. And although wild men, like brutes, are deprived of reason, this proves nothing else than that they were born from a peculiar parent, and did not truly descend from [standard] men. If these things are so, then all other creatures will behave in exactly the same way. If it is objected that there is an **eternal element** <note>the soul</note> within other formed beings, from which men are also named: that is not of such weight as to prove that all men proceeded from a single parent; though they do proceed from one God, who pours the soul into all. That God, who both gives and has given the eternal, and whom Philosophy acknowledges, does not permit men of such varied and manifold forms to be born from one parent, but from many; nor did He ordain anything monstrous and inhuman against nature.

<margin>
*God's equal ordering.*
</margin>
Indeed, He conferred a similar eternal element upon all, but He did not implant a similar form; rather, He produced them from their parents with a wonderful variety of differences. Although it also seems worthy to be recounted in this present preface who the first father of the bipedals might have been, if one were to count backward to the beginning. Yet that is not at all Philosophical, but a kind of playful joke. For as soon as we have grasped that father from whom all men were born, we must stop right there at that mark. For how would Philosophy explain to us in what manner *he* was born? For God created him. By which we also conclude—not consulting the scripture or the letter as to where God created him from—but being entirely persuaded that such things are hidden from all. Concerning which matter, even if something certain could be brought forth and known, it is to be feared whether anyone would understand what that **clod or clay** <note>original: *gleba vel argilla*; a reference to the biblical creation of Adam from the dust of the ground.</note> was, of what kind, or where it was. We shall therefore leave that in parables, and search no deeper into it; but those who do not recognize this parable as such, and think it can be understood or explained by them, we compare to those who seek understanding in the ringing of bells.

<header>PREFACE TO THE BOOK</header>

## THE THIRD PREFACE.

<margin>Bipeds are superior to others.</margin>
**T**HEREFORE, putting aside such discourse, we shall proceed in weighing our proposed subject. Here we will survey how the birth of children was established and ordained by God. We will, therefore, take the father and mother as an example from the bipeds <note>Human beings who walk on two feet.</note>, and through that example, we will philosophize on the cause of why two, and not one, nor three, are required for the formation of a single fetus. We will let this specific argument rest for this preface. However, just as the generation of bipedal humans exists within us, so it is in all other groups <note>original: "sectis"; here referring to different varieties or "species" of human-like beings in Paracelsian lore.</note> according to all their forms. And although these groups are many and varied in their outward appearance, among all of us, nothing is divided except the form, not the nature itself. Wherefore, with good right, we include the generation of all those others under our own generation. For at least one unique nature is found, but that same nature is hidden in various forms. In the inner man, however, all things are situated, and not in his outward appearance or exterior form. For Philosophy is the examination of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World"; the Paracelsian belief that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>, that is, the inner man, and not as he appears to the outward sight; a clearer declaration of this will be established in another place. 

As for why we take the bipedal man as our example, the reason is not because we ourselves are such, or that our blood is found to be of that sort, or that this matter is better known to us than others, or even that this race occupies the largest and most powerful part of the known world. None of these, I say, are the reasons. But the chief reason is this: we deservedly consider ourselves more worthy than the others because Christ himself was of our group and assumed our form. Although he had the free choice and will to choose anything, or even to put on a peculiar form, he nevertheless wished to assume our form, even without human seed. From this, one may suppose that the other groups are not equally perfect according to their forms, but that something of a defect or a "sport of nature" <note>original: "ludicri"; implying a whimsical or less serious creation compared to the bipedal form.</note> lurks within them. In the form of bipeds, however, nothing is lacking. Rather, by this form itself, it is argued that the group of Christ is the most perfect and absolute of all, lacking any blemish, and more worthy than all other groups which have certainly not been raised to this degree of perfection and integrity. 

And although nothing is lacking in the sight of the one-eyed, nor is anything lacking in the running of the cyclopses <note>Paracelsus often treated mythical creatures as actual, though rare, "races" of people created by God.</note>, but they are perfect enough for their own uses and live content with that form, it can nevertheless be fairly gathered that this diversity of form was bestowed upon them to more clearly illustrate the dignity and nobility of the bipedal form, which without this contrast might perhaps be less clearly evident. Nor was that form given to them because of a peculiar soul. Indeed, the interior things of nature, and that which is life itself within nature, exists as the same in all forms, <margin>The life or internal form is the same in all.</margin> neither weaker nor stronger, but differing only in form. This point does not trouble us greatly. Therefore, according to the eternal part, the rational soul, and the light of nature itself, we value them as the same as us and of the same rank, nor do we say anything to the contrary. 

Nevertheless, Philosophy does not allow us to stay silent, but compels us to pronounce—when weighing the manner of their origin—that they exist as monsters and a kind of marvel of creation. Namely, whatever turned out well in nature became a biped, and <margin>Whatever man is not a biped is a monster.</margin> whatever turned out badly became monstrous and assumed either the aforementioned form or any others. For just as in natural operations many things often happen which deviate from the natural mode and form, so also by the will of God in the creation of men, monsters of this kind can arise and occur, so that not all and everyone are contained under the appearance of a single perfect man. Thus, we pronounce them monsters according to such a form, but not according to their eternal nature. For this reason, they also beget children similar to themselves, because they received such a maimed and faulty form during creation. And as they were established in creation, so they remain perpetually, until all creatures are again abolished. However, whatever is made monstrously in nature itself [through accident] and degenerates, this produces nothing and propagates nothing. But on the contrary, that which is made monstrous *in the act of creation* is perfect and capable according to its own form and nature for generating and propagating its own kind.

## THE FOURTH PREFACE.

**B**UT staying within the present text, so that we do not extend our purpose too far, we will finally add the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem"; literally a finishing stroke or conclusion.</note> to the prefaces, presupposing for you the perfection of the generation of all men, with no race excepted. To establish this more conveniently, we shall describe the origin and generation of all those who have the eternal within themselves. Nor will we treat these in any other way than we did in examining the distinction of forms, where we determined the truth regarding monstrous creation. But here we will produce our text concerning the internal nature of all groups or races, which is everywhere similar and one. For the entrance of our book, we will mention that which will then be more clearly finished in the book itself: namely, that we, the aforesaid, are not the only ones who occu— <note>The text breaks off here to the next page.</note>

<summary>Paracelsus explains that while diverse human forms (like cyclopses) exist as "monsters" of creation, they share the same internal nature and soul as bipeds. He argues the bipedal form is superior only because it was the form chosen by Christ.</summary>

<meta>Catchword: then (tum)</meta>

<margin>The four types of Humans according to the number of the four Elements.</margin>
*...we shall proceed: but we affirm that this world of ours is at least a fourth part of the entire universe. Not indeed that the world is three times larger than what is known to us, but that in this world known to us, three parts still remain which we do not inhabit. To help you understand this more clearly, we shall explain it thus: We establish that there is a world in the water, and that humans dwell in it who are also partakers of eternity, and similarly to us, are altogether adorned and endowed with form, nature, and various species, just as we mention regarding the humans of the fourth part of our world. Since we know, therefore, that there is also a world in the water, this shall be our reason and incentive to set about composing a specific book—this following one—concerning their origin and generation; namely, concerning the second part of the world. This same reason will also lead us to write a third book. For we have discovered another remaining part of the world, namely that of the earth: by describing its inhabitants, we shall complete the third book. This finished, we shall hasten to the fourth, and we will explain to you the births or generation of the <term>Vulcanians</term> <note>Beings of the element of fire; in Paracelsian philosophy, these are often associated with salamanders or spirits of the forge.</note>, who inhabit the fourth part of the world and act under the element of fire. In this way we are to be understood: by positing four parts of the world, from which one world is constituted. Nor shall we allow this Philosophy, which teaches and demonstrates such things, to be shaken from us. We shall not be moved by the noise of those who, weighing the conditions of animated beings only from an earthly nature, reject the three remaining parts of the world. For the imaginings they conceive are of no great weight, but are mostly vain and worthless. Therefore, eager and joyful, we shall continue our text under the guidance of our sound Philosophy and with the assent of the words of Christ himself, which act in our favor (as shall be said) and strongly establish our Philosophy. Under the auspices, therefore, of the most true testimony of Christ and Philosophical experience, we shall now seasonably begin the text of our books according to the four generations of the four parts of the world. The first, however, will treat of our world and its natives, namely the aerial ones <note>Humans who live in the air, which Paracelsus considers the "standard" human race.</note>. The second of the <term>Nymphs</term> <note>Beings of the water.</note>, the aqueous ones. The third of the <term>Pygmies</term> <note>Beings of the earth or mountains; also called Gnomes.</note>, the mountain-dwellers. The fourth of the Vulcanians, living in fire. Thus we conclude the generations of all humans in whom the eternal—that is, the soul—dwells, which is the highest good, extreme blessedness, and the ultimate reward: whose sole redeemer is Christ. God and Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, who was the same before birth, and thereafter is, immaculate through all eternity, inserted into the holy Trinity without end.*
<margin>Saint Mary, the mother of Christ, inserted into the Trinity.</margin>

## THE TEXT OF THE FIRST BOOK
### OF THEOPHRASTUS.
#### THE FIRST TREATISE.
##### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Two orders of created things.</margin>
<margin>Sensible creatures do not have a seed from their own nature.</margin>
**A**t the beginning of our text, we make a general discourse about all creatures, so that the understanding of our purpose may be more certain and accessible. We divide the generation of all created things into two modes. One of these is of created things that have the seed of their multiplication implanted in them and so inserted into their very nature that the nature and the seed exist as an indivisible thing; so confused and mixed together that one cannot be separated without the destruction of the other. Such are the <term>insensible</term> <note>Things without animal-like senses or feelings.</note> growing things, like plants, herbs, stones, metals, and others devoid of a sensing soul: as will be more clearly taught regarding their generation. The other mode is that some creatures are <term>sensible</term> <note>Beings that possess senses and feeling, such as humans and animals.</note>, which have no seed established in themselves that arises from their own nature, but they live and exist plainly without any such seed: such as humans and cattle. No man in himself, no woman in herself, contains a seed that is begotten or flows from their own nature in the way we mentioned regarding insensible things. The reasoning is the same for cattle. But keeping silent about cattle, we shall continue only the treatise on human generation. Regarding which we propose this: that all sensible or sensing things in the universe have no seed in themselves or from themselves. Whence the foundation...

<meta>This page begins Treatise I of the work, following the introductory cosmology. The author moves from discussing the elemental inhabitants of the world to the specific mechanics of human generation, focusing on the relationship between nature, the mind, and the "seed."</meta>

# TREATISE I.

<margin>Neither man nor woman possesses seed within their own nature.</margin>
...you ought to understand the purpose of this chapter, which teaches this one thing: namely, that the seed does not grow or emerge from within the human being’s own nature, nor does nature contribute anything to the drawing out or generating of the seed, nor does it even stimulate the human being regarding the seed. Thus, in the human being, nature exists alone, without the seed and without the mixture of nature and seed, just as is understood regarding unfeeling things <note>Non-sentient things like plants or minerals.</note>, in which both are present as a mixture; however, it is not the same in the human being. From this, you ought to gather that in a non-sentient creature, any given thing becomes a <term>matrix</term> <note>original: *matrix*; here meaning a womb or a generative environment</note> by itself, even without a male; and that which is considered masculine among them also exists as a matrix by itself. For it also carries seed. In the human being, however, the matter stands differently. For he who is a man does not contain seed within himself for the purpose of propagating his own kind. So it is also with the woman. Thus, they are without seed and are established in a free nature, in which no condition of the seed has been implanted. By this understanding, therefore, any unfeeling things are a **Matrix**; but sentient things, on the other hand, are different. Thus, the human being exists as a free agent, without an inborn seed, and does not have a mixture similar to or of the same kind as plants.

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Where seed is present, the light of nature is absent.</margin>
**N**ow that it has been demonstrated and settled that the human being does not contain seed within themselves proceeding from their nature, this must now be illustrated by an example, such as this: It is known to all of you that none of you begets anything from nature itself; rather, you are free and empty of all seed, pure and clear in that nature from which you have drawn the light of nature itself. However, where seed exists in nature, there the light of nature does not shine, but is dead. Take this as proof: It is well known to you that a human being occupied by the seed <note>i.e., someone consumed by lust or the physical drive to procreate</note> employs no reason, nor does he live according to reason, but is consumed by mere pleasures and Venusian phantasms <note>Erotic fantasies or delusions associated with lust/Venus.</note>. But why we speak here of the human being carrying seed, when a little while ago we taught concerning a free nature, we shall give you the reason for this in the following chapter. Regarding the previous text, however, pay attention to this:

<margin>The human being was created by God with care.</margin>
Namely, that God created the human being so sublime, lofty, and vigorous, that He willed him alone to turn and live entirely free in the light of nature. Whence, without any contradiction, we can freely philosophize that it is necessary for every philosopher to be simultaneously divine and natural,

<margin>The human being was despoiled by God’s care.</margin>
to live in the light of nature, and by no means in the seed, which is **ALLARA** <note>A Paracelsian term likely referring to the state of physical corruption or the "fleshly" seed that obscures spiritual/natural intellect.</note>. And so that we may explain the matter to you from its foundation, know that God, the creator of all things, established the human being alone in the light of nature so that he might be free and unconstrained. For this reason, He took the seed away from his nature and did not implant it in him, specifically because of the eternal element that flourishes within him. For God demands the human being to be pure, not altered—yet the seed renders him altered if it should persist in his nature. Observe the conclusion of this matter: God created male and female, and put the seed in neither, lest by chance through lust they should be cast out from the light of nature. However, for the sake of the propagation of the species, He granted them free will, and at the same time gave them the seed, so that they might choose whether they wish to beget or not.

<margin>Imagination is the origin of the human seed.</margin>
The seed, however, He placed in their imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> originally and materially, according to all its conditions, in this manner: If a man desires to beget, then his contemplation <note>original: *speculatio*</note> stirs up lust within him. Lust then generates the seed for him, as will be more clearly demonstrated hereafter. Thus, the seed was placed by God into the faculty of contemplation. To contemplation, moreover, free will was granted, either to stir up lust or to let it sleep.

<margin>For what purpose was free will granted to man? What is the Object?</margin>
And nature does not bring this about; rather, only the "Object" does. For it is an "Object" if a man looks upon a woman. But it is within his power whether he wishes or does not wish to comply with that which has been implanted in his reason—namely, what the Object contains within itself. For God bestowed reason upon the human being so that he might know what kind of thing lust is. Yet he himself can either despise it, or crave it, or act upon it, or leave it be; and he can either command his reason or succumb to it. Therefore, God also sowed the seed into the human being's imagination, in which all intellect is situated, along with the knowledge of the Object that ignites and tickles the contemplation. If he does not support this through his will, no seed is present in him, but only the light of nature.

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>How seed is produced in both sexes.</margin>
**W**hat we have said concerning the man applies also to the woman. If she sees a man, she beholds her Object. Contemplation then follows: what is this man? And reason, or rather intellect, is given by God. Now it is within her power either to engage herself lustfully or not at all. If she consents to the lust, she is pregnant with seed. If not, she neither has seed, nor is she carried away into lust. Thus, in the assent of the human being, God [placed] the seed...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that human beings do not naturally contain reproductive seed; instead, it is generated in the imagination through the "Object" of desire and the exercise of free will. He posits that while plants have seed inherent in their nature, humans are created "free" so that they may live in the "light of nature" unless they choose to succumb to lust.</summary>
<keywords>seed, generation, light of nature, imagination, free will, lust, libido, matrix, Paracelsus, phantasia, Allara</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "seed" (femen), which the author distinguishes from physical sperm. The previous page established that humans do not naturally possess seed within themselves like plants do, but that it is a product of the will and imagination.</meta>

...implanted the seed: but He placed the assent within the human will, so that a person can do whichever he wishes. When this assent is pending, it is necessary that it belongs to both—namely, to the man and the woman. Thus, the assent of the will of both completes the work. Such is the mode of generation of the seed, which is neither seen by anyone, nor can it be seen.

<margin>The human seed has never been seen by anyone. A rebuke of the Physicians.</margin>
What cause is there, then, that these blind Physicians hand down entire chapters concerning sperm, asserting that sperm is the seed? In truth, it is by no means the seed. Furthermore, by the help of their art, they prepare various recipes and various broths through which they dare to promise to make women prolific; yet this is entirely impossible for their art to achieve.

<margin>What sort of thing is the seed? That sperm is something else.</margin>
For the seed is not a material substance, but a speculative one <note>original: *speculativum*; in this context, it refers to something existing in the realm of the mind, imagination, or spirit rather than a physical body</note>. These physicians merely increase the sperm, even though sperm is an expulsion of moisture, not of blood. We shall define sperm in its proper place, treating it not as the seed, but as an excrement of nature in which no seed is contained. As for the fact that it is ejaculated with delight and a physical itching, the cause is this: the sense of pleasure opens the veins of that expulsion, which is pushed forward by the force of heat stirred up by the impulse of the imagination. Since they have published many such delusions, let them pass along with their other errors. However, this must not be skipped over without a clear explanation: that the Anatomical Physicians profess that sperm is the seed, and seriously defend the idea that it is produced by nature. In doing so, they both call themselves "men" and act as such, when they ought to be acting as Gods <note>The author suggests that true generation is a divine-like act of will and spirit, not a mere biological function.</note>. Meanwhile, lest their "Deity" become suspect because of their indulgence in lust, they declaim from their chairs that man must act in a human fashion. This opinion greatly tickles that haughty Aristotle when he says that nature is entirely owed its own discharges. We grant this much to Aristotle; however, it is not equally true that this seed flows forth from nature, just as Satanic fornicators protect their malice and lust with this shield.

<margin>Tibullus</margin>
And we cannot help but marvel at that "great God" Tibullus <note>Likely a sarcastic reference to the Roman poet Tibullus, known for his erotic and elegiac poetry, used here to represent those who prioritize physical desire over spiritual purity.</note>, who, while he demands that the light of nature in his followers be pure and unpolluted, allows them such foul excuses. Yet elsewhere he exalts himself in the praise of purity alone, and establishes that only the pure are Prophets, and deems them alone worthy of his grace and mercy. Perhaps he himself is never at home, or he dozes, while his servants twist everything to their own lust. But why do we graze against these "Gods" and Physicians here? Especially since they are not knowledgeable in any philosophy, and the labor we have begun has not yet been brought to its proper goal. Returning therefore to the generation of man, we will continue our text as an introduction.

## CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Things necessary for the human seed and for generating.</margin>
**J**ust as we have established thus far, the seed is placed in the imagination of man, and the counsel or assent of the mind is the begetter or parent of the seed. Yet one person alone is not sufficient for the seed, but has need of another object; that is, one person constitutes only half the requirement for the seed. Therefore, we shall now make it somewhat clearer why God established man as only half of the seed. We propose this cause: because the "object" <note>The person toward whom the imagination and desire are directed.</note> alone works this, just as the man is toward the woman, and she in turn toward him.

<margin>Why the seed of only one was made as a half.</margin>
Now, this is the reason why He placed the object of the man in the woman, and the woman's in the man. Even if the man, through the object, becomes the <term>matrix</term> <note>original: *matrix*; the source, womb, or formative environment where something is generated</note> of the seed: nevertheless, in order for it to work, he can either nod yes or refuse. Thus, if by a hasty <term>fantasy</term> <note>original: *phantasia*; a sudden mental image or impulse</note> a chance should be carried into the seed: if he did not assent, then the seed would perish and die. For it is abolished together with the fantasy. As it emerges through the fantasy, so it dies with it. But if the source itself were capable of full generation—as divine ordinance could easily have established—then the seed would grow out of its own necessity. But He did not wish to burden us with that. For God established man as man, and woman as woman, and made it so that both were one human being: which does not need to be investigated further here. Nor did He wish them to be like trees, in which male and female are mixed and are one. For one sentient thing requires another sentient thing as an opposite.

<margin>Not all are born for propagating.</margin>
But to what end do we bring forth this discourse? For God does not want just any man to be a propagator of his own kind: but He made some without seed, and others with seed, and that in various ways. Therefore He placed the "object" in the woman, so that anyone might either desire it or reject it. For God prefers the light of nature to exist pure, rather than contaminated. For in the pure, the spirit lives; in the impure, foolish and deaf spirits dwell. And with these words, we wish the introduction concerning the seed to be finished, where we have taught what the source of the seed is, and how it is generated. There you ought to attend carefully to the great distinction and that difficult cause, why God [placed] the seed in the will of man in this way...

TREATISE II.

<margin>
Christ alone is the goal for Philosophers
</margin>
...He wished to be deposited and established within man. Whatever He chooses, He does so with respect to the seed. If I were acting as both a theologian and a philosopher, I would surely fill many volumes for our scribes and leaders, so that they might finally learn and understand from the very foundation (which they have not yet reached) that Christ ought to be the end and goal of any philosophy. He loves pure hearts, not contaminated ones; He wants light, not darkness; He demands a free person, not one burdened and oppressed; He requires one who is released, not bound and chained. We complain that we are not yet sufficient for this theology ourselves. Yet we hope, in turn, that nothing will be denied to us by Philosophy.

# SECOND TREATISE

## CHAPTER I.

From our previous chapters, you can gather and remember that you have been forewarned so that you may know the nature of the seed: that is, the seed itself and the nature of physical reality were not created joined together in man, but nature was established separately. Furthermore, the nature of the seed—that is, the "speculation" <note>original: *speculatio*; here meaning the mental image or imaginative power that triggers biological processes</note>—arises from its object, just as God ordained those things: Nature, certainly, for the life of the human body, but the "object" for the seed; and each truly for itself, separately. By this reasoning, whatever possesses an "object" that excites the seed does not have that seed implanted or dwelling within it naturally. Although for the sake of greater understanding it would be fitting here to also introduce the brute beasts, who understand their object and know its nature. For in this way, the "congenital speculation" which is in the beasts causes that operation and rouses the seed, and not their nature itself. God likewise deposited this for them in the object. However, the "reason of the spirit" <note>original: *Ratio spiritus*; the higher intellectual or spiritual faculty</note> flourishes in man alone, and in no other. Therefore, we shall begin to speak of man, how he is generated: and we shall discuss the matter from which he is made, and finally his formation and growth. Attend, therefore, to the text of the following chapters.

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>
The matter of the seed is the will.
</margin>
<margin>
The liquor of life is the whole man, containing the idea of all the members.
</margin>
<margin>
The dignity of the liquor within the vessels.
</margin>
The text of the generation of man, then, proceeds in order as follows. God placed the "matter" of the seed for man within the will, which he takes from his object <note>The "object" refers to the person or image desired by the will</note>. If, therefore, a man has assented to the object and fulfilled his will in speculation, then the "liquor of life" <note>original: *liquor vitae*; a vital, semi-spiritual fluid believed to carry the essence of life throughout the body</note> is kindled by that speculation, and it becomes the seed of another human being. This is how it is in the male, and so it is in the female. Otherwise, the liquor itself remains just liquor and does not become seed. The seed then becomes what it is because it exists distributed and scattered throughout the entire body. Similarly, every nature, property, condition, and species of the limbs is a spirit within it. And just as the body consists in its own formation, so too does the liquor of life. Nor is the liquor of life anything other than the "hidden man": for that which hides it is visible. The liquor of a man can be compared to nothing more aptly than to a shadow on a wall. It is projected by the man and is formed according to his measure. Such also is the liquor. It is a microcosm <note>A "little world" or miniature map of the entire human being and the universe</note>, it is the interior shadow. Yet it has its own substance with it, its own tangibility and sensibility, and the "idea," substance, and nature of all the members of the whole body; it is the most noble of all things that exist in the human body. And although it does not have a soul of its own and borrows its life from the body, rather than having it from itself, it is nonetheless an "other man." For just as someone looks at themselves in a mirror, so nature contemplates itself within this liquor; and thus it is in man, without loss or detriment to the body.

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>
The mode of human generation.
</margin>
<margin>
The amber of the body attracts the seed. The seed withdraws into the spermatic vessels.
</margin>
If, therefore, the human will consents to that object, then that liquor becomes seed. Just as the heat of the sun ignites wood, or as one fire ignites another piece of wood because of the great heat that touches the wood—even if the flame is not yet put forth—so also the "object" ignites the other microcosm <note>meaning the internal liquor/essence</note> so that seed is produced from it, just as fire comes from wood. The seed that is produced in this way, *as has been said*, lies quiet in its own places and seats, just as the seats of the liquor are in the body: namely, hands in the hands, feet in the feet, heart in the heart, brain in the brain, and so forth. There is no one peculiar place into which the seed falls and rests; rather, it is preserved in its own receptacles in which its liquor and matter are contained. It is separated from the liquor of life like foam from broth or from new wine. Since these things are so, know that as long as this "amber" <note>original: *succinum*; likely used here to describe an attractive or magnetic force, as amber was known for its static attraction</note> does not attract the seed to itself, nothing is accomplished in that man regarding his seed. However, the thought may occur to you that the seed, once produced, withdraws into the spermatic vessels...

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The discharge of sperm is misunderstood.</margin>
But let us continue with the text. The sperm, which is poured out from the spermatic vessels, is an egestion <note>original: *egestio*; referring to a waste product or excrement</note> of that liquor of life which is purified and separated, just as dung is separated from food. Thus, the sperm has no other purification than that which occurs through the "kindling of the object" <note>This refers to the "object" of desire mentioned on the previous page which ignites the process</note>. Once this kindling has occurred, the liquor casts the waste into the spermatic vessels and retains the seed within itself. However, the seed from which a human is born remains in the liquor and does not turn into sperm. At this point, we shall discuss a certain argument that might be thrown at us by those blind Physicians and some of the ancient Philosophers who side with them, namely this:

<margin>The objection is cleared away.</margin>
> *We know by certain experience that the image of a man is generated from sperm. Yet that is not sufficient for a human being, but only for a likeness. Although that does not lie in the place where it ought to lie—according to what our adversaries say, who think a human can be made from it, and indeed is made—they are hallucinating. For their thoughts and their art are more intent on money than on the truth.*

But hold this solution to their argument. The sperm is such a waste product of the liquor of life that it has the power, during digestion, to also take on the formation which the liquor contains in its own nature. For the liquor of life is the "form" of the body. Thus, the sperm also retains that same form within itself and has the power of shaping, just like the liquor. Yet you must understand the matter in this way: that nothing else is born from the sperm except the "form" <note>The physical shape or appearance</note> which exists in the liquor. This is a natural operation: there is no life there, no sensibility, no sight, no hearing, no taste, no smell. All these things are in the *seed* perfectly, entirely, and without defect. Therefore, the sperm is a part of the liquor of life, which is the microcosm <note>term: *microcosmus*; the "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note>. And if it shakes out its waste from the kindling, it then clings to a certain part in the property of the liquor—that is, to the form—and nothing further.

### CHAPTER V.

Setting aside the previous discussions, we shall proceed to the consideration of the seed <note>original: *feminis*; a variant for the seed or source of generation</note>. Since you have heard that the aforementioned sperm is merely a waste product and not the true seed—though we would gladly demonstrate this to you more clearly and lucidly, your own intelligence makes us think these remarks are sufficient for now—understand the seed itself in this way. We defined earlier that the seed, after its inflammation, rests unmoved in the place where it dwells; that is, it is distributed throughout the entire body and does not itself beget any human. <margin>Amber feels and attracts.</margin> Only amber <note>original: *succinu*; amber was famously known for its static electricity and "attractive" properties</note> attracts it and carries it toward the places of generation, where it must mature. Understand it thus: first, you must remember that *a man has only half the seed, and the woman has the other half.* Therefore, these two contribute to a complete seed. Now, pay attention to how they are joined. In the matrix <note>term: *matrix*; the womb or uterus, viewed here as an active biological vessel</note> there lies hidden <margin>The attractive power of the womb.</margin> an attractive force, which is like amber or a magnet, being quite powerful enough to attract the seeds. That attractive force of the womb breaks out and exerts itself when the seed has been generated. Therefore, if those works which are stirred up from "speculation" <note>The imaginative desire</note> are set in motion, then the womb attracts the seed of the moisture to itself, both from the man and from the woman: from the heart, from the liver, from the spleen, from the bones, from the marrow, from the veins, from the muscles, from the blood, from the flesh, and from all those things contained in the body. <margin>Every part has its own seed.</margin> For whatever is a specific part in the body also has its own specific seed. However, all the seeds attracted from every member make at least one single seed if they flow together. And thus the womb draws the true seed, mixed with the sperm, from both persons to itself. <margin>Rebuke of the Physicians.</margin> Therefore, mention must again be made of those Physicians who, busy with sperm as if it were the whole of nature, try to make women and men fertile; yet this is a pure and simple invention. For as long as the attractive faculty of the womb does not act out of its own nature, the seed is not carried to those places, and consequently, no infant would exist. Despite their babbling that a fetus could be made without the womb, as was said before, know that the womb is so often drenched and filled that children ought to be born every day if they were right. But they have not looked out carefully enough for their own lie.

the matrix of nature: so hereafter we shall also describe the microcosm for you, in this manner. If all the seeds from all the parts have flowed together into the matrix, then the nature of the matrix separates the seed of the head, the brain, the crystalline <note>original: *crystallinum*; likely referring to the crystalline humor of the eye or clear bodily fluids</note>, and similar things to their own places, and thus disposes the members where they ought to be, not unlike how the architect of a house arranges and places the timbers.
