<margin>The method of arranging the body's members.</margin>
But concerning the "half-seed" <note>original: *semine dimidio*; referring to the contribution of a single parent</note>, observe this: the solitary seed of one human being is certainly not perfect or sufficient for generating a human. The cause is that God wills one human to be born from two, not from one alone.

<margin>The seed of one is insufficient for generation.</margin>
Furthermore, from the inner sanctums of Philosophy we bring forth such a reason: if a human existed in the seed of only one person, then no species would be generated from that person other than exactly what they themselves were. For thus their offspring would be constituted: just as a walnut is born from itself, and for that reason is similar to the one from which it emerged. And so in all trees, like only produces like: just as a walnut tree produces walnuts all similar to one another, with nothing changed in any of them. The same is the logic for a human. If one were generated from a single person: they would become entirely similar to the father, who would be both father and mother at once. And thus humans would be of only one figure, and one would be perpetually similar to another, and one seed, one nature would flourish.

<margin>Whence the dissimilarity of man.</margin>
In the meantime, however, the mixing of seeds performed by women and men introduces that variety, so that one human never becomes exactly like another. For in the union, the seed always converges in an unequal weight, so that it is never so perfectly balanced that a human could be born who exists as an exact likeness of both father and mother. Always one seed or the other breaks the influence of the other: that is, it changes its likeness. And this is the sole reason why one human is never born identical to another.

## ## CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The properties of the seeds and their gathering.</margin>
After the **Matrix** has conceived the seeds and hidden them within itself, the approaching Nature of the man and woman joins and unites them. Whichever of these is the strongest and best shapes the other into its own likeness, either in its entirety or in the greatest part. Let there be an example. The seed from the brain of the man, and likewise from the woman, these two joined together constitute only one brain. Yet whichever of them is most powerful makes and forms the fetus similar to itself. Nevertheless, it never assimilates it perfectly or "by the ruler" <note>original: *ad amussim*; an architectural term meaning with absolute precision</note>. The reason is that an "infraction" <note>a breaking or counter-influence</note> has been introduced by the other seed, through which a change in form immediately occurs. And the further one generation is born from another, the greater and more certain is the variation in likeness.

<margin>The union of the seed and the meeting of the fetus.</margin>
Thus the seed for a nose forms the nose in the fetus according to the proportion and mixing of both parents. So also the mouth shapes the mouth, the limb shapes the limb. From this, even hereditary diseases follow, depending on which seed held dominance. The more one seed surpasses the other in the "goodness of generation," the more the fetus is rendered similar to that parent. However, the matter is handled differently regarding the generation of either a male or a female, in this way:

<margin>The generation of male and female.</margin>
Before nature arranges the seed to produce the fetus, as we have mentioned, a certain operation precedes it, which behaves like this: If the matrix attracts the seed to itself, the first operation is in that seed, and it "tints" the other seed. Thus one surpasses the other, not in the form or figure of the fetus or its members, but only in its nature. And there a natural struggle is joined, not touching the seed itself. This predominance does not happen from the power of the seed, but from the power of the nature of each person compelling the seed into the womb. In this way, whichever seed the matrix first attracts to itself from those two, that seed generates either a male or a female. If the woman's seed is drawn in before the man's: it becomes a female; if the opposite, a male is generated.

## ## CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Why seed and sperm are two different things.</margin>
**F**or the resumption of the text, therefore, note that we have placed the seed within the free will of man. If he wills, he can. Even if these things please others less, we are not at all distressed on their account. For the consideration of things, and the comparison of one with another, gives birth to no other Philosophy. The distinction must also be noted as to how seed and sperm are two different things. For if every bit of sperm were seed, fetuses would be born daily, both in those already pregnant and otherwise. But because the matrix attracts only once, and not multiple times: therefore note that nothing comes from the sperm alone. But from Philosophy we shall communicate a still more subtle instruction to you, in this manner: Because we have discussed the seeds of the matrix, you might gather that as often as an "object" <note>referring to an object of desire or sexual stimulus</note> is offered to someone, so often they exist as fit and ready for the emission of seed. <margin>When the womb acts.</margin>
In this chapter: Whenever a man’s will is overcome by an object and he consents to it, he becomes full of seed. So it is likewise for the woman. However, the female womb <note>original: *matrix*; the term used for the womb as a creative organ</note> does not always attract seed to itself, but only as often as it is robust. A pregnant woman, as we understand it, can generate seed within herself daily. But it is not always led to those places where it ought to be carried. The reason is that it is not attracted by the womb. For because the womb has already enclosed one seed within itself, it does not entice another. As long as it is quiet and empty, it is fit for attraction, until it is cooled too much by advancing age; in which case it strives for nothing further. For the power of attraction <margin>Cold breaks attraction.</margin> is extinguished by cold. You shall seek similar and related Philosophical discourses on generation in Physics <note>original: *Physica*; in this period, "Physics" referred to the broader study of natural science and medicine</note>. Menstruation is not the "flower" of the woman, as a flower is to a tree; rather, it is the excretion of the womb—that is, of those things by which it is nourished. Once nutrition has occurred, the womb casts out the surplus which is unfit for nourishment. It casts it out every month, just as the stomach and liver do daily. Nor is menstruation anything other than dung; it is by no means a "flower." It is the dung of the womb, just as excrement is the dung of the stomach and urine is the dung of the liver, as you will understand in Physics concerning the specific diseases of women.

# TREATISE THE THIRD

## CHAPTER ONE

<margin>How seed is drawn into the womb.</margin>
Furthermore, we must also speak of the seed—what sort of thing it is if it lies stored in the womb, as we have described before. In the beginning, it is so subtle that it can be blunted and hindered by various accidents of ill health, no differently than any other fresh seed cast into the earth. Thus it sustains various impulses and has many impediments before it is conceived. But we refer the examination of these things to Physics, continuing our text on the augmentation of the body. Understand then, that many members exist in the body, such as veins, bones, marrow, and others, just as you know them from the whole human being. Indeed, as many members as exist in the body, so many "seeds" <note>referring to the biological essences or "blueprints" of those specific parts</note> go out from them. But I would have you receive the text in this way: <margin>The fluids of the parts follow their constitutions.</margin> namely, that there is a Liquor <note>original: *Liquor*; a vital fluid or essence</note> which contains the bones of the whole body; another liquor again which preserves the marrow; another the veins; and so on for the rest. This is the rule: If someone’s hand is cut off, a fetus is not immediately born without a hand for that reason. The reason is: that the liquor of that hand was by no means taken away from him, but only the *place* of the liquor was torn away. If, however, the hand becomes diseased from the liquor itself, then the hand of the fetus is also imbued with that vice. For all diseases that proceed from the liquor are transferred by heredity to the fetus, unless perhaps the other seed <note>the seed of the other parent</note> suppresses and overcomes it. Relegating these things to Physics, we shall apply ourselves to continuing our text, in which all the forms, defects, and affections of children shall be described, and from whence they arise.

## CHAPTER II

Hitherto we have discussed enough concerning the operations of the man and woman. And yet, if we begin on the formation of children, we shall add more to them. Know therefore that two seeds wage war with one another for the sake of the form. For out of them one human being is constituted, which is nature's way. But nevertheless, for the sake of generating either a male or a female, a certain struggle occurs. For it must become one of the two, and it is necessary that one be entirely overcome and suppressed by the other. But if not, then the generation of Hermaphrodites occurs, which are both male and female at once in one subject. The cause of this is that the mastery of each seed is then equal, and one does not take away the property of the other. When this happens, a Hermaphrodite is born. <margin>When hermaphrodites are born.</margin> But even among these there is a distinction. For although they are of both sexes, they do not have the properties of both equally; rather, they are so distinguished that they are at least one or the other, never perfectly a woman, nor perfectly a man. And so they are a monster produced from an error of nature; and that sometimes perfectly in one or the other sex, and occasionally in both, though more rarely.

<margin>When twins are generated.</margin>
This is the origin of twins: If the womb has attracted to itself the seed of both the man and the woman, yet has not attracted the whole amount that is in the whole body of both at one and the same time, but rather one portion at one turn, another at a second turn, and a third at a third turn; then, as many portions as are attracted, so many fetuses are constituted. Understand it more clearly in this way: If the womb draws, it draws any seed at one turn as a whole and entire thing. Meanwhile, however, it can become tired, so that if it has attracted half the seed, it later grows faint; and yet immediately in a moment, before the operation of the attractive power fades away, recovering itself, it sucks in or entices the remaining part as well.

And understand this through an example: it should be understood as if a great supply of material is to be drawn, but due to the laziness or weakness of the "drawer," at least half the part is pulled first, and then the second and third parts are drawn one after another. Similar things happen in the womb whenever it begins its work without completing the attraction in one go; instead, it rests a little from the first pull, and while the power has not yet completely ceased, it renews and reintegrates that drawing action. And as often as this happens, nature places and arranges the attracted part into its own private location. This is how twins or multiple fetuses are produced. And the more that are produced, the weaker they are. Although it is also <margin>Twins larger or smaller than each other.</margin> true that twins sometimes grow no less than if they had been made as a single fetus. However, a cause can be given for this outcome: namely, that nature exists so strongly on both sides for growth that no smallness can remain. For the great size of infants and adults does not come from the quantity of matter (as the **Physicians** <note>In the 16th century, "Physicians" often referred to those following the traditional Galenic or Scholastic medical schools, whom the author frequently critiques.</note> foolishly claim). Rather, size and strength emerge from the nature and condition of the **growing power** <term>auctrix facultas: the inherent biological force responsible for expansion and development</term>, which exists strongly in both parents; or from the proportion of the mixture of seeds; or from the health and vigor of the growing power within the fetus itself. Indeed, the manner in which the seed slips into the womb also contributes <margin>Another cause of twins.</margin> something to the production of twins. If the seed falls while slipping into the womb: then sometimes one part is carried into it more precipitously than the other, with the womb not drawing the whole mass at once, but drawing what is left later by its own strength. For in this way, two or more fetuses are established. For any single seed is sufficiently abundant and large to establish one, two, three, ten, or twenty fetuses—which, however, would have no defect or vice in their size, provided that the **growing power** within them flourishes with enough strength and robustness. For from the seed from which two fetuses are produced, full and perfect in every stature, even if only a single infant had been born, it would never have grown to a larger mass than those two.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The cause of monsters.</margin> **H**ere we must also refer to the fact that children are sometimes born with imperfect and monstrous shapes: such as with two heads, with more hands, fingers, and feet, or with members more or less numerous than the fair and established order of nature. The cause of these is that sometimes nature in the **liquor of life** <note>original: *liquore vitæ*; the vital fluid or seed containing the blueprint for the body</note> is not at all whole and perfect. Therefore, whatever limb is held back by some defect of perfection, that same limb of the fetus is afterward perverted and changed in the same way. And this happens in various ways. For sometimes the "capital seed" <note>the portion of the seed destined to become the head</note> is divided alone while slipping in, while the seeds of the other parts remain united and joined. <margin>How two-headed ones are born.</margin> In that case, the fetus is born two-headed. Sometimes the seed for the fingers becomes three-fold, or is divided more or fewer times. And the fingers of the fetus are formed in such a number. For not only are whole twins made, but sometimes "half-twins" and many other monsters of this kind. It also sometimes happens that the seed of some limb, because of the laboring fluid within it, or an obstruction of the pathways, or the weakness of the attracting womb, remains away entirely and is not added. That part is then necessarily missing in the fetus as well. And monsters of nature of this kind are born whenever the seeds are either not attracted equally, or are divided during the slip, or one seed is missing, or another perishes, or something is absent from those things required for a perfect seed. For then fetuses are either born monstrously, or two are joined by one head, or they are deformed in any other way, according to the cause already explained. However, you shall judge these errors in such a way that you determine that twins are a legitimate birth and according to nature, if the **growing power** is present, perfect and strong in the womb, and is instilled into the fetus from there. All other births are faulty and result from some error. For any error admitted during conception produces a faulty and mangled fetus. For if anything happens otherwise than according to the order of nature, then nature is disturbed and precipitated in its functions. Yet she works upon the seed already conceived only as much as is within her power. Hence, faulty births are born afterward. For it was so arranged by God that all things should happen according to nature. If things do not happen according to His order and manner, then the operation is neither whole nor praiseworthy.

Other faulty births are also born in the womb, about which we instruct you thus. <margin>Whence worm-like births.</margin> For sometimes "worm-like" beings are produced, of various shapes and species. The cause of these is mostly a mixture of abuse and petulance <note>likely a reference to illicit or "unnatural" sexual acts in the author's view</note>, through which the womb entices a "foreign seed," from which monsters of this kind are then brought forth against nature, so great...

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The period of the growing fetus.</margin>
Just as we have defined the seed up to this point and the various ways it is placed in the womb, we shall now set aside further explanation of this material and add the doctrine concerning the seed: how it grows and increases in this particular way. God has preordained for the infant its own time for how long it ought to grow, namely 40 weeks; just as He has also defined and fixed the time for cows, doves, and others. Behold, then, the reason how in this interval of time the seed becomes a fetus. First, then, after conception has occurred in the manner described, **Nature** <note>Often personified in these texts as the "craftsman" or "alchemist" of the body.</note> approaches and arranges the seed and separates it as it should: the "head seed" to the head, the "arm seed" to the place of the arm, and so forth. Once this arrangement is properly made, the womb then rests from its labor and does nothing else thereafter. Following this, **material nature** takes over and brings the fetus to growth, so that all the parts that were arranged may grow, increase, and become a body, each according to its own proportion. Thus, what pertains to the flesh becomes flesh; what concerns the bone becomes bone; what is added to the veins

<margin>In what way they are grafted.</margin>
becomes a vein; what is applied to the internal organs becomes an organ. Therefore, if the seed is no longer seed (as it once was) but is now blood and flesh fitting for a human, then material nature itself recedes from the fetus. It is succeeded by the **Grace of God**, which implants and imparts to the fetus—according to the quality of a human—life and those other things owed to a living creature, such as sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell. At that time, the **growth faculty** <term>facultas auctrix: the inherent biological force responsible for physical development</term> is also present in the fetus. Once life has been implanted in the human by God according to the mode of nature, the fetus grows in the mother’s womb until all the limbs have received their proper strength, stability, and solidness. When all these have been introduced, the **spirit** is finally inserted into it, along with the **soul**, **reason**, and **intellect**, and all those things that follow the soul. After all these things, the time of birth finally follows.

<margin>When the soul is given to the fetus.</margin>
For the soul and those things which cohere to it, being impatient with the delay in the mother’s womb, strive for an exit at the appointed time; this happens at the end of the period of the aforementioned weeks. You will find more concerning these parts in the **Paramirum** <note>A reference to Paracelsus’ major work, *Opus Paramirum*, where he discusses the origin of diseases and the soul.</note>, where the origin of the soul will be treated. The method has now been handed down to you: first, how the conceived seed is formed and arranged; second, how it is changed into blood and flesh; then, how the fetus grows and becomes large; and finally, how it is endowed and imbued with spirit and soul.

For as long as it is too weak and feeble to sustain or bear the earth, the spirit is not conferred or implanted into it. For this strength is the maturation of the spirit and the bestowing of the soul itself. For only after the spirit does the soul finally arrive. Indeed, the soul enters no body in which the spirit does not already exist. And this itself is sometimes the cause why, during the period of growth, a fetus can change into a monster: it is not fit for receiving a soul. But when the growth of the fetus has been led to the point where no further error can occur, only then does the spirit enter, which is the precursor of the soul. The soul then follows the spirit. From that time on, the fetus grows and overflows into the union of body and soul, until it can no longer endure the lack of air, nor tolerate the nourishment of the womb any longer. All these things the birth finally follows and concludes.

### TREATISE III.

At the same time, everything required for a perfect and complete human being must be brought together, such as *sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch*, as well as further faculties like *reason, wisdom, understanding*, and other related traits. Lest we forget, it must also be mentioned to you that many people have indeed received a soul, but are either deprived of sight, or devoid of hearing, etc., or they lack intellect or are destitute of wisdom. Concerning all these, we determine the following: in every single human being, all those parts are present. If by chance 

<margin>
How sometimes a certain faculty is lacking.
</margin>

one of these is missing at any time—such as sight—the cause is this: namely, that the seed of the instrument of the eye and the **cells of sight** <term>cells: referring to the medieval medical belief that the brain was divided into specific "cells" or chambers for different senses and mental functions</term> did not concur. Therefore, because no place was provided, no natural operation can occur in that place. God, indeed, did not deny him sight; rather, Nature did not instill it, either because of a defect in the instrument, or because of its own error, or for some other reason. The same judgment applies to hearing. Concerning **reason** <note>original: "ratione"</note>, however, it must be believed that it is withheld from no one, but is given to all, full and intact. If, however, any fault or defect is present, the cause depends on the fact that the cells of reason, memory, and the senses were not arranged and placed soundly, but vitiously, erroneously, and unnaturally. Therefore, because they were poorly placed by nature, the spirit cannot operate properly through them or within them. And since we are speaking of "cells," you ought to understand the matter in this way: that an immature seed of a certain **raw liquor of life** <note>A vital essence or fluid in Paracelsian thought that determines the health and formation of the organism.</note> causes this. Whoever among men has a raw—that is, a polluted—liquor, cannot produce a good and upright seed. If the body of the seed is foul, prideful, or foolish, such children will also turn out and be born. However, a pure liquor grants a pure seed. From this seed, pure and sincere offspring are born, perfect in all members, lacking neither reason, nor sight, nor anything else. But if that purity is lacking, no reason is found. Similarly, this is the same cause for children who are lame, crooked, or born poorly in any other way. From useless and vitious liquor, such children are born according to its condition. But as to where and how such liquor is produced, we refer the matter to the **Physicians** <term>Physicos: natural philosophers or medical doctors</term>. And with these things mentioned, we now wish the universal generations of man to be concluded and finished.

### CHAPTER VI.

**P**roviding a finishing touch to this first book, you must also be fortified and instructed against 

<margin>
How the mother's sight causes harm.
</margin>

certain objections of the common folk, who are accustomed to saying with one voice: *this or that woman received this or that mark from a sight:* which is exactly as if they were to say, *the pregnant woman received a monstrous fetus through sight.* To these, we give this response: that sight does not change the fetus at all, and that the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> of a sight brings no harm to the mother. However, the beginning of the offense can arise from this: either fear, or shock and wonder, or any other more serious **emotion** <note>original: "pathema"</note> so greatly shakes and strikes the woman that the blood—

<margin>
Concussion of the fetus.
</margin>

the nourishment of the fetus—is either violently withdrawn or rushes in and overflows in a mass; thus, the nature of the **womb** <term>matrix: the uterus, seen as an active, formative organ</term> is changed through these more violent accidents. Because of this change, the fetus is then shaken in the womb, which always appears more serious in fetuses than in other people. For the fetus is most tender and soft, so that when the blood leaps forth from consternation more abundantly toward the womb, the fetus can easily be branded with spots. If that same blood happens to become foul, it can foully stain and contaminate the fetus either in some parts or even in its whole body, so that whatever member of the entire body is touched in that place 

<margin>
How various things are branded.
</margin>

becomes discolored and defiled. But this also pertains to Physics. Yet another thing remains in this place. For it often happens that the form of a crab, a fish, an acorn, a mouse, or some other similar shape is imprinted on the fetus. Observe a few things about this. If a woman during the period of pregnancy eats a crab with great desire: that appetite does not press from the **stomach** <note>original: "ventriculo"</note> as in other humans, but 

<margin>
The appetite of pregnant women comes from the womb, not the stomach.
</margin>

rises from the womb. Therefore, as soon as it is ingested, it is joined to the womb. For the womb attracts it with wonderful greed and is so strong and powerful in carrying it that it both eats and digests it. But the **seed** <note>original: "sperma," here referring to the essence of the food consumed</note> that is taken in with the crab is attached to the fetus as something similar; and that eventually even grows into the fetus and is imprinted upon it, just like a shadow on a wall. For whatever the womb most greedily desires, that thing penetrates into it, and is not cooked and subdued in the stomach like other foods. And although the waste is indeed separated in the stomach, the rest is entirely carried into the womb. Therefore, if the pregnant woman does not happen to satisfy such an appetite, then harm is imprinted on the fetus—not the stomach—because the womb has been offended and is "angry" or indignant. This, therefore, is the unique cause of these things: that the essence of the thing eaten is drawn into the womb, and afterwards, in the manner of a seed, degenerates into a vitious mass or form. But because this happens contrary to nature, it can only be compared to shadows; of which more will be said where we discuss **Impressions**.

## PART ON THE HUMAN CONDITION.

### CHAPTER I.

After we have, up to this point, sufficiently dealt with the generation of man, and have put forward the opinion that God certainly created man himself in the beginning—and afterwards attributed seed to him, so that he might sow and plant descendants like himself—now, consequently and rightly, we shall next recount to you several things concerning the state of man, *namely, what it is like and how it is carried out until his dissolution, toward which he is preserved.*

<margin>What the corporeal part of man is.</margin>
Therefore, to make this clearer, we shall divide the state of man into two parts: namely, the *corporeal* part which he has within himself, and the *eternal* part. Thus, there will be two treatments of this part: one on the decaying or mortal, and the other on the *eternal* and *immortal*, both of which nevertheless dwell in one man. The *corporeal* or decaying part is that which sustains the eternal, just as an **Innkeeper** <term>Innkeeper: Latin "Pandochæus," a host who receives all guests. The author uses this as a metaphor for the physical body serving as a temporary lodging for the soul.</term> sustains a guest. To this benefit, another divine gift was added: namely, that which sustains the body itself while it preserves the soul. This, however, is the "life." Concerning this, we shall not take up any special treatment. For life is such a gift, as if a prince were to give a house to someone as an honor—a house he did not owe him—at least for the reason that in that lodging, he might manage his other possessions more safely and pleasantly. We shall not relegate such matters to the boundaries of Philosophy; for there seem to lie hidden beneath them things much greater and more sublime than those which can be discovered through philosophical experience.

<margin>Philosophical matters through experience.</margin>
For in the beginning, before we proceed to the declaration of the following text, we shall teach this concerning the condition of Philosophy: that it draws its entire origin from experience. But that which has escaped experience is merely an "experiment" <note>the author distinguishes between "experientia" (established, reliable knowledge) and "experimentum" (a mere trial or uncertain attempt)</note>. From which it rightly follows...

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Censure of Physicians.</margin>
Now, turning to the text itself, we shall first uncover and make plain to you the unformed nonsense of the Physicians (whom we should by no means deign to call by the name of Physician, but since you call yourselves such, we shall wink at that title). These men, when treating the state and condition of man, define him by **four complexions** <term>complexions: the "temperaments" (Sanguine, Choleric, Melancholic, Phlegmatic) believed in medieval medicine to govern human health and personality</term>, and just as many humors, qualities, and other similar digressions. It would be right, however, for no Physician to utter anything unless he had first worn down the furthest limits of Philosophy, as is appropriate for a Naturalist. But as many of them are born of **Astronomy** <note>here used disparagingly to mean "astrology" or those who rely on stars rather than physical observation</note>, they enter into a league of gestures with charlatans, and on both sides, insofar as they differ regarding the nature of man, they paint and veil their doctrine with no few lies. 

However, so that we may grant True Philosophy its right, we shall propose the state of man as it was brought forth in its generation—a perfect and complete human being. This shall be done in the following discourse. First of all, the first man must be considered, from whom all other things proceed. Here, however, two humans occur, established in the beginning: namely, man and woman. From these two flowed all the nature of other men, and whatever exists anywhere within them (as far as the fragility of life is concerned). But as for his spirit, and the eternal part itself, and his reason, wisdom, and the soul itself, we shall defer that to its own treatise. For although reason, wisdom, and prudence are distributed equally to all men, not everyone perceives all things with equal ease, due to a defect in the shaping and composition of the **bodily instruments** <note>original: "instrumentorum corporeorum"; referring to the physical organs, particularly the brain, which act as tools for the soul</note>. Setting these matters aside here, we shall explain the generation, origin, and reason...

<margin>
Neither man nor woman has seed in their healthy nature.
</margin>
...you ought to understand the meaning of this chapter, which teaches this one thing: namely, that seed does not grow or come forth from the human being out of nature itself. Nature contributes nothing to the eliciting and generating of seed, nor does it even stimulate the human being in regard to seed. Thus, in the human being, nature exists alone, apart from seed and apart from the mixing of nature and seed—just as is understood regarding non-sentient things, in which both are present as a mixture, though it is not the same in the human being. From this, you ought to gather that in a non-sentient creature, any given thing is a **Matrix** <note>In this context, "Matrix" refers to a generative womb or the fundamental environment that gives form to matter.</note> by itself, even without a male; and that which is considered masculine among them also exists as a Matrix by itself. For it also carries seed. In the human being, however, the matter stands differently. He who is a man does not contain seed in himself for the purpose of propagating his kind. Likewise, neither does the woman. Thus, they are without seed and are established in a free nature, into which no seminal condition has been implanted. In this sense, any non-sentient things are a **Matrix**; sentient things, however, are the opposite. Thus, the human being stands free, without innate seed, and does not have a mixture similar to or of the same kind as plants.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>
Where seed is present, the light of nature is absent.
</margin>
**N**ow that it has been demonstrated and settled that the human being does not contain seed in himself proceeding from his nature, it must now be illustrated by the following example. It is known to all of you that none of you begets anything from nature itself, but that you are free and empty of all seed, pure and unmixed in that nature from which you have drawn the **Light of Nature** <note>original: "lux naturae"; a central Paracelsian concept referring to the innate wisdom and divine reason that allows humans to understand the natural world.</note> itself. However, where seed is present in nature, there the Light of Nature does not shine, but is dead. Take this as proof: it is known to you that a human being carrying seed <note>The author here refers to the state of being consumed by sexual impulse or "lustful seed."</note> uses no reason, nor does he live according to reason, but is consumed in mere pleasures and Venusian <note>relating to Venus, the goddess of love; here meaning erotic or sexual.</note> fantasies. Why we speak here of the human being "carrying seed," even though we just recently taught concerning his "free nature," we shall explain the reason for this to you in the following chapter. But regarding the previous text, attend to this:

<margin>
Why man was brought forth by God.
</margin>
God surely created the human being so sublime, lofty, and vigorous that He willed him alone to move and live entirely free in the Light of Nature. From this, we can freely philosophize without any contradiction that it is necessary for every philosopher to be both divine and natural at once,

---

<margin>
Why man was stripped of seed by God.
</margin>
to live in the Light of Nature and by no means in "seed," which is **ALLARA** <note>original: "ALLARA"; a technical term in Paracelsian thought likely referring to the crude, physical matter of generation that competes with spiritual light.</note>. And so that we may explain the matter to you from its foundation, know that God, the creator of all things, established the human being alone in the Light of Nature so that he might be free and unconstrained. For this reason, He took seed away from his nature and did not implant it in him, specifically because of the **Eternal** <note>the soul or divine spark</note> which flourishes within him. For God demands a pure human being, not one who is "altered"—which is what seed makes him, if it should cling to his nature. Note this concluding point: God created man and woman, and He gave seed to neither, lest by any chance they should be cast out of the Light of Nature through lust. Yet, for the propagation of the kind, He granted them **Free Will**, and at the same time He also gave them seed, so that they might choose to beget or not to beget. Moreover, He placed seed into their **Fantasy** <note>original: "phantasia"; here meaning the creative imagination or the mind's ability to visualize.</note> originally and materially, according to all its conditions, in this manner: if a man hungers to beget, then his **Speculation** <note>original: "speculatio"; the act of looking at or contemplating an object of desire.</note> arouses lust within him. Lust then begets the seed for him, as will be demonstrated more clearly hereafter. Thus, seed was placed by God into "speculation." To "speculation," however, free will was granted, either to arouse lust or to let it sleep. And his nature does not toil at this; rather,

<margin>
Why free will was granted to man. What is the Object?
</margin>
only the **Object** does. For it is an "Object" if a man looks upon a woman. But it remains within his power whether he wishes or does not wish to comply with that which is implanted in his reason—namely, what the Object contains within itself. For God bestowed reason upon the human being so that he might know what kind of thing lust is. He himself, however, can either despise or desire it, exercise it or omit it, and either command his reason or succumb to it. Therefore, God inserted seed into the imagination of the human being, in which all intellect is situated, along with the knowledge of the "Object" that ignites and tickles his speculation. If he does not assent to this, no seed is in him, but only the Light of Nature.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
How seed is made in both sexes.
</margin>
**W**hat we have said of the man applies to the woman as well. If she sees a man, she beholds her "Object." Speculation then follows: what is a man? And reason, or rather intellect, is given by God. ## THE SECOND TREATISE.

### CHAPTER I.

From our previous chapters, you can gather and remember that you were forewarned to understand the logic of the seed: that is, the seed itself and the logic of nature were not created joined together within the human being; rather, nature was established separately. Furthermore, the logic of the seed—that is, the <term>speculation</term> <note>original: *speculationem*. In this context, it refers to a "mirroring" or a powerful mental imaging that directs nature.</note>—arises from its object, just as God ordained those things: Nature, certainly, for the life of the human body, but the "object" for the seed; and both truly for themselves separately. By this reasoning, whatever possesses an object that rouses the seed does not possess that seed as something implanted or inhabiting it permanently. Although for the sake of greater understanding it would be fitting here to introduce the brute beasts, who also understand their "object" and know its nature. For in this way, the innate speculation that exists in beasts causes that operation and rouses the seed, and not their nature alone. God similarly placed this within them toward an object. Nevertheless, the logic of the spirit flourishes in man alone, and in no other. Therefore, we shall begin to speak of man, how he may be generated: we shall discuss the matter from which he is made, and finally his formation and growth. Therefore, attend to the text of the following chapters.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The matter of the seed is the will.</margin>

The text of the generation of man, then, proceeds in order. God placed the matter of the seed for man within the <term>will</term>, which he takes from his object. If, therefore, a man has assented to the object and fulfilled the will in speculation: then from that speculation the <term>liquor of life</term> <note>original: *liquor vitæ*. A vital, spiritual fluid that Paracelsus believed contained the blueprint of the entire body.</note> is ignited, and the seed of another human is made. This is how the matter stands in the male, and likewise in the female. At other times, the liquor itself remains merely liquor and does not become seed. However, it then becomes seed because it exists distributed and divided throughout the entire body. Similarly, every nature, property, condition, and species of the limbs is a spirit within it. And just as the body consists in its formation, so too does the liquor of life. Nor is the liquor of life anything other than the hidden man: for that which hides it is the visible part.

<margin>The dignity of the liquor of life.</margin>

Moreover, the liquor of life in a human can be compared to nothing more aptly than to a shadow on a wall. It is projected by the man and formed according to his measure. Such is the liquor. It is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "little world"; the idea that the human being contains the entire universe in miniature.</note>, it is the inner shadow. Yet it has its own substance with it, its own tangibility and sensibility, and the idea, substance, and nature of all the limbs of the entire body; it is the most noble of all things that exist in the human body. And although it does not have a soul and borrows its life from the body, rather than having it from itself: nevertheless, it is that "other man." For just as someone gazes at themselves in a mirror, so nature contemplates itself within this liquor: and thus it is in man, without damage or detriment to the body.

The seed that is produced in this way, *as has been said*, lies quiet in its places and seats, just as the seats of the liquor are in the body: namely, the hands in the hands, the feet in the feet, the heart in the heart, the brain in the brain, and so on. Nor is there any one peculiar place into which the seed falls and rests; rather, it is preserved in its own receptacles in which its liquor and matter are contained. It is separated from the liquor of life, however, like foam from broth or must.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The discharge of sperm is false.</margin>
**L**et us proceed, however, in the context of our argument. The <term>sperma</term><note>The author distinguishes between *sperma* (the physical discharge/fluid) and *semen* (the vital "seed" or spiritual blueprint).</note>, which is poured forth from the spermatic vessels, is a discharge of the <term>liquor of life</term><note>original: *liquor vitae*; the vital fluid that permeates the body.</note>, which is purified and separated, just as dung is separated from food. Thus, the sperm has no other purification than that which occurs through the kindling of the object. Once this kindling has occurred, the liquor casts the discharge into the spermatic vessels and retains the seed within itself. However, the <term>semen</term><note>The true seed or vital principle.</note>, from which a human is born, remains in the liquor and does not pass into the sperm.

<margin>The objection is cleared away.</margin>
At this point, however, we shall discuss a certain argument that might be raised against us by those blind Physicians and some of the ancient Philosophers who agree with them, namely this:
> *It is established for us by certain experience that the image of a man is generated from the sperm. This, however, is not sufficient for a human being, but only for a likeness. Although that might not lie in the place where it ought to lie, as our adversaries speak, thinking that a human can be made from it, and is entirely made from it: in this they are hallucinating. For their thought and art are more intent on money than on the truth.*

But hold this as the solution to this argument. The sperm is such a discharge from the liquor of life that it has the power, during digestion, to also take on the formation which the liquor contains in its own nature. For the liquor of life is the "form" of the body. Thus, the sperm also retains that same form within itself and has the power of forming, just like the liquor. Yet you ought to understand the matter itself in this way: that surely nothing else is born from the sperm but the form which exists in the liquor. And this is a natural operation: there is no life there, no sensibility, no sight, no hearing, no taste, no smell. All these things are in the seed perfectly, entirely, and without defect. Therefore, the sperm is a part of the liquor of life, which is the <term>microcosm</term><note>The idea that the human body is a "little world" reflecting the entire universe.</note>. And if it shakes out its discharge from the kindling, then it clings by a certain part to the property of the liquor—that is, to the form—and nothing further.

### CHAPTER V.

**H**aving set aside the previous discourses, let us extend our consideration to the female.

---

Since you have heard that the aforementioned sperm is at least a discharge, but not truly the seed: although we would gladly demonstrate this to you more clearly and lucidly, your own intelligence makes us judge that what has been recounted so far is sufficient. Concerning the seed itself, understand it this way. We defined above that the seed, after its inflammation, rests unmoved in the place where it is situated; that is, distributed through the entire body, and not yet begetting any human. Only that <term>amber</term><note>original: *succinum*; amber was famously known for its "static" or "magnetic" ability to attract light objects when rubbed.</note> lures and carries it to the places of generation, where it must mature.

<margin>The amber of the female elicits it.</margin>
Understand this thus. In the beginning, you must remember that the man has at least half the seed, and the female has the other half. These two, therefore, contribute the whole seed. But pay attention to how these are joined. In the <term>matrix</term><note>The womb.</note> there lies hidden an attractive power, which is like amber and a magnet, being surely powerful enough to attract the female parts.

<margin>The attractive power of the womb.</margin>
That attractive power of the womb breaks forth and exerts itself when the seed has already been produced. And therefore, if those works—which are stirred up according to the assent of the imagination—are instituted: then the womb lures the seed of the humor to itself, as much from the man as from the woman; and indeed from the heart, from the liver, from the spleen, from the bones, from the marrow, from the veins, from the muscles, from the blood, from the flesh, and from all those things contained in the body.

<margin>Every part has its own seed.</margin>
For whatever is a specific part in the body also has its own specific seed. All seeds, however, attracted from every member, make at least one seed if they flow together. And thus the womb draws to itself the true seed mixed with the sperm from both persons. Therefore, mention must again be made of those Physicians who, occupied with sperm as if with nature itself, try to make women fertile, and the men as well: which is nevertheless a pure and simple fabrication.

<margin>Reproof of the Physicians.</margin>
For as long as the attractive faculty of the womb does not act from its own nature, the seed is not carried to those places, and consequently, no infant is born. And if the sperm were the seed itself, as they trifle, a fetus would be made without a womb; as was said before, know that the womb is so often washed and filled that children ought to be born daily. But they have not looked out carefully enough for their own lie.

TREATISE II.

<margin>The method of arranging the members of the body.</margin>
...the womb-nature: thus we shall further describe the <term>microcosm</term><note>A "little world"; the belief that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note> to you in this way. If all the seeds from all parts have flowed together into the <term>matrix</term><note>original: *matrix*; the womb or the creative environment where life is formed.</note>, then the nature of the womb separates the seed of the head, the brain, the crystalline, and similar parts to their own locations, and thus disposes the limbs where they ought to be, just as an architect of a house arranges and places the wood. Now, if every single seed lies in the womb as it ought to lie, then that is called a Microcosm. For there, all things required to constitute a human being are gathered and joined together—life and the soul alone excepted, as you will hear in what follows. 

<margin>The seed of one person is insufficient for generation.</margin>
Concerning the "half-seed," however, observe this: the solitary seed of one human being is certainly not perfect or sufficient for generating a person. The reason is that God wills one human to be born from two, not from one alone. From the inner sanctuaries of Philosophy, we offer this reason: if a human existed in the seed of only one person, then no species would be generated from that human other than exactly what he himself was. In this way, his offspring would be constituted just as a walnut is born from itself, and for that reason is identical to the one from which it emerged. Thus, in all trees, like is only from like: just as a walnut tree produces all nuts similar to one another, with nothing changed in any of them. The same logic applies to man. If he were generated by one person alone, he would become entirely like the father, who would be both his father and mother. In this way, men would be of only one figure, and one would perpetually be similar to the other, and there would be but one seed and one nature flourishing.

<margin>The source of human diversity.</margin>
However, in the meantime, the mingling of seeds made by women and men introduces that variety, so that one human never becomes exactly like another. For the seed in its union always concurs in an unequal weight, so that it is never so perfectly balanced that a human could be born who would be entirely similar to both the father and the mother. Always one seed or the other "breaks" the other: that is, it changes its likeness. And this is the sole cause why one human is never born identical to another.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The characteristics of the mingled seeds.</margin>
After the womb has conceived and hidden the seeds within itself, the approaching Womb-Nature joins and unites the seeds of the man and the woman. Whichever of these is the strongest and best shapes the other into its own likeness, either in its entirety or for the most part. Let an example be given: the seed from the brain of the man, and likewise from the woman—these two joined together constitute only one brain. Yet, whichever of them is most potent makes and forms the offspring in its likeness. Nevertheless, it never assimilates it perfectly or exactly. The reason is that an "infringement" has been introduced by the other seed, through which a change in form continually occurs. And the further one is born from the other, the greater and more certain the variation from the likeness becomes. Thus, the seed of the nose forms the nose in the offspring according to the proportion and mixture of both parents. So too, mouth shapes mouth, and limb shapes limb. From this also, **hereditary diseases** follow.

<margin>The qualities of their seed are brought together.</margin>
Depending on how the dominance of this or that seed turns out: the more one seed surpasses the other in the "goodness of generation," the more the offspring is rendered similar to it. However, it is prepared differently with the generation of either a male or a female, namely in this way. Before nature arranges the seed to produce the offspring, as we have mentioned, a certain operation precedes it, which works like this: If the womb attracts the seed to itself, the first operation is within it, and that seed "tints" the other. Thus one surpasses the other, not in the form or figure of the offspring or its limbs, but only in its nature. 

<margin>The generation of a male or a female.</margin>
And there, a natural struggle is joined, though not touching the seed itself. This predominance does not arise from the virtue of the seed, but from the virtue of the nature of both parents, compelling the seed into the uterus. In this way, whichever seed the womb first attracts to itself from those two, that seed generates either a male or a female. If the woman's seed is drawn in before the man's, a female is made; if the opposite occurs, a male is generated.

### CHAPTER VIII.

To resume the text, therefore, note that we have placed the seed within the free will of man. If he wills it, he can. Even if these things please others less, we are not at all distressed on their account. For the consideration of things, and the comparison of one with another, does not give birth to any other Philosophy. 

<margin>Why seed and sperm are two different things.</margin>
A distinction must also be noted: how **seed** and **sperm** are two different things. For if every sperm were seed, offspring would be born daily, both in pregnant women and otherwise. But because the womb attracts only once, and not multiple times, note therefore that nothing comes from the sperm. But from Philosophy, we will communicate a still more subtle instruction to you, in this way: because we have discussed the seed of the womb, you might gather that as often as an object is presented to someone, so often he exists ready and prepared for the emission of seed. Understand it thus.

# THIRD TREATISE.

## CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>How the seed is delivered into the womb.</margin>
**F**urthermore, we must speak of the seed and what kind of thing it is if it lies stored in the womb, as we described before. In the beginning, it is so subtle and delicate that it can be dulled or hindered by various accidents of ill health, no differently than any other fresh seed cast into the earth. Thus it endures various impulses and encounters many obstacles before it is conceived. But we refer the examination of these things to Physics, continuing our text regarding growth. Understand, therefore, that many members exist in the body, such as veins, bones, marrow, and others, just as you recognize them from the whole human being. Indeed, as many members as exist in the body, so many "seeds" <note>original: *semina*; the author believes each body part contributes a specific essence to the reproductive seed.</note> depart from them.
<margin>The fluids constitute the fetus at birth.</margin>
But I would have you receive the text in this way: *namely, that there is a Liquor which contains the bones of the whole body; again, another liquor which preserves the marrow; another for the veins.* and so on for the rest. This is the rule: if someone’s hand is cut off, a fetus is not immediately born without a hand for that reason. The reason is that the <term>liquor</term><note>A vital, formative fluid or essence associated with a specific organ.</note> of that hand was by no means taken away from him, but only the *place* of the liquor was torn away. If, however, the hand grows sick from the liquor itself, then the hand of the fetus is also imbued with that defect. For all diseases that proceed from the liquor are transferred by heredity to the fetus, unless perhaps the other parent's seed overwhelms and conquers them. Relegating these matters to Physics, we shall apply ourselves to continuing our text, in which all the forms, defects, and conditions of children shall be described, and from whence they arise.

## CHAP. II.

**H**itherto we have discussed enough regarding the operations of the man and the woman. And yet, when we begin with the formation of children, we shall add more to those things. Know, therefore, that two seeds do not wage war against each other for the sake of the form. For from them one human being is constituted, which is the work of nature. Nevertheless, for the sake of the generation of either a male or a female, a certain contest occurs. For it is necessary that one of the two be made, and it is necessary that one be entirely overcome and oppressed by the other. If this does not happen, then the generation of <term>Hermaphrodites</term><note>A historical term for intersex individuals; here explained as a "tie" between the male and female formative powers.</note> occurs, who are at once male and female in a single subject. The cause of this is that the mastery of both seeds is then equal, and one does not take away the property of the other. When this happens, a Hermaphrodite is born.
<margin>When hermaphrodites are born.</margin>
But there is a distinction even among these. For although they are of both sexes, they do not possess the properties of both equally, but are distinguished such that they are at least one of them; they are never perfectly female, nor perfectly male. And thus they are a "monster" produced from an error of nature; sometimes perfect in one [sex], sometimes in both, though that is rarer.

<margin>When twins are generated.</margin>
This is the origin of twins. If the womb has attracted to itself the seed of both the man and the woman, yet has not attracted the whole amount that is in both their bodies at one and the same time, but rather one portion at one turn, another at a second, and a third at a third: then, as many portions as are attracted, so many fetuses are constituted. Understand it more clearly this way: if the womb pulls, it pulls any seed at one time as a whole and integrated unit. In the meantime, however, it can become tired, so that if it has attracted half the seed, it afterwards becomes faint; and yet, in that very moment, before the operation of the attractive power fades away, it collects itself again and swallows or pulls in the remaining part as well.

...entices. This double traction <note>The "pulling" or magnetic force exerted by the womb.</note> produces a double fetus. For in this way, if the seeds are separated once, they are not united thereafter. And from this example, understand that it should not be interpreted otherwise than if, out of a great abundance to be drawn in, due to the laziness or weakness of the "puller," at least the middle part is drawn first, and then the second and third parts are pulled one after another. These things happen similarly in the <term>matrix</term><note>The womb.</note> as often as it begins its work before the traction is complete; that is, it slackens somewhat from one pull and then, while the power hasn't entirely ceased, it renews and restores that pull. And every time this happens, nature places and arranges the attracted part in a separate location. From this, twins or multiple fetuses are produced. And the more that are produced, the weaker they are. Although it is also true that twins sometimes grow no less than if they had been made as a single fetus.

<margin>From where twins are larger or smaller.</margin>
A reason for this outcome can be given: namely, that nature exists so strongly on both sides for growth that no smallness can remain. For the vastness of infants and adults does not arise from a multitude of matter (as the Doctors <note>Referring to the conventional medical authorities of the time, whom the author often critiques.</note> trifly claim). Rather, greatness and strength emerge from the nature and condition of the <term>nurturing faculty</term><note>original: *auctrix facultas*; the inherent power within the seed and womb that directs growth.</note> existing strongly in both parents, or from the proportion of the mixture of seeds, or from the health and vigor of the nurturing power within the fetus. Indeed, the manner in which the seed falls into the womb also contributes something to twins.

<margin>Another cause of twins.</margin>
If the seed, in falling into the womb, drops in: then one part of it is sometimes carried into it more precipitously than the other, with the womb not pulling the whole mass at once, but pulling what is left behind later by its own strength. For in this way, two or more fetuses are established. For any single seed is abundant and large enough to establish one, two, three, ten, or twenty fetuses—which, however, would have no defect or vice in size, provided the nurturing force flourishes within them with enough strength and robustness. For from a seed from which two fetuses are produced, full and perfect in every stature, if only a single infant had been born, it would never have grown to a larger mass than they did.

...and the established order of nature: The cause of these things is that sometimes nature is not at all whole or perfect in the <term>liquor of life</term><note>original: *liquore vitæ*; the vital fluid believed to carry the blueprint of the body.</note>. Therefore, whatever member is held by some defect of perfection, that same member of the fetus is afterwards perverted and changed in the same way. And this happens in various ways. For sometimes only the "head-seed" <note>original: *semen capitale*; the portion of the seed destined to become the head.</note> is divided during the falling-in, while the seeds of the other parts remain united and joined.

<margin>How the two-headed are born.</margin>
In that case, a two-headed fetus is born. Sometimes the "finger-seed" becomes three-forked, or is divided more often, or even more rarely. And the fingers of the fetus are formed in such a number. For not only are all twins made this way, but sometimes "half-twins" and many other such monsters occur. It also sometimes happens that the seed of some member—due to the liquor suffering within it, or an obstruction of the paths, or the weakness of the attracting womb—fails to flow out totally and absolutely, and is not added. That part is then necessarily missing in the fetus itself. And monsters of nature of this kind are born as often as the <term>sperma</term> are either not attracted equally, or are divided during the fall, or one seed is missing, or another perishes, or something is absent from those things required for a perfect seed. For then fetuses are born monstrously, or two are joined by one head, or they are deformed in whatever other way the cause has already been explained. You shall judge such errors in this way: determine that twins are a legitimate birth, as much according to nature as a single birth, if the nurturing force is present, perfect, and strong in the womb, and is also instilled into the fetus from there. All other births are faulty and arise from some error. For any error admitted during conception produces a faulty and maimed fetus. If anything happens otherwise than according to the order of nature, then nature, hurried in its functions, is disturbed. Yet nature works upon the already conceived seed only as much as is within its powers. From this, faulty offspring are later born. For it was so ordained by God that all things should happen according to nature. If things do not happen according to His order and manner, then the operation is neither whole nor praiseworthy.

...with such great variety and wandering that their number cannot be described. It also happens sometimes that the seeds of animals are taken in either with food or drink and ingested; if these enter the body, the <term>matrix</term><note>The womb.</note> attracts them and fashions monsters within itself. Sometimes animals are even swallowed along with the seed. If this happens to women, such creatures can easily be born within them. Occasionally, little animals of this kind enter through the womb and are mixed with it. However, such defective births reside solely in the seed. For whatever comes from animals are pure seeds. In an animal, there is no <term>liquor of life</term><note>original: *vitae liquor*; a vital fluid or essence that Paracelsus believed distinguished human life from that of lower animals.</note>; rather, all their seed exists as <term>sperm</term><note>original: *sperma*; here used in a technical sense to mean raw biological matter lacking the divine spiritual component found in human "semen".</note>. Whatever seed they have is merely their discarded matter, as we shall relate concerning the seed of animals. 

It can also happen that monsters of this kind are produced from the seed of humans in this way: if, while the act is being performed, the seed is retained in the body so that the womb does not attract the male seed, while the female seed has already been conceived, a defective birth can easily be born from this seed—namely, an imperfect human of animal-like form. For if one seed glides in without the other and takes on growth, then the birth will be born least perfect. Thus, from pure and unmixed seed, a strange and unknown human can be born. And there are many such cases, all of which are included under the aforementioned categories.

### CAP. IV.

<margin>The period of the growing fetus.</margin>
**J**ust as we have until now defined the seed and the various ways it is placed into the womb, so leaving further explanation of this matter, we shall next add the doctrine of the seed: how it grows and increases, namely in this manner. God has appointed for the infant its own time during which it must grow, namely 40 weeks; just as a time for cows, pigeons, and others has been defined and prefixed by the same God. Pay attention, however, to the reason why the seed becomes a fetus in this interval of time. 

First, then, after conception has occurred in the manner described, approaching Nature disposes the seed and separates it as it should: namely, the "head-seed" <margin>How this is introduced.</margin> to the head, the "arm-seed" to the place of the arm, and so on. Once this disposition is properly made, the womb then rests from its work and does nothing further thereafter. This is followed by "material nature," which leads the fetus to growth, so that all things that have been disposed grow, increase, and become a body, each according to its own proportion. Thus, what pertains to the flesh becomes flesh; what concerns the bone becomes bone; what is added to the veins becomes a vein; what is applied to the viscera becomes an organ. 

Therefore, if the seed is no longer seed (as it was) but is now blood and flesh, as befits a human, then the material nature itself withdraws from the fetus, and the Grace of God succeeds it. This Grace bestows and imparts to the fetus—according to the quality of a human—life and those other things due to a living creature, such as sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell. At that time, the <term>augmentative faculty</term><note>The internal power that directs growth.</note> is also present in the fetus. Once life has been implanted in the human by God according to the way of nature, the fetus grows in the maternal womb until all the limbs have received their due strength, stability, and solidness. 

After all these things have been introduced, the spirit, soul, reason, and intellect—and all those things that follow the soul—are finally instilled. After all these things, finally, the time of birth follows. <margin>When the soul is instilled in the fetus.</margin> For the soul and those things which cohere to it, being impatient with the delay in the maternal womb, strive for an exit at the appointed time; this happens at the period of the aforementioned weeks. You will find more about such parts in the <term>Paramira</term><note>original: *Paramiris*; referring to Paracelsus’s major work *Opus Paramirum*, specifically the section on the origin of the soul.</note>, where the origin of the soul will be treated. 

The method has now been handed down to you by which the conceived seed is first formed and disposed, then changed into blood and flesh, then the fetus is increased and grows large, and finally is endowed and imbued with spirit and soul. For as long as it is weaker and more feeble than is necessary to sustain and bear the earth <note>That is, to survive the physical weight and conditions of the world outside the womb.</note>, the spirit is not conferred or instilled into it. For this strength is the maturation of the spirit and the bestowing of the soul itself. For the soul only arrives after the spirit. The soul enters no body in which the spirit is not present. And this itself sometimes acts as a cause for why, during the period of growth, a fetus can change into a monster that is not fit to receive a soul. But when the growth of the fetus has been brought to the point where no error can occur, then for the first time the spirit enters, which is the precursor of the soul. The soul then follows it. From that time, the fetus grows and overflows into the union of body and soul until it can no longer bear the deprivation of air, nor tolerate the nourishment of the womb any further. All these things at last result in and end with birth.

### ->PART ON THE HUMAN CONDITION.<-

### ->CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>
What the corporal part of man is.
</margin>
**S**ince we have thus far treated the generation of man in sufficient abundance, and have put forward the opinion that God created man himself in the beginning, and afterwards attributed seed to him so that he might sow and plant those like himself for posterity: now, consequently and rightly, we shall next recount some things to you concerning the state of man, *namely, of what sort it is and how it is conducted until his dissolution, for which he is preserved.* Therefore, so that we may accomplish this more clearly, we shall divide the state of man into two parts: namely, into the *corporal* <note>original: *corporalem*; relating to the physical body.</note>, which he has within himself, and the other, which is *eternal*. Thus, there will be two treatments of this part: one concerning the *perishable or mortal*, and the other concerning the *eternal and immortal*, both of which nevertheless dwell in one man. The *corporal* or *perishable* is that which sustains the eternal, just as an <term>Innkeeper</term><note>original: *Pandochæus*; a Greek-derived term for a host or hotelier.</note> sustains a guest. To this, however, another divine benefit has also been added: namely, that the body itself, while preserving the soul, is also sustained. This, moreover, belongs to *life*. We shall take up nothing to be treated specifically regarding this. For life is such a gift, as if a prince were to give someone a house as an honorary gift—which he did not owe him—at least for this reason: so that in that lodging, he might live more safely and pleasantly with his other possessions. Truly, we shall not relegate such things to the goal of <term>Philosophy</term><note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to the study of nature and the physical world.</note>; for much greater and more sublime things seem to lie hidden beneath them than can be discovered through the experience of Philosophy. For first, before we proceed to the declaration of the following text, we shall teach this concerning the condition of Philosophy: that it draws its entire origin from experience. But what experience suggests is an experiment. From which it seems right to
<margin>
Experience is the mother of Philosophy.
</margin>
derive that which is born from this mother. Therefore, we conclude with such a discourse: if indeed nothing is defined for us concerning the life and origin of the soul, as is done regarding corporal things, then it must be entirely established that those things do not consist within our experience. Nor shall we cite here those blind orators who, out of the wisdom of their own <term>winged spirits</term><note>original: *volacium spirituum*; likely referring to fleeting, unsubstantiated ideas or perhaps demonic inspirations.</note>, declare and rhetorize many things about these matters. It would be easy for us to put forward an opinion about them, such as we know regarding dreams and dreamers. Although these men also boast loudly of their science in higher matters, they have known and held nothing—absolutely nothing—worthy of note concerning them.

### ->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>
Reproof of Physicians.
</margin>
**N**ow, turning to the text itself, we shall first uncover and make plain to you the unformed nonsense of the Physicians (whom we ought not to deign to call by the name of "Physicians" <note>In the 16th century, a "Physician" was a university-trained doctor, often criticized by Paracelsus for being too theoretical.</note>, yet since you call yourselves such, we shall wink at that title). These men, when treating the state and condition of man, define him by <term>four complexions</term><note>The four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic.</note> and as many <term>humors</term><note>The bodily fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm.</note>, and qualities, and other similar extravagances. It would be proper, however, for no Physician to utter anything unless he had first reached the furthest limits of Philosophy, as is appropriate for a Student of Nature. But just as many of them are "born from Astronomy" <note>Referring to the practice of medical astrology.</note>, so these mimes enter into a league with charlatans; and on both sides, insofar as they differ concerning the nature of man, they paint and veil their doctrine with not a few lies. However, so that we may grant true Philosophy its right, we shall propose the state of man as such: just as he was brought forth in his generation as a perfected and complete human being. This shall be done in this discourse. First of all, the first man comes to be considered, from whom all other things proceed. Here, however, two humans occur, established in the beginning: namely, man and woman. From these two flowed all the nature of other men, and whatever exists anywhere within them (as far as the fragility of life is concerned). But as for his spirit, and the eternal itself, and reason, and wisdom itself—the soul—we shall set that aside for its own treatise. For although reason, as well as wisdom and prudence, are distributed equally to all men, not all grasp all things with equal ease, due to a defect in the shaping and composition of the corporal instruments. Having dismissed these things here, [we turn to] the generation, origin, and reason...
