<header>ON THE STATE OF MAN.</header>

...we will consider in the state of man for what reasons anyone appears as they do, exists as they do, and lives as they do. Concerning these things, we will arm you with a brief instruction against the aforementioned Doctors of medicine and Astronomers, who either possess nothing of solid Philosophy within themselves or do not even care for it. Also annihilated here are those who claim that the heavens <note>original: *caelum*; referring to the influence of the planets and stars.</note> establish and produce so many forms and species, so many heads, so many senses, and various other things.

## C A P. III.

<margin>The four complexions of man.</margin>
**M**an consists of four <term>complexions</term><note>A historical medical term referring to the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, in such a way that one of them is entirely dominant. That one makes him either cold, hot, dry, or moist: but it introduces no property of his essential character. For example, if he is cold and dry, he cannot for that reason be called unfaithful; or if he is <term>sanguine</term><note>The "blood" temperament, traditionally associated with being cheerful.</note>, he does not necessarily exist as a cheerful person. For that which makes people happy and that which makes them sad is something other than the complexion itself. But, so that we may speak before all else about the beginning of the complexions, the matter stands thus. In
<margin>Adam was hot and moist: Eve was cold and dry.</margin>
Adam there was one complexion, namely hot and moist. There was also one in Eve, namely cold and dry. From these two, four were born, by this reasoning: If the coldness of Eve overcame the heat of Adam, she produced an offspring of a cold nature. If indeed the moisture of Adam prevailed over the dryness of Eve, the offspring was born moist. Thus the third complexion emerged, namely cold and moist, and that from the nature of both, and not from one alone. In the same way, we must also judge the fourth complexion. If the heat of Adam conquered the coldness of Eve, the offspring turned out hot. And if the dryness of Eve transcended the moisture of Adam, the offspring was born hot and dry. And this is the completion of the four complexions. God cast Eve into one, and Adam into the other. Thus even after birth, it sometimes happens that the cold and dry complexion overcomes its opposite in turn, and so the birth is named after one alone. In this way, therefore, such a distribution was made among men, so that now every man is allotted his own, and that a single complexion, in which he consists, just like those first parents. Thus therefore
<margin>Equal complexions.</margin>
the complexion is mixed either more or less in men and women, so that there is no longer a unique complexion for either sex, but it is indifferent and similar. A hot and moist complexion in a woman is just as strong and valid as in a man. Likewise, a cold and dry complexion is equally intense in men and women. Although you ought also to note that complexions are not so entirely similar to one another that whoever is hot is entirely similar to another hot person: rather, all are distinct among themselves according to more or less, by weight.

## C A P. VI.

**F**rom this philosophy concerning the four complexions, we nevertheless do not give them peculiar names.
<margin>Melancholy is no complexion.</margin>
For if we were to name the cold and dry "Melancholy," we would be telling a lie. For it is not so. *<term>Melancholy</term> is a collective name*, stitched together from many lies and marked by various properties, which nevertheless are neither found in that complexion nor can they exist there. Similarly, regarding the hot and dry complexion, we can by no means establish the name of <term>cholera</term><note>Often called "yellow bile" in ancient medicine, associated with anger and dryness.</note>: for complexion and cholera are not one thing. But who can stop all the trifles of those for whom lying is a pleasure? You ought to feel the same about the remaining complexions.
**** But now, so that we may speak of the property of man, pay diligent attention. For we describe the other properties of man as being born from those principles from which he proceeds.
<margin>Where cheerfulness and sadness come from.</margin>
For example, cheerfulness and sadness themselves were fathered by Adam and Eve. Cheerfulness was placed in Eve; sadness in Adam. Moreover, these things were in them materially, just like their other essences and conditions. Whichever property overcame the other, the offspring also took on the nature of that winning quality. If, however, a certain mixture occurred—as a mixture could hardly be absent—then necessarily one was the breaking of the other. Therefore, no one is ever born after Eve who has the same cheerfulness as her;
<margin>Eve was the most cheerful of all; Adam was the saddest of all men.</margin>
nor after Adam, one who exists as equally sad as he. For the twin materials of Adam and Eve themselves are now mixed, so that sadness with cheerfulness, and cheerfulness with sadness, now exist as tempered to some extent, and the matter can never return to its original state. From this it happens that as more or less of the "seed of sadness" is contributed, a man becomes more or less sad. This must be understood not only regarding the contribution of the seed, but also regarding the dominance and victory of cheerfulness. Thus, therefore, there is a shifting of these twin materials, so that they do not consist in the woman alone, nor in the man alone (as has been said), but exist mixed in both sexes. Thus, tyranny and fury, as well as gentleness, mildness, and moderation: these also are present from both. The first from Eve.

<margin>What is laughter?</margin>
<margin>What is anger?</margin>
<margin>What is weeping?</margin>
*** Regarding the specific nature of human beings, pay close attention. For we are describing to you (these words also appear a little further up in the text; now follow those through which the author himself drew a line) the <term>material properties</term><note>Physical or bodily traits.</note> and the <term>immaterial properties</term><note>Spiritual or psychological traits.</note>. The material ones are: Laughter, anger, tears, and yawning. **Laughter** is a tickling in the blood, the characteristic of which is recognized and expressed by the mouth; as a person has more or less of this tickling, so are they prone to laughter, as is taught regarding laughter. **Anger** is a boiling produced without bile <note>Paracelsus is challenging traditional medicine here, which claimed anger was caused by yellow bile.</note>; if this boiling bursts forth, anger is generated, as is taught regarding anger. **Weeping** is a constriction in the spleen. When this occurs, weeping happens. And such things, as has been said, are innate in children. For if an "angry seed" and a "laughable seed" proceed to generation, then according to which one overcomes the other, so the human is born. These four natures—sadness, joy, anger, and gentleness—exist materially in the body. But who will show how they lie hidden in the body? We point out to you examples concerning the blood, bile, and spleen for the sake of greater understanding; we do not, however, conclude that they reside in the heart in this way. Yet there is something similar contained in the body in which these four are situated, received into a single matter, which themselves also add their own "seed" during generation. As each one falls, more or less, and either conquers or is conquered, so the specific character of a person is established.

<margin>
All prior things are rendered. Men today are more perverse than the first.
</margin>
<margin>Astronomers are rebuked.</margin>
<margin>Man is a perfect creature even without the stars.</margin>
...since by the generation of the first humans, all of nature and the substance of men was born in sin, and that depravity has subsequently descended from one seed into another, and now continues constantly until the final consummation of those seeds. Although many perverse natures are now found in men that were not noted in the first parents. The reason for this is that they followed reason as their guide, and not the instinct of the body; hence they could not even be driven to those enormities. Similarly, other natures and depravities now spread among men that were not derived from them, such as <term>whoring</term>, gambling, etc. For these arise from an "object" <note>Meaning external temptation or environmental influence.</note>. Whatever objects give birth to did not flow from the first parents. But whatever dwells in us without an external object, all of that was implanted in us from our first parents according to the weight of the mixed seeds. Why then should we be moved by the fictions of those who ascribe all such things to the Planets, the sky, and the stars? For they make one person "Jovial" <note>Influenced by Jupiter; cheerful.</note>, another "Martial" <note>Influenced by Mars; warlike.</note>, a third "Venereal" <note>Influenced by Venus; lustful.</note>, and so on. It is a wonder, however, why they have not also placed a Planet in the heavens that heals the sick, or one that shows itself to be charming and lovable. For they make all of them evil, sickly, and adverse; nor do they themselves establish any planet that assists the Physician, so that what the planet itself breaks and destroys, it might repair and restore. But to those who are captured by playful and jesting things, such ideas can easily be given. Man is a perfect creature in himself, to whom neither the stars nor anything else can add or engraft anything. All things were given and pre-ordained for him from the first man. And just as man can contribute nothing to the stars, so much less can the stars contribute to man in turn. As for the fact that they impart to us rains, heat, and cold, and similar things: all of that is external only, not at all internal, just as rain touches only the skin, not the internal parts. So it is with cold likewise. These things, as we have said, are only external, and can make a man neither good, nor malicious, nor a thief, nor a robber. If the stars are like that, then they prey upon their own things among themselves, not our things upon us. For theft is an internal matter, flowing from the inner man, not from external things. Nothing of this kind enters him. Man was also created in such a way that whatever surrounds him and enters him does not leave him again. For the most powerful protector of all...

Christ, our patron and mirror, testifies that nothing evil enters into man. Therefore, the planets cannot enter either: for it would then be necessary for them to exit again. ### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Good and evil are innate to man from his first parents.</margin> **A**s it has already been said that nothing evil enters into man, so too is no entrance granted to the planets into man. Therefore, it is proper to know that man consists within himself, and that all conditions, of both good and evil, were entirely implanted in him by his primeval parents. But lest we dwell too long on these matters, for the sake of the text of the second treatise, we will touch upon and unfold a few things here concerning the body, the spirits, and the eternal, which ought to govern the body. For whatever we have enumerated as innate to man happens in its own way: such as faithfulness, goodness, and malice, and other similar deeds, both bad and good. <margin>The purpose for which reason was given.</margin> For those are corporal or earthly things which arise from our brute nature. For in the aforementioned things, all transitory matters consist, which must be either good or bad. Beyond these things, however, it must be recognized that an eternal intellect was surely added, so that men would not live according to the nature implanted in them like wood and stones, which do not transcend the nature and condition innate to them but act according to it until the end of all creation. These things, I say, understanding men ought not to follow; rather, they should establish that way of life which the intellect of him who is eternal suggests and shows to them. For he received intellect for this one end: that he might restrain the body's freedom in doing anything it wishes, and shape all things according to the guidance of reason and spirit. For it is altogether necessary that he use reason. <margin>Reason is the moderator of all things.</margin> For whatever else is in man is rebellious and stubborn, and it has an absolute need to be tamed and bridled by reason. But for whatever trait there is no bridle, man feels no power or harm from it—such as a physical distortion, a difficult shape, an unpleasing appearance, and other similar things. These require no moderation of reason; rather, only the innate powers, whether they be good or bad, require it.

So that we may finally bring a <term>colophon</term><note>A finishing touch or concluding note to a work.</note> to the text of this treatise and defer the rest to its proper place: you should know that concerning all the parts which man has within himself according to his state, enough has been sufficiently said thus far regarding what he contains within himself physically. Furthermore, we shall define prudence and wisdom, as well as the spirits and the eternal, in their proper place. <margin>Eve was the most beautiful of all. Adam was also so in his own kind.</margin> And, to briefly add something regarding complexions, know this: in Eve there existed lovely, delicate, and beautiful complexions, all established far beyond all human grasp and loveliness. Similarly, in Adam, the most beautiful complexions of all flourished, yet according to a masculine nature. But through the subsequent mixing of the lineage, those colors were rendered much darker; so much so, that henceforth neither any man nor woman can ever be tinted or endowed with that same beauty of color as they were. The same judgment must be made concerning the other ornaments and beauties of the body and character.

### THERE FOLLOW NEXT
# VARIOUS FRAGMENTS, PERTAINING TO
# THE PRECEDING PHYSICAL MEDICINE,

which we have desired to transcribe from many of Theophrastus’s <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> original manuscripts and print for the use of students. Indeed, it is certain that the Author very often handed down—on a light page, in few but clear words—the very things through which many obscure passages in his books might be explained and more clearly understood. Therefore, let the Kind Reader receive these not with contempt, but with good grace, as if they were certain crumbs, etc. In arranging these fragments, we have industriously taken care that each should fit into its proper Volume, and that books should correspond well to books wherever possible.

## THEOPHRASTUS
### *To the Reader.*

*AS for the fact that I have suppressed my books until now, Reader, and have not sent them out into the public, the blame should by no means be pinned on me, as if I had stood forth as either negligent or in any way envious. For it is common knowledge that no obstacle—whether my frequent or distant travels, or the ridiculous insults of my adversaries, or anything else of the sort—threw me off from continuing to tread the path toward the goal of my undertaken labors. But those who impute the cause of this procrastination to me make themselves the guilty ones: For when I was at Basel, <note>Paracelsus taught at the University of Basel in 1527–1528, where he famously burned the books of traditional authorities like Galen and Avicenna.</note> rightly and deservedly introducing a new Theory and Philosophy in the teaching of Medicine, explaining those things which ought to be declared through the <term>Iliadum</term> <note>A Paracelsian term referring to the first matter or the "chaos" from which everything is formed.</note>, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal, vital force or "chemist" within the body that directs health and growth.</note>, and the <term>Effatum</term> <note>A firm decree or fundamental principle of nature.</note>: it is a wonder how much those clever and sublime Platonists and "Indians" <note>likely a derogatory reference to followers of foreign or outdated traditions</note> immediately insulted me, even though these things were scarcely understood even in a mediocre way; and they caused a division. For one man, striving to extol and sell himself by looking down on me, thrust upon himself the name of Theophrastus <note>original: "Theophrastus" (Divine Speaker)</note>, but upon me the name of <term>Cacophrastus</term> <note>original: "Cacophrastus" (Evil or Foul Speaker), a mocking pun on Paracelsus's given name.</note>. Another, from elsewhere, falsely accused me of stealing my own ideas, which nevertheless never saw the light before me, not even as recently as this morning. For the Reader himself will judge by himself, and I shall demonstrate with the firmest reasons, that none of my works were written before me by either Philosophers or Physicians, nor were such things heard or read by anyone before me. Thus, my own writings themselves prove that I bring forth 600 Inventions in this book, not a single one of which—neither the smallest nor the greatest—is admitted by any Philosopher or Physician, whether ancient or modern, unless he wishes to make a total defection from all the writings of all the ancients. I say nothing of the fact that it is well-known to many that my present library is so thin that I could scarcely fill six written pages from it. Furthermore, my own secretaries will testify under oath that these things are taken directly from my mouth. Indeed, it is manifest that for an entire decade I have read no book. The arrogance and pride of my rivals, therefore, by which they rashly hold me in total contempt, is less than evident; meanwhile one made me out to be a Maniac, another a <term>Necromancer</term>, and whatever else of Magic they could pin on me to my despite. The sole cause of their impudence was that they thought my Inventions were now known to them with less certainty: Thus, to pile up a heap of honor, this one thing now remained: that, ascribing the name of Theophrastus to themselves, they should call me Cacophrastus through their insolence. That thief and rogue, whom they carry about sitting behind their ears <note>a metaphor for being influenced by the devil or a malicious spirit</note>, inflamed them to dare this: Next, that notorious and widely spread dexterity in curing, by which I was wonderfully useful to many kingdoms and provinces above all Physicians and the very marketplace—both patrons and books—and performed such works which they will never be able to imitate from all their books for all eternity. Yet they, in the meantime, lest they be forced to grant me this deserved glory and praise acquired in curing Princes and Great Men, preferred to ascribe it to devils, as if I performed such things by the help of Beelzebub. Of which envy this was the sole cause and end: that they might render me despised everywhere; and so that they themselves might celebrate a solid triumph over me, rejected and cast out in every place and among every people. If ever a single sick person under my care died: they noted that far more eagerly than if ten became healthy. In which case they did not blush at any lie, but went hunting everywhere, begging for many doubtful testimonies to convict me. Since they attempted everything with nefarious cunning in this matter: they found associates like themselves without difficulty—such men, surely, whom partly the virulence of an ungrateful mind, and partly the unjust denial of a justly earned fee, could stimulate quite actively to criminalize me. From whose number Philippus* should not be considered the least...*

*The Margrave of Baden <note>Philip I, Margrave of Baden (1479–1533), whom Paracelsus treated in 1527.</note>, whom I snatched from certain death from dysentery when he had been given up by the care of the Chief Physicians <note>original: "Archiatrorum"</note> and was already in his final death-throes: he certainly kept the royal promise he made to me in a most ungentlemanly way. Indeed, he proved himself much more stingy—to my certain loss—than even that impious Jew, Messe de Thalles, the worst of all charlatans. When I had helped that Jew in some illness, he dismissed me much more generously than said Prince. The ingratitude of this Prince, and his far too stingy payment, just like the plain example of certain other high-ranking nobles, was not only a source of singular joy and pleasure to all my aforementioned adversaries, but they also later attempted to use this same weapon to suppress me everywhere. For wherever on earth the kind Sun seemed to shine upon me, they maliciously pursued me there with both boastful words and printed books. They placed all their defense in flattering tongues and traduced me through slander before wicked counselors, for whom betraying one another for a mere morsel of food is a game. These same people were not only unmindful of the faithful help I provided them, but they also unfairly defrauded me of my earned wages. Furthermore, like plagiarists, they pillaged both my honor and my labors, selling the work of others as their own. The very works I had proposed to write, they attempted to forestall by treating the same subjects themselves, even now when they have sucked dry all my inventions from me.*

*Therefore, if it would not displease you to closely compare what they have written with my own writings, it will become entirely plain and evident to everyone that those men transcribed all their material from mine, or that whatever they know, they learned from me alone, even if they flew the nest too prematurely. Hence, I do not doubt that they will shortly be table-companions, schoolmasters, and lowly servants once again, as they were before. Since they have therefore already made their own disgrace public, I thought that I could now safely publish even my simplest works, with this intention: that I may thereafter proceed to weightier matters and bring to light the books of the <term>Archidoxes</term> <note>One of Paracelsus's most famous works on the "ancient teachings" of alchemy and medicine.</note>, the <term>Meteors</term>, and the <term>Generation of Minerals</term>. By these, I shall not only expose the foul lies of my assistants <note>original: "Amanuensium"</note>, but I shall also break and wash away the rash accusations of those from whom they first fell away in shameful apostasy, and with whom they are now joined again in contempt of me.*

*These things having been prefaced, Good Reader, it is your part to be persuaded that my writings labor exactly in that Philosophy from which flows the origin and principle of Medicine—which shall reveal my truth and the lies of others. Read these things, therefore, with experience and truth, and carefully judge both my stable foundations and the empty trifles of others. Do not approach these readings with the mindset that, having leafed through one book, you are finished; rather, act so that you may penetrate to the very end and the foundation itself with a certain longing. Farewell.*

## REGARDING THE FIVE ENTITIES.
### CONCERNING THE ASTRAL ENTITY.

<margin>
What the Astral Entity is.
</margin>
<margin>
The agreement between the Astral Entity and man.
</margin>
**H**aving set forth the preface to the books on the Entities above, we shall now begin the third paragraph, by which we shall bring them to a close, and concerning which we have decided as follows. The <term>Astral Entity</term> <note>Ens Astrale: The influence of the stars and atmosphere on human health, one of Paracelsus's five categories of disease causes.</note> is the Being of all the dwellings of heaven, and whatever the firmament contains. This is so united with man that, whatever the star suffers, the man himself suffers similarly. Not that the star is sick in itself, since it undergoes no diseases, but because its nature happens to be too strong, powerful, and adverse for the man. By this force, the star weakens its subjects. Since we are commenting briefly on the Stars in this paragraph, we shall explain the doctrine of them more plainly and clearly in the book *On Death*.

<margin>
What heaven is.
</margin>
<margin>
Heaven is established everywhere.
</margin>
If we truly desire to understand briefly what a star is, we must first inquire what heaven is. Heaven is a spirit and a vapor in which we live like a bird in time. Nor do the stars, the Moon, etc., alone constitute heaven; there are also stars among us which we do not see at all, which also constitute heaven. Note here how this happens, for it is thus: just as a <term>hypocaust</term> <note>A room heated from below, like a sauna or Roman heating system.</note>—whether it be hot or cold—either warms or cools those staying within it, so too is the principle of the firmament and the <term>complexions</term> <note>The physical and mental constitution of a person, traditionally governed by the four humors.</note>.

<margin>
The Firmament is twofold.
</margin>
Therefore, just as heaven subsists, and we in it, so attend hereafter to what sort of union exists between heaven and man, in this manner: nothing imprints itself, neither a Star necessitating, nor governing, nor inclining. These things pertain to death, but not to diseases. The <term>Firmament</term> is twofold: of the heaven and of the bodies, and these have a harmony with each other, and not...

# ANOTHER FRAGMENT
## Concerning the Astral Entity

<margin>Whether the stars shape man.</margin>
**T**wo things must be considered here regarding the Astral Entity according to the rules of the Astrologers, who teach that the heaven forms the body, shapes it, and (as I might say) disposes it according to its own nature. But we shall treat nothing of that here, since the matter is not like that at all. For if we wish to speak of the principle of the body’s formation, we consider it by ascending to the fact that the <margin>The material Adam. Man's generation is from the Entity of nature, not otherwise.</margin> material Adam was made, and nothing else is created further. However, that which is conceived in the mother’s womb—namely flesh and blood, or the body of a perfected man—that happens entirely from the <term>Entity of nature<note>original: "Ente naturae." One of Paracelsus’s five causes of health/disease, referring here to biological and hereditary processes.</note></term>, by means of the parents' seed. The seed which is cast into the field grows from its own Entity alone, and from no other: the Star contributes nothing to it of power, or of its proper nature, or of its temperament, etc.; it merely adds time. So too the stonemason who builds a house is helped by no other creature, except that <margin>The stars contribute only time to the generation of man. Life is not from the stars, but from God.</margin> time is given—namely, the deadline for completion. And just as the stars do not build a house in any way other than by producing time, so they also do not build the body in any other way. But lest we omit the rest—that is, life—it must be held that even this is not granted by the stars. For life was divinely given to Adam and implanted in his seed, from which it is never again taken away. Rather, everything that nature forms from its own Entity also receives life from this itself. For once given, it is not thereafter imparted anew. From this comes the growth and strength and other things which man has and ought to have. But reason and conscience <margin>The source of man's reason and sense.</margin> descend from the singular gift of God; prudence, sense, and industry are conferred upon man from an external spirit. Thus, the star itself works nothing in man. 

But to press our point and lead the Physician to Astronomy: it must be known that man must have a <term>Magnale<note>original: "Magnale." A Paracelsian term referring to a vast, invisible medium or "great thing"—often identified with the air or atmosphere—that transmits celestial influences to living things.</note></term>, without which he cannot live. For the <margin>The Magnale was made for the sake of man; the Magnale is twofold. The origin of man's Magnale. The Magnale alters man's nature.</margin> Magnale was made for the sake of man, not man for the sake of the Magnale. This Magnale sustains the Magnale of man. This, moreover, descends from the stars and from nowhere else. If that [external] Magnale is hostile to the body, then it weakens it and breaks its own proper nature. Let this be an example: Water by itself ought to be cold. But if the Magnale of the stars touches the water, then the water exceeds its nature, and the fish living in it perish. For they cannot endure the contrary nature impressed into the water through the Magnale. 

In the same way, man has a quality proper to himself; if this is altered too much through the Magnale—whether in heat, or cold, or humidity, or dryness, or by a Magnale of stench, or acidity, bitterness, etc.—then the nature's quality, having been altered, sheds its own quality. Afterward, even the internal members, such as the heart, liver, brain, spleen, etc., are changed, just as fish are infected in the water. From this change arises the Astral Entity—namely, from such a Magnale. And thus bodies are infected, weakened, and killed through the stars, just as the example of the fish in the water teaches.

<margin>The Sun and all the Planets infect our bodies, and how.</margin>
But so that you may have an even fuller understanding of this Astral Entity, pay attention. We do not make the sun alone the cause of our bodies being infected; but furthermore, we also make a cause of any Planet whatsoever that is established in its exaltation, so that it is powerful in the Magnale, penetrates it, and disposes it according to itself. Thus we believe that if Mars or Saturn, etc., are dominant, they cool the Magnale too much; or the sun's Magnale heats too much; Jupiter's makes it too salty; Saturn's makes it too acidic. From all these things, when they are raised to exaltation, our bodies are infected. If, however, they are positioned too far from us and cannot reach our bodies at all, then that vapor does us no harm. Concerning which <margin>The Reality of Jupiter makes water salty.</margin> observe an example: The Reality of Jupiter. If it alters the water, it makes it salty. This now kills the fish. The Reality of Saturn makes the water acidic, from which the fish also die. The Reality of [others] makes the water bitter, whence the fish are extinguished. Thus, therefore, not only the sun's heat kills the fish, but...

# MEDICAL FRAGMENTS

...but moreover, even infinite other stars, which in their astrological exaltation and joy are much more malicious, do the same. But let us explain the matter by a certain likeness. You see, surely, that it frequently happens that in some river a huge number of fish are caught, such a plenty as none have seen in years past. Following a catch of this kind, a cruel and unheard-of plague usually follows. Now, the cause of this thing ought to be considered. It is surely this: that the saltiness of <term>Realgar</term><note>original: "Realgaris." In Paracelsian thought, Realgar is not just the mineral arsenic sulfide, but a specific "astral salt" or poisonous vapor that can infect the environment.</note> made the waters in the <term>Magnale</term><note>original: "Magnali." This refers to the "Mysterium Magnum" or the great subjective medium (the air or atmosphere) through which astral influences are transmitted.</note> saltier than is right; from this, they are matured into a substance which then seeks the bottom. If, therefore, the fish feel the multitude of the salty *magnale*, they take flight and seek rest at the surface of the water, toward the sun, the day, and the light, and they do not return to the bottom which has become too salty. From this, it happens that they are caught. Just as, therefore, the *magnale* of the fish becomes too salty, so too the *magnale* of humans is salty, and thus the quality and nature of the constitution has overstepped its bounds.

<margin>An unheard-of catch of fish is a precursor to epidemics.</margin>
<margin>The alteration of the *magnale* infects the human body.</margin>
This alteration is then conceived by the heart, the liver, and the brain; death follows afterward. If the fish were to remain in that water, they would die in the same way that men do. Just as the present text has taught concerning the *magnale* thus far, so it must be understood: namely, that this <term>Astral Entity</term><note>original: "Ens Astrale." One of Paracelsus's five causes of disease, referring to influences from the stars.</note> exists, which weakens our body by its own power, without the conspiracy of the other four Entities. To teach these things belongs to the Astronomers. For the exaltations of the stars indicate what and how much they infect in the *magnale*, etc.

### Another fragment, corresponding to the *Paramirum* concerning Diseases from the three primary substances.

### TREATISE II.

<margin>The "Mercury of the commoners" is the image of the first principle.</margin>
Accept now this instruction on how the diseases of the three first principles are divided and born.

The nature of MERCURY as it is in itself is also fashioned and expressed in the <term>Mercury of the commoners</term><note>original: "Mercurio vulgi." Quicksilver or elemental mercury, which Paracelsus uses as a visible symbol for the invisible "Mercury" principle in all matter.</note>. Hence, it is not undeservedly named after this liquor. For none among all things exhibits the nature of Mercury through external signs more expressively than this alone.

<margin>What the volatility of Mercury causes. What the acrimony of volatile Mercury causes.</margin>
To this, it follows that three cases consist in Mercury. For by its **Volatility**, it causes mania, the mortification of ligaments, arteries, and joints, as well as tremors and falls. By the **Acrimony** of its volatility—if it purifies itself and passes too much into a spirit—it begets mania, frenzy, loss of mind, fainting, and that other madness which the common people call Melancholy. Nor is it true that diseases of this kind arise from a multitude or other affection of the blood. For they are generated only from the spirit of Mercury, which, ascending and seeking an exit, harms the brain and the chambers of memory and judgment, as is taught in the specific chapters.

<margin>What the spirit of Mercury produces.</margin>
If, however, it penetrates into the ligaments so that it descends and touches the brain, it excites Apoplexy. If it touches the <term>Nucha</term><note>The nape of the neck or the spinal cord.</note>, it stirs up paralysis. But if it is not so subtle, but has a cold course, it causes tremors in the hands and feet, or in the head alone; similarly, it causes the Lethargic disease and the contortion of the mouth, eyes, nostrils, and the like. All these things happen from the <term>Archeic</term><note>Related to the "Archeus," the internal vital force or "alchemist" within the body that directs health.</note> nature of Mercury, of which there are many kinds, which are explained in the theoretical sections in their own proper chapters.

### II.

<margin>Diseases of Sulfur.</margin>
But SULFUR also has its own diseases: namely, febrile diseases, abscesses, and Jaundice. The generation of these from sulfur occurs because it is not volatile. Yet it putrefies and is corrupted more readily than either of the other two. For **Salt** sustains the other two so that they do not putrefy. **Mercury** does not putrefy unless it is too greatly impressed upon [the salt], so that it is made volatile along with the salt. Whatever Mercury works, it works from the subtlety of its own nature.

<margin>Sulfur putrefies more quickly than the others.</margin>
Sulfur, however, is not so deeply impressed upon the salt, but both subsist more crudely in a single opposition. Therefore, if the salt is separated and recedes from the sulfur, then the sulfur putrefies and produces diseases of its own disposition, according to the various places it falls into.

<margin>How Sulfur procreates its diseases.</margin>
For in the region of the heart it causes pleurisy; in the stomach, fevers; in the liver, fevers; in the head, migraines, pains of the eyes, teeth, and ears, and heaviness, and headaches, and the like. For these diseases are not generated in the way the opinion of the ancient authors decrees. And that hallucination is indeed no light matter—that in these diseases they consider "hot and cold," or "choler and melancholy," and "phlegm or blood." For whoever wishes to act as a Physician with praise, let him bid these trifles a long farewell. For no hot disease was ever cured by cold things, nor cold by hot things.

<margin>Like is cured by like, not by the contrary.</margin>
But "like" has frequently cured its own "like"—namely, Mercury cures Mercury, Sulfur cures Sulfur; and Salt cures Salt.

<margin>The entire world consists of three things.</margin>
The entire body—that is, all the bodies of the world that have ever been at any time, or shall be until the end—are placed in three things: in **Salt**, **Mercury**, and **Sulfur**. These three consist in all the Elements, and in each one separately there is something perfect, and they are called minerals. Those which exist in the Element of Earth are of a singular nature. Those in Water are singular. So also those in Fire and Air. The same reasoning applies to them within man.

<margin>What is the Yliadus.</margin>
Every single body consists of these three, and it is called the <term>Yliadus</term><note>A Paracelsian term (sometimes spelled Iliadus) referring to the fundamental mineral or vital force that creates specific forms out of the elements.</note>: that is, all the species which minerals contain within themselves in that Element are comprised here. This, however, is twofold: one of the Elements, the other of man. <margin>The Yliadus is twofold.</margin>
<margin>The number of the Yliadi is the measure of the parts.</margin>
There are four Yliadi. Since the Yliadus behaves in this way, it must first be known what species the Yliadus has, and how many. According to their number, the body must also be divided into just as many parts, so that not even one is lacking; for the Elements do not suffer the lack of anything. Regarding these things, observe how <term>vitriol</term><note>Metallic salts, usually sulfates, which were seen as the "fruit" of the water element.</note> and <term>ogertinum</term><note>An archaic term for a specific mineral or vitriolic salt.</note> come from the Element of Water. Paracelsus viewed mushrooms as the earthly equivalent of mineral precipitates like vitriol.</note>. Just as there are many vitriols, so also are there many mushrooms. Arsenic is a mineral of the water. So, in turn, in the earth, the fungus is that arsenic. In the same way also lead and others. Therefore, as the species are, so they retain their name: that is, one must speak thus: the "white vitriol of the earth" is a Mushroom; the "vitriol of the water" is the water of vitriol, and so on.

<margin>Arsenic is a mineral of the water according to the philosopher.</margin>

<margin>Internal things are to be named according to external things.</margin>
According to this reasoning, the same species also exist in man—that is, in his own Yliadus, with its minerals. From this, it is manifest to follow: that just as in an Element, vitriol arises in one place, <term>marcasite</term><note>A term then used for various shiny metallic ores, often iron pyrites.</note> in another, <term>cachymia</term><note>An archaic term for an "immature" metal or the dross of an ore.</note> in another, etc., according to how the Yliadus consists and flourishes in that place: so in man also the same thing happens in the same way. In him, it produces such a mineral—that is, a "fruit." For minerals are called "fruits," and are taken for minerals. Therefore, if you see erysipelas, say it is vitriol; if you see cancer, say it is <term>colcothar</term><note>The brownish-red residue (iron oxide) left after the distillation of vitriol.</note>; if you see a <term>wolf</term><note>original: "lupum." For you ought to attend to these species, how external minerals agree so much with them, as will be said later. Know therefore that in this chapter nothing else is treated but the entrance to the philosophy of the Yliadus, what it may be. How indeed all things behave will follow. Likewise, there are as many states of health as there are species, and as many diseases as there are species.

<margin>Salt is fourfold.</margin>
A part of Salt is also sweet, as in the flesh; a part is salty, as in the blood; a part is bitter, as in the bile; and a part is acidic, as in insects. For Salt provides taste.

By this reasoning, therefore, this <term>Yliadus</term><note>In Paracelsian philosophy, the Yliadus is the vital force or spiritual substance that directs the distribution of elements in the body.</note> is divided here into three parts: into color, weight, and taste. That which gives off smoke is Mercury and the salty <term>Alkali</term><note>Originally referring to ashes of plants, here it signifies a basic, salt-like substance.</note>. <margin>Diseases are the fruits of the three primes.</margin>
But if they do bring forth fruit, diseases are immediately present. For all three are essential: it is not that only color, or weight, or taste is present, but rather all are present together and in the specific way they ought to be; that is, every species has its own essence joined to it. From these essences, the fruit now emerges. Just as it is the nature of the <term>Ylech</term><note>A term for the "first matter" or the raw cosmic material from which things are formed.</note> that it can never remain whole. For it consumes death, and one species is forced to perish after another until everything that is malignant within departs. Just as the Element of Earth produces gold. That fruit is "bad" <note>In this context, "bad" or "evil" fruit refers to a deviation or an "extrusion" from the balanced state of the element.</note>.

<margin>Gold is a disease of its own Element: just as all other minerals are.</margin>
For according to the nature of its Yliadus, gold is a great disease of the earth; therefore, like a disease, it is cast out by its Element and is not sustained by it. The same logic applies to other minerals. Thus, this disease is similar to those metals and minerals. And in the Yliadus—that is, in the "house" from which minerals emerge—all diseases are situated. And just as one mineral or another emerges here or there according to the division of the Yliadus, so it is with disease.

<margin>How great the variety of the Yliadus is.</margin>
And just as in one mountain <note>original: "vino monte" - likely a clerical error for "uno monte" (one mountain).</note> there is much gold, and in another something else, so too in men: one disease flourishes in this person, another in that person. From this it happens that in one place a plague dominates, and in another less so. And just as minerals are distributed among the Elements—so that in one place fruits grow, in another trees, and in another herbs—so among men some suffer only this disease, others that one, and the rest endure yet another. And although all men may be in one or more places, they nonetheless carry this "mountain" within themselves; that is, all together they constitute one mountain or one mine. For disease is a single "mine" found in all men. From these things, understand that the sole purpose of our words is that the Yliadus may be rightly understood in its fruits through the example of other minerals, which are one with man—namely, which diseases are usually born from them.

<margin>The principal minerals are three.</margin>
Now truly, understand how many minerals—that is, how many diseases—exist in this way. There are three principal minerals: **Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt.** Therefore, just as minerals require these three, so likewise a disease is generated from these three, but in a wondrous and varied composition, as is taught regarding minerals. However, it is one thing that produces the disease—that is, one species—which is nevertheless threefold. For example, if a disease has arisen from <term>vitriol</term><note>A historical name for various sulfate minerals, often used to describe corrosive or metallic conditions.</note>, then the vitriol of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt are joined, and yet it is one "vitriol" and is called such. In weight, however, they do not agree; one is greater or lesser than the other. But the disease is named after the principal part.

<margin>Vitriol is threefold.</margin>
Thus, if it is of Salt, it is said that "Vitriol of Salt" caused the disease; if of Mercury, "Vitriol of Mercury," etc.; if of Sulfur, it is affirmed that "Vitriol of Sulfur" caused it. The same logic applies to the other species as well, whether they be Alums, Salts, Arsenics, or others. The next step, therefore, is for these species to be known. Once they are perceived—namely, how many there are—it must then be investigated which diseases they produce: that is, what vitriol is, what its diseases are (which are called "vitriolated"), and so on for the others.

<margin>What the diseases are called.</margin>
And finally, how it should be recognized whether a disease ought to be called vitriolated, or plumose <note>likely referring to "Alumen plumosum" or feathered alum</note>, etc., or a fungus, or agaric, or <term>botin</term><note>A Paracelsian term for a type of turpentine or resinous eruption.</note>; that is, how diseases ought to be named according to the four Elements. For example, <term>Alopecia</term><note>Baldness or hair loss.</note> is in the Element of Earth, as is "cetum"—that is, scabies in the bark. In the Element of Water it is called rust. In the Element of Air, "Sanet" <note>A term for a specific atmospheric or spiritual disease.</note>, etc. In the Element of Fire, lightning; in man, Alopecia. And so it is in all other diseases. Once the most necessary types of mineral species are known, and then the diseases, their names now follow.

# ANOTHER FRAGMENT.

The origin of all diseases is either from Resolution or Coagulation.

Ruby, etc. how it is in the blood.

But how is it recognized that blood becomes a Ruby or becomes a crystal? From the fact that the nature of such things is there in a particular way—namely, in the grains of the blood, etc.—just as they are particularly in gems. However, the form is not the same, because it is also not the same as in the earth; but the natures and properties are particularly such as they are particularly in gems. In their particular nature, they do not differ. They differ only in form and figure, etc.

---

### Now regarding the Cure.

**A**nd thus it must be noted concerning the cure of these things: if gold "sins" <note>An alchemical way of saying a substance is pathologically out of balance.</note> by its resolution, then it shall be cured by coagulation. If Salt is resolved, then let it be coagulated. If Mercury is resolved, it is coagulated and "fixed" <note>Alchemical "fixation" makes a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>, just as through Alchemy. In the same way, the things of man are fixed through medicine, and there will be long life. Likewise in Leprosy: if Mercury is lacking, let it be generated and the leprosy will be cured.
But those diseases that are "born" (such as Epilepsy) have their cure subjected to these things: it is the "flower of minerals," etc. Certain things are to be referred to the *Book on the Womb*.

---

<margin>
The womb is the tree of the body.
</margin>
**T**he womb <note>original: "Matrix"</note> behaves like a tree in the earth. And just as a tree draws from the earth and from all the Elements what it needs, so the body also stands as the earth, and the womb as the tree; this is what Philosophy, with its minerals, declares.

<margin>
Mystic diseases of the other are Theories.
</margin>
2. Thus, the womb attracts diseases from the earth—that is, from the body. These "arboreal" diseases, which it conceives in this way, are different and entirely diverse from the remaining corporeal diseases. Therefore, two Theories are given: the Natural, and that of Miscarriage <note>original: "Abortus"</note>.
3. The body, therefore, exists by itself in a manner similar to male diseases. If it becomes ill, it similarly arouses other diseases in the womb, etc.
4. From which it follows that male corporeal diseases may cause the menstrual flow, the <term>mola</term> <note>A "false conception" or mass of tissue in the uterus.</note>, etc. Just as suffocation comes from epilepsy, "precipitation" <note>Likely a reference to sudden onset or collapse.</note> from apoplexy, or discharge from fevers, etc.
5. Therefore, first the body must be rectified; afterwards the womb—that is, the tree.

<margin>
Good earth, good fruits, etc.
</margin>
6. Good earth produces good trees; a good tree brings forth good fruit. Therefore, first the body, then the womb, and finally the infant must be considered.

<margin>
Mystic diseases of the one Theory.
</margin>
7. Since the womb is the tree and the body is the earth, two Theories must be described and handed down in the "Monarchy of Women" <note>Paracelsus's term for the specific anatomical and pathological domain of women.</note>: namely, the corporeal and the arboreal diseases. To these is then added a third Theory of this Monarchy: that is, concerning the recently born infant, not rightly conceived, but behaving like a pear rotting on the tree; from all of which the Monarchy of Men is exempt.

...things do not succeed, or have no power. Regarding these matters, it must be held that unclean spirits, attentive to humans, watch diligently to see upon whom a person bestows their love, so that the spirits might confirm that love with their own help. For instance, if an <term>Idol</term> <note>Here, a physical statue or image used in worship.</note> is at hand, radiant and adorned in itself, and claiming the name of some <term>Saint</term> <note>original: "Diui"</note>—whom the person loves and worships intensely—the unclean spirit, understanding this, adds its help to make the Idol appear even more lovable and commendable to the person's eyes. Thus, the spirit finally enchants the person so that they venerate that Idol above all things.

<margin>How great the power of incantation is.</margin>
This kind of <term>incantation</term> <note>Not just a magic spell, but a spiritual "binding" or obsession.</note> is similar to that by which someone falls in love with a person they previously found harsh or bitter. In this way, people are enchanted so that they pursue and desire things that are strictly forbidden—such as someone deserting their wife to chase after prostitutes.

<margin>A wife is from God; a prostitute is from Satan.</margin>
A wife is from God; a prostitute is from the Devil. What could Satan do that is more harmful than to cast out the divine and put diabolical things in their place? For Satan is so "keen of scent" <note>original: "emunctæ naris," a Latin idiom for being shrewd or sharp-witted.</note> that he easily recognizes that if he were truly known by men, he would not be easily called upon by them. Similarly, a person does not say, "O Satan, help me," but rather, "O God, help me." Therefore, the devil devises a middle ground in these matters, so that he is not invoked under his own name, but under the pretext of the Saints, while in the meantime he himself is hidden behind the mask. For he who seeks someone where they are not—

<margin>Saints are to be sought in heaven, not in wood.</margin>
if he finds the one he seeks there, he is without doubt circumvented by a trick. The Saints, to be sure, dwell in heaven, not in wood. Whoever seeks them in wood will certainly never find them. If, however, they nonetheless obtain their wish, that success is already in conflict with faith. For on earth there is nothing anywhere so excellent or noble that the Saints could comfortably inhabit it—let alone a foolish piece of wood or stone. Now, that granting of a wish is called a healing. But that healing is actually a disease, not health—concerning which healing we will treat in its own proper chapter.

So too the working of signs or miracles comes from the same power and potency; as if someone were to say, "Devil, help me," etc., and he helps. For both are the same. Or if someone were to say, "I wish Saint Anthony would burn this person." If the person is burned following this imprecation, this sign must certainly be ascribed not to the Saint, but to the devil himself. These same spirits also work miracles when some Abbot, or Prelate, or Lord, etc., dies; just as in many places these "heralds" appear three days beforehand. All of these things prove that very powerful spirits dwell there, instilling much superstition in the reckless.

<margin>The Devil is a craftsman of a thousand arts.</margin>
For the craftiness and sagacity of malignant spirits in seducing and deceiving men is so great that they set infinite hiding places and traps for them, such that no industry can avoid them all, unless one protects oneself with this single shield: to believe in the one and only God, and to commit all other things to His protection.

<margin>To believe in God is the "sacred anchor."</margin>
And although the Saints were among men, or could be, and fulfilled the vows of men by their grace, that matter is nonetheless so doubtful and full of danger that, because of the mixed-in Satanic frauds, nothing should be attempted rashly. For this one and safest foundation stands before us against all temptations: that we believe in one God, throw all our trust upon Him, and shake all worldly things far out of our minds. And even if Saint Peter himself were to bestow an entire Kingdom upon you, you ought by no means to accept it—not even, I say, if he spoke to you face to face. For so many articles and conditions are inserted by Satan that it is far better to accept absolutely nothing in any way whatsoever.

<margin>Nothing is to be accepted from the Saints.</margin>
In the same way, if someone were sick and invoked a certain Saint who had a sure supply of help to bring; nevertheless, it would be much holier not to invoke the Saint at all,

…and that illness should be endured patiently, rather than becoming guilty of a **Satanic pact** or foul **idolatry**. Nor should one fail to consider, with the greatest attention and most diligent examination, that Christ gave nothing of this kind to his **Saints** <note>original: "Diuis." While "Divus" can mean a deity, in this context it refers to the Saints of the Church.</note>, such as specific regions, cities, villages, and so on—though he could have done so with little effort. Indeed, for what reason did he not do this? Surely for this one reason: to cut off every opportunity for the recurring frauds of Satan, which he is accustomed to recklessly mix into all things. Thus, **prayer beads** <note>original: "spherulæ precatoriæ," referring to the Rosary.</note> (the Our Father), if carried in the hands, are good. Yet this is not so good that it would not be much better for them *not* to be carried than to be carried.

<margin>Saints are not to be worshipped.</margin>

For the eyes then govern the prayers, which ought not to happen; that was the duty of the heart. If a Saint dies and is buried, and at their tomb the lame, the blind, and the infirm are all healed, that is indeed a great praise and grace of God; yet it would be better if it did not happen, on account of the superstitions and the idolatry of Satan that run alongside it. A Christian person, therefore, who is a worshiper of the true faith, must be certain that all things ought to be ascribed to God, as to the one from whom all things proceed and are divine. Therefore, do not worship [the Saint], but stay within these boundaries: do not constantly seek for this or that to be done further. This is already enough. For he sits nearby, waiting for this. But if God confers this grace upon some Saint on earth, so that bears, lions, crows, and so on perform duties and services for them beyond the nature of animals: let us leave that in its place and regard the matter with indifference. For if we wished to invoke the Saints for this purpose—so that bears, lions, and crows might perform similar services for us—Satan would certainly be ready at hand. Therefore, the judgment of all these things

<margin>Medicine was created to avoid superstition.</margin>
belongs to the **Physician**. For this reason, **created Medicine** <note>Physical medicine derived from nature, as opposed to "miraculous" or superstitious cures.</note> exists: so that superstition and idolatry might be avoided. Let God alone be God, by whose power all hell trembles, but not by the power of the Saints. Therefore, believe in God.

<margin>God's commands are to be kept simply.</margin>
But this also must be held in a mindful heart: that God has given us the mandates of His will, which must be observed **simply**. If they are "corrected"—and (supposing the case) they could indeed be corrected—that must nonetheless be attempted by no one recklessly, because of the consequence that Satan will immediately interfere. Whatever Christ said and commanded,

<margin>True faith.</margin>
must be held simply. And although a more "useful" order might be established through our own wisdom than the one fixed by Christ, it must by no means be done. The reason is that the Satanic power simultaneously mingles with it and creeps in. Thus, the **Lord’s Supper** was administered simply. Now,

<margin>The Lord’s Supper turned into something else.</margin>
indeed, the same has degenerated into something else. What is that, I ask? I grant and concede, of course, that the [modern] rite is more splendid, more pleasant, and more delightful than sitting at a table in the manner of Christ. And yet, it ought not to have been changed, however beautiful and arranged in a better order it may seem. For **Magic**, **sorcery**, and **augury** <note>Divination or interpreting signs.</note> have crept in together, which would not have been introduced if that action had been kept and administered simply according to the example of Christ. For there is a vast distance between

<margin>Simplicity and wisdom are far apart.</margin>
using a thing **simply** and using it **wisely** <note>In this context, "wisely" (sapienter) implies human intellectualizing or "cleverness" as opposed to humble faith.</note>. In this case, the supreme and sole consideration should not be the elegance or the grace of the order, but rather simplicity; nor anything else in any way,

<margin>One must indulge in simplicity.</margin>
lest a window be opened for the insertion of Satan’s frauds. From this also the proverb was born: *The more learned, the more perverse.* For faith has no need of any scholar or wise man. **Simplicity** is a safe refuge, through which one must break through without any doubt.

### Chapter on Desperate Diseases.

<margin>Desperate diseases are difficult to recognize.</margin>
The diseases, however, which are born from **desperation** <note>original: "desperatio." In Paracelsian thought, this is not just a feeling, but a spiritual state of having lost hope or "fallen" from God's simple order.</note>, are manifold and varied, so subtle and hidden that they are recognized with difficulty, except by those who have already acquired a knowledge of them according to their types. Before we speak of desperation, therefore, observe its foundation—what it is—and likewise its beginning. God the Greatest and Best has bestowed upon each person their own **conscience** and a universal property, by which a human possesses all things that they need in intellect, wisdom, integrity, honesty, and the like. And it is fitting

<margin>Everyone should be content with their own intellect.</margin>
for a person to be content with these, and not to probe or inquire after more. But whoever does not rest satisfied with these given things, but seeks something "better" and more "excellent"—namely, another wisdom, a higher judgment, another integrity and honesty—that person indicates that they are already doubting. And therefore,

<margin>How people become "desperate."</margin>
they fall into **desperation**, and the contrary follows.

While he occupies himself with the contrary and investigates too curiously, he subjects himself to all spirits and **Satanic specters**, to all fluttering phantasms <note>original: "phantasmatis," referring to deceptive mental images or apparitions</note>, and to trivial matters. Indeed, as the phantasms are, so he himself becomes. For now a spirit flies into him which makes him doubtful and despairing of wisdom; then another, which tests his integrity; and later another, which suggests hanging, stabbing, suffocation, and so on. Similarly, those who live in such "wisdom" and "integrity" are **children of this world** <margin>Children of the world, etc.</margin>. People of this sort, who wander so far from the true path that God has shown, become something else; they are changed into something other than what God commanded them to be—in their dress, in their doctrine, in their sermons, in their morals, in their counsel, in their actions, and in their whole life. By these things, they separate themselves from the world as if by a divorce; that is, they exhaust and waste away in those things about which God taught nothing. All these have already entered the **path of desperation** <margin>The logic of the thief and the steward is one and the same.</margin> and are entangled in the snares with which they might hang themselves. Just like a thief for whom the gallows is already prepared, who has no other solace or protection except that he does not yet hang there where he ought; so these people also exist like thieves, in that they do not yet hang. And just as not all thieves are hanged, so it is with these: they differ from the others only in that they hang themselves.

And this disease is truly very grave and terrible, and it is widespread. For they undergo various kinds of death and miserable conditions upon the earth. Indeed, they do not walk in the **way of God**, in which they were established. Therefore, one must walk in simplicity after the manner of a dove. Doves do not hang themselves, and yet they have what they need <margin>Simplicity is the one thing necessary.</margin>. For simplicity is of great importance to God. Let us seek nothing, therefore, but simplicity, in which no one despairs. And yet these simple ones exist just as providently and prudently as **serpents**, placing all hope in future things. Now, just as the dove was established by God in simplicity, and the serpent in prudence—which is the proper nature of each— <margin>Man is of a nature both dove-like and serpent-like.</margin> so man also has doves and serpents within his own nature. That is: if God provided for these necessary animals, he will do much more for us. Content, therefore, let us use those things which nature has bestowed upon us to handle all those things which God has commanded us. Beyond this, let us crave nothing, and bind ourselves to nothing. In this way, we shall be safe and immune from this disease. For let no one be 

persuaded that supernatural cleverness, deceits, wisdoms, industries, and the like emerge from the gift of God. For God is a lover and observer of moderation <margin>Supernatural gifts are not from God.</margin>. And excessive or idle chatter is not a gift of God. For God is no babbler, nor does he wish us to be occupied with trifles. Therefore, what God is not himself, he does not make us to be. Whence the brevity of the speeches of Christ and the Apostles should be a sign and a lesson to us that nature consists in things that are brief and moderate. For he who wished marriage to be established or refused with a simple "Yes" or "No" <margin>Nature is brief and moderate.</margin>—leaving aside all long-windedness—pursued that same simple brevity in other matters as well. He who knows the aforementioned prayers, why should we be anxious? He likewise requires from us no <margin>God delights in brevity.</margin> long-windedness, or ornate oratory and rhetoric. All these things, therefore, do not flow at all from the fountain of human property or possession, but rather overflow into the way of desperation. That is, those who attempt to transcend the goals and limits of humanity are subject to desperation, unless <margin>The transgression of humanity is the path to desperation.</margin> God protects them with singular care. And the judgment concerning these people is the same as it is for that commandment of nature: *Love God and your neighbor*. For this commandment is not from the earth, it is not from the borderlands <note>original: "limbo," here likely meaning the fringes or edges of the natural world</note>: it is from God. God is not nature. The commandment is from nature and from God. Indeed, it is from God in such a way that it is implanted in us by him to be so. Therefore it flows from nature—that is, it is inserted into us along with our nature, just as simplicity is given with the dove and prudence with the serpent. Now, therefore, he who does not have the **love of God** <margin>A lack of love for God and neighbor is a sign of desperation.</margin>—according to the degree that nature has been given to him in his strength, power, and mind, all of which are naturally within a man—he is undoubtedly already treading the boundary of desperation. Furthermore, he who does not love his neighbor, just as his inborn nature wills and teaches him, he too is a despairer. For these are those properties which nature has implanted; which we do not learn from others through instruction, but are taught immediately in the very moment of our conception. And this is surely that nature in which we ought to walk soberly.

Thus, anyone who seeks more than what has been given to him by God is subject to that hanging and throat-cutting, etc. For he obtains nothing further from God. He will, therefore, obtain it from the devil. In the same way, he who does not expend what <margin>Gifts received are to be put to use.</margin> he has on that which nature shows (and the inborn logic of his property requires), the devil compels and rules him to suppress it, and finally...

### -> Chapter on the diseases of sleep. <-

<margin>From where the diseases of sleep are born.</margin>
**W**hatever happens to us through a dream also exists as a disease, although it may not hurt or manifest outwardly. For there are many other diseases that are painless, and yet they are diseases nonetheless. The body overcomes them. Every Physician ought to be both knowledgeable and persuaded of this: namely, that the body by itself removes far more diseases than the Physician and Medicine. For unless God had implanted such a "Healing Nature" <note>original: "Naturam Medicatricem," the concept that the body possesses an innate ability to heal itself</note> in man, his life would certainly be only a few years long. The same thing also happens regarding the diseases of sleep; these diseases do not afflict the body itself in its physical form, but rather the congenital spirit in its own body (which is itself also corporeal, since it dies). Here, however, it must be known that human prudence is a foreknower of future events, and knows the past as well as the present. Furthermore, the nature of man, which he brought into the world from conception, is so sublimely endowed that he knows and sees what his kinsmen and friends are doing in foreign regions—which is taught more at length and clearly in the Kabbalah <note>original: "Gabala," likely referring to the Paracelsian tradition of interpreting the signs of the soul and the stars</note>. Since this is the case in man, I would have you know that the dream plays a role in the Kabbalah; and what is judged through it is the shadow of that wisdom and providence of man. But the reason the waking man is ignorant of these humors is this: because he does not seek what has been given to him by God. For God gave us all arts, all wisdom, understanding, and the knowledge of all things—both future things and things happening in foreign places. We, however, do not know that which is within our very selves. For we act insanely or make meaningless gestures in temporary matters, and thus we drowsily neglect what is within us. Each and every person has all arts and sciences within himself, and no one has received more or less than another. But he who does not see what he has in himself, and tells another that the other is a good painter while he himself is a bad one—he speaks truly indeed, but he errs in this: that he thinks more grace has been conferred upon the other than upon himself. For you have no less than the other in yourself, but you have not searched for it. And this is true of all things. For behold, Adam, Moses, and others sought within themselves for what was in man, and they revealed it, just as all the other Kabbalists did; nor was anything foreign <note>The Latin text ends on the word "peregrinum" (foreign/strange), leading into the next page.</note>...

they did not search for anything **foreign** <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: "foreign" things refers to knowledge sought from external demons rather than one's own nature.</note> from demons or spirits, but they drew out what was their own from the light of nature, which they produced and illuminated entirely within themselves. From this they also knew things that we judge to be impossible—which are nevertheless possible because they are within man. But we do not seek what is in us; therefore we are also nothing and know nothing (concerning which I have written elsewhere in my *Secrets* and the *Great Gabalia* <term>Gabalia|A term used by Paracelsus to describe a form of spiritual or mystical knowledge, often related to his unique interpretation of the Kabbalah</term>). Natures of this kind are within man. Since they are in man, yet man is ignorant of them, it happens that future events occur to him, and through sleep there are offered things that are intelligible, obscure, past, future, foreign, and the like. All these proceed from nature, so disposed, and such things are handled in man through sleep. For it is through sleep that such things must happen, not through waking hours. Sleep is the waking state of these arts; therefore they have a spirit that plays the prelude. No one can deny that Satan, in his own science, is a Gabalist, and a very powerful one at that. These innate spirits of men are themselves of such a kind. Hence Satan seduces many in sleep who cling to him, just as has been said of those who are awake. It is therefore right for a man to be pure and immaculate, so that he may have both sleep and waking safe and secure in the light of nature. For the light of nature <term>Light of Nature|The innate, God-given intuition or "inner light" that allows humans to understand the natural world and spiritual truths without formal schooling</term> is that which works in sleep—man existing as invisible, and yet born as a visible and natural man. Yet it has more power in cognition and knowledge than the flesh can know. For what is seen proceeds from the innate spirit. The flesh profits nothing, it is the spirit that gives life <note>original: "caro nihil prodest, spiritus est qui vivificat," a reference to the Gospel of John 6:63</note>: which is the same as saying the flesh can do nothing, but its spirit both can and knows, and it exercises the flesh and gives it life. In that innate spirit the light of nature is placed, which is the Teacher of man, not hearing or formal instruction. This is what the example of Adam and others teaches us. All these things flow from that spirit alone which nourishes and preserves the flesh. It speaks in sleep; it plays within those who slumber. But the fact that not all things proceed pure and exquisite as they ought to is due to the thickness of our ignorance, because we do not know those things that are innate to us. And this is that disease which agitates and holds us in sleep, the nature of which must be treated separately. But it is also true that in sleep God suggests many things to man; that is, He manifests the Gabalia to the innate spirits, and so these things become known to man by divine permission and become familiar. But that man is seduced by this happens because of an unclean spirit, who waylays the innate spirit to deceive it no less lazily than others, especially among those who wish to live, know, and understand from dreams, and yet meanwhile are not pure and immaculate in the light of nature. To the internal spirit of these people, the unclean spirit presents souls, spirits, dances of the dead <note>original: "choreas mortuorum," likely referring to spectral visions or the "Danse Macabre"</note>, and many other such things, so that they might prophesy from them. The genuine Gabalistic spirit is indeed perfectly capable of this, but Satan nevertheless adulterates and corrupts it, just as he depraves reason even in some who are awake.

<margin>Birds possess a Gaballic spirit.</margin>
<margin>The natural omens of birds.</margin>
<margin>The dream-spirit.</margin>
<margin>The source of human prophecies.</margin>
<margin>Human prophecies have no grounds for proof.</margin>
<margin>The innate spirit.</margin>
Furthermore, it must also be known that the auguries of birds come from these innate spirits. To this order belong roosters, which announce the coming storm with their song, and peacocks, which presage the death of their masters, etc. All these things happen by the innate spirit, which is the very light of nature planted within. If this is present even in animals, and naturally so, then man will certainly contain the same within himself and bring it into the world with him. He who is pure is a certain augur, and as natural as the birds. For the omens of birds are by no means against nature, but come from nature itself, according to the spirit of each. These things which the birds announce, sleep also presages. For the dream-spirit is the same thing as the invisible body of nature. At this point it should be known: if a man prophesies, he speaks neither from a demon, nor from Satan, nor from the Holy Spirit, but he speaks from the innate property of the invisible body, which teaches magic, and from which the mage is born. For if a man prophesies who does so neither by divine command nor concerning knowable things (that is, visible and palpable things), then he brings those things forth from himself alone, like a dream—for it is a dream—but the kind that is uttered by the mouth during waking hours. Yet it behaves entirely like a dream, where what is said can be supported by no proof, but whatever the light of the Gaballic spirit suggests is presaged unknowingly. This is what magic further declares, along with the degrees of the great Gaballic wisdom. From this, therefore, it is clear that a dream is the invisible body of man, which is the innate spirit that teaches the flesh—that is, the man—which leads and directs his hands to painting and craftsmanship, which [directs] the brain...

the brain, it stirs it toward wisdom, reason, and diligence: and finally it gives life to the body itself for all things. # THE PARAGRANUM BY PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM, DOCTOR OF BOTH MEDICINES <note>original: "Utriusque Medicinae Doctoris." This title traditionally meant Doctor of both Civil and Canon Law, but Paracelsus used it to claim mastery over both Internal Medicine and Surgery, which were then separate and often unequal fields.</note>.
