## PREFACE TO THE BOOK PARAGRANUM BY DOCTOR THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.

<margin>Theophrastus’s caution.</margin>
**S**ince I recently published certain things about several diseases for no minor reasons, through which I intended to detect many errors and corruptions spreading everywhere throughout Medicine, I now experience—not without grief—that this labor of mine is being unfairly traduced and mocked by those wanderers <note>original: "erronibus." Paracelsus often played on words, calling his opponents "erroneous" or "vagabonds" of thought.</note> beyond all merit. And they do not only do this vigorously on their own, but they also incite and inflame the common people (who are already irrational enough) against me. These people do not have even a shadow of knowledge regarding these matters; instead, driven only by the favor of rivals and the envious, and unmindful of all the benefits I have provided, they rise up to accuse and slander me. Therefore, so that I might offer a solid defense against both these present and any future adversaries, I have resolved to bring this book, called the *Paragranum* <note>The name likely suggests "beyond the grain" or "the core of the matter."</note>, to light. In it, I certainly bring into the open the entire foundation upon which I build all my writings, and without which no one can be made an upright Physician. In this work, I provide such a plain and clear explanation that I have certain hope that my opinion will eventually be favorably known to all; furthermore, I hope to win the assent even of those who, by flattering the opposing side, have hitherto hindered our course and striven with hostile intent to overwhelm us—though they are moved not at all by our excellent counsel, through which they see us so obstinately bringing forth everything for the health of the sick. <margin>Theophrastus’s protest.</margin> Nor is there reason for anyone to complain that they are harmed by slanders and injuries. For our rebukes are not of a civil or judicial nature, but are of that kind and rank which the majesty of truth itself grants and permits to every writer and professor as free and exempt from punishment—namely, that errors and the corruption of the arts might be cut out and uprooted with due severity. <margin>The author’s freedom.</margin> For we know that this right is free to all: that he who brings forth sounder and better things in any matter may also rebuke the contrary falsehoods and harmful opinions, and may even dare to attack them more seriously with "words from a wagon" <note>original: "verbis veluti de plaustro dictis." A classical idiom referring to the coarse, unrestrained insults shouted from wagons during ancient festivals.</note>. In our writings, however, entirely better things are proposed than are found in the traditions of other authors. For not even the smallest stroke has been placed by us without long observation and simultaneously long and accurate experience. By this, I trust I shall be sufficiently safe and defended against anyone. I have written, indeed, what seemed to me too little; yet to my adversaries, the same things seem too much. I have written, I say, for the most part about impostures and the thick and foolish remedies which Physicians extract from woods <note>likely referring to "Holy Wood" (Guaiacum), a popular but often ineffective 16th-century cure for syphilis</note>, from Mercury, wine, and other violent things. I have written about Surgeons—how, with rashness and cruelty, they erode, cut, and burn the sick. Thus, out of zeal for the public good, I have exposed the ignorance of both. <margin>Which works Theophrastus has published.</margin> I have moreover published other works, all of which they also translate into slander: namely, on <term>Tartar|Stony, calcified deposits in the body, which Paracelsus compared to the crust inside wine barrels.</term>, on the origin of pustules <note>A common term for the lesions of the "French Disease" or syphilis.</note>, on the method of preparing medicine, on the method of bloodletting, and other similar things in the books of the *Paragraphs*...

<summary>This page introduces the Paragranum, Paracelsus's foundational text explaining the four pillars of his medical philosophy. In the preface, he defends his work against critics and the "insane" public, arguing that his harsh rebukes are necessary to cleanse medicine of corruption.</summary>
<keywords>Paragranum, medical ethics, four columns of medicine, medical reform, critique of physicians, Tartar, syphilis, mercury, surgical cruelty</keywords>

--- Page 225 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of the Paragranum, where Paracelsus defends his unconventional medical theories against the established academic physicians of his time. He transitions from discussing his previous publications to outlining the four "pillars" of his new medicine.</meta>

...I have delivered, of which they gnaw only the crumbs, but they do not dip their hands into the dish itself. Because of these things, they treat me with such contempt and ignominy that they have nearly banished and exported me to the <note>original: "Insulas Pontii Pilati." A proverbial expression for being cast out into exile or a place of no return.</note> Islands of Pontius Pilate. However, so that I may be safe in Germany and serve my homeland, I now bring forth and lay out for all of you the entire base and foundation upon which the columns of my Medicine are raised and fixed. Once you have read, understood, and weighed these things, you may damn my writings if I have not emerged from the root of <note>original: "Reyri." This may be a Paracelsian term or a reference to a foundational source of truth; in his context, it often refers to the core essence of a thing.</note> Reyri. Judge for yourselves whether it is not right and just to persist diligently in writing with such a foundation, rather than to give up. For this reason, I now also set out to explain in clearer words those things which I previously wrote too briefly and in too narrow a sense regarding the opinions of my adversaries. In this way, I may clearly reveal and set before everyone’s eyes—without deceit or disguise—their folly and mine, their experience and mine, and the foundation of truth for both. For the sole demand of both sides is to explicitly recognize the similarity and agreement between the <term>inner Physician</term> <note>The "inner physician" is a core Paracelsian concept: the body's own natural healing power (the Archeus), which the external doctor must assist.</note> and the outer one.

<margin>Why the style of Theophrastus’s writing is accused.</margin>
While they find fault with me because my writings are not composed according to their standards and methods, the fault is not mine, but lies in their own ignorance. For, as my writings testify, I certainly publish nothing without a foundation; rather, I push out the branches of truth from the root itself during the very time of May <note>Paracelsus often uses organic, seasonal metaphors; "May-time" signifies the natural season of growth and revelation.</note>. As for why they snarl and murmur against my mature writings, there are, by Pollux, no small reasons. For no one cries out unless they are wounded, unless they feel it. No one feels it unless they are mortal and fragile. These men cry out because their art is fragile and momentary. Nothing cries out unless it is fleeting and mortal. Thus, they themselves are 
<margin>The Perpetual Art of Medicine.</margin>
mortal, which is why they vociferate against me. The Art itself, however, does not cry out against me. For it is immortal, and established upon a foundation so solid that it would be necessary for heaven itself to break and perish along with the earth before the Art should die and perish. Since Medicine itself offers me peace, why, I ask, should the noisy clamor of fleeting physicians trouble me? They shout for this reason alone: because they are struck and wounded by me. This very thing is proof that they are "sick" within the field of Medicine. That sickness is the struggle they have brought against me, which they are not at all pleased to see revealed or manifested. They bark and mutter most of all if I touch their pulse in the place where it throbs. They are much more inclined to procure their own destruction than to protect their art, industry, experience, and integrity (which belong to the sick), though it is in these very things that I place the entire "bow and stern" <note>An idiom meaning "the whole" or the most important parts.</note> of my writing. Likewise, they make their various responses and proceed from a double foundation, 
<margin>The foundation of Medicine is one and self-consistent.</margin>
even though the foundation of Medicine is only one, perpetually continuous with itself, and not at all divided. The cause of this fragmentation of theirs is that their art is heaped together and glued from scraps. Hence these frequent voices are heard: *"You, Doctor, answer this; you, Bachelor, defend that; you, Surgeon, cure this; you, Bath-keeper, provide the rest."*

The heaviest charge they twist against me is that I did not emerge from their schools or publish my works according to their canons. However, if I were to do that, I would never escape the fault of
<margin>The discordant ancients.</margin>
lying. For the writings of the ancients themselves are found to be discordant and false. Who can become truthful from such sources? If I wish to write the truth in Medicine, and to comment upon it not only for the
<margin>The occasion and manner of writing.</margin>
students, but also for the masters and teachers themselves, it will certainly be necessary first and foremost that they all be driven into one single yoke by a stable and confirmed truth. And since they are so clamorous, it is appropriate that it first be explained to them what Medicine is; then let it be added what sort of men they are, what their clamor is like, and what their art is. This cannot be done in any other way than by bringing forward those things in which Medicine itself consists, so that it may be clear to all whether I have sufficient right and occasion to write. Thus, led by this necessity, I establish four columns as the foundation of my
<margin>The fourfold foundation of the author.</margin>
writing: namely, <term>Philosophy</term>, <term>Astronomy</term>, <term>Alchemy</term>, and <term>Virtue</term>. Leaning upon these four columns, I will watch any adversaries to see if they can produce anything against me from sources other than these four. They are despisers of Astronomy; they are despisers of Alchemy; they are despisers of the Virtues. How, then, can they not be despised by the sick, when they despise that which must absolutely produce and administer Medicine to the sick? For the measure they use to measure is returned to them, and they are confounded by their own works. Christ was the foundation of salvation, and yet he was held in contempt. That contempt later so oppressed those despisers that neither they nor Jerusalem could stand.

Therefore, I rightly compare this breed of Academic physicians, surgeons, and barbers to buffoons and peddlers of trifles. Among this insolent tribe, you have chosen the first place for yourselves.

<margin>The four columns hand down all Medicine.</margin>
But to return to the foundation: who will ever be a proper Physician if he is not born without blemish from the four things mentioned above? No one. For the knowledge and experience of these four...

<summary>Paracelsus defends his "unorthodox" medical writing, arguing that his critics are merely protecting their fragile, fragmented traditions. He introduces his four pillars of medicine—Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue—as the only true foundation for healing.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, Virtue, four columns, medical education, academic physicians, inner physician, medical foundation, Paracelsus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of the Paragranum. Having previously established that his medicine is rooted in the "Reyri" (the core essence of nature), Paracelsus now directly attacks the academic medical establishment of the 16th century. He introduces his four pillars—Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue—as the only true foundation for a physician, contrasting his "Theophrastian" divine knowledge with the "Cacophrastian" or foul-speaking errors of his rivals.</meta>

# PARAGRANUM. 183

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
*...is required above all else: Medicine is occupied with these things, not in the man himself. In these is the knowledge of disease; in these are the signs of disease; in these is the medicine for disease; in these the hope and health of the sick are placed, just as the resurrection of the dead is placed in the passion of Christ. Yet, because I write from the foundation of Medicine, I am rejected by you. Because you were not born from the true seed and genuine inheritance, you follow bastards <note>original: "spurios." In this context, Paracelsus refers to physicians who follow traditional authorities like Galen rather than the direct observation of nature.</note>, raising and magnifying yourselves higher than a horse. Truly, who among all the learned would ever value the sand more than the rock of their profession? Only the horned simpletons <term>beani</term> <note>original: "cornuti beani." "Beani" was a mocking term for first-year university students; Paracelsus uses it here to suggest the "learned" doctors are mere beginners or fools.</note> of the Academies do not do this; they take their name from the foundation they stand upon, impatient of any correction, and exist as merely shadowy Doctors. If they did not walk about dressed up for the sake of appearance, who would recognize them as Doctors? For they cannot be made manifest through their own works. Thus they shine on the outside, but inside they are filthy, like the images of statues. Who that is truly skilled and learned judges a Physician by his external clothing? No one, unless he is a man of lazy stupidity and simplicity. Now then, this Medicine, which is valued by no learned man—upon what is it finally rebuilt? For it neither smells of Philosophy, nor tastes even a little of Astronomy; it displays nothing of Alchemy, nor is it distinguished by any Virtue.*

<margin>Cacophrastus instead of Theophrastus.</margin>
*But to me, who produces and hammers home such things, a name is smeared upon me so that they call me **Cacophrastus** <note>A mocking play on his name: "Theophrastus" means "God-speaker," while "Cacophrastus" means "Foul-speaker."</note>, though by nature and the right of baptism I am named **Theophrastus**.*

<margin>What each column will hand down.</margin>
<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
<margin>The great spirit of Theophrastus.</margin>
*Furthermore, so that you may more accurately understand my foundation, upon which I shall stand unmoved—namely, Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue—know that the first whole and perfect column shall be the **Philosophy** of the earth and water itself; the second column shall be **Astronomy** and Astrology with absolute knowledge of both Elements, namely air and fire; the third column shall be **Alchemy**, with the perfect and multifaceted preparation and skillful extraction of the four aforementioned Elements; and the fourth shall be **Virtue**, which follows the Physician even unto death, acting as a guardian and preserver of the other three columns. Pay diligent attention to these things. For you will either support yourselves by these four columns, or you will certainly be revealed to all commoners and heathens alike, so that they may finally understand that your art is nothing other than a deception imposed upon princes, nobles, entire regions, and cities—a craft supported by no science, no experience, and no truth. Thus, all the honors with which you have been heaped were, as he persuaded you, bestowed upon mere fools and impostors—that is, upon you Doctors. By the same reasoning that I propose these four columns, they must be entirely admitted by you as well; you shall follow me, not I you. Me, me, I say, you shall follow: you Avicenna, you Galen, you Rhases, you Montagnana, you Mesue <note>These represent the "Old Guard" of medicine: Greek, Roman, and Arabic authorities whom Paracelsus sought to overthrow.</note>. Not I you, but you shall follow me—you Parisians, you of Montpellier, you Swabians, you of Meissen, you of Cologne, you of Vienna, all you whom the Danube and the Rhine nourish, you whom the maritime islands enclose; you also Italy, you Dalmatia, you Athens, you Greek, you Arab, you Israelite. Not I you, but me you shall follow; nor shall anyone hide in the furthest corner where the dogs will not urinate on him. I shall be the monarch; the monarchy shall be mine. I administer this, and I gird your loins. Does that **Cacophrastus** please you now? This is the dung you must eat.*

<margin>Duelech: the third spagyric stone. Galen is sharply attacked.</margin>
*What will be the state of your minds at that time, when your **Cacophrastus** is established as the prince of the Monarchy? Will you, the "heaters," clean the chimneys instead? How will it seem to you if the sect of Theophrastus celebrates a solemn triumph? If you are dragged under the yoke of my Philosophy, and you call your Pliny "Cacoplinian," and your Aristotle "Cacostotle"? If I am to newly initiate or baptize them, along with your Porphyry, Albertus, etc., and all their compatriots in my oil? All these things the mineral power and the generation of minerals shall procure and win for me; and whatever is contained between both poles shall aid me, so that I may drown your Astronomy and your bloodletting calendars in the Lake of Pilate <note>A reference to a legendary lake associated with the ghost of Pontius Pilate, symbolizing a place of cursed exile.</note>. Our Alchemy itself shall cook your Aesculapius, Avicenna, and Galen, and any other writers, burning them into Alkali; and in the <term>reverberatory furnace</term>, it shall reduce them to the very last dregs. With Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, used by Alchemists to represent the transformative power of the furnace.</note> then pouring on Sulfur, pitch, nitre, and oil, you shall be purified through fire more exquisitely than gold itself. Indeed, you shall be passed through <term>stibium</term> <note>Antimony (stibium) was used in alchemy to purify gold, as it consumes other metals; here it is used as a metaphor for a harsh trial.</note>, where I shall observe which king you leave at the bottom. Furthermore, I will have you polished upon **Duelech** <note>original: "Duelech." A Paracelsian term for a stone or tartar formed in the human body, particularly the kidneys or bladder.</note>. Finally, Virtue itself, as the fourth column, will make a far greater spectacle of you than the Jurists have devised for criminals. How greatly your sick will burst into laughter at this sight! Woe, therefore, to the wretched soul of Galen. If he had been immortal in Medicine, his shades would not be buried in the abyss of hell (from whence they sent letters to me, the date of which was given as "in hell"). Never, never would I have thought that such a prince of Physicians should have had to fly into the devil's backside. Here his disciples follow him as well. Shall this man be the prince and monarch of Medicine? Or shall Medicine stand built upon this?*

*Indeed, if I were armed with no other support against you than the testimony...*

He now continues this metaphor, arguing that his medical "monarchy"—his supreme authority based on nature—is the only true path, while the academic establishment relies on flattery and dead traditions.</meta>

-># PREFACE TO THE BOOK<-
->### PAGE 184<-

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence from the previous page: "...tiller] of fields."</meta>

...of fields; how much, I ask you, would I be valued in the <term>Monarchy</term> <note>original: "monarchia." Paracelsus frequently used this term to describe his own supreme, self-appointed authority over the realm of medicine, contrasting it with the "corrupt" authority of the universities.</note>? Because I uncover such a long-standing lie, and overthrow it with solid testimony, and I establish the truth itself and bring it forth clearer than the Sun: how much more certainly and sublimely would I rule in the monarchy, if beyond the cited testimonies of the fields I also convince you with a fourfold faculty, and act so that I teach you, and not you me. For what I learned from you has vanished like the snow of the past year; and I threw the sum of the books of St. John into the fire, so that all misfortune might ascend and be dissipated with the smoke <note>This refers to the famous incident on St. John’s Day in 1527, when Paracelsus publicly burned the "Canon of Medicine" by Avicenna and the works of Galen in a bonfire at the University of Basel.</note>. By this means the Monarchy has been purged; hereafter it is subject to no fire and cannot be devoured. Yet look at what else still awaits you: see truly whose Monarchy it is, mine or yours? For unless you crept so deceitfully into the favor of the Lords through the flattery of words, you would wander more impoverished than Codrus <note>A legendary figure representing extreme poverty.</note>, and, compelled by extreme want, you would be forced to eat your own dung. In this way Galen teaches his disciples to seek their livelihood from the dead and the corrupt. But if the deceased were to return to life, and the corrupt were restored to health, they would pelt you with filth rather than greet you with a bowed knee as they passed.

<margin>
Why Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus's given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> broke away from the Philosophers and Physicians.
</margin>
Now, as for the fact that I am a <term>Philosopher</term>, though not one tuned to your lyre, what do you think is the reason for me? Very much: first of all, that Natural things are described by you without any truth or foundation, and your text with all its explanation stands as mere opinion and a dream, and the true and genuine principle has not yet been touched by the Philosophers even with the tips of their fingernails. Indeed, in Medicine the first thing is this: namely, that the Physician should have investigated that which existed before man.

<margin>
What Philosophy delivers.

Dual Philosophy.

Two spheres and how many Elements.
</margin>
Truly, this is <term>Philosophy</term>, which treats none of those things that came after man, but those which existed before him. These things he ought to know entirely and perfectly as a skilled and industrious practitioner, not merely as a Physician. From this, two Philosophies are established: one of the things of the lower sphere, the other of the things of the upper sphere. And thus I could rightly profess that Philosophy is twofold, and so there is a twofold entrance or a two-headed beginning of Medicine: and furthermore, each of these is again twofold within itself. For each sphere includes two Elements. For this reason, the Astronomer is also a Philosopher of the sky and the air. And what the Astronomer knows, the Philosopher ought to know as well. Conversely, the Astronomer must also be skilled in Philosophy. Both are called Philosophers, both are called Astronomers. Each is an Astronomer, each is a Philosopher. One applies the stars to the lower sphere; the other applies Minerals to the upper sphere. Thus, therefore, a <term>Mineral</term> and a <term>Star</term> <note>original: "Minera ac Astrum." Paracelsus believed that everything in the lower earthly world had a corresponding "star" or celestial essence in the upper world.</note> are one thing.

<margin>
Who should become a Physician.
What is a Physician?

Natural Alchemy as an artificial guide.

What is maturation?
</margin>
But for what purpose do you think I propose these things? Not indeed to deal in trifles, but to establish in order that the Physician must be divided into two spheres, namely the Philosophical and the Astronomical, and the external must be led into the internal. Thus the Physician is an internal Astronomer, and an internal Philosopher, born from external Astronomy and Philosophy. And yet even so, the Physician is not yet ready: truly, just as the calyx in the flower is the matter of the pear, and the pear itself, yet as of yet useful to no one: so also is the Physician, but the harvest does not yet press on. And therefore it is fitting to be an <term>Alchemist</term>. What leads the pears to maturity? What makes the grapes ripen? The Sun alone? No, Natural Alchemy. What produces milk from grass? What brings forth wine from the dry earth? Natural digestion alone. Therefore, just as nature provides an Alchemist outwardly, so also the Physician must be ripened. And just as the preparation of all materials occurs in nature, so also must those things be perfected through the Physician. The maturation of fruits is a natural cooking. Thus, what nature contains, it cooks. That which is fully cooked out is nature herself in her entirety. Thus, if the Physician knows how to "cook" according to the purpose of the aforementioned Philosophy and Astronomy: then he is a Physician, in whom the confidence of health can be boldly placed. Guided by this, you ought to penetrate into Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy. Otherwise, you will achieve nothing fruitful or solid with any labor. Where then do your pharmacists and sycophants hide now? Where has your Astronomy and Philosophy gone? What has your art been until now other than a putrid foundation, from which you have adorned and polished your wives and children? These things must be brought into the light. And even if you were to hide twice as many scorpions under the grass, the poison itself will not choke me, but you; and your fraudulent counsels will break out into the nerves of your own necks.

<margin>
What a Physician is, unknown until the time of Theophrastus.

How certain the portents of urine are.
</margin>
From the first of your writers to the very last, all of you universally have until now been ignorant of what a <term>Physician</term> truly is. Your uncertain and ambiguous arts prove this. You know perfectly well what a Sophist is. And so, what you desire to know, you are not; and you affect to be what you are ignorant of. I say it once: you are not Physicians, but Sophists. This is established by this proof: that all of you together, and all your books together with you, do not have enough foundation and truth to be able to judge truly and aptly what even the smallest sample of urine offered to you portends or presages. What then is this? Or what kind of judgments are held of that fabricated soothsaying? The truth of the Art provides conditions for urine as well-known and conspicuous to a Physician as a <term>last</term> <note>original: "mustricula" – a shoemaker's wooden model of a foot.</note> is to a shoemaker, upon which he fits the shoe. Now, if you lack the perfect art of <term>Uroscopy</term> <note>original: "Vroscopica" – the diagnostic examination of urine, which Paracelsus claimed his rivals did purely by guesswork.</note>, what else shall I judge you to be but household servants, who scrape together alms and interest for Lady Doctoress to buy her sandals—an order in which the Pimp also professes his name. It is necessary for the Physician to be such that, just as...

He fiercely mocks the academic doctors of his time as "sophists" who cannot even perform a basic diagnosis of urine correctly.</summary>

-># PARAGRANUM<-
->### PAGE 185<-

...just as a farmer, having taken up his axe, fells and casts down a tree, so too should the physician himself cut out and strike down diseases. But if, by the same reasoning, I were unable to do this, I should no more be numbered among physicians than you are.

<margin>Medicine is certain; it does not waver.</margin>
For Medicine is so constituted that it exists beyond all ambiguity and falsehood. Nothing created by God is imperfect. He created the Physician to be perfect, not doubtful. Nor can God endure such a deception as to set before man anything imperfect; rather, it is man himself who makes what is perfect, imperfect. And here your "foundation" <note>Paracelsus is mocking the academic foundation of his rivals.</note> comes to light; here your very sides are pierced. It is therefore right that a perfect Physician stand upon the four aforementioned columns: this is the order by which one enters into Medicine. Yet because I urge these things so strongly, am I for that reason a rejected member of the Academy? Am I a heretic of the faculty? A seducer of students? These and similar charges they twist against me from the fictional writings of <term>Galen</term> <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was the standard university textbook.</note>, and they busy themselves trying to trample me into the mud.

<margin>Theophrastus's prophecy.</margin>
Nevertheless, I shall live, and you shall become as dry figs. You have emerged from fictional stars: those stars will fail, and the heavens will avenge their own evil, correcting their own Astronomers. The earth and water will renew their own Philosophers, the light of nature will once more give birth to its own Alchemist, and the sick will scourge their own Physicians. Once this purification has been established, under what banner, finally, will that crowd of ambitious Doctors be counted? Who will grant their wives the money for their headbands and shoulder-cloaks? No one, I think.

<margin>The pride of Physicians.</margin>
For their arrogance has until now been nourished on mere lies; when these vanish, that pride will also go to ruin. How loudly will those "flaming" Doctors <note>Likely referring to the bright red robes worn by doctoral graduates.</note> hiss at that time? Surely no differently than snakes shriek against toads; let their poison penetrate themselves, not me. Let them alone devour their own drugs; it would be much better for them to be choked by them than for me to be.

<margin>What makes a Physician.</margin>
Therefore, it is concluded and settled that healing makes the Physician, and that works themselves create Masters and Doctors—not Emperors, not Popes, not faculties, not privileges, nor Academies. For the things required for a Physician are hidden from these institutions. Therefore, they study only an external veneer so that they might appear great. Until now, not a single Physician has ever emerged from the schools—not even one, I say—who could explain the cause of even the smallest disease from the true principle of actual truth.

<margin>A long reproach of Physicians.</margin>
Why then, you hood-wearers <note>A derogatory reference to the academic or monastic hoods worn by university doctors.</note>, do you slander my writings? You can reject them with no firmer pretext than what you chant against me: that I can write of nothing other than luxury and Venus <note>original: "praeter luxum & Venerem." A reference to his work on "the French Disease" (Syphilis).</note>. But should that be considered a small thing? Or is it so worthy of contempt in your opinion? For as I hand down the knowledge of all wound-related diseases, and how they change into the <term>Venereal plague</term> <note>Syphilis. Paracelsus was one of the first to treat it with minerals like mercury rather than traditional herbal mixtures.</note>—the most virulent disease in the whole world, than which no more cruel has ever emerged, which spares no one, and which especially seizes and invades the highest heads—am I to be held in contempt for that? If I intend the health of princes, nobles, and all the common people, and I expose harmful and obvious errors, and thus by this undertaking I lose the praise and favor of everyone: is it fair or honest that I should be pushed into the filth and bogs because of it? Nor is any respect for the sick maintained in this. For it is the sick, not me, whom you ruin. That health which is provided through my works is not at your heart; rather, for your own sake, the sick are forced to waste away, or become paralyzed, or die. For your sake, they are led to slander me, while having no care in the meantime for their own disease or pain. Indeed, I open and reveal the mysteries and secrets of Nature, hitherto unknown to them, not in one way but in many. Because these secrets overshadow their worn-out "Receipts" <note>The standard, often complex, prescriptions used by traditional doctors.</note>, it is deemed necessary to despise them. Yet in these secrets, the Saracens, Barbarians, Persians, Chaldeans—in short, all tribes and nations—find pleasure, and they clearly experience the gifts and virtues which divine mercy has bestowed upon all who believe. They wish to cast away this mercy of God for the sake of their own impostures, so that by this means not the glory of God, but their own unfaithfulness, may prevail. For by favoring themselves, they remain unfaithful toward the sick.

And these iniquities affect me so that I call them <term>Beans</term> <note>original: "Beanos." A slang term for ignorant first-year students (freshmen), derived from the French "bec-jaune" (yellow-beak/fledgling).</note>, because they surely oppose the true foundation of Nature, and with their shouting they busy themselves selling their Syrups and pills instead of the <term>Arcana</term> <note>The "arcana" were the hidden, essential healing powers of substances that Paracelsus sought to extract through alchemy.</note> themselves. It is not I, but they themselves who betray and reveal what they are, while they deafen the ears of their listeners with wandering noise so that they might refuse to attend to the secrets and mysteries of nature. Thus, they are forced to float in the decoctions and mixtures of Physicians, even if the fear of suffocation must be endured.

You are from the brood of vipers. Why should I expect anything from you but poison? With how much shame you have cast it in my teeth that I am the **Luther of Physicians** <note>original: "Medicorum ego Lutherus sim." Like Martin Luther in religion, Paracelsus sought to overthrow the "papacy" of ancient medical authorities.</note>, adding the explanation that I am a leader of heretics? I am Theophrastus; in time, I will be better and more powerful than those to whom you compare me. I am he, and besides that, I am the **Monarch of Physicians**; I can demonstrate such things to you as you never could. Through me, let Luther defend his own; likewise, I will make my own path clear, and I will outshine all those to whom you compare me, to which my *arcana* shall carry me. Who truly hates Luther? A similar mob harasses me also. And the same evils that you portend for him, you forge for me as well: namely, "To the fire! To the fire!" For no other timely cleansing is to be expected from you.

<header>PREFACE TO THE BOOK</header>

# PREFACE TO THE BOOK

<margin>The heaven does not give birth to the Physician.</margin>
The heaven did not make me a Physician; God created me. The heaven has no power to bring forth a Physician. That art belongs to God; it does not come from the heavens. And I congratulate myself on this: that wicked men hate me. For Truth has no hater except for a liar. By right and merit, I dare to call you impostors. Your own hospitals teach me this. Dare something, I pray, and hurl that same mockery back at me with the truth? What need is there for me to put on armor and breastplates against you? For you do not possess even a shred of knowledge or learning—not even enough to write a single tiny letter against me. If I could protect my bald head from flies with the same ease that I can protect my <term>Monarchy</term> <note>Paracelsus refers to his "Monarchy" as his supreme and sovereign system of medical truth, which he believed would eventually overthrow all others.</note>; if Milan were as secure from its enemies as I am from you, by Pollux, neither the Swiss nor any other soldiers would need to be brought in. I will protect my Monarchy not with slaps or punches, but with the <term>Arcanum</term> <note>The secret, essential healing power of a substance, often extracted through alchemy.</note>. I speak of Arcana, moreover, that are not taken from the apothecary shop, where nothing but boiled mixtures and a medley of juices are dispensed. You, however, defend your cause with sycophancy. How long do you think this will last? What have you not tried? Did you not try to thrust me away to the leather-dressers? Yet these very people will one day scratch your itching backs and drive you into the pits you prepared for others. Will you snatch the palm of victory from me in debate, you who are not even slightly skilled in <term>simples</term> <note>Medicinal plants or herbs used as single ingredients in a remedy.</note>? But you learn those things first from your apothecaries, asking, "What is this?" and "What is that called?" You hunt for glory and yet you are mere apprentices to apothecaries? Begone! Outside of your fine clothes, I wouldn't trust you to mind a dog.

<margin>The pretext of oaths.</margin>
Because I am not, like them, a physician for hire by public contract, nor do I frequent the courts of Princes or the chief cities: am I for that reason of less value? For they grow insolent because of the oath they have taken, and by flaunting that oath, they try to crush me in debate. Such things happen because of the simplicity of the Magistrates who hire such men, expecting them to apply the greatest diligence; yet they do not consider that no diligence or industry can be expected from them. Once these men have been named for an annual salary, they promise I know not what else—to say nothing of so trivial a matter. What is this, whether it be simplicity or honesty on the part of the magistrate, that they bind men of this sort by an oath, when such men cannot even keep an oath? From this system of hiring, nothing grows stronger than heavy impostures. For the unlearned common folk are persuaded that those who have sworn an oath and pledged their word can hardly err; they believe that where there is an oath and a contract, there the art of medicine also flourishes. Thus, because of the oath, they presume that no one else is skilled or truthful except for these sworn doctors. Tell me, I pray, how many simple people are deceived by such oaths? For anyone who considers this will never agree with that external testimony. That testimony is utterly dry and hollow which such an oath produces. It implies that the art is present where it is not, and the oath is meant to veil or atone for all such things. Who ever heard of a Physician being bound by an oath? Is he to be compelled toward honesty by this pact? What is the use of this force or coercion if the art itself is missing? If the coercion is meant to ensure he does not charge an unfair price, he will simply plan a trick to charge for three instead of one, so that his tally remains certain. Such coercion toward an oath is a sorrowful thing. An oath should be offered to no one unless it is first established that it provides no occasion for fraud. It is a harsh testimony indeed that is given to the people to their own prejudice. You affirm that he is honest and fit, yet he is found to be dishonest and unfit. And in the name of the oath, you approve what was hardly fit to be approved. Therefore, take heed of how far the oath will extend. To secure their provisions, they would no doubt swear away their own hands and feet.

Nevertheless, however these things may be, their oath will not protect them against me. They will find it necessary to race with me to the finish line to win the prize. And they will be forced to give up their impostures, even if their courage fails them. They will also say farewell to that excuse where they say, "God disposed it so." They will even restrain themselves from the lie they babble: "if it does not help, it does no harm." For in their "cures" using wood <note>Referring to Guaiacum, or "Holy Wood," then used as a failed cure for syphilis.</note>, mercury, cathartics, and the like, they are accustomed to say, "it does no harm; first take a taste, or anoint yourselves, and see if it does you any damage." I will indeed make you understand what kind of veterinary medicine you practice, even if I am a "heretic" and a "vagabond" to you. Though it is truth, and not your lies, that leads me to wander. For I boldly profess that the downy hair on the back of my head knows much more than all your writers put together. Indeed, the buckles of my shoes are more learned than your very Galen or Avicenna. And my beard has more experience than your entire Academy. I long for that time when they shall be dragged and turned through the mud. And this "foreigner" who now pleases you: what do you think of the Hermit on a Wild Ass? <note>original: "onagro Eremita." Paracelsus likely refers to himself here, using a mocking or cryptic title to contrast his rugged, wandering lifestyle with the pampered academic physicians.</note>

---

Break out at last! What is in you? Are you skilled in debating? Why then do you not make a beginning? Debate will drive you to the point where you must give an account of your patients, and undergo the punishment of the political magistrates. How sweetly it rubs you that you are cherished by the patronage of the lawyers. But what if that protection is someday shattered, and you, like fishermen in the woods, are made into a public spectacle? Do not rise up, saying, "We have Galen for our father, we have Avicenna." Those stones shall be crushed, and the heaven will bring forth other Physicians, who will truly know the four

<header>PARAGRANVM.</header>
<sig>Q 4</sig>

# PARAGRANVM.

To the elements, add also Magic and <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Gabalisticam"; refers to the Jewish mystical tradition which Paracelsus integrated into his natural philosophy</note>, which are like cataracts and stakes in your eyes. These new physicians will be <term>Geomancers</term> <note>diviners who interpret signs from the earth</note>, they will be <term>Adepts</term>, they will be <term>Archei</term> <note>from "Archeus," the internal "alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believed governed the body's functions</note>, they will be <term>Spagyrists</term> <note>alchemical physicians who "separate and recombine" substances to create medicines</note>; they will possess the quintessence, they will be skilled in secrets, they will hold mysteries, and they will know the tinctures. Under this revolution, where will you "cooks" find a place? Who will then tint the tender lips of your wives and wipe their sharp little noses? An evil genius hides in your napkin.

<margin>Theophrastus on those whom he cannot help.</margin>
How gladly you would say to me what I say to you: "Theophrastus, you also lose and kill the sick, no less than we do." Not at all, truly, not at all. While you destroy, I strive to restore. If it does not succeed, the prior corruption came from you. Therefore, I compare you to forest fishers <note>likely referring to poachers who take game they cannot replace</note> who prey upon what they cannot return. Who can pull back death? Who can glue a severed limb back on? In this way, you hack off limbs, albeit without swords or knives. You say: "But even Theophrastus himself cannot help this man." Let it be so. But who could ever atone for or fix such robberies as yours? You have fumigated this man fifteen times; you have anointed that one just as often; you have washed another so many times; you have dragged this one around for two or three years on "the wood" <note>refers to Guaiac wood, a common but often ineffective 16th-century treatment for syphilis</note>. In this book, a quarter-pound of <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyri"</note> is hidden; in that one, a half-pound; in another, a whole pound. Now it sticks in the marrow, now it fluctuates in the veins, now it is fixed in the joints. Here it is seasoned in wine, there in the form of a powder; here it lies sublimated, there calcined, there resolved, elsewhere precipitated. and so it goes with other things as well. But who is there who can cover up everyone's shames? Who can convert or excuse any harlot? How greatly you wish that your disgrace would fall back onto my shoulders, as you have plotted many times! But because I know that you are "wooden Doctors" <note>A pun on their stupidity and their reliance on the Guaiac wood treatment</note>, I fear nothing.

<margin>The cure of the wood has failed.</margin>
Even if you had spent double your age in studies, you would still end your cure with "the wood." That is your only study. Yet those things could be learned in the space of fourteen days—not in Universities, but even in the crossroads. Oh, the shame! Even any blacksmith now knows that your cure is of no importance without the wood. You have the same nature as goats: the higher they climb, the more they show their pride, never considering that the lower place and the higher place are the same. If, therefore, you rest on no other foundation, and your writers and authors have not come any closer to the nerve of Medicine, and if your canons, recipes, and other processes which you use are not established on a more solid ground or certain trust—then it is clearer than the noonday light that true Medicine has not yet been discovered, and you have done nothing until now except what a cat does around a bowl of porridge.

<margin>Sapphire is the medicine for Anthrax.</margin>
Are you so stupid as to think that Fenugreek and Psyllium mucilage, or other things similar to these, are true and genuine "maturatives" <note>substances used to bring a boil or abscess to a head</note>? See how many recipes are prescribed for <term>Anthrax</term> <note>a carbuncle or malignant boil</note>, which by common judgment might seem to lead toward a cure. But such judgment is not enough for a Physician. You see that <term>Sapphire</term> was shown by God as the remedy for Anthrax, and not some white ointment; nor a horse's hoof for the plague. And do you think this foundation exists in your published writings? Not in the least. Medicine is no different than if a carpenter wanted to work using only a knife. Do you think you have written correctly about degrees and compositions? You have wandered far from the target. Medicine embraces such a wide foundation within itself that all such things of yours cannot even be compared to its very beginning. Are you truly so simple as to dwell on urines, even though you swallow daily lies?

<margin>How many signs are contained in urine.</margin>
Urine is indeed good in itself, and provides a great judgment of itself, containing within it the entire Physiognomy and Anatomy with its properties. If these things already exist in the urine, they must certainly be pronounced by the Physician in a complete and solid way, since they are entirely present. If they were not within, the things you are content with would be explained well enough. Life dwells in the body within the pulse, and the pulse indicates this. From this, demonstrate what needs to be demonstrated about life.

<margin>Theophrastus’s defense.</margin>
But I would wish the listeners and readers to be warned not only in these matters, but in many others, lest you perhaps attribute some arrogance or "Martial" <note>war-like or aggressive</note> nature to this preface of mine. Instead, relate like to like, and consider that Medicine was not built or born so lightly from such a shallow foundation as has been believed until now.

<margin>Sapphire is the cure for Anthrax.</margin>
For if Sapphire is the true cure for Anthrax, who, I ask, would put their trust in someone who brought forward something about Fenugreek? Therefore, let these examples and "sword-clashes" always be before your eyes, so that you may penetrate to the sublime Medicines. You should not be forced to linger among those things which neither God nor Nature established so that you might attain true discoveries. I have set before you many volumes of these, described from the following four: <term>Philosophy</term>, <term>Astronomy</term>, <term>Alchemy</term>, and <term>Virtues</term>. In bringing these forward, my purpose was to drive you listeners to accept or admit nothing anywhere outside these four boundaries. For this reason, I shall next proceed to their explanation, so that you may understand the foundation and causes of my commentary, weigh me and my adversaries on an equal scale, and respect and honor each man according to his knowledge and experience. I HAVE SPOKEN.

<summary>Paracelsus concludes his preface by mocking traditional "wooden" doctors and their ineffective treatments like Guaiac wood and mercury. He introduces his four pillars of medicine—Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue—as the only true path to healing.</summary>

# THE FIRST BASIS OF MEDICINE,
## OR THE PILLAR: PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>
What the virtue of a disciple consists of.
</margin>
Since Philosophy is established as the first and principal foundation of Medicine, it is worth the effort for us to know, above all else, by what means the knowledge of medicine can be drawn from Philosophy. But before I explain this, necessity and the facts of the matter demand that I first bring before your eyes those against whom I write: so that you may rightly recognize a false and adulterated Philosophy before I apply myself to describing the true and genuine one. It may be difficult to persuade you to renounce those things to which you are accustomed—indeed, in which you were trained and educated. And yet I have hope for every one of you, if you will compare those things you have practiced with these ideas of ours with a sober judgment. You will find that nothing is so hard that it cannot be softened, nor so soft that it cannot be hardened; and you will be persuaded that in matters of learning, the more recent things always dominate the older and prove to be more powerful.

<margin>
The nature of the old Philosophy.
</margin>
From its very cradle, moss grew upon Philosophy; later, fungi sprouted from it, like <term>glands</term> <note>referring to swellings or tumors</note> in the body.

<margin>
Aristotle
</margin>
Aristotle and his followers have done the same with Philosophy as the <term>dregs</term> <note>original: "feces"; in an alchemical and chemical context, this refers to the sediment or lees that settle at the bottom of a liquid</note> which pull the earth out of wine. And foam, though it is the worst part of what the pot contains, nevertheless floats in the highest place and covers the better things below. Hence, because it covers something better, it retains a hint of that flavor and is even counted among foods—but only for dogs and cats. The same must be thought of the old Philosophy: it deals only with fungi and foam, not the actual material from which it was born. This kind of "fungal" Philosophy is what constitutes <term>Theory</term> in Medicine, from which "foamy" Physicians are later born. These two have taken it upon themselves to establish the nature of things and to describe human afflictions and diseases. But just as the foundation from which they proceed is, so must the fruits be judged by their root. Therefore, I would have you forewarned: nothing is ever so rough or harsh that a <term>mattock</term> <note>original: "dolabra"; a heavy tool for digging or hacking</note> cannot smooth it; nothing so crooked that a hammer cannot straighten it; nothing so savage or wild that a hunter cannot strike it down. What, I ask, could be more honorable or commendable in a worthy student than to lie within a soft shell and not be hardened until he has acquired other solid parts of his discipline, and finally withdraws his hand from the <term>ferule</term> <note>a flat ruler used to strike the hands of students; here it represents elementary schooling</note>? And for such a one, it is a matter of praise and glory if he himself shakes the old and obsolete out of the nest.

<margin>
In art, it is praiseworthy to surpass one's teachers.
</margin>
For art and science, as well as modesty and love, ought to raise themselves above their masters at every moment, and sprout like a blooming beech tree, which obscures the glory of the older trees with its own joyful growth.

<margin>
A praise of Philosophy.
</margin>
But I must turn back to the philosophy I have mentioned, so that you may understand the foundation of true medicine. For it alone bestows that knowledge with which a physician must be equipped to more closely perceive the matter, condition, and nature of all diseases. Indeed, besides this, no other way remains by which the truth and nature of the body—both sick and healthy—can be assessed. Outside of this Philosophy, whatever other investigation or knowledge is drawn from anywhere else must be considered a mere imposture. For the intellect enclosed within our skull is too powerless to give birth to a physician. Indeed, it is right that the Philosophy of Medicine be explained in such a way that the eyes themselves may grasp its sense. It is right that Philosophy be no less loud and ringing in the ears than the rushing fall of the Rhine or the roar of the winds on the Ocean strikes and pierces the ears. It is right that the tongue perceives no less distinct a taste from it than that of honey or gall. It is right that the nostrils also inhale and discern the complete scent of the entire subject. Beyond this exquisite knowledge, whatever is added or applied to nature is offensive and nauseating.

<margin>
Nature is the disease itself, and the only medicine.
</margin>
For the teaching of my Philosophy is this: that nature herself is the disease. Therefore, she alone knows what the disease is. She alone is also the medicine, being well-taught in the afflictions of sick bodies. Without the knowledge of these two, who can eventually become a physician? Indeed, no disease or sickness proceeds from the physician himself. But because he can, by reason, inflict diseases and impart health in the same way—and who is a more ready teacher in this than nature herself? She is the most knowledgeable of all these things; she [provides] the clearest [explanation] of all these universal matters...

<summary>Paracelsus introduces Philosophy as the first pillar of medicine, contrasting his sensory-based "true" philosophy with the "foamy" and "fungal" academic traditions of Aristotle. He argues that nature is both the disease and the cure, and the physician must learn directly from her rather than from outdated books.</summary>

## ON PHILOSOPHY.

...provides the most lucid instruction of all things. By this most clear explanation, the physician is most conveniently informed. Now, if nature alone is conscious and aware of these things, then she alone will also prepare the remedies she has received, and this art of composition will be brought before the physician’s sight by nature alone. The art issues forth from nature, not from the physician. Therefore, it is necessary for the physician's 
<margin>
What perfect knowledge is.
</margin>
knowledge and full diligence to flow from nature itself. Moreover, full knowledge, or perfect understanding, is that which the hands touch and the eyes see—even that which is hidden and presumed within the skull. For that which is grasped obscurely and in secret begets faith; but the works, which are visible, prove and provide the outcome or perfection. Now, if the physician must be born from nature, what else will nature be but Philosophy? What else is Philosophy but invisible nature? He who has known the Sun and Moon in such a way that he knows, with eyes closed, what the Sun and Moon are like: he holds the Sun and Moon within himself just as they exist in the sky or the <term>firmament</term> <note>the heavens or the celestial sphere</note>. This, then, is Philosophy: that those lights should exist as definitely within a human being as they do outside him, no differently than if one were looking at oneself in a mirror. Just as someone looks at themselves according to 
<margin>
The whole Human must be clear to the Physician.
</margin>
even the smallest features, so the physician must carry the human being in his knowledge no less expressly, drawn from the mirror of the 4 Elements. For these exhibit the whole <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "microcoſmum"; the "little world," meaning the human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note> with such an accurate idea that he shines through as if enclosed in the clearest glass. For the human being must be as transparent and lucid to the Physician as distilled dew, in which there is not even the slightest thing that escapes his sight. The Physician must penetrate the human being with his sight no less than a clear and bright fountain, in which he distinguishes and judges even every little stone and grain of sand, along with its natural color and shape. No less conspicuous, I say, should all the limbs of the body be to the physician. It is fitting that those limbs be as transparent to the Physician as polished crystal, in which not even a hair could remain hidden. This is surely that Philosophy upon which the foundation of medicine is built. Not, indeed, so that you see through the human being as such, but rather the nature enclosed in that "heaven." It shows you everything, limb by limb. For

---

<margin>
The human is from nature.
</margin>
the human being was made from nature itself. That matter from which he was made testifies to you about that which was made from it, just as you see a building reflected in polished bronze that shines from the outside. If the external thing is removed, its interior idea does not remain in the mirror. For the external gave birth to the internal. Thus, therefore, the human being is an image from the 4 Elements, impressed into a mirror. When the elements are dissolved, the human being is also dissolved. Because the external part of the mirror is moved away, the internal part cannot remain. And therefore Philosophy 
<margin>
What is Philosophy?
</margin>
is nothing other than a full and absolute notice or knowledge of that which puts the image into the mirror. And just as the image in the mirror can provide no one with knowledge of its own essence and nature—since it is nothing but a dead image—so it is also with the human being through himself. For nothing is drawn from him except what proceeds from the external knowledge of that whose figure exists in the mirror. What the human speaks is uncertain speech; it is at least a voice and a tongue. But should the Physician know no more than if he saw a sick person’s mask speaking to a mirror, and did not hear the voice? The Physician must know the whole and complete microcosm through its own <term>matrix</term> <note>original: "matricem"; the source, womb, or originating environment from which a thing grows</note> from which it was born. For there is not any limb, however small, or even a hair in a human being, which that "shell" does not embrace and exhibit and reflect in many ways. And so, as has been said, true medicine can in no way endure or tolerate the "foam" of Philosophy or a "spongy" Medicine, such as has been babbled everywhere until now.

A great apparatus of words would be needed if one wished to make it clear and manifest 
<margin>
Theophrastus's Philosophy differs from that of the ancients.
</margin>
how great a distance lies between Aristotelian, Stoic, or Platonic Philosophy and this of mine; and again, how much the Philosophy of Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a polymath and teacher of Paracelsus</note> and [the other] Theophrastus would be separated from me, Aureolus Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus's own chosen name</note>. These distinctions have been handed down fully enough from page to page in the description of Philosophy. Nevertheless, regarding what is relevant here for the understanding of what has been said—namely, that this kind of Philosophy is the foundation of medicine—you must know that the matter, species, and essence of the Physician consist entirely of bodies; and the science of the Physician is the cause of constitution and dissolution. In these things, the Physician has his knowledge. Now, as was said before, he has need to grasp the understanding of these things from the matrix from which he was created. In that matrix, he finds his heart and all the joy and sorrow of the heart.

<summary>Paracelsus defines true Philosophy as "invisible nature," arguing that a physician must understand the human "microcosm" as a mirror reflection of the external elements. He asserts that a doctor should be able to "see through" a patient as if they were clear glass, distinguishing his experiential approach from the abstract theories of the Greeks.</summary>

# TRACTATE I OF THE PARAGRANUM

...pain. In that [Philosophy], he finds the brain, and whatever things either restore or affect the brain. Thus also the delights and injuries of the kidneys. Thus the desire and nausea of the liver. Thus the affections of all the other parts as well. In these, this investigation remains: to learn what it is that affects this or that member from within. Here, however, a 
<margin>Critique of Physicians.</margin>
crowd of physicians rises up against me. For they do not know or recognize those parents of humanity; rather, they build their art from a **dead figure in a mirror** <note>original: *mortua in speculo figura*—Paracelsus refers to the study of anatomy through dead corpses or textbooks rather than the living forces of nature</note>, they gape at their own fantasies or speculation, directing and explaining names according to whatever nature they please, which is nonetheless founded in no Philosophy. From this source also emerged those 
<margin>The humors are speculative.</margin>
names **Yellow Bile, Black Bile, Phlegm, and Blood**: <note>original: *Cholera, Melancholia, Phlegma, & Sanguis*—the four humors of traditional Galenic medicine</note> whose foundation is nothing but a wandering and fleeting speculation. For who in nature has ever seen yellow bile? Who has ever found black bile in Philosophy? Who has ever recognized phlegm as an Element? By what thing has blood ever been made similar to the air? Who anywhere taught them to distribute the material heaven and the globe of the earth with its included Elements into the body? They have no more foundation for this speculation of theirs than those who either simply opine or dream about virtue or pleasure. Thus they build upon speculations and conceived dreams; may this be as far as possible from us and from sane physicians. Compose the whole human from the external world. Thus you will find in him the conspicuous bodies of all materials, and in these all the species 
<margin>From where knowledge is given to man.</margin>
of members, health, diseases, and the essences of all these—how, for instance, one relates to another, and what restores it. In this is placed that wisdom which the physician ought to seek. For the physician does not draw wisdom from the sky. Nor does he achieve it by inheritance; rather, it increases within him daily, just as an art does with an honest and sagacious craftsman; and that wisdom is given by the parents of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the "small world," meaning the human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note>, so that their son may know them. If Medicine were born from the human being according to its own origin, it would also be necessary for diseases to be directed or accommodated to the origin and grasp of their Physician. From this, as many origins of diseases would be established as there were physicians. And thus, yellow bile would indeed be rightly called by its own name. Yet this is not permitted. On the contrary, the physician ought to follow the disease just as a cow follows the manger. From which it is concluded that the Physician proceeds from nature, not from speculation. For nature is visible; but speculation is invisible. What is visible 
<margin>Nature constitutes the Physician.</margin>
makes the Physician. The invisible creates nothing. The visible gives birth to truth, the invisible least of all. Whatever is invisible and belongs to man offers itself visibly. From which it is also gathered that you are wrong to profess, *this is Yellow Bile, this is Black Bile.* It 
<margin>How diseases are to be named.</margin>
should have been said: *this is arsenic-like, that is aluminous.* Likewise: *this belongs to Saturn, that to Mars*: but not, *this belongs to black bile, that to yellow bile.* For one part belongs to the sky, the other to the earth, mixed together like fire and wood, where the name of both is abolished and fades away. For they are two things in one. Thus, thus it is said: *This disease is Acorine* <note>related to *Acorus*, a medicinal plant</note>, *this sickness is Anthera*: then, the natural Physician can understand that, just as in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the universe or "large world"</note>, so likewise in the microcosm, Anatomy must be known. If you say: *this disease is of pennyroyal, that of lemon balm, this of savin*: then a certain cure is drawn for you from the names themselves. For as many as there are motherworts <note>original: *matricariae*—plants traditionally used for the uterus (*matrix*)</note>: so many are the passions of the womb. And in this sense, one remedy, and not many heaped together, proceeds against one disease. Do not, therefore, be deceived and mocked by your phantasms, so that you designate the property and number of diseases according to a wandering speculation. External eyes 
<margin>Critique of Physicians.</margin>
ought to establish all these things. Thus you also speak: *this is a vice of the blood, this is a vice of the liver, etc.* But who, I ask, of the Gods imparted to you those **lynx-eyes** <note>proverbial for sight that can see through solid objects</note>, so that you know so properly that either the blood or the liver is the cause—when nonetheless you have not the slightest knowledge or exploration of what blood actually is? In the great anatomy, blood is nothing other than wood. Wood, however, is a single name; and yet some hundreds of species of wood exist. No fewer species of blood itself exist. And as various fruits are brought forth from trees, so also various sicknesses of the 
<margin>Infinite species of blood.</margin>
blood occur. And just as the sky makes the trees grow through the summer, but puts them to sleep through the winter: so by the same governance it also alters and changes the blood. From which it is now proved that the true and genuine Physician 
<margin>How diseases are to be named.</margin>
must speak thus: *this is a turpentine disease, this is a Silermorane disease, that is a Helleborine disease, etc.* and not in this way: *this is phlegm, this is a sore throat, that is a rheum, that is a head cold, that is a catarrh.* For these names are not drawn from the foundation of medicine. For a thing ought to correspond to its like by name as well. For from this likeness proceed works, that is, they manifest secrets in...

...their diseases. For there is not just one colic, but many; indeed, there are as many as there are secrets <margin>What the species of colic are.</margin> hidden within colic. From this follows *Civet-like colic, Musky colic*: <note>original: *colica Zibetina, colica muscata*—Paracelsus named diseases after their "signatures" or chemical odors rather than Galenic humors</note> *not windy colic, not colic of the bile*, or other such names as you designate for their origins.

<margin>A sharp rebuke of physicians.</margin> At this point, I must again touch upon that faction of people who have stood as my adversaries for so long. They have rendered the impressions and influences of fruits and minerals plainly useless and relevant to nothing in medicine; yet they placed their speculation on the humors above these things, convinced that no Philosophy or external art provides any benefit to the afflictions of the body. <margin>The humors do not testify regarding diseases.</margin> Driven by this ignorance, they devised the "four humors," from which they inquire and snatch at whatever concerns the physician regarding the causes and natures of diseases. This fits no better than **a fly on a donkey.** <note>A proverbial expression for something completely irrelevant or absurdly mismatched.</note> The reason is this: because there is nothing at all in the body that does not give its judgment outside the body. You should not be offended by these forms and this bodily appearance. For therein is established the foundation that it concerns you to know. There is no need at all to seek a foundation elsewhere. For God did not establish the art of medicine upon innate knowledge or acquired **Sophistry**. <note>original: *Sophisticam*—Paracelsus used this to refer to the abstract, logic-based learning of the universities which he felt lacked practical, natural truth.</note> 

But you have made a separation from all the truly learned: that is, after physicians declined into frauds and impostures, they meditated on other new ways through which they might appear to be learned and industrious men, yet they remained ignorant of the origin of these faculties and arts—clearly so that they might veil their presumed wickedness under the pretext of singular erudition. Now then, who would dare give you a Jurist as a judge or arbiter? For you have rushed so far ahead—even to the Emperors and Popes themselves—that what you deal with is obscure and hidden. Or how can the Theologians condemn you, when they cannot fish out from your writings whether you adhere more to God or the Devil in your practice? You hide your lies so deeply within the "humors" that no absolution or penance can now be imposed upon you. 

Furthermore, who would now set even the common people as your judge? For your language is entirely exotic; and you construct such strange vocabularies and dictionaries for yourselves that no one can look at them without taking offense. And you even bring these kinds of exotic words into the pharmacies, <note>original: *officinas*—the laboratories or shops where medicines were prepared.</note> when the garden itself would supply much more convenient terms. Thus, medicine is as far separated from learned men as a dog-slaughterer is from honest men; although it would be right for medicine to exist in the <margin>Medicine teaches to be clear.</margin> native language, so clear and sincere that a German could entirely understand an Arab, and a Greek a German. 

Medicine ought to flourish so brightly and conspicuously in its art and science that the singular authority and admiration of all the learned, and of the art itself, would stand before everyone. For whom does the heaven adorn, if not the Doctor who has known it? Whom does the earth decorate, if not its own Philosopher? For the secrets of the firmament and the earth are opened through the Physician. The secrets of nature are open to him of their own accord; and through the Physician, they are imparted to the learned. <margin>What Philosophy embraces.</margin> Thus, Philosophy embraces all parts, all members, health itself, and even sickness, which must be learned outside the "judgment of urine." <note>Paracelsus famously rejected uroscopy—diagnosing solely by the appearance of urine—as a primary diagnostic tool.</note> 

The pulse is contained in the firmament; **Physiognomy** in the stars; **Chiromancy** <note>original: *Chiromancia*—usually palmistry, but for Paracelsus, it meant reading the "lines" and signs (signatures) in minerals and herbs.</note> in minerals; spirits in the East and West winds; fevers in earthquakes; and so with other things in others. If the Physician is skilled in these things word for word, he sees and distinguishes all diseases even outside of man. If, therefore, man with all his affections or illnesses lies thus fashioned and expressed within you: <margin>The internal man can never be judged without the external.</margin> then penetrate to the inner man and act as a Physician. Only then examine the urine, touch the pulse, and judge the person; yet do none of these things without knowledge of the external man, who alone is heaven and earth. 

Never be of such confidence or ambition that you dare to touch any man without such a foundation. Your speculative and "sandy" foundation protects nothing, for it is more movable than a reed shaken by the force of the winds in the waves. But be content with this also: that matters have been brought by you to such a point that faith is now further granted to you even without works, and the fault which is yours is even imposed upon and imputed to God himself.

<margin>The dual Philosopher.</margin> To proceed in illustrating and adorning the Philosopher, it must be known that he exists as a double: one of heaven, the other of earth. Thus, both spheres constitute one part of the Physician; and neither one alone is a whole and complete Physician. This one is a Philosopher who has knowledge of the lower sphere. <margin>Who is a Philosopher; who is an Astronomer; who is Eagle-like.</margin> That one is an **Astronomer** who is ignorant of the upper sphere. <note>Paracelsus often reversed or specialized these terms to show that a true Astronomer must understand the "upper" influence on the "lower" body.</note> In the meantime, however, both have one science, one art, and the mysteries of the four Elements are handled between them. There is one science for him who has known **Mercury**, together with him who...

He argues that a true physician must be both a Philosopher of the earth and an Astronomer of the heavens to understand how external nature reflects internal disease.</summary>
