<page-num>192</page-num>
# TREATISE I OF THE PARAGRANUM

...knows the eagle-stone. <note>original: *Aquilatum*. Likely referring to *Aetites* (eagle-stone) or a sublimated alchemical substance.</note> The science of one who knows **Marcasite** <term>Marchasita: an iron sulfide mineral with a metallic luster</term> is the same as the science of one who is skilled in **Galaxa**. <term>Galaxa: likely *Galactite*, a white, milky stone</term> He who knows **Manna** is similar to the one who knows **Angelica**. <note>Manna is a natural resin/exudate; Angelica is a medicinal plant. Paracelsus links them through their "heavenly" or "angelic" signatures.</note> The **Anatomy** of each divided part is one and the same, differing no more than one arm from another, one foot from another, the right eye from the left, the lower teeth from the upper, or the flesh of the feet from the flesh of the jaws or cheeks. Thus, **Saturn** is one in the heavens as fire, and another in the earth as something terrestrial. Thus, **Sol** <note>The Sun</note> is one in the water and another in the heavens. Thus, every single thing in man is fourfold. And whatever lies in the farthest corner of the earth, its shadow falls into man; whatever is in the deepest sea, it imprints or shapes man; whatever exists beneath the Antarctic pole sends its reflection to the Arctic pole; and whatever lies beneath the Arctic pole strikes its reflection upon the man beneath the Antarctic. What else is the sphere of **Venus** but the matrix <note>the womb</note> of the belly? For the Venus of the world provides the Physician for the womb. What is the conception of the belly if the Venus of the world does not work it? What do the spermatic vessels contribute if the vessels of Venus do not favor them? What is iron, if not **Mars**? What is Mars, if not iron? Both are Mars; both are iron. What is the difference between Suns, between Moons, between Mercuries, between Saturns, between Jupiters? Nothing, if you look toward man, except that here the form excludes it. Therefore, there are not four secrets, but one, yet it is four-angled, just like a tower looking out toward the four winds. And just as a tower cannot lack any of these corners, so much less can a Physician lack one of these parts. One part does not make a Physician complete. Nor do two, nor three; but four make him perfect. For it is proper for him to be whole, and those are the secrets <note>original: *arcana*</note> that consist in these four. And just as the world is prefigured through an egg in a single shell, and a single chick with all its wings is enclosed within it, so it is proper for all universal things, which the world and man encompass, to be established within the physician. And just as a hen changes the prefigured world in the shell into a chick through her brooding, so the secrets that are philosophically placed in the Physician are matured through **Alchemy**. And just as fire prepares and purifies, so these things are also brought forth into the earth or into the open air. But this is where the deficiency lies: we have not yet sufficiently examined the Physician. For if they are ignorant of these things, they will not know the secrets themselves. If they do not know what brings forth copper, or what gives birth to vitriol-like things, then—

---

<margin>External things lead to internal things.</margin>
—they will also be ignorant of what brings forth leprosy. If they do not know what causes rust <note>original: *æruginem*</note> in iron, they will also be ignorant of what brings on ulcerations. If they are ignorant of what stirs up earthquakes, they will also be ignorant of what induces the shivers of fevers. We must learn from external things what harms man; man himself indicates none of these things. But where the foundation is situated, there these sleepy men pass by. It is not that metals are produced from **Mercury** and **Sulfur** as they [the traditionalists] would have it. Nor is it true, as they claim, that pure earth does not produce stones. For stones do not grow from the earth, but from <margin>The generation of stones from water.</margin> water, and they are like the metals of the water. However, in the generation of metals, they forget that which nevertheless coagulates. Not two, but three things constitute metals. <note>Paracelsus refers here to his "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> Upon this true and genuine Philosophy you ought to have built medicine, and not upon that fungal sort, whose nature and appearance is no different than an **Agaric** hanging from a Larch tree. <note>Agaric is a shelf-fungus; Paracelsus uses it as a metaphor for something parasitic and useless.</note>

<margin>The doctrine of humors obscures medicine.</margin>
I know, however, that I shall by no means write these things without the contradiction and barking of all those who nevertheless understand neither me nor my adversaries sufficiently. And it is necessary that the previously mentioned generation of metals be defined and explained by no other discourse than that of the Philosophers. For just as all medicine has been mocked and obscured by the **humors** invented by Physicians, so also has Philosophy itself been corrupted by [the theories of] Mercury and Sulfur. And just as the sick have been rendered distorted by the aforementioned four humors, <margin>The Philosopher is more than unblemished. Who is a fundamental Physician.</margin> so also have Philosophers become distorted by Mercury and Sulfur. As one fits, so does the other. He who strives to act as a Philosopher without blemish or falsehood must establish such a foundation of Philosophy that he includes heaven and earth into one **microcosm**, and does not deviate from it by even a thumb's breadth. Likewise, he who desires to write from the true foundation of Medicine needs to do so without straying by even a single hair from building the Microcosm out of the movement of heaven and earth. So that, surely, in this way the Philosopher establishes nothing else in either heaven or earth that he does not also find the same in man; and the Physician also finds nothing anywhere in man that heaven and earth do not also contain equally. And thus, these two differ in no other way than in the mode of their forms, which form nevertheless is understood to be the same in both. However, from the stirring of our brain, these things...

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence as indicated by the catchword "non" in the original Latin.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that medicine must be based on the structural correspondence between the macrocosm (the universe) and the microcosm (the human body), asserting that diseases like leprosy and fever are understood by observing natural phenomena like rust and earthquakes. He rejects the traditional Galenic four humors and the simplified "Mercury-Sulfur" theory, insisting that a true physician must understand the fourfold nature of all things matured through alchemy.</summary>

<page-num>193</page-num>
# ON PHILOSOPHY.
<margin>R</margin>

<margin>The Light of Nature</margin>
...are not understood, but are illuminated by the **light of nature** <term>Light of Nature: In Paracelsian thought, this is the innate intelligence of the natural world and the human ability to perceive it directly, as opposed to learning from books.</term>, ignited by the **Holy Spirit**. This Spirit manifests the knowledge and understanding of its disciples through their works with such splendor that even beastly reason cannot fail to admire them or gaze upon them without amazement. In this, the fundamental principle of all science is established. And just as the splendor of the **Sun** is poured out over all things—and both bad and good things are produced by the Sun—so are these works born through the noble light of Nature. However, the degeneration of the "avenger" <note>likely referring to the corrupted or "fallen" state of nature</note> is similar; these too are produced from the Sun's splendor. For **Medicine** and **Philosophy** must be so perfect and complete that one knows what it is that melts in lead, what constitutes hardness in iron, what creates the colors in a ruby, and what secrets ultimately exist within it. For these things to be gathered under one science, there is a need for the ignited light of nature, through which all things are presented to the eyes in a way that is visible and knowable. But those who clearly and evidently demonstrate nothing outside this torch of nature are driven by the phantasms of beastly reason. From such a source have come those famous Philosophers and Physicians who, despairing of a true master, have judged that whatever their animal intellect cannot grasp can by no means happen to a man or be conferred upon him. It is as if the entire limit of Philosophy rested in **Aristotle** alone, and the limit of Medicine ended with **Galen** <note>Aristotle and Galen were the traditional "pillars" of university education; Paracelsus famously rejected their authority.</note>—who nevertheless devised nothing other than what fought against the truth.

<margin>Aristotle and Galen are criticized</margin>
And those who do battle against the light of nature have such an excellent shield; yet among us, it would be right to cherish that light as purer than gold itself—with such purity, indeed, that no rust could ever grow upon it. However, because various infections leap in, that foundation is shattered. For who is he who could equal or compare any good thing to copper in this way, if he speaks thus: "What is whole? That which is without rust." That which cannot be without rust is not whole, for rust does not cling to the whole. The supreme light, the Apostle himself, confirms this—in whom no vice, no rust, nor any other blemish can dwell. <margin>Judas</margin> Now, in this sense, if anyone should wish to consider **Judas** as rust: he is indeed not rust, but one chosen for that office, though not according to the supreme light. And although he stood in the number and the name of the light, nevertheless nothing lived in him except the name alone. For this reason, you must pay attention to the distinction of error: that those men fail the true light of nature in such a way that the order is violated.

---

For without the perversion of order, there is no error. And in this way also, we can concede that an intellect has been given to our adversaries, which they so greatly boast to have as pure and uncorrupted. For the order of the light of nature was violated in their infancy, and a beastly intellect took the lead and dominated all their professions. Thus, a modern Philosopher will greatly admire the writings of Aristotle and his like; and in the same way, the first "genuine" Physician will also admire the writings of **Avicenna** and Galen. For neither of these was a true Physician or Philosopher whom we ought to follow as guides in such matters. Therefore, because they strike against the principles and foundations, it is necessary that their art be one of violence—yet art refuses to be forced. <margin>Art is not compulsion.</margin> And just as every art under the Sun rouses faith in itself among the people, so do they establish a forced faith for themselves, and this they interpret as "love" through their diligent labors and works. Thus the body confers a vain and fictitious faith; yet it was not fitting for faith to flow from that fountain, but only from the art itself and the works of the art. Truly, what work is there anywhere by those writers that you can be certain proceeded from the art itself? Therefore, those who take such labors upon themselves build mere phantasms and imaginary works. For six hundred times more diligence and labor is required of a fictitious Physician than from a genuine and native one. Therefore, when placed on the scales, they are compelled by every means and craft to make themselves heavier, lest their lightness be revealed. You ought to know, therefore, that your error can be veiled by no excuse and no testimony; otherwise, the works would be at hand simply because you have the name. Not at all: rather, you are like Judas, whose election you possess. <margin>Truth from the good Spirit, lies from the evil.</margin> For as many truths as proceed from the Holy Spirit, so many opposing lies of the Devil are caught. Thus, Philosophy warns you that you are born from it like **Marcasite** <term>Marchasita: iron pyrites or "fool's gold"; it glitters like gold but contains no precious metal.</term>, which is so shining and glittering that a miner believes it to be the purest gold. Yet when cast into the fire, it is nothing but sulfur and arsenic. Thus you also shine and glitter. But if you were tested in the fire, you would be nothing but **cat's silver** <note>original: "felium argentum", likely referring to mica or a similar worthless, shiny mineral</note> or **mica**. And just as **Orichalcum** <margin>What marcasite is.</margin> <margin>Mica.</margin> <term>Orichalcum: a golden-colored brass alloy.</term> changes its heat <note>or "quality/color"</note> from **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: a cobalt or zinc ore (calamine) used in the production of brass.</term>, so you likewise adopt your art and your Doctorate. If one comes to the sick, that splendor becomes volatile and does not withstand the test, just like **talc** in the fire. <margin>Talc.</margin> You see, however, that nature itself has hidden nothing in colors and forms; but the secret is there where there is neither form nor...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medical and philosophical knowledge comes from the "Light of Nature" rather than traditional academic authorities like Aristotle and Galen. He uses mineral metaphors—marcasite, mica, and talc—to describe false physicians who appear impressive but fail when tested by the "fire" of real-world practice.</summary>

<header>PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.</header>

## PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.

...these two things. If this is the nature’s own genius in such a matter, what do you think, you worthless physician—that structure of a shadowy work, when I add nothing of the sort to the building itself? But why do I use this jest here? It is because I intend to lead you into nature herself, so that you may see yourselves reflected in her, and see that a physician must be born from external things, not from the human being alone. If he detects a disease in a person, then surely he will know what it is and what its quality is, not from the place or seat where the disease clings, but he must experience and learn it from the outside, as has been said more than once. <margin>Peony presents the falling sickness</margin> I repeat this here because the **peony** indicates the **falling sickness** <term>falling sickness: an old term for epilepsy</term>, and not just the disease itself, but also its timing and hour, its paroxysm <note>the sudden onset or worsening of symptoms</note>, and its nature along with all other conditions. All these things must be learned by you from the nature of the peony. If you do otherwise, you are at best a deluded physician, conscious and aware of nothing except what you hear from the sick person—whose mouth, however, is not the physician, nor even the investigator of nature. <margin>Oak mistletoe</margin> Thus you will also recognize the origin of another type of falling sickness from **oak mistletoe**. The same logic applies to all other **arcana** <term>arcana: the secret, transformative healing powers hidden within natural substances</term>. As many arcana as there are, so many species of this disease exist. Furthermore, you will recognize the origins and births of **worms** <margin>Worms from St. John's Wort and Tunella</margin> from **St. John's Wort**, from **Tunella** <note>original: "Tunella," likely referring to shepherd's purse or a similar herb</note>, and other similar plants. If you are not skilled in these things, you certainly cannot be a master of them. For if you attempt to drive them away with either **centaury** or **gentian**, what kind of physician will you prove to be? It will be no different than if someone gave a morsel to another and, to drive him out of the kitchen, ruined it with too much salt. Can this really seem like a foundation to you physicians? It is certainly a crude one, fit for nothing. And so **Philosophy** alone <margin>Philosophy is the mother of the physician</margin> exists as the mother of the Physician, as the explainer of all the human limbs and, at the same time, the definer of all the diseases occupying them. This is the foundation. Where the aid is, there also lies the knowledge, understanding, and science of helpful things. Here, then, one thing will be lacking—that you will be ignorant of what lies hidden in this or that herb. From this it will happen that you will either despair in your art or turn to impostures; and in the name of the Lord—just as you have done until now—you will continue to make patients lifeless, lame, and distorted. How much effort did it take until you gathered a way of compounding—that is, the art of arranging **Recipes**? What was your mind doing then, since you did not understand the logic of nature in recognizing diseases? By what convenience or consideration did you then prepare syrups, pills, and other things from "simples" <term>simples: individual medicinal herbs used on their own</term>, when by that very approach the condition and property of their nature is violated and broken?

---

The art of compounding recipes is founded in nature, and nature herself arranges them. If she put into gold what gold requires, she also bestowed on violets what is due to violets, so that there is no need for you to add sugar or honey—just as you have no idea how to perfect or complete gold itself. If nature <margin>Nature compounds remedies, not the Physician</margin> made pearls without your help, she also perfected **Verbena** <note>vervain</note> without your help in the restriction of blood, so that there is no need <margin>Nature requires nothing to be added by the Physician</margin> for you to add any **Shepherd’s Purse** or **Jupiter’s Beard** <note>houseleek</note>. I would like you to understand this: that any virtue exists whole in a single "simple," not divided into two, three, four, or more, but gathered into one whole. That same simple needs no other accessory, except for **Alchemy**, which is one and the same with the miner and the smelter of metals. The whole matter <margin>Extraction, not composition, is owed to remedies</margin> turns on **extracting**, not on compounding. One must know what lies hidden within, rather than making something different by mixing and adding. What boots are best? Surely those that are whole; those that are torn and patched are the worst. Who, I ask, could be so simple and unrefined as to dare to believe that nature imparted only so much of a single virtue to this or that herb, and commanded you physicians to afterwards compound and gather into one what was scattered? Nature’s wisdom is so precise that she has no need to delegate this task to you. For nothing at all rests in you. Nature herself has effectively gathered the arcana and compounded what needs compounding. It is fitting for you to learn and know this one thing: that what you understand is of no consequence anywhere if nature herself does not understand the same. <margin>Let Physicians act regarding medicines</margin> **Nature is the physician**, not you. You must proceed from her, not from yourself. She compounds; you do not. At least do this: fish out where her workshop is, where her virtues lie stored, and in which jars they are found—not in **Mesue**, not in the **Lumen**, not in the **Praepositus** <note>Reference to standard medical textbooks of the time: Pseudo-Mesue’s *De re medica*, the *Lumen Apothecariorum*, and the *Dispensarium* of Nicolaus Praepositus</note>. For these things are contrary to nature, and you find nothing in them. For they break what is whole, and they say the broken has been made whole. Am I acting unjustly because, in writing about "degrees" <note>the traditional Galenic intensity of a medicine's qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>, I have not strictly followed your method? Not at all. For nature compounds, not the physician. And therefore, it is a single fraud,

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medical knowledge comes from observing nature rather than human textbooks. He asserts that remedies are already perfectly "compounded" by nature in single plants, and the physician's job is to extract these powers through alchemy rather than mixing complex, artificial recipes.</summary>

Paracelsus is currently critiquing the traditional "Recipes" and pharmaceutical compounds used by the physicians of his day, arguing they are based on deception rather than a philosophical understanding of nature.</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
# ON ASTRONOMY <note>original: "DE ASTRONOMIA"; though the header indicates Astronomy, the text continues the discussion on Philosophy as the foundation of medical science</note>

<margin>Uroscopy is noted.</margin> A single fraud heaped with various lies is discovered wherever your **Recipes** are applied; yet, from now on, you will be able to defend them with no further effort, unless it happens that a lie prevails over the truth. However much you twist and turn, you will achieve only one thing: that some of your compounds might be proven effective. But can you really protect your entire art with this shield? For an operator could easily join and heap things together so that he holds the very heavens and the entire earth in his hand. And this matter is clearly the same as your **Uroscopy** <note>the diagnostic practice of examining a patient's urine</note>. In this, you confuse so many and such varied things that it becomes necessary for you to divine one excessive answer out of them all. This is exactly how it stands with these compositions of yours. And what does it seem to you? If I were to take away and exclude only three of your **Recipes**—namely **Theriac**, **Trifera**, and **Mithridaticum** <note>these were famous "universal" polypharmaceutical antidotes and cure-alls used in ancient and medieval medicine</note>—then all the other ingredients, even if there were a hundred of them, would immediately be worth nothing, not even a husk. Where then is your composition? O, you blind men!

<margin>Philosophy is the mother of Medicine.</margin> Thus, therefore, **Philosophy** is the mother of **Medicine**, in which nature must be known. That knowledge is the understanding of the passions and the sicknesses of man, which is like the ultimate purpose for which man exists. And just as it is impossible for anyone to create colors or grow trees without natural knowledge, so it is also impossible that you could see what lies hidden in a human being without this same knowledge. And just as you perceive what is in a seed by the benefit of nature, so through that same nature you must look into, perceive, and investigate the human being himself. <margin>Gall-nuts and vitriol are the causes of ink.</margin> And just as **gall-nuts** and **vitriol** produce **ink** <note>the standard ingredients for iron gall ink in the 16th century</note>, in the same way, you recognize what lies hidden in man. For nature reveals all such things. And just as you can least of all know where blackness comes from out of blackness even if something is written down, so it is with diseases themselves. He who knows what *makes* something black is a **Philosopher**. But he who merely knows that it *is* black is worth nothing; he can do nothing else but stain and paint with that blackness.

<margin>Adapting the external to the internal produces a Physician.</margin> He who is truly such a Philosopher as we have described may then enter the faculty of Medicine and convert the **external** into the **internal**. That conversion produces a **Physician**. If the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: the "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</term> is made from the **macrocosm** <term>macrocosm: the "great world," the universe or nature as a whole</term>, it must be directed in such a way that nothing is drawn from the inner man himself. For this way is purely seductive and is death itself. For before someone can learn the whole inner man without the external, there is a fear that there will not be enough sick people for the Physician to reach the end of his study by considering them from the first to the last. For those who strive to learn from the human being alone, it is required that they have the first, the last, and indeed all human beings placed before their sight. For in all humans, all diseases are situated. In one person, there is but one disease. Now then, if it is necessary for a Physician to be a Physician of all men, how will he know this from one, from ten, or from a hundred? Especially since there is nothing at hand that extends to the entire end or total sum? For what else has been handed down in writings except at most a beginning and an opening? And even this is without foundation. <margin>The world contains within itself all the diseases of men.</margin> Therefore, the world must supply the human being. For that human being who is known through the **greater world** <note>the macrocosm/nature</note> has all diseases within himself—those of people already dead, as well as those yet to be born. Therefore, knowledge gained only from the human being is imperfect; for it has neither an end nor a foundation. And the outcomes that testify to it are lameness, distortion, corruption, and death. This is what Physicians who learn from the human being are capable of; this is what they hold. For unless the **external man** <note>the blueprint of humanity found in nature</note> is situated and explored within you, you will certainly be nothing but an **experimenter**—that is, one who is nourished by eventual hope and ambiguous expectation. Is it the mark of Doctors or of thieves to learn in this way? Let any honest reader weigh within himself whether it pleased God to impart medicine to the human race through this kind of superficial knowledge and investigation, or not. For in truth, that was never God's plan. Away then with that harmful prelude or experiment of your discipline! For those who were created by God for this purpose—to preserve and restore life—are the ones who snatch it away and pillage it. And is it right, I ask you, that we are created as masters or Doctors through such trials and butcheries? Surely it would have been better for the human race if no Physician at all had been created by God. For through these experimentations, more must be killed than could be restored and saved by all the Doctors in the world. <margin>The reason why Philosophy was given.</margin> For this reason, God set **Philosophy** before us, so that we might be born learned and knowledgeable from it, and that we might achieve mastery even outside the human being himself. For Philosophy does not kill; it does not destroy. But such things as these cannot gain a place among you; instead, a thick and constant **Beanism** <note>original: *Beanismus*; a derogatory term referring to the ignorance of raw university freshmen, known as "Beani"</note> stands in the way of those who give sound encouragement. I appoint your own conscience as judge: is not every purpose and effort of yours occupied in mere error and ambiguity? And unless God saved the sick, who would remain alive? Just as you yourselves rightly marvel at this goodness and mercy of God.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that medicine must be based on Philosophy and the study of the "macrocosm" (the natural world) rather than trial-and-error experimentation on patients. He dismisses traditional complex recipes and uroscopy as frauds, claiming that true medical knowledge comes from understanding the external forces of nature that mirror internal human conditions.</summary>

<page-num>196</page-num>
<header>TREATISE I OF THE PARAGRANUM</header>

## THE FIRST TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>How the anatomy of the external man is necessary for the Physician.</margin>
Furthermore, the **Anatomy of the external man** <note>By "external man," Paracelsus refers to the Macrocosm—the entire universe—which he believes mirrors the internal anatomy of the human being</note> must be so totally and perfectly incorporated into the Physician that he should not know a single hair on the head, nor a single pore in the body, which he has not already discovered and most clearly recognized ten times over in the outside world, or the "external man." For from this Anatomy is born the art of **Remedies**, so that limb may be matched with limb, **Arcanum** <note>a term for the spiritual essence or "secret" power of a healing substance</note> with Arcanum, and disease joined with disease. For every nerve and rhythm lies hidden in this; not in the numbering of the "first, second, or third degrees" <note>traditional Galenic medicine categorized medicines by "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>. Let limb be weighed against limb: and thus the disease and the Arcanum are joined. This is the way Nature intends Medicine itself to be handled, and not according to the custom of impostors. For from where did that science emerge, 
<margin>The humors are examined.</margin>
which claims that heat, cold, moisture, and dryness give birth to diseases? And that these same qualities likewise heal them? What is it that "dryness" dries out? What is this "drying out" other than the fact that moisture is transferred from one place to another? For in this way the Sun dries a linen cloth; its moisture does not vanish into nothingness, but is transferred from that place to another. How is cold removed by heat in any way other than it remaining there with at least a lesser weight? Add to this that causes must be weighed from every side, so that what concerns time also pertains to the science of Medicine. Now, therefore, judge for yourselves: since you are so utterly void of **Philosophy**, how can the science of your Medicine stand in the truth? I do not deny that every one of these things requires its own nature. But that is not Medicine, nor is it the Arcana. Rather, what is it that speaks from within a man? What is it that sees from the eyes? What is it that hears in the ears? Is it cold? Is it heat? Indeed, it is none of these.
<margin>Medicine does not attend to qualities.</margin>
But if things are either hot, cold, moist, or dry, what do these have to do with sight? Thus, Medicine itself must be considered in the same way, so that neither cold nor heat is joined with sight; but just as sight is the Arcanum of the eyes, so in turn do the Arcana relate to the eyes and to other things. Therefore, I command that, by right, limb should always be applied to limb. For here the Medical art is established. In these Arcana, the Physician’s Pharmacy is located. For heat remains heat, and cold remains cold; they do not allow themselves to be consumed. Water 
<margin>The Elements are fixed.</margin>
remains water; fire remains fire; for the **Elements** are fixed. And this fixed nature has not yet been considered—that moisture has its own fixed coldness. They wish to expel a "hot" disease with this, yet no disease is fixed in cold or heat, and a fixed thing must fight entirely with something that is not fixed. From this, therefore, the foundation was established: *Opposites are cured by opposites* <note>original: "Contraria a contrariis curari"; the fundamental rule of Galenic medicine</note>, which is to say, cold things are driven out by hot.
<margin>That opposites are driven out by opposites is false.</margin>
This is utterly false, and it never existed as a truth in Medicine. Rather, the matter stands thus: **The Arcanum is health. Disease is the opposite of health.** These two now expel each other, one acting upon the other. These are the "opposites" which drive each other out; and one continuously ejects the other by means of death itself, so that nothing of its opposite remains. This total abolition does not happen in the case of cold and heat. The skill of expulsion lies in the disease not returning. But where has winter or summer ever been so expelled that it did not return? Never, nowhere. Therefore, those things testify only to the movement and nature of time, not to diseases. Disease is one thing; the Elements themselves are another. The Elements do not fall ill; but the body becomes sick.
<margin>Like is cured by like. A scorpion cures a scorpion.</margin>
Thus a **Scorpion** cures a scorpion, and **Realgar** <note>a toxic arsenic mineral</note> cures its own Realgar, **Mercury** its own Mercury, **Melissa** <note>the herb lemon balm</note> its own Melissa, a heart its own heart, a spleen its own spleen, a lung its own lung; not the heart of a pig, nor the spleen of a cow, nor the lung of a goat, but the limb of the great "External Man" joined to the limb of the "Internal Man."

<margin>A reproach of Physicians.</margin>
But lest I detain my listeners longer than is fair: I would have them warned in general that they should first strive to know the **Great Man** <note>the Macrocosm/Universe</note>, and through him, later, the internal man. Do not rashly give your trust and your hand to the words and the doctrinal precepts of your teachers, who repeatedly decree victory for themselves so that they might have an excess of truth and right, and can never lose their case. But let this prejudice move you not at all. Turn your eyes toward their works; from these, you will judge more closely what they are like. Indeed, what can they teach you—they who shamefully fail everywhere, and are publicly caught and convicted in lies so many times? Will they promote you to be "Magnificent Doctors" or create "Masters," when they themselves have never been of any weight or dignity? 
<margin>Believe in works, not in words.</margin>
And fix this seriously in your minds: believe in works, not in words. Words are empty things; but works testify concerning their master. I pray you, read what I write, turn the pages, and weigh them diligently: not with envy, nor with contempt, nor with mockery.

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the Galenic theory of curing diseases with "opposites" (heat vs. cold), arguing instead for the principle of "similars" (like cures like) based on the relationship between the Macrocosm and the human body. He emphasizes that a true physician must study the "external man" (nature) to find specific spiritual remedies (Arcana) rather than relying on empty academic theories.</summary>

<keywords>Macrocosm, Arcanum, Similia similibus curantur, Galenic medicine, Anatomy, Realgar, Elements, Medical philosophy</keywords>

<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>ON ASTRONOMY.</header>

<margin>Man must be known through external things.</margin>
For those things for which I am now an object of your scorn will, in the end, turn into the highest contempt and insult for you yourselves. And if your mind is truly set on acting as my audience, then I beseech you: learn, and listen to both sides, and so select and retain what is good and useful. For if those things which I hand down to you are not chewed over daily, how, I ask you, can a solid foundation of Medicine ever come to you? The same must be done so that you may diligently and curiously come to know and learn the <term>microcosm<note>The "little world"; the Paracelsian belief that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note></term> within external Nature. In her, you will truly comprehend and observe the wonderful and most secret mysteries that have been hidden within man. Do this not for my sake, but for the health of the sick and the praise of God. For who has there ever been who proposed man to himself merely *as* man? In such a person, all faculties are blinded, and no one truly knows him. From this, nothing but harm and ruin emerges. Theologians would certainly be quite faint-hearted if they were to become such Physicians. Lawyers, too, would easily realize how much they truly knew if this truth were to break out. And the same for others. The cause of all these failures is that man is proposed as his own subject; yet no one takes enough care to search out and know him correctly.

<margin>Metals in all the elements.</margin>
For you have metal in the water, and in the earth, and in the air, and in the fire. You have a fourfold Mercury, a fourfold Betony <note>a common medicinal herb</note>, a fourfold <term>Tereniabin<note>original: *Tereniabin*; a term for a type of "celestial manna" or essence that Paracelsus believes exists in different forms across the four elements.</note></term>, and a fourfold Amethyst. And the difference between all of these is nothing other than their form. Likewise, there is a fourfold Celandine <note>original: *Chelidonia*; a flowering plant</note> and a fourfold <term>Orizon<note>A specific Paracelsian term likely referring to a celestial boundary or influence.</note></term>. These are nothing other than what is in man himself. For he is composed fourfold and perfectly formed. In this formation lies the Physician’s knowledge, his art, and the <term>arcanum<note>the secret "soul" or healing essence of a substance</note></term> itself. Toward this, the Physician shall compose and direct himself, and not toward any other profession that does not square or agree with these things.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
With these things having been said, we wish the first foundation of Medicine to be judged, and sufficiently so: namely, that no Physician can exist without this Philosophy. Those who lack it are mere impostors, like moss growing out of the trunks of trees.

It is proper for the whole of man to be proposed and considered by the Physician. It is right for you to know in this second foundation, **Astronomy** [ *which is the superior part of Philosophy through which man is known* ], in what way those bodies ought to be understood—just as in the superior sphere, so also in the interior sphere of the microcosm. You must know how one firmament, one star, one nature, and one essence is present under a divided appearance and form.

<margin>What Astronomy teaches.</margin>
Astronomy, therefore, is the second foundation, embracing two parts of man: namely, his air and his fire. For in the same way, Philosophy embraced two parts: the earth and the water. Just as was said in Philosophy, so in turn—and especially indeed in Astronomy—I would have you consider that the heavens and the air exist within man, no differently than they do outside him. <term>Melissa<note>Lemon balm; used here to illustrate that biological life is as much a part of the "inner sky" as the outer world.</note></term> is no more in the earth than it is in the body.

<margin>Man is body, air, and earth.</margin>
The same **Milky Way** <note>original: *lactea linea* or *Galaxa*</note> that is in the heavens is also within us. As there are two poles in the heavens, so they are within us. As the **Zodiac** is in the heavens, so it is in man, not lacking even a hair's breadth. There is one and the same number of the firmament in the heavens and in the body; and likewise, one number in the air. Since man also contains these things within himself, it is worth the effort for this part of him to be known and not neglected in the slightest. You <term>humoral physicians<note>Doctors who followed the traditional Greek system of balancing the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note></term> may wonder by what logic the Milky Way moves through the belly, or

<margin>Reprimand of Physicians.</margin>
where the upper and lower poles reside, or where the Planets wander, or how the Zodiac rotates. Yet this wonder of yours is of the same kind as wondering how Melissa is born in the belly, or

<margin>Iron in the body.</margin>
how iron in the body is infected by rust. These things are not truly wonders. For you have as much wonder as you have lack of learning. Those who excessively admire everything are counted among the simpletons and fools.

<margin>Wondering is for fools.</margin>
Above all else, the Physician must strive to have man himself well-known in that other part which pertains to Astronomical Philosophy; he must introduce man to this and bring the heavens into him. Otherwise, he will not be a Physician of man. For the heavens, in their sphere, embrace half of man's body and half the number of his diseases. Who truly would profess himself a Physician if the diseases of this half-part were not seen and known by him?

<margin>Man is the son of the air.</margin>
So, furthermore, it must be established that man has his father in the heavens as well as in the air, and that he himself is a son, made and begotten from the air and the firmament.

<header>SECOND TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM.</header>

# SECOND TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM

And the principal hinge of this matter will turn upon this: that I shall demonstrate and complete these points so plainly that you may easily be able to agree with them. Even if, in this place, I do not finish that entire business with perfect accuracy, it will nonetheless be of no consequence. For the amount we produce here does not pertain to the very foundation of Medicine itself. Here, at least, I indicate those things which are necessary for a Physician to know. Seek out the rest in its proper place, in my book *On the Generation of Man*, where they will be more fully handed down. Here, however, you must understand more plainly through my teaching what is lacking in the person who is ignorant of these things, and what sort of person he is who knows them.

<margin>
The woodworm is not from the wood.
The cricket is not from the clay.
The beetle is from the constellation.
Air is not tangible.
</margin>
For as long as man is not perfectly sketched out in the Physician according to this foundation, for so long is there no truth in Medicine, whether in healing or in rightly knowing effects. For diseases do not proceed from the man, but from the father <note>Paracelsus uses "father" metaphorically to mean the origin or generative source of a thing—in this case, the stars or the "firmament."</note> of the disease. Moreover, learn to inquire from that same source from which they proceed. The woodworm is not born from the wood, yet it is in the wood. The cricket is not fathered by the clay of the furnace, yet it lives in it. Caterpillars are not generated from the trees, yet they cling to them. As for where the beetle comes from: it is not from horse dung, but is generated by the constellation. Just as the constellation falls upon it, so it grows or does not grow. In the same way, all things of man likewise proceed from the father.

In the first place, know that air and fire are not tangible bodies, but are sensible and visible. Therefore, just as it is in the heavens, so also those bodies in man grow sick. And just as the Sun either harms or benefits, so also the bodies in man are affected, just as the earth is affected by the Sun. Now, the heart is not the Sun, nor is the brain the Moon, and so on for the rest. For the heart and the brain are the spheres of the other elements. And just as the heavens operate within them, so it must be understood that a similar body exists in man. Indeed, how could you endure to practice medicine without a foundation? You who seek diseases physically <note>original: "corporaliter"</note>, which nonetheless are not physical, nor do they have physical bodies, as far as this part is concerned. How will you take the heat of the Sun away from the earth? You will achieve nothing. For you have no power against it, except to turn away its heat with a shade-covering, or to hide yourself in the dug-out earth like a yew tree. This is not truly to have expelled the enemy, but merely to have turned away its operation. In this very way, and no other, you ought to understand how to approach the foundation of firmamental diseases. Furthermore, that one part of the diseases of the firmament must be known, namely, what they work upon the other part. Because

<margin>
Lower things grow sick from higher things.
</margin>
it is not to be understood otherwise than this: that you should know that the earth and water themselves never grow sick or are affected unless the superior firmaments <note>The "firmament" refers to the celestial sphere and the influence of the stars.</note> are the cause. For if they rot, they rot because of the air and the heavens. If they become sterile, they suffer that from the air and the heavens; and whatever sickly thing they finally receive, they take it from the firmament. Moreover, there is now a peculiar explanation in diseases which also establishes the singular Physician. If the Physician must be divided into categories such as <term>Humoralists<note>Followers of the traditional Galenic medicine based on the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note></term>, <term>Surgeons<note>original: "Chirurgi"</note></term>, and <term>Physicians<note>original: "Physici"; here referring to internal medicine practitioners.</note></term>, the only cause is shame, ignorance, unskillfulness, and pride. If, therefore, as has been said, that part of the physical species exists in the body—just like the two external Elements, earth and water—so you ought to know that a similar part of diseases must be understood in the members of the body. And therefore, once those diseases are understood, there follows in turn another origin from the superior sphere. For it lies within itself; and it must be understood in what way and form something happens in that place. And just as things stand in the heavens—they do not cling, they are not carried, but they poise themselves most freely beyond all earthly reason and power— <margin>The stars poise themselves in the Heavens.</margin> so they are similarly in the body. And just as the stars in the heavens "tinge" <note>An alchemical term meaning to transform or influence the nature of something through a subtle essence.</note>, yet have no physical contact through mixing, so the same happens also in the <term>microcosm<note>The "little world" of the human body, which mirrors the "macrocosm" of the universe.</note></term>. And just as this operation proceeds invisibly and works visibly, the same must be understood similarly regarding Medicine, which works visibly while itself being invisible. <margin>Medicine is invisible.</margin> For this which we see is not the medicine, but it is the body in which that medicine lies. For the <term>Arcana<note>The secret, spiritual "kernels" or healing essences of natural things.</note></term> of the Elements are invisible; likewise also those of man. What is visible is external, and does not belong here.

You see this: that air is the body of the firmament. However, the eyes do not prove it, but rather the human secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note>. And the firmament—that is, the Element of fire—consists in the air. Moreover, we speak according to our opinion, as stated above: namely, that no one carries the heavens and the stars, and no one drives them in their course. For since we are earthly, we speak in an earthly manner. Therefore we say that the Moon carries nothing, just like the Sun. So we also say, *The air is nothing*, since no one sees it. But if the nature of the superior intellect is to be judged and set forth, we find that the thing is one and the same above and below—and it differs in this one way: that we do not comprehend it in an earthly fashion, even though it is an earthly thing, divided by that reasoning which you see.

<summary>Paracelsus explains the second pillar of medicine, Astronomy, arguing that diseases originate in the "firmament" (the stars and heavens) and influence the human body invisibly. He asserts that the true essence of medicine is an invisible power (Arcanum) hidden within physical substances.</summary>

<page-num>199</page-num>
->ON ASTRONOMY.<-

### ON ASTRONOMY.

Just as whiteness is a color, so too is blackness a color. How contrary and different are these two from one another? Truly, in the highest degree. The same logic applies to physical bodies when we say: *Water and earth are bodies; yet heaven and air are not bodies in the same way, and yet they are bodies nonetheless.* Or: *The Moon is a body, and the Sun is a body; but not in the same way as the air, which is also a body.* Now, look at marble. It is dark and obscure, so that it cannot be penetrated by sight—at least only its surface can be seen. Crystal, on the contrary, is transparent, and through it you see what lies beneath it. Thus, marble indicates the nature of earth, while crystal indicates the nature of air. Observe how thick and dark wood is, yet the glass made from it is clear, bright, and not dark at all. In this same way, you ought to know that the two spheres <note>The "spheres" here refer to the celestial (upper) and terrestrial (lower) worlds.</note> are compared and related in this respect. No one should wonder that we walk in the air, even though it is a body. For fish move in water, yet they do not fall to the bottom, nor are they suffocated. So it is with us in the air. An egg preserves life and <margin>The yolk is the center.</margin> essence: the yolk is enclosed in the white, and it keeps to the center, not leaning toward any side. The yolk signifies the lower sphere <note>The Earth and Water.</note>; the white signifies the upper sphere <note>The Air and Fire.</note>. The yolk is earth and water; the white is air and fire. Just as in the egg one is sustained by the other, believe that the same happens in the world outside; be fully persuaded that the air <margin>The yolk is earth and water; the white is air and fire. The egg is heaven and earth. The humors do not match the Elements.</margin> is nothing but a chaos, like the white of an egg, and the egg itself is heaven and earth. If, therefore (*to return to our purpose*), the egg-white—which does not seem like a solid body, and yet (as was said) exists as a body (which only the eyes can distinguish)—produces diseases: by what logic will you recognize them if you are ignorant of Philosophy? For if you are going to say: *"it is phlegm, it is bile, it is blood, it is melancholy,"* <note>The four "humors" of traditional Galenic medicine, which Paracelsus famously rejected.</note> you must remember that these four do not agree with the Elements. It is necessary to match them with the elements so that they themselves are <margin>Humors do not agree with the Elements.</margin> no less elements than the others. From this follows the knowledge of these diseases, and at the same time, the realization that your previous path was a delusion. For the Elements work in one way, and the "phlegms" <note>Referring to the humors.</note> work in another. If you wish to distribute diseases into those four parts, you must enter a different path than the one started by the "Humoralists" <margin>Reproof of Doctors.</margin> <note>Paracelsus's derisive term for traditional physicians who followed the Greek theory of the four humors.</note>, who wish to be submerged in the bilge-water of humors, and seek and handle nothing but filth. For this reason, their entire science is directed toward enemas, purges, and the like. What is omitted here will be more clearly listed in the section on the method of purging. Thus, the humors must be set aside, and the properties of the Elements must be drawn forth; from these, one must learn what diseases truly are. For the humors will teach you nothing, but the Elements will lead you to the innermost foundation of Medicine—you who have wandered so far off course and behave deceitfully regarding all diseases.

Furthermore, you ought to know this: *heaven works within us.* But who will understand this operation if he does not know heaven according to its own essence and nature? What is knowledge other than <margin>The star is the basis of celestial wisdom.</margin> the star? If, therefore, the star is the basis of celestial wisdom, the Physician must be skilled in it. If he is such a man, he has already become a disciple of Medicine and possesses the knowledge to recognize and judge the heaven within man. As soon as he identifies the inner heaven, then he is a Physician; otherwise, not at all. For if he only <margin>How the Physician and Astronomer differ.</margin> understands the heaven from the outside, he acts only as an Astronomer and Astrologer. But if he applies it to man, he knows the "twin heavens." Therefore, two kinds of knowledge make one Physician in that part which pertains to the upper sphere. In a Physician, this must exist without any defect: that he knows the Tail of the Dragon <note>A term for the descending node of the Moon, used here as a metaphor for anatomical/astrological locations within the body.</note>, and Aries, and the polar axis, and the meridian line, and the rising and the setting—within the man. If he is ignorant of these, send such a man away to Pilate! <note>A common Renaissance idiom meaning to send someone to their doom or to wash one's hands of a hopeless case.</note> Regarding these matters, note that the upper and lower stars are one thing, and they are not divided according to their powers. Rather, just as air in a sealed glass bottle moves up and down and changes for good or ill, no differently than the exterior air with which it is one: so you must know that the thing in the body and in heaven is similarly one. The glass breaks, and nothing changes or separates in the Elements, for the Elements existed before the glass, and existed while the glass was being made. Just as the air is one in both places but is merely divided by the glass, so in man the firmament is the same as it is in heaven—not as one single portion, but as two. For the hand that separated light and darkness—the hand, I say, that fashioned heaven and earth—the same hand also established this lower part in the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," meaning man, who mirrors the "Macrocosm" or the universe.</note>, taken from the upper world and enclosed within the skin of man everything that heaven encompasses. Therefore, the exterior heaven is the guide to the interior heaven. Who, then, would boast that he is a Physician if he does not know the exterior heaven? For in that <margin>The Physician is made by the external.</margin> heaven we exist, and it is before our eyes.

<summary>Paracelsus uses the analogy of an egg to explain how the human body mirrors the elemental structure of the universe, arguing that doctors must study astronomy to understand the "inner heaven" of their patients. He rejects the traditional Greek theory of the four humors as a superficial focus on "filth" and "bilge-water."</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, microcosm, macrocosm, egg analogy, elements, humoralism, Paragranum, firmament, medical theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Astronomy as the second pillar of medicine. Paracelsus is arguing that the "inner heaven" of a human being is the true subject of the physician’s study, rather than just the visible, outer body.</meta>

# A TREATISE ON THE PARAGRANUM

is placed before the eyes. However, the heaven which is within us is not placed before our eyes, but is cast behind our eyes <note>Paracelsus means that our internal "astral" nature is hidden from our physical sight, existing in the spiritual or "inner" realm.</note>. Therefore, we cannot see it. For who can see through the skin that stands in the way? No one. Therefore, the Physician is born before the eyes, and he looks through the things in front to see the things which are behind him: that is, he contemplates the interior through the exterior. The exterior things alone provide knowledge of the interior; otherwise, no internal thing can be known.

<margin>The outer man affects the inner.</margin>
<margin>The star is the father; men are the sons.</margin>
Now, if anyone asks about the two firmaments—whether one affects the other—know this: the outer man does not affect the inner, yet this [the inner star] affects the interior. The reason is this: *the son is the heir to the father’s goods, not the father to the son’s.* Now, truly, the star is the father of the son, and man comes from the star. Every infection also begins from the stars, and from there it flows even into man: that is, where heaven ends, man begins. However, heaven itself does not penetrate or strike into man. Therefore, there is no need for fumigations or flavors <note>Paracelsus often criticized traditional cures like incense or complex herbal syrups.</note>; rather, the star itself in man is disposed and ordered by the hand of God to imitate that which the outer heaven begins and brings forth. Therefore, it is necessary that those things which belong to man also follow. And while the Sun may shine through glass, and the Moon may provide a torch upon the earth, this nevertheless contributes nothing to the corruption and diseases of the human body. For just as the Sun itself does not penetrate into that place, so much less do the stars themselves descend into man; nor do their rays pour anything into man. For it is necessary that those bodies be present, not merely their rays. These astral bodies of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>Microcosm: the "little world," meaning the human being as a reflection of the "macrocosm" or the great universe.</note> are what receive the nature of the parent by inheritance.

<margin>A rebuke of physicians.</margin>
<margin>Petrus de Crescentiis.</margin>
Therefore, because man has been made similar to the stars—and the stars were made before him, and he himself was made from the stars—it is necessary that the father’s traits lie hidden in the son, as they do in man. Therefore, the interior does not have business with the exterior heaven; but vice versa. For the son follows the parent, and is neither his herald nor his equal companion. In this way, Mars has his son in the star of man; so Saturn has his son in him; so likewise Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, the Moon, and all other things here too numerous to count. Wherefore, you Physicians, do not by any means despise that which establishes and completes your name. For how pleasant it is, how honorable and excellent, if a Physician is certain and conscious of his art? But there is no art in breathing out snores <note>original: "ronchos spirare," implying both snoring and expressions of lazy scorn</note>, wearing monk-like hoods, or displaying a great and ambitious name. Such things as these torment the sick. Hence you are even called butchers and corrupters, which is your disgrace. I ask you, never persuade yourselves that you are sufficiently learned from <term>Avicenna</term>, or that you will find everything in <term>Galen</term>, or that you can scrape everything together from <term>Mesue</term> <note>Avicenna, Galen, and Mesue were the traditional authorities of medieval medicine, whom Paracelsus famously rejected.</note>. For all these things (if you wish to agree with the truth) benefit you much less than *Petrus de Crescentiis* <note>Petrus de Crescentiis (c. 1233–c. 1320) was an author on agriculture; Paracelsus is saying a farming manual is more useful than the current medical textbooks.</note> benefits the peasants.

<margin>Dannhauser.</margin>
<margin>Adam is not the father, and [Eve] not the mother of men.</margin>
<margin>Man is the limbus.</margin>
It is the same as if someone thought he could become a Musician from *Dannhauser* <note>Likely referring to the legendary Tannhäuser, suggesting someone who only knows the songs or stories but not the science of music.</note>, or from a noble woman of *Weissenburg*. A song indeed sounds sweet to him who is satisfied with a wealth of things; nor does it soothe anyone more deeply than the singer himself. But should not these things be considered by the Physician: whether man is the heir and possessor of his parent's <term>Anatomy</term>? For no one can take this from him; nor can the son be known without the father, but he wishes to be known through him. And father Adam is not the father; nor is Eve the mother of men. For both were humans themselves. But man was not begotten by man. In the first man, there was no prior man, but rather a creature: and from the created things is the <term>limbus</term>; and man was made a limbus, and man remained a limbus <note>Limbus: Paracelsus uses this term for the "Great Mystery" or the primordial chaos/matter from which all things were extracted.</note>. If, therefore, he remained a limbus: he must entirely—since he is enclosed in skin (for through this, as I said, no one sees inside, nor are the operations within him manifest)—be presented and recognized from his father, and least of all from himself. For the outer heaven and his [the man's] heaven are one heaven, but they are nonetheless two parts. So also the father and the son are two, and yet they are one Anatomy. He who knows the one, knows the other also.

<margin>The perfect knowledge of a physician is required.</margin>
Now, regarding the knowledge of the health of the sick, it is not fitting to take man for man in a general sense—that is, for everyone. For his body suffers, not the eternal part which is in him. If the body suffers, that is the limbus. Now, all men are one limbus, and all diseases are one limbus. Therefore, establish it so: that all the diseases of all men are the disease of only one man. And if there were as many Anatomies as there are men (according to the Humoralists <note>The "Humoralists" were doctors who followed the ancient theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note>), who, I ask, could reach the end of it? No one. Therefore, know that the Physician must be powerful in his knowledge in all diseases without any defect. And he takes this from the external father, so that he may know what exists in Arabia, what in Europe, what in Italy, what in Germany, etc. For as far as the world extends, the Physician ought to shine forth, not being devoted to a single man. And these things must be done through the father. He teaches the Cabalistic science <note>original: "Gabalisticam scientiam." Paracelsus refers to his own version of Cabala—reading the secret signatures of nature.</note>, which you must learn.

<summary>This page explains that the human "inner star" is the heir to the macrocosmic "outer star," meaning human health can only be understood by studying the universe. Paracelsus rejects traditional medical authorities like Galen in favor of a universal, astral "Anatomy" and the study of the primordial Limbus.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, macrocosm, microcosm, Limbus, Paracelsian medicine, medical education, Galen, Avicenna, anatomy, astral body</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s argument that the human being (the microcosm) contains the same astronomical structures as the outer universe (the macrocosm). He moves from the general concept of the "inner star" to the specific medical application of "ascendants" and "astral hours."</meta>

# ON ASTRONOMY.

<margin>How many ascendants are in man.</margin>
Since, therefore, there is a heaven in man, and it cannot be denied by any reason: I would have you Physicians know in general that all **ascendants** <term>ascendant: in astrology, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth; Paracelsus believes these are also internal forces</term> also reside within man. Now truly, who will say this: *that man is subject to the Ascendant, except for the lonely, external, dry Astronomer*? It is the Physician's task to make this clear and reveal it. For as many Ascendants as there are in the sky, so many are there in man. Thus man is placed in a nearly infinite nature. From this it happens to him that in this place he is healthy, in that one he is ill; in this place he is of one sort, in that one another; today he is disposed in one way, tomorrow in another. Thus, therefore, every day and at no single moment is he secure in any part of his body, whether in health or in sickness. Because this matter concerns the health and sickness of the body, it is absolutely necessary that the Physician have knowledge of the **Ascendants**, the **conjunctions**, <margin>The Physician's duty.</margin> and the exaltation of the Planets—indeed, of the entire constellation <note>original: "constellationem"; here meaning the specific arrangement of stars influencing an individual</note>—and that he knows and understands it thoroughly. And if he understands it out there in the "father" <note>Paracelsus refers to the outer universe/macrocosm as the "father" of the human "son."</note>, it follows then by what reasoning he should compare man to it—since the number of men is vast and they exist as nearly infinite—and he should act so that he may find in any one individual their own concordance, showing where health is, where disease, where the beginning, where the outcome, where the end, and where death may be. For man is heaven, and heaven is man; and all men are one heaven, and the heaven is one man. Therefore, it must be known here why in this place there is one thing, and in another place something else; why here it is new, there it is old, and elsewhere it is different. This must be understood, however, not in terms of outward form, nor for the sake of heaven's appearance, but in the division of the **impressional virtues** <note>the specific influences or "powers" that the stars "impress" upon the human body</note>. This, above all else, establishes and stabilizes the Physician. For understand it thus: Since we men have only one heaven, and that heaven exists in each person privately—not divided, but whole and singular—what then is the reason that there is not one single movement and one single logic for all men in a similar way? For the efficacy of heaven must be entirely certain. Since, therefore, there is one man, one heaven, and so <margin>Why one heaven does not have one single affection.</margin> on: it seems entirely likely that either all men should exist as healthy in the same way, or ill in the same way. However, this does not happen, but the operation is interrupted at the time of the heaven’s generation. For the infant who is even now being conceived already has its own heaven. If, however, all infants were born in the same moment, there would exist at least one single heaven and one single operation, as was said before. Therefore, know that just as the great heaven holds itself, such a heaven does it impress upon a person at birth. And it is a truly wonderful thing: even if ten thousand infants were born by day or night, they would not all attain the same heaven, but would be as far apart as the East is from the West. For just as a tree in the earth grows and increases daily more and more from a seed: so the hours grow in the earth against the heaven. Just as the tree becomes larger than its seed, so also the **astral hours** are larger than the earthly ones; so much larger, I say, that according to our earthly hours, months cannot be contained within our <margin>How much greater astral hours are than earthly ones.</margin> **minutes**. And a wonderful variety or condition is the cause, so that we are compelled to marvel greatly at this; just as in the fact that heaven and air exist within us, as they do outside with their aforementioned magnitude. For in a single point, a circle exists no less than in the cycle itself. Now, how much larger is the cycle compared to the point? And yet both are complete. Therefore, just as it is possible for the stationary foot of a compass to draw a circle while the moving foot draws a wide perimeter: so there is an equal and similar increase in the magnitude of man in respect to heaven. Similarly also, there is a decrease from heaven toward man, just as rays return from the circumference into their own center point. For just as it is possible for things to be distributed from the highest point, so they can also be distributed from the exterior to the interior. <margin>A circle is also in a point.</margin>

Therefore, because man comes forth from the earth and from the heaven, he suffers those things which they suffer, and he attracts those things which are within them. For he has those things within himself: whence the operation also proceeds from him. For what other reason does man desire to eat, except that he is from the earth? Why does he desire to drink? Because he is from water. Why does he desire to breathe? Because <margin>Why man eats, drinks, breathes, and is warm.</margin> he is from air. Why does he grow warm? Because he is from fire. But someone might say, *what is this to our purpose?* On the contrary, this is the knowledge from which the Physician establishes a regimen. Outside of this, no regimen is pre-ordained. And this is the cause, at least, of external diseases, not of the true **Elementary** ones <note>diseases caused by the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire)</note>. For from this, recognize the cause and reason of diseases: namely, that the **center** gives birth to diseases. <margin>The center gives birth to diseases.</margin> Whence also every disease is generated. And indeed, no disease occurs outside of the center. Therefore, they speak idly of putrid air, and they say, *Close the doors, avoid the fog*. For unless the constellation is within yourself, no-

<summary>Paracelsus explains that the human body contains an internal "heaven" with its own astrological ascendants and astral hours. He argues that disease originates from an internal "center" or constellation within the person, rather than being merely a result of external factors like "putrid air."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Treatise of the Paragranum," where Paracelsus explores the intersection of Astronomy and Medicine. He argues that the internal "heavens" within the human body—the microcosm—are the true causes of health and disease, rather than external factors or traditional humoral theories.</meta>

### SECOND TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM

...if it happens, you will feel no harm. It is proper to know, therefore, that in this case, the origin should not be judged by the external air, as if someone were to speak of the splendor of the Sun and not at the same time of the Sun itself. The Sun harms no Moon, but only the Sun. The Moon affects no Sun, but only the Moon <note>Paracelsus is arguing that like affects like; the celestial forces in the macrocosm affect the corresponding celestial forces within the human body.</note>. From this consideration, do not judge or estimate the generations of diseases from external opinion. This is the same as saying: *As the motion is, so is our health and sickness.* <note>original: "Prout motus est, ita nostra est sanitas & ægritudo"</note> For we are bound to both. We are subject to motion according to diseases and according to health. If we are seized by that motion, it is proper for us to know about it, and not about other things. Outside of this art, who shall judge? In what science is the knowledge of conjunctions, exaltations, and of either good or bad days situated? Who will recognize the so many innumerable fathers and mothers, of whom man consists, without that art?

<margin>The primitive, antecedent, and conjunct causes of medicine are mocked.</margin>
Who will find such varied offspring in man through the humors, through the primitive, antecedent, or conjunct causes? <term>primitive, antecedent, and conjunct causes: standard scholastic medical terms for the origins of disease, which Paracelsus found insufficient</term> O, the ignorance and the insolence! Who taught these fresh-faced fools <note>original: "beanos"; a medieval academic term for first-year students or "greenhorns," used here as an insult for inexperienced doctors</note> to distinguish diseases in such a way? The classification of diseases proceeds from a path that cannot be grasped by any number. One must learn not from the "antecedent," but from the **ascendant**. Diseases possess this: neither heaven knows the antecedent, nor the primitive cause. What is a primitive cause but a father? What is a conjunct cause but a conjunction? And who can find peace in this "knowledge" of the origin of all diseases? Every disease requires its own complete Philosopher and Astronomer. And just as the origin of these things must be understood: so must the origins of the diseases themselves. Who is there anywhere who can bear such a division in the generation of natural things?

<margin>Reproof of the Physician.</margin>
Much less can a Physician bear it. And does this become Academic? O, catchers of lice! <note>original: "captatores pediculorum"; a derogatory term for petty, nit-picking academics</note> Indeed, it would be an easy thing to speak this way, if only it were true. However, Medicine is not fashioned in this manner. Thus you are compelled to constantly cling to your smelly syrups, and you build your cure upon such a morbid foundation. But see how much these things "honor" you. It corresponds to your Theory and also your Practice. Truly I say, if you were to send a dismissal to this ignorance, and if you scrutinized the natures of heaven and earth, it would come to pass that you would burn not just one book, but your entire libraries—and with them, if possible, the very masters and authors themselves. Meanwhile, you will not terrify me with your sophistry. For I still have my most choice arrows hidden in my quiver.

Thus it is also understood, and from here emerges the principle of the causes of future motions: that the **greater man** <note>the Macrocosm or the Universe</note>, who is the father of man, also himself falls into diseases; from these diseases of the father, the diseases of the son <note>the Microcosm or the human being</note> are also estimated and indicated.

<margin>The "lesser man" is not known to the Astronomers.</margin>
Now, however, this is the field of the Astronomer, so that he may speak in common terms and not aim at the individual. For the **lesser man** <note>the human being as a reflection of the universe</note> is not known to him, nor how he relates himself to heaven. This very same thing also escapes the Physician. For even if he knows whom it concerns or whom it strikes: nevertheless, because he is not skilled in the **Cosmography** <term>Cosmography: here, the anatomical and spiritual "mapping" of the human body in relation to the stars</term> of all men, he explains the matter as best he can. For what other end is there for Philosophy and Astronomy, if not man? If, therefore, man is not in the known, the said arts are dead. Similarly, what is a Physician, if he does not conclude with Cosmography, of which he ought to have a singular knowledge, as well as of those things which have already been said? For all sciences are referred back to Cosmography: and without it, nothing happens.

<margin>Heaven heals itself like a dog.</margin>
Now, however, heaven is a Physician to itself, just as a dog is to its wound <note>referring to a dog's instinct to lick and heal its own sores</note>: which, in this case, is lacking in man. For because he is more than a mortal creature: he ought also to be of more science. For if he ought to know what is in heaven, what in earth, what in air, what in water: why does he do it? Surely to this end, that he may know himself, who he is, and from where he is. If this knowledge were not necessary: man would never fall ill. But so that man may see who and of what sort he may be, he must therefore take the place of the "father" <note>the universe</note> in diseases and health. And see, Mars made this member, Venus that one, the Moon this one: this part is **Chaos** <term>Chaos: in Paracelsian terms, this often refers to the atmosphere or the invisible "space" that sustains life</term>: on this side is **Tereniabin** <term>Tereniabin: a Persian-derived term used by Paracelsus for a celestial manna or spiritual exudation from the stars</term>: in this place you have blood and flesh from water, or earth. This is the sole end of these diseases and healths of man: that from them he may know the **limbus** <term>limbus: the "great Limbus" or primordial matter from which all things were created</term> from which he was born, so that he may know the cattle in the forests and fields, and see that he is entirely similar to the cattle, and in no part better.

<margin>Man is similar to the beasts, not better.</margin>
It is fitting, therefore, for man to consider himself, and to be skilled in all universal creatures, so that in this way he may know himself. No one penetrates deeper with this knowledge than the Physician himself: for in him the truth of this knowledge is situated, as its basis. It is right for him to be believed, for him to be held as authentic, and no one else.

<margin>Man is more sublime than all creatures.</margin>
Now because man is more sublime than all other creatures: all these things must be within him. Even the Intellect was added to him as an inheritance from Adam, so that he might judge how great he is...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that physicians must understand "Cosmography"—the internal mapping of the stars within man—because human health is governed by the same celestial motions as the macrocosm. He critiques traditional academic medicine for focusing on superficial causes while ignoring the profound connection between the human "son" and the universal "father."</summary>
<keywords>microcosm, macrocosm, Cosmography, Limbus, Tereniabin, Paragranum, internal stars, medical astrology, academic critique</keywords>

Paracelsus is elaborating on the idea that the physician must look beyond the physical body to the "internal heaven" to understand the true origins of health and disease.
