# ON ASTRONOMY.

<margin>
Why he received it in the intellect.
Why he was made from perishable things.
</margin>
...let him judge, lest he become a companion to the pride of Lucifer, who, being ignorant of this, estimated himself to be equal to God. This is also the reason why man was established and created differently; that is, God foresaw these things in such a way, and established him from the perishable <note>original: "caducis" - things that fall or pass away, emphasizing human mortality compared to the eternal.</note>, so that he would be mindful of his origin. From which it follows now, that it is necessary for man to draw his knowledge from the Physician; for God established him to explain and define to you who you are, by what bond and by what predictions you are bound, and by what thing you ought to be liberated. This whole consideration leads us to understand that man was produced from external creatures for this one reason: so that through his infirmity he might be reminded of whence he was taken and established.

<margin>A sickened heaven transfers evil into man.</margin>
Now, however, as has been said, the heaven itself also falls ill. But it pours itself out further. Man receives this by inheritance. For his own internal heaven imitates its parent [the macrocosm]. Yet the disease is not brought forth directly in that way. For within itself it has a body, which consists of four [elements], not one. That mixture is the subject of the Physician. Indeed, the nature of the subject must be discovered by the Physician: namely, that this heaven mortifies [destroys/corrupts], and that the air mortifies that. This is the reason why it is fitting for the Physician to know why the upper sphere invades so violently, and where, and in what place it invades, and that death alone blunts its attack, so that it cannot break through and penetrate the heaven. This repression is the strangulation of that which is closed within the skin. For it must be observed in this place that the inner stars, which have twin death-bearing bodies within themselves, induce disease because of that twin nature, which must be completely shaken out and extruded outside the skin. But the heaven does not attempt this. For it is not doubled. How shall the Physician avert this mortification if he does not know that these stars break through and cut out their own heaven: and if indeed they have broken through, that death alone is extruded there, not health itself? Regarding these things, read the *Paramirum* <note>The *Opus Paramirum* is one of Paracelsus's major works, dealing with the five causes of disease.</note>, the specific book I dedicated to the causes and origins of diseases.

<margin>Opposites in one science.</margin>
So much therefore lies in the foundation of Medicine, that unless the Recipes are directed against the properties of the stars themselves and the proximate causes of diseases, nothing can be properly cured and healed. For whatever the star is, such is the nature of the disease: and he who knows the star also has the knowledge of the disease. And this knowledge teaches nothing else than to weigh the very nature of Medicine. For if you know the enemy, you also know the friend. If the heaven is the enemy: the lower sphere is the friend. If the hostility comes from the lower sphere: friendship is found in the upper. Not only the productions of the earth [herbs and minerals] help: but also the celestial secrets. Now, however, there is no disease which nature and property alone do not violently attack, and not at all the complexion <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). Paracelsus rejected this as the primary cause of disease.</term>. And so conversely. <margin>Worms not from qualities.</margin> Worms that are born have their origin from a property, and not from cold, nor from heat. And this property has the force of a cause in all diseases. Who, indeed, will apply his hands to this work to describe those diseases whose nature and property he is ignorant of? Or who will teach the method of healing those things, if he is unskilled in that? Therefore, both spheres impart those secrets to their Physician. Now, indeed, this is the difference between the <term>arcana</term> and Medicine: that <margin>How Arcana and Medicine differ.</margin> *arcana* operate in the nature or essence, while Medicine operates in the contrary elements. But the *arcana* of Medicine do not present themselves [openly]. And these are the medicines where cold is understood to be removed by heat, and a multitude by purgation. Thus, then, the substances of the *arcana* are judged, because they are natures directed against the property of the enemy, no differently than a boxer against a boxer. Thus there is also a conflict of nature, so that trickery is anticipated by trickery. And whatever things we possess naturally on earth: the same nature also wants reserved in Medicine. And let this be as an example for the Physician: things are not done here otherwise than as two enemies oppose each other, who are either equally cold, or equally burning, who are both armed, and who intend a struggle with similar weapons. As victory belongs to these: so also you ought to know regarding man, that his twin wrestlers solicit natural help from one mother; that is, from one virtue. When they operate with a similar virtue, it is fitting that the same industry be used by the Physician in suggesting Medicine, and that he put the victorious spears of Medicine into their hands. For Medicine has these things within itself. You, at least, provide the arms of nature: which will protect itself afterwards. <margin>Because nature must be handed over to the Physician.</margin> I produce these things for this purpose, lest anyone trust rashly in the degrees <note>original: "gradibus" - refers to the Galenic system of classifying medicines as "hot in the second degree," etc. Paracelsus argues this is insufficient.</note>, which attack the heaven with such hostility. For every consideration is terminated by such an example: Someone is wounded, and flows with a large amount of blood. The blood cannot be stopped in this man. But out of twenty or thirty remedies applied, one crude thing [a specific arcanum] stops the hemorrhage.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that physicians must understand the internal "stars" of the human body, as diseases originate from astral properties rather than simple humoral imbalances. He introduces the concept of "Arcana"—essential remedies that act like a wrestler against a specific disease-enemy.</summary>

<header>TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM</header>

# TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
Or a hemorrhage ceases of its own accord. In this matter, what is there for a Physician to know or consider? Namely, the single motion of the sphere. A star wishes to proceed, with nothing hindering its course. There are many such motions or courses: there are also many cessations and repressions of bleeding. Now, as many courses as there are, so many are the ways of restraining blood. Therefore, the Art consists in this: that there are many <term>blood-stanching</term> <note>original: "ischæmas" - substances or methods used to stop the flow of blood.</note> things, and as many as there are motions or courses. But to relate a blood-stanching remedy to a motion or course—that is already an <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum" - a secret, higher medicinal essence that works on a spiritual or celestial level rather than a merely physical one.</note>. Thus, a star must be considered alongside its Medicine, and the hot compared with the hot, the cold with the cold. For nothing else is to be considered here than nature with nature. Let every husband be joined to his own wife, and every wife to her own husband. In this lies the very sinew of Medicine, so that a judgment may be made regarding good and bad signs, and concerning the injuries of the limbs. This has indeed been begun to some extent by a few, but physicians who were not sufficiently skilled have not forced it into a proper order. For through forgetfulness, Medicine has been cast aside; nor has anything been proposed except for at most a half-part. The whole, however, has been discarded.

Since, therefore, the power of the heavens is so great that it rules Medicine so potently, it is necessary that this foundation which I propose be finally and stubbornly maintained, and that nothing outside of it be held by anyone. From which it is also fitting that whatever things are produced or published against it should be cast into the midst of a funeral pyre. For there is nothing in them but mere deceptions. And who will 
<margin>Pliny handed down things of no value.</margin>
charge me with a crime because I reject Pliny in his commentaries on the powers of natural things? For he writes nothing that is either true or has any use. I do not deny, certainly, that he has handed down the truth in some places. But who is there who knows in what thing, or when, that truth can be found? The heaven works in its own time. And it is the heaven that brings forth and manifests the powers of things. For powers and virtues are subject to the heaven. Who, then, would dare to hand down anything concerning a virtue, who does not simultaneously add the native hour of that virtue? What else is that but a vain, compiled, and unexamined speech, which resounds concerning empty things? And yet those babblers cling to writings of this sort. 

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
For the herbalists know not how to preach or adorn anything except what happens to be sweet to the tongue, in which all deceits reside. Who will find fault with me because I do not highly value Macer <note>A reference to "Aemilius Macer," the traditional name associated with a popular medieval herbal poem, *De viribus herbarum*.</note> and authors similar to him, and forbid his reading? Is this cause truly slight, that someone should speak and write in a triple-tongued way? That someone should wickedly explain the natures and species of things, and where they tend? Secondly, they are even unmindful of the *process*—which is nevertheless no less necessary to things than the virtue itself. And he who is ignorant of the process, how can he have certain knowledge of the virtue? For the process demonstrates the virtue, and the virtue is explained through the process. Thirdly, because the mind and sense of these authors could never be understood either in diseases or in other matters, should they not be prohibited from being read? For they are mindful neither of Mother Nature, nor of her light, nor of any natural principle or origin. For what else have they ever done anywhere, except give to the public some compiled and begged things, the reason and foundation of which (which they did not understand in the slightest) is found to be far different from what they designated. In the same way the Poets also write, and devise various things, and feign one thing from another, chanting now this, now that; whose pen is nothing other than the poison of Medicine.

<margin>The foundation is poison.</margin>
The foundation of Medicine ought to be produced in such a way that flint is led into Sapphire and Emerald, and Venus into the Sun, not through art alone, but also through the heaven: not only in form, but also in virtue. And so much so must it be taught and written, that all the virtues of Coral are found in marble, and marble in Coral. The work of those who write about colors is easy. Light is the labor of him who collects and writes down the sayings of his neighbor. These can by no right be called writers. He who wishes to comment on the nature of the son ought to derive the matter from the foundation of the mother. And in this way, any thing becomes that which is the other, and nothing becomes better or worse through it. The work of those writers has now reached such a point that Rhubarb and <term>Hermodactyls</term> <note>original: "Hermodactyli" - a root used in the Renaissance to treat gout and joint pain.</note> must now be sought beyond the sea. From this has been born the most blessed <note>Paracelsus is being sarcastic here.</note> recklessness of the pharmacists, who have deserted the nature and knowledge of medicines. This matter is no different than if one were to hire an orator to speak for himself, even though he himself has enough of a mouth and tongue; he lacks only this: that he does not have a mouth equally skilled and practiced. But just as a Doctor can be made from a peasant, so can Rhubarb be made from Gentian. I wish you to be mindful of this: just as anyone's mouth can be shaped and instructed, so nature itself is also subject to discipline.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires aligning remedies with celestial motions and criticizes ancient authorities like Pliny and Macer for lacking this astrological "process." He suggests that the inner virtue of plants depends on timing and that local plants like Gentian can be transformed into exotic ones like Rhubarb through proper alchemical-astrological understanding.</summary>

<page-num>205</page-num>
<header>ON ASTRONOMY.</header>

<margin>Medicine is before your feet: do not bring things from the furthest shores; all things differ by a single opinion.</margin>
For Medicine is born both near gardens and near fields. But after the Experimenters and the Humorists <note>Followers of the traditional "humoral" theory of Galen, which Paracelsus sought to overthrow.</note> arose, they dared to thrust Greek medicines upon the Germans. And it is the same with these as with rags: the further they are brought from, the better they are considered. But domestic ones, which ward off the cold just as well, are cast aside and become worthless. In what way, then, is one better than the other? Only opinion, and will or foolishness makes them differ, and it is only a deception of the eyes: those who are afflicted by a certain defect of vision called "hay" <note>original: "fenum" — likely a metaphor for a clouded or distorted vision that sees distant things clearly but misses what is immediately present.</note> discern a herb six hundred miles away, and do not see what is before their feet. But the heaven is as much before one’s feet as it is beyond a thousand miles. If the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising over the eastern horizon at a specific moment; here representing the specific celestial influence acting on a patient.</note> can find the sick person to slay him, it can also find him to save him. Both are twins: where there is disease, there is Medicine; where there is Medicine, there is disease. For in <term>arcana</term> <note>Hidden medicinal essences or spiritual forces within physical substances.</note>, tartar becomes Hyacinth, red ochre becomes Alabaster, <margin>The power of arcana.</margin> flint becomes Garnet, clay becomes noble Bolus, sand becomes Pearl, glass becomes Manna, and a hoof becomes Balsam. In these things lies the description of matters in which it is proper for a Physician to be well-versed.

Every temporary thing is subject to the heaven. Their decay is the cause. As soon as the course and the end are at hand, the dissolution of the thing is also near. After any single dissolution, a new <term>ascendant</term> and a new entry must be introduced. For hence it happens that often ten or twenty things fall upon one limb before the whole heaven perishes. Thus, therefore, other recent constellations come forth, useful for life, but harmful to health: for one moment breaks and destroys what can never afterwards be restored. Now from this follows the "fortune" of <term>circumcised</term> physicians <note>original: "circumcisorum Medicorum" — Paracelsus often used this term to mock conventional academic physicians who followed rigid, "clipped" traditions without true insight.</note>, <margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin> because with one and the same medicine they help this person and do not help that one, and yet it is one, and now it proceeds, now it recedes. But for these things there is need for the science of Revolution and Alteration, and the change of the Ascendant, and the completion of <term>Exaltation</term> <note>In astrology, the sign in which a planet has its strongest influence.</note>, and a new reckoning of conjunction. In what other way, I ask, can anyone govern and direct with Medicine? You physicians, where then will you seek and establish the base of your fortune? Or whom will you blame if things turn out adversely? Whom will you praise if they succeed according to your wish? What is fortune? What is misfortune? Tell me, what was the face of the Moon, what eyes, what nose did she wear? If you had tasted the doctrine of the celestial motions, you would speak thus: <margin>Fortune is knowledge; misfortune is ignorance.</margin> "Here it is, here it is not," nor would you say, "I will make an attempt, may God favor it." No fortune exists without a foundation or without one experienced in foreknowledge. What else is fortune but order, joined with the knowledge of Nature? What is misfortune but an entry made into nature outside of order? If Nature proceeds correctly, that is fortune. If she goes astray, it is misfortune. These things we profess for the sake of those who are persuaded that fortune is a man doing all things according to the pleasure of humans. Which is false. For we have our <margin>Opinion on fortune.</margin> ordered condition within nature. He who walks in the light is overwhelmed by no misfortune. He who goes through the darkness is not pressed by misfortune either: the lot of both is one. He who does not fall maintains order. He who falls has broken order. Therefore, fortune and misfortune do not behave like snow and wind: but they must be drawn out and known from the inner recesses of nature. And therefore misfortune is ignorance; fortune indeed is knowledge. He who walks in the rain, even if he gets wet, is not unfortunate. He who walks in the Sun is not unfortunate. For both the fortune and misfortune of each are invented only by those who doubt and hope, who both do nothing else but open their mouths wide if some chance thing flies in. Regarding knowledge and science, you physicians ought to labor so diligently that you know the origin or cause of both fortune and misfortune. As long as you cannot do this, take your hands off medicine. For to kill a sick man is not misfortune. Even to heal him is not fortune. It is the end and the goal, according to which each thing acts and operates. For the end testifies to who is engaged in fortune, or misfortune, or knowledge, or ignorance. Who else knows the number of diseases than he who knows the number of plants <margin>Death beyond fear.</margin> and natural arcana? There is nothing more than the other: there is nothing less, that remains more, than death alone, which is included in no number. Therefore, because the number is equal on both sides: who is first in taking the number but the Philosopher for one part? For the other part is the Astronomer: and neither is more than the other, and both keep the number of diseases. It is <margin>Impossible for a physician to experience all diseases.</margin> impossible for a physician to experience them all. For he is a physician at least for one region, for one first year; what then does he know in the second year? He does not have it discovered from himself by what thing names may be unearthed and found. Thus also here is the principle of matter, of nature,

S
knowledge <note>Catchword: "scientiæ"</note>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that medicine should be found locally rather than imported and that clinical success is not a matter of luck ("fortune") but of scientific knowledge of celestial and natural orders. He redefines fortune as the result of following nature's order and misfortune as the result of ignorance.</summary>

<header>THIRD TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM.</header>

situated in knowledge and property.

<margin>A sharp rebuke of doctors.</margin>
Is it therefore unjust that your stupidity, <term>Beani</term> <note>original: "Beanis" — a term for "freshmen" or "novices," used here as a mocking insult for doctors Paracelsus considers uneducated</note>, and your errors, and your deceptions of the sick be uncovered and brought into the light? Or is it right for you to have another foundation: otherwise you must come forward into the public eye as something worse than thieves. Do you think this should be turned into a vice against me, or that I should be cast out of my fatherland because I say such things and reproach you? Which, in the truth of the matter, is nothing else than dragging your robbery out of the darkness and into the open. Your authority will remain stable no longer than until the judgment of the sick. For then, in that time, you will be widely revealed. You will not protect your "freshman-folly" through your colleagues and kinsmen, or through the flattery and fawning of princes: but a completely different fate shall be yours and theirs with you. For unless you establish your foundation in such a way that the names of diseases shall be those of Leo, Sagittarius, Mars, or Saturn: then you will certainly achieve nothing else than to wallow in misfortune. Which of those two foundations will you propose to the sick person as the true one? In truth, if they knew your lies, or had found them out sufficiently, they would heap stones upon your backs much more frequently than they place them beneath your feet. Do not say: this is <term>Melancholy</term>, that is <term>cholera</term> <note>The traditional "humors" of Greek medicine, which Paracelsus rejected in favor of chemical and celestial causes.</note>. For the matter is not so. Borrow true knowledge from the external world: and thus no one will prove you a liar. You will not move or strike me with your threats and slanders. For if one must descend into the arena, my weapons are known to me at home, and are already prepared.

From this, now, O listeners and readers, estimate what foundation I and they use: and judge whether my science depends upon and proceeds from insanity, or necromancy, or the Devil, as they say. Furthermore, weigh the foundation that they themselves have, and from whence it emerges. Mine, in truth, is from Truth. From which you can now recognize its father. Theirs, however, is from a lie: from whence it is easy to guess both its origin and its end. And with so many things commemorated here, I now place an end to this second pillar: intending to add a fuller explanation in those places where nature and man are described. This is not my current purpose here: but it was at least this, to explain from whence Medicine ought to be drawn, and how it ought to be distinguished from the fraud of impostors, who have protected it with words alone until now.

# THE THIRD PILLAR OF MEDICINE
## ALCHEMY.

Insisting upon our purpose, we now next bring forward the third foundation of Medicine, which is *Alchemy*. Truly, unless the Physician is skilled and experienced in this to the highest degree, whatever he spends of his art will be empty and vain. For Nature is so sharp and subtle in her works that she refuses to be handled except with sublime and accurate craftsmanship.

<margin>The way of Nature.</margin>
For she brings nothing into the light that is perfect in itself there, but leaves it to be perfected by man. This perfection is called *Alchemy*. For the Alchemist is a baker in that he cooks bread; a vintner in that he prepares wine; a weaver in that he makes cloth. Thus, whatever is poured forth from the lap of nature for the benefit of man: he who brings it to that state for which it was destined, he is an Alchemist.

<margin>Nothing is perfect in the beginning. What is Alchemy?</margin>
From these things, now learn the distinction of this art from the others by this given comparison. For imagine if someone were to put on a raw sheepskin as a garment and covering for himself; how rude and coarse that would be, if compared with a furrier or a cloth-maker. It is equally rude and coarse if someone takes what is drawn from nature and does not prepare it. Indeed, it is much ruder than the former. For this concerns the body itself, and life, and health. Whence it happens that it must be handled and held much more accurately. Now, however, all crafts have emulated nature, and have learned her properties so well that they can now express nature herself in all things, and draw out what is highest in her.

<margin>Medicine is ruder than other arts.</margin>
But in Medicine alone, where it was most necessary of all, this has been least provided: which for that reason exists as the rudest and most unpolished in this respect. How could a man be coarser than one who devours raw meat, and is clothed in raw hides, and establishes a home for himself under the nearest rocks, or stays out in the rains? In the same way, how could a Physician be coarser, or what preparation of Medicine could be ruder than that which the <term>seplasiarii</term> <note>original: "seplasiarii" — a term for ointment-sellers or common apothecaries, often used disparagingly by Paracelsus to describe those who mix medicines without chemical understanding.</note> use in boiling things down? For nothing is more foul than to thus pound, knead, and mix medicines together, or to pollute them in various ways. And just as that leather adorns him: so does his art adorn the medicine-seller.

<margin>From whence Alchemy is to be drawn.</margin>
Because, truly, in this place the true foundation for preparing remedies—

<sig>S 2</sig>

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The difficulty of the alchemical quest.</margin>
...then, upon which medicine itself consists, is produced and established. Therefore, know that this foundation must be unearthed from the inner secrets of nature, and not truly from an imaginative brain, as if a cook were boiling porridge according to his own whim. For in this preparation, the highest and final point of all things is placed. Thus, if Philosophy and Astronomy are understood here—that is, the nature of diseases and remedies along with their entire composition and conjunction—then the next and most necessary thing is that you decide how to bestow and apply what you know. For nature herself teaches you in these matters what work you should most specifically study so that you may bring your Medicine into effect. Just as summer brings forth pears and grapes, so you must bring forth your Medicine. If it is applied in that way, you will certainly achieve its desired outcome. Therefore, if one must strive so that, just as summer produces its fruits, you also produce your Medicine, then know— <margin>The stars perfect the work of the Physician.</margin> —that summer does this through the stars, and not without them. Now, if the stars provide this, observe in this place that this preparation shall be so directed that it is subject to the stars. For they are what complete and perfect the work of the Physician. And so, if such stars exist, it is entirely right that Medicine be understood and brought to its nature according to them. It should not be said: "This is cold, this is hot, this is moist, this is dry" <note>These are the four "qualities" of traditional Galenic medicine, which Paracelsus rejected in favor of chemical and celestial properties</note>; but rather let it be said: "this is Saturn, this is Mars, this is Venus, this is the Pole." In this way, the Physician walks the right path—especially if, beyond this, he knows how to harmonize and join the astral Mars with the Mars born within the patient. For here lies the <term>shell</term> <note>original: "volua" — a covering or husk</note> or the kernel, which no physician from the first to the latest has bitten into before me. This must be understood as follows: it is necessary for Medicine to be prepared into stars, so that they become stars. For the stars above make ill, they kill, and they also heal. If any of these things are to happen, they cannot happen at all without the stars. If it must happen with the stars, however, it will happen in such a way and path that the preparation is led to the point where, by a similar reasoning, the Medicine is fashioned and prepared by the heaven, just as prophecies and all other deeds are established by the heaven. This is what you see: the stars presage and prophesy a horrid storm; the stars portend diseases and the death of kings and princes; the stars foretell battles and wars, plagues, and famine. The heaven indicates all these things, for it makes and produces them. Whatever it makes, it rightly signals. These things go out from the heaven itself; from it also emerge the arts of this science. Thus, if they are through the heaven or from the heaven, they shall also be governed by the heaven, so that they occur at its nod and will, just as has been said and indicated. Thus the aforementioned things are made by the heaven according to its will; therefore the heaven also leads <margin>Remedies are from the stars and are governed by them.</margin> and moderates them. Furthermore, know this about these things: if Medicine is from the heaven, it will remain subject to the heaven without any contradiction; it will obey it and accommodate itself to the heaven's will. If this is true, it is necessary that the Physician cast out opinions regarding <term>Degrees</term>, <term>Complexions</term>, <term>Humors</term>, and <term>Qualities</term> <note>Technical terms of medieval medicine based on the balance of bodily fluids</note>, and whether he likes it or not, he must recognize Medicine in the stars—that is, he must judge the Nature of Medicine according to the stars, so that he knows the stars both above and below. <margin>Medicine without the heaven is worthless. Medicine is not ruled by the stars unless separated.</margin> And because Medicine without the heaven is worthless, it must therefore be led through the heaven. This "leading forth" is nothing other than the abolition and removal of the "earth" existing within the medicine. For the heaven does not rule it unless it has been separated from that earth. If you have separated it, then the Medicine is in the power of the stars and is governed and protected by them. Thus, that which pertains to the brain is led to the brain through the Moon; that which acts upon the spleen is channeled there through Saturn; that which is bestowed upon the heart is carried to it through the Sun. In this way, the Kidneys are ruled by Venus, the Liver by Jupiter, and the bile by Mars. This should be understood ineffably not only of these, but of all other things. For what is that Medicine which you apply to a woman's womb if it is not directed there by Venus? What kind of remedy would there be for the brain if the Moon did not channel it to that place? Judge the rest in the same way. For otherwise, all things would remain in the stomach and, finally sent out through the intestines, would produce no operation. For from this emerges the cause of why, if the heaven favors you less and refuses to direct the Medicine, you profit very little. <margin>The cause of bad successes.</margin> For one needs the heaven as a moderator. Therefore, let the work of the art be situated in this, so that you do not speak according to this rule: <margin>A rebuke of Physicians.</margin> "Melissa is a womb herb, Marjoram is for the head." For that is how the unskilled speak. Rather, that power is placed in Venus and the Moon. If you wish to experience such things as you presume, it is necessary that you have a merciful and benign heaven for yourself; otherwise no operation will come forth. Here is that foundation of error which has so greatly prevailed in Medicine: "you at least provide the drink; if it helps, it helps." <margin>The favor of heaven is the breath of the work.</margin> Any dull-witted peasant might know an art of this kind, nor [is it necessary] for this...

<summary>Paracelsus defines Alchemy as the process of separating a medicine's "earthly" matter from its "astral" essence, allowing celestial forces to guide the remedy to specific organs like the heart (Sun) or brain (Moon). He mocks traditional herbalism and Galenic humors, arguing that without celestial alignment, medicine remains useless in the stomach.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous page's discussion on Astronomy into the third pillar of medicine: Alchemy. Paracelsus is refuting the traditional medical authorities, Avicenna and Galen, arguing that true healing power comes from the stars and is only accessible through alchemical refinement.</meta>

<page-num>208</page-num>
<header>THIRD TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM.</header>

<margin>Only heaven is the director.</margin>
<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
<margin>One fate for physicians and priests.</margin>
...this [medicine] has need of either Avicenna or Galen. But you physicians, who are the progeny of these men, are accustomed to repeatedly say that <term>Directives</term> <note>original: "Directoria"; substances or forces intended to guide a medicine to a specific organ</note> must be given to the head, to the brain, to the liver, and so on. And yet you dare to establish those Directives when you do not understand the heavens in the least; for it is the heavens alone that direct. Indeed, you have forgotten one thing that entangles you all in folly. To be sure, you have discovered things which you think direct to the brain, the head, the womb, the anus, the bladder, and so forth; but those things which direct to the disease itself, you do not know at all. Now, if you do not know what directs toward the disease, you will also be ignorant of where the disease is located. You deal with the "principal parts" <note>The vital organs according to ancient medicine</note>, which you frequently argue are sick, in the same way that priests <note>original: "sacrifici"; literally those who perform sacrifices, used here as a jab at religious authorities</note> deal with their gods: they thrust them all into heaven, even if many of them lie buried in hell. So it is with you: all diseases are located in the liver and lung, even if they occasionally occupy the backside.

<margin>Medicine must be refined.</margin>
<margin>The "fifth essence," or a certain secret.</margin>
<margin>The stomach is an alchemist.</margin>
<margin>Alchemy is the external stomach.</margin>
<margin>The goal of alchemy.</margin>
Now, because it is heaven that directs through the stars, and not the physician, medicine must be refined <note>original: "subtilianda"; made "subtle" or spiritualized through alchemy</note> into an airy state so that it can be conveniently ruled by the stars. For what stone is lifted up by the stars? None, except only that which is volatile. Hence it happened that many, through Alchemy, have sought out the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintum esse"; the quintessence, the purest and most potent extract of a substance</note>; this is nothing other than the separation of the four bodies from the <term>arcana</term> <note>The hidden, spiritual healing powers within natural substances</note>. Then, whatever remains there is the secret power. This secret power, moreover, is also a <term>chaos</term> <note>A formless, receptive state of matter</note>, as easily led by the stars as a feather is by the wind. Therefore, let the preparation of Medicine be such that the four bodies <note>The physical elements</note> are removed from the secrets. Next, let knowledge be added: specifically, what "star" is within that secret; and then, let it also be known what the "star" of this disease is, and what "star" in the Medicine acts against this disease. From this, finally, proceeds the *Direction*. If you offer a medicament, your stomach is then compelled to prepare it; the stomach is your internal Alchemist. If the stomach can reduce the medicament to such a point that it may be received by the stars, then it is directed. If not, it remains in the stomach and slips away through the bowels. What, I ask, is more worthy of a physician than the knowledge of the concordance of both stars <note>The "star" in the medicine and the "star" in the patient</note>? For in this consists the knowledge of all diseases. Here, then, Alchemy is the "external stomach" which prepares its own for the star—not as those madmen who say Alchemy is for making gold and silver. There is only one work here: Create *arcana*, and direct them toward the disease. This is where the work must end; this is the heart of the matter. For all these things proceed from the guidance of nature and its proof.

<margin>Secrets are volatile.</margin>
<margin>Reproof of pharmacists.</margin>
<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
<margin>What the true secrets are.</margin>
<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
Thus, nature and man wish to be joined, compared, and valued together in health and disease. In this rests the principle of treatment and healing. Alchemy perfects all these things, without which none of this can be done. Now, if all Medicines are *arcana*, and all *arcana* are volatile by nature, by what right, I ask, can that tailor and filthy cook, the <term>Pharmacist</term> <note>original: "Pharmacopoeus"; the apothecary</note>, boast of being a "Dispenser" and a cook? Rather, he is a dispenser and cook of scraps! How great also is the folly of those Doctors who deceive through these rustic cooks, to whom they offer Electuaries, Syrups, Pills, and Ointments, which nonetheless display no foundation, no art, no Medicine, and no science anywhere? Nor would any of you dare to maintain, having taken an oath, that you work with science and truth. The same logic applies to your <term>Uroscopy</term> <note>The practice of diagnosing diseases by looking at urine</note>. For from urine you divine a "blue sky," and you trifle so vigorously that, by your own confession, it is established that these things are nothing other than divinations and conjectures, and nothing ever matches unless it happens by chance. Thus you lie in your shops, and in washing and boiling you display such "mastery" that no one is persuaded otherwise than that the kingdom of heaven dwells with you, while you are actually hiding the mere pit of hell. If you would dismiss those apprenticeships of yours and search for the *arcana*—what they are, what director they have, and how the stars rule disease and health—then certainly you would also know that your "foundation" is mere fantasy and persuasion. The final and single purpose here is that the principle of Medicine should at last consist in these *arcana*, and that *arcana* should seal the physician's foundation. Therefore, know that the <term>colophon</term> <note>The finishing touch or crowning achievement</note> is situated in the *arcana*; it is necessary that Alchemy be the foundation here, through which the *arcana* are prepared. Know, therefore, that the *arcana* alone are those things which are the strengths and virtues. For this reason they are also volatile, empty of bodies, and are "chaos," and are clear, and are transparent, and are in the power of the star. If you know the star, and you know the disease, you fully understand who your teacher is and what your power is. And thus the *arcana* also prove that your Humors, Qualities, and complexions are nothing, and that Melancholy, Phlegm, and Cholera are wrongly introduced...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that medicine must be alchemically refined into a "volatile" or spiritual state so that it can be guided by celestial forces (stars) to the seat of a disease. He attacks traditional physicians and pharmacists for relying on physical mixtures like syrups and pills, which he claims lack the true spiritual "arcana" necessary for healing.</summary>

<page-num>209</page-num>
-># ON ALCHEMY.<-

...in their place [they use] Mars and Saturn, and it is said: "this is the <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: arcanum; the hidden healing essence or spiritual power within a substance</note> of Mars, this is the arcanum of Saturn." And within these things, natural science resides. And who among you, listeners, would dare to reject and oppose this foundation? Only your teachers do this: in this matter they are exactly like those stubborn and hardened old students.

<margin>Requirements of a physician.</margin>
Therefore, if it is right for a Physician to know such things, it is also fitting for him to have discovered what it is to <term>calcinate</term> <note>to reduce a substance to powder by heat</note> and what it is to <term>sublimate</term> <note>to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, purifying it</note>. Nor should he know this merely by the hand's work, but also through the "mutation" <note>transformation</note>, which is of greater value than the manual act. For through these processes, as they are understood in the preparation, "maturations" are often produced of a kind that nature itself could not provide. And the Physician ought to direct his art toward this maturation. For he is the autumn and the summer, and the star of those things which he must bring to perfection. The fire is the earth; man is the order; the object of the work is the seed. And although all these things are understood simply in the world, they are nevertheless various and manifold in their end, just as they are manifold in the place of their completion. Although, 
<margin>All secrets come from fire.</margin>
through a single process, all <term>arcana</term> are born and produced in the fire. This fire is their "earth"; and this earth is also according to the Sun; and thus the earth and the firmament in this second generation are one and the same thing. In this [fire] the arcana are cooked, and in this they are <term>fermented</term> <note>alchemical ripening</note>. And just as a grain rots in the earth before it springs up and bears fruit, so here too a dissolution occurs in the fire, where the arcana are fermented and cast off their [gross] bodies, 
<margin>The times of exaltation.</margin>
and through ascent they depart into their "exaltations," the stages of which are calcination, sublimation, <term>reverberation</term> <note>heating in a furnace where the flame is deflected onto the substance</note>, solution, etc., and secondly into <term>reiteration</term>, which is to say, transplantation.

Now, however, all these operations are brought about by the course or motion which time gives. For there is one time for the exterior world, and another for man. But the operation, or 
<margin>Nature attempts all that the craftsman does.</margin>
force of the celestial motion, is also wonderful. And although the craftsman may highly esteem himself and his work, the sum of it is this: that heaven <term>cooks, digests, imbibes, dissolves, and reverberates</term> just as wonderfully as the Alchemist does. And the motion of the heavens teaches the movement and government of the fire in the <term>athanor</term> <note>original: Athanar; a furnace used in alchemy designed to maintain a uniform heat</note>. Regarding the power that resides in the <term>Sapphire</term>, heaven promises its dissolution, coagulation, and fixation. If heaven is thus constituted in its operations through these three things, bringing them to that point, then it is necessary that the dissolution of the Sapphire itself must likewise consist of these three points. This dissolution is of such a kind 
<margin>Dissolution reveals the secret.</margin>
that the [physical] bodies are excluded by it, and the arcanum remains. For before this, while the Sapphire was whole, there was no arcanum [available]. But afterward, just as life is infused into man, so too is this arcanum infused into this matter from heaven. The body must therefore be removed, as it 
<margin>The body hinders the secret.</margin>
hinders the arcanum. For just as nothing is made or born from a seed unless it is dissolved—which dissolution is nothing other than the <term>putrefaction</term> of the body, not of the arcanum itself—so in this place the body of the Sapphire behaves, unless it has received the arcanum. Now, however, its dissolution occurs through those things by which it grew together. The grain of the field experiences no small industry of nature until it proceeds into an ear of corn. For there is the <term>Elixir</term> and the highest ferment, which is retained above all things in nature. Afterward follows digestion, and from this, its own increase. He who wishes to be such a preparer of nature must pass through this way; otherwise, he will be a mere scullery-boy, or a cook, or a cleaner. For nature requires that the preparation in man be in every way as it is in herself: that is, that we follow her as our mistress, not the 
<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
follies of our own brains. But what, finally, do you Doctors and <term>perfume-sellers</term> <note>original: seplasiarij; a derogatory term for apothecaries who deal in superficial mixtures</note> either ferment, putrefy, digest, or exalt? You have fashioned nothing but a certain varied mixture of broths which you administer, and thus you shamefully deceive men. Who would praise a physician who 
<margin>The office of the physician.</margin>
has not learned the way and reason of nature? Or who would trust him? For a physician ought to be nothing other than a consultant of nature itself, who is excellently skilled in her nature, property, and condition. If he is ignorant of such things regarding the composition of Nature, what, I ask, can he do in dissolution? 
<margin>Dissolution is the reverse path of composition.</margin>
Understand therefore, that dissolution is a certain backward step. Whatever nature has composed step-by-step forward, you must dissolve backward. And as long as you or I remain unskilled and ignorant of this dissolution, we act at the very least as thieves, cut-throats, <term>horned ones</term> <note>cuckolds or fools</note>, and <term>simpletons</term> <note>original: beanos; a term for a raw, uninitiated student</note>.

<margin>Many secrets of Alum.</margin>
What, I ask you, will you produce from <term>Alum</term>, in which so many arcana lie hidden for diseases of the body as well as for wounds? According to your process, who will ever lead it to that use for which it is powerful, in the manner of the pharmacists? And this 
<margin>Mummy.</margin>
we say as much of <term>Mummy</term> <note>original: Mumia; a medicinal preparation, sometimes derived from embalmed bodies, believed to contain vital spirit</note> as of alum. Where do you look for these things? Beyond the Ocean, among the Heathen? O you simpletons: who summon from afar what is ready before your doors and in your own orchards. Truly, because you are ignorant of Alchemy, you are deservedly ignorant of the mysteries of Nature as well. Or are you so persuaded...

He rebukes traditional doctors for being mere 'cooks' who do not understand how to dissolve matter back to its essential spirit.</summary>

<page-num>210</page-num>
->## THE THIRD TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM.<-

<margin>Reproach of the physicians.</margin>
Do you think that because you wear out the works of Avicenna, Savonarola, Valescus, and Vigo <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Giovanni Michele Savonarola, Valescus de Taranta, and Giovanni da Vigo were standard medieval and Renaissance medical authorities whom Paracelsus frequently criticized.</note>, you are already sufficiently prepared by them? Those are mere trifles. Outside of this <term>arcanum</term> <note>the secret healing essence or spiritual power hidden within a substance</note>, no one can fish out what is truly stored within nature. Gather all your doctors and writers into one group and explain to me: what do corals contain and what can they do? If they have babbled much about their powers in a wordy and tedious chatter, they only prove, when those corals are later put to use, that you have not even the slightest experience or knowledge of them. The reason for this is that the process of the *arcanum* has not been handed down in writings. But if the process is completed, then the virtue is ready at hand.

<margin>The process of the arcanum is not written down.</margin>
Indeed, your simplicity is so crude that most of you think everything lies in crushing [ingredients], and that it is enough if you write: "let them be sieved and mixed; *let a powder be made with sugar*." <note>Paracelsus is mocking the "apothecary style" of medicine that relies on simple mechanical mixing and sweetening rather than chemical extraction.</note>

<margin>Reproach of the physicians, especially Pliny and Dioscorides.</margin>
What Pliny and Dioscorides <note>Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides were the primary classical authorities on natural history and herbal medicine.</note> commented upon regarding herbs, they themselves did not prove through use; rather, they received these things from noblemen who knew many such things, and they smeared many books with that womanly chatter. I ask you to endure this: try to prove whether what they hand down is true. You will never be able to reach the end of experimenting and proving! What, however, do Hermes and Archelaus <note>Hermes Trismegistus and Archelaus were legendary figures in the alchemical tradition.</note> hand down concerning <term>vitriol</term> <note>a term for various sulfate minerals, highly valued in alchemy for their transformative properties</note>? By Pollux, they describe immense virtues! And these are truly within it, yet you are ignorant of how they exist in it, whether they are green or blue. Should you be masters of natural things and yet be ignorant of these? Or, regarding what you do know, you have certainly read it, but you achieve nothing or gain no advantage from it. What do the Alchemists and other Philosophers hand down about the powers of Mercury? Something extraordinary, and most true. This is known to you as well, but you do not know how it is to be verified. Therefore, stop your bellowing.

<margin>The vanity of reading.</margin>
For both your Academies and you yourselves are <term>Beani</term> <note>original: Beani; a term for "greenhorns" or first-year university students, here used to call the established doctors mere novices</note> in these matters, and mere beginners. In your reading, you fly through everything and say: *this is in this, that is in that, this is black, this is green.* By God, I know no more; I find it written so. Thus, if it were not written so, would you know nothing of it? Do you truly think that I wrongly place and fix my foundation in the Alchemical art? This art reveals to me what is true, and you are far too inept to prove it. Should such an art not be worthy of coming into the light? And should it not, by right and merit, be established as the foundation of Medicine—the very thing that proves, increases, and stabilizes the knowledge of the Physician?

<margin>Faith in authors is found in the justice of the thing.</margin>
What kind of judgment should we think yours is, when you say: *Serapion, Mesue, Rhazes, Pliny, Dioscorides, and Macer hand down that verbena is useful for this or that.* <note>He lists classical and Arabic medical authorities: Serapion the Elder, Mesue the Elder, Rhazes (al-Razi), and Macer Floridus.</note> You cannot prove that what you say is true. How does such a judgment seem to you yourself? Be the judge: is he not more powerful who can prove that what is within is true? You will by no means be able to do this without the benefit of Alchemy. And even if you read or knew twice as much, all your knowledge is nevertheless worth nothing. And who, reading this work of mine, would have the gall to charge me with a crime for objecting to these things and explaining them to you? For you do not lead into action those powers and virtues which you boast of and glory in knowing.

Answer me: *if a magnet draws nothing, what is the cause of it? If Hellebore does not move you to vomit, what is the cause of that?* You know the things that cause one to defecate and vomit. But as for what the *arcana* of healing are (as mentioned a little earlier), here you are a brother to Ignorance.

<margin>Knowledge without writing is better than writing without knowledge.</margin>
Tell me, in the works and powers of natural things, who is to be trusted? Those who described such things but had no use or experience of them, or those who knew how to prove them but did not describe them? Is it not the truth that Pliny never proved any of his own [claims]?

<margin>Pliny is censured.</margin>
What, then, did he comment upon? What did he hear from the Alchemists? If you do not know who and what kind of people they are, you will be at best a traveling marketplace doctor.

If, therefore, it is of such great importance that Alchemy be properly known here in Medicine, it is because of the great hidden virtue which is located in the things of nature—virtues which are open to no one unless they are opened and brought forth through Alchemy. Otherwise, it is the same as if someone sees a tree in winter but does not recognize it, or is ignorant of what is within it, until summer pushes out one thing after another—now the branches, now the flowers, now the fruits, and whatever else belongs to it. In this way, the power lies in these things, hidden from men.

<margin>Alchemy alone opens the arcana.</margin>
And unless a man knows and experiences these things through the Alchemist alone, as if through the summer, it is impossible for him to explore them in any other way.

Because the Alchemist brings forth in this way what lies hidden in nature, know that there are certain powers in the grasshoppers <note>original: locustis; likely referring to the pods of the carob tree or similar plant parts rather than the insects</note>, others in the leaves, others in the flowers, others in the unripe fruits, and others in the ripe ones. The diversity among these is so evident that the later fruit of the tree is entirely unlike the earlier, not only in form but also in virtues.

<margin>The virtue of each thing varies by time.</margin>
Therefore, by right, such knowledge ought to be that which proceeds from the first to the last.

<summary>Paracelsus critiques traditional physicians for relying on ancient texts without experimental proof, arguing that only alchemy (the "summer" of science) can reveal the hidden healing powers (arcana) within natural substances.</summary>

<sig>S 4</sig>

<margin>The vision of Nature with Alchemy.</margin>
lastly: For that is nature. Now, just as such nature exists in its own manifestation, so too is the Alchemist proceeding in those things where nature leaves off: namely, he preserves the <term>Genesis</term> <note>the process of creation or natural growth</note>—the process of its nature—in the hand of the Alchemist. So it is with Thyme, so with Dodder <note>original: "Epithymus"; a parasitic plant often used in early medicine</note>, and others. Furthermore, a single thing contains not only one virtue, but many. For you see this in flowers, which do not have only one color, and yet they are in one thing, and are one thing: and each color by itself is at its highest degree.

<margin>The vision of the presence of virtues.</margin>
In the same way, the various virtues lurking in these things must also be understood. Now, however, the Alchemy of colors consists in separating art and nature, so that just as it is with colors, a separation of this kind may also occur in virtues. And as often as there is a change of colors, so often is there a change of virtues.

<margin>The example of Sulfur.</margin>
For in Sulfur there is yellowness, whiteness, redness, brownness, and blackness. And in each and every color there is a peculiar power and virtue; and other things, which also have these same colors, do not have the same virtues, but have other virtues hidden within those colors. And here now lies the knowledge of colors, such as is owed to colors; yet there is also another knowledge of virtues, such as belongs to virtues. The manifestation of virtues, however, is only found in form and colors, so that first there are the <term>shoots</term> <note>original: "locusta"; Paracelsus uses this botanical term to describe the first sprouting stage of a substance's development</note>, then the pith, afterward the branches, then the flowers, then the leaves, next the beginning of the fruits, then their middle, and lastly the end. Through this process, if the virtues are thus matured and brought forth again for growth, then the virtues within are changed in their degrees and great numbers every day and minute.

<margin>Elderberry purges.</margin>
For just as time bestows a purgative power upon the Elderberry, and not the mere matter, so the same time confers its powers upon virtues in different ways.

<margin>Acacia and verjuice bind. The observation of time is necessary in Alchemy.</margin>
Just as time grants a <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent or blood-stanching</note> quality to Acacias, which is not natural except by the passage of time, as it is with other verjuice <note>original: "agresta"; the sour juice of unripened grapes</note>; so time here also imparts intermediate virtues before the final limit is reached. For these signs or intervals in Alchemy are to be uniquely noted for the knowledge of when the time of mature or immature virtue ends, and this is more accurately attended to in Medicine. Thus, therefore, those maturations are divided: one into little buds, one into branches, one into flowers, one into piths, one into liquids, one into leaves, one into fruits; and in each and every one there are peculiar beginnings, middles, and ends, divided by three ways or methods into Laxatives, Styptics, and Arcana.

<margin>The three operations of time.</margin>
For those things that loosen and break down are not <term>arcana</term> <note>the "arcana" are the highest, most refined medicinal "secrets" or essences of a substance</note>. Indeed, none of these has been led to its final end, but they stop at the first and middle virtues. How evident this example is in a single <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolo"; a sulfate mineral, like copperas, which Paracelsus championed as a powerful medicine</note>: which is now gradually becoming very well known to everyone, and whose virtues are most open. This very thing I set before myself here, not to obscure its virtue, but to reveal and manifest it more widely.

<margin>Description of Vitriol.</margin>
First, therefore, vitriol brings forth its own laxative, the highest of all laxatives, and the greatest <term>deobstruent</term> <note>original: "deoppilatorium"; a medicine that opens blockages in the body's vessels or organs</note>. For there is no member in the body, whether it be external or internal, which is not penetrated and affected by it. This power of it is present from the first stage of time. A second time bestows a constrictive power upon it. Therefore, as much as it loosened at the beginning of the first stage, so much does it now bind. And yet its *arcanum* is not yet ready, nor have the buds, branches, and flowers broken out. If it turns into branches, what is more excellent in what is fleeting? If it proceeds into flowers, what is more penetrating? For it is like an odor, most readily diffusing itself everywhere. If it goes out into its fruits, what is more sublime for cherishing [vital] heat? And many other things of this kind are also in it, which are counted among its final stages. By these at least we have striven to explain how the *arcana* in one thing withdraw into many parts, and each part is carried into its own time: and that the end of times is the *arcanum* of things.

<margin>Description of Tartar.</margin>
So in the first transformation of <term>Tartar</term> <note>the crystalline deposit found in wine barrels</note>, what surpasses this *arcanum* anywhere in treating itching, scabies, and other similar foulnesses? In the second stage, what is more excellent than it for all opening of blockages? <gloss>not loosenings?</gloss> Finally, what is more powerful in the healing of wounds? And these things Alchemy lays open and manifests.

<margin>Reproof of Medicine and Pharmacy.</margin>
But why should the foundation of Medicine not be built upon it? Therefore, learn from this, and dismiss those filthy, over-boiling sellers of ointments <note>original: "seplasiarios"; a derogatory term for apothecaries who merely mix drugs without chemical knowledge</note>, who do not know a process of this kind, but along with their teachers are double asses, and are so insane that they dare to judge things of this kind to be altogether false and impossible. They are so rude and unskilled that they have not even learned the beginning of "cooking" <note>i.e., chemical digestion or laboratory preparation</note>: and yet must the health and safety of the sick be sought from such people? What else is found among them, but a desire for money, and a thirst for goods? meanwhile it is all the same to them [if] their medica-

<summary>Paracelsus argues that medicinal substances like Vitriol and Tartar possess different healing powers (laxative, styptic, or arcanum) depending on their stage of "ripeness" or alchemical preparation. He mocks traditional apothecaries who ignore these chemical transformations, calling them "double asses" who care only for profit.</summary>

### TREATISE III OF THE PARAGRANUM.

medicaments help or hinder, whether they remove diseases or increase them. And should it not be lawful for ignorance of this kind to be publicly revealed? I do not do this, however, because I hope they will imitate me. For by this approach they will not easily shame themselves; but rather <margin>The vice of malice.</margin> malice and envy will so occupy them that they will persist entirely in their ignorance. And yet meanwhile, whoever wishes to follow the truth itself, he will turn aside into my one monarchy, and by no means into <margin>What the way of truth is.</margin> another. Pay attention, I pray, readers and listeners, to how wretched and distorted a process all writers—both the ancients and those who are now my contemporaries—establish regarding the <term>Falling Sickness</term> <note>original: "Caduco"; epilepsy</note>: such that they are hardly able to rescue or heal anyone. Meanwhile, do I act unjustly by despising such writers and teachers? They demand as if by right that people use their remedies, which are nevertheless of no importance. On the other hand, if someone investigates another way by which help can be provided to the sick, they call him a vagabond, a <term>Polyphemus</term> <note>a reference to the one-eyed cyclops; here meaning a monstrous or unrefined person</note>, and a fool. But this is more true, <margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin> that both their recipes and their causes and reasons regarding the falling sickness and many other diseases stand as mere lies. The outcome declares this, the patients themselves testify to it, the very nature of things cries it out, and the foundation upon which medicine stands proves it. Nor do they know how to cure any other disease with a fixed and constant medicine; since God does not call and choose such uncertain and ambiguous physicians, but <margin>God’s generosity.</margin> certain and skillful ones. If He bestows a certain and skillful farmer or stone-cutter, much more will He give a physician certain and confirmed in his art, in whom alone more is placed than in all the rest. But these men call their very foundation into doubt and place it in the hand of God. Thus the hand of God is held up as a veil for their imposture and ignorance, and they justify themselves while accusing God, saying that their art is indeed upright, but that God breaks and inhibits it. What impiety and imposture would it be, if this is not? See now by what firm reason I establish Alchemy as the foundation <margin>Physicians are ignorant of how to cure many diseases.</margin> of Medicine. Namely in this: that all the gravest diseases, such as *Apoplexy, Paralysis, Lethargy, Falling Sickness, Mania, Phrensy, Melancholy or sadness*, and others like these, can never be healed by any decoction of the <term>perfumers</term> <note>original: "seplasiariorum"; vendors of ointments and simple medicines, used here to criticize unrefined pharmacists</note>. For just as meat cannot possibly be boiled in snow, so much less can such medicine be brought into effect through the art <margin>The preparations of pharmacists are worth nothing.</margin> of the pharmacists. For just as there is a peculiar <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; a high-level alchemical preparation</note> for each thing regarding its purpose, so you ought to judge the same concerning these diseases: that they have unique <term>Secrets</term> <note>original: "arcana"; the hidden healing essence within a substance</note>. From this, they also require unique preparations. Regarding what I say of these preparations, I wish it to be understood that unique secrets have their own unique administrations, and different administrations have different preparations. Now, however, in the workshops there is no preparation other than a certain stirring and boiling, such as cook-shops know. By boils of this kind <margin>Through boiling, the secrets are suffocated.</margin> the secrets themselves are suffocated and brought to no <term>energy</term> <note>active healing power</note>. For nature wishes to be kept in its own mode and temperament. For you see one preparation of bread, another of meat, etc. Judge the same concerning herbs. By equal reason, you ought also to estimate that nature by no means mixes together foods and drinks, meats and breads, into one form by a tumultuous confusion, but each thing separately. This happens for reasons that are not slight, which it would be more laborious than is right to recount here. Now if nature <margin>Nature delights in order.</margin> reminds us through these things that in all matters its own order must be preserved, with that same teacher we are commanded to prepare medicines in another way, and to accommodate each to its own diseases. A thirsty liver demands wine or water. But you, consider how often the wine is prepared, and as if reborn, before it quenches the thirst of the liver. In a similar way, the stomach seeks food. In this, pay attention to how variously food is changed and prepared. Be persuaded no differently concerning diseases. For if you are going to undertake a true and skillful cure, you shall establish no other distinction, nor act otherwise than as if Apoplexy were a thirst, for which there is need of a peculiar medicine and a unique preparation of it. Or think of the Falling Sickness as a stomach, which for necessary uses needs another stomach-like preparation. Or suppose that Mania is similar to the spermatic vessels, which solicit their necessity through other paths. Thus you shall also determine the same concerning medicines and their preparations in Mania. Therefore, I rightly warn you of these things, lest—if by chance you have noble remedies and secrets ready against diseases—you allow those <term>over-boilers</term> <note>ignorant pharmacists who over-process and ruin ingredients</note> to corrupt or drown them. For should these things not be brought forth? Indeed, so that errors of this kind may clearly be avoided, and the sick may be led to the true secrets, <margin>God’s beneficence.</margin> which God has destined for their uses and necessity,

<summary>Paracelsus critiques contemporary physicians for their inability to cure serious diseases like epilepsy and apoplexy, arguing that their simple "kitchen-style" medicinal preparations ruin the active healing secrets (arcana) of substances. He asserts that Alchemy is the only foundation for true medicine because it allows for the specific, orderly preparation required to match the unique nature of each disease.</summary>

<header>ON ALCHEMY.</header>

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but mysteries.</margin>
...destined, let them penetrate. From these things conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my instructions, and by no means according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still hurl more thunderbolts against me, my <term>Monarchy</term> <note>Paracelsus often used "Monarchy" to describe his supreme system of medical and natural philosophy.</note> shall nonetheless stand, while all of yours goes to ruin. I do not write so extensively about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and goal: that from these things you might nearly and solidly recognize what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by this: that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it. Rather, this is what must be carefully seen to: that through alchemy the <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcana"; the hidden, inner virtues or "secrets" of a substance that provide its healing power.</note> may be uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>druggists</term> <note>original: "seplasiariorum"; these were sellers of perfumes and ointments, whom Paracelsus often accused of being fraudulent medicine-sellers.</note> may be exposed, by which the unrefined common folk are deceived, while these men serve them for one florin what they would not redeem for a single penny. So "precious" are their secrets.

<margin>Poison is even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that even in the best things poison lies hidden and dwells within? Everyone is forced to admit it. If this is true, I now ask of you: must the poison not be separated from what is good and useful? Should the good be accepted and the bad left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If it must be so, I pray you, tell me: how is that separation performed in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed together. To be sure, in order to protect your simplicity—if you have been convicted into admitting that poison lies there—and you are asked where it eventually goes, then you bring forth I-know-not-what regarding "corrections," which are supposed to drive out and take away the poison;
<margin>The "correction" of the Physicians is examined.</margin>
just as they say <term>Quinces</term> <note>original: "Cotonea"</note> correct <term>Scammony</term> <note>original: "Scammoneam"; a harsh plant-based purgative.</note>, or as they say of <term>Diagridium</term> <note>A preparation made from the juice of scammony, often baked in a quince to "mellow" it.</note>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you, meanwhile, boast that you have "corrected" it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it vanish to? 
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the proper measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will find that out soon enough! You "correct" <term>Turpeth</term> <note>original: "Turbith"; another potent purgative root.</note> in the same way, and you call it "Diaturbith." Those are your kinds of corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be fed to pack-horses. Try the experiment by exceeding the measure and increasing the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. 
<margin>What "I correct the physician" means.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected thing.* <note>The Latin "Corrigere est correctum sumere" implies that true correction means only using the refined substance after the bad part is gone.</note> He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction extends no further than the will of the one who was punished lasts. These "corrections" of yours are of such a kind; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. For example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same is to be understood equally for all other things: that there is a need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation—unless by chance it happens that nature makes up for your failings, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection remains.

Now, therefore, let us finally look at that true foundation, if it is required, which removes poison, and how Alchemy provides it. For it must be done in such a way that if <term>Mars</term> is in the <term>Sun</term>, Mars is removed; and if <term>Saturn</term> is dwelling in <term>Venus</term>, it is separated from her. <note>Paracelsus uses the names of planets to refer to metals or qualities: Mars (Iron/Choler), Sun (Gold/Vitality), Saturn (Lead/Melancholy), Venus (Copper/Flux). He is describing the chemical purification of mixed elements.</note> For as many "ascendants" and "impressions" as there are in the things of nature, just as many bodies exist within them. Truly, when bodies are contrary to one another, it is absolutely necessary for one of them to be taken away and removed, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is taken away from the good which you seek.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is a Medicine which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into a second generation, through which it ought to benefit and help mankind. And should this not be rightly judged the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to employ poisons, but rather arcana. 
<margin>The Pharmacies are rebuked.</margin>
However, all those preparations of the workshops—as many as there are—do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are occupied simply with "correcting"; as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were put to sleep either by <term>troches</term> <note>medicinal lozenges</note> and incense, or by juniper wood. I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room just as much afterward as before? And although it might not be perceived by the sense of smell, is anyone permitted to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? No, it is there, but "corrected" by the fumigation. Thus, the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who dull the <term>Aloe-mixture</term> <note>original: "Aleopaticum"</note> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their "mastery." In this way, they also "correct" <term>Gentian</term> and <term>Theriac</term> <note>An ancient, complex herbal "cure-all" that Paracelsus often mocked for being a messy soup of ingredients.</note>. Are these not the works of donkey-like ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of Princes. Who is so stupid as not to smell immediately that these things are worthless? Regarding their remedies, what else can they boast, I pray, except to say, *“This Electuary is sweet, made of spices, sugar, and honey”*?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the true purpose of alchemy in medicine is the chemical separation of poisons from healing virtues, rather than the pursuit of gold. He mocks traditional pharmacists for merely masking the bad taste or harsh effects of drugs with sugar or quinces, comparing it to using incense to hide a foul odor without removing the source.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, separation, poison, arcana, pharmacy critique, fire, Mars, Saturn, Diagridium, Scammony, medicinal preparation</keywords>
