<meta>The previous page provided (numbered 215) discussed the specific role of Alchemy in uncovering hidden healing virtues (arcana). This page (numbered 214) appears to be the conclusion or "Epilogue" to the third tractate of the Paragranum, summarizing the three columns of medicine—Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy—and offering a fierce defense of Paracelsus's departure from traditional Galenic medicine.</meta>

# TRACT III OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>
Sweetness: the trap of physicians.
</margin>
...and prepared with honey and all other pleasant things; many praises are certainly circulated about it. Thus you mock the sick with your medicine when you preach nothing but sweetness. Think for yourselves how little it suits to build a foundation out of so many concocted things and to entrust everything to foolish teachers. This method is far removed from the true foundation of medicine; it is nothing but a scraped-together and ridiculous fantasy.

<margin>
Epilogue.
</margin>
Thus, enough has been discussed concerning the three columns of Medicine: namely, **Philosophy**, **Astronomy**, and **Alchemy**. Upon these three, the foundation of any true Medicine rests. He who is not built upon these is cast down by every wave—that is, the wind blows away his work, or the new moon shatters it. Any nearby new moon destroys his building, or a rainstorm softens and pierces it. Now indeed, you yourself judge, reader, concerning Medicine built upon such a foundation: am I a Doctor beyond the order of Medicine, or a heretic, or an eraser of truth, or a mad brain? Do I treat my adversaries deservedly or undeservedly? And by what right do they rise up against me? I could certainly admit without difficulty that everyone cares for their own club <note>The "club" refers to a weapon or a tool of one's trade; Paracelsus argues that most people cling to their old tools even when they are useless.</note>. If it has once grown warm in the hand, it is not easily thrown aside. But only fools do this. A wise man should by no means imitate them. A prudent man throws away the club himself and seeks another.

<margin>
Fools resist; the wise yield.
</margin>
What does it matter to me whether they follow me or persecute me? It will not be my task to restrain them. Yet it will be my task to expose them—to show that they overflow with frauds and impostures, and hold no other foundation than that born from their own brain and fantasy. He who is faithful and honest toward the sick, who wishes to be an imitator of nature in his art, will not flee from me or turn away.

<margin>
Christ was not approved by all.
</margin>
But even Christ himself was not followed by all who lived in that age; instead, many despisers of him arose. Why should this privilege be given to me alone, that I should be despised by no one?

<margin>
Theophrastus was first a Galenist.
Why Theophrastus broke away from the Galenists.
</margin>
In the beginning, I certainly pulled the same plow-handle <note>original: "stivam"; a metaphor for working within the established medical tradition.</note> as they did, no less lazily. But when I perceived that nothing followed from that art except slaughter, death, paralysis, lameness, and other destructions, I was absolutely forced to step back and seek the truth by another way. Afterward, they reproached me, saying that I neither attained nor understood Avicenna or Galen <note>Galen and Avicenna were the ancient and medieval authorities whose teachings dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>, nor knew what they themselves wrote. They, however, boasted that they understood these things. Yet from that boasting, it emerged that they themselves corrupted, twisted, and slaughtered many more people everywhere than I did in my "ignorance." This is the same as if someone said: the work of the intelligent man and the non-intelligent man is the same, but both are worth nothing. However, the more I looked upon their ruin and my own, the more I began to burn with a greater hatred for that art; and I brought myself to the point that I clearly saw it was nothing but a patchwork garment <note>original: "centonem"; a cloak made of scraps, implying the old medical system was a messy collection of unrelated ideas.</note> and a torn collection—indeed, entirely chosen imposture. But I do not wish all such things to be concluded here; I will explain further in my other writings how and in what ways all things are mired in error.

<margin>
Theophrastus’s shipwreck.
</margin>
For daily I discover more and more that not only Medicine, but even **Philosophy** and **Astronomy** themselves, are never supported by any good or praiseworthy foundation, as has been said thus far. But a huge tumult will be stirred up against my head because I reject those who for so many centuries have alone possessed the throne of glory and magnificence. Yet it is clear to me by a certain inner foreboding that it will happen one day that all those "magnificences" will be cast down from their throne. For their strength <note>original: "nervus"; literally "nerve" or "sinew."</note> is nothing other than fantasy. Just as I do not finish with this opinion here, I will continue to testify to it in my writings. If the Universities do not approve of me, what does it matter? For they will eventually fall and be humbled by themselves. Meanwhile, I will expose and beat back your errors with such severity that, until the end of the world, my writings will be both truthful and welcomed; whereas yours, on the contrary, are destined to suffer this: that, full of bile, poison, and the "offspring of vipers," they will be cast out by everyone like toads, trodden underfoot, and avoided. This is not my effort to tear you down and overthrow you in a single year. Is it not more just that in the future you should waste away and expire from your own infamy and shame? Indeed, I will judge more people when I am dead than while I am alive.

<margin>
Theophrastus’s threats.
</margin>
And even if you should demolish this body of mine, you will have devoured nothing but dung. Theophrastus will wrestle with you even without a body. I want those who will be the physicians of the future to be warned to deal with me more cautiously than their teachers did, and to weigh our disagreement with their own diligence and judgment, rather than condemning one and acquitting the other with an immature sentence.

<summary>Paracelsus concludes his defense of the three pillars of medicine—Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy—while launching a scathing attack on the traditional Galenic establishment. He predicts that his work will endure forever while the prestigious medical academies will eventually fall due to their own lack of foundation.</summary>
<keywords>Paragranum, Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, Galen, Avicenna, medical reform, Epilogue, medical errors, legacy</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from page 214, which concluded the discussion on the third column of medicine (Alchemy), this page serves as a final appeal to the reader to trust Paracelsus’s new medical foundation over traditional methods. It introduces the "Fourth Column" of medicine, which focuses on the character and moral duty of the physician.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>
->**ON THE VIRTUE OF THE PHYSICIAN**<-

<margin>The principal works of Theophrastus.</margin>
I ask you to consider carefully with yourselves what you ultimately aim for: namely, the health of the sick. If this is your target and your whole focus, then I ask you to endure me as a teacher, for I act solely to lead you toward the healing of the ill. The foundation and gravity upon which I do this has been stated thus far and will be revealed more abundantly every day. Do not let my writings be a stumbling block to you because I am alone, because I am new, or because I am German. For through these means, and no others, it is necessary for the art of medicine to be discovered and learned. I also want to command you above all to diligently read and study my works, which I shall complete by the favor of divine grace: namely, one volume on **Medical Philosophy**, in which all the origins of diseases will be tracked; a second on **Astronomy**, for the sake of healing; and a third and final one on **Alchemy**, that is, the method of preparing medicinal substances. If you read and understand these three books, you will follow me, even those of you who fell away long ago. I will not make an end of these here, but as long as divine grace shines upon me, I will continually proceed to defend the <term>Monarchy<note>original: "Monarchia"; Paracelsus used this term to describe the supreme, unified sovereignty of his medical system over all others.</note></term>, with several individual booklets published for this purpose. If I were not weighed down by such untimely hatred and the envy of some leaders in Medicine, those booklets would have seen the light of day long ago for the most part. I can easily foresee from my own experience that the astronomers and philosophers will also stand riotously against me. But they will not understand me. They will attack me with premature shouting, but eventually, they will fall silent and retreat to their huts. 

But you, listeners, do not let these things disturb you. Instead, see to it that you read their writings in the meantime, until mine follow in full step. In this way, you will find what you desire. For in this place, I proposed to write at least this: on what ground and foundation I build Medicine, so that it may finally be settled among you what I wish to build upon this base. I present these things to you so clearly that you cannot rightly reject me based on the suggestions of your fathers, teachers, and professors. Beware further, also, that you are not led astray by common physicians, such as <margin>The nature of surgeons and bath-keepers.</margin> surgeons and <term>bath-keepers<note>original: "balneatores"; in the 16th century, these were low-tier medical practitioners who performed minor surgeries, bloodletting, and tooth extractions.</note></term>. These people want to seem great and powerful, and they pour out "foot-and-a-half long" words <note>original: "sesquipedalia"; a reference to the Roman poet Horace, meaning overly long, pompous words used to impress without substance.</note>, which, however, smack of no art, but much ambition and boasting. They are like chanting nuns: they sing the Psalter indeed, but they do not understand a bit of the meaning. Such are these physicians: they continually make a noise and bellow. And just as a nun understands one word now and then, but afterwards turns ten pages without understanding, so too these physicians: occasionally they touch upon the truth, but afterwards they always wander off the track. Weigh these things deeply within yourselves and be the judges of what foundation most of them use to push their studies. Although in Medicine these things are not so new that accusations should offend anyone. For in their own consciences, Medicine is worse than all pimps, directed only toward agitations and insults. All of these, however, are signs of a doubtful and uncertain art. For those who profess this are foul with envy and hatred, and wherever one can be a hindrance to another, he considers this the height of his art. Thus the Devil governs them, from whom they drank this discipline—of which you should have no doubt. This is further witnessed by the frequent slaughterhouses and butcheries <note>Paracelsus is comparing the botched surgeries and ineffective treatments of his rivals to the work of a butcher.</note>, for which the hand of God is not the cause.

***

### THE FOURTH COLUMN OF MEDICINE: 
### ON VIRTUE.

**P**OST-demonstration—having now completed the demonstration of the science and art of medicine, upon which any physician ought to lean firmly and place his profession—it is furthermore necessary that the same physician be equipped with another gift. This gift is a kind of ornament for the previous three; that is, it stabilizes the three aforementioned columns with a kind of strength and confirms them according to the will of God, who alone created Medicine. For a <margin>A physician is a physician for others, not himself.</margin> physician is not one who heals himself, but one who cares for others. Just as a sheep does not bear wool for itself, but for the weaver and the furrier, and is praised if it is weighted with a heavy fleece, so too the <margin>The physician is like a sheep.</margin> physician is like a sheep, who should be useful and profitable not to himself, but to others. Let him not judge this example to be shameful for himself. For even by John the Baptist, Christ the Savior was compared to a sheep, or a lamb. And yet it matters much that the physician also be a lamb. From the lack of this [virtue], many hardships lie open, such as robberies, throat-slittings, distortions, relaxations, corruptions, butcheries, thefts, and plundering. All these things exist in a Wolfish Physician...

<summary>Paracelsus concludes his defense of the first three columns of medicine (Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy) and introduces the Fourth Column: the moral character or "virtue" of the physician. He emphasizes that a true doctor must be selfless and "lamb-like," contrasting this with the "wolfish" greed and ignorance of his contemporaries.</summary>

<page-num>216</page-num>
->### TREATISE IV OF THE PARAGRANUM ###<-

<margin>Lupine physicians, and who they are.</margin> They are recognized by the wolf. For just as a physician ought to be a sheep or a lamb, appointed by God, so is he a wolf who uses medicine against God. From these examples, judge now how execrable a beast the wolf is, and how God compares him to the worst and most destructive things. By good right, all those qualities ought to be attributed to the predatory physician as well. But who are these men? They are surely those who handle medicines and yet are convicted by their own witness of conscience that they know nothing of them, but undertake such things only for the sake of money and gain. These have the same nature as the wolf. The wolf preys upon the sheep, knowing well they are not his; yet for the sake of his private advantage, he snatches them away. Such a physician is a thief. He takes risks, whether the sick die or recover, provided that he may pile up his own profit. And just as a sheep is in the jaws of the wolf, so are such patients in the hands of this kind of physician. Furthermore, they plunder the goods of the sick, devouring their houses and estates, and swallowing whatever comes their way. This is truly to steal and to prey. For he who seeks a living through a false and deceitful art—whatever he scrapes together through it—all of it is robbery and plunder. Thus they kill and slaughter, and there is nothing they will not do. For in all these matters, they know nothing; yet they push their purpose forward as if sails were being struck by the winds. Truly, it is not at all fitting for a physician to be such a man, nor is it decent for him to gape after his own profit. And although <margin>A physician must be free from greed. A rebuke of physicians.</margin> physicians may know this, they nevertheless refuse to know it so that they may acquire pride, pomp, and authority for themselves, and so they might send out their wives burdened with golden necklaces. These wives, though they were previously peasants, cooks, house-maids, servants, and sometimes even harlots, now shamelessly make themselves into countesses through their clothing and finery. All of these are ravenous wolves. However, medicine ought to be founded in the sheep or the lamb, so that remedies are offered or communicated with a purely sheep-like spirit and with faithfulness; and in turn, the faithfulness of the sick may be expected with a peaceful mind. Faithfulness is owed to faithfulness, truth to truth, and equity to equity—but equity is not owed to iniquity, as if a lupine physician should be rewarded with faithfulness, or as if a patient, who is a sheep, should satisfy the voracity of the wolf. Truly, the origin of all such things must flow from the physician. As they show themselves to be in the beginning, so shall they be found by the sick in the end. But if the physician inverts the order, and puts on the wolf while feigning the lamb—or having become unjust, hungers for the just man to bring him wealth while he himself contributes nothing to the sick—and the patient is faithful to him while he is unfaithful to the patient: wherever such things happen, know this! No fever, no wind, no storm is more uncertainly, violently, and intricately confused than the muddle <term>miscellam<note>A "miscella" refers to a confused mixture or medley; here, Paracelsus uses it to describe the chaotic and fraudulent medical practice where truth and lies are blended.</note></term> they make for the sake of that physician, so that no one can sufficiently distinguish what is finally real, while they mix and drench faith with perfidy, deceit with candor, evil with good, worse than gall mixed with sugar.

Should we not then, by the highest right, admit and establish the <term>integrity<note>original: "probitas"; this implies not just moral "goodness" but professional honesty and the reliability of one's results.</note></term> of the physician as a certain foundation and pillar of medicine? But what is this integrity of the physician? *Yes, yes; no, no*—this is his integrity, upon which he must especially lean. If therefore <margin>Integrity is the physician's proper quality.</margin> it is fitting for it to be so, it is truly necessary that he know medicine so precisely from its foundation that it is "so" and remains "so," and is not equally "not so." Therefore, he must also know what is *not* medicine; whence it follows that this integrity of the physician consists in the <margin>Whence comes the certainty of medicine.</margin> certainty of the art. This certainty emerges and comes forth entirely from the aforementioned foundation, outside of which no one can or would dare to profess himself honest in medicine. Now it is certain that God, above all the arts and faculties of <margin>God is the greatest lover of the physician.</margin> men, loves the physician most of all, and commands that he be loved and honored. If therefore God has established such a physician, he must not be a masked or disguised actor, nor an old crone, nor an executioner, nor a liar, nor frivolous, but truthful and constant. For God no more confers the medical art upon such physicians than he permits false prophets to be his disciples and apostles. For you yourselves see that false prophets and apostles or martyrs and confessors neither flourish nor emerge; but if they think they are thriving in the highest place, they fall, and the disciples themselves rise up against their masters and defeat them. For God <margin>False physicians have no success.</margin> does not want His word and mysteries brought forth by false ministers. For if He had decreed to work through the false just as much as through the true, legitimate, and unpainted workers, He would have had no need of any chosen and secret disciples, but would have committed the entire province to the Devil himself. Now, if these things oppose Satan, and they are the organs of Satan himself, then happiness consists entirely in the elect of God, and from this, the false prophets, apostles, and martyrs are excluded, as are all their miracles.

<summary>Paracelsus distinguishes between the "Lupine" physician, driven by greed and fraud, and the true physician whose "integrity" is rooted in the absolute certainty of his art. He argues that medical success is a divine gift that God withholds from those who seek only profit and vanity.</summary>

<page-num>217</page-num>
-># ON THE CHARACTER OF THE PHYSICIAN #<-
<sig>T</sig>

...miracles, signs, works, sermons, doctrines, and prophecies are rejected, and neither "Yes" nor "No" will be accepted by God, but all their good and evil alike will be cast into hell. The same must be established here concerning Medicine: that God does not wish to endow fickle men with it, but demands that it be practiced entirely by the truthful.

<margin>Only truthful physicians are true physicians.</margin>
Since God created the art for the salvation of man—a fact which no one can contradict—it is right that it rest on truth alone, and indeed on certain truth; not in an ambiguous art, but in one that is entirely confirmed and stable. For God wants man to be truthful, not wavering, not lying. God created truth, not a lie.

<margin>The physician's uprightness and truth.</margin>
So too He created the physician, so that he might work in truth and not be polluted by lies. Therefore, truth is the integrity of the physician: so that he may be as constant and sincere in it as the very apostles chosen by God were. For in the eyes of God, the physician is not in a lower position than they. If God Himself is truth, and He established the physician as such, certainly He does not make him a trifler or a speaker of lies, but creates him in truth.

<margin>Upright physicians are from God; the wicked from Satan.</margin>
Upon this, therefore, the fourth Pillar <note>Paracelsus's four pillars of medicine are Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue/Integrity.</note> must be placed. If it does not stand as immovably in truth as God Himself, but sways suspended in the air, then it is certainly built upon Satan himself, just as false prophets also allure men. So too false apostles display signs before the eyes of the world; so false martyrs allow themselves to be killed no less than the genuine and elect ones. So too false confessors pray and fast no less than the just and upright; yet they are not founded on the truth of God or Christ because of these things, but entirely on Satan and the Devil, in whom they perform such works. Thus, following their example, such physicians also boast of their fortune and art, and glory along with those mentioned before:

> *We too are from God. See what we can do? See what we perform? Behold, it is God who works through us!*

Meanwhile they are silent about the truth itself: that these things are produced and carried out through the Devil. If you were to weigh how miraculously these works are done, you would also discover from them from whence your triumphs and praises arose—not through you, indeed, but through him who suffers <note>original: "per eum qui patitur"; likely referring to the patient who endures the disease or the treatment.</note>.

<margin>Property of the Physician 1: Faith or Truth.</margin>
Furthermore, it is fitting for the physician to be of no less good and sincere faith. For he who is of good faith does not lie and is a completer of the works of God. For as he is, so he is a testimony to himself; that is, you ought to be of an honest, whole, and constant faith in God, with all your soul, heart, with all senses and thoughts, with all charity and trust. In respect of this faith and charity, God will not take His truth away from you, but will manifest His works to you trustfully and visibly. But if you are not of such faith toward God, you will fail entirely in your works and labor in their poverty. So afterwards the people will cast no trust in you. From this it will happen that you are openly revealed, as to how you hold yourself toward God by your faith. For if they find you to be a liar, ambiguous, doubtful, and ignorant, they will argue from a plain foundation that your business with God is nothing, but rather that you exist as a <term>meddler</term> <note>original: "ardellionem," a busybody or person of little consequence</note> and a vagabond in Medicine; and thus your art will be of no benefit or use. Just as if someone were to preach and teach the people, and produce many things, yet meanwhile no apostolic works shine forth alongside them: then certainly that letter is dead. For God does not permit that sermon to be fruitful among the little sheep, but tears it out of their hearts. For he who sows is not a true sower, nor does he sow anything except tares. The same reasoning exists for unskilled physicians. For since it is right that Medicine be nothing other than truth, it must be founded upon God Himself and His truth, not upon lies. Or would I be teaching wrongly and be unjust if I established such a foundation for Medicine—that God alone is the Teacher and Institutor of Medicine—that is, according to the manner of creation? Therefore, if the faith of the physician is esteemed among the people, the same is also ratified with God. For God wants all parts to consist and live in truth—from you to God, and from the people to you. And all arts upon the earth are divine; they are from God and from no other principle.

<margin>All arts are from God. The Light of Nature is the torch of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
For the Holy Spirit is the kindler of the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>Lumen naturae: the innate source of wisdom and discovery found in the natural world, as opposed to direct revelation from scripture.</note>. Whence it is not right for anyone to slander anything, whether Astronomy, or Alchemy, or Medicine, or Philosophy, or Theology, or the arts, or Poetry, or Music, or Geomancy, or Auguries, and whatever other similar things there are. Why so?

<margin>Man finds nothing of himself.</margin>
Because man finds nothing at all from himself—not even a small patch to sew onto his boots. What has even the Devil found? Nothing anywhere, not even the smallest bit with which you could kill or catch a head louse. But those things which are discovered through the kindled light of nature in us, those things the De[vil]...

<summary>This page argues that the physician's integrity (truth and faith) is as essential as his technical skill, claiming that true medical knowledge is a divine gift from the Holy Spirit via the Light of Nature. Paracelsus contrasts the God-ordained physician with "Satanic" frauds who boast of miracles but lack true foundation.</summary>

<page-num>218</page-num>
# THE FOURTH TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>The Devil corrupts the arts.</margin>
The Devil, just as he strives to corrupt and adulterate everything given by God, endeavors to turn all things into lies and impostures. From this it happens that all arts and crafts are now corrupted. Thus **Alchemy** <note>In Paracelsus's view, alchemy was not just about making gold, but the art of transforming raw materials into medicine.</note> has been corrupted and handed over to lying tongues and wicked masters. Similarly, **Geomancy** <note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note> has been shifted onto a false foundation. In the same way, **Medicine** has been moved away from its natural steps. Even auguries <note>Ancient practices of interpreting omens from the behavior of birds or other natural signs.</note> have been changed by the Devil, for he alone is a liar and is a lie itself. God, on the contrary, is truth; if He imparts and bestows truth upon us, the Devil immediately rises up to slander God, seeking to make Him a liar. He seduces those who are weak in faith away from God and entangles them in errors, so that they fall away from God, contaminate the arts with lies, accuse God, and waste their time with falsehoods. No matter where they wander or how much they scrutinize everything, they eventually die without any knowledge of the truth. Therefore, the Physician must attend to these things diligently. For he is not instructed upon the foundation of Satan, but upon that of God, so that he may continually and immovably persist and walk in the truth. I openly declare, however, that the faculties and all
<margin>Physicians rebuked.</margin>
physicians walk in lies and are entirely wallowing in them. They recognize fraud as their foundation and die in it, calling that "truth" which is actually a lie. In this way, Satan, the father of lies, is placed as the pillar of Medicine, when they ought to have established God, and not Satan, in that place. Now take heed and see if you are firm enough upon this pillar, and test how closely you stand to God or how far you withdraw from Him. It is beyond doubt that you ascribe lying pillars to God, offer yourselves as slaves to the Devil, and support his kingdom with every effort.

Indeed, a Physician ought to conduct himself as pure, chaste, and continent, not only in the 
<margin>Properties of the Physician: Purity.</margin>
aforementioned virtues of the soul, but also in matters pertaining to the body. He must not employ medicine for the sake of pride. For from pride, a false Physician is born. As soon as he busies himself with turning his profit toward something other than the purity of his heart, he already stands upon a wicked foundation. Therefore, that good earned from medicine should by no means be spent on harlots.
<margin>The different nature of wealth.</margin>
For whatever amount is bestowed upon scoundrels is not produced from a true foundation. God does not allow the goods produced from Himself to turn into something good for either harlots or rascals. For the wealth produced by a Physician is one thing, and that of a soldier is another. The nature of a Physician's wealth is different from the wealth of a King. The wealth of a King has one mandate; that of a Physician has another. Now, the mandate of the Physician is nothing other than that he should spend his wealth on integrity. If he applies it toward this, it is from a good
<margin>Let every use of wealth be praiseworthy.</margin>
foundation. If, however, he does otherwise—whether he dresses his own wife like a harlot or makes his children the equals of the children of Kings—then those goods were not produced from a true foundation; they were acquired, I say, not from the foundation of God, but from the foundation of the Devil. For it is the Devil who rouses the sick and offers them to such a man, and heals them through him. What do you think, Physicians, if you have indeed learned a worthy 
<margin>The Devil rouses the sick for his followers.</margin>
art, but you yourselves are worthless and use that art for luxury: is that not from the Devil? The art itself is from God, but the use and the nature of it are from the Devil. Even if you make an ample income from it, it is the same as if someone were to practice usury with stolen goods and grow rich from it. What is such a man in the eyes of God? He is a thief. Thus you possess certain arts, not as Physicians, but as those who have snatched them away from Physicians by theft. And since it is the desire of your heart to prepare a living by stealing and plundering, God allows that increase of goods to that extent. All men are nourished and sustained by God, and no one besides God knows how to feed us. But just as a master treats and observes his servants according to how each one is minded, so does God. To him who seeks to prepare a living through truth, God bestows enough truth, and through this He also confers the necessary nourishment upon him. He is bound by His own law to supply us with food, which He gives according to what we desire. If we choose to have things through deceit, truth becomes a lie among us, and we live as liars. But God supplies His 
<margin>God nourishes both liars and the truthful.</margin>
nourishment to the lying as well as to the truthful. For we are all to be sustained by Him, the good and the bad alike; just as He wills the same sun, the same earth, and all other creatures to be for the good and benefit of everyone indiscriminately. Thus it is fitting for the Physician to be pure and chaste, and so perfect that he spends his goods on no luxury, pride, wickedness, or any other status. For those who are occupied in these lies manifest their lying works and their wicked labors; everything within them dwells in falsehood, and so they live by mere lies and impostures, which is not a worthy foundation in **Medicine**. The foundation, however, ought to be truth,
<margin>Truth rejoices in purity.</margin>
which rejoices in purity and chastity, and all such good fruits are pure and chaste.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that while all arts originate from God, they are easily corrupted by the Devil into lies and greed. He specifically rebukes physicians who use their divine calling to fund a life of luxury or immorality, asserting that a true physician must maintain personal and professional integrity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the fourth pillar of medicine: Virtue. Specifically, Paracelsus moves into the concept of 'Congruity,' arguing that a true physician must grow into their craft from youth, rather than attempting to learn it through rigid academic 'disciplining' later in life.</meta>

->## ON THE CHARACTER OF THE PHYSICIAN<-

...remain, and no stain of pride, envy, luxury, unchastity, ambition, pomp, vanity, or worldly reputation stands out in them. If I present this foundation of the Physician to you in this way, you proclaim me stupid and insane, and you come close to swearing that I am possessed. Indeed, I strive with the greatest zeal to be properly understood by everyone. But you say that what I say is unknown, and you cry out that my words "have nothing to do with the matter." <note>original: "nihil ad rem & rhombum" — a Latin idiom meaning "not to the point" or irrelevant.</note> But ask the peasants if these things are not relevant: or whether I do not present to you the very material that burns you the most?

<margin>Property of the Physician 4: Congruity.</margin> Therefore, for a Physician to be perfected and to stand on a perfect foundation, know that it is necessary to proceed in all things with a fitting order. Now, this fittingness, which is called **congruity**, is this: <margin>What congruity is.</margin> to proceed according to the predetermined order of Nature, not of men. For the Physician is subject not to man, but to God alone, through Nature. From this it follows that the fittingness and congruity of order must proceed from the condition of the body and the **Light of Nature**. <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "Light of Nature" is an inner wisdom or intuitive knowledge granted by God through the natural world, as opposed to knowledge learned from books.</note> For the body itself has one light, and Nature has another, regarding their constitutions. These natures must now be entirely joined, and like must be united with like. And that, finally, is the congruity by which both entwine with one another, and one sounds and agrees with the other. Thus, the first knowledge must be about the nature of the body.

<margin>What the "schooled body" is and why it is unfit for Medicine.</margin> If the body (if I may say so) is "natured" and "schooled," <note>original: "disciplinatum" — referring to someone trained in traditional, rigid academic theories.</note> it is least of all suited for the Physician. For a schooled and corrected body is something far different, and it never becomes the "child" into whom doctrine can be poured. A schooled body is an adult body in foreign matters. Now, this "adult" is one who has already become master of himself and is thus full of his own knowledge. The "foreigner" is one who moves toward the unknown.

<margin>The principle of the Light of Nature.</margin> Now this is the condition and principle of the Light of Nature: that it is infused or instilled in the cradle; that it is grafted and struck in using rods <note>referring to early education or discipline</note>, as they say; that it is "pulled by the hair" and enters the man so that at first it is smaller than a grain of mustard seed. Later, once growth has occurred, it becomes far larger than the mustard plant itself. And since the mustard shrub, though very small, still bears and feeds its little birds: what else, I ask, should be understood by this, except that something tiny descends into us, which nevertheless grows larger as age progresses? It grows in such a way that it does not merely equal the man himself but towers over others. Because it is necessary for a man to become a tree in this way, and it is fitting to fulfill Christ's teaching about the mustard seed: it is certainly known to everyone that an aged, worn-out, and sapless tree can take in nothing more, but remains entirely dead and withered compared to the mustard seed. Since this is now dead and is nothing—and the example proposed by Christ looks only to the wood and branches as if born from tender youth—how, I ask, can an apple tree produce quinces from a dead fir? Or a young Elder from an ancient Laurel? It is quite impossible. Much less is it possible for an old proofreader from a printing house, or an old porter in a student hall <note>original: "Bursa" — a medieval university dormitory or hostel.</note> or a Logic College, or a "Senior Father" in a school to turn out a Physician. For the Physician must *grow*. But how can old men grow? They have already finished growing and have hardened; they have been reduced to such a state of filth that they can do nothing but turn into mere calluses, knots, and lumps.

<margin>Medicine must be learned from the cradle.</margin> Therefore, if a Physician wishes to be supported by and stand upon a firm root, it is necessary that he be carried in the cradle like a mustard seed, and grow and increase in the same way, just like those who are great and holy before God. Indeed, he must grow in such a way that he progresses in the things of nature like a mustard seed, which turns out larger than all others. And such things must rise and be born through the tenderness of youth.

<margin>Why old men are unfit for Medicine.</margin> If this is so, how, I ask, will those things grow in "adult fathers" who have already grown hard, whose time has passed, who never bloomed, never produced buds or little branches? They never felt any March, nor knew April, nor know whether May is green or blue, but first emerged in July and immediately want to bear fruit. <margin>Colchicum <note>The Autumn Crocus, which blooms late in the year; Paracelsus uses it here as a metaphor for people who try to begin their medical education far too late.</note></margin> And these are true ephemerals or *Colchica*, bursting forth in autumn. Know, therefore, that **congruity** must be present—not the kind they understand, but the kind I teach—namely, that it is necessary for the nature of the body to grow up with the nature of the natural light. For in this way, they are easily united and agree. For man cannot join or unite them himself; here, nothing belongs to him. The foundation must be like this and must be established from tender years. For that which is not sown in its own time fails. These are the Physicians who are grafted and transplanted from wild apples into vines, having neither kernel nor marrow. If they are sown, they become what they can.

Furthermore, it cannot happen but that,

<summary>Paracelsus defines 'Congruity' as the alignment between the physician's body and the Light of Nature, arguing that medical wisdom must be planted in youth like a mustard seed. He critiques older scholars and 'schooled' individuals, claiming their rigid minds are as incapable of growing true medical knowledge as a dead tree is of bearing fruit.</summary>

# TREATISE IV OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>Property of the Physician: Faithfulness.</margin>
<margin>Virtues are undivided.</margin>
Where the foundation for such upright Physicians is laid, let faithfulness also concur, and let it be perfect—not half-hearted, not divided, not partitioned, but full, whole, and absolute. For just as truth cannot be divided or mixed in God, neither can faithfulness. These things are by their very nature indivisible, just as charity is. For faithfulness and charity are one and the same thing. Now indeed, 

<margin>Faithfulness must be practical.</margin>
in what does the faithfulness of the physician consist? Not indeed in this, that he visits the sick diligently; but before he has even seen or known the sick person, he must already possess faithfulness—that is, he must have diligently and faithfully learned those things which belong to his office. For it is a lazy contempt of faithfulness if one learns for the sake of arrogance, or for show, so that he may ambitiously discourse on many things, or prepare some singular name for himself, and be satisfied by such things. All these things are rather against faithfulness and lack the seasoning of charity. For charity in this place is for itself, and not for another. For such a man learns and acts at least so that he may benefit himself, not another. Faithfulness, therefore, is situated in this: that it is known and performed. For he who does not know it cannot impart it to others. It is indeed drawn out and learned through teaching.

<margin>No one is a physician without teaching and experience.</margin>
Because it is acquired through instruction and experience, it is necessary for the beginning of possessing it to occur before the sick arrive. When they are present and standing by, it is necessary for it to be offered and performed. Now concerning the instruction and beginning of works, know that no one can become a Physician without teaching and experience: and that not of a short time, but of a long and lasting duration. For the number and catalog of diseases is so long and manifold that no one can become a Physician without teaching and experience over a long duration. For just as flowers do not burst forth before May, nor do crops ripen before harvest, nor wine before autumn: so these times cannot be shortened or changed in any experience.

<margin>A man is hardly untrained for ten hours.</margin>
Experience begins from childhood, and extends even to old age, and even to death itself, and a man is hardly untrained for ten hours <note>Paracelsus implies that humans are born into the "Light of Nature" and begin learning from the moment of birth; there is no time when a human is not being "taught" by nature.</note>. How then could those decrepit fathers, who approach the harvest or autumn in middle age, reach it? Nor is it a help to them that they think themselves already learned, and well-versed in many arts. For all these things are not faithfulness toward the sick, but they labor for your own benefit rather than faithfulness toward the sick. You, however, must know not that kind of thing, but Medicine. For this is faithfulness toward the sick; all other things are owed to you and your wife, so that you might "swim with the other apples" <note>original: "cum cæteris natare pomis" — a proverb mocking those of little substance who try to float along with more important people.</note>. For in your way, the foundation you lay is sandy, upon which you can build nothing solid. Because every foreign foundation in Medicine is worth nothing, but it is fitting that the pure and solid ground of Medicine be absorbed and implanted from tender years; therefore consider now among yourselves how hard and painful it happens for the sick, that they are forced to commit themselves and their lives to convent-dwellers, schoolmasters, providers, and other "fathers" (who bring nothing but despair).

<margin>All are designated by instruction.</margin>
It is necessary that all craftsmen—cobblers, skinners, and so forth—become accustomed to their art. A greater habituation from tender years is required from painters, sculptors, and goldsmiths. If these things are required from craftsmen, how much more so from Physicians, who have need of far greater and longer instruction. And just as it cannot happen that, from a very learned and skilled Master of Leipzig or Vienna, you could make yourself a more skilled or learned cobbler relative to his level of learning; so much less will such a man become a learned Physician—rather, for this reason, he will become more ignorant. Like an "ass at the lyre" <note>original: "asinus ad lyram" — a classical proverb for someone attempting a task for which they have no natural talent or training.</note>, so are they at the touching of a pulse, or a forehead to see if it burns or not. Know therefore, Physicians, that you can by no means learn faithfulness from such a late start, and your <term>Sophistry</term> <note>Sophistica: Paracelsus uses this to mock the empty, logic-based arguments taught in universities that have no practical application in healing.</note> and Philosophy contribute nothing here. For the Doctorate adorns you like nobility adorns a peasant; that is: "I am a Noble, I am a Doctor." For how can you, old scribes, become faithful, when you wish to learn nothing faithfully in that decrepit old age of yours? For in you, <term>Saturn</term> <note>In medical astrology, Saturn governs old age, rigidity, and the slowing of the spirit; Paracelsus suggests these men are too "set in their ways" to learn the living art of medicine.</note> dominates too powerfully.

<margin>Property of the Physician: Industry.</margin>
Besides all these things, it is also necessary for the Physician to be industrious and skillful. Whoever wishes to be considered industrious, it is right for him to have his own knowledge in all things. For from industry proceeds the foundation of your art—that is, not the foundation of teaching, but of the medicinal art. For how could you judge anything unless you make a judgment based on other things? For a judge must draw his judgment from the outside to turn it inward. He understands art who is industrious: nor can anyone judge it who is unskilled in it. From other things, what must be judged is understood. But what Physician could exist without industry?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medical faithfulness (fidelitas) requires a lifetime of preparation and love for the patient, rather than late-life academic study for the sake of status. He asserts that medicine must be learned from youth through constant experience and industry, mocking university doctors as rigid and unskilled.</summary>

# ON THE PROPERTY OF THE PHYSICIAN

<sig>T 3</sig>

...be possible? Since the greatest secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> should be hidden within him? For great secrets have arisen from the wise. What then, after all, is the industry of the Physician? That he should know what insensible things either help or harm; what is accepted or adverse, what is healthy or unhealthy for sea-beasts, fish, and brute animals. These are matters of skill that relate to nature. What besides?
<margin>The Physician is nothing without industry.</margin>
The consecrations of wounds and their powers—from where or by what force they perform that, and what they are; likewise, what is a <term>Melusina</term><note>In Paracelsian lore, a nature spirit (specifically of water) representing the hidden, transformative powers within the elements.</note>; what is a <term>Syrena</term><note>A siren; Paracelsus often used these terms to describe elemental beings or monstrous births that revealed natural laws.</note>; what is permutation, what is transplantation, and transmutation, and how these should be grasped with full understanding; what is beyond nature; what is above the constitution; what is above life; what is visible and invisible; what makes things sweet or bitter; what gives scent; what death is; what benefits the fisherman, the tanner, the healer, the dyer; what serves the metal-smith, what the woodworker; what belongs to the kitchen; what relates to the cellar; what is owed to the garden, what to the season; what the hunter knows, what the miner knows; what the traveling physician needs, what the stationary one needs; what wars and expeditions require, what peace requires; what gives cause to the church canons, what to the secular world; what each status does, what each status is; what the origin of each is; what God is, what Satan is; what poison is, and what is the opposite of poison; what is in men, what in women; what the difference is between a wife and a virgin; what is between yellow and pale, between white and black, between red and purple in all things; why one color is here and another there; why something is short, why long, and whatever concerns <term>Adeptio</term><note>Adeptship or "Attainment"; the state of having mastered the secrets of alchemy and medicine.</note> in all things. These things are not truly Medicine itself, but at least the properties annexed to medicine. 
<margin>What things the Physician ought to know.</margin>
For just as it is the property of a true and chosen Apostle to heal the sick, give sight to the blind, restore walking to the lame, and bring the dead back to life: so also these things belong to the Physician himself. And how, I ask, will an old man so worn out and decayed—one who has grown old in Casuistics and Temporalities—comprehend all such things? One who would need a long time just to learn the names that he should have soaked up under the schoolmaster’s rod in childhood? Therefore, in these things, all of which the Physician ought to know, the foundation of Medicine is placed. For more is situated in the Physician than in all other faculties and such matters. If, therefore, so much is situated in him, he will be all the greater and know more than others. He ought to be the father of Philosophy and Astronomy. 

How is it possible, however, that
<margin>A rebuke of the Physician.</margin>
such elderly scholars, pharmacists, and others, who finally come to Medicine late in life and attain a degree, can stand upright and be well-founded? By reason of age, nothing would stand in the way. But if you look at the art, there is a massive deficiency. For there, it is not by art, but by money, that one is created a Doctor and Master. It belongs to art to be a Doctor and Master with truth and dignity. And what, after all, do you Doctors and promoters commend in your students? *If they are Doctors, you say: "He was my student at Leipzig, and he heard me lecturing on Avicenna, Galen, and the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, and many good things"* <note>original: "Qui si Doctores sunt, vos dicitis: Is meus discipulus fuit Lipsiæ, & à me legente auscultauit Auicennam, Galenum, & Aphorismos Hippocratis & res multas bonas"</note>—yet neither you nor your affairs contain anything good. What good thing did he finally learn from you? *To make people lame and paralyzed on both sides.* <note>original: "Claudos & reſolutos ex vtroque latere facere"</note> This would be worthy of praise if any Doctor or promoter or Teacher taught his listeners the secrets of truth itself. This would be the mark; here the student could boast and say, *I have this, I know this.* But these things are so rare and thin among you that you should rightly be ashamed of them. 

Thus you rest upon 
<margin>Dead books as Doctors.</margin>
dead books, from which none of you has ever been made a true and genuine Physician. When someone desires to boast of his student with any honesty, he ought to instill and bestow much more upon him than the word-fights <note>original: "logomachiam"</note> of <term>Avicenna</term><note>A Persian physician whose texts were the standard in universities, which Paracelsus famously rejected.</note>, and the trifles of <term>Galen</term><note>An ancient Greek physician whose theory of "humors" Paracelsus sought to replace.</note>, and the "Great Sea" of <term>Jacobus de Partibus</term><note>A 15th-century French physician known for his massive commentaries on medical texts.</note>.
<margin>Jacobus de Partibus.</margin>

Although all these things can moreover 
<margin>The Physician is unfortunate without the patient's aptitude.</margin>
be invalidated by the sick. For you see that their operations must be perfected in those who have a certain aptitude for Medicine. If that does not happen, nothing is achieved. Since, therefore, so much is situated in the Physician, and so too everything that belongs to the Physician, the sick person must be fit for the reception <note>original: "conceptionem"</note> [of the cure], without which aptitude nothing can be done. Therefore, pay attention to what must be present in the sick person: namely, *natural disease, natural will, and natural virtue or force.* In these three
<margin>What things those about to be healed must have.</margin>
the Physician's work to be completed consists. If, however, anything else is in the sick person besides the said three things, then he can expect no healing from the Physician. For those whom Christ healed had to be fit for receiving it. None of the unfit were ever healed. But much more accurately for the Physician himself...

He also notes that healing requires a "natural aptitude" or willingness within the patient to receive the cure.</summary>

# FOURTH TRACTATE OF THE PARAGRANUM

<margin>A hidden dispensation.</margin>
The physician must take care to have patients who are suitable and fit for treatment. For the power of the physician is less than the power of God. There is a certain dispensation <note>The "dispensation" refers to God’s divine plan or the way He distributes events and fates across the world.</note> with God over mankind and over nature, which no one can measure or search out, as to how any specific thing is distributed. With God, this is a great matter; with man, it is hidden. Truly, this is nothing to the physician <note>Meaning it is outside the physician’s control or ability to diagnose.</note>.

<margin>The physician’s duty regarding the dispensation of God.</margin>
This, however, pertains to the physician: that he should veil or excuse nothing under the pretext and accusation of God. For it is possible for no one to search out where God either promotes or hinders. The physician must stand firm in the knowledge of the heaven, the water, the air, and the earth; and from these, he must fashion the <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "microcosmum"; the concept that the human body is a "little world" reflecting the laws of the greater universe.</note>. Upon this knowledge, he must place and defend his certainty, adding nothing to God, nor taking anything away, but at every moment awaiting His grace and mercy. For if He established the **eclipse** of the **Sun** and the **Moon**; if He commanded them to stand and be still; if He brought the **deluge** <note>original: "cataclyfmum"; the Great Flood of Noah.</note> upon the world; if He daily ordained the frost and the hail: then in these medical matters He has likewise ordained His will. Nor does He wish that through these things His **Medicine** and His creature should either be ill-spoken of or accused. For nothing is lacking, but all things are full of virtues. However, at this time, this is His singular will: He wishes to act according to His will, and He does not desire to take away the power of nature, but merely commands it to be still. Just as He does not strip the **Sun** of its light even when darkness falls: at least during that period in which the darkness lasts, its splendor is not seen. Thus, therefore, while God imposes such an impediment upon **Medicine**, death meanwhile creeps in secretly and strikes down life.

<margin>How and when death rushes in.</margin>
**Once the man is dead**, **Medicine** again shines brightly as before, just like the **Sun**. For at night, thieves steal while they are not seen. And those thieves are most industrious who steal in such a way that they are not noticed. So also death creeps in through the night of **Medicine**, and steals away life, the most excellent treasure of man. Unless God commanded **Medicine** to stand still, just as in the time of **Joshua** the **Sun** stood still, who would ever die? He wishes many to be sick in this way, by withdrawing their health just as He withdrew the **Sun**; yet He does not allow Himself to be accused of it. For His works are so hidden that we neither know them nor perceive from whence they come. And God entirely wishes us to be subject to **Medicine**, so that we may be pure in all things, and suspect nothing concerning Him.

<margin>God is not to be accused, even as the source.</margin>
It is fitting that we be so inclined and rightly minded toward God that we do not impute such things to Him, but transfer the cause into nature. In nature, we should continually work through **Medicine** applied by faith, so that whatever the physician does is done, whether those things are perfected by God or hindered. The patient ought to have that faithfulness, belief, hope, and confidence toward God, lest he be driven into the cause of an **Eclipse**, in which death leaps in, in which the **Sun** is withdrawn, or a flood overwhelms. For if He did not spare the entire world, how should He spare a single person? And all these things happen in silence and obscurity.

<margin>The hidden judgments of God.</margin>
Just as the **Deluge** was manifest and visible to all creatures, so on the other hand these sorts of secluded judgments are hidden, so that a man departs from this world from within himself, even without a visible judgment from God.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
Since, therefore, it is fitting for a physician to be of such great authority and esteem, built upon such strong foundations: here also you ought to know that no physician can stand at all unless he is supported by the aforementioned four columns or pillars <note>Paracelsus famously argued that medicine rests on four pillars: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note>. Truly, it is situated in the physician that God works through him, loves him, and imposes upon him both the praise and the disgrace of **Medicine** to be borne. The praise is his if the patient recovers, so that he may celebrate God. The disgrace is his if **Medicine** is hindered and the thief plunders the patient. Know here, therefore, that physicians who wish to support themselves solely through **Medicine** have no need for further investigation or experience. But whatever those physicians—whom God supports according to their own will—perform or destroy through medicine, God by no means wishes that to be blamed on Him, but rather that the homicide be ascribed to the physician. For God does not wish **Medicine** to be preserved through wicked men of that sort. Therefore, it must be diligently considered upon which foundation and path a physician ought to walk.

<margin>A rebuke of physicians.</margin>
I deservedly instill this into you, because you strive to be what you are least of all, and you reject that foundation upon which you ought especially to have been built, and without which you can neither stand nor walk. Now take account among yourselves: from what brain do I speak or write, and what is my foundation, and the foundation of those whom you judge to be of my sect? How much more honorably and solidly are they founded than you, who can do nothing else but point a finger at papers? Yet those papers flow away with any passing water and are composed of mere rags. For such as the material of the paper is, such is that which is written upon it: namely, mere fragments, mere scraps. **Paper** <note>original: "Papyrus"</note>

<meta>The catchword "ager" (patient) at the bottom indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus explains that while God’s will can "eclipse" the power of medicine to allow death to occur, the physician must never use God as an excuse for failure. He rebukes "paper physicians" who rely on books rather than the living foundations of nature and divine grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s critique of conventional physicians, contrasting their superficial knowledge with true medical experience, and introduces a second version of his work, the Paragranum.</meta>

<page-num>223</page-num>
<header>ON THE PROPER NATURE OF THE PHYSICIAN.</header>

[...nor does] the field [belong to the physician], in which fate has sown weeds <note>original: "lolium"; specifically darnel, a weed that mimics wheat and can be toxic.</note>: and you Physicians are entirely weed-like. For you snatch up at least this much: that which is worth nothing. That which is useful, you trample underfoot. Because, however, the weed grows more abundantly than the wheat and appears more beautiful to the eye, you therefore stuff your pharmacies with it. As your simple medicines are, so also are you Doctors. They are foul, eaten away, covered in mold, and decayed; nor is there one among you who knows what lies within them. Just as you know nothing regarding the medicines themselves, so also is nothing to be found in you. In your pharmacies, the paintings <note>Refers to the decorative jars and labels in a chemist's shop.</note> are the best thing. And the best thing in you is also outward show. And because you are built upon such a shifting foundation, you know nothing whatsoever. As soon as even the lightest sweat breaks out on a patient, you are immediately stuck, nor can you know what to do. Thus the **Swiss Doctor** <note>original: "Doctor Heluetius"; Paracelsus is referring to himself here in the third person.</note>, whom you despise, is the Master of you all. You do not waste away from merely reading and learning; and yet you remain ignorant of all things. Whom shall I call you other than those from the number of the **virgins** who, when they had spilled their lamps, turned to their companions to borrow from others? <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25.</note> You Doctors are entirely of that sort. Your jars are all spilled lamps; and as often as a new Doctor comes forth anywhere, you say: *“I beg you, teach me something also; my lamp has ceased to burn, nor is there any oil or liquid left to me.”* Thus, either I myself, or another who does not entirely recognize you as fools, communicates what we have to you, and by our very kindnesses we prepare enemies for ourselves. But if we were to emulate the parable of the prudent virgins by sharing nothing with you—but instead commanded you **City Physicians** <term>Poliatros</term> and **Chief Physicians** <term>Archiatros</term>, who sit idle on your cushions, to be anxious for your own oil—you would see how much commotion there would be in your experience; by the very outcome you would learn what you were finally going to achieve. And unless we **itinerant healers** <note>original: "circumforanei"; literally "those who go around the markets," a derogatory term for traveling doctors like Paracelsus.</note> (with which name you deign to call us) frequently averted it, how many homicides would be committed by you everywhere? For which of those whom you have lost have we not restored? And after you saw how much benefit lies in experience, you then poured out your own weeds to travel abroad, so that now you deceive and defraud not only your own countrymen, but even foreigners.

And if in these things recounted so far, I wish my foundation to be set before you, I am supported by the full hope that you will finally open your eyes more clearly and recognize more accurately what your art and what kind of Medicine it is. We wish the listeners, however, to be forewarned above all, lest they by chance separate themselves from you and become entangled.

## To the Reader, Greetings.

*SINCERE and benevolent Reader, we wish you to know that this book, the **Paragranum**, was arranged and written down by **Paracelsus** two or three times. And although the present treatise is of the same subject as the following one, I wished to add the latter word for word, just as it was written by the author and as much as has been found of it, chiefly for this reason: that in it he introduces many useful Philosophical, Astronomical, and Medical examples not included in the preceding **Paragranum**. If by chance some obscure and less intelligible places are inserted in the first treatise, these can for the most part be explained and clarified by the following ones, as the upright and diligent Reader will easily discover from a mutual comparison.*

*Truly, because this following treatise agrees in several places with the former many times, both in words and in opinions, some might perhaps be offended because one thing is delivered here twice. Nevertheless, we did not think it appropriate that those things should be omitted, or that the arrangement and order of the author’s book should be mutilated. Therefore, let this not be ungrateful to you, and be fully persuaded that these things have been gathered here entirely for your benefit and advantage, which were certainly not printed before. I have no doubt that many diligent students will use and enjoy them with great profit.*

->PREFACE<-

## PREFACE

...I had published. By that act, the opportunity and cause were provided to me to set about uncovering the frauds and errors of those who, though they are utterly ignorant and unskilled in these matters, nevertheless hold everyone else in contempt.

But what I have published seems to them too much, and to me too little—namely, concerning the wood <note>original: "de ligno"; referring to Guaiac wood, a popular but (in Paracelsus's view) ineffective treatment for syphilis.</note> and the three books of impostures. In that explanation, by right and truth, I could have filled a much larger book; however, I gladly cut it short and docked it, so that I might suppress certain disgraces and the ignorance or simplicity of the Doctors and Masters. Yet because I enclosed it within narrow limits and barriers, they complain that there is too little, and that it can be properly understood by no one. Therefore, since those things are too few for them, I am absolutely compelled to publish more abundant works and to compose larger books, so that they can no longer object to my brevity. I suspect, however, that they are pushing for this only so that their own folly may be dragged more fully and clearly into the light <note>original: "sub radium"; literally "under the sunbeam."</note>. In this matter, I justly pledge my labor to them.

They do not obscurely hint that those things which pertain to their own honesty, erudition, and learning have been brought forth clearly enough with the truth—at least those parts that require a more abundant explanation of my own doctrine. Yet these things can by no means be separated from one another, but must be handed down together as one: so that not one part alone, but both together may be understood in this way. Even if they seek only one part, they cannot have it without the other.

<margin>Why all are rebuked in the same way.</margin>
That they interpret my writings poorly is due to their own imprudence. For I have never written anything (as all my works will testify) without a foundation and experience. Moreover, the reason they cry out against me is that I struck the fibers of their hearts when I demonstrated that they are entirely ignorant of those things which it especially becomes Physicians to know. Because I did not emerge from their schools and do not speak according to their prescriptions, they charge me with this as a primary crime. But their own rash prejudice drives me to this. Concerning this, when I am about to write—since under their leadership they can establish the truth neither among the old nor the young—I am forced, willing or unwilling, to oppose them, nor can I agree with them in the slightest thing. If, therefore, the truth is to be written at all, I cannot merely winnow the disciples separately; rather, the situation demands that I drag the masters themselves along with the disciples, and indeed the Teachers of both masters and disciples, under one yoke. Since they are so loud, I shall explain to them first what Medicine is, and then what they themselves are. For it is of no less value to blunt their shouting than it is to reveal the art.

<margin>What the foundations of Medicine are.</margin>
Now, if it is right for Medicine to be derived from a foundation, it will also be necessary for me to put forward those things which constitute that foundation. Thus, I rightly take my foundation from **Philosophy**, and **Astronomy**, and **Alchemy**, and upon these I build and establish all my works. They, on the contrary, are despisers of these three principles: they are despisers of Philosophy, despisers of Astronomy, and despisers of Alchemy; add also the despisers of virtues. They bark at this art for no other reason than that they are ignorant of it and are too shameless to learn.

<margin>Pharisee Physicians</margin>
And so that they may look after their own honor and reputation, they persuade the foolish and simple common people that all my works are mere trifles, when they themselves are mere fools, and asses—indeed, nothing at all. They make themselves similar to the Jews and Pharisees in this, who thought that heaven was theirs while rejecting or despising the one to whom it belonged, namely Christ. Thus they also exist simultaneously as University Physicians, Bath-keepers, and Surgeons. Therefore, I liken them to busybodies <term>ardelionibus: meddlers or people who are busy doing nothing</term> and buffoons <term>balatronibus: jesters or professional rascals</term>, who can do nothing but shout, slander, and make accusations, and that without any shame or fear. Such are our loud-mouthed Physicians.

To speak to the matter: who is there who can be a Physician without these three? Who can be a Physician who is not a Philosopher, an Astronomer, and an Alchemist? No one. He must be entirely practiced in these three. For in these the truth of Medicine is placed. What Astronomy is, they do not know. What Philosophy is, they are ignorant of. What Alchemy is, they have not discovered. Since they are ignorant of these three highest things, they set themselves to attack them. And because I use them, I am rejected and hissed at by them. But no one has ever rejected me unless he was a lazy and "horned" **Beane** <note>original: "Beanus"; a play on "Bejaunus" (yellow-beak), a medieval academic term for a raw, uninitiated freshman. "Horned" refers to the ritualistic "horns" a freshman supposedly wore until they were purged of their boorishness.</note>, such as you all are. For to "Beans," nothing is certain regarding these matters. Nor is anything certain to you. Therefore, you are just like them. Outwardly, in your clothes, you are painted as Physicians; inwardly, you hide faithless Jews, corpses, and the images of statues.

Understand, therefore, what foundation I use in Medicine, and upon what I lean.

<summary>Paracelsus defends his decision to write more extensively against his critics, asserting that true medicine must be built upon the three pillars of Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy, which his contemporaries ignorantly reject.</summary>

->PREFACE<-

The *first* is Philosophy. The second is Astronomy. The last is Alchemy. Add a fourth: specific property <note>technical term: "proprietatem," referring to the unique medical virtues or "signatures" inherent in specific plants or minerals</note>. Truly, note and attend to me diligently. For either you must establish these things for yourselves in this way, or you will be branded by public insult among all people as mere impostors; as those who, without these three pillars, are mockers and babblers of princes, of nobles, and of cities and regions; and you will be seen as those to whom all honor and reverence is paid only by pure, unadulterated fools, hypocrites, and parasites.

But attend to the manner in which I propose these three things. For it will by no means be permitted for you to propose them in any other way, but it will be necessary for you all to follow me alone—along with your Avicenna, Galen, Rhazes, etc.—and I will not follow you. Follow me, you Parisians, you of Montpellier, you of Salerno, you of Vienna, you of Cologne, you of Wittenberg; all of you included in one sum, with not even the most inward corner of a sweating-room <note>original: "Laconici"; a reference to a dry heat bath or sauna, suggesting no one is exempt from his scrutiny</note> left out. For I am the Monarch: I rule the Monarchy, and I administer it, and I gird your loins.

How much will the Horned One <note>original: "Cornutus"; likely referring to the "horns" of a fool’s cap or a mock crown of shame</note> adorn you, when Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus’s given name: Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim</note>, Prince of the Monarchy, shall rule, with you appointed as his furnace-heaters? What will your spirit be at last, if I drive you into my Philosophy and force you to befoul your Pliny and Aristotle, and to piss upon Albert, Thomas, Scotus, etc., and say: "These men were able to lie skillfully and subtly"? How truly certain and lazy fools our ancestors were along with us, that neither we nor they caught the scent of such things! How will it seem to you, if I am to so arrange the heavens that the Tail of the Dragon <note>original: "cauda Draconis"; an astronomical term for the descending lunar node, here used as a metaphor for an omen of destruction</note> devours your Avicenna and Galen? For they themselves are ignorant of the heavens. You also are ignorant of them. Oh, how "laudable" it is that you are foolish Doctors and Masters! How heavily your backs will be pressed if you are to wear ears six ells long <note>A common metaphor for the long ears of a donkey, symbolizing stupidity</note>? For John in the Apocalypse [the Book of Revelation] saw no monsters anywhere more foul or deformed than what you are. How great a disgrace it will be to you that, in curing the sick until now, you have extorted large riches from them, and yet you have not even learned to cook properly, but have offered them raw and uncooked things? From which it is certainly clear that you have killed many. And Alchemy will speak of this more clearly. You must penetrate into this, unless you choose the alternative: that your wives, children, and kinsmen see you struck with the greatest shame.

But if I had no other support against you than this testimony—that you are counterfeit and ignorant—how great do you think I would still be in the Monarchy? I am silent about the fact that I am also uncovering all your lies and trifles, and the ravings of bathhouse-keepers and lousy barbers, and that not in just one book, but in all of them. Indeed, I add this: that I teach you, not you me. For what I drew from you, the fire has long since consumed <note>A likely reference to Paracelsus publicly burning the classic medical texts of Galen and Avicenna at the University of Basel in 1527</note>. On the other hand, what I teach, no fire shall consume; yet it shall eat through and devour you. Whose Monarchy is it then? Mine, or yours? I do not despair, indeed, that there will be some fools and "horned ones" who will act as defenders of your party. But these men and you shall mutually finish and devour yourselves. You prepare friendships for yourselves by kneeling, submitting, and saluting: "Gracious Lord," "Elect Lord," and again and again "Lord." But if lordship is ever confined to a sickbed, you, having pledged the laws of friendship, provide nothing but frauds and impostures. But if the sick whom you have slaughtered could be returned to their lives: <margin>Aboali <note>A name for Avicenna</note>.</margin> they would sooner beshit you and your prince Aboali and Abinschini <note>Corruptions of the names Abu Ali ibn Sina (Avicenna)</note> than pay you any of your former honor. Oh, the shame! That you fantasists consume even as much as six days in reading those trivial authors.

But let this preface not be a source of grief to you. Toward the end, I will toss a morsel to those of Leipzig, and lead them with salt to the wood <note>original: "ad lignum"; a double entendre referring to both the gallows and the "Holy Wood" (Guaiac) used to treat syphilis, which Paracelsus considered a fraud</note>.

### TREATISE ON PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>Philosophy is the foundation of Medicine.</margin> SINCE it is certain and established that the foundation of Medicine exists in Philosophy, we must first know how it should be drawn out from Philosophy. But before these things are explained, it is worthwhile first to shake out the counterfeit Philosophy which might by chance oppose and hinder me. For only those will oppose me who, born of false and spurious Philosophy, nevertheless boast themselves to be legitimate, just as [has been the case] until now...
