# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE PARAGRANUM: TREATISE I. #

<margin>Doctors like foam.</margin>
The outcome has proved it. For only worthless Philosophies—that is, the moss and foam of Philosophy—have risen against me so far. But it is always the nature of foam that, although it is nothing but waste, it floats and sticks out in the pot, and by its bubbling, it obscures the better and worthier thing beneath it. Yet, when finally caught by a spoon, it is shaken out into the ashes; and the broth, as the better part, remains pure in the pot. In the same way, the false Philosophers will also be skimmed off and poured into the swamp; but I will shine forth, remaining with my Philosophy. Those who eat of us will also be satisfied—no longer from the foam, as has happened until now. For all those doctors are foamy, and it is right that they be thrown into the pigs' troughs.

<margin>What Philosophy teaches.</margin>
Philosophy, however, is based on this: that the nature, matter, and condition of all diseases be understood along with their entire essence, and this from Philosophy alone, not from any other art. For wherever any other foundation is taken from except Philosophy, it will be mere imposture and called imposture. For the sick person is deceived by such things; and what nature provides to the sick, is taken away by such a Doctor, who is born of adulterated Medicine. For it is Nature that administers Medicine to the sick. If Nature does this, it must also thoroughly know the sick person. For without knowledge, she can administer nothing to him. This knowledge, however, is not placed in the Doctor, but entirely in Nature. For she knows herself, not the Doctor. Therefore, if Nature alone knows herself thoroughly, she alone will also compose and prepare the prescriptions.

<margin>Nature is both disease and Medicine.</margin>
For disease comes forth from Nature, and the remedy descends from Nature, not at all from the Doctor. If this is true, it is entirely proper for the Doctor to learn from these twins, and whatever both teach him, that he should do. If he is taught nothing by them, he will know nothing and understand nothing. For the Nature of these twins is Medicine, and disease, and the healer of itself. Now, if the Doctor must be born from nature, and he himself is nothing in himself, nor from himself, nor by himself, but everything exists from and in nature, he will also be born entirely from nature—not from Leipzig, nor from Vienna. For let them know that what they learn there is the same as what is taught in Deventer, and Zwolle, and at Uberlingen <note>A town on Lake Constance; Paracelsus implies that university learning is identical and equally stagnant everywhere, from the Low Countries to southern Germany.</note> near the German Ocean.

<margin>Nature teaches the Doctor.</margin>
But Nature teaches the Doctor, not man; since therefore Nature is of such great importance, it seems right to teach what and what kind of thing Nature is: which is the task of Philosophical discourse.

Moreover, it is also worth knowing what Philosophy is. For on this, I have a dispute with my adversaries. For what they consider Philosophy, I judge to be small glands <note>original: "glandulas"; referring to abnormal growths or kernels, like swollen lymph nodes, suggesting their philosophy is a parasitic growth</note>, growing on the outside of the body and bearing its likeness; yet they are by no means that which they resemble.

<margin>Rejection of Doctors.</margin>
Thus, those Doctors too are as worthless as the Philosophers who spring only from the fungus clinging to a tree. For in this way, they also cling to Philosophy, but are not woven into it. As for what they feel about my Philosophy, it need not be very good or great. For horse dung does not care for contempt. Therefore, neither they nor other fools use my Philosophy.

A long speech would be needed if one tried to demonstrate clearly and evidently what the main point and nerve <note>original: "rhombus & nervus"; metaphors for the core or heart of the matter</note> of our disagreement is. To summarize the matter briefly here, I at least propose this: it is entirely necessary for the Doctor to know heaven and earth according to their matter, form, and essence.

<margin>Things a Doctor must know.</margin>
If he is equipped with this knowledge, he has already become one who can further enter Medicine itself. For after the knowledge and comprehension of those things is absorbed, the Doctor truly begins. Therefore, the logic of Medicine is such that it is necessary for the internal Doctor to be born from the external. For if the external is lacking, the internal does not exist at all.

<margin>The internal Doctor does not exist without the external.</margin>
For whatever the internal one either does or teaches from his own subjects, it is all in vain. Now, however, internal Philosophy teaches nothing else but some empty fictions, as when it is said, *“This disease is Choleric, etc.”* For <term>Cholera: in the traditional Galenic system, this was one of the four "humors" (yellow bile), but Paracelsus rejects the humors as imaginary inventions</term> is nothing, nor was it ever known or discovered by any Philosopher. The reason is that it does not emerge from external Philosophy, but from internal; nor does internal doctrine provide any other teaching than the speculative and imaginary theories of man himself. This kind of speculation also gave the name and origin to "cholera."

<margin>Cholera is a fiction.</margin>
External Philosophy, however, does not burst forth from any speculation, but is generated entirely from the external man, and it teaches and shows what the internal man is. Since, therefore, we have obtained such a teacher, it is right to send away all speculation entirely, and to grasp those things which are demonstrated not through speculation, but through truth and nature itself. In this, therefore, our divorce consists: that my adversaries speculate, but I work from the nature of things themselves.

<margin>What is the difference between Theophrastic and ancient Philosophy.</margin>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine is derived from Nature (External Philosophy) rather than academic speculation. He dismisses traditional humoral theories, like "cholera," as imaginary fictions and asserts that a doctor must study the material essence of the world to understand the internal workings of the human body.</summary>

<header>ON PHILOSOPHY.</header>

I teach by nature. Now, to speculate is to deal in phantasms <note>original: "phantasmata"; Paracelsus uses this to mean imaginary theories or mental delusions that have no basis in physical reality.</note>. Phantasms, in turn, give birth to "phantasts" <note>dreamers or those who prefer theory over observation</note>. Indeed, phantasy rests on no foundation; it is left free to anyone to tickle and satisfy themselves with their own phantasms according to their pleasure. In reality, it is no different than if someone were to imagine many things by wishing for them, yet never obtain what they wished for. So too, the phantasms of these dreamers are worthless and empty. It is upon such a foundation that their Medicine is built. Now, compare and weigh my foundation against theirs.

<margin>The discovery of Theophrastus's mind.</margin>
If speculation were good and useful, then wishing would also be useful. In that way, something might be gained against me. But nothing is produced against me that lasts. For the foundation I lay is not speculation at all, but *Discovery* <note>original: "Inuentio"; in a Renaissance context, this refers to the systematic finding or uncovering of natural truths through observation.</note>; it is not, I say, speculation, but the very property of things. For Philosophers recognize in the external <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "Archeus" is Paracelsus's term for the vital force or "inner chemist" in nature that directs the growth and function of all things.</note> that it is not right for you to say, "*This is Choleric, this is Melancholy*." Rather, nature suggests it should be said thus: "*This is Arsenic-like, this is Alum-like*." For if you said, "this is *of Jupiter*" <note>tin</note> or "that is *of Saturn*" <note>lead</note>, then I would have no quarrel left with you.

<margin>How a Physician ought to speak.</margin>
If you were to say, "*This is a stomach sickness* <note>original: "Acoria"</note>, *this disease is a flowering*" <note>original: "Anthera"; referring to a disease manifesting like a botanical extract</note>, then you would hear from me that you are upright and learned Doctors, a truth I could indeed testify to. For such talk proceeds from true Philosophy.

<margin>External things give names to internal ones.</margin>
Likewise, if you asserted, "*This disease is of Fleabane, it is of Lemon Balm*," then at last I would see that you have a certain knowledge of those diseases. But if you continue to say, "*this is yellow bile, this is phlegm*," I know for a certainty that you possess no knowledge, but are born only of speculation and phantasy—which has never produced anything healthy or true. Therefore, such things are not uttered or announced by a true Physician, but only by those who are fantastic and speculative; a license given to fools who dare to invent such foundations. 

In this way, you make blood the cause of dysentery. This is nonsense—as is your claim that it is a *fault of the stomach*. For all those things among you are mere opinions, and you are mere opinion-makers regarding those choleric, phlegmatic, melancholic, and sanguine humors. But if you were to pronounce it thus: "*This is the disease of Meadow Saffron* <note>Hermodactylus</note>, *the disease of Bitter Apple* <note>Colocynth</note>, *the disease of Hellebore*," I would rightly praise and extol you, because you would be proceeding from a foundation and speaking the truth itself. For names ought to be derived from the foundation, not from phantasy. Thus, <margin>Civet-like Colic: Musk-like Iliac.</margin> colic should be called "Civet-like," and intestinal pain should be named "Musk-like." <note>Paracelsus is arguing that diseases should be named after the natural substances—minerals or plants—that act as their "cure" or "counterpart" in nature.</note> For what reason? Surely because External Philosophy teaches and commands it, which bestows and attributes all names, natures, properties, and signs to the internal world. Outside of this, no good Physician is born; instead, they become mere impostors, wanderers, dreamers, and donkeys.

<margin>In what Philosophy consists.</margin>
Since, therefore, the primary science of the Physician must flow from Philosophy, it is appropriate that this science does not consist of man, but rather of heaven and earth, and air and water. In these, the knowledge and understanding of all Physicians lies hidden. For Philosophers speak and treat of these kinds of things—not of yellow bile, or phlegm, or melancholy, or blood. Therefore, all talk of such humors is foolish. All true Philosophers treat only of *minerals*, of *fruits*, of *celestial impressions*, and of *influences*; <margin>The Object of Medicine.</margin> not one of them says even a little word about the Humors. 

But if a speculative Physician should now object: "I am indeed skilled in Philosophy, but it is not enough for me; I must know and seek more, and descend to the four Humors to investigate everything more exactly than those things handed down through Philosophy," etc. <margin>The Solution.</margin> Here, know that he is driven by a grave error. The cause is this: <margin>All things of the body exist more clearly outside.</margin> there is nothing inside the body that cannot be shown to you plainly outside of it. Indeed, all things are more certain and abundant when they lie open outside. Therefore, if you had an accurate and full knowledge of Philosophy, you would have no need to speculate on any other foundation. 

Because you possess only a crippled <margin>Reproof of the Physician.</margin> and imperfect knowledge, you deal in that "patchwork" and act just like butchers <note>original: "carnifices"; this term implies someone who does dirty, bloody work away from the public eye, often used as an insult for executioners or dishonest surgeons.</note> who withdraw from honest men into secret and hidden alleys to conduct business that no one can speak against or oppose. Such are you Doctors as well. You have brought things to such a pass with your speculations that no one is allowed to speak against you; that is, you have so involved and hidden your business that no honest man can understand you. Therefore, no one can easily catch you in a mistake. Yet, if the true nature of your speculation were as well known to other Philosophers as it is to me, they would certainly say, "*Out with these butchers!*" You rightly separate yourselves from other learned men through your jargon and vocabulary. For if these were understood, your imposture would immediately become known to the whole world. For example:

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the traditional "Four Humors" of Galenic medicine (bile, phlegm, etc.) as imaginary phantasms, arguing that diseases should instead be named and understood through their relationship to minerals, plants, and the "External Philosophy" of nature. He accuses university-trained doctors of using technical jargon to hide their ignorance and act like secretive "butchers" beyond the reach of public criticism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s sharp critique of the medical establishment. Having previously argued that academic medicine is built on empty "phantasms," he now exposes how doctors use technical jargon to confuse the public and introduces his core theory: that the human body and the natural world are mirrors of one another, sharing the same "Anatomy."</meta>

# THE SECOND BOOK OF PARAGRANUM: TREATISE I

...on your apothecary jars you write labels like **Rosemary Flower**, **Wallflower**, **Bugloss**, **Speedwell**, and so on. <note>original: "Anthos, Cheyri, Buglossa, Veronica." Paracelsus is pointing out that doctors use fancy names for common weeds to make their work seem more mysterious.</note> If the common peasants knew and understood what these were, they would be utter fools to pay so much money for them! This is a fatal fraud that no one can easily detect. No one understands these exotic terms, even though the things themselves are well known to the peasants. In this way, Medicine has been cut off from all other professions; it has been separated from other learned arts by both its jargon and its methods, so that it is now almost impossible to criticize. But this is not Philosophy—it is mere speculation.

<margin>What Philosophy should teach</margin>
But since my purpose is to explain true Philosophy, I shall define what a Physician ought to be as an introduction to Medicine. I will do this in plain language, so that specific details can be more easily applied to universal truths. For Philosophy must be taught in such a way that the whole, visible man is presented within it. Within this Philosophy, all diseases, accidents, and states of health must be discovered, along with every joint and limb, every part and sub-part that exists or could exist in a human being. These things must be seen and known in nature—seeing all that has happened or could happen from the first man to the last. All of this must be known so perfectly and absolutely that the eyes, ears, voice, and spirit are found mirrored in the world. Even mobility, the organs of digestion, the parts that expel waste, and those that attract nutrients must be seen as clearly as they are in the body, contributing to its well-being. These universal things must be understood, learned, and found externally. They must be tested and judged externally; they must be processed and purified by fire externally. Just as the urine is inspected, the pulse is felt, and the colors of the <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person's character or health from their facial features or body structure.</note> are judged in a patient, these same things must be understood in the outer world. Once you have thoroughly mastered all these things externally, then you may proceed to the "inner man." Only after you have tested and accounted for the greatest things outside the body should you finally inspect the urine, feel the pulse, and apply external Medicine to internal needs.

<margin>A rebuke of the Medical establishment.</margin>
This is the genuine Philosophy that I drum into you so often. If you neither know nor understand this, tell me, where do you get the confidence and arrogance to dispense medicine to such a multitude of people based on such empty speculation and fantasy? How dare you cause so many to become blind, lame, and crippled? One could rightly call such reckless men <term>Beanos</term> <note>original: "beanos"; a term for a raw, uninitiated student or a "greenhorn." It refers to the "Beania," a sometimes violent initiation ritual for university newcomers.</note>, who experiment on everyone. They are not content with deceiving others; they even teach others to do the same, lest their imposture should ever die out. If you persist in doing this, why do you not persist in writing against me? Satan is busy indeed if he allows his wounded sons to suffer. If you truly cared for the health of the sick, you would realize that you must choose a much more certain foundation. But everything you occupy yourselves with is based on trickery. You think it is enough to simply have "faith" in your theories, regardless of what happens with your actual work—whether the patients end up dead or half-alive. Your "kitchen-science" is fine as long as there are people to agree with your nonsense. You possess a "faith without works"—that is, a dead faith. Whenever something fails or turns out poorly, you simply say, "God did it."

<margin>The two-fold Philosopher.</margin>
To truly perfect a Philosopher, know that he is born of two paths. One is in the heavens, the other is on the earth; that is, he is produced from both spheres. Each sphere on its own is only half a principle; joined together, they are a whole principle. Now, although a man who is expert in both parts is called a Philosopher, the name changes depending on the focus. He who is skilled in the lower sphere is specifically called a Philosopher.

<margin>How the Philosopher and Astronomer differ.</margin>
He who knows the upper sphere is called an **Astronomer**. Yet both are Astronomers, and both are Philosophers; both belong to the same science and art. Now, all Astronomers are divided into four parts.

<margin>The four-fold Astronomer.</margin>
The **first** Astronomer knows the origins of metals and the properties of minerals. The **second** understands the fruits of the earth. The **third** understands **Manna** <note>original: "Mannam"; here referring to "Tereniabin" or "honey-dew," believed to be a celestial substance that falls upon plants.</note> as well as anyone who knows the nature of Saturn or Jupiter. In turn, he is also a Philosopher who has learned the impressions, influences, and movements of the heavens. The **fourth** Philosopher is he who understands the Air no less than another understands the Earth. For this is the one Philosophy that concerns nature.

<margin>There is one Anatomy for all things.</margin>
Now, for these four, there exists only one <term>Anatomy</term> <note>For Paracelsus, "Anatomy" is not just dissection, but the study of how the structure of the world (macrocosm) corresponds to the structure of the human body (microcosm).</note>, one essence, and one matter. For **Saturn** <note>The planet Saturn was linked to the metal Lead.</note> is not only in the heavens, but also in the deepest depths of the sea and in the furthest hidden reaches of the earth.

<margin>Lemon Balm in heaven.</margin>
**Lemon Balm** <note>original: "Melissa."</note> is not only in the garden, but also in the air and in the very heavens. What, I ask you, do you think the planet **Venus** is, if not the herb **Mugwort**? <note>original: "Artemisia."</note> And what is Mugwort, if not Venus?

<margin>Mugwort is Venus.</margin>
And what are both of them? The womb, conception, and the spermatic vessels. What is **Iron**? It is nothing but **Mars**. And what is Mars? Nothing but Iron. That is, both are Iron or Mars. The same is true of the **Nettle** and the "fourth manna" <note>original: "Tereniabin"; a Persian-derived term for a type of medicinal manna or resin.</note>—all are one and the same.

Mars...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires a "philosophy" based on the structural correspondence between the human body and the natural world (the macrocosm). He rejects academic jargon and asserts that planets, minerals, and plants share the same essential "anatomy" as human organs.</summary>

He is building toward his definition of the "four pillars" of medicine, emphasizing that a true physician must also be an astronomer and a philosopher to understand the inner workings of the human body.</meta>

->229<-

He who knows Mars, knows iron. He who knows iron, knows Mars. <note>In the alchemy and astrology of Paracelsus’s time, the planet Mars was directly linked to the metal iron. To know one was to know the essence of the other.</note> He who knows these things also knows *Tereniabin* <note>original: "Tereniabin"; a Persian term for "manna" or a sweet dew found on plants, often used in alchemical preparations.</note> and the Nettle. Therefore, the Philosopher who knows one thing in one form knows the same thing in another—save for the difference in outward shape, and nothing else. Thus, these are not four separate things, but one. Who shall judge the rain? The Astronomer. Who shall judge the dew? The Astronomer. Who shall judge Talc? The Philosopher. Who shall judge *Cachmia*? <note>original: "Cachmiam"; a term for the slag or dross of metals, or sometimes ores like cobalt or bismuth.</note> The Philosopher. 

<margin>
The Philosopher judges all things.
</margin>

He who judges one of these is not ignorant of the other. And although their names are indeed diverse, the arts and sciences are by no means separate. For there is one essence in all things. From this, simple Philosophers are made, who are skilled and experienced in only one thing. But these men are worth nothing. Others are skilled in two things, but they too have no value. Even those skilled in three are nothing. Only those skilled in the four <note>Paracelsus refers to his "Four Pillars" of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note> can grasp the conclusion that is at hand: that is, Medicine is the end and the limit of all these. For what use is it 

<margin>
A rebuke of physicians.
</margin>

for an Astronomer to know the rains and the snow if he does not also see clearly what purpose they serve? Thus, he is worth nothing. He ought also to know the properties of his subject; without this, he is otherwise a nobody. The Physician constitutes the whole of this knowledge. Now, however, you must note that until now there have been no complete or certain Physicians. For they have wandered astray in Philosophy; nor have they yet discovered what tin is, what flows within it, or what provides its heat. They have never treated any of these matters, and yet they boast of being Doctors and Philosophers. If they are ignorant of such things, they will be much less capable of investigating what such diseases are. For first of all, it is necessary for them to know from where tin, copper, gold, and iron are born, how they are made, what their attributes are, and to what diseases they are subject, and what afflictions they are forced to endure. <note>Paracelsus believed that metals and minerals were "alive" in a sense and could suffer their own versions of disease (like rust or corruption), which mirrored human ailments.</note> And even if they were to know this, they would still know only a single member in the body of man. If they must learn about a single metal with such great sweat, with what difficulty will they attain the remaining seven, the remaining 

<margin>
A thousand metals.
</margin>

twenty-four, and all the rest, of which there are thousands? That which is most necessary of all in Philosophy, and in Medicine itself, they neglect and omit.

Now, as for what they say regarding the doctrine of the ancient Philosophers—that all metals are generated from Mercury and 

<margin>
Metals are not from sulfur and mercury alone.
</margin>

Sulfur; and likewise, that stone is not born from pure earth—how shamelessly they lie! For who is there anywhere who has found the matter of metals to be only sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; another name for Mercury.</note>, when in fact all metals and all minerals consist of three things, not two? <note>Paracelsus is introducing his famous theory of the *Tria Prima*: that all matter is composed of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. The traditional view held there were only two components.</note> Therefore, this error is manifest. But even their Philosophy itself is openly deceptive; for it teaches nothing of their generation, their end, or other matters. All these things ought to have been thoroughly known to them. Just as they boast that they can know the essences and medicines of all diseases from urine and the pulse, they ought also to make their judgments certain in these matters, so that they might similarly discern the "urine" and "pulse" of the heavens, the earth, and the air. But they have discovered neither the one nor the other. Their Philosophy also asserts that no stones are generated from pure earth; yet stones are never generated from earth anyway, but from water. This is their genital and native element. Therefore, these men are wavering and ignorant of philosophy. Even if this Philosophy of theirs was written by Aristotle, Albertus, and others, who would believe these liars? They do not speak from Philosophy itself—that is, from the Light of Nature—but from mere fantasy. Just as they brought the "four humors" into Medicine from that same source, they have likewise drawn that lie about Mercury and Sulfur with no greater success. One does not fit better than the other. They constantly appeal to Albertus and Thomas. But it is not Albertus, nor Thomas, but you yourselves who will have to stand your ground on this. For Albertus did not drink this doctrine from the Holy Spirit, but rather from idle speculation. Thomas is in the same category, as are Hermes and Archelaus. <note>A list of major medieval and ancient authorities: Aristotle, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, Hermes Trismegistus, and Archelaus.</note> None of you 

<margin>
Where philosophy should be directed.
</margin>

is unaware that the doctrines and arts of this profession are not to be credited to the Holy Spirit, but rather to the Light of Nature. Where, then, is this found, if not in nature? For example: the Holy Spirit teaches faith. Therefore, He is faith. Likewise, these things are nature. Therefore, they must be taught and learned from Nature. They were not established in the Spirit, but in Nature itself. Therefore, you shall be informed about them from nature—of which Albertus, Thomas, Aristotle, Avicenna, or Actuarius had no knowledge other than what was speculative and imaginary. Since it is of such great importance to know what nature is, the foundation of Medicine is proposed to you here with the greatest right. For a Physician ought to know better than his own fingernails what melts in lead...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires a deep philosophical understanding of nature's unity, particularly the correspondence between minerals and the human body. He critiques traditional authorities like Aristotle and Albertus Magnus for relying on speculation rather than the "Light of Nature," specifically challenging their "two-element" theory of metals.</summary>

<header>THE SECOND PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.</header>

# THE SECOND PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.

<margin>Give to the physician who knows.</margin>...how it may be liquefied, or what may be dissolved in wax. What is it that exists so hard in a Diamond? <note>original: "Adamante"</note> What is so soft in Alabaster? If a man knows these things, he might also be able to say what can cause an Abscess <note>original: "Apostema"</note> to ripen or stay immature, or what stirs up carbuncles and the plague. Beyond these things, he can know nothing at all. Therefore, all those writings are false and erroneous, whatever has been handed down concerning these and other diseases. For they have flowed out of speculation, not out of Philosophy. And because those authors were ignorant of Philosophy, their entire labor is in vain. Indeed, they have become like a peasant who threshes the empty straw after the ears of grain are gone, hoping to strike out the wheat. He does it with a good heart, certainly, but the labor is useless. The same is true of those physicians who describe diseases of this sort and yet are ignorant of Philosophy itself; they possess neither art nor any science, indulging only their own fantasies and speculation. Finally, I do not know by what seal their success is confirmed, for all their sick patients bear witness that they are—to speak subtly—fools. To put it more bluntly, the patients call them rascals. Yet these lying Masters or School-regulators, Correctors, Proctors, Visitors, Freshmen, <note>original: "Beani"; a term for new students or novices, often used mockingly by Paracelsus.</note> and Fathers, etc., if they turn into physicians, they behave no differently; they have this one familiar habit.

<margin>John of Garland. Aristotle’s *Meteorics* are examined.</margin>They have one or two books of the *Meteorics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Meteorologica*, a treatise on natural philosophy which Paracelsus considered theoretical nonsense.</note> with many commentaries. These are no better than what was handed down by *John of Garland* <note>A 13th-century grammarian and scholar; Paracelsus uses him here as a symbol of outdated, pedantic academic tradition.</note> who commented on the second part of Alexander. For what are Aristotle’s *Meteorics*? Nothing but fantasy. The reason is this: there is nothing anywhere under heaven where such Exhalations and Impressions can be proven, except that it is mere fantasy and "cyclopean" <note>In this context, "cyclopean" refers to something massive but clumsy or blind.</note> reasoning. That study of Meteors is therefore nothing but a fiction, upon which they nevertheless build their "Masters," who themselves praise and defend these things, though they do not quite understand what they are defending. Yet these men will not lightly provoke a war with me on this matter. For it does not greatly worry them whether a thing is true or false. They are accustomed to doing the same in other matters as well: they have nothing more at heart or in mind than how to extort money through trifles. Whether they know or are ignorant makes no difference—at least let the money be produced, so that the "Lord Doctor" can struggle out of poverty <margin>An exceptional and lengthy rebuke of physicians.</margin> and walk about politely in the streets for the sake of appearances, and his wife likewise can shine brilliantly alongside others. Even if the kitchen of such women is quite cold <note>A metaphor for having no food or being poor despite outward appearances.</note>, they must nevertheless be commended and adorned in the streets, in the church, and at dances—just like a cat about to relieve itself. Physicians of this kind keep their art in whatever place they happen to be, nor do they care much whether they have a foundation and art, or not. For they establish fantasy itself as their foundation.

On the contrary, all this labor of mine is so that a solid foundation may be placed in the art—not built upon "accidental masters," not upon mortar-grinders, <note>likely referring to apothecaries or those who merely mix ingredients without understanding.</note> nor upon hungry convent-dwellers and provosts. For their foundation is nothing other than this: *"He is a learned Master. He is reading Physics now, and this past year he commented on the Heavens and the World. This man is going to turn out to be a good physician. This Convent-dweller will be a Light and a chosen vessel"* (a fool, I think). However, you ought not to bestow any other title upon Convent-dwellers of this sort than to say: *"He is a boor, and a horned beast; he knows nothing, understands nothing, and is only a 'Good Father' fit for wearing a doctoral hood; <note>original: "lirippippio"; the long tail of a graduate's hood, used here to mock academic status.</note> he is stingy and grasping, and a cut-purse."* As he was made in the bursary, <note>The treasury or administrative office of a university.</note> so he has decided to remain in Medicine. But if this is the foundation upon which your medicine is planted and fixed: woe to those sick people who fall into the hands of these Freshmen. They would be handled more gently by the wash-house workers.

Now this is much more serious: that these physicians who oppose me use neither my Philosophy nor that of others, but make a kind of secession from all learned men. Thus, they must be squeezed and repressed in turn, so that neither the Theologian, nor the Jurist, nor the Artist, nor the Astronomer, nor the Philosopher, nor the Alchemist, nor anyone else has any business with them, nor they with others. For this is the veil through which their imposture is not revealed. If things are so, it is necessary that their art be practiced entirely by a kind of force, through violently extorted faith, so that whatever they say is promptly believed, no matter what scripture eventually testifies. If, by some chance, they heal one sick person in a year, they sing about it for a whole decade—even if the patient would have recovered sooner on his own than through the help they provided.

With such crimes and triumphs, as well as with your trifles, and your running about, and your "faithful visitation," you [seek to win] faith for yourselves...

<page-num>231</page-num>
-> ON PHILOSOPHY. <-
<meta>catchword: I am (sum)</meta>

### ON PHILOSOPHY.

...you build and establish for yourselves. Indeed, all these labors are merely for the sake of the kitchen. <note>original: "culinarij"; Paracelsus uses this term to mock doctors who practice medicine only to earn a living—to fill their bellies—rather than to heal.</note> They run about for the sake of money, not for the sake of the health of the sick. For if you possessed genuine and noble remedies at home, what need would there be, I ask, for your running about, your inspections of urine, <note>The practice of uroscopy (interpreting health through urine) was a standard academic tool that Paracelsus viewed as prone to fraud.</note> and other similar works of the staff? All of these things, however, prove that an unlearned physician is skilled and knowledgeable in nothing. Where, finally, does Philosophy teach you to treat the sick in such a way? Where did you learn that from nature? Rather, you do such things out of your own lack of skill and ignorance, so that you may stir up some opinion of diligence and hard work regarding yourselves. Thus it happens that the peasants are persuaded that you do such things out of art, when in fact they arise from sheer ignorance. Even if you were Aristotle himself, or Porphyry, or Albertus, or Avicenna, or Galen, <note>These figures—Aristotle the philosopher, Porphyry the logician, Albertus Magnus the theologian, and Avicenna and Galen the medical authorities—formed the backbone of the traditional university curriculum Paracelsus sought to dismantle.</note> you could not show even the smallest bit of a foundation in which a sick man might dare to trust safely. For who would easily believe in impostures and lies? No one. Therefore, your entire foundation is no foundation at all. For it does not proceed from the evidence of Nature, but from empty fantasy, handed down and funneled as a heritage from one person to another. Whatever is introduced and applied outside of evident and conspicuous Philosophy is all in vain. And whatever Medicine is administered without that foundation is mere imposture and a doubtful risk. Indeed, all their prescriptions, both physical <note>original: "Physica"; here referring to internal medicine.</note> and surgical, are placed upon a wavering scale. And unless they occasionally stumbled upon good fortune, or a gift from heaven, or a suitable time, and a favorable nature, they would cut the throats of everyone they attempted to cure by the same pattern and send them to the underworld. For there is nothing in them but the most destructive and fatal lack of skill, and an ignorant foundation. And just as an executioner lives among honest men, so do these men live with their "art" among the learned. 

<margin>PHILO- SOPHIA</margin>
<note>Note regarding the harassment of Physicians.</note> This is certainly bitter to you now, that your foundation and your Philosophy are rolled out into the mud, and you along with them. Even the sows that wallow you in the filth will find nothing suitable or tasty in you except sheer dung—that is, there is nothing useful in you. Dung is better than everything else you have. Snakes and salamanders stable and nest in your red hoods. <note>Red hoods were the traditional academic dress for Doctors of Medicine.</note>

<margin><unclear>The doctor's dress</unclear></margin>
How great a disgrace will it be to you if, cast into the mud, you are mocked by the taunts of common schoolboys? For you have no foundation in Medicine, but it is built upon the sand. Your status and dignity were once sublime; it shone like glitter, and the whole world judged you to be made of silver and gold and honored you at great expense. Now, however, it will become clear to everyone that all those things were nothing other than glitter and "gold-sand." <note>original: "ammochrysos"; a mineral that looks like gold but is worthless.</note> O Talc, then indeed you keep watch in the Academies! O *Cachymia*, <note>A term for an imperfect or immature metallic ore.</note> then you dwell in Leipzig—you, whom I had believed were hiding in the lungs? O Marcasite, O Magnesia! <note>Paracelsus uses these mineral names (Talcum, Marchasita, Magnesia) as metaphors for things that look precious but are chemically common or deceptive.</note> Thus you glitter alongside gold and resemble gold no differently than Marcasite does. In the fire, however, you are sheer sulfur, and pitch, and arsenic, and antimony. And so, by your copper-like splendor and external pretense, you deceive. In the same way, the sick are also deceived by you. For they are persuaded that you are Physicians, when you are mere mockers. This is *Cadmia*, <note>Zinc ore or calamine, used to color copper to look like gold.</note> which produces brass and tints copper, and yet it is mud. So also you are tinted, and yet you remain "horned" ones. <note>An insult implying stupidity or being cuckolded by nature.</note> O calamine, you will finally become Orpiment, <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; an arsenic sulfide mineral with a golden-yellow color.</note> and at that time a fool will diligently scale you, and pull off one skin after another, so that you may continually shine and glisten. This certainly pleases the peasants. Since you know this, you gratify them all the more. From these things it follows that a Physician must be ornately dressed, walking about cinched in a long, knotted robe with a red hood, so that everything is red. Why red? That color is pleasing to the peasants. Indeed, it is necessary for the hair to be combed and covered by a red cap, and the fingers covered with rings—set with Turkey-stone, <note>Turquoise.</note> Emerald, and Sapphire (if not true gems, then at least glass ones). In this way, some confidence can be stirred up in the sick person toward you. Indeed, there is such remarkable power in these stones themselves that they inflame the hearts of the sick with a certain love toward you: "O my dear, O my Lord Doctor." Is this your Medicine? Is this that celebrated Hippocratic oath? Is this surgery? Is this art? Is this the foundation? O glitter! Truly glitter, which, hidden in the sand, feigns gold and silver by its splendor, as is well known to miners. This truly is to walk about as a Doctor for the sake of appearances. He, forsooth, is learned, he is modest, in his gait...

<summary>Paracelsus denounces the academic physicians of his time, arguing that their "science" is merely a deceptive performance of fancy clothes and mineral-like glitter intended to trick the poor. He contrasts their outward prestige with their inward ignorance of the true, hidden forces of nature.</summary>

<page-num>232</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.</header>

...is a geometric calculation; he is affable toward men, repeatedly humbles himself, and greets everyone he meets. O, you Pharisee! <note>A reference to the biblical Pharisees, whom Paracelsus uses as a symbol for religious and academic hypocrisy—those who follow the letter of the law but lack its spirit.</note> If you knew the things you boast of, you would not be a Pharisee. O, you Simon! <note>Likely a reference to Simon Magus, associated with "simony" or the buying of spiritual influence; here, it refers to those who buy their way into medical authority.</note> This is a heavy and great burden among men: that they do not cease to commit evils until they betray and publicly expose their own disgrace, giving others the opportunity to spread and broadcast those same faults.

<margin>Where the physician should seek the human being.</margin>
Now, however, so that you all may know what Philosophy is—the foundation that supports the entire building of Medicine—recall from what was said above: it is fitting for a physician to search for the human being in the earth, in the water, in the fire, and in the air. In these, he should not look for four different humans, but for the one unique human within them all. He must learn from these elements what happens to a person: in what way he ascends, descends, is exalted, or is saddened; where he is sick, and where he is healthy. If he has thoroughly known and learned this **external human**, then at last he may commit himself to the faculty of Medicine. He may then turn the external human into the **internal**, and recognize the internal within the external. But he must take diligent care not to learn anything from the internal human alone. For there, nothing is found but deception and death. <note>Paracelsus argues that the "External Man" (the Macrocosm or the world of nature) is the true blueprint for the "Internal Man" (the human body). To study the body in isolation—especially through the dissection of corpses—is, in his view, a dead-end path.</note>

<margin>The external human is the mirror of the internal.</margin>
For before the internal afflictions could be known without the help of the external human, how many cemeteries would be needed to prove the art? And yet, these physicians rely on that very foundation, hoping that through such "experience" <note>Paracelsus often mocks "experience" when it means the trial-and-error of academic doctors on living or dead bodies.</note> they can arrive at the art. But which is better? To be a teacher, or to be a robber? Let every prudent man consider for himself whether God willed for the health of men on this earth to be procured through such robberies—especially since in God no robbery, no deceit, and no falsehood is ever found. Yet they babble that God disposed Medicine to be this way, and that a physician must enter into the inner secrets of the art in this manner (namely, through homicides). So they believe. But it was by no means ordained so by God; rather, God intended for the physician to be learned and recognized through **that one** whom it is permitted to corrupt or kill without any sin. <note>The "one" he refers to is the Macrocosm (Nature). Paracelsus believes we should "dissect" the elements and the stars to understand disease, rather than cutting open human beings.</note> If we first know him, and then perfect in the human being what we have learned, then we are skilled in all things beforehand, and we do not run the risk of killing the patient. Make your own consciences the judges of this, and allow them enough time and breath to judge my writings fairly. If you learn from both the interior and the exterior, then your own conscience will convict you that you are not entering through the door, but are descending into the house through the roof, sneaking into the art through robbery.

<margin>Academies are like robbers.</margin>
All the Academies of Germany, and likewise the Universities of Italy, descend into Medicine in this way—through the roof. O, you deceivers! O, you robbers and thieves! You put on a cloak over this entrance of yours; that is, you hide your wickedness.

Now, it is right that the Anatomy of this **external human** be entirely engraved upon the physician, and so universally impressed upon him that he neglects not even a single hair of the head, but sees and understands everything with the utmost clarity.

<margin>How remedies are to be prescribed.</margin>
From this it also follows that the prescription of remedies must be so ordered that member corresponds to member, and one is always directed toward the other—not according to "degrees" 1, 2, 3, or 4, or according to a beginning, middle, and end. <note>The Galenic system of medicine, which Paracelsus opposed, classified medicines and diseases by four degrees of intensity (e.g., "hot in the second degree").</note> For that art of describing recipes according to degrees is false and fraudulent; it is harmful, such that many homicides are introduced through it. For neither diseases nor remedies ought to be forced into such an order; indeed, nature itself trembles and shakes at being confined within such degrees. The true order of nature commands that Anatomy be applied to Anatomy, and member be referred to member—not "stronger," "weaker," "stronger," and "stronger again."

<margin>Diseases and remedies are not graded.</margin>
For diseases are not graded, just as remedies themselves are not. To say they are graded in the "first degree" refers to one member. To say they progress in the "middle degree" refers to another member. To say they are graded at the "end of this degree" refers to yet another member. It is not, as they say, that one member equals one degree. A "degree" is nothing other than speculative and fanatical **Beanishness**. <note>original: "Beanismus"; a term derived from "Beanus," a nickname for a new, unpolished university student. Paracelsus uses it to call academic theories "sophomoric" or "childish."</note> Likewise, what they cast into the second degree is one member, and what they refer to the third degree is another. From this it follows that in this division, member must be referred to member, not degree to degree. For if one member suffers, and then a second, and then a third: then that degree is not "one." For there, three passions exist, requiring entirely threefold remedies—constituted not in one degree, not in one complexion or quality, but in three **arcana**. <note>term: <term>arcana</term> (secret/hidden powers); in Paracelsian medicine, an arcanum is the essential healing virtue of a substance that acts directly on a specific disease, rather than balancing "humors."</note> And this discovery, that...

<summary>Paracelsus defines true Philosophy as the study of the "External Man" (Nature/Macrocosm) and condemns university doctors as "robbers" who learn through the sinful dissection of humans rather than the divine study of the elements. He further rejects the Galenic system of "degrees" in medicine, arguing that remedies must specifically match the anatomy of the disease through hidden "arcana."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s critique of the scholastic medical tradition. Having argued on the previous page that a physician must seek the "human being" within the four elements of nature (the macrocosm) to understand the internal human (the microcosm), he now attacks the rigid Galenic system of "degrees" (hot, cold, moist, dry) used by university doctors, proposing instead a medicine based on the "arcanum" and the anatomical correspondence between nature and man.</meta>

<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>ON PHILOSOPHY.</header>
<sig>V 3</sig>

# ON PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The classification of degrees is amateurish.</margin>
The system of degrees <note>original: "graduum"; refers to the Galenic system of categorizing medicines by four degrees of heat, cold, etc.</note> which the university doctors have put forward for the purpose of ranking medicines is purely amateurish <note>original: "Beanica," referring to "beania," the rough hazing rituals for first-year university students; Paracelsus uses it to call the doctors "freshmen" or "know-nothings."</note>. For if a disease takes hold of someone, and that disease is "hot," and he is cured by something "cold," that healing power must by no means be attributed to that coldness, but rather to the **arcanum** <note>The "arcanum" is Paracelsus’s term for the hidden, spiritual healing essence within a substance, which acts beyond physical properties like temperature.</note>. For it is this arcanum that does the work, not the cold. It is the same as if a man were required to perform a task: how would heat or cold help him do it? Not at all. What does heat contribute to the voice? How does cold help the ears? Nothing at all. These qualities—heat and cold—are present in all things, yet they perform no actual work. And here lies that ignorant
<margin>The error and ignorance of physicians.</margin>
invention which they urge and hammer home in the Academies. In this, they have forgotten what was most necessary: they posit only one kind of heat and one kind of cold. Yet they are forced to admit that even if there were only one heat and one cold, a single and identical operation does not exist; rather, one virtue exists in this cold thing, and another different virtue exists in that hot thing. From this, it is clear that they are hallucinating when they apply the cold to the hot and the hot to the cold. Whatever happens or succeeds in these cases must be credited entirely to the arcanum, of which they themselves have never discovered anything. Therefore, I can more rightly affirm that a bodily
<margin>Member is cured by member.</margin>
organ is "owed" to its corresponding organ <note>The theory that external nature contains counterparts to human organs.</note> according to the method of external and internal Anatomy; degrees should by no means be compared to degrees. Medicine ought to be such as this; it should not fit your invented theories. For this Philosophy is a twin: so that you may know the **external human**, and through him, learn of the **Microcosm** <note>The human being as a "little world" that mirrors the "macrocosm" of the universe.</note>. In this way, you might truly be called a Physician founded upon solid rock—not founded upon moss and swampland, which is what your doctrine smells and tastes of. Phooey, you stinking freshman from Meissen! Clean yourself up at last and get in the bath.

<margin>Why a scorpion cures a scorpion.</margin>
For the sake of this delicate Anatomy, you must now also take up and understand diseases in such a way that you know why a scorpion cures the venom of a scorpion: namely, because it shares the same Anatomy as the other. Thus the external human is the Anatomy of the internal, and the latter of the former. In this way, Arsenic heals Arsenic; thus Realgar <note>A red arsenic ore.</note> heals Realgar; thus heart heals heart, lung heals lung, spleen heals spleen—not the spleen of a cow, nor the brain of a pig, but the brain of a human: that is, the brain which exists as the **external brain** of the **internal human**. From this Anatomy, Philosophy proceeds: and this is Philosophy itself—the very thing from which a Physician is made and born.

I ask all of you physicians: how great is the person of the external human? How great are his arcana, virtues, properties, essences, and powers? What, then, is your speculation and invention? To cleanse, to wipe away, to know a thing rightly from its foundation: from this, you Surgeons and Physicians ought to be born and profess your craft—not from your insane heads, in which nothing but seduction and error lies hidden. Both of you, Physician and Surgeon, must proceed from one single Philosophy and be undivided in your foundation; you shall only be separated in your Practice. Yet each must be both Physician and Surgeon at once, not divided as you are in practice. Go on then, continue to say that your Theophrastus is no Philosopher, nor a Physician, but only a Surgeon—he who is nevertheless destined to be the patron and prince of you all. Consider your blindness rightly and fundamentally, and judge everything according to your conscience. In doing
<margin>Physicians rebuked. Theophrastus the greatest of physicians.</margin>
so, you will find that Theophrastus himself is the greatest of all physicians, who, in the school of Medicine, is going to beat you all with his rod <note>original: "ferulis," referring to a schoolmaster's switch or cane.</note>. Meanwhile, no one forbids you from saying—along with the Jews (for you are indeed Jews in medicine) <note>Paracelsus uses "Jews" here as a derogatory metaphor for those he considers legalistic, stubborn, or "enemies of the truth," reflecting the common prejudices of 16th-century polemics.</note>—that I am a deceiver of the people, that I have a Devil, that I am possessed, that I was taught by Necromancy, that I am a Magician. For the Jews themselves threw all these same charges at Christ. What shall I say?
<margin>How great Theophrastus is.</margin>
I am indeed so great that you are not worthy to untie the laces of my shoes. Let nothing else persuade you but this: whether I be a Geomancer, or a Necromancer, or a Hydromancer, or a Magus—you all shall at last be rolled under my feet. And though you may drag out all your "arts," you will not be safe enough from me. I will send you back home to the Devil whom you say lives in me. For he is yours, not mine. But such is the nature of all impostors, "belly-Pharisees" <note>original: "ventripharisaeorum"; those who use religion or profession only to fill their stomachs.</note>, and hypocrites: they protect themselves with such a fragile shield. For that which is in you, and by which you are possessed, is the very thing you accuse me of. But it matters little. You city asses and "musk-doctors" <note>original: "Moschiatri," likely referring to physicians who rely on expensive perfumes and ointments rather than true cures.</note> of Princes, you "glory-doctors"—nonetheless, you are to be exposed to the whole world. You give testimony about yourselves that you are of this kind, and your testimony in this is honest and just. For you practice a chosen and enormous wickedness when you say:

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the Galenic system of "degrees," arguing that healing comes from the "arcanum" and the anatomical correspondence between the macrocosm and microcosm. He asserts his superiority over university doctors, whom he accuses of hypocrisy and ignorance of nature's true philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophy of Medicine, Arcanum, Microcosm, Like cures Like, Medical polemic, Anatomy, Paracelsus, Galenic critique</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the first treatise of the *Second Paragranum*. Paracelsus continues his attack on traditional Galenic medicine, specifically mocking the idea that certain herbs "purge" specific humors (like black bile or phlegm) based on academic theory rather than the essential nature of the elements. He introduces the concept of the fourfold nature of all things—metals, plants, and humans—as the true foundation of medical knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.</header>

### THE SECOND PARAGRANUM, TREATISE I.

You say that **Lapis Lazuli** <note>A blue semi-precious stone used in ancient and medieval medicine, believed to purge "melancholy."</note> purges Melancholy, that **Hellebore** purges phlegm, and **Rhubarb** purges choler. Who, indeed, revealed to you that these things are so? The matter is certainly easily settled. If those things you teach concerning degrees, compositions, and arrangements were true, who, I ask, would ever be sick? But because those theories of yours are worth nothing, who can ever be healthy?

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
But lest I detain my listeners longer than is right, I shall bring an end to this Philosophy of mine in the manner already stated: namely, so they may know that unless they embrace within themselves those things contained in this philosophy, they must by no means descend into the practice of Medicine. Let them thoroughly weigh in their minds the works of their own teachers—that is, how they provide no help to their sick, heal no one, and destroy many. All these things ought to serve as a commentary for them, so that afterwards they might attend more accurately to the teachers' own doctrine, seeing how a false Physician is hidden beneath it; thus, they may avoid falling into the footsteps of their own deceivers through negligence. Judge their doctrine for yourselves; do not wait for their own judgment. For they never condemn themselves; instead, they constantly attribute so much justice to themselves that there is always a surplus of it. I write these things to you so that you are not led astray. I beg you to read and reread them diligently—not with envy or hatred, since you are students of Medicine by good intention. Learn something even from my books, so that you may make a sound judgment concerning both sides. For the total judgment and choice must rest with you. For as long as you have not progressed far enough to recognize that the four Elements are similar <note>Paracelsus refers to the "archetypal" elements that exist across different realms of nature.</note> and to hold those same elements as the **Microcosm** <note>The "Little World"—the human being seen as a reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>, you will never be able to reach the true foundation.

<margin>Metals in all Elements.</margin>
For you have metals in water, you have metals in the earth, and in fire, and in the air. You have **Mercury** in water, and a similar one in the earth which is "bloody" <note>original: "sanguineus"; likely referring to cinnabar or the "red" state of mercury in alchemical processes.</note>, and a similar one in fire, which is Mercury existing out of itself; and in the air, you have **Manna** <note>In Paracelsian thought, Manna was often considered an "aerial" or celestial sulfur/mercury that fell from the heavens.</note>.

<margin>The fourfold Mercury.</margin>
Thus, there exist four Mercuries and four metals; and in man, they are of a single operation.

<margin>The fourfold Man.</margin>
For Man is fourfold; and Medicine is also fourfold. Therefore, member corresponds to member. Thus, there is a fourfold snow, a fourfold **Melissa** <note>Lemon balm.</note>, a fourfold **Tereniabin** <note>A Persian-derived term for a type of medicinal manna gathered from plants.</note>, and a fourfold **Amethyst**. Unless you are properly instructed in these matters, you will by no means attain your profession without disgrace and imposture. For you must know the four types of **Celandine**, the four of **Verbena**, the four of **Angelica**, as well as **Anthos** <note>Rosemary flower.</note> and **Antheras** <note>The medicinal parts of flowers, specifically the extracts of roses.</note>. If you know these, it is permitted to you by every right to enter into Medicine. For in these lies the knowledge of the heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, brain, and all the members of the body. No truth will ever be found in you if you do not follow the figure designated by nature itself. Just as you see that nothing exists within man that has not been designated externally, whether regarding honesty or falsehood, etc. Nature marks him. But Nature is so subtle that she cannot mark these types of Doctors, Teachers, Masters, and similar Physicians upon their bodies. The reason is that they no longer remain in the womb during the formation of their bodies. If they were to be born with that kind of fantasy and stupid faculty, you would certainly see very wondrous shapes with which nature would have marked them. But now, so that they might not lack their own signs, even though they have already exited the maternal womb, Nature marks them through **magic** in this way: she dresses them in certain garments, hoods, etc. Thus, they carry the signs of fools. And not only the signs of fools, but also of deceivers—Pharisaic <note>In the sense of being hypocritical or obsessed with outward show rather than inner truth.</note> habits, ornaments, fringes, rings, and other baubles, medals, tiaras, and hoods. These external ornaments do not arise from the foundation of Medicine, but from the foundation of the light of nature, which thus marks its foolish deserters. It is true that Nature marks a man. But it is a great thing that they can so industriously hide their signs, taking up one after another. If they were to receive their form anew from nature—along with their art, wisdom, and whatever they know or can do—they would, by God, exhibit a figure wonderful beyond measure. Arabia herself does not nourish more wondrous monsters among all her camels and buffaloes. Indeed, there would eventually be a total lack of shapes, so great is the number of these "cuckoos" <note>original: "cuculorú"; a pun on "cucullus" (hood) and "cuculus" (cuckoo bird/fool).</note>, each of whom is owed his own peculiar sign. It would certainly be a sight worth seeing if such a spectacle were offered to anyone. Magic, however, includes them all under one category, and attaches hoods or caps to them. For his own club or cap is enough for every fool.

<summary>Paracelsus concludes by arguing that true medicine requires understanding the fourfold nature of elements and the "correspondences" between nature and the human body. He mocks academic physicians, claiming nature "marks" them as fools by their ostentatious academic robes and hoods since their inner stupidity isn't visible on their skin.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the second treatise of the *Second Paragranum*. Having established the philosophical foundations of medicine in the first treatise (centered on the four elements), Paracelsus now transitions to the second pillar of his medical theory: Astronomy. He argues that a physician cannot understand human health without understanding how the celestial bodies are reflected within the human "microcosm."</meta>

<page-num>235</page-num>
<header>ON ASTRONOMY.</header>

# TREATISE II.
## ON ASTRONOMY.

**I**f, therefore, man is to be presented as a whole in his composition: you must first know how his place is to be recognized, and how you ought to understand the bodies of the firmament within the body of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—a core Paracelsian concept that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>. For the stars of the body derive their condition, nature, properties, essence, motion, state, and part just like the external ones; they are divided only in form—that is, in substance. For just as it is in the ether, so it is in the Microcosm and in nature itself: both things are one, one single essence. Since, however, my purpose here is to treat the locations of the Planets and stars of the entire firmament which are necessary for a Physician to know, I shall at least provide an Anatomy of both essences, as much of their locations as of their nature.

<margin>The stars wander freely.</margin>
Beyond this, indeed, it is impossible to praise a Physician. Know, therefore, that a star in the heavens has no body. For it neither lies, nor hangs, nor stands; but it poises itself freely, like a feather in the air. This must be understood similarly in man according to nature and its course or motion. And although one thing may hang from another, and it may be one body that stands or lies, etc., that physical attachment is of no more consideration to the Physician than if it did not exist at all. For that belongs to the earthly nature. Nothing of these physical things should block the Physician's path here; rather, he shall recognize the Anatomy just as if nothing were present from which a part might hang or stand.

<margin>How the stars of the body are to be regarded.</margin>
But by the same reasoning that all stars in the heavens are free and depend on nothing else, so the Physician must know the Anatomy in the human body, and must not say: "this hangs from that," "this depends on another," "this sits in that," or "that in another." These are matters of location, not of dependence; they do not advance the Physician, but hinder him. And although you may find upon investigation that a certain vein extends from one part of the body to another, and that this attached vein carries something from one substance into the other, yet you must not take or understand the matter in that way. Rather, just as you see in the heavens that one star affects another even without a physical connection of veins, so too you must not admit the visible passage of veins in the body as the primary cause. For what constitutes the science of a Physician is nothing other than what the heavens themselves show him: that is, just as the radiance of the Sun penetrates glass without substance or body, so the stars also relate to one another; and so it happens equally in man. And that which is not a body, is the disease. And that which is a body, is not the disease.

<margin>Air is a body and not a body.</margin>
You know that air is the body of the firmament. For it exists within the firmament. Now, it is not a "body" in the solid sense, and yet it is that which supports the star, and no one touches it.

<margin>Chaos carries the stars.</margin>
Such is nature and its mystery: that <term>chaos</term> <note>In Paracelsus’s vocabulary, "chaos" refers to the atmosphere or the invisible "ether" that fills space and sustains life, rather than "disorder."</note> supports and carries the stars, the Sun, and the Moon; yet we see no chair or porter carrying them.

<margin>The yolk is carried by the white.</margin>
Now consider the Yolk, which is to be understood similarly to the stars. It is carried by the white, which is its "air." The white, however, exists as something visible and tangible. So it is arranged in nature as well, so that the chaos in an egg is visible, while in the stars it is invisible.

<margin>Where earth and water are carried.</margin>
Thus you ought to know that nothing else is to be understood regarding the sphere of earth and water. It is round, and no one sees what carries it. And we, who are carried by it, go and walk in that which supports it—that is, we walk in the chaos, because chaos sustains that sphere lest it should fall or slip by chance. The Yolk in an egg cannot tilt toward any part or move from its place, but remains motionless in the middle of its white. Thus, just as the Yolk is compelled to rest in the white, so by that same force the earth and water are held immovably in their own "white." For even if that white is clear and limpid, no one sees it and no one touches it, yet it is present, and it is that "white" which sustains the earth. And this is the chaos.

<margin>The chick from the white.</margin>
We walk in this in the same way that a chick is hatched from the white, not from the Yolk. For its life is from the white, its motion is in the white, and in the white it both becomes and lives. Similarly, you ought to know that we humans also walk and live in this chaos like a chick. That was created for the chick according to its nature; for the Yolk according to its nature; and for man according to his nature. Thus the egg remains an egg in its white, and the earth remains earth in its chaos. Therefore, know (since the "place" supplies us with so much, and there is a distinction in the place itself, and yet it is one thing—the egg and the world—and they are two) that the Microcosm must be understood in the same appearance, which I posit to be separate from the air and stars—that is, to be that very thing itself.

<margin>All stars are present in man.</margin>
Truly, in man are the Sun and Moon, all the Planets, and all the stars, and the whole chaos. Regarding this matter, I desire to hand down to you more and more abundant things.

<sig>V 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: Scire (To know)</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus introduces the celestial pillar of medicine, arguing that the human body (the microcosm) contains the same astral forces as the heavens. He uses the analogy of an egg—where the yolk is suspended in the white—to explain how the earth and humans are suspended in and nourished by "chaos" (the atmosphere).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Second Treatise on Astronomy. Paracelsus moves from the general principle that stars are within the human body to explaining the mechanics of how celestial influences interact with the physical form, while launching a sharp critique of traditional anatomical authorities like Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

<page-num>236</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE SECOND PARAGRANUM.</header>

<margin>
The Sun works through harmony.
</margin>
You ought to know, therefore, that the heavens act upon us. It must be understood in what way they act upon us. The Sun from above acts on nothing through a solid wall, but acts at least through its ordinary means—that is, through a window set into the wall. Likewise, the air too must enter and exit through windows. In enclosed things, no operation of the stars is completed. Therefore, if a "window" is needed: see how all these things occur around the man himself. He is enclosed in skin. The skin covers him all around. Thus, the stars could seemingly work nothing within him. Yet now, understand why and how the stars *do* work within him.

<margin>
All the stars are within man.
</margin>
Just as the Sun penetrates through glass into a palace without the glass being damaged at all: in the same way, the Sun also penetrates the body. But as glass also refracts the brightness of the Sun—so that it is not as perfect inside as it is outside—so too a medium lies between the stars and man, which diminishes and breaks their powers.

<margin>
How stars are refracted through the skin.
</margin>
And just as a veil is drawn before windows, so man is also disposed to add to and indulge in such works. Now, besides these things, it is necessary for something to exist in the body that may receive the stars which are to work within the body. For if nothing existed in the body to receive the stars, they would be unable to penetrate inside at all. For example: the Earth receives the Sun. The reason is that a certain attractive force exists in it, by which the Sun is drawn. For thus you see that the earth drinks in the rain, while rocks do not drink it in: because rain is useful to the earth, not to rocks. Thus, if the body itself were a rock in respect to the stars, then the heavens would be unsuitable for the body, just as rain is to a rock. But the matter is not so: rather, the body draws the heavens to itself. You ought to know that this thing which attracts the heavens is a divine ordination.

<margin>
Man is from the four elements.
</margin>
For if man came forth made of the four elements—not according to <term>complexion</term> <note>The traditional medical theory that health is governed by the balance of four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note>, as some say, but according to his own nature, motion, essence, fruit, and property, etc.—then it must be gathered from these things that a "youthful heaven" is located within man. This means that all the Planets in man have their own likeness in appearance and <term>signature</term> <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that the physical appearance of things in nature revealed their hidden healing properties and celestial connections.</note>, and their own children, of whom the father is the heavens.

<margin>
Man consists of heaven and earth.
</margin>
For man was created according to the example of heaven and earth. For he was made from them. If he was made from them, he must be entirely similar to his parents, no differently than an infant to its father, whose every limb he displays. So, man similarly holds with his father. His father is heaven and earth, air, and water. Because heaven and earth are his father, it is necessary that he also contain all their nature and portion within himself, and lack not even a single hair. From this it follows that the Physician must know this: that within man there is the Sun, Moon, Saturn, Mars, Mercury, Venus, and all the other signs, the Arctic and Antarctic poles, the scales <note>The constellation Libra.</note>, and the entire zodiac. For if he does not have all these thoroughly known, he is a total impostor, and he practices medicine like a peasant who soaks <term>colocynth</term> <note>Bitter apple; a powerful and often dangerous purgative plant.</note> in wine and heals all men with it. And with the same judgment that the peasant does this, so also does Avicenna.

Is it then a matter of small importance that it is right for a man to be appraised and anatomized according to his father, and not outside of him? So that, just as the father is, so also the son should be in the liver, spleen, and brain, and one precisely matches the other?

<margin>
A reprimand of Galen.
</margin>
Who then could be a Physician content with that <term>Beanic</term> <note>original: "Beanicâ." A derogatory term derived from *beanus*, referring to a raw, unschooled novice or a first-year university student.</note> anatomical doctrine of Galen? Or who would dare to seek a foundation in those books, in which nevertheless no true anatomy nor anything else is considered, but everything contrary to true Anatomy is handed down? Therefore, I want each and every person who has professed the name of Medicine to be diligently warned: that before all things, they properly build up and recognize the father of man, who and of what sort he is. Surely, in this way, once the father himself has been thoroughly explored, the son himself can then be known more accurately. For the son does not offer himself to be known without the father. And the father reveals the son; the son does not reveal himself. Because the father reveals the son, the heavens and earth, water and air will also reveal the man himself: for they themselves are the father. And if the father is the revealer of the son, who can be a physician who is not properly skilled and conscious of Astronomy? For according to all the parts that exist there, those things must be entirely known.

Is it then now unfair that from these things Avicenna himself, and the hooded Galen, and Trusianus, and Gentilis should be rejected and repudiated? For they do nothing but babble from their own brains, and they prove their ideas from no other source than their own authority.

<margin>
A reprimand of Physicians.
</margin>
For it is right that a Physician write, teach, or apply nothing unless it be found to be highly proven, demonstrated, and established in nature. But men of this sort want to break through rashly, and they neglect those things which they ought to have known right from the beginning.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the human body is a microcosm containing all celestial bodies, and that a physician must understand astronomy to understand human anatomy. He vehemently rejects traditional medical authorities like Galen and Avicenna, accusing them of ignoring the "heavenly father" of the human body.</summary>
