-># ON PHILOSOPHY<-
<page-num>237</page-num>

... what else should I say about them, except that it is only fair that—as all my books reveal about them—all these things should be publicized and manifested through both critique and instruction? Furthermore, besides what has been said, you should know that the heavens must be understood by the physician exactly as they are in themselves. And just as they are in themselves, so too is man within his own <term>Anatomy<note>For Paracelsus, "anatomy" refers not just to physical organs, but to the structural mapping of the internal "stars" and spiritual forces that correspond to the external universe.</note></term>. From this, therefore, proceeds the anatomy of man. And there is at least one part of it which I name here. For the air is another part, <margin>A critique of medicine.</margin> and both parts here are effectively one part. By this, and this alone, must all you physicians be convinced. And indeed, you shall find by experience that here, with all your books—with your Astronomy, Philosophy, Theory, Physics, and so on—you will be strangled just like a bird in a snare. For just as a stag, when it is in heat and most ferocious or proud, falls into the nets: so you too, with your "horns" not yet shed, will fall into that swamp which is the grave of the <term>Beani<note>A mocking term for first-year university students or "greenhorns." Paracelsus frequently used it to insult traditionally trained doctors whom he viewed as ignorant of nature's true laws.</note></term>.

Furthermore, within man lie the "sons of the Ascendants"—that is, of the stars—just as Adam must be understood in relation to his father, which is to say, the heavens and the earth. Just as a man has a different form within himself <margin>*The son from the father, who is different.*</margin> with respect to his father—though otherwise in no way separated or different except for what the eyes can judge—in the same way, the stars conduct themselves within man. And thus man is constituted from some thousands of fathers and mothers; and all those virtues and operations in which the fathers and mothers are powerful also exist within the sons. And unless these sons are perhaps educated otherwise, they will closely emulate their parents and carry out those operations which you call *Impressions*. <margin>What is an Impression?</margin> Now, "Impressions" are of this kind: just as a father teaches his son and raises him according to his own judgment and will, so too an "Impression" is an influence from the "father" (the macrocosm). Thus, in this context, the heavens are nothing other than a father toward a son. And just as a son can fashion or shape himself differently, or be cast into other "Impressions" by others, the same is true here. Let these things be said concerning the <term>mysteries<note>Paracelsus distinguishes between "Mysteria" (spiritual or divine secrets) and "Arcana" (the hidden healing powers within nature).</note></term>. But as far as the <term>arcana</term> are concerned, life is lived in a "forced inheritance": that is, the son cannot cast away from himself even the smallest member received from the father—neither the nose, nor the eyes, nor the ears, nor the teeth, nor the heart, <margin>The origin of hunger and thirst.</margin> nor the lungs, nor the liver—but is compelled to retain all these for himself. Just as these things are compelled to be so in man, you should know that these are also the reason why man is overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, receiving those things by inheritance from the father. This, then, is the relationship of the father to the son, and the son to the father: be persuaded that the stars themselves are also of this nature within man, so that they receive the heavens by inheritance in that "Anatomy," and both eat and drink from it. From this cause it now follows: just as man is a part of the earth, he must therefore also eat of the earth. And since he is also a part of the air, he entirely requires it and draws it in. Thus, he also contains within himself an attractive force from the heavens. If, therefore, the internal Ascendants, Signs, and Planets rule in the motion of the <term>Microcosm<note>The "Little World"—a common Renaissance term for the human being as a reflection of the "Macrocosm" or the great universe.</note></term>, and they fall into a longing for the external firmament and attract it to themselves (just as the earth attracts rain), then if that attraction from the heavens is healthy, it is good; if not, it is poison. For example, if <margin>Goose dung is poison to the sick.</margin> someone heaps goose dung upon a field, he corrupts it; in the same way, diseases are also inflicted here from the heavens—and not only diseases, but health as well. For just as disease falls upon us from the outside, so does health. Therefore, we are not "pre-ordained" for either health or disease; but just as motion makes one either healthy or sick, so he is entirely. All these things are placed in the power of the conjunctions. From these things, therefore, hold it as certain <margin>The attractive force is hidden in man in infinite ways.</margin> that the attractive power from external things lies hidden within us in infinite ways. For the father of man is infinite in his number; the sons of this father within man are also infinite. Just as there is one Father—not many—who made and constituted us, whom we express; so on the contrary, in Nature, from which we were marvelously produced, there exist infinite fathers. For nothing is less than, nor can be less than, Unity. <margin>Nothing is less than the Henad. There is no final number.</margin> But who can know the highest number? Or who has made an end to numbers? Just as it is impossible to count lower than one, it is equally impossible to count the end of numbers. Indeed, nothing can be counted beyond that end. But who knows it? Man was created so great that he is a single man, and cannot be fewer than one; yet in Nature he is endowed and gifted with such excellent fathers and sons that their Arcana, Mysteries, and Great Works are without number. Therefore, not without merit do I judge to the flames <margin>A critique of medicine.</margin> those lying Doctors, Masters, and all other Physicians who try to defend and establish the entire medical art and its whole foundation upon nothing but their "four excrements" <note>A scathing reference to the traditional four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which Paracelsus rejected.</note>. And in these four excrements you will all be merged and suffocated—one, no doubt, in "leek-green bile," another in "egg-yolk bile," and a third...

<-...third->

<summary>Paracelsus argues that man's internal "anatomy" is a direct inheritance from the celestial "fathers" (the stars), creating an attractive force that draws in health or disease. He concludes with a fierce condemnation of traditional doctors who rely on the four humors, which he dismissively calls "excrements."</summary>

<page-num>238</page-num>
->### THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE PARAGRANUM###<-

...the third in scorched bile <note>original: "cholerâ adustâ"—in medieval medicine, this was believed to be yellow bile that had been overheated, becoming toxic and causing melancholy or frenzy</note>, the fourth in false phlegm: and your souls shall prophesy from dung, and fly about like flies around a backside.

<margin>When diseases are subject to medicine, and when they are less so.</margin>
From this foundation it is also understood that the "Great Man" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe at large.</note> himself also falls ill no less than the "Small Man" <note>The Microcosm or the individual human being.</note>. Yet the lesser does not act upon the greater; rather, only the greater acts upon the lesser. From this is built the prediction of future diseases—those which relate to the heavens. Regarding this, one must know: if the higher stars are insuperable and "deadly to themselves," then the diseases of man must be subject to medicine. If not, the heaven is a medicine unto itself. We write or hand down these things because many diseases are often attempted to be treated with medicine, which the heaven itself actually removes, not the medicine. For how great an error do you think it is, I ask, if a physician attempts to heal one whom the heaven has made infirm, when that cure ought to be left to the heaven? 

For in a celestial disease, two things are understood: one, which is subject to medicine. That which is subject to it is the disease alone, which—once the heaven has poisoned it—the heaven then abandons or deserts; it goes elsewhere and cares nothing for it, corrects nothing, amends nothing, but having once made its impression, it withdraws. But that which is *not* subject to medicine is the disease which the heaven retains in its own power, and does not release from its possession. For whether they perish or are healed, it is a matter for the heaven alone. Therefore, know that diseases of this kind, which the heaven does not release from its possession, are not at all subject to medicine, nor should anything even be attempted in treating them. Once this investigation is made, it is necessary for the physician to know what is assigned to medicine and what is not. For if a physician treats a disease which

<margin>Diseases subject to the heaven are treated in vain.</margin>
is still in the power of the heaven, then he certainly will not release its force. For the heaven is the master, it is the Physician, it is the executioner. And if the physician in this case thrusts himself into the office of the heaven, and tries to cure the sick person according to his own judgment, not only will all his medicine be in vain, but it will moreover be poisonous to the patient. And do you not think you physicians should be blamed for this poison, seeing as you rush into curing diseases no differently than peasants rush into puddles? If you are ignorant of the nature of the heaven, let the heaven be, and leave its operation free to it. For if the heaven itself is going to depart from the sick man on its own, you meanwhile have destroyed the patient with your "care"—he who would have emerged free and healthy by reason of the heaven, but could not become healthy through you. For you have slit his throat: you have made his disease more prolonged than the heaven intended. If you do not have knowledge of such things, then what, 

<margin>A rebuke of Medicine.</margin>
and with what, I ask, are you healing? What is your foundation, I pray, that you work constantly with such blindness, and are suddenly swept away into highway robbery <note>Paracelsus frequently compares incompetent doctors to "latrones" or highwaymen because they take money and "kill" their patients.</note> out of such thick ignorance? For knowledge of this kind ought to be most certain in such matters. Wherever it is lacking, there physicians must necessarily grow strong by everywhere filling up the cemeteries. Such is the talent of most Doctors and Masters of the Academies, that they recommend almost nothing until they have each filled several cemeteries. And even if they have filled many cemeteries, they still know nothing even then; rather, after the cemeteries, they fill the fields, camps, and gardens with their errors, and they rabidly slaughter whomever they touch. Therefore, I judge that the best and most most praiseworthy foundation of Medicine is if someone is so skilled and expert in it that he requires no cemeteries because of his ignorance and homicides. Now you judge how rightly they act who wish to pull apart and destroy this foundation of mine: and whether they, or I, are the ones engaged in highway robbery? Or which of us conducts himself more honorably and generously regarding art and truth?

<margin>Diseases from infections of the elements.</margin>
Furthermore, this foundation also emerges from Astronomy if diseases are induced through infections of the remaining elements, provided that they operate in the same way as the heaven: these elements themselves must also be understood through their other parts as the "fathers of men." But if the heaven 

<margin>The same thing is often both a remedy and a poison in the same hour.</margin>
is not understood, neither can those elements be investigated in the foundation of their nature. For it often happens that a medicine is both a poison and a remedy for the same disease in the same hour: specifically because the heaven possesses the medicine and rules it. Since it rules it, then certainly that which rules must be inspected more than that which is ruled: so that, clearly, that which is ruled may be known through that which rules. 

<margin>The variety of Purgative and Digestive remedies.</margin>
From which it follows, that <term>purgatives<note>Medicines used to cleanse the bowels or "purge" humors.</note></term> do not remove diseases, nor do <term>digestives<note>Medicines intended to promote the "digestion" or maturation of a diseased humor so it could be expelled.</note></term> digest diseases, nor do other degrees or other qualities and complexions. These scholastic things are all false. From this it is elicited that one must know in what way the heaven governs diseases, and in what way it governs medicine. For, as has been said once before, the heaven itself rules both diseases and, similarly, the medicines of the remaining elements.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the physician must understand Astronomy because the "Greater World" (the heavens) dictates the course of disease and the effectiveness of medicine. He asserts that many doctors "murder" their patients by interfering with diseases that the heavens would have healed naturally or by treating conditions that are still under celestial control.</summary>

->ON PHILOSOPHY.<-

## ON PHILOSOPHY.

For its secrets are its own. Therefore, if they belong to the heaven, then its <term>Impression</term> <note>the celestial influence stamped upon a physical object</note> and <term>Generation</term> <note>the process by which things are brought into being</note> also exist from it. Furthermore, it must be understood what kind of impression this is and how it proceeds. For if there is a defect in the points <note>the specific degrees of a zodiac sign</note>, you claim that the degrees were not correctly ordered, and you bring forth I know not what other trifles, saying that you arrived too late. If there is no other defect than that an error lies hidden in the degrees, and it is proper for you to know the revolution and operation of the heaven correctly: I ask you to pay attention in this way.

<margin>Shepherd’s purse stops blood and does not stop it.</margin>
In Shepherd's Purse <note>original: "bursa pastoris," a common weed used in folk medicine</note> there is a power to stop the blood of dysentery and menstruation. Yet now, the same plant also possesses the power to stir up a flow of the belly, and not to stop the blood, but often even to promote it. And so there are other things as well which purge and often restrict, or which restrict and yet purge, so that in this way opposites and contraries appear.

<margin>The cause of contrary operations is the heaven.</margin>
What is the cause of this? It is the heaven alone, which exists in man in such a way—in one person like this, in another like that—that it inclines this man one way and another man differently, and thus performs medicine in various ways in different people. For in the "leading down" <note>original: "deductione," referring to the channeling of celestial influence to earth</note> of the heaven, according as it makes them agree and joins them, the operations and virtues of the entire Medicine are placed. If they do not properly coincide, your purpose will not succeed. This is the <term>rhombus</term> <note>the central puzzle or crux of the matter</note>, so that you may discern in all things by what means you may know and apply Medicine according to your purpose: namely, that you join the heaven according to both operations—once in the disease, and once in the Medicine. For those virtues which Pliny, or Dioscorides, and Macer <note>standard classical and medieval authorities on botany and medicine</note> describe to you will not respond to you literally with equally good success.

<margin>Pliny was unskilled in herbs.</margin>
For Pliny, as one unskilled, wrote his commentaries in the manner of mere "experimenters"—which is not how Physicians ought to be trained; they should rather be formed from the foundation that I propose here. Even if you know what is in an herb, you still know nothing unless you have also discovered this: how its power is perfected, how it is moved, and how it wishes to be "led down." If you are ignorant of this, all your efforts are worth nothing <note>original: "nauci," literally "a nutshell" or "trifle"</note>. If the herb provides no benefit or confers no utility, you are immediately struck dumb as if at the sight of some monster, and you say:

> By God, it was written so here and there; this herb worked so for this person or that; this punishment must be from God. For my art is upright and certain.

But the fault is actually yours, in that you are a fool and do not have a perspective on the "concordances" of Nature.

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
Since, therefore, the heaven is of such great importance, and its operation in Medicine must be known entirely: it is necessary that this sole and unique foundation, which I lay down, be held, and nothing else besides this. Thus, the ancient writers should be thrown into the fire. For who will place any trust in the lies of Pliny? Who will think he will attain the promises and judgments of Dioscorides, Macer, and the other naturalists who attribute virtues to herbs—these to this one, those to another?

<margin>In Flint, the power of Sapphire and Ruby.</margin>
Now it is certain that in common Flint <note>original: "Silice"</note> there are "Sapphiric" and "Rubinal" virtues. That these may be uncovered and manifested depends on the motion of the heaven. Likewise, from the motion of the heaven, these same powers are in Sapphire and Ruby. If it pleases the heaven, and such a motion of itself exists, then the power is present in the stones. If it pleases less, the power is absent; that is, if its "concordance" is not present. But since Physicians are not familiar with such cognitions and sciences, being entangled in errors, they have deserted the heaven itself and its motion, and have turned aside to the composition of Recipes.

<margin>Reproof of physicians.</margin>
But every composition of such Recipes is erroneous Medicine and a plainly imposturous art, encompassing nothing but the lies and deceits of writers from first to last. For when Physicians fell into despair regarding the nature of celestial motion, they devised such Phantasms and imaginary rules; yet Medicine can by no means be established by that reasoning. Instead, it demands to be stabilized entirely through the adaptation of the <term>simple</term> <note>a single medicinal herb or substance, as opposed to a "compound" recipe</note> or herb to the celestial motion. For in this way, remedies grow in all gardens. But when science and arts became obsolete and were extinguished among Physicians, it was necessary to sail across the sea and bring remedies from everywhere, from all regions—as if, forsooth, those things which were useful there would help here in a similar way. From this, the <term>pharmacopœi</term> <note>apothecaries or pharmacists</note> later arose. As long as they remain with their mortars, Medicine will be nothing other than coarseness, ignorance, robbery, and pure <term>Beanism</term> <note>original: "Beanismus," a term derived from "beanus," medieval student slang for a raw, foolish beginner</note>. For it is the highest ignorance that anything outside of genuine and decent art should be expended and applied by anyone. And therefore, all you Physicians, diligently enter into a reckoning with yourselves as to how you wish to excuse this or make it valid, while you yourselves admit that your remedies sometimes fail and sometimes help not at all. For what is the cause of that? But if you knew what I propose to you, you could boldly trust your art. What kind of minds are those, I ask, which Pliny and others like him have devised? They are true...

<margin>Pliny is criticized.</margin>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the medicinal power of herbs and stones is not fixed but is activated by celestial movements. He attacks traditional physicians for relying on the "lies" of ancient authors like Pliny and for using expensive, imported compound drugs instead of locally-grown "simples" synchronized with the heavens.</summary>

# THE SECOND TRACTATE OF PARAGRANUM
### PAGE 240

<margin>
In what the knowledge of simples consists.
</margin>
...they are indeed something more, and even those things are present: not only in these, but also in other things of nature, which themselves also possess virtues of this kind. But to know these things is not the essence of the art. This is the art: to ensure that the <term>operation</term> <note>the actual healing process or chemical transition</note> proceeds. Here the pattern is formed, not in the knowing, but in the performing. For this is the art and industry of the physician. And by this skill, <term>Hypericon</term> <note>St. John’s Wort</note> now expels <term>Ascarides</term> <note>parasitic intestinal worms</note>, now other worms, now even serpents. In this way, iron also performs the operations of Gold. Thus Amethyst has the virtue of pearls. Thus marble becomes <term>Hyacinth</term> <note>a precious zircon or sapphire-like stone in Renaissance lore</note>. And this is a celestial operation, such as exists in many other things, which I shall pass down in my work <term>on Astronomical Power</term> <note>original: "de Potentia Astronomica"</note>. It has now been sufficiently declared upon what foundation a physician ought to stand.

Let the listeners at least repeat to themselves what the foundation of medicine is (or is not), upon what medicine itself stands founded, and how it ought to be handled. Every single thing existing in time exists in the heaven.
<margin>
Things that follow time.
</margin>
From this follows putrefaction, dissolution, and regeneration or fruitful birth. For instance, if the heaven has unfolded into a certain constellation, bodies rot. If the heaven has not unfolded, they endure and persist, awaiting its unfolding. Therefore, all things rot after the motion of the heaven, not merely within its motion. In this way things are dissolved; thus they disappear; thus worms are generated in rotting things. For without this motion, nothing becomes rotten, nor is any worm born.
<margin>
Whence worms come.
</margin>
The origin of worms is from motion: and these are born from any rotten matter once the motion is completed. And as soon as another generation begins—such as these worms—know that the Physician must consider the heaven there, not the body. Now, because healing proceeds from the heaven, and a <term>simple</term> <note>a single medicinal herb or mineral</note> is brought or ordained here from the heaven: why, I ask, should I not speak against those who have no knowledge of the heaven, but are occupied only with the earth, and yet do not even know or understand the earth itself? In that context, the constancy of healing must also be considered. For just as you bring down the heaven into that place, so too the medicine is constant and works accordingly. If your work is contrary to the heaven, and you persist only with earthly virtue, "stuffing" and packing <note>Paracelsus uses the term "fartor," meaning a sausage-stuffer or poulterer, to mock clumsy doctors</note> without consideration of the heaven itself: your work is undone, and a common stuffer completes a much more durable work than you. For this reason, one year is more suited for healing than another, and this time is more apt and useful than that. But if you do not know this: what kind of Physician do you think you are? A haphazard
<margin>
Reproof of the Physician.
</margin>
and imperfect one, certainly; one who is convinced that because a thing succeeded once, the same outcome will happen again. Such is your "foundation." The heaven heals many of your patients, yet you assign that work to your medicine. The heaven loses many patients while your medicine achieves nothing, yet you refer their death to some other cause. Should it really be considered a fault in me that I expose your follies and show that your way of healing is worth nothing? You are like fishermen. As luck shines, so the catch proceeds. Upon such a "fisherman’s foundation," you Physicians also build your way of practicing, which you judge has never been better or more certain under the Sun: yet you ought rather to know that nothing more uncertain or fraudulent than that foundation has ever existed anywhere, nor does it have any certainty, whether the work succeeds or fails. This is also why all the streets, houses, and corners are crowded with the sick. Surely, if your practice were true and fundamental, the sick would be seen very little in the crossroads. But in truth, because your art is nothing but bait for catching the rich and swallowing money: therefore, the more destitute sick bear witness that you nourish mere deceptions and are destitute of any solid foundation. There is no disease so grave or <term>fonticus</term> <note>a term for a severe, chronic, or "falling" sickness like epilepsy</note>, provided it is a disease, that does not have a remedy assigned to it. But you remain ignorant of it; you do not find it in <term>Avicenna</term> <note>the 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon" dominated medieval medicine</note>, nor do you read it in the <term>Consilia of Montagnana</term> <note>Bartolomeo Montagnana, a famous 15th-century academic physician</note>. If, therefore, you busy yourself to know this, you will follow this foundation which I propose to you, whether you want to or not. You will follow it out of fear, not of me, for if you do otherwise, you will die an impostor, and enrich your heirs with the fruits of imposture.

If a physician is to explain, enumerate, or name diseases, he has need to be taught this by the heaven.
<margin>
The heaven gives names to diseases.
</margin>
For the heaven indicates the origins, matter, and essence of all diseases. Nor can we know anything else besides what is announced to us by the heaven. If, therefore, the heaven indicates it: then nothing else is given for a foundation, just as grass emerges from its own root, or a stalk is born and comes forth from its own seed. And since in the foundation—regarding what diseases are and how they happen—no other science is provided, we can write nothing else about them than what the stars teach and indicate. From which it follows, that not even in the remedies themselves...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the true "foundation" of medicine is astronomy, asserting that the timing of the heavens governs biological processes like putrefaction and healing. He harshly critiques contemporary physicians for ignoring these celestial influences, comparing their inconsistent results to the mere luck of fishermen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that medicine must be founded on the macrocosm—the "Great World"—rather than the internal humors of the body. Paracelsus is asserting that the stars and the universe are the true blueprints for human health and disease.</meta>

# ON ASTRONOMY.

...or in healings, no other foundation should be placed by our own whim than that which we learn or draw from the judgment of the <term>Great World</term> <note>the Macrocosm; the universe as a mirror to the human body</note>. For diseases are divided into as many parts as there are stars; they have as many origins as the plants, which nevertheless all emerge from a single root—not from the hot, nor the cold, nor the moist, nor the dry <note>Paracelsus is rejecting the traditional Greek "four qualities" used by Galenic medicine</note>. And if a disease is of Saturn, it remains "Saturn"; it neither changes its name, nor its essence and nature. For just as the names of the stars are, such also are the names of the diseases. This one belongs to Mars, that one to the Moon, another to Sagittarius, another to Leo, this one to the pole, that one to the Great Bear. In this way, the nature of diseases can be tracked, and in no other way: not as the defenders of the <term>humors</term> <note>the traditional medical theory that health depends on the balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> indicate or claim when they speak of <term>cholera</term> <note>yellow bile</note>, phlegm, blood, and melancholy.

<margin>External things, like diseases, indicate the nature of things by their character.</margin>
And just as there are diseases of Saturn, of Jupiter, or of Venus, so too has the foundation of their generation, origin, and beginning been found. For a son will not degenerate from his father. Therefore, he who knows the origin, generation, cause, and nature of rains will also understand the origin of the flows of the bowels—such as *Lientery, Dysentery, and Diarrhea*—and the logic and property of all these things. He who knows the origin of thunder, winds, and tempests also knows from whence colic and abdominal twistings arise. He who knows the generation of lightning, hail, and flashes of light, and whatever else of this kind exists, also knows the urine, the stone, the sands <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and whatever <term>tartar</term> <note>Paracelsus’s term for stony "precipitates" or calcifications in the body, named after the hard crust in wine barrels</note> exists or is formed. He who understands conjunctions and eclipses also knows sudden death, <term>Apoplexy</term> <note>a stroke</note>, and all things related to it. He who knows the new movements of the seasons and their changes from day to day and hour to hour also knows what fevers are, how many kinds there are, and the nature of each one. He who knows what the "rust" of the Planets is, and their fire, their Salt, and their Mercury, also knows how ulcers are made and from whence they arise; likewise <term>scabies</term> <note>itchy skin conditions</note>, leprosies, and the like. He who knows what Venus brings and contains also knows the affections, diseases, and health of women, and so on. And such things should not be considered from any other foundation. For if Medicine does not proceed from this single foundation in those chapters where origins and diseases are taught, then in truth everything will be false, and it will be thought that nothing has been described in accordance with truth. For in the aforementioned way alone do all diseases arise, and in no other. And all these things we must know with certainty, not bleating in the manner of foolish Academics. For a Physician ought to know from certain signs what he should judge and say concerning any disease; and at the same time, he must know perfectly the origin and generation of all diseases and the "matter" of the stars—not indeed of fictitious humors.

<margin>The world contains all that the Physician must know.</margin>
For the stars and those bodies are the things that suffer; they are the things that are sick and healthy—not "humor," "cholera," "phlegm," etc. Whatever the entire universe contains that is required for the knowledge of a Physician, that is the "Great World." All other things are frauds and impostures.

<margin>Let the physician be a foreteller.</margin>
Because the Physician is born from external things alone, he must therefore be a prophet and a foreteller of future diseases, as well as present ones, and an indicator of how much strength and power any disease has drawn from the star from which it was born. For just as you can examine and track the growth of forms, so you ought equally to understand the growth of diseases, namely in this way: You see, of course, that a fir tree grows from the seed of a fir, and you know the form and appearance of that fir, what it will be in the future. And although you may know this, you do not know *what* it is that leads it forth into that form, even if you know what the future form will be; the same is true in diseases. You know what the <term>Falling Sickness</term> <note>original: "Caducus"; epilepsy</note> is, and you have recognized it. Just as you have known a plant, so you will also know the Falling Sickness. Yet, what produces and constitutes the "form" <note>the underlying essence or driving force</note>, you do not know. Thus, you have not explored what makes the Falling Sickness. You are permitted, while things are being born, to identify what it is that becomes wood, or turns into leaves or bark. But the "matter" is not discovered by you, nor do you know what it is, until it is present before you.

<margin>The consideration of invisible things belongs to the Physician.</margin>
The Physician, therefore, must speak of that which is invisible. That which is visible, however, ought to be known to him no differently than to one who is not a Physician. The layman discerns a disease and knows what it is from signs alone; yet he is not a Physician because of that. He alone is a Physician who has known the invisible, which has neither a name, nor matter, nor even a visible operation. Who, then, would say that these or those diseases arise from humors, when these are nevertheless visible and not at all invisible? Upon which humors the heaven acts not at all, and impresses nothing? For the heaven...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases are not caused by internal humors but are earthly reflections of celestial movements and the "Great World." He asserts that a true physician must be an expert in astronomy to understand the invisible origins of ailments like epilepsy, stones, and fevers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s argument from page 241, moving from the specific celestial influences on certain diseases (like those of Saturn or Mars) to a broader philosophical claim: that the "inner" health of a human is entirely dictated by the "outer" world of the heavens.</meta>

<header>THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE SECOND PARAGRANUM.</header>

## THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE SECOND PARAGRANUM.

<margin>The cause of all diseases is the heavens. Diseases are invisible.</margin> For the heavens govern diseases: and diseases are invisible. How, then, could a <term>humor</term> <note>the traditional "four fluids" like phlegm or bile</note> be a disease? Or even the cause of a disease? Since heaven alone exists as the cause of all diseases? Just as the wind or the air can neither be touched nor seen, so much less can diseases be. If, therefore, diseases are not tangible, but are like the wind: how, I ask you, can they be purged and drawn out of the body? <margin>The Arcana operate without a physical body.</margin> This is the nature and condition of all <term>Arcana</term> <note>original: "arcanorum"; the secret, spiritual essences of things used in healing</note>: that they perform their operations without any matter or physical body. The reason is this: diseases are not bodies. Therefore, spirit must be applied to spirit. 

If snow vanishes because of the Sun in summer, who touches its body? No one. But if you insist on considering snow as the disease, and try to prove it is a body because of that: nevertheless, that which *makes* the snow is not a body, but a spirit. That spirit is what the snow is. In the same way, that which produces waste, which generates feces in the body (which you call "humors"), those things are not the disease. The disease is that which *acts* and *generates* what occurs. But who sees this? No one. Who touches it? No one. How then can a Physician look for diseases in the Humors, and explain their origin from them, when those humors are actually produced and generated *by* the diseases, and the diseases <margin>Humors come from diseases: diseases do not come from humors.</margin> do not come from them? Snow does not bring about winter: rather, winter produces the snow. For by the removal of snow, winter is not abolished. And even if no snow existed anywhere, winter would still truly thrive. 

In this way, you ought to judge and understand diseases similarly from the "superiors" <note>the stars and celestial forces</note>. If you investigate them in any other way, and treat their origin differently, you are entirely in error in all your books and writings; just as you have continually nurtured such errors up to now, and have recognized that which the disease expels and poisons as the disease itself. From this, it has also happened that you have lost and corrupted so many men; so much so that it is now necessary for heaven itself to finally provide medicine and heal. For it is a much more excellent Physician than you are.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
Since, therefore, Medicine is founded on no speculation other than that which is born and established from the "external man"—that is, the heavens, the stars, and such things—know now in common, all of you, that the entirety of Medicine applied outside of this knowledge exists as a most rotten and deceitful foundation, in which no truth, but a whole "Iliad of lies" lies hidden. For the matter speaks for itself: that outside the proposed foundation, every presumption is mere fantasy, built only on opinions and dreams. Who is there who can see the pestilence through the skin? Or who is there who can discern from which part of the body it arose? Or how it attacks? Or what kind of matter it consists of? No man can truly know these things. 

But he who knows the heavens, who knows the stars, who has discovered <term>Manna</term> <note>a celestial food or substance falling from the sky</note>, who has explored the minerals: he knows perfectly what the plague is, where it hides, and what its nature is. Outside of the heavens and stars, no physician whatsoever can comprehend it. <margin>Why Physicians have been driven into error.</margin> Because Physicians have abandoned the foundation of Medicine—Philosophy and Astronomy—and have retreated into fantasy: therefore, not even a tiny bit of the foundation of even the smallest disease has been handed down and explained by them until now. 

How, without any foundation, have all the chapters of Surgery been handed down by those writers? If I hammer home and punish these errors, they make me a "heretic" in Medicine, claiming I am possessed by Satan and nourish a demon within me. But who is so dull as not to understand that a foundation in Medicine is needed that is entirely different and diverse from what they propose? The same is also true of Surgery, which is entirely pregnant with lies where it treats origin, causes, and matter. Who would not consider those writings a "Beanic" invention? <note>original: "Beanico"; a "Beanus" was a mocking term for a raw, inexperienced student or "freshman"</note> For thus do the <term>Beani</term> peer through a wall, and see things that are hidden and cannot be seen at all. Who would not call such a habit foolishness? 

<margin>The great dignity and nobility of man.</margin> Consider, I pray you, with what great dignity and nobility man was created, and how widely his <term>Anatomy</term> <note>Paracelsus refers to the "spiritual" or "universal" anatomy, not just the physical structure</note> spreads itself out: and how little it is possible for the anatomy of his body and virtues to be fully investigated by any human brain or reason. For the foundation must proceed from external things. Then, whatever is within him will become conspicuous and manifest. For as it is outside, so it is also inside; and what is not outside is not inside either; for <margin>All things are one.</margin> the external and internal exist as one thing, one constellation, one harmony, one body, one metal, one <term>Tereniabin</term> <note>a type of celestial manna or dew</note>, one fruit. For that is the <term>Limbus</term> <note>the primordial "primordial matter" or chaos from which all things were made</note> in which all created things lie hidden: just as the seed in which the whole man exists is the "limbus" of the parents. <margin>What the Limbus of Adam was.</margin> Now, the Limbus of Adam was heaven and earth, water and air. Therefore, man also remains in that Limbus, and contains within himself heaven and earth, air and water, and he himself is those same things.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases are invisible, spiritual forces governed by the heavens, asserting that physical symptoms (humors) are merely the results of disease, not the cause. He concludes that true medicine and surgery must be based on the "Limbus"—the idea that man is a microcosm containing the same elements as the universal macrocosm.</summary>

<header>DEDICATORY EPISTLE.</header>

It is. Who, therefore, without such Philosophy and Astronomy through his own speculations, fantasies, and <term>humoralizations</term> <note>the outdated practice of attributing all illness to the four "humors" like phlegm or bile</note> could sufficiently explore man? For whom would this finally be possible? For no one in any nation. Thus, in no way can it ever be done: I am forced once more to name such men as <term>Beani</term> <note>original: "Beanos"; a term for university freshmen or "greenhorns," often used by Paracelsus as an insult for ignorant academics</note>, who imagine such impossibilities and congratulate themselves on their old-wives' inventions like fools, who shake themselves with both laughter and weeping, and either praise or blame themselves as their mood dictates. Truly, as much power as such Medicine has, so much power does the fantasy of a fool possess. Therefore, all Medicine is lying and fraudulent which does not draw the efficacy of its knowledge from the aforementioned solid foundation. It is also nothing else but bait prepared to deceive both the noble and the ignoble alike.

## OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND EXCELLENT LORD THEOPHRASTUS
## HOHENHEIM, Doctor of both Medicines.

# TO THE MOST REVEREND, REVEREND,

*First, the responses and refutations of certain slanders by his detractors.*

*Third, concerning the Generation and causes of <term>Tartar</term> <note>in Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to the stony deposits or calcifications in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty crystals</note>, and its cure.*

*To the Most Reverend, Reverend, Illustrious, Striving, Distinguished, Noble, Prudent, and Honest, etc. Archbishops, Bishops, Prelates, Counts, Barons, Lords, Knights, Nobles, and the entire province of the Archduchy of Carinthia, etc.*

<margin>Why Theophrastus did not gather the three books into one volume.</margin>
**M**OST REVEREND, Reverend, Illustrious, Generous, Striving, Distinguished, Noble, Prudent, Honest, etc. Let my most devoted and ready services and duties be dedicated especially to Your most Reverend Mercies and to all the rest of you. By good counsel it seemed right to me some time ago that I should write and publish three books on Medicine. However, as to why I did not gather these three books into one volume, but instead reported them in three distinct ones: I had this most powerful reason for my purpose, because the Galenic and Avicennist physicians <note>followers of the traditional ancient Greek and Persian medical systems</note> have everywhere defamed and sold me out as a heretic. Since justice and honesty discouraged me from bearing this injury from those false physicians; and so that I might return to them a just retaliation,

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s "Dedicatory Epistle" to the leaders of Carinthia. Having previously introduced his "Three Books," he now explains his motives for writing and why he has chosen to dedicate this specific work to the province where he spent much of his youth.</meta>

<header>DEDICATORY EPISTLE.</header>

<margin>The saying of Christ is explained.</margin>
*The very same reason that compelled me to report these things also drove me. And although Christ himself urges that we should offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us, and give our tunic to the one who takes our cloak, this command will not be a cross or a source of affliction for me here. For that burden was not placed upon my back. Christ speaks of fleeting and temporal goods, in which it is not right for our treasure to be placed. But this work, this "plow" that I handle—this gift granted to me by divine favor—is directed toward the health and benefit of the lands. Just as Paul commands, no one should boast in Christ if charity toward their neighbor is not fulfilled. What kind of self-denial would that be? Therefore, because of those who hate me and my rivals—who have busied themselves with blocking this gift granted to me by God through their slanders and deceptions (which is the nature of a deceitful tongue)—I could in no way restrain myself from preparing a response against them, and revealing the whole matter publicly for the sake of asserting the truth. And if it is established by example that Christ dissolved the lies of the Jews with a serious response, then this defense of mine should not be held against me as a crime by anyone.*

<margin>The Labyrinth of Physicians.</margin>
*Secondly, so that those men might more fully recognize the beam in their own eye <note>A reference to Matthew 7:3; Paracelsus is calling his critics hypocrites who ignore their own flaws while attacking him</note>, I have composed a second book, titled the "Labyrinth of Physicians." And so that the work might prove the skill of its craftsman, I have taken it upon myself to describe the principal diseases of these regions—namely, the <term>Tartarean</term> <note>Paracelsus’s term for diseases caused by stony deposits or "tartar" in the body, such as gout or kidney stones, named after the crust in wine barrels</note> diseases—according to my own theory and practice (that is, according to their causes and cures). I wished to release these three books publicly, joined into one. As I was thinking about publishing and compiling them in this way, it occurred to me—something I had not remembered before—that among "cats," the trading of lard is difficult <note>An idiomatic way of saying it is dangerous to trade valuable things among thieves or rivals</note>, and that for the most part, "potter hates potter" <note>original: "figulum figulum odisse"; a Greek proverb from Hesiod meaning that people in the same profession are often jealous rivals</note>. I wanted to communicate this plan of mine to men of my own sort; yet they immediately shared these new things about me with others like themselves, so that they might more conveniently forge spears against me from my own iron. The situation itself taught me that it is far safer and more secure that if I am at St. Stephen’s in Vienna, they should walk in the High Market; or if I stand at the watchtower corner, they should pass straight on to St. Lawrence. For their hatred toward me is no light matter; if they could do so by any means, they would seek to harm me even if I were forty miles away. Indeed, they have tied such a knot for me that I have barely been able to come into the light with these works of mine until now.*

<margin>Reason for the dedication.</margin>
*And so now at last, most merciful, kind, noble, and benign Lords—since the Archduchy of Carinthia is a second fatherland to me after my birthplace, where my beloved father lived for thirty-two years and was everywhere affected by many benefits and honors throughout the whole province—it seemed just and right to me, in place of my said father, to show you some specimen of pious gratitude. I find no gift greater or more significant than to consecrate and name these three books to your Illustrious Highnesses, etc., so that the entire province may uniquely rejoice and enjoy the public benefit for all the sick. For although these works are so diligently watched by my rivals throughout all Germany that they can be published and given to the public nowhere in those places, they can by no means keep them out of this Archduchy; indeed, they are altogether forced to favor them for that region. I do not deny that the style is in some places more difficult, the names or terms more obscure, and the <term>Recipes</term> <note>prescriptions or medical formulas</note> themselves are confused in their order. But this was not done out of ignorance or envy; rather, the genuine order and sequence of Medicine requires it. Nevertheless, so that all these things may be understood more clearly and intelligibly, I have added a unique explanation, which everyone should attend to accurately. None of this was done out of a spiteful mind; rather, it was to stay ahead of certain vagabond physicians, who might try to run their profitable markets through our work and mix their poison with our remedies to the destruction of the sick. For Carinthia, Styria, and Carniola are the first regions whose physicians—most highly commended by the public testimony of Italian Doctors—generously practice medicine for men. Let your Highnesses, etc., consider how much better it is to be one's own shepherd than to trust oneself to any passing mercenary. For the difference between a Shepherd and a Mercenary is evident. He who guards himself acts best. Thus, I have a certain and undoubting hope that these works of mine, along with the attached most humble offering of my services, will be pleasing and acceptable to your Highnesses and Nobilities, etc. If in any affliction (such as can hang over us at any moment) my diligence and industry can be of use to you, I offer and devote myself entirely to you. Given at St. Veit in Carinthia, on the 24th day of August, in the year 1538 from the birth of Christ.*

*Of Your Highnesses, Nobilities, and Excellencies,*

->The most humble and ready,<-

->**Aureolus Theophrastus Hohenheim, Doctor of both Medicines.**<-

# CHRONICLE AND ORIGIN
## OF CARINTHIA.

<margin>Origin of the Germans.</margin>
<margin>Tubisico and Theuto.</margin>
<margin>Samo occupied Carinthia. Theuto's insignia are the same as the Swabians'.</margin>
<margin>When Carinthia was made smaller.</margin>
The most ancient chronicles of all—such as the "Rhapsodic Chronicle" of Nauclerus <note>original: "rhapsodicum Chronicon Naucleri"; Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510) was a prominent German historian whose "Memorabilium omnis aetatis et omnium gentium chronici commentarii" was a standard reference for world history at the time.</note>, along with others not yet published—testify to the fact that the Germans, together with the Slavs, descended from Japheth <note>The son of Noah in the Bible, traditionally considered the ancestor of European peoples in early modern ethnography.</note>, and that the first offspring of Japheth occupied Germany. Thus, we Germans have our origin in Japheth. *Tubisico*, one of his children, and *Theuto* are named first in the Chronicles, and from the latter the name of the "Teutonic" nation was bestowed. These two, Tubisico and Theuto, settled in Upper Germany; and *Samo*, also one of the sons of Japheth, occupied the land of Carinthia. Being born of the same blood, they distributed the kingdoms and divided the regions in this manner. Thus Germany was settled, which today stands as the most populous of all other lands. Tubisico and Theuto brought their own arms, insignia, and shields with them: namely, three black lions on a golden field. Because of their kinship, these lions were passed down as a hereditary right all the way to the first Duke of the Swabians. *Samo*, who occupied Carinthia, displayed those same lions for the same reason. It is established that these nations were the very first in Germany. Later, after a long time—for the Chronicles regarding the founding of Germany are not recorded with sufficient accuracy, though the matter is clear from other histories—the first children of Japheth passed away and those regions were distributed among heirs: some into *Slavonia*, some into *Carniola*, others into *Istria*, and so on. In this way, Carinthia was reduced in its borders and size.

<margin>The Romans move into Carinthia.</margin>
How the general title of "Duke Samo" originally applied to all those lands is not sufficiently explained in the Chronicles. However, it is clear that long before the monarchy of the first Julius Caesar, the Romans frequently made incursions into Germany. Because the Romans were always far more arrogant than the Germans themselves and were itching with a strange lust for power, they occupied and seized many kingdoms within the Germanic nation. Carinthia was among them; once occupied, the Romans fortified it with many castles and cities, and chose it as a place to live above all other regions.

<margin>The descendants and families of the Romans among the Carinthians.</margin>
Even the most noble and powerful families of the Romans moved there, and, enticed by the pleasantness of the land, established their seats and dwellings in that place. From these families, the Carinthian nobility later descended, though they are now known by German names. Thus from them arose the *Counts Palatine, such as those of Görz: Counts, such as Sternberg and Ortenberg, etc. Barons, such as Kreyg, Ungnad, etc.* This is besides the other Knights and Nobles, for it would be too long a task to review each of them by name.

<margin>Why it is called Carinthia.</margin>
Since the Romans cherished that land with a singular love above all others, they bestowed a name upon it out of that affection, calling it *Carynthia, as if to say "intimate dearness"* <note>original: "quasi caritatem intimam"; Paracelsus is suggesting a folk etymology linking "Carinthia" to the Latin "caritas" (love/dearness).</note>. The Germans call it by the shortened name *Kärnten*, and the Slavs call it *Quarenden*. The land has retained that name even to our own times.

<margin>The Carinthians receive the Regalia from Charlemagne.</margin>
As for those Dukes who administered the kingdom among the Romans, the Chronicles that have come into my hands do not record the succession of individual generations in order, until one descends to the time of *Charlemagne*, the first Roman Emperor from among the Germans. For it is recorded that the Carinthian Dukes obtained the Regalia <note>The emblems or rights of royalty/sovereignty.</note> from this Emperor, were confirmed by him, and received the title of Dukes. Under the same Emperor, they also came to the recognition of the Christian faith. After they had persisted in this faith for some time, the situation reversed and they were driven from it several times—most notably in the time of *Attila*, the most cruel tyrant of the Huns, who wretchedly devastated and overthrew both their faith and their political society and state.

<margin>Attila, tyrant of the Huns.</margin>
Later, however, through *St. Rupert, Virgilius, and Amandus* <note>Early medieval missionaries and bishops influential in the Salzburg and Alpine regions.</note> along with their deacons, they were finally converted back to the faith and more diligently instructed in it.

<margin>The Duke of Carinthia receives his fief from a peasant.</margin>
The solemnity and custom of this Duchy was once such that the future Duke of Carinthia, in a field under the open sky <note>original: "sub puro Ioue"; literally "under pure Jove," a Latin idiom for being outdoors.</note>, would receive his fief from a peasant. He would have a horse and an ox with him, and would swear that he would defend the Carinthian Duchy with his physical efforts, goods, and all his wealth with the highest loyalty, even to the point of extreme poverty, such that he would reserve nothing more for his own sustenance than that horse and ox. This custom was subsequently confirmed even by the Emperors—

...was confirmed and established. The granting of such fiefs <term>fiefs|land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service</term> was required to take place in Liburnia—now called Solfeldia <note>original: "Solfeldia"; this refers to the Zollfeld plain in Carinthia, a site of great historical importance where the Dukes were traditionally installed on the "Duke’s Chair."</note>—which was their first seat of power. Here, four noble lineages were accustomed to appear to perform their duties, as their own Chronicle relates at greater length. This same source also records that the peasants there were granted more liberal privileges and immunities than the other inhabitants.

<margin>Frederick Barbarossa.</margin>
Furthermore, the Chronicles testify that *Frederick the Great*, surnamed *Barbarossa* <note>Frederick I (1122–1190), Holy Roman Emperor, known as "Redbeard."</note>, who came from Swabia, harassed the Venetians in a fierce war and won a glorious victory over them with the help of the Germans. At this time, the Dukes of Carinthia were still in their prime; because they shared the same coat of arms and ancient origin as *Emperor Frederick*, they maintained a close friendship. Joined by a common treaty, they defended their rights in Friuli <note>original: "foro Iulij"</note>, and together they both destroyed and built various castles and other monuments. At that time, Emperor Frederick the Great, in memory of their kinship, founded a college in the Duchy of Carinthia called *Innichen in the Puster Valley* <note>original: "Ingnigen in Busterthal"; this refers to the Innichen Abbey (San Candido) in modern-day South Tyrol.</note>.

<margin>Innichen in the Puster Valley.</margin>
And, to tell you something truly memorable, the same Barbarossa adorned that temple with various images and stone statues. Among these images, one was more conspicuous than the rest, depicting the form of a monk, with his loins girded and his head bare, just as monks are usually shown. Above his head, certain large letters were seen sculpted in this manner: **LVTERVS**.

<margin>The statue of LUTHER at Innichen.</margin>
Due to their age, these letters were not very noticeable unless one looked closely. What kind of omen this might have been, I leave for others to judge. <note>Paracelsus suggests here that a statue labeled "Luterus" (Luther) existed centuries before the Reformation as a prophecy of Martin Luther.</note> Furthermore, when *Frederick the Great, the Swabian Emperor*, raised the Margraviate of Austria to the status of a Duchy, this was also done in the presence of the Dukes of Carinthia.

<margin>Transfer of Carinthia to Austria.</margin>
No more can be taken from the Chronicles, except that after the Carinthian Dukes died out and were forgotten, that Duchy was transferred to the House of Austria. Thus, it was joined and united to them with all its rights of birth and insignia; that is, it passed into the obedience and protection of the Dukes of Austria.

<margin>Solfeldt, the first seat of the Carinthians.</margin>
In this place you should also know that when they first sought seats and habitations after the time of Japheth, they settled in a certain field now called Solfeldia and built beautiful dwellings for themselves. Among other things, they also 
<margin>Temple of the Sun.</margin>
established a certain temple, which they named after the Sun. For they worshipped the Sun as their deity. 

<margin>Liburnia devastated by Attila.</margin>
But the city itself, called Liburnia, was eventually devastated and overthrown by *Attila* <note>Attila the Hun, who invaded the Roman Empire in the 5th century.</note>, the ruins of which are visible even today. From certain antiquities, monuments, and other remains, it is clear that in those times, very skilled and industrious craftsmen flourished in the fashioning of metals and stone, as can be gathered and discerned from the coins, images, and buildings adorned with wonderful and stupendous workmanship.

<margin>Philistines in Carinthia.</margin>
<margin>Samson.</margin>
It is also clear from some Chronicles that the *Philistines* once lived in these lands in great numbers; it was even told to *Emperor Frederick* as a fact that *Samson* once stayed here. Just as antiquities concerning the *Philistines* are found in other foreign lands, similar ones are likewise found in Carinthia. 

<margin>Metal-bearing Carinthia.</margin>
Indeed, reason itself shows that Carinthia was at that time very wealthy in all kinds of mines and metals, and that the sons of Japheth especially flourished in the metallic arts; it was primarily their love for these things that kept them in those lands. For the events of later times prove the same. 

<margin>Frisians and Saxons migrate to Carinthia.</margin>
For from the North, Frisians and Saxons moved into Carinthia in great numbers for the sake of the metals; from them, the city of *Friesach* <note>original: "Frisacum"</note> was later built—named, as it were, after the Frisians and Saxons. Moreover, miners from Liguria <note>Northern Italy.</note> migrated into Upper Carinthia and founded a city on a certain mountain in the vicinity of *Mooskirchen* <note>original: "Moskirchensi"</note>, which they called *Liguria* after their homeland. However, when the mines failed, the city also perished. But not only these, but many other cities and mines were established in the same way, because many people from distant shores came here as if in a race.

<margin>Carinthia: Germany's first mine.</margin>
Furthermore, it is proven by other documents that Carinthia was the first of all Germanic regions to practice those arts pertaining to mining—namely vitriol, copper, and the rest. The chronicles mention no mines older than these. When these were first found and discovered in these lands, similar ones later became known in other regions by this example, and were built and established in imitation of the Carinthian mines.

<margin>Highly refined medicine in Carinthia.</margin>
It is also clear that throughout Germany, the art of medicine was first treated and cultivated most subtly in this place. This is attested by certain very ancient discovered German books, which...

# OF CARINTHIA

The matter itself shows that records <note>The Latin text uses "Christum," which may be an OCR error or a shorthand for Christian records; the context suggests the collection and writing of historical or medicinal chronicles.</note> had already been gathered and written down at that time. It is also gathered from those very books that the extraction of what they call **Quintessence** <term>Quintessence|in alchemy, the "fifth essence" or purest medicinal extract thought to be the soul of a substance</term> was already flourishing at that time. <margin>The Fifth [Essence]</margin> Indeed, if you properly examine the foundation and the very beginning of both mining and medicine, Carinthia was the first producer of them all. Even today, it is clear that the knowledge of these refined arts is not very great along the tract of the Rhine and among other nations. However, with the passage of time, the old mines have faded away, and new ones have emerged in their place from time to time. Furthermore, since that land was divided after the death of the Carinthian Dukes, part of it fell to Styria, part to Friuli <note>original: "Foro Iulij"</note>, part was assigned to the Church or Archbishopric of Salzburg, and part even to the Bishopric of Bamberg. For as often as a kingdom is divided against itself in this way, such desolations must necessarily follow.

The Archbishopric of Carinthia was split into twin archbishoprics: namely, the Patriarchate of Aquileia and the Archbishopric of Salzburg. Besides these, there are two other bishoprics of that region, Gurk and Lavant, as well as the Commandery of the Knights of St. George, whose leader is called the High Master of Millstatt. <note>The Order of St. George was a military order founded to defend the region against Ottoman incursions.</note> For this order, Emperor Frederick III added a red cross as a distinguished badge, along with the most ample benefits and privileges, so that they might fight strenuously against the Turks and others who frequently used to infest Carinthia and its borders with a hostile hand. This same region is also famous for many other colleges and monasteries. It is clear from the annals of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman geographer and astronomer.</note> that in his time, the primary city in this region was Villach, though it was situated in a somewhat different location. We also read that Claudius the Roman founded the city of Klagenfurt, called by the Latins *Forum Claudii*.

Furthermore, the Annals record that the city of St. Veit was always the metropolis <note>metropolis: the chief city or capital</note> of Carinthia from the earliest times, and that the Dukes of Carinthia held their diets and assemblies there. It is even read that at one time, a certain Duke was captured here and handed over to the Archbishop of Salzburg. However, when he was later restored to St. Veit by the right of *postliminium* <term>postliminium|a legal right where a person who was captured by enemies is restored to their former status upon returning</term>, he punished many with Ducal severity. <margin>The Lavant Valley.</margin> The name of the Lavant Valley in the Duchy of Carinthia was derived from its growth <note>original: "à crescendo"; the author suggests a folk etymology linking the name Lavant to the Latin "lavare" (to wash) or "levare" (to rise/increase), referring to the abundance of gold washed from its rivers.</note>. For in that place, the rivers were most fertile with gold—so much so that many miners and craftsmen from many different nations flocked here in crowds. There, even today, pure and solid gold that requires no fire for refining is found in various places, possessing admirable mass and weight.

In the aforementioned valley, acidic mineral springs of the greatest virtues are also found; they are very medicinal, and I have ventured to comment on their powers, as well as the properties of the other things growing and produced there (which are rare elsewhere), in a specific small book. In old Carinthia, at a distance of one mile from Friesach in deserted places, there are famous acidic springs that are naturally warm. <margin>Warm acidic springs at Villach.</margin> There are not many similar springs known or frequent throughout Germany which retain their acidity while being hot.

To put it briefly, the mines of this region are much more numerous than those of other provinces. <margin>Bleiberg.</margin> At Bleiberg <note>The name "Bleiberg" literally translates to "Lead Mountain."</note> there is a lead-bearing mine, providing more than enough lead not only for all of Germany, but also for Hungary, Turkey, and Italy. <margin>Hüttenberg.</margin> There are also frequent iron mines, especially at Hüttenberg and around its borders, producing a great heap of the most noble steel. Alum-bearing minerals are also found, which are commonly used for buildings. Moreover, minerals of the most excellent vitriol <note>vitriol: a sulfate mineral used in chemistry and industry</note> and the most noble gold are produced in various places; such things were found in a rare form at St. Paternion. Certain metallic veins are also uncovered there, the likes of which Europe itself does not know. That metal is singular and truly admirable for its rarity. Furthermore, cinnabar mines are also common there, which are very pregnant with mercury. Pyrites of a golden color are also dug up there, along with various marcasites and white, red, and black <margin>White, red, and black talc. Lungau.</margin> **Talc**. Indeed, in old Carinthia, as well as near Lungau, garnets are sometimes found, along with many other similar things that cannot all be listed in this place. If the Carinthian mountains could be opened like a chest with a key, what land anywhere, I ask, would be found more packed with treasures? From this it also happens that so many augurs, diviners, "Vitones" <note>likely a local term for a type of folk-seer or dowser</note>, geomancers, crystal-gazers, and similar prophets inhabit those lands, who seek out and explore those riches by a special art through crystals, rods, and other methods. Yet God has defined and preordained a limit for all these things, which they cannot exceed by their art and industry...

# CHRONICLE

...which no one shall cross over. Since so many and such varied **mines** <term>mines|original: "scaptensulae," a rare term derived from Greek for pits or mine shafts</term> are found in those regions, it is believable that a gathering and conjunction of the Planets and the firmament with the three lower parts existing within the Elements themselves flourishes there. These conjunctions of the higher stars and the Elementary bodies finally produce and bring forth those metals in the places established by God for this purpose. Nor is it a wonder that minerals of such great variety, unknown elsewhere, are found here, since the nature and character of the very frequent waters there are also unique. <margin>The number is missing.</margin> For the lakes (.....) are numbered in this land, all famous for their gold-bearing bottoms and surrounded by a sort of rampart, from which the most opulent treasures could be extracted.

As for the other cities, towns, villages, and hamlets, the mines gave the beginning to them all, in various ways according to the nature and condition of the ground. For some of them are famous for being near riverbeds, such as those which run from Lienz <note>original: "Luenza"</note> through the neighboring tract to Lavamünd <note>original: "Lauemunda"</note>. Others are near Lavant; some are noble near Gurk, and Glan, and Gail. Although the Chronicles may recount many more of these, let these accounts handed down to us suffice as an epitome <note>An epitome is a summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note>. We wish for those who are eager to know more abundant and fuller things on these matters to be referred to those Chronicles.

# PREFACE OF THE MOST EXCELLENT
## LORD THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM
### Doctor of both Medicines. <note>In this period, "Doctor of both Medicines" usually referred to a mastery of both internal medicine (physic) and surgery.</note>

<margin>Who were the illustrators of medicine.</margin>
**T**o make it clear to you, benevolent Reader, regarding the causes of the writing and publishing of these defenses, I would wish you to attend only to these few things. God, the highest benefactor, permitted the Genius of Medicine to be brought forth from the innermost shrines through Apollo, through Machaon, Podalirius, and Hippocrates <note>In Greek mythology and history, these figures represent the founding fathers of the medical arts.</note>. He allowed the very light of nature to shine out widely, having expelled every dark spirit, and caused many admirable works—the most brilliant **mighty deeds** <term>mighty deeds|original: "Magnalia," a Paracelsian term for the great wonders of God hidden in nature</term> and amazing miracles—to be perfected from the mysteries of the **Elixir**, the **Secrets** <term>Secrets|original: "Arcana," referring to the hidden healing powers of substances</term>, and the Essences of Nature. Thus, Medicine itself shone forth and was wonderfully illustrated through the aforementioned leaders.

<margin>The deceits of Satan.</margin>
*But since it is the solemn custom of the lurid Satan to sow his own weeds and tares everywhere among the healthy wheat, it happened that medicine also was greatly obscured from its first natural genius. It fell headlong into the hands of **pseudo-doctors** or **anti-doctors** <term>anti-doctors|original: "Antiatri," a term Paracelsus coined for those who practiced medicine incorrectly or opposed his methods</term>, who so involved and entangled it in their sophistry that the works which Machaon and Hippocrates performed in their own time can by no means be provided today with equal success. Indeed, whatever is not demonstrated in medicine by the weight of its works can hardly be proven by disputing and arguing. Answer me, Reader: if someone sends forth an effective or working doctrine against a Legion of Sophists, is it not right and just that such a work should repress and refute their empty trifles?*

<margin>The trifling gods.</margin>
*O Reader, at whom shall I hurl these words? Truly at the "Gods" <note>Here, Paracelsus refers mockingly to the established medical authorities of his day as false idols or "gods."</note> who show no signs of healing. The number and the crowd of those visiting a man might move many to stop rebuking these babblers. But the outcomes and the returns of the sick prove that there is little weight in that crowd. From this is cooked up that lie: that Hippocrates is nothing but trifles and fables. And the Spirit of medical truth is accused of being empty chatter by those Sophists. For what is there anywhere that an unbridled tongue does not dare to say?*

<margin>Reproof of medicine.</margin>
*From this tribe have arisen those who, overcome by the incontinence of their tongues, have tried to protect their cause with slanders. Since they had merely sipped the "juice" of Medicine with their lips, they broadcast the assertion of their art only with their mouths—mouths which have been trained for accusations and detraction. Such deceitful...*

The tongue of such people has also stung me. Thus, custom and the reality of the situation demand that—since they have built their art not upon a true and genuine foundation, but rather upon a culinary rock <note>A "culinary rock" refers to doctors who Paracelsus believed focused only on "kitchen" recipes and superficial treatments rather than the deep secrets of nature.</note>, and have rashly neglected the truth of Medicine itself, while leading me and others about with their sophisticated fables like a masked parade—they should not be dismissed by us without a solid response. Indeed, these slanders would never have been vomited forth by them if they had been established upon the primary center. Their highest art is wordy rhetoric, a wealth of ancestral heritage, and a "virtue" worthy of and innate to such pseudo-physicians. Therefore, several defenses will follow in order, which you should attend to properly and diligently. Although it would be much better for such responses to be omitted and for them to be indulged, so that they might remain "Poetic Physicians," "Rhetorical Receivers of Prescriptions," and worthless preparers. For even these men shall have their fill in their own time. <margin>The work proves the craftsman.</margin> These reminders have been instituted by me for this purpose: so that it may finally be understood that a Physician without works is nothing, and that only the work, not chatter or words, makes a man a Physician. An obstacle was also placed in my way by these people to prevent these and my other writings from being published. Nevertheless, I have at last wished them to be gifted to the Archduchy of Carinthia. From these most praiseworthy lords, you alone—whoever and wherever you receive them—obtain these works. For if they were not in this province, they would never have been placed into your hands. You, Reader, should embrace and love the theory of this book, but much more the works of the art itself. Given at St. Veit in Carinthia, on the 19th day of August, in the year of salvation 1538.

# DEFENSE I.
## Regarding the discovery of the New Medicine of Dr. Theophrastus.

<margin>Why Paracelsus introduces a new method.</margin>
**T**HAT I bring forth in this work a new Theory and Physics, together with new reasons which neither the Philosophers, nor the Astronomers, nor the Physicians have used or understood until now, has been done for those causes which I am about to hand down. This is the first and primary reason: that the ancient theorists proposed the reasons and causes of diseases wrongly and unskillfully, and introduced certain errors with them, which they finally polished to such an extent that they applied no small amount of false coloring to the truth itself. Indeed, they pushed forward with their effort so far that, beyond the foundations proposed by them, no one was ever allowed to inquire about others; and whoever did otherwise was judged to be engaged in open error. This must be diligently impressed upon you here: that such a custom and lack of freedom provides clear evidence of ignorance. For the Heavens, according to the light of nature <term>light of nature|original: "lumen naturae," the inner wisdom or divine intelligence found within the natural world</term> and of talent, continually give birth to and produce new inventions, new arts, and new sicknesses; and should all of these be neglected out of laziness, or esteemed not at all? What use is the rain that fell a thousand years ago? That rain is useful which falls right now. How does the motion or course of the Sun made a thousand years ago benefit this year? Does not Christ himself hold out a torch for us, showing how we ought to judge such things? For he speaks thus:
> Sufficient unto each day is its own care, or its own yoke. <note>Matthew 6:34. Paracelsus uses this to argue that medical knowledge must be current to the diseases of the present day.</note>

It is as if he were saying: it is enough that you do those things which that day demands. For he concludes further: tomorrow's day has also been given its own care. Now, if there is a reason and time for its own care, and if any day consists of twelve hours, then a peculiar operation belongs to each hour. How, I ask, will the twelfth hour inconvenience the first? Or what damage will the first inflict upon the twelfth? For every single thing is established within its own proper Monarchy <term>Monarchy|original: "Monarchia," a Paracelsian term for a specific period of time or a specific realm of natural influence</term>. And it becomes us to be solicitous for the present, not to be tormented by care for things past. Provision has been made for every single Monarchy from the full and perfect light of nature. And those are the miracles of the divine hand: namely, to change the Light of Nature into many Monarchies between the beginning and the end of the world. In this consideration, those men have miserably gone astray, and have not adapted themselves according to the right of this Monarchy. Therefore, by the virtue of the present light of nature, and from a predestined ordination, I wish and demand that these writings of mine be entirely beyond reproach and blameless, so that they may not be attacked or hindered by anyone on account of my instituted refutation of Sophistries, which I rightly call "seductions."

It is necessary that I publish their madness more widely and bring it under the sunbeam for the sake of recognizing both my foundation and their lapses and errors. Nor shall the Academies ruin me for this reason, to whom I propose and explain the matter in this way. Medicine is a work. Therefore, because it is a work: <margin>Medicine is a work.</margin> the work will testify concerning its craftsman. Therefore, judge from the works, in what way and of what sort
