# DEFENSE

...both sides must be judged. The work is the art. The art transmits the teaching of the work: so that the art may operate, and through that teaching, produce the work. Now the question is: is the teaching of the Academic Doctors the true art of Medicine, or is mine? This shall be defined by the works. But it will also be noted alongside this that Christ proposes in our Philosophy—and offers for us to know—the one who has not only renewed the eternal light among us mortals but, beyond this, the light of Nature itself. He speaks thus: *False prophets will arise, false Christs, and they will perform many miracles.* <note>Reference to Matthew 24:24. Paracelsus often links theological warnings about deception to the "false" medical practices of his time.</note> Thus, even if these false physicians also perform signs, as may happen, they do not stand against true medicine. For just as Moses and the Sorcerers were opposed to each other by their respective works, so too are the true and false foundations of Medicine. Now, if I teach that my opposing side and I myself ought to be known by our works—yet works are also found among the false, just as Christ affirms regarding signs and wonders—the matter must be discerned in this way: 

Imagine a patient who suffers from a fever and has a "term" <note>original: *Terminus*; refers to the predestined duration of a disease according to the Galenic theory of "critical days."</note> for the disease lasting twelve weeks; at the end of this period, the disease naturally ceases and declines. If it happens that the patient asks for remedies to strike down his fever before this legitimate term, he then <margin>What the treatment of false physicians is like.</margin> has two doctors at hand: one false, the other true. The false one organizes his cure in this way: he begins to heal slowly and gradually, wasting a vast amount of time by handing out syrups, laxatives, purgatives, oat or barley gruels, gourds, melons, juleps, and other similar things administered slowly over time. Meanwhile, he occasionally applies enemas and performs I-know-not-what else. By these things, added to the flattery of their words, they prolong the disease for the patient until the *Term* destined for it by nature arrives. Even though the illness finally ends of its own accord, they attribute its expulsion to their own art and industry. 

<margin>What the treatment of true physicians is like.</margin> Judge the genuine Physician, however, by this: He divides this period into twelve parts; he spends only one and a half of those parts on his labors or his operation. <note>The author claims true medicine is significantly faster, taking only a fraction of the time nature or "false" doctors require.</note>

But another piece of ignorance also remains, which greatly moved me to write this book. Namely, they pretend that those diseases which I encompass in this work are incurable. Who would not marvel at their impudence? For how can a physician call a disease incurable in which death itself does not exist? <margin>Which diseases are incurable.</margin> *Only those are incurable whom death accompanies.* <note>A classic Paracelsian maxim: No disease is inherently "untreatable" by medicine; only the transition to death is inevitable.</note> They babble the same nonsense, of course, about gout and epilepsy <note>original: *podagra* and *epileptia*.</note>. O truly insane heads! Who commands you to broadcast those things which you neither know nor understand? Why is the word of Christ himself—saying that *the sick have need of a Physician*—not rather a concern and a matter of the heart for you? Are these not indeed "the sick" whom you desert? I certainly judge them to be sick. Therefore, if they are sick, they have absolute need of a Physician. If they need a Physician, why do you say they are incurable? Why should the sick need one from whom they can be helped by no counsel? Or why do they say that medicine profits or benefits them nothing? Truly, it is because they were born from the error of Medicine and conceived by their mother, Ignorance, before being brought forth. 

<margin>Every disease has its own peculiar remedy.</margin> *Every disease has its own proper and peculiar remedies.* For God wishes to be recognized wonderfully in the sick; He wishes to be celebrated in the "falling sickness" <note>original: *morbo caduco*; epilepsy.</note>, in Apoplexy, in St. Vitus's Dance <note>original: *Chorea S. Viti*; a disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements.</note>, and others which it is not necessary to list here. For this is the same God who gave the commandment *that you should love your neighbor as yourself, but love God above all other things.* Now, if you wish to love God, it is necessary that you also love His works. If you are to love your neighbor, you will not say to him, "You cannot be helped"; but you would more rightly speak thus: "I cannot help you, nor do I understand the disease." <margin>Ignorance excuses.</margin> This truth, indeed, excuses you and redeems you from the curse that awaits the false. So, let it be settled: in inquiring and investigating, one must proceed until at last the true art is discovered, from which works may proceed. For if Christ said, *Search the Scriptures,* <note>John 5:39.</note> why should I not also be permitted to say: "Search the natures of things"?

And let these be my defense as to why I now, for the present Monarchy <note>The "Monarchy" refers to the supreme authority or the unified system of his "New Medicine."</note>, rightly and deservedly bring forward and publish a new medicine. If someone should ask: "Who taught you to do these things?" I in turn ask this: "Who today teaches the herbs and grasses to grow?" For He who taught this also said: *Come and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.* From Him flows the fountain of truth. That which does not come from Him is mere seduction. The Devil is a craftsman of a thousand ways, who is pregnant with many signs and wonders; he does not take a holiday, but like a roaring Lion circles us, seeking...

...whom he might carry off into a lie along with himself.

<margin>Christ as the source of both forms of health.</margin>
You should not wonder why, at the conclusion of this defense, I point my finger toward him who said: *I am gentle and humble of heart* <note>original: "mansuetus sum, & animi demissi"; a reference to Matthew 11:29.</note>, so that we might learn healing from him, who at the very least shows us the way to eternal things. For what exists in us mortals that does not fall upon us and is not grafted into us from God? He who teaches us the eternal also grants the mortal or temporal.

<margin>The Physician and Medicine are from God.</margin>
For both flow from the same source. And although celestial doctrine was delivered from his mouth, and not Medicine specifically; nevertheless, if he also says, *The sick have need of a physician* <note>original: "Ægros opus habere Medico"; see Matthew 9:12.</note>, and *The physician is created by God*: how, I ask, should the physician not recognize him as his Teacher from whom he came forth? *For the physician is he who takes the place of God in bodily diseases.* Therefore, it is necessary that he holds from God what he is able to do. For just as Medicine is not from the physician, but from God, so likewise the art of the physician is not from the physician, but from God himself.

<margin>Physicians are of three kinds.</margin>
Although physicians are also of three kinds. The first are born *from Nature*, through the physicians of the heavens in the starry influence of conception. From this same parent are born Musicians, and Mechanics, and Rhetoricians, and the other arts themselves. *The second kind* of physicians are those who are established by men and educated in Medicine according to the precepts of their masters, as much as could be grasped by natural industry. *The third kind* is that which God gives. These are taught and established by God himself, just as Christ says: *Every scribe shall be taught by God.* <note>original: "Vnusquilibet scriba à Deo doctus erit"; see Matthew 13:52.</note> Which is the same as if he said: whatever we are capable of, we have from God.

<margin>Both types of physicians meet at the end.</margin>
If, therefore, Medicine presents its practitioners in a threefold manner and path, care must be taken even if they do not agree in their theory and reasoning. For in the work itself all agree, and conclude upon one end or limit. Nature creates and disposes according as the conception received its influence. So also man himself teaches, according as he is industrious and capable. But God teaches as he wills. Yet the <term>rhombus</term> <note>original: "Rhombus"; here used figuratively to mean a guiding point or the central target toward which all paths converge.</note> for all these is this: that the man who is to teach another should draw his knowledge from God and nature. For from these the instruction of men ought to proceed. But whatever doctrine proceeds from elsewhere than the aforementioned foundation is such as has been defined most recently.

# SECOND DEFENSE

## Regarding New Diseases and Names by Dr. Theophrastus.

<margin>Diseases which are "new" according to Theophrastus.</margin>
For the protection and defense of my character—as to why I describe new diseases, about which nothing has been handed down by anyone before, and why I give them new names, never used before but first introduced by me—pay diligent attention to what follows. Concerning new diseases, hold this to be the case: I write indeed of that insane leaping which the common people call <term>St. Vitus’s dance</term> <note>original: "S. Viti chorea"; a disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements, often associated with historical outbreaks of "dancing mania."</note>. I also treat of those who strangle themselves. I even add diseases inflicted through sorcery or incantation, and similarly regarding possessed men. These diseases have been described by no one anywhere before me. Why they have been neglected ought to seem utterly unworthy and unjust. The cause, however, which incites me to describe them is Astronomy alone, which until now has been treated too lazily by physicians, but has imparted to me the knowledge of all such diseases.

<margin>Contempt for Astronomy as the cause of ignorance.</margin>
But if other astronomers had achieved the same experience as I, those diseases would have been known as fully and perfectly described and explained long before me. Because Astronomy was rejected by physicians, neither these diseases nor others could be rightly recognized or understood from their true principle and genuine causes. Since, therefore, the Medicine of other writers does not flow from that spring in which the foundation of true Medicine is placed—the possession of which spring I can truly boast of—is it not permitted for me to write and comment in a different way than other writers have done? Indeed, to speak, to advise, and to teach is given to anyone. However, to speak and teach with vigor and efficacy is not given to everyone. For you know that the Evangelist himself testifies that *Christ, when teaching, spoke with a certain unique power and efficacy*, unlike the scribes and hypocrites.

<margin>Christ's doctrine is effective.</margin>
And one must pay diligent attention to this kind of power, which is proved through works if credit is not given to words. Just as it is impossible for someone to demonstrate the appearance and form of a thing they have not seen as certainly and fundamentally as the one who has observed it with his own eyes, so I am fully confident that the judgment here will be the same regarding those who...

# DEFENSE

...those who speak without a foundation, and those who use a foundation. It is certainly true that everything that exists in a diseased state is subject to the Physician's consideration, and it is right that he should have all diseases known and explored. However, what he does not know in one person, he must surely know in another. For the gifts bestowed upon the Apostles were also distributed by this measure. And in whatever has been given to each person, his honor flourishes. Yet, if he did not receive a certain gift, it was not a disgrace to him. For as God has established each person, so he is.

<margin>The honorable gifts of God.</margin>
Other writers can by no means boast of having received such gifts. They are intent only on the *Limit* <note>original: "Terminus"; in classical medicine, this referred to the defined boundaries of what was considered treatable or "within the rules" of the art.</note>. And whatever they cannot accomplish through that *Limit*, they immediately pronounce incurable.

<margin>The "Limit" is the refuge of physicians.</margin>
<margin>Why Theophrastus innovates names for diseases.</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that I produce new names and Recipes should not cause you wonder. This is not done out of any simplicity or ignorance; rather, anyone can think to themselves that the names handed down by the ancients, and the remedies assigned to them, can easily be read and recognized from a paper even by a novice. This, however, offends me: that they have constructed names from so many languages that we can never fundamentally grasp or reach the nature and essence of diseases through them. Indeed, they themselves do not correctly understand those same names they have handed down—just as among the Germans, different names are given and applied in different districts. And although some have compiled <term>pandects</term> <note>A term for comprehensive encyclopedias or legal digests; here, Paracelsus refers to massive, uncritical medical compilations.</note> and other such things, yet because they repeatedly stumble into other errors, they do not gain much trust from me, and for reasons that are not slight. My own sincerity and integrity dissuade me from endangering my conscience and accepting an uncertain and ambiguous doctrine as valid. It is clear that no chapter has been handed down by those writers that is not full of lies and error. What use, then, do these authors have for me, or how do they help me? Truly, I do not hunt for Rhetoric or the elegance of the Latin tongue in them, but I seek Medicines, I seek remedies—yet in the delivery of these, they are "dumb dogs" <note>A reference to Isaiah 56:10; Paracelsus uses it to describe doctors who are silent when they should be providing active cures.</note>. Likewise, they object to my Recipes, saying that I prepare them in a new way and by a new process, even though the tenth commandment of God mandates that nothing foreign should be used—just as they have many times objected to me in person: *You shall not covet what belongs to another* <note>original: "Non concupisces alienum"; Paracelsus is being accused of "stealing" or using "alien/unnatural" methods by his rivals.</note>.

<margin>What "foreign/another's" means in the Decalogue.</margin>
Since they accuse me of being a violator of the tenth commandment based on these things, I must altogether unfold and explain in this place what is *foreign* and what is not. It is foreign if someone does not enter through the right door. It is foreign if someone snatches away what is not his own. For example: if someone sells himself as a Physician when he is not; or if someone places Medicine in a thing where no Medicine exists. And let it be held against me as a fault or a crime that I uncover their frauds.

Furthermore, the fact that I also write about possessed people seems plainly crude to them. But I do it for this reason:

<margin>The possessed are to be healed by fasting and prayers.</margin>
Since *fasting and prayers* expel unclean spirits, I judge that it is first and foremost commanded to the Physician that he seek the kingdom of God before all things; afterwards, the things he needs will be given to him. If it is granted to him that he can heal the sick through prayers, let this "purging" not seem contemptible to him. If it is granted to him to heal through fasting, let this be an excellent restorative for him. Answer me truly: does Medicine hide only in herbs, wood, and stones, and not also in words? If you do this, I will also tell you what words are. What is this word: *Do not do it*? As the disease is, so also is the Medicine. If a disease is assigned to herbs, then it is cured by herbs; if to stones, by stones. If it is judged to be for fasting, it is also expelled by fasting. To be *possessed* is a very great disease. If Christ himself proposes the Medicine for this, why should I not search that Scripture which contains and delivers the Recipes for that disease? The heavens give birth to diseases. The Physician drives them away. If, therefore, the heavens themselves are forced to yield to the Physician, the Devil himself will also certainly yield to the legitimate use and order of suitable remedies. Yet the modern physicians deny such things, because naturally the talkative Mesuë <note>Mesuë (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh) was a major authority in medieval pharmacy; Paracelsus views his followers as too reliant on old books.</note> makes no mention of such matters, and for that reason they despise others of whom they are envious.

They have also accused me of imposing new names of this kind on diseases, which no one either recognizes or understands; and they say it would have been better for the old names to be retained.

<margin>Why Theophrastus changed the names of diseases.</margin>
But how could I, or should I, have retained the old names, which do not proceed from the foundation from which the diseases themselves arise? For those names at least...

...were only given in passing <note>original: "obiter"</note>, nor does anyone know if those diseases are correctly and lawfully called by those names. Therefore, since I find that foundation to be so loose and uncertain, why should I be anxious about retaining the names? If a disease is known and explored by me, it will be very easy to initiate it with its own genuine name. And what does it matter if it is called Apoplexis or Apoplexia <note>Stroke</note>? Or why should I be distressed over whether the second-to-last syllable of "Paralysis" is pronounced short or long? Or whether the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note> is called *Epilentia* or *Epilepsia*? Or why should I ask if the word is Greek, Arabic, or Algoic <note>original: "Algoicum"; likely referring to the "Algorists" or foreign logic systems</note>? Time is only wasted by idle chatter on all these matters.

The Heavens,

But as to why I have taken upon myself the task of teaching and explaining new diseases, other reasons have existed besides those mentioned. Namely, there are new operations of the heavens every day, and the sky exists variably from day to day according to its causes and essence. For it also hastens toward its own old age. Just like an infant who is born, who from the first day of birth is altered and changed toward youth, and further toward the very limit of death. Now, even the heavens were an infant and had their beginning at some point; no differently than man, they received a predestined end, and thus are enclosed in death. Just as anything is varied and changed through age, so too its works are changed likewise. And if changes are entirely imminent, why do I need the "schoolmaster's rods" of children <note>Refers to the elementary, outdated teachings of the ancients</note>? Therefore I speak of the Monarchy now present, and of the age of the firmament and the old age of the Elements.

<margin>
Entirely new
customs of
men today.
</margin>
Moreover, even today there exist such natures of people, and such various mixtures, and different pursuits and occupations arising from carnal pleasures, the likes of which have never flourished since the foundation of the world. From these there also emerges such a "pressure of nations" as has never been before. Therefore, it is no help to the Physician when he says, "I truly rest upon those books that were written and published two thousand years ago." For the old causes do not persist even today, but the logic is far different, as both philosophies—that of the heavens as well as of the Elements themselves—most clearly prove. It would be right for those supposed Doctors of Medicine to be more cautious when they clearly see that sometimes even a coarse peasant, plainly illiterate, restores many more sick people to health than they all can heal with their commentaries and red robes. If they realized the difference in this outcome, they would cast off their red robes and dress themselves in a sack full of ashes, <margin>Ninevites.</margin> as we read of the Ninevites <note>In Jonah 3:6, the people of Nineveh repented in sackcloth and ashes</note>. Thus, I am fully and completely persuaded that, according to the tenor of this defense, I am permitted by good right to establish, decree, and describe entirely new names and new diseases based on the aforementioned foundation.

***

### DEFENSE III.

-> *Concerning the description and designation of new Recipes.* <-

<margin>
Whether
Theophrastus's
remedies
are poisons.
</margin>
Besides what has been said so far, those unskilled and ignorant Physicians further bark at me, saying that my Recipes which I prescribe are poisons and corrosives, and therefore the extraction of all the malice and toxins of Nature. Against this accusation, if they themselves were fit to answer, I would first ask them whether they knew or did not know what a poison is? Or whether any mystery of Nature lies hidden in poison? For on this point they are unskilled and ignorant of natural virtues. For what is there anywhere, created by God, that has not been coordinated with wonderful gifts for the curing of man's health? <margin>What should be sought in poison.</margin> Why should poison be rejected and exterminated, when it is not the poison itself, but Nature that is being sought? To strengthen my point, I will bring forward such an example. <margin>The toad as a remedy for the plague.</margin> Turn your eyes toward the toad <note>original: "bufo"</note>, how poisonous and abominable that animal is! But how excellent is its mystery for curing the plague? Now, if this mystery were despised because of the poisonousness and abomination of the toad, how great a disgrace, I ask, would that be? Who is it that ever composed this recipe of Nature? Was it not God who did it? Why then should I reject or despise this composition? <margin>The profound wisdom of God.</margin> And if He indeed composed things that might seem less suitable to me? He, He, I say, is the only one in whose hand all wisdom is enclosed, and to whom it is well enough known where any mystery should be brought...

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus's "Third Defense," where he justifies his use of powerful substances that his critics labeled as "poisons." # THIRD DEFENSE

...to be ordered and placed. Why then should I either marvel at or loathe that which contains poison in some part, especially when this mystery is of the most noble sort? Any thing ought to be employed for that which it is destined, and we should not be driven further away from it by some misplaced disgust. For God himself is the Physician and the Medicine. Within every Physician, there ought to be fixed and engraved the Power of God, which Christ explained to us when he said: *Even if you drink poison, it will not harm you.* <note>Original Latin: "Etsi quidem venenum biberitis, vobis tamen noxium non erit." This refers to Mark 16:18, often cited by Paracelsus to argue that a true physician, acting with divine favor and knowledge, can handle dangerous substances safely.</note> If, therefore, the poison does not prevail but yields without harm when we use it according to the established order and reason of nature, why should poison be universally despised and rejected? <margin>Poisons are not to be retained in medicines.</margin> He who scorns poison is ignorant of what lies hidden within it. For the secret power <term>Arcanum</term> <note>Paracelsus used the term "Arcanum" to describe the hidden, celestial healing essence of a substance, which remains after the physical "impurities" or toxins are removed.</note> that is concealed within the poison is so blessed and effective that the poison itself subtracts nothing from it, nor does it cause harm. But I do not expect you to be satisfied by this paragraph alone; rather, for my defense, it is necessary to bring forth a more abundant explanation, since we have once and for all addressed the handling of poisons.

You note and rebuke in me exactly what you yourselves are overflowing with. You do not tolerate a lentil in me, yet you do not notice the melon in yourselves. <note>A variation of the "speck and the log" parable (Matthew 7:3); Paracelsus suggests his critics focus on his small errors while ignoring their own massive failures.</note> If you mock my recipes, why do you not weigh your own? Your purgatives are of the first order. But what purgative can be brought forth from all your books that does not contain poison? Either it leads to death, or it cannot be administered without harm if the moderation of the dose is exceeded. Now, pay attention to what this point means. Truly, it is not too much, nor is it too little. He who holds the middle path and the measure does not take poison. And even if I were to administer poison—which you will by no means be able to prove—if I offer it in a suitable and lawful dose, would I seem worthy of your rebuke for that? On this point, I easily accept all men as judges. It is known to you that Theriac is prepared from the viper <term>Tyro</term>. <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal" medicine. One of its main ingredients was the flesh of vipers, which Paracelsus uses as proof that even his critics use venomous creatures to heal.</note> <margin>Theriac from the viper.</margin> Why, then, do you not also criminalize your own Theriac, which contains the poison of this serpent within itself? Because you find by experience that Theriac is most useful and possesses nothing harmful, you admit this to be true. Now, if the logic of my medicine is no different than that of Theriac, why should it be rejected simply because it is new? Why should it not correspond in goodness to that ancient remedy? And if it truly pleases you to consider any poison, what, I ask, will you find anywhere that is *not* a poison? **All things are poison, and nothing exists without poison. The dose alone makes it so that it is not a poison.** <note>Original Latin: "Omnia venenum sunt: nec sine veneno quicquam existit. Dosis sola facit, vt venenum non sit." This is the most famous maxim in toxicology, expressing that the toxicity of any substance is determined by the amount administered.</note> <margin>All things are poisons, even to you.</margin> Let this be an example: any food or drink, taken in a dose larger than is proper, is poison. The outcome proves this. Indeed, I even concede that it is poison. But I do not grant that it ought to be rejected because of this. Since, therefore, nothing exists anywhere that is not a poison, why do you perform corrections? <note>In pharmacy, "correction" refers to the process of adding ingredients to a formula to mitigate the harsh effects of a drug.</note> Surely so that the poison does not harm. If I also do this for that same purpose, why do you rebuke me? It is well known to you, I believe, that quicksilver <note>mercury</note> is nothing but poison. <margin>Quicksilver is poison.</margin> Daily experience teaches this as well. Yet it is your custom to smear your patients with it, much more forcefully and laboriously than shoemakers smear leather with grease. You fumigate with its Cinnabar; you wash with its Sublimate; and yet you do not want it to be called poison, though it is poison, and though you drive it into the human body, saying "it is wholesome and good," and that it is "corrected with white lead"—as if, in this way, it were not poison! Bring my recipes and yours to Nuremberg for judgment; <note>Nuremberg was a major center for medicine and pharmacy in the 16th century, and Paracelsus often appealed to its authorities to validate his work.</note> there you will learn which of us offers poisons, I or you. For you know neither the correction nor the dose of Mercury; you simply smear it on until it penetrates. One thing remains to be asked: whether your recipes, which you say lack poison, can heal the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, <margin>The ignorance of physicians rebuked.</margin> or not? Or Gout? Or Stroke? Or do you trust that you can cure St. Vitus’s Dance <note>A disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements.</note> with your rose-sugar, or the "moon-struck" <note>lunatics</note>, or other similar diseases? Not at all. For by those means you have never cured such patients, nor will you ever cure them. If, therefore, other remedies are necessary, why is it attributed to me as a crime that I take up those things which I ought to take, and apply them to those for whom I am meant to apply them—He who created the heaven and earth established and ordained them in such a way. Furthermore, since the art of separation has been given to us to pull apart two contraries from one another: <margin>What is the use of the art of separation.</margin> why should poison be said to be present? Turn over all my recipes, and see whether this is not my primary teaching: that the good should be continually separated from the bad? And is this separation not my "correction"? And so cor-

It then transitions into the "Fourth Defense," where he justifies his constant traveling as a necessary pursuit of medical knowledge scattered across the globe.</meta>

<header>THIRD DEFENSE</header>

<margin>Vitriol, full of secrets, is not a poison.</margin>
...should I then not boldly dare to administer or prescribe a corrected secret remedy <term>Arcanum</term> <note>An "Arcanum" is the refined healing essence of a substance, stripped of its toxic physical dross through alchemical processes.</note>? Especially since the malicious can find nothing wrong in it—neither I, nor you. You throw Vitriol <note>Vitriol generally refers to metal sulfates (like iron or copper sulfate). While corrosive in its raw form, Paracelsus used it to create various medicines.</note> in my face, a substance in which many secrets are hidden; I say to you, there is more utility stored within it than in all your apothecary boxes combined. You cannot possibly assert that it is a poison. If you are going to say it is corrosive, then please tell me: in what 

<margin>Sweetness is innate in corrosives.</margin>
form and in what way? You must reduce it to its essence for it to be so; otherwise, it is not corrosive. If it can be reduced to a corrosive state, it can also be reduced to a state of sweetness. For both qualities exist within the same thing. As the preparation is, so too is the vitriol. Any simple substance, as it is in itself, can be reduced by art into a manifold nature, in much the same way as food served at a table. If a human eats it, it becomes human flesh; if a dog, canine; if a cat, feline. So it is with Medicine: what you make or prepare from it, that is what it becomes. If evil can be made from good, then good can also be produced from evil. No one should rashly pluck at a thing whose transmutation <note>The alchemical process of changing one substance into another.</note> he does not know, and if he is ignorant of the art of separation. Thus, even if this 

<margin>Arsenic is a poison.</margin>
<margin>What the preparation of Arsenic is.</margin>
indeed be a poison, it can nevertheless be easily reduced to a non-poison. We shall take the example of Arsenic, which is the greatest of poisons—where a single drachm <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> can choke and kill any horse. Yet, if you ignite it with saltpeter <note>Original: "sale nitri." Potassium nitrate, used in alchemy to "fix" or alter minerals.</note>, it ceases to be a poison. If you were then to consume ten pounds of it, you would feel no harm. See from this what a difference exists, and what the preparation of things can achieve.

He who takes it upon himself to act as a critic should first take care that, while he criticizes, he does not fall into the same fault himself. I easily recognize your foolishness and simplicity by the fact that you yourselves ignore the things you speak of, placing your only defense in a mocking and 

<margin>Why Theophrastus writes new recipes.</margin>
sniping tongue. I write new Recipes <note>Original: "Recepta." These were the written formulas for medications.</note> for the reason that the old ones are worthless and of no account. Furthermore, new diseases have arisen which absolutely demand new Recipes. But note this one thing regarding my Recipes: whatever I might eventually take up in them contains an entirely hidden power <term>Arcanum</term> within itself, which acts to expel its opposite <note>Paracelsus followed the principle of "Like cures like" (similia similibus curentur), but here he refers to the Arcanum's power to drive out the contrary disease.</note>. Furthermore, note how I proceed. I separate that which is not an *arcanum* from that which is, and I assign to the *arcanum* itself its specific dose. It is certain, then, that I have more than sufficiently defended my Recipes, and that you calumniate them out of sheer envy, preferring your own useless things to them. If your conscience were honest, you would desist from this henceforth. For what the heart is full of, the mouth speaks. In this work, I set down five defenses; by unrolling them, you will understand the reason why I compose Recipes from those simple substances that you consider poisonous. Why 

<margin>That which is useful to man is not poison.</margin>
should I pay the penalty for laying a foundation of a kind that you cannot see or understand? If you had a certain and proper knowledge of those things in which it is absolutely right for a Physician to be skilled, you would adopt a far different perspective. You must know this: that which turns to the good of man is not a poison. For only that is a poison which works to the detriment of man—that which does not help, but primarily hurts—such as most of your Recipes are, which are prepared by no other art than pounding, mixing, and infusing. Let this, then, be the refuge of my defense: that my Recipes are administered and applied according to the order of nature itself, and that you yourselves know not what you say, but spend your tongues on mere fury, unskillfulness, and ignorance.

***

### FOURTH DEFENSE

-> *Regarding my travels and wanderings.* <-

NOW the matter requires that I also defend the fact that, by traveling everywhere, I visit many places and do not stay or remain in any fixed seat. How can I struggle against or resist that which I cannot tame or subjugate to myself? Or what can I either add to or take away from predestination? Because you pursue me with slander, as if I were of lesser value because of my wanderings, let no one be more unfair to me than when I receive that charge with indignation. The fact that I have traveled until now has provided me 

<margin>What the benefits of Theophrastus's travels are. Not all arts are in one place.</margin>
many advantages. For no one learns his Mastery <term>Magisterium</term> at home, nor draws his doctrine from behind the stove. Indeed, the arts themselves *are not all enclosed within one’s fatherland; they are disseminated and distributed throughout the entire world. They are not crowded into one single man, or one single place.*

<header>FOURTH DEFENSE</header>
<sig>a6</sig>

...but they must be gathered from various regions, and taken from the places where they flourish. And the entire firmament acts as a witness for me in this matter, for inclinations are distributed in a peculiar way; they are not gathered or heaped together into a single village, but are cast out toward their own goals in every direction according to the nature of the rays of the upper sphere. Is it therefore not fitting for me to investigate these goals, and to observe what is accomplished in each? If this were a blemish upon me, I could not rightly be called *Theophrastus* <note>Paracelsus’s given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim. Here he asserts his identity as a true seeker of wisdom.</note>, which I nevertheless am.

<margin>Arts do not come of their own accord, but must be sought.</margin>

Is it not established that art does not force itself upon anyone, but must be completely captured and investigated? Therefore, that same necessity lies upon me: that I should seek it out, rather than it pursuing me. Consider an example. If it is our intention to be with **GOD**, we are absolutely compelled to go to Him. For He says, *come to me.* <note>Reference to Matthew 11:28: "Come unto me, all ye that labor."</note> Where we wish to be, there we must go. From this it follows that it is necessary for anyone who wishes to see a certain person, or a land, or a city, or to know the manners and customs of a certain region, or to look upon the nature of the sky and the properties of the elements, to go to that place and consider each thing individually. For it is impossible that all these things should follow him. This logic applies to all those who burn with a passion for experience and the knowledge of things. These must be pursued and inquired after; and once knowledge of them has been received, one must move his seat and location even further.

How, I ask, can a good Cosmographer or Geographer be born behind a stove?

<margin>All things become certain through the eyes.</margin>

Does not the sight of the eyes provide a certain foundation? Let this foundation, therefore, be solidly established in this manner. What do those who merely turn the spit behind the stove <note>original: "pyraversant"—meaning those who stay idle by the hearth rather than working in the field.</note> learn? What could a carpenter know without the testimony of his eyes? Or what is it that can be established concerning the faith of the eyes? Did not God Himself offer Himself to be seen by eyes? Does He not demand testimony from us that we have seen Him with our own eyes? What art, then, or anything else, could lack the testimony of the eyes? I remember once hearing from legal experts 

<margin>The Law of the Ancients <note>original: "Idorum," likely referring to the *Idumaeans* or a corrupted reference to ancient Egyptian/pagan laws Paracelsus often cited.</note> regarding Physicians.</margin>

that they established in their laws that a physician should act as a traveler. How much does this support my cause! For diseases themselves wander and roam across the entire world, and do not persist in one single place. He who busies himself with knowing the greatest number of diseases must travel. The 

further he wanders, the more diseases he will learn, and the more experience of varied things he will drink in. Once this is achieved, even if he should later return to the lap of his mother <note>i.e., his homeland.</note>, he will nevertheless easily recognize such a foreign guest if it ever arrives in his fatherland. If he does not recognize it, he will not escape shame and disgrace. For he could not provide for his neighbor that knowledge which he had previously and improvidently boasted of possessing. Now, if what I labor at and do for the sake of the Commonwealth is turned into a crime, who could help but experience this with indignation? And yet, only the 

<margin>The laziness of physicians is rebuked.</margin>

sedentary ones twist this against me—those who, without sleds, carts, or other vehicles, do not even endure to step outside the gate. Thus, they are the most lazy of strollers. Therefore, they hate more intensely that which they themselves are not. They despise what is better because they themselves are worse. Now it is indeed very certain to me that wandering does not make one worse, but altogether better. Does travel not bring success to any kind of business? 

<margin>Travel makes people better.</margin>

Does travel not cultivate the mind more, and firm up judgment more, than staying at home behind the stove? For a physician to be a domestic servant or a doorman is very shameful. It is fitting that he aspire to greater and weightier things. But what "generosity" is noticed in them in this century? Certainly, travel does not suit them, nor does any experience of things please them. The fault lies with the superstitious common folk, who gild them with gold at home even if they are not worth a hollow nut. And since they realize that the peasants are entirely ignorant of what a physician ought to be, they hide themselves at home in their studies and libraries, and they travel only in a *ship of fools.* <note>original: "naue stultiferâ"—a reference to Sebastian Brant's *Stultifera Navis*, a famous 15th-century satire on human folly.</note>

<margin>The Physician should be an Astronomer.</margin>

*It is necessary that a Physician first be an Astronomer.* Now, the matter demands that the testimony of his eyes prove that he truly is one. Without this testimony, he exists as a mere babbler of astronomical trifles. It is fitting that he also be a Cosmographer—not 

<margin>The Physician should be a Cosmographer.</margin>

so that he may paint nations and what kind of boots <note>original: "caligis"</note> each wears, but that he may pass down something deeper: namely, which diseases usually plague those nations. If you are confident that you can describe the dress of this or that nation without having traveled, what does that matter to a physician? It only proves you are a good tailor. Therefore, because the aforementioned things must be known through experience, travels are absolutely necessary for us along with our assistants <term>Parabolani</term> <note>The "Parabolani" were historically a class of men who risked their lives as nurses to the sick; Paracelsus uses the term for itinerant medical practitioners or assistants who learn through travel.</note>.

<summary>Paracelsus defends his nomadic lifestyle, arguing that because medical and astronomical knowledge is spread throughout the world and diseases travel, a physician must also travel to gain true experience. He mocks "stove-sitting" doctors who remain in libraries, comparing their sedentary expertise to a "ship of fools."</summary>

<header>->DEFENSIO IV.<-</header>

### ->DEFENSIO IV.<-

...with Medicine are so connected that they can by no means be torn apart. Furthermore, it is necessary that a Physician be a 
<margin>The Physician must be a Philosopher.</margin>
**Philosopher**, and that he be established as such by the faith and testimony of his own eyes. If, therefore, he wishes to be such a man, it is necessary that he collect all things from those places in which they are individually stored. For if even a roasted dish is offered to the table: the meat is brought and taken from one region, the salt from another, and the other seasonings from yet another. Since these things are forced to travel before they reach you, you must also think that you must travel in the same way, until you attain that which could not follow you. For the arts do not have feet of their own, that they might be driven closer to you by butchers like cattle. Nor can they be carried to you enclosed in vessels. For what they lack, you must do yourself: namely, what they themselves should have done. English humors <note>In the medical theory of the time, "humors" were bodily fluids and temperaments; Paracelsus argues that people's biological nature varies by geography.</note> are not Hungarian, nor are Neapolitan humors Prussian. Therefore, to know this, you shall take yourself to the place where they are. The more closely you visit and know them, the greater the judgment and prudence with which you shall return to your homeland. Then, it is also right for a Physician to be an
<margin>The Physician must be an Alchemist.</margin>
*Alchemist*. To become one, however, he must necessarily see the mother from whom the minerals are born. Now, the mountains will by no means travel to him, but he himself must make his way to them. Where minerals
<margin>Craftsmen are where minerals are.</margin>
thrive, there the craftsmen flourish. Whoever seeks a craftsman skilled in separating and preparing nature, let him track him down in that place where the minerals are found. For who shall attain the preparation of Nature, unless he follows her to those places where she flourishes? And these things being so established, by whom could it be made a crime against me that I have thoroughly investigated all minerals? That I have learned (so to speak) their very heart and soul? That I have grasped their secrets with my own hands? For those things—those things, I say—taught me so that I now know how to separate the pure from the dross <note>original: "purum à stercore" – literally "the pure from the dung."</note>, by which knowledge I have averted many evils that would otherwise occur. Therefore, I cannot help but cite a Philosophical saying here: *Wisdom
<margin>Wisdom and art are hated by the ignorant.</margin>
is despised by the ignorant alone.* Thus art also has no haters, except the ignorant.

I say nothing here of the other things that come to him who wanders through various regions. For he comes to know various men, learns the customs and rites of many, and experiences many other things, for the sake of seeing and knowing which anyone might deservedly wear out both shoes and hat. I omit other matters even more weighty and sublime than these. We see that even lovers measure out long journeys just to behold a certain beautiful and charming woman. How much more should this be done for the sake of a beautiful and sublime art! Even the Queen <note>The Queen of Sheba.</note> set out from the furthest maritime shores
<margin>The wealth of the Queen of Arabia.</margin>
to Solomon for this one reason: namely, that she might be permitted to hear his wisdom. If, therefore, so powerful a Queen sought the wisdom of Solomon, what was the reason for it? This, surely: that *Wisdom is a gift of God.* To 
<margin>Wisdom is a gift of God.</margin>
wherever He pours it out, there it must be sought. And this knowledge is difficult, if a man understands that the gifts of God are to be sought where they lie hidden, and that it is fitting that we hunt and pursue them, even if compelled. But if even those who are compelled must do this, who, I ask, can rightfully 
<margin>The arts are poor.</margin>
mock him who undergoes and accomplishes it of his own accord? I do not deny that it is true that those who do not dare such things are wealthier than those who do. For those who settle down behind the stove are fattened on partridges and delicacies. But those who hunt the arts abroad are forced to sip a thin milk broth. The "corner-sitters" <note>Paracelsus's term for scholars who never leave their home or study.</note> are adorned and burdened by wealth; they are clothed in silk and fine linen. But the wanderers can scarcely afford coarse linen. Those who hide within their own city walls have both heat and cold ready at their greatest wish. But the seekers of the arts, if the trees should fail, could scarcely find shade anywhere for their bodies. Therefore, he who wishes to serve his belly, let him not follow me; let him follow those who walk in soft garments. These are not fit for traveling. For Juvenal has handed down that only he who travels empty-handed walks joyfully <note>Reference to Juvenal’s Satires: *Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator*—the penniless traveler will sing in the face of the robber.</note>. Therefore, holding this verse as certain, lest they perhaps be overwhelmed by robbers, they hide at home behind the stove and turn half-roasted pears. I am firmly persuaded, therefore, that the travels I have made thus far will not be a disgrace to me, but will be for my highest praise and glory. For I shall prove this from the very nature of things. He who wishes to investigate this nature has need to tread upon and turn over her books <note>original: "codices"</note> with his feet. Scripture is known through letters; but Nature is learned by the feet, by going from region to region. As many lands as there are in the world, so many are the pages of nature. Such is the book of nature; in such a way must its pages be turned.

<header>FIFTH DEFENSE.</header>

# FIFTH DEFENSE.

## Of the Repudiation of False Physicians and their Association.

<margin>Nothing without fairness.</margin>
<margin>Evils outnumber good things.</margin>
**S**ince nothing is ever found so pure anywhere that it is not polluted by some stain, it is worthwhile to teach how to properly discern the polluted from the pure. For this is also true in Medicine: *that more evils than good things are numbered.* If even among the disciples of Christ there was one traitor and degenerate out of twelve, how much more certain will this be among men? Indeed, it is believable that among twelve, scarcely one upright man will be found. The reason is: *that all things must be done by us out of charity.* <note>In this context, "charity" (Latin: *caritas*) refers to the theological concept of selfless, unconditional love for one's neighbor, rather than just giving alms.</note> But now, nothing is done out of charity; instead, whatever is provided is undertaken for the sake of due compensation and reward. This is followed by private interest.

<margin>Charity is dead.</margin>
<margin>Profit is the cause of all evil things.</margin>
From this, base and illegitimate <term>Physicians<gloss>Paracelsus uses the term "Pseudomedici" to describe those who lack the inner moral calling to heal.</gloss></term> are born in Medicine: those who hunt only for gain and fulfill the mandate of charity quite coldly. As soon as the pursuit of one's own profit begins, both the arts and their works are immediately corrupted. For these things ought to flow from charity; otherwise, nothing perfect is available. Just as we know there were two kinds of Apostles—one of whom loved Christ for the sake of his own benefit, for which reason he also took the purse of private gain—so, driven by that same cause, he sold Christ himself; and for that same reason, he delivered Christ to death.

<margin>Christ is betrayed for profit.</margin>
How much more will <term>False Physicians<gloss>original: Pseudomedici</gloss></term> destroy, corrupt, and slaughter men for this reason, so that private gain may be increased and its growth never hindered? For as soon as charity has grown cold in a man, he is no longer fit to bear fruit for his neighbor. Indeed, whatever fruits emerge from this are all heaped together for private benefit.

<margin>Twofold Physicians. The gain of Charity.</margin>
Hence it must be gathered that *the natures of Physicians are twofold. Some work from charity, others from profit.* Both are known by their works. The upright and just are revealed through charity, which they do not recklessly violate toward their neighbor.

<margin>The nature of False Physicians.</margin>
The wicked and base strike against this mandate for a slight reason, reaping where they have not sown, and emulating wolves in all things, scraping together from wherever anything can be scraped, so that the heap of domestic wealth may grow, being otherwise more than unconcerned with the divine mandate. Christ relates the example of the "Pearl" that was bought, and the "field" redeemed through that treasure. By this, He wished to teach that charity is found not in numbers, but in fewness. This is what he meant to say: If you are an upright physician, your "pearl" is the *field*. <note>Paracelsus is making a linguistic pun here: in Latin, *ager* means field, and *aeger* means a sick person or patient. He is identifying the patient as the "treasure" the physician should value above all else.</note> That same "field" is the sick person in whom the treasure is hidden. From this it follows that a Physician ought to sell all he has and restore the sick to health. This is the virtue of charity toward one's neighbor. But if anything is done otherwise, and you do not even keep what is yours but also plunder the sick person of his own, then you are by no means fulfilling the scripture, and thus your art in Medicine cannot be perfect. For this must always be kept before our eyes: that the purse of private gain was handed to Judas, and taken away from the other Apostles, whom it befitted to eat of those things which were set before them. To provide something of one's own accord proceeds from charity. To demand, to solicit, to beg—that is by no means permitted. For what we ought to receive from our neighbor is entrusted once and for all to charity, not committed to our own power. Therefore, it follows from this that for those who walk in the ways of God, perfect works and fruits remain entirely according to the gifts divinely given to them.

<margin>Wicked physicians do not heal.</margin>
Those who work against the ordinance of scripture are hedged in by many miseries and adversities, along with all those upon whom they prey for private gain—unless it happens that God works something in the neighbor against the False Physician’s art and remedies. Otherwise, through the work of their own hands, no one will be made healthy. Let it not seem strange to anyone that I cannot praise private profit in medicine. For since I have found out well how harmful a thing private benefit is—to the point that even the arts are foully corrupted by it and directed only toward outward show and deception—it is certain that such things cannot be performed without falsehood, which falsehood later brings about the corruption of all things.

<margin>All things are corrupted by profit.</margin>
It is fitting, therefore, for a physician to proceed not from profit, but from charity. That charity is free from care, nor is it anxious about tomorrow's food, but thinks thus to itself: *If the lilies of the field are well clothed, if the birds of the sky are abundantly fed, how much more man, who walks according to the heart of the Lord.*

<margin>The miserable petty gains of Physicians.</margin>
Since, however, men of such diverse nature flock to medicine, who [hunt] for profit...

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "cro," which likely completes the word "lucro" (for profit) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine must be practiced out of selfless charity rather than for profit, comparing greed-driven physicians to Judas Iscariot. He asserts that profit corrupts the medical arts and that a physician's primary focus should be the restoration of the patient, whom he likens to a hidden treasure.</summary>

<header>FIFTH DEFENSE.</header>

...they greedily compete for private gain: how, I ask, can my words find a place, when I so diligently call and invite them to charity? For my own part, I am not a little ashamed of medicine when I see how it is now entirely corrupted by impostors. Today, even the most wicked executioner, or

<margin>
Medicine is corrupted by a tribe of scoundrels.
</margin>
pimp, or dog-slayer <note>In the 16th century, executioners and "dog-slayers" (who caught stray animals) were seen as "dishonorable" trades, yet they often sold folk remedies or charms.</note>, attempts to mint gold from human or dog fat, and through it to heal all diseases. This is despite the fact that, as their own conscience bears witness, they are convicted by the reality that they have no permission to cure anything but one disease through the allowance of others. Nevertheless, out of a desire for their own profit, they take on sick people—whoever is offered to them from anywhere. Thus, even the worst and most lazy scoundrels force themselves into the tribe of Physicians, thrusting their remedies like poison, whether they fit the case or simply suit their convenience.

In this way, whoever knows how to chain gold into his pockets immediately gains the praise of a worthy physician. In the same way, even unskillful pharmacists and barbers dare to handle medicine, in which they occupy themselves not without injury to their own conscience; they cast aside the care of their own souls, just so they might grow rich from scraped-together little gains, build houses and halls, and add every ornament to them. Nor do they care much by what right they possess those things, as long as they are at hand.

<margin>
The corrupt custom of Physicians.
</margin>
Indeed, the doctoral custom today has earned (though where Scripture testifies this to be just, I for one do not know) that every single approach or visit to a sick person is rewarded with one <term>florin<gloss>A gold coin of significant value in the Holy Roman Empire.</gloss></term>. Thus, even for looking at a wash <note>Refers to uroscopy, the common practice of diagnosing diseases by examining the color and sediment of a patient's urine.</note> and other things, a fixed ordinary tax is established. However, that one person should be mercifully moved toward another and fulfill the mandate of charity—it seems all too true that no custom wants to become accustomed to that.

<margin>
The law of false physicians.
</margin>
Furthermore, the authority of the laws themselves does not remain intact; instead, the one supreme law is: *Snatch, Plunder, whether it be right or wrong.* <note>original: "Rape, Expila, fas seu minus fit"</note> This is how they wring out necklaces and extort gold rings; hence they go about clothed in silk garments, and thus exhibit their shame and disgrace to the whole world to be looked at, as if that spectacle would bring them honor and commendation. They walk about like brightly painted images, when rather it is a great abomination in the sight of God. And should one not rightly be ashamed of a possession whose nature and dignity is entirely perverted and contaminated by such vile scoundrels? And although the art itself is indeed a great treasure, it is never valued by those worthless men. Thus, many people everywhere handle Medicine, and there is almost no one anywhere who does not claim some knowledge of it for themselves. These, however, are thieves and robbers who do not enter through the door. Their highest art is to trifle, to make words, and to pretend to use technical terms. And by their tricks, they are sometimes even driven out. But once they desert a place, they do not dare to return to it again.

<margin>
Physicians are like couriers.
</margin>
They are like couriers, who, wherever they arrive, spread new news and then repeatedly take up the same song. If they return, they are no longer held in any value.

It is therefore to be deeply grieved that such a great art is handled by such ignorant and trivial men, and is driven to such corruption that even the truth itself is no longer believed. For the matter has now been brought to such wickedness by them that physicians everywhere are all considered to be "of the same flour" <note>An idiom meaning "all of the same sort" or "all bad in the same way."</note>, and even the most skilled does not retain his proper praise. This should be a wonder to no one.

<margin>
Jews are criticized.
</margin>
For since the most lying and treacherous Jews also handle sacred Medicine, and are highly valued by Pharisaical men: who, I ask, would hereafter grant honor to such a profession, which is performed and managed by such criminal scoundrels? <note>Paracelsus reflects the pervasive anti-Semitism of his time, using "Jew" and "Pharisee" as synonyms for deceit and legalism in the medical marketplace.</note>

<margin>
The world wants to be deceived.
</margin>
Meanwhile, since it is the fate of the world that *it wants to be deceived* <note>original: "Mundus vult decipi"</note>: because one saddle <note>original: "ephippium"</note> is fitted to horses of every kind, and the essence of the disease is not known, but whatever falls into someone's fantasy, that is his art. Therefore, no truth is held through experience; and from this it happens that so many corruptions creep in alongside sincere Medicine.

For those who are honest men attempt nothing of that sort. And unless people desired to be mocked back and forth, far more worthy and pure administrators of the medical province would be put in charge. But this is the perpetual custom of the world: that it cannot tolerate good, skilled, and honest craftsmen. Like is easily joined with like and melts together readily.

Should not, I say, any sincere and upright Physician blush to be counted among such scoundrels? Not only because they handle medicine, but because they also exist as craftsmen and advocates of every kind of lust. No religion...

<summary>Paracelsus denounces the greed of contemporary medical practitioners, comparing them to thieves and "dishonorable" tradesmen who prioritize high fees and silken clothes over patient care. He laments that the public's desire to be deceived allows these unskilled scoundrels to flourish while honest physicians lose their reputation.</summary>

<page-num>260</page-num>
<header>FIFTH DEFENSE.</header>
<meta>Catchword: in (from previous page, completing "religionem")</meta>

religion they themselves understand: they judge all things, and according to their own whim they either praise or blame everything; and whatever they wish, they take the most liberal power to act upon themselves. Furthermore, they boast of expertise in all languages. If you look closely, they are blockheads. Nor is there any lack of those who profess that the heavens bring about such things, and that the firmament is the cause of these corruptions. But I, too, have a thorough knowledge of the firmament from a certain perspective; yet I cannot understand in what way such impostures can flow into medicine from the heavens.

<margin>The stars are not the cause of human probity.</margin>
In truth, it is more certain and better proven that the impudence and fickleness of men are the cause of these frauds. There is no reason to cast the blame onto external things. Let each man touch and judge himself. For who today does not strive to fly even before his wings have grown? This deceit consists in this: that they act, yet have no certain knowledge of what they are doing. Their fickleness is placed in this: that a man strives to provide something for which he knows himself to be unequal. For these pseudo-physicians think thus to themselves: 
> Even if the work does not succeed, you will easily find an excuse by pinning your wickedness on God, or by transferring the blame to the sick man. Meanwhile, whatever happens, the money must be paid to you by the patients.

<margin>The medical art must be practiced truly.</margin>
Medicine is an art of such a kind that it ought not to be practiced by anyone except with the most certain knowledge, the greatest experience, and the highest fear of God. For he who does not fear God continues steadily in throat-cutting and thievery. Those who lack a sense of shame have no modesty within them. It is a supreme disgrace—indeed, a fatal punishment—that such criminal men are not recognized; yet, when we know a tree is not fruitful, we strike it with an axe and cast it into the fire. But people are deceived because the magistrates see only the civility shown toward them and the prompt obedience of these pseudo-physicians toward those to whom it is owed. It is necessary, therefore, that a certain distinction be maintained among physicians: namely, between those who walk in the law of God and those who walk in the laws of men. The former looks to charity; the latter makes his own profit. ¶ Let this, then, be the finishing touch <term>colophon</term> <note>The final stroke or crowning touch of an argument or a book.</note> of my defense: that I have no commerce whatsoever with these pseudo-physicians, nor do I support their frauds in the slightest. And if it were up to me that the axe should be set to the useless tree, there would be no long delay.

# SIXTH DEFENSE.

-> An excuse for the austerity and anger of Theophrastus. <-

<margin>Theophrastus's austerity is a virtue.</margin>
**A**MONG the other things they criminally charge me with, this is not the least: that I am of an unconventional <term>heteroclite</term> <note>Literally "deviating from the standard rules." Paracelsus was often mocked for his strange appearance and disregard for academic fashion.</note> head and strange hair; that I answer those who question me with austerity; that I do not offer myself up ready for everyone’s expectation; and that I do not listen to and admit everyone with the proper gentleness. Such things as these they hold against me as a great disgrace and vice. But I know that these things are not so joined to vice that I would not openly profess them to be very close to virtue. Nor would I wish to be anyone else entirely, even if I could do so very easily. This nature of mine is most highly approved by me. Nevertheless, for the excuse of this austerity of mine, take heed thus. Nature did not weave me from a subtle thread; nor is it the custom of my homeland that a great profit is made by spinning silk. We are not nourished on figs, or mead, or similar things.

<margin>Theophrastus's upbringing.</margin>
Our food is cheese, milk, and oat bread. How could these things make men subtle? But also, that which is implanted in us from our tender years, we taste of throughout our whole life; it is something very coarse if compared with those subtle, delicate, and well-groomed men. For we who are nurtured among pine cones cannot be like those who are educated with soft clothes in the women’s quarters <note>original: "Gynæceis." Paracelsus is contrasting his rugged, mountainous upbringing in Switzerland with the "effeminate" or overly-refined courtly doctors.</note>. Whence it happens that a coarse man is judged to be coarse, even if he seems subtle and amiable enough to himself. The same thing happens to me. For what I judge to be silk, they themselves deem to be coarse flax.

<margin>The custom of pseudo-physicians.</margin>
But as for the fact that I give hard and austere answers to men, hold this as my excuse. The physicians opposed to me have little of the art. Therefore, they study "humanity" and devote their efforts to the charms of words; they instruct men with modest and light speeches, and they lead the whole matter through an amiable series of explanations; departing, they dismiss the patient politely and say, *“My Lord, visit me again soon; My little wife, come here, and escort the Master to the door, etc.”* I, on the contrary, burst forth thus: "What is it you ask? I have no leisure now; the matter does not require such haste." By doing this, I have immediately "pissed on my ancestral ashes" <note>original: "in patrios cineres minxi." A Latin proverb from Horace meaning to act irreverently or to violate traditional sanctity/conventions.</note>. Thus, they have hitherto poured such illusions over the eyes of the sick that everyone is now persuaded that in...

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header>SIXTH DEFENSE.</header>

...that the whole height of the art is placed in flatteries, fawning, and trifles. They call these men "nobles" or <term>Junkers</term> <note>original: "Iunckeros," a term for young noblemen or squires, used here mockingly</note>, though they still smell of the shopkeeper. They call those men "Lords" who savor of the cobbler's shop or something even worse. But I, if I consider the benefit of people rather than the favor of an individual, immediately poured out whatever broth was in the pot <note>A common German idiom of the time meaning to speak one's mind plainly and without filter.</note>. And yet my purpose is firm: to gain nothing by a flattering tongue, but to devote myself only to works. This principle they do not share with me; they judge me by the standard of their own character to be strange, <margin>A living gained by fawning is shameful.</margin> and harsh and ungrateful in giving answers. Although I never presumed to earn my living by fawning and flattering. Hence it happens that I cannot practice that to which I previously devoted no effort.

But it is not right that every blockhead of a man should be lifted up by hands, when many of them are not even worthy of being carried on a sled <note>original: "trahâ," a crude transport often used for menial work or dragging heavy loads.</note>. It is fitting for a physician, setting aside all titles and petty flatteries, to give answers in such a way that in a brief speech he gets to the heart of the matter <note>original: "rhombum complectatur," literally "to embrace the turbot," a classical idiom meaning to get straight to the point.</note>, touches the wound, and does not wander off into any nonsense. For works and deeds, not words, are the sinews of counsel. Thus, as far as this accusation is concerned, I trust I have been sufficiently defended and vindicated against whatever rivals I may encounter.

Although they also say I am too harsh toward the patients themselves, while they do not adapt themselves well enough to my prescribed regimen. I do not do this unjustly, but I set this one goal: namely, that medicine itself, true and genuine, may be recognized in this way, so that patients heal more quickly, and I am forced to hear less ill from my adversaries. By this logic, however, even a turtle-dove's stomach could be turned <note>A metaphor suggesting that even the most patient person would eventually be provoked to anger by such behavior.</note>.

Furthermore, they also throw my own servants and some of my disciples in my face, who, weary of my austerity, have departed. <margin>The tragic end of Theophrastus's runaway servants.</margin> To this quibble I respond thus: The executioner has taken twenty-one of my servants from among the living. May God help them all. But how could they stay with me if the executioner took them away? Or what did my indignation do to them? If they had avoided the indignation of the executioner, *that* would have been a true art. 

But if other servants also, of the same batch <note>literally "the same flour"</note> as the previous ones, who have so far escaped the executioner, go about as runaways singing of my anger: what does it matter? Why should I not be angry if a servant does not do a servant's duty, but wickedly tries to act as the master? If, busy with his own advantage, he brings about my loss and disgrace, and insults me on top of the harm done? If they succeed by secretly slandering me to the patients, and without my knowledge take over their care for half the fee, saying they know all my secrets? <margin>All are treacherous toward Theophrastus.</margin> If their insolence becomes known to me, why should I not be indignant? Doctors, surgeons, barbers, disciples, servants, and even boys have committed this crime against me. And yet after all this, am I supposed to be a lamb? It would be a wonder if I did not become fiercer than a wolf. Meanwhile, I must travel on foot while they ride about on horses. This, however, is a constant consolation to me: that I remain consistently myself, while they flee and are caught in enormous crimes. 

That the doctors raise complaints about me is nothing new. For truth is harsh and bitter to the ear of one whose fraud is brought to light. <margin>Truth is bitter to hear.</margin> But how many are there who even commend me greatly for this very thing? These too are doctors themselves. The same lamentation comes from the pharmacists, that I am satisfied with no one's work or industry. Yet anyone who does right has my approval. <margin>Why Theophrastus is accused of being authoritative.</margin> But if they offer *substitutions* <note>original: "Quid pro Quo," a pharmaceutical term for substituting one drug for another, often done for profit rather than efficacy</note>, offering dung instead of musk, I certainly cannot support or give my assent to such a disgrace. 

Furthermore, of what they give me, barely a third part is good and useful. Sometimes it is not even what it ought to be. Should I then, following their reckless example, administer to my patients "this for that," the spoiled instead of the fresh? I would do so certainly if I did not place much value on my own disgrace, the harm to the patients, and finally their very death. So if I behave according to my innate nature (which I nevertheless consider human enough), those gamblers call me angry and strange, unlike all the other doctors, and famous for this austerity alone. Then they also say that I write brief prescriptions, not consisting of 40 or 60 ingredients. They complain that their jars are not being emptied, and no money is being provided for their kitchen. Hence those tears; hence those hateful attacks and slanders. Now you yourselves judge: to which of these do I owe more? To the profit of the pharmacists' kitchen by emptying their jars, or to the health of the patients by providing recovery?

<summary>Paracelsus defends his abrasive personality and direct medical style, arguing that his "harshness" is a necessary reaction to the incompetence of "Junker" doctors, the treachery of his servants, and the greed of pharmacists who profit from bloated prescriptions.</summary>

should I care for you? From this, let everyone now see how <term>irregular</term> <note>original: "Heteroclitus," a grammatical term for words that deviate from standard patterns, used here to mean "eccentric" or "non-conforming."</note> I am, and how intolerable this head of mine appears. For if I wished to go further in rendering the reasons for my anger, by heaven, all those who charge me with this as a disgrace and a crime would be ashamed and confounded. For this accusation of theirs would draw out many outrages about themselves to be betrayed by me, which would be rightfully detestable before all honest judges and listeners. But if I truly wished to manifest the reasons for certain surgeons, on account of which they are hostile to me: I think indeed that their condition would be no more tolerable than was the condition of those about whom we spoke a little while ago. Therefore, from this sixth defense, I would wish each and everyone to be warned that they should weigh these things they hear about me with a fair judgment and an equal scale, and think thus: that these accusations do not flow from a pure and cleansed heart, but rather overflow from the mere bilge-water of envy, so that in this way the outrages of the sources might be veiled, and I, innocent, might become the scapegoat for their wickedness.

# SEVENTH DEFENSE.

->*That I do not know, nor am I able to do, all things that*<-
->*use and necessity might demand of anyone.*<-

<margin>Why Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim is Paracelsus’s given name.</note> does not heal everyone.</margin>
**I** can neither deny nor do I wish to, that I am not that man who can satisfy the petition and hope of everyone conceived about me in all things. For God did not wish Medicine to be granted with such a nature that it is ready at anyone’s whim and prayer, and provides whatever is completed. If, therefore, God does not wish to impart health to some man according to His private counsel: what can I avail against God in that case? I, who can neither compel nor command God. But on whose nod do both we, the sick man and I, depend? Let this therefore be the general answer: if they were a concern to God, and if God wished them to be healed, He would by no means have withdrawn the help of nature from them. Nor does this matter seem different to me than if someone should seem to himself handsome, polished, and lovable, and should demand that he prevail in the love of all women and virgins, even though he was born with such a form that, being both lame and hunchbacked, he exhibits a certain spectacle of deformity of the rest of his whole body to everyone.

<margin>Why many are not favored.</margin>
And how, I ask, could delicate women love this man, whom nature herself did not love? Whom she herself twisted in the mother’s womb and miserably deformed? But so that you may receive the matter even more fully, know that to him whom God does not favor, nature itself confers nothing healthy. Unless these two favors correspond to each other, what can the Physician do? Or who will accuse him of the unhappy success? But they also object this to me: that if I am called to a sick man, I do not distinguish his condition immediately, but have need of a long time to know it. That is true of me. What they judge there and then and instantly, that is a symbol of folly and arrogance. For the outcome finally teaches what they judged precipitously and wrongly: and so it happens that daily they know less, and they themselves basely betray their own lie in this way. On the contrary, it is my intention to increase and be enriched more and more daily in knowledge or certainty.

<margin>Knowledge of diseases is difficult.</margin>
For the knowledge of hidden diseases is not as easy as that of external colors. For while they are open, it is easy to judge which color is black, green, or blue. But if you hold up a veil to them: then you yourself would not discern or judge them. For to see through a veil, that is an art of which they themselves are entirely unskilled and ignorant.

<margin>Where the judgment of the senses is certain.</margin>
What the eyes dictate, that is permitted for anyone to discern instantly. But what is hidden from the eyes, you will strive in vain to judge in that way, as if it were open and exposed outside. Let the <term>coppersmith</term> <note>original: "ærarius," a worker in bronze or copper; Paracelsus frequently uses analogies from mining and metallurgy, reflecting his background in the mines of Villach.</note> be an example for you. However skilled, or artistic, or wise he may be, if he first sees a certain ore, he nevertheless does not know what it is, what it contains, or how it must be treated—whether it must be roasted, or melted, or burned, or prepared in any other way. For first he is forced to make a trial of it and take some assays, so that he may understand more accurately where it will turn out. Once that is properly hammered out and known by the necessary trial, afterward he decides and decrees what he wishes to be made of it.

<margin>Judgment of hidden disease is difficult.</margin>
The same logic applies entirely to hidden and long-lasting diseases: so that a sudden judgment can by no means be made of them, unless perhaps it is attempted rashly and ridiculously by the <term>Humorists</term> <note>Physicians who followed the traditional Galenic system of the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). Paracelsus was their primary critic.</note>. And therefore, the diligent investigation, weighing, balancing, and testing of such conditions [should be] a fault to no one... <meta>The sentence continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that a physician's success is ultimately subject to God's will and that a proper medical diagnosis requires careful testing and time, rather than the "instant" but faulty guesses of traditional physicians.</summary>
