# SEVENTH DEFENSE.
<sig>c</sig>

granted. But if, through trial and examination, the disease is properly understood, and then at last you manfully gird yourself for its healing, you will have performed the duty of a good Physician. For one should by no means proceed with diseases in any other way. Yet the <term>Humorists</term> <note>Followers of the traditional Galenic theory that illness is caused by an imbalance of four "humors": blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note> do not walk this path in testing for diseases. This is the reason why they send so many sick people to the cemetery before they even grasp the "sinew" <note>The essential strength or core principle.</note> of the art; and yet even so, they do not penetrate deeply enough into its secrets. This is the face of their own art. And shall I allow myself to be judged by such craftsmen? So be it: I cannot do everything.

<margin>Reproof of Physicians.</margin>
But what can those men do themselves, who think that nothing is of any importance unless it is sanctioned by the "Sun"—that is, by Avicenna, by <term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Referring to Maimonides, the influential medieval Jewish physician and philosopher.</note>, or by some haphazard method, however it might turn out? These are surely their <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>Short, authoritative principles of medicine, originally popularized by Hippocrates.</note>: by which they construct a shortcut to the cemetery for the sick.

Because I cannot cure those things that are incurable, why do you hurl this at me? You, who do not even know how to lawfully cure light and curable diseases; you, who destroy what I am forced to rebuild and restore? How indeed could I replace a ruined heart, or re-attach and bond together a severed hand? Who in the <term>light of nature</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the innate wisdom and functional laws found within the natural world, accessible through observation rather than just ancient books.</note> was ever so powerful as to unite death and life, so that death might receive life? For this is not a work of nature, but a divine work. Why should I be able to perform such things, when you cannot even heal a small wound—one in which there is no danger or anything lethal, unless you yourselves bring it about? You are surely dim-sighted: you see what is in the distance, but you do not see yourselves right in front of you. Your own conscience will be my witness, against which you sin, because you wickedly desire to veil those things which you are nonetheless not ashamed to commit—

Before you, all medicines have been brought forth by God, by which curable diseases can be removed, yet you do not know how to cure those very things. Why then do you pluck at me because I perform nothing in incurable diseases, when no remedies have been given to us by God for them? But receive the "finishing touch" <note>original: "coronidem," a Greek-derived term for the final flourish or conclusion of a work.</note> of this defense. How, I ask, can I heal curable diseases if hail strikes the pharmacies? If lightning burns the kitchens, who can eat the food? Who can ward off musket balls with a skin, or drive away the cold with a breastplate? How can <term>Substitution</term> <note>original: "Quid pro Quo," a pharmaceutical practice where one drug is swapped for another. Paracelsus argues this is often done with inferior or incorrect ingredients.</note> suffice for me in a cure? For by that practice, you cast down most of your patients. And you have need of good luck, so that no riots or robberies are brought in by that "this for that." Who could accomplish a cure through adulterated spices, which only the genuine and true ones can achieve? Who could obtain a result through herbs corrupted by rot, for which fresh and green ones are required? Who can tolerate that the juice of <term>Spurge</term> <note>original: "Tithymalli," a caustic plant often used as a harsh purgative.</note> be administered instead of <term>Scammony</term> <note>original: "Diagridio," a potent medicinal resin.</note>? Who would endure distilled shoemaker's pitch being offered instead of <term>Blessed Oil</term> <note>original: "oleo benedicto," often referring to "oil of bricks" or a specific holy preparation used in surgery.</note>? Or the pulp of cherries mixed with treacle being provided instead of <term>Mithridatum</term> <note>A famous semi-mythical "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients.</note>? For if I were to begin to examine all your simples and compounds out of necessity: where would they scurry off to?

<margin>It is lawful for anyone to defend himself.</margin>
And let this be the final shield of my defense, until I am provoked by new injuries and slanders. For then we too shall have a sword at home. I wish for all good and honest men to be asked, from a sincere and upright conscience, that they do not judge these writings of mine with an unfair sense. For necessity itself compelled me to this response and defense. Thus even Christ did not keep silent, but resisted his detractors. To defend and protect oneself is honorable, indeed necessary, lest glory and place be yielded to those who place all their protection in a slandering tongue. Unless they were seriously confronted, they would deafen everyone with their shouts, and with their trophies, they would continually bring in new deceptions, scandals, and outrages. Therefore, let this be the manner and end of the response: that present as well as future errors and corruptions may be washed away and prevented, and at the same time, it may be made manifest what "bad hair" <note>original: "mali pili," an idiom suggesting someone of poor character or "a bad lot."</note> these triflers are. Thus my spirit has also rejoiced to defend myself boldly against all those whose hearts overflow with the splinters of envy, so that in this way, we might become known to each other on both sides for what we truly are. For it is necessary that slanders and outrages overflow. But woe to him through whom they are introduced! This is the same as saying: It is necessary that liars speak against the truth. But woe to them! For the lie will be made manifest through the truth. If they had hidden their crimes, I also would not have betrayed the truth about them. But because it is necessary for this to happen: lies and outrages cannot keep silent. But woe to them. It is your duty, Reader, to weigh everything with a fair and candid mind. Thus it will happen that you will certainly feel the sure fruit of your reading.

### CONCLUSION.

<summary>Paracelsus concludes his Seven Defenses by arguing that he cannot be blamed for failing to cure the incurable, especially when his rivals fail at simple cures and pharmacies provide corrupt, substituted ingredients. He asserts his right to defend his reputation against envious detractors, comparing his stance to that of Christ against his accusers.</summary>

## CONCLUSION.

<margin>
Hippocrates, Apollo, and Machaon <note>In Greek mythology, Machaon was the son of Asclepius and a healer of the Greeks at Troy; he represents the surgical side of medicine.</note> are the purest Physicians.
</margin>

**S**o then, Reader, you have for the most part understood these defenses of mine, and you have observed that I have treated the whole matter as modestly as possible. It is now entirely up to you to consider, by your own effort, how much trivial and worthless men are accustomed to boast and chatter. You may also learn from this that the dispute concerns Physicians alone. From this you will know how to predict what kind of men Medicine is practiced among today, and how unequal the match is if Polydorus <note>Likely a reference to the Trojan prince or a legendary figure associated with healing/restoration.</note> and Apollo were to be compared with the moderns. Indeed, Nature herself might shudder at such a spectacle. For she, being most sagacious, senses her enemy much more readily than a dog senses its killer. With what praise Medicine should be celebrated, and with what honors a Physician should be adorned, is abundantly clear from Holy Scripture. And reason itself dictates that Scripture pointed its finger at Hippocrates, Apollo, and Machaon, who, driven by the purest genius of Medicine, exhibited wonders, signs, and works within living beings, and proved themselves the very lights of Nature. However great my simplicity may be, I can nevertheless easily grasp that Holy Scripture did not intend to refer to those who lack works, who are loud-mouthed, and who act as mercenaries; rather, it primarily hints at those who follow in the footsteps of Machaon. From what has gone before, it can easily be gathered that the whole world is full of hardships and labors. Yet I have no doubt that if the magistracy were fired with a zeal for knowing these things, and had suffered the same evil themselves, they would institute a much sharper censorship for the sake of brotherly love. The most praised province of Carinthia <note>A region in southern Austria where Paracelsus found refuge and wrote some of his most important works.</note> has drunk this deeply into its soul; it performs the duty of a <term>Maecenas</term> <note>A generous patron of the arts and sciences, named after the advisor to the Roman Emperor Augustus.</note>, and is the unique refuge, the sole protection and defense of the Hippocratics of our age. May God, in exchange for this heroic virtue, pour back upon it peace, grace, and harmony forever, Amen.

### BOOK SECOND,
# TITLED THE LABYRINTH OF PHYSICIANS.
## THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM, etc., 
->To the Hippocratic Doctors, greetings.<-

<margin>
The medical books of the ancients are a chaos.
</margin>

**I**t now seems to me convenient and timely to finally set forth which books I have used in my speaking, so that in this way the expectation of many may be satisfied. I would particularly wish you to know, beloved lords and friends, that those books which antiquity offered both to me and to you seemed by no means sufficient for my purpose. For they were not perfect, but were a certain confused and indistinguishable chaos, the reading of which showed monsters rather than a clear path. This

<margin>
There is no discipline without a teacher.
</margin>

was also the reason why I shook them from my hands. Meanwhile, it is only too true that a student cannot exist without a teacher. For the student has need of the teacher in order to learn. Hence, that care continually gripped me: where, at last, might a true Master dwell who could teach solid wisdom? For it seemed unsuitable to recognize the ancient writers as such. Finally, I reasoned with myself thus: What if there were no book, no Doctor under the Sun—from where, then, would you learn? And I later discovered through certain proofs that Medicine can be learned by a most ready method without any living teacher. But in what way and by what path that might be done, I am about to explain through certain books, collected and inserted here, which are a certain

<margin>
Medicine must be learned from living books.
</margin>

foremost foundation for finding all things and arts, and for investigating a universal theory. These will be connected later; the sum of them, however, is this: that it be solidly established that a man ought by no means to seek or grab at his health from a man as if from a singular master, but that he ought to be made perfect through the fundamental books by eloquent men. And this is the unique principle of the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>A central concept in Paracelsus's philosophy: the innate wisdom placed by God into the natural world, which a physician must learn to read like a book.</note>, which man can by no means bring forth from himself and his own reason. Man indeed bestows something, but that is quite imperfect. Perfection must be investigated more deeply, namely from that spring from which all men drink. And although God indeed bestowed upon St. Peter and other Saints the power of casting out demons and raising the dead, they nevertheless can by no means confer this power upon others. In the same way, we...

*...we are also compelled to receive these things from God and through God. In Medicine as well, a human being can bestow something, but it is only a simple and crude instruction.*

<margin>Perfect instruction comes from the light of Nature.</margin>
*The perfection itself must be drawn from the light of nature, in the same way that the Apostles received it from God. Let this be the example: the Apostles did not preach Christ from their own power, but from Him who spoke through them with tongues of fire <note>A reference to the Pentecost in Acts 2, where the Holy Spirit descended as fire to grant understanding.</note>, whom they held as their master. This is the kind of school that Physicians must also attend: namely, that the light of nature itself should instruct the Physician through Philosophy and Astronomy, and not a man in whom the natural light shines very little. And so that this may be more easily understood by you, I have decided to set forth the principal books of the light of nature: so that from them you may understand where the school of Philosophy is founded, and in what manner those genuine books ought to be sought.*

<margin>What the Books of the light of Nature provide.</margin>
*Once this is finished, there will be no further need for me or for you to cling to paper books. For if we are willing to listen to every fanatical herald, where will an end or the truth finally be obtained? Through these books of nature, however, no one can be led astray. For in these alone is the truth handed down. Read these, turn their pages. They hand down and teach how we can and should serve our neighbor—not to their harm, but to their benefit.*

*And with these words, whoever you are that shall be the shepherds of bodies, I uniquely commend to you the illustrious and most celebrated leaders of the Archduchy of Carinthia <note>A region in modern-day southern Austria where Paracelsus found significant patronage.</note>, that you may most faithfully provide for them with all the natural help that is within you; and do so specifically out of that same inclination by which you wish for all sick people everywhere to be rescued and healed. Be mindful of what God has spoken: "A wise man will not despise medicine." <note>original: "Vir sapiens non aspernabitur Medicinam" — a quote from Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:4.</note> For there God especially works and dwells. Given on the Kalends of August, in the year of salvation 1538.*

# PREFACE
## INTO THE LABYRINTH
### OF ERRING PHYSICIANS
### By Doctor Theophrastus Hohenheim.

<margin>The Labyrinthine Religion of Medicine.</margin>
<margin>Two kinds of wanderers.</margin>
**T**hose who dwell in error are carried wherever they go by uncertain steps, nor do they have a clear understanding of where they must finally turn. Since errors must be diligently avoided, it is worthwhile to lead those who walk wickedly back from their errors to the right path, and to take care lest more and more people fall into those same trackless wastes. In this way, the "Religion of Medicine" is also (so to speak) entangled in Labyrinths. To err and yet to know it at the same time is a mark of good intellect. But there are two kinds of such wanderers. Some wander and can return neither to the "One-Eyed One" <note>The "Monoculus" or "One-Eyed" represents a person with partial, distorted vision or a false guide who lacks the full "Light of Nature."</note> nor to the gate or entrance; they wander like blind men who know no path. These people go in circles and search, but never find an end. Their path is a pure Labyrinth; they seek where there is nothing, and they find what is not there, and what is nothing. Others penetrate even to the very center of the Labyrinth, and if they reach it, they have found the "One-Eyed One" (whom* <margin>Minotaurs in the center of the Labyrinth.</margin> *they call the Minotaur <note>In Greek myth, the Minotaur was a monster at the center of the Labyrinth; here, Paracelsus uses it to represent the false "authority" at the heart of academic medicine.</note>). He, once found, becomes the King of all those who remain and linger inside. There, then, the One-Eyed One thrives and rules with his science. But the most serious error of all is the one produced by art. And those who walk uncertainly in wisdom are wrapped in a most intricate labyrinth, whom the darkness finally overwhelms.*

<margin>How serious errors in the arts are.</margin>
*Through their errors, however, these people collect many experiments. For they insinuate themselves everywhere into all the winding paths they meet, yet they never find the gate. Such an error causes more dizziness and bile than if one were to go a long way or straight toward the dark stars. In a labyrinth of this kind, they find "experiments of experiments," and all the other foolish labyrinths. As is the Master, so is the disciple. As is the smith, so is the tool. As is the art, so is the work. And whoever dwells under the Minotaur, who is the One-Eyed One, is blind. In the same way, their studies, doctrine, works, speculations, wisdom, science, practice, and visitations must also be blind. Thus they enter the Labyrinth without an eye. So, what the eye does not see, they do not see either. In this error, it is even more serious that even if they did see, and were like the Minotaur, he is nevertheless alone, and has enough work of his own to keep himself from being led into error. Thus he dismisses the others. For a single eye can see only toward one side. The other side is blind.*

<margin>Where the Jews claim Medicine for themselves.</margin>
*Now indeed, see how difficult and dangerous it is to err in the arts, in wisdom, and in sciences. For those who have once fallen into this place are held back until they return to the true and genuine entrance. And in this labyrinth, several thousand run about who are nevertheless unable to extricate themselves. The Jews have also claimed the praise of Medicine for themselves; and they do not even blush at this lie: that the most ancient Medicine is in their possession. Among the nations indeed*

<summary>Paracelsus introduces his critique of traditional medicine as a "Labyrinth" where doctors wander blindly, following the "One-Eyed" Minotaur of false authority. He advocates for a return to the "Light of Nature" as the only true source of healing, rather than relying on "paper books."</summary>

...of all men, these rascals <note>original: "nebulones"; a derogatory term for worthless or deceptive people</note> are the most ancient. But what, and of what sort, is their treatment? What do they know? What do they provide? What do they draw from their books? In practice, they know nothing. They only know how to practice deceptions. They have always opposed God himself and his Son, and they do the same even now. And who, I ask, would possess such great favor of Nature—that which God has nevertheless withdrawn from them, making them shameful and despised men? Just as He has made them infected and corrupted in both body and wealth, so too has He made all those who foster them with their protection or have any business with them. Whatever good they know is from outsiders. <margin>They arrogantly claim the nations intended to practice medicine.</margin> For they were not educated for healing, nor ordained by God for it, but for the worship of God and for serving Him. This was their vocation. Beyond this, whatever else they have attempted anywhere has been mere trickery and imposture. Medicine was given to the nations <note>Referring to the Gentiles or the broader world beyond the specific theological lineage Paracelsus is critiquing.</note>. These are the first and most ancient of physicians. From this it happened that the Greeks rushed eagerly into Medicine for many and various reasons. But they were so deeply submerged in lies that, after the Arabs, they also tried to undertake the same province, just like all the other nations. Yet this was the outcome: the more wisdom, the more of a labyrinth. For the human intellect provides or bestows nothing. <margin>Medicine is from God alone.</margin> He alone gives medicine, in whose hands it has been placed. Finally, the last and newest have also arrived, intending to trample down this labyrinth themselves. And it came to pass that the last were found to be the best. For the first were of no use. Furthermore, salvation lies with the last. Outside of these, it is all over for health. Therefore, so that I might explain and uncover this labyrinth and show its true origin or principle, I have presumed to bring forward those books from which the tangled windings might be known and discerned, and a cleared entrance or way in might be established: not to the one-eyed Minotaur, but to that three-eyed one <note>original: "trinoculum"; likely a reference to divine or spiritual perception as opposed to the blind "one-eyed" logic of the schools.</note>, enclosed within a single Deity. We must stand and walk in His ways. And he who does this is blessed. He who is blessed is free from error and guile, nor is his heart occupied by any imposture.

# THEOPHRASTUS
## GREETINGS TO THE READER.

<margin>The path which is right for Medicine.</margin>
**S**INCE a rumor is spread about me everywhere, Reader, as if I were the one who puts a sickle into another man's harvest <note>A common legal and biblical metaphor for encroaching on another's profession or rights.</note> in Medicine, and do not enter through the right door as is proper: it is fair that I clear myself of this accusation in a timely manner. This I do in this discourse. Let them tell me, what indeed is it to enter into medicine through the right door? Is it through Avicenna, Galen, Mesue, Rhazes <note>Names of the classical Greek and medieval Arabic authorities who dominated university medicine at the time.</note>, etc., or through the light of nature itself? For here two entrances lie open. One is named the entrance of books; the other is of Nature itself. Now, therefore, there is a need for discretion and judgment as to which of these doors should be entered, and which less so. The genuine door, however, is the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>Lumen Naturae: The Paracelsian concept that God’s wisdom is hidden within the physical world and can be "read" by the physician.</note> alone. The other offers a descent through the roof. For these two do not fit together; they do not agree. For the codices of writers are one thing, the Light of Nature is another; the light of the Apothecaries and such things are another. Since these are not of one kind, and yet it seems necessary that there be one way, it is fitting that that book exists as legitimate and authentic which God himself wrote, enriched, and compiled. But the other books, whatever counsels or opinions they have provided according to their own manner, detract from Nature itself in my view. This must be diligently repeated to you, Reader: that Medicine proceeds from a certain single and unique source, namely from God. <margin>As every good thing is from God, so also is Medicine.</margin> For from Him every principle and foundation flows. For He himself testifies that He created medicine wonderfully. What is this other than him saying: I alone have described the medicine of the same in a book; seek and read there, there you will find it. <margin>Who is wise?</margin> A wise man will not despise it, but if it is from God, he will use it entirely. <margin>The wise man admires medicine.</margin> For no one is wise unless he is one to whom the works of God are not an abomination. But he who abominates medicine, in him neither God nor medicine dwells. For where the wisdom of God is absent, then He from whom it proceeds is also not present. Thus, if you wish to become a Physician, first seek medicine where it is, if you are wise; do not track it down or find it from within yourself. For it is not Rhetoric, nor the parts of speech. Take it from here, where it is described. Thus you will not err. And turn over all these described books. Whatever agrees with the light of nature exists as good and durable. But what does not agree with it is a mere Labyrinth, having neither a certain entrance nor exit. Many indeed are persuaded that they have written from the light of nature itself. But it is nothing. They have indeed provided something, but they entered the labyrinth prematurely. It seems likely to me that they borrowed something from those to whom God bestowed this grace. These they suppressed, and found the pearl in the labyrinth. For it had been cast before swine. So, in reading, let it be covered <note>original: "tegere"; perhaps used here in the sense of selecting or sifting through texts.</note> so that the genuine books of the Physician are read first, in which all true medicine is handed down. He alone illuminates the Physician; and without Him, there is nothing.

<summary>Paracelsus defends his unconventional medical approach, arguing that true medicine comes from the "Light of Nature" and God rather than the "Labyrinth" of classical academic texts. He dismisses traditional authorities like Galen and Avicenna as deceptive, claiming they have strayed from the authentic, God-given path of healing.</summary>

# CHAPTER I.

## *Concerning the first and supreme book of Medicine, from which every Physician ought to derive his art and experience, which proceeds from the one spirit.*

<margin>What wisdom is</margin>
**T**he FIRST and highest book of all medicine is called Wisdom. Without this book, no one will accomplish anything good or useful. Moreover, wisdom is to know, not to guess <note>original: "opinari"; Paracelsus distinguishes between certain knowledge and the speculative theories of his contemporaries</note>: so that one may understand all things and handle them with reason, so that there is one science and one understanding, lacking in stupidity and foolishness, and free from error and doubt. In that book, the principle and the truth are contained, as well as the knowledge of all things. For from knowledge, all things are governed, arranged, and brought <margin>God is the source of wisdom.</margin> to their perfection. Furthermore, this book is God himself. For in Him alone, who created the universe, does the science and the principle of all things reside. Through Him, we know how to conduct ourselves prudently in all those things in which we must walk. Without Him, we know how to ask for, decree, or bestow nothing in a just manner. Without Him, all things are foolishness. Just as the Sun illuminates us from above, so all arts must be poured into us from above. For what else is wisdom but a certain art through which everyone may know and recognize his own gift and duty? Just as we cannot produce day and night, or summer and winter, from within ourselves, so much less do we know how to draw that wisdom from our own selves. And although <margin>From whom medicine is obtained</margin> medicine itself is indeed natural—that is, it is found among us on the earth, such as quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, Guaiacum <term>Guaiacum: a medicinal "holy wood" from the Caribbean used extensively in the 16th century to treat the "French Disease" (syphilis)</term>, and so on—the same must nevertheless be shown to us from that supreme book. From this book we may learn what is in medicine, how it is within it, in what way it should be taken from the earth, and how it ought to be applied to diseases, and to which ones. For medicine is not the body; rather, it is the earth. <margin>Medicine is not the body of things.</margin> Medicine is that which exists within the body, which the earth, blood, and flesh do not know. From this it follows that medicine must flow from that spirit which is in man. He who is from Him, to whom he returns, is at last a true disciple of Medicine. It is evident, <margin>Celestial doctrine: what is the first precept.</margin> therefore, that the first doctrine and knowledge is this: *that first of all we seek the kingdom of God.* <note>A reference to Matthew 6:33.</note> Here the treasure is stored; this is the school of the beginning of wisdom for every man in his duty. From here, all other things are drawn for us. For if we seek, and knock, and pray in the kingdom of God, what could be more noble? For we are all earthly, and from this earthly school we carry away nothing other than foolishness. Therefore we are taught to seek and learn in the kingdom of God, in which all sciences are stored. And no physician can tear down this doctrine. If such a person should perhaps think that nature is not established in the kingdom of God, he thinks entirely wrongly. For nature proceeds from God. And although there may indeed be some faithless Physician without having sought the kingdom of God, it nevertheless remains eternally true that nothing happens without God. The spirit gives life and nourishes where it wills; it belongs to no one, and is carried by the freest movement. Therefore, the physician himself must also derive his principles from that spirit. And without it, he is nothing else than a False Physician <note>original: "Pseudomedicus"</note>, wandering and of a straying and fleeting spirit. If he is eager to learn the truth of the art, it is entirely necessary to prepare this very entrance. For unless he enters by this way, he will indeed learn more and more assiduously, but he will never penetrate to the end of truth; just as Paul eloquently hands down concerning these things, and teaches all from where each person should derive his knowledge. For if any Physician lacks art or wisdom, let him seek it, just as the Apostle James teaches, to know and investigate natural virtues and hidden mysteries from God. Moreover, this which has been said by me—*that God himself is the first book*—ought to seem strange or unworthy to no one. For who knows a work better than he who made it? He alone knows how to demonstrate the efficacy of the work. Indeed, who made medicine, if not God alone? Who else is there who knows it, if not <margin>God alone made medicine.</margin> God alone? Thus, therefore, it flows down from God, just as heat from the Sun which produces flowers. In the same way, it is right that our sciences also flow from God. Thus, therefore, say boldly: What has been found anywhere on earth that has not reached us from God? He has enclosed all things <margin>From God all things must be obtained.</margin> in his hands. If we wish to shake these things out of His hands, then it must be done entirely by praying, seeking, and knocking. And this path leads to this school. For nothing at all may be obtained here through force or theft. For He who commanded us to ask for our daily bread, also commands us to be concerned for this very thing,

<summary>Paracelsus establishes that the foundation of true medicine is divine Wisdom (Sapientia) and God himself, rather than human tradition or mere physical matter. He argues that a physician must seek spiritual enlightenment to understand the "spirit" of healing hidden within natural substances.</summary>

## CHAPTER II.

### *Concerning the second book of Medicine, which must be unfolded and read by the Physician, namely, concerning the Firmament.*

<margin>The compulsion to write is criticized.</margin>
**Y**ou ought not to wonder or be indignant that I do not send you away to paper books from which to learn the principles of medicine. The reason for this matter is not worthy of consideration. The good, the bad, the erroneous, and the fanatical all write and comment mixed together; they heap up the depraved and the upright into one chaos, and they corrupt the good with the evil. They make such a foul and confused medley that he who once falls into those waves can hardly struggle out again to a calm sea. They all strive with one zeal to raise themselves up by the feathers of others, and they continually add new things to one another. Through these writers, all Medicine has been corrupted and contaminated, so that those paper books no longer possess any shred of credibility. And even if someone perhaps had one or two experiments, it was such that he was more seduced by it than instructed. And the style itself testifies that great simplicity joined with ignorance has converged in Medicine. Therefore, it is fitting for you to know that there are far different and diverse books available from which the physician must learn, and from which the true foundation flows. And without the books of this true principle, all other things remain a dead letter—that is, they cast the sick more readily toward death than lead them toward health.

<margin>The Firmament is a book, and what it is.</margin>
Now, however, attend to the second book of Medicine, which is the <term>Firmament</term> <note>In Paracelsus's philosophy, the "Firmament" refers to the astronomical and astrological heavens, which he believed directly influenced the human body (the microcosm)</note>. This follows the aforementioned first book in the order of reading. For if, as was said, you seek the kingdom of God, all other things will be added to you. Thus, this is also a certain addition into which he leads us who stands in the Light of Nature. Just as a whole doctrine can be entered and described by letters in a book, so that he who...

so that anyone can read and know it: so also in the firmament a book is placed, which teaches and explains its own virtues, and demonstrates its doctrine. Not that all things take their origin through an Alphabet <note>The author distinguishes between human-made languages (the Alphabet) and the inherent "language" of nature.</note>: but rather that such an origin is plainly nothing. That which is contained in the Alphabet comes to the **Alphabet** from the outside. In the firmament, however, the origin itself and the letter itself are one and the same thing. For example: A tree, which stands here, has the name of "tree" even without an Alphabet, nor does it need an Alphabet. But by its own evidence it testifies to what it is, what it bears, what it holds within itself, and what it is useful for, without any paper, ink, or pen. Therefore, just as a tree describes itself and teaches us what and of what sort it is: so it is also compared with the book of the Firmament, from which the origin or principle is bestowed upon the Alphabet itself. But because man gives and receives the same thing in different ways: it is now clear that one cannot even safely trust what is true and genuine unless it is proven through this second book, just as gold is tested by **antimony**. <note>Antimony was used in alchemy and early chemistry to purify gold, separating it from other metals.</note>

<margin>Why human books cannot be trusted.</margin>
And he who has not learned this book thoroughly can neither be, nor be called, a physician. For this is the task and duty of the Physician: that just as one reads a book on paper, so likewise the stars of the firmament

<margin>The stars are the letters of the Firmament.</margin>
should be read, and gathered together like letters, so that finally a meaning may be constructed from the collected words. For just as every single word has its own peculiar power, and yet does not contain a full meaning in itself since that meaning is completed through many perfect words: so also it is necessary for the stars themselves in the firmament to be collected, and for a "firmamental" meaning—that is, the universal foundation—to be joined and constructed into one. And just as the mind of the sender can be grasped and known from a letter received from the most distant places: so in the same way, the sense and mind of the firmament itself is announced to us. Therefore, you physicians, look diligently now for a suitable messenger who may go there and return from there. And by this reasoning, this second book of medicine ought to be opened and read. This book

<margin>The book of the Firmament was written by God.</margin>
deceives no one: nor did a false scribe compose it. He described it who has no need of any paper for teaching. For He was not ignorant that <term>Pseudo-physicians</term> <note>False or fraudulent doctors who rely on tradition rather than the "Light of Nature."</note> would one day arise, who would write with a dishonest pen. <note>original: "calamo sinistro"; literally "a left-handed pen," a metaphor for something perverse, deceptive, or unlucky.</note>

And such is the way of studying medicine. Such is the book of the Medical Academy. Such is the describer of Medicine. Such diseases are detected in their beginning and end. For if this book of the firmament is smeared onto paper: it behaves no differently than the shadow of a wall, or the image in a mirror, from which perfect knowledge can be given to no one. But he who desires perfect knowledge has need to fix his eyes upon Him from whom the shadow or the image is projected into the mirror. If you look straight at Him, you are not deceived, nor do you have need of a mirror, since you see the living prototype itself. For the principle and foundation arise from the living. 

<margin>Medical books written with a pen are imperfect.</margin>
Thus, books described by the pen are not perfect in medicine, but are as you see them: that is, no tree wishes to be known from a pen or from writing, but from itself. For it is not the external part of the tree that must be known. That which exists internally, *that* is the tree. Food is not food before it becomes blood and flesh: only then does it have the character of food. That which the mouth eats is not food: but that which the blood and flesh eat, that is food. Thus we must not learn from a mirror. For that which must be known does not exist in the mirror. And this is the nature and logic of books, but the firmament is the only one.

<margin>The perversity of Physicians.</margin>
It is a little more than a shame and a disgrace that legitimate Physicians are so stubbornly unwilling to study these books of Medicine, but instead waste all their time uselessly on other fictitious books, whose letter is nevertheless dead, and whose very meaning is lifeless, just as their own works testify to this. For they do not consider this within themselves: that if someone should say, *This book of medicine is false*, they could prove it to be true by no other reasoning than by that letter alone. If a book must be proven: it must be proven entirely from that source from which it originates. Thus the Gospel is from Christ, and is of Christ: and the book of nature is from nature, and is of nature. If, therefore, the natural book of the firmament is not known at all, how can it be proven through a mirror-image and a shadow? Since that from which the image proceeds is not known? What other book could belong to a carpenter than the axe and the wood? What other for a mason than the stone and the mortar? So likewise, what other book ought a Physician to have than this very one which makes men both healthy and sick? It is necessary that this knowledge flow entirely from that which it is, according to which the mirror-image itself must also be judged. This book is the body: this must be read by the Physician. For as Christ says, *where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered*: <note>original: "ubi corpus est, ibi congregari aquilas"; a reference to Matthew 24:28. Paracelsus uses this to mean that true seekers of knowledge (eagles) will find the actual source of truth (the body/reality).</note> this saying applies also to the <term>Light of Nature</term>. <note>original: "lumen naturae"; the innate wisdom and visibility of the natural world provided by God to guide human understanding.</note>

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the third book of Medicine, whose body consists in the Elements.

<margin>How tightly the Elements and man are bound together.</margin>
**B**eyond these things said thus far, it is also fitting for the physician to have known the health and diseases of the Elements. For the Elements and man are bound together by a knowledge much tighter than that of a husband and wife. This is caused by the harmony of union which the Elements have with man, and conversely, the discordance which exists between a husband and wife. And because there is one health, one infirmity, and an equal action in both, one must know what their condition and nature may be. For as the nature exists in the external Elements of the world, such is it also within man. Here, indeed, there is a single action. For just as trees receive their saturation and properties from the earth, so similarly does man. And as you see flowers and various things arise from the earth, so also minerals arise from water, Dew and Hoarfrost from the "Chaos" <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Chaos" often refers to the air or the atmospheric space between heaven and earth.</note>, and Meteoric impressions are produced from fire.

<margin>The Elements exist essentially within man.</margin>
So also in man himself, the four Elements exist essentially, and in them, entirely similar species and generations occur. He, therefore, who has not known external things—as if from the book in which it is fitting for a Philosopher to study—will not know internal things either.

Just as the Astronomical physician is made from the second book, so here the Philosophical Physician is born from the book of the Elements. For what could he know internally (that is, in man)? For man is a **Physical body**, and the Elements are the **body of the Slime**. <note>original: "corpus Limi." This refers to the "limbus" or primordial "mud" from which man was created in Genesis; Paracelsus views this as the extract of all created things.</note>

<margin>The Elements are the body of the Slime.</margin>
And the Physical body arises from the Slime. From this, it also retains the essence of the Slime, just as a son retains the essences of the father in blood and flesh, as is fitting for man.

<margin>The Elements are the matrices of the physical body.</margin>
Therefore, since the four Elements are the **Matrices** <note>Used here in the sense of a "womb" or "mother-source" where things are formed.</note> of the Physical body, and of the things growing from the earth, and of minerals, and of **Tereniabin** <note>A term used by Paracelsus for a type of "heavenly manna" or honey-dew that falls from the air.</note>, and of "impressions," and since from these come both bad and good, both healthy and unhealthy, pure and impure, thorns and roses, gold and talc, hail and dew, manna and mist, etc.; the same happens in the same way in man as well, so that in anyone there resides the virtue of the thistle, and the lily, and of quicksilver, and of orpiment, and of the rest. And similarly, all procreations of that kind proceed from man himself. These, then, are the infirmities of man, and the Physician should perceive and know all those generations—and not from the physical body first, but first from the body of the Slime; afterwards from the physical body, so that, of course, the body of the slime expresses the letter, makes the whole word, and joins the words together so that a meaning is produced. In this way, he should know what the earthy sphere is in the physical body, what the physical cardiac [nature] is in the body of the Slime, and so on for all the others, always maintaining that order: that the body of the Slime precedes the physical, and from these twins, as if through ink and pen, the text and the **gloss** <note>Interpreted here as the "explanation" or "commentary" provided by the physical manifestation of a deeper essence.</note> proceed together. It is fitting for the Physician to know all these things.

<margin>The reasons for health and diseases must be known most exactly by the Physician.</margin>
And just as the hairs of our head are numbered by God, so too the generations of both diseases and health must be precisely numbered for the physician.

<margin>The parts of the Elements: Salt, Resin, Liquor.</margin>
Now, indeed, every Element is divided into three parts, which nevertheless all exist in one appearance, form, color, figure, and reason: namely into **Salt**, which is also called **Balsam**; into **Resin**, which is also called **Sulphur**; and into **Liquor**, which they also call **Gotaronium**. <note>Paracelsus is describing his "Tria Prima" (Three Primes). Usually Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. Here he substitutes "Resin" for Sulfur and "Liquor/Gotaronium" for Mercury.</note> From these three, all things spring forth, namely the procreations of the elements of the Physical body. These three constitute every single body, and no body has more or fewer than three.

<margin>These three mentioned things constitute all things.</margin>
These three generate metals; these three produce minerals; these three produce stones, woods, herbs, and all growing things, both animate and...

He introduces the Tria Prima—Salt, Resin (Sulfur), and Liquor (Mercury)—as the three fundamental components of all matter and health.</summary>

...than those which constitute inanimate things. Yet their nature is one way regarding metals, another regarding flesh and blood, and another regarding wood. The physician, however, values these external forms the least; instead, he looks to the inner substances, which serve as the true subject for him. And these are born from the Elements.
<margin>What things are born from the Element.</margin>
Now, you must know that these four mothers <note>The four Elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> give birth in man according to this logic and condition: namely, from the Element of Earth its own species are produced; from the Element of Water its own species; from the Element of Fire its own species; and from the Element of <term>Chaos</term> <note>original: "chaos"; Paracelsus frequently uses this term to refer to the Element of Air.</note> its own species.

<margin>Contraries are born from each one.</margin>
Just as spearwort and mandrake are born from the earth—which are indeed of contrary natures, yet are born from a single mother—in exactly the same way, diseases are produced in man from the Elements. It should not be said that nothing except what is "cold and dry" comes from the Element of Earth. The same must be understood similarly regarding the other Elements: that not only "watery" things come from water, or only "airy" things from the air. For many things emerge that possess a nature different from their mother. For who would say that the mother contains the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) traditionally assigned to a substance.</note> of these things within herself? No one. Where complexions are born, the complexion does not exist beforehand; rather, it proceeds from the <term>temperament</term>. And that temperament contains within itself all complexions and degrees, which no one has yet numbered or recorded in a system of calculation. For these qualities are within the temperament just as forms are within wood. Whatever forms you choose, you can carve them from the wood, whether they be statues or anything else. The same logic applies to the body, which brings forth complexions, even though the body itself is not a complexion. It is right for a physician to understand these things so that he does not perhaps get stuck on qualities and humors, but rather recognizes the elements themselves (or "mothers"), their procreations, and their species, not the humors.

<margin>The humors are rejected.</margin>
Let it not be asked, "Of which humor?" and answered, "The Melancholic." For <term>Melancholy</term> <note>Black bile.</note> is nothing but a foolish, insane, and fantastical infirmity; it is by no means a pillar of these four Elements.
<margin>Cholera is a disease.</margin>
Likewise, it should not be asked, "Of which complexion?" and answered, "Cholerica" <note>Yellow bile.</note>; rather, it belongs to the "Hot Sect." For <term>cholera</term> is not a pillar of those four elements either, but is a disease. So too, it should not be asked, "Of which quality?" and answered, "Sanguine." For blood is not one of the four pillars, but is the very body of the veins, just as wine is in a barrel. Nor should it be asked: "Of which Nature?" and answered, "Phlegmatic." Since <term>phlegm</term> is merely the mucus of the nostrils, what does that have to do with the belly? Instead, it should be asked in this way: "Of which Element?"—Water, Earth, Fire, or Air. For in this way the answer stands firm. For instance: from which Element was the disease born? From Fire, not from cholera; from Earth, not from Melancholy; from Water, not from phlegm; from Air, not from blood. These things truly match, but the others do not—such as saying "this is Melancholic," when neither heaven nor earth knows anything of Melancholy. Or "this is cholera, phlegm, blood, etc.," when nature itself in its own process has never known any of these. If the physician learns the Elements themselves in this way, he easily finds in the things generated all the diseases with which a man happens to be occupied. And just as the spearwort is what it is, so too is the disease of the spearwort. Why, then, is it necessary for you to leaf through so many books here and there, searching for the origin of blisters? If you have discovered from where marsh-mud, nettles, melons, and feathery things are born, then you will also know the diseases and species of each. Where now is your "burnt cholera" and "melancholy"? You ought to recognize the physical body in its disease through the generated offspring and the sons and daughters of the Elements; you must discern and judge species within species, matter from matter, and man from the Elements.

<margin>How and from where diseases are to be known.</margin>
And those diseases which the generated things exhibit in their first births must be thoroughly learned by the physician. For through the book of the four Elements he will find man described—not the man expressed on the paper of medical volumes, which are by no means produced from the book of the Elements. No one can create a book or a text out of themselves. Nature makes the text; the physician adds the <term>gloss</term> <note>An interpretive commentary or explanation.</note>. Now see how your "gloss" and the "text" of the Elements match: it is like a dog in a bath <note>original: "canis & balneum"; a proverb suggesting two things that are mismatched or do not belong together.</note>. Therefore, take your description as the Elements have it within themselves, judging each body according to its own nature and condition, just as the <term>magnalia</term> <note>The "great works" or wonders of God in nature.</note> of God are ordered and adorned. For what makes wood rot also makes man rot. And what gives birth to worms in man gives birth to them in fruits as well. For this reason, one must learn in this school: where Medicine is handed down according to the lucid truth, not through intricate ambiguities.

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the traditional Galenic system of the four humors (blood, phlegm, cholera, melancholy), arguing that diseases should instead be understood as direct products of the four Elements. He asserts that a true physician must study the "book of nature" to understand how substances and diseases grow, rather than relying on human-authored medical texts.</summary>

## CHAPTER IV.

### Regarding the physical book, from which the Physical body in the Microcosm is known—that is, regarding the book of the Greater Anatomy.

<margin>Everything that exists outside of man is also inside him.</margin>
Next, the Physician must also understand how many various species of bodies exist within a single Physical body. This is to be done, of course, after he has thoroughly learned the third book and understood from it the logic, nature, and condition of all the Elements. Once this is achieved, he must seek and discover that same "Monarchy of the world" <note>The sovereign order and structure of the universe.</note> within man himself. The argument of this fourth book is therefore this: to understand that neither more nor fewer things are found in the Physical body than in the world at large. Just as a Physician ought to know by heart how many species of woods, stones, herbs, and so on exist, he shall likewise establish that all these same species are found in man. However, they do not exist there in the same state as they do in the Elements; rather, they must be found in man either in the mode of health or in the form of a disease. Gold in the Elements is gold and presents as such. In man, it is a "natural fortifier," as is taught in the relevant chapters. The same judgment must be made regarding the species of the other Elements: that they are found in the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>original: "Microcosmo"; refers to man as a "little world" that mirrors the universe.</note> in the same way. Therefore, he who can judge and name the species in the Physical body in this manner—saying, *"This in man is Sapphire, that is Mercury, this other is Cypress, this is the Wallflower,"* <note>original: "flos Cheiri"</note> and so on—is truly well-versed and learned in the book of the Physical body.

<margin>The nature of Medical Theory.</margin>
**If** he knows the bodily species exactly in this way, only then may he act as a Physician and establish his own Theory. This Theory must not be speculative, but must be born from practice—specifically from all those books which I am treating and handing down here. For it is not fitting for practice to flow from speculative Theory; rather, Theory ought to proceed from practice. Thus, this practice is as it has been handed down so far, and as it will be further taught in the following books. If the Physician distributes the concordance of the <term>Anatomy</term> <note>In this context, "Anatomy" refers not just to dissection, but to the structural correspondence between the world and the body.</note> of both fabrications—the machine of the world and the Physical body—into equal parts in this way, and assigns each its proper place, it follows that one disease exists in the bone, another in the flesh, and another in the blood. Likewise, some worms exist in wood, others in herbs, others in leaves, and so on. And as many as there are bodily species, so many types of diseases are counted. That is, similar species exist in each in equal number, with this distinction: they are constituted differently in the Elements than in man in terms of their "corporality" and substance, but not in terms of their properties. Nevertheless, they can fall upon man in a uniform way. For as is the logic of the limb, so is the logic of the disease. Thus, some are worms of the marrow, others of the intestines. And from things of this sort, the cause of diseases in man arises. 

<margin>Whether all blood is uniform.</margin>
Until now, it has been believed and established that blood of only one kind is contained in all veins, and that it is of a single nature, simply because it is all red. For blood is commonly said to be "hot and moist." <note>The traditional Galenic "complexion" of blood.</note> But the matter is otherwise. For just as there are various natures of wood, so there are various natures of blood. Nor should it be thought that a single tree is sufficient for this instruction. Judge this by an example: as when a tree is considered according to its trunk and its out-spreading branches. Such are the branches of the veins in man. And is there only one nature here? But all trees are not the same when joined together, nor are all branches the same. Thus, it is discovered that veins are manifold. So too are the manifold branches peculiar to any trunk. From these now follow the *Cypress-vein, the Berry-vein, the Rosemary-vein,* and the like. Hence, the blood does not remain of a single essence and nature. And this is the genuine book from which Anatomy ought to be drawn: so that a man may know and compare the substances and proportions of the Elements and the Microcosm. For it is not enough to look at a man's body from the outside, then dissect it and look inside again, and finally boil it and inspect it once more. Even peasants know how to do that. Therefore, such a method cannot stand. I offer you this example: as many species as there are in the waters, just as many are in the blood. That is, if we wish to reduce the Physical body to its Element and assign to each Element its own body, then blood will be the Element of Water. And although all blood indeed grows warm, while all water does not grow warm in the same way, nevertheless, not all blood is hot by nature—just as not all waters are hot. Rather, the blood conceives that heat externally from "Physical salt," just as the earth draws heat from the Sun. And just as fire heats, so in man the Elemental fire heats the other Elements, as has been said. The earth grows warm from the Sun. In the same way, the Sun of man warms his Elements of earth, water, and so on. Nevertheless, its nature remains as it was given, nor does it [change] the other...

You ought to judge everything by this rule: before all else, you must reduce the bodies of the Elements, according to their species, back into each individual Element. For the logic of the internal Physical body is the same as that of the external Elements themselves. Thus, when people say that the essence or nature of bones is a single thing, they speak incorrectly.

<margin>Bones are not all of a single nature.</margin>
For just as there are different types of wood, so too do bones have similar and diverse species. Likewise, they talk nonsense about the wind, saying it is of a single nature. The very same is true in man: there are as many types of <term>colic</term> <note>Abdominal pain; Paracelsus argues that symptoms like colic have different elemental origins.</note> as there are causes.

<margin>Where Philosophy ends, the Physician begins.</margin>
<margin>A double Cosmography and Geography.</margin>
In this manner, the book of the Physical body must be accurately divided, and one must pay diligent attention lest we be deceived by the false descriptions that several authors intrude into Philosophy in an unseemly way. For if you were to unroll their works or volumes, you would see that their foundation proceeds from mere fantasy and empty speculation, upon which no Philosophy or Medicine can be built. From this, conclude that it is proper for the Philosopher to precede and the Physician to follow. That is to say: although the "Greater World" <note>The Macrocosm or universe.</note> ought to be placed and explained first in his book, it is nevertheless right that it be immediately compared, not only with the species of the genera, but also so that all the locations and processes of <term>Cosmography</term> and <term>Geography</term> <note>The mapping of the universe and the earth, mirrored here in the mapping of the human body.</note> may be referred back to the Physical body. For it is not enough for there to be only one Cosmography and Geography. Two must be established, just as there are two worlds: *The Greater and the Lesser*. Nor should we allow ourselves to be led astray by the substances and images that the eyes see. Therefore, it has been truly and elegantly said by some: *Where the Philosopher ends, there the Physician begins.* And it happens for this reason: if the Philosopher has properly understood the Greater World according to the heavens and the earth and all their generations, he is then endowed with the diligence required to understand and know the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," or man.</note>. He who does not follow this path of Philosophy is utterly unfit to possess knowledge of the microcosm. Whatever else he writes about the nature of man is no different than what a blind man professes about colors. He only opines; he dreams that "there are mountains of gold in Spain" <note>A proverbial expression for imagining things that are not there.</note>. Now, therefore, judge for yourselves whether I do not provide you with this teaching for grave reasons? For this has more foundation than all the rest of the books that a pen has ever brought forth. For the writers of those books depict man from a mirror, which contains nothing in itself but an external image, and does not present even a tiny bit of the internal or "backside" man. Thus, they do nothing other than a calf staring at a newly built gate. And our pseudo-physicians have clearly established and erected this sort of calf-like appearance and image as if they were "swinish columns" <note>original: "columnis suillis"; a mocking term for clumsy or absurd foundations.</note>.

## CHAPTER V.
### Regarding the book of Alchemy, without which no one can become a physician.

<margin>The Art should be upheld despite its abuse.</margin>
**T**he future Physician must also entirely learn this fifth book: which, however, because of its name, will not be very welcome to many. But what wise man can hate that which some people recklessly abuse? Who would hate the color blue <note>original: "Cyanen"; referring to the pigment or lapis lazuli.</note> because a petulant painter fashions something evil from it? Who would hate a stone because it was ruined by a stone-cutter? Likewise, who would hate <term>Alchemy</term>, which is innocent? Hatred is owed to the one who is guilty—the one who does not grasp the art, nor uses it rightly. Who hates the one who has harmed nobody? Who will blame the dog if, being grabbed by the tail, he bites the one who grabbed him? Does Caesar order the thief to be crucified, or the thing that was stolen? The thief, I reckon. Therefore, science ought by no means to be held in contempt because of the ignorant.

<margin>The utility and necessity of Alchemy.</margin>
<margin>God made all things from nothing.</margin>
Indeed, the science or art itself is such that it is of great use and necessity. Since the art of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>In alchemy, Vulcan represents the power of fire and the "inner alchemist" that transforms raw matter into finished products.</note> is inserted within it, it is necessary to know what Vulcan can do. Alchemy is the art; Vulcan is the artist within it. Now, he who is not an artist does not have its power. So that you may know this art more certainly, it must first be repeated that God created all things from Nothing—from *Nothing*, I say, into *Something*. This "Something" is a seed; that seed gives the end of its predestination, of its office. And although all things were created from *Nothing* unto an end, there is nothing, however, that is complete at the end—that is, it exists until the end, but it is not entirely perfect until the end; rather, Vulcan must perfect it. All things were created to the point that they exist placed in our hands, yet they are not everywhere perfect. Be-

<margin>
Nothing was created perfect unto its end.
</margin>
...wood grows toward its own end, but it does not grow into coals on its own. Clay is born, but it does not become bone by itself. This is also the nature of all growing things. Therefore, get to know this <term>Vulcan</term> <note>In alchemy, Vulcan represents the transformative power of fire and the metaphorical craftsman or "smith" who refines raw nature into a finished product.</note> diligently. We will explain the matter with an example. God indeed created iron, but not as it will eventually be; he did not create the horseshoe, nor the sickle, nor the sword. He gave us at least the iron ore; the rest he entrusted to the fire and to Vulcan, the master of the fire. Because these other things were entrusted to Vulcan, the art of alchemy is noble. For if it were not noble, Vulcan would provide nothing useful. From this it follows that first the iron must be separated from the <term>slag</term> <note>original: *scoria*; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting.</note>, and afterward it must be forged, which the craftsman does. And this is Alchemy; this is the smelter, called Vulcan. Whatever the fire works upon, 

<margin>
The nature of Alchemy.
</margin>
is Alchemy—even in the kitchen, even in the furnace. Whoever governs the fire is a Vulcan, whether he be a cook or a heater. The same logic applies to medicine. It was indeed created by God, yet not prepared for its final purpose, but rather hidden within the slag. Now it is the duty of Vulcan to separate the slag from the medicine itself. What you have understood about iron is equally true for medicine.

<margin>
Medicine is not what the eyes see.
</margin>
What the eyes see in a herb is not the Medicine. Likewise, what they see in stones or in trees is only the slag; but the Medicine is hidden deep within that slag. Therefore, the slag must first be removed from the Medicine. Once this is done, the Medicine will be ready. This is Alchemy; this is the duty of Vulcan, acting as the pharmacist and the one who prepares the medicine. And just as it often happens that gold or silver is found pure in some places, so too is Medicine sometimes found pure, in which case its later separation is much easier—just as even pure gold still requires at least <term>refining</term> <note>original: *fulminatione*; an alchemical process of purification using intense heat.</note> and roasting. When the necessary tasks are done, if the Medicine has been prepared and produced in this way by means of the Alchemical art, it is offered to the sick as a remedy, or to the healthy as food. Let us take the example of bread. The external art of Alchemy in the oven cannot produce the *ultimate matter* from the grain, but only the *middle matter*. That is: nature produces the *first matter* up until the harvest. Then Alchemy reaps it,

<margin>
The matter of things: what is first, what is last.
</margin>
grinds it, kneads it, and bakes it, until it reaches the mouth. Thus, the first and middle matters are completed. Only then does the Alchemy of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "little world," referring to the human body as a reflection of the macrocosm (the universe).</note> begin. It receives the first matter in the mouth—that is, it chews the bread, which is the first task. Afterward, it has it in the stomach, which is the second matter. Finally, the stomach cooks and digests it so that it ultimately becomes blood and flesh. And this is now the *ultimate matter*. Although afterward another Alchemy also approaches, namely infirmity, which is the first matter; this is followed by decline, the second matter. Finally comes death, the ultimate matter. Furthermore, the first matter is putrefaction. Next to this is consumption. The ultimate is dust and earth. Thus nature acts with us through God's creatures. From all this, it follows for my purpose that nothing was created perfectly as its *ultimate matter*. However, all things were created as *first matter*. Afterward, Vulcan takes hold of them, and through the benefit of the Alchemical art, he reduces them to their *ultimate matter*. This is then received by the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The internal "Vital Force" or "Inner Alchemist" that directs the body's internal processes.</note>, the inner Vulcan, who adds the <term>finishing touch</term> <note>original: *colo-phonem*; literally a "colophon," the finishing stroke of a book or work.</note> by circulating and preparing it according to the nature and difference of each thing, through sublimation, distillation, and reverberation. For all these arts are prefigured and active inside a human being no less than they are outside in Alchemy.

<margin>
How Vulcan and the Archeus differ.
</margin>
And in this, Vulcan and the Archeus differ. This is truly Alchemy, which leads toward the end that which has sought its purpose: by leading lead out of the ore into lead, and then by shaping that lead into what it is meant for or what it serves. In this way, there are Alchemists of metals; so too there are Alchemists who work in minerals, and they reduce Antimony to Antimony, Sulfur to Sulfur, Vitriol to Vitriol, and Salt to Salt. Thus, recognize that Alchemy is only that which, by preparing through fire, separates the impure and draws out the pure. Although not all fires burn, they are nevertheless all fires and remain fires. In this way, there are also Alchemists of wood, such as carpenters, who prepare wood for building structures. So too there are sculptors, who remove from the wood what does not belong to the statue. In the same way, there are Alchemists of Medicine, who take from the Medicine what is not Medicine. From this it is now clearly evident what kind of art Alchemy is: it is surely that which separates the useless from the useful and brings it to its ultimate matter or nature. But the reason why I define these things more extensively in this book is that those ink-smeared books of the art contain nothing; they are completely filled with blots and empty dots, and they present such a variable mixture that pigs would rather eat dung than taste even a little of their concoction. Since such disordered mixtures are of no use or importance, God substituted Alchemy in their place...

<margin>Why Alchemy was instituted by God.</margin>
...instituted <note>Continuing from the previous page: "God instituted..."</note> the genuine and sublime art of nature itself. Indeed, that crude and raw preparation of medicines for which the physicians of Montpellier <note>The University of Montpellier was a famous center of traditional medieval medicine; the author frequently criticized their reliance on old Greek and Arab texts rather than chemical experience.</note> pride themselves is by no means to be called an art, but rather mere stuffing and abominable cooking. And yet, they boil their syrups in this manner and mix together laxatives or other similar compounds. The books of pseudo-doctors and "ink-stainers" likewise teach or promote this same craft. Yet, neither syrups nor laxatives should be prepared in the way handed down by those of Montpellier, but rather as the science of Alchemical Medicine teaches. For this is how God has constituted and ordained it. A physician must strive for this: since God created nothing to its final end, but instead committed the "final touch" <note>original: *colophonem*; a Greek-derived term meaning the finishing stroke or crowning achievement.</note> to the <term>Vulcans</term> <note>The metaphorical "smiths" or "alchemists" who use fire and art to complete what nature started.</note>, the physician must fully perfect his medicines, and not force the slag and the iron together into one mass. 

Take bread as an example. Bread was indeed created and given to us by God, but not in the form that the baker gives it. Rather, these three "Vulcans"—the farmer, the miller, and the baker—extract a second form, namely bread, from the primary matter <note>The raw grain.</note>. The same must be done with medications. This is also the logic of the "internal Vulcan" <note>Referring to the archeus, or the body's internal digestive and transformative power.</note>. Therefore, it does not befit a physician to be ashamed of Alchemy; rather, he should proceed in it entirely in the way that has been shown. For if he does not do this, he will be a doctor in name only; or rather, a <term>Beanus</term> <note>A term for a raw, unpolished student or novice, often used mockingly to describe a fool or an "empty" doctor.</note> graduate: a doctor, I say, like the kind of man one sees reflected in a mirror <note>A hollow image without substance.</note>.

## CHAPTER VII.

->*Regarding the book of Medicine, called experience, and the manner in which a physician ought to acquire it for himself.*<-

<margin>
Experience is said to come from universal experiments.
</margin>
<margin>What Medicine is.</margin>
It is right that a physician be entirely empowered by distinguished experience, since Medicine is nothing other than great and certain experience; thus, whatever he does or performs should be founded upon experience. And experience consists of those things found to be good, proven, and true. Whoever has not learned his art through experience, and has not confirmed it by the weight of truth, must be considered an uncertain and doubtful physician. For whatever experience—which is a certain and incorruptible judge—either approves or disapproves, must be entirely accepted or rejected. Therefore, experience must run together with science. For science *is* experience.

<margin>
What experience is, and of what kind.
</margin>
If a trial <note>original: *experimentum*.</note> is once found to be good through experience, and thereafter remains as experience when combined with science, then its further use is entirely recommended. If, however, it is without science, then it is merely a trial without knowledge. For this is how a "trial" and "experience" differ: a trial proceeds by luck without science, whereas experience is joined to certainty, to be applied everywhere with science. For science is the mother of experience, and without science nothing solid exists. 

Thus, <term>Scammony</term> <note>A resin from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, used as a powerful purgative.</note> purges, and that is a trial; <term>Sophia</term> <note>Likely *Descurainia sophia*, known as "Flixweed" or "Physician's Herb," traditionally used to heal fractures and wounds.</note> heals broken limbs and ruptures, and that is a trial. <term>Sapphire</term> <note>Precious gemstones were often ground or used as amulets in Renaissance medicine.</note> cures Anthrax, and that is a trial. Now, although these are indeed trials found through experience, the plurality of diseases makes it necessary for science to be present where those trials might be hindered. For there is no disease that consists of only one single thing; therefore, a trial alone should not be used. If this is so, it is necessary for science to concur entirely.

<margin>
A tree bears fruit from science.
</margin>
Understand this from the following example. A pear tree that bears fruit does so out of science. It has this science from God, and through this science it produces flowers, brings forth leaves, and forms pears. It is a great thing, therefore, for science of this kind to exist stored within wood. For if a man even wishes to paint or write something, it is necessary that it be done through experience and trial. A tree, however, has this art within itself by nature, and that science dwells in the tree naturally. That a tree acts in such a way is seen by our eyes. If we know this, it is a trial for us. We do not have the science of it, but only the trial, because we see it happen this way. And this is taught through experience, and that is experience. But it is the tree that possesses the science.

<margin>
Science must be joined with experience.
</margin>
<margin>
Scammony purges from science.
</margin>
Note this example equally. That scammony purges, it does so with a certain science which God instilled in it—namely, that it purges, *what* it purges, and *how* it purges. If, however, you learn the science of scammony by investigating it so that it exists in you just as it exists in the scammony, then you have experience with science, and not just a trial. But if you have not known the whole nature and property of scammony, then you have a trial without science; nor have you known anything other than that it stirs the bowels. And you know this only as a certain word whose meaning you do not understand. Just so a Frenchman hears the German tongue and understands that it is indeed German, but does not grasp what it signifies. Know that this is the characteristic of a trial...

The author uses the metaphor of the "Three Vulcans" (farmer, miller, baker) to explain how alchemy completes nature's work, turning raw matter into perfected medicine.</summary>
