# LABYRINTH

Know <note>original: "tote," likely a shorthand for "scitote," meaning "know ye."</note> that while the eyes may testify to a matter, the reason and intellect behind it are not necessarily present. For the eyes indicate a **Trial** <note>original: "Experimentum"; in this context, an isolated empirical test or observation without understanding the underlying cause.</note>, not **experience**. Indeed, the eyes do not see experience, since experience exists alongside intelligence. You must know, therefore, that if God bestowed this science upon the pear tree and imparted the same to other woods, how much more and more readily will He grant it to the human being who learns strenuously according to the instruction of the first book? Thus, **Science** <note>original: "Scientia"; here referring to an innate, divinely-implanted knowledge or capacity within a thing.</note> must be an **Influence**. For it is hidden in nature, and yet it must come forth. Otherwise, that which is hidden would be of no use to us, and the talent would yield no fruit. Nothing, however, is so secret or hidden that it shall not be revealed.

<margin>Magic reveals all hidden things.</margin>
From this it follows that **Magic**, in its three methods, brings forth and manifests these secrets—that is, in the school of Physicians, Philosophers, Astronomers, and the like. For unless science is within you in this manner, then it is mere and empty fantasy and foolishness, from which fools are born; it is a pure labyrinth, destitute of any foundation.

<margin>Science and experience differ.</margin>
But note the distinction between science and experience even more clearly than what has been said so far. **Science** resides in that upon which God has bestowed it. **Experience** is the testimony regarding that in which science is proven. For example: a pear tree has its own science within itself; and we, who see its works, have the experience of that same science. Thus, through experience, we give testimony that perfect science exists within that tree. Therefore, having established these points, I now propose this sixth book, and I command that science penetrate you in this very way, so that your patients may testify about you because of the works they have seen—namely, that you possess perfect science. Thus, that which proceeds perfectly with cognition in the true order of nature is science. If this is lacking, only a **Trial** is present, or perhaps experience without science.

<margin>How to trust in proof.</margin>
If someone should perhaps say: *"Listen, I have often put this to the test and proved it to be so; you must therefore admit that this is a Trial,"* I respond to him that such proof is by no means safe or sufficient enough, nor should it be absolutely trusted. But he who possesses the **trial** along with **science** can trust the matter; he can at least say, "Conduct yourself thus, do this, and the outcome will be certain." In this way, the fruits will undoubtedly come forth rightly according to their nature. Such, then, is the difference between science and experience: not that experience is the trial, or that the trial is experience, but that experience is what is found and drawn out from science. And this is their mode: that science must be sought within us, rather than letting a mere trial lead us (which is the rationale of science). For example: I know that a cannon <note>original: "tormentum"; a siege engine or early artillery piece.</note> shakes and casts down a wall. This is a **trial**. But if the cannon is so directed that the casting down of the wall truly happens (and the shot does not miss ten times after hitting once by luck), that is **science**. Thus the artilleryman who possesses both this science and the trial becomes an embodiment of science and experience. For experience includes science. And once science is established, there is henceforth no need for concern or mention of the trial.

<margin>God endowed all things.</margin>
Anyone ought to remind themselves that God has conferred His gifts and endowments upon all natural things. That endowment is science. If, therefore, He has bestowed this science upon trees and herbs so that they might reach their true end in every formation of species and essence, how much more will He grant these to the Physician? Provided the Physician submits himself to God like a herb or a flower, and restores the sick for God's honor and glory. This is not for the Physician alone, but for any other, just as He gave to the Apostles, from whom fruits fell no differently than from a tree heavy with fruit. If He gives such science to the lily of the field, will He not give it much more abundantly to man, who bears the likeness of God? Now, <margin>A perfect gift from God.</margin> every gift from God comes in a state of perfection. From this One Source, therefore, all can be drawn, just as every tree draws its virtue from Him. <margin>Why science is perfect.</margin> Whence it follows that science itself is also perfect. For it proceeds from God, just as the virtue in the vine is from God. Thus, this experience is great.

<margin>Why experience is not a trial.</margin>
Experience, however, cannot be a mere trial, the matter being so considered.

For trials <note>original: "experimenta"; here referring to isolated empirical attempts without a theoretical or spiritual foundation.</note> are imperfect. And just as a pear tree retains its own knowledge and does not share it with an apple tree, so too its own knowledge remains in the plum and the thorns. Think of man in the same way: God has imparted to each their own knowledge. Therefore, it follows <margin>God’s goods are to be cultivated; to each his own.</margin> as right that everyone should bring their gift and knowledge to the highest point and, in the alchemical manner, sublimate <note>To "sublime" or "sublimate" is an alchemical process of heating a substance to turn it into vapor and then back into solid, used here as a metaphor for refining one's inner wisdom.</note> it to the highest degree. That is, a tree must expend much alchemy with its knowledge until it reaches the end of its fruit. If, therefore, a man has the seed of knowledge, it follows that it is entirely necessary for him to act upon it and intensify it until it is led to full ears of grain and the autumn, when its fruits fall just as they do from a tree. And here is the distinction in growing and separating the pure from the impure. For that which works toward growing into knowledge separates nothing. But that which has grown, this separates. Thus, observe that to each one is given their own peculiar nature—that is, a gift with which they are born. In this, he must advance himself so that he may reach its end, and he should not labor to learn his innate knowledge from other creatures. For it was given to you alone, not to the one from whom you wish to learn. For why should a pear learn from a plum? Why a fig from thorns? Why should the sweet devour the sour?

By this reasoning, the book of sciences proceeds, so that we may truly test the sciences that are established and testified through experience. I propose these things with this intent: that you should not only recognize the pear, but furthermore the sciences of medical and natural things—specifically, what kind of knowledge God has given to vitriol-based <note>Vitriol refers to various sulfate minerals, which were central to early chemical medicine.</note> substances, through which the sick are healed. This is so that the vitriolic knowledge, through which the vitriol operates, exists within you yourselves no differently than you imaginatively imprint it upon the vitriol. And this is the impression of the **Light of Nature** <note>original: "Lumen Naturae"; Paracelsus's term for the innate wisdom and divine intelligence present in the natural world.</note>; these are its rays. If they imprint upon you and heal the sick, then it is science. Now, however, that science is not in the physician, but in the medicine. From which it follows that the Physician—since he does not possess the science of healing but only the science of administration—is entirely compelled, because of that administration, to seek and investigate that science in the Medicine where it lies. For the sciences of nature must be in you in exactly the same way they are in nature itself—namely, by the power of impression from the **Light of Nature**. If it is not so, you will waver and doubt in every direction, and you have known nothing but the empty chatter of the mouth. Thus, the books of medicine have been largely indicated, from which the Physician ought to draw his foundation, not to turn pears <note>A colloquialism for wasting time on trivialities or being idle.</note> behind the stove at home, or to ensnare and detain the sick with a sophisticated circuit of words. You must apply diligent effort so that you also read and understand the following books thoroughly and exactly, so that in this way you may have all the books required for Medicine clearly counted and grasped.

### CHAPTER VII.
->*Regarding the Book of Natural Apothecaries and Physicians.*<-

<margin>Nature’s apothecary is the world.</margin>
**I**T HAS BEEN SAID many times until now that all the signs of external nature are directed toward the internal. For whatever nature is on the outside among men, such it is also inwardly within the human being himself. I will give an example. Nature ordains one Apothecary <note>The "Apotheca" was a storehouse or pharmacy where medicinal ingredients were kept and prepared.</note> in the world. Just as herbs are collected and found in an Apothecary—yet in such a way that one herb is better equipped than others either in number or in many species—so also in the world, a certain natural order of Apothecaries has been established, such that all meadows, all mountains, and hills are like certain Apothecaries. Nature herself gives and provides these Apothecaries to us; from her, it is fitting for us to supply what we lack. Now, the whole world is the Apothecary of Nature, which is covered by at least one roof. One person even handles the mortar in it, through which the whole world lies open. A human being has all these things individually, not in the whole; he has something, yet not everything. For the natural Apothecary is more opulent and worthier than the human one.

<margin>Nature’s apothecary is God.</margin>
Furthermore, I have proposed this example to you so that you might understand that in the human being himself there is also a natural apothecary of this kind, in which all things may be found no less than in the workshop of the world—the good as well as the bad, the simple, the material, and however they may finally be named. To this it now follows that every workshop also has its own appointed Physician. For Nature has its own peculiar Apothecary. He, however, is the one who established it himself. Thus, it also has need of some physician. You shall estimate him in this way: just as there is an Apothecary of Nature, after whose example man...

...man also establishes and equips his own: thus the human workshop also needs a Physician to be active within it, and to work within it. Now, the apothecary who is a man is visible himself, and his Physician is likewise visible.

<margin>What the Pharmacy and the Friend of Man are like.</margin>
From these things, it is gathered that within man himself, as if in a <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—the human being seen as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, a Pharmacy also exists, similar to that which the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world"—the universe or the entirety of nature.</note> possesses. Likewise, a Physician is present within him to collect, organize, dispense, apply, and administer all remedies. And since these things are presented to us so abundantly in Nature—so that we may learn from this book and strike down other fantasies or imaginations (which exist only as a volatile spirit and bring nothing good)—learn now from me for what reason I wished to explain these things to you at greater length. The cause is surely this: all remedies were created for the favor and health of the sick.

<margin>Medicine is twofold.</margin>
**Medicine, however, is twofold: one is external, the other is internal.** Man himself attends to and provides the external. Nature perfects the internal. Understand these things in this way:

<margin>Man is subject to all diseases.</margin>
Man is subject to all diseases, both while still hidden in his mother's womb and after he has been brought forth into the world. And it could in no way happen that he would be brought into the world alive unless his internal Physician took constant care of him. Since, therefore, he is full of diseases—and these cling to him by nature—it has been so arranged by God that where there are diseases, medicines and physicians are also ready at hand. Just as disease clings by nature, so also remedies against every disease are present by nature. And just as man received from Nature a destroyer of health, so equally and in turn, he received a preserver of health. Now, just as the destroyer works and aims diligently and constantly toward destruction and corruption to kill the man, so the more active Preserver of Nature, like an innate Physician, restores, repairs, and protects whatever the other destroys or is about to destroy.

<margin>Man has an innate physician.</margin>
The one who destroys has his own instruments in the body with which he demolishes what he encounters. And he finds these within the microcosm itself.

<margin>The Destroyer and the Preserver are naturally within man.</margin>
So, in the external world also, the <term>stone-cutter</term> <note>original: "Latomus"; used here as a metaphor for an artisan or worker who shapes or breaks down structures.</note> who demolishes takes his tools from that environment in which he works. Another stone-cutter, who restores and repairs, also finds the necessary tools for restoring in the external world. Thus, both the destroyer and the preserver have their own instruments for both demolishing and restoring. One pulls out the stakes, the other fixes them back in. And thus, within the same body, the highest art for destroying and the highest art for repairing have been established.

Let us see an example. The Destroyer in the Microcosm takes **Realgar** <note>A toxic arsenic sulfide mineral; here representing a poisonous or destructive force.</note> and attempts to strangle the microcosm with poison. The Preserver, however, offers **Flowers of Antimony** <note>original: "Flores Antimonij"; a white oxide of antimony used in early medicine as a potent purifier.</note> and overcomes it. Thus, the man is made sick and then returned to health. The microcosm undergoes such shifts daily and constantly endures the operations of both the destroyer and the preserver. For these two are perpetually struggling against one another. **The logic of the external world is the same as that of the internal.** In the latter, there are brawlers and peacemakers, the restless and the quiet. For where the firmament and the Elements are present—as they are in the Microcosm—there also wars and peace flourish. Therefore, a man ought to be so persuaded that, unless God had co-created and implanted within him a natural Physician and natural remedies—that is, both a Pharmacy and a Physician—the life of no one could be sustained by the labor of an external physician. For just as the earth is dried out by the Sun, it is moistened again by the rain. Its dryness is a disease; the moisture is the Medicine. And God has disposed things in such a way in the external world. These same two things must also be noted internally within man himself.

<margin>Too much and too little destroy.</margin>
If no rain were given to the earth, everything would dry up. If no rain followed the dryness in man, he would entirely wither away. But then again: excessive rains choke the earth. So also in man: excessive rains choke him. The Sun corrects the rains. The rains correct the harms of the Sun. The Sun is useful, and it is not useful. Equally, rain is both good and not good.

<margin>The nature of diseases of abundance and deficiency.</margin>
From this, you recognize the principle or cause of consumption in man, which perhaps might be called **Phthisis** or **Hectic fever**. <note>original: "Phthisis & Ethica"; Phthisis refers to pulmonary tuberculosis or wasting, and "Ethica" refers to a persistent "hectic" fever associated with it.</note> So also you understand the cause of excessive rains in man, which perhaps might be named **dropsy**, **hyposarca**, etc. <note>original: "hydrops, hypofarca"; clinical terms for the accumulation of fluid in the body (edema).</note> More examples of this kind could be given, but the present space does not allow it. Thus, indeed, cases of dropsy, consumption, and other similar diseases are quite often healed, even when a man does not realize that he is recovering and regaining strength through the benefit and work of the natural medicine innate to him.

<margin>God is concerned for the health of man.</margin>
For God averts the death of man in every way and prolongs his life. For in the longevity of human life, the Lord is well pleased.

Now see how, from this book of the great Pharmacy, a man should judge particulars, and how the external Physician ought to accommodate himself to the internal, innate physician, and learn from him. ## CHAPTER XII.

*> Concerning the book of Medical Theory, and by what reasoning it ought to be established.*

SO THAT you may truly and correctly understand this foundation—from where you ought to take the Theory belonging to Medicine—observe first this example. From where, finally, does Theology take or learn its Theory?

<margin>What is Theology?</margin>
From God. Therefore, it also speaks and speculates about God. Whatever it finds in God, or has, or takes from Him, that is Theology, both practical and Theoretical. For these are not separated. Establish the same rule for Medicine. Where is it? Surely in Nature. Where

<margin>Medical theory is twofold.</margin>
is the disease? Surely in the patient or the sick person. From these two, therefore, *Medical Theory* proceeds, which exists as a double entity. *One is the Theory of the essence of the cause; the other is the Theory of the essence of the cure.* <note>The original Latin repeats "essentia causæ" twice, but contextually refers to cause and cure.</note> From these two, a single Theory must be made; they must not be divided. However, how this Theory ought to be found so that it can be described with pen and ink, you shall know by this reasoning. First, every Theoretical Physician must speak from God. For in Him, and from

<margin>Every principle flows from God.</margin>
Him, every principle flows; and He is all in all. And as the scripture teaches: every perfect gift

<margin>God is all in all.</margin>
proceeds from God. Moreover, medical theory is itself from God. For scripture testifies that He produced both the physician and medicine from the earth. If, therefore, these things are perfect: then the

<margin>Why medicine is perfect.</margin>
physician and medicine will also be perfect. Next, the sick also have need of a physician. If they need a physician, it is necessary that he be perfect; otherwise, he will produce no fruit. If, therefore, he wishes to be a Theorist, he

<margin>From where the Physician must learn Theory.</margin>
must learn to govern his Theory from the said book. First, *from God*. He opens the lips of all and helps us to work in His name. For without Him, all things are nothing. Then all the other books which we have handed down must be properly known and investigated, and nothing else should be brought forward except what they have taught. There, theoretical causes and cures are joined as one. And whatever proceeds and is theorized from those books is whole and perfect. For those books themselves exist as whole and perfect. For God himself founded, described, and bound them, and attached them to His Library as if fastened by certain chains. Therefore, they contain no error in themselves...

contain no dew, no fraud, no labyrinth, and no seduction. And although something excerpted from them may be smeared upon paper, or described and transferred, nevertheless the instruction of those things proceeds from the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>Latin: *lumen naturae*; the innate wisdom or intelligence found within the natural world</note> alone, not from man. For example: we have eternal life described in the Gospel and Holy Scripture according to everything required for it; nor is there need for more traditions for this purpose. Now, even if eternal life is stored within the paper of scripture, it is not yet enough to have it described so; rather, it must be sought and investigated further—namely, at the side of and through Him from whom it was heard, received, and recorded onto paper. <margin>
Eternal life is handed down in Holy Scripture.

<margin>
Literal theory is dead.

The same must be thought regarding the Theory and Practice of Medicine. Even if it can be recorded and inserted into a paper book, it is nonetheless nothing other than a dead letter. Therefore, illumination from the Light of Nature must be added so that the text of the <term>Book of Nature</term> <note>The concept that the physical world is a book written by God to be "read" by the scientist</note> may be understood soundly and properly; without this clarification, no one can be either a Philosopher or a Naturalist. It is vain, therefore, for anyone to trust in paper. Illumination must be received, proceeding from Him who is the Light Himself; and all our doctrines and speculations must be weighed and, if found wanting, cast out.

<margin>
From where the Physician's illumination is to be sought.
</margin>

<margin>
What medical theory is.
</margin>

But it must also be understood what the "Theory of Medicine" truly is. It is that which, with certain and indubitable truth, hands down and explains the principles, origins, materials, causes, natures, essences—in short, all the beginnings, middles, and ends—of each and every sickness. To these it adds the cures for all diseases: in what manner, by what means, and in what order they ought to be performed. Thus, it also recounts the errors associated with them. The matter is entirely the same as if someone were carrying a seed. He who knows the seed knows for certain what will eventually come forth from it. He who grafts a shoot, if he knows it thoroughly, knows beforehand what fruits it will bear. And this is "Rural Theory," or the theory of plants. By the same likeness, if a wound is inflicted on someone, everyone knows how it was inflicted on him. This is "Surgical Theory." Furthermore, to know what will happen regarding the wound, either without medicine or with it, is also Surgical Theory. But how the wound is to be cured, what ought to be applied for its healing, and how individual things are to be prepared and handled—this is "Practical Surgical Theory." Therefore, by the same reasoning that these things are understood, the causes of all diseases must also be scrutinized and unfolded. And just as was said of the seed, so must one theorize about diseases. For every single disease emerges from its own **seed**; if it has grown, it is just like a tree with its fruits. <note>original Latin quote: "Gladius est semen vulneris, sic à semine suo universa sunt."</note> "The sword is the seed of the wound; thus all things are from their own seed." From which it follows that it is necessary for the physician to have the seeds of all diseases known and explored. For once these are known, he can then freely theorize and discourse about diseases, just as a farmer does regarding his field which he has sown. Unless this theory is just as plain and easy for the Physician as his own is for the farmer, he is certainly entangled in a most intricate labyrinth and miserably leads others astray along with him.

<margin>
Diseases arise from their own seed, not from humors.
</margin>

It is common knowledge that many have written and commented on the causes and origin of diseases, and they do not lack followers and disciples. But regarding the "Principle," nothing worthy is handed down. As far as the outward signs are concerned, it is as follows: the very mouth of the sick testifies to it, the eyes see it, the ears hear it. But regarding the principle and origin, a mere labyrinth and seduction is taught. For unless the theory proceeds from the **seed**, and the **humors** are eliminated, all work will be in vain. If humors exist at all, they are nonetheless only generated *by* diseases; diseases are not generated *from* them. It is as if people think that because humors predominate, they must be the causes of diseases. For example: I suppose someone falls into a flux of the bowels and is fatigued by frequent yellow and bilious ejections. If you see these, you say that "cholera" <note>Here referring to yellow bile, one of the four traditional humors, rather than the modern bacterial disease.</note> is doing this or has done it. Meanwhile, you forget that a certain **seed** is present, which suddenly grew into that matter. This seed collapses by itself into bile and expels the bile; the bile itself is not the seed, but the color is from the bile, and the matter is from the seed. Just as wine that tastes of the earth is not therefore *from* the earth, but rather from its own grape—the grape from the wood, the wood from the root, and the root from its seed. Where then is your "cholera" or "melancholic humor"? So also you say of a visible dropsy <note>Latin: *hydropicus*; edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation.</note> that the patient's liver is "cooled," and those so disposed are prone to dropsy. Reasons of this sort are far too cheap. If indeed you were to say...

<margin>
Humors arise from diseases, not diseases from them.
</margin>

<margin>
Matter [comes] from seed.
</margin>

There is a "meteoric seed" <note>original: *semen meteoricum*; a Paracelsian concept referring to the invisible seeds or forces in the atmosphere that produce weather and influence health</note> that turns into rain; the rain drips down from the middle spaces into the lower parts, and in this way, water, or a marsh, or a lake is generated from that seed. so it is also necessary for us as **Theorists** <note>In this context, theorists are those who study the underlying principles or causes of things</note> to understand the cause or principle of Medicine in diseases, just as has been described. And as Theorists, they have a duty to read diligently—not the works of the "Tantaluses," <note>likely a derogatory reference to those who reach for knowledge but never grasp it</note> or Galen, Avicenna, Averroës, Drufianus, Guy de Chauliac, or Roger Bacon—but rather they should leaf through those books which God Himself wrote. From this source, everyone must learn everything. Without Him, all things are dead and lack understanding.

<margin>On what foundation medicine should be established.</margin>
**S**ince, therefore, it is right that Medicine should rest upon a certain and firm foundation—one that does not proceed from one's own brain, but is established through evidence and firm, true doctrine—now remind yourselves that the diseases of men are hidden, just as Medicine itself is. Neither of these two can be performed or discovered through the **earthly body**; rather, it is necessary to establish them through the **sidereal body**, <note>original: *corpus sidereum*; the "star-body" or astral body, which Paracelsus believed mediated between the soul and the physical flesh</note> which penetrates into nature just as the Sun penetrates through glass. Furthermore, it must now also be known by what ways and means hidden things, which are invisible to the earthly body, may be found.

<margin>Magic reveals obscure diseases.</margin>
It is established, therefore, that it is necessary for all these things to be manifested through **Magic** and its various branches, such as **Kabbalah** <note>original: *Gaballiam*; Paracelsus used "Magic" and "Kabbalah" to mean the spiritual science of understanding the hidden virtues and signatures within nature</note> and the Kabbalistic arts, etc. These reveal all the secrets of hidden nature, and thus it is necessary for the Physician to be well-versed and instructed in them. If he is not such a man, he exists in Medicine only as an error and a guesser, devoted more to imposture than to truth, as the facts themselves speak.

<margin>Magic is the anatomy of medicine.</margin>
For **Magic is the Anatomy of Medicine.** And just as a butcher dissects an ox so that all its internal parts become visible and manifest—parts which could not be seen through the skin of the whole animal—so also Magic dissects all the "bodies" of Medicine, in which the remedies belonging to that body are stored. For just as a human exhibits these parts in one place and those in another (as is taught in **Physical Anatomy**):

<margin>These have their own members, as does man.</margin>
so their own "members" are also present within herbs. For in this way, one part is the **heart**, another the **liver**, another the **spleen**, and so on, according to the pattern of a human being. However, it is false to say that all "hearts" which appear as hearts to the eye are a single heart; rather, there is one power and virtue similar to a heart. For example: many properties are perceived in the wind. It dries things out, yet no one sees the "drying" itself. The Sun warms, yet no one sees the "warming" itself. Fire comes from a flint, yet no one sees the fire within the flint. Thus, in one body there are many members, which nevertheless are only one body.

<margin>Multiple properties of a single thing.</margin>
Thus, there is only one herb, and yet manifold virtues exist within it. In the same way, seven members similar to human organs are found in the **firmament**: the heart, kidneys, stomach, lungs, etc. Not indeed as tangible members, but as powers and...

...virtues without a body: just as, conversely, in a man without a body, nothing can be found. So also in a moon-struck woman <note>original: *Lunatica*; a person whose health or mind is influenced by the phases of the moon</note>, the movement of the whole moon is perceived, not visibly, but in the spirit. For medicine is stored in the spirit, not in the body. For the body and the spirit are two different things. The body is not the spirit, which is the true aid of Physicians. Thus, in amber <note>original: *carabe*; likely referring to the resin's "attractive" spiritual virtues</note>, the members of the **Microcosm** <note>The human being viewed as a "miniature universe"</note> are present; that is, virtues of this kind are not in the physical body, but in the remedies—which is to say, in spiritual things.

<margin>The Art of Magic as a discoverer must be zealously learned by the Physician.</margin>
Therefore, since the aid for the sick is, in this way, a Spirit, and is covered or hidden by the **Elemental body**, and lies open only to the **sidereal** <note>relating to the stars or the celestial body of man</note> influence: it is now clear that it is the duty of **Magic** <note>For Paracelsus, Magic is not sorcery, but the "Art" of revealing the hidden, internal powers of nature</note> to teach these things—not the duty of Avicenna or Galen. For Magic alone is the instructor and the Pedagogue who teaches us how to find Medicine and help for the sick, and to do so visibly. Just as the Elemental body, letters, and any form, color, or shape are visible to the eyes: so too the essence of those medicinal aids is rendered conspicuous and distinguishable, just as clearly as a shape lies open to earthly eyes. Indeed, I have many times mentioned Magic, and many times the investigation of the secrets of nature, both in these and other books. I would have you know briefly, therefore, that the Art of Magic, the discoverer, should be diligently and accurately learned by every Physician. For even if all other books throughout the world were lost, and with them all medicine perished: if this art survived, that loss would be considered as nothing. For that "discoverer-book" finds all those things again by a "right of recovery," <note>original: *postliminio*; a legal term for the restoration of rights or property</note> and even much more than those. And this becomes for you the **Anatomy** of the arts.

<margin>How great is the power of Magic in discovery.</margin>
<margin>What the "Signed" is.</margin>
It is not that through this art the members of wood, herbs, or roots are looked into to see what they are like inside; rather, it is that through this art, powers and virtues are uncovered much more clearly and plainly than if the external members were dissected, separated, and thoroughly boiled. This "Anatomy of discovery" first demonstrates the **Signed** <note>original: *signatum*; the theory of "Signatures," where a plant's appearance reveals its healing purpose</note>. Now, as to what is signed and what has performed the signing, that is indicated by **Gaballia** <note>a Paracelsian term for Cabala, here meaning the interpretation of the signs or "signatures" of nature</note>, a species of Magic which is a member of Anatomy. Truly, the art of discovery is not understood in only one way, but also in all species of **Astronomy** <note>The study of how celestial forces influence things on earth</note> and of gifts. And since there are many such members, and even more species—all of which are the discoverers of Magic and the explainers of the Anatomy of sciences, arts, and medicines—it is therefore clear that these members and species must become visible through the operation of "Discovery Astronomy." Just as fire from the Sun becomes visible through a Crystal, or fire in a flint becomes visible through steel, so it is necessary for the **Magical Sun** to become visible through the **Magical Crystal**, so that in this way the **Magical Fire** might become visible through the **Magical Steel**. Now, therefore, Anatomy burns and blazes, and it shows what is at hand, so that what lies hidden in that body may be visibly perceived, no less clearly than fire from the Sun is seen in wood, or fire from a flint is seen in wood. For here, the **Magical wood** is also ignited—that is, the secrets of herbs will burn like wood and bring forth their virtue, showing what they are useful for.

<margin>The schemes of the "Deceiver of a Thousand Arts" in abolishing Magic.</margin>
That **Deceiver of a Thousand Arts** <note>original: *Milleartifex*; a traditional name for the Devil</note> has employed many machines to shake this Anatomy from the memory of men and to bring total oblivion to such a noble art. He has also snatched men away from this art into various trifles, in which there is no art at all, so that they might waste their time idly in those things.

<margin>There is no desire for the unknown.</margin>
For to one who knows nothing, there is no desire. And he who knows nothing, understands nothing. He who is fit for nothing, is nothing. But he who understands a thing, loves it, observes it, and meditates upon it. The Deceiver has striven to lead us away from this desire. For he was not unaware that if a man had knowledge of these secrets, he would not allow himself to be seduced by a book afterward, but would rather stubbornly cling to that treasure. If a man does not know those things, Satan knows that he will follow his belly, lust, gambling, wars, and idleness. For this once is true: he who does not know God, loves Him not at all. He who is ignorant of the Trinity does not believe in it, and therefore does not love it. He who does not know Mary does not love her. He who does not know the saints does not love them. He who does not know nature does not love it. So, therefore, he who knows nothing in this way also meditates on nothing and pursues nothing, but despises all things. The belly alone is his God. But the more certain and penetrating the knowledge of a thing is, the greater the love and affection. He who does not know the poor cares nothing for them. Everything is placed in knowledge. From this, all fruits flow. Knowledge itself bestows faith. For he who has known God believes in Him. Conversely, however, he who has not known Him...

For according to the measure of knowledge, the tranquil...

### CHAPTER X.

->*Concerning the book: how Medicine is brought*<-
->*from the **First Matter** into the **Final Matter**.*<-

<margin>The First Matter of things is formless.</margin>
**E**very single thing that grows is without form, or is formless in its **First Matter** <term>Materia Prima: the raw, chaotic, or undifferentiated substance before it takes a specific shape</term>, and is, as it were, nothing. For example: the Beech, the Fir, the oak; <margin>The seed: when it is nothing, and when it is something.</margin> first it is a seed, in which there is nothing of that which it ought to be. If, however, this seed is cast into the earth, it is necessary that it first **putrefy** <note>rot or break down</note>. Otherwise, nothing is produced from it. If it now putrefies, the whole is dissolved. And while it was still a seed before, it was something. But when it putrefies, it is now nothing more. Furthermore, from that which putrefies, it follows that this putrefaction is the "first matter" which now passes into the plant: and at that time, the form of that tree is implanted in it. First, it received its beginning within the earth. Afterward, it received its second beginning above the earth. And above the earth, it departs into various species, until that becomes what it 

lastly ought to be. However, it is not born all at once, with its form and all things, above the earth as soon as it first emerges from it—just as an infant is brought forth with a full form: I say, plants are not born in that way. But just as plants appear above the earth and pass from one form into another: in such a way you ought to know that the infant proceeds and grows in its mother's womb. Now, as the form increases gradually: so also the Medicine increases, with which that herb or tree is gifted and distinguished. Not that the form is perfectly present [at the start], but it only grows in the perfection of the form, and becomes perfect. <margin>Forms have their ages, like man.</margin> For it is divided by its form into its ages, just like a human. First, he is an infant in the cradle. Such also is the form of plants in the beginning. Afterward, he becomes a boy, becoming accustomed to running and walking, not to other works. The same is the logic of forms and of Medicine. Next, the infant daily tastes and understands more and more. So also plants next increase more and more in their strengths and virtues, and their forms daily escape into stronger ones, until the appointed time. At last, old age and weakness press upon them, by the same decrease with which their vigor had ascended in its increase. <margin>The degrees and ages of Medicine.</margin> In the same way, it is understood regarding Medicine, that it similarly has its degrees, according as its virtue is in youth (or strength) and old age (or infirmity). These things being recognized, now further learn what I am about to say. You see that all bodies have their forms in which they consist. <margin>The form of Medicine is twofold.</margin> So also all Medicines have their forms, established within them: One is visible. The other is invisible. One is corporeal, **Elemental**; the other is spiritual, **sidereal** <note>relating to the stars or celestial influences</note>. From this it is now clear that every Physician ought to be equipped with a spiritual, sidereal **Herbarium** <note>a book or collection of plants</note>, so that from it he may know in what way that Medicine consists in its form: as these examples will teach. <margin>What kind of Herbarium a Physician should have.</margin> Medicine which is taken spiritually in its essence, as soon as it has penetrated into the body, stands in its own form: not otherwise than a rainbow in the sky, or an image in a mirror. Thus, if it has the form of feet, it goes to the feet. If it has the form of hands, it stands in the hands. The same is the logic of the head, back, belly, heart, spleen, liver, etc. But grasp the matter more clearly. Let there be a root which contains all the bodies of men in its sidereal body. If that is taken, then it consists in the human according to all its members in the members of the man. From this it follows,

<margin>Mirror-like feathers in a drink heal the breasts.</margin>

Mirror-like feathers <note>likely referring to iridescent plumage</note> heal the breasts of women when taken in a drink. The reason is that their form corresponds to the breasts and udders; thus, the image of the Medicine moves toward its own matching member where it belongs. Similarly, **Dactiletus** <term>Dactiletus: a finger-shaped stone or fossil, often a belemnite, believed to have healing properties</term> taken in a drink cures cancer. For its own image goes to that place in the body toward which its form looks. For you ought to be persuaded of this: that all surgical diseases can be cured through natural remedies, if the Physician knows and understands the **Anatomy of the essence** <note>the inner, spiritual structure of a substance rather than its physical appearance</note>: of whom, however, I have seen very few. But I have seen a vast number of those who speak of "guiding" and "directing" substances, that is,
<margin>The false opinion of physicians regarding "directing" substances.</margin>
about additives that are supposed to carry and lead the Medicine to its proper seat and natural place; an opinion which, however, lacks any foundation. For they say that Sage, Lavender, and Marjoram are "directors" or "leaders" to the head, which carry the Medicine along with them to that place, not unlike a mail-carrier or a companion leading another who is ignorant of the way to wherever he wishes to go. This is a very **un-medical** <note>original: "aniatron," from Greek, meaning "unskilled in the art of healing"</note> thing to say. For 
<margin>By what power medicine moves to its parts.</margin>
medicine is not carried in that way, but rather promotes itself through the power of its own image. For example: **Eyebright** <term>Euphragia: a common plant traditionally used for eye ailments</term> has the form and image of eyes within itself. Hence it happens that, once consumed, it stations itself in its own matching member and into the very form of that member, so that Eyebright becomes, as it were, a whole and complete eye. What other Medicine is there that could lead another to the eye and into the eye in a similar way, as if by a vehicle? All the members of man have their own completely similar form in growing things, in stones, in metals, in minerals, etc. And because the body is an essence, that image is also within it. If it is consumed, then by the nature of the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: the "little world," or the human being as a reflection of the whole universe</term>, that same image is established in the man. In this way, therefore, the Medicine is carried to the place where it ought to go. For just as a sculptor takes a shapeless piece of wood and fashions from it a certain form until the end: so you 
<margin>Nature is like a sculptor.</margin>
ought to know that nature itself is also such a sculptor, capable of leading any body back into its own form. The food that is eaten is a form in the mouth: but nature is in its **Archeic** <term>Archeus: the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</term> virtues. Now, all members in a man must be nourished. But how? Natural philosophy and the genuine light of nature teach this: that food, when it reaches its essences, goes into its own form and remains there, like an image in the whole body, each thing in the place where it ought to be; that is the "Man of Food." In the same way, likewise, a drink also, if it reaches its spirit, then like a living spirit of a man, it remains in all the members of the man. For these are the perfect forms in all members, with none excepted. The same reasoning applies to Medicine. Where the sickness is, there the Medicine has its form, nature, and property. Here now is the task of the art: that the Spiritual, Essential, and Medicinal man be recognized according to that place in which his cure is located. For *there is a man of cancer, a man of the wolf <note>lupus</note>, a man of the plague, a man of fever, a man of dropsy, a man of flux, a man of monsters, a man of worms*, and so it is for all diseases. If the Physician is ignorant of this—where that **sidereal** <note>referring to the astral or "star-born" influence on the body</note> man is situated within the **Elemental** <note>composed of the physical elements</note> bodies—then all things are established and done outside the order of Medicine. For who could always find a guide and companion for himself to every member? Thus, **Stulentina** <note>possibly a variant of *Stellaria* (Stitchwort) or a similar herbal preparation</note> taken in a drink 
<margin>Stulentina cures whitlows.</margin>
cures a **whitlow** <note>original: "panetitium," an infection of the finger</note>, because its image has its cure in this place. Who is this "Leader" in Medicine who would direct such a cure outward into the fingers? Therefore, they should not be "leading" substances, but "companion-forms" and carriers, and they direct by that which the image produces from itself. That is what the "leader" ought to be. Any other process is merely a shortcut of labor and laziness, nor does it require much art: Physicians learn that from paper at least, nor do they have any need for the book of true art. For Medicine must be understood in this way entirely: how it reaches the final state from its **first matter** <note>the raw, unrefined substance</note>. And if it is led to the final state, then it is a species with all its form and substance, just as the Elemental body itself is. And in the image of the spirit lie the **Secrets** and **Great Works** <term>Arcana & Magnalia: the hidden, most potent powers of nature</term>
<margin>In what the Great Works and Secrets reside.</margin>
of Medicine: where, at last, the true cure is placed. Images of this kind ought to be sought out through the "discoverer" of the Magical art, which the fourth book discusses. For the **Archeus** of Nature ordains this spirit, with its division, into its own form along with all the Secret Power that is to be ordained within it. Surely by this reasoning the "Anatomy of Medicines" ought to be found—not in the compound, not in common things, not in "directions." For all things are already 
<margin>No one can improve the composition of nature.</margin>
ordered within nature, and composed by the best art into a single spiritual form. You will not make this any better than nature itself made it. Use only **Alchemy**, which separates different things. Give your labor to this, therefore...

### CHAPTER IX.

*On the book of the Generation of Diseases, which must be understood through true Philosophy.*

**O**ne more thing remains for you to consider and for me to declare: namely, the generation <note>the origin or birth</note> of diseases according to Philosophical consideration. By now, it is unknown to none of you that the ancients established four **humors** <note>the traditional Greek medical theory that health is governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, from which they claimed all diseases arise. In doing this, they forgot the true and legitimate origin of diseases—that is, the **seeds** <note>original: "feminis," likely a typo for "seminis" (seed). Paracelsus argues diseases grow from specific "seeds" like plants</note> from which diseases are born and produced. 
<margin>The invention of the humors is useless.</margin>
<margin>Man is a Microcosm.</margin>
Moreover, there is no one who would deny that man himself is a **Microcosm** <note>the "little world"; the idea that the human body contains all the elements and powers of the greater universe</note>. From this, it is necessary that he has the four Elements within himself, which are what the Humors lack. Although it would be better if the name "Elements" were retained, for that would make for an easier and fuller understanding. But no paper should be wasted on a quarrel over a name. So that you may grasp my meaning, and so that this book may have its due, apply your mind to what will be demonstrated by the following example. Since the four humors are the four 
<margin>Elements should be substituted for humors.</margin>
Elements, it follows that the understanding of the four humors is exactly the same as that of the Elements. Now, you are aware that the Elements themselves give nothing, but at most receive. Just as a woman cannot be made pregnant without a man, so also the "females" of the Elements only conceive from their "husbands," who are like superior **Vulcans** <note>original: "Vulcanis." In alchemy, Vulcan is the god of fire, representing the transformative power or "inner alchemist" that brings things to completion</note>. This is demonstrated by such an example: An apple is born from its seed; and the seed is the apple, and it is the sperm of Vulcan. But in the Elements it finds its **matrix** <note>a womb or surrounding environment in which something develops</note>, and in that womb it takes its nourishment, substance, form, and perfect nature. There it is able to emerge so that it becomes what it must be according to the manner of its predestination, no differently than an infant who is brought forth perfected by its mother. Thus, the Elements are by no means the 
<margin>The seed is the cause of disease, not the humor.</margin>
cause of diseases; rather, it is the **seed** that is sown within them. It grows there until its final essence and matter. We ourselves grow from this, and from this growth, disease arises; that which has grown or been born is the disease itself. Therefore, he who wishes to know a disease should recognize it like a tree, in this manner: One tree bears apples, another pears, a third nuts, and so on. The same distinction exists in diseases. And diseases must be understood entirely as being born from a seed, not from the humors—from the father, I say, not from the mother. And although the infant is indeed brought forth by the mother, it is nonetheless from the father. Considering these things in this way, who, I ask, would say or grant that diseases should be sought as if they were a "Humor," or that a Humor should be judged or held to be the disease? Since the mother is one thing and the infant who comes from the mother is another: the mother has one disease, and the infant has another likewise. Who would go to great labor to search for the infant’s disease in the mother? For the disease exists only in the infant, who is entirely separated from its mother. And although someone might object that the mother and infant can have the same disease at the same time, the one is nonetheless separate from the other. Thus, the disease must be sought in that in which it exists. But if someone should object: *"Because you hold the Elements to be females, and females themselves are prone to be sick, therefore the Elements can also be sick; thus it seems necessary that the Humor is the disease, etc."* To this, take such an answer: A woman is herself also a fruit from her own matrix, no less than an infant. In this, "Females" and "Elements" differ: for Elements are not fruits, but in the act of conception, they are similar to females. How then can a physician say that diseases themselves are "elemental"? Or how can he be persuaded that if he expels the "element" (the humor), he has also expelled the disease? If the physician must begin where the Philosopher ends, he must certainly be endowed with a far different understanding. For Philosophy does not teach a Physician to begin in this way. For how can one say...

-> THE LABYRINTH <-

Who can say that an apple is merely of the earth, when it actually comes from its own seed? From this it follows that if a Physician wishes to remove a "humor" <note>the traditional bodily fluids believed to cause illness</note> with his remedies, it may happen that he helps the patient, but only in this way: if a mother must be taken away, the infant is taken away along with her. For if the "mother" <note>here meaning the elemental foundation of the body</note> is removed, then the body loses its own Element, and thus falls down dead. 
Thus, from the practice of those doctors follows the killing of the sick and the desolation or overturning of health. For in no way, and by no right, should the body be robbed of its genuine Element. 

Furthermore, note how clear a path Philosophy <note>specifically "Natural Philosophy," what we might now call natural science</note> points out in this matter, as we see that the Elements are the corporeal womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> fit for conceiving a seed and supplying it with its own nourishment and growth. Who, then, would wish to be so unskilled as to dare to administer medicine while not understanding this Philosophy? Let the Physician truly know that without this kind of Philosophy, he claims the name and title of "doctor" unjustly. I would easily grant you this: that every single seed has a **tincture** <note>a quality, color, or essential property</note> within itself. From this, it is possible for the elements themselves to take on a discoloration or alteration. But to say that because of this, the element itself is the disease—that is entirely false. Just as a cloth is soaked with a foreign color, so in the same way does it happen here.

<margin>Color comes from the seed.</margin>
But he who can draw out and extract the color again, so that the cloth returns to its native color: he has performed the proof of it. Let an example clarify the matter. In **jaundice** <note>original: "aurigine," the yellowing of the skin</note>, he who can take away that tincture has removed the seed from which the tincture emerged. In this way, he returns the body to its former and native color. For the color does not come from the body, but only from a foreign seed.

Furthermore, note also concerning corruption: if we speak of putrid air and water, diseases also arise from that corruption. This is indeed true, but for this reason: nothing is broken or dissolved in its entirety that has not conceived a "seed of breaking." From this it follows that seeds corrupt, and they give birth to another kind of disease and corrupt the body, just as snow-water corrupts iron. Therefore, if this seed is removed, its corruption is removed along with it.

<margin>Worms from the earth.</margin>
Example: Beetles, worms, etc., are born from mud. This is not because the dung or mud is changed into worms, but because a seed lies hidden in the dung, from which worms are later produced through **Vulcanian digestion** <note>the process of "ripening" or transformation through heat, named after Vulcan, the god of fire</note>. Thus, the Beetle is something different from the dung; for if it were horse dung, it would resemble it. But since there is no resemblance between them, it has its own entirely peculiar generation by which it is brought forth. A grape has a seed within it, which is wine. From that, wine is produced, not from the seed from which wood grows. The seed from which wood is produced is both visible and tangible. But the seed from which wine is born, no one sees, and yet they exist divided within themselves, just like the body and the soul. 

But pay further attention. If, therefore, every importance is placed in the seed: it is the duty of the physician to study and know it well. For in this way, he will be able to prescribe and direct his remedies against it. And as has been understood, the physician must also know that the **seeds of diseases are twofold: namely, the Illiastrum seed and the Cagastrum seed.**

<margin>Twofold seed: Illiastrum and Cagastrum.</margin>
That is to say, every seed was either established as a seed from the beginning—such as an apple, a nut, a pear, etc.—and this is called **Illiastrum** <note>referring to the "star-like" or primordial, healthy order of nature</note>; or it is born from corruption, and it is named **Cagastrum** <note>referring to seeds of disease or parasites that arise from decay or "bad" stars</note>.

<margin>Which are Illiastrian diseases.</margin>
Thus, **Illiastrian diseases are dropsy, jaundice, gout, etc.**

<margin>Which are Cagastrian diseases.</margin>
**Cagastrian diseases are pleurisy, plague, fevers, etc.**

This "Labyrinth" in Medicine is not to be despised, nor should the physician wander out of bounds in his knowledge of these things. For this error is not merely content with itself; rather, the matter concerns the body and life itself. If this error were free from harm and danger, it might have been tolerated by turning a blind eye until now. But since it is full of extreme danger, must we not say it is unjust that it has flourished for so many centuries? I remain silent about many other more serious things that could also be brought forward here: namely, that all general prescriptions, if they are not directed against the seed itself, are wicked and unfit.

<margin>Prescriptions must be directed against the seed of the disease.</margin>
But once more, give me your ears. What do you think of the fact that diseases arise in this way and increase daily? If you wish to understand this well, turn your step back toward Philosophy, and observe how she teaches you to understand how the grass grows, how wood is produced, and other similar things. Are they not produced from a seed? Indeed. If, therefore, they are from a seed, and the disease itself also emerges from a seed: then one is produced in an entirely equal manner to the other. Why, then, are you so busy taking up the task of describing diseases with such sweat and labor? If you are ignorant of natural Philosophy...

<margin>The Microcosm <note>the "small world" of man</note> is to be compared to the Macrocosm <note>the "great world" of the universe</note>.</margin>

### ->CONCLUSION OF THE LABYRINTH.<-

*That I have so far composed and proposed several chapters from the books of medicine, regarding how they ought to be learned, inquired into, and investigated: no few nor light causes have driven me. The first is that so many people everywhere write commentaries on medicine, teach the same, and prescribe a method of curing. Truly, let everyone know this universally: it is extremely shameful to wish to learn a matter that risks the danger of body and life, and to do so not from a true foundation, but from a labyrinth and mere opinion, which is far removed from the reality itself; and finally to build a method of curing upon this opinion, and to attempt to practice from this fabricated art. For here, a deceptive beginning, middle, and end lie hidden. It is no light thing for an end or a cure to be built from a futile and erroneous beginning. But, since the foundation of Medicine is far different from what they pour out from their labyrinth, is it not much more just that they follow a solid rule and reason, rather than defend that foundation which was not given or placed by God as a foundation? For in that way, we do nothing other than desert this book—the most faithful steward of all medicine and the cure of all universal diseases, established by God Himself—and embrace another book by profession, fighting diametrically against the aforementioned ordinary order.*

<margin>The wicked custom of men.</margin>
*But this is mostly the custom of men: that they almost always praise things that are worthless more than things that are useful; and they show themselves for the most part more inclined toward evil than good. For in this way, the same God, with such accurate meditation, both established medicine itself and signed its books, so that it has no need of another scribe or interpreter, except for one who holds precisely to the text of Nature itself, just as*

I have been exhausted by many long journeys, yet I have attained my wish with a success that was by no means unhappy. As for the elders of whom I speak and write, they have for the most part been snatched away by their fate and have departed to join our ancestors. Thus, today only a very small part of them survives. I finished and polished this book on Tartar when I had set out from Eferding to the Bohemian Marshal. # ON TARTARIC DISEASES: OR,
## THE BOOK
### CONCERNING THE ANCIENT NAME
#### for the stone, or rock and gravel.
#### CHAPTER I.
##### *On the Old Name of this disease: and on the defense of the newly introduced one.*

**W**HOEVER wishes to hand down and teach any matter, it is their duty first of all to propose the material itself, or the thing to be treated; afterward, they should designate its name or title and inquire into the agreement of the name with the thing itself, and finally derive the reasoning for that agreement. Thus, as I am about to hand down the name of this disease, it is incumbent upon me to remind you above all else that the naming used by the ancient writers and modern physicians does not fit or suit those diseases which they designate. From this, it is inevitable that a certain confusion and schism is introduced into Medicine. For whatever a man either does or learns, it ought not to go outside the level, the line, or the circle; nor is it right for anything unequal, gaping, or wandering to occur. That is to say: all things must be reduced to one, and each individual part must be consistent with the others. 

These things being so established, now that I have revealed my intention to write about Tartar <note>original: "Tartaro"; Paracelsus coined this term for metabolic deposits (like kidney stones) by comparing them to the "tartar" or crust left by wine in a barrel.</note>, it will be necessary hereafter for me to explicitly define and properly establish the name of this disease. For since no small dispute grows between us concerning the true name—and indeed the reasoning of the name itself teaches that we agree neither in the beginning, nor the middle, nor the very end—it is worth the effort to establish the foundation of the naming so that the whole matter may be perfectly understood, and the opposing writings about this disease may be accurately judged and decided. However, this foundation which the ancients laid down must be understood metaphorically.

<margin>The ancient physicians named the stone metaphorically.</margin>
For "calculus" <note>stone or pebble</note> is taken from *calculus*, "arena" <note>sand</note> from *arena*, and "fabulum" <note>gravel</note> from *fabulum*. Let an example be set. If Christ says: *I am the light of the world*, a torch or a candle is not immediately to be understood. For there are many lights, and they are understood in various ways. Likewise, if He says: *I am the way*, that "way" which is trodden upon by feet is not to be understood. Though this metaphor may indeed be apt, it is nonetheless too close to a figure of speech; this is because a stone in a human being *appears* similar to the stones of rivers. The same judgment must be made also concerning sand and gravel. Now, however, that which exists outside the human being is something else and is diverse from that which is stored within the human being. Nor should the name of the human stone be derived from external stones. For the reasoning and nature of a stone in a human is one thing, and that of an external stone is another—just as it is one thing to say, *I am the light of the world*, and another, *I am...*

# ON DISEASES

...I am a wax candle in the world. I explain these things more clearly here so that it may be understood that metaphors are used ineptly in Medicine, and that all metaphorical names are the parents of error and ambiguity. This same thing occurs with the metaphors of ancient writers used until now, which should never have been thrust into the art of medicine. Indeed, let such things be far exiled from my writings, with which I adorn this treatment of this disease. For those writers took the name for that human "stone" from the stones paving the streets, and they called human "gravel" from the sand with which buildings are constructed. 

But to call human gravel "sand" is of the same logic as if someone were to bring forth an example from Theology concerning the **Lamb of God**, and then strive to equate this lamb with a woolly lamb and claim they are of the same nature. For one belongs to God, and the other to wool. In the same way, the grit in a human is one thing; the grit in a stream is another. Just as the nature, reason, and essence of that Theological passage are by no means the same as the animal, so too here the name "stone" or "sand" provides nothing of value. Certainly, any lamb is most patient; so too is Christ, who is compared to it. Nevertheless, the true and genuine name is Christ himself, in whom all things are fully understood. Thus, the name of the human stone is something different from the name from which it is borrowed.

<margin>Theophrastus’s naming of Tartar.</margin>

Furthermore, attend diligently. The name that I impose on this disease is *Tartar*, that is, the sickness of Tartar, or the Tartareous disease. This is taken from **Tartar** <note>original: "Tartara"; Paracelsus uses this term to refer to the hard crust or sediment found in wine barrels (cream of tartar), using it as an analogy for metabolic deposits in the body like kidney stones or gouty "chalk."</note> truly so called. It is called Tartar because it produces from itself oil, water, tincture, and salt, and because it inflames and burns the patient no differently than **Gehenna** <note>A biblical term for a place of fiery torment or hell; the author is punning on the similarity between "Tartar" and "Tartarus," the Greek underworld.</note>. Indeed, Tartar signifies Gehenna. The particular logic, essence, property, and nature of this Tartar is distinct from those stones, sands, and grits, which cannot be traced back to that Tartareous heat. 

Therefore, no metaphor can be assumed here that is appropriate for Medicine. For to name a thing according to its external form alone is ridiculous. To the judgment of the eyes, they may agree to some extent because of the process of coagulation; yet the mode of generation is not one, nor is the mode of coagulation similar, nor is their nature and property uniform. Rather, every single thing differs from another according to its nature, just as **Diamond** and **Orizon** <note>original: "Adamas & Orizon"; likely referring to contrasting minerals or precious stones in the author's mineralogical system.</note> differ. And since this disease I am describing—namely how Tartar arises—is produced from the same matter, cause, and logic, such that all things descend from the nature of Tartar and not from the nature of stones and sand: therefore it is right and just that, having shaken off and put to flight the metaphor, I should apply myself more closely to the matter itself, which exists as this disease and gives it its name. 

I will propose a comparison to you. For the naming used by the ancients is no different than if a monkey were called a human simply because it knows how to perform certain gestures similar to humans. From this, it does not follow that one and the same name immediately fits both; rather, the monkey retains the name of monkey, taken from that which it actually is. For since it is a monkey, it is truly and genuinely called a monkey. Thus, everything ought to be known by the force of its name. In that way, a human also retains the name of human, because he is indeed a human, and is that which he is named. From what, from where, and of what kind a thing exists, in that it ought to remain, nor should it rashly step outside its own scale, line, or circle. And it is fitting for all things to be included so strictly and precisely within their own boundaries and limits that they are no more difficult to understand than it is understood that the name Anna indicates a woman, and John indicates a man.

<margin>Why genuine names are given to things.</margin>

Therefore, not without merit, I labor first in this entrance-hall <note>Metaphor for the introduction or preface of a book.</note> regarding the true name, so that the beginning of the treatment may emerge more liquidly and clearly, and a judgment can be more easily made regarding the greater propriety between me and the other writers of Medicine. For it seems to me too coarse and rustic for a certain thing to be called a "stone" which is not a stone. 

<margin>A reprimand of Physicians.</margin>

I judge the same regarding "gravel" and "sand." That these are not gravel and sand is demonstrated both by their primary matter, their operation, and their final matter. Indeed, those physicians betrayed their own ignorance when they did not consider that a stone does not admit **Resolution** <note>In alchemy/medicine, "Resolution" refers to the process of dissolving a solid back into a liquid state.</note>. Yet they nevertheless proceed in the cure of the stone and sand as if they were striving to resolve, dissolve, and pulverize **flints**, 

<margin>Flint cannot be resolved.</margin>

and thus in the same way they try to crush Tartar in a human, even though the works of Nature prove that no comparison or similarity applies here. If they conducted themselves in the cure of Tartar by making that corporeal process a spiritual one, then at last they would walk the right path. For they would observe that the generation...

...the logic of stones serves the coagulation of stone-mucilage; <note>The author uses "mucilage" to describe the sticky, gelatinous substance he believes precedes the hardening of a deposit.</note> however, Tartar does not belong to that specific coagulation of mucilage. And although a certain metaphor can be established here—such as the one comparing an ape to a man—<margin>Speaking figuratively [is what they say] is worthy of a Doctor</margin> it is nevertheless shameful for a Doctor and Master of Medicine to pollute Medicine with those crude and improper names, since one should instead study and cling to the proper nature and the very essence of things. <margin>What Tartar is.</margin> Now that these things have been thoroughly understood, listen further to what Tartar is. Learn the matter through this discourse. Every moisture from the earth conceives a certain incorporated matter, which is naturally inclined and disposed toward coagulation (*if I may put it that way*). <margin>Tartar is in all moist things.</margin> This is clear from this very common example. Wine comes forth from the earth and brings with it a congenital matter of this kind. Now, if it reaches the process of coagulation, then that coagulated material is separated from the wine and adheres to the inside of the vessel or cask. This adhering substance is called *Tartar of wine*. A similar Tartar is also contained in water, which is separated from the water in a subtle way and is called *Tartar of water*. Likewise, that which is secreted from milk is named *Tartar of milk*. In the same way, Tartar is also drawn out from the juices of fruits and herbs, which is named *Tartar of juices and herbs*. So also Tartar is secreted from legumes and all moist things that we eat or drink. And this is the generation of Tartar, not the generation of stones. For the generation and matter of Tartar is one thing, and that of stones is another. From this, understand that the incorporated matter of Tartar does not come from stones, but exists as a different and peculiar thing from the creation of stones; thus, a resolution <note>A breaking down or dissolving.</note> occurs in Tartar, but it performs nothing in stones. <margin>Where the species of Tartar are derived.</margin> Therefore, the name "Tartar" is given to this disease, derived surely from the material of Tartar, the species of which are afterwards established according to the nature and types of individual moistures—that is: there are precisely as many Tartars as there are species of Tartar in the Microcosm. <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human body, viewed as a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>

# CHAPTER II.
## How many kinds and natures of Tartar there are, and by what logic they are found.

**Furthermore**, before we begin the following chapters, we must define and explain what the true and most immediate origin of Tartar actually is. This will be achieved if we weigh more certainly and closely where exactly the matter of Tartar lies hidden, and by what means and path it penetrates into the human being. While we do this, the species of Tartar themselves will also be opened and encountered by us—specifically when we have learned what "body" that is in which the Tartar lies, how that body acts upon us, and what kinship and affinity exists between us and that body through which the matter of Tartar is eventually generated in us. Therefore, this chapter teaches into how many kinds or species these are divided—that is, how many types of bodies there are—to which you should also add the species of the bodies. <margin>As many species, just as many tartars.</margin> You will conclude that just as many kinds of Tartar itself exist. Regarding all of these, however, hold this: that the human intellect, when arising and drawn from within itself, is not at all knowledgeable of natural generations. I say this so you may understand from where I, intending to write about the matter of Tartar, shall draw out and establish my foundation for designating the disease of Tartar. For with these eyes of mine, I can perceive what lies hidden and stored within a certain body no more sharply than other writers on Tartar. This is what you must be forewarned of above all: for a Doctor's own fantasy and imagination teach him very little. But what the eyes see and the hand touches—that, finally, is what teaches him. <margin>The senses provide knowledge.</margin> So that you may comprehend this more clearly, turn your mind to this example. Let us suppose someone raised in a monastery or cloister has spent his entire life there, and has seen nothing else anywhere except the rites and customs of the monastery. What else, I ask, could he know except what he has seen and learned? If other foreign customs and rites should encounter him, he will be plainly ignorant of them and will only know his own tune. To this same man, if you were to propose the disease of Tartar...

Regarding what he might say, he will have nothing other than what monastic speculation suggests to him, which nevertheless proceeds from a human's mere fantasy—just like the Church's regulations on prayer and other matters. For whatever such regulations exist, they flow from human sense and judgment. This is similarly unacceptable in Medicine, and nothing can be successfully built on such a foundation. Therefore, that monk (or unskilled person) cannot grasp the true foundation, because that which is not enclosed within the limits of his speculation emerges anyway. Meanwhile, he can be very knowledgeable in monastic rituals, as those are things he has learned and knows.
