<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s defense of his revolutionary medical system. Having established that a physician must be a "Philosopher of the Firmament" and the earth, he now turns his vitriol toward the academic establishment of his day, defending his specific clinical successes—notably his work on the "French Disease" (syphilis)—against those who rely on the authority of ancient texts like those of Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

# VOLUME II.

A Physician grows if he emerges from Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy. Because I emphasize and cite these things, and build my Medicine upon this foundation, you accuse me of being a bastard member of the medical profession, a heretic, and a deceiver. But since you are lashed by the testimonies of your own lying writers—Avicenna and Galen—should your robberies then overwhelm me? On the contrary, I shall flourish indeed, even when you are suffering the curse of the withered fig tree <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 21:18-22; Paracelsus suggests the unfruitful traditional medical establishment is being cursed by God.</note>. For the axe is now laid to the tree; nor can the heavens endure to look upon their own evil any longer, but will henceforth create their own Astronomers, and the earth will produce its own Philosophers, and the very Light of Nature will bring forth its own Alchemists. When these have taken charge of affairs, they will place you, along with your proud and curly-haired wives, right next to the dog-killers <note>original: "canicidas." Dog-killers were among the lowest social castes in the Renaissance, often associated with executioners and skinners.</note>. Oh, how justly, you wanton and haughty wolves! Every good thing born through fraud will melt away again, lost in that luxury of yours. Woe to you, if a millstone were hung from your necks! For how heavily you will then atone for your refined delicacies—your little "bright-eyes" <note>original: "luciolos," likely a reference to a specific delicacy or perhaps a play on expensive lamp-oil.</note> and Malmsey wine <note>original: "Maluaticum." A sweet, expensive Greek wine popular in the Renaissance.</note>—and likewise your silken and gilded trinkets and headbands. (This is truly the way the devil raises his own; he requires them to be such so that, through their very pride, the "honesty" of their art might be publicly established. For no honest art gains good things through such luxury.) I have no fear but that I shall cut out these windbag Doctors, these lice-munchers and sycophants. I fear rather the serpents and the venomous eyes of the "Lady Doctor," whose tongue hisses like a snake. Away to the sewers with those things, not to me!

<margin>Galen and Avicenna are criticized.</margin>
<margin>The work creates the Doctor.</margin>
<margin>Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus</note> maligned for his writing on the "Venereal Plague" <note>Syphilis</note>.</margin>

Now, if healing makes the Physician, and the work itself creates the doctor and master—rather than His Imperial Majesty, or His Papal Holiness, or a Dean—then you must certainly know that such healing begins from a far different foundation than what you boast of in your Academies. And why do you "healthier" men hurl insults at me for writing about the French Disease <note>original: "Lue Gallicâ." Syphilis, which was a new and terrifying epidemic in Paracelsus's time.</note>, babbling that I know nothing else? Is it truly a slight or contemptible thing if someone describes a massive, most malignant, and most widely dispersed disease, about which no one has commented before? I had hoped that honor would rather be conferred upon me for this work. Although, I have never greatly desired to be praised by you; for I would only be praised by impostors, whose "praise" should be repaid with the cross.

When I wrote about curing pustules, I simultaneously included Emperors, Popes, Kings, Princes, Nobles, Citizens, peasants, men, women, the young, and the old—things both credible and incredible—so that everyone might see and recognize from this the immense mysteries of nature and the stupendous secrets that God has mercifully imparted to us. Now, if I have attained this gift without help, so that God may be glorified in His works (not mine); and if I have sought out the art from Saracens, Turks, Barbarians, Tartars, Germans, and Italians: then you cry out that I am unworthy of the name of Physician because I can cure nothing other than the "Venereal itch." Yet, in that very writing, I show that with all your arts and sciences, you are nothing but pure fools and impostors. For I do not include merely one disease in my method, but whatever exists that is morbid. If, therefore, I encompass all diseases within surgery, excluding none: is that nothing to you? How great an incivility is this—or shall I say malice—that when you see your "Freshman-nonsense" <note>original: "Beanismum." Referring to the 'Beania,' the often-cruel initiation rituals for new university students (beani). Paracelsus uses it to mock the immaturity of academic medicine.</note> is approved neither by Theologians, nor Jurists, nor Linguists, nor Poets, nor any profession, you still do not judge yourselves more accurately within, but persist more stubbornly in piling up your disgrace? But truly, the swamp of your shames will finally be poured out if I am to bring to light those things of which you do not yet dream. For I will not only lash your wickedness there, but I will also twist with a serious censure those new and lying Physicians who will eventually be born. For they will exercise themselves busily in those intricate follies.

However these things may be, above all beware of those listeners whom I left at Basel, who "picked the feathers from my coat" <note>An idiom for stealing someone's ideas or status.</note>, who warmed my urines <note>i.e., acted as medical assistants or servants.</note>, and who smiled at me and flattered and fawned, just as little dogs do for their master. For these are and will be the greatest scoundrels of all, far superior to all impostors and novice physicians. I want you all warned, therefore, to beware of their poison. What they have from me, they use to build glory for themselves if it succeeds. But they deserted the school with too premature a flight; and like a thief, who snatches himself away from the house early in the morning...

<margin>Theophrastus called "Luther" and "Cacophrastus" by his adversaries.</margin>
You are of the brood of vipers, and you do not hide your venom. Wherever you can, you pour it out without delay. Therefore, out of the nature of the Leviathan <note>A biblical sea monster representing chaos or the devil; Paracelsus suggests his enemies possess a monstrous, primordial hatred.</note>, you hate me. Since you had no other ready defense to evade me, you made a "Luther" out of me. Hey you! I am not Luther; I am Theophrastus, whom you called *Cacophrastus* <note>original: "Cacophrastum." A derogatory pun on his name: while "Theophrastus" means "divine-speaker," "Cacophrastus" means "foul-speaker."</note> in Basel, as the doctors of Nuremberg and Frankfurt are accustomed to do. Do you truly think I am merely a Luther? Besides the fact that I am otherwise a Christian, I live privately endowed with an office far heavier and more sublime than an Apostle (that is, I am instructed in Medicine, Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy): am I not more than Luther himself? Indeed, I will make trouble for both him and you. I am not unaware that I leave Luther to his own affairs. I, in turn, will defend my own. For he shall not loosen even the smallest strap of my shoes <note>Paracelsus reverses the words of John the Baptist regarding Jesus (Matthew 3:11) to assert that his own medical-spiritual mission is distinct from and, in his view, more complex than Luther’s religious reformation.</note>. Why do you do this? Clearly, you hope that Luther will be burned. Therefore, you are convinced that the same fate awaits Theophrastus. In this, you have especially betrayed your own simplicity, because you do not know by what fate Theophrastus is to pass away, or for what he is predestined: certainly not for the fire, nor for your will and demand, but he shall die that death which he himself has chosen.

<margin>Theophrastus is more than Luther.</margin>
<margin>By what death Theophrastus will die.</margin>
By this fate Theophrastus shall fall. For blessed are those who choose their own death. Shame is quite necessary for you, because you call me a "Luther," whom the greatest and most numerous villains are hostile toward. So you are toward me. But by introducing that new title, you wished to greet me as a joke. However, the end will testify to this much more certainly than you now hope. It is entirely within my right to pluck at you, to shake you up, and to tear you apart with mockery. For I am safer from you than you—who know nothing—think. I am safe from you, who have experienced nothing as of yet, and are scarcely worthy to sit with the dogs. If Milan were as secure from its enemies as I am from you, it certainly would have no need of Swiss mercenaries or other drafted soldiers. For you are not Astronomers or Philosophers, but triflers; your faculty is no more suited to you than the law is to a brawler, whose entire case is rotten and fragile, and which he seeks to defend only with chatter and hateful noise. You strive for the same in defending your own views. You wish to defend your "cadaver" <note>likely referring to the "dead" anatomical and textual knowledge of traditional medicine</note> with tireless energy, but it smells far too widely of yourselves. Christ truly points his finger at you when he said of the Pharisees: *You decorate the tombs of the dead.* For all your grooming and finery is worth nothing. However much you present yourselves as subtle, eloquent, refined, and polished, the Villain within cannot be so hidden that he does not betray himself by his exhaled stench. I have indeed called you the "apprentices" of the pharmacists. This is the truth. For just as apprentices ask, "Sir, what is this, and what is its name?"—following their example, you also say, "I ask you, is that true? I have read much about this, but by God, I did not know it." Thus your very questioning betrays you as apprentices (*with all due respect to your honor, Lord Doctors*). And if the <term>perfumer</term> <note>original: "seplasiarius," a seller of ointments and perfumes, often used dismissively for a simple druggist.</note> asks again: "Excellent Lord Doctor, do you not know this?" then you, Lord Doctor, reply, "By God, I do not know." This is the truth, by God. Thus you are publicly polished and painted buffoons and fools. Does it not bring shame upon you if the perfumer—who is a <term>newbie</term> <note>original: "beanus," medieval university slang for a raw, uninitiated student.</note> and a "horned" one, indeed nothing at all—is forced to inform and teach you, the Lord Doctors? Is he not an unskilled apprentice who does not know or grasp the very thing he carries in his hands? Judge yourselves.

But because I do not earn my living by public contract in the courts of Princes and cities as they do, more care falls upon me. For they are hired as buffoons and "heaters" <note>original: "calefactores," literally "warmers," likely referring to lackeys or low-level servants who kept the rooms warm.</note>. Such also are the sworn Masters of Surgery of Nuremberg, who (by divine grace) are reckoned to be four in number. Indeed, they are buffoons hired for a salary, those impostors whom I pray you diligently avoid. For they thrust their impostures upon men by force, in which matter they use the promotion and protection of Princes, regions, and cities. It is truly the "ornament" of a city if it nourishes four sworn impostors, who bind themselves by a solemn vow to do nothing other than commit frauds and impostures. In the same way, the Lord Doctors are bound by an oath to commit similar frauds: that they will inspect urines for their own profit, as much as they have learned in the Universities. How wicked is that simplicity of the Magistrate, that he should bind these men to an oath, whom nevertheless...

<header>VOLUME II.</header>

Has it not been well discovered that they are unable to hold fast to their oaths? For no one ought to be bound or obligated by an oath on account of his art. Furthermore, since these same men do not yet know what art is, how, I ask, will they give a sworn vow to the noble practice of art? How will they testify under the faith of an oath what is best? For neither the senate nor princes know what is best in medicine. What, then, should he swear, who immediately swears that poison and gall are the best things? For he does not understand these things, yet you meanwhile bind him with an oath. Judge rather their art and their doctrine, and do not so readily impose an oath on every fool. For they are accustomed to carrying oaths just as donkeys carry sacks. Is it not truly to be rebuked in the Magistrate that, even if they see indeed that their <term>city physicians</term><note>original: "poliatros," referring to state-appointed medical officers</note> are altogether unskilled in <term>judging by urine</term><note>original: "lotio iudicando." Uroscopy, or diagnosing disease by examining urine, was a standard but often abused practice in medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note>, they nevertheless strictly urge them to administer this province skillfully by imposing an oath? And although they know better even with their own fingers that they make many more people crippled and killed by their remedies than they make healthy or rescue, they still force them to swear that they wish to administer their office faithfully and without fraud. Is this truly a well-considered plan? With a similar oath you also burden the hospitals, and you flay wretched men with your robberies. Who can truly bind himself by a vow to diligently execute that which he does not know? Meanwhile, under this pretext, whatever fraud or wrongdoing is committed is entirely excused by the sworn oath, and everything is settled as having been done well:

> *For our Lords hired them for this purpose.*

What kind of absurd oath is this? Certainly, it is no light matter that you apply such an ungenerous deception to the sick—the poor and the rich, the noble and the commoner alike—under the pretext of an oath, so that they think those things are <note>original: "mera Euangelia." Literally "pure Gospels," used here to mean absolute, unquestionable truths.</note> pure truth which you attest to with your oath. Therefore, abolish this corrupt custom; and see to it that no one among the simpler folk is henceforth tripped up by their sworn oath or your public commission. Knock on your consciences, O nobles and magistrates, and value the honest trust of the simple common people, who can do nothing more than believe that those who are commissioned administer everything as rightly as possible. Reflect that no one can swear regarding Medicine; and here your own simplicity is all too manifest. Beware of a false oath and a deceptive commission. Spare the simpler folk and save your consciences, paying no heed to friendships, or favor, or flattery, and so on; nor should you decree an oath so lightly. Weigh instead how great a danger is perjury, and how great a stain it is to testify about a matter that is not understood. As if indeed it were enough to say: "He did well, for he gave an oath to my Lords," and so on. Woe to you swearers! But the Magistrate will by no means blame me for this warning; rather, he will accept it with a grateful heart because I demonstrate what he has not yet understood until now. And so he will not be slow to take care that the simpler folk are not henceforth deceived by these impostures; and he will finally take up a serious thought about suppressing that levity which has its foundation in the useless conscience of lying Doctors and their cursed and <note>original: "meretriciáque," literally "prostituting" or "whorish," implying they sell their services dishonestly.</note> harlot-like medicine. Having received an annual salary, they would swear without hesitation that everything in general is true and right, which they nevertheless know to be the most false and foul of all things. And henceforth, do not impose an oath on all these men; rather, in such a difficult matter, have a distinction of persons. For these men are like hucksters in the marketplace. But they will finally be forced to run the race for the prize with me. And as far as I am concerned, I will see to it that they either finally abandon their ointments, fumigations, <term>wood</term><note>original: "lignum," referring to Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," then a popular but often ineffective treatment for the "French Disease" (syphilis).</note>, washes, incisions, cauteries, and so on, or perish miserably along with them. But if they contend altogether for the preservation of their ointments: come then, let them be anointed themselves, so that the doctrine and the labor may be turned back upon their own heads. For they always and assiduously repeat that those ointments hurt no one, and that the sick man is safe from danger. If they therefore experience them themselves, then at last they will feel what burdens they have placed on the backs of the sick. They accuse me of being their Heretic, their Luther, and so on. If you are just, come forward. For I will not cease to provoke you until I have dragged you "shadow-dwellers" into the light. You will be forced to leap this leap with me even against your will. Am I not enough of a *Cacophrastus* <note>original: "Cacophrastus." A derogatory pun on his name: "Theophrastus" means "divine-speaker," while "Cacophrastus" means "foul-speaker."</note> for you? I would surely have committed perjury if the strap of my shoe were not more learned and skilled than all your teachers—Galen, Avicenna, and so on—and even all the

Universities. If you do not believe this, place both methods of care upon a scale, and you will see soon enough which one carries more weight. Indeed, what skill is there in those useless Doctors of yours? Or what honor do you bring to your teachers? Truly, I will soon bring about that hour when dogs shall urinate on you, and boys shall chase you through the streets, repeatedly crying out, "Fools, fools!" Furthermore, I will see to it that you are finally forced to give a serious account of your crimes and robberies.

Does your <term>Cacophrastus</term><note>original: "Cacophrastus." This is a derogatory play on Paracelsus’s name, Theophrastus. By replacing "Theo" (God) with "Caco" (bad/evil), his enemies mocked him; here, he throws the insult back at them.</note> please you here? I have begun this business under good omens, and I have begun it in such a way that it shall have no end. Your business, however, will neither stand firm nor last to the finish. Indeed, the <term>torture-strings</term><note>original: "fidiculæ," referring to chords used for torture or tight binding, here metaphorically suggesting the doctors will be caught in their own traps.</note> will be so exquisitely tightened upon you that eventually, you yourselves—along with your books, injunctions, fumigations, wood-cures, and waters—will be left hanging in the empty air as a spectacle for all to see.

Do not boast that you have Father Galen, Avicenna, and others acting on your behalf. Do not brag that your custom has been handed down for long ages, and will therefore flourish and remain vigorous far into the future—provided that, in the meantime, no one allows himself to be provoked by Theophrastus, whose sect you claim will utterly perish when yours prevails. 

On the contrary, I proclaim to you that heaven itself is now the Physician, by whom your obsolete custom will be exterminated. The true and genuine arts, such as Philosophy, Astronomy, and <term>Alchemy</term><note>original: "Alchimia." In Paracelsus's view, alchemy was not just about turning lead to gold, but about the chemical preparation of medicines.</note>, will be sought out and brought forth. From the <term>Magi and Cabalists</term><note>original: "Magis Gabaliſque." These were practitioners of esoteric and mystical traditions whom the academic doctors viewed with contempt (as a "deluge" or source of mockery).</note>, the truth shall be dragged out into the sunlight. Together with you, your absurdities shall be poured out and drowned in <term>Pilate’s Lake</term><note>original: "lacum Pilati." A lake on Mount Pilatus in Switzerland, which local legend claimed was the home of Pontius Pilate’s ghost and a place of storms and spirits.</note>, so that neither the Sun nor the Moon nor any other star may ever look upon them again; they shall be cast into a place where even the earth itself cannot receive them. Where then will your custom be? Where will your mistress, "Lady Teacher," receive her kitchen-profit? Upon the Cross, surely, where many more of this genuine sort are gathered. O, woe to you, Lady Teacher!

How gladly you would thrust back upon me what I so often charge you with—saying that I myself lose no fewer patients than you do! Not at all; by no means. Rather, those whom you have ruined, I undertake to restore. If success does not follow as hoped, the fault is yours, for you have plunged the patient so deep that he cannot be healed. For how can that which is near death be restored by nature? Yet how often have you struggled to pin this guilt of yours on me? Thus it is always on your lips: "Even Theophrastus himself cannot restore this one or that one." 

Our thanks to you, Lord Doctors, who have so disgracefully ruined the wretched patient through your ointments, fumigations, blisterings, cuttings, burnings, washings, and bindings! For who could extract such a mass of <term>mercury</term><note>original: "hydrargyri." Paracelsus was a famous critic of the excessive use of quicksilver (mercury) treatments for syphilis, which often led to poisoning.</note> as you stuff into them with your salves and vapors? This man was greased six times, that one ten times, another twenty; this one was steamed so many times, that one washed; to another, the <term>wood cure</term><note>original: "cura ligni." A common 16th-century treatment for syphilis using a decoction of Guaiacum wood (Holy Wood) from the Americas.</note> was applied. You have forced one pound of mercury into this man, two pounds into another, and four into a third. Who, I ask, can fix all your outrages? And yet it is a consolation to you that you can say, "Ho ho, even Theophrastus does not know how to cure the patient." 

Who could wash away that pollution and stain of yours except the Executioner? He is the one who ought to fumigate and grease you. How pleasing would it be to you if you realized your outrages and crimes were being attributed to me? But thus you betray your own evil. Since I have come to know that you act as nothing but "Greaser-Doctors" and "Wood-Doctors," why, I ask, should I fear you? It is certain to me that without your "wood," neither you Doctors nor all your Academies could ever accomplish anything. For whatever you may learn, study, or read, in the end, that single piece of wood is your final refuge. 

Does your Reverence need so much time to learn about a piece of wood? When will you move on to pustules? To birdlime? To barks? It has been fifteen years and more that you have sweated over learning about "the wood." What will be the end of this study? And yet, in the meantime, you haven't grasped even a single scrap of usefulness. When will your autumn come, so that your fruits may ripen? 

Fie! That you do not blush at such a disgrace—that even craftsmen and all the peasants now know that without the help of the "wood," you are all completely foolish. Woe to your art! For if this is what you learn in the Universities, then surely the elementary schools are much better than they. Yet your nature matches the wit of goats: they gnaw at the tops and also climb... <meta>Catchword: "scandunt" (climb)</meta>

<summary>In this fiery polemic, Paracelsus mocks the academic physicians of his day, accusing them of incompetence and of poisoning patients with excessive mercury and ineffective "wood cures." He predicts a future where traditional medical authorities like Galen and Avicenna are replaced by a new medicine based on alchemy, astronomy, and the observation of nature.</summary>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>VOLUME II</header>

The higher they climb, the more "learned" their brains become. They think the lowest things are poison, and they do not realize that the upper leaves flourish no more than the lower ones. For why should a higher leaf be tastier or better than a lower one? It is nothing. Why then are the higher schools better than the lower ones? It is nothing. You can learn frauds anywhere, but integrity is found only in the lowest schools. In the higher schools, only the powerful sit, for whom the truth is a source of shame and a cause for blushing. The lower schools, however, embrace the truth itself more greedily. So you, **Master Doctor Rattler**<note>original: "Doctor Crepitator." A mocking nickname derived from "crepitus" (a rattle or a fart), suggesting the doctor is full of hot air or empty noise.</note>, what are you doing up there in the heights? No doubt you are catching spiderwebs with which to seal your art.

If you "Wooden" Doctors<note>original: "Doctores Lignarii." This refers to physicians who specialized in the "wood-cure" (using Guaiacum wood), which Paracelsus frequently criticized as expensive and ineffective.</note> now grow in number in Tübingen, Heidelberg, Vienna, Leipzig, Ingolstadt, etc., it will certainly be permitted for me to joke and play along with you. For wood is hard, it is not easily split, nor is it suitable for making javelins. Yet a terrible thing can be aptly made from it on your behalf; but for the sick, **Lord, I have loved my soul**<note>original: "Dilexi Domine animam meam." This is a liturgical or biblical phrasing, used here to suggest Paracelsus’s concern for the spiritual and physical well-being of patients over the greed of doctors.</note>. Now, in truth, you ought to consider this seriously: do not make the wood terrible for yourselves, but rather for the sick. He who makes a **Consecration Feast**<note>original: "Encænia." Traditionally a festival for the dedication of a church, used here metaphorically for the celebrations doctors have at the expense of others.</note> for himself out of others is a fraud. The feasts should belong to the one to whom the temple belongs—namely the temple, not the peasants. So it is with the sick. Health, joy, and the **Jubilate**<note>original: "Iubilate," a song of praise or joy.</note> should belong to them, not to you. Yet you claim it for yourselves and enjoy "indulgences" in the manner of peasants, who carry indulgences away from the temple while reserving none for themselves. To be sure, the priest distributes the indulgences and neglects himself. In the same way, you ought to have imparted indulgences to the sick so that they might recover; yet on the contrary, they are forced to provide sacrifices for your kitchens, so that you dance while they weep. But let these things pass.

<margin>Theoph. (Theophrastus') doctrine rests on three things.</margin>
But to press my point, I add this: since there are exactly three things upon which I build my doctrine—namely **Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy**—I shall further treat these three and explain to you how I have them so confirmed and explored from the very foundation that I can in no way be moved or cast down from them. I will cling to this foundation with my teeth, and through it, I will bring you to such a state that you will wallow miserably like pigs in the mud. And since I bring forward entirely new inventions, having despised and rejected all sects, and establish a new **monarchy**<note>Paracelsus famously styled himself the "Monarch of Medicine" (Monarcha Medicorum), claiming a sovereign authority over the art of healing.</note>, I earnestly ask all readers not to pass judgment too hastily or thoughtlessly. Instead, let them diligently read through the volumes of my *Philosophy*, *Astronomy*, and *Alchemy*. Once these have been read and understood, I will explain to you those treatises of my books which you judge to be too difficult to understand: namely, the *Treatise on Wood*, the three books *On Impostures*, the first book of the *Hospital* consisting of four treatises, and the eight books *On the Cause and Origin of the French Disease*<note>original: "luis Gallicæ," referring to Syphilis.</note>. In these, since conflicting opinions must be declared, it will be altogether useful to describe the Physicians and how they are divided among themselves. Once this is done, I shall finish the book on the French disease and turn myself to explaining other illnesses, provided God is present with His help—He who hears the prayers of all crying out to Him, and who Himself created the Physician: not only his flesh, but also the healing to be performed through him, to whom He offers His grace. Indeed, He offers it to no one except the one who knocks and asks. Farewell. In **Beratzhausen**<note>The town in Bavaria where Paracelsus stayed in 1529–1530 and wrote some of his most important works.</note>.

<margin>Man consists of water, earth, and minerals.</margin>
Therefore, since the foundation of Medicine consists in Philosophy, we shall henceforth recognize it by making such a comparison. First, it must be known that man himself, no less than the outer globe, contains within himself **Water and Earth with minerals**, etc. It is clear, therefore,

<margin>Whence diseases are to be recognized.</margin>
that from this we must seek the knowledge of diseases, so that we can truly say: "this disease is **Arsenical**," or "that one is **Aluminous**<note>Aluminous: relating to alum, a mineral salt. Paracelsus classified diseases by their chemical/mineral nature rather than by humors.</note>."

<margin>The Humors are rebuked.</margin>
Since much weight is placed on the knowledge of the disease, just as much will be placed on the knowledge of its properties. As for the fact that it has been believed until now that the sick must be categorized—that is, made into **choleric**, **melancholic**, **phlegmatic**, and **sanguine** types—as if from the knowledge of these four there emerges a full understanding of all things arising from them: that is now a pure lie.

<margin>Who first asserted the Humors.</margin>
For this foundation is neither Physical nor Philosophical, but rather **fanatical**. No philosopher anywhere makes mention of these phantasms; instead, Physicians who have defected from the wisdom of nature introduced these errors. Lest more acute professors see their insanity, they devised those four **humors** and withdrew from Philosophy, just as a dog-killer...

He argues that man is a microcosm containing the same minerals as the earth, and diseases should be identified by their chemical nature (e.g., Arsenical) rather than by phlegm or bile.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from a satirical critique of medical titles to a fundamental attack on the natural philosophy taught in universities. Paracelsus argues that the entire theoretical basis of medicine—rooted in Aristotle and the medieval scholastics—is flawed because it misunderstands the origin and "generation" of natural elements.</meta>

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>MEDICAL FRAGMENTS.</header>

# MEDICAL FRAGMENTS.

-> dog-killer by the citizens <- <note>original: "canicida à ciuibus." This likely refers to a derogatory nickname given to Paracelsus or his followers, or an anecdote regarding his reputation among urbanites.</note>

<margin>What philosophy teaches.</margin>
Since, therefore, a genuine Philosophy is to be set forth here, it must be presented in such a way that it treats the origin and causes of all natural things. If philosophy does not turn within this scope, it is entirely futile and empty. Now, the ancient philosophers handed down many things which were considered entirely philosophical, even if they smelled of nothing less than true Philosophy. Therefore, their philosophy, along with the errors that followed from it, must be examined first, before we give a beginning to our own Philosophy.

<margin>The nature of the philosophy of the ancients.</margin>
A philosopher is born in two ways: one from heaven, the other from the earth. That is, from the sphere of the Firmament (by which he understands Air and Fire) and from the Globe of the earth (by which he understands earth and water). He ought, therefore, to be skilled in describing the nature of both. And yet there is only one Philosophy; however, one person is a Philosopher, the other an Astronomer.

<margin>What a Philosopher is and what an Astronomer is.</margin>
Let us give an example of this Philosophy. It treats two things. Those things which the earth gives are called minerals, under which are contained both minerals and fruits. Those things which heaven gives are contained under the effects of air and fire. From the Earth come minerals, metals, and fruits. From Heaven come the "chaos"—that is, rain and atmospheric impressions <note>The term "impressions" in 16th-century science referred to any atmospheric phenomenon like wind, rain, or lightning.</note>.

<margin>What the Earth gives. What Heaven produces.</margin>
Recognize a twofold Philosopher in each of these: one who considers the growth of a thing, and another who contemplates its nature. And yet both are one Philosopher, not two. This is done in the globe of the earth by one who knows the generation of minerals, metals, trees, etc., and then the nature of both. Likewise, the other knows regarding heaven what is generated in heaven—such as rain, hail, frost, etc.—and also what the stars impress, on one hand; and on the other hand, what the nature, condition, and property of these things may be. In this way, the Philosopher is made complete.

<margin>Philosophy is twofold.</margin>
<margin>Ancient philosophers are criticized.</margin>
Now, the ancient philosophers wrote indeed about the earth and water, and their natures; however, since they did not understand their generations, they omitted them. From this it can be gathered that they did not have a very great experience of nature. By this standard they wrote the *Book of Meteors* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Meteorologica," a standard university text on atmospheric and geological phenomena</note>, teaching the origin of rain and thunder, etc. But they forgot the nature of these things. From this, it becomes manifest that they did not understand those things upon which they commented.

***

<margin>Water is the cause of minerals.</margin>
First, they hallucinated in this: that they produced all minerals from the earth. This is false. For minerals are indeed in the earth, but they are from the water. Furthermore, they forgot the earth in the generation of grass and trees. So also they posited a false generation of rain, thunder, etc.; for they did not observe the knowledge of the four Elements as the mother <note>Paracelsus refers to the "mother" as the creative source or matrix from which things are generated.</note>.

<margin>In what ways the philosophy of the ancients is false.</margin>
Since, therefore, they were entangled in certain and evident errors, and all of Aristotle’s doctrine on minerals and whatever has been handed down about meteors appear false, it will also be necessary for whatever is built upon this foundation to collapse. Such is the doctrine of Aristotle, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, etc., who say that *a stone is not made from pure Earth* <note>original: "De Terrâ purâ non fiat lapis." Paracelsus is quoting a common scholastic axiom to show it is based on a misunderstanding of how elements combine.</note>.

Bear it with a calm mind when I say that those things are false. For all the things they published concerning natural matters are false. This is clear from considering their foundation. But if you ask me whether I truly wish to establish and introduce a new Philosophy? I answer that I do wish it; indeed, this is the one thing I am doing. I will enter into the struggle against the lie, and I will establish a new science of meteors with such clarity that these writings of Aristotle and his followers will henceforth find a place nowhere but in the pigsties. For all of them will be cast down from their throne, and you along with them. For even if you walk through the streets twice as solemn and magnificent, it will nevertheless be publicly trumpeted that all your Medicine and Philosophy is nothing other than veiled wickedness and a shadowy faculty, wickedly devised for deceiving men.

How much this will burn you, that I trample your Philosophy into the muck and mire! But you yourselves will be thrust down into the same wallow, and you will swim there with the pigs. Oh, how great a disgrace that will be! That "Master John" <note>original: "Magistrum Iohannem." A generic name used to represent a typical, unimaginative university academic.</note> has until now lectured to his audience in the Academies on Meteors, on Generations, on the Heaven and the World, etc.—and now it becomes publicly known that Master John is a fool, and has said nothing but mere trifles and lies? You should be ashamed, therefore, that you are about to betray your own disgrace in this way.

<summary>Paracelsus defines true philosophy as the study of the origin (generation) of all things and attacks the Aristotelian tradition for its scientific inaccuracies. He promises to replace their "false" university doctrines with a new, clear understanding of nature, effectively shaming the academic establishment.</summary>

He asserts that the traditional philosophy of Aristotle is a "wooden foundation" that causes the "house" of medicine to collapse, proposing instead a chemical and sympathetic understanding of disease.</meta>

<page-num>341</page-num>
<header>VOLUME II.</header>

<margin>Theophrastus's philosophy is not Aristotle's, etc.</margin>
So that you may be entirely persuaded, and know with certainty, that you cannot in any way do without this Philosophy—and that you have need of it even against your will—I shall next briefly explain what that Philosophy is, and what the Medicine is that rests upon it. Now, I consider Philosophy to be—not that of Aristotle, not that of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval authority on Aristotelian science.</note>, etc., whose Philosophy is nothing but a <margin>Aristotle's philosophy is a wooden foundation.</margin> wooden foundation; whatever is built upon it easily sinks and is suffocated. Their Philosophy is empty, for it has established its theory erroneously. Their Philosophy is empty because they treat minerals erroneously. Their Philosophy is empty because it teaches erroneously concerning the dross <note>original: "stercoribus." Literally "dung" or "excrement," here referring to the impure waste products of natural things.</note> of things. You have been built upon this Philosophy, and through it, you have become confused, foolish, and ignorant.

How can Medicine stand safely on such a fragile foundation? Or what does it help that you have learned to discourse so beautifully and at such length about things? What is your discourse other than babbling, similar to the trifles of shysters and lawyers who, standing before judges, seek to entangle and defend a wicked cause with a wicked and copious circuit of words? Your lot is the same. Your Medicine is bad; therefore, it must be disguised with the seductive charm of words. For unless Philosophy is the complete practice of Medicine, the whole thing is worth nothing.

<margin>What the true philosophy is.</margin>
But what is this practice? It is surely this: that which places all remedies into your hand. And this practice was entirely unknown to the ancients. In this way, Philosophy—which is the foundation of Medicine—ought to be understood.

<margin>Philosophy corresponds to the four complexions.</margin>
Philosophy corresponds to the four complexions <note>The "complexions" were traditionally the four temperaments (sanguine, choleric, etc.), but Paracelsus redefines them here as chemical signatures.</note>: namely, the disease of Arsenic, the disease of the Moon [Silver], the disease of Acorinus, etc. That is, whatever complexion the "wolf" <note>In alchemy, the "wolf" (lupus metallorum) often referred to antimony, which "devours" other metals.</note> possesses; it is said to be from "burnt choler" <note>Choler or yellow bile was one of the four humors; "burnt choler" was the traditional explanation for many skin diseases.</note>. This [traditional view] is nothing; rather, it is Arsenical Mercury from orpiment <note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>.

From this, you should learn to recognize diseases; the other method—based on choler—is a deception. This is my genuine Philosophy. Yours is not Philosophy, but a fantasy. Therefore, strive to become Physicians according to my Philosophy.

<margin>Esthiomenon, cancer, etc., are from Arsenic.</margin>
If you encounter an *esthiomenon* <term>eating sore<gloss>a gnawing or spreading ulcer, often gangrenous</gloss></term>, a cancer, etc., be persuaded that in that place arsenic lies hidden, which produces such a thing; just as with ulcers, that disease must be called "arsenical." For such is its nature. Why then is this Philosophical division established to inform every Physician? Clearly because if the name is established, its property is also established. If you already know arsenic in nature, you will also recognize it in the body. Thus you will also know the nature, property, essence, and origin of all waste products, truly and precisely.

<margin>Arsenic cures arsenic; poison cures poison.</margin>
Once these things are perceived, the cure is also immediately clear. For Arsenic cures Arsenic, Anthrax <note>A generic term for a burning, carbuncle-like sore.</note> cures Anthrax, just as poison cures poison. The scorpion demonstrates this in its kind, but the serpent does so much more evidently. The toad and the spider heal in a much more proven way. <margin>Why the nightingale is healed by a spider.</margin> Why does the nightingale recover by eating a spider? It is because she has "spider-like" diseases and a similar Anatomy <note>Paracelsus uses "Anatomy" to mean the inner chemical or essential structure of a thing, not just its physical parts.</note>. Therefore, one human also heals another; "mummy" heals a human—that is, it stops blood, etc.—because the same and similar Anatomy is present. Thus, Anatomy cures Anatomy. This is Philosophy.

<margin>Gold strengthens the heart.</margin>
Now, if you have recognized that arsenic is present, establish a cure for the "Anatomy of Arsenic" through Arsenic, just as Anatomy teaches you. Gold strengthens the heart and the vital forces for this reason: because in the Anatomy of the Waters, Gold is the Heart, and the Moon [Silver] is the Brain. <margin>Gold is the heart, the Moon is the brain.</margin> If you understand metals in this way, you will also understand Marcasites and Talcs. For the other members are called Marcasites, Talcs, Cachimae, Gems, Salts, etc. <note>These are various mineral and alchemical terms for what Paracelsus considers the "signatures" of different body parts in the mineral kingdom.</note>

This division produces the Physicist <note>The internal doctor or physician.</note>, the Surgeon, and the Medic; and both have one Theory and one cause to learn in their diseases, and they are separated only in practice, not in their foundation. Therefore, those who say that <margin>Theophrastus is wrongly called a surgeon.</margin> Theophrastus is a Surgeon and not a Physicist are lying. For he employs no more than one foundation in both, which is the aforementioned Philosophy. And I myself testify regarding him, that he is both Physicist and Surgeon at once, as has been said, and not as that "offspring of donkeys" brays—those who are ignorant of every medical foundation.

<margin>How philosophy should be explained.</margin>
Philosophy must be explained in such a way that the Physician grows out of it, and Philosophy grows out of the Physician. But look at how those men have grown until now: purely as Sophists and shadowy babblers—something you can by no means deny. For they prove by their own work that they are fools and have drunk in no knowledge of any art.

<margin>External things lead to internal ones.</margin>
Since, therefore, the division stands immovable according to the reason of what has been said...

<sig>Ff 3</sig>

He asserts that the true physician must understand the "Anatomy" (inner essence) of substances like arsenic and gold to treat corresponding ailments in the human body.</summary>

of the sphere, and thus of the man himself, so that external knowledge may give birth to internal knowledge. In what way, I ask, do you—according to your custom—divide and distribute bile <note>original: "choleram." One of the four humors in traditional Galenic medicine, which Paracelsus rejected.</note> and phlegm, and so on? Surely it is just as a dog-butcher carves up hides.

Now, furthermore, you shall learn that the very source from which a disease proceeds is the same source from which a similar "Anatomy" must be established; that is, Medicine follows this path. Now, how will you purge bile? From where do you take the "vapors" of bile—from the bitter apple <note>original: "colocynthide." A powerful and toxic purgative plant.</note>? That cannot be done. For that purges the excrement, not the disease. How, I ask, will you purge melancholy through "Melancholy"—that is, from Lapis Lazuli <note>original: "Lazulum." A blue stone used in medieval medicine to treat "black bile" or melancholy due to its color.</note>? "Welcome, my Lord!" <note>This is a sarcastic greeting to the academic doctors.</note> How is it established for you that Lapis Lazuli *is* melancholy? That is mere smoke and pure trifles, which you sell in your Academies.

One thing more: what kind of melancholy is an "eating sore" <note>original: "Esthiomena." From the Greek for "eroding" or "devouring," usually referring to gangrenous or cancerous ulcers.</note>? What kind of phlegm is in the gall? These are all worthless things, nothing but pure and simple wickedness.

->**Concerning the Philosophy from which the Physician is born**<-

Hold to this: it is necessary for a Philosopher to become great in this science—that is, he must be most skillful in nature, so that he knows the harmony of all things: what a thing is, how it comes to be, and if it is present, what its nature is, both internally and externally.

So that you may understand all these things more exactly, seek out my *Philosophy*. I shall teach you how "growth" should be understood by proposing an example. 

<margin>There are four types of growing things.</margin>
First, divide all growing things in the world into four parts. First are the minerals, which belong to Water. Second are the fruits, trees, and grasses; these belong to Earth. Third are Manna and *Tereniabin* <note>A Persian term for a type of medicinal manna or "honey-dew" found on plants.</note>, and these belong to Air. Fourth are rain, thunder, and frost; these belong to Fire. Thus, those four are divided into the four Elements, into four "Matrices" <note>original: "Matrices." Literally "wombs," used by Paracelsus to mean the source or environment that gives birth to specific substances.</note>, so that to each one its own peculiar growing thing is assigned.

<margin>Four types of diseases.</margin>
If, therefore, there are now four Mothers and four types of offspring, the body must similarly be divided into four types of disease: into metals, into fruits, into mannas, and finally into rain and snow. If you wish to know these accurately in a human being, you must take your knowledge from external things. For there, the growth, the matter, and the effect are displayed; afterward, their virtues—good, bad, and so on—emerge.

Now, if you grasp the divisions of diseases according to their "wombs" (and far be it from you to say
<margin>Bile and Phlegm</margin>
anything about bile, phlegm, and the like, for

---

those are mere lies), then you shall also recognize the types of offspring that each Element gives birth to. If you possess these, you will also know the names, the properties of the diseases, and the essences and natures of their origins. From this is also drawn the name of "Medical Distribution"—that is, the explanation of what the name signifies.

The division of diseases, therefore, must be established according to the "right sphere" <note>A reference to the celestial globe, suggesting that medical classification must align with the cosmic order.</note> and a legitimate knowledge of it.

If you have discovered these things in one Element, you will recognize the same in others: that is, in Earth, Fire, and Air. For just as you have Arsenic in the water, so you have the same also in the Earth (that is, "Persian Fire" <note>original: "Ignis Persicus." A historical term for various skin conditions, ranging from shingles to anthrax.</note>); so also in the Air (the Rainbow); and so in the Fire (that is, the conjunction of Mars).

<margin>Sicknesses are fourfold according to the individual Elements.</margin>
According to the four Elements, therefore, illnesses ought to be divided fourfold; namely, four types of Arsenics, four types of Talcs <note>original: "Talka." Referring to various translucent or foliated minerals.</note>, four types of *Cachimiæ* <note>A term for metallic ores or the "unripe" state of metals.</note>, four types of salts, and so on. Likewise, there are fourfold snows, fourfold hails, fourfold frosts, fourfold lightnings. Similarly, in the earth, there is a fourfold Melissa <note>Lemon balm.</note>, a fourfold Celandine, a fourfold Valerian, and a fourfold *Anthos* <note>The flower of rosemary.</note>. And this is the genuine division of Philosophy; in this way, it is applied to Medicine. Practice medicine according to this, not according to that rotten bile, phlegm, and the rest. Faugh! To the gallows with those Academies! Thus all your art is nothing but imposture and a lie, as your works sufficiently testify. And unless an entrance to high places were given to you through flattery, certainly your noses would be completely defiled with filth thrown upon them.

And how does this Philosophy taste to you? You shall admit it, even if the chains of your hearts crack; or you will endure having your ears publicly nailed to a fool's post—oh, what a sweet "honor" it will be to wear your academic hoods <note>original: "Epomidum." The shoulder-capes or hoods representing academic degree.</note> if they are dashed against your ears!

<margin>Nature's diligence in marking things.</margin>
This is truly a profound thing in the "Light of Nature": that nature marks its subject everywhere. Just as the heavens mark their fools <note>original: "moriones." Mentally disabled people or "natural fools," whom Paracelsus believed were marked by the stars.</note>, shattering their reason; so nature marks the son of man in his root and his malice, and so on. Nature inserts veins and lines into the hand (chiromancy <note>Palm reading.</note>), from which a man is known for what he is; she also imprints signs on the nose, and so on, and on all the members of the whole body. She always designates the internal man through external traces.

<margin>A bitter biting of the Doctors.</margin>
In the same way, she also treats you "hood-wearers" <note>original: "cuculligeros." A derogatory term for the traditional university doctors who wore hoods.</note>. For since fools...

<summary>Paracelsus rejects the four humors of traditional medicine, proposing instead that diseases be classified by the four elements (Water, Earth, Air, Fire) and their "signatures" or external signs. He argues that the internal state of a human being is mirrored in the natural world and visible through physical markers created by nature.</summary>
<keywords>elements, signatures, anatomy, pathology, academic critique, four humors, macrocosm, microcosm, medical botany, chiromancy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s polemic against the medical establishment of his day. Having previously criticized their reliance on ancient "authorities," he now mocks their academic attire (the doctoral hood) as a sign of their folly and introduces the necessity of Alchemy and Astronomy in true medical practice.</meta>

<page-num>343</page-num>
<header>VOLUME II.</header>

...you act like fools <note>original: "moriones." Paracelsus frequently uses this term to mock his academic rivals.</note>, nature has marked you by adding hoods <note>original: "cucullis." The academic or monastic hood, which Paracelsus interprets here as a fool's cap bestowed by nature.</note>, from which you would no doubt otherwise abstain. Nature is far more powerful than you. And since you no longer lie in your mother's womb—that is, you have already escaped nature's formation—she now distinguishes you by adding those hoods. She does this by right, for she considers it your dominant trait: from this, the fool proceeds. Thus must the explanation of your doctoral hood <note>original: "Epomidis." A Greek term for the shoulder-cape or hood worn by academics as a sign of their degree.</note> be brought to light.

<margin>What the power of Magic is.</margin>
For you ought to know that Magic can prefigure its own man, and indicates his form, fate, studies, and so on, by his dress. For this reason, that same magic has also imposed upon you the doctoral hood, which is your firmament and prognosis. Thus, you are to be defined by me magically by your hood, since otherwise I am proclaimed a "magician" everywhere by you.

And regarding these things said so far, I would wish Philosophy to be proposed to you as a foundation, so that you may know that you can nowhere—except by my own Theory or Physics—overthrow or overturn anything with your little staffs <note>original: "bacillis." Likely a reference to the academic scepters or staffs of office.</note>. From this you may learn whether I am a Philosopher or a Surgeon, or whether I am either of these separately, or both, since we are divided in the practice of Philosophy and Surgery. Now, realize who I am, O hooded fools.

The third and last part is Alchemy, in which the Physician must singularly excel. For if he does not take his preparation from this, his practice is worth nothing. For herein lies the entire art of preparation.

<margin>What Alchemy is.</margin>
Moreover, Alchemy is the art that teaches how to separate the "stars" <note>original: "astra." In Paracelsian thought, these are the celestial, spiritual virtues or "inner stars" within physical substances.</note> from bodies, so that those stars may subsequently obey the stars and the Firmament in their direction. For direction is not in the physical bodies, but only in the Firmament.

From which it now follows that everything the brain produces is assigned to it by the course of the Moon; what the spleen produces, Saturn attracts to it; what the heart produces, the Sun. And in this way, the external Firmaments are the directors of the internal ones. Therefore, those who say that Lemon Balm <note>original: "Melissam."</note> benefits the womb, or Sage <note>original: "saluiam."</note> the brain, speak incorrectly. For unless Venus and the Moon ordain them to those places, they will fall into the stomach and pass out through the intestines.

<margin>Medicine does nothing unless directed by heaven.</margin>
Therefore, that which does not work in Medicine is not directed by heaven: that is, the course of heaven is absent; therefore, it effects nothing. Thus, every part has its director from the Stars, and they are called "Stars."

<margin>Heaven directs only the secret essence, not the body.</margin>
Furthermore, heaven directs nothing except what has been separated from the body; that is, heaven directs only the secret essence <term>arcanum<note>The "arcanum" is the potent, spiritual kernel of a medicine, stripped of its physical "husk" through alchemical processes.</note></term>, not the physical body itself. Just as it directs reason for a man, and afterward reason directs the body, so heaven directs medicines. If they lie in the stomach, they are "cooked" in it, and then it directs one thing—that is, the Arcanum.

<margin>The stomach is an alchemist.</margin>
Now, truly, the stomach is an Alchemist; that is, it performs the office of Alchemy. However, it is done with much greater benefit externally, before the substance falls into the stomach. For then the operation will be much more powerful. Unless that is done, it will be like raw meat, which the stomach digests much more exquisitely if it is ingested already cooked. If, therefore, the stomach burns with the desire to prepare the bodies of foods, this will be much more true regarding the preparation of Medicine.

<margin>Whether Alchemy prepares gold.</margin>
Many have despised Alchemy because it vainly attempts the making of gold and silver. But to define this more at length is not our purpose in this place. I have decided to treat at least the preparation—specifically how much power and efficacy there is in Medicine that lacks a physical body. He, therefore, who despises Alchemy even in this regard, despises what he does not understand. Although I know well enough that not even in this way are the apothecaries, barbers, and bath-keepers <note>Paracelsus grouped these lower-tier medical practitioners together, often criticizing them alongside university doctors.</note> abandoned by their "concoctions." Yet even if you place twice as much faith and hope in those medicines of yours, the heap of your recipes sufficiently indicates that you are mere fools. For it is plain enough whom you heal, and how, and where, and when.
<margin>To what extent the author treats Alchemy here.</margin>

<margin>Alchemy is the pillar of Medicine.</margin>
Since, therefore, I have finally resolved to teach concerning Alchemy, because it is itself the foundation and pillar of Medicine, it must be known here that no one can be a Physician without this art. For he who lacks it relates to a Physician as a common cook relates to a prince's cook. Nature, therefore, entirely requires Alchemy, and wants it to be understood by the Physician, and that he be skilled and knowledgeable in it—not merely serving up the same "warmed-over cabbage" <note>original: "cramben recoquere." A Latin idiom (from Juvenal) for repeating a tired, old argument or dish until it is sickening.</note> over and over.
<margin>Alchemy is necessary for the physician.</margin>

Since these things are required of a Physician, it is also required of him that he know what Calcination is, and what power it has. Likewise, etc.

<margin>What Calcination, Sublimation, Reverberation, and Dissolution are.</margin>
Now, truly, the power in calcining is such that the Alkali <note>In early chemistry, "alkali" referred to the ashes or salts left after burning (calcination).</note> comes forth, and its virtues; likewise, in sublimating, the volatile Alkali; likewise, in reverberating, the color of the Alkali; in dissol... <note>original: "dissol-" Catchword for the next page is "uendo," completing "dissoluendo" (in dissolving).</note>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires Alchemy to extract the spiritual "stars" or essences (arcana) from physical substances. He asserts that the human stomach acts as an internal alchemist, but argues that external alchemical preparation makes medicine far more potent.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Arcanum, Astronomy, Calcination, Iatrochemistry, Medical Education, Stomach, Macrocosm and Microcosm</keywords>

->MEDICAL FRAGMENTS<-

...using internal Alkali. Since the virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent healing powers or "active principles" of a substance.</note> lie within these, who would not seek the most subtle forms of them?

Judge now, finally, how much these things differ from the apothecaries and their preparations, and from the powers and virtues of those preparations, etc. The rest is missing. Let the deficiency be filled from what has gone before.

---

## ->Certain other papers follow, pertaining to the *Paragranum*<- <note>The *Paragranum* is one of Paracelsus’s most famous works, where he defines the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note>

<margin>The French Disease is a most evident evil.</margin>
**I** first proposed to write about the French Disease <note>original: "Lue Gallica." A common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note> because this sickness is most frequent among princes, nobles, the poor, and the rich throughout Germany, Italy, France, Spain, England, Denmark, Hungary, and so on. For a just cause, therefore, I have undertaken its description—even though you falsely claim that I know nothing else. I can do this, and I can do more, so that dogs shall urinate on you, and all good men shall spit on you, and all the sick shall cry out against you as fools. I can do and know so much, I say, that through me the time will come when you will be forced to give an exact account of all your robberies in the destruction of the sick. And how does this little broth <note>original: "iusculum." A sarcastic metaphor for the medical theories he is feeding them.</note> taste to you?

You babble, of course, in your usual way: that I also destroy the sick. Not in the least! Those whom you have destroyed, I try to raise up again. Those whom you have so "flayed to the marrow" <note>original: "excarnificastis." Literally "to tear the flesh off," referring to the grueling medical treatments of the time.</note> through quicksilver <term>quicksilver<gloss>mercury, often used in toxic doses to treat syphilis</gloss></term>, through the wood <term>the wood<gloss>Guaiac wood, an expensive imported wood from the Americas used as a popular but often ineffective syphilis cure</gloss></term>, through cauteries, through bloodletting, etc., that it is impossible to restore them to their natural state: these you claim I have corrupted. But what kind of outrage is this, that you pin the destruction of the sick on me? If I wanted to, I could hardly corrupt them further, so thoroughly have they already been flayed by you to the very marrow. For your "cure" (as you call it) with the wood has destroyed all those patients about whom you spread your slanderous trifles. Some have already endured your poisonous ointments ten or fifteen times. Now calculate for yourselves how great this injury, how great this harm is. And who can ever expel all that quicksilver that sticks fast, deeply fixed in the marrow, the brain, and the stomach? You who manage the rudders of affairs, take heed of these things.

Furthermore, when you have "cured" them through smoke <note>fumigation treatments</note> five or six times, through the wood twenty times, through water ten times, etc., can you say with a clear conscience that I destroyed those whom you had already killed? In the meantime, because I do not restore to life those whom they themselves have handed over to death and have slaughtered, they persuade themselves that this will serve as a shield for their slander. Answer me truly: who, by the laws of nature, can anywhere make the dead live again? No one. Who can naturally bring dead limbs to life? No one. Therefore, neither can I. Tell me then, finally: whom have I destroyed? Whom have I killed? O you phantoms! <note>original: "Laruae." This refers to "masks" or "ghosts," suggesting the doctors are hollow or deceptive figures.</note>

Therefore, I will hereafter so manfully direct my vengeance and vindication against you children, that you will find it necessary either to withdraw from your impostures, or certainly to endure being urinated on by cats. I will see to it that you are either driven away by force from your ointments, fumigations, washes, and woods while following at my heels, or certainly that you are clothed in another tunic <note>A metaphor for being forced into a new role or state of disgrace.</note> against your will. Are you not ashamed of your own inconstancy? At first, for ten years, your art was nothing without ointments. Thus, whoever could apply an ointment was immediately elected into the number of doctors. These were succeeded by the fumigators; afterward the washers, etc. Today, he who knows how to use the wood is the only doctor. Unless the wood had been brought to us, I believe you would have remained total asses. And this is your "terrible" doctor—even though the wakeful patient already sings the song of the dead.

Things being as they are, it is necessary that Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy stand out and break through—not by sophistry, nor by empty chatter, but by "Yes, yes; No, no." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:37, advocating for plain truth over elaborate lies.</note> For many craftsmen boast of themselves who are mere phantoms. Many discuss the Elements and yet do not know how to speak of stones. You must press the fight more boldly and strongly if you wish to overthrow me. Otherwise, many arrows will be hurled by me into your breasts.

---

### ->Another Fragment<-

**I** have published several medical books on Pustules, namely three on Impostures, in which I have concealed many things for the sake of avoiding greater shame <note>Meaning he held back even harsher criticisms to be polite.</note>. In addition, I have published a "Hospital Book" <note>original: "Nosocomicum."</note> in four treatises, where I shared a singular explanation and treatment of this disease. Yet doctors, whose minds are held by no love of honesty, defend their cause in their usual way. Besides these, I have again sent out eight other books, where I professedly refute their errors and provide a way of curing...

<summary>Paracelsus launches a fierce attack on the medical establishment's ineffective and toxic treatments for syphilis, championing Alchemy and Astronomy as the true path forward. He accuses traditional doctors of "flaying" their patients with mercury and guaiac wood before blaming him for the patients' eventual deaths.</summary>

<page-num>345</page-num>
<header>VOLUME II.</header>

...I set forth the most convenient way.

Since, therefore, the necessity of writing about this subject has completely fallen upon me: I could certainly obtain nothing from the ancients that would serve as a support for the truth. Much less could I gather anything sound for this undertaking from their disciples. I was therefore forced (if I wished to reach the truth itself) to draw the foundation of doctrine from Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy.

When I proposed these three for consideration: this reasoning, appearing least acceptable to the rest of the Physicians, compelled them to cry out against it, just as the Jews cried out against Christ, *Away with him, away with him* <note>original: "Apage, apage." This is a biblical reference to the crowd's rejection of Jesus.</note>. However, I thought nothing else of it but that these Physicians follow their own custom; no one should doubt that they belong to the order of shouters.

Now truly, I ask, who anywhere can become and be a Physician without the three aforementioned professions? No one. Therefore, among them, there is no Physician. If they bear the name, a scoundrel <note>original: "Nequam"</note> is certainly hidden beneath it. For no Physician is present. He who is present is a Physician's corpse, which they feign and lie about by throwing on a robe and spreading a hood <term>Epomide</term> <note>An *epomis* was a decorative academic shoulder-cape or hood worn by doctors of the era to signify status.</note> over it.

<margin>What Philosophy is.</margin>
Who among you, I ask, is there who can know and describe the nature of earthly things without Philosophy? No one. What is Philosophy? The mistress of knowing what grows from the Earth and Water, and what the nature and virtue of each is. And likewise,
<margin>Who a Philosopher is.</margin>
he is also a Philosopher who has the course of man known and explored. The first is a Philosopher [of the macrocosm]: just like the second [of the microcosm]. That one is of the Earth, this one of man. And yet, he is not yet a Physician.

<margin>Who an Astronomer is.</margin>
Furthermore, an Astronomer is he who knows the sky and the air according to their natures, operations, virtues, and efficacies. An Astronomer is also he who knows the air of man in his own firmament, even if he does not know the sky itself. Thus,
<margin>Two kinds of Astronomers.</margin>
there are two Astronomers: both, I say, are Astronomers: but not even yet is the Physician at hand.

Since, therefore, these four—namely double Philosophy and double Astronomy—do not constitute a Physician, and yet these are the things that consider man and search the sky, earth, air, and water: Who then, finally, will be the Physician?
<margin>Who the Physician is.</margin>
He, of course, is the Physician who knows how to heal the sick. If, therefore, he who knows how to heal the sick is a Physician: he must have a completely certain knowledge of his subject, around which he is occupied. What kind of Physicians are those who know nothing of these things, and yet want themselves to be proclaimed as Doctors and Masters? etc.

If, then, it belongs to the Physician to be able to heal: and the foundation must be taken from the four aforementioned things: with what shall he conclude? With Alchemy alone. <margin>What Alchemy is.</margin> What is Alchemy? The preparer of Medicine, which makes the remedy pure and exquisite, and offers it perfect and whole, by which the Physician's science is completed.

If medicine is now such, and the science of the Physician must be so arranged: how, I ask, do those square and knotty Doctors and Masters (saving their honor) dare to find fault with me for using not trifles, but the truth itself, to establish science more fundamentally and exquisitely? But they hold to their ancient ways, from which nothing good ever came.

Why do they pursue me with such Vatinian hatred <note>original: "Vatiniano odio." A classical term for an exceptionally fierce or visceral hatred, named after the Roman Publius Vatinius.</note> that through the bitterness of envy they call me Luther?
<margin>Theophrastus is called "Luther" by his adversaries.</margin>
I am *Theophrastus*: not *Luther*. *Luther* will defend his own; I will defend mine. For they do this not for the sake of increasing my honor, but to create envy. For you despise *Luther*, as if you were truly more learned than he. So if I am *Luther*, it follows that you exist as more learned than me too. How much shame should really suit you? For you hate me for this reason: because you are ignorant of things. Thus I also know no one who hates *Luther*, unless he is either a fanatic or has felt damage to his kitchen <note>A metaphor for one's livelihood or income.</note> caused by *Luther*. Thus I can also rightly say of you, that this is the cause of your hatred: because you are empty Astronomers, and worthless, useless Philosophers, and mere apprentices of Apothecaries in the art of preparation. Such Physicians you are! Why do I call you apprentices of Apothecaries? Because apprentices in the shops ask, "What is this?" So you also ask, "What is this, Master John?" "By God, I certainly do not know." You speak the truth. By God, therefore, you are a fool and a blockhead.

But what is this, that you boast so haughtily because you are hired and salaried Physicians: and you do not think in the meantime that even the heater for the kitchen, etc., is hired? What is it worth that either you yourselves say, or others say, that you are sworn Masters, Doctors, etc.

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "As if" (Quasi).</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus argues that a true physician must master Philosophy, Astronomy, and Alchemy to understand both the world and the human body, rejecting the empty titles of his academic rivals. He specifically addresses the insult of being called "the medical Luther," arguing that his enemies only hate him because his truths threaten their livelihoods.</summary>

It follows his argument that contemporary physicians are merely hollow shells of authority, lacking the essential pillars of philosophy, astronomy, and alchemy.</meta>

As if indeed, according to your own opinion, you were everything in this way.

What is such an oath other than perjury? Why do you swear? Since you are neither able to do nor know anything? Do you swear to practice your art innocently? But you are ignorant of all arts. Do you swear that you will devote your faithfulness? Yet meanwhile you torture patients worse than an executioner <note>original: "lictor"; an officer attending a Roman magistrate, often tasked with carrying out punishments.</note> himself. Do you swear that you will administer medicine rightly? But you are more twisted than <term>dodder</term> <note>original: "cuscuta"; a parasitic, leafless climbing plant known for its tangled, winding stems that choke other plants.</note>: that is, there is nothing right or just in you.

Princes, Magnates, and Cities, who support such Physicians, will not find fault with me for testifying frankly that they themselves do not understand these matters. For if they understood, they would drive you out with an oath, not entice you in. However, it displeases me greatly that they protect you, and being willing, they are blind despite having eyes. It ought to be the prudence and skill of those in power to know which Physicians are to be sifted and sent through the fire <note>A metaphor for rigorous testing or purification.</note>. Answer me, I pray: what profession anywhere has ever nourished more and more serious <term>scoundrels</term> <note>original: "nebulones"</note>, <term>stage-players</term> <note>original: "ludiones"</note>, impostors, and <term>charlatans</term> <note>original: "Agyrtas"; from the Greek for a wandering beggar or quack doctor.</note>? The founders are now sleeping, while you remain awake.

Moreover, the reckless contempt for those things in which all foundation is placed has violently extorted this writing from me. If I am wrong, why don't you overturn it? Why don't you vomit up the morsel? For I will not let you go as long as this skin of mine lasts. For I know myself to be more than sufficiently fortified by the fates against you and all your "Princes"—Avicenna, Galen, Aristotle, etc. <note>Paracelsus famously rejected the traditional authorities of ancient and medieval medicine.</note> And this bald and hairless crown of mine knows many more and loftier things than either your Avicenna or all the Universities. Come forth, and give a sign of what kind of men you are, and what strength you have. But what are you? Doctors and Masters, combing out lice and scratching your backsides.

# LIST OF THE BOOKS
## CONTAINED IN THE THIRD PART OF THE WORKS OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.

### I.

**O**^N *the powers of the organs <note>original: "viribus membrorum"; in Paracelsian medicine, "membra" often refers to the internal organs or functional parts of the body.</note>, in two books, together with a fragment on the preservation of the four elements in man. 1.*
**II.** *On the three primary essences <term>Tria Prima</term> <note>The "three primary essences" are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the basic building blocks of all matter in Paracelsus’s chemical philosophy.</note>. 11.*
**III.** *On the plague, that is, on the origin and generation of the plague, 18. and the prescribed accurate and genuine cure for this disease. 58. 71. 72.*
**IV.** *Diverse treatises on the plague and its symptoms <note>original: "accidentibus"; in a medical context, these are the secondary symptoms or complications arising from a primary disease.</note>. 80. 90. 109. 123. 130. 144.*
**V.** *Collected writings on the plague. 146.*
**VI.** *On diseases arising from <term>tartar</term> <note>Paracelsus used the term "tartar" to describe stony or gravel-like deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty deposits, comparing them to the crusty "tartar" left in wine barrels.</note>.*
**VII.** *Two books on diseases arising from tartar, with the author’s own explanations.*
   *In the first book’s treatise (1), the different types and locations of tartar are discussed: concerning external and internal tartar.*
   *In the second (II), on the origin of tartar in the stomach and belly; the intestines; the liver and the <term>mesentery</term> <note>original: "Meseraicis"; the membranes attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>.*
   *In the third (III), on the origin of tartar or stones in the kidneys and bladder; the various forms and signs of tartar.*
   *In the fourth (IV), on the origin of internal tartar and its signs: concerning the tartar of the joint-fluid <note>original: "synouia"; the lubricating fluid in the joints.</note>; on tartar arising from the corruption of seed and urine.*
   *In the fifth (V), a treatise on illnesses arising from unhardened <note>original: "non coagulatâ"</note> tartaric matter; on the diet for tartar.*

### THE SECOND BOOK.

**T***reatise I deals with the cure for tartaric illnesses in the belly: on the appetite <note>original: "orexi"</note>; compressions of the chest; on fevers of the stomach; on diseases of the intestines arising from tartar; on colic, intestinal blockage <note>original: "iliaca"</note>, and contractions.*
*Treatise II on the cure of diseases of the liver, namely on the obstructions <note>original: "oppilationibus"</note> formed in its region: on the plague; on medical crises; on pleurisy and <term>prunella</term> <note>A term often used for a severe sore throat or "thrush," likely characterized by a burning sensation.</note>; on the dropsy of the seven principal organs; on fevers of the liver.*
*Treatise III on ailments of the kidneys, such as the diabetic passion <note>original: "Diabetica passione"; an early term for diabetes, characterized by excessive thirst and urination.</note>; on the milk, curd, <note>original: "Nusto" - likely a specific Paracelsian term for a type of sediment</note> and serum of the kidneys; on fevers of the kidneys; and finally on <term>Usnea</term> <note>In this context, Usnea refers to the moss or lichen found growing on the skulls of the deceased, which was used as a medicinal ingredient.</note>, the stone, and "hailstones" <note>original: "Grandine"; a metaphor for small, hard stones in the bladder.</note> in the bladder.*

# THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM
<note>original: "Theophrastus Hohenheimensis"; the birth name of the famous physician, alchemist, and philosopher better known as Paracelsus.</note>

# ON THE POWERS OF THE ORGANS
<note>original: "De Viribus Membrorum"; in Paracelsian medicine, "membra" (organs/limbs) refers to the various functional parts or instruments of the body.</note>

BOOK I. On the powers of SPIRITUAL THINGS.
BOOK II. On the powers of INTERNAL THINGS.
BOOK III. On the powers of EXTERNAL THINGS.
