<header>ON THE PLAGUE</header>

->...animals are governed by two spheres: by the upper, which is Air and Fire, and by the lower, which is Water and Earth.<-

It has already been said concerning Animals that their life is governed by the heavens. How the heavens are, in turn, governed by the life of the animal is to be understood in the manner that will be described hereafter. Whatever lives has need of food. Whatever is eaten, moreover, must be cooked and digested. From this digestion comes the principle of Philosophy. If, however, these things are to be discussed medically: pay close attention to what I bring forth in this medical discourse on the subject. But before the nature of digestion is explained, for the sake of better information, attend to this brief chapter placed beforehand. For I am treating here of the plague, and of its cure.

<margin>The cure for plague is found in frogs, toads, fish, and birds. Plague remedies: 1. The Moray eel. 2. The Frog.</margin>
The cure for it is placed in frogs, in toads, in fish, and in birds. Therefore, let everyone show their spirit. The moray eel <note>original: "Muraena"</note> fish is a cure for the plague under the "wings" <note>An archaic term for the armpits, where plague buboes often appear.</note>, if it is bound there alive before the rising of the Sun; it draws out the poison of the plague. If, however, it is bound behind the ears, it exerts no power. The frog, of whatever kind or color it may be, if bound to the groin of men before the rising of the Sun, takes away the poison of the plague.

<margin>3. Sparrows.</margin>
Live sparrows, plucked of their feathers, if they are bound to the ears, armpits, or groins of men or women, will draw out all the poison, and they themselves will die. If you burn or bury these dead birds, you will certainly cure the plague. This remedy, however, is worth no more than for drawing back the poison that attacks the heart. Afterward, there is need for the plague-sore to be divided and dissipated by surgical processes and plasters: such as the **Oppodeltoch** <term>Oppodeltoch</term> <note>A famous medicinal plaster or liniment, often associated with Paracelsus, composed of various gums and resins.</note> made of four gums and resins, as is handed down in our practical manuals.

<margin>Oppodeltoch plaster.</margin>
These three animals, if applied in the aforesaid manner, preserve a person from deadly poison. Truly, what is greater or more excellent in the whole medical faculty than for him who claims the name of Doctor for himself to rightly understand for what reason these animals draw out poisons? For to know these things is the primary duty of Physicians.

<margin>Many medicines were discovered by the common people.</margin>
The reason is this. Many medicines were discovered by common people, whose names they still bear today, as is well known to Physicians. But such medicines in the hands of the ignorant <note>original: "idiotarum"</note> were no different than an excellent sword in the power and hand of a weakling. For he is unable to manage it: that is, the common folk apply one saddle to all horses. That which is meant for the ears should not be applied to other parts. That which regards the armpits should not be placed on the groin. Each thing must be administered in its proper place and manner. Therefore, such medicines are brought to us, as it were, by the hands of the common people. They are to be accepted by us like an excellent sword from a weakling. And just as a gladiator, if he has seized the sword, vibrates it with wondrous art and gesture, and turns it according to his every will: so it is right that the Physician, given the medicine, should be able to use it more dexterously than the commoner knows how. And in this way, Aristotle and Pliny, and others like them, described many experiments, but only historically, not medically.

<margin>The experiments of the ancients were written only historically, not medically.</margin>
For no trace of either Medicine or Philosophy is found in Pliny. Nevertheless, our doctors follow them, and they write down only the stories of remedies based on the reports of old women, nor do they pursue the very foundation of the matter. For a Physician skilled in Philosophy can, by easy scrutiny, investigate which creatures are destined by God for medicine, and which for food.

<margin>Certain things are both medicine and food at the same time.</margin>
For not all fish were given by God for food: but some of them are food and medicine at the same time, and some are medicine only: such as the moth against the poison of the "golden sickness" <note>Jaundice, or perhaps a yellowing associated with the plague.</note> in the plague; the eel against the colic occurring with the plague; the sparrow against the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>—these exist as both food and medicine.

<margin>The Art of Signatures.</margin>
And such things are taught by the **Art of Signatures** <term>Art of Signatures</term> <note>A philosophical system (Ars Signata) asserting that the physical appearance of natural objects reveals their medicinal purpose.</note> in any given thing. For this reason, the Cabala <note>Here referring to a form of natural mysticism or hidden knowledge of the properties of things.</note> ought to be learned by those who wish to be called and become physicians. For you have an example in earthly things as well. In the little herb *satyrion*, you see the testicles are "signed" <note>The tubers of the Satyrion orchid resemble testicles.</note>.

<margin>Satyrion strengthens intercourse.</margin>
Does it not contribute its power precisely to that member whose anatomy and signature it exhibits? For it is known how much it avails for strengthening intercourse, to say nothing of the remaining mysteries which are innate to this member for its aid and vigor.

<margin>The Water Lily expels the afterbirth.</margin>
In the same way, you see what similarity and affinity the **Water Lily** <note>original: "Nenuphar"</note> has with the navel and the womb in a woman, through its own signature. Now judge what medical power it provides in the expulsion of the afterbirth <note>original: "secundina"</note>, etc. I wanted to insert this chapter here so that if I happen to say more about the art of signatures hereafter, I may be more readily understood.

<margin>The frog is the medicine of the plague, as is the sapphire.</margin>
For why was the frog created, if not to be the medicine of the plague? For this reason, it carries its signature with it. For just as the plague is foul and abominable, so similarly is the frog. The anthrax and the carbuncle <note>Two types of painful, inflamed skin infections or boils characteristic of the plague.</note> are also of the genus of the plague. Thus the lizard is also a cure for drawing out poison, as is the sapphire. For this reason, the lizard also has the color of the anthrax boil.

For these twins seemed to Nature to be a sufficient medicine for wounds. Nor are they enough only for the healing of them: but they also provide protection and help against the **accidents** <term>accidents: medical complications or secondary symptoms that accompany the primary disease.</term> of wounds. But since this chapter—which we inserted for a fuller and easier understanding of the Philosophy of the generation of the plague—has thus far been led to its goal: I will now further approach to uncover and explain the foundation of the Philosophy itself.

<margin>What digestion is. What putrefaction is.</margin>
It was mentioned above concerning Animals, that they have need of food, for this reason surely: because they contain life within themselves. To this was also necessarily added that all food must be **digested** in the stomachs of animals. Now, **digestion is putrefaction**. Putrefaction is the change and alteration of foods into a substance different from the previous one. Attend here for a little while.

<margin>Fire and its own heat are within all things.</margin>
Whatever is eaten has a hidden fire stored within itself, through which the digestion and putrefaction of all things is perfected. You can judge this by the example taken from wine. For unless wine had such fire and heat naturally born within it, it could not exert and rouse such a thing in the stomachs of men. Let the same judgment be made concerning pepper and ginger, regarding which it is nevertheless certain that they contain an inherent heat. Let these be an example to you that those things are truly similar in other things also. For look at straw and heaps of dung. Even if dung is exposed to the most intense cold: yet its innate heat and fire rouse such a powerful smoke that that heat appears like fire. In the same way, if lime is poured over with water, it shows its fire, that is, **sulfur** <note>In the chemical theory of the time, "sulfur" was the principle of combustibility and internal heat.</note>. From these things it is now abundantly clear to you about what I might philosophize and discuss. Now therefore it is certain that it is necessary for living animals to eat. That eating happens in two ways. Observe distinctly and diligently how I would wish that to be understood.

<margin>The substance of the body constantly flows away.</margin>
Every living body loses something of its substance in every moment, and is as it were worn down, no differently than a cloak, which the longer it is worn, the more worn and torn it becomes daily, so that it must be repaired thereafter. In this way, to eat is nothing else than to repair the cloak of life—that is, the body—and through food, to replace what is worn away. I speak of the body of living animals. For this I call the "body." But I call the spirit "life." So truly I think: not only must the body be sustained by food, but much more the **spirit** itself.

<margin>The spirit is sustained by food.</margin>
For the spirit is diminished daily no less than the body in which the spirit or life dwells. Hence my foundation is established, by which I wanted you to understand that food is nothing else than a certain matter and body in which spirit and life dwell; it is administered through food, from which spirit and life are sustained. Thus for frogs, thus for fish, their own food is also offered in a twofold way: in the same way for all other living things, their sustenance and food is appropriate through digestion.

<margin>What food is.</margin>
That indeed which is "food" lies hidden and is within that which we eat. What we eat and break with our teeth, the peasant indeed calls food; but the **Doctor of medicine** calls "food" that which dwells within what we eat and remains in the body. For whatever things spring up are born from their own seed. Now, give your labor to this: weigh a certain seed, whether of grain or wheat; weigh moreover also the vessel in which the earth is put; finally, weigh the earth itself also. These things being done, cast the seed into that earth so that it may emerge and grow. At the appointed time, although the grain has indeed been made larger, yet meanwhile nothing has departed from the earth itself of its own weight. But why do I bring in this example? There is no other cause for this more broadly and deeply introduced Philosophy than that I want you to reach and grasp how, indeed, from invisible and insensible things, by easy work, a certain substance and sensible matter can be made, just as from seed and earth...

Examples of these things are especially visible during the time of a spreading **plague** <note>original: "pestis"</note> in pregnant women and certain men. For however many men dwell in the universal world, they can by no means deny what I testify here: although it is not for everyone to fully and perfectly understand and attain all things. For he to whom the gift of understanding is given, he enjoys it. But nevertheless, I shall comment on these things even more clearly and lucidly in my explanation of the **Apocalypse**. <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> Meanwhile, let such writings not fall into the hands of the unrefined masses. Later, a volume concerning the **soul and spirit of the world** shall also be given. As for that doctrine of how the **plague** <note>original: "pestis"</note> is generated and how it is cured: in delivering that, I shall pour myself out fully, nor shall I omit anything necessary.

<margin>
Heaven governs all things.
</margin>
**Heaven** <note>original: "Cœlum"; often used by Paracelsus to mean the celestial forces or the "Astra."</note> is the perfecter of its own instituted works, which it is accustomed to produce in a lawful series and order, failing in nothing, erring in nothing. Now, however, Heaven governs all things, both living and non-living, which neither any Doctors nor peasants can deny. Let us take an example from wood and earth or clay.

<margin>
Wood should not be cut during the new moon.
</margin>
If wood is not cut at its proper time—such as during the **new moon**, and especially if a **humid sign** <note>A zodiac sign associated with the element of Water, such as Cancer, Scorpio, or Pisces.</note> coincides with it—it is not durable at all. Likewise, any earth, if it is not dug up at the lawful time, begins to swarm with crickets and worms. But what else is earth or clay than a field for **seeds**? <note>original: "feminis," a variant of "seminis."</note> Meanwhile, wood is from a seed, which you will notice. If a field is turned at an unseasonable time, it gives birth to worms, insects, and poisons. But if it is turned at a favorable time, then it also turns its seed into pure, good, and healthful air. For what else is wood than a seed born from its own fruit? Now, if so much importance is placed on plucking the fruits of wood at the right time: how much more will Heaven be a field for the seed that is destined for it? Or if Heaven itself is not the field, it is nonetheless the preparer and the cook, the spirit and the shaper of every seed. The element of water, however, is the field. The imagination of man is the seed.

<margin>
Heaven is the field of its own seed, namely human Imagination.
</margin>
<margin>
Heaven and man daily fashion something new.
</margin>
Heaven and the imagination of the microcosm are the cook and preparer of the seed, reducing it into its ultimate matter, because the seed is produced from the imagination of men. These three will produce the **plague**. The logic of the process is this: Heaven daily works something new. Daily, man also presumes and meditates upon something new. Even the water itself produces new fish and new monsters every day. Heaven...

## ON THE PLAGUE

<margin>The Virgin who</margin>
The heavens are to be compared and likened to a virgin who is chaste—that is, one who has conceived no seed in her body. However, because of the incitement and tickling of lust born from the **imagination**, she can no longer be considered chaste. In the meantime, she possesses no seed, even if she carries the "field" in which the seed of a man ought to sprout and emerge. And although she may imagine various things from time to time, she still does not conceive. Half of the seed is present, but not the whole that is fit for a fetus. In the man resides the other part of the seed. If he then joins with her, a fruit or fetus comes forth from both. Now, the heavens are the spirit and the shaper of the seed, etc., concerning which it is not safe to speak more openly. These three things lead the seed to its growth, and the imaginations are threefold. In this way, the **Sun** and **Moon** are helpers to both the woman and the man. Therefore, a smaller and specific Moon exists within the woman, just as there is also a smaller and specific Sun. If these two are rightly and well-disposed within the woman, so that neither the Sun nor the Moon are bound in chains (that is, if the rays of the **Microcosmic** <note>Microcosm: the human being viewed as a "little world" that mirrors the great universe or "Macrocosm."</note> Sun and Moon are not blocked), the fetus is completed and perfected. If not, and the operation of either fails, then nothing is perfected from that seed; no fetus is produced, but a monster is born, just as the example of wood cut at the wrong time or mud dug up teaches. So now I repeat: the **Venus** of the heavens is chaste, and is the parent of the Microcosmic Venus. But if the celestial Venus is irritated and inflamed by the lustful Venus of a human and their imagination—so that both are now imagining, one good and the other an opposing evil; the one in the heavens striving for purity and modesty, while the other on earth, which possesses the knowledge of what should be done but abuses its imagination—it follows that the "father and mother" in the heavens are martially <note>original: "martialiter," meaning angrily or violently, like the god of war, Mars.</note> inflamed and provoked. Eventually, the Venus of the **Macrocosm** <note>Macrocosm: the great world or the universe at large.</note> punishes and contaminates its daughter, the Microcosmic Venus, with the impure plague.

<margin>How the plague is born and from where.</margin>
<margin>The plague is the comet of the Microcosm.</margin>
<margin>Celestial Venus bound by the chain of divine grace.</margin>
<margin>What the chain of Venus is.</margin>
<margin>By what Adam sinned.</margin>
For the <term>Plague</term> is the <term>comet of the Microcosm</term> <note>Paracelsian medical theory often linked comets (celestial omens) to the plague (a bodily omen). Just as a comet appears in the sky as a warning, the plague appears in the body as a sign of spiritual and physical disruption.</note>. Unless it happens that the celestial Venus is moved to anger through an unchaste imagination, she can cause no harm to any human. For she is bound and tied by a certain chain; this chain is the mercy of God and His command that she should harm no human. But if we humans break and burst that chain, then that which was bound by the chain falls upon us and rushes in. Here it greatly pleases me to discourse by explaining what that thing is which is bound by the chain and remains so. It is nothing other than the **constancy of the human Balsam** <term>Balsam: in old medicine, a natural preservative force within the living body that prevents decay and disease.</term>, which prevents the body from rotting. Now, the first man **ADAM** fell through imagination, following the example of Lucifer, in that he too readily complied with the woman. A punishment immediately followed this sin: namely, ejection from Paradise; likewise the curse that he should eat his bread in sweat and anguish, and give birth to children in pain. In this way, all humans, through the transgression and violation of God’s commands caused by the imagination, incur the punishment due for sins. The longer explanation of this belongs to the Theologian. However, it is the Physician's task to declare, through further philosophizing, the process of how diseases are generated. And it is the Physician's duty to warn men to escape bodily death and diseases, while the Theologian denounces to them the punishment of both bodily and eternal death in a single work.

<margin>What power is in the imagination of a woman.</margin>
<margin>The heavens as the avenger of sins.</margin>
If a woman imagines anything, she forgets herself—to say nothing of God—and through this same self-forgetfulness, she also imprints an absurdity and the shadow of a foul image upon the fetus. Therefore, a woman will be forced to give an account if she abuses her imagination through wandering thoughts. For she has the knowledge not to abuse that which she received from God. Just as a straying horse is whipped by its rider, how much more justly do the heavens themselves avenge it if given knowledge is wickedly abused. What we have said about a woman forgetting herself through imagination must also be applied to the "Great World" (the Macrocosm). For the imagination of the Great World also has its own abuse; when offended by man, it forgets itself—that is, its ordinary course and operation—and imprints monsters upon us, such as buboes <note>buboes: the characteristic swollen lymph nodes of the bubonic plague.</note>, growths, and all diseases.

<margin>Honey eaten with bread in June produces worms.</margin>
For if in an infant, eating honey with bread in the month of June, the heavens so complete the cooking and digestion that earthworms and intestinal worms are born, the same heavens can also infect the Venus of the Microcosm—that is, inflict the plague upon it. Now, all imagination in man proceeds from the heart. The heart is the **Sun** in the Microcosm. And every imagination of men proceeds from the small Sun of the microcosm toward the **Sun**...

# TREATISE I.

...the heart of the greater world—that is, the heart of the macrocosm. <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the entire universe, which Paracelsus believed mirrored the "Microcosm," or the human body.</note> There, the imagination of the Microcosm is the seed, which is material, and it is prepared by the father—namely, the sun of the macrocosm—and cast out into the field of water: which field is nothing else but the Element of water. For this reason, water is infected by the heavens first of all. For no poison can touch a human being so that a plague develops from it, unless it is introduced through two Elements: namely, fire (which is the heaven) and water.

<margin>Water is extremely necessary for man.</margin>
For man cannot live without water. He has a primary need for it for his own sustenance. Therefore, water is the very first thing to be infected and poisoned, as is evident from this example: whenever a painter, or any other artist or craftsman, fashions something that did not previously exist in nature and should not be there, his work is the cause by which the heaven begets and produces a fish in the Element of water that matches the image expressed by the painter or sculptor. The "fruits" of the water demonstrate this, just as many things are taught concerning them in books about animals.

<margin>The world is like an ape.</margin>
For the world, with its imagination, is like an ape. <note>The "ape" (simia) was a common metaphor for nature's tendency to mimic human art or for the world's imitation of higher spiritual patterns.</note> For whatever man does, the ape emulates; in the same way, the soul and spirit of the world, by imagining, emulates and expresses everything that man has done and proposed. Meanwhile, however, the heaven can do nothing through imagination except for this one thing: that which man proposes to himself, which ought not to be proposed at all. Thus the water is also infected, and the "first matter" <note>The *materia prima*, or the fundamental substance from which specific things are formed.</note> is generated within it, having the nature of poison. Indeed, as long as it is mixed and confused with the water, it does not appear poisonous; afterward, however, it becomes poison and plague within the man himself.

<margin>A dog born in the wound of a rabid dog.</margin>
By now you know that if a rabid dog bites someone, a long time after the bite (as experience has many times testified), dogs have grown within that wound. <note>This reflects a historical belief that the "essence" of the disease could physically manifest as miniatures of the cause—in this case, tiny dogs—within the body.</note> And if a rabid dog bites another healthy dog, it drives that one into rabies as well through the bite. In this way, man is also infected and poisoned through the imagination of the heaven, simultaneously in both body and imagination. And as you see a snail's shell take form in the Element of water, so the plague also has its own form. From this it is clear that the snail or the tortoise <note>original: *testudinem*</note> is also attractive, and draws in the poison of the plague. Indeed, the pearls found in that shell are the "incarnative" of the plague. <note>An "incarnative" (*incarnativum*) is a medicine that helps flesh to grow or a wound to heal.</note> Therefore, as many plagues as there are, there are just as many shells. To this also belongs the mountain tortoise because of its power to attract poison. Now, anyone who acts as a Doctor with this reasoning will easily understand me. And in this one thing lies the accepted art of preparing remedies, which specifically concerns the Doctor.

<margin>What the remedies for the Plague are: Deer truffle, Agaric, Ruby, Coral, etc.</margin>
Thus, the Deer Truffle <note>original: *Boletum cervinum*</note> is a restorative in a plague of the earth. Thus, Agaric <note>A type of fungus used in early medicine.</note> is a restorative in a plague of the Air. Thus, the Ruby, Red Coral, Almandine, Amethyst, and Garnet are the "incarnative" in a plague of fire, etc. I leave these to the skill of the Physicians. However, the example of the rabid dog was brought forward so that it might be known that the stars are also infected by man in the same way. Afterward, the water is infected by the stars; finally, man is contaminated and poisoned by the water in a twofold manner. At this point, one who is skilled in Magic will not be deterred by our Philosophy. If a Physician understands it, he can judge and foretell from the "excrements of the stars" <note>This refers to meteorites or atmospheric phenomena like *nostoc* (a jelly-like algae) which were once thought to be waste material fallen from the stars.</note> when and how the plague will invade.

<margin>Stellar excrement foretells future diseases.</margin>
But as for who exactly will be seized by it: that is not for the Astronomer to know. You ought to be persuaded of this: that every single excrement of the stars, in winter as well as in summer, reveals and foretells which diseases are about to loom.

<margin>Intestines cast down from the stars.</margin>
Falling stars of this kind have often been observed by me and my disciples, formed in no other way than like the intestines of a man. When we cut them open or unfolded them, we found them to be true intestines. Not long after that time, a cruel plague invaded Swabia, Switzerland, and Bavaria, with a most severe colic never similarly heard of. This happened in the year 1538.

<margin>Tongues shaken out from the stars.</margin>
Similarly, in Hungary, signs and traces were presented to me, expressing a tongue the thickness of a finger, marked with black spots like a rather large pearl. Afterward, in Hungary, a most ferocious plague followed in the year 1536, with "prunella" or a burning of the throat and tongue. Similarly in Prussia in the year 1532, I encountered fallen stars interspersed with yellow, black, and purple spots; an unheard-of outbreak of smallpox followed these, along with heavy dysentery and plague. And many of these things must be kept silent by me here because of the incredulity and ingratitude of men.

Furthermore, mention was made previously of the digestion of those foods used by every living creature. Much also depends on explaining this. For animals themselves suffer from no fewer defects of digestion than man himself, and this is because of the heaven.

<margin>When the dog, peacock, and deer vomit.</margin>
Thus the Dog, sensing a change in the weather, chews grass and vomits. He also... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Pauo" (Peacock), which begins the next page.</note>

# ON PESTILENCE

The peacock is afflicted by a failure of digestion through the power of the heavens if it perceives a human corpse in the place where it stays. The cuckoo vomits blood if diarrhea is spreading among the people. In the same way, all vomitings that trouble a person during a time of plague arise from the Element of water, as if the person had drunk the "sperm" of frogs <note>In older biology, frogspawn or the reproductive matter of frogs was often associated with the spontaneous generation of life and toxins in stagnant water.</note>.

<margin>The physician must be skilled in distillation.</margin>
It is appropriate, therefore, for the Physician to be strong in solid and remarkable experience—not gathered indeed by hearing and reading, but proven through distillation. For if he is truly skilled in this art, having performed tests on waters, he will easily be able to examine all properties and sicknesses. I am not speaking here of "human water" (or urine) which leaves the person, but of that which enters into him. Now, if water is one part from which sicknesses are brought into man, while Earth is the second, Air the third, and Heaven the fourth: then fourfold digestions and generations of poisons must be understood in the same way. Thus the cure itself will also be fourfold, as will be discussed next.

<margin>Just as the frog is generated, so is the plague.</margin>
The frog is a worm <note>original: *vermis*. In this era, "worm" was a broad category for many small crawling creatures, including amphibians and insects.</note>, not a fish. Its mode of generation is easy to understand. In exactly the same way, the plague is also generated in man, through the process of the power of the Microcosmic Element of Water. If the plague attacks in this manner, then those people are infected by the Stars, and the pestilence seizes them with a deep sleep. Remedies for this kind of plague are frogs and turtles or all snails bound upon the body. Then the plague is healed not with difficulty, but easily, like a wound. I mentioned digestion for this reason: because the frog has no food other than poison. Now, if the frog receives nourishment and poison in place of food, it follows that the frog has digested the poison into a non-poisonous matter.

<margin>The food of the frog is poison.</margin>
Therefore also the Frog, the Toad, the Tench, the Eel, the Moray, the Plaice <note>original: *Passer*. While this usually means sparrow, in this context of water animals, it refers to a flatfish.</note>, the Rooster, the Peacock, the Crow, and the Raven draw out and entice the pestilential poison from the human being.

<margin>A rule.</margin>
<margin>Animals that digest poisons.</margin>
For whatever condition and nature of digestion exists in an animal, and whatever poisons it digests: that same animal—whether it be alive or dead—sucks out and extracts those same poisons and that same matter through the intact skin of a human. For you see the Blackbird digest sands and poisonous worms, just as the hen and the rooster do; and in the waters, the Pike and the stork, along with many other animals. And why are these not an example and proof to you that these animals entice and extract the conceived poison from the human? For what is more powerful in extracting poison through the intact skin—whatever kind it may be—than the stork itself, provided it is correctly applied and laid on, having first been soaked in rose vinegar?

<margin>A prepared stork extracts the plague.</margin>
And there are many such things in nature, all of which can be easily investigated by a Physician.

<margin>A rule of practice.</margin>
Much also depends on use and application. For the plague is manifold. If it is a plague of the Earth, seek medicines from those animals that avoid water and live on the land; if it is a plague of water, seek medicines from animals that delight in water. If it is a plague of the Air, use the sparrow and the stork. If it is a plague of Fire, use Tereniabin <note>A Persian-derived term for a type of medicinal manna or sugary secretion found on plants.</note> or Manna to extract it. And this is the discipline of remedies. And although I ought to list the distinct and pathognomonic signs <note>Signs that are specifically characteristic of a particular disease, allowing for a certain diagnosis.</note>, I omit them here for reasons that are not trivial. For even if I were to describe all the signs by which it would be clear which plague belongs to Fire, or Air, or Water, or Earth: nevertheless, because the plague is rarely solitary in a person but is usually accompanied by many other signs and symptoms, it would still happen that one type or another would be unknown, or would appear to be something other than what it is. It is therefore worthwhile for the Physician to investigate these things among the sick with singular industry and experience. For a sleep of a Narcotic nature is merely an "accident" <note>In historical medicine, an "accident" refers to a symptom or non-essential secondary effect of a disease.</note> of the plague. Likewise, the "falling sickness" <note>original: *caducus*, referring to epilepsy or seizures.</note> itself is nothing but an accident. Those things which I omit here for this reason, I will record elsewhere under the title of the signs of new diseases. From there, your desires shall be satisfied.

<margin>Signs by which each kind of plague is identified.</margin>
Meanwhile, however, the plague that attacks with great heat and inflammation and causes the glands behind the ears to swell—in which, however, the sick do not feel thirst—that is to be judged a plague of fire. In this case, the cure for extracting the poison (which penetrates directly to the heart and brings death) is Tereniabin, Manna, Sugar, Garlic, leeks, and onions.

<margin>The fiery plague and its cure.</margin>
In the plague where there is vehement thirst, little or no sleep, and buboes <note>The painful, swollen lymph nodes in the armpit or groin that are the hallmark of bubonic plague.</note> appear in both groins, that is a plague of water. For this, use fish, frogs, toads, and whatever lives in the waters, and especially the flesh of storks and ducks laid upon the body.

<margin>The watery plague and its cure.</margin>
In the plague where the Buboes are under the arms, and a difficult panting for breath presses, and a squeezing or narrowing of the chest weighs down, and a headache with delirium plagues the sufferer: in that case, apply sparrows, blackbirds, the flesh of hens...

### TREATISE I.

<margin>The Earth and its cure.</margin>
Finally, in that state where there is a deep or narcotic sleep, and no definite tumors or buboes <note>Swollen lymph nodes characteristic of the plague.</note> appear on the body—though the skin of these sick people is often mottled and livid, and crowded with blood-suffused swellings—that is the plague of the earth. For this, use the fat of vipers, badgers <note>original: *melinum*</note>, the flesh of moles, foxes, wolves, and cats. For use and experience dictate that all these things are beneficial. You see, for instance, that serpents are nourished within the body of a wolf.
<margin>Wolves produce serpents.</margin>
Which serves as evidence that the wolf also carries within itself the remedy against their poisons. For the plague is generated in the human body by the stars, and sometimes even without the stars. It is an external poison, the operation of which should be understood in the same way as the bite of a rabid dog drives the bitten dog into madness.
<margin>The wolf is a wild dog.</margin>
For a wolf is nothing but a fierce and wild dog. It is known to you that during the time of the "dog days" <note>The hot summer period associated with the rising of the Star Sirius, historically believed to cause madness or disease.</note>, dogs often become rabid. Even for deer, there is a set time when they become hotter and more ferocious than usual. During the time of this fury, they shake froth from their mouths onto the ground, from which the *cyclamen* <note>Sowbread; a flowering plant used in traditional medicine.</note> is born, shaped like a walnut, without leaves. This is a flesh-making medicine <term>incarnative: a substance that promotes the growth of new flesh to heal wounds</term> for wounds caused by the plague.
<margin>Cyclamen from the froth of deer.</margin>
<margin>Its virtue.</margin>
Furthermore, the internal bone of the deer's heart <note>The *os cordis*, a small bone or cartilage found in the hearts of some deer, historically prized as a heart tonic.</note> exists as a strengthener of the heart during the time of plague. Deer blood taken with *Mumia* <term>Mumia: a Paracelsian term for the vital life-force preserved in remains, used here as a medicinal preparation</term> from a human and a stork acts as a preventative. Thus, just as it was said of deer and dogs that they have set times for their fury and heat, it must be known that such fury is natural to deer, but not at all to dogs. Similarly, the wolf does not always produce serpents and vipers. For
<margin>Orion produces serpents in the wolf.</margin>

<margin>The star Cochab</margin>
However, the star *Cochab* <note>original: *Cochab*, from the Hebrew word for "star"; in this context, it likely refers to a specific celestial influence or Mercury.</note> completes its operation in the Whale at the time when she ejects her seed or sperm. Now, the Sea-Pike and the Salmon greedily seek out the sperm of the Whale, just as dogs almost always pursue a corpse.
<margin>The sperm of the whale is digested into a serpent within the Pike.</margin>
Nevertheless, this sperm is digested and putrefies within the "wolf" <note>likely referring back to the predatory pike or a similar predator</note>, and it turns into an eel and a serpent. Thus, these things arise from the sperm of the whale. The eel seeks the sperm of the Pike at the time when the fish release their seed. Once swallowed, that sperm is changed in the belly of the eel into lampreys <note>original: *murænulas*</note>, which is something especially well-known to fishermen.
<margin>The sperm of the Pike turns into a lamprey within the eel.</margin>

And furthermore, whatever conceives seed through the mouth to produce offspring and thus propagate its kind: all of that is a protection and aid against this savage disease of the plague. For in the same way, a human conceives the seed of this violent disease through the mouth on one hand. On the other hand, one also conceives it through the unbroken skin, by which means someone can be poisoned if they touch a poisoned thing, such as clothing, a home, and other items. Thirdly, it is caught through sight, in the same way that a person is poisoned by the gaze of a Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent said to kill with its glance.</note>. So also women who have an impure menstrual flow during a time of plague infect almost anyone nearby with their eyes and naked gaze. Thus man infects man, and the plague is transferred from one to another in many ways.
<margin>Plague attacks by three ways.</margin>
Against this infection of the eyes, the best of preventatives is the tongue of a serpent, plucked during a full moon. Similarly, the heart of the hoopoe, the wolf, the mole, and the badger have the power of this preservation. For all operations of the stars in any animal tend toward the heart. And the virtue of any living animal is most perfect during the full moon. Learn, therefore, Magical Astronomy, which I otherwise call Cabalistic. In this way, you will be able to prescribe suitable recipes against this and all other diseases.

For consider this example: Bread is the food of many living animals. Even though its power is only one, yet through various digestions performed in the different stomachs of animals, it is converted into the peculiar nature and flesh of each animal. For if a dog eats it, it becomes dog flesh. If a cat, cat flesh. If a mouse, mouse flesh. And yet there is a great difference between dog, cat, and mouse flesh. And what else is this but what I want you to understand: the natures and differences of *Mumia*, and which one is born from another? <header>ON THE PLAGUE</header>

## ON THE PLAGUE

<margin>Are all things one in Essence?</margin>
Essence is undivided; only form makes the distinction. For who would believe that a duck is, in its essence, a female frog? Yet, if you pluck a duck and place it in a cellar—either boiled or roasted and sealed between two dishes—within the space of three or four weeks, it will degenerate into nothing but frogs. For after putrefaction <note>The process of decay, which alchemists believed was the first step toward the transformation of matter.</note>, any thing returns to and is changed into that which it was before its generation. Look closely: the duck feeds on frogs and fish, and thus it degenerates into frogs, not back into a duck. <margin>Putrefaction turns everything into what it was before birth.</margin> This is achieved by the universal Nature of putrefaction and digestion. A frog appears poisonous, and indeed it is. Yet, by the duck, it is changed into something non-poisonous through the power of digestion. Similarly, the food of the stork consists of frogs and snakes. Nevertheless, the stork transforms these into something non-poisonous. <margin>Snakes from the stork.</margin> And although snakes may indeed be born from a rotting stork—such that the bird might seem unfit to be counted as food—nonetheless, in a time of plague, it ought to be both taken internally and applied externally to extract the poison. <margin>A king of bees from a Gudgeon.</margin> A gudgeon fish <note>original: *Gobio*; a small freshwater fish.</note> sealed in a glass becomes a true King of Bees within a few days. That fish itself, when bound to the body, also draws out the poison of the plague. If I were to describe all the things with which my brain is filled, massive books would surely be produced, from which one could judge how coldly and lazily the Philosophy of Medicine has been handled until now. And yet, Theophrastus <note>The author, Paracelsus, often refers to himself as Theophrastus to assert his authority against the established medical schools.</note>, with all his knowledge and skill, is excluded and forced to yield, while the ignorance of others meanwhile raises itself up to the very heavens. Consider, I pray, the lion and the cat: how closely their anatomy matches in terms of form and behavior. It would be well for a doctor who is about to go among those infected with the plague if he knew how to rightly and properly use the skin and tongue of both the Lion and the Cat for the sake of preservation. <margin>The power of the skin and tongue of the Lion and Cat against the plague.</margin> This is a mystery hidden from the great lords by ignorant despisers of the Magical art. <margin>The Lion gives birth to dead cubs.</margin> And if I wished to reveal that great and admirable secret—why the Lion gives birth to dead cubs and brings them to life with a shout or roar—this miracle would surely not torment many of those who are currently hostile toward me. But it is unworthy to publish such things to the common crowd. Our "little scholars," however, are already so knowledgeable in their own eyes that they do not greatly desire to learn such things from us. <margin>The power of the urine and blood of the lion, deer, etc., in the plague.</margin> This I say: if you had discovered how excellent a preservative against the pestilential contagion the urine and blood of the Lion, Deer, and Cat are, and what noble prescriptions could be prepared from them, you would feel more benefit from that than from the entire Galenic art <note>The traditional medical system based on the Greek physician Galen, which Paracelsus famously rejected.</note>. Meanwhile, your contempt causes me to keep these things hidden. In a time of plague, human urine warns the physician about that person's digestion. <margin>A reproach of doctors.</margin> For it is the doctor’s duty to discern whose digestion is more excellent or more powerful than another’s. For a great difference is noted in human digestion compared to others. Let us suppose a case where twelve men lie sick with the plague at the same time. The urine of none of these is like another’s. What is the cause of this diversity? Digestion alone, which varies from man to man. Yet you doctors escape these traps and do not endure the task of judging such urines. From this, it can be gathered how poorly you perform your duty in testing urine. Do you not fear that God will finally demand a severe accounting from you, asking why you were so hesitantly confident in your art? For who is more seriously ill anywhere than those whom this cruel disease has prostrated? Yet you pass them by, just as the priests and the Levite passed by the wounded man at Jericho <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Good Samaritan.</note>. And when someone objects to you about such things, you call him a fool. But if you indeed treat God’s warnings and impending judgment as worthless, how can you accept my exhortations? It is all over for you; no pen and no voice can correct you from now on. <margin>Wall Germander is suited for the plague.</margin> Furthermore, the herb Wall Germander <note>original: *Gamandrea*; likely Teucrium chamaedrys.</note> possesses the "anatomy" of the plague. This is demonstrated by the round fruit born upon it. And what herb among all others is more excellent than this against the plague, if a drink is made from it? Yet it helps no one, nor does it help elsewhere, except for those in the place where it grows. Also, the "apples" growing on an oak <note>Oak galls, caused by insects.</note>, if bound while fresh, are medicine against the plague, etc. <margin>Galls.</margin> So also are galls, if applied and sprinkled in the form of a dry powder. <margin>Nutmeg.</margin> Nutmeg, powdered, steeped in vinegar, and bound externally, draws out the poison. All these things are evident from their "form" <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that the physical appearance of a plant indicates its medicinal use.</note>. You doctors, meanwhile, do not weigh the signs and forms of herbs any more deeply than the peasants do—indeed, you make yourselves even more ignorant than them. For I swear that I have known more than eighty peasants who, from form and "anatomy" alone, were able to skillfully match herbs with diseases, and in my presence and sight, they helped the sick in a marvelous way. So great is the beneficence of God that He teaches us even through common and simple folk, and indeed, through the wild beasts themselves. Blessed is he who takes these things to heart, and does not despise the simple...

Paracelsus critiques the medical establishment for ignoring the "signatures" of nature—such as the lion’s blood or specific herbs like Wall Germander—which provide more effective plague remedies than traditional Galenic medicine.</summary>

<header>TREATISE I.</header>

## TREATISE I.

...deems it a disgrace to emulate the simpler folk. For if we look more closely at the matter—"closer to the torch," as they say—we see that most of the most certain arts were 
<margin>Most experiments were discovered by the common people.</margin>
discovered by the common folk and men of lowly status, and have flowed down to us through a kind of succession. Indeed, if individual experiments were recorded in a single book, pure and unpolluted, without the adulterations of those who merely collect recipes, that work would be far more beneficial than all the commentaries of Galen and Avicenna <note>Galen and Avicenna were the two pillars of traditional medieval medicine, whose authority the author frequently challenges in favor of direct observation and alchemy.</note>. Meanwhile, time speaks and bears witness that bad and counterfeit recipes are frequently concocted from the best <term>simples: Medicines made from a single natural ingredient, rather than complex mixtures.</term>. If you apply your judgment, what is more effective and excellent against the plague than the nettle <note>original: *urtica*</note>, of which there are many species? For those who drink of it experience both certain preservation and a certain cure. The white-flowered nettle, drunk by women, is beneficial if signs <note>original: *signa*; the physical marks of the plague, such as rashes or spots.</note> and buboes have erupted. If these are not appearing, the smaller stinging nettle should be administered to women. For in this way, 
<margin>Cure for the Nettle-Plague.</margin>
<margin>The Rule.
“
“
“
“</margin>
the smaller stinging nettle does not emit flowers. For all herbs that lack flowers should be applied to those diseases which similarly have no signs or "flowers." However, those diseases which break out on the outside of the body with certain signs should be treated with herbs distinguished by their flowers. And it is unworthy of you to say that this is "hot" or "cold" in the first or second degree, and so on <note>The author is mocking the traditional "Galenic" system of degrees, which classified medicines by their perceived temperature and moisture levels.</note>. Form is owed to form; here is the <term>rhombus: A geometric shape used here to suggest a perfect symbolic or structural correspondence between the remedy and the ailment.</term>. Therefore, 
<margin>Which nettle should be used for which plague.</margin>
the larger nettles should be administered to men in this manner: those which lack flowers should be used for the diseases or plagues of men that are not accompanied by visible signs. But if signs and tumors are prominent, Nature has destined the nettle with yellow and white flowers for men. This is the true foundation. If you Medical Doctors and Pharmacists possessed the <term>Magical and Kabbalistic: Here, these terms refer to the study of the hidden "signatures" or divine marks on plants that reveal their uses.</term> knowledge of the form, color, and taste of all herbs, you would label your jars in which you keep your distilled waters like this: *This is the water of the smaller nettle; this is the water of the larger. This one is for this sex, that one for the other; this one is suitable in summer, that one in autumn; this one for a woman, that one for a man, and that one for a maiden.* In this way, you would surely walk the right path. And by this means, the status of the Doctor and the Pharmacist would be one and the same. 
<margin>The same thing does not always work the same way.</margin>
It is easy to believe that Rhubarb purges every day. But I cannot and should not believe that it always purges exactly what it ought to purge every single day. For there is no herb so vile and lowly that it does not have its own peculiar time for administration. If anyone reproaches you for neglecting these things, you flare up and chatter like old women.

It is known to you, and you observe it daily, that men frequently die from consternation and terror. You also know that corals are hung from the necks of infants 
<margin>Corals against the terror of infants.</margin>
to preserve them from terror. For from terror, they are cast headlong into the <term>falling sickness: An old term for epilepsy.</term>. Can an adult man not also be driven into the falling sickness by consternation? For what else is terror but the imagination? And 
<margin>Terror is imagination.</margin>
should imagination—as you say—not have its own cure? What else would faith in Christ be, who is himself the cure for a depraved imagination and for unbelief? And how could the children of Israel have been healed in faith and preserved against 
<margin>The serpent of Moses.</margin>
unbelief, unless Moses had set up and erected the bronze serpent as a figure for their preservation from eternal death? For the same purpose, Nature itself, and God the ruler of Nature, produced many herbs through her by which a man can be preserved from imagination, fear, and terror. For the greatest part of men are infected by the imagination when the plague is raging. But this finds no place among you, even though God and Nature have created infinite means for these things. Is the 
<margin>A herb against imagination. Celandine preserves against the plague.</margin>
herb Celandine <note>original: *Chelidonia*</note> not a distinguished preservative, if it is uprooted at the new moon or full moon and hung as a defense against the plague and the imagination of it? The cause is this: just as a woman has her monthly cycle, so also does this herb and its root, as its "anatomy" teaches. For when cut, it pours out a juice similar to the monthly flow and blood. Whence it is also a preservation against women who are infected by the plague and suffering their cycle at the same time, and who infect others by their very sight. The 
<margin>How it should be interpreted that Celandine benefits the eyes.</margin>
ancients indeed recorded that it benefits the eyes. But that was not their meaning as you impose it upon them. For if you would understand Galen rightly, according to my instruction and the introduction of the examples I have brought forward, you will see that a much more certain and better "Galenic" discovery will be found by me for all of you. For in the city of Braunau in Bohemia <note>Modern-day Broumov in the Czech Republic.</note>, you will find a book in a certain College in which the genuine Commentaries of Galen and Avicenna 
<margin>The genuine commentaries of Galen and Avicenna.</margin>
are held, written entirely and purely, without any disguise, corruption, or addition. That book is longer by six <term>dodrants: A dodrant is a unit of measurement equal to three-quarters of a Roman foot, roughly 9 inches.</term>, three dodrants in width, and one dodrant in thickness.

# ON THE PLAGUE.

<margin>...found in Brunswick and Hamburg and Pelplin.</margin>
...one and a half parts, and has nearly two three-quarter measures: which even today is shown to men, though the Monks do not understand it. Open your eyes and your mind here. It is indeed a great shame and disgrace that a treasure of such value and fruitfulness lies there so basely hidden and entombed. I also happened to see a book similar to this in the Monastery of the city of Brunswick in Saxony: which was nevertheless burned in a fire by those ignorant asses. A copy similar to this is also kept by a certain elderly citizen of Hamburg, along with many other manuscripts of Galen and Avicenna <note>Galen and Avicenna were the foundational authorities of medieval medicine, though the author often views them as outdated compared to his own observations.</note>, inscribed on birch bark and wax tablets. But to what end? As soon as those books are shown to our "little scholars," they will not blush to cry out immediately and say that Necromancy <note>original: *Nigromantia*; here used to mean forbidden or "black" magic.</note> and other trifles or deceptions are therein: because, forsooth, the matter does not seem to suit their palate. For that book, of which I spoke, describes some thousands of humors, and not just four <note>Galenic medicine was based on only four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—while the author argues for a much more complex chemistry of the body.</note>.

<margin>Pelplin Monastery in Prussia.</margin>
A clearly similar book is also found in Prussia in a certain Monastery called Pelplin <note>original: *Polphir*; referring to the Cistercian Abbey in Pelplin.</note>: which itself is destined to perish at last from decay and old age. He who truly knew and understood books of this kind could maintain the title of a diligent, skilled, and expert Physician with dignity.

This place demands that something also be said about the virtue and property of the stars. I will relate a few things regarding this matter. For it is by no means possible to bring the whole matter, with its very foundation, into a short paragraph. However, in that book to which I gave the title, *The Work on the Astronomy of the World* <note>original: *Opus Astronomiæ mundi*</note>, I intend to treat this material more copiously and fully as the subject requires: for it is right that the comparison of the Microcosm and the Macrocosm <term>Microcosm and Macrocosm: The philosophical theory that the human being (the "little world") is a reflection of the entire universe (the "great world").</term> should square and agree. Indeed, to bring forth everything that pertains to this would be a work of infinite labor and immense bulk.

Therefore, you must know this. Every celestial star is nothing else than a spiritually born herb, to which every herb among us, of whatever kind it may be, is similar—except that the stars exist as a kind of <gloss>chaos</gloss> <note>In this context, *chaos* refers to a primordial, unmanifested state or the "atmosphere" from which physical things are condensed.</note>.

This should not be understood in any other way than how a Physician and distiller extracts the spirit from wormwood <note>original: *absynthio*</note>. While this is done, the leaves, roots, and whatever is sensible and material are indeed destroyed through the art of separation; nevertheless, the spirit retains the form and image of that same herb: though only spiritu-

<margin>Stars have tares and Sodomy.</margin>
-ally, so that the leaves, branches, twigs, and roots of the entire wormwood are presented spiritually. In the same way, the stars also exist in heaven. And it should be noted here that the stars themselves also have tares <note>original: *zizania*; a reference to the "weeds" among the wheat in the Biblical parable, signifying corruption or "unnatural" influences.</note> in their own order. For they practice Sodomy and adultery <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Sodomy" and "adultery" among stars refer to "unnatural" or destructive astronomical conjunctions that produce disease.</note> among themselves no less busily than other creatures: which is well enough known to the Magi.

The stars, therefore, are no different than the mold <note>original: *forma*</note> by which a cannonball <note>original: *glans tormenti*; literally "the acorn of the engine of war."</note> is cast and shaped. For in the same way, the Stars themselves are the manner, the form, and the <term>matrices: The "wombs" or blueprints from which physical objects take their shape.</term> of all herbs, etc. Thus, by an attractive virtue, every star draws an herb similar to itself out of the earth. Unless you wish to be blind by choice, you can observe this in very many herbs, that they have an express similarity with the stars and planets, from which both the learned and the unlearned have given them names. But I shall make fuller mention of these in my *Herbarium*.

<margin>Herbs are terrestrial stars turned toward heaven.</margin>
Thus, every herb is an earthly star, turned upward toward heaven. And conversely, every star is a heavenly herb, differing in no way from our native herbs growing on earth according to their spiritual form, but differing only according to their material substance. Therefore, the stars also foretell all future diseases through their "excrements" and their "tossings" <note>This refers to celestial phenomena like comets or unusual planetary alignments.</note>. But these things must be learned and investigated, and so established through one's own experience. Thus it will happen that no one is deceived by pretense or imposture.

In the same way, the heavenly herbs look downward toward the earth, facing their own herbs from which they were begotten. Now, if you had the skill of the art, you would speak in this way:

<margin>The Star of Rosemary, of Wormwood.</margin>
"This star is called the Star of Rosemary; this is the Star of Wormwood, and it has the power of wormwood." Thus, indeed, you would both display the proof of your doctoral knowledge and bring forth a legitimate and true herbarium, more noble than all gold, silver, and gems. You would know which herbs grow under the snow for the feast of the Bacchanalia <note>The "feast of the Bacchanalia" likely refers here to the late winter/early spring Carnival season.</note> and why, which are called *Trellenblumen*, *Schmergeln*, and *Schnegellen* <note>original: German folk names for spring flowers like Globeflowers and Snowdrops.</note> by the Germans. And by that very reasoning, you yourselves would know the constellation of the herbs, and there would be no need to search for this or that herb in Galen or Avicenna and fail to find it. And it is a work of much less labor to learn the whole heaven with all its herbs than to learn the Latin or Greek language. And so it would be more profitable...

# TRACTATE I.

<margin>The proper aspects of the Art must be learned first.</margin>
The first thing is to learn those matters which pertain to the art itself: and afterwards to join Latin to it. But such warnings are in vain among you: for you grasp at languages just as a peasant grasps at nobility.

It would even be fitting to explain certain secrets and more hidden things about the pulses in this place. For this doctrine holds much utility. But it would be too long to insert it here as a formal treatise. Let a brief declaration suffice us here. The rest you will receive more fully delivered in that book titled *The Work of the Astronomy of the World* <note>original: *Opus Astronomiae mundi*</note>.

<margin>What the pulse is.</margin>
The pulse, therefore, is nothing other than a measure of the body's temperature, according to the condition of its six locations occupied by the Planets. For thus, the two pulses visible lower down in the feet belong to Saturn and Jupiter:

<margin>Which pulses belong to which Planets.</margin>
the two in the neck belong to Venus and Mars: the two in both temples belong to the Moon and Mercury. The pulse of the Sun is on the left side under the heart. From this it follows that if ever the pulse is faster than is right, the principal members suffer—these being the Heart, Brain, Liver, Gallbladder, kidneys, spleen, and lung. Whence, as those adversaries and enemies attack,

<margin>A fast pulse indicates strength, a slow one weakness.</margin>
the pulse is provoked and stirred. If indeed some principal member—whether it be the liver, the heart, the brain, or any other—be overcome and as it were cast down by the force of disease, the pulse becomes slower and weaker. And so it often happens that, with the pulse striking more weakly, the air and spirit of life <note>The "spirit of life" or *spiritus vitae* was believed to be a subtle substance that animated the body, distinct from the soul.</note> are obstructed in that place where it is perceived. And the pulse is nothing other than

<margin>The seven pulses of man.</margin>
fire and air, the best part of the spirit of life. These things ought to be understood by you in this way: In man, there are seven remarkable pulses. 

<margin>The seven pulses of the world are the movements of the seven planets.</margin>
These seven pulses have their nourishment from the pulse of the great world. And it is this which moderates those seven pulses of man. Now truly the greater world <note>The Macrocosm or universe.</note> also has seven pulses. These are the movements of the seven planets, just as is taught in Astronomy. These seven rule and govern the air, that is, the spirit of life in the greater world. For air is nothing other than the spirit of life, and the life of the Macrocosm itself. Now, he who wishes to have certain knowledge of the human pulse must be skilled in Astronomy. For from the Sun and 

<margin>All the stars of heaven suffer eclipse.</margin>
Moon, one learns what Eclipses are. And this example is indeed clear. For the same thing is given to even a peasant to see. In the same way, the other five planets of the greater world also suffer their own Eclipses: and with these, similarly, all the remaining stars of the world. Thus, therefore, the inequality of pulses in man is to be judged as nothing other than a certain Eclipse, where the spirit of life in the body completes its course like the external heaven. From this also arises the deep and narcotic sleep in pestilential fevers. I would wish you to know, moreover, that an Eclipse made in heaven is nothing 

<margin>An eclipse is an earthquake of the planets.</margin>
other than a certain (so to speak) earthquake of the planets. For just as through an earthquake a certain shaking occurs, by which all things are moved: so also the pulse in man palpitates, and repeatedly stirs up one shaking after another. Just as earthquakes in the great world are not frequent but fall at an uncertain time: so in man, fever also invades at an uncertain time. And you know, if the temperature of the operation of the planets conducts itself well and rightly, that at that time the stars lack all violent force.

<margin>How thunders occur.</margin>
If indeed their course is interrupted according to the reason and Meteoric manner of the planets—in that the stars have become increased in sulfur, mercury, and salt <note>Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt were the "Tria Prima" or three primary chemical principles in Paracelsian alchemy.</note>—then thunders occur, which exist as certain earthquakes of heaven; that is, a leaping up of the spirit of life of the greater world, or (to speak more truly), a labyrinth and

<margin>The Sun is the master of heat, the Moon of cold.</margin>
wandering of the two qualities of heat and cold, which are governed by the sun, as the moderator of heat, and the moon, as the governess of cold. For thus sulfur is then burdened with too much nitre <note>Nitre or saltpeter was associated with cold and explosive force in early chemistry.</note>, when nitre is nothing other than cold salt, impatient of a fire more vehement or greater than is right; those things which we have said arise and are generated. Nitre or saltpeter can indeed bear a moderate and suitable heat, as if placed in a warm furnace. Nevertheless, if it is 

<margin>Saltpeter is a cold salt.</margin>
commanded and overwhelmed by one more plentiful and vehement, it seeks its own way out and leaps up, and the more tightly it is enclosed, the more violently it shakes. In this way it is ignited by the sun, that is, by the spirit of life of the great world. But the spirit of life by no means rests, but continues its motion and course. But as soon as the spirit of life has departed, then both the shaking and the burning of the saltpeter cease. The same is to be understood similarly concerning the spirit of life in man also, just as is more evidently observed in fevers. For the sinning matter <note>original: *materia peccans*; the traditional medical term for the corrupted substance or "humor" that causes a disease.</note> in a fever is nothing other than

<margin>Fever is a disease of nitre.</margin>
sulfur and saltpeter. And this disease is called by its true and genuine name: the disease of nitre, or of ignited sulfur. For it must be known that saltpeter or nitre, in the great as well as the lesser world...

->## ON THE PLAGUE<-

...in the world there is nothing else than a spiritual essence and the byproduct <margin>Saltpeter is Hermaphroditic.</margin> of all salts; and thus it has a "hermaphroditic" nature <note>In alchemy, a hermaphroditic substance is one that possesses both active and passive, or "masculine" and "feminine" properties, making it highly versatile.</note>, so that it exists neither entirely as a salt nor entirely as sulfur.

<margin>Urine is saltpeter.</margin> Furthermore, even human urine itself is nothing other than pure saltpeter <note>original: *nitrum*</note>. For this reason, it is also very closely joined with sulfur, which is evident from the fact that urine becomes foul and smelly so quickly. Indeed, urine that easily and quickly turns foul contains much sulfur, but has little of the "spirit of salt" mixed in. Urine of this kind is easily disturbed and corrupted.

<margin>Urine as an index of the disease's cause.</margin> If, however, salt predominates in the urine and is present in greater abundance than sulfur, this is recognized by the fact that the urine becomes cloudy more slowly and is more reddish. By this reasoning, a ready judgment can be made regarding any urine: whether sulfur or salt is the cause of the disease.

Furthermore, it must be repeated here that everything we eat and drink is resolved and digested into these three: **salt**, **sulfur**, and **mercury**. We shall remain silent about mercury for now. However, sulfur and salt especially need to be explained here so that the nature of the pulse may be properly understood. Regarding salt, therefore, note this first: if a live fish from the water is bound to a burning plague-sore <note>original: *pesti ardenti*</note>, it draws out the burning or inflaming salt. <margin>Salt is the cause of hardness in buboes.</margin> For salt gives hardness to Buboes <note>The painful, swollen lymph nodes that are a hallmark of the bubonic plague.</note>. Because of this hardness, the sulfur in the flesh is ignited.

This sulfur is like wood that burns and blazes. Yet it is ignited by the power of salt. Almost the same thing happens here as with vitriol <note>Vitriol, or iron/copper sulfate, was a key substance in early chemistry, often associated with the blood due to its color changes when heated.</note>. <margin>A stone is made by the cooking of vitriol.</margin> Vitriol is tender and soft as long as it remains in its green state. But if it is cooked until it loses its moisture, it is changed into a hard stone—so much so that fire can be struck from it. For as soon as its wateriness vanishes, salt predominates over the sulfur in the vitriol, and the vitriol finally turns red. For the same reason—because the blood in human flesh is nothing but pure vitriol—the Buboes arising from the plague also glow and turn red.

<margin>Saltpeter with rose and houseleek juice wards off inflammation.</margin> For while the sulfur in the blood is ignited by the power of salt, a flame and burning are stirred up in the flesh. To extinguish this burning, the best and most powerful remedy is saltpeter (or *nitrum*) soaked in rose vinegar and the juice of the great houseleek <note>original: *sedi maioris*</note>, and bound to the wrists or the locations of the pulses. By this, a feverish swelling, however large it may be, is cooled and softened. Likewise, if finely ground sulfur, enclosed in a linen cloth, is cooked in good wine for two or three hours, and afterwards is well rubbed or ground with the fingers, squeezed out, and dipped into the wine again—and this is repeated until the wine becomes white like milk: <margin>Sulfur cooked in wine removes burning and buboes.</margin> cloths soaked in this liquid and applied to the swelling extinguish and remove the burning along with the pain and the entire swelling more powerfully than anything else. And note, saltpeter should be bound to the pulses. If the same thing is drunk with parsley water <note>original: *aquâ petroselini*</note>, it will extinguish internal burning and drive away narcotic sleep.

What do you think now of the pharmacists' recipes? Sulfur and salt are surely the cure for the plague—not fifty or a hundred "simples" <note>Individual medicinal herbs or ingredients used on their own.</note> heaped together into a single medicine. <margin>Simples should not be heaped together in abundance.</margin> For that attempt is too reckless—to thrust so many ingredients into one recipe. For the unskillful and cruder common folk are persuaded that when so many ingredients are taken in one medicine, it must be that, because of the sheer quantity, if one does not help, another will.

<margin>A rebuke of physicians.</margin> Away with this ambitious "composition" of the art! For they do not remember that the force of one ingredient often blunts and destroys the power of another. A woman does not need more than one man to conceive offspring; indeed, many men and various women corrupt the offspring. See for yourself and test the matter: mix various and different seeds, crush them in your usual way, and bury the crushed mess in the earth. You will produce no fruit from them. It is no different in medicine. For the patient is the field. Medicine is the seed. The physician is the sower. Health is the fruit.

But understand further what I criticize and rebuke in your recipes. In your Herbals, you judge herbs far too clumsily, saying: "this herb is hot in the first degree, moist in the second; that one is hot in the second, dry in the third or fourth; this one is dry in the first, cold in the second, third, or fourth," and so on. Even if you have designated all these things with the utmost exactness, your opinions clash so hostilely with one another that no consensus appears anywhere. This is demonstrated by the variety of your writers and authors, each of whom takes a private judgment for himself, contrary to the others. And yet you constantly cry out that your method is certain, constant, and uniform...

## TRACTATE I.

...to have a form: which, however, exists as more confused than any patchwork quilt <note>original: *centone quouis confutior*; a 'cento' was a poem made of scraps from other works, here meaning the system is a messy collection of fragments.</note>. For if degrees were to be dispensed according to your rules and directed against the four humors <note>The four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were the foundation of ancient medicine, which Paracelsus sought to replace.</note>, it would be necessary to compose a prescription in this manner: **Take** <note>original: *Recipe*</note> a herb hot in the first degree, which is simultaneously moist in the second; to this, add another, moist in the first and hot in the second. In this way, surely, two degrees (namely hot and moist) would be joined, and only two **simples** <note>A "simple" is a single medicinal plant or ingredient, used on its own rather than in a complex mixture.</note> would be used. But if, in truth, a remedy must be accommodated to the four humors, it should be composed like this: **Take** a herb cold in the first degree and dry in the second; add one dry in the first and cold in the second. And this, finally, would be a proper and industrious prescription made from four things.

But how often is it noted in your prescriptions that barely a "one-and-a-half" degree <note>original: *sesquialter gradus*</note> (as you call it) abounds or emerges in them? For if your "certain" degrees are compared by arithmetic, all your prescriptions—fashioned from so many and such numerous simples—appear to be composed only by chance and in the hope of a good outcome; as if, in the composition, if the third ingredient does not help, the twentieth or thirtieth might contribute something. Thus, you fashion no remedy in which there is not either a surplus of one-and-a-half degrees or a deficiency of one-and-a-quarter. Consequently, you corrupt the very degrees established against diseases. Since you bring judgment upon yourselves through your mutual disagreements, who else should eventually judge you?

<margin>Certain remedies should not be many.</margin>
Meanwhile, the experiences of the peasants prove that it is not a multitude of ingredients, but the certainty of simples, established by experience and truth, that settles the matter. He who affects the praise of a legitimate and industrious Doctor should learn what conjunction of herbs—that is, the "stars" in the firmament—the prescription describes and contains; thus, by the same effort, it will happen that he also knows and understands what the conjunction of terrestrial stars—that is, the composition of herbs—actually is.

<margin>A two-colored flower of a herb possesses two virtues, etc.</margin>
For any herb whose flower exhibits a double color is also of a double virtue <note>original: *virtutis*; in this context, "virtue" means the medicinal power or property of the plant.</note>. The same reasoning also applies to three colors and three virtues. And these are the true degrees that exist—not "cold, hot, dry," and so on—but form, color, anatomy, and finally the seven degrees and the taste of salts.

<margin>The degrees of herbs which are true.</margin>
And you ought to make these degrees ready and tested for yourselves. Then, since any herb can also be reduced into three parts by the aid of art—into **sulfur**, into **salt**, and into **liquor** <note>This refers to the *Tria Prima* (Three Primes) of Paracelsian alchemy: Sulfur (the soul/flammability), Salt (the body/solidity), and Mercury/Liquor (the spirit/fluidity).</note>—sometimes a certain herb reduced to sulfur ought to be administered and is required against a disease of that kind; sometimes sulfur and salt from one simple; sometimes all three, having first been reduced into the aforementioned essence. Consult **Alchemy** <note>original: *Alchimiam*</note> regarding these things, and you will be taught them fully and clearly. For, to speak of metals, even if you elicit salt from lead through extraction (which can be done very easily with wine vinegar), you will nonetheless have nothing but **Alum** <note>original: *Alumen*; a type of chemical compound, often potassium aluminum sulfate, used as an astringent.</note>.

<margin>How many and which diseases Theophrastus can cure with a single simple.</margin>
I, however, can cure thirty-two diseases with Alum alone. Thus, the sulfur and Mercury from the lead remain for me: from each of which, separately, I truly know how to heal eighty-seven ailments, etc. And with the salt of **Wormwood** <note>original: *Absynthij*</note>, I can perfectly heal fourteen diseases. With the sulfur of Wormwood, six great ones, and those of contrary types. Through its Mercury, however, which I call the "liquor of Wormwood," I have healed over one hundred and six ailments, as I recall, completely and successfully. And yet, that exists as a single simple. And indeed, in the cities of Saxony—Brunswick, Hildesheim, and Goslar—even the laity and the peasants in the villages know how to prepare it; by which they even excel and achieve more than all of you Doctors. From this, finally, judge what "degrees" are.

For in all your books, nothing else is handed down except that "hot, cold, moist, and dry" are repeatedly hammered in. I do not deny that it is true that every disease is either excessively moist or dry. But if, for that reason, the matter were such that only "cold" were useful against "moist and hot," or "hot" helped against "cold," certainly even then there would be no need for that multitude and heap of simples. Now look: if someone were to read your Herbals, he would note more than 50 or 100 virtues assigned to a single herb. And yet, the prescriptions you write against one disease often take 40 or 50 simples. If it continues in this way hereafter, there is no doubt that your disciples in future years will sometimes heap 300 or 1000 simples into one remedy. For even in my time, this "joining together" has grown so strong, whereas previously only six or at most seven simples were used—naturally, the first for the heart, the second for the liver, the third for the lung, the fourth for the brain, the fifth for the gall, the sixth for the kidneys, and the seventh for the spleen. And these formulas for remedies were the best and most praiseworthy. But afterward, when they had learned to give "three times three" to make nine, they also began to believe...

...also, six times six, to make thirty-six. And indeed, from that trial, multiplication so delighted them that you would not know whether they value summation, addition, or multiplication more.
