# CHAPTER III.

I promised earlier that I would reveal to you the signs of this disease, and especially that which is constant and <term>pathognomonic</term> <note>A medical term meaning a specific sign or symptom that allows for a definitive diagnosis of a particular disease.</note>: it is of this sort. If you wish to discern whether a person is naturally enchanted: take a thread of two or three cubits <note>An ancient measurement; roughly the length of a forearm.</note> and fold both ends together. With the thread thus doubled, encircle the patient’s neck and measure its thickness. Having taken this measurement, lead the single thread from the crown of the head down to the nose. And if this person is chaste and has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, yet the measurement proceeds beyond or sticks out past the nose: whether it be a man or a woman, know that they are truly enchanted. If, however, it happens otherwise, then the disease exists naturally, even without sorcery. But if that measurement is tested in a husband or a wife—that is, one who confesses to being guilty of intercourse—then if the thread led over the crown of the head ends exactly at the tip of the nose, that person is enchanted beyond any doubt. Now that this sign has been pointed out, I trust you have fulfilled your desire. For no more words need to be made about these things, since the matter itself is easily understood when placed in the open. In this way, measurements are also taken of fornicators, adulterers, the chaste, and the lustful. Therefore, many secrets can be revealed to you through this kind of measurement. Only see to it that you do not demand that everything be "pre-chewed" <note>An idiom meaning Paracelsus wants the reader to do their own thinking rather than being spoon-fed every detail.</note> and fed to you.

## OF AUREOLUS
### PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM,
## ON THE PLAGUE, WRITTEN
->*For the city of Sterzing.*<- <note>Modern Vipiteno, Italy; Paracelsus fled here during a plague outbreak after being forced out of Innsbruck.</note>

# THEOPHRASTUS VON HOHENHEIM
Professor of Sacred Theology, and Doctor of both Medicines,
->to the Reader.<-

Not without cause, Reader, has it happened that I have written this book with such great faithfulness. For if you had seen my condition and state, you yourself would not have kept any secret hidden. I do not here express the books of the ancients perfectly and to the letter; nevertheless, I bring the present and modern <term>constellation</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, the "constellation" refers to the current astronomical and environmental conditions that influence the character of an outbreak.</note> back to its own harmony and foundation. Even if the "sons of Minerva" <note>A poetic term for scholars or medical students.</note> born from the schools of Montpellier and Salerno might be knowledgeable in some part of these things, all remedies were by no means found by them immediately in the beginning; rather, a later age finally produced them—individual remedies, to be sure, for each new assault of disease, as Astronomy and Philosophy themselves evidently prove. I have concealed nothing here that could be reduced to a brief compendium, although this present year has involved me in great and intolerable misery. For malevolence, force, and snares had pressed upon me too heavily, and nearly overwhelmed me. Driven by this injustice, I hastened to travel to foreign regions without delay. And (to give you a brief account of my journey) I first visited Innsbruck. Since that place suited my condition well enough, I moved my feet from there and, having reached Sterzing, I encountered among others two patrons and intimate friends: one called Kerner, and Marcus Poschinger. They received me with all duties of humanity and, because the plague was testing that region, they asked me—considering my poverty—that I might teach and communicate a way of averting and turning it away, as much as possible. Oh, truly happy pledge, which returns its master—

Therefore, I decided that no <term>arcanum</term> <note>From the Latin "arcanum" meaning secret; in Paracelsus’s work, these are powerful alchemical secrets or "keys" to nature’s healing power.</note> should be suppressed. I have always followed this moderate rule: that each day should have its own care, and that tomorrow should find its own specific pledge.

But, Reader, do not let my poverty and want offend you. Leave that burden for me to bear. Thus, when I undertook this labor at the request of my friends, I dedicated the little book in the manner you will understand from the following letter. But what happened to me? The same that happens to those who mix themselves with bran: they are devoured by the swine and pigs. Two things were held against me as faults: *poverty and honesty.* My poverty was mocked by their own magistrate, who perhaps once at Innsbruck <note>original: "Oeniponti"</note> had seen Doctors walking in the courts of princes dressed in silks and waved fabrics, rather than parched in the sun, ragged and torn. Thus, the sentence was passed: I was not a Doctor. Because of my honesty, the public crier or Parson plucked at me in a sermon, because I am not a "grandson of Venus" <note>original: "Veneris nepotulus"; a euphemism for a womanizer or someone devoted to lust.</note> nor do I know how to play the market. So I was received with insults—not indeed by the council and the people themselves, but by that man I mentioned. Therefore, having changed my location, I turned toward Meran <note>original: "Meronam"</note> along with *Marcus Poschinger*. There, the doors of both honor and fortune opened wide for me.

From this, Reader, you can judge what forced me to betray and reveal my secrets. For if you were struggling with a similar poverty and hardship, you would surely pour out even a weight three times greater if you had it hidden away. If indeed I had been gifted with professorships, benefices, and similar comforts, I could have been a Harpocrates <note>The Greek god of silence and secrecy, often depicted with a finger to his lips.</note> and kept my mouth shut. Since these were lacking, however, I had to try whether I could ransom myself with a ready pledge and console my poverty. But even this turned out badly. For instead of a pledge, I pawned my very self. Thus, I have poorly scattered my pearls. Yet if this little book of mine had been delivered to the council and the people whole and with as much faithfulness as I wrote it, I would certainly not have paid the penalty for either my honesty or my poverty. But even a wagon is overturned, though it rests on four wheels. Then the saying of Christ came to my mind: "Woe to him who falls and has no one to lift him up." For that was clearly my lot. Therefore, Reader, hold these secrets—drawn from my *Archidoxis* <note>One of Paracelsus’s most important alchemical works, detailing the "arch-doctrines" of medicine.</note>—in high regard, and study the art, its preparation, and experience. Given at Meran.

### TO THE HONORABLE, LEARNED, AND
->prudent Lords, the magistrate and council of the city of Sterzing, etc.<-

Not without merit, prudent and honorable men, have I dedicated this little book to your honor and for the benefit of all the people. For at this time, a significant nursery of the plague is revealing itself, which—as the influence of the heavens and the properties of the lower globe clearly threaten—could break out into a much more foul evil. Here, however, I deliberately reject those certain books about the order and cure of the plague that are circulated everywhere; they lack all foundation and bring no profit to anyone. For those are nothing but empty labor, if one looks at the result. This is something I, as a Doctor, must absolutely warn and bring forward. For since God, the Father of bounty and the giver of health and disease, testifies to His kindness and mercy toward us through medicines—and even confirms us in His word that the Physician was created by Him, and Medicine produced from the earth, as the wise man noted—because of this, since the sick have need of a Physician, I deemed it necessary and useful to write a brief order for the plague with the most proven recipes, as I noticed a significant lack of them among you. My aim here is to describe the virtue and efficacy of the Medicine itself rather than to hunt for the grace of words. If these recipes of mine are prepared, administered, and used according to our instruction and doctrine, I do not doubt that the greatest part of the sick will return to perfect health and wholeness. For they were discovered by me through exquisite investigation, and proven and established through long use. Although I have previously treated this same material in the University of Basel, the use and reason of the matter require that every sky and region be separately brought into one harmony and compared; this I have performed here with singular industry, so that the <term>inclination</term> <note>The astrological influence or "tilt" of the heavens affecting a specific geographical area.</note> agrees and matches perfectly with the recipes themselves.

Thus, prudent and learned men, I have divided this little book into four parts, omitted the idle trifles familiar to others, and set forth every necessary point, so that each thing can be more easily and correctly grasped and understood by all. I trust...

### By what means the Disease should be briefly recognized and cured.

<margin>Two types of plague.</margin>
<margin>Internal and external.</margin>
**F**or the recognition of the disease, take note that the plague is twofold. One lies hidden within. The other breaks out externally. The internal type shows no outward signs. In this kind, a rapid burning heat, an immense headache, and similar symptoms grow strong. The external type appears behind the ears, under the armpits, or in the groin. Thus the cure is also twofold, each type of plague having its own. In the beginning, the signs must be observed in this manner: <margin>Signs of internal plague.</margin> Shivering, heat, delirium <note>original: "phrenitis"</note>, and the absence of marks in the three locations mentioned above denote the internal plague. <margin>THE CURE</margin> In this case, <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The practice of opening a vein to draw blood, a standard medical treatment of the time.</note> is not performed in the same way as it is for the external plague; rather, three veins are to be opened: the one at the thumb for the head, the Median vein, and the one at the little finger for the liver. If all three are not opened, then at least one <margin>Bloodletting.</margin> should be done, or two, according to the Physician’s advice.

Afterward, attention must be paid to other signs, namely the behavior, gestures, and complaints of the sick person, according to which the medicine must be established and directed. And first, the following potion shall be given, from which they will sweat. This sweat should continue for at least four or five hours. In this way, the blood will emerge purer and more sincere, and the infected humors will be driven out through the sweat.

Once this is done, the "accidents" <note>Secondary symptoms or complications arising from the primary disease.</note> occupying the patient must be looked at and considered. <margin>Removal of sleep.</margin> For instance, if they are overwhelmed by a deep, narcotic-like sleep, it must be removed in this way:
$\text{R.}$ <note>The symbol for "Recipe" or "Take."</note> *Betony,*
*Marjoram,*
*Sage,*
*Wild Roses,*
*Elderflowers, one handful of each.* <note>original: "M j" standing for "manipulus unus."</note> Let them be boiled in equal parts of wine and rose vinegar until they bubble somewhat. Wring them out and place the herbs upon the head. When they have cooled, soak or heat them again in the aforementioned wine and vinegar, and apply them once more. This should be repeated frequently. Thus the lethal sleep will soften, it will become natural, and it will vanish without harm.

<margin>Restraining vomiting.</margin> If, however, vomiting should infest the patient, it should be inhibited by these remedies:
$\text{R.}$ *Hops, 3 handfuls.*
*Red Mugwort, half a handful.*
*Juniper berries, 1 handful.* Let all be thoroughly pounded; add a double quantity of wine, work them together with a spoon, and let them boil mixed in a pot. When removed, apply them while hot in the manner of a plaster with a cloth over the <term>praecordia</term> <note>The area of the chest over the heart or the upper abdomen.</note> for the space of half a span. If they cool, let them be heated again and reapplied. All these remedies must be diligently prepared and administered before the potion is given, so that the vomiting of the potion may be avoided.

But if the patient complains of pains in the sides, and these do not soften after the first potion, the same potion must be given to them a second time, four hours after the first sweat has finished. <margin>Mitigation of stitches in the side. Marmot fat, etc.</margin> Thus the "stiches" will be eased, and the body will be further purged by a more profuse sweat. It would also be beneficial to smear the aching side with <term>marmot fat</term> <note>original: "adipe murmentorum." A traditional Alpine folk remedy used for aches and respiratory issues.</note> and to apply warm cloths several times. In the absence of this fat, let <term>Bolus</term> <note>A medicinal clay, likely "Bolus Armena," used to treat inflammation.</note> and Sandalwood be placed in rose water, half an ounce poured into half a pound of water. Add one drachm of Camphor. Soak a red cloth in these and apply it to the side.

<margin>Cure for headache.</margin> If the patient complains of headache and wakefulness, the vein of the big toe of the right foot should be cut if it is a man; the left, if it is a woman. And the following remedy should be applied to the head:
$\text{R.}$ *Outer bark of the root of Henbane, half a handful.*
*Nightshade,*
*Stonecrop, half a handful of each.* Let them boil in half a measure of wine and half a measure of rose vinegar, until a quarter part is consumed. Soak linen cloths in this decoction and apply them warm to the head; when they dry out, soak and apply them again. You will repeat this until rest and sleep overcome them. Cloths of this kind are also to be applied to the right side, so that the heat of the liver may be blunted and drawn out.

<margin>Cure for headache.</margin> <note>The marginal note here repeats "Cure for headache," though the text shifts to treating a mouth/throat condition.</note> If signs of <term>Prunella</term> <note>Likely "thrush" or a severe sore throat/mouth infection common in plague victims.</note> appear (as often happens), take 6 or 8 live crabs and three or four handfuls of stonecrop. Let them be thoroughly pounded together in a mortar and express the juice. With that juice, [moisten] the tongue...

you shall rub and wash the tongue diligently, and also give a little of it to drink. In this way, the <term>prunella</term> <note>original: "prunella." A medical term used in the Renaissance to describe a parched, blackened, or inflamed tongue and throat, often associated with high fevers like the plague; similar to "thrush."</note> will be soothed and removed. Likewise, small white plums, which the Germans call *Zibartlein* <note>The sloe or wild plum (*Prunus domestica subsp. prisca*).</note>, should be distilled in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A chemical apparatus used for distilling liquids.</note>, and a spoonful or two of that water should be drunk from time to time. If these are lacking, larger plums may be substituted.

<margin>Sloe plums; a water against prunella</margin>

Aside from the "accidents" <note>In medical terms of the time, "accidents" were the symptoms or secondary conditions arising from a disease.</note> already mentioned, there are not many others that require internal care. I have reviewed them for this reason: so that it may be known that these same symptoms can sometimes bring about death, even if the plague itself has already departed. Such things, as I have said, are deep sleep, immoderate wakefulness, delirium, vomiting, prunella, and so on.

<margin>Signs of the external plague.</margin>

Furthermore, pay attention to the signs of the **external plague**, if it develops into <term>Apostemes</term> <note>Large inflammatory swellings or abscesses, specifically plague buboes.</note>. In this case, along with the aforementioned medicine, the following should be employed. There are three stages to consider. For it breaks out and tends outward in three places. First, it breaks out like a bubo lurking under the skin, which can be moved here and there by touch. Next, it rises into a swelling, consistent and fixed, either by the power of medicine or by Nature herself, by whom the entire matter of the plague is expelled and driven into a single center. Thirdly, it matures and bursts.

<margin>The Cure.</margin>

In the **first stage**, this process should be followed. Take half an ounce of <term>opopanax</term> <note>A medicinal gum resin obtained from the herb *Opopanax chironium*.</note>, let it be dissolved in vinegar, cooked into the form of a plaster, and applied. By this, the bubo will be drawn out. In the **second stage**, when it is gathered into one center, take a **Toad** that has been thoroughly dried in the air or the Sun. Apply it directly to the swelling. There, it will swell up and extract the poison of the plague through the intact skin, and it will be completely filled. Once thus filled, let it be cast away, and another fresh one applied. No one should be disgusted by this medicine. For it has been so ordained by God that the poison is extracted by the toad. For in this way, **evil is drawn out by evil**.

<margin>The Toad: a wondrous remedy for the plague.</margin>

In the **third stage**, when it is near to maturing, take fir cones, the tips of larch, and marshmallow root. Let them boil in water for two hours. Let the water be poured off or collected and cooked anew: from this, let a plaster be made. When applied to the swelling, it quickly matures it and draws out the pus, nor does it allow any of the plague to return inward to the heart. After the plague has been purged, this medicine must be insisted upon until it is completely healed. Take two egg yolks and two spoonfuls of leather scrapings: let them be thoroughly stirred together until they become an ointment. Let this be spread on linens and applied in the morning and toward night for as long as it takes until it is healed. And this order of remedies must be followed diligently and zealously, so that the medicine applied may be of benefit.

->Preparation of a sweat-inducing potion, to be administered in the plague.<-

<margin>Sweat-inducing potion.</margin>

Take: *One measure of the best sublimated wine <note>High-proof distilled alcohol or "spirit of wine."</note>, which when lit leaves no fat behind.*

| | |
|----------|----------|
| *Best Theriac* <note>A famous ancient "universal" polypharmaceutical electuary used against poisons.</note> | 6 ounces |
| *Myrrh* | 2 ounces |
| *Coltsfoot Root* | 3 ounces |
| *Spermaceti* <note>original: "Spermat. Cati." A waxy substance found in the head cavities of the sperm whale; used in ointments and medicines.</note> | |
| *Sealed Earth* <note>original: "Terra sigillata." Medicinal clay, often stamped with a seal, used as an antitoxin.</note> | ½ ounce each |
| *Swallow-wort Root* | 1 ounce |
| *Dittany, Pimpernel,* | |
| *Valerian Root* | 3 ounces each |
| *Camphor* | 1 ounce |

Let all the mixed ingredients be cast into a clean glass, and let them stand in the Sun for eight days, well-sealed. Give half or a whole spoonful of this to the sick person, according to the person’s condition. Let them be well covered, and let them not take food or drink for the space of six hours; and let the things written above be done.

---

->*An addition by which the prescribed water is made sweeter, its virtue increased, and the potion is taken more easily and safely.*<-

Let good, pure **Tartar** <note>Potassium bitartrate, a sediment from wine fermentation.</note>, finely ground, be distilled twice through a glass alembic. From this water, pour half the amount into the quantity of the previous potion, mix well, and use as was said.

In this drink, prepared in the said manner, the highest defense can be placed. For its power, according to nature, cannot be further intensified. It is known and used by few: but its power and operation are inexpressible.

## CHAPTER II.

->Regarding preservatives; that is, certain unique points on preventing the plague.<-

**A**lthough many preservatives are proposed by many, and adorned with many words: nevertheless, they do not seem to me to be of great value. For some say that the air, which is the enemy of nature, must be corrected. This, however, cannot be done. For the pestilential air is so powerful in its penetration that it creeps in and enters much more along with fragrant things. For it seeks that which is similar to itself within. Therefore, the state of the air should not be considered as much as the proper fortification and strengthening of the internal body. In the same way, neither changed food nor drink can change anything.

<margin>The air is corrected in vain during the plague.</margin>

<margin>In what the preservation of the body consists.</margin>
No mortal plague can be turned away by these external means. Since, therefore, the preservation of the body does not lie in external things, but the whole pivot <note>original: "rhombus"; here meaning the central point or crux of the matter.</note> and hinge of the entire matter turns on fortifying the internal parts: to achieve this, it will be entirely advisable that the "subject" <note>The "subject" refers to the physical state of the body and its humoral balance.</note>—for the plague attacks in three places—be first removed and taken away, in which the plague exerts its power and tyranny. Such things are an *excessive heat of the blood*, and all diseases lurking in the body. To remove these conditions, the best and most concise <margin>The best preventatives.</margin> preventative is to drink hot, on each of six days, one <term>drachm</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce.</note> of the potion prescribed above with wine or similar liquids, and to sweat vigorously in bed. This potion protects for six days.

<margin>Myrrh.</margin>
Furthermore, he who uses Myrrh continuously—either chewed and swallowed in the mouth, or the quantity of a hazelnut drunk in wine every day before dawn—is safe. <margin>Coltsfoot root.</margin> One drachm of <term>Coltsfoot</term> <note>original: "Tussilago." A plant long used in traditional medicine for respiratory issues.</note> root eaten with ginger in the morning on an empty stomach also protects for 24 hours. And although someone using these preventatives might occasionally be attacked by the plague, they are cured with easy labor and safely. Those accustomed to baths and <term>scarification</term> <note>original: "sacrificationi," a likely typo for "scarificationi." This refers to the practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw blood or fluids.</note> should keep that custom, but let it be done separately, away from a gathering of many people.

It is no wonder, however, that those compelled to care for the sick and be near them are infected by the air and breath of the sick. To prevent this, one visiting the sick should chew <margin>Frankincense. Masterwort.</margin> frankincense in the mouth, and place a root of <term>Masterwort</term> <note>original: "Magistrantia," also known as Imperatoria. A herb believed to have great protective powers against poison and infection.</note> in the sick person's mouth. In this way, the root and frankincense will allow no poison to prevail.

And those preventatives are for the elders. However, the preservation of the young, infants, and the like should be established in this way: No food should be offered to them in which some powdered myrrh has not been mixed. For myrrh benefits infants and the young more than adults.

<margin>Garlic. Nut. Rue. Rose vinegar. Theriac.</margin>
There are also known preventatives for the common folk and the populace: such as garlic eaten often in vinegar during the day. Likewise nuts, wild radish, <term>rue</term> <note>A bitter herb used in ancient medicine to ward off contagion.</note>, or a draught of rose vinegar; or even maintaining no memory or imagination of the plague. Furthermore, myrrh and <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "poly-pharmaceutical" ointment or potion used as an antidote to poison.</note> mixed with <term>distilled wine</term> <note>original: "vino sublimato," referring to aqua vitae or brandy.</note>, drunk twice or thrice in a week.

Many are also seized by this disease whose temperament and nature have no affinity with it. For such as these, so that their fear may be removed, they can be strengthened more than they can be tested by other medicines. For them, the most excellent and best preventative is ground <margin>Red coral.</margin> red coral, and a half drachm drunk in wine every twelve hours. If so great a supply of coral were available that everyone could obtain it and use it in this manner, <margin>Praise of red coral.</margin> not even half the people would be infected. But enough now concerning preventatives.

Indeed, a regimen of food, drink, air, and other things, though it does no harm if correctly established by good advice, nevertheless these mentioned are the principal and chief secrets, which, if correctly applied, will undoubtedly allow infection to be avoided.

### CHAPTER III.
->On some other diseases coinciding with the plague.<-

<margin>Diseases that concur with the plague.</margin>
**I**t frequently happens that during a time of plague, three other "foreign" diseases flood in and concur: such as blood-blisters, <term>phlegmons</term> <note>Spreading inflammations of the soft tissue.</note>, and stitches in the side. These are by no means the plague itself, but they erupt during its time, stirred up by <term>celestial influence</term> <note>original: "influentia coelesti." In medieval and Renaissance medicine, the alignment of stars and planets was believed to cause epidemics and seasonal illnesses.</note>, even though they would have erupted on their own at later times anyway. Because these kinds of diseases are uniquely brought forward by the plague before their appointed time, and are no more to be looked down upon than the plague itself, they shall be dealt with as follows.

For the diseases that "pinch the side" <note>likely pleurisy or similar respiratory pains.</note>: the prescribed potion must be administered against them. When the sweating is finished, the vein of the little toe on the same side must be cut immediately, and the blood should not be stopped until it changes to a third color. Although this disease is by no means the plague (though many judge it to be so), it is nonetheless subject to the same remedies as the plague.

With blood-blisters, one must proceed in this way: Take a sapphire, <margin>The use of sapphire.</margin> and move it slowly in a circle around the external tumor for a quarter of an hour. A black circle will appear there. When this appears, stop. The tumor will come to a head <note>original: "suppurabit."</note>, and all the poison will be extracted. If a sapphire is missing, a crystal, shining like the sun, should be moved around in the same way, and the same result as the sapphire will be achieved. Even if a <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "Phrenetis," a brain fever or delirium.</note> or other similar disease should concur, nothing else needs to be specifically applied for them. For in this one way, all things are removed.

### CHAPTER IV.
->In what manner those more desperately infected are to be specifically<-
->recognized: to whom, nevertheless, their own remedies<-
->must also be decreed and administered<-
->during the plague.<-

**Pregnant women** are in a dangerous state during the new moon; they are less at risk when the moon is waning.

For women, the eruption of menstrual flow during a waning moon portends more evil than a flow occurring while the moon is waxing.

If the plague seizes a person in its own <term>zodiac sign</term> <note>Medical astrology was central to Renaissance medicine; each sign governed a specific part of the body.</note>, it is more lethal than if it seizes them in other signs: for example, in Aries or Taurus, it attacks the **Head**; in Gemini or Cancer, the **armpits**; in Virgo or Scorpio, the **groins**; and similarly in Aquarius and Pisces.

If foreigners are infected in Aries, Gemini, Leo, or Sagittarius, they will be in greater danger.

If "ruddy" <note>Those with a sanguine or reddish complexion.</note> men are inflamed in Taurus, Leo, or Capricorn, it is worse.

If those of a darker complexion are infected in Libra, Sagittarius, or Pisces, it is dangerous.

If older adults are attacked during a full moon in Pisces or Aquarius, it is an evil omen.

If the more delicate and infants are overwhelmed by the disease toward nightfall, they will suffer more severely than if they are attacked during the day.

Those who are "rotten inside" <note>Likely referring to a pre-existing state of "putrid humors" or chronic internal infection.</note> will scarcely escape.

Those who are healthy, endowed with "praiseworthy blood," and accustomed to good food and drink, if they are infected in Leo, Aries, or Capricorn, they will fall seriously ill.

Those of a "thicker nature" <note>Referring to a phlegmatic or heavy constitution.</note> accustomed to harder foods, if seized, will be more endangered in the sides than in the two other locations.

An angry Leo, Taurus, and Sagittarius will be ominous.

But the suitable and appropriate remedies for each, besides those handed down above, now follow.

---

The care for pregnant women, beyond what was said above, shall be accomplished by a drink of red wine in which <term>steel has been quenched</term> <note>Red-hot iron or steel dipped into wine was believed to infuse the liquid with strengthening, "astringent" properties.</note>. She shall drink no other drink. She shall also place a **Bloodstone** <note>Hematite, traditionally used to stop bleeding.</note> in her hand, which they shall change from time to time, transferring it from one hand to the other. They shall continue this for a very long time, and she shall not neglect the medicines reviewed above. One should also cast **Coral** into the "steeled" wine, and they shall drink from it. They shall avoid all meat dishes.

Women who are seized during the time of their menstrual flow should be "fumigated"; let them mix **Great Plantain** with its roots and rose water, and drink from it three times, always with eight hours in between. Thus they shall turn away the evil.

Those who are attacked under adverse signs must be succored immediately by the application of **dried toads**. <note>Toads were commonly used in plague amulets or plasters, believed to "draw out" the poison of the pestilence through a sympathetic attraction.</note>

Help will be provided to all the rest in general by the following described powder, which is also singularly beneficial for those with the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>.

Often, "stoppages" or obstructions of the body <note>Constipation.</note> also occur: this should terrify no one; nor should <term>clysters</term> <note>Enemas.</note> or purgatives be used. At the very least, let a drink of **Senna** be taken, and let suppositories be applied made of soap, or egg yolks mixed with salt wrapped in a small cloth.

#### Powder against the childhood disease or Epilepsy.

> ℞. Two <term>drachms</term> <note>About 7 grams.</note> of ground red **Coral**.
> One drachm of burnt **Hartshorn** <note>Deer antler.</note> tips.
> One drachm of the **bone from a stag’s heart**. <note>A small, cross-shaped cartilage found in the hearts of older deer, highly prized as a heart tonic.</note>
> One drachm of burnt **Ivory**.
> Two full spoonfuls of distilled **Lily of the Valley** water. Let them all be mixed;
and if the disease is felt, let the patient drink of this three times, once every hour.

### Concerning Food and Drink.

No meat shall be offered to these sick people, no eggs, no fried things, and no fish: but only, after the first drink, broths made from water mixed with **Rose Vinegar**, or if something similar can be prepared from **Barley**. One should not attempt to achieve anything here with foods. For there is no agreement between food and medicine. Nor can food be of any benefit here. It is better to administer something unpleasant and loathed than what the patient craves.

As for drink, **Barley Water** is most useful. All others should be avoided. However, water of **Speedwell** <note>original: "veronica".</note> or **Blessed Thistle** <note>original: "cardui Mariae".</note> administered instead of barley water or other drinks is also beneficial for the thirst.

### Conclusion.

**S**o then, most prudent and most learned Lords, I have included in this brief little book this counsel concerning the plague—proven and established by long and lasting experience—omitting all trifles. I wished to dedicate and write this to your name and honor for the benefit and profit of all people. If there should be anyone who has decided to undertake the care of the sick according to these prescribed remedies, let him meet with me and hear a fuller instruction, which I offer of my own accord. And although the present day does not yet demand a more <term>exquisite</term> <note>original: "exquisitiorem"; in this context, it means highly refined, complex, or specifically tailored remedies.</note> system of remedies, provision must nevertheless be made for future events. I hope that I have gratified you in no small way by this zeal of mine; and so, I promise myself that you, all and each, will be well-disposed and favoring toward me.
Given at Sterzing <note>A town in South Tyrol (modern-day Italy), where Paracelsus stayed and wrote during a plague outbreak in the 1530s.</note>.

# THE TWO BOOKS 
## OF PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS 
## PARACELSI
## ON THE PLAGUE AND ITS SYMPTOMS
<note>original: "De peste et huius accidentibus." In Renaissance medicine, "accidents" refers to the symptoms or side-effects accompanying a disease.</note>

#### TO THE READER.
#### DOCTOR THEOPHRASTUS.

**R**egarding the plague, benevolent Reader, many things delivered from ancient ages or even 4,000 years ago have undoubtedly come into your hands. But it is only too clearly evident that a true and genuine description—and thus a fundamental explanation of the matter itself—has been delivered by no one as of yet, as it should have been. This is abundantly testified by the same backward care, the disordered regimen, and the unskillful nature of both preservation and cure. Therefore, all those books will not in the least stand in the way of my very free discourse on this matter. And although very many have built their doctrine upon that foundation, it is nevertheless pure and simple sand, which will be minimally constant or durable in a time of rushing storms. 

Indeed, whatever books are to come forth hereafter, if they are built upon that same foundation and do not accommodate themselves to this following basis, they will all be fruitless to the sick. For reflect within yourself, Reader, how many and how immature the books, treatises, and procedures are that have been published and dispersed until now by those spurious doctors of both former and present times. Their entire principle is established upon dreams and fatuous imagination, to which those who boast that they are Masters, Doctors, and even the Gods of Medicine, have later sewn their own useless and fictitious experience. They do this so that their art might be sold everywhere to the people as if it were certain, established on foundations, and consistent with its own principles; and so that a license for talking nonsense might then lie open to them, more certain and abundant. 

You, however, Reader, will not take it with an ill mind that my preface traces these things further back from their origin. For that manifest imposture of theirs must not be hidden—an imposture by which, in their wild state, they would not hesitate (I know well enough) to scoff at this my theory and practice. For to despise and find fault with everything is their one and only art. But if you yourself, Reader, would apply your own judgment and conscience to weighing each point, you will clearly see how many books, polluted by foul impostures, have reached us—those of Rogerius, Bartobalia, Guido, Lanfranc, Theodoric <note>These are "old guards" of medieval medicine and surgery: Roger Frugard, Guy de Chauliac, Lanfranc of Milan, and Theodoric Borgognoni. Paracelsus famously rejected their reliance on ancient Greek and Arab authorities.</note>, and others like them. 

How much more will books published on the plague be impostures, when those which handle the treatment of lighter and daily diseases are so far away from the true foundation? If these men prove useless in understanding the generation and cure of diseases, how much more sterile and dry will be those who promise the consideration and cure of the most grave disease of the plague? In like manner, the <term>Barbers and Bath-keepers</term> <note>original: "Rasores & Balneatores." In the 16th century, these were lower-tier medical practitioners who performed minor surgeries, bloodletting, and basic treatments, often without formal university education.</note> do the same; swollen with pride, they make much of themselves and consider themselves to be without any blemish, even though in all their counsels and administrations they display neither foundation, nor science, nor any experience. In explaining the powers of natural things—which alone the sick person seeks from a physician—they are entirely naked; indeed, they are blocks of wood. Their ambition and audacity have gained such strength that they now dare, without any shame, to describe and treat not just this or that disease, but all of them. Who is there anywhere who cannot judge that from truth itself and a certain understanding of the art—which resides in far deeper matters...

<summary>Paracelsus concludes a brief practical guide on the plague written in Sterzing and introduces a larger theoretical work. He uses the preface to denounce traditional medieval medical authorities and unlearned practitioners as "impostors" who lack a foundation in natural science.</summary>

It maintains the continuity of his argument that true medicine is found in "works" (results) rather than the "empty talk" of established authorities like Galen or Avicenna.</meta>

<page-num>402</page-num>
<header>TO THE READER.</header>

*...and deals with more refined goals, such people do not devise such things, but rather out of mere ignorance, opinion, and confidence? It is indeed lamentable that their dreams are valued so highly everywhere: to which even the Doctors themselves lazily turn a blind eye. Thus, one may gather that they are much more unrefined and ignorant than common barbers and bath-keepers. <note>In the 16th century, "barbers and bath-keepers" were low-status medical practitioners who performed minor surgeries and bloodletting; Paracelsus is insulting university-trained doctors by saying they are less skilled than these manual laborers.</note> And who among these accomplices would dare to pull a speck from another's eye? So, a triumph is deservedly decreed for those "lice-catchers" with their cobbler’s pitch, horse hooves, and the like. So too, the palm of victory is rightly extended to the Doctors themselves, in their sweat-inducing powders, in potions, and in bloodletting. Although these things should not be rashly brought into contempt—for their favor is great, but their merit is thin. However, the greatest victory over them is this: that the Creator of Medicine has arranged all Medicine into signs and works. For only the will and the work make a Physician. But "works" are too truly lacking in them. Why then should they be allowed to speak and declaim about causes and the manner of regimen, counsel, and cure, when they—both by themselves and going back to their first teacher—exist as entirely empty, barren, vain, and void of medical knowledge? Here they will seek some defense and support from Apollo, Machaon, Hippocrates, etc., who performed admirable works in Cos and other regions. But what if I consider such things as "Legends" (as they call them) or not? Let it be so: let those men have performed miracles. Meanwhile, who would believe that those Secrets and Great Wonders <note>original: "Arcana & Magnalia"; Paracelsian terms for the hidden powers of nature and the great works of God.</note>, through which they accomplished so much, were written down by them and have reached us handed down through the centuries? Their writings, which we have received, are mere talk, not very pregnant with art.* <margin>Avicenna and Galen are triflers.</margin> *Who then would fix their foot in them? I say nothing of the fact that Avicenna and Galen are triflers and word-jugglers. <note>original: "Logodaedali"; a term for someone who uses clever language to deceive or distract.</note> And Galen especially, a rhetorician, never reefed or gathered the sails of his "Asiatic luxury." <note>A classical reference to a flowery, over-embellished style of speaking/writing.</note> Thus, Reader, through this introduction I would wish you to be warned, lest through some imprudence you submit your gullible neck to the yoke previously mentioned. Let this always be before your eyes and mind: that a Physician without signs and works cannot stand, nor can he prepare a lasting name for himself. But those "works" are the things to which I now lead you. To smile sweetly and charmingly at the sick is not a "work," it is a deception. Although I could easily be persuaded that, since all medicine has now turned into smooth-talking, the same might not be entirely disagreeable or displeasing to you. If, therefore, you judge trifles and nonsense to be art, you will undoubtedly never follow me here. Meanwhile, I am not unjustly a serious exhorter to you regarding all these things. For God himself is magnified through works; and he likewise created Medicine from the earth. Truly, he did not create it as a spirit, but concealed and hid it in bodily matter. Therefore, the works of the hands will testify to the truth of the mouth. Upon this, my following purpose is founded. Read and re-read these things, and do not let the labor of it weary you. Let the magnitude of the disease (which does not allow itself to be neglected) move you to follow the truth, not trifles. Therefore, act as a fair judge.*
->Given at Nördlingen.<-

## BOOK ONE
# OF THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM,
### DOCTOR OF BOTH MEDICINES.
<note>original: "Utriusque Medicinae Doctoris"; this refers to being a doctor of both Medicine and Surgery, a distinction Paracelsus often emphasized to show his practical experience.</note>
### *On the Plague and its Symptoms.*
#### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>Medicine is twofold.</margin>
**S**ince in Medicine we have found nothing other than what instructive Nature has taught us, it is worth the effort that we, after God, should especially love and consult her. For what is greater and more holy than to love and honor those who, after God, instruct us with good precepts? Since, therefore, not man, but speechless and mute creatures give birth to the Physician, you must know that Medicine is twofold, or consists of two parts: from the Light of Nature; and from the Fragments, which fall like crumbs beneath the table. The distinction for recognizing both types of Physician is placed in this. <margin>The nature of the natural physician.</margin> He who works according to the Light of Nature <note>The "Light of Nature" is Paracelsus's term for the innate knowledge of the physical and spiritual world granted by God to humanity through observation and intuition.</note> abounds in both Philosophies, namely of heaven and of earth. How great a science he is endowed with can easily be gathered from the fact that neither life, nor health, nor disease, nor death are hidden from him. <margin>The nature of the fragmentary physician.</margin> But judge how greatly the other part is defective from this: they have experiments ready and prepared, but they lack the diseases which might match their experiments. That is to say, the art is ready for them...

<summary>Paracelsus finishes his polemical preface by dismissing classical authorities like Galen as "word-jugglers" and then begins Book One by defining true medicine as rooted in the "Light of Nature" rather than academic fragments.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, Plague, Light of Nature, Galen, Avicenna, Medical Philosophy, Nördlingen, Medical Ethics</keywords>

--- Page 446 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the general introduction to the first specific book on the plague. Paracelsus begins to outline his anatomical theory of the plague, specifically targeting the traditional Galenic belief that plague symptoms (buboes) originate from the "principal organs" like the heart, liver, or brain. He argues for a more localized, chemical understanding of the disease.</meta>

<page-num>403</page-num>
# BOOK 1. ON THE PLAGUE.

...they think they are Physicians, provided that suitable diseases are presented. But what kind of art is this, which flows away and vanishes before the required disease even approaches? Therefore, they are not Physicians, but mere experimenters. On the other hand, the nature of Medicine is this: as often as a disease occurs, so often is the art or Medicine ready and prompt against it. If you know the disease, you also know the art. But if you do not know the disease and the art, how easily you can be deceived! Hence it follows that one must first speak and teach about the disease, and afterward about the art or remedy owed to that disease. Thus, these matters are distributed into two books. And unless nature herself taught us by this indication, all diseases would certainly be hidden from us. So here in the plague, through the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lumen Naturae) is a central Paracelsian concept referring to the innate wisdom and visibility of the natural world, which a physician must learn to read.</note>, she teaches us the same from the place she has occupied—what its origin and cause are.

<margin>The location of the plague indicates its origin. Three locations of the plague.</margin>
And if we do not know or understand this place, everything we attempt will be vain and useless. There are three locations of the plague: namely, the regions of the **Ears**, the **Armpits**, and the **Groins**. Before I proceed to declare these, I promise that I will remain on the path of nature herself. It follows, therefore, that it is not at all clear that the plague is a disease or infection of either the brain, the liver, the spleen, the heart, or organs similar to these. The common opinion that has long prevailed is that the plague behind the ears arose from the brain; that under the arms, from the heart; and that in the groins, from the liver or spleen. This is a great error. For if the ailment of those organs were the plague—as they think—how, I ask, could the urine remain silent about them, which nevertheless can by no means hide the diseases of those parts?

<margin>Plague is not a disease of the principal organs.</margin>
<margin>Urine and blood remain good in the plague.</margin>
For this is proved by the established rules of urine, which hunt down and investigate all diseases to the highest degree. Furthermore, the constitution of these parts by nature is such that if infection or plague occupied them, those same parts would exhibit many other signs and indications. In the same way, you also order <term>Minutions</term> <note>original: "Minutiones", a technical term for bloodletting or phlebotomy.</note> of those organs, and yet you find no fault in the blood that is let. For it cannot be said whether those treatments are useful or useless, since they turn out just as they do in healthy people, whether well or poorly.

<margin>The brain and heart are very distant.</margin>
One more thing remains to be pointed out. Consider for yourselves the nature of the brain and the nature of the heart, and see by what great intervals they are distant from each other—truly as different as white and black. Yet, without regarding this, you apply your medicine, which can bring nothing but death. If a medicine were to benefit the brain and conquer its plague, it ought to destroy or throttle the plague of the heart, [but] those two plagues are distant by such a great interval. Understand similarly regarding the liver and spleen. But if you say: the plague is one and the same, in whatever place it occurs, and therefore one medicine benefits all, and there is no need to look to particulars or specifics—know that this has no place in Medicine. For it is necessary to consider the infected body and the medical infection, no differently than wounds, which entirely require knowledge of their site, from which the infection and the medical treatment of the infection may be distinguished. Therefore, the plague is not attributed to those organs.

<margin>The brain is not emptied through the ears. The heart not through the armpits. The liver not through the groins.</margin>
For the brain is not purged through the ears, nor the heart through the armpits, nor the liver and spleen through the groins. For <term>Anatomy</term> does not allow such things. Furthermore, the plague is not a disease of "superfluity" <note>In traditional medicine, diseases were often blamed on a "superfluity" or excess of bodily humors.</note>, nor is it a humor, nor is it an infection, but it is an **intoxication**, from which <term>Apostemes</term> <note>original: "Apostemata", inflammatory swellings or abscesses, referring here to the buboes characteristic of the plague.</note> arise; without this intoxication, no apostemes can be born. And here lies the <term>central core of the art</term> <note>original: "artis rhombus", a Latin idiom for the heart or most difficult part of a problem.</note>. In the same way, you also usually say: "let the choleric beware"; "now infection will touch the sanguine"; "the melancholic will hardly escape"; likewise, "the phlegmatic will be heavily infected." But what do such things matter to the Physician, which were not established by Physicians? For if we wish to speak of the seizure and assault of the plague, we certainly have no surer knowledge by which to say, "*you beware; you protect yourself; you flee*," than what we have concerning a bolt of lightning or thunder. We have found that it is born in the upper heaven. We also know that it will rush downward. We know even the strength of its vibration. Moreover, we are also convinced that everything it strikes, it breaks and burns; yet exactly where it will strike, we are utterly ignorant. Therefore, from the vibration or the throw itself, we can by no means distinguish what kind of person, what temperaments, what cities and houses it will strike separately, unless it is predicted by chance. Therefore, it is not at all proper for us to speak of these things, as they oppose the Light of Nature. And if by chance some astronomical Philosopher wishes to predict that the "*Saturnine*" or "*Martial*" <note>People whose temperaments or fates were thought to be ruled by the planets Saturn or Mars.</note> people should beware, etc., that is rash. For it has never been revealed to any mortal who that Saturnine or Martial person on earth is, at whom the star above aims as if at a target. All these speeches have flowed from imaginary experience. And thus, it is advisable and healthy...

<header>ON THE PLAGUE.</header>

...I judge it necessary that vanities and errors of this kind, which have been held as foundations until now, be cut away and removed, so that the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>The "Lumen Naturae," or the innate wisdom found in the natural world that a physician must learn to observe.</note> itself is not obstructed or disturbed in its works by any stumbling block.

### Chapter II.

<margin>The location of the disease.</margin>
Because it has been demonstrated thus far that it is necessary for the Physician to take his science and art from the evidence of nature, it is clear that the *Location* of the disease itself entices and leads the Physician into its own region; nor should any other part of the body, besides that one, be proposed or inspected. Thus, nothing further is to be sought outside that region, but in the same way that the location of a wound exhibits in itself <margin>He teaches through Theory and Practice.</margin> **Theory and Practice**, and afterwards shows its own symptoms as well; in exactly the same way, the plague must also be understood. For the plague is a wound, inflicted by superior powers <note>Paracelsus refers to the "upper" or celestial forces as the source of the plague's "blow."</note>, <margin>Similarity between a wound and the plague.</margin> which is in no way different from a wound inflicted by men. Indeed, they share one and the same theory, one and the same practice of a single method, and are separated only by the mode of operation and the simple remedies—a distinction that stems from this: that one blow is from the heavens, and the other from men. Now, if the plague is to be called a wound by the Physician, a comparison of both seems necessary. Both can be studied so that the specific property of the location may be known. For there is one Medicine that heals a wound; likewise, there is one that heals the plague. But here such a thing occurs: you see that this wound or that one is mortal. What other cause is there for this than <margin>Location makes a wound lethal.</margin> the location, which is closest to the principle or root of life? This is where the other Medicine looks, which becomes more powerful than <term>Balsam</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Balsam" refers to the internal life-force or preservative fluid of the body that allows it to heal itself.</note>. So too in the plague, a local accident occurs. Now you see, in turn, that many things coincide: inflammation, fevers, paroxysms, delirium, spasms, flowing menstruation <note>This likely refers to hemorrhaging or abnormal discharges associated with the disease's progression.</note>, chronic heat, sometimes obstruction, diarrhea, etc. All these are <margin>The symptoms of a wound.</margin> symptoms of a wound, along with many others. And what are symptoms here are also the symptoms of the plague. From which it follows that the <term>Physician</term> <note>original: "Physicum" — here meaning a doctor of natural philosophy.</note> must practice his physical art surgically. He who removes inflammation from a wound acts surgically. Now, however, the cure is twofold: surgical and physical. From this I conclude that the naturalist-physician is the surgical Doctor and surgeon of the plague, and not a false surgeon.

But leaving these things aside, I want you to be advised by this example regarding the practice to be established. Although I am not dealing with the cure here, this example is nevertheless introduced to more clearly declare and understand my following purpose. Now, in this chapter, I urge this: namely, that the wound must be proved and knowledge of its location compared, so that the plague does not arise in any other place than where it has been said. To demonstrate this, I will propose such an example. You have also learned from other books I have written that the <term>Great Creature</term> <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe.</note> is the <margin>The Macrocosm is the parent of the Microcosm.</margin> parent of the **Microcosm** <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>. From this it follows: there are four parts in the Great Creature. Therefore, there are also four parts in the Microcosm. Furthermore, know that every like thing encompasses its own like, not <margin>Like acts upon like.</margin> something different. This is **Anatomy**, which must be known entirely by the physician so that he can compare the Microcosm and the Great Creature with each other. Now, three of these parts are not to be looked at; but the fourth, however, is a portion of the part of the heavens—that is, near the ears, the armpits, and the groins. Therefore, the heavens seize their own part. And just as there are various parents in the heavens, so too various parts are seized, the number of which we can hardly grasp. Know this about it: that the parent of the Microcosm divides itself into various intoxications. But the point here is to explain and understand the example, in which the location alone is understood, since the boundary and the location are one thing—that is, one Physical Body. It is as if someone said: a wound is inflicted where the sword strikes; that is how it is. The superior weapons, however, strike that which is their own subject; <margin>Action requires a suitable subject.</margin> just as a lightning bolt, if it strikes, burns nothing except wood. For wood is the subject of fire. Rocks feel no damage. This example must be understood in such a way that the Microcosm is led into the parts of the Great Creature. You, however, should not think that the Microcosm is merely flesh; but look at this: that the Globe of the earth has its parts, and yet the earth is one. The Microcosm is the same. Now take this example. Rain falling from the sky <margin>Rain only becomes grass in the earth.</margin> works neither on rocks, nor on sand, nor on wood, but works in the earth alone. It pours its power into the earth, enters it, takes on its property, and becomes grass within it. So it is understood of man also: those impressions are not received unless a suitable subject is ready. Nor is this different from a situation where someone is wearing armor and is struck in that place where he was naked. For thus the whole body is armored against the pestilential impression, except for those <margin>Three locations in the body are naked.</margin> three <insert>places</insert> that are naked.

...those places are naked and open. For there the disease manifests that naked place, from which manifestation we ought to know the cause and the remedy <note>The original OCR reads "ficarium," which is likely a corruption of *pharmacon* or *remedium* (remedy/medicine).</note>. Sudden death or a greater or lesser illness follows this perfusion, just as one wound is larger than another.

## CHAPTER III.

Since, therefore, no cause or infliction of the disease is detected other than the heavens, it must now be understood above all else how the heavens reach us. For there is a different meeting or conjunction of the planets and our bodies when they are to be made ill than that which was said regarding rain and the earth. Although there is a similarity in this: that just as a rainstorm arises from invisible things and becomes visible, so also the weapons of heaven that wound us are invisible, yet they penetrate the body like rain or a storm—not from the outside, however, but from within the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," or the human being, viewed as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>, so that this impression is to be understood no differently than the former. If it strikes a dangerous place, it becomes dangerous and mortal itself. I introduce this chapter with this goal alone: that we may gain certain knowledge of the entry or ingress of the heavens into our bodies. Therefore, consider the matter in this way: The Microcosm was made from the four parts of the <term>Great Creature</term> <note>The "Macrocosm," or the universe at large.</note> no differently than a son from a father. Therefore, the son also retains the properties of the father. Man also shares this likeness with the Great Creature.

<margin>
Man is the son of the Microcosm.
</margin>

The son and the father are divided and constitute two persons. Likewise, man and the heavens constitute two heads—that is, two senses. This is brought forward for the following declaration: thus the heavens consist in a natural conjunction with man, so that man and the heavens are of one nature, differing only in sense. The heat of the sun changes nothing in the nature of the microcosm; likewise, its cold changes nothing.

<margin>
The origin of the plague is not from the natural.
Dropsy and fever are natural diseases, not the plague.
</margin>

For the origin of the plague is not produced from natural humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to control health.</note>; nor is it drawn out from that which is natural within the heavens and man. Indeed, <term>dropsy</term> <note>Edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> and fevers can be produced from natural causes, such as from immoderation in food and drink, which is a natural origin; just as other diseases which can be generated in the four parts of the Microcosm arise and dwell naturally in nature itself. But the reasoning in the plague is not at all the same. For here there is no harmony of natural conjunction. From which it is concluded that here nothing proceeds naturally in such a way as if the blood were infected, by looking to the father and the son—as often happens elsewhere, that a son inherits the diseases of the father. We, however, do not inherit this disease from our first father, the Great Creature; nor does it arise from a natural influence, as if some Physician were to say, "putrid air makes putrid bodies subject to many diseases."

<margin>
Imagination is the principle of every Magical action.
</margin>

It is well enough known to you what a strong <term>imagination</term> <note>For Paracelsus, imagination was not just "make-believe" but a potent spiritual force that could effect physical change.</note> can do and create; it is the principle of every magical action. You also have discovered what power or efficacy lies hidden in <term>characters</term> <note>Sigils, symbols, or written charms used in Renaissance magic.</note> and similar things. Yet the origin of these, as has been said, is not natural; and yet they have the power to inflict a <term>contracture</term> <note>A permanent shortening or hardening of muscles or joints.</note>, etc., and to heal other diseases which they did not previously stir up. A similar judgment must be made regarding the origin of the plague. All these things are laid out so that it may not be carelessly said that Saturn is sick, and therefore his sons will be sick; or that Jupiter is strong and healthy, and therefore his sons must necessarily become so. Rather, this should be said: the heavens are healthy; yet through them, their sons are gravely injured. The same must be understood regarding a strong imagination. For this disease is not recognized here by its origin in any other way than as one is known to be harmed by another without grasping or contact—that is, physical contact—even though a physical boundary exists.

<margin>
Medical Magic is not to be despised.
</margin>

Let Magic never slip from your minds, you Physicians. Nor should it move you that the ancient authors make no mention of it in their commentaries. For mention is nowhere made of the entire <term>Cabalistic art</term> <note>Paracelsus refers to a form of Christian Cabala or mystical wisdom used to understand the hidden signatures of nature.</note>, which is a part of Magic, through which the great and wonderful works of **Apollo** <note>Apollo was the Greek god of both healing and plagues; here he represents the archetype of the physician-magician.</note> were performed.

<margin>
The Cabalistic part of Magic, from whence the works of Apollo were done.
</margin>

Therefore, it is right that their humors be despised, because this disease is not inflicted in a natural way. It is one thing to describe natural diseases, and another to describe supernatural things, of which kind the plague is.

<margin>
What supernatural nature is.
</margin>

For this similarity must be held everywhere: that you attribute to nature itself that which we might call "supernatural," just as if someone were to magically compel, incite, or harm another. For this is the origin to which the plague seems comparable.

## CHAPTER IV.

You are compelled to have known a great force, and also to assign to it a singular power...

# BOOK I.

<margin>
The Intermediary required in the Magical art.
</margin>
...you are compelled [to see] that, just as anger, which conquers its own master, harms his health, so too can another person who strives and thinks upon it harm that same health. Nothing goes out from man himself against another man unless it operates through the *Intermediary* <note>original: "Medium"; Paracelsus refers to an invisible spiritual or astral link between two points.</note> of those two. Whoever can touch or strike the *Intermediary* between himself and his enemy conquers his enemy according to every desire, even without a sword. From man, the operation departs into the influence. And from this, an impression proceeds, just as the *Intermediary* has been touched. In this order, the plague remains.

<margin>
What human emotions produce in the heavens.
</margin>
For all our envy, jealousy, hatred, anger, and lust ascends backward to the superior great mysteries <note>original: "magnalia"; refers to the vast, hidden powers of the universe or God’s works.</note> in which generation is situated. You see by what means a son can provoke and move a father. That anger either breaks out in the father or in the son. If the father does not "digest" the anger, he pours it out upon the son.

<margin>
How supernatural diseases are created in heaven from us.
</margin>
In the same way, it must be known that supernatural diseases also take root. There was never any plague in heaven; but all supernatural diseases arise in and from us, and while still ineffective, they penetrate into heaven. They are generated there, and from heaven they fall back down upon us again.

<margin>
The Astronomer prophesies.
</margin>
To understand these things more easily, note the power of Astronomy, which prophesies the plagues that are about to settle upon us. From where does it predict this? From this alone: that heaven has been infected by men. The Astronomer indeed sees this infection, yet the origin of the infection lies hidden from him. For it ascends from the earth into heaven.

<margin>
Regiomontanus predicted the French disease.
</margin>
By this reasoning, *Regiomontanus* <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a famous mathematician and astronomer.</note> predicted the assault of the French disease <note>original: "lues Gallica"; a common historical term for syphilis.</note>. For this disease first arose in man, was afterward prepared in heaven, and was finally poured out upon the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," meaning the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. From this preparation in the heavens, he prophesied. Note the same thing here concerning the plague.

<margin>
All things happen through the Intermediary.
</margin>
A man who lies sick: death can naturally be predicted for him. This could not have been done at all before the assault of the illness. Thus all things happen through the *Intermediary*, without which man does not have natural knowledge. Therefore, it is clear from this that no power can be ascribed to the stars themselves, since they are a false *Intermediary* in matters of this kind. For unless we ourselves infected the stars through our imagination, no impressions would settle upon us. In the same way, if a son does not provoke his father, he finds him calm and mild. But if he moves him to anger, he creates an *Intermediary* out of the father, which inflicts upon the son that which the son himself impressed into the *Intermediary*.

<margin>
The Microcosm, parent of man.
</margin>
Nor is there any other reason or truth here than that the heaven of the <term>Great Creature</term> <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe at large.</note> is our parent, and we are born from it.

<margin>
Magic reveals supernatural diseases.
</margin>
Therefore, a magical incantation proceeds from us into heaven, and from heaven it returns to us. And thus, magical understanding is the light from which the entire foundation of supernatural diseases is declared. Outside of this understanding, physicians err evidently and enormously in their description of the plague. However, that foundation is different from the one by which Prophets prophesy, being separate from the Astronomers. For instance, if a Prophet predicts a coming plague before the infection of the Intermediary, it is the same as if he said: "You will offend your father." That is: "You men living on earth will infect the stars with your lust; the stars, in turn, will send the plague upon you." That is, they will send you that disease which you yourself generated in heaven. From which it is clear that we ought to think of nothing else than that we men are reserved for the rod <note>original: "ferula"; a schoolmaster's rod or switch used for discipline.</note> of our parent. For God indeed made us men from the Great Creature; but nevertheless, he established us in that parent in such a way that we must die within it. If we now contract a disease from our parent, it is necessary that we also receive the remedies for those diseases from the same source.

<margin>
Death is more than diseases.
</margin>
For death is more than diseases. If the outcome of events itself proves that we cannot be without our parent, nor are we exempted from it by God, it must be known that this same supernatural parent has also received the power of punishment over the son. Because we are not yet liberated from the parent for the sake of death, we shall not be exempt from its rod. We ourselves see the strikes of the rod. But the cause, having arisen in us, strives toward heaven, and from there it is rolled back down upon us again.

<margin>
Twofold diseases: of Blood and of the Rod.
</margin>
Thus, therefore, there are twofold diseases to be borne by us: by reason of heredity (the blood) and by reason of the rod (punishment).

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>
The minerals of the Microcosm are the matter of diseases.
</margin>
Since all parts of the Microcosm are minerals, know that for the sake of finding the causes of diseases, those minerals are what pass into the matter of the plague. Whence it happens that all infections are determined minerally. Now, if the minerals themselves are the matter, the cause of this disease will also be conceived and generated in that place which was spoken of above. Since, however, many minerals exist, it must be known that the "sinning matter" is nothing other than sulfur. For all bodies consist of three things <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>. Their intermediary is sulfur, which will remain established without any contradiction. This at least will be ambiguous and obscure to you: by what means sulfur becomes such matter. What else is *Mars* <note>In alchemy, Mars represents Iron or the aggressive, fiery principle.</note> than a type of sulfur...

<margin>Sulphur is the material of the plague.</margin>
...the spirit of sulphur? The momentum now rests on this: whether a bodily spirit can be made, which occurs only in a supernatural disease. For it is necessary that the spirit becomes corporeal. Yet the spirit remains in its own place. Those are the three places about which we spoke above. This spirit is similar to the heat flowing from the sun and igniting through the Intermediary <note>original: "Medium"; the invisible link between the celestial cause and the physical effect.</note>. The body is the thing that is ignited; the body that sets fire is sulphur; the sulphur that causes burning is Mars <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, Mars is associated with fire, iron, and the "bile" or choleric heat of the body.</note>. Thus, there is not just one sulphur, but many parts of the firmament are involved.

<margin>Various kinds of sulphur.</margin>
And although there is one body that is ignited, the Physician need not concern himself with it. For what is the sinning matter <note>original: "Materia peccans"; a traditional medical term for the substance causing a disease.</note> but sulphur alone? And since Saturn has sulphur, and the Moon and the other rulers <note>referring to the planets that "rule" or govern specific organs.</note> likewise have parts of the body, it follows that many sinning matters are established. Healing is found in sulphur, and from the same, Mars is also pacified. For what power does steel have after the blow has already been struck? The evil is located in the sulphur, and it is this that must be averted. If, therefore, Mars is the steel of sulphur and

<margin>Sulphurs are three principal types, etc.</margin>
sulphur is the plague: now the distribution will be found from these. Generally and in total, three sulphurs are detected. For the groins <note>original: "Inguina"</note> contain *Antimony*, the chest regions *Arsenic*, and the ears *Marcasite*. These, of course, are the materials that the physician must know above all. For this is the plague. If someone were harmed or stung by a scorpion, who, I ask, would say otherwise than that there are two poisons here: one outside, the scorpion itself; one inside, the spirit of the scorpion. For this, it is necessary that the Medicine is not applied to the exterior. I propose this instruction so that you apply Medicine only for the mortification of the spirit of the scorpion. The same reasoning must apply here for knowing the sulphurous types, so that the sulphur itself might be extinguished and the supernatural disease within it cured, without considering the body of the location itself—that is, the vein, nerve, flesh, etc. For these themselves are not the plague. Now, the ignition of Mars is the anger of the great creature <note>original: "magnae creaturae"; likely the Macrocosm or the world-soul.</note>. As for why sulphur is the plague in that place: learn it by this way. Although the signs demonstrate it well enough, there is yet another indication at hand, greater and more powerful, by which the other common signs are proven.

<margin>Twofold sweat.</margin>
It is of this sort. You know that sweat in the body is twofold: flowing through the pores,

<margin>Of Pores and Emunctories.</margin>
and flowing through the *Emunctories* <note>term: "Emunctories"; the lymph nodes and other organs that expel waste. Paracelsus links plague swellings (buboes) to these sites.</note>. That which flows through the pores has nothing to do with the firmament. But that which flows from the emunctories (as in the three mentioned places), that is the sweat of sulphur, which is the plague. Now, the mineral parts are distributed equally in every limb; however, in this place, there is a single subject. The reason why that ignition produces nothing other than the plague is the same as in the Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent that could kill with its gaze; Paracelsus uses it to explain how "unnatural" generation creates deadly poisons.</note>. It is generated from an excellent tincture, against and above Nature itself.

<margin>The Basilisk is born without a mother, from the yolk of the father.</margin>
For it lacks a mother. Thus, if sulphur is ignited, and a mother is not lacking, then nothing but fevers are generated. But if the mother is absent, and the father alone generates, then the sulphur is changed into the plague, just as the yolk born from the father becomes a Basilisk. Poisons that are generated without a mother penetrate through all bodies without contact. The sight of the Basilisk kills; so too

<margin>Comparison of the Basilisk and the plague.</margin>
the sight of Mars. And just as the former's sight operates materially, so the spirit of Mars operates equally. And just as the power of the Basilisk is peculiar and diverse from all poisonous natures, so too a different and diverse poison is created through Mars in the plague. And from this, of course, such great difficulties have arisen in the writings of those authors who undertook to comment on the plague, because they were ignorant of the generation of the Basilisk. It would have been necessary for the man to be a Microcosm <note>term: "Microcosm"; the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, and that his generation did not agree with this. Thus, man is forced to concede that if Mars generates the Basilisk of heaven in its own yolk, which is sulphur (according to the Magical process), then this thing which strikes and sees is the plague itself. For where the eyes are turned, there they look. That gaze which it achieves, it conceives and feels the blow. Happy is he, and he remains unharmed, who withdraws himself from those eyes.

## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>What the signs of the plague are.</margin>
**S**ince signs manifest and betray every disease, know that the signs of this disease are also easy to recognize. For what is it that is betrayed similarly to the Basilisk? The first sign is a change of mind, with public signs impressed and concurrent.

<margin>Change of mind.</margin>
If two of these signs concur, know that the Basilisk has struck. Afterward, the Transmutation begins—that is, the power and property of the poison breaks out to stir up Apostemes <note>term: "Aposteme"; an abscess or swelling, specifically a plague bubo.</note>, which are not only visible on the outside but operate similarly unseen on the inside. By these, the beginning of this blow or infliction is sufficiently known. Since, therefore, no signs other than these are required to recognize the beginning, we must now turn to the accidental signs. The way of recognizing these is no different than that of wounds...
