...of accidental wounds, which are not the wound itself, but merely its accidents <note>In early medicine, "accidents" (accidentia) refers to the secondary symptoms or complications that follow a primary injury or infection.</note>. Therefore, the nature of Medicine is twofold. For just as a wound inflicted by a sword indicates nothing other than the site of the injury, the rest of what follows does not belong to the wound itself, but has both a different origin and a different cure. For this reason, these signs themselves must also be examined, so that they may be brought back to their own proper cure, even outside of the aforementioned poison. Among these accidents is the paroxysm, which is similar to <margin>Shivering.</margin> inflammation, shaking with a shivering like a fever. The cause of this is that the Minerals, through their evaporations, pervade the entire body and cannot find an exit. From this, something similar to an earthquake occurs, and the whole body is <margin>Delirium.</margin> shaken. Likewise, Delirium <note>original: "Phrenitis"; an inflammation of the brain or a state of frenzied madness.</note> is also an accident, occurring if the great heat of the poison has penetrated the brain itself, as well as the veins, the blood, and the reason. For then reason is, as it were, terrified, and the animal nature becomes ferocious, according to the measure and mixture of the poison. These <margin>Dizziness.</margin> are almost always preceded by bouts of dizziness. Similarly, all sulphurous accidents also coincide, in the manner of arsenical poisons; which are followed later by obstructions, diarrhea, and so forth.

<margin>By what signs the Plague may be known.</margin>
But so that you may know those signs exactly and from their very foundation in all these cases, pay attention first to the nature of the signs of the poison of Mercury. Afterward, to the signs of Arsenic. Thirdly, to the signs of the Asp <note>The "Aspis" likely refers to a specific toxic quality or "venomous" mineral characteristic rather than the snake itself.</note>. From these three, all plagues are distinguished. And, as was handed down above, because these signs are common to no other disease—especially regarding the location—they will be easily apparent to anyone, particularly if the timing and the frequency of the outbreak coincide. For since we ourselves provide the cause for this plague, the greatest part of us is also usually seized by it. It does not creep sporadically into a few like other diseases; rather, it rages commonly and popularly on account of a common guilt. These things having been sufficiently explained thus far, we shall bring them to an end, and turn next to the cure of the disease already declared.

# BOOK SECOND.
## Preface.

<margin>They were ignorant of the Ancient Cabala.</margin>
*SINCE in the books of the ancient Authors nothing is found handed down that can truly be of protection and help to us, it is entirely right and necessary that we further refine and illuminate our foundation and doctrine, and finally shake off the errors and poverty of the ancients. For since it is publicly known to everyone that they were utterly ignorant of Cabala and Magic <note>Paracelsus refers here to "Magia" and "Cabalia" as the spiritual and hidden sciences of nature, not "sorcery" in the modern sense.</note>, no one should doubt that they were merely imaginary Physicians, who did not even glimpse the origin of this disease through a lattice window. I will not deny here, however, that some of their Experiments have come down to us, which certainly should not be rejected because of their usefulness; yet those prolific writers were by no means their inventors and authors. They could not weigh those matters more deeply than as they received them from their predecessors, with which they also adorned their own worthless books so that they might gain some dignity from them. These experiments are to be entirely accepted, and the books themselves—the dross—are to be left behind. I have already emphasized many times that* <margin>Chiromancy is the discoverer of arts.</margin> *Chiromancy <note>The art of reading lines, applied here not just to hands but to the "signatures" or patterns in all natural things.</note> is the discoverer of the Arts, if it is treated Cabalistically. Similarly, so are Physiognomy and Anatomy, if they are explained according to a Magical interpretation. For in this alone is the art of composing Recipes established. Furthermore, the ancients' method of composing according to "degrees" <note>The traditional Galenic system of classifying medicines as "hot," "cold," "moist," or "dry" in various degrees.</note> is also found to be erroneous. They were caught up in customs. Therefore, it would be right for the "Discoverer of Arts" to be placed here at the beginning, to more fully understand the teacher of nature herself. But because the Light of Nature requires a separate, universal volume and does not wish to be explained in a piecemeal way, I desist from that plan in this place.*

*I will propose at the beginning certain preparations, as it were, for the preventative regimen and the cure. Afterward, in their own chapters, I will teach the regimen separately: the preventative in its own, and the curative in its own. Finally, a private chapter will be dedicated to the Accidents themselves, and nothing that seems relevant to the matter will be omitted. You, therefore, read these things with attention, and hold in a mindful soul the difficult Theory of the first book—namely, the untamed and invincible Basilisk impressions <note>The "Basilisk" effect refers to the way the plague "strikes" its victim through an invisible, lethal influence, like the gaze of the mythical serpent.</note>; the healthy, fixed, and Etnean flame of Sulphur; and the three harmful minerals of Antimony, Arsenic, and Marcasite. And let this brevity not offend you. For since you sell yourself as a Physician and a Surgeon, there is a presumption that you are also an Astronomer of these four parts, according to the Philosopher. And since practice itself makes the physician perfect, it is necessary that he also be most skilled in the spagyric art <note>The alchemical art of "separating and recombining" substances to create potent medicines.</note>. Nothing, therefore, has been omitted by me. Rather, all things have been handed down according to the requirement of the matter. Your own deficiency, however, could scarcely be supplied by all the treatises in the world.*

# CHAPTER I.

<margin>What medicinal preventatives are like.</margin>
**T**his chapter explains the **Regimen** <term>Regimen: The prescribed way of life, including diet, exercise, and environment, intended to maintain health.</term> and **Preventatives**, the knowledge of which is as follows. However, the errors which have been admitted in these matters until now must first be recognized. Their recipes for preventatives are directed toward protecting the principal organs which are infected in this disease. Therefore, several preventatives are prepared from cold and constrictive substances, with the addition of heart-strengthening remedies. But now, there is no disease in the heart, nor is the heart the seat of the plague; therefore, those medicines <margin>A reprimand of the physicians.</margin> are idle and fruitless. And although they may indeed be effective and powerful in themselves, they do nothing for this disease. Furthermore, they are to be reprimanded for this: they apply preventatives before it is known where the plague will strike, and in what place—whether near the ears, the armpits, or the groin. Thus, they wander as far as possible from the mark, because they treat with their "Pestilential pills" and other electuaries <note>original: "Electuariis"; medicinal pastes or syrups made by mixing drugs with honey or sugar.</note> those who do not yet have need of medicine. Moreover, they subject everyone to a single temperament <note>original: "complexioni"; the individual balance of humors (blood, phlegm, etc.).</note>, forgetting meanwhile the nature of the three principal parts about which they so loudly declaim. This error is therefore a gross one, lacking all probable reason, as even their own rules demonstrate. Nevertheless, it contributes no small amount to the "income of the kitchen" <note>A common idiom meaning the practice was done more for the physician's profit than the patient's health.</note>. Next, they add that after preventatives have been used, a diaphoretic <term>diaphoretic: a substance that induces sweating, believed to expel toxins from the body.</term> power is the medicine for the plague. This entire foundation is empty. For it is clear from this that they have neither correctly understood the disease nor its accidents <note>In early medicine, "accidents" (accidentia) were the symptoms or secondary effects of a disease, rather than the disease itself.</note>, but <margin>The accident [symptom] treated for the disease itself by physicians.</margin> have instead taken the accident for the disease itself. Thus, until now, no suitable remedy for the plague has yet been put forward. Furthermore, they betray themselves and their "accident" when they say that a profound "plague-sleep" follows a narcotic stupefying drug. And so they find it not inconsistent that this narcotic sleep is conquered with sweat through a diaphoretic virtue, by the work of those hot spices which are intensified and sharpened through a repeated degree of alcohol of wine <note>original: "Alcool vini"; highly distilled spirits or concentrated medicinal essence.</note>. Thus, if they have expelled the accidental sleep, they are convinced that the disease itself has been cut out. But they could easily gather even from this that they apply remedies only to the accidents, because it is necessary that they be applied within the first 12 hours. Meanwhile, it is easy to know that the virtue of medicine is by no means restricted to these 12 hours; rather, as long as the disease increases, medicine can be opposed and adverse to it. In this way, many <margin>If, the accidents being removed, nature attacks the disease more strongly.</margin> other remedies are also found which remove the accidental disease; and yet, in the meantime, the plague is not cured unless it vanishes of its own accord, here and there. That is to say, if the accident that is more sharply infesting nature is removed and taken away, then nature, having been restored and made more vigorous, attacks the disease more boldly and powerfully, as if it were an internal enemy and a thief. For the strength and vigor of internal nature drives out the primary cause—that is, the disease itself—without the accident. Regarding this power of Nature, Hippocrates wrote an Aphorism. Whether it belongs to Hippocrates himself or to Apollo, I do not dispute. Certainly, if he had not set it down, he could be regarded by no one as a true and genuine Physician. For in that one Aphorism, more things are contained than in all the rest of his books. Just as we have spoken thus far concerning the preventatives of those Physicians, so also they prescribe and command bloodlettings, baths, theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium.</note>, and other similar electuaries, with many other counsels added. However, it is a mad counsel to preserve the body with such great industry and not to wait for the blow or assault of the disease itself. For they thus send the medicine before the disease, when they do not know in what way, or with what nature and condition, it is about to rush in. For preventatives ought to be directed toward the character and nature of the specific attack. If this venture of theirs should occasionally succeed, well and good. But if it misses the mark, woe to him who has swallowed the preventative. For in this <margin>During a time of plague, nothing should be changed in the regimen.</margin> way, like will be joined to like. Indeed, the contrary advice seems to me sound and healthy: that the body should be preserved in its own strength just as it is, and not be disposed toward receiving diseases. For if one is attentive to this, the highest and safest regimen is to hold to old custom, to change or innovate nothing, to remain with a mind as undaunted as if it were outside the time of plague, to use habitual food and drink, and to change neither house nor chambers. For the imagination, if such new counsels are stirred up, can be so powerful and strong that it arouses within itself a disposition in the subject suitable for receiving the plague.

Having defined these things, I do not yet wish the doctrine of regimen to be concluded. Nor am I yet about to cut off all talk of preventatives. The reason is that I must confess that not only man himself is exposed to the eyes of the Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent whose gaze was fatal; here used as a metaphor for the contagious "gaze" or influence of the plague.</note>, but also all those things which...

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Death in the plague is twofold.</margin>
**B**efore I define anything regarding the cure: it must be known by everyone that death in the plague is twofold. And since death is the final goal of things: its diseases should be considered its forerunners. Thus, two diseases in the plague must be understood. For the plague itself brings about a peculiar death; the **Accident** <term>Accident: In medicine, a secondary symptom or complication—like a fever or a spasm—that is not the disease itself but results from it.</term> also summons a peculiar death. The Physician who does not attend to this distinction is no Physician at all. The death of the plague is not defeated by any Accidental remedies; nor is the Accidental death defeated by pestilential remedies.

<margin>What sort of death is from an accident.</margin>
This example explains how accidents produce a singular death. For there are some whom sleep destroys; there are some whom a spasm throttles; there are some whom a hiccup kills. If none of these accidents are present, know that it is truly the death of the plague. Indeed, I distinguish these things on this day so that the two diseases may be separated from one another, and its own peculiar care may be applied to each separately, so that these Accidental things might be restrained lest they bring into action the death they portend. The reasoning for the death of the plague is similar. <margin>What sort of death is from the plague.</margin> In the plague, however, there is a single death, just as there is a single cause. Therefore, any Medicine is in its proper place. In Accidental cases, deaths are varied, since the accidents themselves also exist in various forms. And their own chapters teach the method of preventing each separately. I wanted to explain these things more fully here so that the preventatives and regimens according to the advice of the ancient authors might hereafter be held in lesser and more humble regard.

Furthermore, the logic of the Regimen is as follows. No Regimen can be prescribed before the disease has occurred and is visible to the eyes. Therefore, in the plague, a regimen should by no means be established as a preventative. For this supernatural disease is different in its logic and manner from all others. <margin>The plague does not admit preservation.</margin> For in the case of dropsy <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema, or the swelling of soft tissues due to fluid accumulation.</term>, which has not yet occurred but is about to, it can be met with suitable preventatives. In the plague, the same is not true; instead, the illustrious time must be awaited. Concerning this, observe such a foundation. By the same logic that a person is infected, those things which nourish the person are also infected. Now if a Regimen is to be established, there is a need to know what is poisonous to us, or what is not. And from this knowledge a Regimen must be established, specifically in this way: that what we are about to consume is not infected. Nor can a Regimen be prescribed here with the same circumstances as is usually established in other diseases—in such a way that either little or much is eaten, this or that is eaten, wine is drunk, water is drunk, in the morning, or in the evening. For all these things must be left to the individuals' own habits, and only that which is infected must be forbidden.

<margin>The internal plague is not changed before the fourth tincture.</margin>
For once the infected matter is consumed, whether it be meat or something else, the disease is carried into the human body. For it is fixed with its poison, nor is anything changed before the **fourth tincture** <note>original: "tincturam quartam"; likely a reference to Paracelsian alchemy or a specific stage in the disease's chemical progression.</note>. Therefore, no **Humoral Regimen** <term>Humoral Regimen: A medical approach based on balancing the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) to maintain health.</term> will work here, but the Decree of Astronomy will be of use, through which it is known what is infected or less so. And he who is ignorant of this acts unjustly while he orders people either to flee or to avoid or eat this or that food—a habit familiar to those Physicians for whom that *Fen* and *Tegni* <note>original: "Fen & Tegni"; terms referring respectively to Avicenna's "Canon" and Galen's "Ars Medica," the standard university textbooks of the time which the author rejects.</note> are so authentic, along with whatever other trifles are similar to these.

<margin>Rule of the Regimen.</margin>
Therefore, the foundation of establishing a Regimen is to take away nothing except the poison. Especially in Accidental diseases, diligent effort must be given so that the aforementioned Regimen is not neglected. For what use is it if you order a barley-water <note>original: "ptisanam"; a traditional medicinal drink.</note> and the barley is infected? Therefore, keep to the prescribed order. However, another Regimen must be introduced here: it is distributed according to its disease, and consists neither in food nor drink. In a disease of this kind, food and drink are left to the judgment and palate of the sick person. For a minimum amount causes no harm, nor does too much hurt. <margin>Nature soon succumbs concerning appetite.</margin> For if Nature is about to collapse into death, it crosses the boundary of health, and either craves nothing or craves too much—which are the preceding signs of a fierce death. Furthermore, the accidental Regimen is not the observation of food and drink, but a diligent consideration of the properties of the accidental disease outside of these things. It consists in this: that you do not administer foods for nourishment, but those which do not undergo digestion. Of these...

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
How the accidents of the plague may be forestalled.
</margin>

**T**he Regimen of nourishment having now been settled, the next step is the explanation of preventatives. Against the impression of the "Great Creature" <note>original: "magnae creaturae"; here referring to the macrocosm or the celestial forces of the universe.</note> indeed, no preventative can be established. For that must be endured entirely. Therefore, the one and highest prudence is the forewarning of that death. However, to provide a preventative against the "Lower Medium" <note>The physical environment or air surrounding a person.</note> is placed within the power of the Physician. Because this agrees with the aforementioned Regimen, it would be idle to repeat it here. Now, however, something else occurs by which the plague may be forestalled in three ways. First, by preserving one from the accidents when the plague is already present. Second, by taking care that we are not infected by others. Third, by working so that we are never seized by a future plague through "caused causes."

<margin>
The noble gold preventative.
</margin>

Regarding the first preventative, understand it thus: As soon as the signs of the plague are noted, the accidents can be prevented by no other thing than the preventative of gold. For as long as that is used, no sleepiness weighs upon one, no excessive heat, no immoderate cold, nor any other similar disease. And thus, the "stroke" of the wound, when it falls, persists by itself alone without any other more serious accident. Perhaps other preventatives could also be brought forth which might prevent another death—one more to be feared than the plague itself—from approaching.

<margin>
Terror from the stroke of the plague kills more than the wound itself.
</margin>

But those things are unknown to me. Truly, as far as use and experience teach, those arts which serve to prevent the accidents have more dignity and praise than the secrets <note>original: "arcana"; refers to specialized alchemical or hidden remedies.</note> directed against the plague itself. For the "stroke" <note>The initial onset or "hit" of the plague infection.</note> moves a person no differently than if someone were struck: and meanwhile, terror kills the one touched, rather than the wound itself. By this evidence, accidental diseases are also distinguished.

<margin>
Man attracts the neighboring chaos and thus perishes.
</margin>

Secondly, it must be known that a singular "attractive virtue" is hidden within man, which must be rightly understood according to the mode or nature of Amber <term>Carabe: A term often used for amber, known for its static or magnetic-like properties.</term>. Note this example of the matter: A magnet attracts iron to itself because the iron hides its vital spirit within itself. And yet, it is not its primary food. Man also carries a similar attractive force hidden within himself, which exists on the same level as the Magnetic force. Now, therefore, man draws to himself from the outside, through that power, the surrounding chaos <term>Chaos: In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to the atmosphere or the air as a medium of transmission.</term>. From this follows the infection of the air in man. From this, understand that this magnet is the vital spirit in man, seeking an infected man if they are united outside with the "chaos." Thus, the healthy are infected by the sick through this magnetic attraction. The preventative for this is not to touch the air of the infected. Learn the matter by example.

<margin>
Sore eyes infect healthy ones.
</margin>

If healthy eyes look upon bleary <note>original: "lippientes"; eyes that are sore, inflamed, or running with fluid.</note> eyes, then the magnet of the healthy eyes attracts the chaos of the damaged eyes. Now the evil has jumped across into the healthy eyes as well. There is a similar judgment regarding other diseases. I have brought this example so that you might more easily understand the Magnetic force, which behaves in such a way.

<margin>
The Magnetic virtue is twofold: of men and of women.
</margin>

One is in men, the other in women. The Magnetic force of women is the womb <note>original: "matrix".</note>. It is that which attracts the chaos of which we have spoken. In men, the spermatic force is the magnetic force, and it is itself that attractive virtue, acting as a womb. Since we have therefore resolved to treat the preventatives of this attracting virtue in this place, it must be explained how it happens. Straw should either not be placed too near the fire, or a preventative must be provided so that the attractive virtue is put to sleep.

<margin>
A magnet does not attract in the presence of a sapphire.
</margin>

For just as a magnet attracts nothing to its beam if one wears a sapphire around the neck, until the sapphire is removed again; so it is with Amber, coagulated gum, Resin, and Turpentine. Such a preventative must also be used here, such as the Zenexton <term>Zenexton: A specialized Paracelsian amulet worn around the neck to repel the plague.</term> being suspended from the neck.

<margin>
Looking to the preventative for the fault of life.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>
The plague is a wound.

What the cure for wounds is.

Balsam of Mumia is the highest Medicine. Spirit of Gold.

Which gems are defensive.

Now, because we must descend to the actual method of curing: recall with yourselves what was said at the beginning, that the plague is nothing other than a **wound**. And this theory is true. For by the same reasoning that wounds are cured, the plague must also be brought under care. Now the cure for wounds is twofold: Internal and External. The internal is more difficult than the external. The external results either successfully or unsuccessfully. Thus, if you approach the cure of the plague in such a way that you begin externally, the matter will go poorly for you. However, if you are well-equipped from external sources with *Opodeldoc* <note>original: "Oppodeltoch"; a famous medical plaster or ointment formula attributed to Paracelsus used for healing wounds and soothing pain.</note>, you will act more safely. But the highest thing in curing all wounds is the internal **Mumia** <term>Mumia: In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to the "vital balsam" or innate healing power found within the living body.</term>. For, to speak briefly, the **Balsam of Mumia** is the supreme medicine. Next to this, the highest remedy is the **Spirit of Gold**. If the "incarnative" <term>Incarnative: A medicine that promotes the growth of new flesh to heal a wound.</term> is recognized and judged in this way, an addition must be made to it, just as in wounds, in which all accidents must be removed along with the formation of new flesh. Now if the accidents <term>Accidents: Secondary symptoms or complications, like fever or spasms, rather than the disease itself.</term> in the plague are to be forestalled, just as in wounds, it shall be done in this case by **Gems**. And just as Agrimony is used, so here use **HYACINTH** <note>original: "hyacinthus"; likely referring to the gemstone zircon or similar orange-red stones.</note>; as Pyrola, so here **RUBY**; as Periwinkle, so here **EMERALD**. For these are defensive, not incarnative. The incarnative is the Balsam of Mumia, which lies within nature itself, and which is stirred up here by the Spirit of Gold. Therefore, take heed that in the cure nothing else is to be considered or managed except that you provide a "wound-drink" for the plague, which drink is a pestilential incarnative. That is the Spirit of Gold of which we spoke, given according to its dose in diaphoretic <note>Sweat-inducing.</note> waters, mixed with the gems we mentioned. And although there are many and various other processes, no mention is made of them here. For all of those are found to be imperfect, and in this Spirit of Gold there is no defect, with which all people can be universally satisfied. I do not doubt that these things will be displeasing to our doctors. But the disgrace will be theirs, because they do not understand that from which a Physician himself is constituted. From which it is clear that, besides a bare name, they possess nothing of the matter.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>
What the cure for the accidents of the plague is.

Juice of corals, etc.

Cure of accidents.

Spasms. Menstruation. Mania. Dysentery.
</margin>

Similarly, I wish to speak of the accidents, if they should encounter you; that is, if you are only summoned after the accidents have been produced, you should proceed according to the order prescribed above, and do not wait for any time or hour, but as soon as the disease is encountered, apply the incarnative without delay according to the prescribed process. Then you shall administer a general defensive, one hour after giving the incarnative. Such a defensive is: one scruple of the **juice of corals**, half a scruple of the **juice of the bone from a deer's heart** <note>original: "succo ossis de corde cerui"; a small, bone-like cartilage found in the hearts of older stags, highly prized in old pharmacy.</note>, and half a scruple of the **juice of spodium** <note>original: "succo spodij"; a technical term for the ash of ivory or bones.</note> in **Betony water**. Through this general defensive you will ward off the accidents, lest they summon death, which they would otherwise bring in. Afterward, if by the benefit of these you are secure from both pestilential and accidental death; then finally approach the accident, whatever it may be, on the third day, if it does not depart of its own accord with its period, and proceed with it according to the nature of the type of disease. That is: in a **spasm**, give **hare’s bone**, so that it grows warm in the hand; in the flow of **Menstruation**, provide **liquid coral**; in **Mania**, give **pearl-laudanum** <note>original: "laudanum perlatum"; a Paracelsian preparation of opium combined with crushed pearls.</note>; in a **dysenteric** flow, give corrected **saffron of Mars** <note>original: "crocum Martis"; a chemical term for iron oxide.</note>; and so let it be done with the rest likewise, according to each one's process. These processes and orders are simple and common administrations, yet not previously enumerated; which have hitherto gone so far out of use that almost no one today wishes to understand them. Because truly these...

These same men will have no other certain remedies, and they are despised by them; let them lean upon their own uncertain experiments to drive away the plague, with no consolation or benefit to the sick. # PHILIPPI THEOPHRASTI
## AB HOHENHEIM.
## ON THE PLAGUE
### Three books, with certain additions by the Author himself.
### INTRODUCTION.

Among other great and serious diseases, I have next decided to treat the nature of the plague. While this is being done, the occasion will be given to us to also mark those who oppose the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: From the Greek 'mikros' (small) and 'kosmos' (world), this is the Paracelsian concept that the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe, containing all its elements and celestial influences.</term>. These men indeed, whose bare name is held out as a pretext, are not to be made much of. This must be managed above all: that the thing which they loathe and turn away from be found and named. For there is no greater protection for a name than
<margin>I mildly reprove.</margin>
its own hatred; incited by this, they try to break through and tear down the boundaries of the arts, which, however, they will never destroy. Many assaults and great noises are stirred up, but by those who are ignorant of where they are going. Therefore, I shall enter this field of treatment regarding the plague and its connected fruits without fear. Neither the whispers and cries of the opposing side, nor the stubborn defense of ancient authors, shall terrify me in the least. For they are unrefined, and lacking in science and experience; they were created and "graduated" in the Academies, and so they remain. Therefore, none of them shall cast me down. Let them direct and redouble their threats as they wish. Who would care a straw for them? For those who die of threats shall be buried by the braying of asses. <note>original: "asinorum crepitibus"; Paracelsus uses a crude pun here, as 'crepitus' can mean a braying sound or a fart, suggesting the doctors' threats are empty and shameful.</note> To defeat snakes, vipers, and adders is too light a matter; but to seize such monsters is too laborious. And it is unworthy that these men, who boast of being Astronomers, Philosophers, masters of the seven
<margin>
Astronomy,
Philosophy,
and Medicine 
are a single
art.
</margin>
liberal arts, etc., fly into Medicine with such unwashed hands <note>original: "illotis manibus"; a Latin idiom meaning to approach a sacred or difficult task without proper preparation or reverence.</note>, with no distinction made between youth or old age, and stubbornly defend that absurd opinion that Philosophy is one thing, Astronomy another, and Medicine another—when, in fact, they are all only one. Even so, Medicine has not yet been established as a whole. He who is an Astronomer ignorant of Medicine is like a carpenter who knows how to plane wood with an adze but does not know how to draw a line with a string. He who is a Philosopher but not simultaneously skilled in Medicine refers to a potter who knows how to knead and prepare clay, but not how to shape the pots. He, finally, who is a Physician and is destitute of the other two mentioned, represents a potter who has indeed learned to shape the pots, but not how to fire them. And to encompass it in a word: these are not three arts, but one art. They constitute one man, not three. Therefore, he who has knowledge of only one is vain and empty.

I bring these things forward to the end that you may know that, in the following process, disease must be understood from these parts, which are by no means separated from each other. For if Medicine, as we have said, is an art, it will not be an experiment.
<margin>
Experiment
is
deceptive.
</margin>
*For Art proves itself and is certain; but experiment is deceptive: therefore it is not even an art.* Art makes the Physician, not experiment: which only that triple Physician understands.

The followers of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicennistæ"; followers of the 11th-century Persian physician Avicenna, whose 'Canon of Medicine' was the standard textbook Paracelsus famously rejected.</note> with their accomplices, the inspectors of urine, will be greatly indignant here, I know well, because these following theorems of mine do not proceed from their own boundaries and furrows. But those furrows of theirs are difficult to thresh, nor do they bring anyone out from their field, which is entirely overgrown with thistles, by which they are repeatedly and more severely pricked. 
<margin>
Leipzig 
is noted.
</margin>
Leipzig swarms with so many and such distinguished Physicians that I know—even if the whole world were still silent everywhere—that they alone would not bear or approve of these things. And what wonder? Naturally, they alone hold the palm of all erudition, if their place is also assigned to asses and fools. But, however these things may be, Reader, put aside the dispute, read and judge, and believe nothing from your teacher without a demonstration. Once their fee is taken, they are not ashamed to lie about anything. It is not a troublesome labor to declaim for the space of one hour every day; that matter brings no callus to their hands, and they have long ago accustomed their tongues, which are naturally voluble, to this work. Therefore, Reader, do not be moved by their malice. They only set sail for their own honor and praise, and they immoderately hunt for the favor of everyone everywhere. You, truly, faithfully, and from the heart, care for your sick; do not seek their favor, but rather their health and benefit. We, meanwhile, shall fight with each other in mutual conflict—the Doctorates, the Academies, and the Professors...

# ON THE PLAGUE.

We shall roll and toss those people of Montpellier <note>original: "Monspelienfes"; Montpellier was home to one of the most famous medical schools in Europe, which Paracelsus frequently attacked for following traditional Greek and Arab authorities like Galen and Avicenna.</note> in the mud along with their "plague." But that plague is already at the gates; it is already making its breakthrough. Come forth, then! Bring out your sack and spread it open; pull out your arts and display them, so that men may see openly what you are capable of. In turn, I too will produce my arts, so that at last your frauds and lies, which you have indulged in for so long, may be brought into the light. Show yourselves as vigorous as you can. We shall fight to the blood—even to the death—over a "cat's tail" <note>original: "De cauda felina"; a Latin idiom meaning to fight over something of no value or a trivial matter. Paracelsus is mocking the petty nature of his rivals' knowledge.</note>.

## ON THE LOCATION.

<margin>Nature's sweat is twofold.</margin>
To examine this disease, nature lights a lamp for us and, furthermore, places the disease in its proper location, so that we may more closely and deeply understand what kind of thing it is. If, therefore, the location is the very first thing to be considered so that the disease may be shown to us through it, then its position and its underlying logic must be known completely. For location alone creates the theoretical understanding here, and instructs the physician on the essence of the disease. Now, regarding the location—why it is in one place and not another—pay attention to this example. Nature sends out a twofold sweat: one through the pores, which has no connection to the plague. For that sweat is merely an evacuation of the superfluous humors of the "dung" <note>original: "stercoris"; here used metaphorically for bodily waste or toxins.</note> in the whole body, which is stirred and governed by nature herself, not by the heavens. The other sweat is of a celestial nature and is pushed out in three locations: near the ears, under the armpits, and at the groin. Nor does it break out in more places than these. For these are the <term>emunctories</term> <note>Emunctories: In traditional medicine, these are the organs or areas of the body—such as the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin—responsible for draining or clearing away waste and "corrupt" humors.</note> of the heavens, as far as its own sweat is concerned.

<margin>Man and the plague come from the stars.</margin>
These, therefore, are the locations of the plague, and no others. For just as the plague is from the stars of heaven, so too is man; therefore, the heaven operates in this part. Where there is nothing of the heaven, there it operates nothing. For out of four parts, there is one <note>Paracelsus refers to his theory that man is composed of four "quarters" or realms: the elements of Earth, Water, and Air, and the "Firmament" (the stars/heavens). The plague belongs to the firmamental quarter.</note>. These three are not celestial, but only the one. That one is the body of the plague.

Because it is proper, therefore, for a physician to consider only a fourth part of man and not the rest, it is right that he should explain this part only through astronomy. He must consider the "heaven" of this part in its own anatomy, and thus compare both anatomies so they become a single structure and essence. Then at last he may be allowed to discourse on the foundation of medicine regarding this disease—if he has exquisitely prepared an anatomy of this kind, and is primarily knowledgeable and skilled in the four parts of man as well as the entire firmament. And he is a true Philosopher who, through that light, understands his own nature. Moreover, the anatomy of the aforementioned philosophy works like this: you must learn the property and nature of things from the "light of growing things" <note>original: "lumine rerum crescentium"; Paracelsus's term for the innate vital energy or "Light of Nature" that reveals the inner workings of the natural world.</note>—not, I say, from your own fantasy and speculation, but from that light which emerges from growing things.

<margin>The secrets of nature must be known by the physician.</margin>
To this, therefore, the Theory of Medicine belongs: in the knowledge of the natural virtues, which are called <term>Arcana</term> <note>Arcana: From the Latin for "secrets." In Paracelsian medicine, these are the hidden, powerful healing forces or spiritual essences contained within natural substances.</note>, and these are the mysteries from which a physician must be born. Therefore, from that light, in which the anatomy of both the [external] heaven and the firmament [within man] consists, you should work in this way. For now, the Middle of the external heaven is the lord of the internal heaven. For the former is more mature—that is, man was born from it. Since, therefore, that heaven is the father of man, the son expects and receives something from the father <margin>Man is the son of heaven.</margin>, not the father from the son.

So, it has now been seen that the heaven is the parent of man according to this <margin>Heaven is the master of man.</margin> part. Therefore, it is also his Lord, and rules and governs him, just as a father directs a son. For this reason, the heaven is also the cause and moderator of all health, disease, poison, good, and evil—and even of death itself, as far as this fourth part is concerned. Therefore, nothing else should be considered here, lest foreign things be taken up and the genuine foundation be corrupted. Now, indeed, there are very many diseases of this kind, not all of which can be listed. Many of them <margin>Diseases either were or will be.</margin> have even disappeared. Many are also yet to come, which we do not yet know. Many present ones pass away which we do not notice, do not understand, and neglect out of ignorance. Therefore, I will not list every single one here, but only those known and manifest to me. However, I warn you at the same time that they are infinite—both the known and the unknown, the present and the future. For so many signs reveal themselves in the diseases described below that from them you can sufficiently understand how much pertains to the "Quarter" of the <term>Microcosm</term>.

If we have properly understood this Quarter of the Microcosm, we must consider, once the division is established, that various diseases exist in this part—not just one, but as many as there are parts of the firmament. And yet they all remain "firmamental," not mixed with the other elements (air, water, earth), but produced from the firmament itself. It is no different than how someone can be struck by this or that man, or speaks whatever he wishes, etc. And yet all these are one part, or proceed from the man, even if they are divided. If...

# BOOK I.

<margin>
Knowing the master of the disease is also knowledge for the medical mind.
</margin>
If, therefore, the divisions of diseases arise from the varied nature of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the heavens and the stars, which Paracelsus believed exerted a direct physical and spiritual influence on human health.</note>, it is first necessary to know which of these is the master <note>original: "dominus"; the governing planetary influence.</note> of the disease. For instance, in the plague, the masters are *Mars, Venus, and the Moon*; in acute diseases, it is *Saturn*, and so on. If we recognize this master, the very foundation of the diseases will be revealed, and the process for describing any given disease will be known—without which all our science is nothing but a dead letter. For if *Mars* is the ruler, we then know what *Mars* is; if it is *Venus*, we know what *Venus* is, and so forth, so that each planet serves as its own light of understanding. In the same way, we immediately understand the "Anatomy" of that disease in terms of Medicine. Now, therefore, we are equipped with both Theory and Practice, and we hold that foundation which a Physician must possess, and in which no small comfort is placed for the sick.

<margin>
The Sun is the heart and reason of the firmament.
</margin>
To further understand the cause of why *Mars*, or any other planet, is the master of this or that disease—setting aside all other illnesses—we shall here treat only the plague and its relatives in this manner. Wood that is set on fire burns. Fire, in turn, scorches. *Mars* is the S.S. <note>original: "S.S."; likely an abbreviation for "Spiritus Solis" (Spirit of the Sun) or a specific alchemical grade of "Sulphur." In Paracelsian thought, Mars represents the "burning" or "combustible" quality in nature.</note>. That which ignites it is the Sun. The "wood" is the earthly part of man—that is, the <term>Microcosm's</term> <note>The "Microcosm" (Small World) is the human being, viewed as a perfect reflection of the "Macrocosm" (Great World/Universe).</note> quarter. Just as wood is subject to fire, so is this human "quarter" subject to Mars. *Mars* is the fire; the Sun ignites it; Man conceives it. No fire exists without wood; likewise, no Mars exists without man. The planet and the human are one thing, not two—just as wood and fire are one thing. If the wood stands in the forest and the fire is made in the kitchen, both are "dead" until they are joined together and burn. The Sun compels them, ignites them, and is the source of heat. Know, then, when the Sun ignites, and which "wood" it strikes: that is, if *Mars* burns, know with what wood it creates heat. The Sun ignites like the steel striker which a man strikes to draw out a spark of fire. That "steel" is the Sun; the man moves it. We must speak more broadly of this. Although these things may seem different from our previous purpose and opinion—wherein we said the father is above the son and is his master—the matter is to be understood thus: A son can provoke his father to such anger that he reaches for his switches <note>A "switch" is a flexible rod or branch used for corporal punishment.</note>. Now, truly, man—

<margin>
Man is the son of the Macrocosm.
</margin>
—is nothing other than the son of the great creature, that is, of the <term>Limbus</term> <note>The "Limbus" in Paracelsian terms refers to the "Limbus Major," the primordial "great mass" or chaotic matter from which the entire universe and humanity were fashioned.</note>. Heaven inflicts no disease upon him unless it is compelled by him, just as a father does not beat his son unless the son has offended him. Thus, man is nothing else but the son of the Limbus, divided into his own parts. In this context, the whole universe is arranged so that the son may be tested—to see whether he provokes or has provoked the father of the Limbus. For no son falls ill because of the heaven, earth, air, or water, unless he has irritated them. Here lies the entire foundation. The truth of this is established in this way: all our works, our disobedience, and our misdeeds go into the Sun. For the Sun is the heart, reason, intellect, wisdom, and grace of the entire firmament. Into this Sun, I say, all our works are directed. Just as we receive the natural light of wisdom from the Sun, as our parent, through all the planets and stars, so the Sun is nothing else than the wisdom of our mortal light, directed toward the stars. Now, therefore, we must return into that from which we came. If we return to him, our deeds irritate him, just as a son offends a father. From this, anger boils up in the "mind" of the firmament, stirred up by us. That anger diffuses and divides itself into its various properties, which are many. Afterward, it hastens toward punishment and pours out the anger it has conceived. That pouring out is the disease of which we complain. Nor is this to be understood only regarding the firmament, but also regarding the other three parts of the "great creature" <note>The "Great Creature" refers to the four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire (the firmament).</note>. They inflict nothing on us unless they are first irritated. But how are they irritated by us? We contain water within us, and a part of the water is hidden in us.

<margin>
Heaven and the Elements do not harm us unless provoked.
</margin>
If we live in that water, we must be nourished and sustained by it: that is, internal water must be sustained by external water. If we irritate or offend the internal water through the external, then we fall ill in that part. In this way, external forces stir up the harms of the internal ones. The same logic applies to air and earth. Furthermore, we do not see heaven itself; we see only water and earth. For the "lower globe" <note>The material, visible world.</note> is materially present in man; conversely, the "upper globe" <note>The celestial or spiritual world.</note> is in us invisibly. Therefore, the two superior parts must be known through their power and virtue.

<margin>
The upper sphere is invisible; the lower is visible.
</margin>
Surely, the word of a man can compel another man. A material word is nothing, and yet it commands a servant and compels him. So too the wind casts down and levels things, yet it is not visible itself. This serves as an example to us that the same logic exists for the firmament. Even though we see and touch nothing, it is nonetheless a "Great Nature." Thus, the matter should be understood regarding all other things in the universe, and especially regarding the firmament: that unless it is specifically irritated by us, celestial diseases cannot afflict us at all. This irritation—

<margin>
Invisible things are known by their works.
</margin>

# ON THE PLAGUE, WITH ADDITIONS.

This is caused by great envy. This envy consists of immoderate greed, hatred, and the like. These things cause offense to the Sun. Therefore, the more we indulge in private gain, wars, dissensions, and so on, the more quickly, heavily, and cruelly the plague attacks us. The reason is that the Father is more heavily offended. While Christ prophesies about future plagues, he first makes mention of wars, dissensions, envy, hatred, and the son rising up against the father. By all these things, heaven is offended; and for us, our earthly parent is the *Limbus* <note>In Paracelsian philosophy, the "Limbus" refers to the "Great Mystery" or the primal matter from which the human body was created, serving as a bridge between the physical earth and the celestial stars.</note>.

<margin>Heaven favors virtues.</margin>
If we devote ourselves to virtue, harmony, and charity, we find the natural heaven to be favoring and beneficial. If not, the opposite occurs, and evil breaks out against us. And from this is built the Prophecy of Astronomy: that this or that year will have such or such an outcome. For heaven declines into an anger that is so heavy and harsh that even man himself may feel the father’s indignation beforehand. There, the lot of the guilty and the innocent is one and the same—just as we see happening in a fight or a war. He who is struck, falls; he who is safe, escapes. However, while we profess that heaven is offended and angry, it is first necessary that the cause be joined to it: from what did it become angry? For it does not behave like the nature of Mars or Jupiter, etc., but is like the anger in a father who is otherwise beneficial and smiles upon his children. Yet, if he is offended by them, he pours out his hidden anger. The same reasoning applies here.

<margin>God does not inflict punishment from himself for evil acts.</margin>
To what end, therefore, does the Astronomer say that Mars is angry? Whom, then, does his anger hurt? Let him be left to himself, and he will not hurt you at all. For you are not subject to his rod, but to God’s. If you offend Him naturally, you make yourself His child. Therefore, He chastises you with a present blow. And this is indeed the highest priority for any Physician: to strive above all to show himself a Christian in all things, and to place God, as the supreme parent, before nature itself in all matters.

<margin>God is to be placed before nature in all things.</margin>
But if we say that God sends us Mars and Eclipses, that is as nothing. We ourselves irritate the stars. Therefore, they are arranged according to our merits. Eclipses would bring no trouble in themselves if we proved ourselves upright and did not irritate the firmament. And this is the Theory of its origin; next follows its process.

In the treatment of the Plague, another Method has been observed by most people until now. Although the criticism and overturning of that method may bring the hatred of many, it should not be of great concern to a wise man who follows the "rhombus of truth" <note>The "rhombus of truth" likely refers to a steady, unwavering direction or a precise instrument of measurement, symbolizing the search for absolute truth.</note>. If they had followed the true Method, there would have been no need for this writing of mine. Since enough has been handed down so far regarding the origin and turning away of the plague, the process must now be described: namely, how this weapon or blow is sent from the hand of God upon earthly men. And this shall be done very briefly. You see that all things coming from above exist as visible and sensible things, such as rain, snow, lightning, etc. But that which inflicts diseases from above is invisible. And this is twofold: *The Anger of God* and *The Nature of the Firmament*.

<margin>The origin of the plague is twofold.</margin>
If God is going to punish, it happens just as if someone were tying together switches from a birch tree. So God also takes up his rods in heaven—Mars, Saturn, etc.—and strikes or lashes with them. Therefore, the plague arises: first from God, and then from Mars, and so on.

<margin>The planet is the rod of God.</margin>
From this it is clear that Mars acts according to its essence, not according to its own will. It works all things according to the pleasure of God, though also by its own nature; and it does so in this manner: just as brightness penetrates through glass from the sun, so also the brightness—not as light, but as a Ray—flows down from on high into that region where that influence has power.

<margin>Heaven acts not according to its will, but its nature.</margin>
Two things are here, therefore: the region, and the hand or power of God. Hence it happens that Astronomers and those wise in the Firmament, and observers of the constellations, know the time of the plague of a particular region from the state of the superior bodies; no differently than we also see what is in serpents—namely, pure poison, nothing healthy. As long as it is not excluded or does not attain life, it is quiet. If it is animated and comes to life, it begins to move, to hiss, to entwine itself in coils, and to generate poison on its tongue.

<margin>The serpent's poison is on the tongue.</margin>
Now, therefore, the Philosopher knows that whatever is bitten by it is poisoned; and as one is wounded, so he feels and is afflicted. The industry of Astronomy is similar if Mars or the other Planets and stars are irritated (of which some books make mention; some by no means list them all, but many still remain unnamed). For whatever is done by these, it proceeds from the hand of God, who rules over them all. For at that time, the irritated stars are like...

<header>ON THE PLAGUE.</header>

# ON THE PLAGUE.

<margin>
Astronomers predict the plague by comparison with the past.
</margin>
...they are driven to madness, they roll about and hiss, and strike the ground, and clash like two roosters. If such things happen, it is easy for Astronomers to foresee that a certain punishment and grave disease is looming. Moreover, if they consult experience—how such things happened before—they can certainly prophesy a future plague. For no one can know the "child" of an infection <note>Paracelsus often uses parental metaphors for causes and effects; here, the "child" is the specific manifestation of the disease.</note>, what kind it will be, unless it was born in such a way before—that is, unless the same thing happened similarly in the past. For there is a presumption that the same thing can happen again in the same way.

Furthermore, just as a man uses hands, a dog its mouth, a bee its sting, or a Basilisk <term>Basilisk: A mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze; here used as a metaphor for invisible, lethal toxins transmitted through the air or light.</term> its eyes: so for the higher stars, their splendor <note>original: "splendor"</note> serves as hands, feet, and eyes. <margin>Heaven’s hand, the star.</margin> This splendor is invisible and untouchable. Yet, just as the splendor of the sun passes through glass, so these splendors of the stars penetrate through a man's skin as if through glass, <margin>What the difference is between the Sun and other stars.</margin> differing from the sun’s splendor only in clarity and the sense of presence—that is, the sun's heat is felt; but the ray of the plague, like the sun's light, is not felt at all, so that one cannot withdraw from it into the shade as one does from the sun. I say it is not the same with other stars: for their impression is not felt until it has already been introduced and has penetrated; nor does it touch just one person, but affects many at once and at the same time—that is, it affects the region of this part, of this land, of this city, according as that star has this or that region more or less subject to it. But why the impression penetrates and persuades everywhere, yet does not infect everyone in a single day: the cause lies in the nature of man, which <margin>Why some are not infected by the plague.</margin> resists and fights back for a time. Those who resist longer are affected later. Those who struggle plainly and constantly are never seized. Everyone is illuminated, but not everyone is struck. For just as the sun attacks some who are naked and covered by no protection, while others are hiding under a wall, or a rampart, or a tree: so there are similar trees or walls in the skin or "bark" <note>original: "cortice"</note> of a man, by which he is closed off and fortified so that the infection cannot penetrate everywhere. And according to what these "barks" of a man are like, so the man is infected.

Know truly that this "bark" is not only the skin we see, but also everything else pertaining to the skin, as well as many other things about which Doctors have thus far written nothing; nor shall we do so here. Therefore, the splendor, if directed against a man, is similar to the nature of a Basilisk, whose venom <margin>What kind of venom the Basilisk has.</margin> is struck and inflicted upon the place at which it looks: no differently than if someone dashed a stone against that place. For the imagination of man is an expulsive power <margin>What imagination is in man.</margin> in that which is imagination: especially in menstruating and hemorrhaging people. But the reason why not all imaginations produce their power into effect everywhere is this: that one person is so fortified under his skin (as if by a wall) that the blows and poisons of others can by no means break through. For as material walls are, and the blows made against them: such also are the invisible walls in the imagination. Just as a man’s imagination cannot always penetrate through another—as Attained Wisdom <margin>Attained Wisdom.</margin> <note>original: "Sophia adepta" — a term for deep, esoteric knowledge or spiritual insight granted by God.</note> teaches and clearly demonstrates—so neither do the heaven and the stars of the firmament always penetrate what they strive to break through. Meanwhile, there are also other reasons for this frustration [of the stars' influence], why God grants such protections and walls to man: namely, so that <margin>God is mindful of the human race.</margin> the whole human race and the entire world would not perish in a single ruin and slaughter. For He is mindful of His promise, by which He guarded man so that his whole race would not again be extinguished as in the cataclysm <note>A reference to the Great Flood of Noah.</note>. And from this source, those protections and walls are originally established. Yet, in the meantime, what the will of God demands and commands happens. And the remission of His anger alone is that bulwark which <margin>The remission of God's anger is the bulwark of the plague.</margin> fortifies us against the assault of the Planets, and naturally protects and saves us. And this the Physician must firmly know and believe: that when divine anger relents, some walls and protections fight and clash with the stars. Meanwhile, those who are either naked, or hide behind walls of glass or wood, are easily overcome and cast down. And indeed, they are liable to the impression even when the anger of God has subsided. Yet to these in turn God has supplied other protections—namely, medicines—by which poisons are conquered by Physicians; just as the Devils were cast out by the Apostles. For if a man can wound someone in a fight and afterward, moved by mercy, heal the same person again: how much more powerfully can God do this, who is goodness and mercy itself?

<margin>There are three locations of the plague.</margin>
The plague falls upon us; there are three open places in which it settles: the Ears, the Armpits <note>original: "Alæ," literally "wings," referring to the axillary region.</note>, and the Groins. Besides these, there are no others. For the other parts of the body are not at all subject to the assault and infection of the plague. This matter is no different than if a man were dressed in scales or a breastplate <note>original: "loricâ"</note> but remained naked in one or two parts. It is there he is struck, and not in the protected places. The rest of the body is like that—fortified as if by a breastplate. Therefore, it is an error and a deception

<margin>A reproof of Physicians regarding the locations of the plague.</margin>
when Doctors assert that the brain, heart, liver, and spleen contract the plague and then distribute it to the aforementioned locations.

<margin>The plague assaults from without.</margin>
For the plague is not brought into the body except from the outside, like a spear <note>original: "teli"</note>. Therefore, its beginning is from without, and the body is afflicted from the outside, not the other way around; this must be especially noted. For if those aforementioned organs were the primary locations of the plague,

<margin>Urine, pulse, and stool behave naturally during the plague.</margin>
how would it happen that no signs of it are detected in the urine, but rather the urine behaves naturally? Nor would the pulse, the stool, or the outward appearance <note>original: "physionomia"</note> change. Indeed, it would be necessary for many other signs to occur simultaneously, yet none of them are exhibited. Instead, all those organs remain unhurt, untainted, and inviolate until the plague penetrates from the external parts into the interior. By this penetration, death is brought in, and the disease ceases. The ears have their own peculiar region and anatomy into which the blow is struck. Likewise, the armpits possess the region of the breasts as their suitable place, which is touched. The same logic applies to the groins. These regions have no commerce with the other "noble" parts <note>The "noble parts" in Renaissance medicine were the heart, liver, and brain.</note> due to the singular anatomy they possess, until the evil is transfused from the former into the latter. For only then do these internal organs also fall sick. Therefore, all the treatments established hereafter, such as blood-reduction <note>original: "minutio," referring to phlebotomy or bloodletting.</note>, etc.,

<margin>Blood-reduction is futile in the plague.</margin>
are attempted in vain. If it were otherwise, the blood would certainly show some evidence of it. From these things, therefore, it is concluded that the plague arises apart from all the causes and theories of other diseases. Now truly, the reason that medicines administered before the twelfth hour and at the beginning confer no benefit yet is because they are meant to prevent or forestall the blow, so that it is not directed from the exterior inward to the heart and liver, etc. If this were not the cause, what would prevent them from being offered later as well—namely, after the twelfth hour has passed? For if the disease were being driven from the internal parts outward, they would certainly use different medicines. Thus, their own accepted practices convict them of error. For Practice—which tests and establishes everything—acts to ensure the infection does not penetrate from the outside to the inside. It is necessary, therefore, for the infection to exist on the outside, not the inside.

## The Imagination of Impression.

<margin>The power of Incantation.</margin>
**T**o understand the origin and manner of the plague even more clearly, consider this example. It is known to you that incantatory faith <note>The power of a focused belief or spell to cause physical change.</note> induces a contraction, kills, sickens, heals, or strengthens. Now, it is not only that faith, but also an "impression," just as the heaven impresses this upon one person and that upon another—striking this man now, or killing another tomorrow. For all these are celestial influences and impressions; they do not compel, but they lead the way for those who follow and comply toward a deed.

<margin>The heaven inclines, it does not compel.</margin>
In this way, man is the "heaven of Olympus" <note>Paracelsus uses "Olympus" to refer to the invisible, spiritual, or astral heaven that exists within the human being.</note>—that is, a Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "little world"; the idea that the human body reflects the structure and laws of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</term>, having been allotted the nature of the Firmament. For by the virtue and power of that Firmament which is within him, it happens that a man, in the manner of Olympus, sets his purpose against an enemy, so that his very imagination becomes an "impression," exerting and perfecting its force upon a weaker person.

<margin>Man is of the heaven of Olympus.</margin>
However, there is a need for a certain medium through which this occurs. For all things have need of a medium, and without a medium, nothing happens. Thus, man is the beginning of that incantation and proposes this or that to himself, which he nonetheless cannot fulfill on his own.

<margin>What the medium of incantation is like.</margin>
By him, however, the "internal stars" <note>The spiritual or vital forces within man that correspond to the planets and stars.</note> are moved; that is, he infects his own constellation so that his will and poison pass into the stars. Once this is done, the medium is born within him. In order for all similar things to meet and be united, the other person—against whom the incantation is prepared—has his own "heaven of Olympus" no less than the one preparing it. If, therefore, the stars of his imagination are brought under subjection, then they clash and contend as if with swords; the stronger wins, and the weaker drinks the poison and is overcome by the other. Such are the courses of the stars. Their origins, however, are imaginations. The "star" in man is the medium without which nothing can be done. Whence it follows that one image infects another—not indeed by the power of characters or similar things, such as virgin wax <note>A reference to "poppet" magic or sympathetic magic using wax figures.</note>, but because the imagination overcomes its own constellation to become the medium for fulfilling the will of the "heaven"—that is, of its own man.

<margin>The stars have reason, and man is from the stars.</margin>
From this, it must consequently be granted that the stars (though beyond our grasping) possess their own reason, wisdom, cunning, anger, wars, and weapons, no less than man himself—

### *Impression into the Heights.*

<margin>The heaven of the world is not against us.</margin>
**T**he previous example must also be understood supernaturally regarding the plague. For the plague would not fall upon us unless we ourselves generated it; that is, I would never become lame or paralyzed unless I made myself lame and contracted. For I myself supply the cause, the seed, and the matter for my own disease. Now, the heaven that is above us is not against us, but for us. Yet we infect it: then, it pours back the conceived poison upon us. The beginning sticks within us. And all our deceits, all our vices, are nothing other than <term>imagination</term> <note>In this context, imagination is not just "fantasy" but a powerful creative force capable of projecting internal states into the physical world.</note>, continually agitated and moved. For whether we sleep or wake, we perpetually dream of envy, greed, and all wickedness.
<margin>Imagination, the mother of all evils.</margin>
And this imagination is such that it penetrates and ascends even into the higher heaven, through both stars, from one to the other. This same imagination conquers and moderates the heaven. If therefore it ascends through our own internal heaven into the higher heaven, what else does it become but the mother of a new operation? For let no one be persuaded of anything else than that the sole origin of these evils and diseases is our imagination, with which we so strongly, enviously, greedily, and hostilely exasperate others. And this so varied imagination of men among themselves generates contention and diseases in the heaven. Nor do they fall back to earth otherwise than if someone, as we have said, had enchanted another. This one rises, that one falls. Thus our own imaginations, which emerged from such an evil beginning, fall back, and become nothing other than plagues, <term>Anthraces</term> <note>original: "Anthraces"; referring to carbuncles or inflammatory skin boils typical of the plague.</note>, <term>Arthetis</term> <note>original: "Arthetis"; a term for joint pain or gout-like symptoms.</note>, <term>Colica</term> <note>Colic or severe abdominal pain.</note>, and similar diseases, all of which are nevertheless understood and comprised under the single name of "plague." From which it follows that general envy excites a general plague. The same is true of the remaining vices. For whatever exists in us that is immoderate and inhuman belongs entirely to the <term>Imaginative Nature</term>, which is powerful enough to make an impression upon the heaven. Once that is done, the heaven in turn is powerful enough to pour that impression back. Therefore, the beginning of all things in man is from the stars, and it is perfected in the "Medium" <note>The midpoint or spiritual bridge.</note> of the superior star. And Christ speaks of the plague alone which arises from such a principle, not of any other. For the others are natural and have natural causes and origins.
<margin>Hatred generates corruption and moves the plague.</margin>

### *Strong Perspicacity.*

**T**his "hailstone" <note>A metaphor for the sudden, damaging strike of the plague.</note> must now be more deeply known and understood. It is invisible and non-material. Yet it becomes matter in the body, which is compared to a serpent. It stings or pierces, yet it does not itself penetrate the limb. So too the <term>Magic Cranium</term> <note>original: "Craniū Magicum"; likely referring to the vault of the heavens acting as the skull of the macrocosm.</note>—that is, the heaven of this place—pierces. To pierce is its blow; which is first invisible, then becomes visible, and becomes our disease and death. Now it is brought down from the heaven above, and is joined with us in no other way than as you see a <term>Basilisk</term> <note>A mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze; here used as a metaphor for radiant infection at a distance.</note> infect someone who is even a great distance away, whom it does not touch at all with its physical substance. In the same way, a certain Basilisic force and nature is generated in the heaven from that anger which it conceived from us; and whatever it sees or concludes with its eyes is immediately touched and infected. Therefore, he who knows the Basilisk of the heaven, and its generation and origin, also knows the manner in which the plague is induced. The sight of this Basilisk directed at us is similar to a celestial ray or lightning, which breaks and burns whatever it touches. Meanwhile, we know very little of where, what, or when it will strike. We know its origin and generation, but where it will rush, we do not know. Such is the <term>Basilisk of the plague</term>. Therefore, from a natural foresight, it can by no means be said: "You, Melancholic, or you, Phlegmatic, take care." For where and what it will strike cannot be known, even though its generation is known. Therefore, the foresight of those men <note>referring to astrologers and physicians</note> is no different than if someone were to say that lightning is about to fall to earth, and yet it would only touch one field; and he ordered everyone to look out for their own field, and in that way all the fields of that region were moved or carried away. For they cannot predict specifically...

### *The Wound.*

<margin>The plague is a wound.</margin>
<margin>The symptoms of the plague are more severe than those of common wounds.</margin>
**N**ext follows the property and nature of the disease: that the plague is a wound, and it should be regarded as nothing other than a plague-wound. Just as if someone is struck from the outside, first his skin is broken, then the flesh, the arteries, and the bones. If the wound penetrates even deeper, there follows an injury to the vital organs, which is followed by death. In this same way, the plague itself occupies a person from the outside. And the blow is indeed celestial, yet it is similar to a human strike. Therefore, before all else, the nature, essence, and condition of all wounds must be known, along with all their accidents and symptoms. For what happens to wounds happens similarly to the plague. There is no difference here, except for what the eyes see: that the blows of the heavens are more violent than human ones, and are accompanied by more numerous and more savage symptoms. This itself proceeds from the greater force and efficacy of the heavens. Now, a common "accident" <note>In medieval medicine, an "accident" refers to a symptom or a secondary condition resulting from the primary disease.</note> of a wound is foulness—that is, when a wound suddenly begins to rot. The same accident occurs in the plague. Spasms occur with wounds; the same happens with the plague. Fever or inflammation accompanies large wounds; the same also accompanies the plague. The plague is also accompanied by dysentery, wasting, heat, cold, etc., all of which also follow wounds. And these symptoms of wounds, and no others, accompany the plague. Therefore, two things must be considered in the plague: the disease itself (that is, the wound) and then the symptoms. For these differ from one another. Furthermore, in every single wound, the state of the heavens must be considered, as well as the signs and the nature of the "weapons"—whether they were more or less poisoned. For in the plague, it is not just one, but many swords that wound; various and diverse 

<margin>The theory of the plague and of wounds is one and the same.</margin>
imaginations exist, some more prone than others to generating different poisons. Once this is understood, the cure follows through art, industry, and natural remedies to suppress and cut out the symptoms of the poison. And here there is no distinction between the periodic and the practical. For the theory of the plague is drawn from the theory of the wound. Therefore, let those trifles about the <term>Humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that traditional Galenic medicine blamed for all disease.</note> and Qualities be exploded and exiled. For from them, nothing but lazy physicians are made; as has been observed until now, they have accomplished nothing else in the plague except to send their patients to the underworld.

### *The Matter.*

<margin>The three locations of the plague.</margin>
**T**he next step is to treat the body of the plague itself, once it has been birthed. Mars is the archer <note>original: "Iaculator Mars est"</note>, by the commerce and mandate of all the stars. His shot behaves no differently than if a spark, struck from a flint by iron, falls into a waiting piece of tinder. Many sparks do not ignite the tinder but vanish. However, three known places in the body act as tinder. Now, if the body is to conceive the disease, it must be disposed toward it. For stones do not catch fire. Therefore, one must know what it is, and of what sort, that catches the flame. From this emerges the knowledge of the wound, from which its medicine must be drawn. And by this same principle, my proposition and theory are established. The three locations are the groin, the ears, and the sides of the breasts. According to these regions, the matter of <term>sulphur</term> <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, Sulphur represents the principle of combustibility and growth within the body.</note> is divided into three parts. In the groin is "antimonial sulphur"; in the armpits is "arsenical sulphur"; and behind the ears is the "sulphur of marcasites."

<margin>The sulphur that is proper to each location.</margin>
These are the three "tinder-boxes" that catch the fire of Mars. Unless these are present, no fire takes hold. Therefore, effort must be given so that these three sulphurs—and their poison, their nature, their disease, and their death—are properly understood; and afterward, the <term>arcana</term> <note>Secret or "hidden" spiritual remedies that Paracelsus believed were the true cures for disease.</note> appropriate to them may be sought. For these cannot be found based on your mere opinion. More is required of a Physician than <term>Galen</term> and <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The two most famous ancient and medieval medical authorities, whom Paracelsus famously rejected in favor of chemical and alchemical medicine.</note>. For they only provide the shops with university graduates, mortar-grinders, and those who merely pound herbs. As far as the theory of this first book is concerned, for your brief information, know that all the aforementioned sulphurs must be understood in this way:

<margin>Man has all minerals within himself.</margin>
Man contains all mineral parts within himself, just like the "greater nature" <note>The Macrocosm or the physical universe.</note>. Now, however, this location is the location of water. Minerals are born from the Element of water. Furthermore, sulphurous minerals are bodies in their "first and ultimate matter" <note>Alchemical terms for the primordial substance of a thing and its final, perfected form.</note>. In this

For in those three locations are the <term>emuntories</term> <note>The organs or sites where the body filters and expels waste; in plague studies, these usually refer to the armpits, groin, and neck (lymph nodes).</note> of water: namely, of the heart, the brain, and the liver.
