# BOOK THREE.
## PROLOGUE.

* **A**s we are about to treat the cure of the Plague, it is right that you recall those things which we spoke of in the second book: namely, that although those who are directly struck by the "blow" <note>The author uses the language of a "strike" or "blow" to describe the sudden onset of the plague, often attributed to divine or celestial arrows.</note> must die, those who are inflamed and infected by them may yet live and survive. For the sake of these people, God grants the gift of Medicine. And the experience of things confirms that many who have been seized by the plague are freed by their medicines for this reason. However, the origin of the plague is not with God, but with ourselves. Furthermore, we ourselves are the cause of medicine not being helpful, because we seek medicine with a cold enough heart, and do not hold it in its proper place of honor. Therefore, we ought to emulate the same love which God exercises toward us. If, at His exhortation, we pray as those who knock: what could finally be denied to us by Him? He gave these gifts to the Gentiles, the Saracens, and the Greeks. How much more generously will He pour them out upon those who worship and venerate Him with their whole heart?*

---

### On the Cure.

**W**hatever afflicts and seizes nature rages like fire in wood, or like nitre <note>Nitre, or saltpeter, was known for its volatile and explosive qualities in early chemistry.</note> in coals. Therefore, the physician must be fully equipped with medicines that are of an equal power. For water does not extinguish this fire, nor does it break its heat: but it is necessary to apply something else that exists above nature <note>This refers to "spagyric" or alchemical medicines that have been refined to a higher state than raw herbs.</note>.

---

### On the Accidents of the Plague.

<margin>
One must not despair of God even in the gravest matters.

What the accidents of the plague are.
</margin>

**A**lthough we said above that a certain, infallible, and proven medicine in which trust can be placed is found only with pain and difficulty—yet, because of the wrath and indignation of God, no one should despair. Instead, one must live entirely with a child-like hope and breathlessly seek the protection of medicine, in case God takes pity on our affliction and allows His course to be swayed by the strengths of medicine. This, however, must be particularly weighed here: that in the cure, the plague is not the only thing to be attended to, but also many other diseases alongside it. For plagues of various kinds rush in. Even if these are not lethal in themselves, the things that happen alongside them (the <term>accidents</term><note>In early medicine, "accidents" are secondary symptoms or complications that follow the primary disease.</note>) are lethal, such as <term>Icteritia</term> <note>original: "Icteritia"; modern: Jaundice.</note>, <term>Hydropisis</term> <note>original: "Hydropisis"; modern: Dropsy or Edema.</note>, <term>Paralysis</term>, and so on. In the same way, surgical diseases also coincide, so that <term>Cancers</term>, <term>Fistulas</term>, and <term>Eating Ulcers</term> <note>original: "Vlcera Estiomena"; refers to corrosive or gangrenous sores.</note> are joined to the plague. It is not that the plague causes these; rather, the origin of these lay hidden elsewhere in the body, and the plague, leaping in, brought them to the surface and enticed the disease out. Just as one who treads on a dog's tail with his foot draws out a bark and a bite, so the pressing plague drives the other diseases of the body into a fury. From this it is clear that if the plague itself is not lethal, these other diseases must be met with suitable remedies.

<margin>Medicine is twofold: for the plague itself, and for its accidents.</margin>

Therefore, the medicine ought to be twofold: one for the plague as it is in itself, and the other for the accident, whatever it may be. You must therefore diligently try and strive to have a <term>Quinta Essentia</term> <note>The "Fifth Essence" or Quintessence: the purest extract of a substance, believed to contain its medicinal soul.</note> ready for any disease, which you can mix and administer according to the nature of the accident.

<margin>What the first medicine of the plague is.</margin>

Know therefore that the first medicine of the plague ought to consist of Pearls, Gold, and Sapphire. For in those stones—as also in <term>Unicorn</term> <note>Usually refers to narwhal tusk or fossilized bone, highly prized as an anti-toxin.</note> and Balsams—a virtue so powerful is hidden that the plague can be entirely overcome and expelled by its strength. For just as God, moved by our daily repentance, turns away His wrath, so He does the same through Medicine if we seek it with the highest veneration, so that clearly Art and His own creation may be praised.

<margin>The "aspects" of the novices contribute nothing to the plague.</margin>

Yet, out of His immense mercy, He permits it that we may search out and collect so many and such difficult secrets from everywhere. These secrets and receipts are those of which we have spoken—not the "aspects" <note>Astrological configurations or planetary alignments.</note>, which have no weight here, but only the preparation of Alchemy. This preparation was first called "Aspects" by the astrologers and astronomers, but today it is more correctly called Alchemy. Thus, what were trifles and delusions at that time are now the "aspects." In this way, things are accustomed to be changed in their own time.

<margin>The preservative of the plague is Balsamation.</margin>

Besides the things said so far, it is right to say something about preservatives. A preservative is nothing other than <term>Balsamation</term> <note>A method of protecting the living body from decay or infection, similar to how a corpse is embalmed or "balsalmed."</note>, which is done through Manna, through <term>Mummy</term> <note>A medicinal preparation made from preserved human remains, believed to hold the "vital balsam" of life.</note>, through Gold, through Balsam, and so forth. Therefore, those things are preservatives which have such a balsamic nature and power.

<header>FRAGMENT ON THE PLAGUE.</header>

# FRAGMENT ON THE PLAGUE.
## IT FOLLOWS

->*A fragment of another book on the Plague, collected from certain papers written by the author's own hand, and arranged as the nature of the fragments allowed.*<-

### PREFACE.

<margin>The ancients knew no diseases.</margin>
**I**n the books of ancient Authors, nothing is handed down that could be of help to me. For they had no true knowledge of any disease. Furthermore, they were neither Magicians nor Cabalists, but stood out as Physicians born from their own brains and opinions <note>The author is likely critiquing traditional Galenic medicine, which relied on the balance of "humors," in favor of a more mystical or chemical approach.</note>. Therefore, we shall say a few things beforehand regarding the art and science of the ancient Physicians. The ancients learned from others and from the "horse's hoof" <note>This may be a derogatory reference to base, animalistic observation, or a reference to the plant coltsfoot, known in Latin as *ungula caballina*, used in folk medicine.</note>. The reason is that the arts proceed from spirits. If a man subdues them, he discovers those arts. Therefore, a trial must be made. For which reason they are also called Experiments.

<margin>Chiromancy is the discoverer of plague remedies.</margin>
But you, Reader, discard the medicine and cold Recipes of the ancients. Depart from them, and support our processes: namely, that you descend into <term>Chiromancy</term> <note>While usually meaning palm reading, here the author refers to the study of "signatures" or signs in nature and the body that reveal hidden properties.</note>, and compare veins to veins. Thus you will have the Recipes for the plague discovered and established. For by that method, you yourself will compose them as well as any other. For he who wishes to be content with the Recipes of others will labor in vain. Driven by this cause, I proposed to first hand down instruction on Chiromancy, from which emerges in this place the art and the discoverer of composing Recipes, and of administering and applying them. Afterward, I will establish the Regimens and preventatives. To these I will join the cure; finally, I will hand down the Accidents <note>In early medicine, "accidents" were the symptoms or secondary conditions produced by a disease.</note> themselves. Show yourself sluggish and lazy in nothing, but watch most attentively. For that is what the Basilisk requires <note>The Basilisk’s gaze was legendary for being instantly fatal; the author suggests the plague must be watched with equal intensity to avoid its deadly "strike."</note>. And so that the poison of sulfur, and Arsenics, Orpiments, and Mercury may be avoided and anticipated, the very necessity of the matter demands diligent study and earnest effort.

I will explain the whole matter briefly, in a plain and least intricate sense. But those things which are of the highest nature [the secrets] are not to be published to the common crowd. I bring them forth for the sake of those whom I favor, and who stand out as learned and skilled. I HAVE SPOKEN.

---

**F**urthermore, then, before all things, it is necessary for the Physician to know the beginning of the matter in which he is occupied. For here is the foundation laid, which is worthy for a Physician to know. The foundation and origin is of this kind: we worldly men are made of heaven and earth, etc. The heaven has its own course, so that it may be regarded as a father. From man, however, it receives its operation in such a way.

<margin>Heaven has no power over man, unless received from him.</margin>
Heaven has no force in itself over man, except that man stirs it up and drives it into anger. Irritated, it burns and becomes wild like a goaded bull, and shakes off from itself that which anger has given birth to within it. The Astronomers have judged wrongly and unworthily, etc.

Only prove what power Imagination has, because the sense can do this.

Mars kindles the sulfur. The heaven, therefore, is the cause.

Because all parts are minerals: therefore know that this kind of influence and impression is mineral. Therefore it is nothing other than sulfur <note>In this chemical philosophy, "sulfur" represents the principle of inflammability and heat within the body.</note>.

By what means can sulfur proceed from anger? Just as fire from the eyes.

->*The Manner of Generating the Disease.*<-

Thus, then, sulfur burns; why does it burn? Man is sulfur that does not burn. Heaven has sulfur that burns. All celestial sulfur burns in its impression like a lightning bolt.

->SIGNS.<-

It is directed and aimed at sulfur.

It is necessary to know the disease before Medicine is applied. ...given with other medicines. Accidents erupt because of those three hidden natures. However, the accidents which the plague possesses by its own nature are inflammation, shivering, burning heat, and the piercing pain of wounds.

Now, if you possess this knowledge, you will also know that in such a case one must hasten directly to medicine. Therefore, first of all, regarding the composition of remedies, one must see how <term>Recipes</term> <note>original: "Recepta"</note> are made, so that you may know their legitimate use. ### Use.

If, therefore, one plague can be generated, then two, three, or many can also be produced: just as more than one spark is struck from a flint, and not just one lightning bolt falls, or one hailstone, but many at once. So, in this case, that point is uniquely notable.

<margin>The Physician must be equipped with three-fold remedies.</margin>
Indeed, if all the sparks fall together into a single piece of tinder and become entangled with one another, who could know their number or distinguish them, except by the various afflictions of the sick person? If, therefore, the pattern of distress and affliction provides the knowledge, one must attend to the signs, both internal and external, and to the accidents—that is, those arising from other diseases. Even if you have grasped these, you are not yet sufficiently equipped. Therefore, labor to have three-fold medicines: this one for internal matters, that one for external, and the other for the accidents. If you make progress by treating these in order—first the plague, second the colic, and finally the <term>Epilepsy</term>, etc.—then finally turn to surgery in this manner.

### I. Regimen.

**W**ho establishes a Regimen where there is no disease? And so, who shall prescribe a Regimen here? For at one time this is healthy, at another time that. And this disease is not <term>Humoral</term> <note>Referring to the traditional theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note> or Natural, but is an "impression" which is comparable to an <term>Incantatory power</term> <note>The author views the plague as a spiritual or "magical" force that "impresses" itself upon the body like a seal on wax.</note>. Therefore, no fixed Regimen can be established for this disease. However, the body must be well fortified and preserved when the disease approaches, so that accidents may be avoided, and so that the plague finds fewer subjects in which to work.

However, this is difficult to find (except by a skilled Physician). For if a Physician could know which accidents were about to erupt, so that he might remove the "subject" <note>The underlying vulnerability in the patient.</note> through food, it would indeed be good and excellent. But who is there who knows these things, or dares to boast that he knows them? For if someone falls into the stupor of sleep, who could have known it before it happened? None but the one from whom sleep is taken away. The same logic applies to other things as well. Therefore, nothing solid can be built upon this, as far as the true disease itself is concerned.

Nevertheless, if a regimen is good and suitable, it helps against the contagion of the plague. For one person can contract this from another, just as one catches <term>bleary-eyedness</term> <note>original: "lippitudinem," likely referring to contagious conjunctivitis.</note> if they look upon it. And such are the "impressions" of the heavens within us. And just as it happens to us, so too can one's own disease be inflicted on others through contagion. Since these things are so, a healthy person draws this disease from a sick one, just as was said regarding the bleary eyes.

Against this, apply such things by which the attraction of the body is hindered. This is where the Regimen comes in. For just as someone looks at "evil eyes" but has a preservative so that the sight does not harm him: so here, similarly, it must be understood.

<margin>Two things attract the plague: the Womb and the Vital Power.</margin>
There are two things which attract the plague: the <term>matrix</term> <note>The womb. In this period, the womb was often thought to have an independent, "magnetic" power to attract influences.</note> of a woman, and the vital power. For the womb draws to itself just like the eyes. From this it also happens that spots and marks are imprinted on children. In the same way, it also lures the plague into its body. By a similar logic, the vital power also attracts through the whole skin that which turns about outside itself. And just as a dry tree attracts earthy moisture, even if it be bad...

# ON THE PLAGUE #

<margin>
The attractive power of the Magnet is the vital spirit.
</margin>
...how good it is: so too the spirit of life attracts the external moisture of the <term>Elements</term> <note>In this context, the four physical building blocks of the world: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>.

Now, this is also an Element. Therefore, it draws the disease to itself. That power which a Magnet has for drawing iron to itself is nothing other than the vital spirit. Indeed, it is not only the Magnet that attracts; other stones and woods also attract things to themselves indiscriminately—this one attracts that, that one attracts another, and so on. In this way, all animals and all humans attract; if not iron, then something else. This is clearly demonstrated by the Magnet and by <term>Amber</term> <note>original: "Carabe"; known for its electrostatic properties when rubbed.</note>. Thus, these two virtues attract the plague from other men: in men, in one way; in women, in a twofold manner. Therefore, the <term>Regimen</term> <note>A prescribed way of life or diet intended to maintain health.</note> must also be directed toward these things.

<margin>
Oil of Mercury extinguishes the power of the Magnet.
</margin>
Thus, he who wishes to prescribe a regimen will do the same as what is done to a Magnet. If a magnet is placed in <term>Oil of Mercury</term>, it loses its power of attraction and, as it were, dies. Something similar must be done for the body. Yet, you should note this: such things may weaken the body. For the attractive power is extinguished and it dries out. However, this is the true Regimen for halting the attractive power, so that it does not admit anything inside itself. Just as with a Magnet, if you place <term>Sophelum</term> <note>A technical term in Paracelsian medicine referring to a substance—often foul-smelling like garlic—that "blinds" or neutralizes the attractive force of the plague.</note> before it, it then draws only as far as the Sophelum and no further. Not Musk, not Ambergris, not Spices, etc., but garlic, onion, and leeks.

<margin>
What is Sophelum?
</margin>
<margin>
Meat to be avoided in the plague; no bread or wine.
</margin>
All animals that agree with the human <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and balance of humors in a person.</note> should be avoided, such as pigs. For they are infected no less than man himself. Therefore, if a man eats their flesh, he eats poison and the plague. Likewise, whatever agrees with man and is changed into flesh and blood is infectious. Thus, bread and wine are flesh and blood. Therefore, they also catch the plague. But who can forbid a man such things? It is necessary to eat and drink. Whence poison must also necessarily be expected. I conclude this Regimen only with those things which have been mentioned, namely garlic and onions. The reason is that these are the medicine for the plague, bread, wine, meat, and so on. Garlic, onions, and similar things are least of all infected. Therefore, the Regimen consists in these alone, and in no others.

Garlic and onions are the medicine for the plague.
</margin>
<margin>
Garlic is not infected by the plague.
</margin>
If it is said, "drink white wine, or red," etc., at this or that time: it is entirely the same thing. For all these things are poisoned. Whence the Regimen is also false. Perhaps there are those who think it is impossible for a man to irritate the heavens and move them to anger. This is the very doubt which <term>Astronomers</term> <note>In the 16th century, this included astrologers who studied the influence of stars on health.</note> have neglected from first to last. For what is the cause of the flood, the plague, famine, earthquakes, and so on? It is the provocation of which Christ speaks, etc.

### Preservatives ###

<margin>
Why cold and astringent preservatives are not suitable for the plague.
</margin>
All preservatives which you use made of cold and constricting things are worth a nutshell—which is to say, nothing. For the place to which you direct them is not the part that is infected, but the "region" of said places. Those things only touch upon certain <term>accidents</term> <note>Secondary symptoms rather than the root cause.</note>, just as one can preserve a wound so that it is not seized by a spasm. But the wound itself is not healed in this way.

<margin>
Which medicines of the ancients are to be rejected.
</margin>
Medicine must be twofold, etc. The <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>Sweat-inducing.</note> medicine which you offer in the plague is wicked and unsuitable. For it only removes the <term>Narcotic</term> accident that causes stupor, and is not at all helpful against the "blow" <note>The initial strike of the infection.</note> itself. Also ill-timed and unsuitable are *Pestilential Pills, Purgations, Theriac, Electuaries, Confections, Diaphoretics, Powders, etc.*—at least according to the description and use of the old <term>Periodica</term> <note>Likely referring to the ancient medical theories based on cycles and humors.</note>. For they do not reach the site of the infection, but only the internal bodies which were, however, healthy and untainted before. For it is uncertain how the invasion or seizure occurs. Therefore, those preservatives are also uncertain and lack reason.

Therefore, since medicines of that kind are uncertain, and sometimes bring help and sometimes do not—depending on mere luck—they are at best medicines for the "accidents," provided a powerful plague does not occur. And since they provide the same thing an hour before the plague invades, it is proof that their medicine is worth nothing. For legitimate and true medicine is good at all times, whether it be given early or late.

<margin>Good medicine is always good.</margin>
Because there has been no good or certain knowledge of the plague until now, you will now understand its foundation and reason in this way: In the plague, there are twin deaths: one of the plague itself, and the other of its "accident." For if the plague itself kills someone, that is a singular death. And then the other death is from the accidents, such as when Stupor, Mania, Epilepsy, Spasms, Inflammation, etc., kills someone. The kinds of this death are infinite. And yet they are all only accidents. So, if the plague attacks and brings on a savage accident, namely stupor: then, if by chance <term>Water of Life</term> <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; high-proof distilled alcohol used as a stimulant.</note> is provided, which removes the accident through sweat, this is merely [removing] the stupe-

...if the active force is warmed and dispersed through aromatic spices, and the sick man recovers, he has entirely escaped what would have been an accidental death. Other remedies of this kind are suitable for removing other <term>accidents</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "accidents" were symptoms or complications that arose from a disease. A patient might survive the disease itself but die from an "accident" like a high fever or secondary infection.</note> as well. For in this way, many deaths are merely accidental. And if by chance such a compound contains <term>simples</term> <note>Individual medicinal herbs or minerals, not yet mixed into a complex formula.</note> that act against that death, then you might rescue the patient from them, provided the plague is not inherently violent and lethal—for many plagues move swiftly and lead to death as quickly as lethal wounds.

Therefore, you ought to know that medicines must be divided in this way between the plague itself and its accidents. And, as is the custom, pay very little attention to the hours, but turn your mind toward the medicine. If you can obtain any effect before the twelfth hour—that is, before the accidents weigh down upon the patient—see to it that you can do the same in overcoming the accidents even after that hour has already passed.

If you have already emerged as the victor over the accidents, see that you also master the plague itself. For that medicine is especially necessary. But beware of saying that God has called away or snatched this or that person. You cannot hide behind this lie. It can be proven that your medicine is worth nothing.

Thus, the other remaining protections against the plague, such as Enemas, Laxatives, and so on, are neither the primary nor the principal treatments, but only "concurring" ones, which I leave to the industrious physicians.

<margin>Medicine in the plague is twofold</margin>
Medicine is directed toward two things: toward the accidents, and toward the disease. First, you must know the nature of the accidents, and afterward the nature of the disease; then see which of these requires more immediate help from your hands.

It must be known, therefore, that he who overcomes the plague itself also drives out the accident. However, the reverse is not true, unless the plague has very little tendency toward death.

The accidents are lethal. Therefore, even if the plague is not lethal in itself, you must take care to remove the accidents above all else, so the patient is not "strangled." For if they grow strong, they overcome and strike down nature, such that they do not leave the body without harm, even if the plague itself has vanished after being properly treated—as happens in milder plagues. If the plague is small and disappears, and returns like a <term>glandule</term> <note>A small swelling or "bubo" in the lymph nodes.</note>, the death that follows it belongs to the accident, not the plague. Then both the accident and the plague reveal themselves separately by their own signs. For two kinds of disease here run together, each of which requires its own peculiar remedy.

<margin>Twofold sweat.</margin>
We are forced to admit that a twofold sweat is poured out by nature: through the pores, and through the <term>emunctories</term> <note>The "cleansing stations" of the body, specifically the lymph nodes in the armpits, groin, and neck, where the body was thought to expel "poisons."</note>. But you neglect these. Nor has anyone until now made mention of the emunctories, in which, nevertheless, the plague is fixed. Who then would praise those writings of theirs concerning the plague?

If one intends to write anything about Medicine, first the Theory must be set forth and the cause explained. Once this is done, the locations must be considered. For they themselves constitute the Theory.

The emunctories behave in this way: the sweat of the first, second, or third degree is not sweat, but is a poison from putrefaction. Where does it emerge from? Not from where the sweat of the pores flows out, but from that place where the <term>Planets</term> <note>original: "Planetæ"; In Paracelsian medicine, the major internal organs were linked to the seven planets. Here, he refers to the internal "astral" forces governing the organs.</note> are purged in their own diseases.

For *it is the virtue which cures the disease, namely its own specific virtue*. By this, what else could Hippocrates have understood than the "proper nature," namely that nature itself both heals and harms through its own emunctory?

And to put it in a word, these members (which are purged through those emunctories) are not the brain, the heart, etc. What are they then? Not the brain near the ears. For no brain can be infected by the plague. What is it then? An invisible chamber. Not the heart. What then? The fluid of the chest. Not the liver, spleen, etc. What then? The fluid, etc.

Thus, these three are the things: they are wounds. Never allow yourself to be led away from this. It is the same as if someone were to strike someone's ears, or hit the "wings" <note>Anatomical slang for the armpits (axillae).</note> and pierce them; and besides these, neither the brain nor anything else, nor the sufferings of the heart—phlegmon, death, wound, etc. This is nothing other than the region of <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostematum".</note>. And just as in wounds, death, fevers, paroxysms, and ulceration are recognized and cured, so it is here too. They are the wounds of the Planets.

Why does it *attack*? Because its quarter-phase is imminent.

The spleen, liver, heart, and brain suffer no harm; it strikes them just as lightning strikes trees, oaks, towers, and so on. From this process, it follows that it is nothing but lightning: there is one cause and one reason. For lightning prefigures it. The lightning of the pestilence is directed toward these emunctories of sweat, just as the other lightning is directed toward oaks and fir trees. For who knows the reason why lightning strikes with such discretion and judgment? No one. Who, indeed, governs it? That is in God's power. So it is with this also. For there is no other disposition. That is why these are the emunctories.

# CONCERNING THE PLAGUE #

Likewise, it burns nowhere except in its own part: that is, even if it strikes the rest of the body, it does not burn there, but only in its own specific place. Just as lightning burns only in the wood it strikes, so the "stroke of heaven" <note>original: "ictus cœli"—a metaphorical term for the plague, suggesting it is a divine or atmospheric strike similar to lightning.</note> burns only in its own place.

> The Chapter on the Cure.

<margin>Remedies for the plague. Gold. Gemstones.</margin>
Now, since the medicines for the plague are divided into those for the <term>Accidents</term> <note>Symptoms or secondary complications of a disease.</note> and those for the Cure of the plague itself: therefore, concerning the cure, know that the Spirit of gold and of gemstones are the medicines by which all plagues are healed, regardless of the location.

The primary remedy is Gold; the second is Gemstones. For gemstones are strengthening and defensive, preventing an accident from being brought on. For this reason, they are taken together in one recipe. For all recipes ought to be so composed that the disease receives the medicine and the defenses at the same time.

<margin>Mummy heals internal wounds.</margin>
Furthermore, the purpose of medicine is that all wounds may be cured and consolidated from within in the best and most skillful way. Thus, for wound-healing potions, no medicine is more successful or more excellent than internal <term>Mummy</term> <note>In the medicine of this period, "Mumia" or Mummy was a substance—sometimes derived from preserved remains, other times an alchemical extract—believed to contain a concentrated life force capable of healing the body's internal "wounds."</note>. For no wound heals from the outside. Internal Mummy cares for it and perfects it.

The greatest medicine, therefore, is to bring about <term>incarnation</term> <note>The process of the body growing new flesh to heal a wound.</note> from the internal parts.

<margin>Gold is the best "incarnative." Gemstones are the best defensive.</margin>
Moreover, there is no "incarnative" more sublime than gold itself. Alongside this, there is no defensive for wounds more outstanding than Gemstones against all accidents, of whatever kind they may be.

Thus, the plague is to be cured through these flesh-growing medicines for wounds. For those are the "Spirits" of these things. Because the imagination generates the body, and the <term>impression</term> <note>The "mark" or "signature" left by the disease on the body or spirit.</note> invades in such a spiritual way, "Spirits" must also be opposed and thrown against them—that is, they must be administered.

But now, these Spirits are made through the alchemical art of extraction. Although this is not in common use, especially among those whose greatest interest should be to know it. Although it is not unsuitable to use the Mercury of gold <margin>Mercury of gold etc.</margin> in its red form, if it is reduced to a precipitate so that it does not provoke vomiting—that is, if its laxative quality is removed. For in every preparation of gold, the highest goal is that what is unnecessary be taken away from it: that is:

In the plague, one must not purge. <margin>The plague does not want to be purged.</margin> Gold, however, is laxative, strengthening, and constricting. Remove the laxative. Keep the rest. The same must be known regarding Gemstones, which are dissolved into a liquor, namely, fixed by heat. Take: Sapphires, Hyacinths, Crystals, etc. I trust that physicians hold and understand all these things well enough, as they are the ones who ought to understand them. If they are ignorant of these things, it is a disgrace to them, not an honor.

# BY AUREOLUS PHILIPPI THEOPHRASTUS, THE HERMIT OF HOHENHEIM.
## TWO BOOKS ON DISEASES ARISING FROM TARTAR.

->*Illustrated by the Author himself in public lectures, which a certain person among the authors took down in haste with singular zeal from the mouth of the professor at Basel, in the year 1527.*<-

---

### FIRST BOOK ON TARTAR, TREATISE I, CHAPTER I.

->*What Tartar is: how many its kinds and conditions: its customary and unusual locations: likewise Frost, Hail, Gemstone, and Guest.*<-

<margin>What Tartar is.</margin>
**TARTAR** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to stony or gravelly deposits formed in the body, named after the hard crust found in wine barrels.</note> is a scaly and stony disease, hindering the effect and virtue of Nature. There are two kinds of Tartar: *Frosty and Gem-like. Frosty is twofold: Usnea-like <note>original: "Usneum"—referring to a mossy or crusty accretion, named after the lichen that grows on rocks or skulls.</note> and Hail-like. Gem-like is threefold: collected, simple, and divided.* All these kinds have similar dispositions: they are either *Alabaster-like*, *Marble-like*, *Scaly*, *Diamond-like*, *Dvelech* <note>A term coined by Paracelsus to describe the "spirit" or essence of stones formed within the human body.</note>, or *Magnetic*, and they have their own locations, which are varied. For the kinds are diverse: and therefore there are many locations in the body; and as many locations as there are, so many are the species.

<margin>How many kinds and species of Tartar.</margin>
For the locations are the Stomach, Liver, Kidneys, Spleen, Lungs, Bladder, Head, Joints, the regions of the Ligaments, all Cavities, Pores, Veins, and parts of the Marrow. Hence there is usnea of the liver, usnea of the stomach, usnea of the kidneys, etc. Also frost of the orifice, frost of the spleen, etc. There follows also the gemstone of the intestines, of the lungs, or the gemstone of the bladder: and likewise for hail. The generation of this disease is twofold, namely natural, from a customary place to a customary place, and "Guest-like" <note>original: "Hospitalis"—meaning a disease that migrates or takes up residence in an unusual part of the body.</note> from an unusual place to an unusual place.

<margin>Phlegm is not the material of the stone.</margin>
**H**ippocrates and others say that the stone has its origin from coagulated phlegm, but falsely: because if it were from phlegm, a stone would also arise in the nose; phlegm does not have the power to generate stone, but phlegm in us is a natural humor, containing no stoniness within itself. For if phlegm were stony, then all those suffering from Gout would also have stones in their feet and joints.

<margin>According to the author, Tartar is stone or sand.</margin>
I, however, call stone or sand "Tartar": because all generations that pass into usnea are called Tartar: thus all dregs that come from water, honey, etc., are Tartar. For everything that the earth produces is stony: for all wine, although it has produced Tartar in the vessel, must nevertheless pass to a second separation in the stomach: if the stomach is weak, it then attracts the stone, etc.

<margin>Everything produced from the earth has Tartar; Nature at least receives the pure.</margin>
So also waters have Tartar, and everything that the earth produces. Thus, therefore, that which we eat and drink, nature does not accept except that which is pure. Since, therefore, what we eat and drink has within it something mucilaginous, muddy, and stony: the stomach, as soon as it receives what is eaten and ingested, immediately separates the impure from the pure, which is the nourishment. If the stomach is strong, the pure passes to the limbs for the sake of nourishment, and the impure exits through the stool. If the stomach is weak, it sends the impure also to the liver, where a separation also occurs. If the liver is strong, it separates correctly, and at the same time sends the mucilaginous matter with the urine to the kidneys. If there is good separation here, it is well; if not, this mucilaginous and stony matter remains here and coagulates into Sand, which I call Tartar.

<margin>From where Tartar comes.</margin>
Therefore phlegm is not the cause, because phlegm does not pass into a stony nature. Tartar, therefore, comes from things ingested, drunk, and eaten.

->*Explanations of the first chapter, taken from the mouth of Theophrastus as he was teaching publicly.*<-

He argues against the Hippocratic view that such stones are formed from phlegm, asserting instead that they are environmental residues.</summary>

...eaten, it arises namely from a weakness in the separation of the limbs. It is therefore generated from things ingested, drunk, and eaten.

<margin>What Lephantean Tartar is.</margin>
*Lephantean* <note>original: "Lephanteus"—likely derived from a term for scaly or elephantine skin, used here for a specific texture of deposit.</note> is the first species; it is a bolus, a "hepatic stone," and is a middle ground between mud and stone that can be cut. Therefore, if something of this Lephantean nature passes through with drink, no small stone is generated from it because it is not a stony material; rather, this Lephantean matter—that is, this mud—where it sits at the bottom of the stomach, constipates the bowels, adheres and fixes itself in the passages of the stool, and suppresses the belly.

<margin>What Stony Tartar is.</margin>
*Stony tartar* <note>original: "Lapillosus tartarus"</note> is that which is stone, not mud; therefore, if a stone is to be generated, stony matter must be present, otherwise it cannot be formed. For this reason, when we drink water, there is a stony power in the water, but it is dissolved; therefore the expulsive power, unless it is as strong as it ought to be, allows tartar to be formed from the water.

<margin>Frost.</margin>
*Frosty* <note>original: "Pruinum"</note> is the first kind, but it is the most widespread among the Tartars. It is a frost which, in the folds of the stomach, attaches a thin and subtle Tartar. The same occurs in the bladder, the urinary tracts, and the liver.

<margin>Gemstone.</margin>
*Gemstone* <note>original: "Gemma"</note> is a stone generated from something translucent and clear.

<margin>Vine.</margin>
*Vine* <note>original: "Vinea"</note> is a very thin and spongy Tartar. Some subtle Tartars cling together and yet are porous like a vine; such a vine grows on a tree or a side.

<margin>Hail.</margin>
*Hail* <note>original: "Grando"</note> is a grain generated from a liquid through a phase. These are "Hailstones of Tartar" if someone passes thin pebbles in their urine.

<margin>Collected.</margin>
*Collected*, that is, composed of all species of Tartar. *Simple* is coagulated from one species. *Divided* is from one into several.
These three pertain to the small stone, not to the bolus.
*Collected* is when a bolus becomes a stone; a coagulation occurs, but it is not yet hard—that is, entirely stony. It is *Simple* when it is entirely stone. It is *Divided* when the bolus is present, but the bolus also has small stones along with the large one, and the "vine."

<margin>Alabaster-like.</margin>
*Alabaster-like* <note>original: "Alabastrinum"</note> is when it comes from the bolus. Stones that come from a bolus, even if they coagulate into a stone, are nonetheless not so hard, nor do they sting as sharply as those made of pure stony matter; rather, they are Alabaster-like, which are suited to be cut.

<margin>Marble-like.</margin>
*Marble-like* <note>original: "Marmoreum"</note>, that is, the hardest among the red stones. There are some red pebbles harder than the alabaster ones, which also allow themselves to be cut.

<margin>Lephantean.</margin>
*Lephantean*, that is, a lemon-colored tartar; yellow pebbles.

<margin>Diamond-like.</margin>
*Diamond-like* <note>original: "Adamitum"</note>, that is, the hardest among the white. These are extremely hard white stones. And *Adamita* is specifically the stone that is found in the bladder.

<margin>Duelech.</margin>
*Duelech* <note>A specific Paracelsian term for a type of painful stone formed in the body.</note> is a spongy stone, and those stones come with the greatest danger and cause the most pain.

<margin>Magnetic.</margin>
*Magnetic* <note>original: "Magnetinum"</note> is the hardest spongy stone. And because there are various species of "calculus" <note>the medical term for a stone or pebble</note>, they therefore have diverse cures and various locations: for there is a location in the stomach, the liver, etc. When the first separation of the stomach is not good, the liver must separate; if the liver is weak, the kidneys or the attractive power must separate. And thus the Tartar comes to the place where the nourishment ought to descend.
(From its accustomed nature into an accustomed place.) As when a "white spot" <note>original: "albugo"—a white opacity of the cornea</note> happens to someone in the eyes, it comes to a customary place; so too deafness, if in the ear, is in its customary place; if it moves to the temples, it is then in an unaccustomed place.

## CHAPTER II.

*The beginning of Tartar: where foreign things come from: what is dissolved with liquid: the final stage is separation. Examples: digestion in place of sequestration. The location matters more than the material: Likewise, what Mucilage, Viscosity, Sapphire, Chalcedony, Bolus, and Pebble are.*

### TREATISE I.

<margin>The origin of Tartar is twofold. From the Elements and the body.</margin>
**N**ow, what is to be thought concerning the Origin of Tartar, or where does it come from? The first is *Elementine*, the other is *Corporeal*. Concerning the elementated nature, it must be noted: For the *Archeus* <note>The "inner alchemist" or vital force that governs digestion and separation in Paracelsian thought.</note> of the elementated nature does not dissolve what is separated from the dissolved liquid, nor what is mucilaginous or muddy. Therefore, the matrix produced two things without seed: the *Liquid* and the *Viscous*. The Liquid is pure; the Viscous is the "sinning" <note>offending or problematic</note> part. The Liquid is food and drink; the Viscous is the dissolved bolus, under one appearance and mixture. This product has two ultimate materials, that is, the external and the internal. The principle of these ultimate things is *separation*. If it is external, it is without harm, and is a philosophical matter. If, however, it is internal, then it is with danger, and is a medical argument. For if nature leads the liquid and the viscous into sequestration, it has two forms: that of the Matrix water, and the earthy, and then also that of the body. Of the water and earth, just as with the flints of the body; of the body, just as with the tartars: if it belongs to the body, look to see whether the "sinning" matter was delivered through food and drink. If the nature of the stomach or digestion is accustomed to it, well and good; if not, take heed; the limb is injured and pained by indigestion—namely, by the non-separation of the pure *Sapphire* from the impure and insulting *Chalcedony* <note>Paracelsus uses "Sapphire" and "Chalcedony" as metaphors for the pure nutrients vs. the impure stony waste.</note>: because it is one and the same Nature that separates the pebble and the bolus. Therefore, the location must be treated—namely, the harmful and foreign location—more than the primary material, which is *Mucilage*.

### *Explanations of the Second Chapter.*

**E**lementine is that which descends from the mothers of the elements.
Corporeal is that which descends from the bodily humors.
Dissolved mucilage is a dissolved bolus or pebble.
Dissolved liquid is that which is liquid from the "First Entity."
The generation of Tartar is twofold: Elementine, that is, External, which is from food and drink.
Corporeal is from the humors.
*All created things*) Created things are either liquid or not liquid: if created liquid, they are pure and unmixed, but many are spoiled, just as water is eventually spoiled by stone. For in water there is Stony Matter, just as if it boils for a long time or is distilled, it adheres like Tartar in a vessel. So too the springs which come from...

<header>CONCERNING TARTAR. BOOK I.</header>

Things that take their origin from mud are muddy, and where they flow, the mud adheres. Thus, when they are drunk, they create mud in the stomach or other members. In this way, all things produced from the earth that are eaten and drunk contain within them a certain <term>Mucilaginous</term> <note>A thick, gluey substance similar to mucus.</note> and viscous quality. Consider bread: it is composed so that no viscosity is apparent, but when it is digested, a slipperiness and viscosity emerge on the surface and fall away; after it has cooked for a long time, it hardens at the bottom. The same happens in the stomach: it performs the separation, but if the stomach is weak, it transmits the impurity to the liver and the remaining members. Nevertheless, bread is the least viscous among all foods. Similarly, fields that are manured have more stones because the <term>Tartar</term> <note>In this context, "Tartar" refers to the stony or sandy deposits left behind by fluids, much like the scale in a kettle or the crust in a wine barrel.</note> present in the manure dissolves and creates stones. <margin>Fields in Bohemia are not manured.</margin> In Bohemia, fields are not manured, and the crops that grow in manured fields are less healthy than those grown in unmanured fields. The "ultimate matter" of a thing is its end; just as a spring in a meadow, arising from a muddy source, makes its channel muddy. If it arises from stones and rocks, it makes its channel stony, as seen when silt adheres and creates stone. Often, if a stone is broken, it has folds or layers because one layer of viscosity settled upon another. In this same way, stone or mud—which is the ultimate matter—is born within us. <margin>Stony springs are good.</margin> If, therefore, as in a spring, the water separates itself in the meadow, it goes well for us because the impurity is separated. If it is not separated within us, it goes poorly. Therefore, springs that contain many stones and sand, and those with viscous stones, are good because the sand and stones attract the viscosity and separate the impurity from the pure water. <margin>How Emperor Frederick tested and improved water.</margin> And Emperor Frederick drank only water, and tested it thus: he dipped a clean linen cloth into the water and weighed it on a scale, then dried it in the sun and weighed it again; by this means, he could judge how much Tartar was being generated within it. He did not drink wine because he feared Tartar in that way, for he had a peculiar "spirit of Tartar" within himself. <margin>If water is distilled, it rots.</margin> But a certain Italian came who said that water ought to be distilled to make it purer; and the Ass did not consider that water does not wish to be distilled. For it immediately putrefies and stinks. Indeed, when the Emperor followed his advice, it led to foulness of the breath, etc. Likewise, every month the Emperor saw to it that new flints were carried to the springs so they would attract the viscosity. Thus, just as viscosity or stony matter adheres in meadows or other places, so too must it be separated in the body. <margin>What urine is.</margin> Urine is dissolved salt generated in the liver, descending to its place of expulsion as a superfluity. <margin>The nature of the transformation of food.</margin> Everything we eat is either Sulphurous, which goes to the excrement; Mercurial, for nutrition; or dissolved Salt, which goes to the urine. Thus, Tartar settles in the urinary passages; where the expulsive force is strong, it is expelled; if not strong, it generates diseases. In short, a separation of the pure from the impure must occur. If the stomach is weak, the matter putrefies, leading to fevers and other diseases. This arises from a stomach weak in its "separative virtue." But the Tartar, or the "matter of the stone," does not putrefy; rather, the nourishment that ought to go to the limbs putrefies. From this come bad vapors, fevers, etc. For the separation of pure from impure must happen; if the separative power fails, the nourishment putrefies. Therefore, fevers are cured by purging, because when the putrid matter is evacuated, health returns.

<margin>Centaury purges fevers. Centaury is a liver herb.</margin>
Thus <term>Centaury</term> <note>A bitter herb (Centaurium erythraea) traditionally used to treat fevers and digestive issues.</note> also helps fevers. For Centaury pertains to the liver; it strengthens and purges the liver’s separative virtue where the liver is corrupt and weak. Centaury is the liver's own herb; it does not cure the stomach. Thus, fevers come from a weakness of the separative power of the stomach or liver, causing the matter to putrefy.

Nourishment is derived from a thing putrefied, and its transformation lies in that putrefaction. (Otherwise: and its putrefaction is into transformation.)

"Sapphiric matter" is that liquid in which there is no "sinning matter" <note>original: "materia peccans"—a medical term for the substance causing a disease.</note>.

<margin>Cacedonius is the worst stone.</margin>
<term>Cacedonius</term> <note>A specific, highly harmful type of internal sediment or stone.</note> is that sinning matter generated from separations by the separative virtue. Cacedonius is the worst kind of stone.

### CHAPTER III.

-> *Three things were given by the <term>Iliaster</term> <note>The primeval force or "star" of matter in Paracelsian thought.</note> into nature: in which bodies: what treatment they receive: The generation of Tartar: The nature of Tartar: Also the evil, the secondary viscosity, Bitumen, and what "congluten" is.* <-

<margin>Three evils from the Iliaster.</margin>
**A**nd thus, from the nature of the body, its own evil is produced—that is, the Tartar of nature. For the Iliaster gave birth to three things in the nature of the suffering person: the viscosity of the second generation (internal blood); a perverse <term>Bitumen</term> poorly reduced (that is, a coagulated liquor); and a "conglutinative" or "congluten" of itself from putrefied matter. Much must be noted concerning this Tartar, for it is found in children, in chaste men, in dry bodies, and is an hereditary disease in heirs and offspring. Note these two generations of tartar: the external receives treatment; the internal treatment requires a strong external one for the internal. Their locations are within the properties of their own substance. Local differences must be noted between the former Tartar and this one: for the first occupies a space in the cavities and from the outside, but the second is within the substance itself. From these two follows a third generation, which is a mixture of the two aforementioned; it accepts treatment, but with difficulty, according to the weight of the other. <margin>In whom Tartar is generated.</margin> The generation of Tartar is sometimes from the nature of the blood, sometimes the flesh, and sometimes other members. This is why we spoke of unusual locations, unusual generation, and unusual cure. What is necessary concerning these signs is known; and what concerns common generation—namely in the urinary paths—we know from common experience.

**T**artar of Nature is a stony mineral, created elementally, received under a dissolved moisture.

The viscosity of the second generation is <term>cruor</term> <note>thick, clotted blood or gore</note>, which descends from salts: for cruor is salt cast out, that is, rejected and separated from the first salt.

<margin>What perverted Bitumen is.</margin>
Perverted <term>Bitumen</term> <note>Usually a mineral pitch or tar; here used to describe a sticky, pathological bodily fluid</note> is a fluid digested in a perverted way, that is, an uncooked fluid which descends beneath the viscosity from its own nutrients.

### Proper vital nutrients.

Congluten, or the conglutinating substance, is that which descends from putrefaction into a colored glue; it is the proper substance of both bodies—namely, the substantial and the vital.

<margin>Two kinds of Tartar.</margin>
There are two kinds of *Tartar*, *internal and external*. Tartar is generated from the external by way of food and drink. The internal is that which is generated within the body, just as stones are often born in children; and this is a hereditary disease.

Therefore, the Physician must observe whether the Tartar is in the person's nature, or accidental, or internal, or external. Internal and Innate Tartar ought to be cured by such [internal] remedies. External Tartar should be treated by ashes and alkali.

<margin>All minerals are in man.</margin>
Man has within himself all generations, that is, all minerals. For example, salt is in the body, as appears in sweat. The fluid also, which sustains the flesh, is salt, but sweet. The salt of the blood is bitter. The salt of the flesh is sweet: and the sweeter the flesh, the better the nature; and the bitterer the blood, the more a man is strong in blood.

But those salts, when they are separated from the ligaments, the limbs, and the muscles, pass there into a stony power, just as ulcers are created from salt: for it corrodes, and when it is coagulated after being dissolved, if it coagulates in the veins, the stone causes an obstruction there, and the limb wastes away, so that an arm cannot be raised. Thus it often happens that an arm or a limb atrophies. This occurs because of Tartar, which obstructs the veins and the pathways of nutrition. In this way come stabs of pain and strokes, so that when the wind or breath cannot break through, wasting is induced. Thus the exhaustion of the veins comes from the obstruction of Tartar within them: and so it often happens that an incised vein does not flow. Then our colleagues say that it is "melancholic blood": This is not true, but it is Tartar; the Tartar obstructs it. Therefore, the vein must be pierced in two or three places behind or further back from the Tartar until it flows, or something must be applied to dissolve the internal Tartar. For if the blood is washed, you will find small stones. Therefore, it is not only sand that passes through the urine, but it is everywhere. Thus, stones are even often born in the eyes: for the salt fluid that is in the head settles in the eye in this way. I have also often seen small white stones in head wounds, clinging to the plasters.

<margin>Tartar hinders the flow of blood.</margin>
Innate salt purges itself mostly through sweat: sometimes from the eyes.

<margin>Leprosy from a lack of salt fluid.</margin>
The fluid of salt is the balsam of nature which sustains the body so that it does not rot. For where the fluid of salt is lacking, leprosy now occurs, and the body rots: for leprosy is nothing other than a mortal putrefaction.

<margin>The bodies in us are twofold.</margin>
Bitumen, etc. We have two bodies within us: the Substantial, which is sustained by nutrients and food; and the Vital, which lives from salt. Therefore, the generation of Tartar comes from this [vital] substance. Thus, internal Tartar ought to be cured by salt.

Congluten, etc. When nature moves toward destruction and fails in the nature of balsam, then it becomes a glutinous mucus. 

<margin>The water of the joints is Synovia.</margin>
For among Physicians, this glue is the "water of the joints"; among surgeons, it is <term>Synovia</term> <note>The lubricating fluid found in the cavities of synovial joints</note>.

The fluid of salt descends from a dissolved bolus and a dissolved small stone: therefore, when it reaches its end, it returns again to its own nature.

<margin>Gore is triple.</margin>
Gore <note>original: "cruor"</note> is triple: the gore of the principal members; of the ligaments or the nape of the neck; and exterior gore.

<margin>Nature is purged through gore.</margin>
When nature wishes to purge itself, it purges itself through gore, that is, through sweat. For example, when the brain wishes to purge itself, sweat passes through the <term>pia and dura mater</term> <note>The delicate inner and tough outer membranes surrounding the brain</note>, as we see in head wounds. And in Anatomy, we see that <term>Usnea</term> <note>Usually a type of moss, but here used for a thin, mossy mineral deposit</note>—a thin Tartar—lies upon the pia mater. And in the Anatomy of the eyes, in the veins from which the eyes depend, little stones are found. Therefore, it often happens that some see nothing even with open eyes, because Tartar has obstructed the visual power. When medicines are used that dissolve the Tartar, they see again. And often they see again of their own accord after several weeks, because the Tartar, through the strength of nature, resolves itself back into water.

<margin>Tartar is twofold.</margin>
Therefore *Tartar* is twofold: dry, which is not dissolved; and liquid, which is sometimes dissolved even if it has hardened. Thus also gore in the ligaments, when it coagulates, becomes Tartar. From this, stabs of pain are excited in the joints.

<margin>Sperm is the subject of the seed.</margin>
The exterior gore, which is in the flesh, passes into external sweat; if you taste it, it is salty, and if you allow it to dry slowly in a glass, you will see stones. It is a hereditary disease, because if the parents have much salt, the sperm is also infected, and the man born from it. In the substance of the sperm is the matter and power of the seed <note>original: "feminis," here likely meaning the germinating seed or semen</note>. Thus, someone is often gouty <note>original: "podagrofus"</note> not from his own diet, but from his parents. The substance does not generate—husks and shells procreate nothing—but the matter of generation descends from the vital substance; this is a tiny thing, and it is most pure. But with that matter, the generative substance runs at the same time and is the "shell" of the seed, and the substance runs together with the seed. And if that substance is infected, it creates internal Tartar. For after it has conceived the seed, which is the generative power, it must be separated from the substance. The substance therefore must putrefy, and it will putrefy. From this it happens that <term>molae</term> <note>Fleshy masses in the uterus, sometimes called "false pregnancies"</note>, suffocation of the womb, and slipperiness often emerge from it.

<margin>Mugwort for purging women.</margin>
Therefore, women after conception ought to be purged with <term>Artemisia</term> <note>Mugwort, a herb traditionally used in folk medicine for uterine health</note>. Even dry people have Tartar, because that dryness attracts and coagulates salt. This happens to chaste men: the superfluities—that is, the dissolved Tartar—do not exit with the sperm and do not purge the kidneys. These variations of the causes of Tartar must be observed by the Physician so that he knows what ought to be applied. The locations of internal tartars are the veins and flesh: thus external Tartar seeks out cavities, while internal Tartar sits in the veins and flesh.

diseases. A deliberation on what they are, and what the ancients said.

<margin>Tartar from external sources is twofold.</margin>
**E**xternal Tartar, if it is taken in liquid form through drink or food—whether it is slimy and resolved from small stones, or viscous and resolved from its own <term>bolus</term> <note>A soft mass of food or medicine</note>—understand that there are two operations: namely, those of **Frost** or of **Gems**. If it is gathered as a "gem," whether it be divided or simple, recognize their dispositions—whether alabaster or marble—and so to the matter at hand. The first is the Tartar of swallowing, taken down to the bottom of the stomach. Concerning this, note that if it is so viscous or slimy that it is easily separated, or if the greater part is dissolved, it follows throughout the entire orifice, just as a vine grows over flint stones or over trees.

<margin>Effects and accidents of the Vine-growth.</margin>
From this "vine" follows burning, <term>heartburn</term> <note>original: "orexes," here referring to an acidic or burning sensation rather than just appetite</note>, compression of the chest, and hot vapor; the appetite for eating recedes. These are all signs of a vine-growth in the orifice or the stomach. And according to whether the pains of the vine-growth arise from wines, peppers, or waters, it is converted more or less into pain. If, however, it is not a "Vine" or "Hail" (which are of one generation and chapter) that has been generated, but a separation of "sapphire" from "chalcedony" occurs in the stomach: now the Tartar is in the stomach, producing a twisting of the <term>pecten</term> <note>The region of the pubic bone or lower abdomen</note>, taking away the appetite, causing nausea, a feeling of burning at the bottom of the stomach, and roughness of the tongue. It grants hoarseness and many daily pains and many fevers. Concerning these diseases, the ancient physicians wrote specific chapters under a different system of reasoning, and they erred abundantly, as practice teaches and indicates.

# ON THE SECOND TREATISE. CHAPTER I.
->Annotations.<-

<margin>How Hail is formed.</margin>
**T**he generation of "hail" occurs through dryness in the salt, when it is segregated from the moisture. The "vine" kind occurs through the smoke of the salt consumed, as if from <term>cruor</term> <note>clotted blood or thick bodily fluid</note>. The "collected" kind occurs through the falling of a small stone, both simple and divided—namely, from resolved stones.

<margin>All ingested things contain Tartar.</margin>
Now we must proceed to treat the locations that Tartar occupies. First, regarding the stomach: everything we eat contains within itself something of either dissolved stone or dissolved bolus.

<margin>Tartar which comes from drink.</margin>
First, concerning drink: what we drink passes through the throat to the stomach. If what we drink has much slime, and the orifice of the stomach is narrow and boiling or hot, then the slime adheres there; the power of the salt consumes the wateriness, and thus the matter adheres, coagulates, and hardens. If it is from a dissolved bolus, it adheres in the manner of a bolus. If from stone, it becomes "hail." Thus the "vine" collects itself, and this sickness is found mostly in women, and less in men unless they are great drinkers. This appears in <term>Anatomy</term> <note>Meaning here the practice of dissection</note>; when they are cut open, something muddy is found in the orifice of the stomach, which, if applied to fire, hardens and becomes mud or stone. Thus, when that power of salt consumes the matter and hardens the viscous substance, it becomes heartburn or burning. When the person drinks, the drink passes through this Tartar. And because a healthy stomach closes itself and cooks like a closed <term>alembic</term> <note>A chemical vessel used for distillation; here a metaphor for the stomach</note>: but because the Tartar has settled in the orifice, the orifice cannot be rightly closed, and so smoke ascends and goes toward the Tartar.

<margin>The power and nature of sweet Tartar.</margin>
Thus there is a "sweet" Tartar that does not burn, and that Tartar comes from wateriness. But if it comes from wine, it is a "sharp" Tartar, which, if first drenched with water or wine (that is, with drink), it is like <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: "calx," calcium oxide, which produces heat when mixed with water</note> that is ignited, and so it burns.

<margin>The source of being "Tartarized."</margin>
Therefore, for one who would cure heartburn, it is necessary to move to the cure of Tartar, so that the Tartar falls to the bottom of the stomach and leaves through the <term>bowels</term> <note>original: "secessum," meaning excretion</note>.

Those, therefore, who drink water do not have this heartburn, but those who drink wine do. Although even those who drink water may have heartburn, this is not from the water, but from the food. Thus heartburn is generated because first the "vine" from the wine adheres to the orifice. When they have drunk and eaten, the orifice of the stomach ought to be closed while it cooks. For those who say they "taste themselves" <note>likely referring to acid reflux or tasting undigested food</note> after they have eaten and drunk, their orifice is corrupted by Tartar; and thus the Tartar, when it is moistened, burns like quicklime. This is the first generation.

<margin>Hail in the stomach orifice.</margin>
The second is that of "hail," where small stones or tiny <term>calculi</term> <note>Small stones formed in the body</note> adhere in the top of the stomach and the orifice. Those who have them say that when they eat and swallow, they feel pain; for those "hails" cut in that way. Those generated in the orifice do not cause heartburn but are felt during swallowing. If you were to see or wash the bowel movements of those who have this, small stones would appear.

The third: if the orifice is healthy, possessing neither heat nor the spirit of salt, it allows the matter to go to the stomach and lie there. If the power of separation and digestion is not strong, and if the matter is viscous, it then sticks to the folds. For the stomach has many folds. Therefore it adheres to the walls or the sides. For the stomach sends the pure parts to the liver, and the impure parts to the <term>monoculus</term> <note>The cecum or start of the large intestine</note> for excretion. If the matter is too viscous to be expelled, it becomes attached. If it is from a dissolved bolus, it becomes muddy matter; if from stone, it becomes stone.

<margin>Stones found in a stomach at Venice.</margin>
Just as in an anatomy performed at Venice, three small stones and rocks were found in a certain person's stomach.

Therefore, burning comes either from Tartar or from an effusion of **Bile**; for both Bile and Tartar stir up burning. If someone complains of feeling a burning around the <term>precordia</term> <note>The region of the body in front of the heart or epigastrium</note>, one should not purge there, but the pain should be soothed.

<margin>A mitigator for pain from Tartar.</margin>
The following is a soothing remedy:

> Darnel, 1/2 drachm
> Mandrake, 4 grains
> Theriac <note>A traditional herbal jam or electuary used as an antidote</note>, as much as suffices
> for a mixture. The dose is 4 scruples.

is the generation of Tartar in the stomach: It is just like the formation of Tartar in a wine barrel. When Tartar is present in the stomach in this way, the stomach cannot digest, and the matter passes into putrefaction <note>The breakdown of undigested food into harmful waste</note>. From this, fevers arise, the belly suffers, the body collapses, and the feverish paroxysms <note>sudden attacks or fits</note> occur in the stomach, not in other members like the lungs, ligaments, or blood.

<margin>The resolution of Tartar as a cure for fever.</margin>
And so the paroxysm lasts until the Tartar is settled. Therefore, the cure for fevers is to dissolve the Tartar. Because the digestive power fails, fevers and paroxysms arise; thus, the cure must address the Tartar. For whatever arises from Tartar causes shaking for a time and eventually presses or twists, because over a long time, the digestive power consumes the moisture of the putrefaction. Thus, it later hardens the Tartar, and then the "torsions" <note>painful griping or cramping</note> attack anew.

<margin>The error of the ancients in the cure of fevers.</margin>
Therefore, in the treatment of Tartar, one understands all types of fevers. What our authors <note>referring to traditional authorities like Galen or Avicenna</note> write regarding the cure of fevers is plainly contrary to the resolution of Tartar. If they occasionally effect a cure, it is not from their medicine, but because nature herself expels the Tartar; thus it often happens that fevers are cured through bowel movements or vomiting. For whatever medicine dissolves or expels Tartar cures the fever.

So it often happens that when Physicians wish to cure fevers, they write prescriptions with many "simples" <note>medicines made of only one herb or ingredient</note> which, if they happen to contain ingredients that expel Tartar, result in a cure. Some fevers depart through bloodletting, but this is rare; it happens because the stomach is strong enough to expel the "sinning matter"—that is, the Tartar—to the liver. In such cases, phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> helps. But this fails where there is a very hard stone or where the Tartar cannot be dissolved.

<margin>Spices as a cure for heartburn.</margin>
*With peppers, etc.*) Those who eat much pepper or spices, as they do in Bohemia, do not suffer from <term>orexis</term> <note>original: "orexi"; here meaning acid reflux or heartburn</note>. The Physician Albertus <note>likely Albertus Magnus</note> advised those in Meissen, Bohemia, and elsewhere to eat pepper because they drink beer, which chills the stomach. Therefore, they eat pepper to warm it. Also, because beer is a viscous substance, that viscosity sticks to the stomach. But they use warm beer with butter, and thus the viscosity is dissolved. They eat butter so that a "slipperiness" is created and the viscosity does not stick; before they did this, they always suffered in the stomach.

<margin>Where stomach pains come from.</margin>
All stomach pains, therefore, come either from putrefied Tartar or generated Tartar. The putrefied kind belongs to fevers; the generated kind leads to other diseases. That Tartar matter is not driven out by purgatives unless the Tartar is first dissolved into a liquid. For just as water or a liquid, if it is to be expelled, must be turned back into a liquid state, then it departs. If, however, it is putrefied Tartar, it causes fevers, and sometimes departs through purging.

# CHAPTER II.

->Concerning what is transmitted to the intestines: The consequence of future and present disease: Anatomy is the teacher of this theory. The error of Physicians regarding the cause of disease, and the true cause of Tartar.<-

<margin>Which intestinal diseases come from Tartar.</margin>
**I**f food is digested in the stomach as food should be, all is well. But if it is not, but is transmitted to the intestines through the dung, and if the hidden "coagulating power" is active in that part and works toward a harmful effect, there follows either <term>usnea</term>, or <term>grando</term>, or <term>gemma</term> <note>Paracelsian terms for different consistencies of deposits: moss-like, hail-like, or gem-like stones</note> of both kinds, Alabaster-like and Marble-like. From this follows constipation of the bowels, swelling, <term>Tympanites</term> <note>bloating of the abdomen with gas</note>, windiness, twisting of the navel, incurable types of colic, vomiting, and similar signs. These are understood through the anatomy of these sick people, in whom the intestine is found abundantly filled with <term>usnea</term>, whether in the <term>monocolon</term> <note>the cecum</note>, the <term>longaon</term> <note>the rectum</note>, or the flanks. Regarding these Tartars, many rules have been handed down for "windy colic" and the cause of disease, and for "marked cholera," but quite poorly. The descriptions of the authors are therefore falsely established: for the cause is neither "cholera" nor gall, nor constipation as they have said, but Tartar offending the site. Therefore, accept the cause of Tartar, not some foreign cause.

## ANNOTATIONS ON THE SECOND CHAPTER.

<margin>What kind of digestion occurs for food.</margin>
When food is taken, whether it be a soft mass or a small stone, if the stomach digests it, the first step is **separation**, then digestion—not the other way around, as Avicenna thinks. The first thing is the separation of the pure from the impure; after separation, it digests the nourishment and imparts it to the members. It sends the impure, which is the waste of the nourishment, through the intestines. This "Sulphur" is the unclean thing that passes through the intestines. If the expelling power is weak, then the coagulating power of the **Salt** creates Tartar. For that viscosity sticks to the intestines and forms Tartar, just as Tartar is formed in the stomach and its orifice. This happens because the power of **Sulphur** does this. For dung is nothing other than sulphur and "wind" <note>gas</note>, which, when it exits, can be ignited and burns just like sulphur; so too does the dung.

<margin>How Tartar is made.</margin>
<margin>Sulphurous dung.</margin>
Therefore, there is a certain Sulphur in the dung: for dung is nothing else but Sulphur, a burning power. When it is in the intestines, it sticks to them: if it is *usnea*, it is somewhat light; if *grando*, also light; if *gemmae*, here there is work and labor required. From this follow diseases and constipation. First, when the matter of Sulphur and Salt are joined and they dry out the matter, they cause constipation. From constipation come other illnesses which are cured by the treatment for Tartar, because when the Tartar is dissolved, the illnesses depart. But chamomile oil or other oils, with which Mesue <note>a famous medieval Arab physician</note> wants to drive away the "torsions" of the belly, do not do this. Nor do the enemas that are given, unless they are made from seeds—linseed, psyllium, fenugreek, etc.—and are mucilaginous. Because in the intestines there is more of the "bolus" <note>soft mass</note> than "stones," and because those seeds are mucilaginous, and the matter in the intestines is of the bolus and mucilaginous kind. Thus, they have added like to like, and "likes are cured by likes."

Bloating <term>Tympanites<gloss>a condition where the belly is stretched tight as a drum due to gas</gloss></term> is a constipation of the belly, not a type of dropsy.

What the cure for Bloating is.

Where there is heat, there is wind; and where it cannot exit due to constipation, the Bloating is not cured except by the dissolution of the Tartar. This is what constipation is; but a hot decoction swallowed whole, or some herb boiled in oil, will not fix this.

Diverse opinions on Colic.
Tartar is of two kinds.

Bloating comes from constipation; Griping comes from the dissolution of the deposits. Some think Colic comes from bile <note>original: "fel"</note> which, when redundant, goes to the intestines and pricks them. Others say it comes from constipation, because the person cannot pass stool. In truth, Colic is nothing other than dissolved Tartar in the intestines; because Tartar is sharp, it stings. As I have said, it is of two kinds: Sweet, which when dissolved causes undigested diarrhea <term>lienteria<gloss>a condition where food passes through the body quickly and unchanged</gloss></term>; and that Sharp kind, which causes Colic. When it is thus dissolved, it lies in a fixed place; because it has no expulsive power of its own, it simply sits there and stings. Its cure, therefore, is to either consume this liquid, or to coagulate it back into Tartar, or to let the body's expulsive power drive it out. This is why people drink oil for Colic: because when the oil reaches the dissolved Tartar, it mitigates the Tartar’s sharpness and leads it to be expelled. Sweet wines do the same. As for why it causes saffron-colored urine, that is due to the bile; it also causes vomiting, because when the intestines suffer, the stomach suffers as well.

# CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the great matters of the Liver: what the disease is, what the signs are, the judgment of the Urine, and further concerning Mesenteric Tartar: Regarding infirmities and the errors of the ancients.

If the food has been digested in the stomach during the first digestion and expelled into the second digestion of the liver: if a separation occurs there into "moss" <term>usnea<gloss>a term used by Paracelsus for a moss-like metabolic residue</gloss></term> or "gem" <term>gemma<gloss>a stone-like deposit</gloss></term>—depending on whether it was resolved from a food-bolus or a small stone—then constipation follows in the liver. This causes hardness, chronic abscesses <note>original: "apostema"</note>, thirst, pains in the right side, stinging sensations, and obstructions <note>original: "oppilationes"</note>. It turns into heat; the lips will appear cracked with an itching of the nose, and the tongue will be dried out. Swellings appear in the feet and especially the shins. Appetite is driven away, and digestion is rejected. The urine is like that of a dropsy patient, as if undigested, pale-grey and plentiful. This generation of Tartar occurs not only in the liver itself, but also in the regions and borders surrounding it. If, however, the separation does not appear during the liver’s digestion, and the matter has moved out to the mesenteric muscles <note>original: "meseraicas lacertosas," the tissues connecting the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, and if such a deposit forms in these mesenteric muscles, then the generation of "moss" or "gem" follows. From this comes pain in the mesentery, constipation of nutrition, a type of wasting fever <term>Ethica<gloss>a chronic fever associated with consumption</gloss></term>, and the beginning of lung disease <term>phthisis<gloss>tuberculosis or similar wasting of the lungs</gloss></term>. There is also pain in the spine, the ribs, and the womb; it makes the seed weak, takes away the desire for reproduction, and causes a drying out of all the limbs, etc. These are great pains involving mineral-like deposits, about which the ancients were utterly in error and wrote false chapters.

When there is an obstruction in the liver, the person loses their color; often the color changes throughout the day. Thirst comes from this because the liver lacks moisture due to the blockage. Because the nutrients cannot pass, they return from the liver to the stomach and spoil; from this arises a convulsion of the stomach, which is to say, hiccups; likewise, cracking of the lips and skin-shedding on the feet. This—along with dryness of the tongue—comes from the obstruction of the liver.
