### Exposition of the Second Chapter.

<margin>What is called compression of the chest.</margin>
<margin>The separation of Tartar is twofold. Tartar is either sweet or sharp.</margin>
<margin>What kind of organ the gall is.</margin>
<margin>Signs of stomach Tartar combined with gall.</margin>
<margin>Gall is not to be purged.</margin>
**I** call these "compressions of the chest," though others call them weakness of digestion, coldness of the stomach, nausea, canine appetite <note>original: "appetitum caninum," a historical term for ravenous, insatiable hunger</note>, heartburn, fainting of the stomach, or foul vapors. All these come from the vice of <term>Tartar</term> <note>Paracelsus's term for stony, mineral-like metabolic waste that crystallizes in the body like the crust in a wine barrel</note> and are cured through the treatment of Tartar. Therefore, I embrace them under one name and call them "compression of the chest." As I have said, "orexis" <note>acid reflux/heartburn</note> comes from coagulated Tartar—stretching from the throat to the mesenteric veins—whereas "compression" happens from resolved or dissolved Tartar. This occurs when the digestive force is so strong that it wishes to separate the waste and turns it into a liquid, which then remains in the bottom of the stomach. This liquid is of two types: either "sweet Tartar," where there is no great pain, or "sharp Tartar," where there is great pain accompanied by bilious vomiting or pains in the spine. When such vomiting occurs—yellow, green, and bitter—it is from the <term>gall</term> <note>bile</note>. This is not because there is an abundance of gall or a defect in the gallbladder itself, for the gall does not exit on its own nor does it generate disease in another organ by itself. Rather, that Tartar lying in the bottom of the stomach attracts the gall. These two opposites cannot exist together, and thus vomiting occurs. Therefore, the gall does not overflow by itself, nor does it go into another organ unless it is drawn there, just as blood remains hidden in its veins and marrow in the bones. The gall is a "fixed" organ; no organ is the cause of disease for another organ on its own. Therefore, when that liquid is separated by the digestive force and lies in the bottom of the stomach, and some of it goes toward the gallbladder <note>original: "fellis siculum," likely referring to the sac of the gall</note>, then these opposites cannot stand together—namely, the calcined mineral and the Tartar, which are like <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> and Tartar, or the bitter and the sour. For Tartar is acidic, just as gall is a most bitter thing. Thus it overflows into the stomach, and it has no other way to be expelled except to return by the path through which the Tartar ran. When the gall comes to the stomach, it burns there, and men waste away; there are pains in the stomach, discoloration, and pains in the back. He who grows pale and feels a twisting in the region of the heart <note>original: "torsiones præcordiorum"</note> shows a certain sign that he has Tartar in his stomach and that the gall has run into it. Vomiting occurs because the gall has entered the stomach, and the stomach cannot endure a substance from a foreign organ. From this gall, they say many illnesses arise, and they think the cure is to "shut" the gall. But how should it be shut? If they shut it, where would one receive nourishment? Nor can the gall be purged—would we then purge the heart as well? There are four organs from which nothing should be taken away: the heart, the gall, the brain, and the lungs. No medicine should be applied to these, because they purge themselves if there is anything superfluous. Therefore, the best medicine is for the Tartar in the stomach to be dissolved and sent through the intestines; then the gall will be quiet. There are many who vomit and have pains in the stomach in this way; their cure is for the Tartar to be removed. Others do not have gall in the stomach; they do not have pains in the spine or vomiting, but they are always shivering and wrap themselves in furs in both summer and winter. This is a sign that the Tartar in the stomach has been dissolved. Furthermore, they have an appetite for eating because the Tartar is dissolved. You should not say that the flux has slipped downward. The one cure is that the stomach be strengthened. Therefore, when those people come saying they have been to the baths at Baden and have thoroughly purged the body, yet it helps nothing, it is a sign that the Tartar is dissolved in the stomach. If their feet begin to grow weary and their faces turn white, the Tartar has moved into the bladder—that is, it has become a stone.

<margin>What are the signs of kidney stones.</margin>
<margin>How the heart trembles.</margin>
<margin>What kind of cure. Bad treatment for heart tremor.</margin>
But when they complain of weariness in this way, and their loins and back ache, and their faces turn red, it is a sign that the stone is in the kidneys. When they turn pale, they say it is a "phlegmatic" condition. It is nothing of the sort; rather, a stone has settled there, and they vomit. But when the digestive force has separated the matter and the expulsive force drives it to the intestines, then "colic" pains occur because the intestines are sensitive. When the dissolved matter of the Tartar descends from the stomach to the intestines and is not immediately expelled through the stool, then it causes griping pains <note>original: "tormina"</note>, though not after the stool is passed. If the griping persists even after the stool, or if it has moved into the <term>monocolon</term> <note>the large intestine or cecum</note>, then it has stuck there. The cure there involves "fervent fevers" and "cooked hemp thread"—specifically when it comes from Tartar. It is called "Iliaca" <note>ileus or intestinal obstruction</note> if the Tartar still lies above the navel; there, hemp thread does not help because the heat cannot reach the offending matter. In this disease, purges are given, not so the Tartar itself is purged (for it cannot be purged), but so the stool may take the Tartar along with it. If it will not pass, another cure must be attempted. *Regarding the tremor of the heart, etc.*) It does not actually move, but stays in its place, though it is thought to move. This happens when the gall enters the stomach, drawn by the Tartar, and the expulsive force cannot drive it out through vomiting. The matter weighs heavily there, causing a fever; it convulses the stomach, presses and burns it, and the paroxysm <note>an attack or fit</note> lasts for 5 or 6 hours. It is nothing but a "stomach fever," except that not all the limbs shake, but only the stomach, and the heart does not actually tremble. The cure involves treating the fever. Other doctors, however, proceed as if it were a tremor of the heart; they give "bone of the stag's heart," <note>a small bone-like cartilage found in the hearts of older deer, once prized as a cardiac medicine</note> corals, and so on. They wish to cure the heart when the disease is in the stomach and the stomach is what is affected. The heart does not tremble; it is caused by nothing but the gall, which cannot be expelled.

<margin>Suffocation of the womb.</margin>
<margin>Gall is purged through the mouth, not the anus.</margin>
**Regarding the "Suffocation of Women," etc.**) <note>historical term for "suffocation of the womb" or hysteria</note> This "suffocation" happens from a sickness of the womb caused by Tartar—namely, that sharp Tartar passes with the gall to the womb and causes disease there, just as in the stomach. When the womb suffers because it cannot endure these opposites, it turns back to the stomach and would gladly expel it; the womb pushes it back into the stomach, and if it returns to the stomach, a "suffocation" occurs that feels as if it wants to strangle the person. For gall is not excreted through the bowels, but only through the mouth. Thus, these women fall in a fit of suffocation just like those with epilepsy, and the paroxysm must last until the gall in the womb is consumed. It causes sterility because, in all women who suffer from Tartar, the womb and the digestions are corrupted; for when the liquid of the Tartar goes there, it corrupts everything. It is called an "interrupted disease" because it does not strike in regular fits, but in different ways, having no certain cycle. Regarding <term>Syncope</term> <note>fainting</note>: they fall into a swoon and cry out. A physician should always judge from the cry that Tartar is present, for it burns and stings like a knife.

**G**angrene) Just as those who have gangrene suffer and burn, so it is in the stomach. They are burned in the stomach just as gangrene burns a limb, and when the stomach is in this state, the disease is present.

# CHAPTER III.
## Concerning Fevers of the Stomach.

<margin>Fevers of the stomach.</margin> Concerning the fevers of Tartar, it must first be known of all that we recognize some are daily, tertian, quartan, etc., while others likewise take place in various regions of the body. But of those which arise in the stomach, we must now speak. For the others [we will discuss] when we treat the second and third digestion. Furthermore, these things are to be noted concerning the fevers of Tartar: through its blockage <note>original: "oppilationem"</note> and the failure of separation, rot <note>original: "putredo"</note> seeks an opportunity. This generation is an infection of the air. Because the air always makes itself clean, it does not tolerate its opposite. Now, if the body itself is infected by it, it suffers a tremor: for because the air carries putrefactions within itself, it seeks to make its exit only through the movement of the body, as if through the earth <note>Paracelsus compares the body to the earth and the internal air to the atmosphere</note>. But if it begins to expel: now there is a movement of the earth—that is, of the body through the limbs—until the rot has been destined for its place (namely, through evacuation); thereafter heat follows, which takes up its cause after the opposing forces. For the whole body grows hot, and the site of the rot is painful for as long as nature shows itself quiet from the air. Every tremor, therefore, is from rot, and the motion itself is through the infection of the air, namely of this element. In this generation is the principle of all fevers; if not in the stomach, they yet have similar natures elsewhere. Therefore, regarding the times of the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the sudden onset or worsening of symptoms, such as shivering or heat</note>, into daily, three-day, or four-day, etc., look to the second declaration of fevers in the treatise on the second digestion, namely concerning the pains and passions of the liver.

**Signs of these fevers from the stomach.**
<margin>Stomach fevers.</margin> Compression in the stomach, nausea, foul vapor, weakness of the head, and discoloration of all members, narcotic sleep, strong tremor, and mania after the heat itself. It is moved by saffron-colored tartars, and by drinking cold tartar. Its cure is twofold: Purgation without digestion. Then, pills of laudanum are to be administered before the paroxysm. Concerning which purgations this is to be noted: every evacuating agent must be arranged so as to work not only downwards, but also upwards. These purgations with vomiting ought to be an Arcanum, not humoral <note>referring to the traditional theory of the four humors</note>. For this Tartar is a specific subject in the Arcana, just as are centaury, hellebore, spurge <note>original: "cataputia"</note>, precious stone <note>original: "pręciatus"</note>, syler <note>possibly mountain-parsley</note>, the pulp of colocynth, and so on for the rest.

<header>TREATISE I.</header>

## TREATISE I.

<margin>The source of feverish tremors.</margin>
From this tartar, which does not allow itself to be coagulated, a fever is created either in the stomach, the liver, or the kidneys; these types are not to be treated [simply] according to whether they are quartan <note>occurring every third day</note>, quotidian <note>occurring daily</note>, and so on. Therefore, the waste products <note>original: "fæces," referring here to metabolic waste or undigested "tartar"</note> which do not reach the expulsive faculty cause a paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or fit</note> arising from that vapor of the waste, which mixes itself with the air that is within us. For there are four elements within us as well. Therefore, when our internal air is so infected, it cannot be pure; thus, when it cleanses itself, it causes such a tremor, and continues until the vapor is consumed. And if the air is not strong enough to expel the infection, it is drawn back and stirs up compressions in the stomach. This is why people say, "It does not shake me, but it oppresses me." When, therefore, the air wishes to cleanse itself, it shakes the body for 3, 6, 10, or 12 hours; after the tremor comes the heat, because the air, through
<margin>How the heat of fever is produced.</margin>
this motion, ignites the sulfur and the spirit of salt, etc. <note>In Paracelsian medicine, Sulfur and Salt are two of the three primary principles of all matter</note>. As for why the tremor comes today, not tomorrow, but the day after, the ancients said that
<margin>Humors are not the cause of paroxysms.</margin>
phlegm, bile, and melancholy <note>three of the four traditional "humors"</note> meet at a certain time and cause the tremors; this is nothing [but a falsehood], etc.

It is certain that fevers come from putrefaction, but humors do not putrefy in any disease except in leprosy. Rather, putrefaction comes from the waste products. Waste is found in the digestions of the stomach, the liver, and the kidneys: in the stomach there is the least heat, in the liver greater, and in the kidneys the greatest.

Why, then, does it cause trembling today and not likewise tomorrow, and why does it have its own period? What is the cause? Because the waste also undergoes digestion, just as the stomach or liver digests. Therefore, when the waste begins to boil, then the vapor ascends and infects the internal air: hence the tremor. For there is a digestive power even in the waste. If the waste is from <term>Mercury</term> <note>the third Paracelsian principle, associated here with rapid change</note>, the digestion of the waste happens in a day. If from salts, after the second day; if from sulfur, the digestion is after the third day; and from this comes the paroxysm. Therefore, it is nothing
<margin>What the cause of paroxysms is.</margin>
that they blame the blood and think it can be cured by bloodletting; likewise, that they give cold things, such as melon, etc., wishing to cool the heat—it is nothing. For the heat is indeed present, but it comes from the waste. Waste that comes from Mercurial things has its daily paroxysm, for they have a digestion that happens daily. For there is no tree or thing that does not have its excretion once in a year. So too the waste has its own digestions; sometimes there was a paroxysm, and this happens because there was a digestion.

<margin>No humor putrefies in the body or is purged.</margin>
And let the physician know that fevers are not from humors and should not be purged [as such]. Humors are not purged; any humor stays in the body in its own place and is not driven out, but it is the waste products that offend.
<margin>A tremor is similar to an earthquake.</margin>
A tremor is like an earthquake, and it cannot happen without air. And because the air cannot immediately penetrate the pores, hence the tremor. It is nothing, what they say about melancholy and phlegm fighting each other. This is a beautiful piece of physics that ought to be applied to the <term>mantica</term> <note>likely referring to divination or speculative arts</note>. Thus, in the plague, the external air does not infect, even if it is in the place where someone dies of the plague. It is true that the air which goes out from the patient—namely, the dead person—infects the air within me. For when someone dies, first the elements depart from him, and that air seeks an exit, hence the ulcers, etc.
<margin>Juniper smoke is useless in the plague.</margin>
Good vapors from juniper are of no value in the plague, because nature attracts the good air that pleases it, but at the same time also the bad, etc. Concerning fevers: if it is in the stomach, I can call it a tertian or daily fever of the stomach, a daily fever of the liver, or a daily fever of the kidneys.
<margin>What the cause of erratic fevers is.</margin>
Erratic fever comes from the fact that often the wastes of Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt are mixed together. Hence the various digestions and various paroxysms. The putrefaction of tartar is not yet a fever, but when it passes into digestion, then it is a fever.
<margin>What a fever is.</margin>
For from the digestion a vapor is produced, and from that the air is infected. Waste from Mercury completes digestion in 24 hours; from sulfur, it takes the same amount of time again.

<margin>Signs of stomach fever.</margin>
The signs of fevers, etc.: First, the physician must know whether the fever is in the stomach, liver, or kidneys, and these are determined by signs. It is from the stomach when they have fevers but not a very great thirst; and although the heat may intensify, they do not drink much, etc. But in the liver the burning is great because it is near the blood; they drink a lot, etc.

Compression of the stomach: If they are sluggish and, weary of all things, they walk loosely and can scarcely lift their feet or open their mouths, being so lazy and heavy: it is a sign that it is in the stomach. For in the liver and kidneys, they are agile. Likewise, when they say they feel a taste as if they had eaten hard eggs, it is a sign of the stomach; vomiting and nausea are common signs of the stomach, liver, and kidneys. But it must also be known whether it is from salt, Mercury, or sulfur, or from salt specifically. If they have an aversion to wine and cannot drink it, it is from Mercurial things.
<margin>Signs of the causes of fever.</margin>
From sulfur: when they vomit, and nothing is returned other than what they have eaten. Those from their own salt do not vomit, but are tested by <term>orexis</term> <note>an abnormal appetite or craving</note>.

<margin>All putrefaction is a form of digestion.</margin>
CURE. They can do what we ought to digest; I ask you, what do we want to digest in fevers, since it is a putrefaction? But putrefaction is already digested; the matter has been digested previously, because all putrefaction is a form of digestion. But it is to accelerate the purging. When we want to purge fevers,
<margin>Fevers are to be purged with Secret Remedies.</margin>
we must move to the <term>Arcana</term> <note>original: "Arcana," secret or higher-order Paracelsian medicines</note>; and peasants in those matters know better how to purge fevers than Doctors do.
<margin>What the Secret Remedies for fevers are.</margin>
And it is centaury <note>a bitter herb</note> that purges fevers, because it only purges putrefactions. So also <term>Catapotia</term> <note>pills</note>. Hellebore, <term>Praeciatus</term> <note>likely a specific prepared remedy</note>, these purge fevers. Those [remedies] like *Alephanginae* or *Arabicae* are foolish. And if they are healed, nature by itself expels the putridness. After purging, strengthening must be given. In fevers of the stomach, no one is perfectly cured except upward through vomiting, because that matter does not wish to go through the bowels; the humors are not purged. When the air is infected, and even the putrefactions have been driven out, the air must also be purged, as you have the description in the booklet. Also <term>Nectar</term>, which is made from corrected and clear wine. "Corrected" is from red or very dark wine that is congealed. "Clear" is from white wine. Also, in fevers, <term>Scarifications</term> <note>small superficial incisions</note> are used on the spine, and the bleeding of the <term>salvatella</term> <note>a vein on the back of the hand between the ring and little finger</note>; I do not reject this, because where the blood is so ignited by motion, it is well that it be opened; but that it is a "cure" is not true. Also, signs of fevers are rigors, as when they shudder as if a horror pervades one who is pricked by a needle. And this is a sign that the fever intends to last a long time. Likewise, for some, a sign is when one stretches and yawns. Then it is a sign of a future fever.

### Explanation of the Fourth Chapter.

<margin>What the Tartaric things are.</margin>
**T**hose things are "Tartaric" which descend from the stomach, from a spirit coagulated with a dry body. A dry body is a body made from coagulated moisture, or from a resolved dry substance. The "wind" <note>gas</note> of the body is a wind generated from periodic cold.

<margin>What periodic cold is.</margin>
Periodic cold is that which is seasonal, whether it be summer-like or winter-like; and its cure is periodic, as described in the chapter on periodic time. Moreover, "regress" is the constriction of the disease against the "emunctorium" <note>an organ that carries off waste</note>, making a return to the first principle.

<margin>The dry body causes two diseases.</margin>
The dry body causes two diseases. Coagulated moisture is the small stone in the intestines, which this present chapter treats. The "resolved dry substance" causes colic or contraction, and this chapter pertains to Tartar in the stomach. But if the stomach is not corrupted by Tartar—because nothing adheres to the stomach, but it correctly separates the pure from the impure—then it is carried to the intestines. In those intestines between the stomach and the "rectum" <note>original: "longaon," an old term for the straight gut/rectum</note>, it adheres. Therefore, we treat here of Tartar from a "coagulated dry substance." Thus, just as in the stomach after the stomach first separates and sends it to the intestines, the intestines themselves (between the stomach and the rectum) also separate things for excretion. They possess the power of separation—not that they separate the pure from the impure (for everything in the intestines is "impure"), but they separate the essential matter from the dung.

<margin>The intestines have their own nutrition.</margin>
They send the dung to the rectum, but they take their own nourishment from the rest. For the intestines have their own specific nourishment. Indeed, all the other members throughout the whole body take their nourishment from the liver; only the intestines do not receive nourishment from there. Therefore, because they can have it from no other member, neither from the liver nor the kidneys (as can be seen in anatomy), it is necessary that the stomach, along with the separated impure matter, also sends the intestines their own nourishment. Just as the other members are nourished by the pure, the intestines are nourished by the impure. That is to say, they attract a juice suitable for themselves from the dung, from which they draw oil or fat (which is scraped or taken from the intestines, even in cattle) and they attract what is good. Likewise, the intestine only separates; digestion does not happen there. Later, when that which is good for the intestines has exited—which is their nourishment—then what remains is dung. Just as when wine evaporates it immediately becomes vinegar, nature does not care for it, but it goes out through the exit. Therefore, where they do not well separate their nourishment from the dung, sicknesses arise; and if they attract too much, diseases also arise from that.

# TREATISE III.

<margin>Vistadius is criticized.</margin>
The body is treated with medicines such as drinkable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile"</note>, dissolved Silver <note>original: "Luna soluta"</note>, iron filings, "sweetness of Lead" <note>lead acetate, often called sugar of lead</note>, extraction of copper, and calcined Tin <note>Jupiter</note>; likewise with white clay <note>chimolea</note>, marcasite, asphalt, antimony, etc. If these are given as medicines, they coagulate in the intestines. For they do not remain in the stomach, nor can they pass to the liver; therefore, they go to the intestines. No metal should be used unless it is made into a true medicine and properly prepared; the same applies to dissolved pearls, hyacinth, sapphire, etc. It is not enough that they be dissolved into water, because they can return to their "first matter"—that is, they can revert to their original solid state—therefore they must not be used in that way. For this reason, Vistadius <note>a contemporary or previous medical author</note> wrote everything incorrectly. And where, then, does the generation of the stone begin? First, a gas and wind comes, and that wind has its own timing. If it is born in summer, it has its own cure; if in winter, its own cure. For instance, if anyone feels gas and twisting pains in autumn, they certainly have a generation of the stone and must be treated by an autumnal or winter medicine; and if in spring, by a summer medicine.

<margin>The stone of the intestines is treated according to the seasons of the year.</margin>
Furthermore, other illnesses arise from this—specifically from the small stone—because it constipates the intestines, and it happens that the feces ascend back into the stomach. From this comes a foulness of the mouth, and feces are expelled through the mouth, which is a most certain sign of death, because the stone has caused a total blockage. It often happens that through a violent purging, matter is driven out, but it is watery, thin, and serum-like, and therefore able to penetrate through; this is a sign of Tartar <note>the stony deposit</note>, but the solid matter—the feces—does not pass. Therefore, it is a sign of a generated stone when only water passes with purging, because the mass of the feces cannot pass due to the stone. Likewise, those who have colic of the belly and wash themselves, yet are not eased or relaxed by the bath, show a sign of a stone in the intestines.

<margin>Signs of a stone generated in the intestines.</margin>
*Griping pains <note>original: "Tormina"</note>)* namely, when accompanied by back pain, are a sign of the stone. If the area is anointed with olive or chamomile oil and the griping pains pass, yet the back pain remains, it is a sign of the stone. Likewise, constipation—where they have one bowel movement in eight days, or sometimes they have a regular movement and then none for three days—all who are so constipated and complain they cannot have a movement show a sign of the stone of Tartar. And you should not say that the stomach cannot digest or that it is "cold"; that is nothing, it is the stone. Likewise, "gall-water," when thin water breaks out from the upper parts during defecation, is a sign of the stone, and shows that it is collected and located very near the stomach.

*Hardness and nodes.)* If something hard is felt in the sides, or when someone touches the belly and it feels as if they are touching an abscess or a gland in the intestines, or "figs" <note>nodules or growths</note>, this is a sign of the stone. And you should not say that the spleen has become hardened. Likewise, if there is a gnawing sensation in the sides, as if from worms, it is a sign not of a pebble, but of "hail" <note>a specific type of smaller, grain-like Tartar</note>. For that gnawing they often give wormseed <note>original: "scriphii semen"</note>, but that is a bad medicine, because that powder often generates worms itself.

*And they move.)* If rumbling occurs, it is a sign of Tartar or the stone. When they drink sharp wine, it moves the small stone; likewise, legumes cause gases because they cannot exit due to the stone; hence they cause griping pains. And when the sick say they feel gases high up in the belly, it is from the stone. The gas-relieving <note>term: carminative — a medication that helps expel gas from the digestive system</note> cure is through cumin-seed <note>diacyminum</note>; it should not be done through a clyster <note>enema</note>, but a gas-relieving cure does not remove the stone, only the "accidents" <note>the secondary symptoms</note>, namely the twistings of the belly, rumbling, and gases.

<margin>What a gas-relieving cure does.</margin>
*Water from the dregs of wine, etc.)* namely, the dregs that are left over from burnt wine; those dregs should be thrown into the fire. Then they become white ash, and that ash does not evaporate or smoke. There is no better cure in the intestines against the stone and all its generations than lemon juice, especially when it is reduced to the "fourth Spagyric grade" <note>term: Spagyric — alchemical processes of separation, purification, and recombination to create more potent medicines</note>. Similarly, orange juice is useful, provided it can be reduced to the fourth grade of the Spagyrics. All the remedies that Avicenna <note>a famous 11th-century Persian physician</note> set down for the cure of intestinal diseases are nothing but gas-relievers; but I have said there is a double cure <note>addressing both the symptoms and the stony cause</note>.

<margin>Lemon juice is best against the intestinal stone.</margin>

<margin>What Colic is, and its seat.</margin>
Colic or the variety known as Iliac passion <note>severe intestinal obstruction</note> is an intestinal disease taking its beginning from resolved Tartar that is "pontic" and "pontagium" <note>term: pontic/pontagium — Paracelsian terms for sharp, stinging, or acrid mineral salts</note>. It has its place throughout the entire region of the intestines. The "pontic" and "pontagium" occupy the center of the disease, rather than the length of the entire intestine. For the center of a disease can be small, like a spot on the foot, but because of our sensitive nature, the pain takes over the whole circle. Therefore, the fault is attributed to the sensitivity of the location, not to the mass of the resolved matter. The matter is from acrid Tartar, arising from the "pontic salt" dissolved in the intestines; it causes contraction through its innate "styptic" <note>binding or contracting</note> quality, and twists the gut through these stinging, ginger-like qualities. From these two assigned causes, Colic and the Iliac passion receive their cause according to their location: namely, through the binding and the stinging. If this small amount of resolved matter is generated, it turns into colic or iliac passion with the greatest twistings and constipations. For by its binding nature, it closes the "one-eyed" intestine <note>the cecum</note> and the other intestines, turns the feces into "air" <note>gas</note>, and harms the intestines by wandering. And if that resolved Tartar of the disease has not been consumed or expelled—because in these stinging salts there is no expulsive force, nor in the binding ones, but rather they corrupt and destroy the exit of the excrement—then the disease extends to the limbs by a "rebound" effect. The gas from the feces then takes on a "three-prime" <note>salt, sulfur, and mercury</note> generation; that gas is nothing but an acidic vapor, traveling beyond the intestinal locations into the stomach, then to the gall, to the liver, then through the veins; from the veins to the external flesh, and from there to the ligaments, in which it causes contraction <note>stiffening of the limbs</note>, just as...

<header>TREATISE I.</header>

# TREATISE I.

<margin>Colic and Iliac are one disease.</margin>
<margin>What Colic is and what it is not.</margin>
<margin>How diseases should be named.</margin>
<margin>Colic is not cured by laxatives.</margin>
...and the cecum <note>original: "monoculon"; referring to the "one-eyed" or blind-ended part of the large intestine</note>, the process of the cure is one and the same. They say that colic comes from "cholera" <note>here meaning yellow bile, one of the four traditional humors</note> and that it burns and stings, but this is nothing. For even if bile comes to the intestines, it nevertheless exits with the dung. Rather, colic is nothing else, when it hangs in the intestines, but dissolved **Tartar** <note>metabolic waste that has crystallized into a stony or acidic deposit</note>: it is this which causes such pains. If it is in the upper part, it is called the **Iliac passion**; if lower down, **Colic**; but the origin is the same. This disease, colic, is a disease of <term>contracture</term> <note>a condition where muscles or tendons shorten and stiffen, causing deformity or loss of movement</note>. Properly speaking, Colic and Iliac are not diseases themselves, but only the beginnings of contracture. Therefore, this chapter is about contracture, not about colic or iliac, as others have distinguished them. This disease is called contracture because it usually ends with the stiffening of the limbs. Just as we call the early stages of leprosy "leprosy"—that is, we do not give it a separate name—and the beginnings of fevers "fevers," so a disease ought to be named by its final state and conclusion. Even if I am here against the established Authors, it does not matter, because their prescriptions for Colic and Iliac reveal their error. Unless you adopt their cure for contracture, you will not cure the colic. You will not drive away colic with laxatives unless the Tartar is so easily dissolved that it goes away on its own. For the Tartar is sharp and causes the colic. Therefore, since contracture is the true disease, you must proceed as you would for contracture.

<margin>The seat and manner of Colic.</margin>
<margin>A single drop is the cause of Colic.</margin>
<margin>Pain of Colic from the pungent; contraction from the styptic.</margin>
<margin>Dung retained in colic becomes wind.</margin>
<margin>Why laxatives are not suitable in colic.</margin>
Therefore, the stinging sensations that are felt are not the disease itself, but the signs and the beginning of the contraction. For even if the external limbs are not yet contracted, the intestines are nonetheless contracted; and when they cry out and shout <note>referring to the loud rumbling or "borborygmi" of a distressed gut</note>, it is only because the intestines are suffering a contraction. That disease is only in the intestines—that is, it begins in the intestines, even if it has not yet reached the outer parts. Therefore, the first contracture, which is colic, is in the intestines, and it is cured if the "pontic" <note>bitter or harsh</note> and "styptic" <note>astringent or drawing-together</note> power of the Tartar is removed. Colic or Iliac should be called the "first contracture." In contractures or colic in the intestines, it is located in a small place, and this is the center. But where a little drop might stick, we do not know the location of that drop; it is now above, now below in the intestines. Wherever it falls, it causes pain. And yet, from that tiny place—that is, whenever dissolved Tartar the size of a pea sticks to the intestines—the intestines are so sensitive that this is felt. If they are affected in one small spot, it is felt everywhere, indeed through the whole belly, which it throws into total commotion. Why would I pour in clysters <note>enemas</note> on account of one tiny drop? How would it help? Perhaps it would not even reach it. Sometimes a clyster soothes the pain by its oiliness, but it does not remove the disease. Therefore, that little drop must be considered by the physician, so that its styptic and pontic power may be removed. Should the physician, because of that one drop, affect the whole body, the stomach, or the liver? In contracture, this is the sum of it: that Tartar which sticks to the intestines contains a stypticity, an acidity, and a pontic power. Wherever it sticks, it corrupts the whole belly there. And just like **Tetanus**, which pulls the limbs together, or a spasm which stretches the limbs, so is this Tartar. That is, the styptic quality in that Tartar forces and contracts, like a sloe-plum in the mouth; and the pontic power in that Tartar causes the pain. It burns so that pain arises from the pontic power, but the contraction arises from the styptic power. For the pontic power causes pain, while the styptic causes the contraction of the intestines, which results in a single pain. Thus the disease can be called "colic" because of the location in the colon, which acts like a host for it; otherwise, it is nothing but contracture. After the contraction arrives, it then hurts, stings, and contracts, and does not allow the dung to exit. Sometimes it drives it back, and when that dung cannot exit, it hides away there and is consumed, changing into air. That is, the dung, unable to exit, is transmuted into another body; it changes its substance into air. Just as those who suppress their bowel movements have much wind, and constipation follows the wind. Therefore, now that the substance of the dung has changed into air, how shall I purge air with laxatives? Thus, laxatives and colocynth <note>a powerful herbal purgative</note> will not purge this, because it is no longer dung.

<margin>Why anger is harmful in colic.</margin>
Therefore, this air, which is caused by the constipation of the dung, does not pass through purges, but other things must be considered. Furthermore, dung does not exit except by the expulsive virtue, just as urine does not exit by itself but by the expulsive virtue. If the dung does not have that virtue, it does not go out. But where there is the styptic and the pungent, there is no expulsive power; therefore, the pungent quality must be removed. Then the dung will exit on its own, because the expulsive power returns—which is the single most important thing in colic: that the dung should pass by itself. Therefore, when dung cannot pass because of stypticity while it is in the intestines, and it changes itself into another body, into air, then the pungent, contagious Tartar rises and mixes with it. It separates itself from the intestines and passes into the "dung-air"—that is, following the body of the dung. When the intestines are thus softened and warmed, as by a Bath, then the intestines and the passages are opened. For through baths, the intestines and the pores are "de-obstructed" <note>original: "deoppilantur"; opened up</note>; then that air passes to the stomach, and from there to the liver, and afterwards it extends itself to all the limbs. That air and wind go to all the pores of the body and cause the contracture of the limbs. First, that air goes into the stomach—having been changed, of course, from the substance of the dung—making the voice thin and weak and constricting it. Afterward, it passes to other limbs and to the flesh, and the flesh becomes loose and spongy, and later it seizes the ligaments. When it comes to the ligaments, it is acidic and pontic; because previously in its first state—that is, while it stuck to the intestines as Tartar—it was styptic, pontic, and pungent. So it is in its second state, that is, in the air. And then the contracture happens, and they are dissolved <note>loosened from their proper function</note>. What will it profit then to purge and loosen? After the ligaments, it passes and penetrates even into the marrow, and there stinging pains persist. So, where Tartar sticks, colic is induced along with the contraction of the intestines. Afterward, when it resolves itself, it becomes air—and this happens especially through baths, which open all the pores throughout the whole body. Where there is colic (that is, internal contracture), the air then exits to other limbs, such as the ligaments, and causes external contracture. Thus, anger is also forbidden in colic, because anger "de-obstructs" or opens the pores just like a bath. Nor has it yet been proven that anger comes from the gall, etc. But I say now: that from anger the pores are opened as if by a bath, and if someone is contracted from anger, it is necessary that colic preceded it.

He explains that trapped excrement turns into toxic "fecal air" which, when mobilized by heat or anger, travels through the pores to cause physical stiffening and paralysis in the limbs.</summary>

...yields, and settles in before; for no organ is moved by anger quite like the stomach, and anger forces the stomach to expel that air—of which I spoke—into the remaining limbs, which results in <term>contracture</term> <note>a condition where muscles or tendons shorten and stiffen, causing deformity</note>.

<margin>Anger affects the stomach most closely.</margin>
Note: In advising the use of baths, it must be observed that if people are catarrhal <note>original: "catarrhosi"; suffering from an excess of mucus or discharge</note>, you should not recommend them, because the bath opens all the pores. But if something must be opened from the outside to draw it out from the skin, etc., then recommend it. Some people suffer contractions only in their hands, and this is because blockages <note>original: "oppilationes"</note> often persist in the ligaments due to **Tartar** <note>metabolic waste that has crystallized into a stony or acidic deposit</note> or some other cause; because anger cannot open or loosen these as a bath does, that limb does not contract. Note: The blood is ignited by the air mentioned above. The ligaments, flesh, and so on are naturally sweet. If acidity invades, they are then corrupted—that is, the naturally sweet liquor in the ligaments is ruined by bitter and acidic qualities, which the ligaments cannot endure. Ligaments possess a sweetness, and as long as they preserve it, they are well; but when they are corrupted and acidity reaches them, it is over: they no longer move, they contract, and the limbs can no longer be supported. The cure, therefore, is to drive out the acidity so that sweetness may predominate in the ligaments. There is no reason to purge, for the specific flavors of the organs must be observed; for instance, blood is naturally salty or bitter.

<margin>Ligaments and flesh are sweet and are offended by acids.</margin>
<margin>Blood is either salty or bitter.</margin>
Every organ must be preserved in its own essence, and it does not want its natural flavor to be corrupted; if that happens, it fails.

<margin>The origin of vomiting from a stone of the bladder.</margin>
<note>The marginal note refers to a stone of the bladder, though the text focuses on colic and the gallbladder.</note>
Signs: often there are "twistings" <note>original: "torsiones"; griping pains or cramps</note> in the belly along with bowel movements; when they have a stool after the twistings, the pains go away—this is not true colic. But when the twistings occur with constipation, then it is a sign of the beginning of colic. There may also be back pain because the organs "suffer together," meaning those neighboring organs are affected. There is also a compression of the chest, which shows the colic is strong and is being carried upward to the stomach. This leads to bilious vomiting, because when the stomach is overwhelmed (by the air rushing into it), the stomach sends it to the gall; the gall cannot bear for its flavor to be corrupted, so it expels it, and vomiting occurs. When they vomit very frequently, it is a sign of "perfect" or fully developed colic. Likewise, a bitterness in the mouth follows, as well as a nausea toward eating. This is not caused by a weakness of the stomach, as people commonly say or as the patients think, and there is no need for "strengthening" the stomach; rather, the "sinning matter"—namely, this Tartar—must be removed. Furthermore, a weak voice follows; when the vocal organs are corrupted, it is a sign that the disease wishes to turn into the limbs, because the trapped air present there swells, blocks the passages, and flows through the vocal organs and larger passages. Because the vocal organs are threefold, that air especially blocks and constricts them rather than resolving, because the ligaments are not present there. Or you could say it contracts them just as it contracts the intestines; a sign of this is when the arms do not move. Therefore, baths and anger "unblock" and resolve the matter, and the third method is through purges, which make the matter return to the stomach.

### *Explanation of the Sixth Chapter, on the Cure.*

<margin>Fatty "Arcana" cure colic.</margin>
**A**s I said yesterday, the cure consists of removing the styptic, acidic, and bitter elements; once this is done, the Iliac contraction and the colic are removed. Laxative enemas do nothing here; instead, special <term>arcana</term> <note>secret, powerful remedies that target the essence of a disease</term> cure colic. Neither cold nor heat, nor the "complexion" <note>the balance of the four humors</note> of the patient, provides the cure. Instead, the arcana for colic or contracture lie hidden in fats and oils. Through these, contractures and their various kinds are cured. Other herbs like mugwort, pennyroyal, and wormwood are cooked and applied to the belly; they take away the pain, but they do not take away the disease. To remove the disease, medicine is required. For there are three things that make the disease styptic, bitter, or acidic; therefore, these must be countered. Tartar is the primary cause of the disease—specifically, dissolved Tartar—but nothing can restrain Tartar except fats and oils. It is like when poison is drunk; drinking oil after the poison "suffocates" and strangles the venom. Or like when a corrosive poison like arsenic is applied externally: if it begins to do too much damage, there is nothing better than to pour oil or butter or anything fatty into the wound, for then it is suffocated. But the barber-surgeons are ignorant of this; therefore, they often kill people with such corrosives.

<margin>Oil and butter suffocate poisons.</margin>
In the same way, those styptic and bitter qualities come from Tartar, and Tartar cannot be suppressed except by oil. For when oil enters the intestines, the Tartar inserts itself into it, the oil moves on, and the disease is restrained. But not all oils are useful for this; for instance, oils from small seeds like poppy oil do not work, but those from larger sources, such as laurel, do.

<margin>Smaller seeds are more watery; dissolved Tartar is an oiliness.</margin>
Oils from small seeds have a great deal of wateriness; just as oil does not take up water—that is, it does not mix with it but floats on top—so dissolved Tartar is nothing but a kind of "oiliness," and where there is water, it does not mix. Likewise, when fats reach the intestines, they attract the dissolved Tartar to themselves and mix with it, since it is also nothing but an acidic oiliness; therefore, they ought to mix. But this must happen without water, because oil, as we see, does not mix with water. When it is mixed in this way, it causes a stool or vomiting; if it causes vomiting, then the Tartar was lying deep. This is what is said of the first stage of the disease, that is, of colic or the first generation of Tartar.

<margin>Why the fat are slower to contract.</margin>
In the second stage of contracture, when the air has dispersed and when that air is also greasy, then fats and oils must be used so that the air may be mixed with them and reduced back into an "oiliness." From this it follows that those who are obese do not suffer contractures, because their own fat does not allow them to contract—unless they are so full that they are like the grapes in the Adige Valley <note>original: "Etschlandia"</note> called **Traminer** in German. Therefore, when the disease is in the "second body"—that is, reduced into air—then fats and oils must be used so that the acidic air may be suffocated in them. For that acidic air betakes itself into them.

<margin>Oily things suffocate. The fat of the badger is similar to human fat.</margin>
The fat of the **badger** <note>original: "Taxi"; in this context of animal fats, it refers to the badger rather than the yew tree</note> and the fox are good medicines. For the badger has a fat within it that corresponds somewhat to our human fat, except that it has too much "earth" in it and is thicker than human fat; but it does no harm. Thus these two are, as it were, the correct <term>mumia</term> <note>the vital curative force or "balsam" inherent in a living body</note>.

<margin>Italians drink badger fat for contracture.</margin>
For this reason, in Italy they drink badger fat for contracture, even if it tastes a bit like wild game. Likewise, fox fat is applied externally, not internally, for it is not drunk. And all things that are fox-colored, such as squirrels, etc., have much *mumia* in them; therefore, a preparation made from them is also good. However, these are specifics; many other things are used, but the principal ones are the badger and the fox.

Distill it again through the alembic in the manner of a balsam. The olive oil can be omitted, for it is superfluous. Therefore, that balsam of galbanetum cannot be prepared without distillation, because in the Botin resin there is an oiliness which is especially relevant to the contracture. This cannot be drawn out except by distillation; for otherwise, Botin resin by itself does nothing except consolidate. But when it is distilled and becomes an oil, nothing is more excellent for a contracture. Laurel oil is also good, but it is thick and "undigested" <note>crude or unrefined</note>, and it cannot penetrate unless it is made subtle; it becomes penetrating through distillation.
<margin>A balsam that cures contracture.</margin>

Because that Balsam is so subtle, it penetrates to the air within the ligaments, and afterwards incorporates itself into that oil, and thus that acidity is also removed. There is another medicine made from **Serpentina** <note>likely Dragon Arum or a similar "spotted" plant</note>, which is a general name among some people, such that they call everything that cures wounds "serpentina." In Switzerland, a herb also grows with a single stalk and one leaf, in the middle of which a "tongue" reaches out. But that is not the serpentina that cures contracture, etc. Nothing surpasses those prepared serpentinas among all medicines for contracture, and this is the preparation.

<margin>Circumscription of the liver region.</margin>
The regions of the liver hold their place from the <term>mesaraics</term> <note>the mesenteric veins or membranes</note> down to the beginning of the kidneys; and on both sides, they maintain a distance between the intestines and the flank. For in these regions, the origin of these diseases must be sought: namely, all <term>oppilations</term> <note>blockages or obstructions</note>, both in the pores of the flesh and veins, and in the "chaos of the air." For among us physicians, these things must be distinguished regarding blockages: those which are of the substance, and those which are of the airs. Indeed, blockage is twofold—as will be discussed in its own chapter following—as are the illnesses, whether from <term>narcotics</term> <note>numbing agents</note> or <term>cicatrizing</term> <note>scar-forming</note> agents, even beyond their own region, namely in the throat, which are of this kind. Furthermore, those illnesses which produce discoloration and "calcetum" blood <note>hardened or chalky blood</note> are placed in this Treatise; and those which cause drying out, provoke thirst, and show stinging pains are referred to the pains of the liver. Likewise, every kind of fever without exception belongs here. If, in its intermittent days, the fever takes away nausea and removes thirst, it means this fever was generated from the liver. Also, those kinds of dropsy <note>original: "hydropisis"; swelling from fluid</note> that occur with inextinguishable thirst take their place and origin there, especially those that are stable around the external regions, namely of the liver: every death occurring from the cause of a "fissure" of the liver. For death of the liver arises from acute causes. Furthermore, in the following chapters, one must take care not to be led astray by opinions taken from the errors of the ancient Canons, because some say one thing, and others say another. The sophists have proposed another way...

<margin>Noble liquid gold in contracture.</margin>

Sixtus of Groningen thus cured Laudenberger, who had been laboring under a contracture for five years. In nine days, he cured him using liquids of gold. So too is "liquid mummy"—namely, mummy transmuted into an oil—a most effective medicament for contracture. What shall I say of <term>clysters</term> <note>enemas</note>? <header>CONCERNING TARTAR, BOOK II.</header>

Sophists <note>a derogatory term the author uses for traditional academic doctors</note> [call it otherwise], but we call it the Tartaric disease, for it is Tartars <note>mineral-like deposits or metabolic waste</note> that cause these conditions. We judge this from the passive organ. We have, however, investigated them from their active sources and made this clear to those who possess the acute quality of Tartar. For in the liver, just as in the stomach and in the kidneys, the same judgment applies: those organs which are responsible for sequestration <note>the separation of nutrients from waste</note> and the primary shared digestive organs do not suffer except from Tartar. Therefore, in the causes of the aforementioned diseases, nothing should be thought of the four humors <note>the traditional Greek medical system of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, nor of the three first principles; but rather entirely of those things which pertain to Tartar.

->*Explanation.*<-

<margin>Triple digestions</margin>
**T**here are three digestions: namely, in the stomach, in the liver, and in the kidneys. We have finished with the diseases of the stomach; now we shall discuss the regions of the liver and the diseases contained therein.

<margin>Which is the region of the liver.</margin>
**NOTE**, the liver itself does not labor, nor does it harbor diseases. Instead, we are going to speak about the diseases that dominate in the *regions* of the liver. Therefore, that distance that extends from the stomach to the liver, and from the liver to the kidneys—that is, the space between the stomach and the kidneys, and from the intestines to the side—is the "region of the liver." Everything in that area pertains to it, and all diseases there are to be referred to the liver. Likewise, whatever lies between the intestines and the side, or between the ribs and the intestines, belongs to the liver. Here the liver produces its diseases; or rather, it is not the liver itself, but the diseases are merely attributed to it.

<margin>The liver is not affected by itself.</margin>
The liver by itself has no quality; it does not cool nor heat—that is, it does not bestow temperaments and diseases on its own. Rather, all those diseases attributed to the liver arise from Tartar. Thus, by themselves, the stomach, liver, and kidneys do not cause ailments, but only Tartar within them causes them. All <term>obstructions</term> <note>original: "oppilationes"</note> of the liver—whether they be in the veins, in the blood, in the passages that go through the liver (for small veins pass through the liver), or in the flesh between the ribs, or within that whole space of the liver—arise from Tartar. Phlegm does not descend here; there is no place for phlegm here. Instead, every region keeps its own disease within itself. Therefore, liver obstructions arise in the regions of the liver and remain there; they do not pass into another place or region. Just as paralysis and apoplexy remain in their own region and do not "fall downward" as the common people say; therefore, things otherwise attributed to the liver are poorly attributed when the disease or obstruction is actually in another location.

<margin>Dual obstruction of the liver.</margin>
There are two kinds of obstructions: one is in substance—that is, through the substance of Tartar, as mentioned before; the other is of the air. For air must pass through the whole body. Elemental air (as it is known that there are four elements in the body) must pass through the entire body. Where Tartar blocks the paths, the air is then retained and turns into a "thickness"—that is, into a secondary generation. That air which exists where the breakdown of Tartar occurs is so thick that it cannot pass through. All liver obstructions in the sides arise from Tartar, and such thick air is carried up and down, now here and now there; it has no fixed place, and that is an "obstruction of air" in the regions of the liver. From this air, <term>plague</term> <note>original: "pestis"</note> arises, just like a pestilence. For that air, which is Elemental by itself, has transitioned into a secondary state and become thick. The wind that wanders here and there and cannot pass through, being thus obstructed, creates the plague. As I have said elsewhere, it is the air *within* us, not external air, that causes plague. They give Armenian Bole <note>a medicinal red clay</note> to comfort the heart in times of plague, and likewise "sealed earth" <note>terra sigillata, a famous medicinal clay</note>, and rightly so; but if such air infects the liver, then there is no longer a cure.

<margin>Internal air, not external, is the cause of plague.</margin>
But as long as it wanders in the surrounding areas of the liver, it does no harm. Furthermore, every <term>narcotic</term> <note>used here to mean "stifling" or "burning"</note> disease—that is, one which burns and smokes so much that it seems to drive one to madness, such as <term>Prunella</term> <note>an inflammatory disease of the mouth and throat, possibly "sloe-throat" or thrush</note>—arises from the fact that this air, when it penetrates by itself and seeks an exit, ascends on high. Then it causes *Prunella* in the throat, a black tongue, and dark pustules. Where this sign is present, I say there is an obstruction of air in the liver, and that trapped air in the liver has made an exit for itself. From this, the neck burns, and the skin of the throat is constricted. It is a mortal disease because that air is pestilential. Therefore, "Prunella water" and those medicines do not help, except to preserve and cool those members. Otherwise, the treatment of the air itself must be undertaken. That internal air also causes pleurisy and the same things that cause plague. Therefore, for all diseases that burn the neck and throat, you should say they are from the liver, not from the blood or any other cause, in this manner: that the trapped air has made its exit. Those diseases are "narcotic," in which the heat eventually drives them to the point where they do not know what they are doing—that is, they become delirious.

<margin>What narcotic diseases are. What Prunella is and from where it arises.</margin>

**And from the cicatrizing [agents].)** That is, those which cause the skin in the palate to be pulled away or torn off, etc.

<margin>All paleness is from the liver.</margin>
**Discoloration, etc.)** All who are pale are pale because of the liver. For color comes from the liver, and for those who have a bad complexion, you should judge that the disease is in the region of the liver; and you ought immediately to ask the patient whether they feel "stings" <note>sharp pains</note> in the right side; and thus judge the urine.

<margin>The cause of thirst in the liver.</margin>
And it is not that we should want to comfort the heart, or blame the stomach or the spleen. All those things do not cause a bad complexion; rather, that bad color comes from the liver. And the fact that a "diabetic passion" <note>diabetes</note> also excites thirst is because it passes from the kidneys through the liver and ascends to the neck.

<margin>Thirst, prunella, and plague differ only by degrees.</margin>
Thus thirst, *Prunella*, and plague come from a single cause—that is, from that trapped air—except that one disease is milder than the other: namely, thirst in the first degree, *Prunella* in the second, and plague in the third. So too with fevers that are from the liver: if after the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the sudden onset or fit of the fever</note>, on the "good days," the urine is good and the patient can eat and drink—in short, if the intervening day is good, with no thirst or heat present—that fever is in the liver, not in the stomach.

<margin>Fevers which are from the liver, and those from the stomach.</margin>
Fevers that are not troublesome except during the "accession"—that is, in the fit—are from the liver. And these things must be observed. For authors have written of many types, such as six kinds of fevers, but they did not observe the "Regions." Furthermore, if it is a daily fever, and even after the fit there are rigors <note>shivering fits</note>, it is always from the liver. If, however, there is nausea, vomiting, etc., it is from the stomach. It often happens that many fevers coincide—double tertian, triple quartan—but this is not to be cared for [here].

<margin>Concerning Dropsy</margin>
There is a certain kind of dropsy <note>edema or fluid retention</note> in the liver, another in the kidneys, in the spleen, from hemorrhoids, from the womb, and so on. A sign that it is in the liver is from an abscess; namely, that if there are ever stabbing pains in the right side, then there is an abscess of the liver—not that the liver itself has an abscess, but the air and "chaos" <note>the surrounding atmospheric or gaseous space</note> that lies around it creates the abscess. So much for diseases; now concerning death. All who are seized in the liver and die, for these, 
<margin>The liver does not rot, but contracts cracks.</margin>
the liver is split. For the liver does not rot in death, but it is cleaved and creates fissures. When it begins to develop these cracks, death follows. Likewise, when these fissures exist in the liver, the swollen feet also become affected by cracks, and this is lethal. Thus, where the liver has fissures, there is dropsy which originates from the liver; the feet also contract cracks, and then death is at hand; then the urine is red, and death is at the door. And when the 
<margin>Cause and signs of liver dropsy.</margin>
private parts swell up with defects during dropsy, it is a sign of death. So also in the plague: when the plague is in the regions of the liver, and the liver begins to be cleaved with cracks, and then the lips and tongue have fissures, then it is 
<margin>Cracks in the feet are a sign of death.</margin>
a sign of death. But if the pain remains in the regions of the liver and the stabbing pains endure, the liver does not rot away or become otherwise affected, but at least it is split. For often even the lips are cleaved, even if it does not come from the plague, but from the heat of the liver. So in the burning of the throat or "prunella" <note>original: "prunella"; a term for throat inflammation or thrush, literally "little plum"</note>, when black blisters appear in the throat, it is a sign of death. So also in long-lasting fevers from the liver: when after the paroxysm <note>the peak of a fever fit</note> they still complain of stabbing pains in the sides and the lips are cleaved, it is a sign of death. So also 
<margin>Black blisters in the throat-fever are a sign of death.</margin>
those who say, "I am always afflicted by thirst and dryness": it is foolishness for me to want to give a medicine against thirst and aridity, because it returns even if you have driven it away once. But one must move to the beginning of the disease; and thirst, aridity, and the cracking of the lips are merely signs that a great disease will follow. Note: It is necessary for the Physician to observe the precursors or foretellers—such as thirst, and elsewhere spasms, etc.—they are not the diseases themselves, but the precursors of diseases. Thus often red tubercles <note>small swellings or bumps</note> and

blisters arise on the face. Therefore, let the physician observe such signs and preludes, and judge from them what disease is going to follow. Those who do not observe the precursors cannot judge. For from these one must recognize the disease they indicate so that we may prevent it. Thus, when they often say, "my feet are swelling and blisters are rising," which then go away and return after half a year or a whole year—these are not the diseases themselves, but only the precursors of future diseases. Now, what I would wish you to consider: these diseases of the liver coming from "complexion" <note>the traditional balance of the four humors</note> or from the three first principles is nothing; rather, Tartar is the sinner here, and all ailments come from it. All ailments in the regions of the liver take their origin from Tartar, not from the liver itself (as if the liver were cooling or overheating), but Tartar is the cause.

### CHAPTER II.
->On the obstructions of the liver and its region.<-

<margin>What an obstruction is, and of how many kinds.</margin>
**O**bstruction is a constriction of the pore and the substance, and it is that which occurs from a physical constriction of one body with another. It is twofold: One is in the circumference of the region; the other is "elementated" <note>composed of elements</note> from the air through a second body. Regarding the first, it must be noted that any obstruction is a compression of its own region, for this reason: on account of the *spiritus yleidum* <note>a technical term for a vital or material spirit that governs growth</note> which, when it has no exit, goes into putrefaction within itself, and this happens without a cause from the external region. Regarding the second: it is pestilential and airy; sometimes it causes plague, sometimes pleurisy, sometimes it prepares a "crisis" <note>the turning point of a disease</note> of the liver. Concerning these, it should be noted: pay attention not to the stabbing and wandering pains, but to those which are plague, those which are pleurisy, and the crisis. For the stabbings are signs, not the disease. The disease is what we are treating here, not some small mineral. 
<margin>What the plague is.</margin>
Now, what is the plague? The plague is the air of its own region, generated from the first body, obstructed without exit, and made of Arsenical and "Oppirmechtiolic" <note>an alchemical term likely referring to a specific mineral salt or poisonous property</note> matter; but concerning that Tartar of rapid transformation, we must speak. 
<margin>The plague arises from the time of digestion.</margin>
For it happens through the digestion of nature. For some develop over two years, others over three, others more, others less, others at a set time. For what must be known concerning the plague are those things which pertain to what is digested over time—namely, this "vitriolated" <note>sulfuric or glassy</note> time, and this is the *prunella* <note>throat-fever</note>; another is *ogertum* <note>a specific Paracelsian term for a salt</note>, which is pleurisy; another is arsenical, which is the plague. For therein is the foundation of the diseases of this region, and those things which are held concerning pleurisy come from "Ogertine salt." For according to whatever the time of the Ogertine salt shall be, there is the generation of pleurisy—that is, a pleuritic obstruction. For those obstructions which are of arsenic belong to the plague; those of *ogertum*, to pleurisy; and those of vitriol, the obstructions of *prunella*. Let this be a magnificent insight for you: what an obstruction truly is. There are three in the matter, as I said before: the alternating body, and the new airy one. But what difference exists in the obstructions according to the text must be noted, based on the differences of the ailments, and this according to the text. Three diseases lead their origins from obstructions: plague of the liver, pleurisy of the liver, and *prunella* of the liver. There is true plague, true pleurisy, and *prunella*, arisen from their own salts according to their digestion. They have their reasons from the minerals according to their digestion, time, and ore. For from these comes the highest authority and medical...

ON TARTAR, BOOK II.

Majesty is introduced for the sake of reason, and rightly so.

For the plague is the same as its own substance; likewise, pleurisy <note>inflammation of the lung lining</note> is the same as its own material and <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: prunella; an inflammatory throat infection</note>, as well as its own being, time, digestion, maturation, and the transformation of its own element’s two-fold nature.

### *Explanation of the Second Chapter.*

<margin>What diseases are caused by obstruction of the liver, etc.</margin>
If an **obstruction** occurs in the liver, it produces pleurisy, plague, and quinsy. In the same way, an obstruction of the heart produces pleurisy, plague, and quinsy; and thus, obstructions of the rest of the principal organs produce plague, pleurisy, and quinsy.
<margin>Pleurisy is not an abscess but an obstruction.</margin>
Others say that pleurisy is an abscess in the midriff <note>original: praecordio</note>, but it is nothing of the sort. It is not an abscess, but an **obstruction**. It can happen that during maturation and completion, it returns to its primary matter, decays, and becomes pus.

<margin>What Yleidus is.</margin>
The "signs" that precede are signs of the process, not the disease. The "crisis" <note>the turning point of a disease</note> also stems from this: just as if a person were not affected by a disease—such as a fatal abscess—after the fourth or seventh day, I can judge from a good or bad crisis what will become of the patient. The "circumference" of the liver is its surrounding region. It is enclosed no differently than an egg, whose yolk and white are surrounded by a single membrane. **Yleidus** <note>a Paracelsian term for the elemental spirit or primordial air</note> is the elemental air; in us, it is the spirit that must pass through all the limbs. Just as there is a thin skin in an egg, so must the *yleidus* pass through all the pores. If these are blocked, then diseases follow. However, the air is obstructed if there is matter, such as Tartar, in that region; if that matter is consumed and passes from the body into the external air, it becomes air alone. That air later produces the plague, pleurisy, quinsy, and likewise the crisis. But if we wish to know correctly about these three—plague, pleurisy, and quinsy—there are three things from which those diseases are generated. There is the spirit of **arsenic**, the spirit of **orpiment** <note>original: auripigmenti; a yellow arsenic mineral</note>, and the spirit of **vitriol**, as stated in the text. These three abound in Tartar. If, therefore, the arsenic (if it grows in anyone) in a plague caused by Tartar is expelled through the urine, the plague does not occur. Likewise, if the orpiment is driven out through the urine via the emunctory <note>an organ that carries off waste</note> and is digested, pleurisy does not occur. Thirdly, if the vitriolic salt passes through the urine, quinsy does not occur. Every thing contains within itself those three spirits: Arsenic, Orpiment, and Vitriol. If they are correctly digested, those acute abscesses do not follow. And nature is so disposed that all minerals are contained in the body, and good and evil are mixed together. It is the same in all herbs. Therefore, the fact that we may know the future from the stars, such as the plague, has a physical reason: Astronomers foresee the plague because the "fumes" <note>metabolic vapors</note> are not yet separated from the elements, and all the mineral elements, etc., are in us just as they are in all herbs. Whatever affects the earth, water, fire, or air also affects man, because what those elements have in themselves is also in our bodies. For all things are in us, just as the elements are in us. Now, therefore, just as gold is spoiled and "dies" through arsenic, so also all minerals that contain orpiment or another spirit are corrupted. In the same way, the **Balsam of Nature** <note>the body's natural healing fluid</note> is corrupted by those spirits and by minerals.
<margin>From where plague, pleurisy, quinsy, etc., arise.</margin>
<margin>All things have within them the spirits of arsenic, orpiment, and vitriol.</margin>
<margin>All things are in man.</margin>

<margin>What Opprimechiolum is. What Plague is.</margin>
An **Opprimechiolum** <note>a Paracelsian term for metallic vapor</note> is any smoke or fume exhaling from a metal or mineral. Minerals have the same diseases as we do, and they suffer in the same way. The **Plague** is nothing other than arsenical air enclosed in the regions of the liver. It is generated when the arsenical spirit separates itself from the *yleidus* (the elemental spirit) and settles into the Tartar. Then it is the nature of arsenic to burn, inflame, and cause swelling, just as happens in the plague: first, a continuous burning heat that steadily increases; then thirst comes. The Tartar, now separated from the Arsenic, causes a febrile paroxysm <note>a sudden attack of fever</note>; heat and cold arrive, and the poison of the Arsenic ascends and breaks out on the surface. It happens like this: the small veins that pass through the body become infected. For the arsenic sets the blood on fire, and it turns to pus. For the plague is within, and it creates abscesses under the armpits. That abscess is not the plague itself, but a <term>phlegmon</term> <note>a spreading inflammatory mass</note>; that is what such an abscess is. Therefore, while bloodlettings are performed, they do not treat the plague itself, but the abscess, and this is beneficial because it diverts the blood, etc.

<margin>How plague and pleurisy differ.</margin>
It cools. Furthermore, **pleurisy** is like the plague, except it comes from **orpiment** that has separated itself from the *yleidus*. it lies in the region of the liver (it lies like an egg in its skin and shell, but it ascends to the upper parts) and it rots. From this comes the stabbing pain in the sides and the loss of appetite for food. There is one cause for both plague and pleurisy, but different material, because the arsenic that causes the plague is stronger than orpiment. Just as if arsenic were applied or bound to someone externally, it causes changes in color and a loathing of food, so it is internally. Therefore, if orpiment is in the regions of the liver and attacks the liver, death occurs. All who die of pleurisy die from orpiment. And if someone has stabbing pains in the left side, it is also pleurisy, but of the spleen; for it also comes from orpiment that has separated from the *yleidus*. Thus, in the seven principal organs, where plague, pleurisy, and quinsy occur, they arise from the same cause. So **quinsy** comes from vitriol: where it separates from the *yleidus*, that vitriolic spirit ascends to the neck, sets it on fire, and produces a swelling.

<margin>What digestion is.</margin>
**Digestion of time**. Just as the <term>Marchio</term> <note>likely referring to a specific person or a titled nobleman known for a medical case</note> had a digestion of time. Digestion means that every thing must be "digested"—that is, it must cast out the evil from itself and remain in its own "Being" <note>original: Esse</note> just as it was created. When it is spoiled, it purges itself and labors to return to its Being.
<margin>From where Astronomers, etc., predict.</margin>
Hence, Astronomers, Hydromancers <note>diviners by water</note>, and Geomancers <note>diviners by earth</note> can know and predict the plague. Because when the earth, water, and the four Elements lose something of how they were created, they suffer, and we suffer with them, because they must be purged and digested. You shall observe this, therefore, in the seven organs: if the spirit of the *yleidus* separates arsenic from itself, it produces the plague. The cure is that it must be resolved so that the air has an exit; **diaphoretics** <note>medicines that induce sweating</note> should be given, which consume the air. But if the "shell" <note>the body's exterior or the organ's membrane</note> is so obstructed on the outside that the arsenical spirit cannot get out, the medicine cannot get in; the liver seeks help, but the medicine cannot penetrate.
<margin>Very strong diaphoretics are suitable for the plague. What "Corrected Burning Wine" is, and how it is made and tested.</margin>
Therefore, the strongest diaphoretics must be used in the plague so that they may penetrate. **Corrected Burning Wine** <note>distilled alcohol/brandy</note> is used because no burning wine is so finely sublimated that it does not have some "wateriness" or water in it. Therefore, after it has been well distilled, it must be put back into the <term>alembic</term> <note>a distilling apparatus</note>. And if half of it has been distilled, one must stop...
