<header>ON COLIC.</header>

# ON COLIC.

<margin>What is the cure for Colic?</margin>
As far as the method of treatment is concerned: it must be known that one part is directed toward the four winds, if they begin to turn into a chronic condition; another part is devoted to the resolution of the salt. But regarding the third part—the contractions themselves—each of these requires its own peculiar care to be applied. In the first treatment, attention must be paid to the four cardinal winds, under each of which their collateral winds are included. The care of the navel, therefore, is placed in **Sibeta** and **Egesus**: and that of the spine in **Saceruola**. <note>These terms (Sibeta, Egesus, Saceruola) are specific Paracelsian remedies or technical terms for localized treatments.</note>

<margin>Sibeta and Egesus cure colic of the navel. Saceruola cures that of the spine.</margin>
For the East, it is in <term>Falernian wine</term> <note>original: "Falerno"; a famous wine of antiquity often used as a medicinal base.</note> with oil; for the West, in <term>Poppy</term> <note>original: "Papauere"</note>, etc. One warm draught is owed to the colic of the East, and likewise two others for the collateral winds. For the Southern colic, a warm anointing of the front parts is required. For the Northern, an internal smearing of the back. And by this reasoning, the winds are conquered, without the use of clysters or purgations, nor by provoked vomiting, nor by the application of baths or "white Greek." <note>original: "albóque Græco"; this refers to *Album Graecum*, the calcined droppings of dogs or hyenas, which was a common, though unpleasant, medieval remedy.</note>

<margin>The salt in colic must be extracted pure.</margin>
However, for the expulsion of the salt (which is a heavier and more laborious cure), it is necessary that after the discussion of the winds, you administer <term>elecampane</term> <note>original: "enulam campanam"; a medicinal plant used for respiratory and digestive ailments.</note>, and do so gradually; do not turn precipitously to Rhubarb, <term>colocynth</term> <note>a powerful and harsh purgative derived from a bitter cucumber.</note>, or similar things. For salt bears no force, and already sticks by itself in the stripped passages. Therefore, you should attempt its expulsion with those remedies that drive out nothing else but salt; if you do so, the effort will succeed well. If, truly, you expel other things along with the salt, you will profit nothing at all. For the salt is rendered less fit for extraction when mixed with dung and other waste. Therefore, it must be left pure and separated from other filth, so that it may be more conveniently drawn out by its own purgatives. When it has been sufficiently drawn out and evacuated, the signs of health will make it clear.

<margin>Dissolved gold strengthens the limbs. Balsam with Galbanum and fox oil cures contraction. Serpent oil, etc.</margin>
Finally, the contraction itself must be removed through "consortive" <note>remedies that act in harmony with the body's nature</note> means, so that the sustaining virtue and strength may be brought from the inside to the outside and diffused. That strengthening agent is <term>dissolved gold</term> <note>original: "aurum solutum"; a high-level alchemical preparation also known as potable gold.</note> in "corrected" concentrated wine. <note>original: "vino centrato correcto"; wine that has been distilled or strengthened.</note> But if the appropriate moisture is lacking in the limbs, Balsam with <term>Galbanum</term> <note>a bitter aromatic gum resin</note> or fox oil with corrected wine will replenish it. Surpassing all these is serpent oil, which not only frees the limbs themselves but also heals them perfectly even without gold.

The other remedies, however, which are readily available from experience itself, I do not eliminate here, but I leave to each its own full praise. I only advise this: that this triple order be studiously observed, and that any experiment be administered in its proper place, lest a certain stain be burned into the reputation of medicine and the patient's state be brought into a worse condition. Let each man, therefore, bring forth remedies from the cabinet of his own conscience. For all things are not in my possession alone. I know many things which are held as proven by others. There are also things which I have never even known. Therefore, I wished to advise here that the best things be selected from everywhere.

---

### PARALYSIS.

<margin>How are the lightnings cooked in the earth?</margin>
All storms and lightnings falling from heaven are prepared and "cooked" in the earth. For that which is a lightning bolt is taken from the earth. Observe its generation in this way: By what means the earth receives leaves, branches, and grasses from heaven—namely from its rain and dew, etc.—so in turn the heaven takes from the earth the liquid by which it is nourished and fed. And just as the earth, unchanged in its nature, becomes grass and leaf while no one sees it: so the heaven also continues its nature, with no one looking on. No one misses or sees on earth that which has flown up into heaven. But the earth cooks this in the earth, and the heaven cooks this in the heaven: that is, what the heaven gives to the earth, the earth cooks; and what the earth sends to the heaven, the heaven cooks.

<margin>The heaven from the earth, and the latter from the former, draws its liquid. A likeness exists on both sides in heaven and earth.</margin>
The reason for that cooking is this: namely, that the Sun, and any Planet, and any star attracts its own liquid from the earth into the heights—one attracts this, another that. Just as a flowering tree draws its flowers, the leaves draw their sage, the green draws its vigor, and the red its redness from the heaven. Conversely, the same must be attributed to the heaven and the individual stars. For what is in the heaven? That which has its likeness on the earth; and there is that on the earth whose likeness flourishes in heaven. Otherwise, it could by no means happen that Saturn should reign in the earth if a similar "Saturn" did not exist in it, and both had their exaltation in the same place. Meanwhile, there are not two Saturns, but one. Hence it happens that the terrestrial serves as nourishment for the celestial, and the latter in turn for the former.

<margin>The cause and origin of lightning.</margin>
That which now pertains to the planets in the earth, from that is generated lightning, not rain. For that which is the food of the earth in the earth was never in the earth, but was newly born from heaven. Therefore rain, dew, etc., are the food of the earth, nor were they in the earth before; they are, I say, the food of the earth, not of the heaven. Therefore, that which is the food of another does not proceed from the same. Lightning, however, is not food: therefore it does not descend from heaven. It does indeed descend from heaven, but it first ascended from the earth into heaven. Thus, like a contrary thing and a cause of disease, it descends into the earth—that is, into the body—like a paralysis which weakens the body. For this is sensible, and is thus man himself. The earth, however, is not man; it is not sensible: therefore it is not a "disease." Concerning lightning, therefore, you ought to know that it emerges from the earth and is the nourishment of the Planets. In these, it turns into lightning—that is, Medically it is Paralysis, Astronomically it is Lightning.

->*A loss of two pages (as I believe).*<-

Therefore He created the Physician, and into his hands He placed the heaven. If, therefore, he must hold the heaven in his hands: it is necessary also that he know the Alchemist himself with all his secrets. For what else is <term>Alchemy</term> but an inferior heaven, <margin>What is Alchemy?</margin> knowing how to separate the Sun from the Moon, day from night, medicine from poison, the useful from the dung: and having done this, being powerful enough to command, "You do this, and you do that." For he who is ignorant of the principles, what will he be in the end or in his works? Indeed, the Planets do the same things, yet in an alchemical sense and process. Whatever man does, those Planets do the same, yet in an alchemical sense and process. Just as the Alchemist seeks saltpeter in niter, Mercury in dung, and sulfur in fire: so the Firmament seeks the same, because it is an invisible Vulcan. <note>In this context, Vulcan represents the transformative power of fire or the internal "artisan" of nature.</note> If it has sought out and prepared these three bodies, a strike arises, which the heaven calls "lightning," but the Alchemist calls a <term>Bombarda</term>. <note>original: "Bombardam"; an early type of cannon or mortar. The author is comparing a thunderclap to the discharge of artillery.</note> For he too has the power of producing lightning: about which in Magic, which is the Philosophy of Alchemy.

Magic, Alchemy, and Philosophy are one. 
Why is Alchemy called Necromancy?
</margin>
[philo]sophy. <note>This sentence completes the word "Philosophy" from the previous page.</note> From the secrets of this philosophy came those madmen who habitually called it Necromancy. But truly, that which has been Alchemy from its first cradles is called Necromancy; and the name is derived from blackness <note>original: "nigtore" [nigritudine]; Paracelsus is making a folk etymology connecting "Necromancy" to the "black" soot of the alchemist's fire rather than the Greek 'nekros' for dead.</note>, because its initiates walked about like charcoal burners. For all those who serve Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here representing the alchemist's forge.</note> are Necromancers. Out of ignorance and lack of skill, therefore, they called those things "Necromantic superstitions" and the "art of the furious army," about which we shall not discuss further in this place.

Yet that "other heaven" <note>The internal, microcosmic heaven within the human body.</note> can provide this, so that, just as water quenches fire, it turns away paralysis from the limb that has not yet lost its physical substance—that is, if the entire house has not yet burned down. # BOOK 
## ON GOUTY PERSONS OR ITS 
### SPECIES AND ANNEXED DISEASES. 
### BY THE AUTHOR THEOPHRASTUS.

#### BOOK I.
->*To the Reader.*<-

<margin>The author: for what cause is he driven to write about gout?</margin>
**I**s it indeed my boldness and confidence that I dare to write about gout, which nevertheless has never been truly described or cured by any Physician? For their chatter has been much, but their works few. This is surely the cause of my daring: that I see my adversaries burdened and heaped with such praises and honors, and so much hope and confidence placed in them, as if they alone poured forth the oracles of truth and their words were pure Gospel, even though all their words and judgments are polluted by foul ignorance and stinking nonsense. This, I say, is what strikes pain into me: because I am forced to see lies valued and worshipped so highly by everyone in public, young and old alike, and that things have come to such a pass that no one is allowed to even whisper against the ignorance, stupidity, errors, and flatteries of those boasters. For if anyone speaks against these things, even in passing, they immediately condemn and deport him with a swift sentence to the furthest prisons, so that in this way the kingdom of Satan and his sons may remain safe and internal.

But what, O Princes and leaders of the fatherland, what I say is your concern in this? Why do you so lazily look after your own health, as well as that of the common people and your subjects, while you are persuaded that those are honest and skilled Physicians, and lack all deceit, who yet do nothing but hatch and thrust in their own most harmful worms everywhere, and miserably oppress the Commonwealth with those evils? Do you not lazily neglect and skip over what was especially worthy of sharp censorship? What is smallest, that you judge, and "prepare a tax from cumin" <note>original: "ex cumino... vectigal paratis"; a proverbial expression for obsessing over trivialities while ignoring important matters, derived from the Bible (Matthew 23:23).</note>, as they say. But what is greatest and heaviest, you observe with no care. For though your conscience will proclaim you as uprooters and cutters-off of all evils, how can you so patiently tolerate the extreme fraud of these "painted" <note>Pretended or superficial.</note> physicians? For what faculty exists anywhere today more damaging and shameful than that which pretends to care for the body and even for reason itself, and this life? What art, I say, is swollen and stuffed with a heap of wickedness? Truly and from my heart I say, none from all of them is found anywhere like this one. 

And will no one finally notice how shameful a life those lead who are created Doctors, yet have never restored any sick person to health? In what rank, I ask, should those be held whom executioners, monks, and nuns nonetheless surpass in art and long success, and who maintain Medicine more laudably by practicing their order? By what right, I ask, by what pretext, or with what spirit do you dare to extol men of this kind, whose faculty nonetheless exists as mere opinion, a pure dream, and an inextricable labyrinth? And what is that blindness and madness of yours, that when they say there is no cure or medicine for Gout, you agree with them? When nonetheless that is only a fiction of those whose donkey-like brain has learned to produce nothing healthier or more suitable? And this same delirium has been raved by the greatest part of physicians for so many centuries until now, whose mind is no healthier than that of their leaders <term>Coryphaei</term> <note>original: "Coryphaeis"; the leaders or heads of a choir or movement.</note>: and so their lineage has brought forth a long succession of fools. But what is that fraud and loss, for so noble a faculty, so excellent for the human race, and such a distinguished praise and utility of it to be obscured, suppressed, and ruined by those sluggish pupils of the Academies? 

And would it be a small thing for you, the Rectors of provinces, to wink so much at so many slaughters and robberies? For I do not speak here only of Gout, but of all other diseases universally, in which they are either mute dogs, or with the deceits of words sought from everywhere, they wickedly penalize you and your wives, children, and subjects in goods, body, and life itself. And why does the pomp and so insolent pride of the Academies themselves keep you as admirers for so long? For these offer nothing else than a veil and ornament of a lie and a purchased testimony. Therefore, open your eyes at last, and no longer allow yourselves to be deceived by empty titles. For it can happen most readily that a Doctor simultaneously plays the <term>fool</term> <note>original: "morionem"; a fool or jester.</note>. In a fool, truly, they might even find a place for a scoundrel. Or is that not enough for a testimony, that while they treat your diseases, for whole days and nights nothing...

<page-num>635</page-num>

-> ON GOUTY PATIENTS <-

...they accomplish absolutely nothing, but repeatedly toss out and sell mere smoke, pleasant trifles, and blind riddles; moreover, they fish out of you the very things they ought to be teaching you. For they perform their first experiments upon your own body. And with what audacity, I ask you, do you dare entrust yourself to these Doctors and Masters who, disagreeing in their own studies about what they should have known long ago, first inquire and cross-examine you? And so, in the meantime, while these "Doctors and Masters" are first made by you, do you think it right that you should be slaughtered by such reckless men? Are these games or jokes? You, Emperor <note>original: "Cesar"; Paracelsus is likely appealing to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V to regulate medical practice.</note>, pay heed. For unless you alone, as is your duty, take notice of this, homicide will be committed with no one to avenge it. Everywhere they fortify themselves with numerous alliances, friendships, and frequent patronages, so that no one dares to speak out or contradict them, unless you, Emperor, do so—you who do not wish to be held guilty for the blood they spill.

<margin>Theophrastus: Why is he opposed to Physicians?</margin>
As for why I write this with a more stirred spirit, let the Reader indicate. For you can easily guess that what I speak of here pertains to many. And why, in publishing on Gout <term>Podagra: A historical term for gout, though Paracelsus uses it here as a general term for various arthritic conditions affecting the joints.</term>, I should particularly hurl such accusations, the reason is not light: it is because, wherever I am called to bestow my counsel and art, they take my presence indignantly. They everywhere render me hated among the credulous with their trifles and flatteries, and by thundering out I know not what lightning-bolts of arguments, they impudently sell their own Medicine to everyone. They despise and belittle my process of curing, which they do not understand even in the slightest degree. Many machines are indeed needed to veil a lie that is notorious. Therefore, they shall at last be put to shame, and in harassing me, they will betray their own art; once the plow has been applied, they will have less opportunity to turn and lay waste to their field so widely, so that it may henceforth bear pure wheat, whereas otherwise they were accustomed to sow it with mere darnel and tares <note>Paracelsus uses a biblical metaphor (Matthew 13:24-30) to compare his rivals' medical teachings to weeds that choke the truth.</note>.

Therefore, Reader, read and turn over these things which I write and send out to you. For they will not only satisfy your desire, but will furthermore provide you a most faithful opportunity to compare my writings with theirs. Meanwhile, I am determined to proceed in my purpose and to wait for their contrary writings. Dated, etc.

# NARRATIVE
## OF THE BOOK.
-> THE ARGUMENT. <-
## By the Author, Theophrastus.

<margin>What are the locations of Gout?</margin>
**I**t is my intention here to treat Gout: which is a disease occupying the joints of the head, or the seams where two bones meet, joined by cartilage or some other medium, such as the bone of the nose and the forehead; likewise that which is divided by the milky pores <note>original: "Galaxicis poris"; a Paracelsian anatomical term referring to porous bone structures or specific marrow passages.</note>, also the bones of the neck, the jaws, the tonsils, the chin, the region of the ears, the eyes, and their orbits. In short, wherever in the head such a joining and division of bones or porous structure appears, there the seat of gout can be.

Likewise, from the neck through the entire spine, and all the bones of the armpits, shoulders, collarbones, and all the vertebrae down to the tailbone <note>original: "coccygis os"</note>; wherever joints of any kind intervene, there Gout can fix its seat. Similarly in the beginnings and ends of the ribs, where the bones are united to the cartilages; likewise in the thorax and the whole chest, wherever two bones touch each other, the wombs of gout can exist. In the same way also in the diaphragm, the upper collarbones, and the skulls of men. For the head is composed of many cartilages, in which gout alone lies; so also in the joint where two bones are joined, or enter into one another, as in the hip and thigh and the sacrum, and the knees, and the pores or "sponges" of the knees, and the lower extremity of the leg, and the ankles, and all other joinings of the bones. For in all these Gout is accustomed to fix its seat. Furthermore, higher up in the arm where the bone is inserted into the shoulder, in the elbow itself and its entire circumference, in the wrist <note>original: "carpo"</note> and all its cavities, in the hands and the fingers of both the feet and the hands, and in all the wrist-bones <note>original: "rastetis"; refers to the carpal or tarsal bones.</note> where two bones are united, both internal and external, according to the length, breadth, and crosswise. Likewise under the nails of the hands and feet, in the palm and the sole, outside and inside. For in these places gout afflicts almost more severely because a certain number of small bones are crowded there. And these are the principal locations of Gout.

<margin>Gout: which parts are affected by sympathy?</margin>
Similarly, it should be known that Gout also resides in the bladder, in the kidneys, in the penis, and other similar parts, as those which to some extent cohere with the aforementioned bones and are joined to them by familiarity. For when those bones suffer, these organs are also frequently afflicted—not because they feel a gout of their own, but because they receive the pains pressing upon them from elsewhere by reason of their connection. Such pains are also detected in the heel and other similar joints, due to the union of the bones situated in that place.

<margin>What are the signs of Gout?</margin>
Furthermore, Gouty pains happen in this way. In the place where the root of the evil is hidden, pain is stirred up—sometimes by food and drink, sometimes by the cycles of the Moon and the seasons, sometimes by night—and that with swelling, heat, cold, and redness. Finally and most recently, a great hardening of the matter follows, by which the joints are led away from each other and pulled apart, and the very geometric proportion of the limbs is perverted and distorted; the joints grow calloused, harden, become roughened with knots and tubers <note>referring to gouty tophi, the hard lumps of urate crystals.</note>, and are rendered immobile, nor can they be bent. Where last of all, grains of salt <note>original: "grana salis"; Paracelsus views gout as a "tartaric" disease where minerals precipitate out of bodily fluids like salt or stone.</note> so large and strong are born in the joints that, on account of their excessive growth, the sick must perish and die.

<margin>Gout: a deceptive and wicked disease.</margin>
In this evil affliction, various kinds of pains also occur, revealing themselves by various signs, and these are almost always dissimilar and do not always agree with one another. From this rank is also the fact that if an unsuitable medicine is applied, but experiments are tried, the disease shows itself no differently than if it were mocking the Medicine and the Physician at the same time. The matter is almost the same as if someone were to show an apple to an infant but not hand it over. For so the disease deceives the Physician. For while it seems to have already receded, it immediately returns with much more atrocious pains. Thus, this disease is the most wicked and craftiest of all, which makes a mockery of the Physician no differently than if it were touching him with a baited hook through pre-arranged words and deceits. And here almost the same thing happens as with a Master playing with his fool...

<page-num>636</page-num>
<header>ON GOUTY PATIENTS.</header>

...to the patient where the Doctor is a fool, but the disease is the Master. <note>original: "morio Medicus est, Dominus autem morbus." This concludes the sentence from the previous page, where Paracelsus mocks incompetent physicians.</note>

This disease afflicts either by itself or alongside other illnesses; it leaves and returns, and even when it seems to vanish, it remains present. However, it kills no one unless it leads to an obstruction: that is, if it cannot be reduced to its own Anatomy. <term>Anatomy: In Paracelsus’s vocabulary, "Anatomy" refers not just to dissection, but to understanding the internal, spiritual, and chemical structure of a disease or substance.</term> For then it plunders life itself. But let us now finish this explanatory part of my project. Next, we shall hand down and describe: **1.** The cause of this disease. **2.** Its connection. **3.** The paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or violent expression of a disease.</note>. Finally, we shall attend to the cure of all these things according to the method of the first craftsmen or Masters, who are still among the living. The pains are therefore distributed in this way: they rage now in this place, now in that; they are not confined to one spot, but are disseminated and divided in various and wondrous ways.

# BOOK
## ON THE INVENTOR OF THE ARTS

<margin>
Man is a naked image in need of instruction.
</margin>
**I**t is admitted by all of you that it is entirely fitting and proper that a man should not hide the master of his speech or the author of his writing. For what, I ask you, has a man received from his father and mother for which he can proclaim himself similar to them, except a hungry stomach and a raw, naked mind—or a nature that exists as nothing but a naked image, similar to death? What, then, will a man eventually make of himself, or how far will he penetrate, when he is nothing but a naked and mute statue of a man? For unless he receives what is given and offered from elsewhere, he can produce nothing from his own home. Rather, he knows and *is* that which is carried and poured into him. Therefore, before I proceed further in the deduction of this begun chapter, it seems necessary to define and establish who it is from whom man learns, and by whom he is shaped in such difficult matters.

<margin>
To admirers, everything is great.
</margin>
<margin>
From where the PHYSICIAN must learn, and from which masters.
</margin>
What it is that commands us to learn—that is, what teaches us the things to be learned—can be understood in many ways. He who is ignorant and unskilled believes anyone he meets. For admiration among the simple-minded is so prone and ready that they easily look up to and value even the most slightly learned person. Therefore, it seems necessary first of all to clear up and establish from whom we ought to learn. If I speak and write according to the pleasure and institute of Avicenna, Galen, Hippocrates, etc., I will remain exactly the same as them. Since they themselves provided nothing, it stands to reason that I myself would provide nothing of greater excellence either. Therefore, one must learn not from those just mentioned, but from the true and genuine Master. For much healthier precepts are drawn from these than from those by whom the aforementioned schoolmen were instructed. From this it is clear that those honest and worthy schoolmen proved themselves to be anything but that; rather, they failed through a premature and foul apostasy, defiling all science and involving all their descendants in that same defection.

<margin>
Three types of authors and masters.
</margin>
And these things are to be pointed out for this purpose: so that we may know which authors we ought to trust, or trust less, lest by chance we be incautiously swept away into error by their precepts. For many speak from the instinct of the heavens. Their writings are mere words, lacking all use and benefit. For deceits, impostures, and overly hidden subtleties do not pertain to the Physician at all. Nor is innate erudition of use to the Physician. For that is not a Master upon whom the Physician can place his foundation. There are also many who compose and write from their own experience. These men, if they put forward and boast of naked experience, provide exactly as much benefit as they have experience in this or that disease. For every experience has a defined limit, beyond which it does not extend. Thus, this is not enough for the Physician.

<margin>
Philosophers and Astronomers are the true masters of those who speak.
</margin>
Since the three things already mentioned are not sufficient for the Physician—though they appear great, difficult, and lacking any defect to our eyes—it is necessary that we prefer a more certain and perfect Master over them, one who lacks every stain and defect. These are the things which Philosophy and Astronomy draw out and perfect from both "globes." <note>Likely referring to the Microcosm (man) and Macrocosm (the universe).</note> Their characters and letters are Chiromancy, Geomancy, Pyromancy, etc. <note>Techniques of divination and natural observation used by Paracelsus to read the "signatures" of nature.</note>

->### ON THE LIMBUS.<-

<margin>
The Limbus is everything.
</margin>
<margin>
The world is from the Limbus.
</margin>
All invisible things existed with God, which now exist as visible. All these, as they were, were encompassed into one Limbus <term>Limbus: A Paracelsian term for the "Great World" or primeval matter, the reservoir of all potentiality from which the universe and man were created.</term>, that is, into one visible body. This body was made the "Great World" <note>the Macrocosm</note>: and from this, man was subsequently fashioned. From which it follows that man can do nothing except that which existed previously. Hence it is also clear that the Angels know all the arts and necessities of men, as do the devils. For they are from that Limbus from which man was constituted. Therefore, good and bad men alike, the truthful and the liars, the humble and the proud, act upon the earth. For like produces like.

<margin>
Why Angels know the secrets of nature.
</margin>
<margin>
The first parents of the Limbus, etc.
</margin>
Furthermore, it follows from this that the first fathers of the Limbus learned nothing from themselves, but received all things proposed to them, both good and evil, directly from God; yet having been seduced in these matters, they made themselves Devils when they wished to prove themselves more truthful than God. From this follows the second creation of Heaven and Earth, Air and Water. They were made from these: and what they possessed in spirit, in the Angelic nature, etc., was distributed into this little globe and sphere. For just as the kingdom of heaven is in itself, in its virtues: so also the heaven was brought down into division corporally, taken from the Angelic.

<margin>
There are no stars in the Angelic world.
</margin>
<margin>
The stars represent the essences of Angels and Devils.
</margin>
<margin>
The Angelic nature of man; from whence comes the excellence of the Angelic man.
</margin>
Now, among the Angels there is no star, but God alone, into whom all things proceed, and from whom all necessary things flow to all creatures. But among men, there are stars. The stars do not indicate God, but the nature of the Angels. And the good stars denote good angels, while the bad denote bad ones. In this way, man assumes an Angelic nature from heaven and becomes like heaven. He who knows the Angels also knows the stars. He who knows the stars and knows the Horoscope, he knows and understands the entire world; he knows how to compose man and Angel himself; he is Lucifer on earth, he is Jupiter in heaven, and so on for the rest.

But lest I reveal things that should not be spoken in this place, I conclude the matter thus: that man is as we have predicted, and that all creatures are one, each...

# BOOK I.
<page-num>637</page-num>

<margin>All creatures are one</margin>
...when comparing any one thing with another, mortality is the only exception. This is the reason why one person knows this, and another knows that. I am speaking of those who learn without mortal teachers <note>original: "sine mortalibus præceptoribus." Paracelsus often argued that true knowledge is an internal gift or a discovery of nature, not something merely memorized from old books.</note> and surpass their fleeting masters. For he who learns from a fleeting master learns more and in a different way than his own Angelic nature requires. But he who profits and progresses by his own means, judge him to belong to that Angel, who is his likeness in heaven itself. 

<margin>For all born of Angels, the last day shall come.</margin>
Thus, the names of the learned are inscribed in the kingdom of heaven or the kingdom of Satan, according to what each person is. Once this number is filled, and all those born of Angels have come to be, the final day will be at hand.

<margin>The two teachers of man.</margin>
Therefore, the Master of whom I have begun to speak must be understood as being of two kinds: the Angelic and the Mortal. What does the Mortal teacher teach other than what I said at the beginning—namely, mere errors and nothing perfect? For what good can come from a fleeting kingdom? From this source also proceed and emerge those false Doctors who provoke me to write. Unless an Angel in heaven is present as the Doctor’s teacher and strength, then nothing at all should be accepted from him. 

<margin>Where does true doctrine come from?</margin>
True doctrine, therefore, is drawn in without a fleeting teacher. If this doctrine flourishes in faithful and constant disciples, it is no wonder that they far surpass those of you who have emerged from fleeting schools. For no one emerges truly or solidly learned from a mortal teacher; rather, we are all born from above, from on high, and not from ourselves. And he who is born from above in this way, as we have said, has disciples who themselves leave their own disciples after them. Now, there is a diversity among these: for disciples are born from various stars and Angels, and everyone judges them according to their own measure.

<margin>A Physician without heaven is like a pilot without a ship.</margin>
But to digress into Medicine, hold to this same principle in the same way. Unless heaven itself, and it alone, produces the Physician, who will have even the slightest knowledge of a toothache? No one. And even if a man who does not belong to that Angel meditates upon and puts forward something seemingly appropriate, who would place any trust in such a fantasy? For hidden things are not at all open to man, except those offered to him through the five senses—and even then, he is not always master of them, nor do they encompass everything indiscriminately. A man should not persuade himself of anything else regarding this heavenly birth. For if he does not participate in it, he will not know or understand even the smallest thing. He will never be advanced by his mortal teacher to the point where he holds the place or rank of an author <note>In this context, "author" implies an original authority or creator of knowledge, rather than just a writer.</note>. And even if he has drained every bit of force and industry from his teacher and learned every doctrine and subtlety, along with all Rhetoric and Sophistry to perfection <note>original: "ad unguem" (to the fingernail), a Roman expression for perfect finish.</note>, his lot will still be no better than that of a thorn next to roses, which no one touches. Just as the flowers of the field grow forth, so too must this "growing forth" be. No nettle produces roses. No rose bears lilies. Each keeps its own kind separate. 

<margin>Man is not changeable or moldable.</margin>
Therefore, just as certainly as a lily remains a lily and a rose remains a rose, so too can a man himself hardly be changed or educated into something else. It would be far easier to turn Sage into Rue. If you attempt to change him with the greatest schemes and believe he has been made better, you will nonetheless see him standing there like a statue or an image on a wall, which knows not how to speak or sing, nor laugh or grieve, nor even how to smell good or bad.

And in this, the very Light of Nature is entirely situated; it shines forth in the fact that such people grow naturally and are not to be molded by us. And if we grow in this way, the seed of this growing thing is divided into two: one part remains in the taste and its own ears of grain; the other becomes tares <note>Weeds that look like wheat.</note>. That second part is the man who wishes to be highly esteemed but has no value, produced outside this condition of "lilies" and entangled with the light of death. 

<margin>The eternal Light of Nature.</margin>
For the light of nature itself is eternal because it descends from the Angels; and it remains in the soul, which does not die. But the mortal light dies out. And this is the "fleeting teacher." For neither the Mechanical arts, nor all Music, nor all Geometry, Astronomy, and Philosophy shall die; rather, after their death, they will stand perpetually in that light, and like the Angels, they will be perfectly skilled in it. Because the Angels are Doctors, Masters, Mechanics, and so on—and we are also such—there is no reason the soul should be ashamed to exist like them and remain so perpetually. Therefore, our works will follow us; that is, in them we shall flourish and grow like a mustard seed, humble indeed on earth, but in heaven our Angels will dwell within us.

Now, however, I will speak of that which stands in my way in Medicine: namely, that the mortal light pushes and sows its frauds with such great effort. I will say nothing here of the higher Authority, of which more will be said elsewhere. For I do not intend to confuse you with those matters in this place. 

<margin>Theophrastus's epithets from his adversaries.</margin>
And yet, I wish to point out my teacher here, in case it bites you so much that I, having been instructed by no [mortal] teacher, am a "rebel of the Academies," the "vagabond’s leg," the "devil of experimenters," <note>original: "Academiarium perduellis, vagantium crus, experimentatorum diabolus." These are insults Paracelsus's enemies used against him.</note> and so on, as you are all accustomed to chant about me everywhere. I already know by heart your future writings and efforts to be published against me. And yet, you shall not triumph over me; rather, I shall set up a certain trophy over you. Meanwhile, let these prefaces of mine, written in the form of chapters, be tedious to no one. For they will propose the genuine teacher to you and lead you into far different schools than those in which the merely "crowned Fools" sit. For what can you eventually mold out of a Donkey? Whatever you place upon it, it will nonetheless continue to bray like a donkey, just as a crow croaks and a cuckoo calls. Thus, those tiara-wearing Fools walk about like crowned storks. <note>original: "Beani." A "Beanus" was a raw, unlicked newcomer at a university, often used as a term of abuse for an ignorant person pretending to be a scholar.</note>

***

### MECHANICS.

<margin>The physician, once removed, is raised up.</margin>
**O**ur first task in this work is to describe the cause and distribution of diseases. Now, the growth of diseases is Theoretical. But no man is such an industrious Physician by himself that he can boast of looking into the very body of the disease, its matter, its increase, and finally its innermost essence. It was fitting for those physicians to know these things, yet they are entirely unskilled and ignorant of them. If, therefore, those things are absolutely necessary to know, there is certainly a need for something far different...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 637, where Paracelsus began to distinguish between true, divinely-inspired knowledge and the false learning of "mortal teachers." Here, he transitions into his specific medical theory regarding gout, grounding it in the observation of nature rather than the traditional academic doctrine of the "four humors."</meta>

<page-num>638</page-num>

-> ON GOUT <-
<note>original: "DE PODAGRICIS"</note>

...the foundation is to be held and placed, rather than (as those others object) the four humors. They imagine these humors so boastfully, as if they had seen them with their very eyes, and as if they had observed them with the sharp sight of a lynx <note>The lynx was a proverbial symbol of perfect, piercing vision in the Renaissance.</note>, watching what and how much they do at every single moment, what business they carry out, how they are altered, and so on. Yet all these things are completely hidden and concealed from the eyes. Most of their lies are of this bold character.

If, therefore, you demand that I hand down the matter and the very foundation of <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagræ." Historically, "podagra" specifically referred to gout in the foot, but was often used as a general term for arthritic pain.</note> in this chapter, I will propose its <term>theory</term> <note>original: "Theoricam." In this context, it refers to the underlying natural principles rather than abstract speculation.</note> to you in such a way that I will not touch upon the specific nature of the attack itself, but rather set before you the core model of the theory by way of an example. He who understands this example has explored the cause and origin of all diseases. This example is as follows: namely, that you should not judge the matter and body of a disease in any other way than how the growing things of the earth and the elements indicate and show. If you know those things, you already know the disease. In this, <term>anatomy</term> <note>For Paracelsus, "anatomy" is not the dissection of a corpse, but the study of the inner structural correspondences between man and the natural world.</note> is established; from this, Medicine itself is drawn. For medicine grows just like the disease itself.

<margin>One similar thing is the theory of another similar thing.</margin>
Indeed, one similar thing is always the certain theory of another similar thing.

Hitherto, I have spoken quite often—and especially in the book on the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>—about the Architect of the heavens (concerning all the structures of heaven, what they build there) and about their operations. I spoke with a specific sense, so that you would not stretch your wisdom further than Philosophy itself teaches.

<margin>As many kinds of diseases as there are species of growing things.</margin>
This is the same as if I were to say: set before yourselves a beech tree or an oak tree and how it grows. Just so much—and nothing further—must you know and understand about the disease itself, as far as is possible. For the principle of growth is the same for both. Just as far as trees and herbs can be understood, so far is it permitted to inquire into diseases, and not a step further. If you pass beyond this established boundary, what do you think you will finally become? Surely nothing but an impostor of Medicine and a reckless violator of practical truth.

## ANATOMY.

I can establish nothing else in this place than that you should understand as much about the "bodies" of these diseases as you can understand about growing things. Therefore, penetrate deeply into Anatomy, so that you may see from the opposite side that nature which is similar to and matches this disease. For the "heaven" of both is one and the same thing. And just as man has his own inner <term>Mechanic</term> <note>The "Archaeus" or internal vital force that directs bodily functions like a craftsman.</note>, so does disease, and so does health. Thus, as many "Mechanics" as there are, so many kinds of men.

<margin>Nature was created for the sake of man.</margin>
Now, to what other end was nature created than that man should exist within it? For what uses were wood and fire established, other than for warming man and preparing his necessities? From this it is clear that the anatomy of the cold and the wood is the same, just as the art of cooking and the art of fire are one. The cook himself 
<margin>The anatomy of similar things is one.</margin>
cooks nothing; fire alone cooks. Therefore, there is one "heaven" in the fire and one in the food. These two are one heaven and share one anatomy.

<margin>Nature takes to itself what is like it.</margin>
Thus, the consumption of things belongs to fire, and such is its heaven; likewise, the heaven of the things to be consumed by it is similar to it. By "fire," we understand the power of its specific property. By "that which is burned," we understand the power of that which is subject to fire. Yet the anatomy of both is the same, just like that of a teacher and a student. It is necessary for the teacher to have the same anatomy as the student. Otherwise, the former will not be able to teach, and the latter will not be able to learn at all. For nature does not take anything unless it proceeds from a nature similar to itself. Surely you see that there is no joining of stone and wood. For there is not one and the same anatomy for both, but two heavens are present with their own elements. Thus, neither are iron and wax joined, for the same reason. Conversely, that which subdues iron has the anatomy of iron. That which suits 
<margin>Iron is subdued by iron and fire.</margin>
and matches wax is of the same anatomy as wax. And in these things, one is often known through the other. For if wax is put into fire, it perishes. But if it enters into the anatomy of diseases, then wax is the "fire" of the diseases and consumes them in a similar way. For as the agreement of external things is to themselves, so it is also toward man and within man. (What subdues iron? Only iron—that is, the hammer. Also fire—that is, its own anatomy. What subdues wood? A knife. What subdues stone? An axe. What consumes everything entirely <note>original: "omnino"</note>? Fire.)

Therefore, know this: roses are the "anatomy" of their specific disease. And just as fire consumes roses, so roses are likewise a "fire" and consume the diseases whose anatomy they bear. For power is to be known from anatomy; without this, no knowledge exists. For power is situated in the anatomy of diseases and in the anatomy of their medicines. 

<margin>Anatomy teaches the power of things. As many fevers as there are species against fevers.</margin>
Therefore, the species of the earth are the species of diseases. Thus, there are not merely seventy fevers; rather, there are as many fevers as there are species of plants that act against fevers. The types of plants give the types of classification. In them are also the divisions of diseases—the same number, the same operation. And just as a carpenter easily discerns what he needs, and what fits here or there so that the "anatomy" of those things is made whole, so also the Physician must be like that craftsman. To build a house is the "anatomy" of the completion or perfection of that house. To "make" a man is the anatomy of the completion of man. Therefore, just as a man completes and perfects a man, while being ignorant in the meantime of where he takes the arms, hands, or feet, so it is fitting for the physician to possess such a "seed" <note>original: "sperma." Here used metaphorically for the essential germ of a cure.</note>—not just any limb as a limb. In this way, he will be an <term>Atomicus</term> <note>One who understands the indivisible, essential building blocks of nature and disease.</note>.

## PHYSIOGNOMY.

<margin>The name is nothing. The external testifies to the internal.</margin>
He who busies himself with knowing growing things will give his labor to know that which he does not see at all. For whatever and however much he sees, it is all weighed by its name. The name is nothing. Thus, that which is seen is also nothing. For the eyes distinguish only the external. But no external exists which is not an index of the internal. Thus, the growth of black hair testifies that a similar nature exists within the man. Likewise, red hair indicates a "red" nature. For a thing must be judged by its...

He asserts that a physician must act like a craftsman, matching the "heaven" or essence of a cure to the "heaven" of a disease.</summary>

...it proceeds entirely from that to which it belongs. Thus, the pear reveals its own tree.

<margin>Everything possesses its own body.</margin>
Indeed, in the hidden properties of the secrets of nature, there is nothing that does not have its own specific body. Thus, a human who is inclined toward the "upward" <note>likely referring to spiritual or intellectual health</note> possesses his own specific body, separate and distinct from one who does not tend toward the upward at all. And the difference here is the same as that between white and black. For as often as a <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "mysterium," referring here to a hidden natural power</note> or secret is given, so often is there also a specific body and its own singular sign within that body. The body provides the evidence of the secrets and mysteries hidden within itself. For just as wood presents and indicates itself as being destined for the fire, so does any body and form indicate through itself where it ought to be categorized. And this should have been the focus of study in the schools—not the Humors, Cholera, Melancholy, Blood, or Phlegm.

<margin>A specific body for mysteries, and its own singular sign in that body. The body provides evidence of the secrets and mysteries hidden within.</margin>
<margin>The form and color are marks of the body's craftsman.</margin>
<margin>To every disease, its own peculiar color.</margin>
You see, of course, that throughout the universe, diseases themselves carry their own *Physiognomy* <note>The art of judging character or health from outward appearance.</note> as well as their own colors and forms across all types. Thus, in Jaundice <note>original: "Ictericia"</note>, the lemon-yellow color of the body betrays the disease. And as it is with this case, so it is with all diseases: a specific color blooms on the face, with no exception. These things are said so that you may accurately know the gradations of colors. If you distinguish these, you will know by sight alone what lies hidden in the body. And just as you see a limb increase and grow so much in Elephantiasis <note>original: "Elephantia," a disease causing gross swelling of the limbs or skin.</note> that it is impossible to recognize it by its original shape, you should likewise consider that there is no disease that does not produce such a body and such a form, more or less. This is because every disease imposes another form upon the body itself, outside of its initial <term>spermatic</term> formation <note>The original biological blueprint or "seed-form" of the person.</note>. (That is, the <term>Formella</term> <note>A "little form" or pattern.</note>, matching the form of the disease and the herb according to *Physiognomy*, such as *Celandine* <note>original: "Chelidonia." This herb has yellow sap and was traditionally used to treat jaundice because it "looked" like the disease.</note>.) Therefore, if forms and colors depart from the norm—not from the nature of the seed, but from morbid bodies—it is entirely right that this be noticed and known in that context. For a man is known by his form, and other things by their color, such as an *Ethiopian* and a *German* and others like them. This same logic of knowledge must prevail similarly in all points of *Physiognomy*, which the entire profession encompasses; the purpose of this teaching is for you to learn to name these signs correctly. Even a peasant knows a fever by the shivering and trembling. However, the physician is ashamed of this level of knowledge. For he proceeds with a more "sublime" knowledge, considering more common things a disgrace to himself if he does not also know the more exquisite and difficult matters.

<margin>The Formella matches the form of the disease and the herb.</margin>
<margin>The physician's knowledge is a higher form of the peasant's knowledge.</margin>
I recount all these things for this purpose: so that, if you wish to stand in this profession with truth and praise, you may understand the foundation from which you must derive your <term>Theory</term>, both in recognizing the causes of diseases and in establishing the method of medicine with certainty. For there is nothing that cannot be proven. Just as any craftsman proves his art through his works, so does any thing testify to its own nature through its form. A chalice testifies to the industry of its maker. Therefore, just as the chalice gives testimony of its fabricator, so any herb indicates its creator—which is the medicine, the secret, and the mystery all at once. It is not that the form of the chalice alone is highly valued, but that through it the fabricator is indicated at the same time, so that those who seek chalices can find and track him down. Therefore, just as any work manifests its own artisan, so likewise here, form and color alone exist as the work of their craftsman. Such is the knowledge of things that the Physician must hold above all.

<margin>The work testifies to the artisan.</margin>

## *CHIROMANCY*
<note>Palmistry, or the study of the lines of the hand.</note>

<margin>Praise of Chiromancy.</margin>
The logic of Medicine is not the same as that of sophisticated quibbling <note>original: "sophisticarum," referring to the abstract logic used in university debates.</note>. For everything ought to flow from the aforementioned "light of nature." Among that order, the art of the hands is also numbered. For it is the witness of those things which *Physiognomy* itself does not demonstrate; that is, it grants judgment regarding life and those things adhering to it from those matters that dwell in its nature and property. For just as you have heard concerning colors and forms in *Physiognomy*, here too, beyond those, there is a certain "shaping" that expresses life and its nature. This shaping also descends from the Angelic nature, formed and expressed through the medium of the "middle star" <note>Refers to the astrological influence on human development.</note>. For he who does not have marked hands is not great (that is, multifaceted) in the stars, but is only marked in some specific part, as the matter itself indicates.

<margin>What is Chiromancy and from where?</margin>
Furthermore, in this matter, the degree of the "points"—namely of size and smallness, etc.—is of such subtle consideration that it can hardly be fully investigated or its cycle accurately obtained. However, the knowledge of "passing through" <note>perhaps referring to the lines crossing the hand</note> is easier. But the Physician’s purpose is not to pursue the *Chiromancy* of the aforementioned cycle pertaining to the nature of life—which is nothing other than the "honor of life"—but rather, setting that aside, to fish out the integrity and wickedness of the nature of the whole body. That is the Physician's subject. This investigation is of such a kind that a likeness of form in natural things is produced from chiromancy; because, indeed, there is nothing in growing things whose line a human does not have impressed upon himself. For whatever lives has its own sign. In common parlance, these are called *Chiromantic Signs*. These signs serve this use: that through chiromancy, the logic of a man's life and character may be recognized, as we said before. Since, therefore, man was created from the <term>limbus</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "limbus" is the "great chaos" or the universal material from which the human (the microcosm) was extracted.</note>, it is necessary that he also seek the *limbus*—that is, that he know how to find the "trace" he carries in his hand in that place where it exists [in nature]. For these traces are the Medicines <note>original: "Medicamina"</note> whose use is required. And if this concordance is not found, all compounds will be useless. For the principle and foundation of all things lies hidden here. Just as you see all craftsmen provide proof of their art through their instruments, in the same way, Medicine itself ought to be proven and established through these types of traces and Philosophy. Yet the Sophist <note>The term Paracelsus used for his academic rivals who relied on books rather than nature.</note> rejects and turns away from this proof, which his "composition" cannot endure; and thus the wisdom of the artisan himself fades away and is blackened by this rejection.

<header>CONCERNING THOSE WITH GOUT.</header>

<margin>The hand is the subject of chiromancy.</margin>
<margin>The Limbo has preserved nature in all things.</margin>
...and of those matters which <term>Chiromancy</term> <note>The art of palmistry, which here is used more broadly to mean reading the "signs" of the body.</note> treats. It is not, however, that these signs are limited to the hand alone, but that they overflow into the further parts of the body. Seek these same signs in the hands of those who are still growing: and there you will find the root of those signs which are also scattered throughout the rest of the body. Now indeed, a similar chiromancy indicates a similar nature: just as a similar <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of assessing a person’s character or health from their outer appearance, especially the face.</note> noted a similar essence. And the Physician ought to be well-versed in this similar nature and essence, and from them he must derive his composition. For such is the principle of the <term>Limbo</term> <note>original: "Limbus." In Paracelsian thought, the "Limbus" refers to the primordial "great world" or matrix from which man was created; it contains the blueprints for all things.</note>: that it has preserved its essence and form in all creatures, with nothing changed or turned around; namely, so that from it, man may see and find that which, when it fails, must necessarily be replaced for himself.

## CONCLUSION.

<margin>God willed the Physician to be perfect.</margin>
*The things I have proposed thus far are all intended to make you recognize from what source a Physician should finally speak and prove his claims. For it is his duty to take nothing from himself, to leave nothing unproven, and to establish both his theory and practice more skillfully and accurately than any carpenter. A carpenter fits and joins everything most exquisitely to the most refined judgment of the eyes. Nor will it profit the physicians here to use the excuse of saying that no Physician can be perfect. For those who make such excuses are hardly Physicians at all; rather, they exist as the errors and outcasts of Medicine. Think, I pray, in your own minds, O Physicians, what the standard is for a smith, a traveler, and a painter, etc., in whom perhaps not as much importance is placed: nevertheless, God created them whole and perfect in their roles. How much more will He provide this in a Physician, upon whom the body and life itself depend—to say nothing of other high matters no less noble? If therefore the Physician were more frequent in his school and more attentive in carrying out his work, bringing with him an honest heart, and progressing in his art no less diligently than the smith himself, he would certainly have no need for these fabricated lies to veil his ignorance. Certainly, whoever labors under some defect of Medicine is entirely lacking in that which I have already proposed. For everything that a man is able to do and knows must flow from the aforementioned Teacher <note>referring to Nature</note>. For what else, I ask, is in man, except what grows in him from above? Certainly nothing at all. Unless he conducts himself in all things according to the prescribed manner, whatever he boasts of will be worth nothing.*

<margin>The light of nature is the teacher of truth.</margin>
*Is this doctrine and art of Medicine not great, which heaven itself teaches? Which the earth itself dictates? Which Chiromancy, Physiognomy, and many other similar arts prescribe? For these are those very <term>lights of nature</term> <note>original: "lumina naturae," the inherent wisdom found in the natural world as opposed to book-learning.</note> from which it is right to learn and be wise. On the other hand, what is that blindness, what is that seduction, to follow one's own brain and opinion? For the brain is by no means a solid teacher. The light of nature alone is the mistress of truth—not the brain, not our senses. Since, therefore, no weight is placed in our own powers and intellect, why, I ask, do we lean so obstinately upon them and grant faith to our own subtleties, as if our reason were an absolute Teacher and Mistress, when it ought to be a perpetual novice and student?*

<margin>Born prophets; that is, nature generates its own.</margin>
*In this place, however, I list very few of these things. Read what is handed down concerning the "born prophets" <note>Those naturally gifted or destined by nature for a specific role or insight.</note> of all ranks and faculties—of war, and of peace. From that, you will recognize in what manner a man uses his arts and his intellect. From those same things, it will also be clear who among them is genuine or counterfeit, what the nature of each person is, and from what source anyone speaks or acts. And so that I may be more rightly understood by you, let it be firmly and always persuaded in your minds that those are the best and most truthful who entangle themselves neither with the Astronomers nor with the natural Geomancers. And let this stand in your mindful memory. For whatever I discuss here serves this purpose: that from these things it may be known from whence a man speaks and lives. For once this is known, what I write hereafter will be understood more fully, not as coming from myself. Therefore, even if you have cast some hatred upon my person (as I suspect), it will not be a loss to my writings. And your rejection will fall back upon your own heads, and the fault for the sick will be imputed to you, and not to the true and genuine Physicians.*

### PROLOGUE.

<margin>Disease is invisible; its body, on the contrary, is visible.</margin>
<margin>Disease is a craftsman.</margin>
Since I must now speak concerning the body of gout: in the threshold of this preface, I would have you know that all things which do us either good or harm, and which wound us, do not do so by their own physical body, yet they perform their work *within* a body. For disease itself exists as something invisible, and has never been seen by anyone’s eyes. Its body, however, is entirely visible—it is surely that which torments us and which we complain about. Furthermore, it now falls to me to explain in what manner the invisible—that is, the disease—ought to be recognized from the visible. But just as we can never see that craftsman with any sharpness or focus of the eyes who fashions the Lavender, the Rose, or the Lily, so that it *is* a Rose or a Lily, etc.; so much less can we see the disease itself with our eyes. For disease, by itself, is the craftsman. I take it upon myself here to explain the work which that craftsman fashions.

<margin>The beauty of the craftsman is known from his works.</margin>
Concerning the body, however, this is established: that any body is nothing other than a thing and a manufactured work. That which comes forth from the craftsman is perishable. In the craftsman himself there is no death, but only in his work, or the thing fashioned. For if the craftsman should cease his fashioning, the protection from death also ceases. For death follows only the end and the completion of a thing. The labor, however, regards the fitness of the work.

<margin>The form of things is for their use; the Body and the office are one.</margin>
Thus a cup, from which one drinks, ought to be the cause <note>of the drinking</note>. It must be fashioned for this office and this use. Thus the Lily must be fashioned into a lily; otherwise its secret virtue perishes. For just as man is fashioned into his own suitable form on account of the soul, so likewise is the principle of all things. For the body and the office—or use—are one thing: and without the formation of the body...

# BOOK II.

There can be no hidden secrets or mysteries here. For the form of the body proceeds from the form of the <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcanorum." In this context, arcana refers to the hidden, spiritual, or essential blueprints of a thing.</note>. Understand the matter in this way: a craftsman certainly thinks that this or 그 that thing ought to be made from iron. Already, the form is within him. This form must be impressed upon the iron. Therefore, as long as the iron is not yet what the craftsman intends, the "office" or function is not yet in the iron. Just as in natural things a "fabrication" is established and a physical body emerges through that fabrication, in a similar way in this second book on Gout, it remains to point out and explain the body of the "craftsman" itself—the principle from which gout is fabricated. For the cause and generation of this disease can by no means be explained or understood except through this comparison.

<margin>
No disease lacks its own form.
</margin>
For there is no disease anywhere without its own form. Even if both the cause and the form exist invisibly, they nonetheless forge a body for themselves. And this is the body that is presented to the eyes and hands of Physicians. For everyone ought to be persuaded that God wishes to be celebrated and praised in diseases and their miraculous works no less than in the flowers of the field—even though diseases are adverse to man.

<margin>
The variety of creatures increases the praise of God.
</margin>
Consider, in turn, that it is entirely to God's praise that He created all the birds, as well as the worms, spiders, and <term>basilisks</term> <note>A legendary serpent-like creature said to kill with its gaze; used here to show that even "harmful" creations have a place in God's order.</note>. For these beasts are of no less praise and glory to God Himself than the nightingale or the peacock. The same God created gold, pearls, and gems—but also, in turn, poisons like Arsenic, Mercury, and so on. For both are to His praise. So also it is to God's praise that He has granted us long-desired health. Yet those diseases He has sent are also to His praise. For there is one "mastery" on both sides—the fabrication of a flower and the fabrication of a disease—and for both, there is one order and one reason. And just as God created things that violate health, He likewise established things that break the sickness. And just as it should be no cause for wonder why a man might die from the gaze of a basilisk, 

<margin>
The basilisk kills by sight.
</margin>
neither should it be a wonder that a sick man is healed and recovers from a single drop of medicine. For in both cases, there is a unique mastery in both breaking down and making whole. Even winter, in its own works, is no less praiseworthy than summer itself, since the consideration of both serves perfectly to illustrate Divine works.

With this goal in mind, winter must be considered so that the Physician, in describing his disease, observes that same order which the Philosopher holds in describing the generation of growing things. For he who treats the generation of natural things also passes down the knowledge of the generation of diseases. By the same reasoning, the Physician also, in describing his disease, teaches and indicates the generation of things in earth and water. For the Philosopher is the only one who writes but does not pass down in his writings those things which pertain to the Physician; and that Physician writes poorly who does not indicate in his works the very hours and minutes, etc., of all natural growing things.
<margin>
How the Philosopher and the Physician differ.
</margin>

Therefore, since the body must be considered entirely in terms of its Formation, and since gout itself is numbered among those bodies—about which many things can be taught—we shall first approach what is most necessary and descend to describing the bodies themselves. For the bodies themselves indicate and betray their own thirst and desire to us.

<margin>
Bodies are either Astral or Earthly.
</margin>
Therefore, since this is the highest consideration for the Physician, I will divide the body into two natures: namely, the **Astral**, which is how the body is generated in the Stars (for all formation is first in the stars, not unlike how the iron is first in the imagination of the craftsman), and the **Earthly**. For you see that all astral works become earth. "Earth," moreover, is whatever is dissolved and perishes, such as Soil, Water, Stone, Metal, etc. Direct your mind diligently, therefore, to this division of bodies. For the types of earth, stones, and metals are various and manifold; and so too are there manifold bodies and various forms. As much as is required here for gout, I am about to enumerate everything fully. However, you shall apply this proposed Theory to other diseases as well. For I do not wish this reasoning to apply only to the disease at hand, but to all others as well.
<margin>
What is Earth?
</margin>

->Farewell.<-

### PYROMANCY.

<margin>
Pyromancy belongs to Astronomy.
</margin>
**F**or what I call <term>Pyromancy</term> <note>original: "Pyromantiam." While it usually means divination by fire, the author uses it here to describe a branch of "fiery" astronomy or the study of celestial influences on the body.</note> here is called **Astronomy** by more recent writers, along with all its related fields. For Astronomy is called Pyromancy according to Philosophy. For the star of heaven is a star of fire. Therefore, this fiery Astronomy alone is the Pyromantic art, discovered and produced by the ancient Magi.

<margin>
What is the origin of Pyromancy?
</margin>
Since the distribution of bodies in diseases was made in the preface, their description must now be joined directly to the explanation of this disease. For Gout is the supreme body among all diseases; because I have undertaken to treat it, it can be understood most easily of all. What is true in this disease must be judged similarly regarding the generation of all other diseases.

<margin>
Every star is an invisible body.
Wood is the body of fire.
</margin>
Everything that is a star has an invisible body, and yet it behaves no differently than a body that exists visibly. For we see fire, and even its body, which is wood. This is visible to our eyes. Such also is the star of fire, though it be invisible; yet it exists as a body.

Now, what is this similarity, that I compare fire and the star of heaven? Let it not confuse you, but let it serve to help you understand the "body" of diseases. You see, for instance, the waters, which have no other body besides themselves, just like rain, etc. Meanwhile, however, from that Element which the water contains within itself, a body is made—that is, stones and metals are generated, etc. This is similarly true of the others, which are discussed separately in their own chapters.
<margin>
From water come stones and metals.
</margin>

Now pay attention here regarding the fiery star. In the sun there is nothing but a dry glow or ray. Yet that ray has a body that we can grasp with our reason. Now, what is our perception or understanding? Nothing, merely nothing. This much is true: we do not detect a body in the splendor of the Sun; yet we see a body in it—that is, *from* it.
<margin>
What the splendor of the Sun is.
</margin>

From where do stones fall? From the sky! Not because they are lifted up from the earth and carried through the air into the heaven, and perfected there in their generation. For all such ideas are vain. The earth itself and the sea maintain their own generation entirely. Nor does anything else come from there, except that they themselves generate the things from which stones, iron, etc., fall. The same is the logic of the Sun or of a Planet itself. It perfects that generation within itself; it is situated in the planet itself, just as the property of those things teaches us.
<margin>
What the generation of celestial stones is.
</margin>

Similarly, the body in Gout is made just as those generations behave. For the body of Gout is not made from the course or motion of physical bodies, but from the course...

<margin>Where the body of gout comes from.</margin> Rather, those bodies are generated by the course of invisible astral bodies. From these things it can be understood that the bodies of diseases are made in an astral manner and logic: just as, if the Sun generates a body, that is where the body is produced. ### NECROMANCY.

<margin>Astral bodies are gouty bodies.</margin> Look to the examples and similarities found through <term>Necromancy</term> <note>In Paracelsus's vocabulary, "Necromancy" often refers to the study of the sidereal or "star-born" spirit and the signs it leaves, rather than simply conjuring the dead.</note>. For these are not inappropriately introduced here. For what is understood concerning the external stars must also be understood concerning the <term>Microcosmic</term> <note>The "Microcosm" is the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note> stars. For Astral bodies are Gouty bodies. And what you have <margin>A body is either parental or non-parental.</margin> observed in the explanation of pyromancy, hold similarly in Necromancy: namely, that there are twofold irons, and twofold bodies of all other things. One is produced from the confluence and "parental" conjunction according to the nature of the seed, and the other is generated without a parental nature. And this latter body is that of which I speak. It is not that a parental cause must be established here in gout; rather, an extraneous cause must be placed entirely against all conjunction, confluence, constellation, Nature, course, and similar things—just as one thing is born from another in a legitimate way and course, and one thing begets another. This "non-parental" condition is that body which I have proposed to treat here, and which I have already partially explained in Pyromancy. For hereafter that body will be defined in a clearer sense, so that you may drink in certain knowledge of those <margin>The interval—the cause of the medium of generation.</margin> bodies which are non-parental.

<margin>What are "Necrocomica" and what is the logic of their generation?</margin> See indeed the marvelous nature of those things which arise from the middle intervals <note>original: "mediis interstitiis," referring to the spaces between the spheres or dimensions of existence.</note> against all natural generation and birth: just as the example of <term>Necrocomia</term> <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe astral impressions or "visions" that manifest physically, often as signs or omens.</note> indicates, which fall in various ways. For they are born neither from a father nor a mother; they are things without any father or mother at all, whose matter has never even existed from the beginning of time. And to instruct you with a similarity, it is no different than if a mute person were to pronounce a certain word with his mouth which had never been heard by him, nor had he ever heard or learned it from others—he would be mute, and yet he would have pronounced the word; and yet, before and after that pronunciation, he would know nothing further of it.

So therefore this is the "Necrocomic" principle: in the heavens there are images, figures, and other similar things, whose beginning—the *father and mother*—is nothing; they are things above and beyond paternal and maternal generation. Nor are these only in the heavens, but they are in the "half-middle" of heaven. And furthermore, they are not only in those intervals, but they even fall down to the earth, upon herbs, leaves, and the like, of trees and similar things. And thus, either with the dew or without it, in their own time many figures and forms <margin>Cocomic signs fall between the heavens and man.</margin> and "concomical" signs are found, which themselves come forth from the same origin as the higher things, and frequently fall upon men walking in such a "line." Thus, he who walks under the clouds is more easily seized by them than another who does not walk there. In the same way, various signs and manifold figures are often found upon clothes—sometimes more conspicuous, sometimes less, sometimes darker—and if any other things fall daily, they are nevertheless minimally visible.

<margin>Gout is a Necrocomic body.</margin> In this way, Gout is truly a Necrocomic body. For by the same logic that Necrocomic forms fall or are made, the "Necro-astrals" also beget such forms in the body—not at all parental, but non-parental from a "Cocomic" nature. According to these things, therefore, in every Theory, the foundation is this "Meteorology." Nor can Medical Theory be established otherwise, unless the Astral philosopher directs it according to the nature of Pyromancy and Astronomy similar to this. For in this Theory, since it is not at all parental, the Necrocomic (or at least the Meteorological) will prevail. In knowing and evaluating this, let no one be moved or offended by that crude and immature description of celestial things left behind by <term>Aristotle</term> and <term>Albertus</term> <note>Refers to Aristotle and Albertus Magnus, whose traditional scholastic views on nature Paracelsus frequently attacked.</note>, those <margin>Aristotle and Albertus are noted.</margin> babblers who entangle students of these matters and likewise obscure and dim the genuine course and art with their subtleties. They do not illuminate these things with the light of nature itself, but extract them from their own frantic brains, and with wonderful boasting, they thrust them upon people like themselves to be admired.

Furthermore, concerning that non-parental body (which also occurs in Pyromancy, a faculty to which I leave the further explanation of this matter), it must also be known that there are *presaging bodies*, which according to true Necromancy are called *Erodenian Bodies*. Concerning these, hold this instruction: that the <term>Erodenia</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for signs or indices that predict a future state or reveal a hidden property.</note> are presages. However, as often as this presage falls, so often follows its "Erodenian History" (as we know has been handed down regarding Troy). Now <margin>What presaging and Erodenian bodies are.</margin> indeed, gout itself is likewise an Erodenian body. For it indicates the "history" of Necrocomic bodies, and thus it <margin>Troy is an Erodenian history. Gout is an Erodenian body.</margin> confers this similarity to that one, and another to this, like a presage and a history. So therefore it is itself also an Erodenian body, or form, or index, or herald of the nature and property of that limb or body.

<margin>What is Erodenium.</margin> So that you may understand this correctly, it should be known that an "Erodenium" is an index of property, so called in the Necrocomic manner. But since the "Erodenium" is not understood by the unlearned, and the history follows afterward, it is therefore called a "presage"—which, however, is not truly a presage.
