<header>ON GOUTY SUBJECTS</header>

<margin>Bodies create diseases, not humors.</margin>
Every thing has its own species and its own specific body. For just as a stone is one kind of body, so too is a metal another, and vitriol <note>A historical term for sulfate minerals, often associated with sharp or corrosive qualities.</note> and similar substances are others, as is demonstrated in water. Therefore, these types of substances exist within a human being. In every category, such species of bodies lie hidden, and every body suffers its own particular disease. For humors <note>In traditional medicine, the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were thought to cause disease if imbalanced. The author is rejecting this ancient theory.</note> do not produce any body; rather, other bodies produce other diseases. Nor should we waste time here on things that merely act upon a disease, for that is a matter of mechanics; instead, we must speak of those things that possess a physical body. For in metals, there is rust; in wood, there are worms; and the cause of these is not a "double humor." It is a single thing that produces both. These, however, are two distinct bodies. And so it is with all other things. Let it be perpetually in your mind that bodies cause diseases—not those trifles you chatter about. For if you weigh the matter deeply within yourselves, you will easily see that everything you have put forward regarding the humors is vain and empty. No one will ever emerge as a good and noble Physician who does not apply his mind to the distinction between these bodies. Nor is a man a single body simply because he is covered by a single skin; rather, he consists entirely of four primary bodies. <margin>4 Primary diseases.</margin> These four principal bodies bring about four primary diseases, aside from all other species. And however many species there are of one, there are just as many of the other.

<margin>Disease is like a painter.</margin>
Whatever the disease may be, it is a "Mechanical Fabricator" that behaves like a painter who sketches or fashions an image with nothing but bare chalk, without pigments. Just as the painter pays no attention to the causes or virtues of pigments in that moment, so too must it be handled in this case. If you were to consider the chalk as the "sinning matter" <note>original: "materia peccans," a traditional medical term for the substance causing a disease.</note>, you would immediately be hindered by the fact that the logic of the image is no different than if it had been drawn with a sharp sword. <margin>The body of the disease must be known from the image.</margin> If the sword is removed, the image remains nonetheless; so that you cannot say that if the color is taken away or the chalk is wiped off, the image itself will be extinguished. On the contrary, you would say to yourself: the color is not there, the chalk is not there, nor are you there who made the image, nor is that thing there which the image was made to be. What, then, is it that constitutes the image? It is surely the "impression" that fashions it. The logic of diseases is similar. Know the body alone, and you will have known the disease itself. For that which creates the disease flees, and it carries away the instrument it used along with it. You will seek in vain for that which has departed. Consider also the Pestilence. Who makes it? The Astral Mechanic <note>A force from the stars or the "inner firmament" that acts as a craftsman to build a disease within the body.</note>. If he has made it, he departs; he leaves his work behind and takes his tools with him. Now, no one has seen this mechanic; no one has found anything left behind other than what he made, what he fabricated. It is no different than a carpenter who carries away his saw, his adze, and his mattock, leaving only the constructed house. The carpenter did not build that house out of humors, but out of bodies. And what does this teach you? In the same way, the Stonemason does not erect a house from humors, but from stones, and he handles pure bodies with his hands. Bodies, not humors, make things. Just as rust is never in a stone, nor decay in iron, so in this case you can never rightly speak of Humors.

<margin>Use of Hydromancy.</margin>
All these things certainly testify to the error in the understanding of gout when it is admitted without the consideration of such bodies. Therefore, in this place, the "hydromantic stars" <note>The internal forces governing the water element within the human body.</note> indicate that all their bodies—which, as is evident, are manifold—serve as a prefiguration, showing that similar bodies exist in the human body and possess a gouty nature. <margin>The body of water is iron, etc.</margin> This you will understand more clearly from the following example. You see, of course, that the "body" of water can be iron, stone, metal, salt, vitriol, alum, and so on—all of which I include under the name of minerals. These bodies "fall" <note>Precipitate or manifest physically.</note> according to the manner and reason of their disposition and anatomical order. The same thing happens in the same way in the number of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," meaning the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>. And just as these minerals are distributed into <term>Ylech</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the primordial, raw matter of the world or the basic building blocks of physical substance.</note> by falling, so also does Gout "fall." Here, pay attention to the arrangement of salts. For in this place, the body will be made of salts, which is the matter and essence of gouty diseases. Therefore, judge the species of diseases and bodies according to the species of the salts. <margin>Gout is a saline body. Differences in what gout is composed of.</margin> For the disease of gout is nothing other than a body of salts. And as salts are divided into their types, so also the types and species of gout are distributed. The pain of salt is one thing, that of alum another, that of saltpeter another, that of vitriol another, and so on.

## ARRANGEMENT

<margin>The body of salts is Gout; salts are the glue.</margin>
Thus, it remains to speak next of the fabrication, which is Mechanical. This will be done through the treatment of the "arrangement" (disposition). Under this arrangement, the "signs" (symptoms) are also included. For the description of the species is the description of the signs. The matter is to be set down thus: What is the body of gout other than a body of salts? What else is it than glue, than <term>synovia</term> <note>The lubricating fluid found in the joints.</note>? Gout lies only where that "glue" flourishes, and not outside of it. What happens outside of this is not gout, but an accident of it. Now, these salts are the glue. Here is the salt of fountains; there, congealed salt; elsewhere, the salt of alum, the salt of vitriol, the salt of saltpeter, and whatever other types there are. <margin>The diversity of salt is the cause of diverse gout. What is the cause of gouty pain?</margin> The pain is different in the salt of the fountain than in the salt of saltpeter, different in alum, and so forth. And who could describe these signs? Surely only the Naturalist, through the evidence of experience. Physicians should not have considered so lazily and listlessly what it is, exactly, that can stir up such atrocious and exquisite pains. For it is certain that neither choler nor phlegm <note>Again, rejecting the traditional humors.</note> can move those pains. Therefore, something else entirely must be the cause. They could easily penetrate to the knowledge and understanding of this, if only they would take enough leisure and time for themselves. But they stumble immediately at the principles, to say nothing of the middle and the end. Therefore, the reason for the pain is far different than what they claim. Truly, here is "saltiness," and nowhere else; here is "vitriol-ness," and nowhere else. <margin>Man is a Microcosm endowed with senses. Minerals are sensible.</margin> The same happens in man. For man is a Microcosm, endowed with sense. It is necessary, therefore, that he feels what is within him. Furthermore, all minerals are "sensible" <note>Meaning they can be perceived or felt by the senses because of their sharp, active nature.</note>, and none is insensible; every sensitivity—good, bad, etc.—is mineral in nature, and the mineral causes it. <margin>
What stirs up Gouty pains.

Regarding the stirring up and the sensation of diseases, what shall I say? It must be known that **Gout** <note>Original: "Podagra."</note> does not have its own manufacturing process in the same way that grass of the field does; for the matter itself remains at rest, in the manner taught by <term>Hydromancy</term> <note>While usually meaning divination by water, here it refers to the specialized study of elemental fluids and their hidden properties.</note>. For unless it is sought out, it is not present. If it is sought, it is found. In the same way, metal provides no use unless it is worked. A salt-pit gives no salt unless it is boiled down. The same must be understood regarding Gout. For if it were planted with "hydromantic" subtlety, none would be found. Indeed, this "planting" consists only in this: that it be sought, that it be built up, and that it be led to that state to which it must be led. Now, this is achieved solely through discovery, through the <term>Anatomy</term> <note>In this context, "Anatomy" refers not just to dissection, but to the chemical and spiritual breakdown of a substance into its fundamental parts.</note> of other bodies and the Elements themselves: just as salts lie in fire, and also in the Air, and even in the Earth. To understand this, consider the example of the Anatomy of wine. Wine contains within itself an **Astral Anatomy of salts**, and salt is that which is called "saline" here in the Element of water. Not only in wine, however, but also in the disposition of animals, the Saline quality lies hidden. And one is the discoverer of the other. For who knows how to find gold better than a metalworker? And why is this? Even if he himself is not gold, he is nonetheless the master of gold; he possesses knowledge of it and knows its nature and property. Therefore, it suits and fits him. For Man, in his thoughts, is similar to all creatures, according to the nature of his arts. A single Art in man is the matter of which that art treats—not indeed materially or visibly—and yet the condition of the one is the same as the other. Now, if a miner, skilled in this matter, seeks gold and finds it, he then prepares, separates, and refines it, and so on. In the same way, the bodies of diseases wish to be sought out by their own bodies.

<margin>
Anatomy of wine? etc.
Saline salt, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
Man is all things according to his arts.

<margin>
Wine brings forth hidden Gout.

Thus the Anatomy of wine and the Anatomy of food from animals (in which the fountain of salts lies) seeks the fountain of salts in its own body, the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>. This is not because wine *is* gout, but because gout already lies hidden in the man, like metal in a mountain; wine acts as a "second mechanic," searching it out and separating it from the "glue," just as a miner extracts metal from a mountain. And just as the metal is not manifest in the mountain, so too Gout is not manifest until it is pushed all the way out. This is done by the "discoverers" in wine, and in similar animals, fish, and meats. If you understand this discovery correctly, then you will fully know the cause and origin not only of this disease, but of all others. For the cause is not always to be assigned to food and drink in all diseases, as if the body or matter were drawn from them; rather, understand that these things are "discoverers," and consider for yourselves, guided by Philosophy, that the Microcosm continually carries his own minerals within himself.

Discoveries of foods.

Foods etc. Discoveries.

[Nature's art] is twofold: one which she places in reason, so that she may work and labor through the industry of the senses and of art. The other is that which she administers herself, and human skill does not abandon it. Thus she works herbs, trees, and iron. Nature therefore works in a **twofold light**, which is nonetheless a single light. One part she completes herself, placing the matter under our hands. For that matter to become what it ought to be, and what it was destined for by nature, requires the light of the Microcosm, which is used by the one who further treats and perfects it. According to this rule, understand that Nature maintains this same custom in diseases; that is, she herself does this in opposition to the "Mechanical craftsman," namely the Physician, who must heal her again. This physician is compared to a Reaper or a Cutter who mows the grass of the meadows. For what nature has produced, he harvests. A Physician, therefore, must be such a "Reaper of diseases." For they grow in the body in the same way as grass in the fields. And what the scythe is in the hand of the reaper, Medicine must be in the hand of the Physician. Since only this one thing remains to be said concerning the "Discoverer"—namely, how the gout in wine and animals finds the gout in man—we shall proceed to describe it next. Therefore, if wine (which is "gout") descends into the body where the mineral of gout lies, it then finds it. For just as one who seeks metal finds it, so here also, by nature, one finds the other. **Like finds its like.** Thus wine is the seeker. If it reaches the body in which gout lies, it then drags it out and puts it into the "furnace"—that is, it brings it into its own operation. And by the same method that metals are usually prepared, wine also prepares and treats its own mineral. Nor does wine do this alone, but also animals of the same nature.

The Physician as a Mechanical craftsman, the reaper, and medicine as the scythe.
</margin>

<margin>
The industry of Gout: Are Wine and foods Gout?
</margin>

<margin>
Wine as the seeker of Gout.
</margin>

No one, even the skeptical, should wonder at this seeking, finding, and separation of these things. For just as you see red things produced from black, black from red, black from white, and white from black, you ought to understand "Mechanical Nature" in the same sense. For what are colors in man or other things but the production of hidden bodies that were obliterated within them? Where bodies of this kind are hidden, there also other diseases lie. And just as nature works in those colors, so too in diseases, the matter is conducted invisibly in both cases. For who will deny this "discovery" if someone, through nature, produces whiteness and then redness from lead? A man does not do this himself. For he can neither give nor take away colors unless nature consents and helps. When she consents, he has the colors ready, not through his own power, but by the power of nature alone, which manifests the hidden and occult bodies there. Just as she is the "discoverer," so it is manifest through the **Light of Nature** <note>Original: "lumen naturae."</note> that man also...

<margin>
What are colors?
</margin>

<margin>
Man neither gives nor takes away colors without nature.
</margin>

---

## THE JOINING.

<margin>
The twofold art of the light of nature.
</margin>

**N**ow, furthermore, learn how that discovery proceeds. For as you see industrious and skillful craftsmen discover their trades and complete their works, all of this must flow from the Light of Nature itself. Now, Art is nothing but the **Light of Nature**; therefore...

<summary>Paracelsus explains that gout exists as a latent "mineral" within the human body and is only triggered or "discovered" by specific external substances like wine or meat, which act like a miner seeking gold. He defines the physician's role as a "reaper" who harvests the disease that nature has grown, operating through the divine "Light of Nature."</summary>

<header>ON GOUTY PATIENTS.</header>

<margin>
Example:
litharge,
lead-white,
etc.
</margin>
Even through nature, one finds the same thing within nature. Thus, one also seeks out diseases that are hidden in themselves. As for food and drink, consider that there is no other art for finding gout than if you were to place lead into a fire and produce from it <term>litharge</term> <note>Original: "molybditem." A lead oxide used in pigments and medicine.</note>, <term>ceruse</term> <note>Original: "cerussam." White lead, used as a pigment.</note>, or <term>minium</term> <note>Red lead.</note>; or from silver, produce <term>lazurium</term> <note>A blue pigment, here likely referring to a chemical derivative of silver.</note>. You do not eat these things. For they belong to the walls <note>i.e., they are painters' pigments for decorating buildings.</note>, not to the body. However, those things—food and drink—belong to the body. If you offer these to nature through your art, then nature takes them up and delivers them where they ought to go. If you thrust these into the stomach, it is no different an art than if you were to cast <term>Antimony</term> into a fire. Once that is done, nature begins to labor and work within it, seeking for as long as it takes until it has extracted its "redness." Such is nature’s search. By the same mechanism, the diseases themselves are sought out.

## THE MATTER.

<margin>
The types
of salts are
the species
of gout.
Notes of
Theophrastus.
</margin>
In order that you may finally and completely understand the matter of both this "discoverer" and the discovery itself, along with its process and order: it must be established that in this context, salt alone breeds diseases. Just as the various types of salts exist, so the species of gout arise according to their specific nature. If, therefore, you desire to know the signs, the symptoms, and other related things, then take them from the nature and properties of salts, of which these are my notes: 16 salts of springs; 5 salts of mountains; and furthermore the types from the sea, according to how each region is constituted in its fluids. Moreover, there are types from stone, of which there are 8; 5 types from rivers; 4 types of <term>plumose</term> salt <note>Original: "plumosi." Likely refers to feather-alum or asbestos-like mineral formations.</note>; 2 types of borax; 43 types of vitriol; and 46 types of <term>natural lime</term> <note>Original: "calcis natae."</note>. I remain silent on those which are not known to me. Nor would I speak against my adversaries if they were to establish many more species of salt based on the division of climates and altitude, from Cosmographic, Astronomic, and Physical considerations. But what I skip over here will be more fully and fundamentally investigated and enumerated in the *Archidoxes* <note>One of Paracelsus’s major works on the fundamental "mysteries" of nature and alchemy.</note>.

<margin>
The cure of
gout regards
only the
general types.
</margin>
Keep this at least in mind: that having considered all these things, there is very little need for more. For the cure itself regards only the general types, and there is no need to be attentive to every single species. Therefore, do not let this heavy matter distress you further, except insofar as you indulge in Philosophy, Astronomy, and Cosmography for the sake of your mind. Such things do indeed adorn a Physician. But you should study rather to serve the sick themselves. For they have no care for these minutiae. Now, what has been said so far is sufficient for any Physician for the recognition of the gouty disease. But if it seems to you that this <term>Theory</term> <note>Here used in the classical sense of "way of seeing" or foundational knowledge.</note> is too narrow: I ask that you act to understand it rightly; there will be no defect in it. Truly recognize and learn also the things that follow. For thus you explain one thing through another. It will be a hard and difficult province for you if you are not well-versed and understanding in these matters. For outside of this knowledge, a defect will appear in everything. For the entire foundation flows from Philosophy, Astronomy, and the other arts born from them. Finally, attend also to the <term>Practice</term>, which is established according to the nature of "inventive medicine," not according to the whim and opinion of ancient writers, but according to the standard of the 64 primary parts from which Medicine arises. Therefore, bestow your most natural and most constant diligence and faith. Thus the matter demands.

## THE CURE.

<margin>
Only the
Saints perform
miracles.
</margin>
I shall not be safe from calumnies, I know, because I separate myself as if by a divorce from the customary care of Physicians, especially and most of all regarding gout. Yet how can I not repudiate such ridiculous cures, which they have conducted with such disgrace until now? Or how, I ask, can I imitate them, when it has even passed into a proverb among the peasants that "only the Saints work signs"? For outside of these, who will believe them? They will certainly persuade me if they perform miracles. Otherwise, they lose all their effort on me. Nevertheless, what was begun long ago, they will turn their venomous masks toward me just as vigorously. For this will not be the first writing to cause them offense. For they have long and hatefully vomited this out: that I am completely unrefined and ignorant in <term>Physics</term> <note>In the 16th century, "Physics" referred to internal medicine and the study of natural causes, not just the motion of matter.</note>, but that I excel as a "Rabbi" in surgery—not that they seriously bestow this praise on me, but so that they may exclude me from the entire order of Physicians through contempt and insult. And regarding Physics, what can they object? Since I myself am the one teaching it to them; and they even learn from me, not I from them?

<margin>
Theophrastus
is called unrefined
in Physics;
a Rabbi in
surgery.
</margin>
<margin>
Medicine
is twofold.
</margin>
What then is the cause for them to repudiate me so hatefully in Physics? This alone, surely: that they neither know Medicine themselves, nor have they learned its distribution. For Medicine is twofold: Physical and Surgical. <term>Physics</term> teaches the knowledge of all diseases; <term>Surgery</term> teaches the treatment of the same. This is the twin division of Medicine. But they, by a plain and manifest error, make a division into Medicine (or care of the body) and the care of wounds. But no mention was ever made of "wound-medicine," but only of Surgery, which is practice itself.

<margin>
The bad
division of
medicine:
and why?
</margin>
Answer me truly: What "wound-medicine" is there, after all, that does not require a Physician <note>Original: "Physicum."</note> for its disease? Or what Physics is there that ought not be healed by a Surgeon? Thus you betray yourselves as being such doctors who do not even know at this very moment what a Physician is or in what he consists. Physics is nothing else than the knowledge of all diseases, of whatever kind they may be. Nor is Surgery anything else than the treatment of all diseases. For just as a woodworker completes his work with his hands, so does the Physician. Dare something, and try or perform it without hands! Your blindness, therefore, is in the open, because you do not know what kind of "Doctor" you actually are.

<margin>
What is Physics?
What is Surgery?
</margin>
But look at how excellently you go about in those diseases which you call "surgical," such as <term>Erysipelas</term> <note>A bacterial skin infection.</note>, <term>Gangrene</term>, <term>Esthiomenos</term> <note>A "gnawing" or corrosive ulcer.</note>, etc. You treat these from practice, that is...

<summary>Paracelsus defines gout as a disease of salts, listing numerous mineral types as its cause, and transitions into a fiery defense of his medical philosophy, arguing that "Physics" (theory) and "Surgery" (practice) are inseparable halves of a single art.</summary>

->### FRAGMENT OF THE THIRD BOOK.<-
<meta>catchword: More (from Latin "Plura")</meta>

is from surgery. But if you are not at the same time a Physician of nature, what will you know or heal in this case? Nothing. Furthermore, if you are compelled to take the science and foundation for curing all wounds from Physics <note>In this context, "Physics" refers to the study of natural philosophy and the internal workings of nature, not just modern physics.</note>, how, I ask, would you dare to establish another faculty and profession out of it? Away with those wooden Doctors and fools! The name proceeds from the first and principal, not from the last. <margin>What Physics and surgery properly are.</margin> Therefore, it must be called Physics, which discerns the causes of diseases; and it must be called Surgery, which engineers the practical application. For in diagnosing you are a Physician, and in curing you are a surgeon.

So also, from the explained Theory, by good right I approach the practice, which is surgery. For the patient requires Surgery, not Physics. However, the Physician himself seeks Physics. This is the same as if I were to say: No surgeon exists without the Physician; for the former is born from the latter: and the surgeon proves the Physician. For the Physician has no other proof by which he can be known and judged in his works. For unless he is a surgeon at the same time, he will stand by the patient like a statue or a **painted monkey**.

And although I lead the cure to its conclusion, so that they might think I am uniquely a surgeon here because I propose an outcome and lead toward it—for so Theory teaches, so Anatomy, so Manual skill, and so the <term>Confluence</term> <note>Original: "Confluentia." Likely referring to the coming together of different medical signs or methods.</note>—nevertheless, note this brief answer to this objection: no significant or physical disease of the body can be healed without Surgery, but it must be entirely reduced (as they say) into "wound-medicine." And because surgery falls into the category of wound-medicine, they think the surgeon is inferior and less noble than a "Noisy Doctor of Leipzig." But if you knew yourselves "under the skin" <note>An idiom meaning to know one's true nature or internal anatomy.</note>, I do not doubt that you would be ready to bite off your own noses.

Is wound-medicine then another profession simply because the cure is instituted through an opening? Oh, fanatics! What have you finally learned, or what have your "Beany" <note>Original: "Beani." A derogatory term for fresh university students or novices, from "bejaunus" (yellow-beak).</note> accounts and polished manners taught you, that you have not even explored what Medicine is? Note this, and revolve it in a lively heart: unless an "exit" is made in astral diseases, you will certainly never heal any patient. And here, divide the star and the body, the heaven and the matter: here make medicine double, and omit the other. Yet make two surgeries, not two wound-medicines. For we ought not to be "wound-healers," but surgeons. Is it not indeed a disgrace and an infamy that so many and such illustrious Academies, both of Italy and <margin>Reproof of Medicine and the Academies.</margin> Germany, nourish so many asses and "arch-beanies"?

Note this as a finishing touch. Whoever attempts to cure gout <note>Original: "podagram."</note>, it is necessary for him to proceed by operating according to the rule of <term>Microcosmic Anatomy</term> <note>The study of the human body as a reflection of the entire universe (the Microcosm).</note>. If this must be done, certainly surgery is required in many ways: in wounds, in burning, in eating away, in cauterizing, in purging, in diminishing, etc. Who, indeed, because of this, would tear this manual practice into several different faculties, so that one is more excellent than another, one to be preferred, and the other rejected as useless and filthy? It is enough that the manual practice is so instituted that the patient recovers from the disease and is healed.

Meanwhile, I do not patronize those impostors who know and are skilled in nothing but liniments, ointments, fumigations, woods, etc.; but I rather defend the cause of those who have known the diseases themselves according to the prescription of Anatomy and the Microcosm, of nature and the instruction of the external world, so that they can shape their practice according to the requirement of the matter. For such knowledge should be neither a disgrace, nor an impediment, nor a harm to the Physician, but rather his highest praise: that he has acquired such great science in the Microcosm and both spheres of Philosophy and Astronomy. Meanwhile, you "calfish" Doctors, when you burst out of the Academies, you immediately reject and annihilate such mysteries and sublime secrets: and yet, when you are about to produce the truth itself, you trumpet nothing but mere trifles and fictions, which are a disgrace to you and an unatonable loss to others.

Furthermore, attend to the cure. You may call this whatever you like. For the matter will not be decided by your calumny. For he whose infamy has ripened finally betrays and shakes himself. For everyone’s testimony is about himself; that is, the man himself testifies what he is like inside. But you, who side with the unconquered truth, attend to the practice itself, and do not despise my process for being drawn out too long, or my method for being introduced through (as it will seem) pathless ways. And let that persuasion be far exiled from your minds, as if I were the kind of man who tires himself out by striving for something new <margin>What Theophrastus instituted.</margin> and foreign. For I have never conceived this plan in my mind: but by a sober institution, I have always meditated and striven for this: by what means I might instruct you most solidly of all, and by producing true practice, most promptly extricate both myself and you from the traps set before us. Recognize and understand what the cause is for judging either side: and act as fair and sincere judges.

### II.

**I**n the description of the cure, note: as many species of diseases as there are, so many are the practices and peculiar cures. Therefore, no single or unique process is to be held: but just as he who, having grasped a cloak with his hands, adjusts and extends it according to the rushing of the wind, so also medicine ought to be placed in the hand of the Physician. Since, therefore, Medicine is placed in the hands of the Physician with such great judgment, who will make only a single practice from it? Who will force it into one chapter? No one, indeed. Much less will it be included in the "four humors" <note>The traditional Galenic theory that health is governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile. Paracelsus famously rejected this.</note>, as those things lack every foundation of knowledge. Therefore, that should not be understood only concerning gout, but also concerning all primary diseases—that is, the vehement and fierce ones. The division of practice, therefore, is to be taken from Theory, and from all those things of which I have spoken. But the practice I institute, I will explain not in the manner of a "wound-healer," but as a Physician, worthy of you. For the "divided Physicians"—that is, the sects of Physicians—exist as the overfowers of Medicine. For here this man knows one thing, that man another: and yet all this knowledge is of no value. For he who holds only one small part holds nothing, nor does he know what he holds. etc.

He critiques the academic establishment and the four humors theory, insisting that medicine must be adapted to each specific disease like a cloak to the wind.</summary>

## TWO OTHER BOOKS ON GOUTY DISEASES FOLLOW.

*However, the second book (under the title, "Second Book: Common Interpretation of Diseases, etc.") was not found among those following here; this was the fate of several other books as well, which were scattered to different places and did not remain joined together. And although the author himself does not note in the title that it is the "Second Book on Gout," his own words clearly testify that it is one of the books on Gout, as when he says shortly before the end of the chapter on <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The study of external appearances (of people or minerals) to determine their internal nature or health.</note>: "As much as is needed for the recognition of Gout, so much do I propose, etc." It is equally clear from the end of the first book and the beginning of the second that they are to be joined. I indicate this here for the reason that there are those who thought the second book belonged to the <term>Paramirum</term> <note>The *Opus Paramirum* is one of Paracelsus's major works detailing his theory of the five causes of disease.</note>, etc.*

# ON GOUTY
### DISEASES AND THEIR KINDRED:
### BY THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM,
### Doctor of both Medicines.

## DOCTOR THEOPHRASTUS.
->*To the Reader.*<-

*Undoubtedly, many will ask what this stubbornness and rashness of my mind might be, that I should undertake to assert and defend those things in which all Physicians everywhere oppose me, and contradict my conceived opinion out of the deep zeal of my soul. At their request: I deem that such a response must be put forward. If my heart toward the sick were not more upright and benevolent, adding a spur to these matters, than I have found the hearts of my adversaries to be inclined toward me, I could certainly withdraw myself from this burden as easily as possible.*

<margin>Avicenna and Galen are criticized.</margin>
*But now, since I cannot undergo the yoke of <note>original: "nugarum Auicennicarum"</note> Avicennic trifles and agree with the empty fictions of Galen without evident disgrace—as they are men who never undertook the care of the sick from their innermost heart—I have thought it altogether necessary to be bold, so that I might withdraw myself from their sterile Theory as well as Practice, and turn aside to those inner sanctuaries from which it is necessary for every solid Physician to be born and proceed. In the meantime, I can in no way skip over in silence the "Iliad of evils" <note>A classical reference to a great or endless series of troubles.</note> which they have brought into the art and faculty until now. But all the power and virtue, which we know to be deeply enclosed by nature herself within remedies, they have allowed to fail and be obliterated through their own negligence. For they have not only miserably defrauded themselves with their dreams until now, but they have propagated the crop of their opinions with great interest unto all posterity.*

<margin>Old things are not immediately to be accepted as best.</margin>
*Whence it has happened that in this age, such obstinate patronage is bestowed everywhere by all upon that bad custom, that they immediately think an enormous crime is committed if anyone should move or attempt anything against those "ancient lights." Meanwhile, they do not consider in their own minds that a donkey indeed walks perpetually in its ancestral and ancient gait, but a more noble horse outstrips it by many <term>parasangs</term> <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, about 3-4 miles; used here to mean "by a great distance."</note>; and yet the horse receives applause, while the donkey receives blows from its master. Should it truly not be lawful for me to write against lying medicine, and to oppose true doctrine to deceitful and disguised custom? This doctrine is drawn from the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>A central Paracelsian concept: the innate wisdom and divine intelligence found within the natural world.</note> itself, and established through the stars, through the Philosophy of both sciences—of heaven and earth—with the concordance of the four Elements themselves supporting all these things. For in this, my whole refuge is placed: that I extend my Theory wider and deeper than theirs. For even those who are otherwise rude and unskilled in the stars, in the sea, and in practice, are nevertheless superior if they take their practice from Theory. But what is it, finally, that could terrify and move me to make a departure from <term>Mechanical Anatomy</term> <note>Paracelsus distinguishes between the mere cutting of corpses and the "mechanical" or "vital" understanding of how nature's structures function.</note>? Or how much is that of which they themselves swell up so much and boast: namely, that they act in the courts of princes and kings? That they associate with the counselors of Metropolitan cities? That they cling to the bosoms and eyes of those whom I, for my part, judge not even worthy of a passing greeting? But what sort of prevarication is it, finally, that you princes, and you consuls and governors of provinces, thrust both your own bodies and the health of your subjects into such a foul prison, and command that a rash custom be held as art on account of its antiquity, as if by a promulgated edict? But what do we have or receive that is more "ancient" than the ancients, other than this: that everything we eat, we discharge through the bowels? And what does this ancient thing, after all, do for or regard the Internal Light? Would it not be more just for these judges to twist their eyes toward the twelve hours of the day and learn from there, so that they might not be anxious about tomorrow? And this demonstrates that what I touch upon here does not proceed from nature—that is, not from the light of the belly—that I should capture tithes, which until now*

<header>PREFACE.</header>

## PREFACE.

This has been done by others who have abandoned that which gives birth to art. But who could say that God is merciful, and that He has placed His own foundation in mercy, if they did not likewise believe that all necessary things can be supplied and restored by God—in diseases, in leprosy, and in the raising of the dead from death to a long and vigorous life through His mercy? Here, then, I once again urge you, O Judges and Presidents, and I ask: what spirit or reason do you have for allowing this excellent art to be oppressed by disorderly custom, and for so readily turning a blind eye to those errors? Even the simplest person can notice and see them: that the confusion of Medicine, to its certain injury, is preferred far above its solid foundation. Yet you nevertheless constantly hold to and chew upon this old rule of yours: <margin>The power of flattery or <term>Self-love</term><note>Original: *Philautia*. A Greek-derived term frequently used in the Renaissance to describe excessive self-regard or narcissistic pride in one's own opinions.</note>.</margin> *our little daughter, whatever she has done, is well done.* Is it truly so? If everything your daughter does is done well without distinction, then come, let this also be "well done" if she were to expose herself as a prostitute in a Venetian brothel. Will no one finally consider seriously within themselves with how much <term>total ruin</term><note>Original: *pantelethria*. A Greek term for utter destruction or annihilation.</note> all of Europe has been contaminated until now by the frauds of Physicians? That sects break out everywhere, each conceiving a new and monstrous opinion and gripping it with its teeth? For who can count them all? Since fanatical spirits have flown out from every side as if from <term>Lerna</term><note>A reference to the Lernaean Hydra's swamp; metaphorically, a source of many spreading evils.</note>, and have rushed upon men in crowds, so that anyone is now free to openly vomit out his own insanity. Meanwhile, how can these wandering spirits be countered when those whose interest it is do not reflect on it even in their dreams? Even those who, being devoted to honesty themselves, conceive and cherish the same hope for others, remain silent. But to what end is this persuasion of honesty? To what end is this tolerance? Rather, you see the confidence and the desperation of so many transgressors who all compete to burst forth as Physicians. But what and of what kind will this art finally be? For if you look down upon the state of all these <term>Hypocrites</term><note>Here used in the older sense of "stage-players" or those who put on a false front of medical knowledge.</note>, you will certainly grasp a number far more abundant than either I or my successors and descendants would wish to hope for or tolerate. Yet I would not even take this indignity to heart, since they could all easily be conquered and overtaken if only we were both weighed in a fair balance, and each given their true value and price by the weights. But until I see that happen—so long as opinions and phantasms are preferred to the light of Nature itself—I can predict with no effort what atrocious schisms are about to slide into Medicine in the coming century.

Who makes you so hopeless in faith, when faith itself solidly and simply encompasses the perfection of God? If He denies us no protection, but brings the fullest aid and help everywhere in infinite ways, why do you not place your trust in this? For what else is the help of Medicine but charity itself? But it is not from man; rather, it is from God. And will you not place your hope and trust in this charity? If so, what else is your faith but an imperfect thing?

I beg you, O judges and princes, finally revolve this matter more deeply within yourselves. For you were not commanded merely to see that the thief who cut a purse yesterday is sent to the cross by you today; but he must be judged entirely worthy of the same punishment who has committed theft through deceit and fraud in any manner whatsoever. Before the avenging sword, the guilt is one and the same: a limb for a limb, for a body, a body. Or is that not a sword which cuts the throat and strips a man of his life? Although it may not be made of iron, and may not be polished, no fewer homicides are perpetrated by it than by iron itself. But why do do I recount these things to you in vain, which are nevertheless notorious and manifest to everyone? Or why is it that you are warned so greatly by those whom I—in all my writings—cry out and proclaim are spreading film and <term>cataracts</term><note>Original: *glaucoma*. Used metaphorically here for something that blinds the judgment or obscures the truth.</note> over your eyes? It is certainly a great realization to see from a mirror what it is that the mirror displays: that is, the splendor that shines out from a man is not that which is hidden within a man. But why and to what end do I extend these points, when I know they will be accepted by no one? Yet I have a most certain hope that those whom you call my followers will drive fixed roots into this foundation; and that their sons, together with the children of princes, will give rise to and bring forth other princes and Doctors who will collect the ancient volumes together with these of ours that fight against us, and with a vengeful spirit will consecrate them all to <term>Vulcan</term><note>The god of fire; the author is predicting that future generations will burn the old, ineffective medical textbooks.</note>. For what <term>North Wind</term><note>Original: *Boreas*. The cold, harsh wind.</note> has ever blown to which the <term>Southeast Wind</term><note>Original: *Vulturnus*. A warmer, more pleasant wind.</note> did not eventually bring a grateful and pleasant splendor? Why do I stir these things up? I wish that those who live under the North Wind would receive this Southeast Wind. But they must wait for a kinder time.

Recognize, fair Reader, whether I do not have enough cause to write irritably. For what I have recounted so far does not pertain only to that disease which I have proposed to describe here, but the business concerns the entire profession itself. Meanwhile, however, let each disease be assigned its own chapter and its own place. Here I have resolved to treat Gout. For there exist four principal diseases—three, that is, besides the Gout to be treated. If I explain these to you, I fully trust that you will approach any sickbeds with a brisk and unshaken spirit.

But let it not be a stumbling block to you, Reader, that I posit Gout to be curable, even though my adversaries deny it. Do not despair of me, even if I seek no remedies from their books. And do not turn away from me because they object that I have been hauled off to prison three times, that I have fought many wars, and that I have severely beaten many people, etc. For no blow was poorly placed by me, except that which did not penetrate the skin. But they ought by no means to be indignant on account of the beatings I gave, provided that the purpose of inflicting them could have been achieved among them. In this way, all things would have been turned to good by God.

You, Reader, accept what I propose to you here, and revolve in your mind what I have warned in the preface. Thus it will happen that by reading these things you may learn what can be of use to both yourself and others.

Moreover, adapt this treatise to a threefold objection. First, that I am unfit to hand down Medicine. I leave this for you to judge. Second, that I ought to attempt nothing new, and should acquiesce to the old doctrine. I entrust this also to your judgment. Third, that "two know more than one." You should evaluate this too, and think to yourself which "two" they mean, or which "one" they understand. With these things I end the preface, having certain hope that God, the Best and Greatest, will grant to both me and you the desired end.

### NARRATIVE OF THE BOOK.

**W**hen about to treat <term>Podagra</term><note>While modern readers know "podagra" as gout of the big toe, in this period it was often used as a general term for any agonizing joint or bone pain throughout the body.</note>, it is necessary above all else to declare at the outset what will subsequently be taught. Regarding the pains of diseases and their signs or indications, however, nothing can be taught through words alone. For the assault of the disease, along with its concurrent signs and their nature and habits, ought not to be entrusted to "silent letters" in such a way that you might think you could be sufficiently satisfied by them. These matters are situated in manifold experience and the practical exercise required of every Physician. Yet, for a brief comprehension of what is to be said, it is necessary that you hold a full and sufficient knowledge of the locations of this disease.

### THE LOCATIONS OF PODAGRA.

<margin>The locations of Podagra.</margin>

**T**hese are the locations of the head: if the "milky line" <note>Original: *linea lactea*. Likely referring to the cranial sutures or specific anatomical markings on the skull.</note> creeps through the cranium, of whatever sort, manner, or figure it may be, it is entirely subject to Podagra. Likewise, wherever a composition of the cranium occurs, or where the joints of the bones are committed like bitumen through interposed cartilage; or where other parts grow onto the cranium, such as the nose, chin, neck, and the like: also the locations of the eye, ears, and teeth—all these provide a seat and place for Podagra.

Furthermore, from the neck through the spine of the back down to the anus, wherever there is a vertebra or a joint, there is a seat of Podagra. So too in the shoulders, wherever bone is joined to bone. Similarly in the ribs where they are fixed to the back and meet in the thorax from the collarbone down to the diaphragm; as also in all bones in which marrow is contained. So too in the hip-joint: wherever a joint, a seam, or a passage is seen, a retreat for Podagra is granted in that same place. Likewise in that union of joints where the thigh bone is inserted into the <term>sacrum</term><note>The triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>, and where the bones of the private parts are united by interposed cartilage, in both men and women. No less in the kneecap and all the hollows of the knees, and in that region where the leg is joined to the bottom of the foot, near the ankles and other neighboring spongy locations.

The same logic applies to the joints of the shoulders and the arm, and of the elbow and the radius, where they are united by interposed cartilage; no less where the arm is joined to the hand, near the knot of the wrist and the prominent bulge visible at the roots of the fingers.

Moreover, in all locations of the hands and feet: in which there are as many seats of Podagra as there are scales or seams, which run between the roots of the fingers all the way to the nails; and this is true in both hands and feet.

But there are also certain hidden locations of Podagra inside the body, namely as far as the bladder or the <term>Ramax</term><note>Original: *Ramax*. A term for a hernia or the inguinal region involving ligaments.</note> with its ligaments encompasses. For here, there are as many seats of Podagra as there are insertions of the ribs.

Although other locations of Podagra are also numbered, such as in the heel, the calf, and other similar parts, these are not properly the locations of this disease; rather, it is only an obstruction of the passage that moves those parts.

However, so that you may more clearly understand what I am treating, I will set before you certain signs and examples from which you may be able to judge the rest. Let the species of pneumonia be an example to you, as well as <term>rheuma</term><note>Rheumatism or "flowing" pains.</note>, which usually occupies the shoulder blades and shoulders and does not pass without diarrhea. Similarly, if pains of the ears, teeth, and eyes concur, these are signs of beginning Podagra; as are tumors of the joints, joined and packed with many <term>pollutions</term><note>Original: *pollutionibus*. In this context, likely referring to morbid discharges or accumulations of "waste" fluids in the body.</note>.

Present Podagra is also known by these signs. Its pain depends on the power of the sky and moves according to the condition of the seasons and the Moon. It is also stirred up by drink, by food, by sexual exercise, and by "martial anger" <note>Original: *ira Martiali*. A reference to a fierce, aggressive, or choleric temperament, often associated with the planet Mars.</note>. For from these things, paroxysms are almost always induced, as they are from other things that inflame this disease from the outside. In this way, once the location of Podagra is established and confirmed, it afterwards turns into "Geometry," and it varies or changes the line of proportion so that the joints are disjointed and pulled apart; this dislocation moves the pains in no other way than if the limbs were being stretched by a rack <note>Original: *fidicula*. An instrument of torture involving cords or strings; the author compares the physical deformity of gout to being stretched on a rack.</note>. The inflowing matter occupies the middle space and is there coagulated and granulated like hail, and is altered in various ways: the mysteries of which mutation ought to be well known to the Physician. For who could sufficiently hand down in writing the nature and manner of raging Podagra in pulling apart and tearing away the joints?

But let these things now suffice for the narrative. With this, I do not at all finish the book itself, but I prepare the way for what is to be said next, which certainly pertains to the cause, generation, and nature of this disease. You, however, will hardly accept my manner of writing. Yet the very logic and nature of explaining the disease demands it. Nor should this be a source of wonder to you, why I do not immediately approach the cause and cure of this disease. For it is fitting that the <term>Matrix of Medicine</term><note>The fundamental womb or source from which medical knowledge is born.</note> be spoken of first of all, so that it may be known from what principles this treatment flows. I hope, moreover, that this my doctrine will find a place among you all the more readily because it is built and fixed upon a more certain and stable foundation.

### On the Origin of the Art.

<margin>The Light of Nature alone gives birth to the Physician.</margin>

**S**ince various spirits here and there write and comment on various things: you ought to know above all else that their doctrine does not flow from a foundation and true principles, but that truth must be dug out from a far different kind of knowledge. For what, I ask, has a man ever received from his father and mother from which he could describe even the smallest disease of the human body? Or what teacher is found anywhere who can make a Physician out of you or me? For even if he indeed has experience in many things, what, finally, does that contribute to either my or your benefit? For in that man operates the <term>Light</term><note>Original: *Lumen Naturae* (Light of Nature). A central concept in Paracelsian medicine suggesting that true knowledge of nature is an inner illumination or a divine gift that allows the physician to "read" the world.</note>, which he cannot thrust or pour into me or you. For they did not draw these things from schools or instruction. Unless the Light of Nature itself forms and fashions the Physician, fragments certainly collected from here and there will render nothing but a pure and simple "experimenter" <note>A term often used disparagingly for those who rely on trial and error without understanding the underlying spiritual or natural principles.</note>, who will never be useful to Medicine. Since, therefore, without such gifts a man cannot shine or excel even in other professions—as one who has nothing from himself but is forced to draw everything from an external teacher—it is especially fitting for anyone to know from what foundation each person writes...

<sig>Iii 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: So</meta>

... [so that he may] teach, lest by any chance the reader be driven headlong into errors, or—what is more—so that the reader may hold and attain the same sense and the same principle as the Author.

<margin>Disciples are not above their Master.</margin>
For as long as a disciple has not achieved such progress that he transcends from his Natural teacher to the supernatural, he is not yet to be thought to have touched the true foundation. For as you remember it is handed down in Scripture, "the disciple is not above his master, but it is enough for him to be equal to him" <note>A reference to Matthew 10:24-25.</note>: in its genuine sense, this must be applied entirely to the invisible Master—namely, that visible teachers are and remain perpetual disciples so long as they speak and write from their own strength and mental perception.

<margin>The Light of Nature is the unique master.</margin>
Since, therefore, our own education or information is nothing on its own, it must certainly be understood a little more deeply what that thing is which instructs and teaches us. You must establish this: the <term>Light of Nature</term><note>original: *Lumen Naturae*. For Paracelsus, this is the intuitive and divine spark within the natural world that reveals true knowledge to the human mind, as opposed to book-learning.</note> itself bestows the foundation and knowledge of every profession. 

<margin>Avicenna, Galen, and Hippocrates are only disciples, not Masters.</margin>
With this granted and conceded, it follows that it is impossible for a solid and learned Physician to be born from the doctrine of Avicenna, Galen, and Hippocrates. For the truth of time itself proves that they were merely disciples; I say nothing of whether certain mastery ought to be sought in them. And so, let this be an unshakable axiom for you: unless you come forth from the Light of Nature alone, you cannot in any way be noble Physicians worthy of praise. Otherwise, all your praise and honor will flow from the vain and dry honor of "experiments." Experiments themselves by no means make a Physician; rather, the Light of Nature alone constitutes him. And just as one who looks at various lands described on a map, but does not travel, unjustly claims the name of a traveler: so no one can justly sell himself as a physician based on experiments alone.

<margin>Which Physicians are the teachers?</margin>
But lest I cause you weariness by detaining you longer than is right: I will finally briefly review those things which bestow knowledge upon any Physician. There are four branches of Philosophy and four of Astronomy, from which, as if from a mirror, all those things are brought forth and taken which can complete and perfect a Physician. Outside these eight "mothers," who could proclaim himself a genuine Physician? For just as it is impossible for an infant to be born without the union of father and mother: so neither can a Physician lack a similar conception or generation for his own knowledge.

<margin>The body is from man; knowledge is from the Light of Nature.</margin>
And from men themselves, he [the physician] ought not to seek or hope for more than the proper proportion of his limbs. But the other thing, which as it were gives life to the body itself, proceeds from the light of nature, as has already been said. While I discuss the eight Mothers from which knowledge flows, pay attention also to what Natural Geometry, <term>Chiromancy</term><note>The art of reading signs in the hands, but here used broadly to mean reading signs in nature.</note>, and <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The study of outward appearances to judge internal nature.</note> teach us. For these are the books from which we must learn.

<margin>Nature is the book of Medicine.</margin>
For even if what is contained on paper is perfectly understood, the book of Medicine itself has not yet been opened. The book of Medicine is Nature herself. And just as you look at yourself in a mirror: so in this mirror of Nature you ought to see all your sciences exactly, no less certainly than you recognize your own face in a physical mirror.

There are many who write from their own experience. Pay attention to what should be thought of this. Experience indeed can be conferred upon anyone: yet its power and operation cannot be passed from one person to another. 

<margin>Experience does not pass from one to another. What is experience?</margin>
True experience, according to the Philosophical and Astronomical sense, is this: that any thing be known in its invisibility. Thus, also for any "dissolutions" <note>Likely referring to chemical or alchemical breakdowns of substances.</note> outside this knowledge, it is true and genuine experience. What was experienced yesterday: how does it benefit today? Or what does today's experience confer upon tomorrow? For today's experience is not like tomorrow's, because the conjunction of circumstances does not remain constant; it is fresh now, and then renewed again and again, even though experience itself remains consistent within its own nature. So that you may more exactly hold and understand the foundation from which one must write, we will thereafter hand down in order—as much as anyone needs to know—from where finally either my writings or those of others ought to proceed and flow.

-> ### ON THE LIMBUS. <-
---

<margin>Man is the lesser limbus. The limbus is twofold. What is the limbus?</margin>
**T**he reason why I treat the <term>Limbus</term><note>A Paracelsian term for the primordial "seed-matter" of the universe. He views it as the reservoir of all potentiality.</note> before all things is not obscure. For in this, those eight "mothers" of which I spoke are hidden and contained. I believe it is unknown to none of you that man is nothing other than the Limbus itself. And since the Limbus is twofold: man, as the "lesser limbus" <note>The Microcosm.</note>, was produced and made from the "greater limbus" <note>The Macrocosm or the Universe.</note>. The Limbus in itself is the seed from which any creatures arise and grow, just as a tree is born from a seed. The difference is this: that the Limbus had its "earth" in the word of God. Thus, the Greater Limbus is the seed from which all creatures came forth. But the Lesser Limbus is the final creature into which the Greater Limbus passed. For when man was built from the Limbus, all of the creatures existed within him.

<margin>The lesser limbus is born from the greater.</margin>
From that, as if from sperm, man—who is now the lesser limbus—was taken and established. Just as a son is born from his father: so the lesser limbus was produced from the greater. And just as a son exhibits all the limbs of his parent: so man also contains all creatures within himself. Since, therefore, the "greater world" was first established from the Limbus, and finally man himself after all creatures: it must therefore be known that the nature, essence, and every property of all the creatures which the whole world contains were again collected and ordered into this one Limbus.

<margin>Man contains the "idea" of all creatures.</margin>
That Limbus became man. From this, it follows that all arts, all sciences, and whatever is in man, or is brought into man, turn and subsist in the knowledge of all the creatures of the greater world. For man knows nothing and can do nothing which was not implanted in him from the Limbus: nor does he have anything higher or more sublime than the Light of Nature itself.

<margin>The Physician's art ought to be like the song of the lark.</margin>
As its line falls upon him, so he grasps and understands nature. Whence I can truly and constantly say: that unless a Physician knows and possesses his art just as the lark has its song and the peacock its painted feathers, nothing can be brought into him from elsewhere, unless he continually and directly immerses himself into that line of nature.

# ON THE GOUTY DISEASE

Thus it now follows from this, that men are able to know and investigate all the knowledge of the Angels and spirits, and are able to obtain all the nature found in the rest of the creatures. For since man was fashioned from these very things, he certainly holds the power and the inheritance of knowing all things which are in heaven and on earth: and just as an infant learns and drinks in speech from its parents, so we also must learn from those things from which we were brought forth. For parents teach the infant everything they know. Similarly, the creatures teach us everything that they themselves know: provided that we avoid seeking an outside parent from whom to learn.

Since, therefore, by the reasons stated, man was formed from the <term>Limbus</term><note>original: *limbus*. In Paracelsus’s philosophy, this refers to the "Great Mystery" or the primordial "soup" containing the seeds of all created things. Man is the "extract" of this entire universe.</note>:

<margin>The Limbus is the sole cause of human variety.</margin>
Moreover, since the Limbus embraces all the creatures of heaven and earth: it is clear from this that no one should be filled with wonder at the wisdom, or the stupidity, or the spirituality, or the brutality of men.

For from whatever nature a man is born, such a one he necessarily becomes, nor can he escape the condition of his own origin and parentage. From this it happens that some have the nature of a donkey, and others of a falcon.

<margin>Cosmography is threefold.</margin>
From these things, I personally judge (as it ought to seem to you yourselves) that one must seek and investigate that which is to be known concerning man. For if his nature and character, in both good and evil, are to be described: the same must first be understood from the "Great Limbus" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe at large.</note>. And in place of <term>Cosmography</term><note>original: *Cosmographia*. Usually the mapping of the world, but here Paracelsus uses it to mean a systematic mapping of human nature against the rest of creation.</note>, this nature of man, which is diverse, ought to be judged and estimated, so that once the nature of the beast is understood and placed into its own Cosmography, it may finally be understood: which beast and which man correspond to one another? And this is now one Cosmography. The second is that the Angels and man be "cosmographized" in their own right. And then, through that Cosmography, the faculty will be given to us of knowing and recognizing with what knowledge or wisdom anyone is endowed. Furthermore, there is a third Cosmography: that the spirits of the Great Limbus and the spirit of man (the <term>Lesser Limbus</term><note>The Microcosm, or man himself.</note>) be compared. By this reasoning, the very division and distribution of spirits will be laid open. For it is from here <margin>From whence comes the variety of men?</margin> that some men are teachable, others crude, others beastly, others humane, others good, others evil. From here you will also find men who perform miracles, and who command spirits and Angels. And this matter is no different than if a son were to surpass his father and compel him, so that the father complied with the son’s will. For that man was born from those who have power of this kind. And unless it is provided through the father himself: this man certainly has no such power of his own.

Thus, he who obeys the Angels obeys his own parent. He who learns from the spirits learns from his own father. He who recognizes the beasts recognizes himself. He who understands the Elements knows him who was created as a <term>Microcosm</term><note>Man as a "little world" that mirrors the "big world" of the universe.</note>. For in this way, one thing proceeds from the other in succession. But to continue my intended work, having now relegated these sayings to Philosophy: I would have you understand for what purpose I have brought up this discussion of the Limbus.

It is nothing other than <term>Podagra</term><note>Gout.</note>, through which other diseases of this kind are also to be understood. <margin>Nothing is to be granted to dead Masters.</margin> Concerning this, it must be noted above all that we should place no trust in dead Masters <note>Referring to ancient authorities like Galen or Avicenna whose books were the standard of the time.</note>, but it is right to attend only to the immortal teachers. For the reason of a dead master is nothing other than a cloth soaked in water. For the cloth is indeed wet, and it reflects the water, and water is even in it: but no one can drink from it more than enough to slightly and briefly cool the tongue. Therefore, just as a man drinks from the fountain itself, not from the cloth: so let us also draw our knowledge from the angels, not from mortals, who are scarcely tinted and imbued with water by the sun. And whom can these people eventually satisfy, when they themselves have a penury of water?

In the preceding chapter, I taught that a physician ought not to grow in that way. Indeed, those who are made in this [new] way are the most learned of all. For here "Fortune" is placed, so that a Physician who is born from above in the aforesaid manner performs many miracles, and has a gathering and a success much more fortunate than others. For these men work such great signs and miracles of man, that others, who are placed outside this influence, almost regard and worship them as gods and divine beings, and thus they readily fall away from the true God.

<margin>Fortune is not to be waited for by the Physician.</margin>
Nevertheless, to return now to the beginning of this verse, it is fitting that the Physician does not trust in "Fortune," or attribute anything to fortunate stars: but art itself ought to compel and lure Fortune as if by force. For this reason, you say that the Physician ought to exercise himself, lest he stand on the fickle wheel of fortune. For spirits are volatile or fleeting: while on the contrary, art is not at all fleeting, but remains standing for you with a solid foot. Hence, that you may possess the art, the way I am showing you will teach you. Thus, however, the doctrine is conferred upon you from the *Limbus*—that is, from the "third body," namely of animals and growing things. For these things have a likeness with the body of man, because they have the same rationale as those bodies in which diseases—of which <margin>Gout is a primary disease.</margin> gout is a certain primary one—lie hidden and concealed. Moreover, regarding what I proposed in the introduction: even if it is not necessary for Medicine, it can nevertheless serve as a preface, so that one may have a true recognition of a true physician, and judge the vanity of those Physicians who decree such arrogant triumphs for themselves outside of this art. Yet all of them should not be estimated or placed elsewhere by me or by you than as "Saints" who perform miracles not in the name of the Lord, but in the power of their own birth, in which they exalt themselves with too much rejoicing. But I do not even reject or repudiate this kind; I only command that roses be preferred to nettles, and that their own place be left to these, and their own place also to the thistles.

Now, while the things said so far serve as a cursory instruction for the Physician: yet at the same time, this must also be held: what is the particular method for recognizing diseases? <margin>All things of animals are in man.</margin> For all diseases which belong to animals, just like all their temperaments, qualities, and the like, are also present in man himself. From this also the principle and science of Physicians proceeds in the same way. If a Physician understands nothing of animals: what, pray, will he know of man? In animals there are species: in man there are universals. For in him the conjunctions of diseases meet. But what in species...

<header>BOOK I.</header>
<sig>Iii 3</sig>

First, it must be understood that this knowledge is not taken from man himself, but from that source from which we have already said it is derived. From this it is now clear that the reasons, causes, and all similar things taught by the Physicians are mere fabrications. For they begin their learning from man, who is actually the *end* of the teaching. The principle must be taken from outside of man himself: and that external principle is to be found within him. Those who strive to learn from within the man—which ought to be sought outside of him—are the "Heretics of Medicine." They are wandering in open error, seeking a way to describe man while remaining ignorant of his very <term>Limbus</term><note>The "Great Mystery" or primordial matter from which Paracelsus believes the universe and man were created.</note>.

<margin>The Limbus is for unlearning [the old view of] man.</margin>
Learn the Limbus, and so it will be that you recognize the things that are in man. He who learns not from the Limbus, but from the man himself, learns nothing other than how to rob and lie; thus he sets his sails toward mere sophistry and every kind of wickedness.

<margin>How diseases are aired out.</margin>

### ON THE MECHANIC <note>original: *De Mechanico*. Here, Paracelsus refers to the "Internal Craftsman" or architect of nature.</note>

It has been the custom until now, and not without evident cause, that the description of all diseases should be derived from their generation. Why should I discuss this more deeply here, since the things handed down so far do not agree with my opinion at all? Nevertheless, to press on with my purpose, it is fitting in this place to explain the present disease more accurately alongside others, so that the universal declaration concerning the "smith" of the disease may become clearer and more intelligible. Since a man is not such a certain Physician that he can boast of seeing the very "body" of a disease with his own eyes, surely the "smith" who forges the body for the disease is hidden much more deeply. It is my purpose to define this more explicitly now, so that the Academies may have no reason to teach anything different or contrary regarding the causes of diseases.

<margin>The body of a disease is invisible to the eyes.</margin>
Since, therefore, nothing is open to human eyes in this case, but everything depends on the eyes of Nature herself: it will be entirely right for me to leave behind the visible mechanical laborers and proceed in explaining the order of Nature itself. Meanwhile, I do not exclude the visible here, for the invisible works according to its pattern. For the invisible must be known from the visible. Thus, Theory is invisible, but the Mechanic <note>The practical application or the internal "builder."</note> is visible, even though both are one thing. The reason I call it invisible is this: because invisible things are not seen. But what shall I say of them here? My intention is to explain the becoming or the generation of disease, so that you may finally understand more deeply in what way diseases themselves are produced. 

In these matters, the logic is the same as that of a carpenter, an axe, and wood, which are directed toward multiple ends and used in many ways—for houses, for stables, for barns. What carpenter will restrict his method so much that he observes only one "Geometry" and no more? Furthermore, you make as many opinions as there are heads, so that not even one simply fits or agrees with another. By these things, I consider it proven that it is impossible for only one process to be held and observed from which one may not depart. For just as a craftsman daily practices new and diverse works, so also is that "smith" who forges the gout varied and diverse. And who could announce a daily horoscope for everyone? Can I help but burst into laughter when I see the <term>sophists</term><note>Paracelsus's derogatory term for traditional academic doctors who relied on logic rather than nature.</note> have their diseases so "ready at hand"? I speak of such men as those. Truly, what shall I say? They speak of the "wood," when yet there is no wood; and meanwhile, they make no mention of the "smith" himself? This is especially true since any disease does not grow from matter, but is born from a master and a smith, of whom they do not mention even a word. Now, a "humor" <note>In traditional medicine, one of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to cause disease.</note> is no more than wood. Who, then, has ever seen wood form and erect itself into a house? Much less can the humors by themselves become a disease. For what is a disease other than a constructed building? Look at a snail: who taught it to build its own house? It builds a house for itself from an innate art.

<margin>Mechanical knowledge of disease.</margin>
In the same way, every disease is the craftsman and builder of a peculiar form. For all diseases are fitted to Geometry. In this same sense, the very buildings of diseases must be understood. For the fabricator who forges the diseases is invisible. And it is he who must be renewed, not the wood itself. Pay attention to me, you <term>Humorists</term><note>Doctors who believe all diseases are caused by imbalances of fluids.</note>. Are houses not built from "worked" wood rather than from rotten, broken, or decayed wood? And who would construct these? No one but a smith or a craftsman. Therefore, take hold of this fabricated matter, and by tearing apart the joints, break the structure itself, and knock the axe out of the craftsman's hands. Only then will it happen that the building collapses, and a new one is not erected again by the fabricator. This craftsman, who ruins the wood and builds his own dwelling, must be approached and driven out. 

Now, consider among yourselves whether you grasp this number in a set of four so that you omit nothing. For if you wish to discuss diseases as affirmatively as you boast of seeing into the matter, you ought to approach it much more deeply in spirit, joining it to the visible, so that your faith cannot be shaken. I grant you much, looking at the nature of the <term>Microcosm</term><note>Man, viewed as a "miniature universe" that mirrors the macrocosm of the stars and elements.</note>, of which you are ignorant and unskilled. But what shall I recount finally, so that you may briefly understand what disease is born in the "Mechanic"—that is, by the secret and hidden carpenter whom we do not see with our eyes? Certainly, just as human reason works in many ways toward various ends, so you ought to know that the Mechanical fabricator behaves in the same way. If you wish to strip away from him reason, ascent, or human wisdom, then group him with the spiders; compare the works of spiders with the industry of a silk weaver, and give him his place. But if not, and you would rather take away animal operation from him, place before your eyes a thorn or a thistle growing in a field.

<margin>The human garden.</margin>
How much reason is in that? What is born from it? Just as a garden is flowery with various herbs that have sprung up, so man is a similar garden. But if you still do not understand that "Mechanic" through these things, I ask you to judge for yourselves how moths and little worms are born. For they are not produced from themselves, unless they are brought forth by their own craftsman and smith.

<margin>Putrefaction does not act.</margin>
And if this example is not enough for you, but you wish to credit this generation to "putrefaction," yet this stands in the way: that putrefaction is nothing by itself, nor does it do or produce anything, unless...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases like gout are not caused by physical fluids (humors) alone, but are "built" by an internal, invisible force or "Mechanic." He critiques traditional doctors for focusing on the symptoms (the wood) rather than the internal builder (the smith).</summary>
