<header>ON THE DISEASE OF GOUT</header>

<margin>What decay is</margin>
...unless it is forged and led back into something else. For what else is decay <note>original: *putredo*</note> but a thing that has departed from its own nature, or rather, the death of that thing? Therefore, it is of no use for a Physician to write about this [the state of death]. Instead, recognize the cause, so that I may explain this <term>Mechanic</term><note>In Paracelsus's view, the "Mechanic" or "Archeus" is an internal artisan that shapes life and disease within the body.</note> to you, so that you may learn to master and restrain him. For just as you can cut down an entire tree while it is still in the seed, so too can the same be achieved here. For the same reason that a pear grows from the root and not from the branch—because, of course, the "pear-maker" lives in the root and not in the branch—so here too, the generation of the thing ought to be credited to the craftsman, not to the wood. And with these things delivered so far, I believe the generation of disease has been sufficiently explained to you. Regarding those things which can be extracted more deeply from Philosophy and Astronomy, I shall deliver them more at length in their proper sequence in the <term>Archidoxis</term><note>One of Paracelsus's most famous works, "The Archidoxes of Theophrastus," which deals with the "ancient dogmas" of alchemy and medicine.</note>.

## BOOK TWO.
### *The Common Interpretation of Diseases, on the Discovery of Causes, the Cure, and the Qualities of Things.*

<margin>Nothing lacks its concordant form.</margin>
It has been established and demonstrated thus far that all growing things, and indeed the entire universe, must be reduced to a single form; nothing exists without its own form, which is not shaped into its own concordance <note>original: *concordantia*; a state of harmony or "fitting" together</note>. Let us take an example. A man [is fashioned] by a mechanical craftsman into a calf <note>original: *vitulum*; this likely refers to a mold or a specific transitional shape in alchemical creation</note> for which he was made. Now, truly, this work is not yet whole or such as it ought to be, but it requires further crafting to be fully completed—namely, the "woman" who is forged into the likeness of the "man" and completes that work.

<margin>A man is not whole without a woman.</margin>
Set such a man before yourselves; even if he has already been crafted in this way, he is not yet whole, since something is departing and missing from his health. It is no different than how a woman is missing to a man, a deficiency which is mended and restored by the arrival of the woman. In the same way, in this place, a human

<margin>The human is not whole.</margin>
(whether it be a woman or a man) is by no means whole, but their perfection and integration—or their completion—lies hidden, forged within the Elements. In these Elements, the human finds his concordance, through the union of which he is made whole and perfected. Take note, however, that I am speaking here of health. For according to health, a human is by no means whole; that is, in the state of health, something is missing from every person. This deficiency should be judged by you as if

<margin>The "Woman" of health, etc.</margin>
the "woman of health" were missing—she who lies hidden and established within herbs, roots, and stones. It is now my purpose that she (understand this as the "woman" or the "cure") be recognized and found within the four Elements in which she is established, as the third book will explain. For before all things, it must be believed that a man is not whole without a woman, but is whole with her. Now, the woman is from the earth. The man is also from the earth; and so both are from the earth, and both become one whole—that is, from one earth. Thus also,

<margin>The Human and Medicine are one.</margin>
the Human and Medicine are both from one earth and constitute one whole human.
Furthermore, I wish it to be understood from this that I am speaking of the person—that is, the "woman"—whose form 

---

must agree with the form [of the man], so that it may be known what ought to mend the deficiency of the other. Therefore, it is necessary that the form be present; nothing exists without form. In this way, surely, the woman and the man are not only one thing, but also one image. For the deficiency of the man and of his woman requires this; for she herself does not exist as a whole without the man, so that form is no less present than property, and property no less than the form itself, and thus both become one thing. I want this to be understood in this way: unless the form itself is found, the foundation of the property

<margin>The properties of forms are found.</margin>
which I am emphasizing here will certainly never be discovered. And whoever decides to speak of the property must also discuss the form itself—that is, the same <term>Anatomy</term><note>To Paracelsus, "Anatomy" is not the study of dead tissues, but the "inner blueprint" or essential structure of a living thing.</note>. For there is one Anatomy: man and woman. By a similar reasoning, a disease and its remedy are also one Anatomy. One Anatomy is one thing, which is one in both form and property. Diseases are forged and fabricated just like the human himself. Therefore, every disease is a "human"—that is, in the property and form of a single human. Likewise, so is Medicine itself. From this it is now clear that a disease demands its own "woman"—that is, the Medicine. Here must be found the "concordance" of diseases: that is, the union of both into one Anatomy,

<margin>What is "One Anatomy"?</margin>
just like a man and a woman. When that is found, the physician is whole and perfect. To this end, therefore, which

<margin>Disease is a human.</margin>
I indicate, it is now required that in what follows I explain those arts to you by which you may find and understand this concordance. For without the knowledge of these, the Anatomy

<margin>What should the physician know of Anatomy?</margin>
can by no means be found. What, in the end, is it that you see when you examine a naked man and his limbs so curiously? What do you observe in him that could make you more equipped or fit for a cure? Not a single thing! You labor only over the bones and the substance of the body, when it is actually necessary that you penetrate into the Anatomy of the diseases themselves. For nothing is missing from the limbs themselves, to which you can neither add nor take away anything by your own power.

Since, therefore, it is the duty of all of us Physicians that, when asked for the reasoning of our art, we know how to give an account of everything; therefore, if someone asks where we get this or that from, it is by no means enough to answer that this or that person handed it down so. For time, having slipped away over such a long interval, shatters that truth; a careless scribe shatters it; and the discrepancy between our opinions and theirs shatters it, so that we can by no means agree on a single opinion. Here, what is most serious is that in those authors (I exclude Hippocrates and 

<margin>Praise of Hippocrates and Apollo.</margin>
Apollo), no other foundation is discovered than that which consists of their naked opinions and imaginations, which no one could believe without being flawed. With equal daring, many also write and comment from their own daily experience, though that same experience is uncertain and conceived outside the genuine "mother of experience" <note>likely referring to Nature or the divine light</note>. Such experience is surely nothing but a mere and naked crutch, providing nothing else than to bargain for the favor of inconstant fortune. For what kind of experience is that which either the state of the heavens annihilates or reason shatters...

<summary>Paracelsus introduces a revolutionary concept: that disease and its cure share a single "Anatomy" or essential blueprint, comparing the relationship between a patient and their medicine to that of a man and a woman who together form a single whole. He criticizes traditional physical anatomy as useless for healing, arguing instead for a deeper understanding of the "Internal Mechanic" and the harmony of nature.</summary>

<page-num>655</page-num>
<header>BOOK II.</header>
<sig>Iii 4</sig>

<margin>Who is the mother of experience?</margin>
...the logic of the earth, or how it might spoil a drink, or evade foods; for those who possess such experience without it being strengthened by the true mother of experience, find themselves easily suppressed and defeated when the desired success does not breathe upon them. For the mother of experience is that which provides the way, the method, the order, and the art—without which Medicine is nothing. It is rightly said by those who are not Physicians that Medicine is nothing but experience, which is to say, it is not an art. For whatever daily experience provides to anyone, that is his "art." This truly applies to those who have not known the mother of experience. I, on the contrary, feel that one must descend entirely to the principles and the very foundations, and learn from the deepest causes from which father any given thing proceeds. For once this is accurately understood, all things that ought to be known are known without doubt. Just as a knight seeks the shoeing of his horse from a blacksmith, and the smith in turn seeks iron from the smelter, and the smelter from the mines, and so on, each acting according to his own experience: so must we also think backward. We must not stop at the blacksmith's shop, merely looking at the herbs as they have already been made or produced; rather, we must go back to the very beginning to see what they were before they were made—before the production of their seed, while they were still <term>metals</term><note>Paracelsus believed that plants and minerals shared a "metallic" spiritual root or "liquor" before they took their final physical form.</note>. From this, I say, we must learn with great zeal.

<margin>Conjunction is either natural or by art.</margin>
The core of this entire instruction is that we be skilled and knowledgeable in <term>Anatomy</term><note>In this context, Anatomy refers not just to dissection, but to understanding the "concordance" or energetic relationship between different parts of nature.</note>, which is to say, that we know the "concordances" of those things which are to be joined. This joining is called the "conjunction of art." For those things which nature herself joins, that is a natural conjunction. Those things which man joins are called the conjunction of art. I speak of the art that is to be produced. If this art is to be found, it is necessary that <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The practice of judging character or properties from outward appearance.</note> be the small part that teaches us the discovery.
<margin>Physiognomy: the mother of discovery.</margin>
For we ought not to place anything in our own subtle heads, but rather prove all things through nature alone. Just as our own reason cannot make even the smallest blade of grass, so likewise we cannot achieve even the slightest thing by mere chance. And just as the reason that lives within us must follow nature—that is, it must sow and plant according to nature’s way—so too must Medicine follow her.
<margin>Likewise Chiromancy and Anatomy.</margin>
Thus, Physiognomy is one of those things that teaches us. So too is <term>Chiromancy</term><note>Commonly known as palmistry, but for Paracelsus, it meant reading the "lines" and signatures of any natural object to understand its inner power.</note>. And so also is Anatomy, which ultimately proceeds from the two aforementioned. Pay diligent attention to what the process of these things is: for if we say,
<margin>The letter is of no importance.</margin>
"this thing is useful for that," etc., the matter is certainly not to be proven by the "letter" (book learning), but by our art, which breaks through the letter itself. For just as there is no place for the "letter" in Holy Scripture, but rather for the spirit and faith, so it is in this art. If, therefore, art is required to prove a thing, it is clear that the letter itself must be set aside; we must prove it just as a blacksmith proves his workmanship. That is, we must know the workmanship of anatomy, conjunction, and concordance. Physiognomy and Chiromancy lead us to these as if they were rules, 
<margin>Anatomy is proven through Physiognomy and Chiromancy.</margin>
and through them, Anatomy itself is proven. From this, the art of Medicine is subsequently confirmed, so that I may then boldly say we are Physicians. To be certain of this, grasp the thing itself; do not just read books. For the blacksmith and the carpenter accomplish or perfect nothing through writing, but through knowledge. Now, Medicine is also a knowledge. Therefore, the Physician will yield where the Mechanic yields—whom he also understands deeply—and he will not follow his own dizzying brain, out of whose twenty inventions scarcely one turns out well, and even then, not always. With these things understood thus far, now pay attention to what Physiognomy and Chiromancy are, and by what reasoning a Physician must learn them. For without this path, his entire education is nothing.

### PHYSIOGNOMY.

<margin>Every disease is a man and a microcosm.</margin>
Before I pass on the teaching of Physiognomy, I want you to know at the threshold that every disease is a "complete man," having an invisible body; it is thus a body of the <term>Microcosm</term><note>The "Little World"—the idea that the human body reflects the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note> and the Microcosm itself. So that you may grasp what I intend, attend to this example from which you may know the form of the Microcosm of disease. Consider <term>Jaundice</term><note>original: *Icteritia*</note>. This arises from the center of the body, <margin>Jaundice arises from the center of the body.</margin> which is to say, from the gall. However, it inflicts no harm until the "whole man" has grown out of it—that is, until Jaundice has become a "whole man," or stands at his boundaries. <margin>When and how does Jaundice become a body?</margin> From this it follows that the entire "body" of Jaundice is extended as far as the entire Microcosm is extended and bounded—namely, into the hands, feet, ears, eyes, and all the ends and limits of the body. Once that body is completed in this way, it has reached its full growth and possesses all the members that a man ought to have. Therefore, member corresponds to member everywhere, in the same proportion and similar distance. From this it is again clear that diseases produce "hand-like" hands, "foot-like" feet, "eye-like" eyes, "stomach-like" stomachs, "intestine-like" intestines, and so on. This is where that bad "experience" of the secrets of Jaundice emerged, where one man boasts he knows a stomach remedy for the "stomach" of Jaundice, and another for its "eyes." These are by no means the arts of true Medicine, but merely experiments applied without any judgment or reason. <margin>Two bodies, of disease and man: how are they together?</margin> Therefore, the Microcosm in such a disease is now double, and it has a double body, even though it is one man: for two bodies are folded together or combined in no other way than if you were to pour water into ashes enclosed in a vessel. No matter how much liquid you pour in, the ash does not swell because of it, nor does it occupy a greater space; rather, the same place remains for both the ash and the water as was there before, and the distance is not doubled by the joining. <margin>Why disease is called a "man."</margin> In a similar way, you ought to understand disease in its own form. Furthermore, now attend to the Physiognomy of the man—that is, of the disease itself, which I call "man" in this place for this reason: because not only the aforementioned disease, but every other disease as well, grows and flourishes with the man until it dies or is abolished. If, therefore, the disease is a "man," albeit an invisible one, its Physiognomy must be accepted by both in the way shown, and afterward compared with Medicine so that one single Physiognomy stands for both. And one must look primarily to this, not the Physiognomy of the [physical] body itself, although the logic and process of both are very nearly the same...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine is an "art" based on nature's internal logic, requiring the use of Physiognomy and Chiromancy to understand how a disease—which he describes as an invisible "man" or microcosm—occupies and grows within the patient's body.</summary>

<header>ON GOUTY DISEASES</header>
<meta>catchword: so</meta>
<sig>tt</sig>

...exists as the least.

<margin>Medicine is the female of the disease.</margin>
In the same way, one must understand regarding Medicine that it is the "female" of the form, just as was said above. In all growing things produced by nature, we must labor to understand that which is the internal spouse: the form of the Medicine, which indicates a similar <term>Physiognomy</term><note>Physiognomy here refers to the art of reading the internal nature or "character" of a substance by its outward signs and signatures.</note> through its power and appearance. For disease, as you have heard, builds an "internal man." It is this man who dies, not the external one. This same internal man also rules the external one. For death does not reside in the external man, but in the internal; nor does the external man putrefy <note>Paracelsus argues that the spiritual or "astral" body is the seat of life and disease; the physical body merely reflects what happens to this inner template.</note>. Therefore, for the sake of these things, you owe that [internal] man his own spouse in the form of medicine. For just as the "man of the disease" lies and exists within the body, so there is a similar "man" within the medicine, possessing its own hands, feet, head, eyes, belly, and all other parts. And whatever the internal man is like, such is his spouse [the medicine] also.

<margin>The man of the disease and the medicine are not alike.</margin>
But you will note here that the "man of the disease" may touch one limb more clearly (as it seems to us) or more severely than another. Thus, he is felt more in one limb and less in another. And yet, there is only one single "man," complete in all his limbs, bringing a similar death to all members. It is by this very reasoning and by such a Physiognomy that Medicine itself must be known and drawn out. If you do not recognize it in this way, the same thing will happen to you as to a fool who, looking at a beautiful woman, is ignorant of why and for what purpose she exists, and instead of the woman, grabs a crust of bread. As long as you are not skilled in the Physiognomy of the internal man, it will be impossible for you to truly know what the external man is like.

<margin>A reprimand of Doctors.</margin>
You will be far less able to profess yourselves as Physicians while you remain ignorant of the true art. Therefore, your teaching is not science, but a mere <term>farrago</term><note>original: "farrago" - a confused mixture or hodgepodge.</note> of experiments, which could be just as ready in the hands of a crude peasant. It was not necessary for you to be created Doctors for the sake of such trivialities, or to waste your lives at the Academy of <note>The University of Leipzig and the University of Ingolstadt were prestigious centers of learning that Paracelsus frequently criticized for their traditionalism.</note>Leipzig or Ingolstadt. An "art" of this kind (if it even deserves to be called an art) can be more aptly sought from old women, monks, and nuns. Meanwhile, as you must endure this just reproach, let it be sung everywhere that I am a "magician," "delirious," and a "fanatic." But if you have no better ability or strength to defend your ignorance and lies than to repeatedly cry out that I am a magician, an impostor, and a stage-player, then you yourselves will remain worthless impostors hereafter, just as you have been—men who will not rashly abandon what you have learned. In the meantime, it is enough for me that it is proven everywhere to all people that you know and hold nothing other than how to jeopardize lives, court luck, propose riddles, and sell the allurements of words to everyone: which is the graphic sign of Hypocrites.

<margin>The man of disease who becomes visible.</margin>
Now, if you have grasped the matter and agree with the proposed doctrine of the "two men" (the disease and the medicine) hidden within, then attend also to this: although that man is indeed hidden, he nevertheless becomes visible, much like a shadow, or a rainbow (the celestial arch), or other "impressions." For such impressions, rainbows, and celestial appearances are themselves nothing other than the internal figure of their own body. Just as these things are in the heavens, so too is that "impression" in man. Medicine has this [internal figure] constantly and perpetually within itself. Man, on the other hand, only has it when he is sick. Just as you see that impression made in the sky, so you can perceive it made in man. Thus, a future Physician must necessarily be an <term>Astronomer</term><note>For Paracelsus, medicine and astronomy were inseparable; the "stars" in the macrocosm corresponded to the "stars" or spiritual forces within the human body.</note>. For it is impossible for you to become a Physician without Astronomy. Furthermore, you shall consider and inspect these two personas (which you will see with your eyes like an impression) in the same way you look at an external man and, having recognized his Physiognomy, say: "this man is a thief," "that one is a liar," "this one is a predator," etc.

<margin>Heaven imprints the Physiognomy.</margin>
For if you can do this outwardly, you will also learn to do it inwardly. What are those external things? Surely, it is Heaven that imprints that Physiognomy from which you divine. In exactly the same way, Heaven gives to the internal parts what it gives to the external. Therefore, the internal things must be inspected no less diligently than the external.

<margin>Physiognomy as the index of temperament.</margin>
For if you recognize the "complexion of Mars" outwardly in a martial face, you will also be able to judge the internal complexion of the man—whether Mars or Saturn imprinted that Physiognomy. And indeed, it is the internal man who is sick, not the external one whom you see. The external man is simply the one being "conquered" or overcome. Do not concern yourself with the conquered, but speak of the one who conquers him.

<margin>A red beard is more deceitful and dark.</margin>
It is known to all peasants that those clothed with a red beard are more unfaithful or deceitful than those with black beards, and that the latter, in turn, are more prone to anger than the former. But what "art" is there in a Doctor who only knows this?

<margin>Grey eyes are better than black.</margin>
It is also commonly found by everyone that grey eyes are healthier than black ones, and that bald men are better or more refined than those with hairy foreheads.

<margin>Bald men are better than hairy ones.</margin>
<margin>Sharp noses are angrier than flat ones.</margin>
So too, a sharp nose is judged to be angrier than a blunt one. But what does this contribute to the glory and ornament of a Doctor? Enter into the body itself, penetrate it, and look upon *it*, not the external. Whatever the outward appearance may be, you will notice nothing from it that is of use to you, other than what is deformed and diseased. But what harmed him? Who made him weak? This is what you must truly look into.

Since Nature demonstrates the internal man—and it is he of whom I discourse here—it is primarily from this that you must determine which limbs in him are sick. For those same limbs labor and ache in the body of the <term>Microcosm</term><note>The "Little World"—the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>. Now, he who complains of a "place" [of pain] does not indicate what excites the pain, but only what hurts or feels the pain.

<margin>The external man feels pain, not the internal.</margin>
The internal man feels no pain; yet the external man does. But the one who feels no pain [the internal cause] is the one who must be considered. If you focus only on that which feels the pain, look at what you do: you apply <term>Narcotics</term>. These are your "medicines" for the flesh. A fine medicine indeed, a fine doctrine! Eventually, you even add <term>erosives</term><note>Caustic substances used to "eat away" diseased flesh.</note>. Oh, what charming "eaters" you are! It is no wonder you are called "Medics," given how you understand the matter. Having performed these things, you then purge "choler" [yellow bile] where none exists; you purge "melancholy" [black bile] which you have never seen in your entire life, and so on. From all this, it is evident that you have no idea what a disease actually is. Hence, you insist on external medicines and omit the internal ones that truly constitute a Physician. Thus, we have begun to teach that Physiognomy must be understood from its very foundation.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that disease is an "internal man" whose spiritual form must be matched by a corresponding "internal medicine," critiquing academic doctors for treating external symptoms like pain with narcotics rather than understanding internal causes. He emphasizes that a true physician must use "Physiognomy" and Astronomy to read the hidden signs of the internal body.</summary>

...so it is necessary that you see the eyes, ears, and nose of the internal man, and prepare for this <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The art of judging character or internal nature from outward appearance or "signatures."</note> its own spouse [the medicine], whose own Physiognomy you must also have recognized with no less certainty. For who first indicated the virtues of herbs? Surely only he who had explored such things as these. For no one could have known these from their outward face alone. Nor did this knowledge 

<margin>
The excellence of Physiognomy.
</margin>
flow from taste or smell. Therefore, these powers were explored through the art of Physiognomy alone. But the art that found these things, or taught how to find them, was later wiped away by forgetfulness; however, the fragments and crumbs falling from its mouth were collected and preserved. From those fragments comes this fact which you know: that from

<margin>
Wintergreen, a wound herb.
Comfrey, a wound herb.

<term>wintergreen</term><note>original: "pyrula"</note> a wound-healing potion is prepared. But what further virtues it may have is by no means discovered by you. So also you have known concerning <term>comfrey</term><note>original: "consolida"</note> that it heals and consolidates. But what exactly it consolidates, you do not know at all. Thus you know something and nothing at the same time, nor have you penetrated to true knowledge. And in respect to these medicines, your reasoning is the same as that regarding a woman or a virgin. You see her indeed—that she is of a womanly nature and mind—but to whom she has devoted her love, that you do not see; yet in this lies the hidden basis of all knowledge. For if you join her to another whom she does not favor in her heart, you would stir up strife and quarrels. The same is the reasoning for Medicine itself, if you join and couple it in a similar way.

<margin>
A rebuke of Medicine.
</margin>
Since, therefore, Medicine requires a true, genuine, and fundamental Physiognomist in the recognition and cure of diseases—not one who is ignorant and unskilled in things, who turns over the trifles of old women, as our Doctors and those like them do, who, arising from books, refine the secrets of fish-wives, their experiments, trivial collections, and various <term>handbooks</term><note>original: "Vade mecum," literally "go with me," referring to portable manuals of the time.</note>—whom, then, shall we say are the Masters of the seven liberal arts? Shall we believe them to be more fit for Medicine? For since their seven liberal arts do not pass down even a scrap concerning these things, what fruits will a Poet finally take from Medicine, whose art is mere fiction, whose craftsman is born only to catch the laughter of men? From these things, another who is slightly more sane perceives nothing hot, nor cold, nor sweet, nor sour; and so those mockers tickle themselves most of all. And yet these ridiculous men boast that they alone preside over the medical faculty and moderate it with their scepter. These men fit Medicine like a fist fits an eye. Meanwhile, those who seriously undertake the patronage of such an excellent faculty are immediately proclaimed Mages and sorcerers; furthermore, they are called <term>Geomancers, Pyromancers, Hydromancers, and Chaomancers</term><note>Diviners by earth, fire, water, and the "chaos" or atmosphere; here used as insults for those studying the elemental forces of nature.</note>, though in a sense much more wicked and harsh than the reality. For if they themselves had skill in these four arts, they would certainly have known everything that a Physician ought to know. But, as 

<margin>
The proverb of a certain Consul.
</margin>
the proverb goes: an old dog does not easily get used to the leash. This was the complaint of a certain man who, in the city of Meissen, flocked to his famous Academy, taking it poorly that his deceits and frauds were being brought into the light of day. It is a wonder, indeed, how much I long to see those common people over whom such a leader 

---

is the consul. It is believable, however, that "like lips have like lettuce"<note>A Latin proverb meaning "like attracts like" or "to each his own," often used to describe someone getting exactly what they deserve.</note>. Meanwhile, one might not undeservedly wonder that a <term>dullard</term><note>original: "Beonum"</note> of this kind, a wandering hypocrite of Medicine, is extolled to such great honors. I believe there is a shortage of better men there. Thus it goes: this is nothing new, that among the blind, the one-eyed man is king. Meanwhile, for honest and wise Physicians, it ought to be settled that the disease itself gives the beginning to Medicine, from which science flows: of which one part is Physiognomy, one is Chiromancy, and others which cannot or should not be recounted here. For in this place, only those things are brought forward which are required for the knowledge of <term>Gout</term><note>original: "Podagræ"</note>. But if there are those who think these things are either too few or too unclearly delivered: let them also leaf through our other books. For the defect of one is patched by another, so that in various places all things are fully delivered. This, however, is necessary above all else: that you have the "inventress of Medicine" as an explored and familiar friend. For without her, truly no one can become a Doctor, if it were possible. Otherwise, he would not know the name he professes. Therefore, your degrees, and "Excellence," etc., serve for nothing else than to veil hypocrisy, and to better commend your sycophancy, fawning, gestures, and impostures, until you have cheated the sick themselves of their money.

## CHIROMANCY

<margin>
What is Chiromancy?
</margin>
**T**hose who think that Chiromancy is directed and intended for the hands alone are involved in a clear error. For not only the lines of the hands, but also the lines of the whole body pertain to Chiromancy. But the art is named from the more prominent part, because the lines of the hands are the most evident of all. Therefore, the art ought to be practiced not only on the hand, but also on the trunk. Just as a herb that grows puts forth leaves, those leaves have their own Chiromancy. For every leaf is the "hand" of its own body. A human has twin hands. 

<margin>
Man has more hands than these; the lines of Chiromancy are twofold.
</margin>
Herbs have more or fewer. And yet any leaf is like any hand, and has its own manual <term>Anatomy</term><note>original: "Antomiam"</note>. Furthermore, lines are exhibited in two forms: in the feminine and masculine way; for there is a distinction between women and men. Just as various lines are shown in various leaves, so it is likewise in man. For every peculiar thing shows its own peculiar signs. Furthermore, not only the leaves, but also the body or trunk ought to be considered according to its lines, as in the ash, beech, or fir, whose trunks exhibit Chiromancy itself. For the logic of these is the same as that of man, whose "stem" or trunk is the length of the body.

<margin>
What the "Architect Lines" denote.
</margin>
But if you have not known this Chiromancy, you are by no means Physicians, but collectors of crumbs and fragments. For in the manner of dogs, you scrape together what falls from others. Now, this knowledge of Chiromancy is such that you may discern and comprehend the **Architect lines** in the hand. He who has these dies and perishes from <term>colic</term>. Therefore, the "architect line" of leaves is the remedy for that colic. In the same way, the **Anchor line** is the line of <term>Apoplexy</term>. For which reason, the "anchor line" in <term>Sweet Flag</term><note>original: "Acoro"</note> is the medicine for Apoplexy; and so consequently in others. Medi-

<header>ON THE GOUTY DISEASE</header>

<margin>No disease exists without a body.</margin>
For <term>Medicine</term><note>The original OCR reads "cina," likely a fragment of "Medicina."</note> must be drawn from <term>Chiromancy</term><note>The art of reading the "lines" or "signatures" of a thing to understand its inner nature; usually applied to palms, but here applied to the whole body and disease.</note>. If you compose your remedies outside of <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The practice of judging the internal character or essence of something based on its outward appearance.</note> and Chiromancy, you will certainly go far astray in every art. In exactly the same way, Physiognomy has its own "body" in Gout: that is, unless Physiognomy itself provides the body of the gout, the gout is not present. For the body must be present. So too, in the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>, its own body must be present; otherwise, no case of the falling sickness will be produced. The same reasoning applies to all other diseases as well. Now, if bodies must be present, and nothing exists without a body: then unique bodies will have entirely unique diseases, which is to say they will also have unique signs. And it is about these signs that I speak, from which we assert a Doctor must learn everything.

<margin>The necessity of Chiromantic signs.</margin>
For without signs, who learns anything? Signs, you see, testify to the craftsman. From signs, one must come to know what a thing is. Without them, nothing can be known. I rightly lead you, therefore, into Chiromancy and Physiognomy. For these bring forth the signs of all future diseases. Now, just as the "body" designates the "man"—that is, the disease—so also Nature has designated its "female"—that is, the Medicine—with the same sign. If you "synagogue-attending" Doctors <note>A term Paracelsus uses to mock academic doctors who gather in lecture halls rather than observing Nature.</note> are ignorant of these things, you are ignorant of everything.

<margin>Usage.</margin>
<margin>Chiromancy is either external or internal.</margin>
But I am not speaking here of external Chiromancy alone, but also of the internal kind. For just as Physiognomy emerges from the inside to the outside, it must be understood both inwardly and outwardly. The same logic applies to Chiromancy. Not only the external, but the external and internal together must be known. Now, if there is also an internal Chiromancy, it is proper that it be drawn from the external, which testifies to the internal. Thus the branch and the leaf of a tree testify to its root, with no less certainty than if we were seeing it with our own eyes. This, therefore, is the reasoning of Chiromancy, as well as Physiognomy: that we might know and evaluate the internal from the external, and thus recognize the entire state of the whole body from both. For if we have the external knowledge, and that man dies and we bring him to <term>Anatomy</term><note>In Paracelsus's view, Anatomy is not just dissection, but the study of the structural blueprints of life.</note>, we will surely find everything inside that we indicated by looking at the outside. These things must be known before all else. For diseases lie hidden, concealed within. By a similar method of perception and knowledge, their "female"—that is, the medicine—must also be understood.

<margin>Every disease is born from its own body.</margin>
Every disease is born from its own body: and the body of that which is born bears signs that are ordered and arranged. From these, the <term>arcanum</term><note>A secret or "hidden virtue" within a substance that contains its healing power.</note> must be drawn. A similar order and arrangement exist in Medicine itself: the goal of which is that the Doctor should learn and experience from it—not so that he follows his own exhausted brain, but that he consults the true teacher from what has already been said, and begins nothing except from such prior knowledge. For whichever of the Doctors and Masters has not come forth from the school of Nature, he is a mere impostor and deceiver. And if something occasionally turns out well for them, it should be ascribed to luck, not to their own knowledge; the same thing happens to them as to a blind man who finds a coin by chance.

## ANATOMIA.

*These notes are found as follows in the original Autograph: for he did not progress further in writing on these pages. However, those things which now follow, written separately on two other pages, were found among the papers and fragments, previously unpublished.*

### 1.

<margin>What does Anatomy teach?</margin>
**S**ince a Doctor can know and do nothing of himself but is forced to learn entirely from external things, **ANATOMY** above all others provides him with a foundation and knowledge. Now, Anatomy is the art that teaches one to know the form of any thing, how it holds itself, how it is constituted and composed: what condition and state it maintains; and this applies to a human, to wood, and to a tree.

<margin>How is the form of Anatomy to be known?</margin>
We speak of the "form" which is necessary for a Doctor to know. For Anatomy offers knowledge of form through the properties of those things. You see that nothing exists without its own form. Thus, diseases themselves are not formless, but are entirely shaped. Therefore, they have their own Anatomy and, so to speak, their own peculiar "man." The form of Anatomy in diseases is this: that they are entirely known and explored through pain, through color, and through location. Color indicates what and of what kind a disease is; so does the location of the disease. These two demonstrate the Anatomy of the disease itself.

Once these are known, the Anatomy of herbs and growing things must be done in the same way: so that, in this manner, you may collect and reduce the Anatomy of herbs and a similar Anatomy of diseases into one order. For this similarity provides the knowledge of the cure in which one must proceed and advance.

<margin>Celandine, centaury, and lice as remedies for Jaundice.</margin>
Why is <term>Celandine</term><note>original: "Chelidonia"</note> a medicine for <term>Jaundice</term><note>original: "Icteritia"</note>? Surely because of its Anatomy. So too with <term>centaury</term>; so too the <term>beetle</term>, so too <term>lice</term>, etc. Now, for as many kinds of medicines as there are for Jaundice, there also exist that many species of Jaundice: and you ought to have just as many Anatomies—that is, understandings of them—in the differences of the diseases. The same difference exists even in those diseases which you cannot find outside of Anatomy.

Thus, why do similar members comfort other similar things? Because they have the same Anatomy. The same is true in other things where the forms and essences of medicines and diseases clearly agree.

The knowledge of these things was given to instruct the Doctor with greater certainty. For these are his books, not mute letters. For if he knows these things, he knows all things necessary. If not, he is certainly entirely full of ignorance. And whoever trusts and commits himself to such a person is hopeless and foolish.

Regarding Anatomy, it has pleased me to discuss it here so that you might understand Gout—from what principle and with what end it should be described. If the ancients before me had devoted faithful labor to this matter as was proper, this writing of mine would now be unnecessary—

He emphasizes that true medical knowledge comes from observing Nature's signs rather than academic theory.</summary>

<page-num>659</page-num>
<header>BOOK II.</header>

->II.<-

<margin>Physiognomy is a part of Anatomy.</margin>
**S**ince any given thing reveals itself—just as you are accustomed to say that a man has the face and shifty eyes of one who is not to be trusted (for the external <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The art of judging internal character or medicinal properties from outward appearance.</note> always testifies to the internal state)—it is therefore a requirement of the art to first know the external man. Following this path, I establish my Physiognomy so that you may know the foundation from which my writing proceeds.

<margin>Eyebright benefits the eyes.</margin>
Indeed, Physiognomy is a part of <term>Anatomy</term><note>In Paracelsus’s view, "Anatomy" refers not just to dissection, but to the essential structure and relationship between things in nature.</note>. For it has its own evidence: that which is dry, that which is knotted, that which is cracked, or that which is of this or that sort. The form always indicates what a thing is for or what it might benefit. <term>Eyebright</term><note>A common flowering plant (Euphrasia) used since the Middle Ages for eye ailments.</note> benefits the eyes. Why? Because it possesses the Anatomy of the eyes. For there is no cloudiness or form in the eye that is not also contained within the flower of the Eyebright.
<margin>Tormentil, Cornelian, [and others] stop the flow of blood.</margin>
<term>Tormentil</term><note>A herb (Potentilla erecta) known for its red roots and astringent properties.</note> stops the flow of blood. Why? Because its Anatomy is similar to blood. So too with <term>Cornelian</term><note>A reddish-brown mineral (Carnelian).</note>, so with <term>Hematite</term><note>Bloodstone.</note>, and so with <term>Coral</term>: each of these restrains the specific blood whose Anatomy it carries.

Regarding these matters, a singular book must be composed for all of them, as well as for diseases, so that Anatomy may be related to Anatomy, Physiognomy to Physiognomy, art to art, and <term>Chiromancy</term><note>The reading of "lines" or "signatures" on any object, not just hands.</note> to Chiromancy. These arts are granted to the whole man so that they may be known and spoken of by him; without knowledge of them, his learning is worth nothing.

This proof is worthless if a Doctor says that <term>cholera</term><note>Yellow bile.</note> must be purged with <term>Colocynth</term><note>Bitter cucumber, a harsh laxative.</note>, or <term>phlegm</term> with <term>Turbith</term><note>An Ayurvedic root used as a purgative.</note> and the like. For these men are mere <term>Sophists</term><note>A term of abuse for those who rely on academic theory and rhetoric rather than practical experience and natural observation.</note>, whose refuge is mere opinion. The proof against these things is only true and genuine if Anatomy is referred to Anatomy, Physiognomy to Physiognomy, and Chiromancy to Chiromancy. In this way, you will have a legitimate concordance that will not deceive you in the least.

If, therefore, the Nature of these things is the conqueror of such diseases, it must be thoroughly explored by the Doctor. It becomes explored by him if he is knowledgeable and skilled in this art. For this knowledge is the same as that by which it is known that wood and iron share one Anatomy in their Essence. For iron splits and cuts wood. And in turn, wood is the "Anatomy" of iron. For what reason? Because wood burns [smelts] iron and sharpens it.

Unless the medical profession is brought to the point where the art is as certain as the art of craftsmen or mechanics—who prove their art themselves—then surely all Medicine must rightly be judged as mere pretense and imposture.

# PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS
## PARACELSUS'S BOOK
# ON THE FALLING SICKNESS.
### PARAGRAPH I.

<margin>Charity is the root of Medicine.</margin>
**I**n the entrance of this arduous work and labor which I have undertaken to explain the <term>Falling Sickness</term><note>Epilepsy.</note>, it is first of all necessary that I discuss something of the Mercy that ought to be innate to the Doctor. For if they examine the matter thoroughly, I notice a lamentable lack of mercy prevailing everywhere among all Doctors. This testifies against them: that they bear no charity toward the sick. Where charity is exiled, there no ready art exists.

Since, therefore, Medicine has such presiding officers who love neither themselves nor the patient, I cannot help but address them regarding such a deadly disease and cry out for them to finally wake from their sleep. For they lie buried, as it were, in slumber and snoring; yet the care of these arts (the theory and practice of which I propose here) ought to be entirely close to the Doctor's heart. In doing this, I did not wish to omit this necessary preface. For in this preface, the argument of the things to be treated is enumerated, and at the same time, those who have hitherto undertaken to treat such a cruel disease with such yawning and negligence are stirred from their sleep. It would be right here for me to pursue the habitual neglect of Doctors with many serious complaints—those who have only undertaken the healing of minor diseases, and very few of those at that. This is clear evidence that they have by no means sought the health of the sick from the bottom of their hearts, but have rather much more breathlessly affected private tranquility and profit. If they had not done so, they would surely have bestowed more diligent care upon the sick, and in writing and compiling their books, they would have applied greater experience and a far more certain and constant foundation for the public health of everyone. But their deficiency was too great. And so, regarding the true Doctor—because I am undertaking this explanation—I believe I am attempting an entirely necessary and useful thing; and I hope that I will be given praise by those of sounder mind for more clearly explaining in this place what a Doctor and what sort of Medicine there ought to be.
<margin>What the Doctor and medicine are.</margin>
For neither the Doctor nor Medicine is anything else than the mercy given and offered by God to those in need. Therefore, the use of the place and the subject demands that mercy be treated more extensively here. For it is the work of charity, from which the art that the Doctor must openly show flows forth as if from a fountain.
<margin>What mercy is.</margin>
Since, therefore, mercy ought to abound in the Doctor, and since he is nothing other than its steward and mediator (I speak of that mercy which flows from God into man), it is entirely fitting and right that the same Doctor be equipped with no less charity and mercy than that which God exerts toward man. If, however, the Doctor does not exercise this charity and mercy toward the sick—of which he ought to be the executor in God's place—how, I ask, can God thereafter entrust and mandate to him that charity which he does not dispense according to God's pleasure?
<margin>Why the Doctor was created.</margin>
For the Doctor and Medicines were created for this end alone: so that through them, the sick may manifesty feel and understand the love and mercy of God toward themselves. If the Doctor is not inclined toward these virtues, he is blocked by God and even robbed of those things which are especially worthy and necessary for a doctor to know. For by what reasoning...

<page-num>660</page-num>
<header>ON THE FALLING SICKNESS.</header>

# ON THE FALLING SICKNESS.

<margin>Daily bread is a gift of God, not a human merit.</margin>
By reason we pray, and by Christ we are commanded to pray, that our <note>original: "panis nobis detur quotidianus"</note> daily bread be given to us: thus, through this prayer, we bear witness that we do not ask for it by any righteousness of our own, nor that God owes it to us by right. Rather, it shows that we are so unworthy of it that at any moment it could and should be taken from us by God. Ultimately, whatever we receive of it is entirely extended to us out of divine love and mercy. Now, if bread is placed within the mercy of God and is by no means our right or merit, we ought to be much more persuaded of the same regarding medicine.

<margin>Two types of daily bread.</margin>
For just as that bread is the bread of nutrition, so this bread <note>meaning medicine</note> is the bread of health and well-being. Both types of bread are included under the same petition: just as the hunger of the healthy is restrained by it, so too are the limbs of the sick refreshed by it.

<margin>Mercy is the Teacher of the Physician.</margin>
Thus far I have discussed Mercy as if it were the Teacher of Physicians, to the end that it may be known that all physicians ought to be born merciful, so that by this mark they may turn out more learned and excellent than they are by themselves. For out of mercy, God chooses for Himself the Physician whom He created. The Physician differs from the other essences of the world in this: that other things act to nourish themselves, but the Physician acts not for himself, but for others.

<margin>How the Physician differs from other things.</margin>
<margin>What duty the Physicians perform.</margin>
Now, the duty of the Physician is nothing other than to distribute mercy to others. This mercy is not his own, nor is the operation of Medicine his own. Since, therefore, he has nothing of his own—and yet through him, or through his own person, these things are perfected—his work certainly must not be homicide, destruction, slaughter, or distortion. Instead, it must be the restoration of the sick through that same mercy and love with which God is moved toward mankind. It is a grave lack of mercy if someone, ignorant of his own duty, abandons the one who was committed to his care. For what are the duties commanded by God other than the fulfillment of the divine will? His duties arise from the grace of mercy. Because of this, God wills that through these duties we receive the <term>expiation</term><note>Here meaning a balancing or compensation for our physical failings.</note> of our defects. For no one is exempt from living under God’s ministries: I am under a master, the master is under me; I am under him outside of my own office, and he is under me outside of his. Thus, one person continually acts under the office of another, and in mutual love, each is subject to the other.

<margin>All men are subject to the Physician.</margin>
In this way, all men are subject to the mercy of the Physician. It is not that the man himself is mercy, but he is the medium through which nature is brought into effect. Now, who could contradict or be displeased if I describe the Physician in this way, since praying for such a person is a command of Christ Himself? For even if Medicine grows of its own accord without being asked, and bursts forth from the earth without us worrying about it at all, what use is it if it stays in the soil, if we are ignorant of it? Or how would it help if we held it in our hands but had no knowledge of where to apply it?

<margin>Medicine is a gift from God.</margin>
<margin>The opinion of the Nations regarding Medicine.</margin>
Therefore, we must pray. If we do otherwise, we shall never learn medicine through any righteousness of our own. If we do not learn it in this manner, we shall never restore any sick person through it. Indeed, the <term>Nations</term><note>Refers to non-Christians, specifically "Gentiles" or "Pagans" in the worldview of the time.</note>, as well as the Tartars, the Muslims, etc., claim to possess it by right of inheritance, as a brute logic seems to dictate nothing else to them.

<margin>Physicians should acknowledge the mercy of God.</margin>
But we who have given our name to Christ, having condemned those others, freely profess that we possess Medicine entirely out of mercy, and by no means out of our own righteousness. The Nations think in a pagan way, being persuaded that these things happen entirely out of an inviolable constitution and order of nature—things which God actually arranged and granted out of singular love. Christians, however, understand more "Christianly," confessing that nature itself does not help, nor does man have command over it, but that God the Best and Greatest has, out of singular mercy, bestowed such a <term>dowry</term><note>Latin: "dotem." Paracelsus views the healing properties of nature as a marriage gift from God to humanity.</note> upon nature. Thus, the art and the teacher is not man, but God Himself, who out of His immense love and mercy provides and bestows Medicine upon all.

If we now acknowledge and profess that it flows down from God, who, I ask, would contradict that it is fitting for us not only to accept it with great affection and love, but also to dispense it and distribute it to our neighbor with that same love and mercy with which God looked upon us? For just as the mercy and grace of God is never idle, but works continually and perpetually in deeds of love, so it is entirely right and pious for us to hold and follow the divine footsteps more swiftly than the Rhine or the Nile. And just as fire works in wood, so we too should work unceasingly in these matters, and thus it is fitting to look into and learn all things with great care.

<margin>The heavy duty of the Physician.</margin>
And so let all things be directed to this: that we think nothing is available from the man himself. For what the Physician does is by no means the work of the Physician himself. It is incumbent upon him that on the Day of Judgment he render a precise account of his office, whether he distributed it with the same measure by which he received it. For concerning the <term>talent</term><note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> received, each person must pay back their own interest.

<margin>Medicine is equal to the Physician's heart.</margin>
The practice of this art is located in the heart. If your heart is fraudulent, your Medicine is likewise fraudulent. If the heart is upright, the Medicine is also upright. And the lot of Physicians here is the same as that of the Prophets, of whom some were true and others were false. You shall act entirely faithfully in the office received from God.

<margin>What is the Physician's office?</margin>
As for the things you have from yourself, conduct yourself in them according to your own judgment. But now, your duty is to know all diseases with all their accidents. Here, however, I propose only one <term>movement</term><note>Latin: "motum." In early medicine, diseases were often described as types of internal motions or disturbances.</note>, namely the <term>Falling Sickness</term><note>Latin: "Caducum." Epilepsy.</note>, for the sake of knowing and curing which we ought never to rise from our bended knees. But what is this fraud and madness of ours in medicine, that we usually know least of all these diseases, which are the most serious and difficult? While on the contrary, those which heal on their own, we treat more carefully and arrogantly, and we cannot spread enough praises about those cured cases. Meanwhile, regarding those diseases through which the glory of God was to be preached—such as fevers, epidemic delusions, and the like—we do not understand even the smallest part. In these cases, we often turn to lies, proclaiming them to be incurable; yet with this word, we proclaim nothing but our own lies and disgrace.

<header>SECTION I.</header>
<sig>Kkk</sig>

...reveal these limbs.

<margin>What the effect of mercy is</margin>
Furthermore, in this place, this concluding point regarding Mercy must be held: If we are merciful and inclined from the heart toward the sick, we learn and progress entirely through that love and charity. If these are absent, we learn nothing at all. And even though our grandfathers and great-grandfathers may have learned through that charity and recorded their progress in books, we cannot rejoice in those writings for our own sake, because all things are still established in the hand of God. Even if I had grasped all the arts of the whole world and completed all their works, and described every single thing precisely in a book or volume, I would still have taught no one anything, nor would any of you have accomplished what I performed. Since, therefore, the Master of Medicine is not a man, you will by no means be able to save yourself with that excuse if you say, "No one taught me those things," or "I read that nowhere," or "nothing about these things has been handed down in writing." For the heathens also shroud themselves in this pretext. But to a Christian, it is known that medicine flows entirely from mercy—so much so that mercy itself is the Physician. If mercy is great, the Physician is also great. If charity is great, the work of the Physician is also great.

<margin>Mercy itself is the Physician.</margin>
If, therefore, love and mercy make a physician industrious (since these act like fire in wood, and bestow both art and experience, along with other necessary things for both), the Physician will surely see to it that he thrusts and pushes himself toward charity by force and effort. Having given this advice, I now propose this disease, the **Falling Sickness** <note>original: "Caducum"; a historical term for epilepsy</note>, so that the physician may be moved and swayed by the one who presents such a sad and pitiable spectacle to his eyes. Let him consider his duty within himself: that he is bound to heal and restore this person, whom God has cast before his sight as a fountain of misery, so that through this restoration, the praise and glory of God may be heaped up and spread more widely. Let the Physician not say, like the ghastly Satan, "*It is impossible*"; but let him place a greater and more certain trust in God, and know that God has established and provided his own medicines for each and every disease, which it is your task to track down and recognize in the manner we have described. If your heart were upright and faithful, surely before your arts failed you through ignorance, the very herbs and roots in which the powers you need lie hidden would offer themselves to you of their own accord and speak with you. But if, driven to despair and becoming a fugitive from the aforementioned school, you place your trust and protection in human instruction, then even the things you hold in your hand will fall silent.

<margin>Every disease has its own remedies.</margin>
<margin>Even the most cruel diseases must be attacked by the Physician.</margin>
For although it is an arduous and sad thing that God inflicts such a formidable disease upon us, the Physician must not despair in the face of it.

You see clearly from this, kind readers, what the reason and purpose of this Preface of mine is: namely, that I may cry out to you with just indignation and commiseration, because for so many centuries past, such trust and hope in God—and such charity and faithfulness toward one's neighbor—has not flourished among physicians in general. They have not weighed such a grave and atrocious disease more sharply in their minds, nor described or cured it with greater truth and severity.

<margin>A reproof of Physicians.</margin>
What a great stain is burned into the entire medical faculty because (I will remain silent now about that violent disease, the falling sickness) they have so far made so little progress in art and truth that they have not even been able to investigate the true causes of toothaches, or cure that so frequent evil with suitable remedies? What else shall we say of this, except that they have pursued this one thing with the worst example: to provide a fertile harvest for their kitchens with their lies, or to dazzle the minds and eyes of all who consult them with ornamented nonsense. From these things, Reader, it is now clearer to you than the midday sun with what benefit and profit you might call upon these Physicians, who, with so many cunning pretexts and machinations of words, openly betray their desperate ignorance and wickedness at once. For all these things ought to be certain, discovered, and explored beyond any doubt by a true and genuine Physician.

<margin>What kind of Physician.</margin>
For the Physician has tasted of that banquet to which the invited guests did not appear. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Great Banquet in Luke 14, where guests made excuses to avoid attending.</note> Beware, therefore, of saying that you have bought a yoke of oxen; beware of saying that business weighs upon you in your village. For only those who are not worthy of the prepared banquet use these excuses, saying they have read none of these things, or that nothing has been written about this or that.

Impostor physicians cry out such diversions everywhere, pretending that they find nothing handed down in books about this or that—though books are things meant for burning, while true Physicians are not. Their fate, therefore, is the same as that of those virgins who had poured out their oil. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25.</note> Now truly, Reader, that heart must be made of stone and iron which, at the sight of a patient so miserable (whether he be Jew or Turk), does not take up a serious thought about providing help and aid. Yet these men, despairing at such a sight, are not moved or stirred in the slightest. However, everything I explain more fully in this place, I prescribe for this end: that you may strive to administer your duty sincerely and with truth, and that you may know and be able to perform what is proper to your calling. May you not fail in help or knowledge in the gravest diseases—for whose sake the Physician was chiefly created by God—but with a ready and strong hand, may you solemnize and soothe the distress of the sick.

<margin>Remedies are created even for the most serious diseases.</margin>
For not only for a cough, or a fever, or a catarrh, but also for the falling sickness and other more savage diseases, remedies have been entirely established and fitted by God. Therefore, no physician could say with any face or conscience that this disease is incurable. For a speech of that kind is witness that such a transgressor atrociously slanders both God our creator and the creature itself in all its virtues. Thus, he is nothing but a pure and simple "kitchen physician," <note>original: "medicum culinarium"; a pejorative for a doctor motivated only by food and profit</note> who grows arrogant over curing those diseases which otherwise would have subsided on their own, without any medicine added.

From all of which you Physicians ought finally to see...

He asserts that God has provided a remedy for every ailment, including the most severe, if the physician is spiritually prepared to find it.</summary>

<page-num>662</page-num>

# ON THE FALLING SICKNESS.

<margin>Why was medicine created?</margin>
Know that Medicine was not created for your greed, your pride, your insolence, nor for your lovers and little nephews, etc., but rather for the purpose of securing the health of the sick. For who anywhere is more sick and afflicted, or who is ever in greater need of the help of Medicine, than one who is struck down by the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "caduco"; a historical term for epilepsy, so named because the sufferer falls to the ground during a seizure</note> or a similar disease? Nor do I speak here only of this present disease, but also of others which are of the same sort. For the more grave and violent a disease is, the greater is the necessity for medicine.

<margin>Are no diseases incurable?</margin>
Meanwhile, regarding diseases of this kind, you hang this "ivy" <note>An "ivy bush" was a traditional sign hung outside a tavern; here, the author suggests physicians use the claim of "incurability" as a sign or advertisement for their own limited business</note> upon your houses: that they are lethal, and that they are incurable. By this word, what are you doing other than slandering the great <term>secrets of nature</term> <note>original: "arcana naturae"; the hidden inner workings or healing powers of the natural world</note> and the mysteries of created things? On the contrary, let every Physician know for certain that in sudden diseases—such as apoplexy, the falling sickness, and the like—Medicine is not one bit weaker than it is in a toothache or other light ailments, which are the only ones you "experts" have the courage to tackle.

<margin>The glory of God from difficult things.</margin>
And yet, from the cure of chronic diseases, the praise and glory of God shines forth more greatly than from the healing of the slightest ones. For there is no disease so savage and monstrous that God has not established a medicine to oppose it, so that His wonders might shine forth all the more clearly. Therefore, do not lose heart in the least, but invade any disease whatsoever with a fearless breast, quite differently than you have done until now. Therefore, allow yourselves to be taught; act so that you may learn. Let this matter not be a joke to you, nor should you despair of the perception of Medicine.

<margin>Of what kind and from where are the writings of physicians?</margin>
For just as remedies emerge from the hidden depths of the disease, so too do the remedies themselves arise and spring forth. But let no one trust too much in "Scripture" <note>Here referring to traditional medical textbooks rather than the Bible</note>; for it is not only imperfect, but it even provides the occasion for all kinds of despair—a thing surely devised by Satan, not by God.

I cannot at all deny that many Recipes, both compound and simple, have been written down, whose secrets and mysteries I would not dare to reject. But I wish to God that these had never fallen, by some evil fate, into the style of **Avicenna**, **Galen**, **Rhazes**, or **Mesue**, but had remained as they first came forth from nature. If that were so, the affliction of the falling sickness would not lie so violently upon us. But Satan and the **Leviathan** <note>A biblical sea monster representing chaos or evil</note> have corrupted them, and through false Physicians have set them up as the "lights" <note>likely referring to "Lumina," a common title for medical or pharmaceutical guidebooks of the era</note> of the apothecaries. Away with those lights! For he whose eyes have been gouged out can still see much more sharply than the eyes of those very pharmacists.

<margin>The Holy Spirit is not effective in only one person.</margin>
Meanwhile, the obstacle to the art is this: they think that the Holy Spirit flourished only in **Avicenna**, **Galen**, **Mesue**, etc., and that the same Spirit cannot exercise its power in other Physicians as well. Surely these men are detestable apostates and transgressors. Tell me finally, oh you followers of Avicenna and Galen! In what line, in what Recipe anywhere among those authors, do you catch the scent of the Holy Spirit? Oh, you fanatics! Is this the extent of your skill in discerning the Holy Spirit: that you think a passing crow is a dove?

<margin>The sign of the Holy Spirit's presence. A sharp rebuke of the Physician.</margin>
Rather, recognize the writing of the Holy Spirit by these signs: *the sick are healed, the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, those with the falling sickness rise up.* <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 11:5, applying Christ's miracles to the ideal work of a physician</note> Dare to do something, and strive to emulate such things from the teachings of your writers, if you can. But what can you do, you wretch? Not even enough to coax a rumble from a belly, or to quiet a toothache, or to heal a bleary eye—and meanwhile, you thunder out I know not what pompous sermons about graver matters. This is surely the "Holy Spirit" by which you are ruled. I will say it in one word: all your arrogance is mere despair and a seduction away from the true arts which God has bestowed upon us from heaven. For God did not create the Physician for the sake of your toothache, or your enema bag, or your pills, but much more for the epileptic, for the leper, and for others like them. Does this pill taste bitter to you?

Step forward at last, you masked Physician, and show yourself to be looked at. For who are you, you most "faithful" **Judas**? That having been reborn through holy Baptism, you fall away from its virtue—that is, away from the Holy Spirit—as if He were entirely dead and had no medicine left? It would be much better for you to have a millstone tied around your neck with chains and be sunk deeper than Crete itself lies, than for you to so foully contaminate the secrets of nature with your stinking trifles, and to testify to a scarcity where the greatest abundance clucks <note>original: "glocit"; like a hen calling out</note>. Because you yourself, an idiot, are ignorant of these things, do you think it is right that everyone else should also be ignorant of them, and simply believe you, and not investigate the truth further for themselves? Now, see and take notice, all you readers everywhere: how great a tyranny the raging Devil exercises through these men, while they so stubbornly stand in the way, lest the wretched sick seek out and hunt for their health further than the lies of these men allow? Now, if God should repay us according to the measure of our mercy and charity, how, I ask, could He bestow the art upon these impostors? Rather, God clearly deprives them of His charity for its own sake, so that they now have nothing left but frauds and impositions—even though, being ignorant of true art and experience, they are nonetheless honored by the unskilled. Medicine must be handled entirely with a Christian soul, not a Heathen one. And in this way, you will turn out learned. But as for God sometimes bestowing knowledge upon Heathens as well: who knows whom and where He has His own? He Himself fulfills charity, as is evident in the Sun, which shines without distinction upon enemies and friends, those to be saved and those to be damned alike. But you, impostor, if you have obtained knowledge and art, you exercise it in your own way—that is, like a market-peddler—and you mix your frauds into it, and you deck the matter out with such a dye that you seem to offer pure gold, when meanwhile you sell nothing but adulterated ginger and saffron. Suffer it, therefore, that I sing this truth to you.

I know well enough that you are busy opposing me here with many arguments. But they will find no place. You see, of course, that Baptism is denied by God to no one, but is conferred upon all who are in need, as it stands as the true entrance to the blessed life.

<margin>God gives gifts without distinction.</margin>
If, therefore, those things which regard eternity are offered to all, why should He not also bestow bodily things upon the needy just as much as Baptism? For these are lighter than the eternal things themselves. And what finally do you think of these things, oh you impostors and despairers! Does not God Himself also baptize with such a Baptism? Or does man alone have the power of baptizing? And has God reserved no power for Himself?

<margin>God baptizes with the Holy Spirit.</margin>
