# TRACTATE FOURTH.
## *On the Cure of Metallic Disease.*
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>The work reveals the craftsman. Experience is far from trifles.</margin>
**H**ENCEFORTH, therefore, I must no longer speak with the learned and the philosophers, but with experience itself. I must consider the benefit of the men who work with metals, so that I may drive the metallic disease away from them. Now, it is the nature and habit of any skilled and experienced man not to speak many empty words with another expert. For among experts, the focus is on the cure of the disease, and that is done with few words. For words and speeches do not cure diseases, nor do they please the sick man. Furthermore, such is the condition of experience that its works may be understood and perfected by anyone without nonsense and long-winded tales. Therefore, we must attend further to practice, so that it may defend itself by its own works and win trust for medicine. For the works are so clear that they require very little dispute. What sort of works they are will follow. Nevertheless, let <margin>The discoveries of the youth are no obstacle.</margin> everyone’s experience be free. Who cannot find the end of medicine, especially since the school of medicine is, by its own creation, infinite?

### CHAPTER II.

IN the matter of metallic diseases, therefore, these articles are to be considered and organized into chapters in order.
First, how they may be prevented from those mineral spirits, so that they do not infect their metallic miner, and how the miners might not be made subject to them.
Second, it is useful to know that in the progress of time, the limbs of a man—the lungs, liver, kidneys, stomach, intestines, etc., and however many <margin>Mineral spirits corrode the principal parts.</margin> parts the body has—are gnawed away by poisonous mineral spirits, and especially the principal organs, whence they tend toward putrefaction. Those things which are truly putrefied cannot be healed by the restoration and reintegration of the corrupt and consumed part. However, preservatives can be made so that the evil does not creep further, just as in <term>esthiomenic</term> <note>Corroding or "eating" ulcers.</note> and "wolf-like" ulcers.

Third, after the preservatives, follows the chapter on diet and its order, through which a man ought to guard himself, lest he give the mineral spirits an occasion to predominate over him.
Fourth, the physical cures and medicines driving away natural asthma are to be set down. For these are also the medicines for the metallic disease, as follows.
Fifth, concerning the handling of secret remedies, it follows (as has been said) how, namely, every good thing brings forth triple "pearls" to drive out triple evils.
Sixth follows the conclusion of the first book on metallic diseases.

## *On the Preservative of Youth.*
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>How the influence of the heavens may be turned away.</margin>
**A**CCEPT an example: it is the Heaven that infects us through the stars, as much as it is permitted to harm us, nor are we strong enough to resist it. For it is not placed in our hand—that is, we cannot forestall the influences, just as we cannot turn away the snow or the rain. So also, we must leave the mineral spirits to leave their own impression freely. Nevertheless, a roof is held up against the rain, and a shade against the Sun; so also a "stove" is found through which the impression cannot penetrate, which you should understand thus: He who is not yet infected is preserved <margin>Description of the essence of tartar.</margin> by the essence of <term>tartar</term>, taken once every month and applied to stir up a sweat. Its composition is as follows:

| | |
|---|---|
| Take | Liquor of tartar, 2 ounces. |
| | Oil of <term>colcothar</term> <note>Iron(III) oxide, often derived from vitriol.</note>, 1 scruple. |
| | Purest <term>laudanum</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, a potent compound of opium and minerals.</note>, half a drachm. |

Let them be mixed. The dose is three grains. However, according to the reason of a healthy constitution, to offer it once in six months is also sufficient, which I leave to be weighed by a skilled physician. But "Pearl-matter" <note>original: "Perlatum"</note> surpasses this and all other things.

## *On the Other Preservative of Putrefaction.*
### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>What is Pearl-Calabrian Manna? Its powers.</margin>
**F**OR those, however, who have already fallen into putrefaction, <term>Calabrian Manna</term> <note>A sweet sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a mild laxative and restorative.</note> treated with pearls is exceedingly beneficial. Now, "Manna" is any sweetness that is extracted from any thing. And this Manna is from the species of Balsam: wherefore it also has this power, that it allows nothing to putrefy. By this manna, the body must be preserved lest it rot, and it alone resists those metallic putrefactions. Now, so that we may reveal that <margin>Species of Manna.</margin> Manna, it must be known that there is one in <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfuric acid or its sulfate salts.</note>, one in the nettle, and one in the Magnet. The mannas of these three are those balsams which preserve against these diseases of putrefaction, as has been said.
Manna of vitriol is made thus: Let its <margin>Manna of vitriol.</margin> phlegm be drawn away from the vitriol for so long until it becomes like sweet honey and inclines toward a purple color. Its dose is one drop in <term>Veronica water</term> <note>Water distilled from the Speedwell plant.</note>, daily.
The description of the Manna of Nettle is this: Let the nettle be <term>alcoholized</term> <note>Reduced to its finest essence or spirit.</note>, <margin>1. Manna of the nettle.</margin> afterwards let it be rectified in its own wateriness for so long by means of a <term>horse's belly</term> <note>A method of providing gentle, constant heat by burying the vessel in fermenting horse manure.</note> until an oiliness is seen, which should be separated from its dregs. Its dose is four drops daily, as above.
The extraction of the Manna of the Magnet is that it be reduced to <margin>2. Manna of the magnet.</margin> "alcohol" <note>Here meaning a very fine powder.</note> and stratified with steel filings in equal weight, and in a glass vessel with <term>lute</term> <note>A clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels.</note>...

# On the Manner of Diet.
## CHAPTER V.

<margin>How the metallic disease is produced.</margin>
Until now, it has been the custom of physicians to prescribe food and drink to men with the greatest diligence. This may be granted to them in those diseases which they understand; but here, in metallic diseases, that cannot be done. For here there is another "heaven"—not the exterior or upper heaven, but a heaven that is the earth itself. Therefore, you should know that every heaven has the power in its own kingdom to prescribe a diet. Thus, whatever is on the plain looks to its upper heaven; however, whatever is contained under the terrestrial heaven is compelled to direct its diet—that is, its food and drink—according to that very heaven. But since man was not born to nourish himself from the terrestrial heaven, but is closer to the plain, he maintains an exterior diet and preserves himself from the "exterior asthma" so that the "interior" ones do not join together. Therefore, he guards himself from those things that produce asthma, as enumerated in the previous tractate. And note here that heat, extinguished by water in the caverns of mountains, produces not an exterior, but an interior metallic disease; and so it is with others. But the diet in the mountains, which must be observed alongside the other, is this: that metallic men should strive, as much as possible, to salt their foods with that salt which is boiled and prepared from the "salt of the rock" <note>Saltpeter or rock salt</note> born in the mountains, just as common salt is processed. Similarly, in place of spices, let them use salt which is boiled in a similar way from alum; for it imparts no saltiness, but makes the food well-seasoned.
<margin>Salts and spices of mineral men.</margin>
I only wish to suggest that salts and spices lie hidden in minerals more than I am expressing here, which I leave to the expert to find better examples.

# On the Cure of Asthma Above and Below Ground.
## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>The cure of asthma.</margin>
If, therefore, nature is to be considered above all things in these matters, and these things must be done through her, it is necessary that we do not only accept writers and their plausible interpretations <note>original: "glossas"</note>, but that we also further explore nature, from which true doctrine and instruction flow. We find, therefore, that in asthma only *arcana* <note>Concentrated medicinal virtues or "secrets" extracted from substances.</note> are to be considered, and not complex mixtures. Therefore, since man is ordered under these arcana, they must also be used in metallic disease. For although the "heaven" is different, yet because man is from the upper world, he can defend himself through such arcana so that not even metallic spirits can resist, provided that the natural arcanum is directed toward the mineral condition. And although minerals have their own proper medicine, just as the plains have their own medicine, yet man sustains himself from both sides and inclines to either side,
<margin>Man is overcome by arcana.</margin>
<margin>Sowbread water is diaphoretic.</margin>
since he subjects himself to both habitations. Now, **sowbread water** <note>original: "aqua panis porcini"; water distilled from Cyclamen.</note> is a singular arcanum which corrects all non-putrefying asthma. For nothing benefits the lungs better than if they are reduced to a diaphoretic <note>Sweat-inducing</note> nature, etc. Understand this also regarding the liver, stomach, and other organs. For if they can be preserved in a state of diaphoresis <note>Healthy perspiration or "breathing" through the skin/membranes</note>, no mineral spirit will harm them; and if any damage has been brought in, they expel it through that diaphoretic force. For whatever sweats will not be clung to by mucilage, resin, or tartar—three things which the sweat-inducing force does not tolerate. And this is true not only of the said organs, but also in a diaphoretic bladder and a diaphoretic region of the kidneys: no stone or sand is collected there. This diaphoretic power, here very briefly described, is treated more widely in other places, and it can do greater things, as those skilled in nature know. Enough has been said about the institution of the cure, even if the practice is not fully detailed. What must further be known in the heaven or the mineral world follows next.

# On the Cure of Three Species of Metallic Disease from Arcana.
## CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The utility of sweat in metallic diseases.</margin>
But to proceed to the minerals of the interior earth, it must similarly be known that there is a single foundation: that the injured organs be reduced to a sudorific <note>Sweat-producing</note> power; that is, that they should sweat just as the skin does in a bath when it opens itself. For if they are encrusted with tartar like a wine vessel, or covered with viscous bitumen, or hardened by alkali, none of these will henceforth stick to the skin if a sufficient sweat emerges from them. Therefore, one must only consider the diaphoretic nature of those organs which are covered by these three: **Realgar**, **Antimony**, or **Alkali**. <margin>What Realgar is.</margin>**Realgar** is soot. <margin>What Antimony is.</margin>**Antimony** is mucilage—or that you may understand it better, *sirnisium* <note>A Paracelsian term for a specific mineral secretion or "slime."</note>. **Alkali** is tartar. These are the three things with which the spiritual organs are burdened. Therefore note, that from metals three-fold **Pearly Arcana** <note>original: "Arcana perlata"; highly refined or distilled essences.</note> are extracted, any of which retains its diaphoretic virtue, which alone pertains to the three said species—namely, so that the organs of the spirit may be led into their own proper humidity, through which the three things mentioned above are washed away and directed to the exit through their own "cleansing channels" <note>original: "emunctoria"</note>. Since, therefore, the metallic Apothecary has no other species except its own metals, such a cure is taken from there. <margin>The resolution of gold and other metals into their three first principles, which are the pearly arcana.</margin>Let vitriol and sulfur be extracted from gold by the press, and let its "first matter" be exhibited, just like liquefied quicksilver, of a color almost purple, not wetting the hand, until it is resolved by itself in the moisture. Just as you have heard concerning gold, so also in the remaining six metals you have a single process, but under different preparations, as is sufficiently treated in the *Death of Things* <note>Referring to the process of alchemical "mortification" or breaking down substances.</note>. For this reason, there is no need to repeat those things here.

# BOOK II

Thus, everything in the first three treatises has been correctly explained. # THE SECOND BOOK
## ON METALLIC DISEASES
### First Treatise.

### *On the diseases of smelters, refiners, silver-purgers, and other mineral craftsmen.*

#### *On the things that harm such men, and first concerning the smelters of ores. Chapter I.*

<margin>The fragile body in the separation of minerals harms the man who is not fixed.</margin>
**E**very thing that is cast into the fire has a twofold consideration within itself; one by reason of the **fixed body**, the other by reason of the **fragile body** <note>In alchemy, "fixed" substances resist fire, while "fragile" or "fugitive" substances evaporate or transform into smoke.</note>. There is no need to speak of the fixed body here. For nothing harmful comes out of fixed bodies; indeed, they remain in the fire without damage to the working man. But the matter and purpose of this book will be concerning the fragile body, which is always joined to the fixed, and that alone is distinguished and found in the fire. For through fire, the separation of the fugitive and the constant takes place. Since, therefore, man now brings these things to separation, those things which happen to him in this work must be noted. For fragile things are not without poison and malice. For it is necessary that every good thing we wish to obtain be separated from the evil, and this is its condition: that it is by no means acquired happily and without pain. For the enemy is so powerful around the good that whoever wishes to obtain the good is compelled to expect evil as well. Nevertheless, man seeks metals so anxiously, having no regard for the injury to his body, and pursues these things so boldly that he casts himself, as it were, into the midst of enemies, so that he sees enemies all around him, and yet he remains for the sake of that good which lies hidden in that poison. For everyone who melts down ores sees the smoke of the ores and knows that it is poisonous, and that it is...

<margin>Fire separates the fugitive from the fixed.</margin>
<margin>Good is extracted with danger. How great is the audacity of men regarding metals.</margin>

# CHAPTER II.

<margin>Sulfur and Mercury mixed in the air lie hidden in metallic things.</margin>
**T**he fragile body, therefore, is of such a nature that it contains three bodies within itself: namely, **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** <note>The "Tria Prima" or Three Primes of Paracelsus, believed to be the fundamental components of all matter.</note>. These three are separated in the fire, and although the fixed body also consists of these same three, yet in the fixed they are not separated. When, therefore, the fragile body tends toward separation in the fire, a part of it falls back into Salt, that is, ash and slag. **It is not my intention to write about this.** Furthermore, the body of sulfur and the body of mercury: these two are the subject of this book. Truly, the body of sulfur is fire; for otherwise nothing burns except sulfur. But the body of mercury is the smoke which departs from the fire. These two bodies inflict their diseases upon men who handle fire. First, however, it must be considered here what that body is which is cast into the fire: for from it arise the species of fire and smoke. For every metal gives its own fire and its own smoke. For the smoke of **Zwitter** <note>original: "Zwitteri"; an old German mining term for tin-ore (cassiterite) or mixed ores.</note> is one thing, that of copper-stone another, and that of lead ore another; and although only sulfur burns and only mercury smokes, yet their species are various, just as the ashes and slags are various.

<margin>What is the body of sulfur?</margin>
<margin>Burning comes from sulfur alone. What is the body of Mercury?</margin>
<margin>Every metal gives its own smoke and fire. Zwitter etc.</margin>
Experience and association give the knowledge of these things. Hereafter, therefore, only that which burns and that which smokes must be treated, in this manner: Every fire has its own air, which is innate to it and arises from the sulfur. That air has a nature like the air in which there is an **impression** <note>An "impression" in this context refers to a characteristic quality or "signature" imprinted on the element.</note>. This impression arises from the sulfurous ore. For just as a lily sends out a scent, which is a natural impression inseparable from the body, so there is also a similar odor in sulfur, which indeed is called "air." From which it follows that those who labor in the fire draw in that air which comes out of the fire, and not that which is of the world—just as when a mist rises, which is also a peculiar kind of air.

<margin>The air of sulfur is inhaled in place of common air.</margin>

## ON METALLIC DISEASES.

<margin>The Salamander lives by the power of fire from the air.</margin>
Know, therefore, from these things that fragile bodies emit a peculiar kind of air within the element of fire. A person can live from this air just as well as from common air, as is demonstrated by **Salamanders** <note>In Renaissance natural philosophy, the salamander was a mythical creature believed to live within and feed upon fire.</note>. These are not sustained by the same air that humans live on, but rather by that air which is specific to fire. It is from the virtue of this element that the Salamander has its respiration, for it has no life outside of fire. Understand, then, that from a sulfurous ore a peculiar element of air is born; and although this air exists only within the fire and not outside it, nevertheless, when the fire spreads its heat, it also emits the property of that air, just as a lily emits its scent. For whatever can naturally be said about the scent of a lily must also be understood regarding the heat of fire, insofar as it contains the mixed element of air.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Mercury flees the fire.</margin>
Similarly, understand further regarding the body of **Mercury** <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Mercury" refers not just to the liquid metal, but to the principle of volatility and fluidity in all matter.</note>, which remains neither in sulfur nor in salt, but flees the fire. Therefore, know that when it desires to depart, it becomes smoke. This is caused by destruction, which happens through fire. It is the nature of Mercury to be so changed by fire that it becomes unrecognizable to everyone. For this purpose, we discuss here how this smoke gathers itself together. From this, it can be known that it is not reduced to nothing, nor does it vanish. For when the fire, sulfur, and salt have "lost" it, it then moves to colder places and congeals.

<margin>All smoke is Mercury.</margin>
The species of the matter is recognized from that substance. For every smoke is Mercury. Since it is recognized and found, and does not vanish but remains, it can also be known from the substance itself what kind of poison it is: thus there are various types of smoke from the metal-workers' shops arising from their ores,

<margin>Various metallic soots. Mixed smoke or mineral Mercury is inhaled.</margin>
such as **arsenic**, **realgar** <note>A red arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, **orpiment** <note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, and many similar things along with their species. Now, since we know that this smoke is Mercury, and similarly that this Mercury is arsenic, realgar, and orpiment, we must also know how evil those poisons are, and with what danger they seek our lives, for their very nature is unhealthy. For this smoke, before it even sticks to a surface, is no less effective a poison than after it has adhered. Thus we see clearly that the air and the smoke become one, coming together into an indivisible mixture.

<margin>As the air is encountered, so it is inhaled.</margin>
But since man is forced to use the air, he is undoubtedly also forced to take in this Mercury. It is impossible for humans to separate the air. Rather, in whatever state it is joined, in that state it must be inhaled.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Mineral Mercury is established by the stars and produces fevers.</margin>
But this question must also be introduced: Since it is impossible for man to separate the air, and whatever the fire expels into the air remains in the air—for the air does not consume that smoke—since the Mercury remains, it is attracted by the upper stars, from the earth into the upper region, just as the needle of a compass turns toward the northern magnet. When the stars hold that fugitive Mercury, expelled by the fire, with them—having held it even before it was fully prepared and "cooked"—they then prepare it anew and turn it into a constellation along with an "impression." This impression is a union and the mother of feverish plague. But since it is not my purpose to declare those things here, but only those pertaining to men who handle fire, I leave their fuller explanation to their own proper books. Furthermore, since the smoke along with the air provides breath to the man, one must consider the evil that arises from such inhaled breath, which is nothing other than a "sinning" Mercury. Note here, therefore, a two-part division. True air performs its proper duty, unhindered by Mercury. Just as if someone's water is tainted, and it is drunk to quench thirst, the water fulfills its duty and quenches the thirst without the help of the thing tainting it: so the same must be understood regarding this air, which is separated from the evil, but within the man himself—that is, in the lungs. This separation produces several "final matters"; that is, the Mercury enters, and in the lung, the sides and the region of the lung dry out over time: after its own specific drying process, the Mercury finally adheres to the lung.

<margin>Inhaled Mercury is digested into a final matter in the lung.</margin>
And since the lung and its region are compared to the **Horse's Belly** <note>term: "Horse's Belly" (Latin: *venter equinus*). In alchemy, this refers to a gentle, moist, fermenting heat, traditionally achieved by burying a vessel in a heap of horse manure. Paracelsus uses it here as a metaphor for the internal heat of the body's digestive and transformative processes.</note> in all its properties, it is necessary for the Mercury of the "Horse's Belly" to be transmuted into another form than it would otherwise take in the smelting shop. Just as you see with food, which is beautiful and pleasant, but when it comes into the stomach, it acquires a loathsome alteration, which the "Horse's Belly" of the stomach alone performs; and if it then passes into the intestines, it takes on another change caused by the "Horse's Belly" of the intestines.

<margin>The Horse's Belly is the digestive power.</margin>
<margin>The Horse's Belly transforms things.</margin>
Therefore, just as such digestions are various and manifold in the whole body, so also a specific one exists in the lung.

### CHAPTER V.

It is fitting to speak more of these things. After the Mercury has come into the lung, it chooses a wall there to which it adheres, as chance or order brings it. One need not inquire much about the place of adhesion. In **Anatomy**, however, such **sublimations** <note>The process of a solid turning into gas and then back to solid; here, Paracelsus describes the metallic vapors re-solidifying inside the body.</note> are found in many ways, which it is useful for every physician to learn.

<margin>The type of matter resulting from the digestion of Mercury.</margin>
When Mercury has entered the lung, its "Horse's Belly" works in this way: It putrefies one Mercury into an oiliness or fat; another into a spermatic slime; another into a "false" matter; another into a gum-like resolution; another into a mucilage of Fenugreek; another into a leathery or horny glue, and many other similar kinds. It must be known, therefore, once such putrefaction has occurred, what kind of matter the "Horse's Belly" of the lung has reduced the Mercury into. For every thing that comes into a region and is not the food of that region cannot be digested.

<margin>Indigestion is the mother of putrefaction.</margin>
Therefore, a putrefaction of the "Horse's Belly" follows, whether thick or thin, or in whatever way it can happen.

It should also be noted whether that putrefied resolution resides in the windpipe or in its sides. For in that region it often happens that such resolutions, by the sharpness of their putrefaction, become so penetrating that the putrefied liquids pass through the pores and tend toward the regions of the kidneys; because of this penetration, that final matter is found in the urine sometimes,

# SECOND TREATISE.
## BOOK II.
### On the Diseases produced by the first three metals for their craftsmen.

### I.

<margin>Which are the semi-fixed bodies.</margin>
**B**ut to finish the matters we have begun, just as it was said regarding the fragile body that occurs in the separation of good from evil, so also must we speak of the evil that has hidden and insinuated itself into the "good" in such a way that it cannot be separated. For the smoke of metals—as well as their fire and dross—are the only three fragile bodies, as has been said; but they are called "semi-fixed" because of the fixed body to which they are united. Thus, in all metals, there exists a semi-fixed Salt, a semi-fixed Sulfur, and a semi-fixed Mercury. From these three it follows that the fixed nature is dragged away and removed from all metals, and through these three, any metal whatever is consumed. For these three are the death of metals. That which glows is Sulfur; that which smokes is Mercury; the remainder is dross <note>original: *scoria*; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting.</note>. <margin>Metals already separated still provide three fragile bodies.</margin> Since they are so closely related to "fixation" <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable in fire.</note>, they are worn down by a metallic and seemingly fixed consumption; this happens so that the three fragile bodies, in the progress of time through fire, consume the metals. <margin>Gold and silver which do not eject dross or rust.</margin> Although gold and silver do not behave like the rest of the metals—that is, they do not give off dross or rust—nevertheless know that even if the eyes do not see the salt of gold and silver, a reduction is still perceived in their weight. This reduction is visible in copper and iron because it happens in a coarse manner. In gold and silver, however, the subtraction is subtle, yet in the end, the whole is consumed in this way. The sulfurous body is consumed in the fire. For the "flowers" <note>Sublimated vapors that collect as powder.</note> appearing in the ash-pit and the closing sparks or flashes come from the sulfur within the gold and silver; they represent the consumption of the metals, and such fiery colors appear according to their sulfurous nature. The body of Mercury flees in the manner of smoke. For any thing lying in the fire gives off its smoke, according to the condition of its metallic fixation. Thus, know that while metals are glowing and being treated in the fire, such sulfurous and Mercurial spirits depart from them—but so subtly that without diligent observation, they are not felt.

<margin>The power and nature of the metallic spirit.</margin>
Their power in the lung cannot be recognized as easily as the smoke of the metal-shops. Because these spirits are so closely allied to "fixation," the **Horse's Belly** <note>Here referring to the human digestive/metabolic power.</note> cannot overcome them. Therefore, they are themselves the "ultimate matter." They penetrate the lung and those parts like a <term>tincture</term> <note>In this context, a "tincture" is a powerful chemical essence that dyes or transforms the substance it enters.</note>, which is so entirely absorbed into that body that they become one, and the body assumes the property of the tincture—just as copper receives its color from calamine <note>The process of making brass.</note>. Because of this, it is thereafter governed by the property of the calamine, even though the copper remains copper. For the calamine cannot corrode it. But when the lung is "dyed" by this tincture, it cannot resist; rather, the tincture corrodes it gradually, just as nitric acid <note>original: *aqua fortis*.</note> consumes linen cloths. A similar thing happens to the other members that catch the tincture, namely the regions surrounding the lungs and the stomach. Furthermore, this metallic spirit penetrates the body and works in those places where it fixes its seat, as I said above. <margin>Various diseases arise from the spirits of metals.</margin> For this reason, many diseases happen here which should not be categorized except as has been said: they must be recognized by their corroding nature. They have various and wonderful signs which cannot be written down because of their variety, and they are so manifold in their species that only long and great experience can teach and indicate them. This, however, the physician must know: that all the diseases of such men must be referred to a metallic nature. <margin>Tinctures of sulfur and Mercury: what kind of medical knowledge of tinctures is required.</margin> For the tincture of these two—Sulfur and Mercury—is so dry and parched that it consumes all natural Humors, Qualities, and temperaments, and dyes them all into its own nature. Therefore, it is fitting for the physician to be skilled in "tinctures" and not in "Humors." For although various ailments may concur here—such as dropsy, jaundice, arthritis, fever, etc.—nevertheless they are all governed by metallic tinctures against their native condition. Therefore, there is a need here for the physician to be somewhat more skilled than has been their common custom until now. For metallic diseases are not diseases of the Humors, etc.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Mercury and sulfur of metals are not digested like minerals.</margin>
**S**ince, therefore, there is a "fragility" in fixed metals which is not as light as the former kind, know that those who work with metals fall upon enemies that are indeed more subtle and penetrating than the previous ones. Therefore, it must be further noted that because of the subtlety...

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>By what means metallic spirits are attracted. On metallic disease.</margin>
**T**hese spirits, therefore, cannot be separated by man. For while people move in the air, they also move within these spirits. Indeed, this air is drawn in not only through the channel of the lungs, but also through the nostrils. <margin>The brain needs air. Metallic spirits infect the brain and transform old diseases into new ones.</margin> The most subtle part of that which is drawn through the nostrils does not flow back into the throat, but seeks higher ground and ascends into the brain and its region. For you must know this: the brain requires air just as much as the lung does; and just as was said of the lung, so you should understand regarding the brain. Whence also in the brain, putrefactions, **Tartars**, **Realgars**, **Soots**, etc., are made and generated. For the nostrils were made for this purpose: to be a channel through which the more subtle air passes into the brain. The coarser air descends into the lungs. And even if the nose were blocked and did not transmit the breath, the air would still ascend from the throat through the internal nostrils. From this, therefore, arises Headache <note>original: *Cephalalgia*.</note>, abscesses of the head, Mania, and other diseases of the head, as well as paralysis, lethargy, twisting of the mouth <note>original: *tortura oris*; likely Bell's Palsy or stroke symptoms.</note>, etc.

<margin>Mineral paralysis, etc.</margin>

Although these diseases show and manifest themselves according to the common description, they are nevertheless like "white copper" or brass—that is to say, if the tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a subtle, transforming essence that gives a substance its specific properties, such as color or medicinal effect.</note> were absent, they would be those old and common diseases. But the tincture, which is not separated from them, gives them another name. Therefore, such a paralysis is not called simply "paralysis," but is called **Mineral Paralysis**. The same applies to mineral lethargy and other similar conditions. For as many diseases as are found in the "old nature" <note>Referring to traditional medicine or diseases of non-mineral origin.</note>, just as many metallic tinctures can exist.

<margin>Even the subtler mineral spirits enter the brain.</margin>
Furthermore, it cannot be denied that the same reasoning applies to the brain regarding those prior spirits found in metallic workshops. This is because among those spirits, there are many subtle ones that can mix with that subtle air which alone is suited to the brain. From this comes "brancha" <note>A hoarseness or throat ailment.</note>, phlegm, head colds, catarrh, and others. Just as has been said of the brain and lung, you may also expect such effects in the stomach itself. And although this matter could be argued against in many ways, the anatomy of the stomach demonstrates to the eye that soot, tartar, and realgars <note>Arsenic sulfide minerals, here referring to toxic mineral deposits in the body.</note>, as well as bitumens, mucilages, and other things listed above, break into the stomach along with the hidden descending air. These things can hardly be noticed without demonstration, nor can they be believed by bare reason alone.

## CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Which fumes each craftsman is subject to.</margin>
But to proceed in declaring these things more fully, moving from one craft to another: know that every trade falls into its own peculiar metallic spirit. For instance, those who work iron fall into the **spirit of iron**; those who heat copper fall into the **spirit of copper**, and so with the others. Those who work in brass fall into the **calamine** <note>Zinc ore used to make brass.</note> and **copper spirit**; so too those who work in "white and red" <note>Likely referring to silver and gold/copper alloys or stages of the alchemical work.</note> are cast into those metallic and tinctural spirits. Furthermore, there is no need to better describe or declare these spirits here, for that requires the further experience and skill of those craftsmen who work in metals. Thus, those who part the metal of silver perceive the fume of silver and lead, and the properties they possess. Roasters of silver breathe in only the fume of silver. Those who make minium <note>Red lead pigment.</note> breathe the fume of lead; those who make ceruse <note>White lead pigment.</note> draw in the sharpest fume of lead. For when a metal is destroyed <note>i.e., smelted or chemically broken down.</note>, it emits the strongest fume. Those who smelt antimony fall into an evil sulfurous and Mercurial fume. Those who smelt zinc fall into fourfold subtle fumes: copper, iron, tin, and the fume of immature *Zwitter* <note>original: *Zvvitteri*. A German mining term for "mixed" or "hybrid" ores, particularly tin-bearing rock.</note>. Those who prepare *Lazurium* <note>Lapis lazuli or azurite blue pigment.</note> are subject to the sharpest silver fume, or a spirit mixed with additives. Those who work with litharge <note>Lead monoxide.</note> fall into the worst pneumonia. Those who mine and handle cinnabar <note>Mercury sulfide.</note> fall into the spirit of quicksilver and sulfur. Understand the same for metallic trades: how they infect and attack their craftsmen and the "servants of Vulcan" <note>A poetic term for blacksmiths, smelters, and chemists.</note> in so many ways and paths. And the more refined or exquisite the art is cultivated, the more species and genera of enemies and symptoms are created. For if we do not use the fire with subtlety, it does not infect us subtly. But if we seek subtleties within it, then the fire finds much subtler poisons against us. For example, the **Stellio** <note>original: *Stellio*. A spotted lizard or newt, used here as a metaphor for a hidden danger that becomes aggressive when provoked.</note> crawls into its cavern and harms no one; but if we wish to seek many things within it, we must on the other hand expect many evils from it, even to the point that body and life are in danger before we learn from it what it does, etc. So it also happens to all those who delight and cheer themselves in the fire, that in the end, everything turns to grief. In these matters, the same thing happens as with "Epicurus’s pigs" <note>A classical idiom for those devoted to physical pleasure and gluttony.</note>, who, if they delight themselves too long in eating and drinking, are finally forced to breathe out their perceived pleasure in poverty and disease. Thus, there is no happiness without grief, etc.

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>The three seats of metallic diseases.</margin>
<margin>The brain, lung, and stomach are affected by metallic spirits.</margin>
Note, therefore, that (as has been said) there are three regions in the body in which these diseases arise: namely, the **brain**, the **lung**, and the **stomach**. It must also be known that those parts do not keep their evils within themselves, but send them further into the body. Therefore, mineral diseases must be investigated most diligently. For you see that if the brain suffers a mineral disease, the whole body suffers with it. For such is the nature of spirits, that they gnaw in a similar way to a worm in the finger. Such is the **Mercurial power**, that it erodes and stabs like burning coals wherever it has its center. And this twitching and gnawing is the cause of many symptoms, such as **Mania**, frenzy, etc. So it also happens that in the lung a longing <note>original: *orexis*. Usually meaning appetite, here likely a morbid craving or a specific type of irritation.</note> arises similar to a *paneritio* <note>original: *paneritio*. A whitlow or painful inflammation of the finger, used here metaphorically for internal inflammation.</note>. So too in the stomach, where Mercury perpetually gnaws and bites around the pit of the heart, just as if a biting worm lay there. But not only do those twitchings, gnawings, and stabbings occur, but many other species of diseases arise from this, whose names have not yet been found; for which reason this is not the place to list them. Let everyone, however, strive to have the diseases of the "old nature" well-known. Afterward, let him seek to investigate these mineral diseases through experience in those places where they reside. For from such exercise and experience, a physician emerges skilled and learned. For even if I were to put all diseases here, no one would understand them without the aforementioned experience.

<margin>To be learned not from books, but from experience. Experience is the seeker of truth.</margin>
If anyone wishes to experience these things, let him do so among those where they are found—that is, among the mineral-sick. For who could become excellent in experience from paper? Paper has this one unique property: it makes a man lazy and sleepy, yet at the same time arrogant and proud. For it teaches him to persuade himself of many things, and to fly without wings—all of which are contrary to the physician. Therefore, hurry toward experience; this is the best foundation, etc.

<margin>Three kinds of salts are to be understood. The utility of the spirit of salt within the body.</margin>

If not, it then penetrates to the brain and dissolves waste, mucus, and abscesses <note>The original Latin "apostemata" refers to any inflammatory swelling or gathering of "bad humors."</note>, lest they accumulate; it dries the head internally so that the heads of those men are healthy. If it reaches the lung, it dissolves those things within it which would produce a cough and distress; furthermore, it wards off incipient tumors in the lung.

<margin>The spirit of salt is like a balsam warding off putrefaction.</margin>
It is like a <term>balsam</term> <note>In early medicine, a "balsam" was a substance that preserved the body from decay or "putrefaction."</note>: for it allows nothing to rot, nothing to stick; whatever begins to coagulate and thicken in the form of air, that humid air dissolves. Likewise, if it descends into the stomach, it cleanses the same in its humidity, although that is not otherwise the nature of salt if it is taken by itself.

<margin>The essence of the spirit of salt is most subtle. The benefit of the spirit of vitriol.</margin>
However, the cause of these operations is that its highest essence, which lies hidden in the salt, is mixed with the air; it is a most subtle essence which is reduced into air. Similarly, it assists the stomach in digestion and guards it from phlegm and <term>pituita</term> <note>A watery or mucous humor believed to cause sluggishness.</note>; it preserves the appetite, besides the fact that it also benefits the eyes, ears, and teeth.

Besides these, however, hidden <term>arcana</term> <note>Secret or powerful medicinal virtues.</note> are within it against many abscesses and great diseases, such as jaundice, the overflowing of gall, a lost appetite, and excessive fatness. Similarly, it penetrates from the stomach into the liver and expels "sand" <note>Referring to kidney or gallstones.</note> and similar conditions, if one dwells perpetually in that air. Nay, it even purges the lungs through the upper and lower passages, prevents pleurisy, and likewise epilepsy, convulsions, contractions, spasms, etc.

<margin>The benefit of the spirit of Alum.</margin>
Furthermore, note concerning alum that if it passes into the air and is inhaled in the manner described, it also possesses the properties of salt, even if it is not so strong in its balsamic power; moreover, it consolidates whatever tends toward opening <note>That is, it helps "knit" together tissues or wounds that are threatening to gape open.</note>. Indeed, it also removes <term>esthiomenic</term> <note>original: "esthiomenos," referring to corrosive or "eating" ulcers that spread rapidly.</note> flows, lest they be diverted into the external ducts.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The utility of salts outside the body.</margin>
Furthermore, when the three already explained are reduced into air, they do not harm the exterior either, except that by long-continued and too-fervent handling they are [harsh] to the eyes and kidneys. Rather, their nature, if administered in the right way and time, is so composed that they cure many external evils. For from these three salts any <term>scabies</term> <note>A general term for itchy skin eruptions or mange.</note> is healed, if the "concordance" between the disease and its medicine is observed. For the "Air of Alum" heals itching. The "Air of Vitriol" heals <term>alopecia</term> <note>Hair loss, often attributed to "corrosive" humors in this period.</note>; the "Air of Common Salt" heals scabies. Moreover, they also cure ulcers inside and out like a "vulnerary potion" <note>A healing drink for wounds.</note>, provided a good external plaster is applied, so long as that ulceration is contrary to them in its disposition. Therefore, not much can be written concerning their poison.

<margin>Salt is temperate and suits all natures.</margin>
For they are of a nearly temperate nature, like common salt, which is suitable for all complexions, qualities, and diseases. Therefore, also know regarding the trades that handle salt: if they moisten themselves in salt, wash, and use it externally in other ways, it wonderfully consumes all "fluxes" and superfluous humidities of the body.

<margin>Workers handling salt are most healthy.</margin>
Indeed, the same happens to other craftsmen who use it, such as dyers, soap-boilers, and the like. For they are very healthy workers, who do not fall ill without a notable cause.

<margin>Dangers of salts. Impure minerals are harmful; purified are harmless.</margin>
However, after we have noted the benefits of the said three salts: on the other hand, it is also proper to explain the poison that is caught within them; and that in this way. Any mineral not yet purified <note>original: "deputata," meaning separated or refined.</note>, but still placed in its mixture, contains poison in itself; just as vitriol in its raw ore produces scabs and itching, and draws corrosive flows out of the body. Salt in its raw mixture produces a subtle scabies, <term>impetigo</term> <note>A contagious skin infection characterized by crusting sores.</note>, and bad teeth. But alum, still clinging to its earth, produces all those things that "plume alum" <note>A fibrous form of alum or asbestos.</note> does. Inside the body, however, those three salts work no evil. Moreover, the diseases they cause externally do not descend deeper into the body, so that no internal malice is brought in by them as it is externally. As soon as they are prepared, however, they give off nothing bad, as said above.

<margin>How do Salts, Vitriols, and Alums differ?</margin>
Here also know that there are many kinds of salts, such as saltpeter, etc. There are also many kinds of Vitriol, and similarly of Alum. Nevertheless, the understanding of each kind is one and the same, nor do they differ in anything except the degree of their nature, which is stronger in one species than in another.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Through what things separation occurs. Saltpeter is not salt nitre. How the spirits of "strong waters" harm. From where are strong waters prepared?</margin>
But so that those things pertaining to salts may be sufficiently explained, we must also speak of "separations." For those things which they use are fashioned from the three aforementioned salts. In place of common salt, they take <term>saltpeter</term>, or rather <term>salt nitre</term>, which is boiled and fashioned from nitres; it is not saltpeter, yet it turns toward the genus of minerals. Therefore, it is right that its nature also be explained, namely that it is like a Salt. It should be noted, therefore, that from the three mentioned—or more or fewer—are made <term>Aquae fortes</term> <note>Nitric acid.</note>, "Waters of Giving," <term>Aquae regis</term> <note>Nitro-hydrochloric acid, famous for its ability to dissolve gold.</note>, and the like, of which there are various names. Now, understand what evil these bring to man in this way: as "composites," so that we need not speak further of each separately, but according to the form of any composition. Since this is indeed varied—such as *Aqua fortis*, which is made from Saltpeter and Vitriol, or from Alum and Saltpeter, or from "Visionary Alum" and Saltpeter—the effectiveness of any "water" is estimable from the entry of mineral spirits.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>How other alchemical works cause harm. How Royal Water is prepared.</margin>
Much of what was said above should also be understood regarding **Royal Waters** <note>original: "Aquis Regum," better known as *Aqua Regia*, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids used by alchemists to dissolve gold.</note>. However, since they are prepared with other additions, such as eggshell lime or egg whites and the like, they become weaker than the aforementioned waters; nevertheless, they belong to the "grading waters" <note>Used in metallurgy to refine or "grade" the purity of metals.</note>.

It should also be known here that in distillations, besides salts, many things are taken in hand, such as the refinement of honey, the refinement of tartar, and similar things. These are of such a nature that they never allow themselves to be driven away from the place where they have stuck. The diseases they produce have their own peculiar signs and properties, which experience itself makes known. Judge similarly of other distillations according to the foundation of the **ultimate matter** <note>The final form or residue of a substance after it has been processed.</note>, which signifies their power. Understand the same for other salts and distilled things. For it often happens that good things become sheer poison in distillation, <margin>Salt and Honey, though good, become bad through distillation.</margin> such as honey and salt. Indeed, salt burns the blood with its smoke for those who handle it—such as coin-smelters, alchemists, and the like—during the processes of reverberation, cementation, calcination, and similar labors. Salts act in this same way if they are added to ores by those who smelt ores privately. The same happens to glassmakers and similar workers, goldsmiths and minters, who seek and perform such additions, fluxings, gradings, cementations, and the like; not only in the **Royal cement** <note>A process for refining gold using salt and heat.</note>, but also in all **particular** operations <note>In alchemy, "particulars" refers to processes aimed at specific metallic transmutations rather than the "universal" philosopher's stone.</note>. Such are also the alchemists who seek, do, and prepare various things in such minerals—in the universal, the particular, and the like—in all of which it is only necessary to know what things they are handling and how to act according to them. <margin>Why alchemists are long-lived.</margin> Yet many alchemists are found who live long lives, from which it might be guessed that the spirits of the things they handle cause this. But I cannot believe that; rather, I attribute this to <margin>Source of longevity.</margin> abstinence, hunger, exercise, travel, etc., all of which of themselves make a man long-lived. If good spirits also happen to be present, as mentioned, their health is all the greater; but those who do not follow such a diet, as mentioned, reach that age for those reasons. For order and diet are necessary here.

### CHAPTER V.

But let us proceed to speak of such laborers as those who handle sublimations. They can hardly be without harm. In the air of Mercury, all the virtues of Mercury lie hidden. Therefore, those who handle its sublimation are not infested by pustules. Such also are the precipitations, reverberations, calcinations, burnings, and many similar preparations, in all of which an aerial spirit ascends, which possesses the same nature and property as that from which it is raised. How that air and the disease of the laborer agree, however, must be left to the physicians who live near them and ought to use daily experience.

However, not with as much malice and infection as the metals. Truly, the physician who wishes to have these things well known should exercise himself in this **mineral school** by experiencing them. Of this, nothing should be said or written without the eyewitness testimony of these **Great Works** <note>original: "Magnalia," a Paracelsian term for the great medicinal or alchemical powers hidden in nature.</note>; nor can anything be learned of these things unless the teachers and students have been raised and well-versed in the mineral world. In short, pictorial perfections and representations achieve nothing perfect; nothing is properly handed down, nothing is right, unless it flows from the very springs of the river, from which those who truly thirst drink, etc.

<margin>Two-fold care of the second book.</margin>
a two-fold care: one for diseases arising from minerals; the other for diseases arising from salts. ### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The element of fire to be considered in the diseases of the second book.</margin>
In order that you may be taught the compositions of recipes for diseases which arise from minerals, it must first be known that under the "Air," of which we spoke above, the **element of fire** alone ought to be included and understood. This is because in this place a certain elemental operation occurs, just as you see in a flame which consumes as an element, and not merely as 
<margin>Heat and fire are different things.</margin>
heat—the way the sun dries things, not as a fire, but as a hot thing. That heat and fire are different: for one is an element, the other a quality. We are not speaking here of the quality, but our purpose concerns the Element. For just as the fire of a flame works upon wood, so also these spirits work within the members to which they cling. And that they are not burned as quickly as wood is due to the **vital force** <note>original: "vis viuida"</note>, which contains within itself a growing humidity, by which the power of the fire is weakened for as long as that power of growth is not consumed.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Element overcomes element, temperament overcomes temperament. Element and quality differ. Like is cured by like.</margin>
From this it now follows that a medicine in the virtue of an element must be opposed to this fire, just as water alone extinguishes fire and nothing else. For effective elements must be overcome by effective elements. For an element is one thing, and a quality is another: heat is one thing, fire is another. Heat is not considered here, but fire. Therefore, a temperament <note>original: "complexio," the balance of qualities in the body</note> is not to be directed against a temperament. For fire is not overcome by a temperament, but a temperament overcomes its like, and an element likewise overcomes its like. For example: let there be some disease that is hot in itself. Now the disease must have innate to it either humidity or dryness as its **disposition** <term>diathesis: a physical condition or constitution that makes one susceptible to certain diseases</term>, as is understood from the books on *Degrees and Compositions*. From that it follows that the medicine must also be prepared according to such a disposition. But here, since we are dealing with an element, these things are not to be considered. For in an element there is no "disposition," but one property of nature is the master over another—just as the humidity of water
<margin>The humidity of water is against fire, not coldness or heat.</margin>
rules over fire, and neither cold nor heat does so. Therefore, water is humid, and neither cold nor hot <note>In this alchemical theory, the "elemental" nature of water is pure humidity, while temperature is merely an "accidental" or temporary state.</note>. If water is called cold, suppose that to be an accidental coldness which does not remain in the operation of the humidity, nor does it assist it. For cold is as foreign to water as heat is. For instance, if you make water boil over a fire, then when the fire is no longer present, the water returns to its original temperature; so likewise, when the foreign cold leaves the water, the water returns to the same middle state as after boiling.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>A metallic disease is an element, not a quality. The difference between humid and moist. What is truly humid?</margin>
Therefore, know that this disease is an Element, and not a quality or a temperament. If, therefore, it is an element—namely fire—it is also necessary to constitute and direct the medicine in such a way that the element of **humidity** resides in it, and not a "moist" temperament or quality. For it is one thing to be **humid**, and another to be **moist** <note>original: "madidum," meaning superficially wet or damp</note>. And this is the difference: the Humid is not consumed, but the Moist can be dried out. That which can be dried out is worthless against an element; only that which is not consumed prevails. This is to be recognized in this way: that which is least subject to **coagulation** is the truly Humid. Whoever wishes to know these things must be skilled and practiced in the transformations and preparations of the **Artists** <note>meaning Alchemists</note>, to whom I commend these things in this place. In man, therefore, this is the condition of fire and humidity: that the humidity is not coagulated like that which is merely moist. For if the moist is administered against such a fire, it is coagulated. Thus, one dryness is joined to another, and wood is added to the fire. But that which is of a humid nature, even if it is distilled into vapor by the fire, nevertheless its element remains uncorrupted. For it is re-distilled for as long as the man can endure his own **Alembic** <note>The body is here compared to a distillation vessel (alembic), processing its own internal fluids.</note>.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Error can be committed in elemental medicine. The cause of Dropsy. The cause of Hectic fever. The four Elemental diseases.</margin>
But to speak further of this medicine, know that there is another power in it, which the elemental force produces in natural things. If an error is made through negligence in this, and the humidity is corrupted, **dropsy** <term>hydrops: an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</term> is born, which arises from no other cause. If the dryness is corrupted, **hectic fever** <note>original: "Ethica," a wasting fever associated with consumption</note> and its species follow. For if it can be said, "You have corrupted that person by purging" (which is something done outside the element), it can also be said, "You have sinned against the element of fire and led the patient to **wasting**" <term>Marasmun: a severe form of malnutrition or wasting away</term>. If you err in the element of **Air**, you make the patient colicky and contracted; if in the element of **Earth**, you lead the patient into the exaltation of **quartan fever** <note>a fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, historically linked to the "earthy" humor</note>. And just as these four diseases are elemental and do not arise from the humors, so it is proper to describe them in this **monarchy** <note>referring to the "Monarchy" or sovereign realm of medical knowledge</note> and to proceed according to it. As has already been said, a middle path must be kept here, and one must not progress further, lest the said diseases follow. The sum of it is this: a mineral disease is a **material fire**, just as its world and specific nature indicate. Therefore, the medicine must also be a **material humidity**,
<margin>Radical moisture is to be preserved.</margin>
such as we have described above, so that through this process of medicine, the **radical moisture** <note>the essential life-fluid of the body</note> may be preserved in its quality. While this is done, no disease can be found. The recipe for this elemental humidity follows hereafter.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Alum contains elemental humidity against the fire of the microcosm.</margin>
Therefore, let medicines be chosen that are free from coagulation, such as **Alum** <note>original: "Alumen"</note>, in which humidity and coagulation exist together. If these two are separated from one another, the quality departs to one place, and the element likewise to another. The element of alum is very close to the element of water. For the element of water also consists in its **Hyle** <term>Hyle: primordial or fundamental matter</term>, just as Alum does after its boiling, and after being separated from its coagulated parts...

...it has passed into its own pure and proper element, yet it is stripped of its medicinal <term>arcana: secret, concentrated essences or spiritual powers within natural substances</term>. ### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Sea-water etc. against mineral diseases.</margin>
<margin>Preservative & conservative from herbs & milk-butter.</margin>
**B**esides the mentioned secret, there are certain "simples" <note>medicinal plants or ingredients used on their own</note> which are similar to the element of water—namely, if their coagulation is removed from them. This present chapter will speak of these. They are, namely, the water of Horehound, the water of Jupiter’s Beard <note>Houseleek</note>, Betony, and Water Lily. Since the art of preparing them is not commonly used by apothecaries, the method follows for how they are to be prepared, so that the craftsmen who are inflamed by such spirits may be preserved; likewise Alchemists, smelters, and others spoken of in this treatise, so that they may look after themselves. The teaching of the cooking is this: that the said herbs, or those similar to them, are bruised while they are still green, mixed with an equal quantity of cream of milk, and cooked in a jar in a <term>bain-marie: a water bath used for gentle heating</term> for one hour, and thus eaten on an empty stomach.

This food preserves, maintains, defends, and cures Alchemists, goldsmiths, minters, smelters, and the rest of whom we have spoken in this book. Note here that on one side the body is butter, or at least fatty milk, and on the other side the aforesaid herbs, or similar ones, or their juice or liquor. Indeed, they can even be boiled down, and afterwards cooked with the cream of milk, as above: outside of this process, mineral diseases are by no means overcome.

<margin>Quick-silver, both good and evil.</margin>
...at the same time it holds them united, so that they are not separated. For which reason it follows that whatever evil is here, it must be attributed to both the good and the evil simultaneously; likewise, whatever good occurs must again be imputed to both the good and the evil. By the example of <term>theriaca: a famous ancient medicinal paste used as an antidote and panacea, often containing poisonous elements like viper flesh</term> we can understand that here, good is worth nothing without the evil. Thus, Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> is a born theriaca, to which nothing must be added, nor anything taken away, but only by preparation is it to be transmuted into a theriaca. Therefore, know that Mercurial infections of the "perfected" metals <note>Gold and Silver</note> are a harsh impression. For those things which proceed from a sharp and vehement impression surpass others in the malice of their infection. For everything that comes to its perfection is without poison and well-tempered.

<margin>Mercury is a born theriaca. Why Mercurial infection is more serious.</margin>
<margin>Everything perfect is tempered; in contrast to the imperfect.</margin>

However, that which does not reach perfection, but finds its limit in the middle-time—in which limit perfection cannot be generated—is of a different nature than something perfect, and it is more to be desired in both good and evil things than those whose generation has been led to its end. Thus also Mercury is a sown fruit, not yet progressed to its perfection, but in the middle of its generation it acquires that power which ought to be produced from it.

### On Diseases from Quicksilver.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>How diseases of quick-silver differ from others.</margin>
**S**o that the mineral diseases may be gathered into one work, Book Three now follows: in which are comprised all the diseases which arise from quicksilver, which have been collected from singular observation and experience. For the diseases mentioned above required their own peculiar books. Wherefore, at the beginning of this book, know that diseases from quicksilver have nothing in common with sulfurous and salt diseases, or others termed Mercurial, nor are they related to other metals or minerals. Likewise, it should not be considered here that what is separated from the quicksilver—as if one were to say the evil separated from the good—is what produces diseases here. For quicksilver is such that it holds the good and the evil...

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>All metals were Mercury. From Mercury all metals can be produced.</margin>
**T**he sole cause, therefore, why Mercury brings so many harms is that it is not coagulated into a metal. And because coagulation is lacking to it, it is therefore "half-generated": and whatever is similar to it, the same is understood of it as of Mercury. Every coagulated metal contains within itself the nature of Mercury. But because it is coagulated, that power is no longer present. For in the half-generation, and up to the half-generation, all metals are Mercury, after which follows the operation toward perfection, in which the distribution of metals begins, wherever each is directed. From this it follows that from Mercury, through the fires of Vulcan, any metal can be generated, as is found in the *Book of Generations*. This is indicated so that you may well understand the distinction of Mercury—namely, the coagulated and the non-coagulated—and that all those things which are not coagulated, and yet whose end and "ultimate matter" is coagulation, have all kinds of poisons and medicines within them.

<margin>Coagulation is the end of all metals except Mercury.</margin>
<margin>Gold is coagulated Mercury. How all metals have the power of Mercury.</margin>
Now truly, there is nothing whose end and limit is coagulation, and which has not been led to it, except Mercury alone. For many things are liquid, but their final condition is not coagulation, but liquidity. Wherefore a distinction must be observed here regarding Mercury, whose nature it is that it is not born perfect, but living in its substance it contains those properties which dead metals have. For gold is only Mercury: but because it is coagulated, it no longer has that <note>mercurial</note> nature; and although the properties of Mercury are in it, they are nevertheless dead. Understand the same of silver, iron, copper, etc., all of which have Mercurial power in them: but just as someone can be submerged and suffocated in fluid water, yet cannot be when it is coagulated <note>as ice</note>. Just as, therefore, the coagulation of water removes the danger: so also the coagulation of Mercury takes away its power.

### CHAPTER III.

**W**hat other reason could there be that this metal did not reach its perfection, other than that the physician should seek his pharmacy in this liquid? This is not because of the evil that arises from it, but rather because of the great <term>art: the alchemical process of transformation</term> which lies hidden here, so that those things which drive away both their own and others' evils may be investigated. If, therefore, for the sake of this art, the nature of metals is reserved by nature—from which those six more perfect metals <note>Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead</note> can be made, and furthermore the <term>Essences and Arcana: the pure spiritual or medicinal cores of substances</term> which lie hidden in those six metals can be found in its substance—I shall omit those things here as being too lengthy and will recommend them to their own school. For here my only purpose is to reveal the evils that arise from it, as well as the medicine for the evil born from it. Therefore, so that you may well understand its liquidity and its <term>coagulation: the process of a liquid becoming solid</term>, you must consider that from a substance which ought to be coagulated and is on the path to coagulation, yet remains liquid, a smoke rises, just like humidity from water. And although that smoke does not appear to be water, it is nevertheless invisible water. For when water boils in a vessel until nothing remains, that which exhales does not seem to be water, but only vapor; yet in a <term>distillatory: a glass vessel used for distilling</term> it condenses back into water, so that afterwards the eyes may see that vapor was indeed water. So it is with Mercury, which emits from itself an exhalation by the power of the upper firmament <note>the macrocosm or celestial influences</note> like water, which is dried out from it. Now this vapor of Mercury passes into the air, and through the air enters into man. Thus Mercury is now in man, just as some vapor of water in the air is inhaled: and just as water becomes water again, so Mercury becomes Mercury once more. Moreover, its distillation is not only caused and ruled by the external firmament, but also from within itself by the fire it carries with it. For just as every liquid is consumed by itself through the power of its own destructive fire, so also Mercury drives and distills itself in the mountains, caves, and veins of the earth, in which its "soot" cannot break out in a mass because of the obstructing earth. From this it happens that those who live in that region of the earth are forced to be polluted <note>original: "fœdere"; likely referring to being saturated or fouled by vapors</note> by those vapors, just as someone would be polluted in a bath-house sweat-room. It is the same as if he were entirely drenched in Mercury itself. For he who is drenched in a bath is made wet by the vapors no less than if he were drenched in a wash-basin of water.

<margin>On the vapors of stones, metals, woods & herbs. The coagulation of stones is most useful.</margin>
<margin>The stench of Rebis is stilled by heat and suppressed by cold.</margin>

### CHAPTER IV.

**N**ow, such wickedness is not only in Mercury, which infects man so badly, but also in stones; if they were not coagulated, who could live on earth without evil—that is, without disease? For if their Mercury remained as imperfect as the Mercury of metals, those distillations would certainly infect the earth so much that nothing healthy would grow in it. But the coagulation of stone removes all these things. For just as you see that the stench of <term>Rebis: an alchemical term for the "two-fold thing," often referring to the foul-smelling matter of the "Great Work" during its black stage</term> is the worst and foulest of all, so that no one can bear to be near it, yet cold congeals and hardens it, through which coagulation all those adverse qualities are lost: so it also happens in the coagulation of stones, which does not allow their wickedness to dominate. Indeed, if there were as much "Mercury of metals" as there is "Mercury of stones," and if metals lay on the surface of the earth just like stones, then certainly the earth would bear no useful fruit because of the distillation of its vapors; indeed, it would infect men no less than the earth itself. For the regions that are near these Mercurial fumes, and the refiners of quicksilver, live in greater danger of diseases than other regions. Where Mercury is stored, those places are unhealthy. But understand also that metals emit no poison without fire. For fire drives them into their "fixed" Mercury. And although their coldness is unhealthy, yet by its operation it is compared to frozen water. The same must be judged regarding stones. But other generated things, which are not so violently coagulated, are less harmful, such as wood, which is closer to its <term>prime matter: the original, undifferentiated substance of all things</term> than metals are. Therefore, the smoke of wood is not so much to be avoided, since its liquid matter has not been brought to the firmest coagulation. Likewise, herbs have an even lesser coagulation, which is why their smoke surpasses all others in goodness. Therefore, they have a good prime matter, which is not as opposed to men as metals are, etc.

### CHAPTER I.

**I**f these things are to be understood from a true foundation, as is proper, it cannot be done without <term>physical Astronomy: the study of how the "stars" within the earth and the human body interact</term>. For the physician is dedicated to all natural arts and sciences, all of which he must gather into one; and after he has embraced them all, only then is he permitted to approach the medical task and the administration of the sick. Therefore, recall those things which were said in the first treatise about semi-perfect natural generations, among which is quicksilver, which is not brought into solid compaction but is left in liquidity. Furthermore, it should be known that any natural thing which is "open," such as quicksilver, is like an unlocked house into which anyone can enter. Thus Mercury also lies open, so that any Physician can take from it what he wishes. But it is not so with gold, silver, tin, etc. For their door is closed by coagulation, until an opening, dissolution, and reduction into the prime matter is made by art—which things certainly have many obstacles. But all those obstacles are not present in Mercury. For it is open, and needs nothing other than direction in the <term>Vulcanic preparation: alchemical processing using fire</term>. But all these things will be omitted for now, and henceforth we shall speak of Mercury, regarding what it is in its earthly constellation. For the earth contains its own heaven within itself, and its stars are minerals. Thus, one of those stars is quicksilver. Know then what sort of thing it is, etc.
