but it arrives too late, so that time rules over it, and the certain medicine is not in his hand: from this it follows that no good judgment can be delivered. For in all the principal branches of the art there is doubt and not certainty. But when the four aforementioned columns <note>The "four pillars" of medicine according to Paracelsus: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note> are well known to someone, then the matter is quite different. For then, life is long, the art is short, time is bent and governed, experiment is bound by a bridle, and in this way a judgment can be made that is not doubtful, dangerous, or reckless, but certain, by which the physician can restore health.

<margin>Medicine is an art.</margin> Medicine is an art. Since it is an art, it ought to be as round as a circle, so that everything considered in a circle is also considered in Medicine. Just as a compass performs its work, so too must medicine perfect its own. For an equal power is within it, though they do not speak of it similarly. The compass is visible, as is evident from its work. Medicine is not visible. This has its own reason: nevertheless, both the compass and medicine are destined for their works. Since Hippocrates did not bring the compass to mind or compare it to medicine, it follows that there must be despair in medicine:

<margin>Medicine, once born, ought to be as certain as Geometry.</margin> But if the condition and nature of Medicine, such as it is, were reduced to Geometry, who, if he only wished, could err or be in doubt? Those who do not act in the manner of a compass err even against their will, like stone-cutters or carpenters. So too does the physician in his profession.

*It is not enough, however, for the physician to have done his duty, unless the patient also does his, and the attendants do theirs, and external things are properly arranged.*

Hippocrates wishes for the patient to be obedient and do all that is commanded and prescribed by the physician. But he alone should not perform his duty, as he is only one person; indeed, others also—those who take care of him, serve him, cook, carry him here and there, and make the bed—should have the heart, mind, and desire of the patient within themselves, so that altogether there is one and the same heart. Moreover, this saying is pious and just, according to the command: *Love your neighbor as yourself.* Since the one who serves you is the patient and your neighbor, you should rightly have one heart with him, so that you do for the patient what you would wish done for you if you were lying ill. One can appreciate why Hippocrates wrote this Aphorism, namely because of things that still happen to many today. For often someone is sick whom his wife would gladly see die, or a husband his wife, a servant his master, a master his servant, a brother his brother, a companion his companion. Why? There is no need to list the reasons. When a family is thus set against the head of the household, what can the Physician hope for there? Even if he wishes the patient well and prescribes good things as they ought to be done, yet because those mentioned are differently minded than the patient, the physician's art is confounded, the patient is lost, the heirs rejoice, the physician is harmed, and the art is dishonored. Therefore, there must be one heart; then the health of the sick begins. For it is necessary that help be brought and administered to the patient by himself, by the physician, and by those who live in his house, all of whom ought to be endowed with a similar heart.

### ## Second Aphorism.

> *In disturbances of the bowels and vomitings which occur spontaneously, if such matters as are necessary are purged, it is beneficial and they bear it easily; if otherwise, the opposite occurs. So also is the emptying of the vessels; if it happens as it ought to happen, it is beneficial and they bear it easily; if otherwise, the opposite happens. Therefore, one must take account of the region, the seasons, the ages, and the diseases, to determine whether such evacuations are appropriate or not.*

Hippocrates’ opinion is that all flows and vomiting through the upper parts <note>i.e., the mouth</note> which arise on their own without a purgative should be considered to see whether they need to be purged or not, and where nature is perceived to be expelling too much, so that she is not assisted but stopped. This saying pleases me.

<margin>The cure for Dysentery.</margin> For in dysentery, this is the highest medicine: to draw down through the lower parts with a powerful medicament. For in this way, dysentery is most usefully cured. Similarly, in vomiting, it is proper to approach the matter with the strongest emetics. For experience itself proves that in any flux through the upper or lower parts, if a medicine suitable to that matter is administered, present help is at hand. However, in such a cure, great knowledge and observation must be present, so that the very medicament is chosen that is fit to expel that flux, lest something else be expelled. Otherwise, death would be brought in. Furthermore, care must be taken that the limit of quantity is not exceeded, so that the dose is equal to the disease in its efficacy. It must also be noted that if the signs of strength have receded too much and are not present but failing, then this process ought not to be followed; rather, constipation <note>In this context, "constipatio" means the binding or stopping of a flow, not digestive blockage.</note> and the swiftest binding should occur. Therefore, Hippocrates spoke rightly in this place, and if you obey him, you will find it to be so by experience. As an example and testimony, I offer these:

<margin>Scammony, etc. Alkali of Serapio.</margin> *Scammony <note>A resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, used as a drastic purgative.</note> cures dysentery; alkali of Serapio <note>Likely referring to a preparation described by the physician Serapion the Younger, an 11th-century Arab physician.</note> cures a discharge; the spleen of a castrate <note>A traditional remedy used in early medicine for hormonal or systemic regulation.</note> stops the menstrual flow; an extract of Hellebore <note>A poisonous plant used as a powerful emetic or purgative.</note> removes phlegmatic vomiting; and all these things work through an expulsive power.*

<margin>Spleen cures. Extract of Hellebore.</margin> Hippocrates also testifies that if everything has been purged of its own accord so that nothing more remains, then binding must occur. Let that be done through **SPIRIT OF WINE** <note>Distilled alcohol</note> taken with precious fragments and corals, which stops all these things. Indeed, this is also true,

<margin>Spirit of wine with corals binds.</margin> that other binding agents—which should by no means be used for such a constriction—produce colic, tumors, dropsy, paralysis, and many similar diseases against the order of nature after their binding. Therefore, the most suitable constrictives must be used so that these things are avoided.

*So also is the emptying of the vessels; if it happens as it ought to happen, it is beneficial and they bear it easily; if otherwise, the opposite happens.*

When emptying <note>original: "inanitio"; refers to the depletion of bodily fluids or "vessels"</note> occurs in a man, which is just as possible as the beginning of flows, then one must proceed similarly as with the flows. Namely, if something remains to be dried out and exhausted, it ought to be done. If not, it ought to be hindered. For nature often finds something superfluous in itself and strives to consume and dry it out on its own. When this operation begins, the patient decreases in body, which ought not to happen. Yet the physician should not try to hinder this consumption; rather,

<margin>When the physician ought to help nature.</margin> he should instead help nature so that it can better attain its intended goal, and thus that consumption is a Medicine which should in no way be hindered.

But if nature were excessive in consuming, then it ought to be turned away and directed from that purpose to another. Hippocrates, therefore, hands down an excellent doctrine in this place, but he does not attach the medicines of this doctrine. I

<margin>The strengthening of nature by gold.</margin>

<margin>The Physician's Prudence.</margin>
Therefore, account must also be taken of time. In this operation of the Physician, according to the doctrine of this aphorism, Hippocrates offers an admonition regarding what the physician must consider: namely, the time and the hour—that is, how any given hour is not established by itself alone. For the times change daily. One must also weigh what nature brings, what medicine brings, what the signs bring, so that the Physician may compose himself in every way according to them. He should resist or follow them, not recklessly or by chance, but with prudence, knowledge, and a good understanding of true and suitable Medicine.

### And of Time.

<margin>The Stars of the Elements.</margin>
**T**he stars rule time: moreover, the stars are within the elements and dwell in the elements, just as the soul is in flesh and blood, and as the spirit is in the body, and medicine is in the herb. For the herb is not the Medicine, the body is not the soul; likewise, the elements are not the stars. Nevertheless, the operation and effect proceed from the four elementary bodies. Therefore, it befits the physician to be a skilled Astronomer <note>In this context, astronomy includes astrology and the study of celestial influences on health</note>, so that he may know what time brings, takes away, completes, or breaks in natural things, so that he may be able to withstand it.

### And Regions.

<margin>Each region has something specific. The Physician should be a Cosmographer and Geographer.</margin>
**F**urthermore, the physician must also consider in what region the sick person is; that is, what singular property and nature that region has. For one province differs from another, one land from another; so too do stones, wines, bread, meats, etc. That is to say, every region has a peculiar and specific nature beyond the general property which the whole world possesses. The Physician ought to consider this property well. For this reason, it is necessary for him to be both a Cosmographer and a Geographer, and to know those arts perfectly. However, what those arts are and what they teach, together with Astronomy, there is no need to describe in a commentary. For these things are to be sought in their own volumes—namely, how they pertain to the Physician.

### And of Age.

**T**ake an example of this kind. Suppose a case where a boy suffers from a quartan fever <note>A malarial fever characterized by paroxysms every 72 hours</note>, and likewise a youth, a man, and an old man. Each of these requires a peculiar cure, yet since the cure itself is one and the same, there are nonetheless some distinctions in adding or taking away. The physician, therefore, must consider the distribution of the ages of man, as well as the age of the medicine, the age of the diseases, and the age of time itself. For when the world had stood for a thousand years, men could be cured more easily; two thousand years ago, better still; three thousand years ago, even better; and the closer it comes to our time, the worse the diseases become. All ages, therefore, must be well considered: namely, those of the hours, of the time of man, of the world, of diseases, etc.

### And of Diseases.

**L**ikewise, the disease itself must be considered—what it is and of what kind. And let these things be known exactly, not by opining or supposing. For he mentions <term>episteme</term> <note>original: "ἐπιστήμην" - certain, scientific knowledge</note>, which in Medical terms means to recognize deliberately, to know, and not to doubt or waver. For where this certainty is lacking, there the cure is also uncertain.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
Hippocrates wants the physician to understand the five aforementioned articles in this way, not only in this aphorism, but rather in all other diseases these articles are necessary. Let the physician know, therefore, where he ought to apply diligence and where not, when and when not, lest he be diligent and curious where it is not needed, and negligent where it is. It befits the Physician to be such that he practices his art with good and right contemplation of those things which pertain to the sick person, and that with the zeal of healing the sick. For thus he will enjoy a good outcome from his contemplation: for he is guided by the supreme physician, who prospers it and directs it along the right path.

### Third Aphorismus.

The fuller bodily condition of athletes, if it is brought to the highest degree of fullness, is slippery <note>meaning unstable or precarious</note>. For it cannot remain or stay in the same state; and since it does not stay, and can no longer progress for the better, it remains for it to fall back for the worse. For which reason, that fuller bodily condition must be dissolved with deliberation <note>original: "cunctanter"</note>, so that the body may take the beginning of new nourishment. However, I would not want the evacuation to proceed so far that the vessels collapse within themselves; for this is not safe, but one must proceed as far as nature allows. Likewise, extreme evacuations are dangerous; and extreme repletions are similarly dangerous.

<margin>Severe diseases: sudden rest is not good.</margin>
**S**ince Hippocrates speaks of diseases: in this aphorism, he makes mention of those diseases which tend toward the highest point, and when they are at the highest degree, they then soften and become tolerable in appearance, but they are deceptive: for they eventually return. For although such sick people seem to be cheerful, they cannot remain in that quiet and joy, and that rest, if any is present, does not turn out for the good, but for the worse. For they fall back into the tyranny of the disease. Know, therefore, that Hippocrates has spoken correctly in this place. For any serious disease endowed with foreign signs is difficult to cure. For example, when epileptics first begin to enjoy rest with a joyful sign, then the disease soon returns; likewise in **St. Vitus' dance** <note>original: "morbo S. Viti" - a disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements</note>, when the disease is at its highest degree, then they exult, and so in many other diseases that tend toward death. Where they seem to be at their best, death stands by the bed. For death and the rest of health cannot exist together. That rest comes, however, happens by reason of nature, which thinks it has overcome death or disease, while death or the disease rests in the meantime, waiting for the limit of its purpose. But when the patient rejoices, then the disease rises up again and fights against health. When the disease has progressed a little in this way, it then rests again, and good health seems to be present, but it is deceptive. These joyful conditions are signs of long-lasting disease or of death.

<margin>Recurrence of epilepsy: what sign. St. Vitus' dance.</margin>

<margin>From where rest in serious diseases comes.</margin>

*For which reason, that fuller bodily condition must be dissolved with deliberation.*

Therefore, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, the cure is that those joyful signs, which are of such good hope, be broken—that is, that they be transformed back into the disease, so that nothing joyful is seen anymore, and this must be done quickly. For whether the matter is inclined toward death or toward a fixed disease, one must hurry. For as soon as the signs in fixed diseases last half a year, no longer than common...

->*So that the body may receive the beginning of new nourishment.*<-

The reason why one must hurry is so that the body, according to its nature, may receive food before the disease arrives and infects the food before the body can enjoy it. For if the body is secondary in the consumption of food, then the matter is handled perversely; for in that case, the disease will feed the body and not nature, as ought to happen ordinarily. To be nourished by disease, however, is to have the entire body infected.

I would not wish, however, to proceed with purging to the point that the vessels completely collapse within themselves, for this is not safe; rather, one must proceed only as far as nature will bear. Thus, extreme evacuations are dangerous.

It is also not a good sign, like the things mentioned above, if compression or coagulation occurs, whether from the disease or from the Medicine. Similarly, if purging is done because of "accidents" <note>In early medicine, 'accidents' refers to secondary symptoms or complications rather than the disease itself</note>, that also would not be appropriate. For the disease is disposed either toward death or toward a fixed nature. If, therefore, you try to remove those accidents, those things which are in the whole body will penetrate to the heart, and the matter will be worse than before.

->*And on the contrary, repletions <term>repletion: an excess of bodily fluids or over-fullness, the opposite of depletion</term>, if they are extreme, are similarly dangerous.*<-

Even if some health follows after taking medicine, it is nonetheless not constant. For as soon as any of the prior signs return, no one can erase them again as in the beginning; rather, it is necessary to leave the matter and commit it to God. For nature here is worn away, weakened, and vanishes, and it withdraws without any help.

### Fourth Aphorism.

> *A slender and delicate diet is always unsafe in long diseases, and in acute ones where it is not appropriate; and again, a diet that has reached extreme thinness is troublesome, since repletions that have reached the highest point are also troublesome.*

<margin>Where diet should be studied.</margin>
**I**t is the opinion of Hippocrates that in the most difficult and longest-lasting diseases, a moderate and decent diet ought to be maintained. But if that is not sufficient, there is a danger that the patient may be cured with difficulty. If you still wish to tighten and restrict the diet even more subtly and strictly at the end, it is to be feared that this too will be done in vain. And finally, if repletion is induced so that the disease fills itself and not the diet, that too is a bad sign. It is certainly true that any disease, whether it be mortal or otherwise long-lasting, does not require a peculiar diet. For nature does not crave food; rather, it is entirely full of disease. Therefore, when a moderate diet does not help, it is a sign that one must act not with diet, but with medicine. For where the disease feeds itself, there is no need for diet, but for medicine alone. For diseases fill themselves just as if someone were overwhelming himself with too much food; in the same way, the disease is satiated. Hippocrates, however, speaks of no Medicine in this place, nor does he attach the names of diseases, but he only makes a general aphorism that applies to all diseases, as if he were saying: if it happens in great diseases that diet accomplishes nothing, then diet should not be the focus, but rather all effort should be spent on medicine. For nature feeds itself so much that it is full. This Aphorism teaches nothing else.

<margin>Diet is useful in no [active] disease.</margin>
<margin>When diet is needed, and when less so.</margin>

### Fifth Aphorism.

> *Sick people err in a thin diet; whereby it happens that they are more harmed, since any error here is more serious than in a slightly fuller diet: for the same reason, a very thin, fixed, and exquisite diet is not very safe even for healthy people, because they bear errors more heavily. Therefore, a thin and exact diet is for the most part more dangerous than one a little fuller.*

<margin>Diseases are to be cured not by hunger, but by Medicine.</margin>
**H**ippocrates wants, in this place, for sick people not to use a severe diet or attribute much to it. Those who do the opposite and wish to accomplish much through diet corrupt themselves further. Observe the reason why he says this: a disease that is cured by such a diet is not truly cured. For when the diet ends, the disease returns and grows anew. For it is not diet, but Medicine that ought to cure. Therefore, patients sin against themselves when they try to drive out diseases by hunger. For no disease is driven out by hunger. A diet should indeed be maintained, not so that it may cure, but so that it may preserve a fit nature so that it can better perform its actions.

<margin>The use of diet.</margin>

->*Since any error here is more serious than in a slightly fuller diet.*<-

<margin>Where the diet should be more liberal. Thickness is better than thinness. * From small plums, which are called Jujubes. Plums are not for the thin nourishment of the healthy.</margin>
Therefore, when some error is committed in medicine, just as has been said regarding diet, then that error will cause no small evils; indeed, it will bring in great inconveniences, and greater ones indeed if the patient is "subtle" <note>meaning thin, fragile, or refined in constitution</note> by nature than if he is "thick" <note>meaning robust or sturdy</note>. Note, therefore, that being thick is better here than being subtle. For thickness has more strength than subtlety. Where there is strength, therefore, nourishment must be offered, and it should by no means be denied. If, therefore, there is more [strength] in turnips than in * <note>referring to the jujubes mentioned in the margin</note>, then turnips ought to be given, not *, that is, the sick person ought not to be cured by subtle diets, but rather by the kind of foods in which there is more strength.

->*For the same reason, a very thin, fixed, and exquisite diet is unsafe even for the healthy: because they bear errors more heavily.*<-

Furthermore, we must take this as an admonition: not to nourish healthy men with such a subtle diet, but rather with more effective food. Nor should a diet be maintained exactly according to a measured number; rather, let us permit various things to be granted, not certain fixed things. For when they fall into diseases, they can better bear thicker foods and will be cured more quickly than subtle men. For as the food is, so the nature becomes: if it is nourished by subtle food, it helps little in medicine; but if it is fed by more robust food, then it excellently supports the medicine.

<margin>Thicker people are cured more quickly than slender ones. To the extent that the food is such as the one being fed.</margin>

->*Therefore a thin and exact diet is for the most part more dangerous than a slightly fuller one.*<-

Therefore, the physician will not study subtle diets much, nor will he try to accomplish much through them; rather, he will think this: that diets are deceptive and trick the physician when they are subtle. For he neglects the help due to medicine. Hippocrates does not, therefore, teach that the physician or

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates. The previous page discussed the dangers of over-purging and how to recognize signs of recovery. Here, the author explores the relationship between the severity of a disease and the potency of the medicine or diet required to treat it, emphasizing that medicine, not just diet, is the true healer.</meta>

ON THE APHORISMS OF HIPPOCRATES

<margin>
The method of prescribing diets; it is medicine that heals, not diet.
</margin>

The patient should rely on the diet and strive to achieve much through it, but the physician must prescribe a diet that is suitable for nature to strengthen it, and let that be a more substantial <note>Latin: *crassior*, meaning a thicker or more nourishing diet</note> diet. However, he should place his chief study in the medicine which has the power of healing the patient. This was created for that purpose, not the diet.

### Aphorism Six

->For extreme diseases, extreme remedies, exquisitely prepared, are the best.<-

<margin>
Diseases of later years are worse than earlier ones.
</margin>

**H**ere in this place, Hippocrates sets down a kind of prophecy, namely that in the final times, extreme medicines will be applied; and this is to be understood in this way: From its beginning to its end, any thing always becomes more and more mature, stronger, and more stubborn, and the closer it is to the end, the more vehement it is. For example, an acorn is planted in the earth. It grows more and more until finally, after many years, it becomes a great tree. In the beginning, this tree could have been cut down with a small knife, while it was still a sapling; but later, a great axe is needed to cut it. In the beginning, a boy could have split it; but later, two or three grown men have enough labor to cut it down. In the beginning, it could have been split in the blink of an eye; later, it can hardly be cut and split in several weeks. It is the same with diseases, which begin to arise quite lightly, and finally grow up so that they become more and more vehement, until they eventually reach their <term>exaltation: the state where a disease or medicine reaches its highest potency or peak intensity</term>. In the beginning, a light medicine would have cured them, but later it can do very little. Therefore, Hippocrates says that medicine ought to be applied according to grades: that is, for a disease of the first grade, a first-grade medicine; for a middle disease, a middle medicine; and for an extreme disease, an extreme and most powerful medicine is required.

<margin>
The grades of diseases and medicines should be equal. See Serapinum; also, gums cure beginning dropsy.
</margin>

Know, however, that the grading of medicine ought to be understood according to this example: if someone were suffering from <term>hydrops: dropsy, or the swelling of soft tissues due to excess fluid</term>, and it was in the beginning, it follows that he should be cured by a light and easy way, namely through pills of <note>original: "de Serapino," likely referring to sagapenum, a bitter resin used as a laxative</note> Serapinum, of gums, etc. However, when the disease increases and reaches its middle stage, and the swelling becomes greater, then the previous medicine is no longer strong enough. It is necessary, therefore, to apply something stronger. For the disease is stronger, and besides, it has some symptoms which must themselves be considered in the cure. But when it reaches the highest grade, then the patient swells all over, his breath is short, and his head and other limbs ache severely. All these things must be considered together, and thus a medicine must be prepared which is beneficial for the thirst, the breathing, and all the limbs—and that will be an "extreme" medicine.

<margin>
Diseases differ in their quantities.
</margin>

Thus, the medicines for diseases when they are at the beginning differ from those which are at the end. For the beginning is one way, the middle another, and the end another. It therefore suits the physician to know how the medicine is to be reduced <note>processed or distilled</note> so that it is effective even in extreme diseases. For example: pills of Serapinum and <note>original: "de mezereo," referring to the Daphne mezereum plant</note> mezereon help in the beginning, but not in the end. But if you transmute them into a <term>quintessence: the purest and most concentrated essence of a substance, achieved through alchemical distillation</term> and place them in a higher grade, then they will heal even an extreme disease. For if some disease grows even to the extreme, and has its natural medicine in the beginning, know for certain that this medicine can also be "exalted" through art, so that it is always on an equal grade with the disease. The physician, therefore, ought to know that which medicine—

---

<margin>
Alchemy is the formula of nature.
</margin>

—reveals, which he must imitate, namely through Alchemy, which is the art that teaches how to prepare and perfect all these things.

### Aphorism Seven

->When, therefore, a disease is very acute, it brings extreme distress immediately, and a very thin diet must be used. But when it is not so, but a fuller diet may be offered, one should relax the extreme thinness of the diet in proportion as the disease is less extreme.<-

<margin>
In sudden and intense diseases, thin food is appropriate.
</margin>

**E**very acute disease, which attacks with the greatest distress like death itself—such as the plague, mania, and many others—when it invades someone, it immediately brings with it extreme exhaustion and the greatest pains. For example, a fever is mild in the beginning, but its force increases more and more until it finally becomes very bad. So it must be understood of these diseases: when they invade someone, then the greatest pains are present immediately at the start, so that the disease and the pain in the beginning and the end are one and the same—that is, death is present immediately with its beginning, along with all its conditions. Hippocrates says, therefore, that when acute diseases of this kind begin, which are worst at the start, then the patient must be fed with the thinnest and lightest food.

<margin>
The cause.
</margin>

The cause is that where such a disease is present, there all the forces of nature are fighting with the disease. If, therefore, nature were not fed with ordinary food and fed cautiously, then the food could not be digested; for nature does not desert the patient in the fight with the disease. But if the food remained undigested in the stomach, another disease would follow from it, and the disease would thus be doubled.

<margin>
Which foods are light.
</margin>

Therefore, the food given must be thin and light, which passes through of its own accord, not needing much digestion, such as broths, legumes, and porridges; such things do not hinder nature in its care and its fight. But if the vehemence of the disease is not so great, then food can be given more liberally according to the condition of the patient.

<margin>
The best food and drink is that which is also a medicine.
</margin>

It is necessary, however, to know one more thing, although Hippocrates makes no mention of it: namely, that in such diseases, the diet or food ought to be a medicine at the same time, to help nature. For example: if someone were seized by the plague or pleurisy, then it is necessary to expel the food so that nature may be unburdened and freed, and that ought to be done through Diaphoretic Gold <note>a chemical preparation of gold intended to induce sweating to "sweat out" a disease</note> and through Diaphoretic Tartar; although these may not seem to be foods but medicines, yet they are both food and drink.

<margin>
Diaphoretic Gold for the plague. Diaphoretic Tartar, etc. See the prologue of the *Archidoxa*.
</margin>

For he who is nourished by them does not die of hunger even if he eats nothing else, however little of the aforementioned things he takes. It should be known, therefore, that these are medicines and nutrients at the same time, and in such a nutrient a great secret <note>Latin: *arcanum*</note> lies hidden.

### Aphorism Eight

->When the force of the disease is at its peak, then the thinnest diet must be used.<-

<margin>
Exaltation of medicines.
</margin>

**E**very disease which is at its highest grade must be treated very delicately in food and drink, so that the patient is not given food that penetrates or delights the body, such as aromatic or delicate foods, fish, chicken, etc. For where there are such good cooks, nature is delighted and deserts the disease in its conflict, and hungers for delicacies, and thus is led astray. Non-delicate foods are the best in this diet. Similarly, one should give no strong or "leaping" wine. For just as this wine intoxicates and weakens the brain, so it also weakens all the limbs. Therefore, a light wine should be given, in which nature seeks no—

Indeed, you must also note this, although Hippocrates does not say it, that dairy products and other foods which draw disease toward themselves actually remove the disease when they carry it out through the urine and stools, as in the case of jaundice <note>Latin: *icteritio morbo*</note>.
<margin>Foods ought to be medicine at the same time.</margin>
<margin>Juniper berry.</margin>
<margin>Cherry water.</margin>
The juniper berry is an excellent food for nourishing the sick along with other foods; likewise, cherry water has a particular power if it is drunk within another beverage. It therefore suits the physician to be so prudent that he does not merely establish a diet by a certain weight of food and drink and select the most delicate foods, but rather that he chooses those foods which are at the same time medicine, and let the sick person enjoy them. These are suitable for those diseases that are in the state of their full strength.

### Aphorism Nine

> *But one must also make a conjecture from the patient, whether he can hold out with the prescribed diet until the peak of the disease, and whether he might fail beforehand, and being unequal to the task, succumb to such a diet before the disease yields and is blunted.*

<margin>What the word "diet" signifies.</margin>
**I**t is also necessary for the physician to consider, when a certain diet is of no help, that he should not persist in it any longer, but should apply medicine, whether that be food or not. For that is most necessary, however it is handled. Since Hippocrates says so much about "diet," you must know that it is not to be understood only as food and drink, which the Italian and French physicians study so intensely. Rather, "diet" is to be understood differently here. For Hippocrates requires a diet not only to correctly nourish the body, but rather to cure it. It therefore suits the physician to consider what power resides in any food, so that he may choose those foods which are simultaneously medicine. He should order the diet not for the sake of nutrition, but rather for the sake of medicine, and prescribe abstinence only because of the medicinal power inherent in the food, not because of the filling or lack of nourishing food.
<margin>Medicated foods and their dosage.</margin>
<margin>From where the dose of medicinal foods is to be estimated.</margin>
For example, if someone suffers from a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria.</note>, a diet should be prescribed for him that is both food and medicine. You shall gather the "dose" of the diet—how much the patient ought to eat—during its administration according to the strength and power of the medicine within the food, not according to the nutrition within the food. Thus, the salt for one suffering from quartan fever should be salt of wormwood <note>Latin: *sal absinthij*; a chemical salt derived from the wormwood plant, used for digestive and feverish complaints.</note>; let its stalks be laxative, and let its flesh draw out, digest, and purge through the bowels. Similarly regarding drink: let his wine be medicine; that is, let it be prepared with those things which drive out that disease. Therefore, nothing should be offered to the patient in which some medicinal power does not reside.

### Aphorism Ten

> *To those, therefore, for whom the peak of the disease will occur immediately, one must immediately provide a thin diet. But for those whose peak comes later, one must subtract from the diet at the time of the peak itself and a little before it. Before that, however, they are to be nourished more fully so that they may be able to endure it.*

**I**t also behooves the physician to know when the patient should be given food and drink, and this must be determined from the disease itself, according to how it is affected. Understand it this way: since nutrition does not cure the patient, but medicine alone does, the foundation of the diet will also be found there. Therefore, Hippocrates wants to say how medicine is to be administered, at what times, and how strong. For nature does not always embrace medicine, but only sometimes, and at other times not at all; thus the hour should be chosen in which nature craves medicinal drink and food. For when the paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in the intensity of symptoms.</note> is at its height and the disease has swelled, then nature accepts no diet. She is fastidious. Hippocrates therefore wants the physician to notice the suitable time for administering to nature. He speaks of these things, not whether pears, apples, broths, or other things are to be given.

### Aphorism Eleven

> *In the paroxysms themselves, one must withhold food. For to provide it is harmful. And when diseases return in cycles, one must abstain during the attacks themselves.*

**T**his aphorism, like the ones above, is to be understood as follows: when nature refuses, food is not to be given to her, but only at that time when it is convenient for her. For there is an adverse time, and there is a constant time.

<margin>Why nothing should be attempted during paroxysms.</margin>
<margin>A paroxysm is the anger of nature.</margin>
<margin>Period, attack, paroxysm, etc., are different things.</margin>
<margin>What a paroxysm is.</margin>
For when a disease exerts its nature and its force, it is not good to deal with it, just as nothing can be done with an angry man. But when something must be done with him, one must wait until the anger has passed; then he is rational, so that he can perceive your speech and responses and reply briskly, etc. All these things cannot happen during the "anger of nature." This is likewise to be understood regarding exacerbated diseases. Note therefore that periods, paroxysms, and attacks are all the anger of nature and its fury. Although a "period" is one kind of anger, an "attack" another, a "paroxysm" another, and an "exacerbation" yet another; nevertheless, all these are the anger of nature, arising from the offenses which nature is forced to suffer from the disease, or which the disease is forced to suffer from nature. For anger arises from both sides. Let the physician know, therefore, that there is one anger of nature—which is another time, or that of health—and another anger of the disease when it shows itself. It suits the physician to look at these things, so that he may act according to the time and hour, and begin nothing at an unsuitable time.

### Aphorism Twelve

> *The attacks and the constitutions of diseases will be indicated by the diseases themselves, the seasons of the year, and the observation of the proportions of the periods relative to each other, whether they happen daily or at a greater interval. But indications are also taken from those things which appear later, as in pleurisy, if sputum appears immediately at the beginning, it announces that the disease will be short. But if it is produced later, it will be long. Also, when urine, fecal matter, sweats, and crises—whether difficult or easy—occur, they demonstrate whether the diseases will be short or long.*

<margin>The disease itself has its own certain attacks and distensions. Time.</margin>
**S**o that the physician may recognize the anger of nature in paroxysms, constitutions, periods, attacks, etc., let him first of all set the disease before himself and investigate it thoroughly. Once it is known, he will know the hour and day when the anger of nature begins, or even that of the disease; and from this it will be known to him how he must anticipate it, and when, so that by means of medicine the anger may be avoided on both sides. However, the disease alone does not do this, but even the time itself signifies the anger of nature and the disease. For example, you know someone is suffering from a fever, and from art and experience you recognize it to be a tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day.</note>. Now, therefore, you must know the habit of the fever from the beginning to the end, when rest will not be forthcoming. Similarly, if a fever happens in autumn or winter, then it is a quartan fever; the season teaches this. Thus, every disease has its own certain time in which it arises,

-># ON THE APHORISMS OF HIPPOCRATES<-

<margin>The firmament is the cause of the seasons, and these are necessary things for the Physician to know.</margin>
...from month to month, from one Moon to another, and so concerning all the firmaments, which indeed are time itself. For light and darkness are only night and day; they are not time but merely the divisions of time. The firmament gives the seasons of the year. Therefore, he who understands the firmament also knows which diseases are destined to come in individual years. It is fitting for a physician to consider these things, as well as the orbits of the planets, and the movements and departures of the wandering stars, which hold their course in one way or another, birthing new seasons and either increasing or weakening things—specifically, how their effects are mingled. Diseases behave in a similar way, for they are governed by the stars, like some foolish person; and just as the stars are and behave, so also the fool wanders inconstantly here and there with his affairs, always appearing as someone else. Therefore, the physician ought to know such diseases. In this way, he must anticipate the "anger" <note>Referring to the "paroxysm" or peak intensity of a disease, often called its "wrath" in early modern medicine.</note>, as has been said, which can happen daily or every third day.

<margin>The signature of diseases.</margin>
Furthermore, the physician must know this: that diseases give their own signs from which the physician can understand whether they will be long-lasting or not. For there is no disease that does not bring signs of its own end and transformation, from which it can be recognized, just as nature makes itself known and designated in other ways. For there is a certain signature <note>term: *signature* — The theory that the external appearance of a thing reveals its internal character or medicinal use.</note> in a disease just as there is in a man; as it is said, "red-haired men are treacherous," or that "the weaker man is the more ferocious." Nature made signs of this sort so that a man might be known. Similarly, every disease is marked by its own signs, which it suits the physician to know. Hippocrates says, therefore, that if the disease does not come immediately after the signs, it signifies a short illness; but if it comes immediately, it signifies a long-lasting one. The reason is that maturation <note>original: *maturatio* — the "ripening" or processing of the disease by the body's heat.</note> ought to happen first, not last. That which must be ripened cannot ripen in a short time. <margin>The ripening power is most potent at the beginning.</margin> For the ripening power is almost at its most effective at the beginning.

<margin>Excrements, that they may testify to the condition of diseases. What the Physician should know. Let the Physician be different from the commoner.</margin>
The urine also denotes where the disease is tending, as do the stools and sweats. For all these are the excrements of those things which are the disease itself. Since they come from the disease, it can be known from them what is happening regarding the disease or because of it. Just as a messenger coming from foreign regions is usually asked how those regions are doing, so it is necessary for the physician to have his experience and observation in every way, so that he stands before the sick person as one who is knowledgeable rather than ignorant, so that he can turn away diseases, and so that he knows whether it will be long or <margin>The signature of diseases must be especially known to the Physician.</margin> short-lived, and whether it will have a good or bad outcome. The physician ought to have learned all these things well in all diseases and should least of all follow general custom, as the common people do, who speak only according to their own opinions. <margin>The signature of diseases and the influence of the stars must be known to the physician.</margin> The physician, however, must not speak recklessly, but knowledgeably and according to the medical art. For he must be so learned that he knows how he ought to behave from the beginning to the end. In summary, it is fitting for the physician to recognize the signature of diseases in a man, and similarly the firmaments—what they pour into the seasons themselves. Then all things will go well.

## Aphorism Thirteen

> *Fasting is endured most easily by old men who are not decrepit; second to these, by those who are of a steady age; less so by adolescents; least of all by children, and among them, least of all those endowed with a sharper and more vivid spirit.*

**I**n this aphorism, note above all this example. A tender tree is inclined toward growing and increasing. But if it truly must grow, it is necessary for it to have something by which it is helped in growing, and that it may grow: for without that, it will not become heavier. From this it follows that nature, which possesses the potential for growing, desires that very thing from which it is nourished. Therefore, the younger ones must have this, because they must grow until they reach their perfect age. For this reason, a child requires more moisture than an adult until he stops growing, which is until the twenty-fourth year. Hippocrates says, therefore, that elders can bear hunger better than <margin>Double hunger in the young.</margin> younger people. For the young are afflicted by a double hunger: namely, the hunger for growing and the hunger for sustenance. Since elders no longer grow, they are not stimulated by the hunger of the growing power. But the young are provoked by the hunger of growth; therefore, they cannot endure fasting like elders, who, if they ate for a double hunger, would fill themselves in vain and unnecessarily. By reason of the power of growing, therefore, the young are stimulated by hunger, and they can least of all tolerate it without falling into disease. But when they cease to grow, then they are afflicted by true hunger, and then they begin to be fit for fasting. Before that, however, it is necessary for them to have eaten more than elders for this reason: that their nature is more vivid and more burning than that of elders. For old age is more and more <margin>Old age is more sluggish than youth.</margin> afflicted by aversion and weariness, and their nature desires less and less. For it decreases like a tree which, as winter approaches, loses one leaf after another, and one virtue after another; and the closer it is to autumn, the less nourishment it requires, and thus it can better do without it than when it was younger, namely, when summer was at hand.

## Aphorism Fourteen

> *Those who grow have the most innate heat; therefore, since they need abundant nourishment, it must be supplied to them plentifully, otherwise the body is consumed. In old men, however, there is little heat, and for that reason they need few things to be kindled; for indeed, their heat is extinguished by many things. For the same reason, fevers in old men are not as acute, for their body is cold.*

**H**ere Hippocrates says that those who grow abound in innate heat <note>term: *calor natiuus* — the "vital heat" or internal fire believed to drive all life processes in ancient and early modern medicine.</note>, and therefore they require much food and are less suited for fasting. As for why he calls the power of being born "innate heat," this is the reason: just as the Sun urges all things on, and all things grow through the Sun, and the Sun <margin>The Sun is the secret of nature.</margin> is the supreme secret <note>original: *arcanum*</note> in fire, and the purest and highest degree of the element of fire—so much so that no species in the element of fire is as clarified and prepared as the Sun, and therefore all things grow most through the Sun— <margin>Innate heat is like the sun in the world.</margin> so also is the innate heat in man, who is the Sun of the element of fire in the microcosm <note>term: *microcosm* — the human being viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>. Through this Sun, man grows. Therefore, where this Sun is strong and effectively strikes the earth, it is necessary that there be many...

# COMMENTARIES.

<margin>The Sun of the Microcosm.</margin>
<margin>The Sun and man generate man.</margin>
...there are dampenings, rains, and dews. A similar thing happens in a person while they are growing. For the Sun of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "little world"; the idea that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note> must have much moisture—namely, abundant "rain and dew," which is to say, plenty of food and drink. Hence the famous saying, *The Sun and man generate man* <note>original: "Sol & homo generant hominem"</note>, so that the man is the father from whom the seed comes, but the Sun provides the power of growing in size and strength. Therefore, the human seed must be given its proper nourishment. For otherwise, it is dried out like a tree that withers due to dryness and is deprived of moisture.

<margin>Old age is cold like winter.</margin>
For this reason, the elderly possess a "Sun" no differently than winter does; and just as the Sun in winter allows the earth to grow cold, so also does the Sun of the microcosm in old age. Old age is cold, like autumn: therefore, it is poorly dealt with; and just as nature made the Sun behave in winter and autumn, so it is arranged in old age. Winter does not need much rain or dew, for it cannot consume them.

<margin>Why the elderly do not require much nourishment.</margin>
So also in old age: if much food were given to it, all of it would freeze into ice—that is, into death. Since, therefore, the elderly have passed from "spring" into "winter," they are no longer "spring-like" or "summer-like," nor do they belong to the dog days of heat; instead, they become and remain "autumnal," like October and November, etc. For that reason, they are compared to cold seasons, not to spring, summer, or the high heat of August.

### Aphorism Fifteen.

> Nature’s bellies are hottest in winter and spring, and sleep is longest. Therefore, during those times, more food must be given, since they have more innate heat, which requires more nourishment. Evidence is found in ages and athletes.

<margin>Why bellies are fuller in winter.</margin>
Know this natural cause for why bellies are fuller <note>The Latin "pinguiores" literally means "fatter," but here refers to the richness of the digestive power and the physical fullness of the organs.</note> in winter and spring: the higher the Sun is, the more it cools bodies. This is because, like a magnet, it attracts its like to itself—that is, it draws out the Sun of the human microcosm.

<margin>The exterior Sun weakens the interior sun of man in summer by attraction.</margin>
For like associates with like. When, therefore, the exterior Sun is stronger than the interior one, it draws the interior heat entirely out of the person. For example, the Moon dominates the "Moon" of a man, which is in the brain, so that a person feels the actions of the Moon within their own brain.

<margin>The Moon rules the brain.</margin>
The same must be understood regarding the Sun: it extracts a man’s own "Sun" from him—that is, it takes away his heat—so that it becomes less effective by several degrees, and by that many degrees, the Sun within the man grows cold. In winter, however, the Sun is not so effective upon the earth, but much weaker; therefore, it draws nothing out of the man. From this it follows that the Sun of the microcosm remains entirely within him, with all its heat, nature, and powers. Therefore, a man is stronger in winter than in summer. Indeed, all the members of the body rejoice in that "Sun" when winter arrives, since the Sun is present in the body in its entirety and with its perfect effectiveness. To this Sun, therefore, enough food and drink must be given through the winter; for that internal Sun consumes them all, just as the exterior Sun exhausts the water from a pool or a pit.

<margin>How youths, younger people, and the very young differ.</margin>
The ages of men and the dispositions of their bodies must also be noticed. For there is a distinction between youths, the younger, and the very young. Similarly, there is a difference between adults, the elder, and the extremely old—those who are purely decrepit and those who are purely children. According to the proportion of age, that interior Sun works more, and therefore demands more nourishment. Furthermore, athletic bodies require this observation, according to whether they are fat or lean. Their Sun is also strong and effective.

### Aphorism Sixteen.

> A moist diet is useful for all those with fevers, but especially for children and those accustomed to such a diet.

<margin>What the Heat of Fever is.</margin>
The heat that all fevers possess has almost no name; it is not from the "Sun" of the man, but is another heat, much more ravenous and insatiable than a wolf, if compared to a man. Moreover, all febrile heat is like fire. And just as the heat from a fire is different <note>referring to a controlled or natural heat</note>, so also is that febrile heat different from natural heat.

<margin>How febrile and natural heat differ. Why moist food should be given to those with fevers.</margin>
From this it follows that febrile heat is like a ravenous wolf, consuming and swallowing everything, and it feeds only on moisture. Know, therefore, that many moist foods must be given to those with fevers, so that the febrile fire does not invade the natural moisture of the body and dry it out—even the marrow of the bones and limbs, etc.—just as a wood fire consumes everything present, leaving nothing but coals and ashes. It is therefore fitting for the physician to consider the degrees of fire according to youth and old age as the work requires; for there are truly degrees of heat: more in one constitution than in another, and greater in children and the younger than in the elder.

### Aphorism Seventeen.

> One must also see for whom food should be given once or twice, more or less, and gradually. Something must truly be granted to the time, the region, the age, and custom.

<margin>What must be observed in giving food.</margin>
Hippocrates wants us to consider not only the disease in a diet—so that food is given to the sick person once, twice, or three times a day according to the stage of the illness—but also the demands of age must be inspected, and the diet ordered accordingly. Besides old age or youth, the conditions, properties, nature, and essence of the region must also be considered, and food and diet must be established for those as well.

<margin>A winter diet is not suitable for summer.</margin>
For the nature and custom of the region must be watched and followed, and not broken in the choice of food and drink; and as often as nature hungers, it should be given. Also, the season must be observed. For summer diets are worth nothing in winter, nor winter ones in summer. Each has its own time; therefore, let what is customary for that time be preserved in the diet, and let nothing foreign be mixed in.

<margin>Praise of Hippocrates for his sincerity.</margin>
In this way, the dietary regimens of the sick must be established, just as Hippocrates teaches, and nothing should be introduced against this aphorism. For Hippocrates in this place had the sincere spirit of medicine. However, those "clever" physicians of ours want to turn Germany into Italy <note>A critique of physicians who try to apply Mediterranean medical customs (like specific diets or timings) to the colder climate of Germany.</note>, which they do only out of sheer pride, not thinking about what Medicine really is; otherwise, they would better preserve the doctrine of Hippocrates.

### Aphorism Eighteen.

> In summer and autumn, they bear a bounty of food with great difficulty; in winter, most easily; in spring, less so.

<margin>Why digestions are worse in summer and autumn.</margin>
The reason why summer and autumn digest food with the most difficulty of all is because their Sun...

is taken away from a person who has not yet been "exalted" <note>Raised or strengthened in vitality.</note> in winter and spring. For where the Sun is not present, there digestion is not good. The heat is not there, and the fire of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Roman god of fire; here used as a metaphor for the internal "cooking" heat of the stomach.</note> is not present to crave, cook, and prepare the food. If, therefore, too much is eaten, much undigested food remains in the person, from which rot is born, and from this come diseases—namely worms, <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostemata," referring to swellings or gatherings of pus.</note>, and other similar troubles.

### Aphorism nineteen.

> *In those cases where the attacks occur through periodic cycles, nothing should be given, nor should they be forced; but food should be withheld before the crises.*

<margin>Nature is forced with danger when it is unwilling, especially before a crisis. Appetite is of great importance. Immoderation is an enemy to nature.</margin>
If anyone suffers from a disease that returns in cycles, so that the disease must be expected with a doubtful mind, Hippocrates wants no food to be given to that person, nor should they be forced to eat. For a nauseated Nature receives food poorly, and what she receives unwillingly, she considers an enemy; she fights against it and refuses to digest it. Therefore, care must be taken that Nature is not burdened with enemies, but is allowed to act according to her own will. Indeed, this is also true: if food is taken beyond measure, Nature does not digest it, but instead constantly hinders it as her own enemy; from this it follows that the food, in turn, harms Nature. The food desires to be in the stomach, but the stomach rejects it; the food wants to be digested, but Nature does not want to digest it. Thus, the food vexes Nature, and the person becomes much more miserable. If this happens just as the disease is accelerating its period or <term>paroxysm</term> <note>The peak intensity or sudden "attack" of a fever or disease.</note>, know that nothing but great misfortune is to be expected. <margin>Nothing is ruined by fasting, but by too much feeding.</margin> Therefore, no sin is committed by fasting, but rather by feeding; even if it is done with good intentions and with good food, it can nonetheless be the cause of death at such a time. One must follow the safer and more certain path.

### Aphorism twenty.

> *In those things which are reaching a judgment or have already been judged, nothing should be changed, whether by medicines or other irritants, but they are to be left alone.*

<margin>Nature, when striving for victory, must not be bothered by ill-timed medicines.</margin>
When a <term>Crisis</term> <note>The "turning point" of a disease where the patient either begins to recover or decline toward death.</note> occurs in a disease, the Physician ought to see and recognize whether that crisis has begun or is completely finished, and whether the crisis is worse than the state itself or in balance. For then the Physician should begin nothing, nor use his medicines, nor introduce any new things, but should commit the labor to Nature alone. For when she has obtained the victory and the crisis is in balance, it is to be hoped that Nature will henceforth also be the superior force. If, therefore, she were changed or perverted, she would lose her advantage, and thus a labyrinth would be created; the disease would take up strength anew, and something worse than the previous disease would be born. The Physician must note this. <margin>Nature is the Doctor.</margin> For Nature herself is a doctor, having her own medicines and her own pharmacy; the physician must not hinder her, but help her. <margin>The Medicine and the Physician are twofold.</margin> For Medicine is twofold, the pharmacy is twofold, and the Physician is twofold: one within nature, and the other outside nature—that is, one within the man himself, and the other outside the man. The external physician ought to yield to the internal one, unless he sees that it is necessary to help the internal one. For the inner fortress is granted to the internal physician so that he may hold and fortify himself there; the external one must only assist him.

### Aphorism twenty-one.

> *If something must be expelled, it should be expelled by the way toward which it most tends, and through the appropriate places.*

<margin>How many ways there are for the expulsion of harmful things.</margin>
In this place, Hippocrates gives good advice on how those things which do not suit Nature are to be expelled. For some want to expel everything adverse to nature through the bowels; others through vomiting; others through urine; others through sweat, etc. All of these things should not be done indiscriminately. For those thoughts which are not medicinal must be abandoned. Know, therefore, that the physician first of all must recognize where Nature is tending. For she is the primary Doctor; man is the secondary and subordinate one. <margin>Nature is the primary Doctor; man is the secondary. Sepsis and pleurisy are to be cured through sweat.</margin> Where Nature begins, there the Physician ought to help her; that is, Nature is the better Doctor, knowing best where the most convenient exit should be sought. If, therefore, Nature wants to expel through sweat, and you find signs of sweating in the expulsive power, then help so that the expulsion happens through sweat. For <term>pleurisy</term> <note>Inflammation of the lungs/chest.</note> and <term>sepsis</term> <note>original: "septis," referring to putrid infections.</note> are not expelled through the anus, urine, vomiting, eyes, ears, or mouth, but most conveniently through sweat. These, therefore, are to be promoted; for the <term>emunctorium</term> <note>An organ or duct that removes waste from the body (like a pore or a lymph node).</note> of these diseases is through sweat, so that they may depart through the pores. Therefore, things pertaining to sweat should be led out through sweat; and similarly, things that should be expelled through the bowels should be diverted through them, and likewise for urine.

Nature has her own tracks; wherever you find them, expel that way and do not establish another path. If you feel pain in any place, know that Nature wants to have an exit point there. <margin>Where Nature gives a sign of expulsion, there an exit for the disease must be made.</margin> If it has not yet been made by Nature herself, you make it. For it will be necessary for Nature to have it in that place; thus Nature will hasten only toward that exit. Even if no exit points were open anywhere, when you see Nature tending and gathering there and seeking an exit, you should quickly open it and leave Nature an exit in the place where she wishes. See, therefore, that you are ready to make an exit according to the condition of the matter: through <term>corrosives</term> <note>Chemicals used to create a sore or opening in the skin.</note> in gout, sciatica, arthritis, etc. For the physician who knows how to direct the expulsive power according to Nature's will possesses nearly a third of the art of medicine. Often there is also a "superfluity" present, as in <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydrope," an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, where at the beginning it helps somewhat if exit points are made; but when the superfluity is too great, it no longer does any good. For Nature leaves the matter as it is, and therefore shows no sign of an exit. When, therefore, she gives no sign, no exit point should be made. For if exit points are made without Nature’s indication and will, then lethal diseases arise, or long-lasting and durable ones. <margin>The abuse of corrosives.</margin> Know, therefore, that it is great folly to apply corrosives where Nature does not seek an exit; she might wish for an exit to be made in another place, but those people want to rule her, even though she is the master. <margin>Nature is quite commanding.</margin> The Physician, however, is a servant. And indeed, Nature is such a master that she does not yield to any servant; therefore, these things are attempted in vain. Let every physician consider where Nature tends, and expel there and help the expulsion. He who is skilled and knowledgeable in these things perfectly knows a third part of Medicine, and he should not be ashamed to be called a physician. For he can be one worthily and honorably. ->COMMENTARIES.<-

Note this: even if it seems to a physician that there is an <term>emunctory</term> <note>original: "emunctorium"; an organ or canal that carries off waste, like a sweat gland or the bowels.</note> somewhere, he must nevertheless obey nature. For he will lose nothing by it, except that he cannot lead nature elsewhere, unless by greater sweats and the like. Those physicians are misguided who seek only a single emunctory—whether it be only sweats, or only bowel movements, or only vomiting. For what nature wants, the physician should also want.

### Aphorism twenty-two.

> *It is proper to treat and move things that are cooked and ripe, not raw; and this should not be done at the beginning, unless they move by their own impulse, which happens very rarely.*

<margin>Immature things are not at all manageable.</margin>
No one can use an immature thing. For what use is an immature apple or pear? Likewise, nothing can be started with an immature disease. An <term>abscess</term> <note>original: "apostema"; a swelling or gathering of humors.</note> accepts no medicine unless it first ripens. Once ripening has preceded, its cure follows, etc. This also happens in the whole body. For if someone were to open an abscess that was not yet ripe, it would not happen without great harm and pain, besides the fact that many evils would have to be feared afterward. This would also happen in the whole body. Therefore, Hippocrates rightly says that only those things which are ripe ought to be expelled, not the immature. Furthermore, it should be known that what is not ripe must be made to ripen. Understand how that is done in this way:

<margin>By what means ripening is to be done.</margin>
A certain Art knows "Attractives," <note>Medicines or treatments intended to draw humors toward the surface.</note> which draw out "nails" <note>likely referring to "clavus," a type of hard skin growth or corn.</note>, etc. These can ripen things that otherwise would scarcely ripen in two or three months. Some diseases even ripen in the hour of their star, so that they are ripe in four or six hours. Many such things are possible for nature, which the physician ought to know, so that in this way he himself can also ripen diseases to hasten their expulsion. There is also another way of ripening diseases: namely, so that the *Hard becomes soft*—that is, what is hardened is resolved into water, just as iron is resolved in water. These are indeed the "destructions" of natures, so that they tend from hardness into softness, as happens in man; and these things are afterward expelled through sweat, or through urine, or through the bowels, according as the disease suits its own emunctory.

<margin>Ripening is fourfold.</margin>
<margin>Syrups contribute nothing to ripening.</margin>
Such "corruption" is indeed good and useful if it is rightly understood as true ripening, which certainly cannot be achieved through syrups. For they do not resolve in their corruption, and therefore they should not be discussed here.

<margin>Diseases are twofold.</margin>
Hippocrates also places two kinds of diseases here: the "savage" and "pleasant," and the "non-savage." By the savage, he understands those which have stabs and pains joined to them—that is, he speaks of diseases (not only in this aphorism, but also in others) that are hardened and not "furious," such as the plague, pleurisy, and gout, all of which are exceptions. But those which are not so savage and painful are to be ripened and afterward expelled. In "furious" <note>meaning acute, violent, or rapidly progressing.</note> diseases, however, one must proceed as they are, according to how they show themselves. For they are almost ripe by themselves and do not need any medicine for their ripening.
<margin>Where ripening is not to be expected.</margin>

### Aphorism twenty-three

> *Evacuations are not to be judged by their quantity, but by whether those things which ought to be evacuated have been, and whether the sick bear it easily; and if it is necessary to expel even to the point of fainting, it should be done, provided the patient can endure it.*

<margin>Laxatives are of two kinds.</margin>
The quantity of excrement, urine, sweat, etc., is not to be considered; rather, one must see whether those egestions are suitable and proper. For if much comes out, but the egestions are not proper, then peculiar diseases are present, namely flux of the belly, dysentery, diarrhea, etc. Know, therefore, if the egestions are proper and suitable, and there is a need, then one must proceed with the expulsion, and it will be beneficial. But if those egestions are not right, one must stop the expulsion. If, therefore, the stools are "true," <note>meaning they contain the actual harmful matter of the disease.</note> then the water should be vigorously expelled so that the patient is diligently purged, provided he can bear it. And even if some weakness follows, it is not to be cared for. For great health will follow it. Therefore, let the physician not boast of the multitude of bowel movements, but rather of the true egestion. For there are certain laxatives that expel both good and bad together; but others which eject only the good and none of the bad. Therefore, great discretion is needed so that the suitable is taken and not the unsuitable. Take an example in dysentery: if a proper purgation is made, which finds the true offending cause, then the sick person is immediately healed. But if he takes an unsuitable one, the patient's death is at hand. In purgations, therefore, proper simples and compounds are to be offered to the patient, which move the true matter and not the false. But the folly and ignorance of physicians is so great that they do not understand this aphorism, and yet they boast about it daily. For they say: "How can this man be sick, when he has been purged so many times, has swallowed so many enemas, and had so many bowel movements?" What kind of talk is this? Truly, you glory in your own disgrace—that you do not understand the matter, and you give your attention to the internal stools rather than to the true recognition of the disease, upon which depends what is suitable and what is not. And so many, if they were dealt with according to public law, would be convicted of being treacherous.
<margin>Ancient doctors as boasters.</margin>

### Aphorism twenty-four.

> *In acute diseases, medicine should be used rarely and at the beginning, and that must be done with diligent circumspection.*

In the plague, in "stabbings" <note>sharp, localized pains.</note>, and similar sudden diseases, one should not purge at the beginning. For the material cause is not in the stomach. That which is not placed in the stomach, but in another place, ought not to be purged. For purgation is not its emunctory; and thus purgation would be done in that place where the disease does not hide, and the disease would rather be strengthened in this way. Sometimes, however, purgation is suitable even in these diseases, as in the plague and some others, where the stomach is often full of "raw" <note>undigested or corrupt.</note> humors; if therefore that superfluous matter wishes to join and associate itself with the disease, you may remove that filth—not, however, by reason of the disease itself, but rather because of the dregs. But proceed differently with the disease itself.

### Aphorism twenty-five and the last of the first section.

> *If such things as ought to be purged are purged, it is beneficial and they bear it easily; but if the opposite, they bear it with difficulty.*

It becomes a physician to recognize diseases with discretion, and not that alone, but rather the disease in its own...

# FRAGMENT OF THE COMMENTARY OF THE GERMAN THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS ON THE SECOND SECTION OF THE APHORISMS, EXPLAINING THE FIRST SIX APHORISMS.

## SECTION TWO.

### Aphorism First.

> If in any disease sleep is troublesome, it is deadly; but if it is beneficial, it is not at all lethal.

<margin>Sleep is necessary for man.</margin>
In this place, Hippocrates encompasses all diseases together, excluding none, saying: If in any disease whatsoever, sleep—even if it seems appropriate to the disease—goes badly, or weakens or sickens the patient, it is a sign of death. But if it does not do these things, but instead benefits the sick person, there is no danger. The cause of this matter is that we require sleep, which <margin>Six hours must be slept.</margin> we must enjoy once in twenty-four hours, usually for six hours. That sleep restores rest to the body, takes away the weariness and exhaustion of labor, and refreshes it so that it can be sufficient for work once again. Besides this, there are <margin>Causes and types of sleep.</margin> also other kinds of sleep which are not of the nature and company of the aforementioned natural sleep, but come upon a person from elsewhere: namely, first through food and drink; second through diseases, so that it is brought upon the sick person by the nature and property of the diseases themselves; third through time and the stars, which can themselves induce sleep and burden a person with a strange and unusual sleep; fourth through certain medicines, such as those that are sleep-inducing, narcotics, stupefying agents, etc., about <margin>Sleep so that it may testify about the disease.</margin> all of which there is no need to speak. You should therefore understand Hippocrates in this place to mean that sleep, which creeps in along with the disease, shows in the sick what the purpose of the disease is, and gives its sign, either toward death or toward health, and this through its own nature. For it expels the natural sleep owed to rest and succeeds it. Once true sleep is driven out, this disease-sleep itself obtains dominion. There are, however, in the sleep of the stars, of diseases, of food and drink, and of medicine, two properties: one good and prosperous, signifying good health; the other unfortunate, the hour and time and sleep leading toward death. The physician will discern these two from their signs. For even to one who fills himself with an immoderate amount of food and drink, the sleep that follows can be good or bad; for example, <term>gout</term> <note>original: "gutta"</note>, paralysis, or a contraction might seize him, or he might even be cheered and awakened. If therefore <margin>Sleep is a blind and obscure thing.</margin> it does not suit him but harms him, he should abstain from it. Similarly, a heavy sleep hides within wine; if this produces pains in the sick person, let him avoid it and not drink, lest sleep come upon him. But if it does you good, there is no need for you to flee that sleep. So also there are certain medicines that contain sleep within them, if you use them rightly according to their property. If it profits you, then the medicine is good. If not, omit it, otherwise it will kill you. Hippocrates therefore says of sleep that it is a blind and obscure thing, and for that reason only its signs are to be considered—what they are like and where they tend.

### Aphorism Second.

> If sleep calms delirium, it is good.

Hippocrates continues to speak and affirm regarding sleep: if in any <term>maniacal</term> <note>original: "maniaco"; referring here to any state of mental frenzy or madness</note> disease, or another that disturbs the reason, sleep acts as a remedy and settles the delirium, it is a good sign. But if the disease is increased through sleep, it is not good. Understand Hippocrates in this way: <margin>Balance is the cause of natural actions.</margin> the human body has its own <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperaturam"; the balance of qualities or humors</note> which it must retain, so that every member may perform its duty and have its own property. When this happens, then a man is strong in his powers and is healthy. In the brain, therefore, there is also a certain commanding power that preserves the reason and thought of a man. When this is disturbed, and a discord falls between that power and the reason, then the reason is perturbed, and thus the man becomes delirious; just as if two people were of one mind, and of one purpose and counsel, then the thing they want is accomplished. But when they disagree, and each wants to keep his own measure, then a disturbance follows, which flows from a certain insane lust of both. When therefore <margin>A mutual will between two does not lack effect.</margin> these two are calmed and reconciled through the interventions of neighbors, so that the matter is finally given over to oblivion, then the matter goes well. But when those reconciliations accomplish nothing, then those two remain enemies until death. In a similar way, understand Hippocrates in this place: if such a fury arises in the brain, no reconciliation helps, and nothing else will be of use except sleep. If sleep can be the reconciler, it is the best one, as the only thing able to cure. But if sleep accomplishes nothing, then it is a sign of fixed and perpetual insanity, which is resisted in vain. Regarding sleep, therefore, know that the physician must apply the greatest diligence, so that he may deal with it industriously, artistically, and skillfully. For SLEEP is such a great <margin>Sleep is a wonderful secret.</margin> <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum"; a profound medical secret or a potent, hidden remedy</note> in medicine, that I would gladly learn from someone (let there be no error in the saying) whether and what medicine exists that is such <margin>Praise of sleep and sleep-inducing agents. Sleep-inducing agents must be diligently known.</margin> a present and sudden help in all diseases, and so greatly leads the body to health, as much as sleep does. Sleep-inducing agents, therefore (by whatever name they are called), must be most highly considered by every physician. For sleep is a medicine surpassing all the secrets of gems and precious stones. He who knows how to rightly apply the SLEEP-INDUCING SECRET of Nature, drawn from the appropriate essence, is to be highly valued among the sick. Therefore, Hippocrates does not speak here only of natural sleeps, but it is necessary that you understand him as an experienced physician, who from the spirit of medicine...
