-> COMMENTARIES <-

<margin>The Humorists are rebuked.</margin>
...[he] is [described], not as a <term>Humorist</term> <note>original: "Humorista"; Paracelsus uses this term disparagingly for traditional physicians who relied solely on the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) without understanding deeper natural principles</note> who does not know what is sleep-inducing, but as a master craftsman.

### Aphorism Third.

-> *Both sleep and wakefulness, if they exceed moderation, are bad.* <-

<margin>Sleep is medicine.</margin>
Hippocrates continues regarding sleep and, at the same time, wakefulness, which is the opposite of sleep; if either is utilized more than is necessary, it is harmful. Understand this as if he were saying: sleep is a medicine, whether it arises from wine, from bread, or from a medical drug, etc., and it contributes to the health of the sick person if it is not excessive. That is to say, the sick person must carefully weigh the <term>sufficiency</term> <note>original: "sufficientiam"; the exact amount required for health, neither too much nor too little</note> of each thing. For the highest point in medicine is to know sufficiency. For it is not only fitting for the physician to know how much the sick person has eaten or drunk, but also that he knows how much is excreted and how much remains in the body, lest it become too much. For if medicine is intended to expel a disease, and no disease is present, it does not remain ineffective; rather, it attacks something else with which it does not harmonize and destroys it, and from this, a new disease arises.

<margin>The harms of immoderate sleep.</margin>
It must be understood similarly regarding sleep: if it exceeds moderation and necessity, it harms the person, hinders the function of the limbs, and disturbs nature. Regarding excessive wakefulness, know that a person must hold the middle ground in all things, taking a little of anything up to its limit—once that limit is passed, one must stop.

<margin>How long should one sleep?</margin>
A person, therefore, ought to be awake from the fourth hour of the morning until the eighth hour of the evening, more or less, according to the requirements of each person’s <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific physical makeup and temperament of an individual</note>. But if a person does not do this, but rises not at the fourth hour but only at the tenth, and spends the whole night sleepless, then the true and natural order is broken.

<margin>The sun demands wakefulness, night demands sleep.</margin>
For the sun requires wakefulness while it provides heat; when it sets, then the person should also lie down, and rise again with the sun and lie down with it.

<margin>The inconveniences of perverted sleep and wakefulness.</margin>
All regimens pertaining to sleep and wakefulness should be established according to this order. If the opposite is done, "foreign" diseases arise which do not behave according to the order of nature, but against it. From this, it follows that even the natural order of medicine is of no use; for the disease did not arise in a natural way, since all things should have their own order.

<margin>Just as with diseases, so medicine has its own order.</margin>
For example, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydrops"; an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> arises in its own way, and a fever in its own. Therefore, the medicine for dropsy is of such a kind, and so on, so that all things have their own order.

<margin>Every excess is an evil.</margin>
When, therefore, no order is observed in this matter, it follows that the medicine is also disordered, wandering, and uncertain, in which one can place very little trust. For nature has been destroyed and wanders without its order. Hippocrates says, therefore, that it is an evil if excess occurs, whether in sleep or in wakefulness, such that death can arise from it, or a perpetual disease which no one can cure or would dare to boldly tackle. For nature itself trembles in such irregular people.

<margin>Nature is balanced.</margin>
All things ought to be certain and fixed, and not exceed moderation. And indeed, he [Hippocrates] considered the matter well when he said there ought to be equality and nothing in excess. For God created all things in such a way that nothing should depart from its own nature, and nothing should be in excess against the order of its creation and nature, [setting] a limit for each thing, so that every excess is a poison.

<margin>Excess is against nature.</margin>
One foot, therefore, ought to be as heavy as the other, etc.; so it is with the fingers; one foot ought to have as many fingers as the other. Whatever exceeds in weight or number is superfluous and is a disease. For if someone drags one leg heavier than the other, it is a foul sight.

<margin>Through immoderation there is either too much or too little.</margin>
In a similar way, things ought to be inside the body, so that every limb has its own weight and measure. Hippocrates proposes two things by which all superfluities and defects can be understood, namely excessive <term>repletion</term> <note>filling up/overeating</note> and excessive <term>inanition</term> <note>emptying/starving</note>. That is, if someone fills himself today with more than nature can bear, and tomorrow takes away from himself more than nature can suffer, neither is of any value. For a certain measure must be kept in number and weight, so that in the beginning there is an equilibrium and equal weight with the filling. Whatever, however, exceeds the other, acts against nature, nor can nature endure it. For if we consider nature in its essence, we will see all things keep their own order, their own number, their own weight, their own measure, their own circle, etc., so that they neither exceed nor fall short.

<margin>Equilibrium must be maintained in man.</margin>
It is just as if Hippocrates were saying: you physicians, see to it that you direct all your efforts so that there is equilibrium in man, and nothing exceeds or falls short in diet, regimen, etc., so that all things are certain, fixed, and equal on both sides. Unless you consider this, what you do, you do in vain.

<margin>The fasts of monks are harmful.</margin>
Note, therefore, some examples. Monasteries have such laws where fasting occurs at a fixed time and hour against nature, so that nature is deprived of its due at that hour. At another hour they have too much, so that the measure of nature is exceeded. These two weights break the scales of nature. For one is too heavy, the other too light. Or the entire scale is in error, such that they fill themselves for the whole week, but on Friday and Saturday they eat only bread and fast; or through the whole rest of the year they stuff themselves with meat, but during the time of <term>Lent</term> <note>original: "quadragesimali"; the 40 days of fasting before Easter</note> they devour no meat at all. This scale is unjust in the eyes of nature. But they act this way not only in this, but also in labor and leisure, and other similar things, all of which there is no need to review.

It is therefore fitting for the physician to distribute and arrange all these things and place them in a just balance, lest nature have too much on one side and too little on the other.

Similarly, it must be understood concerning all things wherever inequality is found: especially concerning the physician’s medicine, of which Hippocrates speaks here, where the physician ought to take inequality as the greatest detriment to nature and balance it, lest nature be hindered.

whatever they may be. For the word "Spontaneous" <note>original: "Spontaneæ"; referring to sudden or unprovoked weariness</note> is not to be so greatly regarded; for this is the cause and foundation: when any disease, whether good or bad, has arisen in a man, he can perceive it no better than if he were laboring. For the disease then gives some sign of itself, which sign must be attended to by the physician, who ought to be skilled in this matter, so that he may know which disease is present. However, this aphorism was placed only because of those diseases which do not betray themselves otherwise than through restlessness and labor, by which they are forced to give signs. For example: someone suffers from a stone, from sand, or from a <term>bolus</term> <note>original: "bolo"; in this context, it refers to a mass or clump of morbid matter within the body</note>, etc.

Yet he does not feel this disease, suspecting nothing of the sort. But if he is exhausted by too much travel, or bends himself too much, or moves his body in some other way, so that the clump, stone, or sand is moved from its place and rolled around in that commotion, etc., then the signs of the stone betray themselves: back pain, and biting pains in the legs, sides, and hips, etc. From these signs, the physician will gather what they signify. And these things are not only to be understood regarding external physical labor, but also regarding internal labor—namely, that of nature laboring within itself, which also betrays its own signs through spontaneous labors. For example: someone eats and drinks; nature is forced to digest these, in 
<margin>Pains indicate that diseases are present.</margin>

<margin>Signs of diseases from the obstruction of nature's actions.</margin>
around the stomach; that compression is a sign of disease. Likewise, <term>orexis</term> <note>original: "orexis"; a Greek term for appetite or a sudden craving, often viewed here as a morbid symptom</note> invades someone, and this is a sign of disease; likewise vomiting and <term>tormina</term> <note>original: "tormina"; sharp, twisting pains in the bowels, like colic</note>, etc. All these are signs of some hidden disease. It is fitting for the physician to notice all these things, so that if someone comes saying, "as soon as I eat, then I am affected in such and such a way," and another says, "as soon as I eat milk and cheese, I feel pain in this or that place," etc., and another, "as soon as I am joined to my wife, then dizziness invades me," etc. From these, O physician, judge what those signs signify. If, therefore, you are skilled in these matters and recognize where the signs come from, then you will know what you must answer, and what kind of diseases you ought to cure. It is fitting, therefore, for the physician to observe the labors of a man, not only those which a man performs of his own will, but also those which nature has, as has been said. For in this way the physician ought to demonstrate his science, his art, and his experience, and investigate further causes from the signs. In this aphorism, therefore, understand Hippocrates thus: namely, that he speaks of things far different than what the Humors of Galen teach; Galen is worthy of 
<margin>Galen is censured.</margin>
derision in his explanation, because he lacks both taste and smell <note>Paracelsus often accused traditional Galenic doctors of being "blind" to the chemical and sensory realities of nature, such as the actual properties of substances</note>.

### Aphorism Sixth.

> *Those who feel pain in some part of the body, and almost do not perceive the pain, their mind is sick.*

In this place, the opinion of Hippocrates is that the body suffers from no disease which is not felt and does not produce pains. But if any disease is without pain, the fault is located in the mind; that is, that disease is not corporeal, but spiritual.

# THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS 
## THE GERMAN’S 
## Explanations of the fourth section, a fragment, comprising the last nine aphorisms.

### SECTION FOUR.

#### Aphorism LXXV.

> *If anyone passes blood or pus in their urine, it signifies an ulceration of the kidneys or the bladder.*

<margin>Urine as an indicator of kidney defects.</margin>
If an ulceration occurs in the bladder or in the kidneys, it is their nature to purge themselves through the urine. For urine is collected and exits in these places; thus, that matter which causes ulcerations passes into the urine, and as much as is mixed with the urine also exits with the urine, and so it is seen in the urine whether an ulceration is present or not.
<margin>Blood is the cause of ulceration because of the salt of the bodies.</margin>
However, Hippocrates says that either pus or blood will exit: the cause of this thing is that blood is the origin of every ulceration because of the <term>salt of the bodies</term> <note>original: "sal corporum"; in Paracelsian alchemy, 'salt' is one of the three primary principles (with sulfur and mercury) representing the solid, tactile, and often corrosive elements of a substance</note> which resides in it. Therefore, when the 
<margin>Internal parts of the bladder are denoted by pus; those of the kidneys by gore in the urine.</margin>
urine reaches the said places, it also becomes sharp and opens them, just as if someone touched a known ulcer somewhat roughly, then it begins to emit blood. The same must be understood regarding the kidneys. For no gore flows from the bladder, rather only pus; that is the sign of an ulceration of the bladder, whereas gore denotes an ulceration of the kidneys. For any ulceration of the kidneys is easily made bloody, especially if some amount of sand and stony matter is mixed in, and it passes through that ulceration, then it opens it by biting/gnawing at it and makes it bloody. These two are therefore the most certain signs of ulcerations, one indeed in the bladder, the other in the kidneys.

#### Aphorism LXXVI.

> *If with thick urine passing, small fleshy bits and like hairs flow forth, those are secreted from the kidneys.*

<margin>What the filaments in urine indicate.</margin>
When the kidneys become "lacinious" or "plumose" <note>original: "lacinioſi vel plumofi"; meaning ragged, fringed, or feathery, referring to the shredding of the kidney tissue</note>, just as can happen on the outside—namely, that ulcers are born which are consumed in the form of hairs or like fibrous tears of flesh, as "plumose" ulcers are accustomed to do—when, I say, the kidneys are subject to such ulcers and are thus scraped away, all those things pass into the urine, often in such quantity that the passages are obstructed and the urine is hindered, and so they are seen in the urine after its exit. If, therefore, such "fringes" are 
<margin>Signs of "plumose" viscera in the urinary passages.</margin>
found in the urine, it is a most certain sign that a "plumose" ulcer lurks in the urinary passages. And although Hippocrates speaks only of the kidneys, nevertheless it also happens in the bladder. This is certain: that some ulcer lies hidden in those places through which the urine passes. But the location cannot be certainly defined unless a distinction between the kidneys and other parts is found through the putrefaction of the urine.

#### Aphorism LXXVII.

> *Those who have passed something bran-like with thick urine, their bladder is scabious.*

Inside the body, a disease similar to bran or moths <note>original: "tineis"; likely referring to skin-like scales or lesions resembling those caused by clothes-moths</note> is also produced. For where scales or "moths" are born...

<header>COMMENTARY.</header>

<margin>What scales in the urine indicate.</margin>
...are born; in that same place, there is also a certain fatness that clings to them like an ointment. For this is the nature of <term>tineae</term> <note>original: "tinearum"; literally "moths," but used here to describe skin-like eruptions or parasitic growths</note> or <term>saphatum</term> <note>original: "saphatorum"; a term used in medieval medicine for scaly or crusty skin conditions</note>, that they arise and persist with a certain oiliness. Therefore, when such scales are produced within the body, the urine washes them away, and thus carries that oily substance out with it, and sometimes the scales as well. For this reason, an oily fatness is seen in the urine, so that the entire urine appears fatty and thick, mixed with large and small flakes that have the form of scales. For such flakes have the same nature and origin as those scales.

### Aphorism LXXIIX.

<margin>Where the passing of blood comes from and what it signifies.</margin>
*If someone spontaneously urinates blood, it signifies that a small vein in the kidneys has ruptured.*

**V**eins that are within the body are often thicker by nature than they ought to be; often they are also thinner. Indeed, one person’s veins are thicker than another's, or thinner. Therefore, when the blood boils and rages in the veins, and the veins are too thin, it then bursts the veins. Similarly, this happens in the kidneys; whenever a vein is ruptured in the urinary passages, blood flows out—sometimes without urine, sometimes with urine—for it can happen that the blood is expelled of its own accord.

### Aphorism LXXIX.

*In those whose urine has sandy deposits, their bladder is stony.*

**T**artar <note>original: "Tartarus"; in the Paracelsian system, this refers to the stony mineral deposits formed within the body from food and drink, analogous to the crust in a wine barrel</note> which is in water and other drinks, and even in food, when it coagulates into its final form, then whatever its nature is, such does it exit through the urine—at least as much as nature is able to expel. In that expulsion, sandy materials are secreted. Therefore, when these are found in the urine, it is a sign that the person is subject to the stone and sand.

However, as for the fact that if such sands are red, they denote a red stone, and if purple, a purple one: the cause lies in the kidneys, which alone impart such colors to it. For by itself, no stone is naturally red or white, but in the bladder, the tartar retains the color it received from nature itself.

### Aphorism LXXX.

*If someone urinates blood and clots, and suffers from a dribbling of urine, and pain falls into the lower abdomen and the perineum, then the areas around the bladder are suffering.*

<margin>Erysipelas of the bladder</margin>
**W**hen the bladder is disturbed from its healthy state and tends toward destruction, it gives signs and knowledge of itself to the physician through the urine—namely, if it emits blood through the urine, and that by drops, and with clots, and so on. For the cause is that the bladder suffers a kind of <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "erysipelas"; while usually a skin infection, here it refers to an acute, red inflammation and swelling of the internal membranes</note>, specifically with a swelling of the veins and inflammation, so that the bladder becomes swollen and ulcerated inside. From these occurrences, the urine assumes a different nature. And since the bladder is weak in its power to expel, the urine comes out drop by drop. And where there is such swelling, the areas above the private parts are afflicted with pain, as if an abscess or a <term>bubo</term> <note>a swollen lymph node or inflamed swelling</note> were lurking there. These are the signs of a certain erysipelatous disease, which must be treated just like erysipelas.

### Aphorism LXXXI.

*If someone urinates blood or pus, or small scales, and a foul odor is present, then an ulceration of the bladder is signified.*

<margin>Signs of putrid ulcers in the urinary passages.</margin>
<margin>Foul smell of urine as an index of rot.</margin>
**T**here is also another kind of affection, when hollow ulcers arise from the putrefaction of the ulcers themselves. For not all things rot, but when they do, it is a sign that other things are rotting along with the bladder. Therefore, when the urine passes through, it absorbs that stench in the bladder, which afterwards exits with the urine; for this reason, these signs are in the urine. From this it follows that when the urine stinks, something in the man is rotting. If these signs concur—blood, pus, or scales—then the rot is in the bladder. If not, it will be in other places: namely, in the womb for women, but in a similar region for men.

### Aphorism LXXXII.

*If a swelling in the urinary passage should suppurate and burst, relief will follow.*

Missing. <note>original: "Deest"; the commentator notes this aphorism is absent or not discussed in the source manuscript</note>

### Aphorism LXXXIII. & the last of the fourth section.

*If someone urinates a great deal at night, it signifies little excrement.*

<margin>Why stools become drier.</margin>
**W**hen nature has received food, it separates it in such a way that it sends the urine to the liver along with its nourishment, while the dung tends toward the bowels with its like. More often, however, nature in digestion takes away too much moisture from the dung and assigns it to the urine; hence follows the dryness of the stool. For its moisture, which it ought to have, is secreted through the urine. This is why much urine and little stool are expelled, and that especially at night, for this reason: when nature is at rest, the urine then trickles into the bladder more forcefully than if one were not sleeping. For while one is awake, thoughts, business, labor, and anxiety hinder many operations, and thus they delay the stool and urine, so that they are not so easily moved toward the exit as happens at night. Conversely, overly moist stools signify little urine. For just as much is taken from the urine by the stool, so it happens to the stool by the urine.

### Another explanation of the first Aphorism of Hippocrates, from the Autograph of Paracelsus.

->Life is short.<-

<margin>What sort of man Hippocrates was</margin>
**I**n this place, Hippocrates declares the mortality of the physical body. And he places this first not without merit. For of all his treatment, this is the one end. Rightly, therefore, in the beginning, he describes the years of nature. Let this be an admonition to us, that we may proceed all the more hastily in arts and business and strive toward the end, not by following long winding paths, but by hurrying straight to the goal. Here he also alludes to labor undertaken in vain, by which either health, longevity, or immortality is sought. From this it is clear that he himself was utterly ignorant of the Mysteries of nature, the Arcana, and other Great Works, and thus he stood forth only as a guardian and preserver of a fleeting and short life. And so it is established that he felt concerning the limit of death as if that goal cannot be leaped over, but must be endured entirely.

Foolishly, therefore, do those act who think that from the instruction of Hippocrates they can extend the limit of death, since this opinion of his never...

<header>ON THE APHORISMS OF HIPPOCRATES</header>

what it was: but he will have subjected himself, along with his medicine, entirely to the hour appointed by nature.

remains. We do not know that time itself causes things to be hot at certain times. We know that the same remedies work one day; the next day they do not work; today they help, tomorrow they harm. Where we despair, there they are useful; where we hope, there they fail us. Today they are certain, tomorrow they exist as uncertain. For those things are not in our power. Moreover, that which is not in our power is deceptive.

->*Art is long.*<-

<margin>
The Great Year of Plato.
The Month of Archelaus.
</margin>

We humans indeed learn from the ages of Adam even unto this hour, and so even to the very last man, yet we do not reach the goal of the arts we have begun. If we set them forth universally, the <term>Great Year of Plato</term> <note>original: "Annus Platonis"; a cosmic cycle of roughly 25,000 years after which the stars return to their original positions</note> will not finish them. If we set them forth in detail, the <term>Month of Archelaus</term> <note>original: "Menis Archelai"; likely referring to a shorter astronomical or alchemical period of time used as a contrast to Plato’s cycle</note> does not terminate them. Therefore, it is rightly to be considered that so long an art does not suit so short a life. Thus, they rightly seem to be omitted. Furthermore, while we seek out the arts, one here, another elsewhere, we die twice over before we reach the foundation or even half-knowledge.

->*Judgment is indeed difficult.*<-

We judge what we do not see, and what we imagine. Moreover, we imagine what we are ignorant of. While we judge this, we hallucinate. For why do we imagine internal things as if they stood outside us? And why do we imagine what we do not see as if it were exposed to our eyes? We name things we do not know. We argue about things we cannot witness. For in nature, those things which are secret are not manifested to man. Therefore, our judgment is deceptive. We cannot even make a judgment in an open wound. For our eyes see only the body, but not likewise the spirit, in which the foundation is placed.

->*Time is fleeting.*<-

<margin>
Time rules over medicine.
</margin>

Time rules seriously and powerfully over both art and life, and it breaks the operation of medicine, and cuts off the goal, property, element, essence, form, and whatever else belongs to the art. If therefore time breaks these things: it must be understood entirely, nor should so much trust be placed in the apothecary shops, books, herbs, etc. For all these things are subject to their master, time, which commands us while we sleep. Add to this that time repeatedly produces new diseases—today of one kind, tomorrow others—with both the sick and the medicines of the sick being changed.

->*It is necessary not only, etc.*<-

This aphorism teaches nothing other than that it is proper for the sick person, the attendants, and the Physician to do their duty simultaneously, and that things be done for the sick person accordingly. The sick person, in turn, must be obedient to these. Moreover, the nature of the sick person must be known to the attendants, so that they know what he requires, what things ought to be offered to him, and what things less so. It also suits the Physician to be such a man who knows, and does not merely have an opinion. When these three are correctly disposed, a happy hour can be hoped for, etc.

->*Experience is deceptive.*<-

We have some experience, but it is not complete. We know the natures of some <term>simples</term> <note>original: "Simplicium"; medicinal plants or minerals used on their own rather than in a compound</note>, which exist as cold, etc.

->The End of the Commentaries of Paracelsus on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.<-

### TREATISE

# ON BLOODLETTING AND SCAR-
## IFICATION, BY THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM,
### Doctor of Both Medicines.

In which are explained the abuses and errors admitted into these practices until now, which were subsequently followed by the dissolution of limbs, paralysis, contraction, and death; how these may be avoided and corrected is set forth here.

Similarly, the absurdity of the <term>Almanacs</term> <note>original: "Ephemeridum"; astrological calendars used by physicians to determine "favorable" days for surgery</note> is uncovered, by which bloodletting is decreed against nature and the course of the heavens: where also the true explanation is handed down, in what way signs ought truly and genuinely to be observed, with an enumeration added of which diseases especially may be cured through bloodletting, which is explained with its own figures.

Finally, the manner of purging is also handed down, namely how both the Physician and the sick person ought to conduct themselves regarding it.

->ON BLOODLETTING.<-

## FIVE TREATISES, BOOK I.

->DOCTOR THEOPHRASTUS ON THE ABUSE OF BLOODLETTING, WITH AN EXPLANATION OF THE TRUE<-
->use according to the indication of the celestial course,<-

### Greetings to the Reader.

<margin>
An old dog does not get used to the leash.
</margin>

ALTHOUGH the arrogance and pride of bastard Physicians (who decree triumphs for themselves over me everywhere) compelled me in no small way to describe this abuse: yet the more powerful cause for this writing was the account of the sick themselves, from whom I have chiefly taken this argument, so that I might indicate the errors of the "Almanac Physicians," who can do nothing but make things up. Although they themselves will not greatly understand this foundation: nevertheless, those who are wise and skilled will perceive its utility without delay, where I likewise warn them to acquire for themselves hereafter a fuller knowledge of the Stars, lest they be considered merely "three-legged" Physicians. For that which walks on three legs walks badly and awkwardly. To you, however, who are sick, I am an exhorter, that hereafter you consult these writings of mine more than such Physicians. For since those old dogs do not easily get used to the leash, you meanwhile could easily suffer the loss of your health. And so, judge from these things how rashly they have presumed and prejudged so many things for themselves, not from true and solid science, but from mere—

<header>PREFACE.</header>

...purely by opinion. It would be appropriate for a Physician to be no less tormented by his own intellect than a patient is wasted away by disease; if that were so, opinions would be set aside, and they would devote much more of their gasping effort to learning the art. Meanwhile, they have brought the matter to such a point that, whatever they say, they think it must be accepted entirely as an Elementary Gospel. But how solid and great the knowledge and cognition of these men is, I leave to all of you to judge. If they have received three pennies anywhere as payment: by putting these out to interest, they gain whole houses in a short time. In his own art, however, everyone ought to progress daily, so that it may repeatedly be more and more an honor to him. Therefore, kind Reader, you will labor to enter the true path in knowing the art, and grant trust to the experienced, since coarse errors regarding bloodletting are flickering and spreading everywhere.

<margin>Various opinions on bloodletting.</margin>
For some judge and value bloodletting as a cure for completed diseases, others hold it as a mitigation of the same; some pronounce it useful because of habit; some measure its utility according to the four parts of the year; many seek safety and long life through it. And thus, opinions of this kind about bloodletting are varied, though all are indeed destitute of certain counsel and solid reason.

<margin>Things to be considered in bloodletting.</margin>
Therefore, just as nothing can be certainly known or understood without a true foundation, nor can any healthy counsel be offered; so here also the origin and distribution of the <term>Veins</term> <note>original: "Venarum"</note> themselves must be known, and the nature or condition of the blood drawn out, and finally the very adherence of the diseases. From these things compared among themselves, it can be known and understood in which case bloodletting is either advantageous or harmful.

## TREATISE I.

<margin>Marking of a bad custom.</margin>
**S**ince the <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>original: "Ephemerides"; astronomical calendars used to predict the positions of celestial bodies</note> of the old Physicians are sprinkled with entirely empty doctrine regarding the time for cutting a vein: it is necessary to rebuke and reject them above all. For by suspended linens or displayed <term>bloodletting-manikins</term> <note>original: "imagunculis phlebotomicis"; anatomical charts showing which veins to bleed based on the zodiac sign</note>, almost the greatest part of men is lured to cutting a vein. So that this error may be better recognized, first indeed against the authors of the Ephemerides, you ought to know that in the signs of Aries, Cancer, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius, and Pisces, etc., cutting a vein is not indeed harmful. But because those signs are not damaging, they are therefore persuaded that a vein is usefully pierced, and they establish the manner so that they perform "Middle Bloodletting" (as they call it) and then "Full Bloodletting," though they make not even a <term>jot</term> <note>original: "gry"; the smallest possible unit or a trifle</note> of mention of the first. They think it therefore necessarily exists as useful because it is not harmful. Meanwhile, however, nothing else is obtained than that bloodletting is not harmful at least in those defined members. From this, I ask, how can they infer that it is absolutely advantageous for that reason? Especially when the timeliness or utility of bloodletting should be attributed to the Physician, not to the heavens? Nor do we so readily grant that a thing will be immediately good and healthy which does not exist as noxious and harmful.

<margin>From whence the time for bloodletting should be judged.</margin>
From these things, this error can now be understood: that they sell what is not good as good, to the great loss and detriment of those who, led by this custom, use bloodletting. Here you ought also to understand this as well: that the time for bloodletting must be sought and decided from the exigency and necessity of the body, not by attending to the state of external things. For internal nature overcomes external nature.

<margin>Bad distribution of the body to the 12 signs.</margin>
By common custom, it happens that according to the 12 signs, the body itself is also distributed into 12 parts. However, this attention to and avoidance of that member is entirely vain and ridiculous. Likewise, the aspects of the Moon itself, whether new or full, ought not to be attended to at all. For all these things pass without error of judgment in bloodletting in this way: namely, if in an adverse sign, with a bad aspect existing, and the Moon showing itself either new or full, some harm should arise from a prescribed bloodletting, that happens entirely from the ignorance of the Physician who advised the untimely bloodletting. For neither the heaven, nor the firmament, nor the aspects, nor that full or new moon inflicted that evil, but the bad and inconvenient treatment of the disease.

<margin>Aspects not to be attended to in bloodletting.</margin>
But if the adversaries say that such damage follows least of all if bloodletting is instituted in good signs: and thus they think their opinion is stabilized by this momentum, as if a right and true distribution of the Stars has been made, and because of this my opinion lies defeated; to these I respond, those signs betray their foolishness no less than the aforementioned, yet not so quickly, but over a longer time.

<margin>Disease, not heaven, to be looked at in bloodletting.</margin>
Understand this also as well: if in good signs nothing bad happens, the same will also happen in a full moon. If there is damage in a full moon, the same will also happen in good signs. For the disease of the body is more powerful here than the heaven. The disease must be watched, not the heaven, nor should it be judged and treated according to the condition of the heaven.

But for the conclusion of this argument, I will bring forward one thing still. Choose a good sign for yourselves, and under that very sign cut the vein of fifty men at once: there you will find that fifty varieties also occur. This diversity, however, is not from the signs themselves, but from the disease of the men. Since you cannot grasp these things, what other things will there finally be that you think you can understand? Where also this seems to be driven home to you. For if ever, while cutting a vein under chosen signs, contractions of the arms, tumors, and swellings are brought on: that certainly ought least of all to be imputed to the heaven, but you yourselves accuse the surgeon, saying either that he pierced the whole vein or applied an infected scalpel. Yet I publicly excuse him, and say that you, you I say, have counseled badly, and from bad counsel that evil has emerged. But if the same had happened in a new moon, then you would have imputed that fault to the heaven and to Astronomy. See also that the same reasoning applies to some wounds, which are small and light, and near neither the heart nor the brain, which seem in no way lethal, and yet quickly and suddenly bring on death. Now let this be the hollow excuse of the Physician, if he says the patient was struck and wounded in a bad sign. For even if besides this, others also...

He mocks physicians who use zodiac signs to justify their procedures, asserting that the "internal nature" of the body is more significant than the "external" influence of the stars.</summary>

-> ### ON BLOODLETTING <-

<margin>Why does a very slight wound sometimes bring death?</margin>
Now, if twenty men were wounded in the same spot and in the same way, yet that wound would be fatal to none but this one man. The cause of this is not the <term>heavens</term><note>original: "cælum"; here referring to astrological influences or the position of the stars.</note>, but a lethal disease lying in that specific limb, which was not present in the other wounded men, but was struck and stirred up in this one. This is undoubtedly the genuine cause of that danger, not the stars. This same principle must likewise be understood regarding other matters which are usually blamed on the heavens out of a sheer lack of astronomical knowledge and an ignorance of medicine. From your own judgment, it is clear how you possess no real science in either Medicine, Astronomy, or Physics itself. For the error of your judgment betrays your uncertainty, especially when you wrongly attribute to the <term>Zodiac signs</term> what ought to be ascribed to the disease of the body.

I ask you to place before your eyes a certain battle-line or a fight, in which 20,000 men are beaten with weapons and bullets, wounded, pierced, or harmed in some other way. In the care of these men, no one considers the heavens; they consider only the puncture and the wound as it is in itself. How many of these men are wounded in places corresponding to the same astrological sign, yet for whom the matter heals for the better? Conversely, how many are wounded in a place where a sign does *not* rule, yet those wounds—though light and contemptible—end in the greatest harm? Therefore, an outcome of this kind must be attributed not to the signs or the heavens, but to the body and its own properties and diseases, whether manifest or hidden. Care ought to be turned toward the body, not directed toward the sky. Meanwhile, however, that [the stars] is the excuse of the unskilled Physician. If he applied himself to the art of Medicine with as much zeal as he devotes to his foolish excuses, he would surely experience a much more successful outcome in his care than otherwise happens. Furthermore, concerning these types of dangerous diseases or wounds that frequently occur, just as with <term>phlebotomies</term><note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note>, take note of this example.

If the site of a <term>Mania</term><note>original: "Maniæ"; here referring to a localized "frenzy" or specific pathology in the brain.</note> hidden in the brain is harmed by a wound or a bloodletting during a paroxysm, it becomes lethal. The same must be judged for other cases. Therefore, the heavens should not be blamed at all. Regarding this matter, as has been said, I rightfully take up this discussion. For this doctrine is not sufficiently explained in the <term>Ephemerides</term><note>Astronomical tables used to predict the positions of celestial bodies.</note>, since one must act not according to the signs, but by attending to the disease itself.

<margin>In what does the judgment of blood consist?</margin>
From the first error already mentioned, a second one follows and flows out. For once a bloodletting has been performed, those Physicians gird themselves for the observation and judging of the blood: they examine its color, its substance, and its wateriness. From these they bring forth many and diverse judgments, which are nevertheless established by no certain knowledge or understanding. First, what you see in the blood is nothing other than the coagulation of salt and an external fullness. What will you predict from these? For salt shows a thing doubtfully and reveals nothing definitely. Moreover, that "incidental fullness"—that is, what sweats from the body into the veins—what else does it show you but a foreign guest in the blood? Since it lies in the blood, will you seek the cause in the blood for that reason? Not at all. Rather, seek it where it subsists, outside the veins, and act so that it no longer crosses into the veins; in that way, the blood will surely be pure. You, meanwhile, produce massive judgments from those things and accuse the blood in many ways, as if those things were the causes of certain diseases, when they are contained in the blood only as guests. Various things must be considered regarding blood: namely, whether a disease lies hidden in it, or not; and then, whether the blood is judged correctly. Many times you pronounce blood unhealthy because it settles quickly; yet that does nothing to prove the cause of the sickness. Furthermore, if the blood does not stain, or if it comes out drier or more watery, it seems morbid to you, even though that is the healthy state for that specific man, and it could not be otherwise in him. Indeed, if it were otherwise, *that* would be the certain cause and indication of a morbid constitution. In the same way, you examine the blood immediately and think a perfect knowledge of all diseases can be drawn from it; yet that blood you are inspecting is not from the site of the pain, and it shows the pollution and affection of that site either not at all, or certainly very slightly, while the total cause of the whole disease consists entirely in the <term>origin of the veins</term>.

<margin>What it means if blood settles quickly.</margin>
<margin>In the plague, the blood is often very pure.</margin>
For you very often observe that in the plague, the blood of the vein in which the plague lurks is pure and whole, and nothing at all can be known or judged from it. In that case, I ask, how has the vein-cutting helped, since the pestilence lies hidden in the origin of the veins and does not move from its place, but remains fixed, constant, and clinging?

I say these things to this end: that you do not wander blindly in the judgment of blood, seeing as you can by no means attain the highest goal of your institution. Whatever you do obtain is a mere dream and lacks a goal. Although this too is established: that the condition and nature of blood is varied and wonderful. If you consider a tree, you will see that all its fruits hang at the ends of the branches. The logic of blood is the same, if it is left to itself and is solitary in its operation, as it ought to be: that is, if the blood exists healthy in and of itself, it brings forth flowers and fruits from the beginning to the end and shows the signs of its own nature.

<margin>The same reasoning for blood and a tree.</margin>
But for the "fruit" of the blood to desire to break out in the same way as fruit usually does in a pear tree—that is far from the truth. For nature itself pushes it out, and it disappears and falls away without us knowing. Therefore, you cannot place a great refuge in the blood in this instance. For whatever you collect is only the refuse, not anything stained <note>The author argues that what is removed during bloodletting is the "rejected" matter, not the actual seat of the disease.</note>. Although, just as the tip of the branches indicates what the tree is called, so also the blood, if it is healthy, indicates what it should be named. But if the blood is sick, you do not have the branches from which you can estimate the condition of the blood. Just as you cannot diagnose a tree's disease from a single branch, so you know much less how to judge the disease of this vein. We comment more at length on these matters in the book *On Diseases Arising from Blood*.

<margin>One judgment for healthy blood, another for the sick.</margin>
From these errors already listed, it follows that men are poorly advised. From which the damages and dangers of bad counsel are to be expected; among their number is the <term>contracture</term><note>A permanent shortening or hardening of muscles or tendons, leading to rigid joints.</note> of limbs, just as you very often see that the loss of use of an arm or another limb, or a spasm, arises from so small a wound, with other accidents also accompanying it.

<margin>Contraction from bloodletting.</margin>

<header>TREATISE.</header>

# 768 TREATISE.

with many lethal accidents: all of which could be avoided with little effort if the true and genuine cause were understood.

<margin>Whether bloodletting is a perfect cure or merely mitigation.</margin>
Furthermore, it must also be understood here whether <term>Phlebotomy</term><note>The practice of opening a vein to draw blood, a common medical treatment in the 16th century.</note> ought to be a perfect cure for a disease, or something less—namely, just a certain mitigation and a way to prolong the situation. If it is meant to be a cure, it is necessary for you to know accurately how you might draw out the root of the disease into the furthest tips of the branches, meaning the hands and feet. For if you do not know this, what use is your bloodletting? However, if it is to be a mitigation, then again you must know how to make that mitigation last. For unless it lasts, what benefit, I ask you, can it provide? That is, if you have provided relief through bloodletting, you must arrange the blood so that it does not slide back again. Unless you observe and provide these two things—in both the cure and the mitigation—you cannot boast at all of your skill in bloodletting; rather, you have merely punctured a vein by trial and error, hoping for a good outcome. Those bloodlettings are entirely dangerous in which the incision alone is considered the whole of the art. If you cut a vein merely for the sake of stalling, then you are entrusting the success to luck, being doubtful of your own art. No good counsel can emerge from such a place.

Therefore, one must think diligently here about how many people—both men and women—have been misled until now by this stalling and inconsistent mitigation. When they felt the slightest bit of relief from the mitigation, they continued to follow this habit constantly. Yet it was never indicated to them whether the disease was truly *in* the blood, or whether it merely lived there as a <term>guest</term><note>original: "hospes"; Paracelsus distinguishes between diseases that are inherent to a substance and those that have "moved in" from elsewhere.</note>. Nor was the art applied so that, if the disease were in the blood, it might be drawn out from its origin to the branches, or so that the mitigation might be brought to a lasting state. Furthermore, if it had crept in like a guest, they did not take care to drive it out and lead it away from the veins. Instead, they fixed one single rule for all of you: that if a piercing pain is felt in the sides and a tightness in the chest, the evil necessarily sticks in the lungs, and the <term>pulmonary vein</term> should be cut. Or if pain is felt in the region of the liver, then the <term>hepatic vein</term> provides and completes the greatest power of the cure. In this, they do not consider what the "guest" is doing in that place, so that the disease might be removed from the outside, preventing the need for treating the internal parts. From this follow those "mitigations" resulting from the lessening of blood, so that the fierce disease does not afflict the patient so much. Yet, in the meantime, the growth and the recurrence of the disease have not yet been taken away.

<margin>What is the cause of blood only dripping during bloodletting?</margin>
Furthermore, if the blood does not flow out from the wounded vein, they have very little understanding of why that happens, unless they say this one thing: that either the blood is too thick or the wound is too small. Neither of these, however, should be accepted as the genuine cause. The true cause is this: it is not appropriate for blood to flow out at just any hour, since it is not always <term>windy</term><note>original: "ventosus"; referring to internal gases or pressure that Paracelsus believed drove the movement of bodily fluids.</note>. For if it lacks "wind," it is unfit for exit. The second cause is that in the opening of these veins, the blood is pushed backward, turning its path inward instead of outward. In these matters, specific knowledge is required so that no impediment occurs. Moreover, they do not even know the mode and measure for extracting blood, except for as much as they gather by the judgment of their eyes—which consists in the change of the blood's color, which nevertheless always appears red both inside and outside. But if it first bursts out black, and then red follows, they then close the wound, being persuaded that since the black blood has been evacuated, everything is now in a safe place. They do not consider, meanwhile, that the incision itself gave the color to the blood, and that it was not such by its own nature. Therefore, nothing should be attributed to the change in the blood's color. For that is induced by the cut. And yet they all dream that they have fulfilled every part of their duty if they decide and define the whole matter based on the evidence of their eyes.

Add to this that the standard of judgment is not at all legitimate when they assess the nature and property of the blood. For when it has settled and clotted, they first contemplate the <term>serum</term> of the blood, then its body or substance, and finally the color of both. The error concerning these things is as follows:

<margin>Extracted blood dies immediately.</margin>
All blood that is evacuated or drawn out dies immediately. Who shall judge the living from the dead? Consider for yourselves a man who is healthy, what he is like in himself. If he later becomes sick, how much will you see him differ from the healthy man? Finally, if he is dead, he undergoes such an evident change that no one can rightly or truly judge who he once was. The same must be thought regarding blood. As soon as it is extracted from the body, it is dead. Who, therefore, can judge matters of such great importance from the dead thing itself? Especially when that same blood was already sick even before extraction? Or what finally does it help if you stare quite intently at its water or its substance? For you can see nothing from the deceased thing that you might use to benefit the living. But if you truly wish to babble much about those things, by that very fact you will show that you have very little knowledge of the nature and condition of a dead thing; and from that ignorance, you will bring forth nothing other than what strikes against Nature itself, against which nothing should be rashly decided or spoken.

<margin>Nothing should be decided against nature.</margin>
Therefore, an examination of dead blood can say nothing other than its own present condition. In the same way, nothing solid can be judged about a disease from the "flower" or the foam, etc. For a dead man also often emits foam.

<margin>Multiple types of rot.</margin>
What, then, should be done? Your judgment of the living must be taken from the living. How great the difference is between these can be seen from this: you see, to be sure, a thousand men die, each one having his own private <term>putrefaction</term><note>Decay or rotting. Paracelsus viewed disease as a form of internal decay.</note>, which is also betrayed by its own peculiar signs. Similarly, as soon as blood slips out of the body, it undergoes putrefaction and loses the spirit of life—in which, however, the source of judgment lies, from which the Physician ought to draw his pronouncement, not from a little bowl filled with blood. For just as any dead body can rot, so can any blood.

<margin>Anything dead is subject to rot. From where does rot come?</margin>
Now, truly, rot arises from dissolution—that is, from the spirit of life. If that spirit is already dissolved, who would look for anything whole within it? Now, a certain type of rot can occur if it turns white like mucus in water, which it has from its own property. Outside of water, it changes into various colors. For in this way rot begins, and nothing can be divined from it except by mere chance.

<summary>Paracelsus critiques the medical practice of diagnosing diseases by inspecting clotted blood in a bowl, arguing that once blood leaves the body, it loses its "life force" and begins to rot, making it a useless indicator of a living patient's health.</summary>

<note>The text on this page is affected by some ink bleed-through from the back of the paper, but the core arguments remain legible.</note>

You see, for certain, that when something is snatched up by fire, it is changed in a brief moment from its <term>Elemental</term><note>In this context, the essential nature or "Element" that makes a substance what it is.</note> essence into something contrary. The same principle applies to blood. As soon as it seeks the air, it defects from its native constitution into a foreign nature. Now, just because blood emits serum or "water," it does not mean that water as such exists in the body; rather, water and blood are one thing. However, the reason that one part becomes blood and the other water is this: every single body has its own innate <term>salt</term><note>For Paracelsus, "Salt" was one of the three primary substances (along with Sulfur and Mercury) that made up all matter, representing the solid, physical principle.</note>, without which no body can thrive. <margin>Nothing thrives without salt.</margin> This salt separates itself as soon as it changes its natural essence. Take evidence of this from wood. It burns, indeed, but it does not burn entirely. One part admits the fire; the other part rejects it. And this [latter part] is the Salt, which you call "ash." Just as wood is coagulated and hard in its body, so blood is dissolved and moist; for this reason, its salt becomes watery, whereas the wood's salt becomes ashen. But what will you judge from these things regarding bodies that are not <margin>No judgment of the unmixed.</margin> united and joined? In this way, you can never judge a joined thing. But that which is in the water, you will understand in the same way as that which remains as blood—as if its nature were no different than the flame from a fire. Indeed, one can never hope for a diagnostic judgment from the color, the thinness, or the thickness. For its nature is determined by its own putrefaction. Therefore, see to it that you order bloodletting correctly without even considering the [appearance of the] blood. Indeed, inspection of the emitted blood will lead you far from the truth. The less the substance is divided—and the visible colors that follow in the blood exist only as long as it is joined with the spirit of life—the less you will be able to judge the diagnosis of diseases within it. What you say—that the blood is "putrid"—is true in the bowl, but it is not true in the man.

Therefore, the errors previously demonstrated are of great importance, especially if they are not considered with reason. For even if the defenders of those opinions have spent much effort protecting their "order of words," they are nevertheless compelled to admit my writings, and are forced to confess here and there that my preceding arguments cannot be refuted or <margin>Book on Pulses.</margin> disproven in any way. As for their contention—with a great show of truth—that this blood indicates this or that disease by its color: how true and well-tested that is will be explained more clearly hereafter in the book *On Erroneous Judgments of the Pulses*.

But let these points we have listed suffice regarding the errors usually committed concerning the letting of blood. Furthermore, as for what pertains to phlebotomy, it will be handed down in the specific explanation of the veins: where the virtue and condition of each vein will be more clearly revealed and defined, as well as what opportunity it finally holds for bringing either help or harm, and any other matters required here.

## SECOND TREATISE.

<margin>Censure of doctors.</margin> It is entirely right and proper for me to hand down and teach the method and manner of cutting a vein. For the reasoning you have established until now regarding bloodletting is entirely worthy of severe correction. The writers who have commented on phlebotomy left their years of apprenticeship and training before they were mature, and took up the title of "Master" prematurely. Therefore, their writings should by no means be accepted as true and confirmed. For a student's Rule and Canon is not to be held as authentic. From this, it is gathered that the common Faculty of Medicine arose and was born from these very apprenticeships, and remains obstinately stuck in them. That I take it upon myself to bring such things forward should not be blamed on me as a fault. For it is only too truly established that the doctrine of the ancients is insufficient and not solid; rather, an entirely deeper knowledge of Philosophy, Medicine, and Astronomy is required. Thus, since you hold no foundation in Astronomy, you claim its name and works in vain, while you do nothing but gather bits from calendars like bastards, bringing them into the public eye—which is quite shameful and disgraceful for a Doctor. Therefore, since you are clearly empty of the art and science of Astronomy: please do not think it beneath you to learn. For your works and writings testify to what you have actually established; and since I see many more people being cast down by you than raised up, due to your ignorance and the rudeness of your art: I think it is right for me to pluck and criticize you, until you can actually perform and complete with your work what you boast of in words.

But in the first place, it must be held for what purpose bloodletting is instituted. For you have never even entertained a thought about this; instead, you have relied on mere opinions, as is notoriously clear from your writings. Understand it in this way: The Sky <note>original: "Cœlum"; Paracelsus uses this to mean the macrocosm/stars and their influence.</note> has power over a fourth part of the governing of the body—that is, the blood. According to this, therefore, all diseases that occur in the blood do not originate *from* the blood. Just as you see that a field produces no fruit unless seed is placed in it, so no disease is generated in the blood unless it is first sown. Moreover, that "Sower" is the sky. Therefore, the nature of this sower must first be understood by the Physician. This knowledge is followed by the essence of the disease, the cure, and other matters, except for those things which I have written regarding "proper corruptions." A Physician who is ignorant of these things and does not know that "Sower" should by no means be called a healer of those diseases. For the duty of the Physician consists chiefly in this: not that he knows how to make "bloodletting calendars" <note>original: "Ephemerides"; typical 16th-century almanacs that told people when to bleed based on simple moon signs.</note>, but rather that he understands what the sky is doing in one quarter of the man—that is, in the blood. Nor should it be absurd for any Physician to believe that the body exists as a four-fold entity in the generation of diseases, not a simple one, as those [other doctors] might argue from their "Sophistical Philosophy." On this, read the book *On the Origin of Blood Diseases*. An ignorant and immature Physician is one who, being ignorant of the four parts of the body, places his foundation in speculation, which is built from the fantasy of the "four complexions" <note>The traditional Galenic theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile).</note>.

<margin>The doctrine of the ancients is insufficient.</margin>
<margin>The sky is the sower of diseases, which a Doctor ought to know.</margin>
<margin>The 4 parts of man.</margin>

I know well that these things will seem strange to you upon hearing them. For it is clear to me that you decree no bloodletting from certain knowledge, but rather...

->TREATISE<-

...you err not in one way, but in many. And what, finally, shall I say of you, since you delight in the name [of physician] alone, while in your works you are mere novices <note>original: "tyrones"</note>? It is surely by this custom that you so often command bloodletting <term>phlebotomy</term><note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a standard treatment in pre-modern medicine.</note> even when a disease occupies the stomach. From this, one can see that you are searching like a man who has lost something in a certain city; he knows it lies somewhere in that city, but he remains ignorant and stuck as to where it actually lies. You are exactly like him, to the great shame of both yourselves and the art of medicine itself. For how often do you investigate a disease in the blood, when it actually resides in the intestines, and so forth? Therefore, this "subtlety" of yours is mere coarseness, through which you think it matters little whether you follow the true foundation. For it is easy to judge that the hard penance of a forced retraction awaits the proud and the unskilled. To restrain such men is like trying to train old dogs with leashes. Their thinking only looks backward, never forward.

<margin>Those who seek their own glory go astray.</margin>
Moreover, this vice is innate to all who wander: they capture praise, reputation, and popular applause much more greedily than they seek true glory from their required duty. And since we have reached a point today where novices occupy positions that are scarcely suitable for Masters, it follows that their Medicine must also be the kind that puffs itself up with a name, while remaining mere nonsense and a tall tale.

<margin>The body has 4 parts.</margin>
But to continue the teaching we began regarding bloodletting, it must be known that every incision of a vein ought to be so organized that it is proposed as a complete cure. One should not seek help from medicines elsewhere; the whole cure should be sought there, without turning to other treatments. This is because four parts exist in the body, which produce four types of diseases and, for that reason, four modes of practice. Among these, the practice that deals with blood alone is a complete and perfect system in itself. And the physician is taught this practice by heaven itself, not by philosophy or any other speculation. For this reason, I teach here that the physician who deals with blood must have recognized and explored the "Sower in heaven" <note>The "Sower" (seminator) refers to the celestial or planetary forces that "plant" the seeds of disease in the human body.</note> along with all his properties—a knowledge of which I have not found even once among any of you. Since heaven itself teaches what disease lies in the blood (and it is not the blood itself, for blood is merely that which is produced and does not know its own enemy, whereas heaven alone knows it), what then are you looking for in the blood when you describe blood diseases like <term>Anthrax</term><note>A generic term for a black, burning skin lesion or pustule.</note>, <term>Carbuncle</term><note>A cluster of boils or a deep-seated infection of the skin.</note>, and other abscesses <note>original: "Apostemata"</note>, whether external or internal? For heaven impresses its influences on the blood alone; thus, those diseases of the blood are governed, arranged, and emerge according to the nature and property of the stars of heaven, which I have called the "Sower." Without this perfect knowledge, not one of you will ever make progress in the medicine of the blood.

<margin>The process of physicians for purging.</margin>
It is appropriate, therefore, that an entirely different order and process be established in this matter, one that is distinct from the others. For every part requires its own separate practice, even though you confuse them all into one. So that you may understand this, consider the following example. You have one process used for "purging the bowels" <note>original: "cacandum," a blunt term for defecation.</note>. In this, you first administer

syrups, then pills, then unsalted pea broth, and finally a tonic. This order is established by you for the sole purpose of discharging the bowels, looking to nothing else. Therefore, if a disease does not lie in the excrement, your "order" is useless. But if it is hidden in the stool, then the order is good. Furthermore, if you are busy moving and expelling urine, you establish a completely different order from the first. Finally, you use another when you are about to cure <term>quartan fever</term><note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms that occur every fourth day.</note>. In the same way here, regarding the blood, you must keep a specific, entire, and distinct order from the others. For heaven requires that which is contrary to the other three parts, according to its own nature and property.

<margin>The various kinds of physicians.</margin>
It is not fitting for physicians to be only of one kind. There are Phlebotomist Physicians, from whom the deceptive use of the signs of the "fish" and the "artery" arose. There are also physicians who deal with <term>Chaos</term><note>In Paracelsian terms, "Chaos" usually refers to the element of Air or the atmosphere.</note>; there are those assigned to Earth, and those to Humor; however, all of these are foreign to your Theory and Physics. Besides these, one kind still remains: those who attend to distillation alone. And with these five, the whole of Medicine is completed.

<margin>Who the specialized physicians are.</margin>
From these come the "particular" <note>specialized</note> physicians, each occupied in that specific part where the "root" of that part is given.

<margin>Who the natural physicians are.</margin>
Beyond these are also the "Natural Physicians," who have recognized and discovered the virtues of natural growing things without needing a formal knowledge of diseases.

This division or partitioning of physicians is thrust upon you for this purpose: so that you may know that a different order must be established in the blood—one that indicates a complete cure—and so that you may distinguish which writings of the ancients are sound or erroneous. For I understand that the writers you embrace are completely opposed to me. And since I see that you, their followers, by no means fulfill or perfect what you boast you can perfect, I rightly trample upon your foundation and reduce it to ashes. You cannot defend it, nor will I ever admit your fictitious medicine. Although, to cast it down, there is no need for great effort, since it tends toward collapse on its own. For it is most true that heaven acts as the Sower in diseases of the blood. It is necessary, therefore, that before you cut even the smallest vein, you first of all know what is in it, and that it comes from heaven. You should believe that the administration of bloodletting comes from heaven. If, therefore, you cannot by any reasoning break the fact that you are so greatly bound and beholden to heaven, then certainly whatever you have written about this will collapse and be cast out as empty trifles. For you will never be able to deny the four aforementioned types of physicians; indeed, all your foundations will be overturned by them.

<margin>The wise man rules the stars; and the physician [rules] the heavenly infection.</margin>
Furthermore, just as the "Wise man rules the Stars," <note>original: "Sapiens dominatur Astris," a common medieval proverb suggesting that human wisdom and will can overcome astrological fate.</note> so also the Physician overcomes heaven in the "infection" it has placed in the blood. But if it is the Physician’s job to overcome heaven, he must necessarily know it. From this knowledge flows the indication of the hour that is suitable for bloodletting. For some diseases are impressed upon the blood from heaven, such as certain cases of <term>Falling Sickness</term><note>Epilepsy (original: "Caduca").</note>, some of <term>Gout</term><note>original: "Podagra"</note>, some of Fevers, and similarly with others.

Now, if such a disease increases or decreases with the Moon,

<page-num>771</page-num>
# ON BLOODLETTING.

<margin>When a vein should be cut.</margin>
...even if [the physical state] fails, the Moon certainly indicates the hour for bloodletting in that disease. For at whatever point the Moon is ignited <note>original: "incenditur"—Paracelsus uses terms of "ignition" or "burning" to describe when a celestial body reaches a point of maximum influence or activation over a specific part of the body or a disease</note>: in that same point also the diseases which the Moon impresses are ignited. It is clear, therefore, that it is necessary to know which veins and which diseases are being ignited? And for the sake of this knowledge of the point of ignition, the order of bloodletting ought to be established. From this emerges the practice observed in the celestial arrangements. In this way, any disease of the blood is admitted just as its star ignites it. You who would be physicians, therefore, ought to have a proven and exact knowledge of the heavens—namely, by which star the blood is separately ignited, whence so many various diseases assault the blood. Unless this knowledge is established and certain, you ought not to boast of your Medicine at all. And this is undoubtedly that foundation from which is revealed what no one has described until now: namely, what an abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note>—even the smallest one—actually is, and from what it arises. This is also the reason why you have not yet been able to penetrate to the end of this disease. Although Mallow and Marshmallow <note>original: "Malva & Althæa"</note> have provided you some solar benefit <note>original: "solarij quid"—likely referring to the soothing, "sunny" nature of these herbs</note>, without them this disease would have reached its full completion regardless.

<margin>Good signs must be used in five cases.</margin>
Indeed, I cannot deny that in some diseases one must act according to good signs, at least for the sake of mitigation and support—specifically in five ways and cases. First, in internal causes of diseases that show themselves outwardly. Second, in diseases that show themselves internally and remain there. Third, in diseases stirred up by a flux <note>A discharge or abnormal flow of fluid in the body.</note>. Fourth, in diseases occurring according to the seasons of the year. Fifth, in diseases of which we ourselves are the cause.

Diseases which reach a crisis <note>original: "paroxyfinant"</note> internally are: Cancer, Fistula, and other similar open ulcers. Under the second genus are included dropsy <term>hydrops</term><note>An old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid in the body's tissues.</note>, jaundice <term>ictericia</term>, the menses, and all diseases generated from the principal organs. In the third are contained the diseases of apoplexy, "star-blasting" <term>syderatio</term><note>A term for a sudden stroke or paralysis, believed to be caused by a malignant celestial influence.</note>, gout, and the arthritic passion. In the fourth are included diseases that come forth for a time, such as in spring, summer, autumn, or winter; as well as those of all the "ascendants" as they are contained in the heavens. In the fifth are those which arise from a fullness <note>An excess of "humors" or blood.</note> or commotion of disease, or are generated from food and drink.

Even though you may be able to provide mitigation and soothing in these aforesaid diseases according to the order of your Ephemerides <term>ephemerides</term><note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies, used by physicians to time treatments.</note>: nevertheless, as I indicate everywhere, true cure is not contained here. Instead, what is handed down is only the corruption of diseases and the stirring up of their malice, so that the patients either die more quickly or are afflicted more vehemently. Furthermore, you admit an error even in this: that you seek the mitigation of diseases through bloodletting when those diseases are not contained in the blood at all. And since the blood fights back with its own strength—which causes a particular pain to the body—if you then wish to restrain or remove that strength through bloodletting, the disease wins because you have removed the body's friend.

<margin>All diseases are to be sought in the blood.</margin>
Concerning all these things, however, you ought to know that all diseases of the "first part" are rightly sought in the blood. For this reason, I do not reject bloodletting at all, provided it is done according to the logic of the firmament, so that the point of the ascendant—that is, of the regeneration itself—is observed. For if bloodletting is instituted in this way, the principle of that disease...

<margin>Hereditary diseases.</margin>
...will have been thus removed. It is necessary to consider, therefore, that the "ascendants" operate over many years, whence an hereditary evil emerges, which a son contracts from his father by reason of the blood. This is also the reason why some diseases of wicked ulcers do not admit of care or healing, namely because their star is in its heat <note>original: "in fervore"</note>; whereas, on the contrary, some heal easily because their star has departed.

<margin>Phlebotomy is twofold.</margin>
Bloodletting, therefore, must be recognized as twofold in these diseases: one leads to a complete cure, which is done according to the stars that ignited this type. The other is for the sake of preservation, which eventually happens in many ways. Here I would have you take note: that in that increase of diseases, bloodletting is recommended by you, yet it accomplishes nothing except the removal of matter which nonetheless remains fixed in its place at the root.

<margin>Phlebotomy does not remove fixed things.</margin>
This is certainly no light error when you attempt to take away what can by no means be removed. From this your ignorance becomes notorious: either you did not know the essence of the disease itself, or you were intentionally practicing a deception. Think deeply within yourselves how much this becomes "learned men," such as you boast yourselves to be.

<margin>Dropsy is not cured by phlebotomy.</margin>
In the same way, you also strive to remove dropsy and the like through bloodletting. Yet you cannot prove where dropsy resides from any other source than from books and letters, which contribute nothing to this matter. For they are of neither such weight nor certainty that I myself could safely trust or believe them. You, however, sparing yourselves the labor, agree with them without hesitation, however the outcomes may fall. But how much honor and dignity redounds to you from those things—and how much utility to the sick—can be heard and inquired of from the patients everywhere.

And so your Medicine rests upon such a solid foundation that not one of you in your entirety can demonstrate with truth even the smallest letter of the ancient writers regarding Theory. For in the true uncovering of true Medicine, the deceitful sophist <term>sophista</term><note>Paracelsus used "sophist" as a derogatory term for traditional academic physicians who followed Galen and Avicenna without practical, chemical, or astrological insight.</note> immediately broke in and oppressed and clouded the brilliant splendor of the art itself. If we were to inquire seriously into the first origin of medicine, we would surely find that the first physicians were the simplest of men, infected by no frauds or impostures.

<margin>What is a sophist?</margin>
Through this very simplicity of theirs, as if through a door, the sophist slipped in, dulled the truth itself, and brought it into contempt by "correcting" it, as is the habit of liars.

<margin>What is the duty of an interpreter?</margin>
From this sophistry, which confuses truth with lies, writers later emerged along with their commentators. They forgot what was most necessary of all in the text: namely, to separate truth from lies. And although they did not do this at all, but mixed the false with the true, it is you who gave your faith to these subtleties and embraced their foundations. Among other things, they also neglected to teach the causes of diseases in the blood, because the sophists lacked a true knowledge of the heavens and rightly gaped at speculations, which later burst forth into bloodletting Ephemerides. Therefore, you will diligently take care hereafter that you neither believe nor agree with anyone regarding anything without your own experience.
