<page-num>772</page-num>
<header>TREATISE</header>

You make bargains. But what else are you doing in the end than—since you are ignorant of all things—snatching up whatever is in your way from anywhere, since your title must be disguised by some veil or another?

<margin>The Ascendant <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> must be carefully known in bloodletting.</margin>
You follow the same process in the "defluxions" <note>An old medical term for the downward flow of "bad humors."</note> of gout and other ailments, cutting a vein under a "good sign" rather than under the sign of the gout itself. For your authority must prevail in this, even if it comes at the risk of the patient’s life. Truly, all the skill in this matter lies in your knowing the "Ascendant" of that ailment. Likewise, if you wish to preserve someone from apoplexy <note>A sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke.</note>, you consider bloodletting performed under Pisces to be the most useful of all—as if the fish itself were the apoplexy! However, the genuine sign for bloodletting against apoplexy is neither the Fish nor the Ram <note>Aries</note>, since even in the middle signs, the cutting of a vein may be necessary. From this ignorance, many foul errors emerge, to the point that you do not even have a discovery of the "place" of apoplexy, nor has there been any mention in all your writings up to this hour of the appropriate vein—to say nothing of the *Go-with-me* <note>original: "Vade mecum"; a common title for a portable reference manual.</note> and other secret writings. Who, in such a great defect and poverty of true art, ordered you to write about apoplexy? If you are indeed unskilled here, you certainly can have no knowledge regarding its origin and causes. From this it follows that your entire chapters on this matter are either mute or false, whether you discuss the underlying reason, or "precious waters," or gems, ointments, balsams, and all other similar things.

Your wisdom is entirely similar when you command bloodletting for the four seasons of the year. For a spring-time cutting, you add no other pretext than that it will result in newer and purer blood being born. For just as the leaves and grasses are renewed at that time, so you wish the human being to be similarly renewed. And so, there is not one among you who has yet considered that leaves and grass are green, while blood is red—that is, you have never understood the nature of blood, not even through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam"; meaning even a glimpse or a slight understanding.</note>. And although bloodletting may sometimes do good, it nonetheless exists as neither a helper nor a healer. That which the different seasons of the year cause is the "firmament" <note>The heavens or the overarching celestial influence.</note>. Yet none of you has until now understood the cause of why blood is expelled in the spring, etc., which is evident from your books and your tongues.

<margin>In disease of the blood, what the true cure is.</margin>
From these things you can now judge for yourselves what sort of "advice" yours is if you persuade someone to undergo bloodletting who has either overfilled himself or consumed unwholesome food. For in this case, your error is manifest. To be sure, all diseases that come from our body into the blood ought to be "blood-let" <note>Paracelsus is using wordplay here: instead of removing the blood, the disease should be removed *from* the blood.</note> in the body; that is, they ought to be drawn from the blood back to their native place, and one should not attempt to seek them in the veins through bloodletting. For their true cure is that they should slip back as easily and briefly as possible, if you apply the true medicine. But if, through ignorance, you wish to extract the blood by performing bloodletting, you are now—by disturbing the place in which the disease was born—causing a path to be prepared in the blood. For bloodletting does not only draw in the vein, but also draws from outside it, as far as it can reach. In this way your lack of skill is betrayed, and your imposture becomes known: namely, that you are not industrious enough to be able to extract a disease that has gone from the body into the blood back out of it again. And these errors committed regarding bloodletting—which you partly conceive from your own speculations and partly drink from books composed to suit your own palate—had to be entirely uncovered and shown to you. Thus, if perforce you seem to yourself to have some support or shield against us, you may boldly bring it into the light, so that the foundations of both sides may stand more clearly, and so that the lie and the truth may be separated from one another.

### THIRD TREATISE.

<margin>Bloodletting is not a purging of the body.</margin>
A few of your books are in circulation in which bloodletting is treated in various ways. Although I both ought to and conveniently could bring forth the errors contained in them, I must instead at this point deliver, in a brief teaching, both the abuse and the use of bloodletting, which we now proceed to provide directly. Regarding the abuse, many things have been said thus far. Let it remain, therefore, that we treat the veins specifically and that the errors which occur in those cuttings be partially pointed out. You are certainly persuaded that bloodletting is a "purging" of the body; this is clearly erroneous. The reason for this is not that every purging takes nothing away from the body and substance, but that it only takes away that which is opposed to the substance in general, as far as the substance extends.

Now, for whomever you cut a vein, you take away that part of the substance, yet you lead out no more of the "evil" than that which the substance contains. But what of the rest of the cure? That which flowed out is "cured" <note>Paracelsus is being sarcastic: once the blood is out of the body, it doesn't matter if it's healthy or sick.</note>; but what does that benefit the body? You are therefore wandering in a heavy delusion by calling the removal of substance a "purging." And even if an abundance exists in the blood, on account of which putrefaction could arise from its own causes, your order of bloodletting is in no way useful to it. For bloodlettings which ought to purge in that manner must be done in an entirely different way than by catching the gore in small bowls.

<margin>Yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> is not to be sought in the blood.</margin>
<margin>The humors are fictitious.</margin>
In that blood, you look for yellow bile, which nevertheless can by no means be generated in the blood. But all those things serve your purpose quite well when they are commended—that you should repeatedly vomit up now yellow bile, now phlegm, etc. For whatever it may be, you seem to lie hidden quite safely under those names. There is a need for a much different account of truth than that we should rest in those imaginary "Qualities," "Humors," and "Complexions." Furthermore, you should by no means attribute this purging to the idle and the laborers alike. For this is mere opinion. If you should respond that the laborer expels from himself what the idle man retains: on what foundation, then, will that argument of yours rest? Since neither labor nor idleness is the cause of diseases of the blood. Therefore, they can neither excuse nor accuse it. Regarding the time when it ought to be done, you have established it well. But the "time" is not that which is indicated in your bloodletting charts.

->ON BLOODLETTING<-

# ON BLOODLETTING

<margin>The evils of excessive evacuation of the veins.</margin>
This is not what is indicated in the bloodletting tables. Even if you knew which vein was appropriate, it would still be stated poorly. Why, in the end, do you swear by the doctrines of those masters who have not yet even completed their years of apprenticeship? That the immoderate evacuation of blood is not a good thing is something already known to everyone. But how much does that contribute to the actual foundation of medicine? What does it contribute to a person's health? If you are truly skilled in bloodletting, you will easily know what to do. For too much of anything is harmful: it is the cause of the dissolution of that genuine <term>concordance</term><note>The harmonious balance of the body’s elements and forces which Paracelsus believes constitutes health.</note> in which the integrity of the body and life consists. As much as is taken away from this concordance, that is how much strength is lacking in that limb—a matter that is extremely useful and necessary to consider. And this knowledge should not merely rest in generalities, but must be guided through every specific case: thus <term>Apoplexy</term><note>A stroke or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> is inflicted on one, <term>dropsy</term><note>original: "hydrops"; an old term for swelling or edema caused by fluid retention.</note> on another, the <term>falling sickness</term><note>original: "caducus"; epilepsy.</note> on a third, and so on.

<margin>Two kinds of Phlebotomy. What is "Chosen." What is "Compelled."</margin>
To you, there seem to be two suitable times or types for administering bloodletting: one you call *Chosen*, the other *Compelled*. But what will you say regarding "Chosen" bloodletting? That is the kind which removes the <term>vices of the blood</term><note>Impurities or imbalances within the blood that Paracelsus believes cause disease.</note> according to the requirements of the season and the person's constitution. As for "Compelled" bloodletting, as far as can be understood, you assign it to times of plague and similar crises. But what you mean by "Choice" is easily understood: you intend it as a foundation so that, if you recommend annual purgings, they are established to remove <term>defluxions</term><note>The supposed downward flow of harmful humors or fluids in the body.</note>. Thus, in all your advice, you join substance and matter together, where your manifest error is understood—namely, that you only take away the *weight* of the blood, but you never reach that which *gives* the weight in the first place. What do you think of this example?

<margin>Treatment of paralysis should be established before the paroxysm.</margin>
When someone is gripped by paralysis, at what time do you think it is most convenient to treat them? Is it when the paralysis has already set in, or rather when it is still hidden and has not yet broken out into action? Mark this objection diligently. I urge nothing else here than that diseases existing in any man ought to be recognized and treated while they are still fresh or "young." You, however, try to drive them out when they are already "adults." What you attempt in "young" diseases only amounts to the removal of weight, by which the <term>paroxysm</term><note>The sudden onset or worsening of symptoms; a crisis point in an illness.</note> is merely delayed. It would bring more honor to you and the ornament of your art if you performed in the developing stages of a disease what you later attempt once the paroxysm has already occurred. Therefore, be diligently persuaded of this: it is entirely proper that the cure be established before the paroxysm. You, however, having forgotten this, have instead thrust upon us <term>cochia pills</term><note>original: "pilulas cochias"; a common Renaissance laxative or purgative pill made with aloes and other bitter herbs.</note> for the sake of that "maturation."

<margin>The "point" to be noted in bloodletting.</margin>
<margin>The indication for letting blood is not taken from the Liver.</margin>
<margin>Whether a vein should be cut after labor.</margin>
Why is it that you choose a "clear day" and seek a vein to be cut through many roundabout paths, when all these things contribute nothing to a person's health? For nothing else should be considered except the <term>point</term><note>The specific moment of medical necessity.</note> alone, whether it falls in autumn or spring, or on a holiday or a workday. For any bloodletting ought to be done out of necessity, which breaks your entire system. This same necessity teaches one to find the right time, hour, and convenient minute. Although one necessity may be greater than another, all such necessity exists. For every disease, whether it is fresh or adult, known or unknown, is entirely subject to the necessity of the cure. Furthermore, you add a rule for how a man should know whether he ought to submit himself to bloodletting or not. Here again, your massive error shines through. For you require that the person about to have a vein cut should have a healthy liver, and one that is not "chilled." If the liver is cold, it has no need of bloodletting. If it is healthy, the reasoning is the same. A far different judgment must be made about these things. For diseases contained in the blood are to be estimated by a far different judgment than stopping a bloodletting based on such a trivial consideration of the liver. Do you judge the stomach in the same way? What does the blood have to do with the stomach? If the blood is vicious, it will pay for its own evil; the stomach, in turn, will also suffer its own damage. If something stands in your way in bloodletting, why do you not take it away and remove it? Or why do you betray your own ignorance here? It is the same with what you add: that a vein should not be cut after labor. For will you pay attention to labor or movement instead? Thus you do not decree bloodletting if something from a bath or other connected diseases causes affliction. Rather, remove the things that should be removed and take away what acts as an impediment. You should not allow the blood to conquer or overflow just because you know some disease exists in another limb. On the contrary, act as a perfect Physician, and do not be driven away by that which you yourself ought to expel. For if that which should be afraid of you strikes terror into you instead, you certainly betray a significant defect in your Medical art—one that is, nevertheless, very familiar to you all.

<margin>The nature of Almansor's teaching on bloodletting.</margin>
I cannot entirely contradict the teachings of <term>Almansor</term><note>Refers to the Persian physician Rhazes (865–925 AD) and his famous work "Liber ad Almansorem."</note>, who hand down documents that are not inept regarding which man should have a vein cut. But he truly only decides concerning those who do not necessarily *need* it, but for whom it is merely a relief and a strengthening for taking food and drink. For he concerns himself with swollen and full veins; from which it is evident to anyone that he intended very little regarding the diseases themselves, so as to seek them in their origin, as the cure itself requires. And although he did name some diseases—such as those made heavy by <term>apostemes</term><note>An old word for an abscess or a localized collection of pus.</note> and pustules and other evils—he did not ascend any higher, nor did he urge anything other than an annual relief. From this, it is not difficult to judge what he understood about these matters. This he clearly declares himself when he hands down an "annual preservative" in the cure of fevers. From this, it can be gathered how "dry" <note>Lacking in substance or true insight.</note> he was in this doctrine. In no way, therefore, should a Physician depend upon his authority.

<margin>One should not be bled when desiring food.</margin>
Furthermore, you also set an order for those who should least of all be bled. Among these are numbered those who have no appetite for food. But answer me: who is it that has an appetite for food when they are sick? For if the sick have to wait so long through the presence of their diseases until their appetite is provoked, what, in the end, would become of them? For even you yourselves must admit that diseases...

He rejects the authority of Almansor (Rhazes) and insists that treatment must occur when a disease is first developing, not after it has become "adult."</summary>

<header>TREATISE 10</header>

...diseases of the blood both cast down the appetite and restore it, provided the cure is performed within the blood itself. These doctrines of yours are fine enough and self-contained. However, when the flow of blood must be stopped, you follow the doctrine of <term>Avicenna</term><note>A Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe, though Paracelsus frequently attacked his authority.</note> and attend only to the thickness of the blood. This reasoning for restraining the flow lacks any foundation in truth.

<margin>
The source of the thickness and blackness of the blood.
</margin>
For the black blood leaping out of the veins is by no means like that while inside the blood vessels; rather, it is rendered so by the incision or the wound that was made. Thus, a sudden change is the cause of both this and other colors. So, you remain in doubt as to what you have actually achieved. Furthermore, you say that if the blood flows white and thin, not much of it should be evacuated.

<margin>
He is ignorant of Avicenna's art of bloodletting.
</margin>
Here you should note that Avicenna understood nothing regarding the recognition of blood, judging blood as if in <term>locusts</term><note>original: "locustis"; Paracelsus likely uses this as a derogatory comparison, suggesting Avicenna's observations were as insignificant or as alien as those of insects.</note>. And of this kind, as you say, there are many canons among you. One of them is this, when you say to the sick: "Let blood again shortly, for your blood is quite black." Or: "If you feel well from the bloodletting, return to me soon." What kind of "art" is this? Surely, even a blind man might be so wise as to say that. Truly, how each person should conduct themselves regarding the labor of healing ought to be understood in its own specific order, according as the disease reveals itself in the blood, telling your common rules—which are the same for everyone—to stay far away.

What kind of regimen is yours regarding food and drink, in which you consider nothing else except the safety or protection of the wound? Yet, the disease itself ought to be considered much more, and the wound not at all. This manifold order proceeds from the very foundation of those diseases. For unless that is considered individually, you cannot help but strike a heavy blow against your own devised plan. For the matter is not so easy and safe as you dream in your established "Bloodletting Diet." Everything must be directed entirely toward the business at hand. Do not throw everything into one and the same regimen. For you know how the blood clings to food; and you seek singular virtues and strengths which, nevertheless, cannot be introduced into the blood without food and drink. In this case, therefore, that food must simultaneously be the medicine. They cannot deny that they believe good blood can only be produced from suitable food and drink.

<margin>
Where good blood comes from, and what it provides.
</margin>
Good blood performs this: it frees the blood from its own diseases, it provides a cheerful and serene mind, and so forth; it by no means binds one to a sad and dark hunger, and so forth. For all these things are considered by those who undertake the care of the least serious matters.

It must be known in these cases that if bloodletting is performed and no disease appears in that blood, you should have free use of food and drink, whatever you desire for the body's use. This is where the regimen and order of the "wound-doctors" takes its origin.

<margin>
The parts of the year do not indicate Bloodletting.
</margin>
Your singular error, however, lies in this: that you set the four seasons of the year as the indications for bloodletting. In this matter, you act partly like the <term>Egyptians</term><note>A common Renaissance term for astrologers or practitioners of "superstitious" arts.</note>, because you establish a time for the cutting of a vein and forget the time of the diseases. By doing this, you betray yourselves as "shears-men" <note>original: "fortices"; likely a derogatory term for barber-surgeons who cut without medical knowledge.</note>, because you flatter those who live more delicately and lazily, and you fish for the favor of those who especially enjoy your trade. You persuade people to this four-part bloodletting so that you too may enjoy a share of those profits from the patients. And how much the care of bloodletting matters to you is abundantly declared by the days of <term>St. Blase, St. Philip and James, St. Bartholomew, and St. Martin</term><note>These saints' days (Feb 3, May 1, Aug 24, Nov 11) correspond to the four seasons, showing how medicine had become tied to the church calendar rather than biology.</note>, at all of which times it is "good to be fattened." But if those four times are perhaps not enough for you, add to them the days of St. Valentine and St. Stephen. If even that is not enough: add the whole of Lent, and after Easter betake yourselves to the thermal baths. For if bloodletting is determined in this way, no time for applying it will be more convenient than when the <term>capons</term><note>Fattened roosters.</note> are the fattest and most stuffed of all, and most fit for indulging the appetite.

You even prescribe an order for when blood should be let while fasting and when after a meal. That is well done indeed—so that your ignorance may leak out to the common people! For from this it shines through how great your knowledge of the <term>firmament</term><note>The heavens or stars; Paracelsus is mocking their reliance on astrological timing.</note> is. Driven by the same spirit, you even forbid certain <term>conjunctions</term><note>The alignment of planets.</note> and the body parts in which the <term>Zodiac sign</term><note>original: "signum"</note> is turning. From all this, it is certain that you know neither a point nor a minute concerning bloodletting. Thus you judge, now of summer, now of winter; meanwhile not thinking of what kind of diseases are birthed in summer or autumn.

<margin>
Whether cutting the forehead vein cures the eyes and head.
</margin>
You claim that cutting the vein of the forehead helps in the ulceration of the eyes and headache. How poorly considered and ill-advised such counsel is, is clear from the fact that ulceration of the eyes by no means arises from that vein which you point out on the forehead, nor does headache. And if indeed the evil is somewhat lessened by its cutting, that is only from the cooling, which its own inflammation later follows again. I will say nothing of the fact that the primary causes which conspire to stir up the pain are not considered by you. You say the same cutting works against <term>Lypothymia</term><note>original: "Lypothymiâ"; a historical term for fainting or swooning.</note>. But who ever dared to say that fainting has any kinship with these veins? As for <term>Mania</term><note>Madness or delirium.</note>, it helps only if it happens to help by chance. For nothing durable and constant is achieved if a boiling pot is removed from the fire and immediately moved back to it again. It would even work for sleep, if the "commotion of sleep" lay hidden in the veins. Here you err significantly in that you do not consider the manifold nature of the aforementioned diseases, which lie in the veins of the head, not the forehead.

<margin>
Temporal veins.
</margin>
Likewise, you decree the temporal veins for ear pain. But you did not mention at the same time how "certain" that bloodletting is, and that it harms more people than it helps. From all this, it becomes known that you truly have no knowledge of Anatomy regarding the veins located near the ears. I will say nothing of the fact that the eyes are also included here.

<margin>
Veins of [two] colors. Veins of the back of the head.
</margin>
The veins at the back of the head, when cut, are said to benefit convulsions of the head; yet their nature is such that they actually produce and generate them.

<margin>
Veins of the tongue.
</margin>
Similarly, the veins of the tongue are believed by you to serve many evils. But the anatomy of the tongue has been poorly considered by you, namely that the damage is greater than the benefit in...

# ON BLOODLETTING.

<margin>Veins of the chin.</margin>
On this side: you also observe the veins under the chin as a remedy against nosebleeds.
<margin>Veins of the neck.</margin>
In this, you fail to consider that the blood is extracted in one and the same way; the extraction performed at the chin is no less harmful than that performed in the nose, except for the difference in location. In the same way, the veins in the neck are cut to treat mucus or phlegm, even though the phlegm does not seek an exit at this location, but has found a more certain <term>emunctory</term><note>An organ or body part that carries off waste (like the nose or armpits).</note>. But the heart will not be strengthened by the cutting of a vein either. For its diseases, more is required than mere bloodletting. Furthermore, the veins in the palate or
<margin>Veins of the throat.</margin>
throat do not help in any other way than how an **abscess** is opened, so that the pus may flow out.

<margin>Veins of the thumb.</margin>
Any bloodletting, if administered according to your training, is no different than if a ripe abscess were opened with a scalpel. Thus, you say that cutting the vein next to the thumb helps in all diseases of the head. Yet there is not one among you who can say that any disease was ever removed by cutting it. You feel the same way about the
<margin>The liver vein.</margin>
**Median** and **liver** veins<note>original: "Mediana & iecoraria"; traditional names for specific veins in the arm believed to correspond to specific organs.</note>. Why indeed do you Doctors torment surgeons with that empty curiosity, leading them about on both sides like unskilled men, when you see nonetheless that all your work is empty and frustrated. You treat the
<margin>The Cephalic vein.</margin>
**Cephalic** and **Median** veins as having the exact same use, but the foundation of your opinion is far too shaky. "Many diseases are called, but few are chosen"<note>A parody of Matthew 22:14; Paracelsus implies many diseases are identified, but few are actually "chosen" to be cured by these methods.</note>. The same is likewise
<margin>The spleen vein.</margin>
true of the hepatic [liver] vein. What is useful today is forgotten tomorrow. You say the **splenetic vein** removes many things. Even if it were to act perfectly, whatever it removes was never actually a disease. Furthermore, you testify that the
<margin>The lumbar vein.</margin>
**Lumbar vein** [of the loins] acts against the <term>calculus</term><note>A stone in the kidney or bladder.</note>. In this, who would not believe that your advice is very well-intentioned? For it is easy to think that the stone itself certainly does not exit through a vein. Therefore, as much as you succeed in this case, so much do you benefit by all your bloodlettings. You provide similar proof of this in <term>hydrops</term><note>Dropsy, or edema; an accumulation of fluid in the body.</note>, which
<margin>The umbilical vein.</margin>
at no time was ever led out through a vein, just as you have struggled to extract it through the **umbilical vein**. Since the diseases do not lie within these veins, how, I ask, can opening them help? You assert that many veins act against the stone, etc. How good your opinion truly is, I myself do not know; yet I greatly fear it is more harmful than beneficial. And the
<margin>Veins of the legs.</margin>
**veins of the legs**—how many things they are preached to be useful for! Since these many diseases do not emerge from a single cause and origin, how, I ask, can one simple remedy restrain and tame many ailments at once? Similarly, you say that the cutting of other veins is beneficial, meanwhile considering nothing as to whether the diseases are in the veins themselves or not. You seek the neighbor of the disease, but you leap over the enemy’s own house, thinking peace is sufficiently provided for if you join a good neighbor to the disease.

<margin>The lower veins draw from the upper ones.</margin>
It is indeed true that many things are drawn downward through the cut lower veins, such as those of the ankles and feet. Yet you understand nothing further—whether that cutting is beneficial to the foot itself, or less so. From this it is clear enough that, being anxious only for today, you take no care for tomorrow,
<margin>Veins of the knee.</margin>
thinking of one place but not the other. The **popliteal veins** [behind the knee] are quite healthful for women. But that which matters most here, you dismissively neglect. From this, your progress can easily be judged. You strike the vein of the
<margin>Vein of the outer ankle.</margin>
**outer ankle** to mitigate the upper members of the body. This is no less erroneous and harmful than can be proven regarding other lower veins. For in this way, upper ailments descend into the lower parts; and from the wounded limb, its own blood (which is good) is withdrawn, and in its place bad blood—even worse—later succeeds. Thus a new disease must be generated, ending either in **arthritis** or in **ulcers**, which would have remained much more safely in its own place than being dragged there. In this way, you change many diseases by reason of their location, and while you judge that you have healed one part, you kindle a new fire in other parts. The
<margin>Veins of laughter.</margin>
**veins of laughter**<note>original: "Venæ risus"; Paracelsus refers to veins near the mouth (related to the zygomatic/risorius muscles) which were mythologized to cause death by laughter if cut.</note>, because of which a man might die from laughing, are not equally certain in everyone, but many obstacles stand in the way. If you are going to send a soul to heaven with such laughter, it will be necessary for you to know those veins with much more exploration than is evident from your writings thus far. Furthermore, you posit that the vein of the smallest toe acts against **paralysis**. How, I ask, will you prove that? For even if you were to draw the paralysis away from its seat, it is so fashioned by nature that it rises up high again, and is never drawn downward in such a way that it remains constantly below. From this, your ignorance shines forth again, because you have not understood the essence of paralysis at all. Therefore, since you can without difficulty match some vein to everything a person complains about, you make it so that the burden and trouble must be borne by a neighbor, while that part to which the disease itself belongs goes free.

<margin>The true way of cutting any veins.</margin>
But so that you may have a brief instruction for cutting all veins, it must be known that this cutting ought to be done for no other reason than from the knowledge of those diseases which arise from the blood. At the same time, one must recognize blood-borne diseases and what damage they can inflict outside their own region. This is what must be averted in the veins—not through <term>scarification</term><note>The practice of making many small superficial incisions in the skin.</note>, but according to the legitimate rule of the art: that is, that those veins are selected in that place where the **root of the disease** exists. Before that happens, the blood must be brought back to a **temperament** and moderation, so that it follows our purpose. In this place, I want both Doctors and surgeons (or barbers) to be warned: that, bidding farewell to the art of bloodletting as it has been practiced, you consider a little more attentively how much grave harm and damage you introduce through ignorance of it, while you demand neither knowledge of the hour, nor the end of the disease, nor have the slightest notice of the sky or the earth itself. It is a thing to be lamented that, as soon as someone complains to you of an illness, you immediately resort to bloodletting,
<margin>Every wound is bad in itself.</margin>
even though you have already learned that all wounds are harmful to the body. For the healthier the blood was, the more severe the illness that follows. Therefore, your bloodletting...

# TREATISE IV.

<margin>What must be noted regarding bloodletting.</margin>
Now, so that you may know the subsequent process and order in which bloodletting must be instituted so that it may be healthful and useful, four things above all are especially to be noted by you: namely *Time, Place, Diet,* and the *Specific.*

<margin>Time.</margin>
For the knowledge of **time**, it should be noted that it only indicates at what hour bloodletting should be instituted: whether it be at the recent birth of the disease, or in the fury of an incipient **paroxysm** <note>A sudden attack or increase in the intensity of a disease's symptoms.</note>. For in this lies the art: taking away the root of the disease.

<margin>Place.</margin>
Secondly, one must inquire after the seat or **location** of the vein in which the disease has taken up residence; for where the root of the disease flourishes, there it must be attacked entirely.

<margin>Diet.</margin>
Thirdly, the **Diet** must be established according to the nature of the disease: not according to the condition of the wound, but of the disease.

<margin>Specifics.</margin>
Finally, you ought to know that there is a certain medicine called a <term>specific</term><note>A medicine specifically targeted to a particular organ or disease, rather than one that balances the whole body's humors.</note>. This has power if the hour of bloodletting was too unproductive. You will learn the method of administering this in the book on *Terrestrial Diseases* and *Diseases of the other Elements.* For understand the nature of bloodletting, and how far it reaches, in this way:

The cause and foundation for why bloodletting must be understood in this way is as follows. I mentioned writing a certain book in which all diseases arising from the heavens are contained, and which teaches how they dominate the blood; likewise, which blood ought to be let for the perfect cure of those diseases. As for that written book, it does not pertain much here. For here, at least, the cause of the following order of bloodletting must be described: namely, the irritation which the blood inflicts upon nature to remove it. And although others have attempted the same before me, with what success and foundation they performed it has been sufficiently declared in the previous treatises.

<margin>N.B. What a Chronic Disease is and its nature.</margin>
You will understand this irritation in relation to that about which I have written a specific book. If a disease is generated in the blood that can be called **Chronic**, it will admit no medicine, as I have shown in the book on *Diseases from Blood*. The reason for this is that its cure proceeds with the **influence** <note>original: "influentia"; the Renaissance belief that celestial bodies "flowed into" the physical world to affect health.</note>. If the influence has passed, and it leaves behind a fixed generation in the blood, it must be known that this disease retains the nature of a star; it is governed according to the Moon and follows the regimen of other stars. Therefore, a perfect cure of this disease cannot happen after the influence has passed, for the reason stated above. Thus, it at least provokes and irritates. That irritation proceeds from the left-behind impression, which the paroxysms obey. The following treatise serves to take this away.

## Example.

<margin>Cancer is a disease from influence.</margin>
I would like you to notice such an example. **Cancer** is by itself a disease of influence. And because it does not "chronify" <note>Become a fixed, long-term condition independent of its original cause.</note> itself, it must therefore be divided by influence; otherwise, it will admit no established medicine. Or if it does admit any, it is nonetheless conquered and blinded, like a heap of coals that lies hidden, covered by ashes. And regarding a cancer of this kind, I treat nothing here. If it truly becomes chronic, then it escapes the heavens, and thus it is itself both the "heaven" and the disease. This malice of cancer, which it naturally received from the heavens, accompanies it like a celestial motion or course. To take this away, observe this order in all those diseases whose cause is first the heavens, but which are afterwards separated from the heavens by reason of "chronification." Hold this brief lesson concerning these: that the impression imparts its own nature to the body. As long as the body is not yet conquered, Medicine must proceed from the heavens. But if the body in that place is already conquered, a two-fold medicine is available:

<margin>The impression on the body, the Nature of a Disease of a double element.</margin>
one in bloodletting, the other directed according to the nature of the body. For a double element produces this present disease. But those medicines which pertain here besides bloodletting are called **specifics**, because they are outside the nature and property of the other element.

<margin>What is a specific medicine? Double diseases.</margin>
Furthermore, four things also pertain to what was said above. Time, of course, is contained in practice. Location indicates the practice. The Regimen is handed down in the books of such diseases; the specific is also found there. Hence, diseases are further divided into two kinds: for they are either **Physical** or **Surgical**.

### On Cloudy Diseases.

<margin>Cloudy diseases etc., how they may be cured.</margin>
If a <term>cloudy disease</term><note>original: "morbus nubilis"; likely referring to wandering, vague, or "shadowy" symptoms, or certain skin conditions that appear like clouds or mists on the surface.</note> has passed into a chronic state, retaining the likeness of astral motion, then remove it by this path. If a sign manifests in the body with a roughness of the skin, and its incident paroxysm is already known by habit: then seek it three days before that time, and perform bloodletting (paying very little regard to the sign of the heavens or similar things) in two veins which exhibit their anatomy through the cloudy affliction. Those are the veins that appear black, knotty, and swollen below and above the cloudy disease. Perform the incision below, and when enough blood has flowed out, bind the wound. Afterwards, on the following second or third day, cut the vein higher up and extract a just weight. On the eighth day at the most, apply bloodletting again. Once these things are finished, one must rest from the final bloodletting. Thus the "course" which has already inserted itself as a fixed thing will be taken away. Since it returns annually according to its custom, especially around the beginning of autumn: therefore, you shall take care to open the vein occasionally once above the remaining disease.

# ON BLOODLETTING

<margin>Ulcers of the internal organs, etc., how they are to be cured.</margin>
<margin>Flixweed, etc., for eating sores.</margin>
<margin>A plaster of coral stops the blood.</margin>
...you shall carry out [the treatment] to cleanse the ulcer, and you shall cause the veins above and below the ulcer to swell, and you should apply <term>Flixweed</term><note>Latin: *herba sophia*. A plant historically used in wound healing; its name "wisdom of the surgeons" reflects its high regard in early medicine.</note>, boiled in wine, while hot to the ulcer. As for the cutting of the veins, you shall pierce as many as are found, caring nothing for the astrological signs, but attending only to the hour. And if the <term>paroxysm</term><note>The point at which the symptoms of a disease are at their most intense.</note> is seen to be at its height, you shall allow the blood to flow until the full sign of it reaches its end. Afterward, you shall stop the blood by applying a plaster of coral, and you shall rest for three days. When that time has elapsed, whatever veins appear black or leaden-colored, either above or below the evil, you shall open them in this sequence: first the lower ones shall be cut in order, according to the severity of their appearance, and afterward the upper ones shall be pierced, according to the condition of the person. Always keep this diligently in mind: do not overwhelm the sick person too much, but according to the balance of nature, administer one after another in succession. Once these bloodlettings are performed, the "solemn courses" <note>Paracelsus refers to the regular, rhythmic flow or "influx" of humors and celestial influences.</note> which the blood has received from the stars will be removed, and the malignancy of the erosion or <term>eating sore</term><note>Latin: *exesio*. A corrosive or consuming wound.</note> which resists healing and consolidation will be rooted out. If every bloodletting is instituted according to this prescribed rule, then the operation of any medicine will follow successfully at the end.

### On Fistulas

<margin>How a fistula is to be cured.</margin>
Above all, you shall take care to reach the end of the fistula, and you should know to what place it extends. After that, discern the veins running toward it from your knowledge of anatomy; for without this knowledge, you will inquire into nothing conveniently. Once the true veins are thoroughly recognized, ascend further to their very origin—that is, as high as you can track or hunt them down. Then, when they are swollen, open them during the <term>conjunctions of Saturn</term><note>An astrological alignment where Saturn and another planet appear in the same part of the sky; Paracelsus believed this timing influenced the "heaviness" or blockages in the body.</note>. On the fourth day following, open them a little lower, yet still above the fistula. Finally, cut those same veins below the fistula, as low as you can. Draw the blood according to the nature of the disease and the patient. Meanwhile, you shall press on daily with medicines. For the cure of the evil is swift once the "solemn" downward flow is abolished.

### On Common Abscesses or Phlegmons.

<margin>How phlegmons are to be cured.</margin>
If a bloody <term>abscess</term><note>Latin: *apostema*. A localized collection of pus or swelling.</note> arises in the flesh or elsewhere, observe no other sign than the **full moon**, when it is at its greatest strength. Afterward, discern which veins are passing through the area, and do not care if they seem unsuitable to you. Cut them at the highest point toward their origin, and draw blood according to the condition of the disease and the patient. Once that is done, in that same <term>quarter</term><note>Referring to the lunar phase or the four-day interval mentioned previously.</note>, pierce the vein located above the abscess; and during the **new moon**, pierce below the abscess, always having respect for the person and the malignancy of the disease. When these things have been performed, attend to the fullness or abundance of blood in the abscess. If you have detected full signs, then at the very next full moon, open the lowest veins. In this way, the force of the movement or flow will be broken, so that the blood does not thereafter hinder the healing, regardless of which suitable medicines are applied to attempt the cure.

### On Growing Evils.

<margin>How growing defects are to be cured.</margin>
The origin or root of "growing evils" <note>Likely referring to tumors or spreading malignant growths.</note> must be removed in this way. First, inquire within the circuit of that entire region how many veins you find passing through the growing evil. Once found, pierce them as close to their origin as you can, and spare no region, whether it be the head or another more dangerous part. Having cut them in order, let them bleed thoroughly, which is most conveniently done during the **full moon**. Once the blood has been thus extracted according to the patient’s tolerance, rest until the ninth day, at which time you shall open the veins again. Afterward, discern what sort of veins they are. Search for their "locusts" <note>Likely a term for the branching ends or small nodes of the veins.</note> in the lowest place—that is, if they pass through, then hunt the extremities of those veins and let out the blood. Once these things are finished, attack the ulcer or growing evil itself with the kindly application of medicine. Thus it will happen that it begins to die away little by little. Indeed, as much of it as has grown excessively will die off. But if from the first attempt the evil does not seem to want to die, then you shall take care to break the "influence" <note>The celestial or internal "flow" sustaining the growth.</note> again in the aforementioned manner, and thereafter you shall observe those two times for opening the veins every year, according to the nature and requirement of the evil.

### On Collected Tumors.

<margin>How collected tumors etc. are to be cured.</margin>
<margin>Flixweed causes the veins to swell.</margin>
Intercept the accustomed downward flow of those tumors which are formed by accumulation in this way: First, make the veins swell by applying **Flixweed**. Afterward, seek them out within the tumors, or in the red lines near the accumulations. Those which you find hard, full, and as if filled with small grains, pierce them in the middle of the accumulations, and let the blood flow according to the nature of the person and the disease. On the third day, renew the swelling of the veins again, and inquire which ones have more of the aforementioned signs. Open these also in the prescribed manner where they can be most conveniently reached. And if you have detected similar veins even near the accumulations, pierce those as well, until no such traces remain in the veins. Furthermore, on the ninth day, open those veins below the accumulation. Finally, when five days have passed since that opening, pierce those same veins at the highest point that you are able to track. In this way, the influence impressed by the stars will be driven out, so that your remedies may thereafter have a more evident effect; whereas otherwise, that evil could not be removed or taken away by eroding, nor by cutting, nor by any other effort. For by this art, the flow is intercepted, which would otherwise soon overflow again and would not yield to erosion or incision.

### On Chronic Pustules.

<margin>How chronic pustules are to be cured. Flixweed etc.</margin>
If you are troubled by chronic pustules born of the blood, capture the origin of the veins from them, which you will easily reach. Once investigated together, open them all on one day in the lowest region during a **new moon**. Afterward, in nearly the middle region, cut them again after they have been swollen with **Flixweed**, and extract the blood according to the nature of the matter. Afterward, during the next following **full moon**, open them again lower down. When these things are finished, make the veins swell in a <term>Laconicum</term><note>Latin: *Laconico*. A dry sweating-room or sauna used to stimulate circulation and open the pores.</note> with **Flixweed**; and wherever you have detected veins similar to one another, whether in hardness, or leaden color, or in other things which are contrary to the nature of veins, [you shall pierce them]...

### On Cancer.

<margin>
How cancer is to be cured.
</margin>

**IF** a cancer has become chronic, you must take care to seek it out first of all in the "feminine veins," that is, in the veins of the menstrual flow. Open these veins in their <term>junctions</term><note>Latin: *locustis*. In Paracelsian anatomy, these are specific points or branching areas of the venous system.</note> three times in a single month. Meanwhile, cut the intervening veins that are visible along the red lines in the healthiest part of the area, in order, according to the condition of the person. Afterward, open the menstrual veins again, following the method we explained for <term>eating ulcers</term><note>Latin: *esthiomenis*. These are "phagedenic" ulcers that appear to "eat" the surrounding flesh.</note>. For the poison that sends itself into a cancer is sometimes driven back only with great pain and difficulty. Care must be taken, if possible, that these and other bloodlettings are established at the beginning of the month.

Cancer in men is to be treated in the same way in the hemorrhoidal veins, especially in that place where you can most conveniently reach them. Without this process of bloodletting, no cancer will be uprooted with its "seed," nor will it easily allow even a superficial cure.

### On Lupus.

<margin>
How lupus is to be cured.
</margin>

**BL**oodletting in <term>Lupus</term><note>In historical medicine, "Lupus" (the wolf) referred to any devouring skin ulcer, most commonly what we now call Lupus Vulgaris or skin tuberculosis, so named because it "eats" the face like a wolf.</note> must be performed internally, within the ulcer itself, so that it swells up with the aid of "tumefying" herbs. For then many clustered veins will break out, appearing leaden, black, or red from inflammation. Whichever veins show these colors, open them until they emit fresh blood. Do not be concerned even if the veins must be wounded with a large cut; the condition of the blood requires this. On the third day, repeat the opening, and do not stop as long as the pain lasts. For that pain is an indicator of many hidden veins. It is proper to know, moreover, that these veins can be struck nowhere else but in the ulcer itself. For the center and the root are situated there. As soon as the pains cease, you shall begin the healing and closing of the wound. Finally, you shall open those veins in their junctions once a year. Similarly, also at the half-year mark. Afterward, open them a second time in the middle of the vein toward its beginning; and thus you shall continually change the site, according to the condition of the person and the malignant infection of the blood.

# ON THE DISEASES OF THE BODY OR PHYSICAL DISEASES.

### On Bloodletting for Gout.

<margin>
The paroxysm of gout is from the firmament.
</margin>
<margin>
How gout is to be cured by bloodletting.
</margin>

**I**t is right that you should understand that the heavens insert their impressions into the diseases of the body (or "physical" diseases) no less than into surgical ones. Therefore, pay attention hereafter to those diseases which, having already become chronic, must be removed through the extraction of blood. Indeed, <term>Podagra</term><note>Gout, particularly of the foot.</note> can by no means be brought to its <term>paroxysm</term><note>The peak intensity of the disease's symptoms.</note> without the influx of the <term>firmament</term><note>The sphere of the stars. Paracelsus believed the timing of diseases was dictated by the movement of the stars and planets.</note>. Therefore, its first treatment must begin with bloodletting, without which no cure for gout should be expected. This is the process for removing it: First, at the <term>conjunction</term><note>An alignment of astronomical bodies.</note> of the Moon and the Sun, before the paroxysm invades, you shall cut the four lowest <term>cephalic veins</term><note>While "cephalic" usually refers to the arm, in this period's anatomy, it refers to specific "head-related" drainage points in the extremities.</note> in both feet, and extract blood according to the exigency of the disease and the tolerance of the patient. Afterward, in the following quarter, you shall pierce the same veins in the legs, below the knees; and at the full moon, in the spine of the back. By this process, if the gout has not yet become fully chronic, it is immediately removed and uprooted. But if it is chronically fixed, you shall repeat the prescribed process again in the third following new moon. If, however, it is most vehemently fixed, repeat the bloodletting immediately in the next following new moon: thus the influence of the firmament will be intercepted, and so the full operation of the applied medicines will be felt. For unless the firmamental course is first removed, let no one think that this disease can be expelled by any other means. For no disease weighs upon us without a celestial impression.

For the impressions weigh upon us not in one way, but in many. For this reason and matter, I wrote the book *On the Origin of the Diseases of the Blood* <note>Original: "De origine morborum sanguinis"</note>. Once the impression has been explored, and focusing on that conjunction, cut the cephalic vein in the hands before the remission of the paroxysm, and on the following second day open the two cephalic veins in the feet. If these things are done around the time of the paroxysm, then cut the cephalic vein under the tongue. This being done, wait for the time of the defluxion. If the defluxion falls, repeat the bloodletting afterward in the aforementioned manner. Meanwhile, attend diligently to the signs of the defluxion. If it occupies the regions of the ears, stirring up ringing; or invading the region of the teeth, provoking pain in them; or if it brings on Asthma, or arthritis, or <term>lippitude</term><note>Bleary or inflamed eyes.</note>, or hoarseness, and similar things: in all these cases you shall take care to find the vein proper to each affection. Therefore, at the beginning of that conjunction, cut the veins of the ears, of the eyes, and similarly both the pulmonary and hepatic veins, and many others, having respect in each case to the person suffering the defluxion and the necessity of the matter itself. For defluxions of this kind reach their peak when incited by celestial power. And since the heavens find a body in harmony with them, it prevents any remedy from being helpful or useful while their course persists. This is the reason why men are tested daily by flows of this kind, even if they use many and various medicines at once. For the heaven prevails everywhere.

### On Erysipelas or Red Jaundice.

<margin>How erysipelas is to be cured.</margin>
Regarding this, it should be known that there is little difference between this <term>Erysipelas</term><note>A bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red, swollen rash, often called "St. Anthony's Fire."</note> and Mania. The difference lies only in the location and that the veins differ. For if such great heat and "exhalation" were driven into the region of reason, it would certainly stir up a far more serious Mania.

The origin of Erysipelas must therefore be sought in the veins. For in some who conceive Erysipelas from the interior of the body, the evil sinks down into the legs; in others, it runs through the veins that are distributed from the body into the arms; in some, the evil leaps into the veins of the head. Here again, there is a distinction: some are irritated by the course of the heavens, others by being wetted by water.

Concerning these, it must be held that those moved by the motion of the heavens ought to be bled during the conjunction. Those, however, which are irritated by moisture ought to be opened after the conjunction, once their veins have been sought out in this manner: namely, if the Erysipelas is from moisture, all the cephalic veins in the head must be cut, as they are subject to that course. The rest, however, are to be treated only in those veins which look toward the origin. For in the exterior veins, which have no common part with them, the disease increases. Rarely, however, does a disease of this kind occur which does not lead to ulceration.

### On Menstrual Fluxes.

<margin>How menstrual fluxes are to be moved.</margin>
It must be known regarding these fluxes that the <term>Menstruum</term><note>Menstrual flow.</note> is an outflow of specific veins. These veins must therefore be known above all else, so that you may know how to stir up and move suppressed menses through bloodletting. Although no specific hour of the heaven's course determines the time for this bloodletting, that course is nonetheless to be recognized from the motion of the natural flux, which is similar to the superior motion <note>i.e., the movement of the planets and stars.</note>. Therefore, if the time of the flux presents and indicates itself, then cut the menstrual veins during that impulse; without their opening and perfect evacuation, the operation of medicine does not proceed. Here you will note that such bloodlettings are even performed frequently in pregnant women. In which case, diligent care must be given that you **never** open a vein until the hour of the woman's labor is imminent, even if menstrual fluxes show themselves in the blood. For if that hour is not imminent, bloodletting must be strictly avoided. If, however, it is imminent, that health pertains to both the fetus and the mother.

### On Fever.

<margin>What fever is, and its cure.</margin>
Furthermore, you ought to hold that Fever exists not only outside the blood, but also within it: which is nothing other than a **putrid ignition** caused by the <term>firmament</term><note>The heavens or the stars. In Paracelsian medicine, diseases were often thought to be "ignited" by celestial influences mirroring the macrocosm.</note>. Whence bloodletting also must be instituted according to the reason of the heavens. To observe this, one must distinguish what kind of fever it is. For from this prior knowledge, it will be clear which veins in that place are infected. Once this is perceived, direct the cure so that at the beginning of the <term>paroxysm</term><note>A sudden attack or increase in the intensity of symptoms, like a fever spike.</note> you cut the appropriate vein, and look to nothing else. And although the heaven indeed may be quite powerful by its presence, you should nevertheless diligently act to strike the paroxysm during the New Moon, and afterward, if the paroxysm occurs at the beginning. For through such bloodletting, <term>Quartan</term><note>A fever that returns every fourth day.</note>, <term>Hectic</term><note>A wasting fever, often associated with tuberculosis.</note>, and others called <term>Septane</term><note>A fever that returns every seven days.</note> etc., are cured; otherwise, without a preceding vein-cutting, they in no way accept or agree with Medicine.

### On Paralytics

<margin>How paralysis is to be cured.</margin>
Regarding paralysis, you shall first know this: which veins contain the matter of the paralysis. This having been investigated, cut them in the extremities of the junctions during the **New Moon in Aries**. Afterward, open them in the middle part of the next quarter. Thus it will happen that, as much as the heaven causes, so much of its irritation is taken away. If any other paralytic thing occurs in that place, it is produced by the remaining three parts of man. If you are therefore skilled, and you see a paralytic flux in that region, then take away its paroxysm in the hour of its constellation or conjunction, without which prior knowledge you will otherwise medicate in vain. For this reason it is called "incurable," since it must be said of such a person: "The Doctor is not infallible."

<header>TREATISE</header>

...be drawn out significantly. However, even if the goodness of the blood is apparent from the start, do not let that turn you back from the procedure. Afterward, at the next new moon, open the veins in their proper, correct locations, and once again release a just quantity. Furthermore, at the next new moon following that, cut the vein of the chin and the one under the tongue. In this way, the influence of <term>chronications</term><note>The process by which an illness becomes chronic or settled into the body over a long period.</note> is driven out. But if the evil has endured for a longer time, you shall observe the seasons of the year as it seems convenient to your judgment.

->Conclusion.<-

**T**hus far, we have cleared away the errors and abuses commonly committed in <term>phlebotomy</term><note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood for therapeutic purposes.</note>; and subsequently, we have explained the rationale and method that ought to be observed in certain diseases. This has been done primarily for these reasons:

You see, surely, that God did not complete or perfect the pot as a whole, but produced only the clay, and entrusted the remaining work to the potter, or the disciple of the <term>firmament</term><note>The heavens or the sky; Paracelsus views the physician as a student of the stars.</note>. This same purpose was mine also: to lead those unskilled men into the school. Although they may seem so learned to themselves that they imagine they can divine the end of a matter from its very first letter, they will undoubtedly reject these teachings as useless and worthless because they do not understand them. This rejection is itself a testimony to the weakness of their own intellect. For if they possessed a higher science, they would certainly bring forth a far more sound response.

<margin>The Stars produce the Physician.</margin>
<margin>Galen, Avicenna, etc. are criticized.</margin>
Many of the ancient authors have indeed commented on bloodletting, and the younger ones have imitated them. Yet their own conscience and equity convict them, for they cannot defend that doctrine of vein-cutting in any other way than by saying it was handed down to them as such. From our discourse, it is also understood that the knowledge of bloodletting must be sought from <term>Astronomy</term><note>In Paracelsus's view, medicine and astronomy were inseparable, as the "inner stars" of the human body responded to the outer stars of the heavens.</note> alone. For the Stars themselves complete the fourth part of a Physician; yet the solid ancients taught nothing fundamental about them. Since they labored with such an itch for writing, surely if they had possessed any knowledge of the <term>Astral growths</term><note>The way celestial influences "grow" or manifest within the biological body.</note>, they would not have failed to carve it out more at length with their pens. I speak of Galen and Avicenna, and their ignorant commentators: Gentili, Jacobus de Partibus, Turisanus, and the rest.

As for the fact that they occasionally made mention of certain veins, I believe they learned this from the barbers, yet they never fully understood the matter itself—as they clearly reveal in other arts as well. Therefore, let their writings, being of no importance, not greatly disturb us.

And although it might seem that many more diseases should have been added here beyond those already discussed, nevertheless, since these must be sought from a deeper foundation, we have preferred to designate a specific book for them. In that volume, what is lacking here will be more clearly declared. All these things, however, must be learned like a craft and not judged by a foolish head.

->THE END OF BLOODLETTING.<-

# ON THE PURGATION TO BE INSTITUTED IN BLOODLETTING.

## On the use of Bloodletting in purging.

**C**ertain laws and customs have arisen from the <term>Sophistic Physicians</term><note>A derogatory term Paracelsus used for university doctors who relied on logic and traditional Greek texts (Sophistry) rather than the "light of nature."</note> which have even passed into stubborn habit: namely, the belief that a proper <term>purgation</term><note>The use of laxatives or other means to "cleanse" the bowels or humors.</note> must precede bloodletting so that the subsequent cutting of the vein might bring more benefit and profit. If this were indeed true, who would not praise such counsel? But since the reality is otherwise, who shall approve of it?

Since I have thus far treated the cutting of the vein, it is entirely fitting that I also say something about purgation, its companion. I do not doubt that these views of mine will seem strange to both the sick and the Physicians. For old and confirmed customs are not easily changed, especially when Physicians, through long usage, have persuaded the people that it was well done—when in fact it is done entirely poorly.

It will therefore be a work of great labor to abolish this custom. And the entire weight of this abolition seems to rest on this one thing: that henceforth, Physicians be more diligently watched, and what they do—and from what basis—be more circumspectly weighed. For many counsels are brought forth from custom alone. Whether these help or harm, they think the ancient custom must be held to regardless. Thus also many remedies are taught by Physicians out of simplicity; they are persuaded that a remedy which helped before them, and helps now, and will help hereafter, must necessarily be healthy in this or that disease. Thus many command purgations so that profit may return to the Doctors and the <term>apothecaries</term><note>Original: *pharmacopolas*. Sellers of drugs and medicines.</note>. If you were to force them by an imposed oath, they would certainly never do or undergo themselves what they command to others.

You, therefore, all you sick people in general who are about to have a vein cut, consider first of all the simplicity, custom, and greed of the Physicians. Allow nothing to be commanded to you by these men, nor believe anything from those who are far more unskilled than yourselves; who seek and hunt for their entire food and clothing from the empty persuasion of old custom. I will enumerate in a few words what damage will finally return to you from this, so that from these things you may be certain of what purgation is, what it provides, and what concerning it ought to be admitted or rejected.

Before we explain this, it seems we must define what bloodletting is and what it contributes to. Afterward, we will explain how purgation fits with it, and how both agree with each other.

<margin>What bloodletting is. What purgation is. The difference between purgation and bloodletting. Internal.</margin>
Bloodletting proceeds and is instituted from the knowledge of the heavens, acting upon celestial diseases. Purgation proceeds from the knowledge of earthly bodies, and is employed for removing diseases of this kind. Now see the relationship between them: one is from above, the other is internal.

<summary>Paracelsus concludes his instructions on bloodletting by critiquing ancient authorities like Galen and Avicenna for lacking astronomical knowledge. He then begins a new section challenging the traditional practice of administering a purgative before bloodletting, attributing the practice to physician greed and ignorance.</summary>

hell. Each is a medicine, looking toward its own individual disease, not another’s. For the disease of the heavens does not admit the earth, nor does the disease of the earth admit the heavens. Each removes its own ailments privately. The <term>humoralists</term><note>Physicians following the traditional system of Galen and Avicenna, which focused on balancing the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, however, shamelessly confuse the two. For however they may try to align them, if it certainly contributes to the profit of their "kitchens" <note>A common metaphor used by Paracelsus to describe physicians who prioritize their income and livelihood over the health of the patient.</note>, it is not considered a bad art even if the sick are forced to both defecate and bleed at the same time.

But, so that you may understand the matter more clearly, know that <term>purgations</term><note>Medicines or treatments used to cleanse the digestive tract.</note> evacuate the stomach and carry away the phlegm of the belly and other filth. Now, how these cleansings relate to the blood is easy to understand. For defecation clears the belly; <term>phlebotomy</term><note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, commonly known as bloodletting.</note> unburdens the head. But there is a <note>original: "Diomedea... necessitas"</note> harsh necessity <note>A reference to "Diomedian necessity," an ancient idiom for an unavoidable or forced obligation.</note> which dictates that whenever bloodletting is performed, the belly and stomach must also be sick, and medicines must be taken at the same time. Certainly, purgation contributes no more to bloodletting than it is useful to sweep the streets and temples when a festival is approaching—only to have them more abundantly fouled the next day. Who indeed is so stupid and senseless that he does not immediately see it is nonsense for purgation and the cutting of a vein to be performed at the same time? But they are not even content with these; they add thermal baths on top of it. What kind of counsel of impostors is this? It certainly fits no better than if someone wanted to forge an iron horseshoe out of lead, tin, and copper. If two diseases are present in the body, one of which requires purgation and the other bloodletting, so that both might indeed be advised: what does one have to do with the other? It is as if, were I to have fevers, I should ask whether purgation and bloodletting both contribute to them? Perhaps. Yet both should not be done at the same time; rather, each one by itself 

<margin>
Bloodletting is an <term>arcanum</term> <note>A secret, powerful, or essential healing principle or remedy in Paracelsian medicine.</note> by itself, just as purgation is also an arcanum by itself. Too much of a good thing is poison.
</margin>

is a sufficient cure on its own. For in bloodletting, there consists an *arcanum* for fevers so powerful that it suffices without purgation. Likewise, in purgation, there consist *arcana* which remove fevers and heal them entirely. Why then should a physician perform a double treatment? Too much of a good thing is poison. You should neither remove nor pile up *arcana*. But if you do this, you betray yourself as being ignorant of the purgations in which such *arcana* consist. And although you may dream something about them, you know nothing solid. Regarding bloodletting, you have heard as if in a dream that fevers are driven out through it. Yet you do not understand the *arcana* of bloodletting itself. Hence it happens that you miss the mark and offer ill-advised counsel. Without doubt, you join both together—namely, purgation and bloodletting—so that at least one of them might help, if not both. By doing so, you testify to your own simplicity, rudeness, and lack of skill in medicine, showing that you do not give advice based on the art, but only bring forth what you have heard or seen in your dreams.

Should you not be rebuked for this, that while you boast of being Doctors, you give such weak and dry advice, which flows not from the truth of knowledge, but from pure and foul opinions, by which you cast yourselves entirely upon blind fortune? Does this madness of yours not publicly prove 

that you are skilled neither in purgation nor bloodletting—for what uses each is employed, and what the efficacy and virtue of each may be—and yet meanwhile, according to old custom, you rashly decree whatever you please? Doubtless, this art is so beautiful to you because it pays such high interest to your "kitchens" and continually piles up new profit.

But yet another more damaging custom of yours must be brought forward: that you decree purgations even for healthy people, just as you command bloodletting. To be sure, those who are healthy are those who resist the lower and upper spheres, and whose <term>constellation</term><note>In Paracelsian medicine, "constellation" refers to the internal and external astrological and spiritual forces that govern health.</note> prevails in health. You, however, do the exact opposite, and while you command the healthy to be sick so that they have need of medicines—namely, purgation and bloodletting. Your stupidity is no less than if you were to subject a piece of wood that has no flaw to a lathe just to make it come out "healthy," or as if you were to offer a colic medicine to one who is not distorted by colic, but by a kidney stone.

You constantly babble many things about "corrupt blood," and yet not one of you has discovered what corrupt blood actually is. So too your entire speech is of clotted, burnt, or putrid blood, and so on. In the same way, you put forth I know not what miracles regarding purgations. But what does it matter to sing so many songs about a single pile of dung? How can you prove or agree that the filth which your syrups digest and your purgations lead out were removed before the bloodletting was started, and are no longer fluctuating in the belly? Or how, I ask, will you make the blood pure by what passes through the anus? Since no blood, nor anything else within it, can be expelled through the intestines? And yet you claim to purify the blood by purging, and at the same time you perform bloodletting. In this, what else are you doing but attempting two purgations for one thing, when, if you held true knowledge, one would suffice. Let it be concluded, therefore, that purgation should by no means be performed according to the old custom. For there is no consensus between the blood and the stomach. On the contrary, it is a waste to expend two labors on one matter. This counsel was therefore forged and cooked up in the "kitchens," not drawn from the art itself.

Lest you should think that nature perhaps performs no purgations in the blood, or that if it can perform them, it has not yet reached them: I meet you with this response—that nature designs many ways of purifying the blood. Of this kind are the purging of the blood through ulcers; the purging of the blood through salt; the purging of the blood through wateriness; the purging of the blood through thickness; the purging of the blood through putrefaction; and the purging of the blood through all the diseases born within it. And just as other cures exist for other diseases, so there are similar ones in the blood.

And these are the true and genuine treatments of the blood; these are the true bloodlettings, performed without iron <note>That is, without a surgical knife or scalpel.</note>, which nevertheless do not exit through the anus, nor through the intestines, nor pass out through the stomach. But if it is determined by you physicians to write or [act] from the foundation itself...
