...to speak of the blood, what purpose it serves, and so (as you do) you wish to dismiss the heavens: it will be altogether right that, as I say, you have a thorough knowledge of Natural things and know in what manner nature itself both bleeds and heals itself. If you tread this path, only then can you give counsel on phlebotomy <note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note>, as it ought to be administered by the scalpel. Meanwhile, you must desist from purging, as well as from phlebotomizing, which you have hitherto thrust forward with such shame and ignorance, and with no small loss.

You pretend very foolishly, as if ignorant of true medicine, that I point out to you things which (as you trifle) I myself do not know or am ignorant of. But that Demon of yours is not at all simple, by whose instinct you busily try to elicit such things from me. Lest I dismiss you meanwhile with an empty response, I repeat and emphasize this: that henceforth, just as I have done until now, I shall altogether save patients in blood-related diseases through natural phlebotomy, and (even if you resist) I shall snatch them from destruction. Inquire among these people about your own stupidity. Even if I had intended to teach these very things: nevertheless, they are withheld until we have sufficiently and more than enough clashed our horns against each other, and until your envy—with which you pursue me undeservingly while you yourselves lean on too loose and fluid a foundation—becomes publicly known to all. Finally, then, it is simply true that your purgations and bloodlettings, as they have been established until now, lack all foundation, nor do they contribute anything to the goal of health; they savor of nothing else but culinary gain <note>original: "quæstum culinarium"; a metaphor for medical practices designed purely to provide income for the physician's "kitchen" rather than to heal the patient.</note>, where the defect of art and skill is patched over only by custom, or the enticement of words, or greed for profit, or that tyrant, Custom, which is a stumbling block to many praiseworthy things.

### On Scarification.

Just as with bloodletting, so also in <term>scarification</term><note>A procedure involving making small, shallow cuts in the skin, often used in conjunction with cupping to draw out blood or "vitiated" fluids.</note> certain customs and rites have been introduced by the <term>Bath-keepers</term><note>original: "Balneatoribus"; in the Renaissance, bath-house attendants often performed minor surgical tasks like cupping, scarification, and bloodletting.</note>. For to say it in one word, scarification certainly has neither "sour nor sweet" in it, except that it boasts of custom alone. But this must be challenged first: they are accustomed to say, "here is a great abundance of blood: therefore it must be taken away and extracted." They add: that there is a flow <note>original: "fluxionem"; a pathological movement of humors to a specific part of the body.</note> into the eyes, into the ears, into the dentes: which, unless removed by scarification, will allow no rest or peace. They claim scarification benefits all members and renews one's age, making it easy. Which certainly, if they were true, would deservedly be numbered among good things.

<margin>
Blood is in the flesh in its proper weight.
</margin>
First, blood is born in the flesh according to its own weight, and the flesh is not deprived of it as long as it is healthy. If you take blood away, the flesh attracts its proper weight back again. You, therefore, are not slightly opposing nature. For what she attracts as her proper weight, you extract.

<margin>
The harms of scarification.
</margin>
Now let us see which side defends a more just cause. If you take away Nature’s weight and intercept her purpose, then through a strong attraction you create a certain flowing stream and extract watery blood, similar to the pus extracted from ulcers. You are moving this material, no doubt. Thus, from genuine blood, you come to "flows" [fluxes], as you call them: nor do you consider that Nature herself, if she contains anything evil or fluid, seeks her own <term>Emunctory</term><note>An organ or canal that carries off waste or secretions from the body.</note>. While you struggle with your cupping glasses, you do nothing else but hunt for money, which is characteristic of your "art." You yourselves should estimate how grave it is to struggle with that attraction of the root, which is the origin of things. He who advises this traction knows neither the measure of Nature, nor her motion, nor her vices, nor her needs; he boasts of mere custom, devised not by Physicians, but by imposters born for inventing these arts.

Is that medicine honest and praiseworthy which, while it prepares to remove "flows," repeatedly attracts new and heavier ones? To whom could it seem honest? How could it be called good? They say, to be sure: "Unless I scarify, I feel no peace in this or that place," etc. But does scarification become Medicine because of this saying? Away with these Doctors! How much "art" is in this that you boast of? Where did you learn it? Or why do you hide it, lest you lose it? Which seems better to you: to remove that "flow" through its own <term>Arcanum</term><note>In Paracelsian medicine, the "Arcanum" is the secret, essential healing power of a substance that acts directly on the disease, rather than just balancing humors.</note>, or through scarification?

<margin>
Flows are to be removed through secret remedies.
</margin>
Through an Arcanum, I believe. Since you are ignorant of this, what else do you do but repeat scarification again and again?

Is it a good and useful thing because it lightens the body? Cut off your hands and feet, and you will be lighter by several pounds. Just as much as this method of lightening does not please you, so much it does not please your nature—that you could not bear that little bit of blood, but say you abound in blood that must be evacuated. If you had never even begun scarification, who would have given you occasion to complain about this abundance or lack of blood? You are forging an evil for yourself.

### On Scarification against Diseases.

Since there are some diseases whose outcome is useful and good by reason of soothing rather than curing? If the soothing suggests scarification no differently than in the end—with a multiplication of those pains and diseases—then it is a true and genuine art to know here that the advice for scarification is nothing else than a delay of the gallows <note>original: "suspendij dilatio"; a metaphor for a temporary reprieve that does not prevent an inevitable bad end.</note>. Therefore, it is not Medicine at all, but destruction, which those Physicians nevertheless take as praise. Acquiescing to any kind of soothing, they leap over the deeper sanctuaries of the art itself and willingly dwell in desperation.

### Morphea:

Of this kind of disease is Morphea <note>A skin condition characterized by painless, discolored patches; historically sometimes confused with forms of leprosy or other dermatological issues.</note>, in which scarification, etc., is useful—not regarding a cure, but for appearance and a brief delay. However, it is the duty of any Physician to heal toward a cure, not toward the delay of the gallows, as Jurists [lawyers] do.

<margin>
It is the Physician's job to cure the disease, not to prolong it.
</margin>
You ought to be Physicians, not Jurists: nor should you operate like them, but proceed from the very foundation. That is, the cure for Morphea is completed without scarification. There is no other reason for scarification than if from some swollen...

...from someone whose tumor weighs a hundred pounds, you might draw ten pounds today, yet tomorrow he receives that same weight back again. Indeed, what does scarification <note>The practice of making superficial incisions in the skin, often used in conjunction with cupping.</note> in Morphea <note>A term used historically to describe skin discolorations, often associated with leprosy or localized scleroderma.</note> provide, other than increasing the disease itself and piling on new evils? Furthermore, Morphea is not produced from that blood which is drawn out by scarifying; rather, the disease has another place and seat where it ought to be sought. In such a case, certainly no one suggests scarification except one who is ignorant of the disease. For such a man, this one thing is enough: to fleece money from the credulous by pretending to offer relief. The medicine for Morphea is an <term>Arcanum</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, an "Arcanum" is the "secret" or essential healing power of a substance, a highly concentrated spiritual or chemical essence.</note> existing in the blood: and the arcanum acts upon the blood. And because it is an arcanum for the blood, it is therefore an arcanum for Morphea. Its medicine, therefore, is placed in this, not in scarifying.

<margin>The medicine for Morphea is an Arcanum.</margin>
The reason I repudiate scarification is this: I see that it flows from the ignorance of Physicians. For they have no clear understanding of what disease it is they are treating. They decree poison while meanwhile boasting of nothing but honey and sugar. Should such wickedness be tolerated in them? Or is it not an evident crime that, having despised and neglected the arcana, they thrust forward counsels and remedies so bloody and butchery? Therefore, scarification must be abolished, and the Arcanum must be substituted in its place. This is the true method of medicine. Nor should you ever apply scarification when you could apply the Arcanum itself.

## Scabies, Prurigo.

**But** furthermore, the "Doctor Bath-keeper" <note>original: "Doctor Balneator"—a derogatory reference to physicians who relied on the simple methods of bath-house attendants.</note> has adapted this cleverness from the teaching of Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose works were central to traditional medieval medicine, often criticized by Paracelsus.</note> to suit the profits of his own kitchen, pretending that scarification works for scabies and itching. By this act, they remind me of those "Baths of Mary" <note>likely a satirical reference to different types of medicinal baths or the "bain-marie" apparatus.</note>, one of which works for flies, another for gnats, and a third for hornets. For there is no other logic to this habitual scarification. He who wishes to give counsel for scabies will by no means intend scarification, but will handle arcana. For there is no more reason for scarification than if someone were to tear a scab from the head today, only for a new scab to be reborn in the bleeding wound tomorrow. In the same way, scarification draws blood only to generate a future scab. Let this be a warning to you, so that you do not rashly follow counsels of that sort. For if you dare to obey them, they know well how to "shave" your money away. The same thing happens here as happens in recommending thermal baths. For any Physician who lacks skill commands that the baths be visited. There is no other cause for these counsels except that the sick should die in the baths—which is indeed more "honorable" than dying at home. Thus, the blame is always pinned on others, never on the Physician.

## Dropsy.

<margin>Dropsy is cured by arcana, not scarification.</margin>
**In** this way, occasions for scarifying are also taken from swelling diseases, among which number is dropsy <note>original: "hydrops"—an old term for edema or the swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note>. How great a madness this is can easily be gathered. For it is common knowledge that arcana, not scarification, cure dropsy. In such cases, scarification is useless. For who, I ask, would say anything other than that the medicine for dropsy is not in cupping glasses—by which that which is drawn out is later poured back more abundantly and reborn more stubbornly.

---

<margin>Menstruation.</margin>
**So** also in women’s diseases, they seek many remedies from scarification. If there is anything in that blood that is less than good, it does not exit by this path. Furthermore, that blood is not the blood that manifests as the disease. In truth, the disease lies in another place, which scarification can by no means reach. How then does your puncture help? Moreover, you betray your own boorishness while you look for the disease where it is not, and extract that which is not sick. From this it is abundantly clear that you either know nothing or understand nothing. Meanwhile, it is well for you that you studiously take care in all things lest your stupidity become known. For if the peasants sensed your deceit, they would keep their own skin whole, and with a driven blade, they would shear your own hide.

<margin>Menstruation is not cured by scarification.</margin>
## CONCLUSION.

**Concerning** scarification, therefore, hold this: that it is a mere trap and imposture presented to the incautious common folk. For every counsel regarding scarification is rash and foreign to the foundation of Medicine. Meanwhile, for you "little Doctors," it is not enough for praise (as you think) if you pretend you have "done what you could." For what is this "utmost effort" to the benefit of others? First, learn what is best. Then, perform the same, not according to your opinion, but according to the art. For your fantasy is worth nothing. It has pleased me to advise you of all these things briefly here, so that you might finally abandon this evil custom. For even the peasants know this custom; meanwhile, they are ignorant of the arcana, which they seek from you. It is fitting that these things be understood by you. If you do otherwise, you are by no means Physicians, but etc. <note>The author leaves the insult to the reader's imagination.</note> So, be off with your "arts."

->THE END.<-

# SCHEDULE.
### On Purgations in the Diminution of Blood.

**I** must make mention of the custom observed by Physicians in purging, which they themselves preach as useful and healthy: namely, that purging should be done first, and afterwards phlebotomy <note>The surgical opening of a vein to draw blood.</note> should be instituted. For they say these things are good.

To us, however, the contrary seems true: namely, that this process is by no means good. They call "good" that which is not good. Meanwhile, they prove nothing except through the "written letter" <note>i.e., by quoting old books rather than observing nature.</note>. That it is not good, gather as follows.

Purging must first be understood in this way: Why is the diminution of blood instituted? It is done so that it may force a path through the "heavens" <note>Refers to the internal "microcosmic" atmosphere of the body.</note> to the exit—that is, to expel the "wind" of the blood.

Now, if the cause of the exit is the wind of the blood—not the matter, not the body, not the substance—what will purging do? For purging is only owed to the body, the substance, and the matter: it does not expel wind, but generates winds. What use, then, is purging? It is poison.

If, therefore, it carries away the substance of the blood (as they say), what purpose does phlebotomy eventually serve? A shortcut for this should have been made by skilled Physicians. But purging is worthless. Therefore, it is necessary to follow with phlebotomy. You say, however, that purging disposes the blood for a more successful emission. # THEOPHRASTUS BOMBAST OF HOHENHEIM
## Hermit, Doctor of both Medicines. <note>Referring to both Medicine and Surgery, or perhaps earthly and spiritual medicine.</note>

# A LITTLE BOOK ON THE JUDGMENTS OF 
## URINES AND PULSES:

->Also<-

# ON PHYSIOGNOMY,
## AS MUCH AS IS NECESSARY
### for the Physician:

Lectured by Dr. Theophrastus in the year 1527 at Basel (while he was professing there by public salary to the greatest admiration of all) privately to his disciples during the Dog Days <note>The "Dog Days" (dies Caniculares) are the hottest weeks of summer, usually when universities were in recess; Paracelsus used this time for private instruction.</note>, and illustrated with types and annotations by the Author himself.

### Preface.

**S**ince some of my disciples have now often urged me, and indeed contended with prayers, that I should write a little book on the inspection of urine: in this, most honest listeners, I shall undertake that burden quite willingly and of my own accord, both to gratify you and to look out for posterity. And that leisure, which through the summer holidays is granted to be indulged not in letters, but otherwise in one's own inclination, I shall spend on this labor, so that we may pass no day "without a line" (as they say). Moreover, I wished to gratify you, partly so that I might earn the favor of those most studious of me by this service, and partly also that I might look out for the dexterity of your wits in many other matters. For who does not know how coldly the common crowd of Physicians has handled the judgment of urine until now? Aside from the fact that they fill pages with their innumerable dreams about humors and other trifles of that kind, they also miserably overwhelm the excellent minds of youths with the same, so much so that even a man's whole lifespan would not suffice for this part alone. Therefore, most studious listeners, it seemed best to distribute the method of urine in a certain fixed order, and as it is more succinct, so it is also more true: a fact which those comparing the old ways to ours will easily judge. I will, however, take it as a favor if the studious—should I use any word anywhere less accepted by other authors—remain persuaded that it was done so that I might more expressly delineate both the logic of colors, which is required in this place, and the property of things. Furthermore, if anything occurs that is more obscure than is right, my industry, however small, will not leave it unexplained. But to the matter itself.

---

### BOOK ONE.
## FIRST TRACTATE.
### CHAPTER I.
#### Definition and Division of Urine.

<margin>How many parts of urine.</margin>
**I** shall define urine, which is divided into three parts—namely, the exterior, the blood-related, and the mixed—as being nothing else than the salt separated from the ingested nourishment, and a certain neglect of the <term>Three Primes</term> <note>The Tria Prima: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed were the fundamental components of all matter.</note> by nature. This indeed uses these specific faculties of separating, concocting (or digesting), and expelling in each of the three principal organs. Therefore, the urine of each individual faculty of any organ indicates both the prosperous and the adverse health of a person. Furthermore, it receives its name from these: now "separated urine," now "digested urine"; and both its color and that equal measure of symmetry declare that it possesses the expulsive force correctly. In the next three chapters, I have also decided to speak about urine as an indicator of correct health, so that we may more easily detect the signs of adverse health in what follows.

### CHAPTER II.
#### Concerning the Urine which declares the condition of the stomach’s faculties.

<margin>Signs of good digestion of the stomach.</margin>
**T**he separating faculty of the stomach, which also holds the first place among the rest, is distinguished by the colors of the urine. For once the raw sulfur has been separated, a color or Tincture similar to Topaz, or rather reflecting the thickness of <term>Colophony</term> <note>A dark, translucent resin (rosin) obtained from pines.</note>, remains in the stomach; if the urine also reflects this in any way, we do not doubt that the separation in this part is just. But if either the colors of Salt or Mercury <note>In this context, colors representing the other two of the Three Primes, likely indicating chemical imbalances.</note> prevail in it, it is to be loathed. For the urine of a healthy man, by [only]...

...is tinted with sulfur: but for others, the reasoning will be different. Indeed, you will recognize the complete separation of the <term>Salt</term> <note>One of the "Three Primes" in Paracelsian medicine, representing the solid, earthy principle of a substance.</note> from this part both by the precisely formed sediment <note>Original: "hypostasi." In traditional uroscopy, this refers to the sediment that settles in the middle or bottom of the urine glass.</note> and by its color, which is halfway between dark and sky-blue. Regarding <term>Mercury</term> <note>The second "Prime," representing the volatile, soulful, or vaporous principle.</note>, it should be judged no differently; since by its own nature it is heavy and seeks the bottom, it nonetheless appears most similar in both substance and color to the topmost part of the urine, and therefore its separation is best.

<margin>Signs of digestion in the stomach.</margin>
The signs of digestion <note>Original: "Concoctio." The process by which the body "cooks" or matures food into nutrients.</note> are as follows. Urine that is transparent in substance and color indicates the digestion of <term>Sulfur</term> <note>The third "Prime," representing the combustible, fatty, or oily principle.</note>; however, a sediment of a sky-blue and clear color reflects the exact digestion of the <term>Salt</term>. In the same way, when those things contained at the bottom, the sediment, and the uppermost part of the urine are separated by a proper interval, you may judge the <term>Mercury</term> to be well-digested.

The expulsive faculty <note>The body's ability to rid itself of waste.</note> should then not be neglected; the quantity of urine along with the sediment demonstrates that this power has not been exceeded in any part. Specifically, it should maintain a balance: the sediment should occupy a third part of the urine in young people, but a fourth part in the elderly. If you find either of these diminished, it is a sign of poor health. From these signs, finally, you will judge the afflictions that can happen to the stomach.

### CHAPTER III.

*On Healthy Urine, in Relation to the Liver.*

<margin>Signs of a healthy liver temperament.</margin>
**Y**ou will detect a good condition of the liver by these marks: that the contents of the urine shine through as translucent, bright, and clear. That urine is especially praised which reflects rays of light poured into its center, demonstrating that the <term>Sulfur</term> has been optimally separated by the liver. In a similar way, a sediment that is distinct from the other parts and transmits light into the depths testifies to the <term>Salt</term> being separated in the liver. Furthermore, if what remains at the bottom is so clear that its rays appear through the very base of the glass, it denotes that the <term>Mercury</term> has been perfectly separated.

Digestion, or "boiling," is noted by these signs: the urine should not be of a thick color, so that even when shaken, it perpetually maintains a clearer appearance, which provides a sign of digested <term>Sulfur</term>. Likewise, a sediment that is not dissolved by shaking portends the same for the <term>Salt</term>. Furthermore, that which resides fixed at the bottom, not broken into tiny parts, signifies that the <term>Mercury</term> is excellently digested. Additionally, when the three things contained in the urine are present together, excellently arranged in order and position, they show that nothing is lacking in these three faculties.

### CHAPTER IV.

*On Urine, Declaring the Condition of the Kidneys.*

<margin>Signs of the kidneys from urine.</margin>
**W**hen the color, the sediment, and the contents of the bottom are in their proper state and are not disturbed by any agitation, we can affirm that no faculty at all is failing in the kidneys. However, in this case, while the proper position and order are maintained, their quantity is somewhat reduced. Finally, by way of a summary, we must add that the signs of entirely healthy urine are a sediment that is both porous and not exceeding proper proportions, with a color that extends to both sides and is reflected in the upper part. Ultimately, whatever occurs that is unlike these things, I judge to be an ill omen. Let these things said regarding healthy urine suffice for the present.

### Annotations follow ON THE FIRST TREATISE.

**A**t what time and in what manner urine is to be collected and sent to the Physician: It should be noted that urine collected immediately after lunch is not suitable for judgment. For when nutrients first enter the stomach, they cast off a certain superfluous wateriness to the bladder, from which nothing can be judged. Nor is that which is ejected two or three hours later of much value; for then the <term>Liver</term> draws out its own wateriness: the same happens in the kidneys. But the fourth discharge that follows, however small it may be, must be collected. Similarly, the first urine ejected at night when going to bed is not valid; nor that which is emitted before the third hour; but that which follows afterward must be collected. This is the "true urine" from which a Physician can make any judgment. If someone does not urinate through the night, it is necessary to take that which is emitted in the morning; though it may be foamy and not very colorful (which must be excused), for it comes from both the true urine and the wateriness. It should also be noted that the urine which comes from the interior is more colored than that which comes at night. Likewise, those who are hungry—that is, those who are immediately affected by hunger—will be able to give urine sooner than others. These things concern the "exterior" urine.

If you wish to collect the "blood urine" <note>Original: "Cruoris vrinam." Paracelsus distinguishes between urine reflecting the digestive system (exterior) and urine reflecting the internal vital state (blood/cruor).</note>, it is necessary that you eat and drink nothing, or at most only dry bread or dry meat (such as roasted meat); then that urine is collected which comes after midnight, yet before the seventh hour. But if it happens that the patient is suffering from some acute disease and eats nothing but drinks heavily in the meantime, he must be advised to drink nothing for at least one night, so that the certain blood urine can be collected; otherwise, the judgment of the urine would be falsified. For even if you abstain from both food and drink, nature by itself daily gives its own blood-essence. For those things which are minerals in nature send out this blood-essence daily. Let these things said about collecting the two types of urine suffice. For it does not matter much at what time you collect the "permitted" urine, although it is advised to be collected in the same manner as the exterior urine.

### Notes on Chapters I. & II.

<margin>How many kinds of urine.</margin>
**I**t is necessary that you know beforehand that there are three types of urine: namely, the Exterior, the Blood, and the Mixed. First, therefore, regarding the Exterior urine.

Exterior urine arises from those things which we either eat or drink—that is, from nutrients. It indicates nothing other than what pertains to the stomach, liver, or kidneys. It is also called the urine of <term>Tartar</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to the stony or gravelly waste products that deposit in the body, causing stones, gout, or blockages.</note>, because it comes from Tartar that is coagulated, putrefied, or from an obstruction. It is of two kinds: healthy and unhealthy.

<margin>How many types of Tartar urine.</margin>
The healthy kind is present with the tint of <term>Sulfur</term>, though it is not always golden. For sometimes it appears yellow, and at other times somewhat paler.

The urine of <term>Tartar</term> is recognized by the "circle" <note>The ring or "crown" (corona) formed at the top of the urine in the glass.</note>. For if there is a single ring of a leaden color, it is a most certain sign of tartaric urines. This urine indicates the separation—specifically that which occurs in the three principal members—of the pure from the impure, and the digestion and expulsion. In this way, the three Primes—that is, the <term>Salts</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Sulfur</term>—can be distinguished in any urine. For the sediment denotes the quality of the <term>Salt</term>, the tint denotes the <term>Sulfur</term>, and the bottom denotes the <term>Mercury</term>.

It should be noted, however, that the urine of <term>Tartar</term> indicates no mineral sickness, but only that of <term>Tartar</term> pertaining to the stomach, liver, and kidneys.

If the sediment—that is, the tint of the salt—is of a sky-blue or azure color, it is a sign of good salt. Note, however, that it should be viewed against a wall, slightly in the shade.

<term>Mercury</term>—that is, the liquid of the nutrient—if it has been well separated, the urine will then be yellow, as the nature of each kind and region requires, not always golden.

The "blood urine" <note>Original: "vrina cruoris."</note> occurs when the ring is somewhat more colored and tends toward redness.

From this urine, the most serious diseases can be judged, especially those that come from Nature herself, such as the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>.

It should be noted that unless it is blood urine, nothing certain can be pronounced from the ring concerning a headache. For it indicates nothing else than the quality of the urine—that is, whether it is exterior. From the blood urine, those things pertaining to the liver or kidneys can also be judged, but nothing of the stomach and its...

and its ailments: likewise, nothing certain can be determined about pleurisy or dropsy <note>Original: "hydro-pisi." An old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> from the urine of the blood.

### On the quantity of urine.
**T**he quantity of urine is to be noted in relation to the expulsive power, and it must be observed according to the amount of drink and food consumed. If the urine is abundant and pale (certain things are lacking), it means that the <term>Archeus</term> <note>Original: "Archeitas." In Paracelsian medicine, the "Archeus" is the internal "alchemist" or vital force that directs digestion and health.</note>, that is, the specific nature of the stomach, is failing, and too much nourishment has been taken.
If the <term>sediment</term> <note>Original: "hypostasis." This refers to the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine glass.</note> is white, the urine is deceptive, as are all judgments made from it, if nothing else can be discerned within it.
Similarly, one should not judge much from "gluttonous" urine, since it lacks perfect digestion, separation, and expulsion. For it is like the equivocal urine of Archelaus, who urinated exactly according to what he ate and drank. This is called "permitted" urine, which is identified by two circles, and it occurs when the organs expel their waste, food, and drink; it is composed of both the exterior and the blood-related parts. This concludes the section on "permitted" urine.
It should be noted regarding the bottom of the exterior urine that it should always be somewhat thicker than the upper part, yet still clear and transparent.

### On Chapters III & IV.
**I**f the digestion of the liver is perfectly completed, the upper sediment does not touch the lower bottom.
If the sediment in the upper part is wide, there is a deficiency in the expulsive power. For the sediment ought to taper upward into a point, touching the upper regions with its peak.
Let the urine be of a golden color when a good separation has been performed in the kidneys; but if the bottoms cannot be well discerned, it is a sign of poor separation.
Truly, a good clarification of the bottom—and when there is a double reflection, to the hand, one paler than the other, yet both yellow—is a sign of good separation. Likewise when the urine is not foamy.
It should also be noted that urine is first correctly colored in the kidneys, and the more colored it is, approaching a golden hue, the better the sign of the separation performed. This must also be observed: foam in the exterior urine signifies <term>gout</term> <note>Original: "podagram." A painful form of arthritis often associated at the time with rich diets.</note> absolutely, and nothing else.

### On the urine of ages and sexes.
**T**he urines of young women are always more manageable <note>Original: "habiliores." Likely meaning easier to read or more consistent for diagnosis.</note> than those of young men.
Let the sediment be longer, somewhat smaller, and altogether thinner; that of young men is always thicker.
The urine of women shows a small sediment at the bottom, although to those not paying close attention it may seem continuous with the upper part; the <term>womb</term> <note>Original: "matrix."</note> gives this its own character, yielding a very tiny but distinct sediment, which is not present in the urine of men; this is a sign of a healthy and fertile woman. However, when <term>menstruation</term> <note>Original: "Menstruo."</note> ceases, this sediment disappears, and it is a sign of a formerly fertile woman, although afterward she may always feel heaviness and fatigue; their sediment tends toward whiteness, and around the glass it appears leaden, like a circle, even though the women are nonetheless healthy; it is otherwise in men. For there, the urine should remain the same, except in the very elderly, where the colors also change.
If the tint of the <term>Sulfur</term> <note>One of the Three Primes, representing the oily or combustible principle.</note> becomes paler, the sediment also becomes smaller day by day, which should be attributed to their weakness, not merely to old age.
If you divide the urine into four parts, three parts belong to the young, and the fourth to the elderly, etc.
But, to conclude at once: the most certain sign of perfectly healthy urine is when it is vigorously stirred and moved by the physician, and the foam caused by the motion immediately vanishes, with the sediment standing properly in the middle and the bottom being well-disposed.
In the urine of women, when moved, small bubbles also form between those two small sediments. And this is the most certain sign of female urine. Let these things be said regarding healthy urine.

# SECOND TREATISE ON THE
# JUDGMENTS OF URINES,
### which is about unhealthy urine
### of the exterior Tartar and Ruby.

### Treatise II.
### CHAPTER I.

### *On the division of unhealthy urine and its sub-*
### *divisions, namely Tartar, Ruby,*
### *Alkalita, Scatea, Tremula, Faecula,*
### *and Formula.*

<margin>It is the physician's duty to foresee the future.</margin>
**N**ot without reason did Hippocrates judge that prudence and the knowledge of future events were necessary for a physician. Since it belongs only to the physician—one who is indeed prudent and practiced—to know the nature and parts of a man, and his health both in prosperity and in adversity. However, since some of these things are located in the deep hiding places of the body and can only be discerned through excrements, it is my intention to pursue them here in style and order. First, however, we deal with the urines that hold the marks of the principal organs in ill health—that is, the stomach, the liver, and the kidneys. For some are of <term>Tartar</term>, others of <term>Nutriment</term>.

<margin>Urine which indicates adverse health.</margin>
That which is of Tartar is divided strictly into three parts. For I think one part should be ascribed to "congealed" things, and that sort which are contained only in the members destined for digestion; this is called <term>Alkalita</term>, because the judgments of <term>Tartar</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to the stony or gravel-like deposits formed from metabolic waste, named after the crust left by wine in a barrel.</note> depend exactly upon it.

<margin>The threefold urine of Tartar.</margin>
Another, moreover, shows the putrefaction of Tartar, by which those members are affected, and it is called <term>Scatea</term>. For this brings the judgment of both universal putrefaction and of the Alkalita.

<margin>What is Alkalita urine. What is Scatea urine. What is Tremulous urine.</margin>
The third is <term>Tremulous</term>, and this predicts to the wise physician both the obstructions and the diseases born from them in the aforementioned parts.

<margin>The manifold Rubine urine.</margin>
That which is from the <term>Ruby</term> <note>Original: "Rubino." Refers to the "ruby" or vital red essence of the nourishment and blood.</note>, that is, from the nourishment which is separated from those things we take in, is likewise twofold.
One is called <term>Faecula</term>, from dregs <note>Original: "faecibus."</note>, and it occurs when the urine is corrupted or broken—a sign of nourishment when it lies in the liver as it should, yet is not attracted by the limbs: for it lacks the attractive power.
The other is called <term>Formula</term>, from "distributed form," and it occurs when the urine exits with its own proper color, such as an ochre color (that is, the color of the body) or red—a sign of the Ruby exiting together with the urine.

->Annotations on the first Chapter.<-

<margin>The urine of a sick person is fourfold. What Tartar is.</margin>
The urine of an unhealthy man is twofold: of <term>Tartar</term> <note>Original: "Tartari." In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to metabolic waste that hardens into "stones" or "gravel" within the body, much like the deposits in a wine barrel.</note> and of <term>Ruby</term> <note>Original: "Rubini." This refers to the portion of the urine derived from the blood and nutrients.</note>, that is, of the nourishment which is separated from those things we have consumed, namely from the stool and the urine.

Whatever is generated from that which is not "Ruby" is called Tartar. The urine of Tartar indicates all its own ailments, or those flowing from it, such as the stone, the <term>calculus</term> <note>Small stony mass.</note>, and sand.

In short, it indicates all <term>congelations</term> <note>Hardening or solidification of fluids into solids.</note> in the three principal organs. And it is threefold: a certain type is called <term>Alcolita</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for specific urinary sediments, often appearing as fibrous or "lint-like" material.</note>, which consists of excrement—and it is nothing other than excrement—the sign of which is "alcohol," that is, Tartar resolved into minute parts, which is a false dissolution, and it happens in many ways.

For sometimes white granules come out with the urine; sometimes a <term>vine-like formation</term> <note>Original: "vinea." Likely referring to branching, tendril-like patterns in the sediment.</note> is seen in the urine; sometimes frost, as can be seen in the <term>urinals</term> <note>Original: "matulis." The glass flasks used to inspect urine.</note> when sand lies at the bottom.

Truly, if this <term>alcola</term> <note>The sediment itself.</note> is hidden, a whitening lint is seen in the urine, like plucked wool; sometimes it passes into the liquid and gives a certain thickness at the bottom, which is the worst of all, like a certain <term>bolar</term> <note>Clay-like.</note> or mucilaginous slime, and it is a certain sign of a stone in the bladder or a calculus. Likewise, when you allow the urine to stand for six or seven hours in the flask until it is cooled, you see how it attaches itself to the flask; this is the frosty alcohol or the vine-like formation which can be seen in the urinal.

<margin>What "scatea" urine is.</margin>
The second species of Tartaric urine is called <term>Scatea</term>, a name taken from the stench; it is indicative of all putrefactions arising from Tartar, and its sign is "Scatea," that is, the stench of the urine. From this, the putrefactions of the three principal organs are judged, as well as the diseases generated from that putrefaction. The taste also pertains to the sign of *scatea*; if it is salty or sharp, then it has its own signs as well.

<margin>What "tremula" urine is.</margin>
The third type they call <term>Tremula</term> <note>Trembling or quivering urine.</note>; this is when the urine is placed on a table or another immovable place, and yet the urine moves of its own accord, appearing to boil as it rises and falls. This is a sign of <term>obstructions</term> <note>Original: "oppilationū." Blockages in the "vessels" or organs.</note> and ailments arising from those indications. The species of Ruby are clear from the text. Likewise, it should be noted that if the urine appears very milky and does not have its proper parts, it is a sign of resolved Tartar, and it exits with great pain.

<margin>What "rubinea" urine is.</margin>

->## CHAPTER II.<-

->On the judgments and signs of the Alcolita, the parts of which the following table will declare.<-

**The Alcolita either designates Tartar:**
* **Of the Stomach: <term>Hypostasis</term>** <note>Sediment that stays in the middle or floats; here defined specifically by location.</note> { Appetite / Pressure / Burning / Piercing pain } -> **Signifies.**
* **Of the Liver: <term>Divulsions</term>** <note>Original: "Diuulsiones." Cloud-like sediments that appear torn or fragmented.</note> { Vehement thirst / Pressure / "Hailstones" <note>Hard, granular deposits.</note> } -> **Signifies.**
* **Of the Kidneys: <term>Sediment</term>** { Urine-sands / Frost / Calculus } -> **Signifies.**

->Annotations on this Diagram.<-

First, it should be noted that all ailments indicated by the Alcolita must belong either to the stomach, the liver, or the kidneys. *Hypostasis* always indicates Tartar in the stomach. *Divulsion* indicates it in the liver. *Sediment* indicates it in the kidneys.

<margin>What "divulsion" urine is. What "sediment" urine is. What "hypostasis" is.</margin>
*Divulsion* is when the sediment of the urine is torn apart here and there, like a cloud scattered in different directions.

*Sediment* belongs to the bottom, and is like a mist, or like a thick cloud residing at the bottom.

If the *Hypostasis* belongs to the Alcolita, it is porous and lies in one place and not in another; in those pores or holes lies the "Alcola," that is, the lint-like fibers. This is a sign of Tartar in the stomach, and it can be a judgment of stomach burning, appetite <note>Often meaning a "false" or morbid hunger.</note>, or pressure in the <term>pit of the stomach</term> <note>Original: "furcula pectorali." Literally the "little fork of the chest," referring to the xiphoid process area.</note>, which things ought to be predicted to the sick.

But if the *hypostasis* is red, it is a sign of a vehement disease and pain in the stomach. If it falls in pieces and is torn and full of holes, it is a sign of Tartar in the liver; hence "compunctions," that is, pains in the right side. If that *divulsion* is red, it is a sign of a vehement disease; thirst is always present, and they are cold in the hands. If the *divulsion* resides toward the bottom, it signifies Tartar in the lower regions of the liver, beneath the ribs, downwards.

When the *sediment* resides at the bottom, it then predicts Tartar in the kidneys. If this also is red, the disease is more vehement. Likewise, if the urine with the sediment is red, it is a sign of frost or vine-like formations in the kidneys; they have pain in the thickness of the upper foot <note>Possibly the instep or ankle area.</note> or in the hip.

However, if sand comes out with the sediment, judge it to be pressure in the pit of the stomach. For say that the stomach is not healthy. But if it reflects hailstones or frost, all is in the kidneys, and it is the generation of "red marble" according to the <term>spagyrists</term> <note>Alchemical physicians who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances.</note>.

But, so that these things may be known more clearly, we will combine some of them. For instance, when the urine is white and contains sand, it indicates a stone in the bladder.

Truly, a perforated *hypostasis*, in which "alcola" (that is, lint) is contained, signifies the drying of the bones.

A *divulsion* of the *hypostasis*, in which there are both holes and "alcola," signifies pain of the right side. If these are red, it signifies the vehemence of the disease, which either thirst or coldness of the hands accompanies.

The *hypostasis* which seeks the bottom is an indication of pain that is between the Liver and the Kidneys.

If something dense lies at the bottom, it indicates a disease of the kidneys. If it is red, it signifies a more vehement one. In the pit of the stomach, it betrays malignancy and a corrupted stomach.

->On the form of Alcola in particular, the accidents from the same, and the signs.<-

->Diagram.<-

**ALCOLA**

**I. Threefold Form.**
* **Resolved** { White, milky like the whey of milk, watery; signifies a calculus made of small stones. / Generation toward a stone occurs. / Red, reddish, lemon-colored, saffron-colored, tinted; signifies sand and "marble."
* **Sandy** { White like flour, bran-like; signifies a calculus of small stones with <term>bole</term> <note>A type of medicinal clay or earthy pigment.</note>. / Red, lemon-colored; signifies the form and matter as it appears.
* **Mucilaginous**, bituminous, viscous; signifying Tartar not well-confected, and many other things.

**II. Accidents** <note>Symptoms or secondary occurrences.</note>
* **Blood**: signifies injury from Tartar in another part.
* **Pus**: ulceration according to the location.
* **Sanies** <note>A thin, greenish-red discharge of blood and pus.</note>: putrefaction according to the location.
* **Restriction**: a blockage of the blood.

**III. Signs**
* **External**: Involuntary emission; signifies the ingress of Tartar.
* **Dripping burning**: signifies the sharpness of the Tartar.
* **From experience** { Spirit / Salt. } **Urine**: signifies an impossible cure, when the prior signs (such as mucilage) concur.

<header>ON THE JUDGMENTS OF URINES.</header>

# Annotations on this Type.

When the dissolved form of **Alcolae** <note>A Paracelsian term for certain fatty or filmy sediments in urine.</note> is entirely hidden, and does not emit any of its earlier parts or signs, then <term>Tartar</term> <note>Metabolic waste that hardens into "stones."</note> is being dissolved and is separated from the urine distinctly; and when it is distinct, it signifies something above the rest.

Take the urine from the urinal, set it aside for four or six hours, then you will see that it thickens and becomes sticky. If sandy urine has a sediment, if there are any "hailstones" <note>Original: "grandinum," referring to larger, hard granules or small stones.</note> to come, they will cling to the sides. If white sand-granules appear with white urine, it is a sign of a stone in the bladder.

"Mucilaginous" urine—when mucilage is found in the urine—sometimes comes from the sperm. If it is white, it is a sign of a severe stone. But if it is golden, it can be from the sperm. Likewise, if there is sand with the mucilage, it indicates many stones; although that mucus is not itself a stone, it is nonetheless an indication of a stone.

If there is blood with the urine—that is, if it tints it, such as when urine is poured into water—it is a sign that <term>Tartar</term> has opened some vein in the kidneys, and then it exits without pain. Sometimes it heals again by itself, and sometimes it opens again. But if it comes out in small pieces, it is a sign of coagulated blood, which sometimes kills a man.

It should be noted here, outside the usual order, that when blood is poured into water, one must observe carefully how and how long it stands, and when mucus collects and when it does not. For sometimes mucus comes out, or it forms like pieces.

Pus is a discharge which has a foul odor; it is thicker, however, more viscous, and more tenacious than <term>sanies</term> <note>A thinner, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer.</note>.

<margin>What sanies is.</margin>
Sanies is that which exits daily from a discharge or an ulcer. If the pus is red, know that the diseases are still in the kidneys; but if it is white, then it is in the bladder. Sanies occurs when the urine putrefies within itself; it lies in the urine like pus, dense and clear.

"Restriction" is when the urine is held back and blocked; then one must be made to sweat.

Involuntary emission is when someone sometimes passes urine and does not feel the sign of <term>Tartar</term> penetrating through the pores, nor does it enter the bladder by the right and proper way (otherwise, emission happens when <term>Tartar</term> is dissolved and passes through the pores). "Guttated burning" <note>Original: "Ardor guttatus," known as strangury: painful urination drop-by-drop.</note> is when one urinates drop by drop, a sign of <term>Tartar</term>. If it is white, it tends toward a stone; if red, toward "hailstones."

The spirit of the urine is sometimes beautiful, and they can find nothing in it, yet the patient seems to suffer from a stone; this experiment must then be used: The urine is to be distilled. Put what comes from the distillation into cold water; if it casts down atoms to the bottom, like those of such a stone, and they quickly rise again in the glass, it is a certain sign of the "Alcohol of Tartar." (The spirit of the urine is extracted by distillation; place it moreover in the cold, and it produces a "stiria" <note>An icicle-like or crystalline formation.</note> similar to such a stone).

The salt of the urine, when the urine stands for two or three days, deposits <term>Tartar</term> (as nitre does) all around the urinal—sometimes white, sometimes the color of ochre, sometimes red everywhere in the urinal. These two signs are of an incurable case, unless sand, or mucilage, or other aforementioned signs are added.

# Annotations on the same Types.

<margin>Putrefaction of urine is twofold.</margin>
It should be noted that there is a double foulness in urine; so too there is a double putrefaction of urine: of the body, and of the nourishment.

If it is a putrefaction of the nourishment, then the urine putrefies alone; it comes out white and smells foul. But if it has other colors, then the body itself is putrefying, and the urine smells foul.

If it is pale, but not milky, then it is a putrefaction of the stomach; the breath smells foul. If it is red and smells foul, it is a putrefaction of the liver.

If saffron-colored, of the kidneys.

If turbid—that is, having no proper color—then there is putrefaction in all three members.

As for what pertains to the odors, the Physician must observe through experience.

If it comes from Sulphur, then let it be treated with frankincense, mastic, and myrrh, as in the *Iliad* <note>Likely a reference to a specific medical text or a metaphor for internal "warfare," though possibly referring to Homeric cleansing rites.</note>.

If from Mercury, let it be treated with distilled turpentine, or with the "Oil of the Philosophers," or with centaury. If it smells foul from Salts, let the cure be made with vitriols. Urine which smells like dung indicates a sulphurous putrefaction.

To better understand the foul odors, note: Of Pitch (it is like when shoemaker's pitch is burned over a coal). Of Oil (when you cast it into the fire, you will have the foul odor). All three odors of Mercury tend toward leprosy; they signify a strong Mercurial putrefaction. "Ireos" is a species of Lily.

Of Flesh (like meat broth). Of Herbs (as when hay is brought in, or when you approach the meadows, etc.).

But if one of the colors mentioned above is also present, it is a bad sign of putrefaction. Of Raw Salt (when you cast it upon a fresh glowing coal, you will notice the odor of the smoke). Of Arsenic (do the same as with the salt; for it is almost the flavor of onions). Of Spirits (such as when you cast vitriol into the fire, notice the foul odor of the smoke, and you will have the foul odor of spirits). This concludes Scatean urine.

->FIRST BOOK<-

### A Brief Note on the Preceding Diagram.

<margin>What urine contains.</margin>
**A** blockage of the stomach occurs when the pathway between the liver and the stomach is obstructed; a blockage also occurs in the mesenteric veins <note>The vessels that transport nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note> even without "contents"—that is, the urine remains like pure distilled water. For every urine ought to contain something significant, such as a suspension <note>original: "hypostasin," a cloud-like sediment</note>, the fluid body, or a settled sediment.

Transparent urine, if it is pale, signifies a blockage of the stomach.

If it is red, it signifies the liver; if saffron-colored, the kidneys. But given a sediment at the bottom, it is an indication of color.

Pale urine with foam is a sign of a feverish fit <note>original: "paroxysmi febrilis"</note>.

Red urine with foam also signifies a fever. However, if the ring <note>The "corona" or top layer in the urine glass.</note> is clear and lacks foam, it most often signifies the plague. If it is turbid with foam and lacks contents, it signifies pleurisy.

Therefore, since the "urine of nourishment" <note>Urine resulting from the first stage of digestion.</note> cannot generally indicate all diseases, it has seemed best to describe the "urine of the blood" <note>original: "cruoris urinam." In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to urine influenced by the deeper metabolic processes of the blood and internal minerals.</note> here in the second place.

Red urine lacking contents and which is thick is a sign of death. For when nature wishes to die, she ceases to digest.

When urine begins to spoil, the physician then has two indications: one from when it was whole, and another from when it is already spoiling.

When urine spoils within five or six hours, health is no longer present, and this is usually followed by consumption or a wasting fever <note>original: "phthisis, Ethica."</note>.

The specific locations of disease cannot be judged in such urine unless "sand" <note>Metabolic precipitates or grit.</note> should also appear.

"Fleshy" urine must be similar to meat, not a stew, and it possesses the color of flesh. This is usually followed by dysentery or diarrhea.

Let these things be said regarding the exterior urine.

# THE SECOND BOOK ON THE JUDGMENTS OF URINES.

## CHAPTER I. or Diagram.

### *On the urine of the blood of minerals, and their colors.*

The urine of the blood is recognized by three things:
- **By Colors**, and this is on account of the specific limb or location.
- **By Substance**, on account of the nature of the minerals.
- **By Contents**, on account of the symptoms and the quality of the disease.

**The color of the blood has three ranks, namely:**

**1. Of the individual limb, of which there are six colors:**
*   **Of the Brain** — White, yet not milky, and it has a glassy foam; from this, diseases of the head and brain are judged.
*   **Of the Lungs** — Reddish or liver-colored with foam; from this, things pertaining to the lungs.
*   **Of the Gall** — Yellow, bordering on white with foam of the same color; from this, things pertaining to the gallbladder.
*   **Of the Liver** — Of the same color but without foam; pertains to the liver.
*   **Of the Spleen** — Deeply purple, like the "Saffron of Mars" <note>original: "crocus Martis," a term for iron oxide (rust) used in alchemy and medicine.</note> with a little foam; pertains to the spleen.
*   **Of the Kidneys** — More transparent than those of the lungs, spleen, liver, and kidneys, but with a fatty film.

**2. Of a neighboring part, of which there are seven colors:**
*   **Of the Flesh, that is, the muscles** — Like the water used to wash raw meat.
*   **Of the Fat** — Pale with a fatty film on the surface.
*   **Of the Ligaments, Intestines, and Cartilage** — White with foam, more translucent than the foam of the brain; foam with a white ring. The color of transparent distilled water, and usually in the middle. Like lead with large bubbles.
*   **Of the Skin** — The same color as above but without foam; pertains to the skin.
*   **Of the Blood** — Brick-colored, thick at the bottom, clear at the top; it does not resemble any typical urine; sometimes blue, green, or even black.

**3. From the excrements, of which there are six:**
*   **Mucus** — White with mucus at the bottom.
*   **Sweat** — Thin with a wide, watery ring.
*   **Fugilis** — A yellow, waxy substance in the urine <note>A specific Paracelsian term for an earwax-like metabolic byproduct.</note>.
*   **Tears** — The color of the brain, and it has small bubbles.
*   **Dung** — Red with a little white foam.
*   **Urine** — Somewhat pale, which happens when it is held for a time, spoils, and loses its color.

# ON THE JUDGMENTS OF URINES.

->Notes on the Second Diagram.<-

<margin>The substance of urine is threefold.</margin>
The consistency <note>original: "substantia"</note> of urine is of three kinds: **Thick**, when one cannot see through the urine, regardless of its color (others define this as when light does not pass through it). **Clear** and **Transparent** when held near the hand, but not from a distance (others say the hand is visible through it). 

**Transparent**, which is entirely see-through (others say even bread can be seen through it). The "substance of urine" refers to the urine as it is in itself. **Distress** <note>original: "Angustiæ"</note> means nature is in a state of danger; the patient’s condition reflects how the physician operates in that moment.

**Regarding the Crisis:** that is, the patient dies on the same day the disease reaches its peak.
**Chronic:** that is, the ailment tends toward a long-term illness.
**3. Good:** for the patient is cured without any medicine.
**5. Deceptive:** resulting in a bad outcome.
**7. Interval:** that is, the crisis does not occur immediately, nor according to the stated Rule.

---

### CHAPTER III.
->On the Contents.<-

->**Diagram.**<-

<margin>The order of the contents is held in three parts.</margin>

*   **Salts:** (Alums, Vitriols, Common Salts, Feathery Salts) } **indicated by a bubble** 
*   **Mercurials:** (Liquids, Juices, Waters, Fixed substances) } **indicated by foam** } *three contents*
*   **Sulfur:** (White, Red, Essential) } **indicated by a ring** <note>The "ring" or "corona" refers to the colored band at the top of the urine in the glass.</note>

Everything in the urine that lies upon the surface—such as Foam, Bubbles, and the Ring—is called a "content." (Others say: Contents are those things which float in the urine; all other things belong to the substance and the suspension <note>original: "hypostasim," the cloud-like sediment</note>).

---

->Notes on the Third Diagram.<-

A **Bubble** in the urine is an indication that the disease arises from salts; judge such a disease to be caused by winds <note>original: "ventositates," likely meaning gas or bloating</note>, or the beginning of colic. If it is a woman’s urine, it portends a "suffocation of the womb" <note>An ancient term for various uterine or hysterical disorders.</note>.

If the bubble is colored differently: if **green**, it indicates the falling sickness <note>original: "morbum caducum," or epilepsy</note>. If **red**, it indicates a continuous fever or a burning fever <note>original: "Causonem"</note>.

If **saffron-colored**, it indicates jaundice. An **azure** bubble signifies leprosy.

When two or three bubbles rise together along with small bubbles, it denotes a defect of the head; it is a fixed disease and does not descend to other limbs. This is the difference between a Bubble and Foam.

If two or three bubbles are atop the urine but do not touch the glass, then it is a true bubble. Foam, however, clings everywhere, while a bubble remains floating on the urine.

In **Foam**, if the grains are very small (others say: very tiny blisters in white foam), it is a sign of paralysis (others say: they signify future paralysis); the smaller they are, the more certain the indication.

If these grains descend well below the ring into the urine, it is a sign of paralysis resulting from a fall, or a fall that has already occurred, provided the foam is white.

If the foam does not go away but remains on the urine for a long time, it is a defect of the lung caused by phlegm (others say: foam that does not vanish for four or five hours belongs to the lung).

If foam appears above the ring and produces yet another white ring inside itself, the foam is a sign of apoplexy <note>A sudden loss of consciousness, similar to a stroke.</note>.

If the foam has large bubbles, it is a sign of "plethora"—that is, a thick and full body—even if no illness is present.

If a bubble appears together with foam, it is a sign of wasting disease <note>original: "phthisis," usually tuberculosis</note>.

If it is colored with a yellow heat, it is the beginning of jaundice.

If the foam lies hollow and clings to the glass, but does not touch the ring, and the ring beneath it is black while the foam is white, it is a sign of death.

If the foam sinks to the bottom because of its weight and settles there, it denotes tremors of the heart or a "night-mare" <note>original: "incubum," a feeling of pressure on the chest during sleep</note>.

The **Ring** <note>The colored band at the top of the urine sample.</note> comes from sulfur.

If a small "trough" or depression is seen in the ring, it denotes a chronic disease.

If this occurs in women, it is a sign of pregnancy or a "uterine mole" <note>A non-viable mass or growth in the uterus.</note>.

If the ring is colored with various hues like a rainbow, it is a sign of the worst kind of epilepsy.

If the ring falls below the urine and becomes a distinct circle, it is especially a sign of "leonine" leprosy <note>A severe form of leprosy that causes facial features to resemble a lion's.</note>. If the ring is large and joined with another, and small grains lie in the middle of the ring, it is a sign of apoplexy.

If the outer ring is green, it is a sign of fatal jaundice. These things are said concerning the accidental ring. Likewise, in "suffocation of the womb," it is also fatal.

If it is celestial or azure in color, as happens very often, it pertains only to women; it is then a sign of putrefaction in the womb, which tends toward leprosy.

A halved ring signifies paralysis on one side of the body.

If the ring, the foam, and the bubble are all the same color, it demonstrates an incurable disease and a continuous chronic illness. Likewise, in healthy and good urine, if these same three adhere to one another and hang together, it means the patient feels no heat in the internal organs or around the chest, even if the urine comes out colored.

A very thick ring, especially if the urine itself is thicker and red or brick-colored, denotes "lethargy" <note>A state of profound drowsiness or unconsciousness</note> already present or coming soon.

But if the ring is clear and the urine is thicker than the ring, it signifies dropsy <note>original: "hydropisin," or swelling from fluid retention</note>.

If all the contents lie above the urine and immediately vanish and dissolve into a watery ring and grow larger, it is a sign of true "hyposarca" <note>A type of dropsy where fluid collects under the skin.</note>.

When a foamy ring appears three finger-widths back from the glass, it signifies pregnancy in women.

If that ring is "impregnated" <note>likely meaning clouded or heavy</note>, it is a sign of a difficult birth and a defect in the womb. (Others say: A ring in the "nose of the thigh" <note>likely a specific location in the urinal</note> is a sign of pregnancy. And if it does not have its natural color, it signifies a weak fetus.) A celestial-colored bubble formed in the middle of the urine is a sign of present leprosy, and sometimes also "alopecia" <note>mange or hair loss</note>.

Those who suffer from St. Vitus' Dance <note>original: "morbo S. Viti," a disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements.</note> have urine that is a beautiful red, and above they have a double ring, purple and yellow—one above and another below—and this lasts as long as the fit continues.

In short, whatever is most severe among diseases is drawn out from the contents of the urine.

Let these things be said concerning the "urine of the blood," its accidents, and its contents.

# SECOND TREATISE: ON MIXED URINE, and its conditions, Pulse, and Physiognomy.

### *On the conditions of mixed urine, both intrinsic and extrinsic.*

### Diagram I.

<margin>Mixed urine <note>Urine that contains elements of both the "urine of nourishment" and "urine of the blood."</note> has four conditions.</margin>

**From its own condition, two:**
*   **In six colors** (Red, White, Green, Lemon-yellow, Black, Violet) — each of which has three types:
    *   Transparent <note>original: "Diaphanam"</note>
    *   Clear <note>original: "Lucidam"</note>
    *   Thick <note>original: "Spissam"</note>

    *   Clear, or otherwise shadowy
    *   Thick

**From an extrinsic condition, one:**
*   **In the pulse, by which four properties arise:**
    *   Of the external limbs.
    *   Of the sides.
    *   Of the neck.
    *   Of the temples.

    *   The eyes,

*   **In the "accidents" [symptoms], those things mentioned regarding Tartar** <note>In the medical theory of Paracelsus, "Tartar" refers to stony or gravel-like deposits formed in the body, like kidney stones or gouty deposits.</note> **with three external signs.**
    *   **From the Mouth, and these also from three sources: from**
        *   The air
        *   The speech
        *   The breath — *Each has its own signs.*
*   **In the proportions, of which there are four species.**
    *   Foam: an indication of an excess of fluids <term>plethora: an overabundance of blood or bodily humors</term> in the upper part of the body.
    *   A bubble: an indication of depletion <note>original: "inanitione"</note> in the upper part.
    *   A ring: an indication of the center, that is, the navel and around the hips.
    *   Urine [sediment]: of the womb and the hips <note>original: "Schiae," referring to sciatica or hip pain.</note>.

---

### *Commentaries on the same Diagram.*

**M**ixed urine is that which is mixed from both sources, as was also said before—namely, from the exterior fluid and from the blood <note>original: "cruoris"</note>. It has a double ring of different colors in the upper part. To this, the author attributes four conditions: colors, substance, accidents, and portions or parts. Regarding the substances, these indicate whether the patient's urination is significant or not, as with Tartar, or from *alcolita* <note>A Paracelsian term for the precipitate or dregs in urine</note>, or whether it is frothing or quivering—that is, the sediment, when it forms a bottom on its own.

**Red transparent urine** is that where the redness is see-through.
**Clear** is half-red, yet can still be transparent. **Thick** is a saturated, deep red. And the other colors are to be judged in the same way. **Green transparent urine** is a sign of pain in the spleen.

If there are shadows or "clouds" <note>Nebula: suspended particles in the urine</note>, it overcomes death <note>This likely suggests a fatal prognosis.</note>. Likewise, green urine is a sign of a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria.</note>.

But back to the red again. The species of red urine indicates great heat, and consequently a "hot" disease [fever or inflammation]. Next, one must note the nature of the substance and the portions. If the urine is shadowy/dark, it is a sign of health. If it has foam, it is a sign that the disease is present with a great "repletion" or overfullness.

**White** is the opposite, and signifies a "cold" disease. If it is transparent—that is, purely white—it is a sign of good urine and health. If it is clear, it is even healthier. But the healthiest of all is the thick white. It should also be noted that it is a certain sign of death when the urine inclines toward neither white nor red fully.

If it produces foam or a "cloud" atop the urine, it is the same sign [of death]. Most especially, dropsy <term>hydrops: swelling caused by excess fluid</term> and *hyposarca* <note>A form of dropsy where fluid collects under the skin</note> are judged from this urine.

**Lemon-yellow** <note>original: "Citrina"</note> urine, if it has a thick cloud, is a sign of death.
If it has foam or a bubble, it again points toward death from the upper parts of the body. If it has sediment, the patient dies from the kidneys. Or from the hips <note>original: "Schia"</note> in these cases. **Black** urine, if it has a cloud, leads to death; if it has no cloud, it is a sign of an abscess <note>original: "apostematis"</note> that is being expelled and passing away.

**Violet and transparent** urine leads to death if it belongs to a weak man; but if he is healthy, it tends toward leprosy.
**Clear**, that is, purple: if in acute diseases, death; if in chronic diseases, a sign of health.
If it is **thick**, regardless of the color, it is a sign of health, unless it tends toward leprosy. But if it has a cloud above the thick (that is, coarse) urine, it is a sign of health.
Likewise, concerning clear shadows, transparent ones, etc., they portend certain things.

If the **sediment** is white, then an excessive menstrual flow is present.
If it is red, there is a restriction or blockage of the same. If the sediment tends entirely to the bottom and is neither red nor white in a way that can be discerned, it is a sign of hip pain <note>Schia</note>. The same applies when the urine forms its own bottom or sediment.

Let these words on urines suffice. For the "accidents" are explained in the following sections. Now follow some notes on the pulses and medical Physiognomy.

## ON THE PULSES.

**I**t often happens that the urine appears to be that of health, yet in the meantime the patient is doing poorly. Therefore, other signs of health and death must be observed, such as the Pulse and Physiognomy. First, then, concerning the pulses. When the urine thus deceives, it is necessary that you also see the infirm person and take the pulse in four places to see if they agree.

For it is not enough to touch the pulse of the arms or the external limbs.
Let the pulse of the external limbs be touched first, such as the hands and feet; second, the neck; third, the sides; then under the armpits; and finally the temples.

If the pulses agree with one another at the same time, the matter is well; but if not, one must pay attention, as the following indications of the first figure or diagram declare.

## On the Pulses, that is, the movement of the soul.

The pulse has four virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent qualities or diagnostic categories of the pulse.</note>:
- **Of Tartar** <term>Tartar: In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to metabolic waste or stony deposits (like gout or stones) formed from the "salt" of food and drink.</term>
    - Globular
    - Thick
    - Constricted
    - Obscure
    - [Result:] **Hard.**

    - Subtle
    - [Result:] **Subtle.**

    - Equal
    - [Result:] **Medium.**

    - **Extrinsic** { of Heat } is a sign { **of Tartar.** / **of Mineral.** } according to the element.

->Annotations on the same Diagram.<-

**Of Tartar** (with this pulse, one must not despair in that disease. For it arises from Tartar. **Of the Mineral**) the pulse is subtle, so much so that it can scarcely be touched; it has a soft beat.

A sign of a mineral pulse is when cold water is poured over it, and the pulse stops for a little while; this is the best kind of pulse. **Of Disease**) When the pulse is hotter than the skin, it is a true and certain sign of a present disease, even if the physician feels otherwise. Or when the pulse gives off a certain heat to the fingers of the person touching it. A very sharp test to see whether the disease in the blood is also that hot: let a scrap of silk be moistened, especially in rose water; let it be placed over the pulse. If the disease is indeed that hot, you will see the cloth dry much faster over the pulse than in other places, even if the cloth was first well wrung out; it will then leave a mark or trace under the pulse where it has dried.

Likewise, when you press down with two fingers on the substance of the pulse after the joint, and then also lower down on the arm, and the pulse gives way, it is a sign of disease.

**Health** (which is to be judged not by touch alone, but also by color.

If the pulsing veins are well-colored, that is, appearing violet, it is a sign of a good and healthy pulse.

However, as soon as they lose color, it is a bad sign.

Likewise, when you have placed all four fingers upon it and press down strongly, yet it still touches [the fingers], it is healthy, and it does not become hotter than the skin is.

**Again, regarding the Tartaric pulse.**
**Globular**, that is, knotty. When it becomes soft during an acute disease, it is a sign of resolution <note>The "breaking" or ending of the crisis.</note>; then a bloodletting <note>original: "minutio"</note> should be performed. And when it becomes thick again, it tends once more toward health.

**Hard** when it is felt along its length, and it becomes entirely hard in one place and soft in another, it is a sign of a chronic disease.

Likewise, when the arteries are felt to be hard in the pulse, and it gives a hard touch, like globular and thick, it is a sign of a Tartaric pulse even in a healthy man; however, the "Tartar of the blood" is being diminished, and the blood becomes sandy after bloodletting.

**Thick** (that is, if it pulses more forcefully).

**Mineral-constricted**) when the elbow is placed in cold water: and afterward it nevertheless still beats, it is a sign of health. Likewise, if it stops, but the color remains. But if it loses both—that is, both the pulse and the color—it is a sign of death.

Likewise, when the arm is tied tightly above the elbow and is touched in two places, and it gives the same pulse, it is a sign of health. It should be noted that all pulses need to be in harmony with one another—that is, they must beat at the same time—or it leads to death. Likewise, when it is trembling or leaping; likewise, when you see the pulse beating and the arteries leaping in a healthy person, it is a good sign; in a sick person, it is deceptive.

Note this also: when the pulse tends toward death, it is strong in the temples, weaker in the neck, even weaker in the sides, and also more weak in the hands; then in the feet it is most loose, and then death is at hand.
" For man dies from the lower parts upward.

**The order of the pulse's weakening as it tends toward death.**

<margin>Man dies from the lower parts.</margin>

| Location | Pulse |
|-------|--------|
| Temples | Strongest |
| Neck | Stronger |
| Sides | Strong, yet weak |
| Hands | Weaker |
| Feet | Weakest, and death |

In all things generated from "the drop" <note>original: "gutta" - likely referring here to gouty or apoplectic conditions.</note>, such as apoplexy <note>Stroke or sudden loss of consciousness.</note>, the stronger the pulse is felt, the worse the condition. In these cases, the pulse of the neck must be noted; if it is globular and the "globules" are felt, they die. As long as it is flat, it is a good sign.

Likewise, when the pulse is felt in the neck, death is already in the hands.

In Phrenesy <note>Delirium or brain fever.</note>, Epilepsy, and Mania: if the pulse is felt regardless of the peak of the paroxysm having ended, it is a good sign and one of health; if it is separated, it is bad.

Likewise, when the pulse is felt in the neck during phrenesy and the sick person falls asleep, the disease is curable.

In "dissolved" diseases—that is, in Dysentery, Diarrhea, flux of the belly, etc.—if the pulse remains with the same touch and does not change, and even a single sign of death appears, it is already over. For the pulse remains until death, and sometimes for a quarter of an hour after death. For the pulse of the blood indicates that death has not yet occurred.

The same applies in the plague. The pulse of the sides is the pulse of women; if it is "elemental"—that is, hot or cold—it is a sign of a pregnant woman. In pains of the womb, it is likewise felt in the sides, and nowhere else.

A pulse affected by the element of heat gives a strong and fast beat.

And a pulse affected by heat shows an abundance of fire. A pulse of coldness is slow, without a sense of heat.

Note this also: in the "falling disease" <note>Epilepsy.</note>, the pulse is most vehement and strong.

And so, let these things said about the pulses suffice.

## The head, or the final diagram.

Medical Physiognomy <note>The practice of diagnosing internal health by observing external physical features.</note> consists of five members, namely:

- **The Eyes** with { The Foreskin, the Navel, the Pores, the Tenesmus <note>A distressing urge to evacuate the bowels.</note> } — It descends into depth with colors, especially rice-white and azure-blue.
- **The Nostrils** with { The Ears, the Face, the Mouth, the Lips } — It turns into a lead-white color and roughness.
- **The Teeth** with { The Nails, the Hair, the Soles of the feet } — It turns into a reverberation with discolored roots.
- **The Forehead** with { The Skin, the Breast, the Chest } — It turns into a pale and sickly state with a general weakening of the limbs.
